en: The Madhyama Āgama, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra at Dongting Monastery during the reigns of Emperors Xiaowu and An of the Eastern Jin dynasty,
from the eleventh month of the first year of Long’an to the sixth month of the second year.

The Discourse on Wholesome Qualities (Saddhamma Sutta) (1) Chapter Seven: The Seven Dharmas, Discourse One: The Wholesome Qualities Thus have I heard: Wholesome qualities, the *jambu* tree, The city, the water, and the heap of wood;
The simile of the good person going forth, Worldly merit, the sun, the chariot, and the exhaustion of outflows—these seven.
1. The Discourse on Wholesome Qualities (Saddhamma Sutta) (1) Middle Discourses, Chapter Seven: The Seven Dharmas, Discourse One: The Wholesome Qualities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there is a bhikṣu who accomplishes seven qualities, he shall attain the joy and happiness found among the noble ones and proceed rightly toward the exhaustion of the outflows.”
What are the seven? They are:
a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, knows the meaning, knows the time, knows moderation, knows himself, knows the assembly, and knows the relative superiority of others.
"What is it for a bhikṣu to be one who knows the Dharma?

It means that a bhikṣu knows the discourses (sūtra), chants (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), causal narratives (nidāna), aphorisms (udāna), legends (itivṛttaka), birth stories (jātaka), past lives (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), and expositions of the meaning (upadeśa). This is what is meant for a bhikṣu to be one who knows the Dharma."

If there is a bhikṣu who does not know the Dharma—meaning he does not know the discourses (sūtra), chants (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), causal narratives (nidāna), legends (avadāna), birth stories (jātaka), past lives (itivṛttaka), extensive explanations (vaipulya), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), and expositions on the meaning (upadeśa)—such a bhikṣu is one who does not know the Dharma.

If there is a bhikṣu who is well-versed in the Dharma—meaning he knows the discourses (sūtra), songs (geya), prophecies (vyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), causal narratives (nidāna), legends (avadāna), birth stories (jātaka), past events (itivṛttaka), expanded expositions (vaipulya), marvelous accounts (adbhutadharma), and explanations of the meaning (upadeśa)—this is called a bhikṣu who is well-versed in the Dharma.
“How does a bhikkhu come to know the meaning?
It is when a bhikkhu knows that the meaning of this or that teaching is such-and-such a meaning and such-and-such a meaning; this is called a bhikkhu who knows the meaning.”

If there is a bhikṣu who does not understand the meaning—that is, one who does not know that the meaning expressed in various teachings is this particular meaning or that particular meaning—such a bhikṣu is said to be one who does not understand the meaning.

If there is a bhikṣu who well understands the meaning—that is, knowing that such-and-such an explained meaning is this particular meaning and that particular meaning—this is called a bhikṣu who well understands the meaning.
"How is it that a bhikṣu knows the proper time?

It means that a bhikṣu knows this is the time to cultivate the sign of inferiority, this is the time to cultivate the sign of loftiness, and this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity; this is what is meant by a bhikṣu who knows the proper time."

If there is a bhikṣu who does not know the proper time, it means he does not know that this is the time to cultivate the sign of the low, this is the time to cultivate the sign of the high, and this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity; such a bhikṣu is one who does not know the proper time.

If there is a bhikṣu who well knows the proper time—meaning he knows that this is the time to cultivate the sign of inferiority, this is the time to cultivate the sign of loftiness, and this is the time to cultivate the sign of equanimity—he is called a bhikṣu who well knows the proper time.
"What is it for a bhikṣu to know moderation?

It means that a bhikṣu knows moderation whether drinking or eating, going or staying, sitting or lying down, speaking or remaining silent, or when defecating or urinating; he casts off sleep and practices right wisdom—this is called a bhikṣu who knows moderation."

If there is a bhikṣu who does not know moderation—meaning he does not know moderation in drinking or eating, in going or staying, in sitting or lying down, in speaking or remaining silent, or in defecating and urinating—and who does not cast off sleep to practice right wisdom, such a bhikṣu is one who does not know moderation.

If there is a bhikṣu who well knows moderation—meaning he knows [the measure] whether drinking or eating, whether going or staying, whether sitting or lying down, whether speaking or remaining silent, or whether defecating or urinating—and who casts off sleep, practicing right wisdom, this is called a bhikṣu who well knows moderation.
“What is it for a bhikṣu to be one who knows himself? It means that a bhikṣu knows for himself:
‘I possess such-and-such faith, morality, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, scriptural knowledge (āgama), and attainments. This is what is meant for a bhikṣu to be one who knows himself.”

If there is a bhikṣu who does not know himself—that is, one who does not know for himself: "I possess such-and-such faith, ethical discipline, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, scriptural knowledge (āgama), and attainments"—such a bhikṣu is one who does not know himself.

If there is a bhikṣu who well knows himself, it means he knows for himself: "I possess such a measure of faith, precepts, learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, scriptural knowledge (āgama), and attainments. This is called a bhikṣu who well knows himself.
“What is meant by a bhikṣu who knows the assembly?

It means that a bhikṣu knows: ‘This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas. He knows: ‘In that assembly, I should go thus, stay thus, sit thus, speak thus, or remain silent thus. This is called a bhikṣu who knows the assembly.”

If there is a bhikṣu who does not know the assembly—meaning he does not know, "This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas"—and thus does not know: "In that assembly I should go in such a way, stay in such a way, sit in such a way, speak in such a way, or remain silent in such a way"—such a bhikṣu is one who does not know the assembly.

If there is a bhikṣu who is skilled in knowing assemblies—that is, he knows: "This is an assembly of kṣatriyas; this is an assembly of brahmins; this is an assembly of householders; this is an assembly of śramaṇas"—and he knows: "In that assembly, I should go thus, stay thus, sit thus, speak thus, or remain silent thus"—this is called a bhikṣu who is skilled in knowing assemblies.
“What is a bhikṣu’s knowledge of the superiority of persons?
It means that a bhikṣu knows there are two kinds of persons: those with faith and those without faith;
the one with faith is superior, while the one without faith is inferior.”
It is said that there are two kinds of people who have faith: those who go frequently to see bhikṣus and those who do not go frequently to see bhikṣus.
Those who go frequently to see bhikṣus are superior; those who do not go frequently to see bhikṣus are inferior.
Regarding those who frequently go to visit monks, there are two kinds: those who pay homage to the monks and those who do not pay homage to the monks.
Those who pay homage to the monks are superior; those who do not pay homage to the monks are inferior.
Regarding the two types of people who pay respect to bhikṣus: there are those who inquire about the sūtras and those who do not inquire about the sūtras.
Those who inquire about the sūtras are superior; those who do not inquire about the sūtras are inferior.
Regarding those who inquire about the sutras, there are two types: those who listen to the sutras with a single-minded focus and those who do not listen with a single-minded focus.
Those who listen to the sutras with a single-minded focus are superior; those who do not listen with a single-minded focus are inferior.
Regarding those who listen to the sutras with a single-minded focus, there are again two kinds: those who retain what they hear and those who do not retain what they hear.
Those who retain what they hear are superior; those who do not retain what they hear are inferior.
Regarding those who hear and uphold the Dharma, there are further two types: those who hear the Dharma and contemplate its meaning, and those who hear the Dharma but do not contemplate its meaning.
Those who hear the Dharma and contemplate its meaning are superior; those who hear the Dharma but do not contemplate its meaning are inferior.

Regarding those who hear the Dharma and contemplate its meaning, there are again two kinds: those who know the Dharma and know the meaning, who are oriented toward the Dharma and its sequence, who accord with the Dharma, and who practice in accordance with the Dharma;

and those who do not know the Dharma and do not know the meaning, who are not oriented toward the Dharma and its sequence, who do not accord with the Dharma, and who do not practice in accordance with the Dharma.
If one knows the Dharma and knows its meaning, proceeds toward the Dharma and its sequence, conforms to the Dharma, and practices in accordance with the Dharma, such a person is superior;

if one does not know the Dharma, does not know its meaning, does not proceed toward the Dharma and its sequence, does not conform to the Dharma, and does not practice in accordance with the Dharma, such a person is inferior.

That is to say, knowing the Dharma and knowing its meaning; following the Dharma and the sequence of the Dharma; being in conformity with the Dharma; and being a practitioner who acts according to the Dharma. Furthermore, there are two kinds of such persons: those who benefit themselves and also benefit others, benefiting many people, having compassion for the world, and seeking what is meaningful, beneficial, peaceful, and happy for both gods and humans;

and those who do not benefit themselves nor benefit others, not benefiting many people, lacking compassion for the world, and not seeking what is meaningful, beneficial, peaceful, or happy for either gods or humans.

If one benefits oneself and also benefits others, benefiting many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness—such a person is the foremost among those people; they are the great, the superior, the most excellent, the preeminent, the venerable, and the sublime.

For example, from a cow comes milk; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the essence of butter. Of these, the essence of butter is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the supreme, the most wondrous, and the most sublime. In the same way, if a person benefits themselves and also benefits others, benefiting many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.

These two persons, as described above, as analyzed above, and as designated above—this is the first, the great, the superior, the foremost, the most excellent, the noblest, and the most sublime; this is called a bhikkhu’s knowledge of the superiority of persons.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Sūtra on Wholesome Dharmas* ends here, totaling one thousand four hundred and twenty-three characters. 2. The *Śāla Tree Sūtra* (2), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter Seven: The Section on the Seven Dharmas. The second *Śāla Tree Sūtra*. First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“When the leaves of the pārijāta tree in the Heaven of the Thirty-three wither and turn yellow, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are joyful and delighted, thinking, ‘The leaves of the pārijāta tree will soon fall.’”

Furthermore, when the leaves of the Pārijāta tree have fallen in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, at that time the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are joyful and delighted, thinking: "The leaves of the Pārijāta tree will soon grow back."

Furthermore, when the leaves of the pārijāta tree have regrown in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, at that time the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three are joyful and delighted, thinking: "The net of the pārijāta tree will soon appear."

Furthermore, when the pārijāta tree has produced its blossoms, at that time the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are filled with joy and delight, knowing that before long the pārijāta tree will produce buds like the beaks of birds.

Furthermore, when the pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has produced buds like bird beaks, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods are joyful and delighted, for the pārijāta tree will soon open like a bowl.

Furthermore, when the pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has blossomed like a bowl, at that time the Trāyastriṃśa gods are filled with delight and joy, for the pārijāta tree will soon be in full bloom.

When the pārijāta tree has fully blossomed, its light shines, its colors reflect, and its fragrance permeates for a hundred yojanas. At that time, during the fourth month of summer, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven enjoy themselves, fully endowed with the five celestial sensual pleasures; this is called the assembly and recreation of the Trāyastriṃśa gods beneath the pārijāta tree.

"In this same way, the noble disciple is likewise; when he contemplates going forth, at that time the noble disciple is said to be 'yellow-leaved,' just as the leaves of the pārijātaka tree in the Heaven of the Thirty-three turn yellow."

Furthermore, when a noble disciple shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, at that time the noble disciple is said to have "fallen leaves," just as the leaves fall from the Pārijātaka tree in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple, having detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome and evil states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is said to have "regrown leaves," just as the leaves of the pārijātaka tree regrow in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.

Furthermore, when the noble disciple has stilled directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*), and with internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, becomes free from directed thought and evaluation, attaining and abiding in the second dhyāna which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss—at that time, the noble disciple is said to have produced a "net," just as the pārijāta tree produces a net among the Trāyastriṃśa devas.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple, detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity, free from seeking, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing bliss with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells in bliss"—and attains and abides in the third dhyāna, at that time the noble disciple is said to be "born with a beak like a bird," just as the pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods has a beak like a bird.

Furthermore, when the noble disciple, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity—at that time, the noble disciple is said to be "born like a bowl," just as the pārijātaka tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is "like a bowl."

"Furthermore, when a noble disciple has exhausted all taints and is liberated in mind and liberated by wisdom, he dwells having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is. At that time, the noble disciple is said to be fully blossomed, just like the pārijāta tree of the Trāyastriṃśa gods when it is in full bloom."
He is an Arhat, a monk whose taints have been exhausted. When the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens assemble in the Sudhammā Hall, they praise him, saying:

"A certain noble disciple from such-and-such a village or town has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith has gone forth from the home life into homelessness to study the Path. His taints are exhausted; he is liberated in mind and liberated by wisdom. In this very life, he has known and realized it for himself, having personally attained and dwelt in that realization: 'Birth is ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."
"This is what is called the assembly of Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, like the assembly of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven beneath the Pārijāta tree.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second discourse, the Jyotiṣka Sūtra, ends here, totaling seven hundred and fifty-two characters. 3. The Discourse on the Simile of the City (The Third in the Seven Dharmas Section of the Madhyama Āgama). Recitation for the First Day. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Suppose a king’s border city is fully equipped with seven things and has an abundance of four kinds of food, which are easy to obtain and not difficult to find; for this reason, the royal city cannot be destroyed by external enemies, except in the case of internal collapse."
"What are the seven things by which a royal city is fully endowed?

It is said that when a king’s border city constructs watchtowers and battlements, builds its foundations solid so they cannot be destroyed, and thereby ensures internal security while restraining external enemies—this is called the first thing by which a royal city is fully endowed."

Furthermore, just as a king’s border city digs moats and ditches that are made exceedingly deep and wide, which are maintained and prepared as a reliable defense for the sake of internal security and to restrain external enemies—this is called the king’s city being endowed with these two matters.

Furthermore, just as a king’s border city has thoroughfares all around that are cleared, level, and spacious, serving both to ensure internal security and to repel external enemies—this is called the king’s city being complete with these three things.

Furthermore, it is like a king’s frontier city that assembles the fourfold military forces—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—to ensure internal security and to subdue external enemies; this is called the king’s city being endowed with the four requisites.

Furthermore, just as a king’s frontier city prepares military weapons—bows, arrows, spears, and halberds—to ensure internal security and to subdue external enemies, this is called the king’s city being endowed with the five requirements.

Furthermore, it is like a king’s frontier city appointing a great gate-guarding general who possesses clear strategy, wisdom, eloquence, courage, and extraordinary counsel; he permits entry to the good and prohibits the wicked, ensuring internal peace and security while subduing external enemies—this is called the king’s city being fully endowed with the six requirements.

Furthermore, it is like a king’s frontier city that builds high walls, making them extremely solid, plastered and whitewashed, for the sake of internal security and to repel external enemies; this is called the king’s city being endowed with the seven requirements.
"What is meant by saying that the four kinds of sustenance are abundant and easily obtained without difficulty in a royal city?

It means that the king’s border city has provisions of water, grass, and firewood prepared in advance; this serves to ensure internal security and to restrain external enemies. This is called the first kind of sustenance that is abundant and easily obtained without difficulty in a royal city."

Furthermore, just as a king’s border city collects much rice and stores up barley to ensure internal security and to repel external enemies, this is called the king’s city having an abundance of two kinds of food, which are easily obtained and not difficult to find.

Furthermore, just as a king’s border city accumulates large quantities of mung beans, black gram, and other legumes to ensure internal security and repel external enemies, this is called the third abundance of food in a royal city—plentiful, easy to obtain, and not difficult to acquire.

Furthermore, it is like a king’s border city that stores ghee, oil, honey, sugarcane, sugar, fish, salt, and dried meat—all things being fully provided for the sake of internal security and to repel external enemies; this is called the abundance of the four kinds of food in a royal city, which are easy to obtain and not difficult to find.

In this way, the royal city is endowed with these seven things; the four kinds of sustenance are abundant and easily obtained without difficulty, and it cannot be destroyed by external enemies, except through internal collapse.
"In this way, if a noble disciple likewise attains the seven wholesome qualities and achieves the four states of higher mind, they will do so easily and without difficulty.

For this reason, the noble disciple does not provide an opportunity for Māra the King, nor does he follow evil and unwholesome states; he is not defiled by defilements and shall no longer undergo further rebirth."
"How does a noble disciple attain the seven wholesome qualities?

It is when a noble disciple attains firm faith, is deeply devoted to the Tathāgata, and having established the faculty of faith, never follows other recluses or brahmins, whether gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world; this is called the noble disciple’s attainment of the first wholesome quality.

Furthermore, the noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame and dread of blame; being capable of shame and knowing what is shameful, he recognizes that evil and unwholesome states are defiling afflictions that result in various evil retributions and constitute the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple’s attainment of two wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, the noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing; he knows what is shameful and feels shame regarding evil and unwholesome states—those defilements and afflictions that result in various evil retributions and constitute the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple’s attainment of the three wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, the noble disciple constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he always rouses his own mind, making it one-pointed and firm as the foundation for all virtues, never relinquishing skillful means. This is called the noble disciple’s attainment of the four wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, the noble disciple is extensively learned and well-versed, maintaining what he has heard without forgetting, and accumulating vast learning. Regarding these teachings—those which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; which possess both meaning and phrasing; which are perfectly pure and reveal the holy life—he extensively studies and hears them, practicing them until he has mastered them a thousand times. He contemplates them with his mind, seeing them clearly and penetrating them deeply. This is called the noble disciple’s attainment of the five wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, the noble disciple constantly practices mindfulness and achieves right mindfulness; he constantly recollects and does not forget what was practiced long ago and what was heard long ago. This is called the noble disciple attaining the six wholesome qualities.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple practices wisdom and contemplates the phenomena of arising and passing away, he attains such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear-sighted, and discerning—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering. This is called a noble disciple who has attained the seven wholesome qualities.
"How does a noble disciple attain the four higher mental states (adhicitta), easily and without difficulty?

It is when a noble disciple, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome, evil states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna; this is called the noble disciple attaining the first higher mental state, easily and without difficulty."

Furthermore, when the noble disciple’s directed thought and evaluation have subsided, and he becomes inwardly tranquil and one-pointed, free from directed thought and evaluation, experiencing the joy and happiness born of concentration, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna; this is called the noble disciple attaining the second higher mind, which is easily obtained and not difficult to attain.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple, having become detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity and seeks nothing, experiencing pleasure with mindfulness and clear comprehension—of which the Noble Ones say, "Equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in pleasure"—he attains and abides in the third dhyāna. This is called the noble disciple’s attainment of the third higher mind, which is easily obtained and not difficult to find.

Furthermore, when a noble disciple, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity—this is called the noble disciple attaining the fourth higher mind, which is easily obtained and not difficult to attain.
“In this way, the noble disciple attains the seven wholesome qualities and reaches the four states of higher mind; these are easily attained and not with difficulty.
He does not provide an opportunity for Māra, nor does he follow evil and unwholesome states; he is not defiled by defilements and shall no longer undergo rebirth.”
Just as a king’s border city constructs watchtowers and battlements,夯实s the ground so it is firm and indestructible, for the sake of internal security and to restrain external enemies;

in the same way, a noble disciple attains firm faith and is deeply attached to the Tathāgata. Once the faculty of faith is established, he will never follow other recluses or brahmins, nor gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world. This is called a noble disciple who has attained the watchtower of faith, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas.
"Just as a king’s border city digs moats and trenches, making them exceedingly deep and wide, and maintains them well-prepared and reliable for internal security and to restrain external enemies."

In this way, the noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame and dread; he knows what is shameful and feels shame regarding evil and unwholesome states—those defiled afflictions that result in various evil retributions and constitute the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple attaining the moat of the pool of shame, whereby he eliminates evil and unwholesome states and cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
"Just as a king’s border city has roads running all around that are cleared, level, and spacious, so as to ensure internal security and to repel external enemies;

in the same way, a noble disciple constantly practices a sense of shame (*hrī*), being ashamed of what should be shamed in evil and unwholesome states—those defiled afflictions that result in various evil retributions and constitute the root of birth and death. This is called the noble disciple attaining the level path of shame, whereby he eliminates evil and unwholesome states and cultivates all wholesome dharmas."
"Just as a king's border city assembles the fourfold military forces—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—to ensure internal security and to subdue external enemies."

In this way, the noble disciple constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas. He always rouses his own mind, making it one-pointed and firm for the sake of all roots of goodness, never relinquishing skillful means. This is called the noble disciple attaining the power of the army of diligence to eliminate evil and unwholesome states and cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
"Just as a king’s border city prepares military weapons—bows, arrows, spears, and halberds—to ensure internal security and to subdue external enemies;

so too, a noble disciple is widely learned and possesses great erudition, maintaining it without forgetfulness and accumulating extensive learning. That which is called the Dharma is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, perfectly pure, and reveals the holy life."

Thus, having extensively studied and heard these various dharmas, practicing them until they reach a thousandfold, contemplating them with the mind, seeing them clearly, and penetrating them deeply—this is called the noble disciple acquiring the weapon of much learning to eliminate evil and unwholesome states and to cultivate all wholesome dharmas.

"It is like a king’s frontier city that appoints a great gate-keeping general, one who possesses clear strategy, wisdom, and eloquence, as well as courage and extraordinary counsel; he permits entry to the good and forbids the wicked, thereby ensuring internal peace and security while restraining external enemies."

In this way, the noble disciple constantly practices mindfulness and achieves right mindfulness; what was practiced long ago and heard long ago is always remembered without being forgotten. This is called the noble disciple attaining the gatekeeper and great general of mindfulness, who eliminates evil and unwholesome states and cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
"Just as a king's border city erects high walls, making them extremely firm, plastered and whitewashed, for the sake of internal security and to restrain external enemies."

In this way, the noble disciple cultivates wisdom, contemplates the phenomena of arising and passing away, and attains such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering. This is called the noble disciple attaining the wall of wisdom, which eliminates evil and unwholesome states and cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
"Just as a king’s border city, having prepared supplies of water, grass, and firewood, remains secure within and restrains external enemies;

so too, a noble disciple, detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna. Thus abiding in happiness without lack, secure and blissful, he personally realizes nirvāṇa."

"Just as a king’s frontier city stores much rice and hoards barley for the sake of internal security and to repel external enemies, so too, when a noble disciple has stilled directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*), with internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss. Thus, dwelling in bliss without lack, secure and happy, he personally realizes Nirvāṇa."

"Just as a king’s border city stores large quantities of mung beans, black gram, and other legumes to ensure internal security and to repel external enemies, so too, a noble disciple, detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing bliss with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, 'He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and blissful'—attaining and abiding in the third dhyāna. Thus he dwells in bliss without lack, secure and happy, attaining Nirvāṇa for himself."
"Just as a king's border city stores clarified butter, oil, honey, sugarcane, molasses, fish, salt, and dried meat—all in abundance—to ensure internal security and repel external enemies."

In this way, the noble disciple, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity—and having attained it, he abides therein, free from want, secure, and happy, personally realizing nirvāṇa.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third *Nagara-upama Sūtra* ends here, totaling one thousand nine hundred and two characters. 4. *Vāri-upama Sūtra* (IV) The Fourth Discourse in the Seven Dharmas Section of the Madhyama Āgama: The *Vāri-upama Sūtra*. First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now explain to you the seven types of persons who are like water.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?
There may be a person who constantly lies within the water;..."
Furthermore, some people emerge from the water and submerge again; some emerge from the water and remain there;
and some emerge from the water, remain there, and having remained, look around.

Furthermore, there may be a person who emerges from the water and stands; having stood, they look around; having looked around, they cross over. Or again, there may be a person who emerges from the water and stands;
having stood, they look around; having looked around, they cross over; having crossed over, they reach the other shore.

Or again, there may be a person who emerges from the water and stands; having stood, they look around; having looked around, they cross over; having crossed over, they reach the other shore; and having reached the other shore, they are called one who dwells on the bank.
In this way, I shall further explain to you the seven analogies of persons compared to water.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon them well.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?"
Some beings remain constantly submerged;
some emerge and then submerge again;
and some emerge and then remain stationary.
Furthermore, there may be someone who, having emerged, stands;
having stood, looks around. Or there may be someone who, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks around; having looked around, crosses over.
Or there may be someone who, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks around; having looked around, crosses over; and having crossed over, reaches the other shore.

Furthermore, there may be someone who, having emerged, stands; having stood, observes; having observed, crosses over; having crossed over, reaches the further shore; and having reached the further shore, is called a brahmin dwelling on the bank.
These seven similes of water regarding persons have been briefly explained by me.
As has been stated above, as has been established above:
what meaning do you understand from this?
"What is it that is being discriminated?
What are the causes and conditions?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that he will explain it, so that having heard it, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well."
"I shall analyze its meaning for you.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
“What is meant by a person who is always lying down?

It refers to a person who is shrouded by unwholesome states, defiled by what is corrupting, receiving the retribution of evil dharmas, and creating the root of birth and death; this is called a person who is always lying down.”

It is like a person who has drowned and lies submerged in water; I say that such a person is just like this. This is called the first analogy of a person in water, which exists as a truth in the world.
"What is meant by a person who, having emerged, sinks back down?

It refers to a person who, having emerged, acquires faith in the wholesome Dharma and practices the wholesome Dharma through observance of precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom; yet at a later time, their faith becomes unsteady, and they lose their firmness in the observance of precepts, generosity, learning, and wisdom. This is called a person who, having emerged, sinks back down."

It is like a person drowning in water who, having emerged, sinks back down; I say that such a person is just like this. This is called the second analogy of a person in water, which exists as a reality in the world.
"What is meant by a person who, having emerged, remains?

It refers to a person who, having emerged, attains faith in wholesome dharmas, maintains ethical discipline, practices generosity, cultivates learning, and develops wisdom; they cultivate wholesome dharmas so that later their faith remains firm and is not lost, and their ethical discipline, generosity, learning, and wisdom remain steadfast and are not lost. This is called a person who, having emerged, remains—just as a person drowning in water emerges and remains. I say that such a person is also like this; this is called the third simile of the person in water, which exists truly in the world."
"What is meant by a person who, having gone out, stands; and having stood, observes?

It refers to one who, having gone out, attains faith in wholesome dharmas, upholds the precepts, practices generosity, possesses much learning, and possesses wisdom, cultivating wholesome dharmas. At a later time, his faith remains firm and is not lost; his observance of the precepts, generosity, much learning, and wisdom remain steadfast and are not lost. Abiding within wholesome dharmas, he knows suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are."

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his three fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—are completely exhausted. With these three fetters exhausted, he attains the stage of *srotāpanna*; he does not fall into states of woe, is destined for full awakening, and will undergo at most seven more existences. After seven cycles of coming and going between the heavens and the human realm, he shall reach the end of suffering. This is called the person who, having emerged, abides; and having abided, observes.

"Just as a person drowning in water, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks about—I say that such a person is also like this. This is called the fourth person in the simile of water, who exists truly in the world."
"What is it for a person to emerge and stand, having stood to observe, and having observed to cross over?
It means that once a person has emerged, they attain faith in wholesome dharmas, and practice the wholesome dharmas of observing the precepts, giving, extensive learning, and wisdom."

At a later time, his faith remains firm and is not lost; he maintains his precepts, practices generosity, cultivates much learning, and possesses wisdom, all of which remain steadfast and are not lost. Abiding in wholesome qualities, he knows suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are. Knowing thus and seeing thus, the three fetters—namely, the view of a self, adherence to rites and rituals, and doubt—are completely destroyed. With these three fetters destroyed, lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated. He attains the state of "once-returning" to the heavenly and human realms; having returned once more, he then reaches the end of suffering. This is called the person who, having emerged, abides; having abided, observes; and having observed, crosses over.

It is like a person drowning in water who, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks about; and having looked about, crosses over. I say that such a person is just like this; this is called the fifth simile of a person regarding water, which exists as a reality in the world.
"How is it that some people, having emerged, remain; having remained, observe; having observed, cross over; and having crossed over, reach the further shore?
It is when a person, having emerged, attains faith in the wholesome Dharma, maintains the precepts, practices generosity, cultivates learning, and develops wisdom.
They practice these wholesome qualities, and at a later time, their faith remains firm and is not lost; they maintain the precepts, practice generosity..."
Through generosity, learning, and wisdom, remaining firm and undeterred, one dwells within wholesome qualities;
one knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
Knowing thus and seeing thus, the five lower fetters—namely, sensual desire, ill will, and [the conceit of] the body—are exhausted.
Having abandoned the five lower fetters—namely, views, attachment to precepts and rituals, and doubt—one is reborn in that intermediate state and there attains parinirvāṇa;
having attained the dharma of non-retrogression, one does not return to this world. This is called the person who, having emerged, abides;
having abided, contemplates; having contemplated, crosses over; and having crossed over, reaches the further shore.

"Just as a person drowning in water, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks around; having looked around, wades across; and having waded across, reaches the further shore—I say that such a person is also like this. This is called the sixth person in the analogy of water, who exists truly in the world."

"What kind of person is one who, having emerged, stands; having stood, observes; having observed, crosses over; having crossed over, reaches the further shore; and having reached the further shore, is called a brahmin dwelling on the shore?"
It means that once a person has emerged [from the world] and attained faith in the wholesome Dharma— practicing morality, generosity, learning, and wisdom—
and having cultivated these wholesome qualities, their faith remains firm and unlost at a later time;
their morality, generosity, learning, and wisdom remain steadfast and unlost as they abide within the wholesome Dharma and come to know suffering.

Knowing as it truly is the origin of suffering, knowing as it truly is the cessation of suffering, and knowing as it truly is the path leading to the cessation of suffering—knowing thus and seeing thus, the mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, and the mind is liberated from the outflows of existence and ignorance.
Being liberated, one knows: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established."
Having done what was to be done, and no longer undergoing further existence, one knows this as it truly is. This is called the person who, having emerged, stands;
having stood, observes; having observed, crosses over; having crossed over, reaches the further shore;
and having reached the further shore, is called a brahmin standing on the bank.

It is like a person drowning in water who, having emerged, stands; having stood, looks about; having looked about, crosses over; having crossed over, reaches the further shore; and having reached the further shore, is called one who stands on the bank.
I say that such a person is likewise; this is called the seventh type of person likened to water, who exists in the world as a reality.
What I previously mentioned—that I would explain to you the seven types of persons likened to water—was spoken for this reason.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Fourth Sūtra on the Simile of Water ends here, totaling one thousand three hundred and eighty-eight characters. 5. The Simile of the Woodpile (V), Madhyama Āgama, Chapter on the Seven Dharmas, The Fifth Sūtra on the Simile of the Woodpile, for the First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Kosala among the people, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus.

At that time, while on the road, the World-Honored One suddenly saw a place where a large pile of wood was burning fiercely and intensely. Having seen this, the World-Honored One stepped off to the side of the path, went toward another tree, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down cross-legged.
When the Blessed One had sat down, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see that great pile of wood burning with a hollowed-out flame, blazing intensely?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus again, saying:
"What do you think?

Suppose there were a great pile of wood, burning with a hollowed-out blaze and glowing intensely; suppose one were to embrace it, sit upon it, or lie down upon it. And suppose there were a Kṣatriya woman, or a Brāhmaṇa woman, or a householder’s daughter, or a craftsman’s daughter, in the prime of her youth, bathed and perfumed, dressed in bright, clean garments, and adorned with flower garlands and necklaces. If one were to embrace her, sit beside her, or lie with her—of these two, which would be more pleasant?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One,
it would be extremely painful to embrace, sit upon, or lie down upon a great pile of wood that is hollow-burning and blazing with intense heat."
“World-Honored One!

Suppose there is a daughter of a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman, in the prime of her youth, who has bathed and perfumed herself, put on bright and clean garments, and adorned her body with flower garlands and necklaces; whether she is being embraced, seated, or lying down with him, she finds it exceedingly pleasant.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
“I shall speak for you, so that you who train as śramaṇas do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.”

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*), it would be better for you to embrace a pile of wood burning with a fierce, blazing fire while sitting or lying down; though you might suffer or die because of this, you would not, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to a miserable destination or be reborn in hell.

This is unlike a foolish person who violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states, claiming to lead the holy life when he does not, and calling himself a *śramaṇa* when he is not.

If one embraces the daughter of a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a householder, or a craftsman—she being in the prime of her youth, having bathed and been perfumed, wearing bright and clean garments, and her body adorned with flower garlands and necklaces—and whether sitting or lying with her, that foolish person, because of this, will for a long night experience what is unwholesome and unrighteous, receiving the retribution of evil dharmas; at the breaking up of the body after death, he will go to a miserable destination and be reborn in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both. You should reflect thus:

"My life as a renunciant student is neither in vain nor empty; it bears fruit and retribution, and brings supreme peace and happiness. It leads to birth in auspicious realms and long life, and by receiving from the faithful the offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, it causes all donors to obtain great merit, great rewards, and great radiance."
"You should train yourselves in this way.
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

Suppose there were a strong man who, using a tight cord or hair rope, bound and constricted his calf until it cut through the skin; having cut through the skin, it cut through the flesh; having cut through the flesh, it cut through the sinews; having cut through the sinews, it cut through the bone; and having cut through the bone, it reached the marrow and remained there. If, from such a state, one were to receive faithful offerings from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen, and have one’s body, limbs, joints, hands, and feet massaged—of these two, which would be the pleasure?
Then the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One: “World-Honored One!

Suppose there were a strong man who, using a tight cord or hair-rope, were to constrict and bind one’s calf until the skin is severed; having severed the skin, he severs the flesh; having severed the flesh, he severs the sinews; having severed the sinews, he severs the bone; and having severed the bone, he reaches the marrow and stops—this would be extremely painful.”
"World-Honored One!
If one receives the faithful offerings of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen, and has them massage the body, the limbs, and the hands and feet, it is exceedingly pleasant."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
“I shall speak for you so that you who study as śramaṇas do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.”

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better for a strong man to bind your calf with a tight cord of hair and twist it so that it cuts through the skin; having cut through the skin, it cuts through the flesh; having cut through the flesh, it cuts through the tendons; having cut through the tendons, it cuts through the bone; and having cut through the bone, it reaches the marrow and stops there. Although you might suffer or die because of this, you would not, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to an evil destination or be reborn in hell.

If a foolish person violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states; if they are not of the holy life yet claim to be so, and are not a śramaṇa yet claim to be one; and if they receive the faithful offerings of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—such as massages for the body, limbs, hands, and feet—that foolish person, because of this, will for a long night experience what is unwholesome and unrighteous, receiving the retribution for evil dharmas. At the breaking up of the body after death, they will go to an evil destination and be born in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both; you should think thus:

"My renunciation and study are neither in vain nor empty; they bear fruit and yield reward, leading to supreme peace and happiness, birth in virtuous realms, and long life. By receiving from others the offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, I cause those donors to obtain great merit, great rewards, and great radiance."
"You should train yourselves thus.
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

If a strong man were to sever one's thigh with a polished, sharp blade, and if one were to receive alms, prostrations, respect, and hospitable reception from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or artisans—of these two, which would be the greater pleasure?
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One,
if a strong man were to cut through one’s thigh with a polished, sharp blade, it would be extremely painful.”
“World-Honored One!
It would be most joyful for me to receive offerings of food, prostrations, and respectful greetings from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied,
“I shall speak for you, so that you who study as śramaṇas do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.”

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life (*brahmacarya*), it would be better for a strong man to sever your thigh with a polished, sharp blade; though you might suffer pain or die because of this, you would not, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to a miserable destination or be reborn in hell.

However, if a foolish person violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states—claiming to lead the holy life when he does not, or claiming to be a recluse (*śramaṇa*) when he is not—and yet accepts offerings of food, prostrations, respect, and hospitality from Kṣatriyas, Brahmins, householders, and artisans, that foolish person will, because of this, experience the retribution of unwholesome and unrighteous dharmas for a long night; upon the breakup of the body after death, he will go to a miserable destination and be reborn in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both. You should form this thought:

"My life as a renunciant student is not in vain and not empty; it has its fruit and its reward, and it possesses supreme peace and happiness. It leads to birth in auspicious realms and the attainment of long life, and by receiving from people the offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine, it causes all donors to obtain great merit, obtain great rewards, and obtain great radiance."
"You should train yourselves in this way.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

If a strong man were to wrap his body with sheets of iron or copper that were glowing and blazing with heat, and if he were to receive robes as a gift of faith from a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman—of these two, which would be more pleasant?
Then, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
"World-Honored One!
If a strong man were to wrap his body with sheets of iron or copper that were hollowed out and blazing with intense heat, it would be extremely painful."
"World-Honored One!
It would be most joyful for us to receive robes offered out of faith from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen,
World-Honored One!"
The Blessed One said:
"I shall teach you so that you, who train as śramaṇas, do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better for a strong man to wrap your body with iron or copper plates that are hollowed out, glowing, and blazing hot; though you might suffer or die because of this, you would not, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to a miserable destination or be reborn in hell."

If a foolish person violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states, claiming to be one of pure conduct when he is not, or claiming to be a śramaṇa when he is not, and accepts gifts of clothing offered in faith from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen—because of this, that foolish person will for a long night experience what is unwholesome and unjust, receiving the retribution for his evil deeds; at the breaking up of the body after death, he will go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both;

you should reflect thus: "My life as a renunciant student is neither in vain nor empty; it bears fruit and reward, and brings supreme peace and happiness. It leads to rebirth in auspicious realms and the attainment of long life. By receiving from people the offerings of faith—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—I enable those donors to obtain great merit, great rewards, and great radiance."
"You should train yourselves in this way.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

Suppose there were a strong man who, using hot iron tongs, forced open one's mouth and placed therein an iron ball that was glowing and fiercely burning. That hot iron ball would burn the lips; having burned the lips, it would burn the tongue; having burned the tongue, it would burn the gums; having burned the gums, it would burn the throat; having burned the throat, it would burn the heart; having burned the heart, it would burn the intestines and stomach; and having burned the intestines and stomach, it would pass through and out. Compared to this, if one receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen food given as alms consisting of immeasurable varieties of flavors, which of these two is more pleasant?
Then, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One: “World-Honored One!

Suppose there were a strong man who, using hot iron tongs, forced open one’s mouth and placed therein an iron ball that was glowing and blazing with heat; that hot iron ball would burn the lips, and having burned the lips, it would burn the tongue; having burned the tongue, it would burn the gums; having burned the gums, it would burn the throat; having burned the throat, it would burn the heart; having burned the heart, it would burn the intestines and stomach; and having burned the intestines and stomach, it would pass through and out below—this would be extremely painful.”
“World-Honored One!
If one receives from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or artisans the food offered in faith, consisting of immeasurable varieties of flavors, it is most delightful, World-Honored One!”
The Blessed One said:
“I shall speak for you so that you who train as śramaṇas do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better for a strong man to pry open your mouth with red-hot iron tongs and place into your mouth an iron ball glowing and blazing with heat; though that hot iron ball might burn your lips, and having burned your lips, your tongue, and having burned your tongue, your gums, and having burned your gums, your throat, and having burned your throat, your heart, and having burned your heart, your intestines and stomach, and having burned the intestines and stomach, pass through and out below—even if one suffers pain or dies because of this, one will not, upon the breakup of the body after death, go to a miserable destination or be reborn in hell. Why is that? Because this suffering is finite and has an end.”

If a foolish person violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states; if they claim to practice the holy life when they do not, or claim to be a śramaṇa when they are not; and if they receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans the food offered out of faith, consisting of immeasurable varieties of flavors—then that foolish person, because of this, will for a long night experience what is unwholesome and unrighteous, receiving the retribution of evil dharmas. When the body breaks up at the end of life, they will go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both; you should think thus:

"My life as a renunciant student is neither vain nor empty; it has its fruit and its reward, its ultimate peace and happiness, and leads to birth in auspicious realms with long life. "You should train yourselves in this way.

"What do you think?"

"Blessed One!

The Blessed One said:

"My life as a renunciant student is neither in vain nor empty; it bears fruit and reward, and brings supreme peace and happiness. "You should train yourselves in this way.
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What do you think?"

Suppose there were a strong man who took a large iron or copper cauldron, glowing and blazing with heat, lifted a person up, and cast them head-first into it.
