Which of these two would be more pleasant?
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
"World-Honored One!
If a strong man were to take a person with a large iron or copper cauldron, glowing and blazing intensely, lift them up, and turn them upside down into the cauldron, it would be extremely painful."
"World-Honored One!

If one receives a dwelling as a gift of faith from a kṣatriya, a brahmin, a householder, or a craftsman—one that is plastered and whitewashed, with doors and windows securely sealed, and warmed by a glowing hearth—it is truly pleasant."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
“I shall speak for you so that you, who train as śramaṇas, do not lose the way of the śramaṇa.”

If you wish to accomplish the unsurpassed holy life, it would be better for a strong man to take you up, after you have been seized, and place you head-downward into a large iron or copper cauldron that is glowing and blazing with fire; though you might suffer or die because of this, you would not—upon the breakup of the body at the end of life—go to a miserable destination or be reborn in hell.

If a foolish person violates the precepts and lacks diligence, giving rise to evil and unwholesome states; if they are not of the holy life yet claim to be so, and are not a śramaṇa yet claim to be one; and if they receive from kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen the gift of a dwelling—plastered, whitewashed, with well-secured doors and sturdy windows, warmed by a glowing hearth—that foolish person, because of this, will for a long night experience what is unwholesome and unrighteous, receiving the retribution of evil dharmas. When the body breaks up at the end of life, he will go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell.
Therefore, you should contemplate your own welfare, contemplate the welfare of others, and contemplate the welfare of both; you should think thus:

"My life as a renunciant student is neither in vain nor empty; it has its fruit and its result, and it brings supreme peace and happiness. It leads to rebirth in favorable realms and long life, and by receiving from others the gifts of faith—robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—it enables those donors to obtain great merit, great rewards, and great radiance."
"You should train yourselves in this way.
When this Dharma was spoken, sixty bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and were liberated from their fetters; sixty bhikṣus abandoned the precepts and returned to lay life.
Why is this? The World-Honored One’s instructions are extremely profound and extremely difficult; the study of the Path is likewise extremely profound and extremely difficult.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
When those bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The fifth discourse, the *Kāṣṭhasaṃghāta-sūtra*, ends here, totaling 2,644 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume One, totaling 8,109 characters. First Day’s Recitation.
*Madhyama Āgama*, Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Sūtra on the Departure of the Good Person (6), Chapter Six: The Seven Dharmas, Sūtra on the Departure of the Good Person, Number Six. Recitation for the First Day.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now explain for you the seven destinations to which virtuous persons go, as well as nirvāṇa without remainder.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?
O bhikṣus!"
One should practice in this way:

"I am without self, nor do I possess anything; in the future I shall be without self, nor shall I possess anything. What has arisen is severed; having severed it, one attains equanimity. One is not defiled by existing pleasure, nor does one cling to what is encountered."
A practitioner who acts in this way perceives through the wisdom of the unsurpassed cessation of the traces [of defilements], yet has not yet attained realization.
Bhikṣu! If one practices in this manner, where will one go?
It is like parched grain husks: as soon as they catch fire, they are extinguished.

You should know, bhikkhus, that it is just so for one who has not yet eliminated even a slight degree of conceit, but whose five lower fetters have been severed; such a person attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state. This is called the first destination of the virtuous, which truly exists in the world.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus! Your practice should be as follows:

'I am not-self, nor do I possess anything; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything possessed by a self. Whatever exists, one should sever it; having severed it, one attains equanimity. One is not defiled by existing pleasure, nor does one cling to its occurrence."
One who practices in this way sees with the wisdom that perceives the unsurpassed state of cessation, yet has not yet attained its realization.
Bhikṣu! Practicing in this way, where will you go?
It is just as when iron is heated until it glows with intense heat; if one strikes it with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and are extinguished as soon as they reach the heights.
You should know this, bhikṣus!

It is also like this: with a slight degree of conceit yet unexhausted, but having already severed the five lower fetters, one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; this is called the second destination for a person of virtue, which exists as a reality in the world.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus! One should practice in this way:

'I am not-self, nor do I possess anything; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything possessed. What already exists, I shall abandon; having abandoned it, I shall attain equanimity. Toward existing pleasures I shall not be stained; toward conjunctions I shall not be attached.'"
One who practices in this way perceives through the wisdom of the unsurpassed state of cessation, yet has not yet attained its realization.
Bhikṣu! Practicing in this way, where does one go?
It is as if iron were burning and glowing intensely throughout; when struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air, and one that falls back from above is extinguished before it reaches the ground.
You should know this, bhikṣus!

It is likewise so: with a small amount of conceit yet remaining and the five lower fetters already severed, one attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; this is called the third destination for a person of virtue, which truly exists in the world.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! Your practice should be thus:

'I am not self, nor is there anything belonging to a self; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything belonging to a self. That which has arisen, you should abandon; having abandoned it, you attain equanimity. You are untainted by the pleasure of existence and do not cling to its conjunction."
One who practices in this way sees with the wisdom of the unsurpassed cessation of the traces [of defilement], yet has not yet attained realization.
Bhikṣu! If one practices in this way, where will they go?
It is like iron that is glowing and blazing all over; when struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall to the ground where they are extinguished.
You should know this, bhikṣus!

It is also like this: one who has a slight degree of conceit remaining but has already severed the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) and attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth—this is called the fourth destination of a superior person, which exists as a reality in the world.
"Furthermore, bhikṣus! Practice should be as follows:

'I am without self, nor do I possess anything; in the future I shall be without self, nor shall I possess anything. That which has arisen, one should abandon; having abandoned it, one attains equanimity. One is not defiled by existing pleasure, and does not cling to what is encountered."
One who practices in this way perceives through the wisdom of the unsurpassed cessation of the traces [of defilement], yet has not yet attained realization.
Bhikṣu! Practicing in this way, where will one go?

It is like iron that is thoroughly heated until it glows with intense heat; when struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a small amount of wood or grass, where they either smoke or burn, and having burned, they are immediately extinguished.
"Monks, you should know that it is likewise so:

when a person has little conceit remaining and has not yet exhausted it, but has already severed the five lower fetters and attains *parinirvāṇa* upon entering the realm of form, this is called the fifth destination for virtuous persons, which exists truly in the world."
"Furthermore, bhikṣus! Your practice should be as follows:

'I am not self, nor do I possess anything; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything possessed by a self. What has arisen is now severed; having severed it, one attains equanimity. One is not defiled by existing pleasure, and does not cling to what is encountered.'"
One who practices in this way has the vision of the wisdom of unsurpassed tranquility, yet has not yet attained its realization.
Bhikṣu! Practicing in this way, where will one go?

It is like iron that is thoroughly heated until it glows with intense heat; when struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a heap of firewood and grass, where they either smoke or burn, and having consumed the fuel, they go out.
"Monks, you should know that it is likewise so:

when a person has little conceit remaining and the five lower fetters are already severed, they attain parinirvāṇa without exertion; this is called the sixth destination for a superior person, which truly exists in the world."
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! Your practice should be as follows:

'I am not-self, nor do I possess anything; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything possessed by a self. What already exists, I shall sever; having severed it, I shall attain equanimity. Toward existing pleasures, I shall not be stained; toward conjunctions, I shall not be attached.'"
One who practices in this way perceives through the wisdom of the unsurpassed cessation of the traces [of defilements], yet has not yet attained realization.
Bhikṣu! Practicing in this way, where will one go?

It is like iron that is thoroughly heated until it glows with intense heat; when struck with a hammer, sparks fly into the air and fall upon a great deal of firewood and grass, where they either smolder or ignite, and having ignited, they then burn down villages, towns, cities, mountains, forests, and wildernesses.
"Monks, you should know that after burning down villages, towns, cities, mountains, forests, and wildernesses, the fire may be extinguished upon reaching a road, a body of water, or level ground."

It is likewise so: with a slight degree of conceit not yet exhausted, but having already severed the five lower fetters, one attains parinirvāṇa in the Akaniṣṭha heaven by ascending through the realms; this is called the seventh destination for virtuous persons, which exists in the world as a reality.
"What is nirvana without remainder?
Monks! One's practice should be thus:"

The self is non-self, nor is there anything belonging to a self; in the future there will be no self, nor will there be anything belonging to a self. What has already arisen is severed; having severed it, one attains equanimity. One is not defiled by existing pleasure, and does not cling to that which is encountered.
For one who practices in this way, that which is seen by the wisdom of unsurpassed cessation and traces has already been realized.
I say of such a person, bhikkhu:

he does not go to the east, nor to the west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below; rather, within this very life, he attains cessation and parinibbāna through the stilling of traces.
"That which I have spoken of as the destination reached by the seven types of virtuous persons, and as nirvana without remainder—it is for this reason that I have so spoken.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth sutra of the *Sappurisa-vagga*, consisting of one thousand one hundred and three characters, is concluded. 7. *Lokādhamma-sutta* (The Discourse on Worldly Merit), the seventh in the *Sattadhamma-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Recitation for the first day. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Kauśāmbī and staying at the Ghoṣita Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahācunda rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, and having arrived, paid homage and sat down to one side. He said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"Can worldly merit be established?
The World-Honored One replied, "It can."
Cunda! There are seven worldly merits that bring great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.
What are these seven?
Cunda! There are faithful sons and daughters of good family who give dwellings and halls to the community of bhikṣus. Cunda!
This is called the first worldly merit, which brings great blessing, a great reward, great renown, and great virtue.
"Furthermore, Cunda!
There are faithful sons and daughters of noble family who, within their dwellings, provide couches, seats, woolen rugs, felt carpets, blankets, and bedding as offerings.
Cunda! This is called the second worldly merit, which brings great blessing, great reward, great renown, and great virtue.
"Furthermore, Cunda!
There are faithful sons and daughters of good family who, within their dwellings, bestow all kinds of new, pure, and exquisite garments as gifts."
Cunda! This is called the third worldly merit, which brings great blessing, great reward, great renown, and great virtue.
"Furthermore, Cunda!

There are faithful sons and daughters of good family who, within their own dwellings, constantly provide the community with morning gruel and midday meals; they also provide park-attendants to serve them, and when there is wind, rain, cold, or snow, they personally go to the park to increase their offerings and support."

"Once the community of bhikṣus has finished eating, they are not troubled by wind, rain, cold, or snow soaking their robes; day and night they dwell in peace, practicing dhyāna and contemplation. Cunda!"
"This is called the seventh worldly merit, which brings great fortune, a great reward, great renown, and great virtue. Cunda!"

O son or daughter of good family who has already attained these seven worldly merits, whether going or coming, standing or sitting, sleeping or waking, by day or by night, their merit constantly arises, increasing and expanding further and further.
Cunda! It is just as the waters of the Ganges, flowing from their source and entering the great ocean, become increasingly deep and increasingly vast along the way. Cunda!

Thus, for a son or daughter of good family who has gained these seven worldly blessings through faith, whether they are walking or coming, standing or sitting, sleeping or awake, by day or by night, their merit constantly arises, increasing and expanding further and further.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahācunda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"Is it possible to designate supramundane merit?
The World-Honored One replied,
"It is possible."
Cunda! There are further seven blessings that arise in the world, which bring great fortune and protection, great rewards, great renown, and great merit.
What are the seven? Cunda!

There are faithful sons and daughters of noble family who hear that the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is traveling in a certain place; having heard this, they rejoice and feel extreme exultation.
Cunda! This is called the first supramundane merit, which brings great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.
"Furthermore, Cunda!

There are faithful sons and daughters of good family who hear that the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata intends to come from that place to this one; having heard this, they rejoice and feel extreme exultation."
Cunda! This is called the second supramundane merit, which brings great blessing, great fruit, great renown, and great virtue.
"Furthermore, Cunda!

There are faithful sons and daughters of good family who hear that the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata has come from there to here. Having heard this, they rejoice and are filled with extreme exultation; with a pure mind, they go in person to see him, pay homage, and make offerings. Having made their offerings, they take the three refuges in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and receive the precepts."
Cunda! This is called the seventh supramundane merit, which brings great blessings, great rewards, great renown, and great virtue.

"Cunda! If faithful sons and daughters of good family were to obtain these seven worldly merits, as well as the further seven supramundane merits, those merits would be incalculable; there would be such a measure of merit, such a measure of the fruit of merit, and such a measure of the retribution of merit, such that they could only be described as limitless, immeasurable, and beyond the reach of any calculation of great merit."
Cunda! It is just as there are five rivers flowing from Jambudvīpa:

first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarabhū; fourth, the Aciravatī; and fifth, the Mahī. They flow into the great ocean, and the water within them is incalculable; it consists of so many *śoṇa* and *droṇa* measures that it is simply limitless, immeasurable, and its total volume of great water cannot be determined.

Cunda! If a son or daughter of good family who possesses such faith should obtain these seven worldly merits, as well as the further seven supramundane merits, those merits would be incalculable. There would be such a quantity of merit, such a result of merit, and such a retribution of merit, that it could only be described as limitless, immeasurable, and beyond the reach of any calculation of great merit.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The River Gaṅgā is pure and easy to cross;
the ocean abounds with rare treasures, the king of all waters.”
Just as the river waters, which the people of the world revere and honor,
flow from all streams and are led into the great ocean;
so too with such a person, when one bestows upon them clothing and food, [the merit likewise flows forth].
Couches, stools, rugs, and mats, as well as various sitting implements—
through immeasurable meritorious rewards, one shall reach the wondrous realm,
just as river waters flow into the great ocean.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Mahācunda and the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Seventh Discourse on Worldly Merit ends here, totaling nine hundred and ninety-three characters. (8) The Discourse on the Seven Days (8), from the Section on the Seven Dharmas in the Madhyama Āgama, the Eighth Discourse on the Seven Days, for the First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī and staying at the Āmrapālī Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not delight in or cling to these formations; one should find weariness in them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them."

Why is this? There are times when it does not rain; when it does not rain, all trees, the hundred grains, and medicinal plants wither away, are shattered and utterly destroyed, and cannot remain permanently.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are phenomena that do not endure for long, phenomena that change rapidly, and phenomena that cannot be relied upon. One should not delight in or cling to such formations; rather, one should find weariness in them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.
"Furthermore, there comes a time when two suns appear in the world. When the two suns appear, all the ditches, canals, and rivers completely dry up and can no longer remain."

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure for long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon. One should not delight in or cling to such formations; rather, one should find them wearying, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.
"Furthermore, there comes a time when three suns appear in the world. When the three suns appear, all the great rivers are completely exhausted and can no longer remain permanent."

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure for long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not delight in or cling to these conditioned phenomena; rather, one should find weariness in them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.
"Furthermore, there comes a time when four suns appear in the world.

When the four suns appear, the great springs from which the five rivers of Jambudvīpa flow—namely, first the Gaṅgā, second the Yamunā, third the Sarabhū, fourth the Aciravatī, and fifth the Mahī—all those great springs will completely dry up and can no longer remain."

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are things that do not endure for long, things that change rapidly, and things that cannot be relied upon. Thus, one should not delight in or cling to these formations; rather, one should find weariness with them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there comes a time when five suns appear in the world. When five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean recede by one hundred yojanas, and continue to recede until they have diminished by seven hundred yojanas;
when five suns appear, the remaining waters of the ocean decrease from seven hundred yojanas down to one hundred yojanas;
when five suns appear, the waters of the great ocean recede by the height of one tala tree, and continue to recede until they have diminished by seven tala trees."
When five suns appear, the seawater remains at the height of seven *tāla* trees, and it continues to diminish until it is only one *tāla* tree high;
when five suns appear, the seawater recedes by the depth of one man, and it continues to diminish until it is only seven men deep;
when five suns appear, the seawater remains at the depth of seven men, and it continues to diminish until it is only one man deep.

When five suns appear, the seawater recedes until it reaches the neck, the shoulders, the waist, the hips, the knees, and the ankles; at times the seawater is completely exhausted, not even enough to submerge a finger.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure for long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon. One should not delight in or be attached to such formations; rather, one should feel weary of them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there comes a time when six suns appear in the world. When the six suns appear, the entire great earth and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all emit smoke, which merges into a single mass of smoke—just as when a potter first fires his kiln, everything emits smoke that merges into a single mass of smoke."
When these six suns appear, the entire great earth and Sumeru, the king of mountains, all emit smoke until they merge into a single mass of smoke.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure for long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon. One should not take pleasure in or become attached to such conditioned phenomena; rather, one should grow weary of them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.

"Furthermore, there comes a time when seven suns appear in the world. When these seven suns arise, the entire great earth and Sumeru, the king of mountains, burn through and forth with intense heat, merging into a single conflagration.

Thus, when the seven suns arise, the entire great earth and Sumeru, the king of mountains, burn through and forth with intense heat, merging into a single conflagration; the wind blows this fire until it reaches as far as the Brahma-heaven."

At that time, those gods born into the Radiant Heaven (*Ābhāsvara*), being unacquainted with the formation and destruction of the world, not having seen the formation and destruction of the world, and not knowing the formation and destruction of the world, became terrified upon seeing the great fire; their hair stood on end as they thought:
"Has the fire not come here?"
"Will the fire not come here?

The gods born in previous lives, who were well-versed in the formation and destruction of the world, having seen the formation and destruction of the world and knowing the formation and destruction of the world, saw the great fire and consoled the other gods, saying:
"Do not be afraid; by the nature of fire, it reaches only that far and will never come this way."

When the seven suns arise, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, will crumble, disintegrate, and be utterly destroyed for a range of one hundred *yojanas*; it will crumble, disintegrate, and be utterly destroyed for two hundred, three hundred, and even up to seven hundred *yojanas*.

When the seven suns arise, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, and this great earth will be scorched, ruined, and extinguished, leaving no remaining embers or ashes; just as when ghee or oil is burned, it is boiled away and consumed until not even smoke or soot remains;
in this way, when the seven suns arise, the King of Mountains, Sumeru, and this great earth will leave behind no remaining embers or ashes.

Therefore, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are things that do not endure long, things that change rapidly, and things that cannot be relied upon. One should not take pleasure in or become attached to such formations; rather, one should feel weary of them, seek to abandon them, and seek liberation from them.
"I now tell you that Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, shall crumble and perish entirely; who is there capable of believing this?
Only those who have seen the Truth. I now tell you that the waters of the great ocean shall dry up and be utterly exhausted; who is there capable of believing this?"
Only those who have seen the Truth can hear this.
When I now declare to you that the entire great earth shall be consumed by fire until it is utterly exhausted, who could believe it?
Only those who have seen the Truth can hear this.
Why is that? Bhikṣus!
In the past, there was a Great Teacher named Sunetra, who was revered as the master of non-Buddhist seers; he had abandoned sensual desire and attained the bases of psychic power.

The Great Teacher Sunetra had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. The Great Teacher Sunetra taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world to his disciples; when the Great Teacher Sunetra taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world, among those disciples there were some who did not fully practice the Dharma, yet after their lives ended, they were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

When the Great Teacher Sunetra expounds the Dharma of the Brahma-world, if among his disciples there are those who fully practice the Dharma, they cultivate the four Brahma-abodes and abandon sensual desire; at the end of their lives, they attain rebirth in the Brahma-heaven.
At that time, the Great Teacher Sunetra thought to himself:
"I ought not to go to the next world and be born in the same place as my disciples; it would be better for me now to further cultivate superior loving-kindness."
"Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of his life he was reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas.

At that time, the Great Teacher Sunetra subsequently cultivated superior loving-kindness once more; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of his life he was reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas.
"The Great Teacher Sunetra and his disciples have not studied the Path in vain; they have attained great fruits and rewards.
Bhikṣus, what do you think?"
In the past, the Great Teacher Sunetra was revered as a master by the non-Buddhist seers; having abandoned sensual desire and attained the bases of psychic power, do you think he was someone else?
Do not harbor such thoughts; you should know that I was that very person.
At that time, I was known as the Great Teacher Sunetra, who was revered as a master by the non-Buddhist sages. Having abandoned sensual desire, I attained the bases of psychic power.
At that time, I had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples, and for those disciples, I taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world.

When I teach the Dharma of the Brahma-world, there are among my disciples those who do not fully practice the Dharma; at the end of their lives, they are reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

When I teach the Dharma of the Brahma-world, if among my disciples there are those who fully practice the Dharma and cultivate the four Brahma-abodes, abandoning all desire, they will, upon the end of their lives, be reborn in the Brahma-heaven.
At that time, I had this thought:
"I should not go to the next world and be born in the same place as my disciples; I would rather now further cultivate superior loving-kindness."
"Having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of my life I was reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas.
At a later time, I again cultivated superior loving-kindness; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of my life I was reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas."
At that time, both I and my disciples practiced the path not in vain and attained great fruit.

At that time, I personally practiced this path for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others; for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is righteous and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking security and happiness. Yet at that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate end; it was not ultimately pure, nor was the holy life (brahmacarya) ultimately fulfilled. Because the holy life was not yet brought to completion, at that time I was not free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had I yet been able to attain liberation from all suffering.

“Monks! I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat.

I now benefit myself and also benefit others; I benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking for the sake of gods and humans that which is meaningful and beneficial, seeking peace, security, and happiness.”
I have now taught the Dharma that reaches the ultimate, which is ultimately pure and the ultimate holy life;
having completed the ultimate holy life, I am now free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Rājagṛha and staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, where he observed the rains retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus; the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was also observing the rains retreat in his native land.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka, having completed their summer retreat and finished mending their robes after the three months had passed, took up their robes and bowls and departed from Sthūlakoṣṭhaka. Traveling by stages, they arrived at Rājagṛha and stayed at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves in greeting, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One asked them: "Bhikṣus!..."
"From where have you come?
Where did you spend the summer retreat?
The bhikṣus from his native land replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have come from my native land and shall observe the rains retreat in my native land.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Among the bhikṣus born in that land, which bhikṣu is universally praised by the other bhikṣus for being himself of few desires and contented while praising fewness of desires and contentment;
for being himself secluded while praising seclusion;
and for being himself diligent while praising diligence?"
Being themselves established in right mindfulness, they speak of right mindfulness;
being themselves established in single-mindedness, they speak of single-mindedness;
being themselves established in wisdom, they speak of wisdom.
Having personally exhausted the outflows, one proclaims the exhaustion of the outflows;
having personally inspired aspiration and achieved joy, one proclaims the inspiration of aspiration and the achievement of joy.
The bhikṣus of his native land said to him:
"World-Honored One!

The Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is universally praised by the bhikṣus in that native land; he himself is one of few desires and contentment, and he speaks in praise of fewness of desires and contentment."
Dwelling in seclusion oneself, one speaks in praise of dwelling in seclusion;
being diligent oneself, one speaks in praise of diligence;
maintaining right mindfulness oneself, one speaks in praise of right mindfulness.
From one's own single-mindedness, one proclaims single-mindedness;
from one's own wisdom, one proclaims wisdom;
from one's own exhaustion of outflows, one proclaims the exhaustion of outflows.
"One should encourage oneself to aspire and achieve joy, and one should praise and encourage others to aspire and achieve joy.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was seated among the assembly, and the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has questioned those bhikṣus from his native land regarding this matter, and those bhikṣus from his native land have praised the worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra most highly, saying that he is himself of few desires and contented, and he praises and speaks of being of few desires and contented."
Dwelling in seclusion oneself, one praises dwelling in seclusion;
being diligent oneself, one praises diligence;
possessing right mindfulness oneself, one praises right mindfulness.
From one's own single-mindedness, one proclaims single-mindedness;
from one's own wisdom, one proclaims wisdom;
from one's own exhaustion of outflows, one proclaims the exhaustion of outflows.
"One should encourage oneself to arouse longing and achieve joy, and one should speak in praise of encouraging oneself to arouse longing and achieving joy.
Then, the Venerable Śāriputra thought again:
"When shall I be able to meet with the worthy Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to inquire about a small matter of meaning? Perhaps he will listen to my questions."

At that time, the World-Honored One, having completed his summer retreat in Rājagṛha and passed the three months, finished mending his robes; he then took up his robes and bowl, departed from Rājagṛha, and proceeded toward Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, having completed the summer retreat at his birthplace and the three months having passed, finished mending his robes. The Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated himself in salutation, spread out his sitting mat before the Tathāgata, and sat down cross-legged.

"Virtuous ones!..."
"Who is this worthy one, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra?
The bhikṣus replied to the Venerable Śāriputra:

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having observed the physical appearance of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, took note of it well.

When the night had passed and at dawn, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. After he had finished eating and returned from his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣadana) over his shoulder, and went to the walking path in the Andhavana forest.

The Venerable Śāriputra, having also passed the night, dressed in his robes and took up his bowl at dawn; he entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Having finished his meal after midday, he returned, put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣadana) over his shoulder, and went to the walking-path in the Andhavana forest.
At that time, the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra went to the Andhavana forest, spread out his sitting mat beneath a tree, and sat down cross-legged.
The Venerable Śāriputra also went to the Andhavana forest; not far from Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, he too spread out his sitting mat beneath a tree and sat down cross-legged.

Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his meditation, went to where the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and asked the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"Worthy friend!..."
"Does he practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?
He replied, "It is so."
“How is it, worthy one?
Is it because of the purity of your precepts that you practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?
He replied:

"No. "Is it for the sake of purity of mind, purity of view, purity from the veil of doubt, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, and purity of knowledge regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal that one practices the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"I asked the venerable one, 'Do you practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?
and you replied, 'I do.
Now I ask the venerable one: Is it for the sake of purity in moral discipline that you practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"
He replied, "No.

Is it because of purity of mind, purity of view, purity from the veil of doubt, purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, and purity of knowledge regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal that one practices the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?"
He replied, "No.
For what purpose, then, would one practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?
He answered:
"Venerable sir!
It is because of parinirvāṇa without remainder.
He asked again:
“How is it, worthy one?
Is it because of the purity of his ethical discipline that the ascetic Gautama designates unconditioned nirvana?
He replied:

"No. "Is it because of the purity of mind, the purity of view, the purity regarding the hindrance of doubt, the purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, and the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal that the ascetic Gautama designates nirvana without remainder?"
He replied, “No. He asked again:
"I asked the Venerable one: 'How is it that the worthy one, on account of the purity of his precepts, declares the Nirvāṇa without remainder for the Śramaṇa Gautama?
The Venerable one replied, 'No.'"

Is it because of the purity of mind, the purity of view, the purity regarding the removal of doubt, the purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is and is not the path, the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, and the purity of knowledge regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal, that the śramaṇa Gautama designates nirvāṇa without remainder?
The worthy one said, "No.
What is the meaning of what the worthy one has spoken?
How is this to be understood?
He replied:
"Venerable sir!

If the World-honored One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, were to designate parinirvāṇa without remainder on account of the purity of ethical discipline, then he would be describing that which has a remainder as being without remainder."

Because of the purification of mind, the purification of view, the purification by overcoming doubt, the purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, the purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and the purification by knowledge and vision of the abandonment of the way—when the World-Honored One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, designates "Nirvana without remainder," he is actually describing "with remainder" as "without remainder."
"O Worthy One!

If the Blessed One were to designate parinirvāṇa without remainder as being apart from these phenomena, then even ordinary worldlings would attain parinirvāṇa, for ordinary worldlings are also apart from these phenomena."

"Venerable sir! It is by means of purity of virtue that one attains purity of mind; by means of purity of mind, one attains purity of view; by means of purity of view, one attains purity regarding the overcoming of doubt; by means of purity regarding the overcoming of doubt, one attains purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path; by means of purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path, one attains purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal; by means of purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, one attains purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal; and because of this purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment of the way leading to the goal, the Blessed One, the Śramaṇa Gautama, designates it as Nirvāṇa without remainder."
“Wise one! Listen further.
Formerly, King Pasenadi of Kosala was in Śrāvastī when he had business in Vājīmatī. He thought to himself:”
"By what means can one travel from Śrāvastī to Vālukṣetra in a single day?
He further thought:
"I should now arrange seven chariots between Śrāvastī and Vālukṣetra."
At that time, he traveled from Śrāvastī to Vājīmatī, having arranged seven chariots along the way. Having set up the seven chariots, he departed from Śrāvastī and reached the first chariot;

he mounted the first chariot and proceeded to the second chariot, where he left the first and mounted the second. He proceeded to the third chariot, left the second and mounted the third; he proceeded to the fourth chariot, left the third and mounted the fourth; he proceeded to the fifth chariot, left the fourth and mounted the fifth; he proceeded to the sixth chariot, left the fifth and mounted the sixth; and he proceeded to the seventh chariot, mounted the seventh chariot, and arrived at Vājīmatī within a single day.
"Having completed his business at Vārāṇasī, he sat in the royal hall surrounded by his ministers, and the assembly of officials said to him:
'What is it, O Great King?'"
"Could one travel from Śrāvastī to Vālukṣetra in a single day?
The King replied, "Indeed."
"How so, Great King? Could one riding the first chariot travel from Śrāvastī to Vājīmatī in a single day?
The king replied:
"No. "Did you travel from Śrāvastī to Pāṭaliputra by means of the second chariot, the third chariot, and so on up to the seventh chariot?
The King replied:
"No. "In that case, worthy one,
when King Pasenadi of Kosala and his ministers question you again, what will you say?"
The king replied to his ministers:
"While I was in Śrāvastī, I had business in Vājīvatī. I thought to myself:
'By what means might I travel from Śrāvastī to Vājīvatī in a single day?'"
I further had this thought:
"I should now rather travel from Śrāvastī to Vāsavagrāma, arranging seven carriages along the way."
At that time, I departed from Śrāvastī for Vajjī, arranging seven chariots along the way. Having arranged the seven chariots, I set out from Śrāvastī;

I mounted the first chariot and reached the second, where I left the first and mounted the second; reaching the third, I left the second and mounted the third; reaching the fourth, I left the third and mounted the fourth; reaching the fifth, I left the fourth and mounted the fifth; reaching the sixth, I left the fifth and mounted the sixth; reaching the seventh, I mounted the seventh and arrived at Vajjī within a single day.
"In this way, worthy one,
King Pasenadi of Kosala answered the questions posed by his ministers.
Thus it is, worthy one."

Because of the purity of ethical conduct, there is purity of mind; because of the purity of mind, there is purity of view; because of the purity of view, there is purity regarding the overcoming of doubt; because of the purity regarding the overcoming of doubt, there is purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path; because of the purity of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path, there is purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal; because of the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the way leading to the goal, there is purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment through the way leading to the goal; and because of the purity of knowledge and vision regarding the abandonment through the way leading to the goal, the Blessed One designates it as "nirvana without remainder."
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra asked the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"What is your name, worthy one?
How do your fellow practitioners in the holy life address you?"
The Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra replied:
"Venerable friend!
My name is Pūrṇa."
"My mother's name was Maitrāyaṇī; therefore, my fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
The Venerable Śāriputra praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"

The worthy Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is a disciple of the Tathāgata; his wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence are decisive, secure, and fearless. He has accomplished mastery over himself, attained great辩才 (eloquence), and grasped the banner of the Deathless. Having personally realized and attained the realm of the Deathless, he is able to answer all questions regarding the profound meaning of the worthy one’s teachings.
Worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra!

Fellow practitioners of the holy life obtain great benefit by meeting the worthy Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, visiting him at the proper time, and paying him homage at the proper time; I too have now obtained great benefit by visiting him at the proper time and paying him homage at the proper time.

Fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes and carry the Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra upon their heads; this will bring them great benefit, and I too now obtain great benefit by going to see him and paying him homage from time to time.
The Venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra asked the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Worthy one, what is your name, and how do your fellow practitioners in the holy life address you?"
The Venerable Sāriputta replied: "Friend!
My name is Upatissa, and my mother’s name was Sāri; therefore, my fellow practitioners of the holy life call me Sāriputta."
The Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra exclaimed:

"Now, while debating with a disciple of the World-Honored One, I have failed to understand; while debating with the second most honored one, I have failed to understand; while debating with the General of the Dharma, I have failed to understand; and while debating with a disciple who turns the wheel of the Dharma and turns it again, I have failed to understand."
If I had known the Venerable Śāriputra, I would not have been able to answer even a single sentence, much less such a profound discourse!
Excellent, excellent,
Venerable Śāriputra!

As a disciple of the Tathāgata, one possesses wisdom, eloquence, and intelligence that are decisive; one dwells in peace and fearlessness, achieves mastery, attains great辩才 (eloquence), and gains the banner of the Deathless. Having personally realized and accomplished the realm of the Deathless, one wanders therein—this is because of the Venerable One’s exceedingly profound and deep questions.
Venerable Sāriputta!

Fellow practitioners of the holy life gain great benefit by encountering the Venerable Sāriputta, visiting him at the proper time, and paying him homage at the proper time; I too have now gained great benefit by visiting him at the proper time and paying him homage at the proper time.

"Virtuous companions in the holy life should wrap their robes and carry the Venerable Sāriputta upon their heads; they will thereby obtain great benefit, and I too shall now obtain great benefit by going to see him at the proper time and paying him homage at the proper time."
Thus these two worthies praised and commended one another; having done so, they joyfully received and practiced [the teaching], rose from their seats, and each returned to his own dwelling.

The *Saptasūryodaya Sūtra*, Chapter Nine, ends here; 2,508 characters. 10. The *Āsravakṣaya Sūtra* (10), the tenth discourse in the Section on the Seven Dharmas of the Madhyama Āgama. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Kuru country, staying at the Kuru capital of Kalmāṣadamya.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is through knowing and seeing that all outflows (āsrava) are exhausted, not through not knowing and not seeing."
How is it that through knowledge and vision the outflows (*āsrava*) are brought to an end?

There is right reflection (*yoniso-manasikāra*) and wrong reflection (*ayoniso-manasikāra*). If one reflects wrongly, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen will arise, and that which has already arisen will increase and expand; the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that have not yet arisen will arise, and those that have already arisen will increase and expand.

If one reflects rightly, the outflow of sensual desire that has not yet arisen will not arise, and that which has already arisen will be extinguished; the outflow of existence and the outflow of ignorance that have not yet arisen will not arise, and those that have already arisen will be extinguished.

"However, ordinary foolish people do not hear the True Dharma, do not encounter true spiritual friends, do not know the noble Dharma, are not disciplined by the noble Dharma, and do not understand the Dharma as it truly is."

For one who engages in improper reflection, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases and expands; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that have not yet arisen arise, and those which have already arisen increase and expand.

One who possesses right reflection ensures that the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*) which has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is extinguished; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*) which have not yet arisen do not arise, and those which have already arisen are extinguished.

Because they do not know phenomena as they truly are, they attend to phenomena that should not be attended to and fail to attend to those that should be attended to. By attending to what should not be attended to and failing to attend to what should be attended to, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases and expands; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that have not yet arisen arise, and those which have already arisen increase and expand.
“The well-heard noble disciple hears the True Dharma, meets with true spiritual friends, is disciplined by the Noble Dharma, and knows the Dharma as it truly is.

For one who engages in improper reflection, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen arises, and that which has already arisen increases and expands; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that have not yet arisen arise, and those that have already arisen increase and expand.”

One who possesses right intention does not give rise to the outflow of sensual desire that has not yet arisen, and brings to cessation that which has already arisen; likewise, they do not give rise to the outflow of existence or the outflow of ignorance that have not yet arisen, and bring to cessation those which have already arisen.

Having known the Dharma as it truly is, one should not attend to things that should not be attended to; rather, one should attend to those things that should be attended to. Because one does not attend to what should not be attended to and attends to what should be attended to, the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*) that has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is extinguished; likewise, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those that have already arisen are extinguished.
“There are seven methods for abandoning outflows, afflictions, and states of grief and distress. What are the seven? There are outflows abandoned through vision;

there are outflows abandoned through guarding; there are outflows abandoned through detachment; there are outflows abandoned through utilization; there are outflows abandoned through endurance; there are outflows abandoned through removal; and there are outflows abandoned through reflection.”
"How are the outflows abandoned through vision?

An ordinary person, a foolish man, who has not heard the true Dharma, has not encountered true spiritual friends, does not know the noble Dharma, is not disciplined in the noble Dharma, does not know the Dharma as it truly is, and because of improper reflection, forms this thought:
'Did I exist in past lives? Did I not exist in past lives? By what cause did I exist in past lives? How did I exist in past lives?'"
"I shall have a future existence," "I shall not have a future existence," "By what cause shall I have a future existence," "How shall I have a future existence?"—
thus one harbors doubts within oneself as to what this self truly is and how it exists.
From where have these sentient beings come, and to where will they go?
By what causes did they originally come to exist, and by what causes will they come to exist?

Thus he engages in such improper reflection; among the six views, whichever view arises, it may arise as: "There truly is a self"; this view arises; or it may arise as: "There truly is no self"; this view arises; or it may arise as: "The self perceives the self"; this view arises; or it may arise as: "The self perceives what is not-self"; this view arises; or it may arise as: "What is not-self perceives the self"; this view arises; or it may arise as: "This is the self, which is able to speak, able to know, able to act, able to teach, able to initiate action, and able to instigate others to act; it is born in various places, receiving the retribution of good and evil; it certainly has nowhere from which it comes, it certainly does not exist, and it certainly shall not exist. This is called the corruption of views; one is moved by views and bound by the fetters of views.
It is for this reason that ordinary, foolish people undergo the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

A well-heard noble disciple hears the True Dharma, encounters true spiritual friends, is disciplined by the noble Dharma, and knows the Dharma as it truly is: they know suffering as it truly is; they know the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are.

Having known this as it truly is, the three fetters are exhausted: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Once these three fetters are exhausted, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*; one does not fall into states of woe, is destined for full awakening, and will undergo at most seven more existences.

After seven往返 (comings and goings) between the heavens and the human realm, one then reaches the end of suffering. If one does not know and see [this], then afflictions and lamentation arise; if one knows and sees, then afflictions and lamentation do not arise. This is called the cutting off of outflows through vision (*dṛṣṭiprahāṇa*).
"How are the outflows abandoned through restraint? Bhikṣus!

When the eye sees forms and one restrains the eye faculty, it is by means of right reflection and the contemplation of impurity; when one does not restrain the eye faculty, it is due to wrong reflection and the contemplation of purity."
If one does not guard [the senses], then afflictions and distress arise; if one guards them, afflictions and distress do not arise.

It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind in their cognition of phenomena. One who guards the faculty of the mind does so through right reflection and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); one who does not guard the faculty of the mind does so through improper reflection and the contemplation of purity (*śubha-bhāvanā*).
If one does not guard [the senses], then afflictions and distress arise; if one guards them, then afflictions and distress do not arise. This is called the abandonment of outflows through guarding.
"How are the outflows abandoned through avoidance? Bhikṣus!

Upon seeing a wicked elephant, one should keep far away; likewise with a wicked horse, a wicked ox, a wicked dog, a venomous snake, a dangerous path, a ditch or pit, a privy, a river, a deep spring, or a mountain crag."

If there are evil associates, evil friends, evil paths, evil neighborhoods, or evil dwellings, and if those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) live with them such that people who were without doubt come to have doubt, a bhikṣu should depart from them.

One should completely distance oneself from evil associates, evil friends, evil paths, evil neighborhoods, and evil dwellings; likewise, if those who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) associate with such people, they cause doubt where there was none, and thus one must avoid them all.

If one does not separate from them, then afflictions and distress arise; if one separates from them, then afflictions and distress do not arise. This is called the severance of outflows through separation.
"How is it that outflows are abandoned through usage? Bhikṣus!

If one uses robes, it is not for the sake of profit, nor for the sake of arrogance, nor for the sake of adornment; rather, it is for the sake of warding off mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, cold, and heat, and out of a sense of shame."

If one uses food and drink, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of pride, nor for the sake of physical plumpness and pleasure; rather, it is solely to maintain the body for a long time, to eliminate afflictions and sorrow, to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), to bring about the cessation of old ailments and prevent new ones from arising, and to abide long in peace and freedom from disease.

If one uses dwellings, rooms, beds, mattresses, or bedding, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of pride, nor for the sake of adornment; it is solely so that weariness may find rest and that one may attain quiet sitting.

If one uses medicinal decoctions, it is not for the sake of profit, nor out of pride, nor for the sake of physical plumpness and pleasure; rather, it is solely for the purpose of eliminating the affliction of illness, for sustaining the life-faculty, and for attaining peace and freedom from disease.
If one does not employ them, then afflictions and grief arise; if one employs them, then afflictions and grief do not arise. This is called the severance of outflows through employment.
“How, bhikkhus, are the outflows abandoned through patience?

A bhikkhu, through diligence in abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating wholesome states, constantly maintains the perception of exertion; he is single-minded and diligent, such that his body, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, blood, and marrow all become withered away. He does not relinquish his diligence until he has attained what he seeks, only then does he relinquish his diligence.”

"Monks! Furthermore, you should be able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and lice; you must also be able to endure the afflictions of wind and sun, harsh words, and the striking of staffs. When the body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point where life is about to cease, you must be able to endure all such unpleasant things."
If one does not endure, then afflictions and sorrow arise; if one endures, then afflictions and sorrow do not arise. This is called the severing of outflows through endurance.
"How are the outflows abandoned through removal? Monk! When thoughts of sensual desire arise and are not removed, severed, or relinquished;

when thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm arise and are not removed, severed, or relinquished—if they are not removed, then afflictions and distress arise; if they are removed, then afflictions and distress do not arise. This is called the abandonment of outflows through removal."
"How are the outflows abandoned through contemplation? Bhikṣus!

One contemplates the first factor of enlightenment, mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, leading to liberation. [One contemplates] the factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, and concentration. One contemplates the seventh factor of enlightenment, equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, leading to liberation."
If one does not contemplate, then afflictions and distress arise; if one contemplates, then afflictions and distress do not arise. This is called the abandonment of outflows through contemplation.

"If a bhikṣu causes the outflows that are to be abandoned by vision to be abandoned by vision; the outflows that are to be abandoned by guarding to be abandoned by guarding; the outflows that are to be abandoned by dissociation to be abandoned by dissociation; the outflows that are to be abandoned by using to be abandoned by using; the outflows that are to be abandoned by enduring to be abandoned by enduring; the outflows that are to be abandoned by removing to be abandoned by removing; and the outflows that are to be abandoned by cultivation to be abandoned by cultivation—this is called a bhikṣu whose all outflows are exhausted and whose fetters are already untied, who is able, through right knowledge, to reach the end of suffering."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The First Discourse in the Saṃyukta Āgama on Karma, the Simile of Salt. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“One receives retribution according to the actions one has performed.”

In this way, if one does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya), one will not attain the end of suffering; if one were to say that one receives retribution according to the deeds one has performed, it would be so.
In this way, by practicing the holy life, one attains the end of suffering.
Why is this so? If there is a person who commits unwholesome karma, they will inevitably experience the retribution of the hells as a fruit of suffering.
How is it that a person who commits unwholesome karma will inevitably experience the retribution of the hells as a fruit of suffering?

It refers to a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is exceedingly short; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and will inevitably receive the retribution of suffering in the hells.
It is like a person who throws one *liang* of salt into a small amount of water, wishing to make the water so salty that it cannot be drunk.
What do you think?
Can this one *liang* of salt make the small amount of water so salty as to be undrinkable?
He replied, “It is so,
World-Honored One!”
"Why is this? Because there is much salt and little water, it becomes so salty that it cannot be drunk.
In the same way, when a person performs unwholesome deeds, they will inevitably suffer the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit."
What is meant by a person who performs unwholesome karma and must inevitably experience the retribution of the hells as its painful fruit?

It refers to a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate morality, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely short. This is what is meant by a person who performs unwholesome karma and must inevitably experience the retribution of the hells as its painful fruit.
"Furthermore, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life.
How is it that some people perform unwholesome deeds and must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life?

It refers to a person who cultivates the body, cultivates ethical discipline, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is exceedingly long; this is called a person who, having committed unwholesome karma, must experience the retribution of that fruit in the present life.
It is as if someone were to throw one *liang* of salt into the waters of the Ganges, wishing to make the water so salty that it could not be drunk.
What do you think?
Could this one *liang* of salt make the waters of the Ganges so salty as to be undrinkable?
He replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
"Why is this? Because the waters of the Ganges are vast and the two catties of salt are few; therefore, they cannot be made salty enough to be undrinkable.
In the same way, when a person performs unwholesome karma, they will inevitably experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life."
What kind of person performs unwholesome karma and necessarily experiences its painful fruit as a retribution in the present life?

It refers to a person who cultivates the body, cultivates virtue, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely long; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and necessarily experiences its painful fruit as a retribution in the present life.
"Furthermore, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit.
In what way do such people perform unwholesome deeds and inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit?"

It refers to a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely short; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as its painful fruit.
It is just as if someone were to seize another’s sheep.
How does one seize another’s sheep?

It means that the one who seizes the sheep is either a king or a royal minister of great power and authority, while the owner of the sheep is poor, lowly, and powerless. Because he is powerless, he must wait upon the other in various ways, joining his palms and entreating him, saying:
"Venerable sir!
You may take back the sheep, or you may accept its value.
This is called a person who has stolen another's sheep.
In this way, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit.
What is meant by those who perform unwholesome deeds and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit?

It refers to a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely short; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as its bitter fruit.
"Furthermore, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and necessarily experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life.
How is it that someone performs unwholesome deeds and necessarily experiences the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life?

It refers to a person who cultivates the body, cultivates virtue, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely long; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in the present life.
It is just as when someone steals another’s sheep, yet the owner recovers them.
How is it that someone steals another’s sheep, yet the owner recovers them?

It means that the thief is poor, lowly, and powerless, while the owner of the sheep is either a king or a royal minister who possesses great power and authority; because of this power, he binds the thief and recovers the sheep.
This is called the case where a person, though having stolen another's sheep, has it taken back by the owner.
In the same way, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life.
What kind of person performs unwholesome karma and necessarily experiences its painful fruit as a retribution in the present life?

It is said that there is a person who cultivates the body, cultivates virtue, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely long; this is called a person who performs unwholesome karma and necessarily experiences its painful fruit as a retribution in the present life.
"Furthermore, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and will inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit.
In what way do such people perform unwholesome deeds and inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as their bitter fruit?"

This refers to a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely short; such a person is said to have performed unwholesome karma and will inevitably experience the retribution of the hells as the fruit of suffering.
It is just as if there were a person who owed another five coins and was bound by his creditor, or even one coin and was bound by his creditor.
How is it that a person who owes another five coins is bound by his creditor, and even one who owes one coin is bound by his creditor?

This refers to a debtor who is poor and lacks power; because he is poor and powerless, he owes another five coins and is bound by his creditor, or even for as little as one coin, he is bound by his creditor.
This is called a person who owes another five coins and is bound by the creditor, or even one coin and is likewise bound by the creditor.
In the same way, there are people who commit unwholesome deeds and will inevitably suffer the retribution of the hells as the fruit of their suffering.
What is it that causes a person who performs unwholesome karma to inevitably receive the retribution of the hells as a fruit of suffering?

It is said that there is a person who does not cultivate the body, does not cultivate ethical discipline, does not cultivate the mind, and does not cultivate wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely short; this is what is meant by a person performing unwholesome karma who inevitably receives the retribution of the hells as a fruit of suffering.
"Furthermore, there are those who perform unwholesome deeds and necessarily experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life.
What kind of person performs unwholesome deeds and necessarily experiences the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life?"

It refers to a person who cultivates the body, cultivates morality, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely long; this is called a person who, having committed unwholesome karma, must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in the present life.
It is just as if there were a person who, though owing a hundred coins, is not bound by his master, and even if owing ten million, is still not bound by his master.
How is it that a person, though owing a hundred coins, is not bound by his master, and even if owing ten million, is still not bound by his master?

This means that if a debtor possesses immeasurable assets and great power, for that reason, even though he owes a hundred coins, he will not be bound by his creditor; even if he owes ten million, he still will not be bound by his creditor.
This is called a person who, though owing a hundred coins, is not bound by their owner, and even if owing ten million, is likewise not bound by their owner.
In the same way, there is a person who, having committed unwholesome karma, must experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in this very life.
What is it that causes a person who has committed unwholesome karma to necessarily experience the fruit of suffering as a retribution in the present life?

It is said that there is a person who cultivates the body, cultivates virtue, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom, and whose lifespan is extremely long; this is what is meant by a person who, having committed unwholesome karma, necessarily experiences the fruit of suffering as a retribution in the present life—for such a person, even if they do experience the retribution for wholesome and unwholesome karma in the present life, it is slight.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
