The *Vatrabhū-sutta* (The Discourse on Vatrabhū), Second in the *Karmavarga* (Chapter on Correspondence with Karma) of the *Madhyama Āgama*. First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas at Kapilavastu and was staying in the Nyagrodha Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, together with a community of bhikṣus, had gathered and sat in the lecture hall after the midday meal for some business.

At that time, there was a disciple of the Nirgranthas belonging to the Śākya clan named Upatiṣya. In the afternoon, while wandering about, he approached the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana; having exchanged greetings with him, he sat down to one side.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahā-Maudgalyāyana asked this question:
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭhas?
If there is a bhikkhu who guards his body, speech, and mind, do you see any occasion where, because of that, unwholesome taints arise which lead to future existence?"
Vairaṭī replied: "Mahā-Moggallāna!
If there is a bhikkhu who guards his body, speech, and mind, I see a possibility that, because of this, unwholesome taints may arise and lead him to future lives."
"Mahāmoggallāna! If one has performed unwholesome deeds in a previous life, because of this, unwholesome taints arise that lead to future lives.

Later, while the Blessed One was sitting in seclusion, with the pure divine ear surpassing that of humans, he heard the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna conversing in this manner with the Nigaṇṭha disciple Sīhapaññaka.
Having heard this, the Blessed One rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to the lecture hall before the assembly of bhikṣus, prepared a seat, and sat down.
Once seated, the Blessed One asked: “Maudgalyāyana!
"What was the subject of discussion you were having just now with the Nirgrantha disciple Śreṇika Bimbisāra?
And for what reason have you all gathered here in the lecture hall?
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:

“Bhagavān! Today, together with the community of bhikṣus, after the midday meal, I gathered in the lecture hall for a certain purpose. This disciple of the Nirgrantha, Śreṇika Vatsagotra, came wandering about after his own midday meal and approached me. We exchanged greetings and sat down to one side.
I asked him this: ‘What do you think, Śreṇika?’”
"If there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, do you see any possibility that, because of this, unwholesome outflows (āsrava) might arise and lead to future lives?
The Nirgrantha disciple Śīlabhadra immediately replied to me, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu who guards his body, speech, and mind, I see such a possibility where, because of this, unwholesome outflows might arise and lead to future lives."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If one has performed unwholesome deeds in a previous life, because of this, unwholesome outflows arise that carry over into future lives.
"World-Honored One! [he replied.]
"Just now, I was engaged in such a discussion with the Nigaṇṭha disciple Sīha; for this reason, we have gathered here in the lecture hall.
Then, the Blessed One said to the Nigaṇṭha disciple Sīha:
"If what I say is correct, you should say it is correct; if it is not correct, you should say it is not correct. If you have any doubts, you may ask me about them."
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
What is the matter here? What is the meaning here?
If you can accept what I say, I shall discuss this matter with you.”
Vatsa replied: "Śramaṇa Gautama!
If what you have said is correct, I shall say it is correct; if it is not correct, I shall say it is not correct. If I have any doubts, I shall ask Gautama about them."
"Gautama! What is the matter here? What is the meaning here?
I shall accept and uphold whatever the śramaṇa Gautama says; let the śramaṇa Gautama simply engage me in discussion on this matter.
The Blessed One asked:
"What do you think, Vappa?

If a bhikkhu gives rise to unwholesome bodily conduct, taints, fever, and distress, and at a later time those unwholesome bodily conducts cease, he does not create new karma but abandons old karma; thus, in this very life, he attains the ultimate state free from fever, remaining constant and unchanging—this is what is seen by noble wisdom and known by noble wisdom."

When one has produced unwholesome states of body, engaged in unwholesome conduct of speech, and engaged in unwholesome conduct of mind—characterized by ignorance, formations, taints, fever, and distress—and later those unwholesome formations of ignorance cease, such that one no longer creates new karma and abandons past karma, one attains finality in this very life and is free from fever, abiding eternally and unchangingly; this is what is seen by noble wisdom and known by noble wisdom.
"How is it, Vappa!
When a bhikkhu thus guards his body, speech, and mind, do you see any occasion where, because of this, unwholesome taints arise that would lead to future lives?"
Vappa replied: "Gautama!
If a bhikkhu thus guards his body, speech, and mind, I do not see any possibility that unwholesome taints could arise on that account and persist into future lives."
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Vappa!"
"What do you think, Vappa!

If a bhikkhu has exhausted ignorance and wisdom has arisen—having exhausted ignorance and having wisdom arisen—he knows when a feeling of a future body arises that it is a feeling of a future body, and he knows when a feeling of a future life arises that it is a feeling of a future life. When his body breaks up at the end of life and his lifespan is fully completed, all that was felt ceases and comes to rest right here in this present world; you should know that it has reached ultimate coolness."
It is just as, Vappa!

Because of a tree there is a shadow. Suppose someone were to come with a sharp axe and cut down that tree at its root, hacking it into pieces, breaking it into ten parts or a hundred parts, burning it to ashes with fire, or blowing it away with a great wind, or casting it into water.
“What do you think, Vappa?
When a shadow exists because of a tree, if that tree—the cause of the shadow—is cut off, does the shadow cease and fail to arise?
Vappa replied:
"So it is, Gautama! 'Upāli! [he replied].
"Upāli! [said the Buddha].

It should be known that it is the same for a bhikkhu: ignorance has been exhausted and true knowledge has arisen. Because ignorance has been exhausted and true knowledge has arisen, when he experiences the feeling of a future birth, he knows he is experiencing the feeling of a future birth; when he experiences the feeling of a future life, he knows he is experiencing the feeling of a future life. When the body breaks up and life ends, and his lifespan is fully completed, all that was felt ceases and comes to rest in this very life. It should be known that he has reached ultimate coolness.
Vappa! When a bhikkhu’s mind is thus rightly liberated, he attains six bases of wholesome abiding.
What are the six? Vappa!
When a bhikkhu sees forms with the eye, he is neither glad nor sad; he maintains equanimity, seeking the unconditioned, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, Sāḷha!
When a bhikkhu’s mind is thus liberated through rightness, this is called attaining the first excellent abiding.

In this way, Vappa, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cognize phenomena, one is neither glad nor sad; relinquishing seeking, one dwells in the unconditioned with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. Vappa!
Monks, when one’s mind is thus liberated through right concentration, this is called attaining the sixth ground of excellence, Vappa.
Monks, when one’s mind is thus liberated through right concentration, one attains these six grounds of excellence.
Vatsa replied, "It is so,
Gautama! A well-taught noble disciple whose mind is thus rightly liberated attains six bases of stability."
What are the six? Gautama!

A well-taught noble disciple, upon seeing a form with the eye, is neither glad nor sad; he maintains equanimity, being free from seeking, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension. Gautama!
The learned noble disciple whose mind is thus rightly liberated is said to have attained the foremost state of secure dwelling.

In this same way, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind perceive their respective objects, they are neither glad nor sad; they remain equanimous, seeking the unconditioned with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
"In this way, Gautama,
a learned noble disciple whose mind is thus rightly liberated— this is called attaining the sixth ground of stability.
In this way, Gautama!"
"A learned noble disciple whose mind is thus rightly liberated attains these six bases of wholesome abiding.
Thereupon, Vappa addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Gautama!..."
"I have understood, Sugata; I have comprehended, Gautama.

You, Gautama, are like a man with clear vision who turns upward what was overturned, reveals what was hidden, shows the way to those who were lost, and provides light in the darkness, so that those with eyes may see forms;
even so, Śramaṇa Gautama, have you taught me the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, manifesting its meaning according to the various paths."
"World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
“World-Honored One!
It is just as if someone were to raise a poor horse, hoping to gain profit from it; they would only exhaust themselves in vain without obtaining any benefit.
World-Honored One!”

I am also like this: those foolish Nirgranthas do not understand well, they cannot comprehend, and they fail to recognize the fertile field; without self-examination, they spend the long night honoring, making offerings to, and serving me, hoping thereby to gain benefit, yet their toil is in vain and brings no advantage.
"Bhagavān!

I now once again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I only pray that the Bhagavān will accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live."
“World-Honored One!
Previously I was ignorant; I had faith and reverence for the foolish Nirgranthas, but from this day forth I sever them. Why is this? Because—”
"Because you have deceived me, World-Honored One!

I now take refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Licchavi Vajji-putta and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second *Vajji-putta Sūtra*, totaling one thousand five hundred and two characters, is finished. 13. *Taraṇa Sūtra* (13), Chapter on Correspondence with Karma in the Madhyama Āgama, Third in the *Taraṇa Sūtra*, First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are three cases where one may correctly receive, thoroughly retain, and explain to others teachings that differ in lineage, name, school, and doctrine; yet, though possessing wisdom, such a person does not obtain any benefit.”
What are these three?
There are some śramaṇas and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus: "Everything a person does is caused by what was created in past lives.
Furthermore, there are other śramaṇas and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus: "Everything a person does is caused by a supreme deity."
Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus: "Everything that a person does is entirely without cause and without condition.

Among them, if there are recluses and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus, saying, "Everything that a person does is caused by what was done in a previous existence," I go to them, and having arrived, I ask:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do you truly hold such a view and speak thus, saying that everything a person does is caused by what was created in their past lives?
He replied, "Yes."
I spoke to them again:
"If that were so, then all of you, worthy sirs, would be killers of living beings. Why is this?"
Because all of these are caused by what was created in previous lives.
In this way, worthy ones, all of you have engaged in taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so forth, up to wrong view.
Why is this so? It is because all things are caused by what was created in past lives.
O worthy ones!

If everything were produced solely by the causes of past lives, then for one who perceives things as they truly are, there would be no desire and no effort regarding what is done or not done within the internal sphere.
"Venerable friends!

If one does not know, as it truly is, what is done and what is not done, then one loses right mindfulness and lacks right clear comprehension; thus, there is nothing by which one can be instructed. Only when a śramaṇa speaks in accordance with the Dharma of a śramaṇa can he be subdued by reason, O śramaṇas and brahmins."
"Among them, if there are any recluses or brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus, saying that everything a person does is caused by a supreme creator, I go to them and, having arrived, I ask:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Is it truly your view and your teaching that everything a person does is caused by a supreme creator? He replied, "Yes."
I spoke to them again:
"If that were so, then all you venerable ones would be killers of living beings. Why is this?"
Because all these things are created by a supreme creator;
likewise, O worthy ones, all these involve taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and even wrong view.
Why is this so? Because all things are created by a supreme creator.
O worthy ones!

If one perceives that all things are created by a supreme lord and regards this as the truth, then regarding internal causes within oneself—whether in action or non-action—one would have neither desire nor the means [to act].
"Venerable friends!

If one does not know, as it truly is, what is done and what is not done, then one loses right mindfulness and lacks right clear comprehension; thus, there is nothing by which one can be taught. Only when a śramaṇa speaks in accordance with the Dharma of a śramaṇa can he be subdued through reason by other śramaṇas and brahmins."

"Among them, if there are any śramaṇas or brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus, saying that everything a person does is entirely without cause and without condition, I go to them; having arrived, I immediately ask:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Is it truly your view and your teaching that everything a person does is entirely without cause and without condition?
He replied, "Yes."
I spoke to them again:
"If that were so, then all of you, worthy sirs, would be killers of living beings. Why is this?"
Because all these things are without cause and without condition.
In this way, worthy sirs, all these [actions]—from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, up to wrong view—are likewise [without cause and condition].
Why is this? Because all things are entirely without cause and without condition.
O worthy ones!

If all things were entirely without cause and without condition, and one perceived them as they truly are, then regarding internal causes and internal factors, whether an action is performed or not performed, there would be no desire at all and no application of means.
"Venerable friends!

If one does not know, as it truly is, the doing and the non-doing of actions, then one loses right mindfulness and lacks right clear comprehension; thus, there is nothing by which one may be instructed. Only when a śramaṇa speaks in accordance with the Dharma of a śramaṇa can he, through reason, subdue those other śramaṇas and brahmins."

“The Dharma that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I proclaim to you—neither any ascetic or brahmin, nor any deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, is able to subvert it, defile it, or restrain it.”

What is this Dharma that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I teach to you—a Dharma that cannot be overcome, defiled, or restrained by recluses, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world?

I have a teaching concerning the six sense bases that I have personally known and realized for myself, which I shall declare to you; it is not something that can be overturned, defiled, or suppressed by recluses, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world.

Furthermore, there are six elements that I have known by myself and realized by myself, which I shall teach to you; they cannot be overcome, corrupted, or constrained by recluses, brahmins, gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world.
"What is the teaching on the six sense bases that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I proclaim to you?
They are the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. This is the teaching on the six sense bases that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I proclaim to you."
What is the teaching on the six elements that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I declare to you?

They are the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. This is the teaching on the six elements that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I declare to you.

“Through the conjunction of the six elements, one is conceived in the mother’s womb; because of the six elements, there are the six sense bases; because of the six sense bases, there is contact; because of contact, there is feeling.”

"Monks! If one possesses discernment, one knows suffering as it truly is; one knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are.
How does one know suffering as it truly is?"

That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—this is called knowing suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is?
It refers to this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight in this or that; this is called knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is?

It is this: regarding this craving that leads to future existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking here and there for such existence—its abandonment without remainder, its relinquishing, its vomiting out, its exhaustion, its fading away, its cessation, its stilling, and its disappearance; this is called knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to and including right concentration—these are the eight. This is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.

“Monks! You should know suffering as it truly is; you should abandon the origin of suffering; you should realize the cessation of suffering; and you should cultivate the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

If a monk knows suffering as it truly is, abandons the origin of suffering, realizes the cessation of suffering, and cultivates the path leading to the cessation of suffering, he is called a monk whose taints are all exhausted, whose fetters are already untied, and who has reached the end of suffering through right knowledge.”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third sūtra, "The Crossing," ends here, totaling one thousand one hundred eighty-four characters. 14. The Rāhula Sūtra (14) Middle Āgama, Section on Correspondence with Karma, The Rāhula Sūtra, the Fourth, for the First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Rājagṛha and staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Park.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was also traveling through Rājagṛha and staying in the Hot Springs Forest.

Then, at the end of the night, when dawn had broken, the World-Honored One dressed in his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. Having finished his almsround, he proceeded to the Hot Springs Grove, the dwelling place of Rāhula.

When the Venerable Rāhula saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he immediately went out to meet him, took his robes and bowl, prepared a seat for him, and drew water to wash his feet. After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat upon Rāhula’s seat.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One took up a water vessel, poured out most of the water until only a small amount remained, and asked:
"Rāhula! Do you now see me taking this water vessel and pouring out the water until only a small amount remains?"
Rāhula replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"My description of that path as 'small' is likewise so: namely, knowing yet speaking falsely, without shame or remorse, and without a sense of moral dread or integrity, Rāhula!"
There is no evil they would not do.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus:
do not utter false speech through frivolous joking.
The Blessed One again took this small water vessel and, having emptied it completely, asked: "Rāhula,
did you see me take this small water vessel and empty it completely?"
Rāhula replied,
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Rāhula:

"Rāhula, my teaching that such a person has utterly abandoned the path is likewise true of one who, knowing the truth, speaks falsely, feels no shame, feels no remorse, and lacks both moral dread and a sense of propriety."
"There is no evil they would not do.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: do not speak false words even in jest."
The World-Honored One again took this empty water vessel, turned it over upon the ground, and asked:
"Rāhula! Do you see me taking this empty water vessel and turning it over upon the ground?"
Rāhula replied,
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula:

"I say that the obscuration of that path is likewise so: namely, when one speaks falsely after knowing the truth, yet feels no shame and no regret, being without a sense of moral dread or shame, Rāhula!"
"There is no evil they would not do.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus:
do not utter false speech through frivolous laughter."
The Blessed One then took up that overturned water vessel, turned it upright, and asked: "Rāhula,
do you see me taking this overturned water vessel and turning it upright?"
Rāhula replied, “I see them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rāhula:
"I say that this path is likewise 'upward-facing,' namely, when one speaks falsely after knowing the truth, yet feels no shame, no remorse, no modesty, and no sense of guilt, Rāhula!"
"There is no evil they would not do.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus:
do not utter false speech even in jest."

"Rāhula! It is just as when a king’s great elephant enters the fray of battle, it employs its forefeet, hindfeet, tail, haunches, back, flanks, neck, forehead, ears, and tusks—using them all—yet it protects only its trunk. When the elephant trainer sees this, he thinks:
'This great elephant of the king still cherishes its life.'"

Why is this? When this great royal elephant enters the fray of battle, it employs its forefeet, hindfeet, tail, hips, back, flanks, neck, forehead, ears, and tusks—utilizing them all—while guarding only its trunk.

"Rāhula! When a king’s great elephant enters the fray of battle, it employs its forefeet, hind feet, tail, hips, back, flanks, neck, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk—utilizing them all. Upon seeing this, the elephant trainer thinks:
'This king’s great elephant no longer cherishes its own life.'"

Why is this? When this great royal elephant enters the fray of battle, it employs its forefeet, hindfeet, tail, hips, back, flanks, neck, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk—utilizing them all without exception.
"Rāhula! When a king’s great elephant enters the fray of battle, it employs its forefeet, hindfeet, tail, haunches, back, flanks, neck, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk—employing them all, Rāhula!"
I say that when this great royal elephant enters the fray of battle, there is no evil he will not do.
In the same way, Rāhula, one who speaks falsehood after knowing the truth, and who feels no shame, no remorse, no sense of propriety, and no dread of blame—Rāhula! [is such a person].
I say that such a person is capable of doing no evil whatsoever.
Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself thus: do not utter false speech even in jest.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"When a person transgresses one dharma— namely, the telling of lies—
and fears not the future world, there is no evil they will not do."
It would be better to swallow an iron ball, blazing hot as fire,
than to violate the precepts while receiving the faithful offerings of the world.
If one fears suffering and has no affection [for the Dharma], [how could one accept such gifts]?
In both hidden and manifest places, do not commit evil deeds.
If unwholesome karma has been committed or is being committed now, one can never escape it; there is no place of refuge.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he again asked Rāhula:
"What do you think?
For what purpose does a person use a mirror?"
The Venerable Rāhula replied:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to observe his face to see whether it is pure or impure.”
“In this way, Rāhula!
If you are about to perform a bodily action, you should examine that bodily action:”
"Rāhula, one should reflect: 'I am about to perform a bodily action; will that bodily action be pure or impure? Is it for my own sake or for the sake of others?
Rāhula, if upon such reflection you know:

'I am about to perform a bodily action; that bodily action is impure, whether for my own sake or for the sake of others, being unwholesome and resulting in suffering, leading to the experience of painful retribution,' [you should refrain from it]."
Rāhula! You should abandon those bodily actions you are about to perform. Rāhula!

If, at the time of observation, one knows: "I am about to perform a bodily action; that bodily action is impure, whether performed for myself or for another, and it is wholesome, resulting in happiness and receiving a pleasant retribution."
"Rāhula! You should undertake those bodily actions that lead to future existence. Rāhula!"
If you currently perform a bodily action, you should immediately observe this bodily action:
"As I currently perform this bodily action, is it pure or impure? Is it for myself or for another?"

"Rāhula! When you observe at that time, you will know: 'I am currently performing a bodily action; this bodily action is pure, whether performed for my own sake or for the sake of others, yet it is unwholesome and results in suffering, leading to the experience of a painful retribution.'"
Rāhula! You should abandon this present bodily action. Rāhula!

If one observes at the time [of action], one knows: "I am now performing a bodily action; this bodily action is impure, whether performed for myself or for another; it is wholesome and yields a pleasant fruit, resulting in the experience of a pleasant retribution."
"Rāhula! You should receive this present bodily action. Rāhula!"
If you have already performed a bodily action, you should then contemplate that bodily action:
"This bodily action which I have performed has already passed away, ceased, and changed; was it pure or impure? Was it for my own sake or for the sake of others?"

"Rāhula! When one observes at that time, one knows: 'I have performed a bodily action; that bodily action has already passed, ceased, and changed. That bodily action was pure, whether performed for myself or for another; it was unwholesome, resulting in bitter fruit, and its painful retribution has been experienced.'"

Rāhula! You should approach spiritual friends and those who practice the holy life; they have already performed physical actions, so you should confess them with a sincere heart, speak of your transgressions with remorse, and take care not to conceal them, but rather maintain and protect yourself well thereafter.

Rāhula! If, when observing, you know: "I have performed a bodily action; that bodily action has already passed, ceased, and undergone change; that bodily action was impure, whether performed for my own sake or for the sake of others, yet it was wholesome and brings about a pleasant result, receiving a pleasant retribution."
Rāhula! You should dwell in joy day and night, abiding in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; the same applies to your verbal karma. Rāhula!
Because of past formations, a mental action has already arisen; he then contemplates that mental action:
"If, because of past formations, a mental action has already arisen, is that mental action pure or impure? Is it for oneself or for another?"

"Rāhula! If, when observing, one knows that because of past actions, a mental karma has already arisen—and that this mental karma has already passed away, ceased, and changed—then that mental karma is pure, whether performed for oneself or for others; yet it was unwholesome, resulting in bitter fruit and receiving a bitter retribution."
Rāhula! You should abandon that past mental karma. Rāhula! When you observe it, you will know:

because of past formations, the mental karma that has already arisen has passed away, ceased, and changed. That mental karma was impure; whether performed for oneself or for another, it was wholesome and resulted in happiness, receiving a pleasant retribution.
Rāhula! You should receive that past mental karma. Rāhula!
Because of future formations, mental karma will arise; he then contemplates that mental karma:
"If, because of future formations, mental karma will arise, is that mental karma pure or impure? Is it for oneself or for others?"

"Rāhula! When observing at that time, one knows: 'Because of future formations, mental karma will arise; that mental karma is impure, whether performed for oneself or for another, it is unwholesome and results in suffering, leading to the experience of a painful retribution.'"
Rāhula! You should abandon that future mental action. Rāhula!

If one observes at that time, one knows: "Because of future formations, mental karma will arise; that mental karma is impure, whether performed for oneself or for others, it is wholesome and yields pleasant results, receiving a pleasant retribution."
"Rāhula! You should receive that future mental karma. Rāhula!"
Because of present formations, a present mental action arises; he then contemplates this mental action:
"If, because of present formations, a present mental action arises, is this mental action pure or impure? Is it for oneself or for others?"

"Rāhula! When observing at that time, one knows: 'Because of present volitional formations, a present mental action has arisen; this mental action is pure, whether performed for oneself or for another, yet it is unwholesome and results in suffering, leading to the experience of a painful retribution.'"
Rāhula! You should abandon this present mental action. Rāhula!

If one observes at the time [of action], one knows that because of present formations, a mental karma arises in the present; this mental karma is impure, whether performed for oneself or for another, yet it is wholesome and yields the fruit of happiness, receiving a pleasant retribution.
Rāhula! You should undertake this present mental action. Rāhula!

If there were recluses or brahmins in the past whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions had already been examined and were being further examined, and had already been purified and were being further purified—all those were precisely these same bodily, verbal, and mental actions that had already been examined and were being further examined, and had already been purified and were being further purified.

Rāhula! If there are future śramaṇas or brahmins whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions they should contemplate and thus contemplate, and whose [actions] they should purify and thus purify—all those are precisely these same bodily, verbal, and mental actions that they should contemplate and thus contemplate, and should purify and thus purify, Rāhula!

If there are any present śramaṇas or brahmins whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions they observe through direct insight and purify through direct purification—all those are simply these very bodily, verbal, and mental actions which they observe through direct insight and purify through direct purification.
Rāhula! You should train yourself in this way: regarding these very actions of body, speech, and mind, I observe them through direct insight and purify them through direct purification.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Physical action, verbal action, and mental action, Rāhula!
Regarding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, you should constantly observe them.”
Knowing this, do not speak falsely, Rāhula;
you are a shaven-headed one who lives off others—how can you speak falsely?
It obscures the Dharma of the śramaṇa and is empty, devoid of reality.
To speak false words and fail to guard one's mouth—therefore, do not speak falsely.
This is the Dharma of the śramaṇa for the Son of the Perfectly Awakened One; Rāhula, you should train in this.
"May all directions be abundant and joyful, peaceful and free from fear.
Rāhula, when you arrive there, do not cause harm to others.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Rāhula and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fourth discourse on Rāhula ends here, totaling one thousand eight hundred and thirty-two characters. 15. The Discourse on Volition (Sañcetanika Sutta) The fifth discourse in the Section on Karma Correspondence within the Madhyama Āgama. First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one performs an intentional action, I say that one will certainly experience its retribution, whether receiving it in the present life or in a future life;
if one does not perform an intentional action, I say that one need not necessarily experience its retribution."
Within this, through the body one intentionally performs three types of action; if they are unwholesome and result in suffering, one undergoes the retribution of suffering.

Regarding the mouth, there are four types of action, and regarding the mind, there are three types of action; if these are unwholesome and result in suffering, one undergoes the retribution of suffering.
"What are the three physical karmas that, being unwholesome, result in suffering and lead to the experience of painful retribution?
The first is killing: it is an extremely evil act of drinking blood; one desires to cause harm and lacks compassion for sentient beings, even down to the smallest insects."
The second is taking what is not given: being attached to another’s property and taking it with a thieving intent.

The third is sexual misconduct: approaching a woman who is protected by her father, or protected by her mother, or protected by both parents, or protected by her sister, or protected by her brother, or protected by her husband’s parents, or protected by her kin, or protected by those of the same clan, or one who is another man’s wife, or one for whom there is the threat of flogging and punishment, or even one who has been betrothed by the offering of a flower garland—to thus violate such a woman.
This is called intentionally performing three types of bodily karma that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruits and receiving bitter retribution.
"What is meant by intentionally performing four types of verbal karma that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruits and receiving bitter retribution?"

The first is false speech: whether he is among a multitude, among his kinsmen, or in the royal court, if he is summoned and questioned, "If you know it, speak; if you do not know it, say so; if you have seen it, say so; if you have not seen it, say so," yet for his own sake, for the sake of others, or for the sake of wealth, he knowingly speaks falsely—claiming to know what he does not know, claiming not to know what he knows, claiming to have seen what he has not seen, or claiming not to have seen what he has seen. This is false speech.

The second is double-tongued speech: desiring to cause separation among others, one hears what is said here and wishes to destroy those over there, or hears what is said there and wishes to destroy those here; one seeks to separate those who are united and further alienate those who are already divided, forming factions, delighting in factions, and praising factions.

The third is harsh speech: if one utters words that are coarse and violent, with an evil tone that is grating to the ear, which is disliked by the multitude and unloved by the multitude, causing others distress and preventing them from attaining concentration—such is the speech one utters.

The fourth is frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): speaking at an improper time, speaking what is untrue, speaking what is meaningless, speaking what is not the Dharma, speaking without restraint, and furthermore, praising things that do not lead to restraint; it is contrary to the proper occasion and constitutes neither skillful instruction nor skillful rebuke.
This is called the four types of intentional verbal karma that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruits and receiving bitter retribution.
"What are the three types of intentional mental karma that are unwholesome, yielding bitter fruits and receiving bitter retribution?"

The first is covetousness: seeing the wealth and various articles of daily life belonging to others, one constantly watches for opportunities, seeking and hoping that they might be obtained by oneself.
The second is ill will: harboring hatred and envy in the mind, one forms this thought:
"That sentient being should be killed, bound, seized, exempted [from protection], or driven out."
"Desiring to cause them to undergo immeasurable suffering.
The third is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is a perverted perspective; such a person holds this view and speaks thus: 'There is no giving, no sacrifice, and no recitation of spells;

there are no wholesome or unwholesome deeds, nor any retribution for wholesome or unwholesome deeds; there is neither this world nor a world beyond; there is no father and no mother; in this world there is no true person who has gone to a good destination, one who has fared well, one who has attained a right path, and who, having personally known, realized, and witnessed for themselves, dwells having accomplished [the goal] regarding this world and the world beyond.'"
This is called performing the three types of karma intentionally through the mind; being unwholesome, it yields bitter fruit and one experiences a painful retribution.

"The well-versed noble disciple abandons unwholesome bodily karma and cultivates wholesome bodily karma; he abandons unwholesome verbal and mental karma and cultivates wholesome verbal and mental karma."

That learned noble disciple, thus endowed with the virtue of diligence and morality, accomplishes pure bodily action and accomplishes pure verbal and mental action; he is free from ill will and free from contention; he has removed sloth and torpor; he is without restlessness and conceit; he has severed doubt and crossed over arrogance; possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he is without delusion. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he dwells having pervaded one direction, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, encompassing all everywhere. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness—free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, exceedingly vast, sublime, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
He reflects thus:
"In the past, this mind of mine was limited and poorly cultivated; now, this mind of mine is immeasurable and well-cultivated.

When a learned noble disciple has thus cultivated his mind immeasurably and well, even if he previously associated with evil friends, acted with negligence, or committed unwholesome deeds, they cannot carry him away, they cannot defile him, and they no longer follow after him.

If there were young boys or girls who, from birth, were able to practice the liberation of a compassionate mind, would they ever again commit unwholesome deeds of body, speech, or mind at a later time?
The bhikkhu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this so? If one does not personally commit evil deeds, from what source could evil karma arise?

"Therefore, whether men or women, whether householders or those who have left the home life, should always diligently cultivate the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-vimokṣa*). If those men or women, whether householders or those who have left the home life, cultivate the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness, they will not depart for the next world with this body; rather, they will simply go from here according to their minds."
A bhikṣu should reflect thus:
"I was formerly heedless and committed unwholesome karma; all of this shall now receive its retribution, and never in a future life."

"If one practices such liberation through the mind of loving-kindness (maitrī-cetovimukti) to an immeasurable degree and cultivates it well, one will certainly attain the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin), or even attain what is higher than that.

Likewise, with compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and the mind accompanied by equanimity (upekṣā)—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill-will, and free from contention; vast, sublime, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—one dwells having pervaded the entire world and accomplished this state.
Then one reflects: 'Formerly my mind was limited and not well-cultivated; now my mind is immeasurable and well-cultivated.'"

When a learned noble disciple has thus cultivated his mind immeasurably and well, even if he previously associated with evil friends, acted with negligence, and committed unwholesome deeds, those [deeds] cannot carry him away, cannot defile him, and will no longer follow after him.

If there were young boys or girls who, from birth, were able to practice the liberation of the mind through equanimity, could they, at a later time, ever again commit unwholesome deeds of body, speech, or mind?
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this so? If one does not personally commit evil deeds, from what source could evil karma arise?
"Therefore, whether men or women, whether living as householders or as renunciants, you should always diligently cultivate the liberation of the mind through equanimity."

If those men or women, whether householders or renunciants, cultivate the liberation of the mind through equanimity, they do not take this body with them when going to that other world; rather, they depart from here solely by means of the mind.
A bhikṣu should reflect thus:
"I was formerly heedless and committed unwholesome karma; all of this shall now receive its retribution, and never in a future life."
"If there is one who thus practices the liberation of mind through equanimity and cultivates it immeasurably and well, they will certainly attain the stage of Anāgāmin, or even attain what is higher.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
When those bhikkhus had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Sūtra on Thought*, the fifth, ends here; it contains one thousand one hundred and seventy-four characters. 16. The Kālāma Sūtra (16), the sixth in the Section on Correspondence with Karma within the Madhyama Āgama. Recitation for the First Day. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Kālāmas together with a great assembly of bhikkhus. He arrived at Kesaputta and stayed in the Simsapā Grove to the north of the village of Kesaputta.

At that time, the people of Kajaṅgalā heard that the ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, having renounced his kinsmen to leave the household life and study the Way, was traveling through Kajaṅgalā with a great assembly of bhikṣus and had arrived here at Kajaṅgalā, staying in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of the village of Kajaṅgalā.

That ascetic Gautama possesses great renown that has spread throughout the ten directions; the ascetic Gautama is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.

In this world, among its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and realized for himself through direct experience.

If he were to preach the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing; complete and pure; clearly manifesting the holy life—and if one were to see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and honor, prostrate to, make offerings to, and serve him, one would swiftly obtain great benefit.
"We should go together to see the śramaṇa Gautama, to pay our respects, serve him, and make offerings.

Having heard this, the Kālāmas of Kesaputta each followed their respective peers and kinsmen out of Kesaputta; they traveled north to the Śiśumāragiri Forest, desiring to see the World-Honored One, pay their respects, serve him, and make offerings.
Having approached the Buddha, some of those from the Kālāma clan bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side;
some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat to one side;
and some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side.
Having seen the Buddha from afar, they sat down in silence.

At that time, once the people of Kālāma were all seated, the Buddha taught them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; having taught them the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, he remained silent.

At that time, the people of Kālāma, having been taught the Dharma by the Buddha, inspired to aspiration, filled with longing, and established in joy, each rose from their seats, bared one shoulder, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Gautama!
"A certain śramaṇa or brahmin has come to the Kālāmas!
He merely praises what he himself knows and sees, while disparaging what others know and see,
O Gautama!"
Furthermore, another śramaṇa or brahmin came to the Kālāma community and likewise praised what he himself knew and saw, while disparaging what others knew and saw.
"Gautama!
Having heard this, we have become doubtful:
'Of these śramaṇas and brahmins, which is true and which is false?'"
The World-Honored One said:
"Kālāmas! Do not give rise to doubt or confusion."
Why is this? Because due to doubt, hesitation arises. Kālāmas!
"You yourselves lack pure knowledge; do you know whether there is a future life or no future life?
Kālāmas! You also lack pure knowledge; do you know whether your actions are blameworthy or blameless?"
"Kālāmas!
You should know that there are three types of karma, which exist by virtue of habitual practice from the beginning.
What are these three? "
Kālāma! What is called craving is the cause of these karmas; it exists inherently through habitual practice. Kālāma!
Hatred and delusion are the causes of these various karmas; they have existed since beginningless habituation. Kālāmas!

One who is greedy is overwhelmed by greed and finds no satisfaction in the mind; such a person may kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods knowingly, or drink intoxicants.
"Kālāmas!

One who is subject to hatred is overwhelmed by hatred; with a mind that knows no satisfaction, they may kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely knowing it to be so, or drink intoxicants."
"Kālāmas!

One who is deluded is overwhelmed by delusion; his mind knows no satiety, and he may kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods with full knowledge, or drink intoxicants."

"Kālāmas! A learned noble disciple abstains from killing and abandons killing; laying aside the sword and staff, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he benefits all beings, even down to the smallest insects. Thus, he purifies his mind regarding the taking of life."
"Kālāmas!

A well-taught noble disciple abandons taking what is not given and severs the practice of taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, delights in giving, is ever fond of generosity, rejoices without stinginess, and does not look for reward; thus, he purifies his mind regarding taking what is not given."
"Kālāmas!

A well-learned noble disciple abandons unchaste conduct and severs unchaste conduct; he diligently cultivates the holy life, exerts himself in sublime conduct, remains pure and undefiled, and, being free from desire and having severed lust, he purifies his mind of unchaste conduct."
"Kālāmas!

A well-taught noble disciple abandons false speech and severs false speech; he speaks the truth, delights in the truth, abides in the truth unshakably, is entirely trustworthy, and does not deceive the world. He purifies his mind of false speech."

“Kālāma! A well-taught noble disciple abandons divisive speech and severs divisive speech; he practices non-divisive speech, does not cause dissension among others, does not repeat here what he has heard elsewhere with the intent to divide those people, nor does he repeat there what he has heard here with the intent to divide those people. He seeks to reconcile those who are divided and rejoices in those who are reconciled. He does not form factions, does not delight in factions, and does not praise factions. Thus, he purifies his mind regarding divisive speech.”
"Kālāmas!

A well-taught noble disciple abandons harsh speech and severs harsh speech. Whatever he may say, if it is rough and violent in tone, offensive to the ear, disliked by the multitude, unloved by the multitude, causing others distress, and preventing them from attaining concentration—he severs such speech."

If one speaks words that are pure, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; that are pleasant to the ear and enter the heart; that are delightful and lovely; that bring peace and happiness to others; that are articulated with clarity; that do not cause fear; and that lead others to attain concentration—one speaks such words, thereby purifying the mind of harsh speech.

"Kālāmas! A well-taught noble disciple abstains from frivolous speech and abandons frivolous speech; he speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks in accordance with the Dharma, speaks meaningfully, and speaks for the sake of tranquility. He delights in speaking for the sake of tranquility; his discourse is timely, appropriate, well-instructive, and well-reproving. Thus, he purifies his mind regarding frivolous speech."
"Kālāmas!

A well-taught noble disciple is free from covetousness and has abandoned covetousness; his mind harbors no contention. Seeing the wealth and various articles of daily life belonging to others, he does not give rise to covetousness, desiring 'May I obtain this. He purifies his mind of covetousness."

"Kālāma! A well-taught noble disciple leaves behind ill will and abandons ill will; possessing a sense of shame and a dread of blame, he possesses a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, seeking the welfare of all beings even down to the smallest insects. Thus, he purifies his mind of envy and ill will."
"Kālāmas!
A learned noble disciple abandons wrong view and severs wrong view; he practices right view without perversion, seeing thus and speaking thus:
'There is giving, there is sacrifice, and there is the efficacy of incantations.'"
There is the retribution of good and evil karma;
there is this world and the world beyond; there is father and mother;

there are in the world true persons who have reached the excellent destination, who have gone well and are directed toward what is good, who know for themselves, awaken to themselves, and dwell having realized through their own direct experience both this world and the world beyond, and who have purified their minds of wrong views.

"In this way, Kālāmas! A well-learned noble disciple accomplishes pure bodily action, accomplishes pure verbal and mental actions; he is free from ill will and free from contention; he has removed sloth and torpor; he is without restlessness and haughtiness; he has severed doubt and crossed over conceit; with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he is without delusion. His mind, imbued with loving-kindness, dwells pervading one direction, accomplished and suffused."

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
"In this way, Kālāmas!
A learned noble disciple, whose mind is free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention, attains four abodes of security."
What are the four?

There is this world and the other world; there is the retribution of good and evil deeds. Having attained this right view and having fully undertaken and maintained the corresponding karma, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will certainly reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
In this way, Kālāmas!
A learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the first abode of peace and security.
Furthermore, Kālāmas!

There is no this world nor a world beyond; there is no result of good or evil deeds. Thus, regarding this present life, I am not disparaged by others on this account, but am praised by those of right knowledge—by diligent people and those with right view—who declare that such things exist.
In this way, Kālāmas!
A learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the second abode of peace.
Furthermore, Kālāmas!
If there is anything to be done, one must certainly not do evil; I do not contemplate evil. Why is that?
"If one does no evil oneself, from what source could suffering arise?
In this way, Kālāmas, a well-versed noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the third abode of peace."

Furthermore, Kālāmas! If there is anything to be done, one must certainly not do evil. I shall not commit what is feared or unfeared by the world; I shall always maintain compassion for the entire world. My mind shall not contend with sentient beings; it shall be free from turbidity and full of joy.
In this way, Kālāmas, a learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the fourth abode of security.
In this way, Kālāmas, a learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the four abodes of security.
Kālāma said to the Blessed One: "It is so, Gautama!
A well-taught noble disciple, whose mind is free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention, attains four bases for dwelling in security."
What are the four?

There is this world and the other world; there is the retribution of good and evil deeds. Having attained this right view and having fully undertaken and maintained the corresponding karma, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will certainly reach a good destination, even as far as the heavens.

"In this way, Gautama, the well-learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; this is called attaining the foremost abode of security."
Furthermore, Gautama!

Even if there were no this world or the other world, and no retribution for good or evil deeds, I would not be reviled by others on account of this in the present life; rather, I would be praised by those of right knowledge, and those who are diligent and possess right view would say that I exist.
"In this way, Gautama, the well-learned noble disciple has a mind free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention; this is called attaining the second abode of peace."
Furthermore, Gautama!
If there is anything to be done, one must certainly not do evil;
I do not harbor thoughts of evil. Why is that?
"If one does no evil oneself, how could suffering arise?
It is thus, Gautama!
A well-learned noble disciple whose mind is free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—this is called attaining the third abode of peace."
Furthermore, Gautama!

If there is anything to be done, I shall certainly not do evil. I shall not commit offenses against what is feared or what is not feared in the world; I shall always maintain compassion for all the world. My mind shall not contend with sentient beings, remaining untainted and joyful.
"In this way, Gautama,
a learned noble disciple whose mind is free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention— this is called attaining the fourth abode of security."
"In this way, Gautama, a well-heard noble disciple has a mind free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; this is called attaining the four abodes of security."
"Gautama!
I have understood; Sugata, I have comprehended.
World-Honored One!"

We all take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. We pray only that the World-Honored One accept us as upāsakas; from this day forth until the end of our lives, we take refuge for as long as we live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, all the people of Kālāma and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth *Kālāma Sūtra* ends here; it contains one thousand nine hundred and eighty-seven characters. 17. The *Gāmiṇī Sūtra* (17), from the Madhyama Āgama, Section on Correspondence with Karma, the seventh *Gāmiṇī Sūtra*. Recitation for the first day. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Nanda Grove, staying in the Mango Grove of the village of Bhārgava.

At that time, the son of the deva Asura, named Gāmiṇī, who was of magnificent appearance and radiant splendor, went to the place where the Buddha was as the night was turning toward dawn. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The devaputta Asita Kāmāyana addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The brahmins exalt themselves and serve various deities; when living beings pass away, they claim they can cause them to go freely to a good destination and be reborn in the heavens. World-Honored One, you are the Lord of Dharma; we pray that the World-Honored One will cause these living beings, upon their passing, to reach a good destination and be reborn among the gods."
The Blessed One said:
“Gāmaṇi! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"Gāmaṇi! What do you think?

Suppose there were men or women in a village who were indolent and lacked diligence, who practiced unwholesome ways and accomplished the ten courses of unwholesome action—killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view—and when they were at the point of death, a multitude of people came, each with palms joined in reverence, praising and entreating them, speaking thus:"

"You, men and women, though indolent and lacking in diligence, have practiced unwholesome dharmas and accomplished the ten paths of unwholesome action—killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view. Yet, because of these and by reason of these, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you will certainly reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavens."
"In this way, Gāmaṇi!

Suppose those men and women were indolent and lacked diligence, yet practiced unwholesome dharmas and accomplished the ten paths of unwholesome action—killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view. Would it be possible that, because they each joined their palms toward the multitude, praised and entreated them, and by reason of this and through this cause, at the breaking up of the body after death, they would reach a good destination and be born in the heavens?"
Kāmaṇḍuka replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Gāmaṇi!"

Why is this so? Because those men and women are indolent and lack diligence; they practice unwholesome dharmas and accomplish the ten paths of unwholesome action—killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view. If, for the sake of a multitude of people, they were to join their palms and praise [the Buddha] while making requests, and by reason of that and through that cause, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were to reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavens—such a thing is impossible.

"Kāmaṇḍa! Suppose there were a deep pool of water not far from a village, and someone were to cast a large, heavy stone into it. Then, if a crowd of people were to come and, with palms joined, offer praises and entreaties, saying:
'May this stone float up!'"
"Kāmaṇḍa! What do you think?
Would this great, heavy rock ever emerge because of the many people joining their palms together, praising it, and making requests for its sake?"
Kāmaṇḍuka replied:
"No, World-Honored One."

“It is so, Gāmaṇi! Suppose those men and women were indolent and lacked diligence, practicing unwholesome dharmas and accomplishing the ten paths of unwholesome action— killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view— and yet, if for the sake of being praised and entreated by a multitude of people with their hands joined together, they were to reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavens upon the dissolution of the body after death because of that and on account of that, such a thing is impossible.”
Why is that? It is because these ten unwholesome courses of action are black and have black retribution; they naturally lead downward and inevitably result in an evil destination.
"Kammāra-putta!..."
"What do you think?

Suppose there were men or women in a village or town who practiced with diligence and vigor, conducting themselves according to the sublime Dharma and accomplishing the ten paths of wholesome action—abstaining from killing and severing the habit of killing; abstaining from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech; and so on, up to abstaining from wrong view and severing wrong view, thereby attaining right view. When such a person’s life comes to an end, if a multitude of people were to come, each with palms joined in reverence, praising and entreating him, speaking these words:"

"You, sons and daughters, though you practice with diligence and exertion, performing the sublime Dharma and accomplishing the ten paths of wholesome action—abstaining from killing, abandoning killing; abstaining from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, up to abstaining from wrong view and abandoning wrong view, and attaining right view—nevertheless, because of these causes and conditions, when your bodies perish and your lives end, you shall go to an evil destination and be born in hell."
"Kāmaṇḍa! What do you think?

If those men and women were diligent and energetic in their practice, conducting themselves according to the sublime Dharma, accomplishing the ten paths of wholesome action—abstaining from killing and severing the habit of killing; abstaining from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech; and so on, up to abstaining from wrong view and severing wrong view, thereby attaining right view—would they, because of this and on account of this, upon the dissolution of the body after death, reach a miserable destination and be born in hell, even if all the people were to join their palms toward them, praising and entreating them?"
Kāmaṇḍuka replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
"Excellent, Gāmaṇi!"
Why is that? Gāmaṇi!

Suppose those men and women are diligent and energetic in their practice, conducting themselves according to the sublime Dharma, accomplishing the ten paths of wholesome action—abstaining from killing, abandoning killing; abstaining from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech; and so on, up to abstaining from wrong view and abandoning wrong view, attaining right view. If, for such people, when a multitude of others join their palms toward them, praise, and make requests on their behalf, they were nevertheless to undergo the breaking up of the body after death and be reborn in an evil destination, in the hells, this would be impossible.
Why is that? Gāmaṇi!
It is because these ten courses of wholesome action are bright and have a bright result; they naturally lead upward and will certainly reach a happy destination.

"Kāmaṇḍaka! It is just as if there were a deep pool of water not far from a village, and someone were to throw a jar of ghee into it and break it; the shards and dregs would sink to the bottom, while the ghee would float to the surface."
In this way, Gāmaṇi!

Those men and women, practicing with diligence and exertion, carry out the sublime Dharma, accomplish the ten paths of wholesome action, and—abstaining from killing, abandoning killing, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and so on up to abstaining from wrong view, abandoning wrong view—they attain right view.

At the time of his death, that which is called the coarse physical body—the elements born of father and mother, nourished by food and clothing, maintained by sitting, lying, massaging, bathing, and endurance—is of a nature subject to destruction, a nature subject to extinction, and a nature subject to dissolution.

After his life has ended, it may be pecked by crows and birds, devoured by tigers and wolves, burned, or buried, until it is entirely reduced to dust. Yet his mind, intellect, and consciousness have been constantly perfumed by faith, and perfumed by diligence, learning, generosity, and wisdom; because of this and conditioned by this, he naturally ascends and is reborn in a happy realm.
"Kāmaṇḍa! That person who has abandoned killing and put an end to killing follows the path of the garden-vision, the path of upward progress, and the path to a good destination."

"Kāmaṇḍa! One who refrains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, up to and including wrong view—by abandoning wrong view and attaining right view, this is the path to the pleasure grove, the path of advancement, and the path to a happy destination."
Kāmaṇḍa! Furthermore, there is the path to the pleasure groves, the path to higher advancement, and the path to a happy destination. Kāmaṇḍa!
What, then, are the path of the garden-villa, the path of upward progress, and the path to the wholesome destination?
They are the Noble Eightfold Path, from right view up to right concentration; these are the eight.
"Kāmaṇḍuka! This is what is called the path to the pleasure groves, the path of upward progress, and the path to a happy destination.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Gāmaṇi and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
