18. Siṃha Sūtra (18) Chapter on Correspondence with Karma, Sūtra Eight: The Lion First Day’s Recitation Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī and staying at the Gabled Hall on the edge of the Monkey Pond.
At that time, a great multitude of Licchavis of Vaiśālī had gathered in the Assembly Hall, repeatedly praising the Buddha and repeatedly praising the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Nigaṇṭha disciple, the Great Minister Siṃha, was also present in the assembly.
Then, desiring to go see the Buddha to make offerings and pay him homage, the Great Minister Siṃha first went to where the Nigaṇṭhas were and addressed them, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I wish to go and see the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, the Nirgrantha Siṃhasikha said:
"Do not wish to see the śramaṇa Gautama."
Why is that? Lion, the śramaṇa Gautama takes that which is unconditioned as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches the dharma of the unconditioned to others. Lion!
"If one sees that the fundamental principle is 'it cannot be done,' it is not auspicious; even making offerings and performing rites of worship will likewise not be auspicious.
Then those many Licchavis of Vaiśālī gathered repeatedly in the assembly hall, praising the Buddha many times, and praising the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus many times.
At that time, the Licchavi minister Siṃha, a disciple of the Nirgranthas, was also present among that assembly two or three times.
Then, the minister Siṃha likewise desired to go and see the Buddha, to make offerings, and to pay him homage on two or three occasions.
The minister Siṃha did not take leave of the Nirgranthas, but immediately went to the Buddha. Having exchanged greetings with him, he sat down to one side and spoke these words:
"I have heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama holds as his fundamental doctrine 'the un-doable' (akriyā), and he also teaches this doctrine of the un-doable to others."

"Gautama! If this is what you say—that the Śramaṇa Gautama’s fundamental doctrine is that which cannot be done, and that he also teaches others the practice of that which cannot be done—does he not thereby slander and defame the Śramaṇa Gautama?"
Does he speak what is true?
Does he speak this Dharma?
Does he speak the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma?
"Is it in accordance with the Dharma, without fault, and beyond reproach?
The World-Honored One replied: "Sīha!"

If one speaks in this way—that the Śramaṇa Gautama takes that which is unconditioned as his fundamental principle and also teaches others the practice of the unconditioned—then they do not slander or revile the Śramaṇa Gautama!
What he says is true; what he says is the Dharma; what he says is in accordance with the Dharma. There is no fault in his teaching, nor is there any ground for censure. Why is this so?

"Siṃha! There is a reason for this matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes 'the un-doable' as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches others the practice of the un-doable."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes what is 'to be done' as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches others the dharma of what is 'to be done.'"

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [claiming]: 'The śramaṇa Gautama takes annihilation as his fundamental tenet, and he also teaches the doctrine of annihilation to others.'"

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely accuse the Tathāgata of the following: that the śramaṇa Gautama takes what is loathsome as his fundamental doctrine and teaches such loathsome dharmas to others."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes the Dharma and Vinaya as his fundamental basis, and he also teaches the Dharma and Vinaya to others."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes asceticism as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches the dharma of asceticism to others."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is: that the Śramaṇa Gautama does not fundamentally enter a womb, and he also teaches others the Dharma of not entering a womb."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, there is another matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes peace as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches the Dharma of peace to others."

“Sīha! What is that matter by reason of which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [saying]: ‘The ascetic Gotama takes as his fundamental principle what should not be done, and he also teaches others to do what should not be done’?”
"Siṃha! I say that bodily misconduct must not be committed; verbal and mental misconduct must also not be committed. Siṃha!"
If such immeasurable unwholesome and defiled phenomena are the basis for future existence, the retribution of feverish suffering, and the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Siṃha! I say that this Dharma is entirely beyond being fabricated. Siṃha!"

This is called having a basis for this reason: regarding the Dharma as it truly is, one cannot falsely disparage it, for the śramaṇa Gautama takes what is "un-doable" as his fundamental principle and also teaches to others that which is un-doable.

“Sīha! Furthermore, what is that other matter by reason of which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [claiming]: ‘The ascetic Gotama takes what can be done as his fundamental doctrine, and he also teaches others the doctrine of what can be done’?”
"Siṃha! I say that wholesome conduct of body should be practiced, and wholesome conduct of speech and mind should also be practiced. Siṃha!"
"Siṃha, if such immeasurable wholesome dharmas as these result in the fruit of happiness, one experiences the retribution of happiness, is born in a good destination, and attains long life. Siṃha,
I say that all these dharmas should be practiced."

"Siṃha! This is the matter, this is the reason why one cannot falsely accuse the ascetic Gautama of teaching that what can be done is the fundamental basis of his doctrine, and of preaching to others the dharma of what can be done."

“Siṃha! Furthermore, what is that other matter by reason of which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [claiming]: ‘The śramaṇa Gautama takes annihilation as his fundamental tenet, and he also teaches the doctrine of annihilation to others’?”
"Siṃha! I say that bodily misconduct should be abandoned and extinguished; verbal and mental misconduct should also be abandoned and extinguished. Siṃha!"
If such immeasurable unwholesome and defiled phenomena are the basis for future existence, the retribution of feverish suffering, and the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Siṃha! I say that this dharma should be completely abandoned and extinguished. Siṃha!"

This is called having a basis; on account of this matter, one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [saying]: "The śramaṇa Gautama takes annihilation as his fundamental tenet, and he also teaches the doctrine of annihilation to others."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, for what reason and on what basis could one not falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is by saying: 'The ascetic Gautama holds what is loathsome as his fundamental doctrine, and he also teaches to others doctrines that are loathsome'?"
"Siṃha! I say that bodily misconduct is loathsome, and verbal and mental misconduct are likewise loathsome. Siṃha!"

If such immeasurable unwholesome and defiled phenomena serve as the basis for future existence, resulting in the retribution of feverish suffering and the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Siṃha! I say that this Dharma is entirely loathsome. Siṃha!"

This is what is meant by having grounds for which, on account of those grounds, one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, saying: "The ascetic Gautama takes what is loathsome as his primary doctrine, and he also teaches to others doctrines that are loathsome."

“Siṇa! Furthermore, by what further reason and on account of what matter can one not falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is, [saying]: ‘The śramaṇa Gautama takes the Dharma and Vinaya as his primary basis, and he also teaches the Dharma and Vinaya to others’?”
"Siṃha! I teach the Dharma and the Vinaya for the sake of severing sensual desire; I teach the Dharma and the Vinaya for the sake of severing hatred and delusion. Siṃha!"
If such immeasurable unwholesome and defiled phenomena are the basis for future existence, the retribution of feverish suffering, and the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"Siṃha! It is for the sake of abandoning those [defilements] that I teach the Dharma and the Vinaya. Siṃha!"

This is called having a basis; for this reason, one cannot falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is, nor can one say that the śramaṇa Gautama relies on his own invention of Dharma and Vinaya, or that he teaches people a Dharma and Vinaya that are merely his own fabrications.

“Sīha! Furthermore, for what reason and on what basis can one not falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is, saying: ‘The ascetic Gautama is fundamentally devoted to asceticism and also teaches the doctrine of asceticism to others’?”

"Siṃha! There are some śramaṇas and brahmins who go naked and without clothing; some use their hands as clothing, some use leaves as clothing, and some use beads as clothing. They do not take water with a water-pot, nor do they take water with a ladle. They do not eat food obtained by force of weapons or plunder, nor do they eat food obtained through deception. They do not go in person, nor do they send a messenger; they do not accept invitations from those who are honored, nor from those who are well-born, nor from those who are established in high status."

If there are two people eating together, one does not eat among them; one does not eat in a household where a woman is pregnant; one does not eat in a household that keeps dogs; and even if a dung-fly flies into a house, one does not eat.
He does not eat fish, does not eat meat, does not drink alcohol, and does not drink foul water; or he drinks nothing at all, training in the practice of non-drinking.
Or he eats a single mouthful, considering that one mouthful sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, considering those seven mouthfuls sufficient.
Or he eats a single morsel, considering that one morsel sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven morsels, considering those seven morsels sufficient.

Some eat once a day, taking that single meal as sufficient; or they eat once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once every half-month or month, taking that single meal as sufficient.
Some eat leafy vegetables, or millet, or foxtail millet, or mixed grain, or *tuntula* food, or coarse food.

Some go to secluded places and dwell in seclusion, eating roots, or fruits, or naturally fallen fruit. Some wear patched robes, or woolen robes, or *tusha* grass robes, or *tusha-wool* robes, or whole skins, or perforated skins, or both whole and perforated skins.

Some wear their hair loose; some wear it braided; some wear it both loose and braided. Some shave their heads; some shave their beards; some shave both beard and hair. Some pluck out their hair; some pluck out their beards; some pluck out both beard and hair.

Some remain standing while others sit; some practice the squatting gait; some lie upon thorns, using thorns as a bed; some lie upon fruits, using fruits as a bed. Some serve water, drawing it with their hands day and night; some serve fire, keeping it burning throughout the night; some serve the sun, the moon, or those who are honored, noble, and virtuous, joining their palms toward them. In such ways, they undergo immeasurable suffering, practicing asceticism with feverish intensity.
"Siṃha! As for these ascetic practices, I do not say they do not exist. Siṃha!"
However, this asceticism is a base occupation; it is extremely painful and exhausting, practiced by commoners, and is not the noble path. Siṃha!
If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding that method of asceticism, know it to be completely extinguished, cut off at its root, and ultimately non-arising—I call that true asceticism.

"Siṃha! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has known, abandoned, and exhausted those practices of asceticism; he has uprooted them so that they shall never arise again. For this reason, I practice asceticism."

"Siṃha! This is the matter, for this reason, that one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama takes asceticism as his fundamental principle, and he also teaches the dharma of asceticism to others."

"Siṃha! Furthermore, what is the other matter by which one cannot falsely slander the Dharma as it truly is, [claiming]: 'The ascetic Gautama's fundamental doctrine is that he did not enter a womb, and he also teaches others the doctrine of not entering a womb'?"

"Siṃha! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding future rebirth in a womb, know its cessation and extinction, uprooting it so that it shall never arise again, I say that they do not enter a womb."

"Siṃha! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has known the cessation and extinction of future rebirth in a womb; he has uprooted it, so that it shall never arise again. For this reason, I do not enter a womb."

"Siṃha! This is the matter, for this reason, that one cannot falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is: the śramaṇa Gautama does not fundamentally enter a womb, and he also teaches others the dharma of not entering a womb."

“Sīha! Furthermore, for what reason and on account of what matter can one not falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is, [saying]: ‘The ascetic Gotama’s fundamental principle is peace, and he teaches the Dharma of peace to others’?”

"Siṃha! For any son of good family who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Way—having reached the culmination of the unsurpassed holy life—I have, in this very life, known it for myself, realized it for myself, and attained it through my own direct experience. Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence; I know this as it truly is. I am at peace, and I bring peace to other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."

I have established them in that state, which is the nature of birth; yet sentient beings are liberated from this nature of birth, and from the natures of aging, illness, death, and the defilement of sorrow and affliction—sentient beings are liberated from these states of sorrow and affliction.

"Siṃha! This is the matter by which one cannot falsely disparage the Dharma as it truly is: the Śramaṇa Gautama is fundamentally established in peace, and he also teaches the Dharma of peace to others."
The minister Siṃha addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Gautama! I have understood.”
Well-gone One!
I have understood. Gautama!
It is like a person with clear vision who rights what is overturned, uncovers what is covered, shows the way to the lost, and brings light into the darkness; so that those with eyes may see forms.
The śramaṇa Gautama is likewise; for my sake, he has taught the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means and revealed its meaning according to various paths.
World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live.
World-Honored One!
It is just as if someone were to raise a poor horse, hoping to gain profit from it; they would only exhaust themselves in vain without obtaining any benefit.
World-Honored One!

I am also like this: those foolish Nirgranthas do not understand well; they cannot know themselves, they do not recognize a fertile field, and they lack self-examination. For a long night they have paid homage, made offerings, and performed services, hoping thereby to gain benefit, yet their toil is in vain and without profit.
World-Honored One!

I now once again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live.
"Bhagavān!
I was formerly ignorant; I had faith and reverence for the foolish Nirgranthas, but from this day forth I sever it. Why is that? Because—"
"Because you have deceived me, World-Honored One!

I now take refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the minister Siṃha and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The eighth discourse, the Siṃha Sūtra, ends here; it contains two thousand four hundred and thirteen characters. 19. The Nigaṇṭha Sūtra (19). Middle Āgama, Section on Correspondence with Karma, the ninth discourse, the Nigaṇṭha Sūtra. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas in the city of Devadaha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "The Nirgranthas hold such a view and speak thus:

'Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past deeds. If those past karmas are extinguished through asceticism and no new karma is created, then all karma will be exhausted. Once all karma is exhausted, suffering will be exhausted; once suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.'"
I went to them, and having arrived, I asked: "Nigaṇṭhas!

Is it truly your view and your teaching that whatever a person experiences is all caused by past deeds; that if those past karmas are extinguished through asceticism and no new karma is created, then all karma will be exhausted; that once all karma is exhausted, suffering will be exhausted; and that once suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering?"
He replied to me, saying: "It is so, Gautama!"
I further asked those Nirgranthas: "Do you yourselves possess pure knowledge such that you know:

'The self exists by nature,' or 'the self does not exist by nature'; 'the self has acted evilly in the past,' or 'it has not acted evilly'; 'my suffering is exhausted to this extent,' or 'my suffering is not exhausted to this extent'? And having exhausted it, do you then attain its exhaustion, whereby in this very life you sever all unwholesome states, acquire various wholesome dharmas, and cultivate them to realization?"
He replied to me, saying: "No, Gautama!"

I further said to those Nirgranthas: "You yourselves possess no pure knowledge; yet you claim, 'The self exists by nature,' or 'The self does not exist by nature'; 'The self has acted evilly by nature,' or 'It has not acted evilly by nature'; 'So much suffering has been exhausted by the self,' or 'So much suffering has not been exhausted by the self. Once it is exhausted, one then attains its total exhaustion; that is, in this very life, one cuts off all unwholesome states, attains various wholesome dharmas, cultivates them, and realizes them, making this declaration: 'Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past actions. If former karma is extinguished through asceticism and no new karma is created, then all karma will be exhausted. When all karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted. When suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering.'"
"Nigaṇṭhas!

If you yourselves possessed pure knowledge regarding whether the self existed in the past, or did not exist in the past; whether the self performed evil deeds in the past, or did not perform evil deeds in the past; and whether such suffering as this has been exhausted, or such suffering as this has not been exhausted—and if, having been exhausted, it were to be further exhausted—then you would immediately, in this very life, abandon all unwholesome states, attain various wholesome dharmas, cultivate them, and realize them through direct experience."

"Nirgranthas! You may indeed say this: that whatever a person experiences is entirely due to past deeds; if those past karmas are extinguished through asceticism and no new karma is created, then all karma will be exhausted. When all karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering."

"Nigaṇṭha! It is just as if there were a man whose body had been pierced by a poisoned arrow; because of that poisoned arrow, he experienced extreme suffering. Out of compassion and pity for him, and desiring his benefit and well-being, his kinsmen would immediately call for a physician skilled in extracting arrows."

When the surgeon arrives, he uses a sharp blade to open the wound; while the wound is being opened, intense pain arises. Once the wound is opened, he seeks the arrow-head; while seeking the arrow-head, intense pain arises again. Having found the arrow-head, he immediately extracts it; while it is being extracted, intense pain arises again. Once the arrow-head has been removed, he applies a thin bandage to wrap the wound; while wrapping the wound, intense pain arises again. After the arrow-head has been extracted, the man regains his strength and is free from affliction; his faculties are no longer impaired, and he is restored to his former state.
"Nigaṇṭha!
That person possesses pure knowledge of his own, and thus he thinks: "

"Originally, I was struck by a poisoned arrow. Because of being struck by that poisoned arrow, extreme suffering arose. My kinsmen, seeing me and feeling pity and compassion for me, wishing to benefit and bring me peace and security, immediately summoned a physician skilled in extracting arrows. When the physician skilled in arrows arrived, he used a sharp blade to open the wound for me; while the wound was being opened, further extreme suffering arose. Once the wound had been opened, he sought the arrowhead; while seeking the arrowhead, further extreme suffering arose. Having found the arrowhead, he immediately pulled it out; while it was being pulled out, further extreme suffering arose. Once the arrowhead had been extracted, he dressed the wound with a bandage; while the wound was being bandaged, further extreme suffering arose. After the arrowhead was extracted, I regained my strength and became free from affliction; my faculties were no longer impaired, and I was restored to my former state."
"Thus it is, Nigaṇṭhas!

If you yourselves possess pure knowledge regarding whether 'I existed in the past' or 'I did not exist in the past,' or whether 'I performed evil deeds in the past' or 'I did not perform evil deeds in the past,' or whether 'my suffering has been exhausted to this extent' or 'my suffering has not been exhausted to this extent,' and if, having reached its end, you attain that end—then in this very life you would sever all unwholesome states, acquire various wholesome dharmas, cultivate them, and realize them."

"Nigaṇṭhas! You may indeed say this: 'Whatever a person experiences is all due to past deeds; if those past deeds are extinguished through asceticism and no new ones are created, then all karma will be exhausted. When all karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering. Yet, when I asked them this, I did not see any of the Nigaṇṭhas able to answer me, saying: 'Gautama!'"
"It is so," or "it is not so. Furthermore, I asked the Nirgranthas:
'If the Nirgranthas possess supreme renunciation and supreme asceticism, at that time, do the Nirgranthas experience supreme suffering? "
He replied to me, saying: "It is so, Gautama!"
"If there were an interruption or moderate ascetic practice, would the Nigaṇṭhas at that time experience moderate suffering?
He replied to me, "It is so, Gautama!"
"If there is a lower severance and lower ascetic practice, at that time do the Nigaṇṭhas experience lower suffering?
He replied to me: "It is so, Gautama!"
Thus, for these Nirgranthas, there is superior renunciation and superior asceticism, at which time the Nirgranthas experience superior suffering;
there is middling renunciation and middling asceticism, at which time the Nirgranthas experience middling suffering;
and there is inferior renunciation and inferior asceticism, at which time the Nirgranthas experience inferior suffering.
If the Nigaṇṭhas possess superior abandonment and superior asceticism, at that time the Nigaṇṭhas cease superior suffering;
if they possess middling abandonment and middling asceticism, at that time the Nigaṇṭhas cease middling suffering;
if they possess inferior abandonment and inferior asceticism, at that time the Nigaṇṭhas cease inferior suffering.

If, by acting in such a way or not acting in such a way, one brings to rest extreme suffering and very heavy suffering, then it should be known that the Nirgranthas are creating suffering for themselves in this very life.
However, the Nigaṇṭhas, being shrouded by ignorance and entangled in ignorance, make this claim:

"Whatever a person experiences is all caused by past deeds; if those past karmas are extinguished through asceticism and no new karma is created, then all karma will be exhausted. When all karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted; when suffering is exhausted, one reaches the end of suffering."
When I questioned them in this way, I did not see any of the Nirgranthas able to answer me, saying: "Gautama! It is so; it is not so."
"Furthermore, I asked the Nirgranthas: 'Nirgranthas!
If there is karma that results in pleasant retribution, could that karma, through renunciation or through asceticism, be transformed into karma resulting in painful retribution?'"
He replied to me, saying: "No, Gautama!"

"O Nigaṇṭhas! If there is karma that results in painful retribution, could that karma, by means of its abandonment or through asceticism, be transformed into karma that results in pleasant retribution?
They replied to me:
"No, Gautama! [O] all Nirgranthas!"
"If there is karma that is to be experienced as retribution in the present life, could that karma, by means of its abandonment or through ascetic practices,
be transformed into karma to be experienced as retribution in a future life? He replied to me, "No."
"Gautama! O Nigaṇṭhas!

If there is karma that results in retribution in a future life, could that karma, by means of its abandonment or through asceticism, be transformed into karma resulting in retribution in this present life?"
He replied to me, saying: "No, Gautama!"
"O Nirgranthas! If there is karma that is to be experienced as an unripened result, could that karma possibly be transformed into a ripened result through its abandonment or through asceticism?"
He replied to me, saying: "No, Gautama!"
"O Nirgranthas! If there is karma that is to be experienced as a ripened result, could that karma possibly be transformed into something else through its abandonment or through asceticism?
They replied to me:
"No, Gautama! [This applies to] all the Nirgranthas!"
This is an action that results in a pleasant retribution; that action cannot, through renunciation or through asceticism, be transformed into one that results in a painful retribution.
O Nigaṇṭhas!
An action that results in a painful retribution cannot, through renunciation or through asceticism, be transformed into one that results in a pleasant retribution.
"O Nirgranthas!
Karma that ripens in the present life cannot, through its abandonment or through asceticism, be transformed into karma that ripens in a future life.
O Nirgranthas!"
Regarding karma to be experienced in future lives, that karma cannot, through renunciation or through asceticism, be transformed into karma to be experienced in the present life.
O Nirgranthas!
Regarding unripened karma, that karma cannot, through renunciation or through asceticism, be transformed into ripened retribution.
"O Nigaṇṭhas!
Matured karma cannot be altered by means of renunciation or through asceticism.
For this reason, O Nigaṇṭhas!"
"False expedients lead to empty severance with no attainment.
Those Nirgranthas then replied to me,
saying, "Gautama!..."
"I have a venerable teacher named Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, who speaks thus: 'O Nigaṇṭhas!

If you have previously committed evil karmas, all such karma can be completely extinguished through this asceticism; if you now guard your body, speech, and mind, you will not further commit evil karma because of this.'"
I further asked those Nigaṇṭhas:
"Do you have faith in your venerable teacher, the son of the Nigaṇṭha, and are you free from doubt?
They replied to me:
"Gotama! I believe in my teacher, the son of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, without any doubt.
I then spoke again to those Nigaṇṭhas, saying:
"There are five things that yield results in both the present life and the next: faith, delight, hearing, mindfulness, and wise observation. O Nigaṇṭhas!
Can a person’s own false speech be something that is trustworthy, delightful, worth hearing, worth remembering, and worthy of wise observation?"
He replied to me, saying: "It is so, Gautama!"
I further said to those Nirgranthas:
"These are false words; how can they be trusted? How can they be found pleasing? How can they be heard? How can they be remembered? How can they be rightly observed?"
"It means that a person himself utters false speech, yet possesses faith, joy, learning, mindfulness, and skillful discernment.
"If the Nirgranthas make such a claim, they incur five points of censure within the Dharma and become objects of loathing."
What are these five?
"The pleasure and pain experienced by these sentient beings now are all caused by their past actions. If that were so, then the Nirgranthas and others must have committed evil deeds in the past."
Why is this so? Because of them, the Nigaṇṭhas now undergo extremely heavy suffering; this is what is called the first thing about the Nigaṇṭhas that is loathsome.
Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings all arise from conjunction; if that is the case, then the original conjunction of the Nigaṇṭhas was an evil one.
Why is this? Because of that, these Nigaṇṭhas now undergo extreme suffering; this is called the second abhorrent quality of the Nigaṇṭhas.

Furthermore, the pleasure and pain experienced by sentient beings all have their cause in the life-force (*jīva*); if that were so, then these Nigaṇṭhas originally practiced evil for the sake of the life-force.
Why is this? Because of that, the Nigaṇṭhas now undergo extremely heavy suffering; this is called the third loathsome quality of the Nigaṇṭhas.
Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings are all due to views.
If that were so, the Nirgranthas would have possessed evil views from the very beginning. Why is this?
Because it is due to those [views] that the Nirgranthas now undergo such extremely heavy suffering; this is called the fourth loathsome quality of the Nirgranthas.

Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings are all created by a supreme lord (*īśvara*). If this were so, then the Nirgranthas and others would have originally had an evil supreme lord. Why is this?
Because of that, the Nirgranthas now undergo extreme suffering; this is called the fifth thing about the Nirgranthas that is loathsome.

Furthermore, because the Nirgranthas, due to their past evil karma, evil associations, evil livelihoods, evil views, and evil deities—having been created by those evil deities—and because of those things, the Nirgranthas now undergo extreme suffering; it is for these reasons that the Nirgranthas are considered loathsome.

"The Dharma that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I have taught to you, cannot be overcome by any śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world; it cannot be defiled, nor can it be restrained."

What is this Dharma that I have known for myself and realized for myself, which I teach to you, and which cannot be overcome, corrupted, or restrained by recluses, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world?

If there is a bhikṣu who abandons unwholesome bodily karma and cultivates wholesome bodily karma, and abandons unwholesome verbal and mental karma while cultivating wholesome verbal and mental karma, he will know for himself regarding future suffering: "I shall have no future suffering. Thus, having attained happiness in accordance with the Dharma, he does not abandon it.

He may, desiring to sever the cause of suffering, practice the desire for action; or, desiring to sever the cause of suffering, he practices the desire for equanimity. If, desiring to sever the cause of suffering, he practices the desire for action, he cultivates that practice of desire, and once it is severed, suffering is then brought to an end.
If he wishes to sever the cause of suffering by practicing the relinquishment of desire, he then cultivates that practice of relinquishing desire; once it is severed, suffering comes to an end.
If that bhikṣu should think:

"Whatever I do, whatever I practice, unwholesome states arise and wholesome states perish; whereas if I were to personally sever my own suffering, unwholesome states would cease and wholesome states would arise—I should now surely sever this suffering myself."
"Thus, one cuts off suffering for oneself.
Having cut off suffering for oneself, unwholesome states cease and wholesome states arise, such that one no longer needs to cut off suffering. Why is this so?"
“Monks! That which was to be done has been accomplished; for it to be necessary to further sever suffering—that is not possible.
“Monks! [he said.]
It is just as when an arrow-maker uses a straightening tool to straighten an arrow; once the arrow is straight, he no longer uses the tool. Why is this?
Because that person’s original purpose has already been accomplished; if he were to use the tool again, it would be inappropriate.
Thus, a bhikkhu reflects:

"In accordance with what I do and what I practice, unwholesome states arise and wholesome states cease; whereas if I were to personally bring an end to my suffering, unwholesome states would cease and wholesome states would arise. I should now rather personally bring an end to my own suffering."
Thus, one cuts off suffering for oneself.
Having cut off suffering for oneself, unwholesome states cease and wholesome states arise;
one no longer needs to cut off suffering. Why is this?
The purpose for which this was undertaken has already been accomplished; therefore, it would be impossible for suffering to be further severed in this regard. Bhikkhus!

Suppose there were a man who cherished, was infatuated with, and held in high esteem by a certain woman, yet that woman conversed with another man, exchanged greetings with him, and stayed overnight with him. Would that man, on account of this, experience mental and physical suffering and intense grief?
The bhikṣu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”

Why is this? Because that man feels love and attachment for the woman, treating her with the utmost respect; yet that woman converses with others, exchanges greetings with them, and stays overnight with them. How could his body and mind not give rise to suffering, affliction, and grief?
“Bhikṣus! Suppose that person were to think:

‘I have loved, cherished, and respectfully attended to this woman in vain, yet she converses with others, exchanges greetings with them, and stays overnight with them. Would it not be better for me now, on account of my own suffering and grief, to sever my love, affection, and attachment for her?’”
"Later, because that man tormented himself and grieved over it, he severed his affection for and attachment to that woman.

If that woman were to subsequently speak with another man, exchange greetings, come and go, or stay overnight with him, would that man’s body and mind thereafter again give rise to suffering and distress, or experience extreme sorrow and grief?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”

Why is this so? Because that person no longer has any affection or feelings of attachment toward the woman. Even if that woman were to intentionally converse with others, exchange greetings, come and go, or stay overnight with them, it is impossible for that person’s body and mind to consequently experience further suffering, distress, or extreme grief on that account.
"In this way, a bhikkhu reflects:

'Whatever I do, whatever I practice, unwholesome states arise and wholesome states perish; yet if I were to personally bring an end to my suffering, unwholesome states would cease and wholesome states would arise. I should now surely bring an end to my own suffering.'"
"Thus, one cuts off suffering for oneself.
Having cut off suffering for oneself, unwholesome states cease and wholesome states arise, such that one no longer needs to cut off suffering. Why is this so?"
"The purpose for which I undertook this has already been accomplished; if there were further suffering to be abandoned, that would not be the case.
He then thought again:
"If there is a cause through which suffering is abandoned, I have already abandoned that. However, I have still not abandoned desire. I should now seek to abandon desire."
He then sought to abandon sensual desire.

For the sake of abandoning sensual desire, he dwelt alone in seclusion, in a remote place, or went to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet spot, a mountain crag, a stone cave, an open space, a heap of straw, or to a forest grove, or to a cemetery. Having gone to such a remote place, or to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet spot, he spread out his sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, straightened his body and set his intention, and with mindfulness directed inward, he eliminated covetousness; his mind was free from contention. Seeing the wealth and various possessions of others, he did not give rise to covetousness, desiring to obtain them for himself; he purified his mind of covetousness.

In this way, having abandoned ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and having cut off doubt and crossed over confusion, he has no hesitation regarding wholesome qualities; thus, he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.

Having attained such concentration, his mind was purified, free from defilement and affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable; he directed it toward the realization of the superknowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā*). He then knew this suffering as it truly is; he knew the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are. He also knew these outflows as they truly are; he knew the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as they truly are. Having known and seen thus, his mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), and his mind was liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyāsrava*). Being liberated, he knew he was liberated; birth had been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) was established, what was to be done was accomplished, and there would be no further state of existence—this he knew as it truly is.
"The Tathāgata, having thus attained liberation through right mind, attains five kinds of renown; he is in accordance with the Dharma, free from dispute, lovely, and venerable.
What are these five?..."

Those sentient beings experience whatever suffering or pleasure they undergo solely because of their past actions. If this were so, then the Tathāgata, having possessed sublime karma from the beginning, would now—by virtue of that very cause—experience the realization of bliss through the peaceful cessation of the noble, untainted bliss; this is called the Tathāgata attaining the foremost renown.

Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings all arise from conjunction. If this is so, then because the Tathāgata was originally endowed with sublime conjunction, he now, through that cause, experiences the perception of bliss within the noble, untainted bliss of tranquil cessation. This is called the Tathāgata’s attainment of the second praise.

Furthermore, the pleasure and pain experienced by sentient beings all have life as their cause. If this is so, then since the Tathāgata’s original excellence is his very life, it is because of that life that the Tathāgata now experiences the perception of bliss—bliss that is noble, untainted, tranquil, and stilled. This is called the Tathāgata attaining the third praise.

Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings all arise from views. If this is so, then because the Tathāgata possesses the fundamentally sublime view, he now, through that very cause, experiences the noble, untainted bliss of tranquil cessation and attains the perception of bliss; this is called the Tathāgata’s attainment of the fourth praise.

Furthermore, the suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings are all created by a supreme creator (Iśvara). If that were so, since the Tathāgata was originally a sublime supreme creator, then by virtue of that, the Tathāgata now experiences the perception of bliss—bliss that is noble, untainted, tranquil, and stilled. This is called the Tathāgata’s attainment of the fifth praise.

This constitutes the Tathāgata’s original sublime karma, sublime convergence, sublime life-force, sublime vision, and sublime sovereign grace; it is created by that sublime sovereign grace. Because of this, the Tathāgata now experiences the noble, untainted bliss of tranquil cessation and attains the realization of bliss. For this reason, the Tathāgata now receives five kinds of praise.
“There are five causes and conditions by which sorrow and suffering arise in the mind.
What are these five?
For one who is entangled by sensual desire, because of that entanglement by sensual desire, sorrow and suffering arise in the mind.”

In this world, there are truly two kinds of persons.
What are these two?

There is the person with internal fetters who is a non-returner (anāgāmin) and does not return to this realm; and there is the person with external fetters who is not a non-returner and does return to this realm.
Venerable friends!
How is it that a person who has internal fetters becomes a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and does not return to this world?

Suppose there is a person who cultivates the precepts so that they are unbroken, untorn, unstained, and unclouded; they are extensively practiced without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well-cultivated, and fully perfected.

Because he has cultivated the precepts so that they are unbroken, flawless, unstained, and untainted—being extensive, free from difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well-practiced, and fully perfected—he further trains in the weariness with desire, the absence of desire, and the abandonment of desire.
By training in disenchantment with desire, freedom from desire, and the abandonment of desire, one attains tranquility and liberation of mind.

Having attained this, one cherishes it and does not let go; yet, failing to attain ultimate knowledge in the present life, at the breaking up of the body after death, one passes beyond the gods who subsist on edible food and is reborn among the other mind-made gods.
Having been born there, he then thinks:

"In my former life as a human, I cultivated the precepts—unpierced and unbroken, unstained and unturbid, extensively practiced without difficulty, praised by the noble ones, well-cultivated and well-perfected."

Because he practices the precepts—unbroken, unimpaired, unstained, unturbid, exceedingly complete, and beyond reproach, being praised by the noble ones and well-cultivated and well-perfected—he further trains in the disenchantment with desire, the absence of desire, and the abandonment of desire.
Because he trains in disenchantment with desire, the absence of desire, and the abandonment of desire, he attains tranquility and liberation of mind.

Having attained this, he cherishes it within his pleasure and does not let it go; consequently, he does not attain final knowledge in this present life. "Venerable friends!

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu is accomplished in morality, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, it is certainly possible that he will, in this very life, enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, then at the breaking up of the body after death, passing beyond the devas who subsist on material food, he will be reborn among the other mind-made devas; there, it is certainly possible that he will enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was present in the assembly, and he said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
It is impossible for a bhikkhu who has been reborn among the gods of mind-made bodies to enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
The Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus a second and a third time:
