The Venerable Sāriputta again addressed the bhikkhus a second and a third time:

"If a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, it is certainly possible that he will, in this very life, enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, then at the breaking up of the body after death, passing beyond the devas who subsist on physical food, he will be reborn among the mind-made devas; there, it is certainly possible that he will enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
The Venerable Udāyin also spoke a second and a third time, saying:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
It is absolutely impossible for a bhikkhu who has been reborn among the gods of mind-made bodies to enter and emerge from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling."
The Venerable Sāriputta then thought to himself:
"This bhikkhu has thrice contradicted what I have said in the presence of the Blessed One, yet not a single bhikkhu has praised what I have said; it would be best for me to remain silent."
Thereupon, the Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin! Do you say that the mind-born devas possess form?"
The Venerable Udāyin addressed the Blessed One, saying: “It is so,
Blessed One.”
The World-Honored One rebuked Udāyin face to face, saying:
"You foolish man!
You are blind and without eyes; for what reason do you discourse upon the profound Abhidharma?"
Thereupon, having been rebuked by the Buddha to his face, the Venerable Udāyin felt inward grief; with his head bowed and in silence, he was rendered speechless and remained as if lost in thought.
Having rebuked the Venerable Udāyin face to face, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"When a senior, renowned, and virtuous elder bhikṣu is being censured by another, why did you neglect him and fail to restrain him?"
"You foolish men!
You lack a heart of compassion; you have abandoned the Venerable Elder, who is supreme in name and virtue.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyin and the Venerable Ānanda face to face, addressed the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikkhu is accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, and accomplished in wisdom, it is certainly possible that he will, in this very life, enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.

If he does not attain final knowledge in this very life, then at the breaking up of the body after death, passing beyond the devas who feed on solid food, he will be reborn among a certain class of mind-made devas, where it is certainly possible that he will enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.”
When the Buddha had spoken thus, he entered his meditation chamber and sat in silent seclusion.
At that time, the Venerable Śuklodana was present among the assembly, and the Venerable Ānanda said to him:
"This was done by another, yet I am the one who has been rebuked."
"Venerable Pāṇḍava!
In the afternoon, the Blessed One will surely emerge from his meditation chamber, go before the assembly of bhikṣus, seat himself upon a prepared seat, and discuss this matter with them."
"Venerable Pāṭikāputta should answer this matter; I am deeply ashamed before the Blessed One and my fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Thereupon, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One emerged from his meditation chamber, went before the assembly of bhikkhus, spread out a seat, sat down, and said: "Pāṭikāputta!"
“By how many qualities, World-Honored One, is an elder bhikṣu loved, revered, and respected by his fellow practitioners of the holy life?
Venerable Śuklodana replied:
“World-Honored One!”
“Venerable sir, if an elder bhikkhu possesses five qualities, he is loved, respected, and revered by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
What are these five?
Venerable sir!”

The elder bhikṣu cultivates the precepts and guards the code of liberation; furthermore, he properly maintains dignified deportment and etiquette, regards even the slightest transgression as grave, and constantly harbors a sense of dread toward it, upholding and training in the rules of discipline.
"World-Honored One!
An elder bhikṣu who is senior in years and observant of the precepts is loved, revered, and respected by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!"

The elder bhikṣu is one who has studied extensively and heard much, who maintains what he has learned without forgetting, and who has accumulated vast erudition. Regarding those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life—he has studied such teachings extensively and heard them much; having practiced them repeatedly up to a thousand times, he contemplates them with his mind, seeing them clearly and penetrating them deeply.
"Bhagavān!
A learned elder bhikṣu of high standing is loved, revered, and respected by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Furthermore, Bhagavān!"
“Venerable sir, an elder bhikkhu attains the four higher mental states, dwelling in happiness in this very life, easily and without difficulty. Venerable sir,
an elder bhikkhu who practices meditation and reflection is loved, revered, and respected by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.”
Furthermore, World-Honored One,

when a senior bhikṣu practices wisdom and contemplates the phenomena of arising and passing away, he attains such knowledge— noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning— thereby bringing an end to suffering through right means.
"Bhagavān!
A wise elder bhikṣu who is senior is loved, revered, and respected by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Furthermore, Bhagavān!"

The elder bhikṣus have exhausted all taints; they are free from further fetters, with minds liberated and wisdom liberated. In this very life, they have known it for themselves, realized it for themselves, and having personally attained realization, they dwell therein. They know according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Bhagavān!
The elder bhikṣus who have exhausted the outflows are loved, revered, and honored by their fellow practitioners of the holy life. Bhagavān!"
“An elder bhikkhu who is endowed with these five qualities is loved, respected, and honored by his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Blessed One asked: “Vimala!”
"If an elder bhikṣu lacks these five qualities, for what reason should his fellow practitioners of the holy life feel affection,
respect, and reverence for him? Venerable Śuklodana replied,
"World-Honored One!"

If an elder bhikkhu lacks these five qualities, there is nothing else by which his fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacariya) would love, revere, or respect him; he is loved, revered, and respected solely because of his old age—his hair turning white, his teeth falling out, his vigor declining day by day, his body bent and limbs crooked, his body heavy and breath labored, walking with the aid of a staff, his flesh shriveled and skin sagging, wrinkled like hemp seeds, his faculties decayed and matured, and his complexion ugly. It is for this reason alone that his fellow practitioners of the holy life love, revere, and respect him.
The Blessed One said: "It is so, it is so.

If an elder bhikkhu lacks these five qualities, there is nothing else by which his fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) might love, revere, or respect him, other than his being aged, with white hair and fallen teeth, his vigor having declined day by day, his body bent and limbs crooked, his frame heavy and breath labored, walking with the aid of a staff, his flesh shriveled and skin wrinkled like a hulled hemp seed, his faculties decayed and matured, and his complexion ugly. It is for this reason alone that his fellow practitioners of the holy life might love, revere, and respect him."
"Śuklodana!
The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses these five qualities; you all should love, revere, and respect him. Why is this so?"
"Śuklodana!

The bhikṣu Śāriputra cultivates the precepts and guards the liberation through them; furthermore, he is well-restrained in his deportment and etiquette, perceives even the slightest fault as a sin, always harbors fear and dread toward it, and upholds the training rules."
Furthermore, Śukra! The bhikṣu Śāriputra has studied extensively and heard much;

he maintains it without forgetting and accumulates vast learning. Regarding what is called the Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life—he has studied such teachings extensively and heard them much; he has practiced them until they reach a thousand repetitions, contemplating them with his mind, seeing them clearly, and penetrating them deeply.
Furthermore, Śukra!
The bhikṣu Śāriputra has attained the four states of higher mind, which provide a dwelling in happiness in the present life, and they are easily obtained, not with difficulty.
Furthermore, Śukra!

The bhikṣu Śāriputra cultivated wisdom and contemplated the law of arising and passing away; he attained such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning—thereby bringing about the complete extinction of suffering.
Furthermore, Śukra!

The bhikṣu Śāriputra has exhausted all outflows (āsrava) and is free from further fetters (saṃyojana). His mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated; in this very life he has known it for himself, awakened to it for himself, and having realized it through his own direct experience, he dwells therein. Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows according to reality that there will be no further existence.
"Śuklodana!
Since the bhikṣu Śāriputra has accomplished these five qualities, you all should together love, revere, and respect him.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Śuddha and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second chapter, "The Sūtra on the Accomplishment of Precepts," ends here, totaling one thousand seven hundred and forty-six characters. 23. The Sūtra on Wisdom (23). The Third Sūtra on Wisdom in the Saṃyukta Section Corresponding to Śāriputra. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna abandoned the precepts and left the holy life. When the bhikṣu Kaḷārakhattiya heard that the bhikṣu Moliyaphagguna had abandoned the precepts and left the holy life, he immediately went to the Venerable Sāriputta, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and having sat down, said:
"Venerable Sāriputta!..."
"You should know that the bhikkhu Moliyaphagguna has abandoned the precepts and ceased his practice.
The Venerable Sāriputta asked:
"Does the bhikkhu Moliyaphagguna take delight in this Dhamma?"
The bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya asked:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
Do you find delight in this Dhamma?"
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"Kāḷadanta! I have no doubt regarding this Dhamma."
The bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya then asked again:
"Venerable Sāriputta,
what do you say regarding the future?"
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"Kāḷadanta! I have no hesitation regarding the future either."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu Kṛṣṇadanta rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!

"Venerable Sāriputta now declares for himself that he has attained knowledge: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."
Having heard this, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Go to where Sāriputta is and say to him: ‘Sāriputta!’”
“The World-Honored One calls for you.
Having received these instructions, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed. He went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was and said to him:
“The World-Honored One calls for the Venerable Śāriputra.”
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra went at once to the Buddha, prostrated himself in salutation, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The World-Honored One asked him: "Śāriputra!"

Do you truly declare for yourself that you have attained knowledge, that birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and that there will be no further existence, knowing this as it really is?
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"World-Honored One!
It is not by means of these words, nor by means of these phrases, that I speak; I speak only of the meaning."
The World-Honored One said:
“Sāriputta! According to the skillful means by which a son of good family expresses himself, one who has attained knowledge speaks of having attained knowledge.”
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have already stated that I did not do so by means of these words or these phrases; I spoke only of the meaning.”
The Blessed One asked:
“Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!

How do you know and how do you see that you claim to have attained knowledge—knowing truly that birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence?"
“Śāriputra! Having heard this, how would you answer?
Venerable Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
If various fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me, saying:
‘Venerable Śāriputra! [What is the cause and condition for the arising of the mind of renunciation?]’”

How does one know, how does one see, such that one declares for oneself: "Knowledge has been attained; birth is exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence," knowing this as it truly is?
"World-Honored One!
Having heard this, I would answer thus:
'Virtuous ones!'"

Birth has a cause; when this cause of birth is exhausted, having known that the cause of birth is exhausted, I declare of myself that I have attained knowledge: "Birth is ended, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—this I know as it truly is.
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If fellow practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such things, you should answer them in this way.
Why is that? Because when it is spoken in this manner, one should understand its meaning accordingly.
The Blessed One asked:
"Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you: '...'"
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause and what is the condition for birth? From what does it arise, and what is its root?
Having heard this, how would you answer?
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me:..."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition for birth? From what does it arise, and what is its root?
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
Having heard this, I shall answer thus:
"Venerable friends!
Birth has existence as its condition; it arises from existence, and existence is its root."
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If various fellow practitioners of the holy life should come and ask you such things, you should answer them in this way. Why is that?
Because when it is spoken in this manner, you should understand its meaning accordingly.
The Blessed One asked:
“Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause and what is the condition for 'existence' (bhava)?
From what does it arise, and what is its root? Having heard this, how would you answer?
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
“Blessed One,
if practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition for existence; from what does it arise, and what is its root?
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
Having heard this, I shall answer thus:
"Venerable sirs!
Existence has feeling as its cause, feeling as its condition; it arises from feeling and has feeling as its root."
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask such questions, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If fellow practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such a question, you should answer in this way.
Why is that? Because when it is explained in this manner, one should understand its meaning.
The Blessed One asked:
“Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause and what is the condition for feeling? From what does it arise, and what is its root?
Having heard this, how would you answer?
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
“World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is the cause, what is the condition for feeling; from what does it arise, and what is its root?
"World-Honored One! [he replied.]
Having heard this, I shall answer thus:
"Venerable sirs!
The experiencer is caused by craving, conditioned by craving, born from craving, and has craving as its root."
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If fellow practitioners of the holy life come and ask you such questions, you should answer them in this way. Why is that?
Because you should understand the meaning as it is thus explained.
The Blessed One asked:
"Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you: '...'"
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is craving?
Having heard this, how would you answer?"
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"World-Honored One, if practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me: [what would I say?]"
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What is craving? "World-Honored One! [he replied.]
Having heard this, I would answer thus:
"Venerable friends!
There are three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. That which seeks delight in and clings to these is called craving."
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If fellow practitioners of the holy life come and ask you such things, you should answer them in this way. Why is that?
Because when it is spoken in this manner, you should know its meaning.
The Blessed One asked:
“Sāriputta, if fellow practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask you:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
How do you know and how do you see that among the three types of awakening there is no delight, desire, or attachment?
Having heard this, what would you say in reply?"
The Venerable Sāriputta replied:
“World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me:”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
How do you know, and how do you see, so that among the three types of awakening there is no desire for or attachment to them?
"World-Honored One! [Sāriputta replied.]
Having heard this, I would answer thus:
"Venerable friends!

These three perceptions are phenomena that are impermanent, phenomena that are suffering, and phenomena that are subject to cessation. That which is impermanent is suffering; having seen it as suffering, one then has no desire for or attachment to these three perceptions."
“World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask such a question, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!"
If fellow practitioners of the holy life should come and ask you such things, you should answer them in this way. Why is that?
Because when it is explained in this manner, you should understand its meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Sāriputta! This teaching has further meanings that can be answered briefly."
Śāriputra! Furthermore, for what reason can this be answered briefly?
Whatever is perceived and whatever is done is itself suffering.
“Sāriputta! This is what is meant by ‘there being another meaning,’ such that this teaching may be answered briefly.
The Blessed One asked:
“Sāriputta! If practitioners of the holy life should come and ask you:
‘Venerable Sāriputta!’”

How does one, turning away from what is not the goal and proclaiming for oneself, declare with true knowledge: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence," knowing this as it truly is?
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life were to come and ask me:..."
"Venerable Sāriputta!

How is it that one turns away from and does not incline toward self-proclamation, yet truly knows as it really is: 'My knowledge has been attained; birth is exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence'?"
"World-Honored One!
Having heard this, I would answer thus:
'Virtuous ones!'"

If I personally turn my back on and do not face these internally, then all cravings will be exhausted; there will be no alarm, no fear, no doubt, and no delusion. Practicing such protection, and having so protected myself, unwholesome outflows will not arise.
"World-Honored One!
If practitioners of the holy life should come and ask such questions, I would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
If fellow practitioners of the holy life come and ask you such things, you should answer them in this way.
Why is that? You should know that the meaning is as follows when it is spoken in this manner.
The Blessed One said:
"Sāriputta! Furthermore, there is a point regarding this teaching that can be answered briefly."
Whatever fetters have been spoken of by the Śramaṇa, those fetters do not belong to me; I practice such guarding, and having guarded myself thus, unwholesome outflows do not arise.
"Śāriputra! This is what is meant by 'there being another meaning,' such that this teaching may be answered briefly.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation.
Not long after the Blessed One had entered his room, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Venerable friends, before I had even applied my mind to it, the Blessed One suddenly asked me about this matter. I thought to myself:"
"I fear I shall not be able to answer.
"Venerable ones!
When I first spoke this single point, it was immediately approved by the Blessed One, and I further thought to myself:"

"If the Blessed One were to question me on this matter for one day and one night using different words and phrases, I would be able to answer the Blessed One for one day and one night using different words and phrases;

if the Blessed One were to question me on this matter for two, three, four, or up to seven days and seven nights using different words and phrases, I would likewise be able to answer the Blessed One for two, three, four, or up to seven days and seven nights using different words and phrases."
When the bhikkhu Kaḷārakhattiya had heard what the Venerable Sāriputta had said, he immediately rose from his seat, went quickly to where the Buddha was, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One, not long after you entered your chamber, the Venerable Sāriputta made a most sublime statement, delivering a resolute lion’s roar:
'O worthy ones!'"
"Venerable friends! Before I had even begun to reflect upon it, the Blessed One suddenly questioned me on this matter, and I thought to myself:
'I fear I shall not be able to answer.'"
When I first explained this meaning, it was immediately approved by the World-Honored One, and I further thought:

"If the World-Honored One were to question me on this meaning for a day and a night using different phrasings and expressions, I would be able to answer the World-Honored One for a day and a night using different phrasings and expressions."
"Venerable friends!

If the Blessed One were to question me on this matter for two, three, four, or even seven days and nights using different phrasings and different expressions, I too would be able to answer him on this matter for two, three, four, or even seven days and nights using different phrasings and different expressions."
The Blessed One said: "Kāḷadantī, it is so, it is so."

If for one day and one night I were to question the bhikkhu Sāriputta on this matter using various phrases and various expressions, the bhikkhu Sāriputta would certainly be able to answer me on this matter for one day and one night using various phrases and various expressions.

"Kāḷa! If I were to question the bhikkhu Sāriputta on this matter for two, three, four, or even seven days and seven nights using various phrases and expressions, the bhikkhu Sāriputta would likewise be able to answer me on this matter for two, three, four, or even seven days and seven nights using various phrases and expressions."
Why is that? Kāḷadantī,
it is because the bhikkhu Sāriputta has profoundly penetrated the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Śāriputra and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third discourse on Wisdom ends here; it contains one thousand one hundred and sixty-nine characters. 24. Siṃhanāda Sūtra (24) Śāriputra Saṃyukta Section, Fourth Discourse: Siṃhanāda Sūtra First Day’s Recitation Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, was observing the rains retreat in Śrāvastī; the Venerable Śāriputra was also traveling through Śrāvastī and observing the rains retreat there.

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, having completed his summer retreat in the kingdom of Śrāvastī and the three months having passed, finished mending his robes; he then took up his robes and bowl, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"World-Honored One, I have completed my summer retreat in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
World-Honored One,
I wish to travel through the human world."
The Blessed One said:

"Sāriputta! Go; act as you wish. Let those who have not yet crossed over cross over; let those who have not yet been liberated be liberated; let those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa attain parinirvāṇa."
“Śāriputra! Go, as you wish.

Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha had said, received and retained it well. He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Returning to his own dwelling, he put away his bedding, gathered his robes and bowl, and immediately went out to wander among the people.

Not long after the Venerable Sāriputta had departed, a fellow practitioner of the holy life committed an act contrary to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Today, the Venerable Sāriputta has slighted me and is now wandering among the people."
Having heard this, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
"Go to where Sāriputta is and say to him:
'The Blessed One calls for you.'"
Not long after you had departed, a fellow practitioner of the holy life stood before me and committed an act contrary to the Dharma, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Today, the Venerable Sāriputta has slighted me and departed to wander among the people."
Having received these instructions, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda stood behind the World-Honored One, holding a fly-whisk and attending upon him.
Not long after that bhikṣu had departed, the Venerable Ānanda took the keys and went from room to room; seeing the bhikṣus there, he spoke these words:
“Excellent!
"Venerable ones!

Proceed quickly to the lecture hall; today the Venerable Sāriputta shall deliver a lion’s roar before the Buddha. Whatever the Venerable Sāriputta speaks—that which is profound, the most profound among the profound, and the most sublime among the sublime—if he speaks thus, you venerable ones and I, having heard it, shall properly recite and master it, and shall properly receive and uphold it."
At that time, having heard the words of the Venerable Ānanda, all the bhikṣus went to the lecture hall.
Then, a certain bhikṣu went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was and said to him:
"The World-honored One calls for you."
Not long after you had departed, a fellow practitioner of the holy life stood before me and committed an act contrary to the Dharma, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Today, the Venerable Sāriputta has slighted me and has gone forth to wander among the people."
Thereupon, having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, went back to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Sāriputta!
Not long after you departed, a fellow practitioner of the holy life stood before me and committed an act contrary to the Dharma, speaking these words:"
“World-Honored One!
Today, the Venerable Śāriputra has slighted me before departing to wander among the people.
“Śāriputra! [the Buddha said.]
“Did you indeed travel among the people after having treated a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
Venerable Sāriputta replied,
“World-Honored One, [I did].”
"If one were without mindfulness of the body, he would indeed treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among humans.
World-Honored One, I am well-established in mindfulness of the body; how could I treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among humans?"
World-Honored One!

It is like a hornless ox that has reached the state of patience and gentleness; well-trained and well-governed, as it travels from village to village and from lane to lane, it does not cause offense anywhere in its wanderings.
"Blessed One!

I am also like this: my mind is like an ox with its horns cut off—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
"Bhagavān!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
Bhagavān!"
“I possess the excellent mindfulness of the body. How could I, while practicing this holy life, travel through the human world with such contempt for another practitioner?
“World-Honored One!

It is like the son of a caṇḍāla who has had both hands cut off; his mind is utterly humbled, yet as he travels from village to village and town to town, he does not commit any offense wherever he goes.”
World-Honored One!

I am also thus: my mind is like that of a Caṇḍāla’s son whose hand has been severed; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein.
"Bhagavān!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
Bhagavān!"
"I possess a well-developed mindfulness of the body; how could I, while wandering among human beings, treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One!

It is just as the earth receives both the pure and the impure—feces, urine, mucus, and spittle—all of which it accepts. The earth does not harbor hatred or affection because of this; it feels no shame, no embarrassment, and no sense of disgrace."
"Bhagavān!

I am also like this: my mind is like that earth—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
“World-Honored One!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body as body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
World-Honored One!”
"I possess this excellent mindfulness of the body; how could I wander among human beings while treating even one fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One!

It is just as water, whether clean or unclean—washing away excrement, urine, mucus, or spittle—the water does not harbor hatred or affection because of this; it feels no shame, no embarrassment, and no sense of disgrace."
"Blessed One!

I am also like this: my mind is like that water—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
“World-Honored One!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
World-Honored One!”
"I possess this excellent mindfulness of the body; how could I, while wandering among humans, treat even a single fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One! It is just like fire:

whether pure or impure—whether it be excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva—it burns them all. Fire does not harbor hatred or affection because of these things; it feels no shame, no remorse, and no sense of disgrace."
"Bhagavān!

I am also like this: my mind is like that fire—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
"Bhagavān!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
Bhagavān!"
"I possess the excellent mindfulness of the body; how could I, while wandering among humans, treat even a single fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One! It is just as the wind:

whether it encounters the pure or the impure—whether excrement, urine, mucus, or saliva—it blows upon them all. The wind feels no hatred or affection because of this; it is neither ashamed nor abashed, nor does it feel any sense of disgrace."
"Bhagavān!

I am also like this: my mind is like that wind—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
"Bhagavān!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
Bhagavān!"
"I possess the excellent mindfulness of the body regarding the body; how could I, while wandering among people, treat even a single fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One!

It is just like a broom that sweeps away both the clean and the unclean—excrement, urine, mucus, and spittle—the broom feels neither hatred nor affection toward them because of this; it is not ashamed, not abashed, and feels no sense of disgrace."
"Bhagavān!

I am also like this: my mind is like a broom, free from fetters and enmity, without ill will or contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
“World-Honored One!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
World-Honored One!”
"I possess the mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) well; how could I, while wandering among people, treat even a single fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt?
"World-Honored One!

It is like the *puñchanī* cloth, which wipes away both the pure and the impure—excrement, urine, mucus, and spittle. Because of this, the *puñchanī* feels neither hatred nor affection; it is not ashamed, not abashed, and has no sense of disgrace."
"Bhagavān!

I am also like this: my mind is like that of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as I dwell therein."
"Blessed One!
If one lacks mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they will treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among human beings.
Blessed One!"
"I possess this well-developed mindfulness of the body; how could I wander among human beings while showing contempt for even a single fellow practitioner of the holy life?
"World-Honored One!
It would be like an ointment jar that is cracked all over; though filled with ointment and placed in the sun, it leaks, drips, and flows out everywhere."

If a person with sight were to come and stand to one side, they would see that this oil jar is cracked and broken in many places; though filled to the brim with oil and set out in the sun, it leaks, drips, and flows all over.
"Bhagavān!
I am also like this; I constantly contemplate how this body has nine orifices that are impure, leaking and overflowing with secretions from every pore.
Bhagavān!"
"If one were without mindfulness of the body regarding the body, they would treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among people.
World-Honored One!
I am well-established in mindfulness of the body regarding the body; how could I treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among people?"
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a certain self-satisfied youth who has bathed and washed himself, anointed with fragrant unguents, dressed in pure white garments, adorned with necklaces, shaved his beard and groomed his hair, and wears a crown of flower garlands. If he were to have three corpses—a dead snake, a dead dog, and a dead human—bluish and bloated, extremely foul and putrid, decaying and oozing impurities, tied around his neck, he would feel ashamed and find them utterly loathsome and filthy.”
“World-Honored One!
I am also like this; I constantly contemplate this body as a foul-smelling place of impurity, my heart filled with shame and deeply loathing its filthiness.
World-Honored One!”
"If one were without mindfulness of the body as body, they would indeed treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among humans.
World-Honored One!
Since I am well-established in mindfulness of the body as body, how could I treat a fellow practitioner of the holy life with contempt while wandering among humans?"
Thereupon, that bhikṣu rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One:
“I repent, World-Honored One!
I confess my fault, Sugata!”
I am as foolish, as deluded, as unstable, and as unwholesome as one could be. Why is this?
Because with false and deceptive words, I have slandered the pure practitioner, the bhikkhu Sāriputta.
“World-Honored One!
I now repent my transgression; I pray that you will accept it. Having seen my error, I confess it openly and shall not do it again.
The World-Honored One told him:
"So it is, bhikkhu! You are indeed foolish, deluded, unstable, and unskilled."
Why is this? It is because you have, with false and empty words devoid of truth, slandered the pure practitioner, the bhikkhu Sāriputta.
You are now able to repent, having recognized your fault and confessed it, so that you will not do it again in the future.
If one repents, having seen [the fault] and confessed it, and does not commit it again thereafter, then one thus nurtures the Noble Dharma and Vinaya so that they do not decline.
Thereupon, the Buddha said to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Accept quickly the confession of that foolish man; do not let that bhikṣu have his head split into seven pieces right before you."
Out of compassion for that bhikṣu, the Venerable Śāriputra then accepted his confession.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Śāriputra and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, Chapter Four, ends here; 1,977 characters. 25. The *Vārī-upama Sūtra* (25). The *Śāriputra-saṃyukta-varga*, *Vārī-upama Sūtra*, Fifth; First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!
I shall now explain to you five methods for removing affliction."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
Those bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Venerable Śāriputra said:
"What are the five?
O worthy ones!"
Suppose there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or vexation, they should eliminate it.
Furthermore:
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or vexation, they should eliminate it."
Furthermore, venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person whose conduct is impure in body and impure in speech, yet possesses a slight degree of purity in mind. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or distress, they should eliminate it.
Furthermore, worthy sirs!
There may be a person whose bodily conduct is impure, and whose verbal and mental conduct are impure. If a wise person sees this and gives rise to resentment or vexation, they should eliminate it.
Furthermore, worthy friends!
There may be a person whose conduct is pure in body, speech, and mind. If a wise person sees such a one and gives rise to anger or resentment, they ought to eliminate it.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or distress, how should they eliminate it?"
"Venerable friends!

It is just as when a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, wearing robes made of discarded rags, sees a piece of worn-out cloth cast away in a heap of refuse—perhaps defiled by feces, or urine, mucus, saliva, or other impurities. Having seen it, he takes it up with his left hand and spreads it out with his right hand; if there is a spot not defiled by feces, urine, mucus, saliva, or other impurities, and which is not torn, he then tears that portion off."
In this way, worthy sirs!

Suppose there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure but whose verbal conduct is pure; do not dwell upon that person’s impure bodily conduct, but rather attend only to that person’s pure verbal conduct. If a wise person sees such a case and resentment or affliction should arise, it should be eliminated in this manner.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or distress, how should they eliminate it?"
"Venerable friends!

Suppose not far outside a village there is a deep pool of water covered with straw and grass. If a person were to come along—extremely heated, distressed, exhausted by hunger and thirst, and oppressed by the heat of the wind—and upon reaching the pool, were to take off his clothes and place them on the bank, then enter the pool, part the straw with both hands, and bathe to his heart's content, thereby removing his heat, distress, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion."
In this way, worthy friends!

Suppose there is a person whose verbal conduct is impure but whose bodily conduct is pure. One should not dwell upon that person’s impure verbal conduct; rather, one should dwell only upon that person’s pure bodily conduct. If a wise person perceives this and anger or resentment should arise, they should eliminate it in this manner.
“Virtuous ones!

Suppose there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, yet whose mind possesses a slight degree of purity. If a wise person sees this and feels resentment or distress, how should they eliminate it?”
"Venerable friends!
It is as if there were water in a cow's footprint at a crossroads.
Suppose a person were to come along, extremely distressed by heat, exhausted by hunger and thirst, and oppressed by the wind and sun, and he were to think thus:"

"In this crossroads, the water in the cow's footprint is scant; if I were to take it with my hand or with a leaf, I would disturb and muddify it, and thus I could not relieve my extreme heat, distress, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion."
"I would rather kneel, pressing my hands and knees to the ground, and drink water with my mouth.
He then knelt for a long time, pressing his hands and knees to the ground, and drank water with his mouth; immediately, he was freed from the heat, extreme distress, hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.
In this way, worthy ones!

Suppose there is a person whose bodily conduct is impure and whose verbal conduct is impure, yet whose mind possesses a slight degree of purity. You should not dwell upon that impurity of his bodily conduct or verbal conduct; rather, you should dwell only upon that slight degree of purity in his mind.
"Venerable friends!
If a wise person perceives that anger has arisen, they should eliminate it in this way:
'Venerable friends!'"
Suppose there is a person whose conduct is impure in body, speech, and mind; if a wise person sees this and feels resentment or distress, how should they eliminate it?
"Venerable friends!

It is just as if there were a person traveling along a long road who fell ill midway; he was utterly exhausted and weary, alone without a companion, with the village behind him growing ever more distant while the village ahead had not yet been reached."

Suppose someone comes and stands to one side, seeing this practitioner who has traveled a long distance and fallen ill midway, utterly exhausted and alone without a companion, with the village behind him still far away and the village ahead not yet reached. If that person finds an attendant who can lead him from the desolate wilderness to a village or town, provide him with excellent medicinal decoctions, nourish him with fine food, and care for him well—then this person’s illness will surely be cured; it is because that person possesses a heart of profound compassion and loving-kindness toward this sick man.
In this way, worthy friends!
Suppose there is a person whose conduct of body is impure, and whose conduct of speech and mind is impure. If a wise person sees this, they would think:

"This worthy one’s conduct of body is impure, and his conduct of speech and mind is impure; may this worthy one, because of this impure conduct of body, speech, and mind, not—upon the breakup of the body after death—go to a state of misery or be reborn in hell."

If this worthy person gains a virtuous friend, they will abandon impure conduct of body and cultivate pure conduct of body; they will abandon impure conduct of speech and mind and cultivate pure conduct of speech and mind.

In this way, because this worthy person has practiced purity of bodily conduct and purity of verbal and mental conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly reach a good destination and be reborn in a heavenly realm.

That is to say, this virtuous person has a heart of supreme compassion and loving-kindness toward that other virtuous person; if a wise person should feel anger or resentment upon seeing this, they should eliminate it in this manner.
"Venerable friends!
Suppose there is a person whose conduct is pure in body, speech, and mind. If a wise person sees such a one and feels resentment or irritation, how should they eliminate it?"
"Venerable friends!

Suppose not far outside a village there is a fine pool of water, both clear and beautiful, its depths level and full, with emerald grasses covering its banks and flowering trees surrounding it. If someone were to come along, scorched by intense heat, distressed and weary, parched with thirst and exhausted, oppressed by the hot wind, and upon reaching that pool, were to take off his clothes and set them on the bank, then enter the pool to bathe as he pleased, thereby dispelling his heat, distress, weariness, thirst, and exhaustion."
In this way, worthy ones!

Suppose there is a person whose conduct of body is pure, and whose conduct of speech and mind is pure; he should constantly attend to that purity of conduct of body, speech, and mind. If a wise person sees him and gives rise to anger or resentment, they should eliminate it in this manner.
"Venerable friends!
It was for this reason that I spoke previously of the five methods for removing vexation.
Thus spoke the Venerable Śāriputra.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

26. The Ghoṣita Sūtra (26) The Sixth Sūtra in the Section Corresponding to Śāriputra, the Ghoṣita Sūtra, for the First Day’s Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Rājagṛha and staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.

At that time, the bhikṣu Guṇṇisa was also traveling through Rājagṛha and staying in a secluded hut; he was prone to jesting and arrogance, restless and easily forgetful, his mind like that of a monkey.

The bhikṣu Goniṣa arrived in Rājagṛha on account of some minor business. At that time, after the midday meal, the Venerable Śāriputra, together with a community of bhikṣus, had assembled in the lecture hall for a small matter.
Having finished his business in Rājagaha, the bhikkhu Guṇaṅgiya went to the lecture hall.
When the Venerable Sāriputta saw Guṇaṅgiya approaching from afar, he addressed the bhikkhus because of Guṇaṅgiya’s arrival:
“Venerable friends!...”
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train himself to be respectful and to practice contemplation in accordance with the teaching.
Venerable friends,

if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest is often disrespectful and does not practice contemplation in accordance with the teaching, he will incur the censure, reproach, and rebuke of his fellow bhikkhus.
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice this inactivity? Why is this so?

Because this worthy one, while practicing inactivity, is for the most part disrespectful and lacks proper reflection; thus, when he enters the assembly, he incurs the censure and reprimands of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu practicing seclusion should train in reverence so that his contemplation proceeds accordingly.
Worthy ones!"
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train himself not to engage in frivolous chatter or to be restless and agitated.
Venerable friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest frequently engages in frivolous chatter and is restless and agitated, he will incur the censure, reproach, and rebuke of other bhikkhus.
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice this inactivity? For what reason?

This worthy one, though inactive, practices inactivity while engaging frequently in frivolous joking and agitation; when he enters the assembly, he likewise incurs the censure and reprimands of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, venerable friends!
A bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion should train himself not to engage in frivolous joking, so as not to become restless and agitated.
"Venerable friends!"
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train himself not to engage in talk concerning animals.
Venerable friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest engages frequently in talk concerning animals, he will incur the censure and reproach of his fellow bhikkhus:
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice this inactivity? For what reason?
This worthy one, though inactive, practices inactivity while engaging in much talk about cattle; even when he enters the assembly, he incurs the censure and reproach of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A monk who dwells in seclusion should train in not engaging in talk concerning animals.
"Worthy ones! [he said.]
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train in being free from arrogance and in speaking little.
Venerable friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest is full of arrogance and speaks much, he will incur the reproach and censure of his fellow bhikkhus:
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice this inactivity? Why is that?

This worthy one, though inactive, practices inactivity while frequently acting with arrogance and engaging in much talk; thus, when he enters the assembly, he incurs the reproach and censure of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion should train in being free from arrogance and in speaking little.
"Worthy ones! [he said.]
“Monks living in seclusion who practice seclusion should train in guarding the sense faculties.
Venerable friends!
If a monk living in seclusion who practices seclusion frequently fails to guard his sense faculties, he will incur the censure and reproach of other monks.”
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice inactivity? For what reason?
Because this worthy one, though inactive, practices inactivity while failing to guard his sense faculties. Thus, when he enters the assembly, he incurs the reproach and censure of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu practicing in seclusion should train in guarding the sense faculties.
Worthy ones!"
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train in knowing moderation in eating.
Venerable friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest is greedy for abundant food and lacks contentment, he will incur the reproach, censure, and rebuke of other bhikkhus:
"This worthy one is supposedly 'one who does nothing,' yet why does he practice doing nothing? For what reason?

This worthy one, though claiming to do nothing, practices doing nothing while being greedy for excessive food and lacking knowledge of moderation; thus, when he enters the assembly, he incurs the reproach, censure, and reprimand of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion should train in knowing moderation in eating.
Worthy ones!"
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu who practices in the forest should train himself to be energetic and not indolent.
Venerable friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who practices in the forest is often lacking in energy and is indolent, he will incur the censure, reproach, and reprimand of his fellow bhikkhus.
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice non-action? Why is this so?

This worthy one, being inactive, practices non-action, yet for the most part lacks diligence and instead succumbs to indolence; if he enters the assembly, he likewise incurs the censure, reproach, and rebuke of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A monk who dwells in seclusion should train in vigor and not be indolent.
Worthy ones!"
"A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train in right mindfulness and clear comprehension. Friends,
if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest lacks much right mindfulness and lacks clear comprehension, he will incur the censure and reproach of his fellow bhikkhus."
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice inactivity? For what reason?

Because this worthy one, though inactive, practices inactivity with a lack of right mindfulness and a lack of right clear comprehension; thus, when he enters the assembly, he also incurs the censure, reproach, and rebuke of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu living in seclusion who practices seclusion should train in right mindfulness and right situational awareness.
Worthy ones!"
A forest-dwelling bhikṣu who practices the life of seclusion should train to know the proper time and the opportune moment.
He should not enter the village for alms too early, nor should he depart too late.
"Venerable friends!
If a monk who is supposed to be practicing in seclusion enters a village early for alms and leaves late, he will incur the censure, reproach, and rebuke of other monks:
'This venerable one claims to be in seclusion; why does he practice seclusion? "
Why is this? This worthy one is indolent and practices indolence;
he enters the village for alms too early and leaves too late, and when he arrives among the assembly, he is likewise subjected to the censure and reproach of the bhikṣus.
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A monk who dwells in seclusion should train in knowing the proper time and the opportune moment.
Worthy ones!"

A forest-dwelling bhikṣu practicing in the forest should train in knowing how to sit and sitting properly; he should not crowd the seat of an elder bhikṣu, nor should he be censured by junior bhikṣus.
"Venerable friends!

If a monk who practices in solitude should sit so as to encroach upon an elder while practicing in solitude, and is thereby rebuked by a junior monk, he will incur the censure and reproach of the monks, who will say:
'This venerable one claims to practice in solitude; why does he practice in solitude? "

Why is this? This worthy man, being one who ought to be inactive, practices such inactivity that he intrudes upon the seat of an elder and is rebuked by junior bhikṣus; even when he enters the midst of the assembly, he likewise incurs the frequent rebukes and censures of the bhikṣus.
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A monk who dwells in seclusion should train himself to know how to sit and how to sit well.
"Worthy ones! [he said.]
"Monks who dwell in seclusion, while practicing in seclusion, should train together in discussing the Vinaya and the Abhidharma.
Why is this so, worthy ones?"
When a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is practicing the life of a forest-dweller, someone may come to question him regarding the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma.
"Venerable friends!

If a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, while practicing the life of a forest-dweller, does not know how to answer questions on the Vinaya or the Abhidhamma, he will incur the censure and reproach of other bhikkhus."
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice inactivity? For what reason?

This worthy one, being inactive, practices inactivity, yet he does not know how to answer regarding the Vinaya or the Abhidharma. If he enters the midst of the assembly, he will likewise incur the censure and reproach of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion should train himself to engage in discussion regarding the Vinaya and the Abhidhamma.
Worthy ones!"
"Venerable friends, a monk who dwells in seclusion should train in discussing the liberation through tranquility, from the transcendence of form up to the formless attainments. Why is that?
Venerable friends!"

When forest-dwelling bhikkhus are practicing in the forest, there may be those who come and ask about the liberations through stillness (*samāpatti*), from the transcendence of form up to the formless attainments.
Venerable friends!

If a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, while practicing in the forest, does not know how to answer regarding these liberations through stillness from the transcendence of form up to the formless attainments, he will incur the censure, reproach, and interrogation of other bhikkhus.
"This worthy one is inactive; why does he practice this inactivity? For what reason?

Although this worthy one is inactive and practices inactivity, he does not know how to answer regarding the cessation of the mind and liberation, nor the detachment from form up to the formless attainments. Thus, when he enters the assembly, he is subjected to the censure, reproach, and interrogation of the bhikṣus."
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A monk who dwells in seclusion should train in discussing together the liberation through cessation, from the transcendence of form up to the formless attainments."
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu practicing in seclusion should train in the discourse on the superknowledge of the destruction of the taints. Why is that?
Venerable friends!
When a bhikkhu who dwells in seclusion practices that seclusion, someone may come and ask him about the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Venerable friends!

If a forest-dwelling bhikṣu dwells in the forest but does not know how to answer regarding the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, he will incur the reproach, censure, and interrogation of other bhikṣus:
"This worthy one is a forest-dweller; why does he practice forest-dwelling?"

Why is this? This worthy one is inactive and practices inactivity, yet he does not know how to answer regarding the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows; if he enters among the assembly, he will likewise incur the censure and reproach of the bhikṣus.
"Therefore, worthy ones!
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest should train in the shared discourse on the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was also in the assembly, and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said:
“Venerable Sāriputta!
Is it only for forest-dwelling bhikkhus practicing in solitude that one should train in such a Dhamma, and not for bhikkhus living among people?”
The Venerable Śāriputra replied: “Venerable Mahāmoggallāna!
If even a forest-dwelling bhikkhu practicing in the forest must train in such a Dhamma, how much more so for a bhikkhu living among people?”
Thus these two venerable ones conversed with one another, praising each other’s words as excellent; having heard what was said, they rose from their seats and departed.
They were respectful and free from levity; they avoided talk of worldly matters;
they guarded their sense faculties; they were moderate in eating; and they were diligent, possessed of right mindfulness and wisdom.
Knowing the proper time, and sitting well; discussing the Vinaya, the Abhidharma, and explaining the cessation and liberation;
the supernormal power of the destruction of the taints is likewise.

Thus ends the sixth discourse, the Goṇisādi Sutta, consisting of one thousand seven hundred and forty characters. 27. He replied: "It is so,
Venerable Sāriputta!"

He replied: “It is so, Venerable Śāriputra!”

The assembly of upāsakas and the assembly of upāsikās dwelling in Rājagṛha are physically robust, at ease and free from illness; their movements are light and agile, their strength is as usual, and they desire to see the Buddha frequently and all delight in hearing the Dharma.

He replied: “It is so, Venerable Śāriputra.”

Several heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins who had spent the summer retreat in Rājagṛha were in good health, at ease and free from illness; their movements were agile and their strength was as usual. Desiring to see the Buddha frequently, they all delighted in hearing the Dharma.
He asked again:

The brahmin Dhānañjāni is not diligent and has transgressed the precepts; he relies upon the king to deceive the brahmins and householders, and he relies upon the brahmins and householders to deceive the king.

The Venerable Sāriputta said:

"Brahmin Dhoṇa! What do you think?
Between the hells and the animal realm, which is superior?"
Dhānañjāni replied,
“The animals are superior.
He asked again:
“Dhānañjāni!
Between animals and hungry ghosts, which are superior?
Dhānañjāni replied:
"The hungry ghosts have won," he said.
He asked again,
"Dhānañjāni!..."
"Between hungry ghosts and humans, which is superior?
Dhaññaka replied, "Humans are superior."
He asked again:
"Dhānañjāni!

Dhānañjāni replied,
“The Heaven of the Four Great Kings is superior.
He asked again:
“Dhānañjāni!

Dhānañjāni replied:
"The Heaven of the Thirty-three is superior.
He asked again:
"Dhānañjāni!..."

Dhānañjāni replied,
"The Yāma Heaven is superior."
He asked again:
"Dhānañjāni!

Dhānañjāni replied,
"The Tuṣita Heaven is superior.
He asked again:
“Dhānañjāni!

Dhānañjāni replied:
“The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is superior.
He asked again, “Dhānañjāni! What do you think?”
"Between the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven,

He asked again:
"Dhānañjāni!
Between the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods and the Brahmā gods, which are superior?"

Venerable Sāriputta said to him:

"Udayin! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who possesses knowledge and vision, has taught the four brahma-vihāras. That is to say, when a son or daughter of good family cultivates and practices them repeatedly, they abandon desire and relinquish thoughts of desire; at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among the Brahmā devas."
"What are the four? Tāṇa!

A well-versed noble disciple dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), accomplished and pervasive; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, all around and everywhere, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—dwelling pervading the entire world. In the same way, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated."
This is what is meant, Dhoṇa!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who possesses knowledge and vision, has taught the four brahma-vihāras; that is to say, when a son or daughter of good family practices and cultivates them repeatedly, they abandon desire and relinquish thoughts of desire, and at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among the Brahmā gods.
Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta, having instructed Dhoṇa and taught him the Dharma of the Brahmā-world, rose from his seat and departed.

While the Venerable Sāriputta was traveling from Rājagaha and had not yet reached the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, on that intervening path, the brahmin Dhoṇa cultivated the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*); he abandoned desire and relinquished thoughts of desire, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, was reborn in the Brahmā-world.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a vast assembly of immeasurable followers as he preached the Dharma. Seeing from afar the Venerable Śāriputra approaching, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses wise intelligence, swift intelligence, nimble intelligence, sharp intelligence, expansive intelligence, profound intelligence, intelligence of liberation, penetrating intelligence, and eloquent intelligence; the bhikṣu Śāriputra has perfected true wisdom."

This bhikkhu Sāriputta has come after converting the brahmin Dhānañjāni and teaching him the Dhamma of Brahmā; had he converted anyone further than this, they would have quickly understood the Dhamma as it truly is.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The World-Honored One said to him: “Śāriputra!
"Why do you not teach the brahmin Dhānañjāni the Dhamma that transcends the Brahmā world? If he were to be transformed by it, he would quickly understand the Dhamma as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta replied:
"World-Honored One!"

Those brahmins have for a long night been attached to the Brahmā world, delighting in the Brahmā world, making the Brahmā world their ultimate goal; they regard that Brahmā as venerable, believing that Brahmā truly exists, and that Brahmā is their own.
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
I shall act accordingly.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Sāriputta and the assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was gravely ill and near death. Thereupon, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika addressed a messenger:

"Go to the Buddha and, on my behalf, prostrate yourself at the World-Honored One's feet. Inquire after the World-Honored One’s health, asking: 'Is your holy body robust and strong? Are you at ease and free from illness? Are your daily activities light and convenient? Is your physical strength as usual?'"
He spoke these words:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada bows his head at the feet of the Buddha and inquires after the World-Honored One’s welfare:
'Is your holy body healthy and strong? Are you at ease and free from illness? Is your daily life light and convenient? Is your physical strength as it usually is?'"

"Once you have inquired after the Buddha's health on my behalf, go to where the Venerable Sāriputta is; having prostrated at his feet on my behalf, inquire after the Venerable One, asking whether his body is healthy and strong, whether he is at ease and free from illness, and whether his daily activities are light and convenient, and whether his strength is as usual?"
He spoke these words:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bows his head at the feet of the Venerable Śāriputra and inquires after the Venerable’s welfare:

"Venerable Sāriputta!

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika is gravely ill and now in a critical condition. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika sincerely desires to see the Venerable Sāriputta; however, his body is so exceedingly weak that he lacks the strength to come to where the Venerable Sāriputta is."
Excellent,
Venerable Śāriputra!
Out of compassion, please go to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Thereupon, having received the instructions from the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the messenger went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:

Thereupon, the messenger, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and retained it well; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Venerable Sāriputta was, prostrated at his feet, sat down to one side, and said:
