The householder Anāthapiṇḍika bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Sāriputta and inquired after the Venerable’s welfare:
"Is your holy body healthy and strong? Are you at ease and free from illness? Is your daily life light and convenient? Is your physical strength as it usually is?"
"Venerable Sāriputta!

The householder Anāthapiṇḍika is gravely ill and now in a critical condition. The householder Anāthapiṇḍika sincerely desires to see the Venerable Sāriputta; however, his body is so exceedingly weak that he lacks the strength to come to where the Venerable Sāriputta is."
Excellent,
Venerable Śāriputra!
Out of compassion, please go to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
The Venerable Sāriputta accepted his request by remaining silent.
Thereupon, the messenger, knowing that the Venerable Sāriputta had accepted by his silence, rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
When the night had passed and at dawn, the Venerable Śāriputra dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the home of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada.
Seeing the Venerable Śāriputra approaching from afar, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada immediately rose from his couch.
Seeing that the householder was about to rise from his bed, the Venerable Sāriputta stopped him, saying:
"Householder, do not rise!
Householder, do not rise!"
"There is another seat; I shall sit elsewhere.
Venerable Sāriputta then sat upon that seat. Having sat down, he asked:
"Householder, how is your ailment now? How much do you eat and drink? Is your suffering diminishing and not increasing?"
The householder replied, "My ailment has become extremely grave; I have no appetite for food or drink, and my suffering only increases without showing any sign of abating.
Venerable Śāriputra said to him:
"Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings possess a lack of faith, at the breaking up of the body after death, they go to a miserable destination and are reborn in hell.

Today, the householder has no lack of faith; he possesses only supreme faith. Because of this supreme faith, the householder may have his suffering extinguished and experience extreme happiness; because of this supreme faith, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to unwholesome precepts, at the breaking up of the body after death, go to a state of misery and are reborn in hell;

the householder has no unwholesome precepts, but possesses only wholesome precepts. Because of these wholesome precepts, the householder may extinguish suffering and pain and give rise to supreme happiness; because of these wholesome precepts, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If a foolish worldling, due to a lack of extensive learning, at the breaking up of the body after death, goes to a miserable destination and is born in hell;

the householder is not one who lacks extensive learning, but rather one who possesses extensive learning. Because of this extensive learning, the householder may extinguish suffering and pain and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this extensive learning, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to stinginess and greed, at the dissolution of the body after death, go to an evil destination and are born in hell;

the householder has no stinginess or greed, but only practices giving. Because of this giving, the householder may extinguish suffering and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this giving, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder had already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* from the outset.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to their lack of wisdom, at the dissolution of the body after death, go to a miserable destination and are born in hell;

the householder has no lack of wisdom, but possesses only wholesome wisdom. Because of this wholesome wisdom, the householder may extinguish suffering and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this wholesome wisdom, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder had already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* from the beginning.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, go to an evil destination and are born in hell;

the householder has no wrong views, but possesses only right view. Because of his right view, the householder may extinguish suffering and give rise to supreme happiness; because of his right view, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder had already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* in the past.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to wrong intention, at the breaking up of the body after death, go to a state of misery and are born in hell;

the householder has no wrong intention, but possesses only right intention. Because of this right intention, the householder may extinguish suffering and pain and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this right intention, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to wrong understanding, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, go to an evil destination and are reborn in hell;

the householder has no wrong understanding, but only right understanding. Because of this right understanding, the householder may extinguish suffering and pain and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this right understanding, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder had already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* from the beginning.
"Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to wrong liberation, at the breaking up of the body after death, go to a state of misery and are born in hell;

the householder has no wrong liberation, but only right liberation. Because of this right liberation, the householder may extinguish suffering and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this right liberation, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already previously attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
“Do not fear, householder! Do not fear! Why is this?
If foolish worldlings, due to wrong knowledge, at the breaking up of the body after death, go to a state of misery and are born in hell;

the householder has no wrong knowledge, but only right knowledge. Because of this right knowledge, the householder may extinguish suffering and give rise to supreme happiness; because of this right knowledge, he may attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or the fruit of *anāgāmin*. The householder has already attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Thereupon, the householder’s illness was immediately cured; he recovered as before, rose from his bed, and sat up, exclaiming in praise of the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent! You have preached the Dharma for the sake of the sick.
How marvelous!
"How extraordinary!
Venerable Śāriputra!
Having heard this teaching on the method for attending to the sick, my suffering has been extinguished and I have experienced supreme happiness."
Venerable Sāriputta!
My illness has now subsided, and I have recovered as before.
Venerable Sāriputta!
In the past, when I had some business, I went to the city of Rājagṛha and stayed overnight at the house of an elder.
At that time, that elder was to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus on the following day.
Then, when the night had passed and dawn was approaching, the elder instructed his sons, grandsons, servants, and kinsmen:
"All of you, rise early and together prepare everything."

They each accepted the instruction and together prepared the kitchen staff to provide various kinds of exquisite and delicious delicacies. The elder personally arranged a high seat, adorned with immeasurable ornaments.
“Venerable Sāriputta!
Having seen this, I thought to myself:

‘Is this householder preparing for a marriage, or for a festival to welcome a bride, or has he invited the king, or summoned the ministers, or is he holding a sacrificial assembly and making great offerings?’”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
Having reflected thus, I asked the householder:
'Is it for the sake of a marriage, or for a festival to welcome a bride, or to invite the king, or to summon the ministers, or to prepare a sacrificial feast and provide great almsgiving?'"
Then that householder replied to me, saying:

"I have no marriage to arrange, nor am I welcoming a bride; I am not holding a festival, nor am I inviting the king or summoning the ministers. Rather, I am preparing a great offering for a vegetarian assembly, as tomorrow I shall provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I have never heard the name 'Buddha' before. Upon hearing it, the hairs on my entire body stood on end, and I immediately asked:
'Householder, you speak of a Buddha; what is meant by the term "Buddha"? "
Then that householder replied to me, saying:
"Have you not heard?

There is one born of the Śākya clan who has renounced his Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of supreme faith has left home for the homeless life to study the Way. He has attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he is called the Buddha."
I asked him again:
“Householder, you speak of a ‘multitude. What is meant by a ‘multitude’?
At that time, the householder replied to me:

"There are those of various surnames, different names, and diverse lineages who have shaved off their hair and beards, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith have left home for the homeless life to study the Way under the Buddha; these are called the Saṅgha. This Buddha and this Saṅgha are whom I invite."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I then asked that householder once more:
'Where is the World-Honored One now? "
"I wish to go and see him.
Then, that householder replied to me again, "The World-Honored One is currently here in Rājagṛha, at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground; you may go there as you please."
"Venerable Śāriputra!
I thought to myself:
'If it becomes light quickly, I shall go swiftly to see the Buddha.'"
"Venerable Śāriputra!

At that time, with a sincere heart desiring to go and see the Buddha, I immediately perceived it as daylight during that very night. I then departed from the householder’s home and proceeded to the city gate."

At that time, there were two gatekeepers at the city’s Ximén Gate: one was on duty during the first watch of the night to ensure that visiting envoys entering from outside met with no obstruction, and one was on duty during the final watch of the night to ensure that visiting envoys departing likewise encountered no hindrance.
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I further had this thought:
'The night has not yet dawned.'"

Why is this so? Within the city of Śrāvastī there are two upright officials: one attends during the first watch of the night to ensure that visiting envoys entering from outside meet with no obstruction; the other attends during the last watch of the night to ensure that visiting envoys departing likewise meet with no obstruction.
Venerable Sāriputta!
Not long after leaving the city gate of Isipatana and going outside, the light vanished and it returned to darkness.
Venerable Sāriputta!
I was terrified, my hair stood on end all over my body, and I thought, "May no human or non-human come to disturb me.
At that time, a deva from the city of Rājagṛha went from Rājagṛha to the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, illuminating everything with his radiance, and came to speak to me, saying:
"Householder, do not be afraid!
"Elder, do not be afraid! Why is this?
In a former life, I was your friend, named Ghaṭīkāra; we were young and held one another in the utmost affection."
"Householder!

In the past, I went to the place where the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana preached the Dharma to me, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening me. Having used immeasurable skillful means to preach the Dharma to me, and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened me, he granted me the three refuges and bestowed upon me the five precepts."
"Householder!

Because I took refuge in the Three Jewels and observed the five precepts, at the dissolution of my body after death, I was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and now dwell here within the Gate of Rest."
"Householder, go quickly! Householder, go quickly! To go is truly better than to stay.
That deva exhorted me and spoke this verse:
"A hundred horses, ministers, and women; A hundred chariots filled with precious jewels;"
A single step taken toward the Buddha is not worth even a sixteenth part [of the merit of other deeds].
A hundred supreme white elephants, adorned with saddles and bridles of gold and silver—
even a single step taken toward the Buddha on such elephants is not worth even a sixteenth part [of the merit of other deeds].
A woman of a hundred beauties, adorned with necklaces and flowers,
would not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit gained by taking a single step toward the Buddha.
She is honored by the Wheel-Turning King as the foremost among the precious jade women.
"Taking a single step toward the Buddha is not equal to even a sixteenth part [of its merit].
After the deva had spoken this verse, he further exhorted him, saying:
"Householder, go quickly!"
"Householder, go quickly!
It is truly better to go than to stay.
Thus spoke the Venerable Śāriputra.
I further had this thought:
"The Buddha is honored and possesses sublime virtue; the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus are likewise honored and possess sublime virtue. Why is this so?"
“...and even up to the heavens, I wish to make them see.
“Venerable Śāriputra!
By means of this light, I went to the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.”
At that time, World-Honored One, as night was turning toward dawn, he emerged from his meditation chamber and walked back and forth in the open air,
waiting for me, Venerable Śāriputra!

From afar I beheld the Buddha, upright and most beautiful, like the moon among the stars; his radiance was brilliant and dazzling, resplendent as a mountain of gold. He was endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, his majestic power was sublime, his faculties were tranquil and settled, free from all obscuration or hindrance; he had perfected the art of self-mastery, his mind stilled in profound silence.

Having seen him, he was filled with joy; he approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and followed the Buddha as he walked back and forth. Following the custom of householders, he addressed him with a verse of greeting:
“Is the World-Honored One sleeping in peace? Is your sleep truly refreshing?”
Just as a brahmin who has attained parinirvāṇa, being unstained by desire,
Has abandoned all aspirations and reached ultimate peace;
With a mind free from affliction and fever, he sleeps happily in joy.
"Then, the Blessed One went to the head of the walking path, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.
Venerable Śāriputra!"

I prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side. The World-Honored One taught me the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening me; having used immeasurable skillful means to teach me the Dharma, he exhorted, inspired, and gladdened me.

As is the custom of all Buddhas, he first taught the preliminary Dharma, which brought joy to those who heard it; that is to say, he spoke of generosity, spoke of ethical discipline, and spoke of the way to rebirth in heaven; he censured sensual desire as a calamity and birth-and-death as a defilement, and praised freedom from desire as the sublime path and the pure, white qualities.

When the Blessed One had taught me the Dharma in this way, the Buddha knew that I possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a supple mind, a patient mind, an uplifted mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free of doubt, and a mind free of hindrances; that I was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma—namely, the essential method as taught by all Buddhas—and so the Blessed One then taught me suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Venerable Sāriputta!

Just as a piece of white cloth is easily dyed with color, even so, while sitting right there, I saw the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. I saw the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—just as one would see them while seated.
“Venerable Sāriputta!

I have seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma; I have awakened to the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, transcended delusion, and have no further reliance on others. No longer following anyone else, free from hesitation, I abide in the realization of the fruit and have attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the Blessed One. Then, rising from his seat, he paid homage to the Buddha, saying:
“Blessed One!”

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I then joined my palms and said to him:
'World-Honored One!'"
"I pray that you will accept my invitation to observe the rains retreat together with the community of bhikṣus in Śrāvastī.
Then the Buddha asked me:
"What is your name?"
"What do the people of Śrāvastī call you?
I replied, "My name is Sudatta;
because I provide for those who are orphaned and solitary, the people of Śrāvastī call me 'Givaka' (the Provider for the Orphaned and Solitary)."
At that time, the World-Honored One again asked me:
"Are there any dwellings in the kingdom of Śrāvastī?
I replied once more:
"There are no dwellings in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to me:
"Householder, you should know!
"If there are dwellings, bhikṣus may come and go, and they may stay and reside.
I replied again:
"Indeed, so be it."
"World-Honored One!
I shall construct a dwelling for this purpose so that the bhikṣus may come and go and reside within the city of Śrāvastī. I only pray that the World-Honored One will appoint an assistant to aid me."
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately appointed the Venerable Śāriputra and dispatched him to provide assistance.
"At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, I received and retained it well; I then rose from my seat, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed."

Having completed his business in Rājagṛha, he went together with the Venerable Śāriputra to the kingdom of Śrāvastī; without entering the city of Śrāvastī nor returning home, he instead traveled all over the ground outside the city to find a place where it would be most convenient for coming and going, which was not noisy by day and tranquil at night, free from mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas, and neither too cold nor too hot—a place where a dwelling could be built to be offered to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
Venerable Sāriputta!

At that time, I saw only that Prince Jeta’s Grove was excellent for coming and going; it was not noisy by day and was tranquil at night, free from mosquitoes and gadflies, and without flies or fleas, being neither cold nor hot.
Having seen this, I thought to myself: "Only this place is suitable;
one may build a dwelling here to offer to the Buddha and the assembly.
Venerable Śāriputra!
At that time, I entered the city of Śrāvastī and did not return home; instead, I went first to where the youth Jeta was and said to him:
"Young man!"
"Would you be willing to sell this grove and give it to me?
At that time, the youth said to me:
"Householder, you should know that I do not sell the grove."
Thus, he asked a second and a third time:
"Young man!
Would you sell this grove and give it to me?"
At that time, the youth again spoke to me twice or thrice, saying:
"I will not sell the grove, even for a price as vast as a billion times ten million. I then replied:
"The boy has now settled the price; you need only take the money.
Venerable Śāriputra!

Whether I said the price was settled with the boy or that it was not, we fell into a great dispute and immediately went together to the Great Court of Justice in Śrāvastī to have this matter adjudicated.
At that time, the man of great legal acumen from Śrāvastī said to the youth Jaya:
"The youth has already determined the price himself; you need only take the money."
"Venerable Śāriputra!

I immediately entered the city of Śrāvastī, returned home to fetch money, and used elephants, horses, chariots, and porters to carry it out. I spread billions upon billions of pieces of cloth across the ground, yet there was still a small area that remained uncovered."
Venerable Sāriputta!
I had this thought:
"From which storehouse should I take [earth]—neither too much nor too little—that might be brought here from elsewhere to fill it?"
Then the youth Jeta said to me:
"If you, Householder, regret it, let the money be returned to you and the park grounds restored to me.
I said to the youth:
"It is indeed not regrettable," he replied.
"I was merely thinking:
'Which treasury should I take—one that is neither too large nor too small—so that it may be carried to this other place and fill it?'"
At that time, the youth Jeta thought to himself:
"The Buddha must be most venerable and possess great merit; the Dharma and the community of bhikṣus must also be most venerable and possess great merit."
Why is this? It is because he has caused the elder to provide such great almsgiving, disregarding his wealth to such an extent.
I should now, right here, construct a gateway house to offer to the Buddha and the assembly.
Then the youth Jeta said to me:
"Householder, stop!
Do not spend any more money to spread it over this site; I shall build a gatehouse here as a gift for the Buddha and the assembly."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
Out of compassion, I have granted this place to the youth Jeta.
"Venerable Sāriputta! [he continued.]
During this very summer retreat, I constructed sixteen large halls and sixty small huts.
The Venerable Sāriputta assisted me at that time; yet, how extraordinary it is that the Venerable Sāriputta teaches the Dharma for curing illness!
How extraordinary!
Having heard this teaching on the method for curing illness, my most severe sickness and suffering have been immediately healed, and I have experienced supreme happiness.
Venerable Sāriputta!
"I am now free from illness and have attained great peace; I pray that the Venerable Śāriputra will partake of this meal.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Thereupon, the householder, knowing that the Venerable Śāriputra had accepted by remaining silent, rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and with his own hands served a variety of most excellent, pure, and exquisite foods—both solid and soft—in great abundance until the Venerable was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels had been cleared away, he prepared a small seat and sat apart to listen to the Dharma.

Once the householder was seated, the Venerable Śāriputra taught him the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having used countless skillful means to teach him the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma. Seeing from afar the Venerable Śāriputra approaching, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The bhikṣu Śāriputra possesses wise intelligence, swift intelligence, quick intelligence, sharp intelligence, expansive intelligence, profound intelligence, intelligence of liberation, penetrating intelligence, and eloquent intelligence; the bhikṣu Śāriputra has perfected true wisdom."
Why is this so? While I have briefly explained four types of stream-enterers, the bhikkhu Sāriputta has elaborated upon them in ten ways for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

29. Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra (29). Chapter on the Correspondence with Śāriputra. Mahākauṣṭhila Sūtra, Number Nine, Part One.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his meditation and went to where the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita was. They exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Sāriputta said to the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita:
"I wish to ask you something; will you listen to my question?
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:
“Venerable Sāriputta!
Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
Venerable Sāriputta asked:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there any ground by means of which a bhikkhu, having accomplished view, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and enters the true Dhamma?”
He replied, “There is, Venerable Śāriputra!”
It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows what is unwholesome and knows the roots of the unwholesome.
How does he know what is unwholesome?
It means that bodily misconduct is unwholesome, and verbal and mental misconduct are unwholesome; this is called knowing what is unwholesome.
How does one know the unwholesome roots?
They are the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion; this is what is meant by knowing the unwholesome roots, Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikṣu who thus understands what is unwholesome and the roots of the unwholesome, he is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished right view; he has attained right view, has gained indestructible purity regarding the Dharma, and has entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: “There is, Venerable Śāriputra!”
It refers to a bhikṣu who knows what is wholesome and knows the roots of the wholesome.
How does he know what is wholesome?
It means that bodily conduct is wholesome, and verbal and mental conduct are wholesome; this is called knowing what is wholesome.
How does one know the roots of goodness?
It refers to the root of goodness that is non-attachment, and the roots of goodness that are non-hatred and non-delusion; this is called knowing the roots of goodness.
Venerable Śāriputra!

If there is a bhikṣu who thus knows what is wholesome and knows the roots of wholesomeness, he is called a bhikṣu who has accomplished right view, attained right view, achieved unwavering purity regarding the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Mahā Koṭṭhita!
Having offered this praise, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Venerable Sāriputta then asked again:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra!"

It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows nutriment as it truly is, knows the origin of nutriment, knows the cessation of nutriment, and knows the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is.
How does he know nutriment as it truly is?

It is said that there are four nutriments: first, edible food, both coarse and subtle; second, the nutriment of contact; third, the nutriment of mental volition; and fourth, the nutriment of consciousness. This is called knowing nutriment as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of nutriment as it truly is?
It means that because of craving, there is nutriment; this is called knowing the origin of nutriment as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of nutriment as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of craving, nutriment ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of nutriment as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of right view through to right concentration as the eight factors; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of nutriment as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who thus knows nutriment as it really is, knows the origin of nutriment, knows the cessation of nutriment, and knows the way leading to the cessation of nutriment as it really is, this is called a bhikkhu who is accomplished in view, who has attained right view, who has gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and who has entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Venerable Sāriputta then asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and enters the true Dhamma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra!"

It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows the taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of the taints, he knows the cessation of the taints, and he knows the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is.
How does he know the taints as they truly are?
It is said that there are three taints:
the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance; this is called knowing the taints as they truly are.
What is knowing the origin of the taints as it truly is?
That is to say, because of ignorance there are taints; this is called knowing the origin of the taints as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of the taints as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of ignorance, the taints cease; this is called knowing the cessation of the taints as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If a bhikkhu thus knows the taints as they really are, knows the origin of the taints, knows the cessation of the taints, and knows the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it really is, he is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and entered into the true Dhamma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu accomplishes view, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and enters the true Dhamma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Sāriputta!"

It means there is a bhikṣu who knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
How does he know suffering as it truly is?

That is to say: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging—this is called knowing suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is?
It means that because of old age and death, there is suffering; this is called knowing the origin of suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of aging and death, suffering ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of right view through to right concentration as the eight factors; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who thus knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is—this is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and enters the true Dhamma?"
He replied: “There is, Venerable Śāriputra!”

It refers to a bhikṣu who knows old age and death as they truly are, knows the origin of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is.
How does he know old age?

That is to say, one is aged and decrepit, with white hair and fallen teeth; the prime of youth has daily declined, the body is bent and the legs are crooked; the body is heavy and the breath is labored, walking with the aid of a staff; the muscles shrink and the skin slackens, wrinkled like hemp seeds; the faculties are impaired and matured [with decay], and the complexion is ugly—this is called old age.
What is meant by knowing death?

It refers to those sentient beings, within their respective classes of sentient beings, reaching the end of their lives, undergoing impermanence, passing away, dispersing, and perishing; their lifespan being exhausted and destroyed, and the life-faculty being obstructed—this is called death.
This explains death; what was explained previously is aging. This is called "aging and death," and this is known as knowing aging and death as they truly are.
What is knowing the origin of aging and death as it truly is?
That is to say, with birth as condition, there is aging and death; this is called knowing the origin of aging and death as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of aging and death as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease; this is called knowing the cessation of aging and death as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who thus knows old age and death as they truly are, knows the origin of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death as it truly is—this is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished right view, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra!"
It refers to a bhikṣu who knows birth as it truly is, knows the origin of birth, knows the cessation of birth, and knows the path leading to the cessation of birth as it truly is.
How does he know birth as it truly is?

That is to say: those sentient beings, belonging to this or that class of sentient beings—when they are born, they are born; when they emerge, they emerge; when they are formed, they are formed; they give rise to the five aggregates and have acquired the life-faculty (jīvitendriya). This is called knowing birth as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of birth as it truly is?
It means that because of existence (*bhava*), there is birth; this is called knowing the origin of birth as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of birth as it truly is?
That which arises ceases as soon as it is born; this is called knowing the arising and cessation of birth as it truly is.
What is knowing the path to the arising and cessation of birth as it truly is?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path to the arising and cessation of birth as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If a bhikkhu thus knows birth as it really is, knows the origin of birth, knows the cessation of birth, and knows the path leading to the cessation of birth as it really is, he is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Sāriputta!"

It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows existence as it truly is, knows the origin of existence, knows the cessation of existence, and knows the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is.
How does he know existence as it truly is?
It is said that there are three kinds of existence:
existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm; this is called knowing existence as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of existence as it truly is?
That is to say, because of feeling there is becoming; this is called knowing the arising of becoming as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of becoming as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of feeling, becoming ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of becoming as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to cessation as it truly is?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to cessation as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If a bhikkhu thus knows existence as it truly is, knows the arising of existence, knows the cessation of existence, and knows the path leading to the cessation of existence as it truly is, he is said to be a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, achieved unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Having praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by means of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: “There is, Venerable Śāriputra!”
It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows feeling as it truly is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, and knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
How does he know feeling as it truly is?
It is said that there are four types of clinging:
clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to precepts and vows, clinging to views, and clinging to a self; this is called knowing clinging as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of clinging as it truly is?
That is to say, because of craving there is feeling; this is called knowing the arising of feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of feeling as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of craving, feeling ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing, as it truly is, the path leading to the cessation of feeling.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who thus knows feeling as it really is, knows the arising of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, and knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it really is, this is called a bhikkhu who is accomplished in view, who has attained right view, who has gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and who has entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita.
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Venerable Sāriputta then asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Sāriputta!"
It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows craving as it truly is, knows the origin of craving, knows the cessation of craving, and knows the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is.
How does he know craving as it truly is?
It is said that there are three kinds of craving:
craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless; this is called knowing craving as it truly is.
What is knowing the origin of craving as it truly is?
That is to say, because of feeling there is craving; this is called knowing the origin of craving as it truly is.
How does one know the cessation of craving as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of craving as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who thus knows craving as it truly is, knows the origin of craving, knows the cessation of craving, and knows the path leading to the cessation of craving as it truly is, this is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and entered into the true Dhamma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Mahā Koṭṭhita!
Having praised him thus, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Venerable Sāriputta then asked again:
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Sāriputta!"
It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows feeling as it truly is; he knows the arising of feeling, the cessation of feeling, and the path leading to the cessation of feeling as they truly are.
What is knowing feeling as it truly is?
It is said that there are three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; this is called knowing feeling as it truly is.
How does one know the arising of feeling as it truly is?
That is to say, because of contact (*phassa*), there is feeling (*vedanā*); this is called knowing the arising of feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of feeling as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of feeling as it truly is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If a bhikkhu thus knows feeling as it really is, knows the origin of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, and knows the way leading to the cessation of feeling as it really is, this is called a bhikkhu who is accomplished in view, who has attained right view, who has attained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and who has entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhila!
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and enters the true Dhamma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Sāriputta!"
It means that there is a bhikṣu who knows contact as it truly is, knows the arising of contact, knows the cessation of contact, and knows the path leading to the cessation of contact as it truly is.
How does he know contact as it truly is?
It is said that there are three kinds of contact-feelings (*phassa-vedanā*):
pleasant contact-feeling, painful contact-feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact-feeling. This is called knowing contact-feeling as it truly is.
What is knowing the arising of contact-feeling as it truly is?
That is to say, with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; this is called knowing the origin of contact as it truly is.
How does one know the cessation of contact as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of contact as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of contact as it really is?

It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path leading to the cessation of contact as it really is.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If a bhikkhu thus knows contact as it really is, knows the origin of contact, knows the cessation of contact, and knows the path leading to the cessation of contact as it really is, he is called a bhikkhu who has accomplished vision, attained right view, gained unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and entered into the true Dharma.
Having heard this, the Venerable Śāriputra exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Mahā Koṭṭhita!
Having praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita!
Is there yet another matter by reason of which a bhikkhu achieves vision, attains right view, gains unwavering confidence in the Dharma, and enters the true Dharma?”
He replied: "There is, Venerable Śāriputra!"

It means that there is a bhikkhu who knows the six sense bases as they truly are; he knows the arising of the six sense bases, he knows the cessation of the six sense bases, and he knows the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is.
How does he know the six sense bases as they truly are?
That is to say: the sense base of the eye, and the sense bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—this is called knowing the six sense bases as they truly are.
What is knowing the arising of the six sense bases as it truly is?
That is to say, with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be; this is called knowing the arising of the six sense bases as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is?
That is to say, with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; this is called knowing the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is.
What is knowing the path leading to the cessation of the six sense bases as it truly is?

That is to say, because of consciousness, there is name-and-form; this is called knowing the arising of name-and-form as it truly is.

That is to say, with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of name-and-form as it truly is.
