He contemplates this contact as impermanent; he contemplates feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as impermanent. His mind dwells upon the elements, abiding in stillness with a unified mind, concentrated and immovable.

At a later time, if a youth, a middle-aged person, or an elder comes and performs an improper act—whether by striking with a fist, throwing stones, or inflicting blows with knives or staves—he reflects thus:

"I have received this body, which is material in nature, coarse in substance, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished by food and drink, constantly covered by clothing, requiring sitting, lying down, massaging, bathing, and endurance; it is subject to disintegration, subject to extinction, and subject to dissolution. It is because of this body that I am subjected to being struck with fists, pelted with stones, and assaulted with knives and staves."

For this reason, he exerts himself with extreme diligence and without indolence; with body upright and mindfulness established, he is neither forgetful nor deluded, his mind settled in one-pointed concentration. He reflects thus: "I exert myself with extreme diligence and without indolence;

with body upright and mindfulness established, I am neither forgetful nor deluded, my mind settled in one-pointed concentration. Even though I may receive blows from fists, stones thrown at me, or the application of swords and staves, I shall simply continue to apply myself with diligence to training in the Dharma of the World-Honored One."
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus:
'If bandits were to come and, with sharp knives and saws, dismember one's body limb by limb.'"
If, when bandits were to dismember your body limb by limb with sharp knives and saws, your mind were to undergo change or you were to utter evil words, you would then fall away from your progress.

You should form this thought: "If bandits should come and, with sharp knives and saws, cut my body limb from limb, because of this I shall not allow my mind to change, nor shall I utter harsh words. I shall arouse a heart of compassion for those who cut my body limb from limb; for their sake, my mind shall be imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and I shall dwell having pervaded one direction, thus achieving it. Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below—pervading all everywhere, my mind shall be imbued with loving-kindness, free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; exceedingly vast, sublime, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, I shall dwell having pervaded the entire world."
"Venerable friends!

If that bhikkhu, because of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, does not abide in equanimity associated with the wholesome, then, venerable friends, that bhikkhu should feel shame, remorse, and revulsion, thinking:
'I have neither gained profit nor merit; for I, because of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, do not abide in equanimity associated with the wholesome.'"
"Venerable friends!
It is just as when a newly arrived bride sees her mother-in-law or her father-in-law, or sees her husband; she then feels abashed, ashamed, and weary.
Venerable friends!

It should be known that a bhikṣu is also like this: he should feel shame, remorse, and revulsion, thinking, "I have neither profit nor lack of profit, neither virtue nor lack of virtue; yet I do not dwell in equanimity associated with the wholesome because of my reliance on the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Because of that shame, remorse, and revulsion, he then dwells in equanimity associated with the wholesome. This is sublime tranquility—namely, the relinquishing of all existence, the departure from craving, the absence of desire, and its total cessation without remainder.
"Virtuous ones!
This is called the great learning of a bhikkhu.
Virtuous ones!"
"Just as, by means of timber, clay, and water-grass, one encloses empty space and the designation 'house' arises;

so too, O worthy ones, you should know that this body is likewise: by means of sinews and bones, by means of skin, and by means of flesh and blood, it encloses empty space, and the designation 'body' arises."
Venerable friends!
If the internal eye-base is impaired and external forms are not illuminated by light, then there is no attention, and eye-consciousness cannot arise.
"Venerable friends!
If the internal eye-base is unimpaired, and external forms are illuminated by light, and there is attention, then eye-consciousness arises."
"Venerable friends!
The internal eye-base and forms, as well as the external forms known by eye-consciousness, belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

If there is feeling, it is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*); if there is perception, it is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*); if there is volition, it is the aggregate of volition (*saṃskāraskandha*); if there is consciousness, it is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Thus one contemplates the coming together of the aggregates."
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus:
'If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma; if one sees the Dharma, one sees dependent origination.'"
Why is this so? Venerable friends!

The Blessed One has taught that the five aggregates of clinging arise from causes and conditions: the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Venerable friends!

If the internal bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind were to perish, then external phenomena would not be illuminated by light; consequently, there would be no mindfulness, and consciousness could not arise.
"Venerable friends!
If the internal sense-base of the mind is unimpaired, and external phenomena are illumined by light, then mindfulness arises and the mental consciousness is produced.
Venerable friends!"

The internal sense-base of mind and mental phenomena are known by the consciousness-element; these belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). If there is feeling, it is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*);

if there is perception, it is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); if there is volition, it is the aggregate of volition (*saṃskāra-skandha*); if there is consciousness, it is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). In this way, one contemplates the coming together of the aggregates.
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus:
'If one sees dependent origination, one sees the Dharma; if one sees the Dharma, one sees dependent origination.'"
"Why is this so? Venerable friends! The Blessed One has taught that the five aggregates of clinging arise from causes and conditions:

the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One becomes weary of these past, future, and present five aggregates of clinging; being weary of them, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated; being liberated, one knows one is liberated. One knows truly: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence.'"
"Venerable friends!
This is called the great learning of a bhikkhu.
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, the tenth, ends here; it contains three thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven characters. 31. The *Satyavibhaṅga-sūtra* (31). The *Madhyama Āgama*, Śāriputra-saṃyukta-varga, *Satyavibhaṅga-sūtra*, the eleventh. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"This is the teaching of the Dharma of right practice, namely, the four noble truths, which are extensively encompassed, extensively contemplated, analyzed, revealed, opened up, established, displayed, and directed toward."

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also possessed this same teaching of right practice, namely: the four noble truths, which they extensively gathered, extensively contemplated, analyzed, revealed, opened up, established, displayed, and directed toward.

The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future will also have this same teaching of the right practice, namely: the thorough inclusion, thorough contemplation, analysis, disclosure, exposition, establishment, manifestation, and guidance regarding the Four Noble Truths.

I, who am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, likewise possess this correct practice of teaching the Dharma, namely: the four noble truths, which are extensively gathered, extensively contemplated, analyzed, revealed, opened up, established, demonstrated, and directed toward.

“The bhikkhu Sāriputta possesses keen wisdom, swift wisdom, quick wisdom, sharp wisdom, expansive wisdom, deep wisdom, wisdom that leads to liberation, penetrative wisdom, and eloquent wisdom; the bhikkhu Sāriputta is endowed with true wisdom.”

Why is that? Because, Śāriputra, when I have briefly taught these Four Noble Truths, the bhikṣu Śāriputra is able to extensively teach, extensively contemplate, analyze, reveal, expound, establish, manifest, and lead others toward them.

When the bhikkhu Sāriputta extensively teaches and demonstrates these Four Noble Truths—analyzing, revealing, elucidating, establishing, manifesting, and directing them—he causes immeasurable people to attain insight; the bhikkhu Sāriputta is able to lead and guide them by means of right view.
The bhikkhu Moggallāna is able to establish others at the supreme limit of reality, namely, the ultimate exhaustion of the taints.

The bhikkhu Sāriputta gives birth to the various holy life practices, like a biological mother; the bhikkhu Moggallāna nurtures and raises those holy life practices, like a foster mother. Therefore, all practitioners of the holy life should serve, support, honor, and pay homage to the bhikkhus Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣus Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana seek for the sake of their fellow practitioners of the holy life meaning and benefit, and they seek peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, having spoken thus, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in private meditation.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."

The Blessed One has appeared in the world for our sake; that is to say, he has extensively taught, extensively demonstrated, analyzed, revealed, disclosed, established, manifested, and directed us toward these Four Noble Truths.
What are the four?

They are the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
O virtuous ones!
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering?

It refers to the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and in brief, the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Venerable friends!
When it is said that birth is suffering, on what basis is this said?
Venerable friends!

Birth refers to those sentient beings, and the various classes of sentient beings; being born, they are born; emerging, they emerge; being formed, they are formed; the five aggregates arise, and the life-faculty is obtained—this is called birth.

"Venerable friends! As for 'birth is suffering,' it means that when beings are born, they experience bodily painful feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience mental painful feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience both bodily and mental painful feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully. They experience bodily burning feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience mental burning feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience both bodily and mental burning feelings—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully. They experience bodily feelings of intense heat, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience mental feelings of intense heat, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully; they experience both bodily and mental feelings of intense heat, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, sensing them, and sensing them fully."
"Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that it is said: 'Birth is suffering.
Venerable friends!"
Regarding the statement that "aging is suffering," for what reason is this said? Venerable friends!

"Aging" refers to those sentient beings, within their respective classes of beings, becoming decrepit; their hair turns white and their teeth fall out; their prime declines day by day; their bodies bend and their legs become crooked; they are heavy of limb and short of breath, walking with the aid of a staff; their muscles shrink and their skin slackens, wrinkled like hemp seeds; their faculties are impaired and matured [with decay], and their complexion becomes ugly—this is called aging.

Venerable friends! As for the suffering of old age: when sentient beings are old, they experience bodily painful feelings—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience mental painful feelings—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience both bodily and mental painful feelings—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them. They experience bodily sensations of fever—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience mental sensations of fever—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience both bodily and mental sensations of fever—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them. They experience bodily sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience mental sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience both bodily and mental sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them.
"Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that 'aging is suffering' is said.
Venerable friends!"
Regarding what is called "the suffering of illness," for what reason is this said?
Venerable friends!

"Illness" refers to headache, eye pain, ear pain, nose pain, facial pain, lip pain, tooth pain, tongue pain, palate pain, throat pain, wind-induced asthma, coughing, vomiting, hoarseness, epilepsy, abscesses, goiters, excessive menstrual flow, jaundice, high fever, emaciation, hemorrhoids, and diarrhea; or whatever other various kinds of illnesses there may be, which arise from contact with sensory experience, are inseparable from the mind, and are established within the body—this is called illness.

Venerable friends! As for the suffering of illness, when a person is ill, they experience bodily painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience mental painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience both bodily and mental painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully. They experience bodily sensations of fever, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience mental sensations of fever, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience both bodily and mental sensations of fever, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully. They experience bodily sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience mental sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience both bodily and mental sensations of intense fever, affliction, and distress, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully.
"Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that one speaks of the suffering of illness.
"Venerable friends! [he said.]
Regarding the teaching on the suffering of death, for what reason is this taught?
Venerable friends!

"Death" refers to those sentient beings, within their respective classes of beings, reaching the end of life, impermanence, passing away, dissolution, extinction, the exhaustion of the lifespan, its destruction, and the cessation of the life-faculty; this is called death.

"Venerable friends! As for the suffering of death: when beings die, they experience bodily painful feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience mental painful feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience both bodily and mental painful feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over. They experience bodily feverish feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience mental feverish feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience both bodily and mental feverish feelings—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over. They experience bodily feelings of intense fever, affliction, and dejection—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience mental feelings of intense fever, affliction, and dejection—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over; they experience both bodily and mental feelings of intense fever, affliction, and dejection—feel them, feel them all over, perceive them, perceive them all over."
Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that the suffering of death is spoken of.
Venerable friends!
Regarding the statement that "association with the disliked is suffering," for what reason is this said?
Venerable friends!

"Association with the disliked" refers to the fact that sentient beings truly possess the six internal bases (*āyatana*): the eye-base, which is not beloved, as well as the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases. When these come together, there is grasping, blending, and habitual association; their union constitutes suffering. It is the same for the external bases, as well as for contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving.

Venerable friends! Sentient beings truly possess six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. These come together as one; they are gathered, blended, and practiced together, uniting to form suffering. This is called "association with the disliked."
Venerable friends!

Regarding the suffering of association with the disliked: when sentient beings associate with those they dislike, they experience painful feelings in the body—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; they experience painful feelings in the mind—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them; and they experience painful feelings in both body and mind—experiencing them fully, perceiving them, and being fully aware of them.
"Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that it is said: 'The suffering of association with the disliked.
"Venerable friends!"
Regarding the statement on the suffering of separation from the beloved: for what reason is this said? Venerable friends!

The suffering of separation from the beloved refers to the fact that sentient beings truly possess the six internal sense bases (*āyatana*): they are attached to the eye base, and to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. When these become diverse, disperse, fail to correspond, are separated and do not meet, are not gathered, not practiced together, and are not in harmony, it constitutes suffering. It is the same for the external sense bases, as well as for contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving.

"Venerable friends! Sentient beings truly possess six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element. When these are separated from one another, they cannot remain in association; they become distinct, disjoined, and do not meet. Because they are not gathered, not cultivated, and not unified, this constitutes suffering. This is called 'suffering from separation from the beloved.'"
"Venerable friends!

As for the suffering of separation from what is loved: when sentient beings are separated, they experience bodily painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience mental painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully; they experience both bodily and mental painful feelings, experience them fully, perceive them, and perceive them fully."
"Venerable friends!
It is for this reason that it is said: 'The suffering of separation from what is loved.
Venerable friends!"
Regarding the statement that "the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks" is taught, for what reason is this said?
Venerable friends!

It is because beings are subject to the nature of birth and cannot escape the nature of birth; yet they desire, "May I not be born," but this truly cannot be obtained by mere wishing. Beings are subject to the nature of aging, the nature of death, and the nature of sorrow, lamentation, and despair, and they cannot escape these natures of sorrow and despair; yet they desire, "May I not be sorrowful or despondent," but this also cannot be obtained by mere wishing.
"Venerable friends!
Sentient beings truly experience suffering that is unpleasant, disagreeable, and not to be cherished. They think to themselves:
'If I experience suffering that is unpleasant, disagreeable, and not to be cherished, I wish to transform this so that it becomes agreeable and to be cherished.'"
"Furthermore, this cannot be obtained through desire.
Venerable friends!
Sentient beings truly experience pleasure that is lovely and desirable, and they form this thought:"
"If I were to experience pleasure that is desirable and agreeable, I would wish for it to be permanent, eternal, long-lasting, and subject to no change.
This, too, cannot be obtained through mere wishing.
"Venerable friends!
When sentient beings give rise to thoughts that are truly unpleasant and not to be cherished, they think:
'If I am giving rise to thoughts that are unpleasant and not to be cherished, I wish to transform them so that they become objects of affection.'"
"Even this cannot be obtained through desire.
Venerable friends!
Sentient beings truly give rise to thoughts that are lovely and desirable, and they form this thought:"
"If I give rise to thoughts that are lovely and desirable, wishing for them to be permanent, eternal, long-lasting,
and unchanging phenomena"— this too cannot be attained through desire.
"Venerable friends!
When it is said that 'the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks' is taught, it is for this reason that it is so stated.
Venerable friends!"
Regarding the brief explanation of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), for what reason is this said?
It refers, O Venerable Ones, to the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Regarding the brief explanation of the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging, it is said for this reason:

"Venerable friends! In the past, this was the Noble Truth of Suffering; in the future and the present, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering. It is a true reality, not false, not departing from suchness, and not inverted. It is a true reality that is examined and verified, consistent with such truth—belonging to the noble ones, known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, understood by the noble ones, attained by the noble ones, and perfectly awakened to by the noble ones. Therefore, it is called the Noble Truth of Suffering."
"Venerable friends!
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering through the origin of craving?

It refers to the fact that sentient beings truly possess craving for the six internal sense bases: the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. Within these, if there is craving, attachment, defilement, or clinging, this is called the origin."

"Venerable friends! A learned noble disciple knows: 'I know this Dharma thus; I see it thus; I have understood it thus; I have perceived it thus; I have awakened to it thus. This is called the noble truth of the origination of craving, which is the origination of suffering; he knows it thus."
How is this known?

If one has attachment toward wife, children, slaves, servants, kinsmen, fields, houses, shops, and interest-bearing wealth, and performs actions for their sake, being possessed of love, fondness, defilement, and clinging—this is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).

One knows that this clinging is the noble truth of the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya-āryasatya*). It is the same for the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), as well as for contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Venerable friends!

Sentient beings truly have craving for the six elements: the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. In this regard, if there is craving, attachment, defilement, and clinging, this is called "conditioning."
"Venerable friends!

A learned noble disciple knows: 'I know this Dharma thus, I see it thus, I comprehend it thus, I perceive it thus, I am awakened to it thus. This is called the noble truth of the origin of craving as the origin of suffering; he knows it thus."
How is this known?

If one has attachment toward wife, children, slaves, servants, retinue, fields, houses, shops, and capital for interest, and performs actions for their sake with love, affection, defilement, and clinging—this is called "clinging" (*upādāna*). He knows that this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering through clinging (*upādāna-samudaya-duḥkha-satya*).

"Venerable friends! In the past, this was the noble truth of the origination of suffering through the origination of craving; in the future and the present, this is the noble truth of the origination of suffering through the origination of craving. It is a true reality, not false, not departing from suchness, and not inverted. This true reality is examined and verified; it accords with such truth. It is that which belongs to the noble ones, that which is known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, understood by the noble ones, attained by the noble ones, and perfectly awakened to by the noble ones. Therefore, it is called the noble truth of the origination of suffering through the origination of craving."
"Venerable friends!
What is the noble truth of the cessation of craving and the cessation of suffering?

It refers to the fact that sentient beings truly possess craving for the six internal sense bases—namely, the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind base. If one is liberated from these, being neither defiled nor attached, having abandoned, relinquished, vomited out, and exhausted them, such that there is no desire, cessation, and their subsiding and disappearance, this is called the cessation of suffering."
"Venerable friends!

A learned noble disciple knows: 'I know this Dharma thus, I see it thus, I comprehend it thus, I perceive it thus, I am awakened to it thus. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of craving, which is the cessation of suffering; he knows it in this way."
How is this known?

If there are things one does not love—such as wife, children, slaves, servants, retinues, fields, houses, shops, or interest-bearing wealth—and one no longer performs actions for their sake; if one is liberated from these, being unstained and unattached, having abandoned, relinquished, vomited out, become desireless, extinguished, ceased, and vanished, this is called the cessation of suffering. One knows that this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering through the Cessation of Craving. It is the same for external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*), as well as contact, feeling, perception, volition, and craving.
"Venerable friends!

Sentient beings truly possess craving for the six elements: the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. If one is liberated from them—being unstained and unattached, having abandoned, relinquished, vomited out, exhausted, become desireless, ceased, and come to an end—this is called the cessation of suffering."

"Venerable friends! A learned noble disciple knows: 'I know this Dharma thus; I see it thus; I comprehend it thus; I perceive it thus; I awaken to it thus. This is called the noble truth of the cessation of craving as the cessation of suffering; he knows it in this way."
How is this known?

If there are those who do not love their wife, children, slaves, servants, relatives, fields, houses, shops, or interest-bearing wealth, and they do not perform actions for the sake of these things; if they are liberated from them, being neither stained nor attached, having abandoned, relinquished, vomited out, and exhausted them—being without desire, ceased, stilled, and vanished—this is called the cessation of suffering. They know this as the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering through the cessation of craving.

"Venerable friends! In the past, this was the noble truth of the cessation of craving and the cessation of suffering; in the future and in the present, this is the noble truth of the cessation of craving and the cessation of suffering. It is a true reality, not false; it does not deviate from suchness, nor is it inverted. This true reality is examined and verified; it accords with such truth. It belongs to the noble ones, is known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, understood by the noble ones, attained by the noble ones, and perfectly awakened to by the noble ones. Therefore, it is called the noble truth of the cessation of craving and the cessation of suffering."
"Venerable friends!
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
Venerable friends! What is right view?

It is when a noble disciple, while recollecting suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; or while contemplating what was previously done; or while training in the recollection of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); or while seeing the peril in all conditioned phenomena; or while seeing the stillness of Nirvāṇa; or while, with an unattached mind, recollecting and contemplating the liberation of the wholesome mind—within this, there is discernment, thorough discernment, sequential discernment, the discernment of dharmas, viewing, thorough viewing, observation, and clear penetration. This is called right view.
"Virtuous ones!
What is right intention?

It means that when a noble disciple recollects suffering as suffering, origin as origin, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; or when he contemplates what was done in the past, or trains in the mindfulness of all formations (*saṃskāra*), or sees the peril in all formations, or sees the stillness of Nirvāṇa, or when he recollects with non-attachment and contemplates the liberation of the wholesome mind—at that time, there arise in his mind discursive thoughts, pervasive discursive thoughts, and conformable discursive thoughts. He recollects what is worth recollecting and aspires to what is worth aspiring to. This is called right intention."
"Virtuous ones!
What is right speech?

It means that when a noble disciple reflects upon suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; or when he contemplates his former deeds, or trains in the mindfulness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), or perceives the peril of all conditioned phenomena, or perceives the stillness of Nirvāṇa, or when he dwells with non-attached mindfulness, observing the liberation of the virtuous mind—at that time, he abandons, cuts off, does not practice, does not perform, does not engage in, and does not associate with all other forms of verbal misconduct, setting aside the four types of sublime verbal conduct. This is called right speech."
"Venerable friends! What is right action?

It is when a noble disciple, mindful that suffering is suffering, origination is origination, cessation is cessation, and the path is the path; or when he contemplates what was previously done; or trains in mindfulness of all formations (*saṃskāra*); or sees the peril in all formations; or sees the stillness of Nirvāṇa; or when, with an unattached mind, he contemplates the liberation of the virtuous mind—at that time, setting aside the three types of bodily good conduct, he distances himself from all other bodily misconduct, abandons it, does not practice it, does not perform it, does not engage in it, and does not associate with it. This is called right action."
"Venerable friends! What is right livelihood?

It means that when a noble disciple recollects suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation, and the path as the path; or when he contemplates his former deeds, or trains in the mindfulness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), or sees the peril in all conditioned phenomena, or sees the stillness of Nirvāṇa, or when he dwells with non-attached mindfulness upon the liberation of the wholesome mind—within this state, he does not seek by improper means, nor does he act out of excessive desire and lack of contentment, nor does he maintain his life through various arts, incantations, or false livelihoods. Rather, he seeks robes only by lawful means and not by unlawful means; likewise, he seeks food and bedding only by lawful means and not by unlawful means. This is called right livelihood."
"Venerable friends!
What is right effort?

It is when a noble disciple, mindful that suffering is suffering, that its origin is its origin, that its cessation is its cessation, and mindful that the path is the path; or when he contemplates his former deeds, or trains in mindfulness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), or perceives the peril in all conditioned phenomena, or perceives the stillness of Nirvāṇa, or when, with unattached mindfulness, he contemplates the liberation of the virtuous mind—whatever diligent effort he applies therein, striving single-mindedly, possessing the power of progress, remaining focused and undeterred, and rightly subduing the mind: this is called right effort."

"Venerable friends! What is right mindfulness? It is when a noble disciple, mindful, contemplates suffering as suffering, origination as origination, cessation as cessation; or when he contemplates the path as the path; or when he reflects upon what was done in the past; or when he trains in the mindfulness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); or when he sees the peril in all conditioned phenomena; or when he sees the stillness of Nirvāṇa; or when, with an unattached mind, he contemplates the liberation of the wholesome mind. In this regard, if the mind follows mindfulness, does not turn away from it, is pervasive in mindfulness, is mindful, remembers again and again, attends to each thought, and does not forget what the mind ought to do—this is called right mindfulness."
"Venerable friends!
What is right concentration?

It is when a noble disciple, mindful that suffering is suffering, origination is origination, cessation is cessation, and the path is the path; or when he contemplates his former deeds, or trains in mindfulness of all formations, or sees the peril in all formations, or sees the stillness of Nirvāṇa, or when he dwells with an unattached mind, contemplating the liberation of the wholesome mind—at that time, if the mind abides therein, abides in dhyāna, abides in accordance [with the object], being undisturbed and undistracted, having collected and stilled it in right concentration—this is called right concentration."

"Venerable friends! In the past, this was the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; in the future and the present, it is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. It is a true reality, not false; it does not deviate from suchness, nor is it inverted. It is a true reality, verified and real; it accords with such a truth. It is that which belongs to the noble ones, that which is known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, understood by the noble ones, attained by the noble ones, and perfectly awakened to by the noble ones. Therefore, it is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has clearly realized all phenomena; He perceives immeasurable virtuous qualities.
Regarding the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, He has skillfully manifested and analyzed them.”
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta.
Having heard what the Venerable Sāriputta had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The eleventh discourse, the *Saccavibhaṅga Sutta*, ends here, totaling 3,425 characters. The seventh fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* ends here, totaling 11,369 characters. The third section, the *Sāriputta-saṃyukta-varga*, of the *Madhyama Āgama* ends here, totaling 27,512 characters. First Day’s Recitation.
