Chapter Four: Unprecedented Dharmas (Adbhutadharma-varga). This chapter contains ten sūtras; First Daily Recitation.
The Unprecedented, the Attendant, Bakula, the Asura, the Earthquake, and Campā; Ugra, with two hands each.
(32) The Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra (32), from the Adbhuta-dharma Varga of the Madhyama Āgama, the First Adbhuta-dharma Sūtra. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One, under Kāśyapa Buddha, first resolved upon the path to Buddhahood and practiced the holy life—if the World-Honored One, under Kāśyapa Buddha, first resolved upon the path to Buddhahood and practiced the holy life—I uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was under Kāśyapa Buddha, he first resolved upon the path of Buddhahood, practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; since the World-Honored One, when under Kāśyapa Buddha, first resolved upon the path of Buddhahood, practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, I uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."

"I have heard that during the time of the World-Honored One Kāśyapa Buddha, he first aspired to the path of Buddhahood, practiced the holy life, and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. Later, when the World-Honored One was reborn there, he surpassed those previously born in the Tuṣita Heaven in three respects: celestial lifespan, celestial appearance, and celestial renown. For this reason, all the devas of the Tuṣita Heaven were filled with joy and exultation, and they marveled at this son of heaven, saying, 'How truly extraordinary! "
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?

That he was born later and surpassed those previously born in the Tuṣita heaven by three things—namely, celestial lifespan, celestial form, and celestial renown—and that when the World-Honored One first aspired to the Buddha-way during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, practiced the holy life, and was born in the Tuṣita heaven, he later surpassed those previously born in the Tuṣita heaven by these same three things: celestial lifespan, celestial form, and celestial renown.
For this reason, the gods of the Tuṣita heaven rejoiced and leaped for joy, exclaiming in praise of this devaputra: "How marvelous!
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority."

Why is that? Because those born later surpass those previously born among the Tuṣita devas in three respects—divine lifespan, divine appearance, and divine renown—I have received and upheld this unprecedented quality of the Blessed One.

"I have heard that the Blessed One was in the Tuṣita heaven; having passed away there, he is known to have entered his mother’s womb. At that time, the entire earth and heavens shook, and with a great, wondrous light, he illuminated the world universally, so that even the most remote and dark places were left without obstruction. Even those regions where the sun and moon possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority—places their light does not reach—were all bathed in its radiance. Because of this wondrous light, those sentient beings each gained knowledge, realizing: 'A being of extraordinary nature has been born! A being of extraordinary nature has been born!'"

If the Blessed One, while in the Tuṣita heaven, passes away there and is known to enter the mother’s womb, at that time all the earth and heavens tremble, and a great, wondrous light universally illuminates the world, such that even the most remote and dark places are left without obstruction. Even those regions where the sun and moon—possessing great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority—do not shine, are all bathed in its radiance. The beings there, because of this wondrous light, each give rise to the knowledge: "A being of extraordinary character is born! A being of extraordinary character is born! This, I maintain, is a marvelous quality (*abhūta-dharma*) of the Blessed One.

"I have heard that the Blessed One, while dwelling in his mother’s womb, was aware and reclined on her right side; since the Blessed One was aware and reclined on his mother’s right side while dwelling in her womb, I uphold this as an extraordinary quality of the Blessed One."

"I have heard that the World-honored One dwelt in his mother’s womb with his body extended; since the World-honored One dwelt in his mother’s womb with his body extended, I uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-honored One."

I have heard that the World-Honored One dwelt concealed within his mother’s womb, unstained by blood, nor stained by semen or any other impurities. If it is true that the World-Honored One dwelt concealed within his mother’s womb, unstained by blood, nor stained by semen or any other impurities, then I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was known to emerge from his mother’s womb, at that time all the heavens and earth shook, and a great, wondrous light universally illuminated the world, such that even the most remote and hidden dark places were left without obstruction. It was said that although these sun and moon possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, there were places their light did not reach; yet now, all those regions are bathed in radiance. Because of this wondrous light, those sentient beings each gave rise to knowledge, exclaiming: 'A being of extraordinary nature has been born! A being of extraordinary nature has been born!'"

When the Blessed One knew he was emerging from his mother’s womb, at that moment all the earth and heavens trembled, and a great, wondrous light universally illuminated the world, such that even the most remote and hidden dark places were left without obstruction. Even those regions not reached by the light of the sun and moon—possessors of great psychic power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority—all were bathed in its radiance. The sentient beings there, through this wondrous light, each gained knowledge, realizing: "A marvelous being has been born! A marvelous being has been born! This, I uphold as an unprecedented quality (*abhūta-dharma*) of the Blessed One.

"I have heard that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother’s womb with his body fully extended; if it is true that the World-Honored One emerged from his mother’s womb with his body fully extended, I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One emerged from his mother’s womb, he was concealed and not defiled by blood, nor was he defiled by semen or any other impurities. Since the World-Honored One, when emerging from his mother’s womb, was concealed and not defiled by blood, nor by semen or any other impurities, I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."

"I have heard that at the time of the World-Honored One’s birth, four deva-sons held extremely fine garments in their hands and stood before his mother; they caused her great joy and marveled at this boy, exclaiming, 'How truly marvelous! "
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.

When the World-Honored One was first born, four deva-sons held fine garments in their hands and stood before his mother, causing her joy as they marveled at this boy, exclaiming, "How most marvelous!"
How extraordinary!

That one possesses such great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual authority—this, I uphold as an unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One.

"I have heard that when the World-Honored One was first born, he immediately took seven steps, neither terrified nor afraid, nor even fearful, as he surveyed all directions. Since the World-Honored One, upon being born, immediately took seven steps, neither terrified nor afraid, nor even fearful, as he surveyed all directions, I uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."

"I have heard that at the time of the Blessed One’s birth, a great pool arose before his mother, its waters overflowing the banks, so that she might use them for purification. If, at the time of the Blessed One’s birth, a great pool arose before his mother, its waters overflowing the banks, so that she might use them for purification, I uphold this as an extraordinary quality of the Blessed One."

“I have heard that when the Blessed One was first born, rain poured down from the sky above, one portion cool and one warm, bathing the body of the Blessed One. If, at the time the Blessed One was first born, rain poured down from the sky above, one portion cool and one warm, bathing the body of the Blessed One, I uphold this as an unprecedented quality of the Blessed One.”

"I have heard that at the time of the World-Honored One’s initial birth, the devas above played celestial music and scattered celestial blue lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, white lotuses, celestial mandārava flowers, and fine powdered sandalwood incense upon the World-Honored One."

If, at the time of the Blessed One’s initial birth, the devas above played celestial music and scattered celestial blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, white lotuses, celestial mandārava flowers, and fine powdered sandalwood incense upon the Blessed One—this, I uphold as a marvelous quality of the Blessed One never before seen.

"I have heard that at one time the Blessed One was staying at the home of his father, King Śuddhodana, supervising the agricultural work during the day; sitting beneath a jambu tree, he—detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states—with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna."

At that time, after midday, the shadows of all other trees had shifted, yet the shadow of the Jambu tree alone did not move, shading the body of the World-Honored One. Thereupon, Śuddhodana went to observe the field laborers; arriving at their place, he asked: "O laborers!"
"Where is the youth?
The laborer replied,
"The divine youth is now beneath the Jambu tree."
Thereupon, Śuddhodana went to the Jambu tree.

At that time, after midday had passed, Śuddhodana saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted, yet the shadow of the Jambu tree alone did not move, continuing to shade the body of the World-Honored One. He then thought:
"How truly marvelous this youth is!"
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?
"After midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted, yet the shadow of the Jambu tree alone did not shift, shading the body of the youth.

"If, after midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted while the shadow of the Jambu tree alone did not shift, shading the body of the World-Honored One, I shall uphold this as an unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."
"I have heard that at one time the Blessed One was staying in the Great Forest near Vaiśālī.

Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī for alms. Having finished his almsround, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣadana) over his shoulder, and went into the forest. Arriving beneath a tala tree, he spread out his sitting mat and sat down cross-legged."
At that time, after midday, the shadows of all other trees had shifted, yet the shadow of the *tāla* tree alone did not move, shading the body of the World-Honored One.

Then, as the afternoon progressed, Śreṣṭhin Mahānāma was strolling about when he went to the Great Forest. After midday, Śreṣṭhin Mahānāma saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted, yet the shadow of the *tāla* tree alone did not move, shading the body of the World-Honored One; thereupon, he thought to himself:
"How extraordinary is the ascetic Gautama!"
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?
After midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted, yet the shadow of the tala tree alone did not move, continuing to shade the body of the śramaṇa Gautama.

"If, after midday, while the shadows of all other trees have shifted, the shadow of this tāla tree alone does not move, continuing to shade the body of the Blessed One, I shall uphold this as an unprecedented quality of the Blessed One."
"I have heard that at one time the World-Honored One was traveling through the Great Forest of Vaiśālī. At that time, the bhikṣus had placed their bowls on the open ground.
The World-Honored One’s bowl was also among them, when a monkey took the Buddha’s bowl away. The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying, 'We fear he will break the Buddha’s bowl.'"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Stop! Stop!"
“Do not, Mahā!
Do not break the bowl!

At that time, the monkey took the Buddha’s bowl and went to a *sāla* tree. He slowly climbed the tree, filled the bowl with honey from atop the *sāla* tree, and slowly descended. Returning to where the Buddha was, he immediately offered the bowl of honey to the World-Honored One, but the World-Honored One did not accept it.
Then, that monkey stepped aside, removed the insects from the leaf, and having finished removing them, brought it back to offer to the Buddha; yet the Buddha again did not accept it.
The monkey went back to one side, took some water and poured it into the honey, then returned to offer it to the Buddha, who accepted it.
Seeing that the Buddha had taken the bowl of honey, the monkey leaped for joy; he walked backward while dancing and frolicking, circling away as he departed.

If, after the World-honored One has caused that monkey to see him take the bowl of honey, the monkey leaps for joy, retreats while dancing and frolicking, and then turns back to depart, I shall uphold this as an unprecedented quality of the World-honored One.

"I have heard that at one time the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī by the Monkey Pond, at the lofty pavilion on the edge of the water. At that time, the Blessed One was drying his sitting mat, shaking it out, and brushing it clean."
At that time, a great unseasonable cloud arose, covering the entire sky; it hovered as if about to rain, waiting for the World-Honored One.
After the World-Honored One had dried his sitting mat in the sun, shaken it out, brushed it clean, and set it aside in one place, he took up his broom and stood upon the foundation of the dwelling.
"In this case, as soon as that great cloud saw the Blessed One fold up his sitting mat, it sent down a heavy rain, which poured forth until the low and high ground were completely level and filled.

If the Blessed One caused that great cloud to send down a heavy rain, pouring forth until the low and high ground were completely level and filled, as soon as it saw him fold up his sitting mat, I hold this to be an extraordinary quality of the Blessed One."
"I have heard that at one time the Blessed One was traveling among the Vajjis, sitting beneath the king of sāla trees in the Hot Springs Forest.
Then, after midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted, yet the shadow of the king of sāla trees alone did not shift, shading the body of the Blessed One."

Then, while the owner of the Rāma Garden was inspecting the garden after midday, he saw that the shadows of all other trees had shifted, yet the shadow of the king of sāla trees alone did not move, continuing to shade the body of the World-Honored One. He then thought:
"How extraordinary is the śramaṇa Gautama!"
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?
After midday, the shadows of all other trees shifted, yet the shadow of the King of Śāla Trees alone did not move, continuing to shade the body of the śramaṇa Gautama.

"If, after midday, while the shadows of all other trees have shifted, the shadow of the King of Śāla Trees alone does not move but continues to shade the body of the World-Honored One, I shall uphold this as an unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."
"I have heard that at one time the Blessed One was staying in the Ābhū shrine hall.

Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and entered the village of Ābhū to beg for alms. Having finished his almsround, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and entered the shrine hall to sit in meditation."

At that time, there was a great storm with thunder, lightning, and hail, which killed four oxen and two plowmen. When they were being carried to the cemetery, the great crowd was clamorous; their voices rose so high that the sound vibrated and shook the air.
Then, at the time of the afternoon, the Blessed One rose from his meditative seclusion, emerged from the shrine room, and walked back and forth in the open air.

At that time, among the great assembly, there was one person who saw the Blessed One rise from his afternoon meditation, emerge from the shrine room, and walk back and forth in the open air; he immediately approached the Buddha, prostrated himself in salutation, and followed the Buddha as he walked.
The Buddha, seeing them from behind, asked those people:
"For what reason is the great assembly so noisy, with such loud voices and a clamor that shakes the air?"
That person replied:
"World-Honored One!

Today there was a great thunderstorm with lightning and hail, which killed four oxen and two plowmen. When they were being sent off for burial, the great crowd was clamorous and noisy; the sound was so loud that its resonance shook the earth."
“World-Honored One!
Did you not hear the sound just now?
The World-Honored One replied:
"I do not hear sounds.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"Did you just sleep? He replied, "No."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One,
were you not awake at that time and did you not hear this great sound?"
He replied, “It is so.
At that time, that person then had this thought:
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!
This is the practice of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—utterly tranquil and supremely quiescent."
Why is that? Because although he has awakened, he does not hear this great sound.
If the World-Honored One, having awakened, does not hear this great sound, I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One.
"I have heard that at one time the World-Honored One was staying by the Nerañjarā River in Uruvelā, beneath the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree, having newly attained the Way of the Buddha."

At that time, there was heavy rain for seven days, until the high and low ground were completely filled; the flooded waters flowed everywhere, yet the World-Honored One walked back and forth upon the bare earth in their midst, and dust rose from that place.

If, when floods overflow and flow across the land, the Blessed One walks back and forth upon the open ground therein, and dust rises from that place, I uphold this as an extraordinary quality of the Blessed One never before seen.
"I have heard that for six years the Māra King pursued the Buddha, seeking his flaws, but being unable to find an opportunity, he grew weary and returned.

If it is true that for six years the Māra King followed the World-Honored One, seeking his flaws, but being unable to find an opportunity, he grew weary and returned, then I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the World-Honored One."
"I have heard that for seven years the Blessed One practiced mindfulness of the body, maintaining it constantly without interruption.
If the Blessed One, for seven years, maintained mindfulness of the body constantly without interruption, I shall uphold this unprecedented quality of the Blessed One."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said:
"Ānanda! From me, the Tathāgata, you shall further receive and uphold this unprecedented teaching."
Ānanda! The Tathāgata knows the arising of perception, he knows its abiding, and he knows its cessation; he knows it constantly, and there is no time when he does not know it. Ānanda!
The Tathāgata knows the arising of thought, he knows its abiding, and he knows its cessation; he knows them constantly, and there is no time when he does not know them.
Therefore, Ānanda, you should receive and uphold this unprecedented teaching from the Tathāgata once again.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Adbhutadharma Sūtra* ends here, totaling two thousand nine hundred and seventeen characters. 33. The Discourse on the Attendant (*Upasthāyaka Sūtra*). The second discourse in the *Adbhutadharma* Section of the *Madhyama Āgama*. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were many renowned and virtuous, highly esteemed elder bhikṣus and great disciples, namely:
the Venerable Kauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, and the Venerable Bāhuna, the Śākya King.
The Venerable Mahānāma Kolita, the Venerable Khemaka, the Venerable Yasas,
the Venerable Bakkula, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Suddhika,
the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Aniruddha, and the Venerable Nandiya.
The Venerable Kumbhīra, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahācunda,
the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Elder Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, and the Venerable Yaśas.
The Elder Gaṇaka-Moggallāna, as well as other renowned and virtuous monks, highly honored elders,
and great disciples, were likewise traveling through Rājagaha and all took up residence near the Buddha’s leaf-hut.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I am now old, my body has become increasingly frail and decrepit, and my life span is nearly at its end. It is necessary for me to have an attendant; you should select one for me who can look after my needs regarding what is appropriate or inappropriate, and receive my teachings without losing their meaning."
Thereupon, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I vow to serve you whether it is appropriate or inappropriate, and to receive your teachings without losing their meaning.
The World-Honored One said: "Kauṇḍinya!"
"You yourself are old; your body has grown increasingly frail and decrepit, and your life span is nearly at its end.
You, too, must have someone to look after you.
Kūṭadanta, return to your original seat."
Thereupon, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his seat.

Likewise did the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bādi the Śākya King, the Venerable Mahānāman Kolita, the Venerable Bhadra, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimālakīrti, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Suddhipanthaka, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, and the Elder Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra.
The Venerable Elder Yaśas, who was distributing the voting sticks, rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to serve you in both what is appropriate and what is inappropriate, and to receive your teachings without losing their true meaning.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Yaśas! You yourself are old, your body is increasingly frail and worn out, and your life is nearly at its end; you too must surely have someone to look after you."
"Yasa! Return to your original seat.
Thereupon, the Venerable Yasa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and returned to his seat.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was in that assembly and thought to himself:
"Whom does the World-honored One wish to seek as his attendant?
On which bhikṣu does his mind rest, wishing for him to observe what is appropriate and inappropriate, and to receive his teachings without losing their meaning?"
"I should enter the concentration corresponding to the image [of their minds] and observe the minds of these monks.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana entered the concentration corresponding to the image and observed the minds of those monks.

The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately knew that the World-Honored One desired the worthy Ānanda to serve as his attendant; his intention was directed toward Ānanda, wishing for him to observe what was appropriate and what was not, and to receive the teachings so as not to lose their meaning.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration and addressed the assembly of bhikṣus, saying:
"Do you know, worthy ones?

The World-Honored One desires to have the worthy Ānanda as his attendant; his mind is set upon Ānanda, wishing that he may observe what is appropriate and what is not, and receive the teachings so as not to lose their meaning."
"Venerable friends!
We should now go together to the Venerable Ānanda and exhort him to become an attendant to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahā-Maudgalyāyana and the other bhikṣus went together to the Venerable Ānanda; they exchanged greetings with him and sat down to one side.
At that time, after the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had sat down, he said:
"Venerable Ānanda,
do you know now?"

The Buddha wishes to have you as his attendant; his intention lies with Ānanda, so that you may look after me to determine what is appropriate or inappropriate, and receive my teachings without losing their meaning.
Ānanda! It is just as if there were a multi-storied pavilion not far outside a village, with its door facing east; when the sun rises, its light shines upon the western wall. Wise Ānanda!

The World-Honored One was likewise; desiring to have the worthy Ānanda as his attendant, his mind was set upon Ānanda so that he might attend to him to determine what was appropriate or inappropriate, and receive his teachings without losing their meaning.
"Worthy Ānanda!
You should now serve as the attendant to the Blessed One.
Venerable Ānanda replied, saying:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
I am not capable of attending upon the Blessed One. Why is that? Because—"
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are difficult to serve and difficult to attend upon as their attendants.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It is just like a great royal elephant, sixty years of age, full of pride and vigorous strength, with tusks, feet, and body complete; it is difficult to approach and difficult to tend to.
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna!
It is likewise with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he is difficult to approach and difficult to serve as an attendant.
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
For this reason, I am not fit to be your attendant.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke again, saying:
“Venerable Ānanda!
Listen as I speak a parable; for the wise, upon hearing a parable, immediately understand its meaning.
Venerable Ānanda!
Just as the udumbara flower appears in the world only at rare intervals, O Venerable Ānanda,
so too does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha appear in the world only from time to time.
"Venerable Ānanda!
You should quickly become the attendant to the World-Honored One; the Gautama shall surely attain the great fruit.
The Venerable Ānanda replied again, saying:
“Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If the Blessed One would grant me three wishes, I would then serve as the Buddha’s attendant.
What are these three?
"I vow not to wear the Buddha's new or old robes; I vow not to eat food specially invited for the Buddha; and I vow not to see the Buddha at improper times.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
“If the Blessed One grants me these three wishes, I shall serve as the Buddha’s attendant.

Thereupon, after the Venerable Mahā-Maudgalyāyana had exhorted the Venerable Ānanda to be the attendant, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda, and departed for the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have already exhorted the worthy Ānanda to serve as the Buddha’s attendant.
World-Honored One!
The worthy Ānanda has requested three vows from the Buddha."
"What are these three?
I vow not to wear the Buddha’s new or old robes; I vow not to eat food offered to the Buddha by private invitation; and I vow not to see the Buddha at improper times.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
"If the Blessed One grants me these three wishes, I shall then serve as the Buddha's attendant.
The Blessed One said,
"Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!"
The bhikṣu Ānanda is clever and wise; he foreknows that there will be criticism or that those of the holy life might say:
"The bhikṣu Ānanda attends upon the World-Honored One for the sake of robes."
"Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
If the bhikṣu Ānanda were clever and wise, he would have anticipated that there would be criticism, or that fellow practitioners of the holy life might say:
'The bhikṣu Ānanda attends upon the World-Honored One for the sake of robes.'"
This, Ānanda, is called the extraordinary quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
The bhikṣu Ānanda is clever and wise; he foreknows that there will be censure or that fellow practitioners of the holy life might speak thus: [and so forth].
“Ānanda the bhikkhu attends upon the Blessed One for the sake of food. Mahāmoggallāna!

If the bhikkhu Ānanda were wise and discerning, he would have foreseen that there would be such criticism, or that those of the holy life would speak thus: [‘Ānanda the bhikkhu attends upon the Blessed One for the sake of food.’]”
"That the bhikṣu Ānanda serves the World-Honored One for the sake of food" refers to the extraordinary quality (abhūta-dharma) of the bhikṣu Ānanda,
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

The bhikṣu Ānanda is skilled in knowing the proper time and skilled in discerning the occasion; he knows when it is the right time for me to go and see the Tathāgata, and he knows when it is not the right time for me to go and see the Tathāgata.

He knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs are going to see the Tathāgata, and he knows when the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs are not going to see the Tathāgata.

He knows when the assembly of upāsakas and the assembly of upāsikās are going to see the Tathāgata, and he knows when the assembly of upāsakas and the assembly of upāsikās are not going to see the Tathāgata.
He knows when many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins have gone to see the Tathāgata, and he knows when many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins have not gone to see the Tathāgata.

He knows which of these many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are able to engage in debate with the Tathāgata, and he knows which of these many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are unable to engage in debate with the Tathāgata.

He knows that by eating, chewing, swallowing, and digesting this food, the Tathāgata will be at ease and find benefit; he knows that by eating, chewing, swallowing, and digesting this food, the Tathāgata will not be at ease and will not find benefit.

Knowing that this food is being chewed, swallowed, and digested, [he perceives] that after the Tathāgata has eaten it, he will attain eloquence and preach the Dharma; knowing that this food is being chewed, swallowed, and digested, [he perceives] that after the Tathāgata has eaten it, he will not attain eloquence and preach the Dharma.
Ānanda, this is called a marvelous quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda. Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

Although the bhikṣu Ānanda does not possess the knowledge of others' minds, he skillfully knows that when the Tathāgata rises from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon, and he proclaims in advance for the sake of others: "Today the Tathāgata has acted in such a way; today the Tathāgata dwells in such a state of happiness in the present life. What he says is indeed accurate and without deviation.
"This, Ānanda, is called the unprecedented quality of the bhikṣu Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda spoke thus:
'O Worthy Ones!'"
"I have served the Buddha for twenty-five years, and it has never happened that such a mind as this gave rise to arrogance.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!
I have attended upon the Buddha for twenty-five years, and from the beginning, I have never seen the Buddha at an improper time."
"If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda spoke as follows:
'O Worthy Ones!'"
I have served the Buddha for twenty-five years and have never been reprimanded by him, except for one single transgression, which was committed for the sake of another.
"If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke as follows:
"Virtuous ones!..."

"I have received eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma from the Tathāgata; I have received and maintained them without forgetting. Yet, if one were to give rise to arrogance on account of this, such a sign would not exist in me.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!
From the Tathāgata I received eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma; I did not ask for clarification even once, with the single exception of one phrase, which was likewise not easily understood."
"If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called an unprecedented quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda spoke as follows:
'O worthy ones!'"
"I have received and upheld eighty thousand clusters of Dharma from the Tathāgata; from the very beginning, I have never seen myself receiving the Dharma from another.
If the Venerable Ānanda makes this statement, it is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!

From the Tathāgata I have received and upheld eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma, yet from the very beginning I never had this thought: 'I receive these teachings for the purpose of instructing others.'"
"Venerable friends!
It is simply because they wish to govern themselves, to find rest for themselves, and to attain parinirvāṇa for themselves.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality (abhūta-dharma) of the Venerable Ānanda.
"Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus:
'Worthy ones!
This is most wonderful!'"
"How extraordinary!

When the fourfold assembly comes to me to hear the Dharma, if I were to give rise to arrogance because of this, such a sign would not exist at all; nor do I premeditate, thinking, 'If someone comes to question me, I shall answer in such and such a way.'"
"Venerable friends!
But while sitting here, one should respond according to the meaning.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus:
"Virtuous ones!
This is most wonderful!..."
"How extraordinary!

When many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins come to question me about such matters, there is not the slightest sign of fear, dread, or horripilation in me; nor do I beforehand deliberate, thinking: 'Should anyone come to question me, I shall answer in such and such a way.'"
"Venerable friends!
But while sitting here, one should respond according to the meaning.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality (abhūta-dharma) of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, at one time, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the Venerable Ānanda were staying on Mount Pāṭali in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra asked:
"Venerable Ānanda!
Having attended upon the Buddha for twenty-five years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of desire?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I am a trainee who has not yet abandoned desire."
The Venerable Sāriputta spoke again, saying: "Worthy Ānanda!

I am not asking you about the state of training or the state beyond training; I am simply asking you: having served the Buddha for twenty-five years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of desire?"
The Venerable Śāriputra asked a second and a third time:
"Worthy Ānanda!
Having attended upon the Buddha for twenty-five years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of desire?"
The Venerable Ānanda also spoke a second and a third time, saying:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I am a learner who has not yet abandoned desire."
The Venerable Śāriputra spoke again, saying: "Worthy Ānanda!

I am not asking you about those in training or those beyond training; I am simply asking you: having served the Buddha for twenty-five years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of desire?"
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Worthy Ānanda!
Answer quickly, answer quickly!"
"Ānanda! Do not disturb these most venerable elders.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
I have attended upon the Buddha for twenty-five years, yet I do not recall ever having given rise to a desire-based thought. Why is this? Because..."
"I always maintain a sense of shame and remorse before the Buddha and toward all wise fellow practitioners of the holy life.
If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
"Furthermore, at one time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha, dwelling among the mountain crags.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed [Ānanda], saying: 'Ānanda!'"
"You should lie down according to the lion’s method of lying down.
Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the lion, the king of beasts, method of lying down?
The World-Honored One replied: "Ānanda!

The lion, king of beasts, goes out for food during the day; having finished his meal, he enters his den. When he wishes to sleep, he places one foot upon the other, extends his tail behind him, and lies down on his right side. At dawn, after the night has passed, he turns back to look at his body.
If the lion, the king of beasts, has an ill-proportioned body, one does not rejoice upon seeing it; if the lion, the king of beasts, has a well-proportioned body, one rejoices upon seeing it.

When that lion, the king of beasts, rises from his sleep, he emerges from his cave; having emerged, he lets out a frequent roar; having roared, he examines his own body; having examined his body, he looks around in all four directions; having looked around, he roars two or three times; and having roared two or three times, he goes forth to seek food—such is the manner in which the lion, the king of beasts, lies down and rises.
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"World-Honored One!
Such is the way the lion, the king of beasts, lies down; how then should a bhikṣu lie down?"
The World-Honored One replied: “Ānanda!

Suppose a bhikkhu, residing in a village or town, rises at dawn after the night has passed, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl, enters the village for alms, well-guarding his body, restraining his sense faculties, and established in right mindfulness.”

Having finished his alms-round in the village or town, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, and placing his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, goes to a secluded place—either to the foot of a tree, or into an empty dwelling—where he either practices walking meditation or sits in dhyāna, purifying the mind of all obstructive dharmas.

During the day, he either walks in meditation or sits in dhyāna, purifying the mind of all obstacles; then, during the first watch of the night, he again either walks in meditation or sits in dhyāna, purifying the mind of all obstructive states.

During the first watch of the night, whether walking in meditation or sitting in dhyāna, he purifies the various hindrances within his mind. During the middle watch of the night, when entering his room wishing to lie down, he spreads his uttarāsaṅga fourfold upon the bed, folds his saṃghāṭī to serve as a pillow, and lies on his right side with one foot overlapping the other. He fixes his mind on the sign of light, maintaining right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, constantly keeping the thought of rising in mind.

During the latter part of the night, he quickly rises from his reclining position, either walking in meditation or sitting in dhyāna, purifying the obstructive states within his mind; such is the lion’s posture for lying down of a bhikṣu.
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"World-Honored One!
Such is the lion’s posture for lying down of a bhikṣu."
The Venerable Ānanda further spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!
The World-honored One taught me the method of lying down in the lion’s posture. Since then, I have never again lain on my left side."
“If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, at one time, the Blessed One was wandering in Kuśinagarī and staying in the Śāla Grove of the Mallas of Upavattana.”
At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter final parinirvāṇa, he said:
"Ānanda! Go to the space between the twin sāla trees and prepare a couch for the Tathāgata with his head to the north; the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa at midnight."

Venerable Ānanda, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, immediately went to the twin trees. Between the twin trees, he prepared a bed for the Tathāgata with the head facing north. Having finished preparing the bed, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!...”
“I have already prepared a bed for the Tathāgata between the twin trees with the head toward the north; I only wish that the World-Honored One would know the time himself.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One took the Venerable Ānanda to the space between the twin trees. He folded his uttarāsaṅga robe in four layers to spread upon the bed, folded his saṃghāṭī robe to serve as a pillow, and lay down on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, awaiting the time of his final parinirvāṇa. As the Venerable Ānanda stood attending the Buddha holding a fly-whisk, he wiped away his tears with his hand and thought to himself:

“Monks from various directions who have come wishing to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings, and to pay him homage, are all able to see, make offerings to, and pay homage to the World-Honored One at their convenience; however, once they hear that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, they will no longer come to see, make offerings to, and pay homage to the World-Honored One, and I too shall not be able to see the Buddha, make offerings to him, and pay him homage at my convenience.”
Then the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus:
"Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
The Venerable Ānanda, holding a fly-whisk while attending the Buddha, wiped away his tears with his hand and thought:

‘Originally, there were assemblies of bhikṣus from all directions who would come wishing to see the World-Honored One, to make offerings, and to pay their respects; they were all able to attend upon, make offerings to, and pay respects to the World-Honored One at their convenience. But once they hear that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, they will no longer come to attend upon, make offerings to, and pay respects to the World-Honored One, and I too shall not be able to see the Buddha, make offerings, and pay respects to him at my convenience.’”
"Then, the World-Honored One said:
'Ānanda! Do not weep, nor be sorrowful.'"
Why is this so? Ānanda!
You have attended upon me, practicing loving-kindness through your body, speech, and mind, without ever having a dual intention, bringing immeasurable, boundless, and limitless peace and happiness.
Ānanda! In the past, among all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones who had attendants, none was superior to you, Ānanda.
If there are those who serve any future Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there will be none superior to you. Ānanda!
As for me, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, if there is anyone who serves as my attendant, there is likewise none superior to you.

Why is this? Ānanda well knows the proper time and well distinguishes the proper time; he knows when it is the right time for me to go and see the Tathāgata, and he knows when it is not the right time for me to go and see the Tathāgata.
He knows when it is the proper time for the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs to go and see the Tathāgata;
he knows when it is not the proper time for the community of bhikṣus and the community of bhikṣuṇīs to go and see the Tathāgata.
He knows when it is the proper time for the assembly of upāsakas and the assembly of upāsikās to go and see the Tathāgata;
he knows when it is not the proper time for the assembly of upāsakas and the assembly of upāsikās to go and see the Tathāgata.
He knows when it is the time for many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins to go and see the Tathāgata;
he knows when it is not the time for many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins to go and see the Tathāgata.
He knows that these many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are able to engage in debate with the Tathāgata;
he knows that these many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins are unable to engage in debate with the Tathāgata.
He knows that when this food is eaten, chewed, swallowed, and digested, the Tathāgata, having eaten it, attains peace and benefit;
he knows that when this food is eaten, chewed, swallowed, and digested, the Tathāgata, having eaten it, does not attain peace and benefit.
Knowing that this food is being chewed, swallowed, and digested, the Tathāgata, having eaten it, attains eloquence to preach the Dharma;
knowing that this food is being chewed, swallowed, and digested, the Tathāgata, having eaten it, does not attain eloquence to preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

Although you do not possess the knowledge of others' minds, you know in advance that the Tathāgata will rise from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon and speak to people beforehand, saying: "Today the Tathāgata has practiced in such a way; thus he dwells in the happiness of the present life. This is exactly as he has said; it is true and without any discrepancy.
"Then, wishing to gladden the Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
'A wheel-turning sage king attains four unprecedented qualities.'"
What are the four?
When the kṣatriya assembly goes to see the wheel-turning monarch, they rejoice upon seeing him if he remains silent, and they rejoice upon hearing his speech when he speaks.

When the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, and the assembly of śramaṇas go to see the wheel-turning monarch, they rejoice upon seeing him if he remains silent, and they rejoice upon hearing his speech when he speaks.
The bhikṣu Ānanda was likewise thus, having attained four unprecedented qualities.
What are these four?
When the assembly of bhikṣus went to see Ānanda, they were filled with joy upon seeing him if he remained silent; they were also filled with joy upon hearing him speak when he did so.

When the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the community of upāsakas, and the community of upāsikās go to see Ānanda, they rejoice upon seeing him if he remains silent; they rejoice upon hearing what he says when he speaks.
"Furthermore, Ānanda, when preaching the Dharma to the assembly, there are four things that are unprecedented.
What are these four?
The bhikṣu Ānanda preaches the Dharma to the assembly of bhikṣus with a sincere mind, never without sincerity."
That assembly of bhikṣus also thought:
"May the Venerable Ānanda preach the Dharma constantly and not let it cease.
Although that assembly of bhikṣus never grew weary of hearing the Venerable Ānanda preach the Dharma, the bhikṣu Ānanda himself remained silent.
He preached the Dharma with a sincere heart to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the assembly of upāsakas, and the assembly of upāsikās, never failing to do so with sincerity.
The assembly of upāsikās also thought to themselves:
"May the Venerable Ānanda always preach the Dharma and not let it cease."
“The assembly of female lay followers (upāsikā) heard the Venerable Ānanda preach the Dharma and were never weary of it; yet the Bhikṣu Ānanda remained silent.
Furthermore, at one time, not long after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling through Vajjī and stayed in the village of Vajjī.”

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was surrounded by a retinue of countless hundreds of thousands who were listening to him preach the Dharma. The Venerable Vajrīputra was also present in the assembly, and this thought arose in his mind:
"Is this Venerable Ānanda still a learner (*śaikṣa*), one who has not yet abandoned desire?"
"I would rather enter the concentration corresponding to the object (tathatā-samādhi), and by means of that concentration, observe the mind of the Venerable Ānanda.

Thereupon, the Venerable Vajjiputta entered the concentration corresponding to the object and, by means of that concentration, observed the mind of the Venerable Ānanda; the Venerable Vajjiputta then knew that the Venerable Ānanda was still a trainee (śaikṣa) who had not yet abandoned desire.
Then, the Venerable Vajjiputta arose from samādhi and addressed the Venerable Ānanda in verse:
“Meditating in quietude within the mountain forest, He has caused nirvāṇa to enter his mind.
Gautama’s dhyāna is undisturbed; Before long, he shall realize the state of cessation.”

"Then, having received the instruction of the Venerable Vajjiputta, the Venerable Ānanda left the assembly and practiced alone, with diligence and without distraction. As he practiced alone with diligence and without distraction, that son of noble family—who had shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith had gone forth from the home to homelessness to train in the path—brought the unsurpassed holy life to its completion."

Thereupon, in this very life, he knows it for himself, realizes it for himself, and dwells having attained realization for himself: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
Having realized the Dharma, Venerable Ānanda even attained arhatship; Venerable Ānanda then declared: "Virtuous ones!
While I was sitting upon my bed, before my head had even reached the pillow, I severed all outflows and attained liberation of mind."
“If the Venerable Ānanda speaks thus, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Ānanda.
Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda spoke as follows:
‘O worthy ones!’”
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa while sitting in the full lotus posture.
Then the Venerable Ānanda sat in the full lotus posture and entered parinirvāṇa.
That the Venerable Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa while sitting in the full lotus posture is called the Venerable Ānanda’s unprecedented quality.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second *Śrāvaka-sūtra* ends here; it contains four thousand three hundred and ninety-nine characters. 34. The Bhārgava Sūtra (34) The Third Sūtra in the Section on Unprecedented Dharmas of the Madhyama Āgama: The Bhārgava Sūtra, for the First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, not long after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Bakula was wandering in Rājagṛha, staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time, there was a certain heterodox practitioner who had been a close friend of the Venerable Bakula before he went forth. In the afternoon, while wandering about, he approached the Venerable Bakula; they exchanged greetings, and the practitioner sat down to one side.
The practitioner said: “Worthy Bakula!...”
"I wish to ask a question; would you grant me leave to do so?
The Venerable Bakula replied, "Heterodox teacher! [Please do so]."
"Ask whatever you wish; having heard it, you shall reflect upon it.
The wanderer asked: "Venerable Bakula!"
"How long has it been since you began training in this True Dharma and Discipline?
The Venerable Bakkula replied,
"O seeker of other paths!"
"I have been training in this True Dharma and Discipline for eighty years.
The heterodox practitioner asked again:
"Venerable Bhaddiya!"
"You have been training in this true Dharma and Discipline for eighty years; do you recall ever having engaged in sexual misconduct?
The Venerable Bakula said to the wanderer, "Do not ask such a question; ask me something else."
“Venerable Bakula!
Having practiced the path within this True Dharma and Vinaya for eighty years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of sensual desire?”
“‘O follower of another school!
You should ask this question.
Thereupon, the follower of another school spoke these words:”
“I now ask you further, worthy Bakkula:
having practiced the path within this True Dharma and Discipline for eighty years, do you recall ever having given rise to a thought of sensual desire?”
Thereupon, Venerable Bakkula, in response to this question from the wanderer, addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
It has been eighty years since I began training in this True Dharma and Discipline; yet, regarding this, I have never had the slightest thought of conceit."
“If the Venerable Bakula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakula made this statement:
‘O worthy ones!’”
"Since I have been training in this True Dharma and Discipline for eighty years, I have never once had a thought of sensual desire.
If the Venerable Bakula makes this statement, it is called the Venerable Bakula’s marvelous quality.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula spoke thus:
"Virtuous friends!
For eighty years I have worn robes made of discarded rags; yet, as for arising any sense of pride on account of this, there is no such thing at all."
“If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement:
‘O worthy ones!’”

For eighty years I have carried the paṃsukūla robes, yet I do not recall ever having accepted a robe from a householder; I have never cut cloth to make a robe, nor have I ever asked another bhikṣu to make one for me; I have never used a needle to sew a robe, nor have I ever used a needle to sew even a single thread into a bag.
"If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement:
'O worthy ones!'"
"I have come for alms for eighty years, yet if I were to give rise to arrogance because of this, such a sign would not exist at all.
If the Venerable Bakula speaks thus, this is called the Venerable Bakula’s extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!

For eighty years I have come for alms, yet I do not recall ever having accepted an invitation from a householder; I have never bypassed the practice of begging for alms; I have never begged at great households where I might have obtained pure, excellent, most wonderful, and abundant food to eat and digest; I have never looked upon the face of a woman; I do not recall ever entering a bhikkhunī’s dwelling; I do not recall ever exchanging greetings with a bhikkhunī, nor even speaking with one on the road."
“If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement:
‘O worthy ones!’”

Since I have been training in this True Dharma and Discipline for eighty years, I do not recall ever having kept a śrāmaṇera, nor do I recall ever having preached the Dharma to a white-robed householder, even so much as a four-line verse.
"If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality (abbhuta-dhamma) of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement:
'O worthy ones!'"

Since I have been training in this True Dharma and Discipline for eighty years, I have never been ill, not even for as long as a finger-snap; nor do I recall ever taking medicine, not even a single *harītakī* fruit.
“If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula made this statement: ‘Virtuous ones!’”
"I have sat in the full lotus posture for eighty years without ever leaning against a wall or a tree.
If the Venerable Bakula makes this statement, this is called the extraordinary quality of the Venerable Bakula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula spoke thus: "Virtuous ones!
Within three nights and days, I attained the realization of the three types of supernormal knowledge."
“If the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement, this is called a marvelous quality of the Venerable Bakkula.
Furthermore, the Venerable Bakkula makes this statement:
‘O worthy ones!’”
"I shall enter parinirvāṇa while sitting cross-legged.
Then the Venerable Bakkula sat cross-legged and entered parinirvāṇa.
That the Venerable Bakkula entered parinirvāṇa while sitting cross-legged is called the Venerable Bakkula’s unprecedented quality.
Thus spoke the Venerable Bakkula; having heard what he said, the heterodox practitioners and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Bakkula Sutta, the third, ends here with nine hundred and eighty characters. 35. The Asura Sutta (35), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Unprecedented Phenomena, the fourth discourse in this section for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in Verañjā, staying at the Yellow Reed Grove.

At that time, the Asura King Pāramārtha and the Asura son Mūliśa, their forms majestic and their radiance brilliant, approached the Buddha’s dwelling as night was turning toward dawn. They prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Blessed One asked: "Bālaru!
Among the asuras in the great ocean, there is no decline in the asuras' lifespan, the asuras' complexion, the asuras' pleasure, or the asuras' strength; do all the asuras delight in the great ocean?"
The Asura King Pāra and the Asura son Mūliça replied:
"World-Honored One!
Among the asuras in our great ocean, there is no decline in their asura lifespan, asura appearance, asura pleasure, or asura power; all the asuras delight in the great ocean."
The Blessed One asked again:
"Bālaruci! How many marvelous qualities does the great ocean possess that cause the asuras to rejoice upon seeing them?"
Bharadvāja replied:
"World-Honored One!
Within my great ocean there are eight extraordinary qualities, which cause all the asuras to rejoice upon seeing them."
"What are these eight?
World-Honored One!
My great ocean, from its depths to its surface, widens gradually as it extends outward; it rises evenly and uniformly to form its shores, and its waters are always full, never overflowing."
“World-Honored One!

If my great ocean, from its bottom to its surface, gradually widens as it circumscribes itself, rising evenly and uniformly to form its shores, and its waters remain perpetually full without ever overflowing—this is called the first unprecedented quality within my great ocean, which the asuras delight in upon seeing.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
My great ocean tide never fails its appointed time.
World-Honored One!"
If my great ocean tide never misses its appointed time, this is called the second extraordinary quality within my great ocean, which the asuras behold and take delight in.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
My great ocean waters are profoundly deep and bottomless, extremely vast and boundless.
World-Honored One!"

If my great ocean is profoundly deep and bottomless, and exceedingly vast and boundless, this is called the third extraordinary quality within my great ocean, which all asuras behold and take delight in.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
The waters of my great ocean are salty and all possess a single flavor.
World-Honored One!"
If my great ocean water is salty and all of one single flavor, this is called the fourth unprecedented quality within my great ocean, which the asuras delight in upon seeing.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Within my great ocean there are many precious treasures, immeasurable and extraordinary, all kinds of rare and wonderful gems filling it. As for the names of these treasures, they are: gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, maṇi-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, spiral shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and jade beads."
“World-Honored One!

If my great ocean contains many precious treasures—immeasurable, extraordinary, and diverse rarities filling its depths; and if the names of these treasures include gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, spiral shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *śaṅkha-śilā* beads—this is called the fifth unprecedented quality of my great ocean, which all asuras behold and take delight in.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

My great ocean is the dwelling place of great deities. As for the names of these great deities, they are: asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, makaras, tortoises, crocodiles, śiśumāras, timis, timingalas, and timitimingalas."
Furthermore, the great ocean is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!
There are sentient beings whose bodies measure one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and even up to seven hundred yojanas, all of whom dwell within the ocean.
“World-Honored One!

If there are great deities dwelling within the great ocean, the names of these great deities are as follows: asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, makaras, tortoises, crocodiles, vāruṇīs, timis, timingalas, and timitimingalas.”
Furthermore, within the great ocean there is something most marvelous!
Most extraordinary!

There are sentient beings whose bodies are one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and even up to seven hundred yojanas in length, all of whom dwell within the sea. This is called the sixth unprecedented quality of my great ocean, which the asuras behold and take delight in.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!
My great ocean is pure and does not tolerate corpses.
If there is one whose life has ended, by the next morning the wind shall blow them onto the shore."
“World-Honored One!
If my great ocean is pure and does not harbor corpses,

such that any who have passed away are blown onto the shore by the wind after the night has ended— this is called the seventh extraordinary quality within my great ocean, which the asuras behold and take delight in.”
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

Within my great ocean in Jambudvīpa there are five great rivers: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarabhū; fourth, the Aciravatī; and fifth, the Mahī. All enter the great ocean, and once they have entered it, each abandons its original name and is simply called the 'great ocean.'"

“World-Honored One! In my great ocean within Jambudvīpa there are five great rivers: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Yamunā; third, the Sarabhū; fourth, the Aciravatī; and fifth, the Mahī. All enter the great ocean, and once they have entered it, each abandons its original name and is called simply ‘the great ocean. This, World-Honored One, is the eighth unprecedented quality of my great ocean, which the asuras behold and take delight in.”
“World-Honored One!
These are the eight extraordinary qualities within my great ocean, which the asuras behold and take delight in.
World-Honored One!”
"In the Buddha’s true Dharma and Vinaya, how many wonderful qualities are there that cause the bhikkhus, upon seeing them, to find delight therein?
The Blessed One replied: "Bālaru!"
In my true Dharma and Vinaya, there are likewise eight marvelous qualities, which, having seen them, cause the bhikṣus to delight therein.
What are these eight? Bālaru!
Just as the great ocean, from its depths to its surface, gradually widens in circumference as it ascends in even proportions to form its shores, its waters are always full and never overflow.
Bāvarī! My true Dharma and Vinaya are also like this: they are practiced gradually, learned gradually, brought to completion gradually, and taught gradually. Bāvarī!

If, within my true Dharma and Vinaya, there is gradual practice, gradual training, gradual exhaustion, and gradual instruction, this is called the first unprecedented quality within my true Dharma and Vinaya, which causes all bhikṣus to rejoice upon seeing it.
"Furthermore, Bālaruci!
Just as the tide of the great ocean never misses its appointed time,
so it is, Bālaruci!"

My True Dharma and Discipline are likewise: for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, I have established prohibitions and precepts such that these sons of noble family will never violate the precepts until the end of their lives.

"Bhāradvāja! If, within my True Dharma and Discipline, I have established prohibitions and precepts for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, such that those sons of noble family do not violate the precepts even unto the end of their lives—this is called the second unprecedented quality within my True Dharma and Discipline, which causes the bhikṣus, having seen it, to take delight therein."
"Furthermore, Bāvarī!
It is like the water of the great ocean, which is exceedingly deep and bottomless, vast and boundless. Bāvarī!"
My true Dharma and Discipline are likewise thus: all phenomena are profound, profoundly bottomless, and immensely vast and boundless. Bālarūpa!

That within my true Dharma and Discipline all phenomena are profound, profoundly bottomless, and immensely vast and boundless—this is called the third unprecedented quality within my true Dharma and Discipline, which causes the bhikṣus, having seen it, to find joy therein.
"Furthermore, Bālaruci!
Just as the water of the great ocean is salty and has but a single taste, so too, Bālaruci, is my true Dhamma and Discipline:
it has the taste of dispassion, the taste of awakening, the taste of tranquility, and the taste of the Path."

"Bhāradvāja! If, within my true Dharma and Discipline, there is the flavor of dispassion, the flavor of awakening, the flavor of tranquility, and the flavor of the path, this is called the fourth extraordinary quality within my true Dharma and Discipline, by which the bhikṣus, having seen it, take delight therein."
"Furthermore, Bālaruci!

Just as the great ocean contains many precious treasures—immeasurable, extraordinary, and various rare jewels filling its depths—the names of these treasures are: gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewel, pearl, green jade, white conch-shell, shell-disc, coral, amber, agate, tortoise-shell, red stone, and *śaṅkha-śilā*."

Bhāradvāja! My true Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: they abound with treasures, immeasurable wonders, and various rare jewels that fill them. As for the names of these treasures, they are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path.

"Bhāradvāja! If my true Dharma and Vinaya abound with treasures, immeasurable wonders, and various rare jewels that fill it—where these so-called 'jewels' refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—this is called the fifth marvelous quality of my true Dharma and Vinaya, which causes all bhikṣus to rejoice upon seeing it."
"Furthermore, Bālaruci!

Just as the great ocean is the dwelling place of great beings—those great beings being called asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, makaras, tortoises, crocodiles, śiśumāras, timis, timingalas, and timitimingalas."
Furthermore, the great ocean is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!
There are sentient beings whose bodies are one hundred yojanas in length, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and even up to seven hundred yojanas; all such beings dwell within the ocean.

"Bhāradvāja! My true Dharma and Vinaya are likewise; the great divine beings all dwell therein. Those called 'great divine beings' are: the Arhats, those practicing for Arhatship, the Anāgāmins, those practicing for Anāgāminship, the Sakṛdāgāmins, those practicing for Sakṛdāgāminship, the Srotāpannas, and those practicing for Srotāpanna-ship."

"Bhāradvāja! If within my true Dhamma and Discipline, the great divine beings of the noble Saṅgha all dwell therein—those great beings being known as the Arhats, those practicing for Arhatship, the Anāgāmins, those practicing for Anāgāminship, the Sakṛdāgāmins, those practicing for Sakṛdāgāminship, the Srotāpannas, and those practicing for Srotāpanna-ship—this is called the sixth unprecedented quality within my true Dhamma and Discipline, which causes the bhikṣus, having seen it, to find joy therein."
"Furthermore, Bālarūpa!
Just as the great ocean is pure and does not tolerate a corpse, if there is one whose life has ended, by the next morning the wind blows it onto the shore."
Bhāradvāja! My true Dharma and Vinaya are likewise; the noble Saṅgha is pure and does not admit corpses.

If there is an indolent person who is evil-minded—one who is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to be so, or one who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be so—even though he may fall among the noble Saṅgha, he is far removed from the noble Saṅgha, and the noble Saṅgha is likewise far removed from him.
"Bhāradvāja! In my true Dharma and Vinaya, the noble Saṅgha is pure and does not accept corpses.

If there is a person who is not diligent, one of evil birth, who is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to be so, or who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be so—even though such a person may fall among the noble Saṅgha, they are far removed from the noble Saṅgha, and the noble Saṅgha is likewise far removed from them. This is called the seventh unprecedented quality within my true Dharma and Vinaya, which, when seen by the bhikṣus, causes them to rejoice therein."
"Furthermore, Pāṭaliya!

Just as there are five great rivers on Jambudvīpa that flow into the great ocean—the first called Gaṅgā, the second Yamunā, the third Sarabhū, the fourth Aciravatī, and the fifth Mahī—once they have entered the great ocean, they each abandon their original names and are all simply called the 'great ocean.'"
Bhāradvāja! My true Dhamma and Discipline are likewise:

a son of noble birth from the Kṣatriya caste, having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the path, abandons his original name and is called simply a "śramaṇa. Likewise, a son of noble birth from the Brahmin caste, the householder caste, or the artisan caste, having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the path, abandons his original name and is called simply a "śramaṇa."

"Bhāradvāja! In my true Dhamma and Discipline, when a son of noble kṣatriya lineage shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path, he abandons his original name and is called equally a 'śramaṇa. When a son of brahmin lineage, a householder lineage, or a craftsman lineage shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path, he abandons his original name and is called equally a 'śramaṇa. This, Bhāradvāja, is the eighth marvelous and unprecedented quality in my true Dhamma and Discipline, which causes all bhikkhus, upon seeing it, to rejoice therein."
"Bhāradvāja! These are called the eight wonderful and marvelous qualities within the True Dharma and Discipline, by which the bhikṣus, having seen them, take delight therein. Bhāradvāja!"
What do you think?

Between these two kinds of unprecedented phenomena—the eight unprecedented phenomena within my true Dharma and Vinaya, and the eight unprecedented phenomena within your great ocean—which is superior, more excellent, more sublime, and most supreme?
Bharadvāja said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One!

My great ocean possesses eight marvelous qualities, yet they do not equal the Tathāgata’s eight marvelous qualities; they are not even a thousandth or ten-thousandth part of them. They cannot be compared, they cannot be illustrated, they cannot be measured, and they cannot be numbered. Only the Tathāgata’s eight marvelous qualities are supreme, preeminent, exquisite, and foremost.”
"Bhagavān!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the Bhagavān accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Asura King Pāyāsa and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
