36. The Earthquake Sūtra (36). Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas. The Earthquake Sūtra, Fifth. First Day’s Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vajra, at a city named Bhūmi.

At that time, the earth shook violently; as the earth shook violently, great winds arose from the four quarters, comets appeared in the four directions, and all houses and walls collapsed and were utterly destroyed.

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda saw the great earth tremble; as the great earth trembled, great winds arose from the four quarters, comets appeared in the four directions, and all houses and walls collapsed and were utterly destroyed.
Having seen this, the Venerable Ānanda was struck with terror; his hair stood on end as he approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
Now the great earth shakes violently; when the great earth shakes, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls are all utterly demolished.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “It is so, Ānanda!
Now the great earth trembles.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
When the great earth quakes, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls are all utterly destroyed.
Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “World-Honored One,

how many causes and conditions are there that cause the great earth to shake so violently, such that when it shakes, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are utterly destroyed?”
The World-Honored One replied: “Ānanda!

There are three causes and conditions that cause the great earth to tremble. When the great earth trembles, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and crumble away.”
What are these three? Ānanda!
This earth rests upon water; the water rests upon wind; and the wind depends upon space.

Ānanda! There is a time when a great wind arises in the sky; when the wind arises, the waters are stirred; when the waters are stirred, the earth shakes. This is called the first causal condition that causes the great earth to shake violently. When the great earth shakes violently, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and crumble away.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
A bhikṣu possesses great supernormal power (ṛddhi), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; he possesses the supernormal power of mastery over the mind."

He forms a limited perception of the earth and an immeasurable perception of water; because of this, this earth, according to his desire and according to his intention, trembles and trembles again, quakes and quakes again.

The deva who protects bhikṣus is likewise so: he possesses great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, with mastery over his mind through supernormal power.

He forms a limited perception of the earth and an immeasurable perception of water; because of this, the earth trembles again and again, quakes again and again, according to his desire and his will. This is called the second cause and condition for the great shaking of the earth. When the earth shakes greatly, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and crumble away.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If the Tathāgata is to enter parinirvāṇa in no more than three months from now, for this reason the great earth will tremble violently. When the great earth trembles violently, great winds will arise from the four quarters, comets will appear in the four directions, and houses and walls will all collapse and be utterly destroyed. This is called the third cause and condition by which the great earth trembles violently; when the great earth trembles violently, great winds arise from the four quarters, comets appear in the four directions, and houses and walls all collapse and are utterly destroyed."
Thereupon, having heard these words, the Venerable Ānanda wept with tears streaming down his face; joining his palms toward the Buddha, he said:
"World-Honored One!"
How marvelous! How extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished meritorious virtues and attained a state never before experienced.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata will, before long—after three months have passed—enter parinirvāṇa. At that time, the earth will shake violently; when the earth shakes violently, great winds will arise from the four quarters, comets will appear in all directions, and houses and walls will all collapse and be utterly destroyed.
The Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda:
“So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda!”
How marvelous! How extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished meritorious qualities and attained a state of dharma never before seen.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa before long, after three months have passed; at that time, the earth will shake violently. When the earth shakes violently, great winds will arise from the four directions, comets will appear in the four quarters, and houses and walls will all collapse and be utterly destroyed.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

I once went to visit assemblies of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kṣatriyas, sitting with them in conversation to accord with their inclinations. Once we were seated together, my physical form was just like theirs, and my voice was just like theirs."
Just as his deportment and etiquette were, so too were my deportment and etiquette;
when he asked about a meaning, I answered him regarding that meaning.

Furthermore, I taught the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having used immeasurable skillful means to teach him the Dharma and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, I vanished right there. Once I had vanished, he did not know who it was—whether a human or a non-human.
Ānanda! How truly marvelous!
How truly extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has accomplished meritorious virtues and attained unprecedented dharmas;
so too have these assemblies of brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas.
“Ānanda! I went to visit the assemblies of the Four Great Kings, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, and sat together with them in conversation, making myself agreeable to their minds.
Once we had sat down together, my physical form became just like theirs, and my voice became just like theirs.”
Just as their deportment and etiquette were, so too was my deportment and etiquette;
when they asked about the meaning of the Dharma, I answered them regarding that meaning.

Furthermore, I taught the Dharma to them, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; having used immeasurable skillful means to teach them the Dharma and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, I vanished from that very spot. Once I had vanished, they did not know who it was—whether it was a deva or another deva.
Ānanda! How truly marvelous!
How truly extraordinary!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has accomplished meritorious virtues and attained unprecedented dharmas.

Likewise, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, the Brahmakāyika heaven, the Brahmapurohita heaven, the Parīttābha heaven, the Apramāṇābha heaven, the Ābhāsvara heaven, the Parīttaśubha heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, the Anabhraka heaven, the Puṇyaprasava heaven, the Bṛhatphala heaven, the Avṛha heaven, the Atapa heaven, the Sudṛśa heaven, and the Sudarśana heaven [have likewise attained them].

“Ānanda! I went to the assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of gods of Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where we sat together and conversed, pleasing their minds. Once we had sat together in composure, my physical form was just like theirs, and my voice was just like theirs.”
Just as their deportment and etiquette were, so too were my deportment and etiquette;
whatever meaning they asked about, I answered with that same meaning.

Furthermore, I taught the Dharma to them, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Having used immeasurable skillful means to teach them the Dharma and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them, I vanished from that very spot. Once I had vanished, they did not know who it was—whether it was a deva or another deva.
Ānanda! How truly marvelous!
How truly extraordinary!
"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has accomplished meritorious virtues and attained dharmas never before obtained.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Earthquake Sūtra*, Chapter Five, ends here; one thousand two hundred and thirty-three characters. 37. The *Campā Sūtra* (37), from the *Adbhutadharma-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Campā Sūtra*, Chapter Six. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Campā and stayed by the side of the Gaṅgā pool.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, when it was time to recite the *Prātimokṣa*, the World-Honored One prepared a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down.

Once seated, the World-Honored One immediately entered meditative concentration and, with the knowledge of others' minds, observed the minds of the assembly. Having observed their minds, he sat in silence until the end of the first watch of the night.
Thereupon, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed; the Buddha and the assembly of bhikkhus have been seated together for a long time. We only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *pātimokkha* (the code of liberation).”
At that time, the Blessed One remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again sat in silence until midnight.
That one bhikkhu rose from his seat once more, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed and the middle watch is drawing to a close. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been sitting together for a long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*.”
The Blessed One likewise remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again sat in silence until the end of the night.
That one bhikkhu rose from his seat three times, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has concluded, and the last watch is nearly spent; dawn is approaching and the light will soon appear. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for a very long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"In this assembly, there is one bhikṣu who has already become impure.
At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also present in the assembly, and he then had this thought:
“For what reason has the Blessed One said that among this assembly there is one bhikkhu who is already impure?
I shall enter a concentration corresponding to that [state], and by means of the knowledge of others’ minds through a concentration corresponding to that, I shall examine the minds of the assembly.”

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered the concentration of the corresponding form (*tathatā-vimokṣa-samādhi*). With the knowledge of others' minds within that concentration, he examined the minds of the assembly. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew what the Blessed One had said regarding the bhikṣu: "Among this assembly, there is one bhikṣu who has become impure."
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from his meditative concentration, went before that bhikṣu, took him by the arm, led him out, opened the door, and placed him outside, saying:
"Foolish man, depart far away! Do not dwell here anymore; you shall no longer be able to join the assembly of bhikṣus. From this day forward, you are no longer a bhikṣu."
He closed the door, locked it from within, and returned to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One, regarding that which you have taught for the bhikṣus: there was a certain bhikṣu in this assembly who had already become impure; I have already expelled him.”
"World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has concluded, and the last watch is nearly spent; it is about to dawn, and the light will soon appear. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been sitting together for a very long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*."
The Blessed One said: “Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
That foolish person shall incur great demerit for having provoked and disturbed the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus.”
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if the Tathāgata were to preach the liberation through realization to an impure assembly, that person’s head would immediately split into seven pieces.
Therefore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
From this day forward, you all shall speak of liberation through understanding; the Tathāgata shall no longer speak of liberation through following.
Why is that? Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Just as that great ocean, from its depths to its surface, gradually widens in circumference and rises evenly to form its shores, its waters are always full and never overflow.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
My true Dharma and Vinaya are also like this: they are practiced gradually, studied gradually, brought to completion gradually, and taught gradually.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

If my true Dhamma and Vinaya are practiced gradually, learned gradually, brought to completion gradually, and taught gradually, this is called an extraordinary quality within my true Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Just as the tide of the great ocean never misses its appointed time,
so it is, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"

My True Dharma and Discipline are likewise: for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, I have established prohibitions and precepts, such that these sons of noble family will never violate the precepts even unto the end of their lives.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

If, within my true Dharma and Vinaya, I have established prohibitions and precepts for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, and noble sons therein do not violate those precepts even unto the end of their lives, this is called an unprecedented phenomenon within my true Dharma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
It is like the waters of the great ocean, which are profoundly deep and bottomless, and extremely vast and boundless.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
My True Dharma and Discipline are also like this: all phenomena are profoundly deep, bottomlessly profound, and immensely vast and boundless.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

If the various phenomena of my true Dharma and Vinaya are profound, bottomless in their profundity, and vast and boundless, this is called an unprecedented phenomenon within my true Dharma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Just as the water of the ocean is salty and has but one single taste,
so it is, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
My true Dharma and Discipline are likewise thus: they have dispassion as their flavor, the flavor of awakening, the flavor of tranquility, and the flavor of the path. Mahāmoggallāna!

If my true Dharma and Discipline have dispassion as their flavor, the flavor of awakening, the flavor of tranquility, and the flavor of the path, this is called a marvelous quality within my true Dharma and Discipline.
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

Just as the great ocean contains many precious treasures, immeasurable wonders, and various rare marvels filling its depths—those precious treasures being named gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and spinel beads."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
My true Dharma and Vinaya are likewise: they contain many treasures, immeasurable wonders, and various rare jewels that fill them completely."

The names of the precious jewels refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

If my true Dharma and Vinaya were filled with many treasures—immeasurable wonders and various rare jewels—and if the names of those treasures were the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, this would be called an unprecedented quality within my true Dharma and Vinaya.
"Furthermore, Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

Just as in the great ocean there dwell great beings, and the names of these great beings are: asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, makaras, tortoises, crocodiles, śiśumāras, timis, timingalas, and timitimingalas."

Furthermore, the great ocean is most marvelous and extraordinary; there are sentient beings whose bodies measure one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and even up to seven hundred yojanas, all of whom dwell within the ocean.
Mahāmoggallāna! My true Dhamma and Vinaya are likewise; the great divine beings all dwell therein.

As for the names of these great beings, they are: the Arhats, those practicing for Arhatship, the Anāgāmins, those practicing for Anāgāminship, the Sakṛdāgāmins, those practicing for Sakṛdāgāminship, the Srotāpannas, and those practicing for Srotāpannaship.
"Mahā-Moggallāna!

If within my true Dhamma and Vinaya, the great beings of the noble Saṅgha all dwell therein—those great beings being the arahants, those practicing for arahantship, the non-returners, those practicing for non-returning, the once-returners, those practicing for once-returning, the stream-enterers, and those practicing for stream-entry—this is called an unprecedented quality within my true Dhamma and Vinaya."
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Just as the great ocean is pure and does not tolerate a corpse,
if there is one whose life has ended, the wind blows it onto the shore by dawn."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana! My true Dharma and Vinaya are also like this: the noble Saṅgha is pure and does not admit corpses.

If there is a person who is not diligent, who has given rise to evil, who is not a practitioner of the holy life yet claims to be so, or who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be one—even though such a person may dwell among the noble Saṅgha, they are far removed from the noble Saṅgha, and the noble Saṅgha is likewise far removed from them.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If the noble Saṅgha of my true Dharma and Vinaya is pure, it does not accept corpses.

If there is a person who is not diligent, one of evil birth, who claims to be a practitioner of the holy life when he is not, or who claims to be a śramaṇa when he is not, even though he may dwell among the noble Saṅgha, he is far removed from the noble Saṅgha; and the noble Saṅgha is likewise far removed from him. This, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is called an unprecedented phenomenon within my true Dharma and Vinaya."
"Furthermore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

Just as there are five great rivers in Jambudvīpa that flow into the great ocean—the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sarabhū, the Aciravatī, and the Mahī—and as the water from the dragons in the great ocean falls from the sky in drops as large as carriage-rims, all these waters cannot cause the great ocean to increase or decrease."
"Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

My true Dharma and Vinaya are also like this: a son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path; he attains the unshakable liberation of mind, realizing it for himself and dwelling in its fulfillment."
"Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

The immovable liberation of mind neither increases nor decreases within my true Dharma and Vinaya. Likewise, sons of noble family from the brahmin caste, the householder caste, or the artisan caste shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path; they realize for themselves and dwell having accomplished the immovable liberation of mind."
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
The immovable liberation of mind neither increases nor decreases within my true Dharma and Vinaya.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

If, in my true Dharma and Vinaya, a son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, he attains the unshakable liberation of mind, realizes it for himself, and dwells having achieved it.
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

The unshakable liberation of mind neither increases nor decreases within my true Dharma and Vinaya. Likewise, sons of noble families from the brahmin, householder, or artisan castes shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to train in the path; they realize for themselves and dwell having attained the unshakable liberation of mind.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

That the liberation of mind which is immovable neither increases nor decreases within my true Dharma and Vinaya—this, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, is called an unprecedented phenomenon within my true Dharma and Vinaya."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Mahā-Maudgalyāyana and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth *Campā Sūtra*, totaling one thousand eight hundred and fourteen characters, is complete. 38. The Discourse to the Householder Ugga (38) *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas (*Adbhuta-dharma-varga*), the seventh discourse, the *Ugga Gṛhapati Sūtra*. First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī and staying in the Great Forest.

At that time, the householder Ugga, accompanied only by female attendants and preceded by his women, departed from Vaiśālī. Between Vaiśālī and the Great Forest, he entertained himself with female musicians and amusements like a king.

Thereupon, the householder Ugga, having become greatly intoxicated from drinking wine, left his women and went into the great forest. While the householder Ugga was thus drunk with wine, he saw from afar the World-Honored One among the trees of the forest, upright and beautiful, like the moon among the stars, radiant and resplendent, shining like a mountain of gold. He was endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence; his majestic power was sublime, his faculties were tranquil and settled, free from obstruction, perfected in self-mastery, and his mind was stilled in silent serenity.

Upon seeing the Buddha, he immediately sobered up from his intoxication. Once the householder Ugga had awakened from his drunkenness, he went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma for him, exhorting him to aspire with longing, bringing him to fulfillment and joy; having used immeasurable skillful means to teach him the Dharma and having exhorted him to aspire with longing and brought him to fulfillment and joy, [he continued].

As is the custom of all Buddhas, he first taught the Dharma of upright conduct, which brought joy to those who heard it; that is to say, he spoke of generosity, spoke of ethical discipline, and spoke of the way to rebirth in the heavens. He censured sensual desire as a calamity and birth-and-death as a defilement, while praising the absence of desire as sublime—the pure and bright factors of the path.

When the Blessed One had taught this Dharma to him, the Buddha knew that he possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a supple mind, a patient mind, a superior mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free of doubt, and a mind free of hindrances; that he was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma, namely the essential points of the True Dharma as taught by all Buddhas.

The Blessed One then taught him the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At that moment, the householder Ugga perceived the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—while still seated, just as a piece of white cloth easily takes on dye; even so, the householder Ugga likewise perceived the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—while remaining in his seat.

Thereupon, the householder Ugga had seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the pure Dharma, cut off doubt, transcended uncertainty, and no longer relied on others. Being free from hesitation and having established himself in the realization of the fruit, he attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the World-Honored One. He rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth, for as long as I live, with the holy life as my foremost priority, I shall receive and uphold the five precepts from the World-Honored One.

Having received and upheld the five precepts from the World-Honored One for as long as he lives, with the holy life as his foremost priority, the householder Ugga prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Returning to his home, he immediately gathered all the women together. Having assembled them, he said: "Do you understand?

From this day forth, I shall follow the World-Honored One for as long as my life lasts, making the holy life (brahmacarya) my primary concern and upholding the five precepts. If you wish to remain here, you may stay and practice generosity to cultivate merit; if you do not wish to remain, you may each return to your own homes. If you wish to be married off, I shall provide for your marriage."
Thereupon, the senior wife said to the householder Ugga:
"If you, sir, shall follow the Buddha for as long as life lasts, taking the holy life as your primary practice and undertaking the five precepts, then you may give me to that such-and-such person."
The householder Ugga immediately summoned that man; grasping the arm of his chief wife with his left hand and holding a golden water-pitcher in his right, he said to him:
"I now give my chief wife to you as a wife."
Having heard this, the man was seized with great terror; his hair stood on end, and he said to the householder Ugga:
"Householder!
Do you wish to kill me?"
"Do you wish to kill me? The elder replied, "I do not wish to kill you;
however, I have followed the Buddha for as long as my life lasts, taking the practice of celibacy as my primary vow and upholding the five precepts."
"Therefore, I give my chief wife to you as a consort.
Having thus given his chief wife to the householder Ugga, at the very moment of giving, he felt no regret whatsoever.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands; amidst them, he praised and extolled the householder Ugga, noting that the householder Ugga possessed eight extraordinary qualities.

Then, at dawn after the night had passed, a certain bhikkhu dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of the householder Ugga. Seeing the bhikkhu approaching from afar, the householder Ugga rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the bhikkhu, and said:
"Welcome, venerable sir!"
"The Venerable One has not come here for a long time; please sit upon this seat.
At that time, the bhikṣu sat upon the seat, and the householder Ugga prostrated at the bhikṣu’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The bhikṣu said:
“Householder!
You have gained a wholesome benefit; you possess great merit.”

Why is this so? It is because the World-Honored One, surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands, has praised and extolled you, saying that the householder Ugga possesses eight extraordinary qualities.
"Elder! What Dharma do you possess?
The householder Ugga replied to the bhikṣu:
“Venerable sir!
The Blessed One has never spoken anything different from the beginning; yet I do not know for what reason the Blessed One speaks thus.
Listen, venerable sir, for I have a teaching.”
At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling through Vaiśālī and staying in the Great Forest.
Venerable Sir!

At that time, I was attended solely by female followers; I was the very first to leave Vaiśālī, and throughout the middle of the Great Forest of Vaiśālī, I entertained myself as a king with female musicians and dancers.
"Venerable sir!
At that time, being greatly intoxicated from drinking liquor, I abandoned my women and went into the great forest.
Venerable sir!"

At that time, I was deeply intoxicated; from afar, I saw the World-Honored One among the forest trees, upright and beautiful, like the moon among the stars. His radiance was brilliant and dazzling, shining like a mountain of gold. He was fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks, his majestic spirit was towering, his faculties were tranquil and settled, and he was free from all obscurations. Having achieved mastery as a tamer, his mind was stilled in silent serenity. Upon seeing the Buddha, my intoxication immediately vanished.
"Venerable sir!
I possess this Dharma.
The bhikkhu exclaimed:
“Householder!
If such a thing exists, it is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!”
“Venerable sir!
I do not possess only this quality. Furthermore, Venerable sir, once I had sobered from my intoxication, I went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.”
The Blessed One taught me the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening me; through immeasurable skillful means he taught me the Dharma, having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened me.

As is the custom of all Buddhas, he first taught the Dharma of the fundamentals, which brought joy to those who heard it—namely, discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, and discourse on rebirth in the heavens; he censured sensual desire as a calamity and birth-and-death as defilement, while praising freedom from desire as sublime and the factors of the path as pure and bright.

When the Blessed One had taught me the Dharma in this way, the Buddha knew that I possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a pliant mind, a patient mind, a superior mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free of doubt, and a mind free of hindrances; that I was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma.
That is to say, just as the Buddhas proclaim the essentials of the True Dharma, the World-Honored One then taught me suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that time, while still seated, I perceived the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—just as a piece of white cloth is easily dyed with color, O Venerable One!
"I am also like this; while sitting right here, I have seen the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Venerable sir, I possess these dharmas.
The bhikṣu exclaimed:
“Householder!
If such a teaching exists, it is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!”
“Venerable sir!
I do not possess only this quality.
Furthermore, venerable sir!”

I have seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma; I have awakened to the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, and transcended delusion. There is no other superior teacher; I no longer rely on others, and I am free from hesitation. Having already abided in the realization of the fruit, I have attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the World-Honored One.
"Venerable One!
At that time, I immediately rose from my seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and said:
'World-Honored One!'"

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall receive and uphold the five precepts, with the holy life as my primary commitment.
“Venerable one! [The Buddha said.]

"Venerable sir, if I have, from the time I received the five precepts from the Blessed One— vowing to observe the holy life for as long as I live— never known myself to have committed a transgression against those precepts."
“I possess this Dharma.
The bhikṣu exclaimed:
“Householder!
"If such a dharma exists, it is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!
"Venerable sir!"
"Venerable sir, it is not only that I possess this quality.

Furthermore, at that time, having received the five precepts from the Blessed One—vowing to observe them for as long as life lasts, with celibacy as the foremost—I prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Returning to my home, I gathered all the women of the household; having gathered them, I said to them:"

"Do you know? From this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall observe the five precepts with the holy life as my primary practice under the World-Honored One. If you wish to remain here, you may stay and perform acts of giving to create merit; if you do not wish to remain, you may each return to your own homes. And if you wish to be married, I shall provide for your marriage."
Thereupon, the chief consort came and said to me:
"If you, my lord, follow the Buddha for as long as life lasts, making the holy life your primary pursuit and undertaking the five precepts, then you may give me to that such-and-such person."
"Venerable One!
At that time, I immediately called that man; taking the Great Lady’s arm with my left hand and holding a golden water-pitcher in my right, I said to him:
'I now give the Great Lady to you to be your wife.'"
Upon hearing this, that man was seized with great terror; his hair stood on end, and he said to me:
"Does the householder wish to kill me?
Does the householder wish to kill me?"
"Venerable sir!
I said to him:
'I do not wish to kill you; however, I have followed the Buddha for as long as my life lasts, taking the holy life as my primary practice and upholding the five precepts.'"
"Therefore, I have given my chief consort to you as a wife.
"Venerable sir!
I have already given my chief consort; when I gave her, I had no regret whatsoever."
"Venerable sir!
I possess this Dharma.
The bhikkhu exclaimed:

If such a teaching exists, it is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!”
“Venerable sir!
I do not possess only this quality.
Furthermore, Venerable sir!”

When I go to the assembly grove, if I first see a single bhikṣu, I pay him homage; if that bhikṣu is walking in meditation, I also walk in meditation alongside him; if he is sitting, I also sit to one side, and having sat down, I listen to the Dharma.

That venerable one taught me the Dharma, and I also taught the Dharma to that venerable one; that venerable one questioned me on certain matters, and I also questioned that venerable one on certain matters; that venerable one answered my questions, and I also answered his questions.
Venerable sir!
I do not recall ever having shown disrespect toward elder bhikkhus, whether they be superior, middling, or inferior in seniority.
Venerable sir!
"I possess this Dharma.
The bhikṣu exclaimed,
"Householder!..."

It is most extraordinary!

while I was practicing giving amidst the community of monks, a deva dwelling in the sky addressed me, saying:"

"Householder! This one is an Arhat; this one is one who is practicing toward Arhatship; this one is an Anāgāmin; this one is one who is practicing toward Anāgāminship; this one is a Sakṛdāgāmin; this one is one who is practicing toward Sakṛdāgāminship; this one is a Srotāpanna; this one is one who is practicing toward Srotāpannaship; this one is diligent; this one is not diligent."
"Venerable sir!
When I gave to the community of bhikṣus, I do not recall ever having had a discriminatory thought.
Venerable sir!"
"I possess this Dharma.
The bhikṣu exclaimed,
"Householder!"
"If such a teaching exists, it is most marvelous!
It is most extraordinary!
"Venerable One!"
"Venerable sir, it is not only that I possess this quality.
Furthermore, Venerable sir,
while I was practicing generosity among the community of bhikṣus, a deva dwelling in the midst of the sky addressed me, saying:"
"Householder!
There is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, a World-Honored One who has well expounded the Dharma; the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata is rightly directed."
"Venerable sir!

It is not out of faith in those devas, nor out of desire for them, nor because of what I have heard from them, but rather through my own purified wisdom, that I know there is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, a World-Honored One who has well expounded the Dharma, and that the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s noble disciples is practicing rightly."
"Venerable sir!
I possess this Dharma.

"Venerable sir!
I possess this Dharma.

Why is this? Now, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have assembled in the Dharma Hall for the sake of the householder Haṃsa, praising and extolling him:"
“Householder Hatthaka has great benefit and great merit.
Why is that? O worthy ones!”

After the Buddha had taught the Dharma to the householder Hatthaka, exhorting him to aspire with longing and bringing him to a state of joy, the householder rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed to return to his home.
Having reached the outer gate, if there were anyone there, he would preach the Dharma to them all, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them;

at the middle gate, the inner gate, and upon entering within, if there were anyone there, he would likewise preach the Dharma to them all, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Having done so, he ascended the hall, prepared his seat, and sat down cross-legged, his mind imbued with loving-kindness, pervading one direction and dwelling therein in its accomplishment.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
At that time, the householder Hatthaka remained silent and did not speak, nor did he look toward the Great Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. Why was this?
It was because he respected meditative concentration and guarded meditative concentration.
Thereupon, the householder Hatthaka said to the bhikkhu:
"Venerable sir!
At that time, were there no white-robed laypeople?"
The bhikṣu replied,
"There are no laypeople.
He asked again:
"If there were a layperson [among them], what fault would there be?
The elder replied,
"Venerable sir!"

There may be those who do not believe the words of the World-Honored One; they shall, for a long night, dwell in unrighteousness and impatience, being born in an extremely evil state and undergoing immeasurable suffering.
If there are those who believe the words of the Buddha, because of this matter, they will be able to revere, respect, honor, and serve me.
Venerable sir!
I also do not wish for that to happen.
Venerable sir!
"I pray that you will take your meal here.
For the sake of the householder Hatthaka, that bhikṣu accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Knowing that the bhikṣu had accepted by his silence, the householder Hatthaka rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and with his own hands served a variety of most pure, exquisite, abundant, and nourishing foods—both solid and soft—until the bhikṣu was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished, the vessels were cleared away, and after providing water for washing once more, he took a small stool and sat to one side to listen to the Dharma.

That bhikṣu taught the Dharma to the householder Hatthaka, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and bringing him to a state of joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to teach him the Dharma and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down to one side, and related to the Buddha in full everything that had been discussed between himself and the householder Hatthaka.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"For this reason, I have proclaimed that the householder Hatthaka possesses seven marvelous qualities.
Furthermore, you should know that the householder Hatthaka also possesses an eighth marvelous quality: the householder Hatthaka is free from seeking and free from desire."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The ninth Sūtra on the Householder Hatthaka ends here, totaling two thousand six hundred and fifty-eight characters. 41. The Sūtra on the Householder Hatthaka (41), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on Unprecedented Dharmas (*Adbhuta-dharma-varga*), the tenth Sūtra on the Householder Hatthaka, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Āḷavī and stayed in the Sārandada Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The householder Hatthaka possesses eight extraordinary qualities."
What are the eight?
Householder Hatthaka possesses few desires, has faith, has a sense of shame, has a sense of dread, has diligence, has mindfulness, has concentration, and has wisdom.
Regarding the statement that "the householder Hatthaka has few desires," for what reason is this said?

The householder Hatthaka himself has few desires, yet he does not wish others to know that he has few desires. He possesses faith, a sense of shame, a dread of blame, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; the householder Hatthaka himself possesses wisdom, yet he does not wish others to know that he possesses wisdom.
Regarding the statement that "the householder Hatthaka has few desires," it is for this reason that it was said.
Why is it said that "the householder Hatthaka has faith"?

It is because the householder Hatthaka has attained firm faith; he is deeply devoted to the Tathāgata, the faculty of faith is firmly established within him, and he will never follow other recluses or brahmins, nor gods, Māras, Brahmās, or anyone else in the world.
"The householder Hatthaka possesses faith"—it is for this reason that it is said.
"The householder Hatthaka possesses a sense of shame"—for what reason is this said?

The householder Hatthaka constantly practices a sense of shame; he knows shame regarding that which is shameful. Evil and unwholesome states, defiled afflictions, lead to various evil retributions and constitute the root of birth and death. Thus it is said.
“Householder Hatthaka possesses a sense of shame”—it is for this reason that it is said.
“Householder Hatthaka possesses a sense of dread”—for what reason is this said?

Householder Hatthaka constantly practices shame; he feels dread regarding what is to be dreaded, namely, evil and unwholesome states, defiled afflictions, and the experience of various evil retributions, which constitute the root of birth and death.
Regarding the statement that "the householder Hatthaka possesses a sense of shame," it is for this reason that it is said.
As for why it is said that "the householder Hatthaka possesses diligence":

the householder Hatthaka constantly practices diligence to eliminate evil and unwholesome states and to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; he always rouses his own mind, remaining single-minded and firm, establishing the roots of all goodness and never abandoning skillful means.
As for the statement that "the householder Hatthaka possesses diligence," it is for this reason that it is said.
Why is it said that "the householder Hatthaka possesses mindfulness"?
The householder Hatthaka contemplates the internal body as body; he contemplates internal feelings, mind, and phenomena as feelings, mind, and phenomena respectively.
"Householder Hatthaka possesses mindfulness"—it is for this reason that it is said.
"Householder Hatthaka possesses concentration"—for what reason is this said?
Householder Hatthaka, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
“Householder Hatthaka possesses concentration”—it is for this reason that it is said.
“Householder Hatthaka possesses wisdom”—for what reason is this said?

Householder Hatthaka cultivates wisdom, contemplates the phenomena of arising and passing away, and attains such knowledge: noble wisdom, clarity, discernment, and thorough understanding, whereby he rightly brings an end to suffering.
"It was because the householder Hatthaka possesses wisdom that this was said.
It was because the householder Hatthaka possesses eight marvelous and unprecedented qualities that this was said.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Handadhipati-sūtra*, the tenth, ends here with four hundred and seventy-three characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, scroll nine, totaling twelve thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight characters; the fourth section, the *Adbhutadharma-varga*, ends here with nineteen hundred and forty-six characters.
Scroll ten of the *Madhyama Āgama* for the first day’s recitation.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Sutta 42: On What Purpose (Kimatthiyasutta) The First Sutta in the Chapter on Practice of the Madhyama Āgama Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"What is the purpose of upholding the precepts?
The Blessed One replied,
"Ānanda!..."
"Observing the precepts" means bringing about the state of being without regret. Ānanda!
If there is one who observes the precepts, they will attain freedom from regret.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of 'freedom from regret'?"
The Blessed One replied:
“Ānanda! ‘Absence of regret’ means the sense of being gladdened.”
"Ānanda! If there is one who feels no regret, they will attain joy.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of ‘joy’?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! To be gladdened means to bring about joy. Ānanda!”
"If there is joy, one then attains rapture.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of 'joy' (pīti)?
The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda!"
Joy has the meaning of bringing about stillness. Ānanda!
If one possesses joy, one attains stillness of the body.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of 'cessation' (nirodha)?"
The Blessed One replied:
“Ānanda! ‘Cessation’ (nirodha) means the sense of bringing about happiness.”
“Ānanda! If there is one who attains stillness, they will experience the awakening of bliss.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of ‘pleasure’?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! Pleasure brings about concentration. Ānanda!”
"If there is joy, one then attains a concentrated mind.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What, Ānanda, is the meaning of 'concentration'?
The Blessed One replied: "Ānanda!"
Concentration causes one to see according to reality and know according to the true meaning.
Ānanda! If one possesses concentration, one will then attain seeing according to reality and knowing according to the true.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of 'seeing according to reality' and 'knowing according to truth'?"
The Blessed One replied:
“Ānanda, for one who sees according to reality and knows according to truth, it leads to the sense of disenchantment.”
"Ānanda!
If one sees according to reality and knows according to truth, one will attain disenchantment.
He asked again:
“World-Honored One,
what is the meaning of ‘disgust’?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! To be weary of [the world] means to bring about the state of being without desire. Ānanda!”
"If there is one who feels weary [of the world], they will attain freedom from desire.
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of 'freedom from desire'?
The Blessed One replied, "Ānanda!"
Freedom from desire means liberation. Ānanda!
If one is free from desire, one immediately attains liberation from all lust, anger, and delusion.
It is thus, Ānanda! By means of upholding the precepts, one attains freedom from remorse;

by means of freedom from remorse, one attains joy; by means of joy, one attains rapture; by means of rapture, one attains tranquility; by means of tranquility, one attains happiness; and by means of happiness, one attains concentration.

"Ānanda! A learned noble disciple, by means of concentration, attains seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are. Because of seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are, he attains disenchantment. Because of disenchantment, he attains dispassion. Because of dispassion, he attains liberation. Because of liberation, he knows liberation: ‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,’ knowing this as it really is."

Ānanda! This is what is meant by dharmas mutually benefiting one another and dharmas being causes for one another; in this way, this precept leads to the supreme state—namely, crossing over from this shore and reaching the other shore.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Arthavargīya Sūtra* ends here, totaling five hundred and twenty-nine characters. 43. The *Acintiya Sūtra* (43), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Practice (*Cariyā-vagga*), The Second *Acintiya Sūtra*, First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed them, saying: “Ānanda!”
"One who upholds the precepts need not think, 'May I have no regret.
Ānanda! It is simply the natural law that one who upholds the precepts will attain freedom from regret."
Ānanda! One who is free from regret need not think, "May I be gladdened. Ānanda!
But the nature of phenomena is such that one who is without regret attains joy.
Ānanda! One who has attained joy should not think, "May I be glad."
Ānanda! It is simply the nature of things that one who possesses joy and gladness attains rapture. Ānanda!
"One who possesses joy need not think, 'May my body become tranquil. Ānanda,
it is simply the natural law that for one who possesses joy, the body becomes tranquil."
Ānanda! One who has attained stillness should not think, "May I be happy. Ānanda!
But such is the nature of phenomena: one who attains stillness immediately experiences the joy of awakening. Ānanda!
One who possesses this joy should not think, "May I become concentrated."
Ānanda! It is simply the nature of phenomena that one who possesses joy attains a concentrated mind. Ānanda!
"One who possesses concentration need not think, 'May I see things as they truly are and know them as they really are. Ānanda,
it is simply the nature of phenomena that one who possesses concentration shall see things as they truly are and know them as they really are."
Ānanda! One who sees according to reality and knows according to truth should not think, "May I become weary. Ānanda!
But the nature of phenomena is such that one who sees them as they truly are and knows them as they really are attains disenchantment.
Ānanda! One who has attained disenchantment need not think, "May I be free from desire."
Ānanda! It is simply the nature of phenomena that one who feels revulsion attains freedom from desire. Ānanda!
One who is free from desire need not think, "May I be liberated. Ānanda!
It is simply the nature of things that one who is free from desire attains liberation from all lust, anger, and delusion.

“Ānanda! This is how, by means of upholding the precepts, one attains freedom from remorse; by means of freedom from remorse, one attains joy; by means of joy, one attains rapture; by means of rapture, one attains tranquility; by means of tranquility, one attains happiness; and by means of happiness, one attains concentration of mind.”

Ānanda! When a learned noble disciple possesses a concentrated mind, he sees according to reality and knows according to truth. Because he sees according to reality and knows according to truth, he becomes weary [of suffering]; because of weariness, he becomes dispassionate; because of dispassion, he attains liberation; because of liberation, he knows he is liberated. He knows according to truth: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

Ānanda! This is what it means for phenomena to mutually benefit one another and for phenomena to be causes for one another; in this way, this precept leads to the foremost state—namely, crossing over from this shore to reach the further shore.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second discourse, the Acintiya Sutta, ends here, consisting of four hundred and fifty characters. 44. The Discourse on Mindfulness (44), Middle Length Discourses, Chapter on Practice: The Third Discourse on Mindfulness, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a bhikṣu is forgetful and lacks right knowledge, he thereby harms right mindfulness and right knowledge.”

If there is no right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one harms the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation;
and if there is no liberation, one harms nirvana.
If a bhikkhu is not forgetful and possesses right knowledge, he practices right mindfulness and right knowledge;

if he possesses right mindfulness and right knowledge, he practices guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation;
if there is liberation, he practices for nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third *Nāṇamoli Sutta* ends here, totaling one hundred and fifty-one characters. 45. The *Hiri-ottappa Sutta* (45), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Section on Correspondence with Practice, the fourth *Hiri-ottappa Sutta*. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If a bhikṣu lacks a sense of shame and a lack of remorse, he will destroy his affection and reverence.”
If there is no affection and respect, it harms one's faith;
if there is no faith, it harms right reflection;
if there is no right reflection, it harms right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If there is no right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one then harms the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
If there is no liberation, one harms nirvāṇa.
If a bhikṣu possesses a sense of shame and a dread of blame, he practices affection and reverence;
if he possesses affection and reverence, he practices faith.
If one has faith, one practices right reflection;
if one has right reflection, one practices right mindfulness and clear comprehension;

if one has right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one practices guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they truly are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
"If there is liberation, one then practices for nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Hrī-ottappa Sutta*, the Fourth, ends here with two hundred and four characters. 46. *Hrī-ottappa Sutta* (46), Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on Practice, *Hrī-ottappa Sutta*, the Fifth; for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
If a bhikṣu is without shame and without dread of blame, he harms his affection and reverence."
If there is no affection and respect, it harms one's faith;
if there is no faith, it harms right reflection;
if there is no right reflection, it harms right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If there is no right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one harms the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation;
and if there is no liberation, one harms nirvana.
Venerable friends!

It is just as with a tree: if its outer bark is damaged, the inner bark cannot form; if the inner bark does not form, then the trunk, heartwood, pith, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit will all fail to develop.
Virtuous ones!
You should know that it is the same for a bhikkhu: if he lacks a sense of shame and a dread of blame, he destroys affection and reverence;
if he lacks affection and reverence, he destroys his faith.
If there is no faith, it harms right intention;
if there is no right intention, it harms right mindfulness and right clear comprehension;

if there is no right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, it harms the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
If there is no liberation, one harms nirvana.
"Venerable friends!
If a bhikkhu possesses a sense of shame and a sense of dread of wrongdoing, he practices with affection and reverence."
If there is affection and respect, one then cultivates faith;
if there is faith, one then cultivates right reflection;
if there is right reflection, one then cultivates right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If one possesses right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one then practices the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, bliss, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation;
if there is liberation, one then practices for nirvana.
Venerable friends!

It is just as with a tree: if its outer bark is not harmed, then the inner bark will develop; when the inner bark has developed, then the stem, trunk, heartwood, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit will all reach full development.
Venerable friends!
You should know that it is the same for a bhikkhu: if he possesses a sense of shame and a sense of dread of wrongdoing, he will cultivate affection and reverence;
if he possesses affection and reverence, he will cultivate faith.
If one has faith, one practices right reflection;
if one has right reflection, one practices right mindfulness and clear comprehension;

if one has right mindfulness and clear comprehension, one practices guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
"If there is liberation, one then practices for nirvana.
This is what the Venerable Śāriputra said.
Having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Hrī-apatrāpya Sūtra*, the fifth, ends here with four hundred and sixty-two characters. 47. The *Śīla Sūtra* (47), the sixth in the Section on Practice (*Āgama-samyukta-varga*) of the *Madhyama Āgama*. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu violates the precepts, he thereby harms freedom from remorse, joy, gladness, tranquility, bliss, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation; and if there is no liberation, he thereby harms nirvāṇa."

If a bhikkhu maintains the precepts, he practices freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, vision, knowledge according to reality, knowing things as they truly are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation; if there is liberation, he practices nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth Sutta on the Precepts ends here, totaling one hundred ten characters. 48. The Sutta on the Precepts (48), Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on Correspondence with Practice, the seventh Sutta on the Precepts, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."

If a bhikṣu violates the precepts, he thereby harms freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation; and if there is no liberation, he thereby harms nirvāṇa.

It is just as with a tree: if its root is destroyed, then its trunk, stem, heartwood, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits can all no longer come to fruition.
Venerable friends!

“Venerable friends!

If there is liberation, he then cultivates nirvana.”
Venerable friends!
It is just as with a tree: if its root is not harmed, then its trunk, stem, heartwood, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all reach full development.
Venerable friends!

Having heard what the Venerable Sāriputta had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh Sutta on the Discourse on Precepts (Sīla-vagga), consisting of three hundred and nine characters, is concluded. 49. The Discourse on Reverence (Gārava-sutta) (49). The Middle Length Discourses, Chapter on Practice (Vagga), The Discourse on Reverence, the eighth, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, you should practice reverence and careful observation, honoring and respecting those who lead the holy life.”

If a bhikṣu does not practice respect, does not observe with skillful discernment, and does not revere his fellow practitioners of the holy life, it is impossible for him to be fully endowed with the rules of dignified conduct.
Once one has failed to fulfill the rules of decorum, it is impossible for one to fulfill the rules of training.
Once one has failed to fulfill the rules of training, it is impossible for one to fulfill the aggregate of morality.
Once the aggregate of ethical discipline is not fulfilled, it is impossible for the aggregate of concentration to be fulfilled.
Once the aggregate of concentration is not fulfilled, it is impossible for the aggregate of wisdom to be fulfilled.
Once the body of wisdom is not possessed, it is impossible for the body of liberation to be possessed.
Once the body of liberation is not possessed, it is impossible for the body of knowledge and vision of liberation to be possessed.
It is impossible that one who lacks the body of knowledge and vision of liberation should possess nirvana.

However, it is certainly possible that a bhikkhu who practices with respect and careful observation, honors his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and possesses the rules of decorum, will possess nirvana.
Once one is endowed with the dharma of dignified conduct, it is certain that one will be endowed with the dharmas of training.
Once one is endowed with the dharmas of training, it is certain that one will be endowed with the aggregate of ethical discipline.
Once the aggregate of morality is perfected, it is certainly possible to perfect the aggregate of concentration.
Once the aggregate of concentration is perfected, it is certainly possible to perfect the aggregate of wisdom.
Once one has perfected the body of wisdom, it is certainly possible that one will perfect the body of liberation.
