What is meant by "the food of associating with virtuous friends"?
The answer is: "Virtuous persons are the food.
The great ocean also has its food; it is not without food.
What is the food of the great ocean?
The answer is: rain is its food.
At times there is heavy rain; once it has rained heavily, the mountain crags, mountain torrents, and marshlands become filled with water.
When the mountain crags, ravines, and streams are filled with water, the small rivers are filled.
When the small rivers are filled, the great rivers are filled.
When the great rivers are filled, the small seas are filled.
When the small rivers are full, the great rivers become full.
When the great rivers are full, the great ocean becomes full.
In this way, that great ocean gradually becomes full through successive stages.
"When a person of virtue is thus endowed, they become endowed with the practice of associating with spiritual friends.
Being endowed with the practice of associating with spiritual friends, they become endowed with hearing the sublime Dharma."
Having fully heard the wholesome Dharma, one then fully gives rise to faith.
Having fully given rise to faith, one then fully possesses right reflection.
Having fully possessed right reflection, one then fully possesses right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
Having possessed right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one then possesses the guarding of the sense faculties.
Having possessed the guarding of the sense faculties, one then possesses the three types of wholesome conduct.
Having possessed the three types of wholesome conduct, one then possesses the four foundations of mindfulness.
Having fulfilled the four foundations of mindfulness, one then fulfills the seven factors of enlightenment.
Having fulfilled the seven factors of enlightenment, one then fulfills clear knowledge and liberation.
In this way, this clear knowledge and liberation are successively and completely accomplished.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Bhojana Sutta*, the twelfth, ends here; it contains nine hundred and thirty characters. 54. *Khīṇāsavasutta* (54), the Thirteenth Discourse on the Knowledge of Destruction (*Khīṇāsavasutta*), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, the Section on Practice (*Vagga*), for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Kuru country and stayed at the town of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikkhus:
"One who knows and sees attains the destruction of the taints; it is not by not knowing and not seeing."
How does one know and see so as to attain the destruction of the taints?
It means that by knowing and seeing suffering as it truly is, one attains the destruction of the taints.

By knowing and seeing the origin of suffering, knowing and seeing the cessation of suffering, and knowing and seeing the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are, one attains the destruction of the taints.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for the knowledge of exhaustion?
The answer is: liberation is its condition.
Liberation also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for liberation?
The answer is: non-attachment is its condition.
Non-desire also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for non-desire?
The answer is: disenchantment is its condition.
Disenchantment also has its condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for disenchantment?
The answer is: seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are is its condition.
Seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are?
The answer is: concentration is the condition.
Concentration also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for concentration?
The answer is: pleasure is its condition.
Pleasure also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition of pleasure?
The answer is: tranquility (*śamatha*) is its condition.
Calm abiding also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for calm abiding?
The answer is: joy is its condition.
Joy also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for joy? The answer is: gladness is its condition.
Joy also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for joy?
The answer is: non-regret is its condition.
Non-regret also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for non-regret?
The answer is: guarding the precepts is its condition.
The guarding of the precepts also has its cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of guarding the precepts?
The answer is: guarding the sense faculties is the cultivation.
The guarding of the sense faculties also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for the guarding of the sense faculties?
The answer is: right mindfulness and right clear comprehension are its conditions.
Right mindfulness and right clear comprehension also have a condition; they are not without a condition.
What is the condition for right mindfulness and right clear comprehension?
The answer is: right intention is their condition.
Right intention also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for right intention?
The answer is: faith is its condition.
Faith also has a cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of faith?
The answer is: the patience of observing dharmas (dharmānusāri-kṣānti) is its cultivation.
The patience of contemplating phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) also has its cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of the patience of contemplating phenomena?
The answer is: the repeated recitation and study of the Dharma constitutes its cultivation.
The practice of reciting and studying the Dharma also involves cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of reciting and studying the Dharma?
The answer is: receiving and upholding the Dharma constitutes its cultivation.
The practice of upholding the Dharma also has its cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of upholding the Dharma?
The answer is: contemplating the meaning of the Dharma is its cultivation.
The contemplation of the meaning of phenomena (*dharmārtha*) also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for the contemplation of the meaning of phenomena?
The answer is: the auditory element (*śrotadhātu*) is its condition.
The ear-element also has a condition for its arising; it is not without a condition for its arising.
What is the condition for the arising of the ear-element?
The answer is: hearing the sublime Dharma is its condition.
Hearing the wholesome Dharma also has its cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of hearing the wholesome Dharma?
The answer is: approaching [the teacher] is the cultivation.
Approaching also has its condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition for approaching?
The answer is: service is the condition.

"If there are those who serve a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they shall hear what they have not heard and benefit from what they have already heard; if one does not serve such a spiritual friend, it will harm the practice of service."
If there is no honoring and serving, it obstructs the cultivation of approaching [the teacher].
If there is no approaching, it obstructs the cultivation of hearing the sublime Dharma.
If one does not hear the sublime Dharma, it obstructs the cultivation of the ear-element.
If there is no ear-element, it undermines the practice of contemplating the meaning of the Dharma.
If there is no contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma, it undermines the practice of receiving and upholding the Dharma.
If there is no receiving and upholding of the Dharma, it undermines the practice of reciting and studying the Dharma.
If there is no practice of recitation, it harms the cultivation of the patience of contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā-kṣānti*).
If there is no patience of contemplative insight, it harms the cultivation of faith (*śraddhā*).
If there is no faith, it harms the cultivation of right reflection (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
If there is no right reflection, it obstructs the cultivation of right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If there is no right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, it obstructs the cultivation of guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, freedom from remorse, joy, rapture, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
If there is no liberation, one harms the cultivation of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).

"If one serves a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), one hears what has not been heard before, and having heard it, one practices accordingly; if one serves such a spiritual friend, one cultivates that service."
If there is service and attendance, one then practices going to visit [the teacher].
If there is going to visit, one then practices hearing the sublime Dharma.
If there is hearing the sublime Dharma, one then practices the ear-element (*śrotradhātu*).
If there is the ear-element, one then practices contemplating the meaning of the Dharma.
If there is contemplation of the meaning of the Dharma, one then practices receiving and upholding the Dharma.
If there is receiving and upholding the Dharma, one then practices reciting and rehearsing the Dharma.
If one plays with and recites the Dharma, one then practices the patience of observing the Dharma (dharmakṣānti).
If one has the patience of observing the Dharma, one then practices faith.
If one has faith, one then practices right reflection (samyaksaṃkalpa).
If there is right reflection, one then practices right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

If there is right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one then practices guarding the sense faculties, guarding the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
"If there is liberation, one then cultivates the knowledge of exhaustion.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Kṣayajñāna Sūtra*, the thirteenth, ends here; 868 characters. 55. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (55), Middle Āgama, Chapter on Correspondence with Practice, the fourteenth, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Nirvāṇa has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is called the condition for nirvāṇa?"
The answer is: liberation is its nutriment.
Liberation also has a nutriment; it is not without a nutriment.
What is the nutriment of liberation?
The answer is: non-desire is its condition (*pratītya*).
Non-desire also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition for non-desire?
The answer is: revulsion is the condition.
Revulsion, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition for revulsion?
The answer is: seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are is the condition for cultivation.
Seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for seeing things as they truly are and knowing them as they really are?
The answer is: Concentration is the practice.
Concentration also has a practice; it is not without practice.
What is meant by the practice of concentration?
The answer is: pleasure is the condition for its arising.
Pleasure, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition for pleasure?
The answer is: Cessation is cultivation.
Cessation also has cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by the cultivation of cessation?
The answer is: joy is the condition for it.
Joy, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for joy?
He replied: "Joy is its condition.
Joy, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for joy?"
The answer is: non-regret is its nutriment (*āhāra*).
Non-regret also has a nutriment; it is not without a nutriment.
What is meant by the nutriment of non-regret?
The answer is: guarding the precepts is the practice.
Guarding the precepts also has a practice; it is not without a practice.
What is meant by the practice of guarding the precepts?
Answer: Guarding the sense faculties is the practice.
Guarding the sense faculties also has a practice; it is not without a practice.
What is called the practice of guarding the sense faculties?
The answer is: Right mindfulness and right clear comprehension are the practice.
Right mindfulness and right clear comprehension also have a practice; they do not lack a practice.
What is the practice of right mindfulness and right clear comprehension?
The answer is: Right intention is the practice.
Right intention also has a practice; it is not without a practice.
What is the practice of right intention?
The answer is: faith is the practice.
Faith also has a practice; it is not without practice.
What is meant by the practice of faith?
Answer: Suffering is the condition.
Suffering also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition of suffering?
The answer is: old age and death have a condition.
Old age and death also have a condition; they do not lack a condition.
What is the condition for old age and death?
The answer is: birth is the condition for clinging.
Birth, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is meant by the condition for birth?
Answer: Conditioned phenomena have cultivation;
existence also has cultivation; it is not without cultivation.
What is meant by "having cultivation"?
The answer is: feeling is the condition for clinging.
Feeling, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for feeling?
The answer is: craving is the condition.
Craving, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for craving?
The answer is: Feeling is the condition.
Feeling, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is said to be the condition for feeling?
The answer is: contact (*sparśa*) is the condition for feeling.
Contact, too, has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for contact?
The answer is: the six sense bases are the condition.
The six sense bases also have a condition; they are not without a condition.
What is the condition for the six sense bases?
The answer is: name-and-form is the condition.
Name-and-form also has a condition; it is not without a condition.
What is the condition for name-and-form?
The answer is: consciousness is conditioned by habitual tendencies (*saṃskāra*).
Consciousness, too, has conditions; it is not without conditions.
What is meant by the condition for consciousness?
The answer is: volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) have a condition.
Volitional formations also have a condition; they do not lack a condition.
What is the condition for volitional formations?
The answer is: ignorance is the condition. Thus, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations;

conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth are old age and death; and conditioned by old age and death is suffering.
By practicing the contemplation of suffering, one gains faith;
by practicing faith, one gains right reflection;
by practicing right reflection, one gains right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.

By practicing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, there arise the guarding of the sense faculties, the guarding of the precepts, freedom from remorse, gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness, concentration, seeing things as they truly are, knowing things as they really are, disenchantment, dispassion, and liberation.
"By practicing liberation, one attains nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen, ends here with six hundred and sixty-three characters. 56. The *Meghiya Sūtra* (56), the fifteenth in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Section on Practice, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, staying at the Maṅgura Cave in the Jaṭu Village.
At that time, the Venerable Māgandiya was his attendant.
Then, when the night had passed and at dawn, the Venerable Māgandiya dressed, took his bowl, and entered the village of Jaṭu to wander for alms.

Having finished his almsround, he went to the banks of the Kimikālā River. He saw that the ground was level and even, known as the Subhaga Mango Grove; the waters of the Kimikālā were exceedingly wonderful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, their temperature temperate and pleasant.

Seeing this, he rejoiced and thought to himself: "This place is level and even, known as the Subhaga Mango Grove; the waters of the Kimikālā are exceedingly wonderful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, their temperature temperate and pleasant. If a son of good family wishes to train in severance, he should do so here. Since I too have something to sever, might I not train in severance in this secluded place?"

Thereupon, Makhādeva, having finished his meal, rose after midday, set aside his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat over his shoulder, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
This morning, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered the village of Jaṭila to beg for alms. Having finished begging, I went to the banks of the Kimikālā River.

There I saw a level and even ground called the Pleasant Mango Grove (Supratiṣṭhita-āmra-vana), where the waters of the Kimikālā were most wonderful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, their temperature perfectly temperate. Seeing this, I was filled with joy and thought:

"This ground is level and even, called the Pleasant Mango Grove, and the waters of the Kimikālā are most wonderful and delightful, with clear springs flowing gently, their temperature perfectly temperate. If a son of good family wishes to train in the cutting off [of defilements], he should do so in such a place. Since I too have something to cut off, might I not train in the cutting off here in this secluded spot?"
“World-Honored One!
I now wish to go to that secluded grove of mango trees to practice the cultivation of abandonment.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
“Māgandiya! Do you know this? I am alone and have no one;
I have no attendant. You should wait a while until a bhikkhu comes to serve as my attendant. Then you may go and practice in that secluded place in the mango grove.”
The Venerable Mihika said to the Blessed One a second and even a third time:
“Blessed One,
I now wish to go to that secluded grove of mango trees to practice the cultivation of cessation.”
The Blessed One also repeated this a second and a third time, saying:
"Mekhila! Do you know now?"

"I am alone and have no one; I have no attendant. You should wait a moment until a bhikṣu comes to serve as my attendant. You may then depart and go to that secluded place in the mango grove to practice."
Mekhila spoke again, saying:
"The World-Honored One is unconditioned and inactive, and has nothing upon which to gaze.
World-Honored One!"
“I have something conditioned, something volitional, and something to be observed.
Blessed One!
I went to that secluded grove of mango trees to train in abandonment.”
The Blessed One said:
“Mekhila! Since you desire to seek cessation, what more need I say?”
"Mahānāma! Go, as you wish.

Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Mahānāma received it well, retained it well, and recited it well; he then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed for that mango grove.
Having entered the forest, he went beneath a tree, spread out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and sat down cross-legged.

While staying in the Āmra Grove, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita gave rise to three evil and unwholesome thoughts: thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness. Because of these, he then called to mind the Blessed One.
Thereupon, at the time of the afternoon, Makhādeva rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

When I went to the Āmra Grove and sat in a secluded place, three unwholesome and evil thoughts arose within me: thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harm; it was because of this that I called to mind the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said: "Mekhila!
For one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured and who wishes to bring it to maturity, there are five practices to be cultivated."
What are the five? Māgandiya!
A bhikkhu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends.
"Mahānāma!
For one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured and whom one wishes to bring to maturity, this is called the first practice.
Furthermore, Mahānāma!"

A bhikṣu cultivates the precepts and guards the code of liberation; furthermore, he properly maintains dignified deportment and decorum, viewing even the slightest transgression with constant fear and dread, and upholds the training rules.
"Mahānāma!
When the liberation of the mind is not yet matured and one desires to bring it to maturity, this is called the second practice.
Furthermore, Mahānāma!"

A bhikkhu is one who speaks what is noble and meaningful, which makes the mind supple and removes hindrances from the mind; that is to say, he speaks of virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, gradual reduction, non-delight in society, fewness of desires, contentment, relinquishment, dispassion, cessation, solitary meditation, and dependent origination. Such speech as this, spoken by a śramaṇa, is easily obtained and not difficult to obtain.
"Mahānāma!
When the liberation of the mind is not yet matured, and one desires to bring it to maturity—this is called the third practice.
Furthermore, Mahānāma!"

A bhikṣu constantly practices diligence, severing what is evil and unwholesome, and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he perpetually arouses his own resolve, remaining single-minded and steadfast, making it the root of all virtues and never abandoning skillful means.
"Meghiya!
When the liberation of the mind is not yet matured and one desires to bring it to maturity, this is called the fourth practice to be cultivated.
Furthermore, Meghiya!"

A bhikṣu practices wisdom, contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away; attaining such knowledge, with noble insight and clear penetration, he discerns and understands them thoroughly, thereby bringing an end to suffering through right means.
"Mahānāma!
When the liberation of the mind is not yet matured, and one desires to bring it to maturity, this is called the fifth practice.
Having cultivated these five practices, he further cultivates four dharmas."
What are the four?
Cultivating the meditation on foulness to sever desire;
cultivating loving-kindness to sever ill will;
Cultivate mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation to sever distracted thoughts;
cultivate the perception of impermanence to sever the conceit of "I am. Makhādeva!

If a bhikṣu is himself a virtuous friend, associates with virtuous friends, and dwells in harmony with virtuous friends, it should be known that he will certainly cultivate the prohibitive precepts and guard the Pratimokṣa; furthermore, he will properly maintain dignified conduct and etiquette, regard even the slightest transgression as grave, always harbor a sense of dread toward it, and undertake the training rules.

"Mahānāma! If a bhikkhu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will certainly obtain the noble and meaningful teachings that are spoken—teachings which make the mind supple and free from hindrances. That is to say, he will obtain teachings concerning virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation; teachings on gradual reduction, on not delighting in social gatherings, on fewness of desires, on contentment, on relinquishment, on dispassion, on cessation, on solitary meditation, and on dependent origination. Such teachings as these, spoken by the śramaṇa, will be easily obtained and not difficult to obtain."

“Meghiya! If a bhikkhu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will certainly practice with diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he will constantly arouse his own intention, being single-minded and firm, establishing the roots of all goodness and not relinquishing skillful means.”
"Mahānāma!

If a bhikkhu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will certainly practice wisdom, contemplate the law of arising and passing away, and attain such knowledge—noble, penetrative, lucid, and discerning—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering."
"Mahānāma!
If a bhikkhu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will surely practice the meditation on foulness to abandon lust;
he will practice loving-kindness to abandon ill will."
Mendhaka! Cultivate mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation to sever distracted thoughts;
cultivate the perception of impermanence to sever the conceit of "I am."
Mendhaka! If a bhikkhu attains the perception of impermanence, he will certainly attain the perception of non-self.
Mendhaka! If a bhikkhu attains the perception of non-self, he will, in this very life, sever all conceit of "I am," and attain tranquility, cessation, extinction, the unconditioned, and nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Māgandiya and the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifteenth discourse, the Māgandiya Sutta, ends here, totaling one thousand three hundred twenty-three characters. 57. Bhikkhu Sutta (57) The Madhyama Āgama, Section on Correspondence with Practice, Discourse Spoken for the Sake of a Bhikkhu, Number Sixteen. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“For those whose liberation of mind is not yet matured and who wish to bring it to maturity, there are five practices to be cultivated.”
What are the five? Bhikkhus!

When one is oneself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends; and when one’s liberation of mind is not yet matured, desiring to bring it to maturity—this is called the first practice of the Dharma.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Cultivate the prohibitive precepts and guard the liberation through them; moreover, properly maintain dignified conduct and etiquette, viewing even the slightest transgression with constant fear and dread. Uphold and train in the precepts so that the mind’s liberation, which is not yet mature, may reach maturity—this is called the second practice.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!

There are teachings that are noble and meaningful, which make the mind supple and free from hindrances. These are: discourse on the precepts, discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation, discourse on gradual reduction, discourse on not delighting in social gatherings, discourse on few desires, discourse on contentment, discourse on relinquishment, discourse on dispassion, discourse on cessation, discourse on solitary meditation, and discourse on dependent origination. When one obtains such teachings as these spoken by the śramaṇa—attaining them fully and easily, without difficulty—and seeks to bring the unripened liberation of the mind to maturity, this is called the third practice of the Dharma.
Furthermore, bhikṣu!

One should constantly practice diligence, severing evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas. Always rousing one's own intention, with single-mindedness and firm resolve, one takes up the roots of all goodness and does not abandon skillful means. For one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, desiring to bring it to maturity—this is called the fourth dharma of practice.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!

One cultivates wisdom, contemplating the law of arising and passing away. Having attained such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning—one rightly brings an end to suffering. If the liberation of the mind is not yet matured, and one desires to bring it to maturity, this is called the fifth practice.
"Once he has cultivated these five practices, he further cultivates four dharmas.
What are the four? He cultivates the meditation on foulness (aśubha-bhāvanā) to bring about the severance of desire."
Cultivate loving-kindness to sever ill will;
cultivate mindfulness of breathing to sever distracted thoughts;
cultivate the perception of impermanence to sever the conceit "I am."

If a bhikṣu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, it should be known that he will certainly cultivate the prohibitive precepts, guard the code of liberation, and further properly maintain dignified conduct and decorum; seeing even the slightest fault as a sin, he will always harbor a sense of dread and uphold the training rules.

If a bhikṣu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will certainly obtain what is to be spoken by the noble ones—meaningful, leading to the softening of the mind, and clearing away the hindrances of the mind. That is to say, he will obtain discourses on morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation; discourses on gradual reduction, lack of delight in social gatherings, fewness of desires, contentment, relinquishment, dispassion, cessation, solitary meditation, and dependent origination. Such teachings as these, spoken by the śramaṇas, he will easily obtain and find them not difficult to acquire.

If a bhikṣu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, you should know that he will certainly practice diligence, severing evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he will constantly arouse his own resolve, being single-minded and steadfast, establishing the roots of all goodness and never abandoning skillful means.

If a bhikṣu is himself a good friend, dwells together with good friends, and associates harmoniously with good friends, you should know that he will certainly practice wisdom, contemplate the law of arising and passing away, and attain such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering.

If a bhikṣu is himself a good friend, associates with good friends, and dwells in harmony with good friends, it should be known that he will certainly cultivate the meditation on foulness to sever desire;
cultivate loving-kindness to sever ill-will;
and cultivate mindfulness of breathing to sever distracted thoughts.
Cultivate the perception of impermanence so as to sever the conceit "I am.

If a bhikṣu attains the perception of impermanence, he will necessarily attain the perception of non-self. If a bhikṣu attains the perception of non-self, he will then, in this very life, sever all conceits of "I am," and attain tranquility, cessation, extinction, the unconditioned, and nirvāṇa.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

58 The Discourse on the Seven Treasures (58), Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on Kings, The First Discourse on the Seven Treasures. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, you should know that seven treasures likewise appear in the world.”
What are the seven?
They are the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the minister-of-war-treasure; these are called the seven.
Just as it should be known that when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, these seven treasures appear in the world;
so too, it should be known that when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, the seven factors of enlightenment also appear in the world.
What are the seven?

They are the treasure of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the joy factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment; these are called the seven.
"When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, you should know that these seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment appear in the world.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after the midday meal, the bhikṣus gathered and sat together in the lecture hall, discussing this matter:
"Venerable friends!
How extraordinary!..."
"How extraordinary!

The Dharma King, in accordance with the Dharma, possesses the seven treasures. These seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure; these are the seven. He is endowed with a full thousand sons who are handsome in appearance, valiant, and fearless, capable of subduing all opposing hosts. He will surely rule over this entire earth as far as the great ocean, not by means of the sword or staff, but through instruction in the Dharma, bringing about peace and happiness.

If one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and with deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, one will surely attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame shall spread and be heard throughout the ten directions.

At that time, the Blessed One was sitting in seclusion; with the pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall after the midday meal, discussing this matter together:

“World-Honored One!

Furthermore, the toes of a great man are slender and long; this is called a mark of a great man.

Furthermore, between the eyebrows of a Great Man grows a tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa), pure white and curling to the right; this is called a mark of a Great Man.
“Monks! When a Great Man is endowed with these thirty-two marks, there are two certain and infallible destinies for him.
If he remains at home, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), intelligent and wise, possessing a fourfold army that governs the world under his own sovereign authority.

The Dharma-King who acts in accordance with the Dharma accomplishes the seven treasures. At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was in a quiet place, sitting in meditation and reflecting, when this thought occurred to him:
"Very few people in the world are able to find satisfaction in sensual desires; few are those who meet their end having grown weary of and disgusted with sensual desires."
"It is extremely rare for people in this world to have a sense of satiety regarding sensual desires, yet to pass away while feeling weary of and averse to those desires.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, and having arrived, he paid homage, stood to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
"Today, while sitting in quiet seclusion in meditative composure, I reflected and had this thought:
'Among the people of the world, there are very few who possess a mind of contentment regarding sensual desires; there are few who pass away having grown weary of sensual desires.
It is extremely rare for a person in the world to both possess a mind of contentment regarding sensual desires and to pass away having grown weary of them.'"
The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is.
Among the people of the world, there are very few who can find satisfaction in sensual desires; there are few who pass away having grown weary of and disgusted with sensual desires."
Ānanda! It is extremely rare for people in the world to have their desires satisfied and yet, having grown weary of those desires, pass away. Ānanda!
It is extremely rare for people of the world to find satisfaction in sensual desires, and even rarer for them to pass away while feeling weary of and disgusted with those desires. Ānanda!

However, people in the world are exceedingly numerous; they have no sense of satiety regarding sensual desires and pass away without having grown weary of or felt aversion toward them. Why is this so?

Ānanda! In the past there was a king named Mūrdhaja, who was a Cakravartin king, intelligent and wise. He possessed a fourfold army and governed the world with sovereign mastery. As a Dharma-king acting in accordance with the Dharma, he had accomplished the seven treasures. Those seven treasures were: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the minister-of-war-treasure; these are the seven. He was endowed with a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, valiant and fearless, capable of subduing all other hosts. He surely ruled over this entire earth as far as the great ocean, not by means of the sword or the staff, but through the teaching and commands of the Dharma, bringing peace and happiness to all.
Ānanda! After a very long time had passed, King Mūrdhaja thought to himself:

"I possess the continent of Jambudvīpa, which is exceedingly wealthy and pleasant, and I have many people; I possess the seven treasures and am endowed with a full thousand sons. I wish to rain down jewels from my palace for seven days, until they accumulate up to my knees."

"Ānanda! That King Mandhātu possessed great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. As soon as he formed this thought, there was a rain of treasures within his palace for seven days, accumulating until it reached his knees."
“Ānanda! After a very long time had passed, King Mūrdhaja again thought to himself:

This is the Hall of the True Dharma of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; within this hall, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, the Trāyastriṃśa gods reflect upon the Dharma and its meaning for the sake of both devas and humans.

I also possess the continent of Aparagoyānī, as well as the continent of Pūrvavideha, and the continent of Uttarakuru.

Furthermore, Śakra, Lord of Devas, offered me half of his seat; having already sat upon half of Śakra’s seat, I am entirely indistinguishable from Śakra. "I would now rather drive Śakra away, seize half of his seat, and become the king of gods and humans, acting with sovereign mastery.
Ānanda, as soon as King Mūrdhaja conceived this thought, he was unaware that he had already descended to Jambudvīpa; he immediately lost his supernormal powers and fell gravely ill.
When his life was about to end, the ministers went to King Mandhātu and said to him:

If there should be brahmins, householders, ministers, or subjects who come and ask us:..."
"What did King Mandhātu say when he was about to pass away?
O Great King!
How shall we answer the brahmins, householders, ministers, and the people?"
Then, King Mūrdhaja said to his ministers:

'What did King Mūrdhaja say when he was on the verge of death?'—[how would you answer]?"
"You all should answer him thus:
'King Mūrdhaja attained Jambudvīpa, yet his mind was not satisfied when he passed away.
King Mūrdhaja attained the seven treasures, yet his mind was not satisfied when he passed away.'"
King Mūrdhaja possessed a full thousand sons, yet he passed away with his mind still unsatisfied.
King Mūrdhaja had rain of jewels for seven days, yet he passed away with his mind still unsatisfied.
King Mūrdhaja obtained the continent of Aparagoyānī, yet he passed away with his mind still unsatisfied.
King Mūrdhagata attained the continent of Pūrvavideha, yet he passed away with his mind still unsatisfied.
King Mūrdhagata attained the continent of Uttarakuru, yet he passed away with his mind still unsatisfied.
When King Mūrdhagata saw the assembly of the devas, his mind was not satisfied, and he passed away.
King Mūrdhagata, though possessed of the five qualities of sensual pleasure—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—his mind was not satisfied, and he passed away.
"If brahmins, householders, ministers, or common people should come and ask you:
'What did King Mandhātu say as his life was coming to an end? "
"You all should answer him in this way.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The heavens rain down exquisite treasures, yet those with desire are never satisfied."
Sensual desires are suffering and devoid of joy; the wise should understand this.
Even if one were to obtain a heap of gold as vast as the Great Snowy Mountains, there would still be no satisfaction for each individual; thus the wise reflect.
Having obtained the five sublime sensual pleasures, one does not find delight in these five joys;
having severed craving and become unattached to desire, such is a disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said:
“Ānanda! As for King Mūrdhaja of old, do you think he was someone else?
Do not entertain such a thought; you should know that he was none other than myself.”

Ānanda! At that time, I acted for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others; I benefited many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate conclusion; it was not ultimately pure, nor was the holy life (brahmacarya) brought to its ultimate conclusion.
At that time, one was not yet free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had one yet attained liberation from all suffering.

Ānanda! I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One.

I now benefit myself and also benefit others; I benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
I have now taught the Dharma that reaches the ultimate; it is ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life.
I have now escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

"Is there perhaps any form that is permanent and unchanging, which is exclusively pleasant and exists eternally?"
"Is there perhaps any feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness that is permanent and unchanging, exclusively pleasant, and eternally enduring?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

Thereupon, the Blessed One took a small amount of cow dung with his fingernail and said: "Bhikkhu,

The bhikkhu replied:

World-Honored One.”
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In this way, there is not even the slightest form that is permanent and unchanging, which is exclusively pleasant and eternally enduring."

In this way, there is not even the slightest feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness that remains eternally unchanging, characterized by exclusive happiness, and exists forever. Why is this so?
"Monks! I recall that in the past, for a long time I performed meritorious deeds; having performed them for a long time, I have for a long time experienced the fruit of happiness. Monks!"

In the past, I practiced loving-kindness for seven years; during seven cycles of the world's formation and destruction, I did not return to this world. When the world was being destroyed, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when the world was being formed, I descended to be born within an empty Brahmā palace. There, among those Brahmās, I became a Mahābrahmā. In other places, I was the King of the Gods (Indra) a thousand times; thirty-six times, I was Śakra, the Lord of Devas; and countless times, I was a Kṣatriya king born from the crown of the head.

“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand great elephants, equipped with fine trappings, adorned with various jewels, and covered with white pearl ornaments, headed by the elephant king Uposatha.”

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand horses, well-equipped with harnesses and adorned with various jewels, with gold and silver necklaces, headed by the horse-king Valāha."
“Bhikṣus!

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand great cities, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with vast populations, of which the royal city of Kusāvatī was the foremost."

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand palaces made of four kinds of jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with the Palace of Righteous Dharma as the foremost."

“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand state thrones made of four kinds of precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. They were spread with woolen carpets and rugs, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with under-linens, and furnished with pillows at both ends, including those from Kalinga, Pārasīka, and Vārāṇasī.”
"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand pairs of garments: garments of fine linen, brocade, silk, cotton, and kāliṅgapravāraka."

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand women whose bodies were radiant, pure, and bright; their beauty surpassed that of humans and only slightly fell short of that of the gods. All were of the Kṣatriya caste, and those of other lineages were immeasurable."
"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand kinds of food that were constantly provided day and night, prepared specifically for me so that I might eat."
“Bhikṣus! Among those eighty-four thousand kinds of food, there is one kind of food that is most exquisite, pure, and possesses immeasurable flavors; this is what I constantly eat.”
"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand women, there was one Kṣatriya woman who was most beautiful and lovely, and she constantly attended upon me. Monks!"
Among those eighty-four thousand pairs of garments, there was one pair—whether it were a *kṣauma* cloth, a brocade, a silk, a cotton, or a *kāliṅgapravāraka* cloth—that was what I regularly wore.

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand state couches, there was one couch made of gold, or silver, or beryl, or crystal, spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades and silken gauzes, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and upholstered with Kalinga-paveṭṭha and Pāṭaliputtaka cloth; this was where I usually lay."

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand palatial towers, there is one tower made of gold, or silver, or beryl, or crystal, named the Hall of Right Dharma (Saddharmaprāsāda), which is where I constantly reside."
“Bhikkhus! Among those eighty-four thousand great cities, there was one city that was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a vast population, named Kusāvatī; it was my constant dwelling place.”

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was one chariot adorned with many fine things, with the spotted skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, woven in variegated colors, and decorated in every way; it was extremely swift and named the 'Chariot of Delightful Sound. "Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was one horse with a body of deep blue-black, a head like that of a crow, named the King of Horses, Kanthaka. This was the one I constantly rode when I went to visit the Lumbinī Grove."

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand great elephants, there was one whose entire body was pure white and whose seven limbs were perfectly aligned; it was named the Elephant King Uposatha, whom I constantly rode when going to the Udena Park for recreation."
“Bhikkhus! I had this thought:

‘What is the fruit of this karma, what is the retribution of this karma, that causes me today to possess such great supernormal power, such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual authority?’”
"Monks! I further had this thought:

"Monks! If a learned noble disciple contemplates in this way, he becomes weary of form; he becomes weary of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. In this very life, he knows it for himself, realizes it for himself, and attains realization through his own direct experience, dwelling therein: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.

First Daily Recitation. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—exactly one thousand bhikṣus who were all free from attachment and had attained the state of Arhat. Originally, they had all worn matted hair; they proceeded toward Rājagṛha, a town in Magadha.

Thereupon, King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus—one thousand in number—all of whom were free from attachment and had attained the state of Arhat; they had all formerly been hair-tying ascetics and had now come to this city of Rājagṛha, a district of Magadha.

Having heard this, King Bimbisāra of Magadha immediately assembled his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having assembled these four divisions, he set out for the place where the Buddha was, accompanied by a vast multitude extending one yojana in length.

Then, the World-Honored One, seeing from afar King Bimbisāra of Magadha approaching, cleared a path and proceeded to the foot of the noble Nyagrodha tree king, where he spread out his sitting mat and sat down cross-legged together with the assembly of bhikṣus.

King Bimbisāra of Magadha saw from afar the World-Honored One among the trees, upright and beautiful, like the moon among the stars, radiant and brilliant, shining like a mountain of gold; endowed with the primary and secondary marks, majestic and sublime, his faculties serene and composed, free from all obstruction, perfected in self-mastery, his mind stilled in silent tranquility. Having seen him, he descended from his chariot.
If a Kṣatriya king, having been consecrated by the sprinkling of water upon his crown, attains the status of a sovereign and governs the great earth, he possesses five regalia:

first, a sword; second, a parasol; third, a celestial crown; fourth, a fly-whisk with a jeweled handle; and fifth, ornate sandals. Having set all these aside, as well as his fourfold army, he proceeds on foot to the Buddha.
Having arrived, he paid homage and three times announced his name and lineage:
"World-Honored One!
I am Seniya Bimbisāra, King of Magadha."
Thus it was repeated up to three times.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said:
“Great King!
"So it is, so it is. You are King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
Thereupon, after King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had three times declared his own name and lineage, he paid homage to the Buddha and sat down to one side.

Some of the people of Magadha prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; and some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat silently.
At that time, the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa was also seated in the assembly.
The Venerable Uruvela Kassapa was the one upon whom the people of Magadha relied; they regarded him as their great teacher, an Arhat free from attachment.
Thereupon, the people of Magadha all thought to themselves:
"Is the ascetic Gautama practicing the holy life under Uruvelā Kāśyapa,
or is Uruvelā Kāśyapa practicing the holy life under the ascetic Gautama?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, addressed the Venerable Uruvela Kāśyapa with these verses:
"Uruvela, what have you seen, That you have abandoned the fires and come here?"
Kāśyapa, tell me why you do not tend the sacrificial fire.
It is for the sake of various flavors of food and drink that one tends the fire;

Kāśyapa’s mind finds no pleasure in the various flavors of food and drink;

"Seeing the peace of cessation and extinction, Unconditioned and desiring no existence, There is no other deity more venerable; Therefore, I do not serve the sacrificial fire.
The World-Honored One is supreme; The World-Honored One has no perverse thoughts."
"Having understood and awakened to all phenomena, I have received the most supreme Dharma.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Kāśyapa!"
"You should now manifest your supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) so that this assembly may all attain faith and joy.

Thereupon, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa immediately performed such supernormal powers as he had envisioned: he vanished from his seat and appeared in the east, soaring through the air and manifesting the four modes of deportment—first walking, second standing, third sitting, and fourth reclining.

Furthermore, he entered the fire-concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). Fire issued from the lower part of his body while water issued from the upper part; fire issued from the upper part of his body while water issued from the lower part. The World-Honored One said: “It is so,

At that time, the Venerable Uruvela Kāśyapa, speaking on account of himself, uttered these verses:

"I have now seen the supreme track, taught by the Unsurpassed Dragon;
it is the unconditioned, the complete liberation from suffering. Having seen this, birth and death are exhausted.
When the people of Magadha saw this, they thought to themselves:
"The ascetic Gautama did not learn the holy life from Uruvela Kassapa; rather, it is Uruvela Kassapa who learns the holy life from the ascetic Gautama."

The Blessed One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, then preached the Dharma to King Bimbisāra of Magadha, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and establishing him in joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to preach the Dharma for him, and having exhorted, inspired, and established him in joy, [he continued].

In accordance with the Dharma of all Buddhas, he first taught the introductory Dharma, which brings joy to those who hear it—namely, the discourse on giving, the discourse on ethical discipline, and the discourse on rebirth in the heavens; he censured sensual desire as a calamity and birth-and-death as a defilement, and praised the absence of desire as the sublime path and the pure white factors. The World-Honored One expounded these for that great king.

The Buddha, already knowing that he possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a pliant mind, a patient mind, an uplifted mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free from doubt, and an inexhaustible mind, and that he was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma—namely, the essential teaching as spoken by all Buddhas—the World-Honored One then preached to him the Suffering, the Origin, the Cessation, and the Path.
“Great King!
Form arises and ceases; you should know the arising and ceasing of form.
Great King!”
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise and perish; you should understand, Great King, that these arise and perish.

"Great King!

"Great King!
If a son of noble family knows the arising and ceasing of form, he then knows that he will no longer give rise to future form."
"Great King!
If a son of noble family knows the arising and passing away of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, he then knows that consciousness will not arise again in the future.
Great King!"

"Great King!

"Great King!

If a son of noble family does not cling to form, does not reckon form, is not stained by form, does not dwell in form, and does not delight in form as being 'self,' then he will no longer undergo future form."
"Great King!

"Great King!
This son of noble family has attained immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless tranquility; once he has abandoned these five aggregates, he will no longer undergo further aggregates."
Thereupon, the people of Magadha thought to themselves:
"If form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, then who is it that lives?"
"Who experiences pleasure and pain?
The World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, addressed the bhikṣus:

"The foolish worldling, lacking what he has heard, perceives 'this is me' and clings to a self; yet there is no self and nothing belonging to a self—it is empty of a self and empty of anything belonging to a self."

When dharmas arise, they arise; when dharmas cease, they cease. All suffering arises from the convergence of causes and conditions; if causes and conditions are absent, all sufferings are extinguished.

Because sentient beings encounter and continue with causes and conditions, the various dharmas arise. Having seen that sentient beings arise through such continuity, the Tathāgata speaks thus: "There is birth and there is death.

With the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I see these sentient beings at the time of their death and at the time of their birth—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, whether excellent or inferior, and as they pass to good or bad destinations according to the karma performed by those sentient beings—I see this as it truly is."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish good conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and possess right view and perform deeds of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination, even unto the heavenly realms.

"I know this of them, yet I do not speak to them. This is my capacity for awakening, my capacity for speaking, my making of instruction, my making of instigation, and my teaching of instigation—namely, that in various places one experiences the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma.

Within this, there may be some who think: 'This is inconsistent; this cannot endure. Their conduct is according to the Dharma: because of this, that arises; if this cause were absent, that would not arise. Because of this, that exists; if this ceases, that likewise ceases.'"
