63. The Vepacitti Sutta (63). Middle Discourses, Chapter on Kings, The Vepacitti Sutta, the sixth, for the first day’s recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering through the kingdom of Kosala.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling along with a great assembly of bhikṣus; midway on the road, he smiled with joy.
Seeing the World-Honored One smile, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason do you smile?
Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas never smile without cause or condition;
we pray that you will explain its meaning.
At that time, the Blessed One said: "Ānanda!
In this very place, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa sat and taught the Dharma to his disciples."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda immediately prepared a seat at that spot, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

I pray only that the World-Honored One will also sit here and teach the Dharma to the disciples, so that this place may become a site frequented by two Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”
At that time, the Blessed One sat upon the seat prepared for him by the Venerable Ānanda at that very spot. Having sat down, he addressed him, saying: “Ānanda!”

In this place, there was a lecture hall belonging to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa; having sat therein, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa preached the Dharma to his disciples.
Ānanda! In this place there was formerly a village named Vebhaḷiṅga, which was extremely prosperous and pleasant, with a great many inhabitants. Ānanda!

In the village of Vebhaḷiṅga, there was a brahmin great householder named Aśoka (Unwrathful), who was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous; his assets were immeasurable, his livestock and enterprises beyond counting, and he possessed all manner of fiefs and manors.

Ānanda! The brahmin mahāsālā Aseṇa had a son named the young brahmin Uttara. He was highly esteemed by his parents, born of pure descent, and so on, up to: for seven generations back through both his paternal and maternal lines, his family lineage remained unbroken; in every birth he was free from evil. He was widely learned and possessed of total retention (*dhāraṇī*); he had recited the four Vedas and deeply mastered the five modes of exposition: causal analysis, conditional analysis, textual analysis, philological analysis, and etymological analysis.
Ānanda! The youth Uttara has a good friend named Nandipāla the potter, whom the youth Uttara always cherishes and loves, never wearying of seeing him.

“Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; he does not doubt the Triple Gem, nor is he deluded regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He has attained faith, maintains the precepts, possesses extensive learning, practices generosity, and has perfected wisdom. He abstains from killing and has severed killing; having laid aside the sword and staff, he is possessed of a sense of shame and dread of blame, and with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he benefits all beings down to the smallest insects. Thus, he has purified his mind of the taking of life.”

Ānanda! Nandipāla the potter abstains from taking what is not given; he has abandoned taking what is not given. He takes only what is given, delights in giving, is ever fond of bestowing gifts, rejoices without stinginess, and does not look for reward; thus, he purifies his mind regarding taking what is not given.

Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstained from unchaste conduct, abandoned unchaste conduct, and diligently cultivated chaste conduct; he was energetic in sublime practice, pure and stainless, free from desire and having severed lust; thus, regarding unchaste conduct, he purified his mind.

“Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from false speech and has abandoned false speech; he speaks the truth, delights in the truth, abides in the truth without wavering, is entirely trustworthy, and does not deceive the world; he has purified his mind regarding false speech.”

Ānanda! Nandipāla the potter abstains from divisive speech; he has abandoned divisive speech, practices non-divisive speech, and does not cause dissension. He does not repeat here what he has heard there with the intent to divide these people, nor does he repeat there what he has heard here with the intent to divide those people. He reconciles those who are divided and encourages those who are united; he does not form factions, does not delight in factions, and does not praise factions. Thus, he purifies his mind regarding divisive speech.
Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from harsh speech and has abandoned harsh speech.

Whatever words he utters that are coarse and rugged, foul-sounding and grating to the ear, unpleasant to the multitude, unloved by the multitude, causing others distress, and preventing them from attaining concentration—such speech he has abandoned.

If one speaks words that are clear, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; which are pleasing to the ear and enter the heart; which are delightful and lovely, bringing peace and happiness to others; whose speech is articulate and complete, causing no fear; and which enable others to attain concentration—speaking such words, one purifies the mind of coarse speech.
Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from frivolous speech and has abandoned frivolous speech.

He speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks according to the Dharma, speaks according to the meaning, speaks of tranquility, and speaks with a delight in tranquility. His words are timely, appropriate, well-instructive, and well-reproving; he purifies his mind of frivolous speech.

“Ānanda! Nandipāla the potter abstains from trade, has abandoned trade, has cast aside scales and measures, has discarded the acceptance of goods for sale, does not bind others in service, does not hope for short-measures or over-weighing, and does not deceive others with petty profits; he has purified his mind regarding trade.”

Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from accepting widows and young girls; he has renounced accepting widows and young girls, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of widows and young girls.

Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from accepting slaves and servants; he has abandoned the acceptance of slaves and servants, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of slaves and servants. Ānanda!

Nandipāla the potter abstains from accepting elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; he has renounced the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstains from accepting chickens and pigs; he has severed the acceptance of chickens and pigs, and he purifies his mind regarding the acceptance of chickens and pigs.
Ānanda! Nandīpāla the potter abstains from accepting fields and shops; he has severed the acceptance of fields and shops, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of fields and shops.

Ānanda! Nandīpāla the potter abstains from receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans; he has abandoned receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans, and he has purified his mind regarding the receiving of raw rice, wheat, and beans.
“Ānanda! Nandīpāla the potter abstains from liquor and has abandoned liquor; he has purified his mind regarding the drinking of intoxicants. Ānanda!”
Nanda the potter abstained from high and luxurious beds; he had renounced high and luxurious beds, and he purified his mind regarding high and luxurious beds. Ānanda!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from flower garlands, necklaces, scented ointments, and cosmetics; he has renounced flower garlands, necklaces, scented ointments, and cosmetics, and he has purified his mind regarding flower garlands, necklaces, scented ointments, and cosmetics.

Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla abstained from song, dance, actors, and performers, as well as going to see or hear them; he had abandoned song, dance, actors, and performers, and going to see or hear them, and he purified his mind regarding song, dance, actors, and performers, as well as going to see or hear them.

Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla has abstained from the enjoyment of precious objects of fine form and appearance, has severed the enjoyment of precious objects of fine form and appearance, and has purified his mind regarding the enjoyment of precious objects of fine form and appearance.

Ānanda! Nandīpāla the potter abstained from eating at improper times, having abandoned eating at improper times; he ate only once a day, did not eat at night, and practiced eating only during the prescribed time. In this way, he purified his mind regarding eating at improper times.

“Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla, for as long as he lives, keeps his hands away from the plow and the spade; he does not dig the earth himself, nor does he instruct others to do so. However, if there is soil from the collapse of a riverbank or soil disturbed by rats, he takes it to make vessels, sets them aside, and says to potential buyers:
‘If you have peas, rice, barley, large or small mung beans, pigeon peas, or mustard seeds, pour them into the vessel and take it with you as you please.’”
"Ānanda! The potter Nandipāla served his parents for as long as he lived. His parents were blind and relied entirely upon others; therefore, he served them."
“Ānanda! After the night had passed, at dawn, the potter Nandipāla went to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa was; having arrived, he paid homage and sat down to one side.”

The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, taught the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having taught the Dharma to him through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he remained silent.
"Ānanda!

Then, Nandipāla the potter, having been taught the Dharma by the Tathāgata Kassapa—the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One—who inspired him, roused his longing, and established him in joy, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Kassapa—the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One—and after circumambulating him three times, departed."

At that time, the youth Udāyin, riding in a white horse-drawn chariot together with five hundred youths, emerged from the village of Vebhaḷiṅga at dawn after the night had passed. He went to a secluded place, intending to instruct the various disciples who had come from many countries and have them read the Brahminical scriptures.
Then, the youth Uttara saw the potter Nandipāla coming from afar; having seen him, he asked: "Nandipāla!
Where are you coming from?"
Nandipāla replied:
"I have just come from making offerings and paying homage to the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Uttara! You should go with me to visit the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, to make offerings and pay him homage.
Thereupon, the youth Uttara replied:
"Nandipāla! I do not wish to see a shaven-headed śramaṇa; a shaven-headed śramaṇa cannot attain the Way, for the Way is difficult to attain.
Thereupon, Nandipāla the potter seized the topknot of the youth Udāyin and pulled him down from the carriage.
Thereupon, the youth Uttara thought to himself:
"This potter Nandipāla is never frivolous, nor is he mad or deluded; yet now he seizes me by the topknot of my hair—there must surely be a reason for this."
Having reflected thus, he said:
"Nandipāla! I shall go with you; I shall go with you."
Nandipāla Khāṇuvāsin replied, "It is very well that you go.

Thereupon, the potter Nandipāla went together with the youth Uttara to where the Tathāgata Kassapa—the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One—was staying. Having arrived, they paid their respects and sat down to one side.
The potter Nandipāla addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This youth Uttara is my friend; he always loves me and always delights in seeing me, never growing weary of it."
"He has no faith or reverence for the Blessed One; may the Blessed One please preach the Dharma well for him, so that he may become joyful and attain faith and reverence.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, preached the Dharma to the potter Nandipāla and the youth Uttara, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and bringing them to joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to preach the Dharma to them, exhorting, inspiring, and bringing them to joy, he remained silent.

Then, after the Tathāgata Kassapa—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—had taught the Dharma to the potter Nandipāla and the youth Uttara, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and bringing them to a state of joy, they rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata Kassapa—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—and departed after circumambulating him three times.
Then, before the youth Uttara had gone far, he asked, "Nandipāla!
Having heard such a subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa— the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— what is your intention for remaining at home?"
"Is it not possible to abandon [them] and train in the Noble Path?
Thereupon, the potter Nandipāla replied: "Uttara!"

"You yourself know that for as long as I live, I have made offerings to my parents; my parents were blind and relied solely upon others, and it was for the sake of making offerings to and serving my parents."
Thereupon, the youth Uttara asked Nandipāla:
"May I go forth from home under the Tathāgata Kāśyapa—the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—to study the Path; may I receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life?"

Thereupon, the potter Nandipāla and the youth Uttara went from that place back to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa was; having arrived, they paid their respects and sat down to one side.
The potter Nandipāla addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This youth Uttara has not gone far back when he asked me:..."
"Nandipāla! Having heard such a subtle and wondrous Dharma from the Tathāgata Kāśyapa—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—what is your intention in remaining at home?"
"Is it not possible to abandon them and train in the Noble Path?
"World-Honored One!
This is what I said to him:"

“Uttara! You yourself know that for as long as I live, I shall provide for my parents; for my parents are blind and rely entirely upon others, and it is for the sake of providing for and attending to my parents.”
Uttara asked me again: "Nandipāla!
May I go forth from the household life under the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, receive full ordination, become a bhikkhu, and practice the holy life?"
“I pray that the World-Honored One will deliver him, allowing him to leave the household life to study the Way, bestow upon him full ordination, and enable him to become a bhikṣu.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, silently accepted Nandipāla’s request.

Then, knowing that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa had accepted [the invitation] by remaining silent, the potter Nandipāla rose from his seat, prostrated himself in salutation, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Then, not long after Nandipāla had departed, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa ordained the youth Udāyin, granting him full ordination to enter the homeless life and study the Path.

Having conferred full ordination, he stayed for several days in the village of Veṭhadīpa. Then, taking up his robes and bowl, he set out on a journey together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, intending to go to the city of Kāśi in Vārāṇasī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at the city of Kāśi in Vārāṇasī and stayed in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.

Then, King Kikī heard that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa was wandering through the country of Kāsi with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and had arrived at this city of Vārāṇasī, staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
Having heard this, King Kiki said to his charioteer:
"Prepare the carriage; I now wish to go to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa."
Then, having received the King’s command, the charioteer immediately prepared the carriage.
Once the preparation was complete, he returned and addressed the King, saying:
"The fine carriage is ready; it is at Your Majesty’s disposal."
Thereupon, King Kiki, having mounted his fine chariot, departed from Vārāṇasī and proceeded to the Deer Park, the abode of the sages.

At that time, King Kikī saw from afar, amidst the trees, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa—exquisite and beautiful, like the moon among the stars; his radiance was brilliant and magnificent, shining like a mountain of gold; he was fully endowed with the primary and secondary marks, his majestic power was sublime, his faculties were tranquil and settled, free from all obstruction, having achieved mastery as a tamer, his mind at rest in profound silence.

Having seen him, he descended from his chariot and approached on foot the place where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa was; having arrived, he paid homage and withdrew to sit at one side.

Once King Kiki was seated to one side, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa taught him the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having taught him the Dharma through countless skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he remained silent.

Then, King Kiki, having been taught the Dharma by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa—having been inspired with longing and brought to a state of joy—rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, saying:
“I pray that the World-Honored One will graciously accept my invitation, together with the community of bhikṣus.”
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, accepted King Kikī’s invitation by remaining silent.

Thereupon, King Kikī, knowing that the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, had accepted by his silence, prostrated himself in salutation, circumambulated him three times, and departed to return to his home.

During that night, he prepared various kinds of most beautiful, pure, and exquisite foods—both solid and soft—to be chewed and swallowed; having completed the preparations by that very night, at dawn he spread out the seats and proclaimed:
"World-Honored One!..."
"The time has now arrived and the meal is prepared; we only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to visit us at this hour.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having passed the night, dressed in the early morning and took up his bowl. Attended by the assembly of bhikṣus, he proceeded to the residence of King Kiki and sat upon the seat prepared for him at the head of the assembly of bhikṣus.

Thereupon, King Kīṭāgira, seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were seated, personally provided water for washing. With his own hands, he served a variety of most excellent, pure, and exquisite foods—both solid and soft—in great abundance, until they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels had been cleared away, and after the water for washing had been offered, he spread out a small seat and sat apart to listen to the Dharma.

Once King Kapphiṇa was seated, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa taught him the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having taught him the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he remained silent.

Then, King Kiki, having been taught the Dharma by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa—having been inspired with longing and established in joy—rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for the summer retreat here in Vārāṇasī, together with the community of bhikṣus. I shall provide the World-Honored One with five hundred dwellings and five hundred couches and mats, and I shall offer *koccha* rice such as this white non-glutinous rice."
"The various flavors of the king's own food shall be used to feed the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, addressed King Kiki, saying: "Stop!
"Stop! Great King!
Be content in your heart alone."
King Kiki repeated this request a second and a third time, joining his palms in reverence toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, and said:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept my invitation for the summer retreat here in Vārāṇasī, together with the community of bhikṣus. I shall construct five hundred dwellings and five hundred beds and mattresses for the World-Honored One, and provide *kuñcikā* such as this white non-glutinous rice."
"The various flavors of the king's food shall be used to feed the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha also spoke to King Kiki a second and third time, saying: "Stop!
"Stop! Great King!
Be content in your heart alone."
Thereupon, King Kikī, unable to endure it and unwilling to accept it, was deeply distressed in mind, thinking:
"The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, cannot accept my invitation to observe the rains retreat here in Vārāṇasī, along with his community of bhikṣus."
Having thought this, King Kiki addressed the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps any other layperson in white robes who serves the World-Honored One as I do?”
Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, addressed King Kikī, saying:
"There is, within your realm, the village of Vebhaḷiṅga, which is exceedingly prosperous and joyful, and populated by many people."
"Great King!
In that village of Vebhaḷiṅga, there was a potter named Nandipāla.
Great King!"

The potter Nandipāla has taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks; he is without doubt regarding the Triple Gem and without confusion concerning suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. He has attained faith, maintains the precepts, possesses extensive learning, practices generosity, and has perfected wisdom. Having abandoned killing and severed the act of killing, he has laid aside the sword and staff; possessed of shame and remorse, he possesses a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, benefiting all beings down to the smallest insects, and has purified his mind of the taking of life.
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstained from taking what is not given; he abandoned taking what is not given. He took only what was given, delighted in taking what was given, always loved to practice giving, rejoiced without stinginess, and did not look for reward. Thus, he purified his mind regarding taking what is not given."
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla has abstained from unchaste conduct and severed unchaste conduct; he diligently cultivates the holy life, exerts himself in sublime practice, is pure and free from defilement, and having abandoned desire and cut off lust, he has purified his mind of unchaste conduct."
“Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from false speech and has abandoned false speech; he speaks the truth, delights in the truth, abides in the truth without wavering, is entirely trustworthy, and does not deceive the world; regarding false speech, he has purified his mind.”

"Great King! The potter Nandipāla abstains from divisive speech; he has abandoned divisive speech and practices non-divisiveness. He does not cause dissension among others. He does not repeat here what he has heard there with the intent to cause dissension among these people, nor does he repeat there what he has heard here with the intent to cause dissension among those people. He seeks to reconcile those who are divided and delights in the harmony of those who are united. He does not form factions, does not take pleasure in factions, and does not praise factions. Thus, he purifies his mind regarding divisive speech."
"Great King!
The potter Nandipāla is free from harsh speech and has abandoned harsh speech.

If there should be any utterance that is coarse and violent in tone, foul-sounding and grating to the ear, disliked by the multitude, unloved by the multitude, causing others distress, and preventing them from attaining concentration—he has abandoned such speech."

If one speaks words that are clear, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; which are pleasing to the ear and enter the heart; which are delightful and lovely; which bring peace and happiness to others; whose speech is articulate and complete; which do not cause fear in others; and which enable others to attain concentration—one speaks such words as these, thereby purifying the mind of harsh speech.
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla has abstained from frivolous speech and severed frivolous speech. He speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks according to the Dharma, speaks according to the meaning, speaks for the sake of tranquility, and speaks with delight in tranquility. His words are timely, appropriate, well-instructive, and well-reproving; he has purified his mind regarding frivolous speech."
“Great King!

The potter Nandipāla has abstained from trade and cut himself off from trade; he has discarded weights and measures, as well as receiving goods for barter, binding people with debt, seeking to over-measure or over-weight, and defrauding others of small profits; he has thus purified his mind regarding trade.”
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from accepting widows and young girls; he has severed the practice of accepting widows and young girls, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of widows and young girls."
"Great King!
The potter Nandipāla abstains from accepting slaves and servants; he has severed the acceptance of slaves and servants, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of slaves and servants.
Great King!"

Nandipāla the potter has abstained from accepting elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; he has renounced the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, and has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla has abstained from accepting chickens and pigs; he has severed the practice of accepting chickens and pigs, and he has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of chickens and pigs."
“Great King!
The potter Nandipāla abstains from receiving fields and shops; he has severed the practice of receiving fields and shops, and he has purified his mind regarding the receiving of fields and shops.”
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans; he has severed the practice of receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans, and has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of raw rice, wheat, and beans."
“Great King!
Nandipāla the potter abstains from liquor and has abandoned liquor; he has purified his mind regarding the drinking of liquor.
Great King!”
Nanda the potter, Great King, abstains from high and wide beds; he has abandoned high and wide beds, and he purifies his mind of them.
Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from garlands, jewelry, scents, and unguents; he has renounced garlands, jewelry, scents, and unguents, and he has purified his mind regarding garlands, jewelry, scents, and unguents.
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from song, dance, actors, and mimes, and from going to see or hear them; he has abandoned song, dance, actors, and mimes, and going to see or hear them, and he has purified his mind regarding song, dance, actors, and mimes, and going to see or hear them."
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla has abstained from the acceptance of gifts consisting of precious forms and images, has severed the acceptance of gifts consisting of precious forms and images, and has purified his mind regarding the acceptance of gifts consisting of precious forms and images."
"Great King!

The potter Nandipāla abstains from eating at improper times and has severed the habit of eating at improper times. He eats only once a day, does not eat at night, and trains in eating only at the proper time; he has purified his mind regarding eating at improper times."

“Great King! The potter Nandipāla has, for as long as he lives, kept his hands away from the plow and the spade; he does not dig the earth himself, nor does he instruct others to do so. Should there be soil from a crumbling riverbank or earth disturbed by rats, he takes it to fashion vessels which he sets aside. Then he says to potential buyers:
‘If you have peas, rice, barley, large or small mung beans, pigeon peas, or mustard seeds, pour them out and take the vessel with you, as you please.’”
"Great King!
The potter Nandipāla served his parents for as long as he lived. His parents were blind and relied entirely upon others; therefore, he served them."
"Great King! I recall that in the past, I was traveling through dependence upon the village of Vebhaḷiṅga.
Great King!"

At that time, at dawn, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the village of Vebhaḷiṅga to beg for food. Proceeding from house to house in due order, I went to the home of the potter Nandipāla.
At that time, Nandipāla had gone out on some minor business and was away.
Great King!
I asked the parents of the potter Nandipāla, saying:
"Elder! Where is the potter now?
He replied to me:
“World-Honored One!
The attendant has gone out for a minor matter and is temporarily away. Sugata!”
"Your attendant has gone out briefly on a small errand and is not present.
World-Honored One!
There is barley rice in the basket and bean soup in the cauldron; we only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will take what you please."
"Great King!
I then accepted the custom of Uttarakuru and took the rice-soup from the basket and the pot before departing.
"Later, when the potter Nandipāla returned home, he saw that the rice in the basket was diminished and the soup in the pot had decreased. He said to his parents: "
“Who is taking the soup and rice?
His parents replied,
“O virtuous son!”
"Today the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has come here for alms; he has taken rice and soup from this basket and pot and departed.
Upon hearing this, the potter Nandipāla thought to himself:
"I have gained a great benefit and possess great merit, for the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has been at ease and at his own disposal within my home."

Filled with this joy, he sat cross-legged, his mind stilled and silent for seven days; within fifteen days he attained great bliss, and his parents at home also experienced great bliss during those seven days.
"Furthermore, Great King!
I recall that in the past, I was wandering in dependence upon the village of Vebhaḷiṅga.
Great King!"

At that time, at dawn, I put on my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the village of Vebhaḷiṅga to beg for food. Proceeding from house to house in due order, I went to the home of the potter Nandipāla.
At that time, Nandipāla was away on some minor business.
Great King!
I asked the parents of the potter Nandipāla, saying:
"Elder! Where is the potter now?
He replied to me, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The attendant has gone out for a moment on a minor errand and is not present. Sugata!”
"Venerable One, the attendant has gone out briefly on a small errand and is not present.
Venerable One, there is boiled rice in the large cauldron and soup in the small cauldron; we pray that for the sake of your compassion, the World-Honored One will take as you please."
"Great King!
I then adopted the practice of Uttarakuru; I simply took the soup and rice from the large and small pots.
"Later, when the potter Nandipāla returned home, he saw that the rice in the large pot was diminished and the soup in the small pot had decreased. He said to his parents:"
“Who took the rice from the large cauldron and the soup from the small cauldron?
His parents replied,
“Worthy son!”
Today the Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, came here to beg for alms; he took the soup and rice from the large and small cauldrons and departed.
Having heard this, the potter Nandipāla thought to himself:
"I have gained a great benefit and possess great merit, for the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One, has come to my home and dwells there at his own pleasure."

Filled with such joy, he sat cross-legged, his mind stilled and silent for seven days; he experienced delight throughout fifteen days, and his parents at home likewise experienced delight for seven days.
"Furthermore, Great King!
I recall that in the past, I observed the rains retreat in dependence upon the village of Vebhaḷiṅga.
Great King!"
"At that time, my newly built house was not yet roofed, while Nandipāla the potter’s old pottery house had been newly roofed.
Great King!
I said to the attendant bhikṣu:"
"You all may go and demolish the old pottery kiln of the potter Nandipāla, and bring [the materials] here to cover my house.

The attendant bhikṣus immediately accepted my instruction; they went at once to the home of the potter Nandipāla, tore down the old pottery kiln, bundled the materials together, and brought them back to use for covering my house.
When the parents of the potter Nandipāla heard that his old pottery shed had been destroyed, they asked:
"Who has destroyed the old pottery shed of Nandipāla?"
The bhikkhus replied, "Venerable sir!

We are the attendant bhikkhus of the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. We have dismantled this potter’s workshop of Nandipāla the potter to use the materials for binding and roofing the dwelling of the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
Nandipāla’s parents said:
“Venerable ones!
Take it as you please; there is no one to restrain you.”
“Later, when the potter Nandipāla returned home, he saw that his old pottery shed had been pulled down and ruined.
He said to his parents, ‘Who has pulled down my old pottery shed?’”
The parents replied:
"Worthy son!

Today, the bhikkhus attending upon the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, tore down an old clay hut and carried away the bundles to use for covering the dwelling of the Tathāgata Kassapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Having heard this, the potter Nandipāla thought to himself:
"I have gained a great benefit and possess great merit, for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa—the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—has come to my home and dwells there at his own pleasure."

Filled with this joy, he sat cross-legged, his mind stilled and silent for seven days; he experienced great delight for fifteen days, and his parents at home also experienced great delight for seven days.
“Great King!
The old pottery workshop of the potter Nandipāla did not suffer from any leaks throughout the entire four months of the summer rains. Why was this? Because...”
"By the power of the Buddha's majestic authority,
O Great King,
the potter Nandipāla felt no impatience, no reluctance, and his heart was free from sorrow."
“Kāśyapa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has been dwelling at his own will and ease within my home.
Great King! You have found it unbearable; you do not desire this, and your heart is filled with great sorrow.”
“The Tathāgata Kāśyapa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has not accepted my invitation, but has instead accepted the rains retreat here in Vārāṇasī, together with the community of bhikṣus.”

Thereupon, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa taught the Dharma to King Kiki, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and bringing him to a state of joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to teach him the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he rose from his seat and departed.
"At that time, not long after the departure of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa—the Arhat, the Fully Enlightened One—King Kikī commanded his attendants:
'You should load five hundred wagons with white non-glutinous rice and all kinds of flavors for the King’s food, and transport them to the home of the potter Nandipāla, and say to him: "Nandipāla!'"

"These five hundred wagons are filled with white non-glutinous rice and various flavors for the King’s own consumption; King Kapphiṇa has sent them as a gift to you out of compassion, so you should now accept them."

Then, having received the king’s command, the attendant filled five hundred wagons with white non-glutinous rice and various kinds of delicacies for the king’s consumption, and sent them to the potter’s house at Nandipāla.
Having arrived, he said:
"Nandipāla, potter!

These five hundred carts are filled with white non-glutinous rice and various delicacies for the king’s consumption, sent by King Kikī as a gift for you out of compassion; you should now accept them."
Thereupon, the potter Nandipāla declined and would not accept, saying to his attendant:
"Venerable sirs!
The royal house of the Śākyas has many great affairs of state and extensive expenditures; I am aware of this, and for that reason I will not accept."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What do you think?
Do you consider that the youth Uttara at that time was someone else?"
Do not harbor such a thought; you should know that it was I myself. Ānanda!

At that time, for my own benefit, and for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, I sought what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate conclusion; it was not ultimately pure, nor was the holy life (brahmacarya) brought to its ultimate conclusion.
At that time, one was not yet free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had one yet attained liberation from all suffering.

Ānanda! I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One. I now bring benefit to myself and also benefit others; I bring benefit to many, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is righteous and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
I have now taught the Dharma that reaches the ultimate, which is ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life; the ultimate holy life has been fulfilled.
I am now free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth *Vepacitti Sūtra* ends here, totaling 5,734 characters. 64. The Discourse on the Divine Messengers (64) The Seventh Discourse on the Divine Messengers in the *Rāja-saṃyukta-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. First Day’s Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, whether they are sublime or not, and as they pass away from or go toward good or bad destinations. I see them, exactly as they truly are, according to the karma these beings have performed.”

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a state of misery and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish the karma of right view—then by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens.
"Just as when it rains heavily, bubbles arise and perish upon the water, and a person with sight standing in one place observes them as they arise and perish;

so too do I, with the pure divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether of beautiful or ugly appearance, whether sublime or not, passing away from or being reborn in good or bad destinations—and I see this truly, according to the karma performed by each of these beings."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, speech, and mind; have reviled the noble ones; and, holding wrong views, have accomplished the karma of wrong views—then by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish karma of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
"Just as when it rains heavily, the drops of rain fall either upward or downward, and a person with eyes standing in one place observes them as they rise and fall;

so too do I, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, and whether they pass away from or are reborn in good or bad destinations—and I see this truly, according to the karma performed by each being."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they have reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish the karma of right view—then by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in a heavenly realm.
"It is like a lapis lazuli gem, pure by its very nature, born without flaw or impurity, with eight facets well-polished, strung upon a wondrous cord that may be blue, yellow, red, black, or white."

Suppose there were a person with sight who, standing in one place, observed this lapis lazuli bead: it is naturally pure and free from blemish, well-polished into eight facets, and strung upon a fine cord that is either blue, yellow, red, black, or white.

In the same way, I—with the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans—see these beings as they die and are reborn: their beautiful and ugly forms, their excellent and inferior states, and their passing to good or bad destinations; I see them exactly as they are, according to the karma these beings have performed.

If these sentient beings accomplish evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; revile the noble ones; hold wrong views and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will inevitably go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish karmic actions of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens.
"Just as two houses share a single door through which many people enter and exit,
and a person with sight stands in one place observing them as they come out and go in;

so too do I, with the pure divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings at the time of their death and birth— whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, sublime or not sublime, and whether they proceed to a good destination or an evil destination— and I see them truly according to the karma these beings have performed."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and possess right view and perform deeds of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
"Just as a person with sight standing atop a high tower observes people below coming and going, moving about, sitting, lying down, walking, or leaping;

so too do I, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings at the time of their death and birth—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, excellent or inferior, and whether they go to good or bad destinations—seeing them truly according to the karma performed by those beings."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish karmic actions of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a good destination and be born in the heavenly realms.

"If there are beings born among humans who are unfilial toward their parents, who do not know how to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, who do not practice according to reality, who do not perform meritorious deeds, and who do not fear the retribution of future worlds—due to these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the realm of King Yama."
The messengers of King Yama arrest and escort the being to the King’s presence, reporting:

"O Heavenly King! When this being was formerly a human, he was unfilial toward his parents; he did not know how to revere śramaṇas and brahmins; he did not act according to reality; he did not perform meritorious deeds; and he did not fear the retribution of future lives. We pray only that the Heavenly King shall adjudicate his offense."
"Then, King Yama, with the first divine messenger, questioned him well, examined him well, instructed him well, and rebuked him well:
'Have you ever seen the first divine messenger come? "
That person replied:
"I do not see them,
O Heavenly King!"
King Yama asked again:

"Have you never seen in a village or town a boy or girl, a small infant, whose body is weak and tender, lying on its back in its own excrement and urine, unable to speak to its parents? Have you not seen the parents take the child in their arms and move it away from the place of impurity, bathing its body to make it clean?"
That person replied,
“I have seen them,
Your Majesty!”
King Yama asked again:
"When you later regained your consciousness, why did you not think:
'I am subject to the nature of birth and cannot escape it; therefore, I ought to perform sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind'?"
That person replied:
"O Heavenly King!
Am I utterly ruined, to suffer long-term decline and eternal loss?"
King Yama said: "You have come to ruin and destruction;

you suffer long-term decline and eternal loss. Now I shall examine you as one treats those of negligent conduct and negligent persons. This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by kings, nor by devas, nor was it wrought by śramaṇas or brahmins; you yourself originally committed these evil and unwholesome deeds."
"Therefore, you must now certainly undergo retribution.

Having thus questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with these words regarding the first divine messenger, King Yama further questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with the second divine messenger:
"Have you ever seen the second divine messenger come?"
That person replied:
"I do not see them,
O Heavenly King!"
King Yama asked again:

"Did you not previously see, within a village or town, men or women who were aged and extremely old, whose lives had reached their ultimate limit and whose end was near, with fallen teeth and white hair, bodies bent and stooped, walking while leaning on a staff, and trembling?"
That person replied:
"I have seen them,
O Heavenly King!"
King Yama asked again:
"When you later regained consciousness, why did you not think:
'I am subject to the law of aging and cannot escape it; I ought to practice sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind'?"
That person replied:
"O Great King!
Am I utterly ruined, forever declined, and eternally lost?"
King Yama said: "You have come to ruin and destruction;

you suffer long-term decline and eternal loss. Now I shall examine you as one treats those of negligent conduct and negligent persons. This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by kings, nor by devas, nor by śramaṇas or brahmins; it was originally committed by you yourself through your own evil and unwholesome deeds."
"Therefore, you must now certainly undergo retribution.

Having thus questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with this second divine messenger, King Yama further questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with the third divine messenger:
"Have you ever seen the third divine messenger arrive?"
That person replied:
"I do not see them,
O Heavenly King!"
King Yama asked again:

"Have you never seen in a village or town men or women who were gravely ill and bedridden—whether lying on a couch, a bed, or the bare ground—suffering extreme and heavy pains that are loathsome and cause their lives to be cut short?"
That person replied:
"I have seen them,
O Heavenly King!"
King Yama asked again:
"When you later possessed the capacity for discernment, why did you not think:
'I am subject to the nature of illness and cannot escape it; I ought to perform sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind'?"
That person replied:
"O Heavenly King!
Am I utterly ruined, to suffer long-term decline and eternal loss?"

King Yama said: "You have come to ruin and destruction; you suffer long-term decline and eternal loss. Now I shall examine you, as one treats those of negligent conduct and negligent persons. This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by the king, nor by the devas, nor was it wrought by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself originally committed these evil and unwholesome deeds; therefore, you must now inevitably undergo their retribution."

"Having thus questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with this third divine messenger, King Yama further questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with the fourth divine messenger:
'Have you ever seen the fourth divine messenger come? "
That person replied,
"I do not see them, O Deva!'"
King Yama asked again:

"Have you never seen in a village or town a man or a woman at the time of death, after one or two days, up to six or seven days, being pecked by crows and vultures or devoured by jackals and wolves; or being burned with fire, or buried in the ground, or becoming putrid and decayed?"
That person replied,
“I have seen them,
O Heavenly King!”
King Yama asked again:
"When you later possessed the capacity for discernment, why did you not form this thought:
'I am subject to death and cannot escape it; I ought to perform sublime deeds of body, speech, and mind'?"
That person replied:
"O Heavenly King!
Am I utterly ruined, forever declining and lost for all eternity?"

King Yama said: "You have come to ruin and destruction; you are long-decayed and forever lost. Now I shall examine you, as one examines those of negligent conduct and negligent persons. This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by the king, nor by the devas, nor was it wrought by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself originally committed these evil and unwholesome deeds; therefore, you must now surely undergo their retribution."

"Having thus questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with this fourth divine messenger, King Yama again questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him well with the fifth divine messenger:
'Have you ever seen the fifth divine messenger come? "
That person replied:
"I do not see them,
Your Majesty!"
King Yama asked again:

"Did you not originally see the king’s officers seize criminals and subject them to various forms of torture and punishment—cutting off their hands, cutting off their feet, or cutting off both hands and feet;
cutting off their ears, cutting off their noses, or cutting off both ears and noses; or..."
They are cut into pieces; their whiskers are plucked out, their hair is plucked out, or both whiskers and hair are plucked out;
they are placed inside a wooden cage and wrapped in cloth before being burned with fire; or they are covered with sand and bound in grass before being burned with fire;
or they are thrust into the belly of an iron donkey, or placed in the mouth of an iron pig, or set within the mouth of an iron tiger to be burned, or placed inside a copper cauldron.
Some are boiled in iron cauldrons; some are cut into pieces; some are pierced with sharp forks; some are hooked with hooks;
some lie upon iron beds drenched with boiling oil; some sit in iron mortars and are pounded with iron pestles;
some are bitten by dragons, snakes, and vipers; some are whipped with whips; some are struck with staves; and some are beaten with clubs.
"Is he being beaten, or impaled on a high stake, or has his head been decapitated?
That person replied,
"I have seen it."
"O Heavenly King!
Yama the King asked again:
"When you later regained consciousness, why did you not think this?"
"I now clearly see evil and unwholesome states.
That person replied:
"O Great King!"
"Am I utterly ruined, fallen into long-term decline,
and lost forever? King Yama replied,
"You are utterly ruined, fallen into long-term decline, and lost forever."

I shall now examine you, as one examines those who act with negligence and those who are negligent. This evil karma of yours was not created by your parents, nor by the king, nor by the devas, nor was it created by śramaṇas or brahmins. You yourself originally committed these evil and unwholesome deeds; therefore, you must now inevitably undergo their retribution.
"Having thus properly questioned, examined, instructed, and rebuked him with this fifth divine messenger, King Yama hands him over to the wardens.
The wardens then seize him and cast him into the Great Hell of Four Gates. Thereupon, a verse says:
'Four pillars and four gates, Walls square with twelve edges.'"
With iron walls surrounding it, its surface covered with iron;
the ground within the hell is of iron, spread over with blazing iron fires,
extending for immeasurable *yojanas* deep down to the very bottom of the earth.
Extremely evil and unbearable, its fiery color difficult to behold;
upon seeing it, the hair on one's body stands on end, and one is seized by such intense fear and suffering.
That person falls into the earth-hell, with feet upward and head downward.
“They slandered the noble ones, those who are well-tamed, virtuous, and pure.
Then, after a very long time had passed, for the sake of those sentient beings, the eastern gate of the great four-gated hell opened.

Once the eastern gate has opened, those sentient beings run toward it, seeking a place of peace and a refuge. When they have gathered there in numbers of hundreds of thousands, the eastern gate of the hell closes again by itself. Therein they undergo extreme suffering, wailing and crying out, their hearts oppressed as they lie prostrate on the ground; yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.
After an extremely long time, the south gate, west gate, and north gate open again.

Once the north gate has opened, those sentient beings run toward it, seeking a place of peace and a refuge. When they have gathered there in numbers of hundreds of thousands, the north gate of the hell closes once more. Therein they undergo extreme suffering; weeping and crying out, their hearts are oppressed as they lie upon the ground, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

“Furthermore, after a very long period of time has passed, those sentient beings emerge from the great hell with four gates and are reborn in the Hell of Rocky Peaks (Śiloccaya), which arises adjacent to the great hell with four gates. Fire fills its interior, smokeless and flameless, causing them to walk upon it, coming and going and circling about.”
The skin, flesh, and blood of his two feet are completely exhausted when he sets them down, yet they regenerate when he lifts them, returning to their former state.
He is treated in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet he never dies until that evil and unwholesome karma is fully exhausted.

“Furthermore, after a very long period of time has passed, those sentient beings emerge from the Peak Rock Great Hell and are reborn in the Subsequent Excrement Great Hell, which is filled with excrement to a depth of immeasurable hundreds of fathoms.”

All those sentient beings fall into it; within that Great Hell of Excrement, many worms are born. These worms are named *Aṅgulika*; their bodies are white and their heads are black, and their snouts are like needles. These worms bore through the feet of those sentient beings. Having broken their feet, they break the bones of the calves and thighs. Having broken the bones of the calves and thighs, they break the hip bones. Having broken the hip bones, they break the spinal vertebrae. Having broken the spinal vertebrae, they break the shoulder blades, the neck bones, and the skull. Having broken the skull, they devour the brain entirely.
Those sentient beings are thus oppressed for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma has been exhausted.

“Furthermore, after a very long period of time has passed, those sentient beings emerge from the Great Hell of Excrement and Feces and are reborn in the Great Hell of the Forest of Iron Sheets. Upon seeing it, they conceive the notion that it is cool and think to themselves:
‘Let us go there; we shall find refreshing coolness.’”
Those sentient beings run toward it, seeking a place of safety and a refuge; once they have gathered in numbers of hundreds of thousands, they enter the great hell of the Iron-Plate Forest.

In that great hell of the Iron-Plate Forest, hot winds blow from the four directions; when these hot winds blow, the iron plates fall away. As the iron plates fall, they sever hands, sever feet, or sever both hands and feet; they sever ears, sever noses, or sever ears, noses, and other limbs and joints. Thus, with their bodies severed and smeared with blood, they undergo extreme suffering for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

Furthermore, within that great Avīci hell of the Iron Sheets, there arise enormous dogs with extremely long fangs; they seize those sentient beings and, starting from the feet, flay their skin down to the head and devour them, or starting from the head, flay their skin down to the feet and devour them.
Those sentient beings are thus tormented for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma has been exhausted.

Furthermore, within that great Avīci hell of the Iron Sheets, there arise large crows with two heads and iron beaks; they perch upon the foreheads of sentient beings, plucking out their eyes to swallow them, and pecking through the skull to take and eat the brains.
Those sentient beings are thus oppressed for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma has been exhausted.

"Furthermore, after a very long time has passed, those sentient beings emerge from the Great Hell of the Iron-Plated Forest (Ayastambāraṇya). Next, they are born into the Great Hell of the Iron-Sword Tree Forest (Asipatravana). Those great sword trees are one yojana in height, with thorns sixteen inches long. They cause those sentient beings to climb up and down them; when they climb the tree, the thorns point downward, and when they descend the tree, the thorns point upward."

Those sword-tree thorns pierce and impale sentient beings—piercing their hands, piercing their feet, or piercing both hands and feet; piercing their ears, piercing their noses, or piercing their ears, noses, and other limbs and joints. Pierced by these, their bodies are smeared with blood for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering without ever dying, until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted.

Furthermore, after a very long time has passed, those sentient beings emerge from the great hell of the Forest of Iron Swords. Immediately following the great hell of the Forest of Iron Swords, they are born in the River of Ashes (*kṣāranadī*), whose banks are exceedingly high and covered all over with thorns, and which is filled with boiling ash-water. It is pitch-black within; having seen it, those sentient beings conceive the notion that it is cool water and think, "There must be cool water here."
Having formed this perception, they then thought:
"Let us go there, bathe therein, drink our fill at will, and enjoy refreshing coolness."

Those sentient beings run toward it in competition and enter within, seeking a place of happiness and a refuge. Once they have gathered there in immeasurable hundreds of thousands, they then fall into the Ash River (Kṣāranadī).

Having fallen into the Ash River, they go with the current, against the current, or both with and against the current; as those sentient beings go with the current, against the current, or both with and against the current, their skin matures and falls away, their flesh matures and falls away, or their skin and flesh mature and fall away simultaneously, leaving only the skeletal framework remaining.

On both banks of the Ash River dwell hell-wardens who hold in their hands swords, great clubs, and iron forks; when those sentient beings attempt to cross over to the shore, the wardens then push them back into the midst of the river.

"Furthermore, on both banks of the Ash River (Kṣāranadī) there are hell-wardens who, grasping hooks and nooses in their hands, hook and pull sentient beings out from the Ash River and place them upon a ground of glowing red-hot iron that blazes with intense heat. They seize those beings and violently throw them down upon the ground, where they roll about, while the wardens ask them:
'From where have you come?'"
Those sentient beings all answered together, saying, "We do not know where we have come from; we are currently afflicted only by great hunger.

Then the hell-wardens seize those beings and place them upon glowing, fiercely burning iron beds, forcing them to sit upon them. They pry open their mouths with glowing, fiercely burning iron tongs and thrust glowing, fiercely burning iron balls into their mouths.

That glowing iron ball burns the lips; having burned the lips, it burns the tongue; having burned the tongue, it burns the gums; having burned the gums, it burns the throat; having burned the throat, it burns the heart; having burned the heart, it burns the large intestine; having burned the large intestine, it burns the small intestine; having burned the small intestine, it burns the stomach; and having burned the stomach, it passes out through the lower part of the body.
Thus they are tormented for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma has been exhausted.
"Furthermore, the hell-wardens ask the sentient beings:
'Where do you wish to go?
The sentient beings reply:"
"We do not know where we are being led; we suffer only from great thirst.

Then those hell-wardens seize the beings and place them upon a glowing iron bed, blazing with intense heat, forcing them to sit upon it. With hot iron tongs, they pry open their mouths and pour boiling molten copper into them. That boiling molten copper burns their lips; having burned the lips, it burns the tongue; having burned the tongue, it burns the gums; having burned the gums, it burns the throat; having burned the throat, it burns the heart; having burned the heart, it burns the large intestine; having burned the large intestine, it burns the small intestine; having burned the small intestine, it burns the stomach; and having burned the stomach, it passes out through the lower part of the body.
Thus they are tormented for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, undergoing extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma has been fully exhausted.

"If those sentient beings have not entirely exhausted their evil and unwholesome karma in hell, nor completely exhausted it without remainder, those sentient beings will again fall into the River of Ashes; they will again go up and down in the Great Hell of the Forest of Iron Sword-Blades, again enter the Great Hell of the Iron Shards Forest, again fall into the Great Hell of Excrement, again come and go within the Great Hell of Rocky Peaks, and again enter the Great Hell with Four Gates."

If those sentient beings have completely exhausted all their evil and unwholesome karmas of the hells—exhausted them entirely without remainder—then thereafter they may enter among animals, fall among hungry ghosts, or be born among the devas.

If those sentient beings were formerly human beings who were unfilial toward their parents, did not know how to respect śramaṇas and brahmins, did not practice according to reality, did not perform meritorious deeds, and did not fear the retribution of future lives, they receive such unpleasant, disagreeable, and joyless bitter retribution, just as it is within that hell.

If those beings were originally human, they were filial and obedient toward their parents, knew how to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, practiced deeds in accordance with reality, performed meritorious karmic actions, and feared the retribution of future worlds; thus they receive such desirable, praiseworthy, and delightful rewards, as if within the celestial palaces of the deities of space.
"Formerly, King Yama was in his garden pavilion and made this vow:
'When my life here ends, may I be reborn among human beings.

May I be born into a noble family of extreme wealth and happiness, possessing immeasurable assets and livestock and industries beyond counting, fully endowed with fiefs, food-supply villages, and all manner of things.'"
What are they? They are the great clans of Kṣatriyas, the great clans of Brahmins, and the great clans of householders.

Or, there may be other such clans that are exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable assets and livestock and industries beyond calculation, fully endowed with various fiefs and food-grant villages; one is born into such a family.

Once born, his faculties were matured; he attained pure faith in the True Dharma and Discipline taught by the Tathāgata. Having attained pure faith, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep conviction left the home life for homelessness to study the Path. As for the son of noble family who shaves his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep conviction leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path—he brings the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion, realizing it for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, attaining realization and dwelling therein: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
"In the past, King Yama was in his garden pavilion and made this vow, uttering these verses:
'When one is rebuked by the messengers of heaven, Because that person was formerly heedless,
They shall suffer grief throughout the long night, Being shrouded by base desires.'"
Rebuked by the celestial messengers, truly there are superior persons who will never again be negligent;
they skillfully expound the wondrous and noble Dharma.
Seeing that the messengers cause terror, they seek the end of birth and old age.
When there is no further remainder of feeling, birth and old age are brought to an end.
Having reached secure bliss, one attains parinirvāṇa in this very life;
having crossed over all terrors, one also crosses over the world’s flood.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Discourse on the Parable of the Crows (65). Middle Āgama, Chapter on Kings, First: The Discourse on the Parable of the Crows. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, when a Wheel-Turning King wished to test his jewel-treasure, he would assemble the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having assembled these four forces, he would set up a tall banner in the darkness of night and place the jewel upon it. He would then go out to the park for inspection; the radiance of the jewel would illuminate the fourfold army, and the extent of its light would reach half a yojana in every direction."
At that time, there was a brahmin who thought to himself:
"I should go to see the Wheel-turning King and his fourfold army, and observe the lapis lazuli gem."
At that time, the brahmin again had this thought:
"Setting aside for now the sight of the Wheel-Turning King and his fourfold army, and even the observation of the lapis lazuli gem, I would rather go to that forest grove."
Thereupon, the brahmin went to the forest; having arrived and entered it, he went beneath a tree and sat down. Not long after he had sat, a water-fox came along.
Seeing it, the brahmin asked: "Welcome, water-fox!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"

"This pond was originally overflowing with clear spring water, abounding in lotus roots and many flowers, and filled with fish and turtles; it was my former place of reliance, yet now it is parched and withered.
O Brahmin, you should know this!"
"I wish to depart and enter that great river; I now desire to go, yet I fear only man.
Then, having finished this discussion with the brahmin, the otter left, while the brahmin remained sitting as before.
Furthermore, a *kumma* bird arrived; having seen it, the brahmin asked:
"Welcome, *kumma* bird!
From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?"
He replied: "Brahmin!

This pond was originally overflowing with clear spring water, abundant with lotus roots and many flowers, and filled with fish and turtles; it was that upon which I formerly relied, yet now it has withered away."
"Brahmin, you should know!

I wish to depart and dwell in dependence upon a place where dead oxen are gathered, or in dependence upon dead donkeys, or in dependence upon a place where dead people are gathered; I now wish to go, fearing only human beings."
After the *kumma* bird had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed, and the brahmin remained seated as before.
Then another vulture came; seeing it, the brahmin asked: "Welcome, vulture!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"

"I have come from one great cemetery to another, killing and coming; I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, dead horses, dead oxen, and the flesh of dead humans. I now wish to depart, fearing only man."
At that time, after the vulture had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed, while the brahmin remained seated as before.
Then, a bird that eats vomit came along; seeing it, the brahmin asked:
"Welcome, bird that eats vomit!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
"Did you see that vulture depart just now?
I fed upon its vomit; I wish to leave now, but I fear only man.
After this bird that feeds on vomit had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed, while the brahmin remained sitting as before.
"Furthermore, a jackal came along; having seen it, the brahmin asked: 'Welcome, jackal!
From where have you come, and where do you intend to go?'"
He replied: "Brahmin!

I have come from deep ravine to deep ravine, from thicket to thicket, and from secluded place to secluded place. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, dead horses, dead oxen, and the flesh of dead humans; I am now about to depart, fearing only man."
At that time, after the jackal had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed and left, while the brahmin remained seated as before.
Then a crow came; seeing it, the brahmin asked: "Welcome, O crow!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
"You are a stubborn, deluded fool;
why do you ask me, 'From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
" At that time, having rebuked the brahmin with these harsh words, the Crow-Faced One departed, while the brahmin remained seated as before.
Furthermore, a śarabha deer came along; having seen it, the brahmin asked it:
"Welcome, śarabha deer!
Where have you come from, and where do you intend to go?"
He replied: "Brahmin!
I have come from garden to garden, from pavilion to pavilion, and from grove to grove, drinking clear spring water and eating fine fruits. I now wish to depart; I am not afraid of people."
"After that śarabha beast had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I have told this parable desiring to make its meaning understood; you should know that this teaching possesses a profound significance."
Then, having finished this discussion with the brahmin, the otter departed.
What is the meaning of this parable that I have spoken? Suppose there is a bhikkhu who dwells near a village or town;

at dawn, he puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village for alms. He does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. Yet he preaches the Dharma—whether spoken by the Buddha or spoken by a disciple—and thereby gains profit in the form of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various articles of daily life. Having obtained these gains, he becomes stained by them, becomes attached to them, fails to see their peril, and is unable to relinquish them; he uses them according to his own whims.

That bhikṣu practices evil precepts and accomplishes evil dharmas; he stands at the very extreme, born of corruption and decay. Not being a brahmacārin, he claims to be a brahmacārin; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa. It is just as when a brahmin sees a otter and asks it: "Welcome, otter!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
This pond was originally overflowing with clear springs, abundant in lotus roots and flowers, and filled with fish and turtles; it was my former refuge, yet now it is parched and withered.
O Brahmin, you should know this!
"I wish to leave and enter that great river; I now wish to go, yet I fear only man.

I say that it is the same for a bhikṣu who enters into evil, unwholesome, and defiled states—those which are the basis for future existence, the causes of feverish suffering, and the roots of birth, aging, sickness, and death. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like otters, and do not rely on what is contrary to the Dharma to sustain your lives.

You should purify your conduct of body, speech, and mind; dwell in non-action; wear rag-robes; always practice alms-gathering, begging from house to house in regular order; be of few desires and content; delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence; establish right mindfulness, right clear comprehension, right concentration, and right wisdom; and you should always remain detached, training yourselves in this way.
“After that *kumma* bird had finished this discussion with the brahmin, it departed.
What is the meaning of this parable I have told?

If there is a bhikkhu who dwells in dependence upon a village or town, and at dawn he puts on his robes and takes his bowl to enter the village for alms, yet he does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness; and if he enters the homes of others to teach and preach the Dharma—whether spoken by the Buddha or spoken by the disciples—and thereby obtains gain consisting of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites for life; and having obtained such gain, he becomes stained by attachment, relishes it, fails to see its peril, and is unable to relinquish it, using it according to his own whims. This is the meaning.”

That bhikṣu, possessing bad precepts and accomplished in evil dharmas, stands at the very extreme; he is born into corruption and decay. Not practicing the holy life, he claims to practice the holy life; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa. It is just as when a brahmin sees a *kaumāra* and asks him: "Welcome, *kaumāra*!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"

This pond was originally overflowing with clear springs, abundant in lotus roots and flowers, and filled with fish and turtles; it was that upon which I formerly relied, yet now it has withered and parched.
O Brahmin, you should know this!
I now wish to depart and dwell for the night near a heap of dead oxen, or near a dead donkey, or near a heap of dead people; I now wish to depart, fearing only human beings.

"I say that it is the same for a bhikṣu: if he relies on evil, unwholesome, and defiled dharmas, these become the basis for future existence, resulting in the retribution of feverish suffering and the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like the *kumuda* lily; do not rely on what is contrary to the Dharma to sustain your lives. You should purify your bodily conduct, purify your verbal and mental conduct, and abide in non-action.
