Wear robes of discarded rags, always practice alms-gathering, and beg for food in regular succession. Be of few desires and know contentment; delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence. Establish right mindfulness, right clear comprehension, right concentration, and right wisdom. You should always remain detached and train yourselves in this manner."
"At that time, after the vulture had finished this discussion with the brahmin, he departed.
What is the meaning of this parable I have told? Suppose there is a bhikkhu who dwells in dependence upon a village or town.

At dawn, the bhikkhu puts on his robes, takes his bowl, and enters the village for alms, failing to guard his body, failing to restrain his sense faculties, and failing to establish right mindfulness. He enters the homes of others to teach and preach the Dharma—whether spoken by the Buddha or spoken by the disciples—and thereby gains profit in the form of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and other articles of daily life. Having obtained these profits, he becomes stained by attachment, relishes them, fails to see their peril, and is unable to relinquish them; he uses them according to his own whims."

That bhikṣu practices evil precepts and accomplishes unwholesome dharmas; he stands at the very extreme of depravity, being corrupt and putrid. Not practicing the holy life, he claims to practice the holy life; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa. It is just as when a brahmin, having seen a vulture, asks it: "Welcome, vulture!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"

"I have come from one great cemetery to another, killing as I go. I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, dead horses, dead oxen, and the flesh of dead humans; I am now about to depart, fearing only man."
"I say that a bhikkhu is also like this: therefore, a bhikkhu should not act like a vulture, nor should he rely on what is unrighteous to sustain his life.

He should purify his bodily conduct, purify his verbal and mental conduct, dwell in non-action, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-gathering, and beg for food in regular order. Having few desires and being content, he should delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence. Establishing right mindfulness, right clear comprehension, right concentration, and right wisdom, he should always remain detached; thus should he train."
"After that vulture that eats vomit had finished this discussion with this brahmin, it departed.
What is the meaning of this parable that I have told?"

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who lives in dependence on a village or town. At dawn, he puts on his robes and takes his bowl to enter the village for alms, yet he does not guard his body, does not restrain his sense faculties, and does not establish right mindfulness. He enters the quarters of the bhikṣuṇīs to teach and preach the Dharma—whether it be what was spoken by the Buddha or what was spoken by the śrāvakas. Those bhikṣuṇīs then enter various households to speak of good and evil, receive gifts of faith, and bring them back to give to the bhikṣu. Because of this, he gains profit in the form of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and various requisites for life. Having obtained these profits, he becomes stained by attachment and indulgence; he fails to see the danger and is unable to relinquish them, using them as he pleases.

That bhikṣu practices evil precepts and accomplishes evil dharmas; he stands at the very extreme of depravity and corruption. Not being of the holy life, he claims to be of the holy life; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa. It is just as if a brahmin, having seen a vomit-eating bird, were to ask it: "Welcome, vomit-eating bird!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
"Did you see that vulture depart just now?
I ate its vomit; I now wish to go, fearing only man.
I say that a bhikṣu is also like this: therefore, a bhikṣu should not act like the bird that eats vomit, nor should he rely on what is unrighteous to sustain his life.

One should purify bodily conduct, purify verbal and mental conduct, abide in non-action, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-gathering, and beg for food in successive order. Having few desires and being content, one should delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence. Establishing right mindfulness, right situational awareness, right concentration, and right wisdom, one should always remain detached; thus should one train.
"At that time, having finished this discussion with the brahmin, the jackal departed.
What is the meaning of this parable I have told?

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a poor village, and he learns that within that village or city there are many wise and energetic practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin), he immediately avoids it; but if he learns that within that village or city there are no wise and energetic practitioners of the holy life, he comes to dwell there for nine or ten months."
When the bhikṣus saw him, they asked:
"Venerable one,
where have you been wandering?"
He replied: "Venerable sirs!
I have been traveling through a certain poor village."
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣus immediately thought to themselves:
"This worthy one practices what is difficult to practice. Why is that?"
"This worthy one is indeed able to travel to such-and-such a poor village.

Then the bhikṣus, out of respect, honored, served, and made offerings to him; because of this, he obtained profit in the form of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various articles for living. Having obtained these profits, he became stained by attachment, indulged in them, failed to see the danger, was unable to relinquish them, and used them according to his own whims.

That bhikṣu practices evil precepts, accomplishes evil dharmas, and stands at the very extreme; he is born into corruption and decay. Not being a brahmacārin, he claims to be a brahmacārin; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be a śramaṇa. It is just as when a brāhmaṇa sees a jackal and asks him: "Welcome, jackal!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"

"I have come from deep ravine to deep ravine, from thicket to thicket, from secluded place to secluded place; I now wish to eat the flesh of dead elephants, dead horses, dead oxen, and dead humans. I now wish to depart, fearing only man."
"I say that a bhikṣu is also like this. Therefore, a bhikṣu should not act like a jackal, nor should he rely on what is unrighteous to sustain his life.

He should purify his bodily conduct, purify his verbal and mental conduct, dwell in non-action, wear rag-robes, always practice alms-gathering, and beg for food in regular order. Having few desires and being content, he should delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence. Establishing right mindfulness, right clear comprehension, right concentration, and right wisdom, he should always remain detached; thus should he train."
"At that time, after the crow-faced one had rebuked the brahmin, he departed.
What is the meaning of this parable I have told?

If there is a bhikṣu who takes up the rains retreat in a poor and secluded place, and if he knows that within the villages and cities there are many wise and diligent fellow-practitioners of the holy life, he should immediately avoid it; however, if he knows that within the villages and cities there are no wise and diligent fellow-practitioners of the holy life, he may come to dwell there for two or three months."
Having seen him, the bhikṣus asked:
"Venerable one,
where did you spend the summer retreat?"
He replied:
"Venerable sirs!

I am now observing the rains retreat in a certain poor and secluded place. I am not like those foolish people who prepare beds, dwell within them while fully equipped with five things, and from morning until evening and from evening until morning, let their mouths follow after flavors and flavors follow after their mouths, seeking and searching for them again and again."
At that time, having heard this, the bhikṣus immediately thought:
"This worthy one practices what is difficult to practice. Why is this so?"
"This worthy one is able to dwell for the rains retreat in such-and-such a poor and secluded place.

Thereupon, the bhikṣus together showed him respect, paid homage, and made offerings to him. Because of this, he obtained gains of robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various articles of daily life. Having obtained these gains, he became stained by attachment, indulged in them, failed to see their dangers, was unable to relinquish them, and used them as he pleased.

That bhikṣu practices evil precepts and accomplishes unwholesome dharmas; he stands at the very extreme of depravity and corruption. Not being a practitioner of the holy life, he claims to be one; not being a śramaṇa, he claims to be one. It is just as when a brahmin sees a crow and asks it: "Welcome, crow!"
"From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?
He replied, "O Brahmin!"
"You are stubborn, deluded, and mad;
why do you ask me, 'From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?'?
My teaching for bhikṣus is likewise: therefore, bhikṣus, do not act like crows, and do not rely on what is unrighteous to sustain your lives."

One should purify bodily conduct, purify verbal and mental conduct, and dwell in non-action. One should wear rag-robes, always practice alms-gathering, and beg for food in regular succession. Having few desires and being content, one should delight in dwelling in seclusion and practice with diligence. Establishing right mindfulness, right situational awareness, right concentration, and right wisdom, one should always remain detached; thus should one train.
"After that śiṃśumāra beast had finished this discussion with this brahmin, it departed.
What is the meaning of this parable I have told?"

If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in dependence upon a village or town, that bhikṣu, at dawn, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl to enter the village for alms; he well guards his body, restrains his sense faculties, and abides in right mindfulness. Having finished begging for alms in the village or town, and having eaten his meal, after midday he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, and placing his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, he goes either to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or into an empty house. There he spreads out his sitting mat, sits cross-legged, with body erect and mind set on its goal, turning his attention inward and not toward the outside. He eliminates covetousness and harbors no contention in his heart. Seeing the wealth and various articles of daily life belonging to others, he does not give rise to covetousness, desiring, "May I obtain this."
He purifies his mind of covetousness;

likewise, he purifies his mind of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. Having transcended perplexity and overcome uncertainty, he is free from hesitation regarding wholesome states. Having thus purified his mind of doubt and abandoned these five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he becomes detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, and attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.

Having attained such a state, his mind was concentrated, pure, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and having attained an unshakable mind, he directed himself toward the realization of the superknowledge of the exhaustion of the taints (*āsrava*). He then knew this suffering as it truly is; he knew the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. He knew these taints, the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Having known thus and seen thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
It was just as when a brahmin, having seen a śiṅśumāra, asked it:
"Welcome, śiṅśumāra! From where have you come, and where do you wish to go?"
He replied: "Brahmin!
I have come from garden to garden, from pavilion to pavilion, and from grove to grove, drinking clear spring water and eating fine fruit. I am now about to depart; I fear no man."
"I say that a bhikṣu is also like this.

Therefore, a bhikṣu should not act like a otter, nor act like a *kūrmāsa*, nor act like a vulture, nor act like a bird that eats vomit, nor act like a jackal, nor act like a crow; he should act like a *śiṃśumāra*."
"Why is this? Because among those in the world, the True Persons who are free from attachment are like the śiṃśumāra.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Sāraṅgama-sūtra* ends here; it contains three thousand one hundred and seventy-eight characters. 66. The *Pūrvakalpa-sūtra* (66), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on Kings (*Rāja-saṃyukta*), the second discourse in the second recitation section of the Small Earth-City (*Kṣullaka-māṇḍalika*). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana.
At that time, after the midday meal, a number of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall for some minor reason and sat together to discuss this matter:
"What do you think, venerable friends?..."
"Householder, when staying at home, which is superior:
for a bhikṣu to maintain the sublime Dharma of the precepts, perfect his dignified deportment, and enter a house to receive food;
or to increase one's wealth morning after morning by hundreds of thousands of millions of times?"
Or there may be a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
"Venerable friends!
What is the use of benefits a hundred, a thousand, or ten million times greater? Only this is the ultimate essential."

If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the sublime Dharma of the precepts and is perfected in dignified deportment, his entering a household to receive food is not merely for the sake of gaining benefit a hundred, a thousand, or ten million times greater every morning.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous friends!..."
What use is there in gaining profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten million times over?
Even if it were more than that, this alone is the most essential.

If a bhikṣu upholds the sublime Dharma of the precepts and perfects his dignified deportment, entering lay households to receive food, this is not for the sake of daily gain and profit a hundred, a thousand, or ten million times over.
Why is this? I recall that in the past, while living in this country of Vārāṇasī, I was a poor man who subsisted solely by gleaning ears of grain and carrying loads for hire.

At that time, this country of Vārāṇasī suffered from drought, early frosts, and locusts; the crops did not ripen, and the people were destitute and impoverished, making it difficult even to obtain alms.
At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha named Aṅgaṇa who resided in this city of Vārāṇasī.
Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the pratyekabuddha Aṅgaṇa put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered Vārāṇasī to wander for alms.
"At that time, for the sake of gathering alms, I had gone out early from Vārāṇasī.
Venerable friends!
As I was going out, I encountered the Pratyekabuddha Aṅga entering the city."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha Aśoka entered with his alms-bowl clean; he emerged with his alms-bowl as clean as it had been before.
"Virtuous ones!
When I returned from gathering alms and was entering Vārāṇasī, I again saw the Pratyekabuddha Aśoka coming out."
Having seen me, he thought to himself:
"When I entered this morning, I saw this person coming out; now that I am coming out, I see this person entering again."
"This person might perhaps not yet have obtained food; I should now follow this person.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha pursued me like a shadow follows a form.
"Venerable friends!
Having gathered these gleanings and returned home, I set down my burden and looked back; I then saw the Pratyekabuddha Aśoka coming after me, following behind like a shadow follows a form."
Having seen him, I thought to myself:

"When I went out this morning, I saw this seer entering the city to beg for food; perhaps this seer has not yet obtained any food. It would be better for me to forego my own meal and share it with this seer."
Having formed this thought, he immediately took his portion of food and gave it to the Pratyekabuddha, saying:
"O Seer! You should know that this food is my own portion; out of compassion, I pray that you will graciously accept it."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha replied to me, saying:

"Householder, you should know that this year there has been a calamity of drought, early frosts, and locusts; the five grains have not ripened, and the people are suffering from famine and scarcity, making it difficult to obtain alms."
"You may give half to me in my bowl and eat the other half yourself; thus we shall both survive.
This would be well. I spoke again, saying: "O Seer!"
"You should know, O Seer, that while I am living as a householder, I have my own cauldrons and stoves, I have firewood and grain; furthermore, there is no fixed time for my morning or evening meals."
‘For the sake of compassion for me, please accept this food in its entirety.
Then, out of compassion, the Pratyekabuddha accepted it all.
‘O worthy ones!’”
"By virtue of the merit from giving that single bowl of food to him, I was reborn seven times among the devas as a king of gods, and seven times I was reborn among humans as a king of men.
O virtuous ones!"

"By virtue of the merit from giving a single bowl of food to him, I was born into this Śākya clan, possessing great wealth and abundance, with many livestock, fiefs, and appanages; my resources are immeasurable and I am fully endowed with precious jewels."
"Virtuous ones!

Because of the merit from giving him a single bowl of food, I have renounced a kingdom with hundreds of thousands of millions of gold coins to leave the household life and study the Path; how much more so for other various kinds of goods?"
"Venerable friends!

Because of the merit from giving that single bowl of food, I am recognized and treated with courtesy by kings, royal ministers, brahmins, householders, and all the people; furthermore, I am held in high esteem and respect by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās."
"Venerable friends!

Because of the merit from giving him a single bowl of food, I am constantly requested by others to accept food and drink, clothing and bedding, woolen rugs and carpets, couches and mattresses, cushions and hangings, medicinal decoctions for illness, and all the necessities of life; it is not that they do not request me."

If, at that time, I had known that the śramaṇa was a true person free from attachment, the merit and reward I would have obtained would have been many times greater; I would have received a great fruition, with most wondrous virtues, a penetrating illumination, and an extreme vastness and magnitude.
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha—the one free from attachment, the true person, who has attained right liberation—spoke this verse:
"I recall in the past I was poor, Living solely by gleaning;
I failed to provide for myself The one free from affliction, the most supreme virtue."
Thus he was born into the Śākya clan, named Aniruddha;
skilled in song and dance, he took delight in making music.
Having encountered the World-Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One who is like nectar, [he found true joy].
Having seen this, I gave rise to faith and joy; I abandoned the home life to study the Way.
I attained the knowledge of past lives and knew my former births:
I was born in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, dwelling there seven times.
Seven here and seven there, fourteen births in the world—
among humans and in the heavens— I have never fallen into an evil realm.
Now I know death and birth, and the places where sentient beings come and go.
Knowing the right and wrong of others' minds, the noble ones enjoy the five delights.
Having attained the five-factored meditative concentration, they always rest their minds in silent stillness;
having already attained this tranquil and upright abiding, they then master the pure divine eye.
For the sake of which I now study the Way and have distanced myself from and abandoned the household life—
I have now attained this meaning and entered the realm of the Buddha.
I do not delight in death, nor do I wish for birth.
According to the time and as circumstances permit, I shall establish right mindfulness and wisdom.
Following the Yea-li Bamboo Grove, my life will end there;
beneath that bamboo grove, I shall attain parinirvāṇa without remainder.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was sitting in seclusion, he heard with his purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, that the bhikṣus had gathered in the lecture hall after the midday meal and were discussing this matter together.
Having heard this, the Blessed One rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to the lecture hall before the assembly of bhikṣus, took a seat, and asked the bhikṣus:
"For what reason have you gathered here today in the lecture hall?"
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One!
Today we gathered in the lecture hall because the Venerable Aniruddha was teaching the Dharma by means of past events.”
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish today to hear from the Buddha a teaching on the Dharma based on future events?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time. Sugata!”
Now is precisely the right time.
If the Blessed One were to teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus by way of future events, the bhikṣus, having heard it, would properly receive and uphold it.
The World-Honored One said: “Monks!
Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall explain it to you in detail.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The World-Honored One said:

“Monks! In the distant future, there will be people with a lifespan of eighty thousand years. When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa will be exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a great multitude of people whose villages and towns are so close together that they are within the range of a single cock’s flight.”
"Monks! When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, girls shall not marry until they are five hundred years old. Monks!"

When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there are only these afflictions: namely, cold and heat, excrement and urine, desire, food and drink, and old age; there are no other ailments besides these.

“Monks! When the lifespan of humans was eighty thousand years, there was a king named Śaṅkha who was a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin). He was intelligent and wise; possessing the fourfold army, he governed the world with sovereign mastery.”

The Dharma King, in accordance with the Dharma, possesses the seven treasures. These seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-treasure of the military commander—these are the seven. He is endowed with a full thousand sons, who are handsome in appearance, courageous, fearless, and capable of subduing all opposing hosts.
He shall rule over all this earth, even unto the great ocean, not by the sword or staff, but by teaching the Dharma, bringing peace and happiness to all.
There is a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, a thousand cubits in height and sixteen cubits in circumference; he shall hoist it aloft.

Once it has been erected, he then distributes gifts below to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars who have come from afar—namely, food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, embroidered coverlets, attendants, and bright lamps.

Having given this gift, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the path. Regarding that which a clansman does when shaving off his hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaving the home life for homelessness to study the path—namely, the unsurpassed holy life—he, having reached its consummation, realizes it for himself through direct knowledge in this very life; he dwells having personally attained realization: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence," knowing this as it truly is.
At that time, the Venerable Ajita was seated among the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ajita rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, pressed his palms together toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!

"In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, I shall become a king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who is intelligent and wise; possessing the fourfold army, I shall govern the world with sovereign mastery."

The Dharma-King, in accordance with the Dharma, achieves the seven treasures. These seven treasures are: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the minister-of-war-treasure; these are the seven. I shall possess a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, capable of subduing all opposing hosts. I shall rule over this entire earth, even unto the great ocean, not by the sword or staff, but through the teaching of the Dharma, bringing peace and happiness to all.
There is a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, standing a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference; I shall raise it up.

Once it has been raised, I will first practice giving to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars who have come from afar, providing them with food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, embroidered cushions, attendants, and bright lamps.

Having given this gift, I shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path. As for those sons of noble family who shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path, they do so for the sake of the unsurpassed holy life. Having reached its consummation, I have realized it for myself through direct knowledge in this very life; I have attained realization and dwell therein, knowing according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Thereupon, the Blessed One rebuked the Venerable Ajita, saying:
"You foolish man!
You should have died once more, yet you seek another end."
Why is this? It is because you have formed this thought:
"O World-Honored One!..."

In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, I shall become a king named Śaṅkha, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who is intelligent and wise; possessing the fourfold army, he will govern the world with sovereign mastery.

As a Dharma King who has attained the seven treasures, those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure—these are the seven. I shall have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, capable of subduing all opposing hosts. I shall rule over this entire earth as far as the great ocean, not by the sword or staff, but by teaching and command according to the Dharma, bringing peace and happiness to all.
There is a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, standing a thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference; I shall erect it.

Once it has been erected, I will first bestow alms upon śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars who have come from afar—giving them food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, embroidered coverlets, attendants, and bright lamps.

Having given this away, I shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path. As is done by sons of noble family who shave their hair and beards, don saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path—having brought the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion, I have in this very life known it for myself, realized it for myself, and attained it through my own realization; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I know according to reality that there will be no further existence.
The World-Honored One said: "Āyīda!

In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, you shall become a king named Śaṅkha. You will be a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin), intelligent and wise, possessing the fourfold army; you shall govern the world with authority, exercising sovereign power over it."

As a Dharma King who has attained the seven treasures, those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure—these are the seven. You shall have a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, capable of subduing all opposing hosts. You shall rule over this entire earth, even unto the great ocean, not by the sword or staff, but by teaching through the Dharma, bringing peace and happiness to all.

There is a great golden banner, adorned with various jewels, standing one thousand cubits high and sixteen cubits in circumference; you should raise it up. Once it has been raised, you should then give alms below it to śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars who have come from afar—namely, food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, embroidered cushions, attendants, and bright lamps.

Once you have given this gift, you shall shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path. Such is the practice of a son of noble family who shaves his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path: he brings the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion; in this very life, he knows it for himself, realizes it for himself, and attains realization through his own experience, dwelling in that attainment. He knows truly: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there shall be a Buddha named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat—just as I have now become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."

In this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans to devas, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized for himself; just as I now, in this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans to devas, dwell having personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized for myself.

He shall preach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it shall possess both meaning and phrasing, be complete and pure, and manifest the holy life—just as I now preach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, and manifesting the holy life.

He shall extensively propagate and disseminate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), with an immeasurable great assembly from humans to gods, manifesting it excellently, just as I now extensively propagate and disseminate the holy life, with an immeasurable great assembly from humans to gods, manifesting it excellently; he shall have an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, just as I now have an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Maitreya was present in that assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Maitreya rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!"

In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, I shall attain Buddhahood, known as Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat—just as the present World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.

In this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods—I have known it for myself, awakened to it for myself, and attained realization through my own direct experience, dwelling in that accomplishment; just as the World-Honored One now dwells in this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods—having known it for himself, awakened to it for himself, and attained realization through his own direct experience.

I shall preach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it possesses both meaning and phrasing, is complete and pure, and reveals the holy life—just as the World-Honored One now preaches the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, possessing both meaning and phrasing, being complete and pure, and revealing the holy life.

I shall widely expound and disseminate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), with a great assembly as limitless as that from humans to gods, skillfully manifesting it, just as the World-Honored One now widely expounds and disseminates the holy life, with a great assembly as limitless as that from humans to gods, skillfully manifesting it.
"I shall have a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, just like the retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus that the World-Honored One has now.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised Maitreya, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Maitreya!
Your resolve is most sublime, in that you lead this great assembly. Why is this so?
As you have thought thus:
"O World-Honored One!

In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, I shall attain Buddhahood, named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat—just as the present World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."

In this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, from humans to gods—I have realized it for myself through direct knowledge, awakened to it for myself, and attained it as my own realization while dwelling therein; just as the World-Honored One now dwells in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, from humans to gods—having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, awakened to it for himself, and attained it as his own realization.

I shall preach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, it reveals the holy life—just as the World-Honored One now preaches the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, and revealing the holy life.

I shall extensively propagate and disseminate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), with an immeasurable great assembly from humans to devas, skillfully manifesting it, just as the World-Honored One now extensively propagates and disseminates the holy life, with an immeasurable great assembly from humans to devas, skillfully manifesting it.
The Buddha spoke again, saying: “Maitreya!

In the distant future, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, you shall become a Buddha, named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—just as I am now a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”

In this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, from humans to gods—you have known it for yourself, awakened to it for yourself, and dwell having realized it through your own direct experience, just as I now dwell in this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, from humans to gods—having known it for myself, awakened to it for myself, and realized it through my own direct experience.

"You should preach the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life—just as I now preach the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life."

"You should widely expound and disseminate the holy life (brahmacarya) to an immeasurable great assembly, from humans to devas, manifesting it excellently, just as I now widely expound and disseminate the holy life to an immeasurable great assembly, from humans to devas, manifesting it excellently."
"You shall have a retinue of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, just as I now have an immeasurable retinue of hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One turned back and said, "Ānanda!
Bring me the robe woven of gold thread; I now wish to give it to the bhikṣu Maitreya."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, immediately took the robe woven of gold thread and presented it to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, after the Blessed One had accepted this robe woven of gold thread from the Venerable Ānanda, he said:
“Maitreya!”
"Take these robes woven with golden thread from the Tathāgata and offer them to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Why is this so? Maitreya!"
"The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas act as protectors for the world; they seek its welfare and benefit, seeking its peace and happiness.
Thereupon, the Venerable Maitreya, having received from the Tathāgata the robe woven with golden threads, offered it to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama is staying in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana near Vārāṇasī; he is teaching the Dharma to his disciples concerning the future. I should go there and disturb him."
Then, Māra Pāpīyān went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, he addressed the Buddha in verse, saying:
"He shall certainly attain it— A countenance most exquisite and supreme, His body adorned with flower garlands and necklaces, And bright pearls fastened upon his arms."
"If you are in the city of Kikata, within the realm of King Śaṅkha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This Māra Pāpīyas has come to my presence, wishing to disturb and confuse me."
The World-Honored One, having understood this, spoke these verses for Māra Pāpīyas:
"He shall certainly attain it, Free from subjugation and free from doubt;
Having severed birth, old age, sickness, and death, He has exhausted all outflows and completed what was to be done."
"If one practices the holy life, they shall dwell within the realm of Maitreya.
Thereupon, the Māra King spoke again in verse:
"He will certainly obtain, garments of renown, most excellent and fine."
"His body is anointed with sandalwood; his form is smooth, straight, and beautifully tall.
He is as if in the city of Kāśī, within the realm of the Śaṅkha King.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"He shall certainly attain it: without master and without home,
with no gold or jewels held in hand, unconditioned and free from anxiety—
if one practices the holy life, one will dwell within the realm of Maitreya."
Thereupon, Māra spoke again in verse:
"He shall certainly obtain Fame, wealth, and fine food and drink;
He will be skilled at song and dance, Making music and always rejoicing."
"If one is in the city of Kikata, within the realm of King Śaṅkha.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"He shall surely cross to the other shore, like a bird breaking through a net and escaping."
"Attaining mastery over dhyāna, I travel at will; endowed with bliss, I am ever joyful.
You, O Māra, must surely know that I have already subdued you.
Thereupon, King Māra again thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata sees me.
Distressed and sorrowful, unable to remain there, he suddenly vanished from that place and was no longer seen.
The Buddha spoke thus.
Maitreya, Ajita, the Venerable Ānanda, and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The second section of the *Mūlasūtra*, totaling 4,001 characters, concludes here. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 13, totaling 7,179 characters, [concludes].
Within the recitation of the Second Small Earth-City [Section], the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 14, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
67. The Mahādeva-Āmra-vana Sūtra (67). Middle Discourses, Chapter on Kings, The Mahādeva-Āmra-vana Sūtra, Third, Second Recitation Section of Kṣudrakasāṇḍaka. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Vidiśā country with a large community of bhikṣus; he arrived at Miśrikā and stayed in the Mahādeva-Āmra grove.
At that time, while traveling along the road, the World-Honored One smiled with joy.
Seeing the World-Honored One smile, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason do you smile?
Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas never smile without cause; we pray that you will explain its meaning.
At that time, the Blessed One said:

“Ānanda! In the past, at another time, in this Mithilā forest, there was a king named Mahādeva who was a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin). He was intelligent and wise; he possessed a fourfold army and governed the world with sovereign mastery. As a righteous Dharma-king, he had accomplished the seven treasures and attained the four kinds of human supernormal powers.”
Ānanda! As for that Great King Mahādeva’s accomplishment of the seven treasures, what are they called?
They are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister of the army treasure; these are the seven.
“Ānanda! In what way is that Great King Mahādeva said to have accomplished the wheel-treasure? Ānanda!”

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the Great Heavenly King was reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, he bathed and washed himself and ascended the main hall. Then the divine Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*) came from the east; the wheel had a thousand spokes, all complete, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, its color like a blazing fire, its radiance brilliant and dazzling.
Upon seeing this, the Great Heavenly King was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking to himself:

"A noble wheel-treasure has been born! A wondrous wheel-treasure has been born! I have also heard this from the ancients: when King Mūrdhaja, a Kṣatriya, on the fifteenth day of the month during the time of the *prātimokṣa* recitation, bathes and washes himself and ascends to the main palace, there comes from the east a divine wheel-treasure—a wheel with a thousand spokes, complete in every respect, pure and natural, not made by human hands, its color like a blazing fire, its radiance brilliant and dazzling; he shall surely become a Wheel-turning King."
"Shall I become a Wheel-Turning King?
"Ānanda! In the past, the Great Heavenly King (Mahādeva-rāja) was about to test the divine Wheel-Treasure (cakraratna) himself."

At that time, he assembled the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having assembled the fourfold army, he proceeded to the place where the divine wheel-treasure was located; with his left hand he stroked the wheel and with his right hand he turned it, speaking these words:
"Follow the divine wheel-treasure! Follow wherever the divine wheel-treasure rolls!"
"Ānanda! Once that divine wheel-treasure has rolled forth, it proceeds toward the eastern direction.

At that time, the Great King Mahādeva also follows behind it with his fourfold army; wherever the divine wheel-treasure halts, there the Great King Mahādeva and his fourfold army likewise halt and take up residence."
Thereupon, the minor kings of the eastern regions all came to the Great Heavenly King and addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, O Heavenly King!"
"O Heavenly King!

These lands are exceedingly prosperous and joyful, and they are populated by many people, all of whom belong to the Heavenly King. We pray only that the Heavenly King may instruct them according to the Dharma; we, too, shall assist the Heavenly King."
Thereupon, the Great King Mahādeva addressed the minor kings, saying:

"Each of you shall govern your respective realms according to the Dharma and not by what is contrary to the Dharma; do not allow any unwholesome deeds or those who lead lives contrary to the Brahma-faring to exist within your kingdoms."
“Ānanda! That divine wheel-treasure travels eastward, crosses the great eastern ocean, and returns to the south, the west, and the north.”

Ānanda! As the divine wheel-treasure revolves and proceeds, the Great King himself follows behind it along with his fourfold army; wherever the divine wheel-treasure halts, there the Great King immediately stops to stay overnight together with his fourfold army.
Thereupon, the minor kings of the northern regions all came to the Great Heavenly King and addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, O Heavenly King!"
"O Heavenly King!

These lands are exceedingly prosperous and joyful, and they are populated by many people who all belong to the Heavenly King. We only pray that the Heavenly King will instruct them according to the Dharma; we, too, shall assist the Heavenly King."
Thereupon, the Great King Mahādeva addressed the minor kings, saying:

"Each of you shall govern your respective realms according to the Dharma and not by what is contrary to the Dharma; do not allow any evil deeds or those who lead lives contrary to the holy life (abrahmacarya) within your kingdoms."

"Ānanda! That divine wheel-treasure travels northward, crosses the great northern ocean, and immediately returns swiftly to the king’s capital city. There, the Great Heavenly King sits upon the main hall to adjudicate matters of wealth and property."
At that time, the divine wheel-treasure remained suspended in the air; this is called the Great Wheel-turning King’s accomplishment of such a divine wheel-treasure.
"Ānanda! How is it that the Great Wheel-turning King is said to have accomplished the elephant-treasure?"
Ānanda! At that time, the Great King Mahādeva was born with the elephant-treasure; that elephant was exceedingly white and possessed seven limbs, and its name was Uposatha.
Having seen this, King Mahādeva was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking, "If he can be tamed, he shall become most excellent.
Ānanda! At a later time, that Great King Mahādeva said to the elephant trainer:
"Quickly train the elephant so that it becomes perfectly well-disciplined; once the elephant is trained, come and inform me.

At that time, having received the king's command, the elephant trainer went to the place where the elephant-treasure was and quickly trained the elephant-treasure until it was perfectly well-disciplined.

At that time, the elephant-treasure was subjected to extreme training and quickly became well-disciplined, just as in the past a noble elephant with a lifespan of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, having been subjected to extreme training for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years, quickly became well-disciplined; that elephant-treasure was likewise subjected to extreme training and quickly became well-disciplined.
"Ānanda!
At that time, the elephant trainer quickly drove the elephant-treasure and made it thoroughly well-trained. Once the elephant-treasure was trained, he went to the Great Heavenly King and said:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"You should know that I have trained it with the utmost care; the elephant-treasure is now disciplined and follows the will of the Heavenly King. "Ānanda!

Formerly, when the Great Heavenly King tested the elephant-treasure, at dawn as the sun rose, he went to the place where the elephant-treasure was, mounted that elephant-treasure, and traveled across all lands even unto the great ocean, then immediately and swiftly returned to his own royal city. This is called the Great Heavenly King’s accomplishment of such a white elephant-treasure."
“Ānanda! In what way is that Great King Mahādeva said to be possessed of the horse-treasure? Ānanda!”

At that time, the Great Heavenly King was born with the Horse Treasure. That Horse Treasure was of an intensely deep blue-black color, its head resembling that of a crow, and its body was adorned with fine hair; it was named the King of Tawny Horses.
Having seen this, the Deva King was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, thinking, "If he can be tamed, he shall be made most excellent.
Ānanda! At a later time, that Great Heavenly King addressed the horse trainer, saying:
"Quickly break in the horse and ensure it is thoroughly tamed; once the horse is well-trained, come and inform me.
At that time, having received the king's command, the horse trainer went to the place where the horse-treasure was and quickly broke in the horse-treasure, ensuring it was thoroughly tamed.

At that time, the horse-treasure, having undergone the most thorough training, quickly attained excellent discipline; just as in the past, a noble steed lived for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years and, through that immeasurable period of training, quickly attained excellent discipline, so too was this horse-treasure: having undergone the most thorough training, it quickly attained excellent discipline.
"Ānanda!
At that time, the horse trainer quickly drove the horse-treasure and brought it to perfect training. Once the horse-treasure was fully trained, he went to where the Great Heavenly King was and said:
'Heavenly King!'"
"You should know that I have trained it with the utmost care; the Horse-Treasure is now disciplined and follows the will of the Heavenly King. "Ānanda!

Formerly, when the Great Heavenly King tested the Horse-Treasure, at dawn as the sun rose, he went to where the Horse-Treasure was, mounted that Horse-Treasure, and traveled across all lands even unto the great ocean, then immediately returned swiftly to his own royal city. This is called the Great Heavenly King’s accomplishment of such a dark-blue horse treasure."
“Ānanda! In what way is that Great Heavenly King said to be ‘accomplished in the jewel-treasure’? Ānanda!”

At that time, the Great Heavenly King produced a jewel-treasure. That jewel-treasure was luminous and pure by nature, uncreated by any artisan; it had eight facets, was free from impurity, and was exquisitely polished. It was strung with cords of five colors: blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
Ānanda! At that time, when the Great King desired light within his inner palace, he used jewel-ornaments for it. Ānanda!

Formerly, when the Great King Mahādeva tested the jewel treasure, he assembled his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry. Having assembled these four divisions, he erected a tall banner in the darkness of night and placed the jewel upon it. He then went out to the park, where the radiance of the jewel illuminated the fourfold army; the extent of its light reached half a yojana in every direction. This is what is meant by the Great King’s accomplishment of such a precious great luminous pearl.
“Ānanda! How is it that the Great King Mahādeva is said to have attained the jewel of a woman? Ānanda!”

At that time, Great King Mahādeva gave birth to the Woman-Jewel (*strī-ratna*). This Woman-Jewel possessed a radiant and lustrous body, pure and immaculate; her beauty surpassed that of humans, falling only slightly short of that of the gods. Her features were upright and graceful, bringing joy to all who beheld her. From her mouth issued the fragrant scent of blue lotuses, and from all the pores of her body emanated the aroma of sandalwood. In winter her body was warm, and in summer it was cool.
She serves the king with a sincere heart; her speech is pleasing, her actions are swift, she possesses intelligence and wisdom, and she joyfully practices virtue.

She thinks of the king constantly, never departing from him in mind, let alone in her physical and verbal conduct. This is called the Great Heavenly King’s possession of such a jewel of a beautiful woman.
“Ānanda! How did that Great King Mahādeva come to possess the householder-treasure?
Ānanda!...”

At that time, the Great Heavenly King produced the Householder Jewel (*gṛhapati-ratna*). That Householder Jewel was exceedingly wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and vast herds of livestock; he held many fiefdoms and estates, and was fully endowed with the fruits of various meritorious deeds, having attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

He beheld all treasuries—both those empty and those full—and saw those that were guarded and those that were unguarded; he saw all gold treasuries and coin treasuries, whether they had been prepared or not yet prepared.
"Ānanda! That Householder Jewel approaches the Great Heavenly King and says:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"If you wish to obtain gold, coin, and treasures, O Great King, do not worry; I myself know the proper time. Ānanda!
In the past, when the Great King tested the Householder Jewel, the king boarded a boat and entered the Ganges River, saying:
“Householder!
I wish to obtain gold and precious coins.
The householder replied:
"O Great King!
May the ship reach the shore.
Then, the Great King replied:
"Householder!
One truly desires to attain it right here; one truly desires to attain it right here.
The householder replied:
"O Heavenly King!
We pray that you cause the ship to stop. Ānanda!

Then, the Householder Jewel went before the prow of the ship, knelt down for a long time, and reaching out his hand, lifted four treasuries from within the water—treasuries of gold, treasuries of coin, treasuries of wrought goods, and treasuries of unwrought goods—and said:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"According to his wishes, he may freely use the gold, coins, and treasures as he pleases.
Having used them, he returns the remainder to the water.
This is called the Great Heavenly King’s accomplishment of such a householder-treasure.
“Ānanda! How does that Great Heavenly King possess the treasure of the minister of the military? Ānanda!”

At that time, the Great Heavenly King produced the Treasure of the Commander-in-Chief. That minister-commander was intelligent and wise, possessed of eloquence and skillful speech, and was highly learned and discerning.

As the Treasure of the Minister-Commander, he established for the Great Heavenly King the benefits of the present life, exhorting him to be established therein; he established the benefits of future lives, exhorting him to be established therein; and he established both the benefits of the present life and future lives, exhorting him to be established therein.

That minister of the army, for the sake of the Great Heavenly King, can assemble the military forces when he wishes to do so, and disband them when he wishes; he ensures that the fourfold army of the Great Heavenly King does not become exhausted and provides them with encouragement and assistance. The same applies to the other ministers. This is called the Great Heavenly King’s accomplishment of the treasure of the minister of the army.
Ānanda! This is called the Great Heavenly King’s accomplishment of the seven treasures. Ānanda!
How did that Great King Mahādeva obtain the four kinds of human supernormal powers?

That Great King Mahādeva lived for an exceptionally long life of eighty-four thousand years: he spent eighty-four thousand years as a youth in play, eighty-four thousand years as a minor king, eighty-four thousand years as a great king, and then, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the saffron robes, out of deep faith he left the home life for homelessness to study the path; he studied under the King of Sages and practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) here in Mithilā, dwelling in the Mahādeva Mango Grove.
"Ānanda!

If the Great King Mahādeva lives for an extremely long life of eighty-four thousand years—spending eighty-four thousand years as a youth in play, eighty-four thousand years as a minor king, and eighty-four thousand years as a great king—and then, shaving off his hair and beard and donning the saffron robes, out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Way, training under the King of Sages and practicing the holy life here in Mithilā, dwelling in the Mahādeva Mango Grove—this is called the first wish-fulfilling virtue of the Great King."
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

That Great King Mahādeva was free from illness; he had perfected the way of balanced digestion, neither too cold nor too hot, peaceful and without conflict. For this reason, whatever food and drink he consumed was easily digested."

Ānanda! If the Great Heavenly King is free from illness and has perfected the way of balanced digestion—neither too cold nor too hot, peaceful and without conflict—for this reason, whatever he eats and drinks is easily digested. This is called the Great Heavenly King’s second quality of mastery.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

That Great Heavenly King’s body was radiant, pure, and bright; his exquisite complexion surpassed that of humans, falling only slightly short of that of the devas. He was so upright and handsome that all who beheld him were filled with joy."

Ānanda! If the Great King Mahādeva’s body is radiant, pure, bright, and clean; if his beauty surpasses that of humans, though slightly inferior to that of the devas; if he is upright and handsome, bringing joy to all who behold him—this is called the Great King’s third quality of mastery.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
That Great King Mahādeva always cherished the brahmins and householders as a father cherishes his sons, and the brahmins and householders likewise revered the Great King as sons revere their father."
"Ānanda! In the past, while in his pleasure garden, King Mahādeva said to his charioteer:
'Drive the chariot slowly; I wish to gaze long upon the brahmins and householders.'"
The brahmins and householders also told the charioteer:
"Drive the carriage slowly; we wish to gaze long upon the Great Heavenly King. Ānanda!

If the Great Heavenly King constantly cherishes the brahmins and householders as a father cherishes his sons, and the brahmins and householders likewise revere the Great Heavenly King as sons revere their father, this is called the Great Heavenly King’s fourth quality of wish-fulfilling power.
Ānanda! These are called the four kinds of human-like qualities of mastery possessed by the Great King Mahādeva. Ānanda!
At a later time, that Great King Mahādeva said to his barber:
"If you see white hairs growing on my head, you must inform me.
Having received the king's command, the barber subsequently washed the king's head; seeing that white hairs had grown, he informed him, saying: [He then spoke.]
"O Great King!
You should know that the divine messengers have arrived; white hair has grown upon your head.
Then the Great Heavenly King again addressed his barber:
"Take the golden tweezers and slowly pluck out the white hairs, placing them in my hand.
At that time, having heard the king's command, the barber immediately took the golden tweezers and slowly plucked out the white hairs, placing them in the king's hand.
"Ānanda! That Great Heavenly King held his white hair in his hands and spoke this verse:
'White hair has grown upon my head; My lifespan is now waning.'"
"The messenger of the gods has already arrived; now is the time for me to study the Way. "Ānanda!
Having seen the white hair, that Great Heavenly King addressed the crown prince, saying:"
"Prince! You should know that the divine messengers have arrived; white hairs have grown upon your head. Prince!"
"I have already obtained the desires of the human world; now I shall seek the desires of the heavens. Prince!
I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave my home for the homeless life to study the Way."
"O Prince!

I now entrust these four continents to you; you should govern and transform them according to the Dharma, not by means of what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow various evil deeds or those who do not practice the holy life (abrahmacarya) to exist within the kingdom."

"Prince! If you later see that the divine messengers have arrived and white hair has grown upon your head, you should again entrust the governance of this kingdom to your crown prince and instruct him well.
Having entrusted the kingdom to your son, you too should shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Way."
"O Prince!
I now turn for you this Dharma of succession; you, in turn, shall also turn this Dharma of succession, lest the people fall into the extreme peripheries."
"Prince!
How is it that I now turn for you this Dharma of succession, and you too shall in turn turn this Dharma of succession, so as not to let the people fall into the extreme limits?"
"O Prince!
If the transmission of the Dharma in this land were to be severed and no longer continued, it would be called the people falling into the extreme periphery.
O Prince!"
For this reason, I now turn [the wheel] for you. Prince!
I have already turned this dharma of succession for you; you, in turn, must also turn this dharma of succession, so that the people do not fall into the extreme limits.

“Ānanda! Having entrusted the administration of this kingdom to the crown prince and having given him excellent instructions, that Great King Mahādeva shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Way. He studied under the Royal Sage and practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) here in the Mahādeva Mango Grove at Mithilā.”
He too was a wheel-turning monarch who possessed the seven treasures and attained the four kinds of human sovereign powers.
In what way did he possess the seven treasures and attain the four kinds of human sovereign powers?
As previously described, one who possesses the seven treasures attains four kinds of wish-fulfilling virtues.
"Ānanda! At a later time, that wheel-turning king also addressed his barber:"
"If you see white hairs growing on my head, you may inform me.
Thereupon, having received the king's command, the barber later washed the king's head; seeing that white hairs had grown, he informed him, saying:
"O Great King!"
"You should know that the celestial messengers have arrived, for white hairs have grown upon your head.
Then the Wheel-turning King again addressed the barber:
"Take golden tweezers and gently pull out the white hairs, placing them in my hand."
Then, having heard the King’s command, the barber immediately used golden tweezers to gently pull out the white hairs and placed them in the King’s hand.
Ānanda! Holding the white hairs in his hands, that Wheel-turning King spoke this verse:
“White hairs have grown upon my head, and my lifespan is steadily declining;
the messenger of the gods has already arrived—now is the time for me to study the Way.”
“Ānanda! Having seen his white hair, that wheel-turning king said to the crown prince:
‘Crown prince!’”
"You should know, Prince, that the divine messengers have already arrived; gray hairs have grown upon my head.
I have already obtained the desires of the human world; now I shall seek the desires of the heavens."
"Prince!

I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Way. I now entrust these four continents to you; you should govern and transform them according to the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma, and ensure that there are no evil deeds or those who do not practice the holy life within the kingdom."

"Prince! If you later see that the divine messengers have arrived and white hairs have grown upon your head, you too shall entrust the administration of this kingdom to your crown prince and instruct him well.
Having entrusted the kingdom to your son, you too shall shave off your hair and beard, don the saṃghāṭī robe, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Way."
"Prince!
I now turn for you this Dharma of succession; you, in turn, shall also turn this Dharma of succession, so that the people do not fall into the extreme limits."
"Prince!
How is it that I now turn for you this Dharma of succession, and you too shall in turn turn this Dharma of succession, so as not to let the people fall into the extreme limits?"
"O Prince!
If the transmission of the Dharma in this land were to be severed and no longer continued, it would be said that the people have fallen into the extreme periphery.
O Prince!"
For this reason, I now turn [the wheel] for you. Prince!
I have already turned this dharma of succession for you; you, in turn, must also turn this dharma of succession, so that the people do not fall into the extreme limits.

“Ānanda! That wheel-turning king, having entrusted the governance of this kingdom to his crown prince and having given him excellent instructions, then shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Way. He studied under the King of Sages, practicing the holy life here in the Mahādeva-tāla Grove of Mithilā.”

“Ānanda! Thus, from son to son, from grandson to grandson, from clan to clan, and from generation to generation, there were eighty-four thousand successive wheel-turning kings who shaved off their hair and beards, donned the saṃghāṭī robes, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Way. They studied under the King of Sages and practiced the holy life here in this Mahādeva Mango Grove at Mithilā.”

The last of those kings was named Nimi, a righteous Dharma-king who practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma. Together with his crown prince, queen, concubines, ministers, subjects, śramaṇas, brahmins, and even down to the insects, he observed the Dharma-fast on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practiced generosity by giving to destitute śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar—providing food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, mattresses, woolen rugs, fine carpets, attendants, and bright lamps.
"At that time, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three were assembled and seated in the Sudharma Hall, praising and extolling King Nimi, saying:
'O worthy ones!
The people of Videha possess great benefit and great merit.'"
Why is that? That last king was named Nimi;

he was a righteous Dharma-king who practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma. Together with his crown prince, queen, concubines, ministers, subjects, śramaṇas, and brahmins—even down to the insects—he observed the Dharma-fast on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practiced giving, bestowing upon those in need—śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar—food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mats, woolen rugs, embroidered coverlets, attendants, and bright lamps.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, Śakra, the Lord of the Devas, addressed the gods of the Thirty-three, saying:
"Virtuous ones!..."
"Do you wish to see King Nimi right here?
The gods of the Thirty-three Heavens replied,
"Kauśika!..."
"We wish to see King Nimi right here and now.
Then, Śakra, like a strong man bending or extending his arm, suddenly vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and appeared instantly at King Nimi’s palace.
Thereupon, King Nimi saw Śakra, the Lord of the Devas; having seen him, he asked:
"Who are you? Śakra replied:
"Great King!
Have you heard of Śakra, the Lord of Devas?
He replied:
"Having heard that there is Śakra," he said, "I am he."
Great King, you possess great benefit and great merit.
Why is this? Because the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have assembled in the Sudharmā Hall and, in unison, have praised and extolled you, saying:
"Venerable friends!
The people of Vedeha possess great benefit and great merit. Why is that? Because..."

That last king was named Nimi; he was a Dharma-king who ruled according to the Dharma, practicing the Dharma as it truly is. For the sake of his crown prince, queen, concubines, ministers, subjects, śramaṇas, and brahmins, and even down to the smallest insects, he observed the Dharma-fast on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month. He practiced generosity by giving to those in need—śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar—providing them with food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, fine carpets, attendants, and bright lamps.
"Great King!
Would you like to see the Heaven of the Thirty-three?
He replied:
"I wish to see it.
Śakra then addressed King Nimi, saying:
"When I return to the heavens, I shall command that a carriage drawn by a thousand elephants be prepared for you; Great King, mount the carriage and enjoy yourself as you ascend to the heavens."
At that time, King Nimi silently accepted [the invitation] from Śakra, Lord of the Devas.

Then, knowing that King Nimi had silently accepted, Śakra suddenly vanished from King Nimi’s palace in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and returned to the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
When Śakra had arrived, he said to his charioteer:
"Quickly prepare the chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and go to welcome King Nimi.
Upon arrival, say to him:"
"Great King!
You should know that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has sent these thousand-elephant chariots to welcome you; you may mount these chariots to enjoy yourself and ascend to the heavens."
Once the King had mounted the chariot, he spoke again to the King, saying:
"By which path do you wish me to escort you? Shall it be by the path of evil that leads to the experience of evil, or by the path of excellence that leads to the experience of excellence?"

"Then, having received the instructions of Śakra, the charioteer immediately prepared the chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and went to where King Nimi was. Upon arrival, he addressed him, saying:
'Great King!'"
"You should know that Śakra has sent this chariot drawn by a thousand elephants to welcome the Great King; you may mount this chariot to enjoy yourself and ascend to the heavens.
Then, after King Nimi had mounted the chariot, the charioteer addressed the king again:
"By which path shall I convey you?"
"Is it that one receives a bad retribution from evil, or does one receive a good retribution from what is sublime?
Then, King Nimi said to his charioteer:
"Drive me between these two paths—neither toward the bad retribution for evil, nor toward the good retribution for what is sublime."

Thereupon, the charioteer drove the king along the middle path between the two tracks—the path where evil receives its evil retribution and the path where excellence receives its excellent retribution.
Then, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven saw King Nimi approaching from afar; having seen him, they exclaimed in praise:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"Welcome, Great King!
You may dwell and enjoy yourself together with the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Then, King Nimi spoke these verses for the sake of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three:
"Just as one might temporarily seek a borrowed carriage for a brief moment, so it is in this case as well:
[the body] is regarded as belonging to another."
‘When I have returned to Mithilā, I shall perform immeasurable good deeds;
by this cause I shall be born in the heavens, making merit my provision. Thus, Ānanda!
"Ānanda, do you think that King Mahādeva of old was someone else?
Do not conceive such a thought; you should know that he was none other than myself."

In the past, from son to son, from grandson to grandson, from clan to clan—through eighty-four thousand successive generations of wheel-turning monarchs descending from me—they shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron robes, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Way. They studied the practice of the Brahma-faring under the King of Sages here in this Great Heavenly Mango Grove of Mithilā.

Ānanda! At that time, I acted for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others; I benefited many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate conclusion; it was not ultimately pure, nor was the holy life (brahmacarya) brought to its ultimate conclusion.
At that time, one was not yet free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had one yet attained liberation from all suffering.

“Ānanda! I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One.

I now act for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others; I benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.

I have now taught the Dharma that reaches the ultimate; it is ultimately pure, the ultimate holy life, and having completed the ultimate holy life, I am now free from birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.

“Ānanda! I now transmit to you the Dharma of successive succession; you, in turn, must also transmit the Dharma of successive succession, so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed. Ānanda!”
How then shall I now turn to you the Dharma of succession, and you too shall in turn turn the Dharma of succession, so that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed?
It is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of eight factors from right view up to right concentration.
"Ānanda!
This is what I now call the Dharma of successive transmission for you; you, in turn, must also transmit this Dharma of succession, so that the lineage of the Buddha shall not be severed.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Third Discourse on the Great Heavenly Nyagrodha Forest ends here, totaling four thousand seven hundred and thirty-nine characters. 68. The Discourse on King Mahāsudassana (68) The Fourth Discourse on King Mahāsudassana, from the Section on Kings in the Madhyama Āgama, recited in the Second Sub-section on Small Earthly Cities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kuśinagara and stayed in the Śāla Grove of the Malla clan of the Sūbhadra.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was about to enter final parinirvāṇa, he said:
“Ānanda! Go to the space between the twin śāla trees and prepare a couch for the Tathāgata with its head toward the north; the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa at midnight.”
Venerable Ānanda, having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, immediately went to the twin trees and, between them, prepared a bed for the Tathāgata with its head toward the north.
Having finished preparing the bed, he returned to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have already prepared a bed for the Tathāgata between the twin trees with the head toward the north; I only pray that the World-Honored One will know the proper time.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One took Venerable Ānanda to the space between the twin trees. He folded his *uttarāsaṅga* robe in four layers and spread it upon the bed, folded his *saṃghāṭī* robe to serve as a pillow, and lay down on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, intending to enter final *parinirvāṇa*.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk. With palms joined toward the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda said:
