“World-Honored One! There are other great cities: first, Campā; second, Śrāvastī; third, Vaiśālī; fourth, Rājagṛha; fifth, Vārāṇasī; and sixth, Kapilavastu.”
“World-Honored One, why is it that you do not attain parinirvāṇa there, but instead right here in this small town, which among all cities is the most inferior?
At that time, the World-Honored One said: “Ānanda!”
Do not say that this is a mere small earthen city, the lowest among all cities. Why is this?
In the past, this city of Kuśī was called the Royal City of Kuśī; it was exceedingly prosperous and joyful, and its population was vast.
Ānanda! The royal city of Kuśinagara is twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide. Ānanda!
Towers and battlements were constructed, reaching a height of one man, or two, three, four, up to seven men. Ānanda!

Around the perimeter of the royal city of Kuśinagara, there were seven tiers of moats. These moats were lined with bricks made of the four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and their bottoms were strewn with sands of the four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Ānanda! Surrounding the royal city of Kuśinagara on its exterior are seven tiers of walls; these walls are likewise constructed by stacking bricks made of the four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Ānanda! The royal city of Kuśinagara was surrounded by seven tiers of rows of *tāla* trees made of four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden *tāla* trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of silver; the silver *tāla* trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of gold; the lapis lazuli *tāla* trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of crystal; and the crystal *tāla* trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of lapis lazuli.
“Ānanda! Between those tāla trees, various lotus ponds are made: ponds of blue lotuses, red lotuses, crimson lotuses, and white lotuses.”

Ānanda! The banks of that flower pond are built up with bricks of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; its bottom is spread with sand of four kinds of treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Ānanda! Within that pond there are stairways made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with gold steps and silver treads, silver steps and gold treads, lapis lazuli steps and crystal treads, and crystal steps and lapis lazuli treads.

Ānanda! Surrounding that pond are railings made of four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden railings having silver hooks, silver railings having golden hooks, lapis lazuli railings having crystal hooks, and crystal railings having lapis lazuli hooks.

Ānanda! That pond is covered with a net, and bells are suspended within it. Those bells are made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden bells have silver tongues; the silver bells have golden tongues; the lapis lazuli bells have crystal tongues; and the crystal bells have lapis lazuli tongues.

“Ānanda! In that pond, various kinds of water flowers are planted—blue lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, and white lotuses—which are always present with water and flowers; there is no one to guard them, and they are open to all people.”

Ānanda! On the banks of that pond are planted various kinds of terrestrial flowers: sumana flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mahāsugandhika flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pāṭala flowers.

"Ānanda! On the banks of that lotus pond there are many women whose bodies are radiant, pure, and bright; their beauty surpasses that of humans and falls short of that of the gods. Their features are upright and graceful, bringing joy to all who behold them, and they are fully adorned with necklaces and ornaments made of various jewels."
He practiced generosity, providing whatever was required—food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, dwellings, mattresses, woolen rugs, attendants, and bright lamps—all of which he gave away.

“Ānanda! When the wind blows through the leaves of those tāla trees, there arises the sound of most sublime and exquisite music, like the performance of five kinds of master musicians playing together in a most wonderful, superior, and harmonious melody.”
Ānanda! When the wind blows through the leaves of those tāla trees, it is likewise so, Ānanda!

Suppose there were a person of base and extremely low character within the city of Kuśinagara who desired the five kinds of musical entertainment; he would immediately go together with others to the grove of tala trees, where they all obtain their desires at will and enjoy themselves to the fullest extent.

Ānanda! In the royal city of Kuśinagara, twelve kinds of sounds were constantly present, never ceasing: the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of foot-soldiers, the sound of conch shells being blown, the sound of drums, the sound of paṇava drums, the sound of kettledrums, the sound of singing, the sound of dancing, the sound of eating and drinking, and the sound of giving alms.

“Ānanda! In the city of Kuśinagara there was a king named Mahāsudassana, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), intelligent and wise. He possessed a fourfold army to govern the world, exercising sovereign mastery through his own power. As a Dharma-king in accordance with the Dharma, he had accomplished the seven treasures and attained the four kinds of human excellence that accord with his wishes.”
How does one accomplish the seven treasures and attain the four kinds of human-like sovereign powers?
These are as previously described regarding the seven treasures and the four kinds of human-like sovereign powers.
"Ānanda!
Then, the brahmins and householders of the royal city of Kuśinagara took many jewels and kampilaka gems, loaded them onto vehicles, and went to King Mahāsudassana, saying:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"These many precious jewels and kampilaka gems, O Heavenly King, please accept them out of compassion for us.
King Mahāsudarśana said to the brahmins and householders:
"I have no need for what you offer; I already possess these myself."
"Ānanda! Furthermore, eighty-four thousand minor kings went to King Mahāsudassana and said to him:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"We wish to build a palace for the Heavenly King.
King Mahāsudarśana told the minor kings:
"You wish to build a main palace for me, but I have no need for one; I already possess a main palace."
The eighty-four thousand minor kings all joined their palms toward him and said repeatedly:
"O Heavenly King!
We wish to build a palace for Your Majesty; we wish to build a palace for Your Majesty."
Thereupon, King Mahāsudarśana remained silent and listened for the sake of the eighty-four thousand minor kings.

When those eighty-four thousand minor kings realized that King Mahāsudarśana was listening in silence, they paid their respects, took their leave, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Each returned to his own kingdom and loaded eighty-four thousand chariots with gold—both wrought and unwrought—together with the precious jewels. Carrying one pillar made of each kind of jewel, they proceeded toward the city of Kuśinagara. Not far from the city, they constructed a great and magnificent hall.
“Ānanda! That great assembly hall is one yojana in length and one yojana in width. Ānanda!”
That Great Hall was constructed with bricks of four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Ānanda!

That Great Hall had staircases made of these four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden steps and silver treads, silver steps and golden treads, lapis lazuli steps and crystal treads, and crystal steps and lapis lazuli treads.

Ānanda! Within the Great Hall of Righteousness there are eighty-four thousand pillars, fashioned from four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden pillars have capitals and bases of silver; the silver pillars have capitals and bases of gold; the lapis lazuli pillars have capitals and bases of crystal; and the crystal pillars have capitals and bases of lapis lazuli.

Ānanda! Within the Great Hall of Justice stand eighty-four thousand towers, constructed of four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The gold towers are capped with silver; the silver towers are capped with gold; the lapis lazuli towers are capped with crystal; and the crystal towers are capped with lapis lazuli.

“Ānanda! Within the Great Hall of Justice, eighty-four thousand royal thrones were set out, likewise fashioned from the four precious substances: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. In the golden pavilions, silver thrones were set up, spread with woolen rugs (*kūrma*) and carpets (*tūla*), covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauze, provided with under-linens, and furnished with pillows at both ends, as well as *kāliṅga-pauṣkara* and *pāṭala-syandana* cushions. Likewise, in the silver pavilions, golden thrones were set up; in the lapis lazuli pavilions, crystal thrones were set up; and in the crystal pavilions, lapis lazuli thrones were set up. These were spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauze, provided with under-linens, and furnished with pillows at both ends, as well as *kāliṅga-pauṣkara* and *pāṭala-syandana* cushions.”

Ānanda! That great hall of audience was surrounded on all sides by railings made of four kinds of jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden railings having silver hooks, silver railings having golden hooks, lapis lazuli railings having crystal hooks, and crystal railings having lapis lazuli hooks.

Ānanda! That great hall of justice was covered with a network of nets, with bells suspended within them. Those bells were made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden bells having silver tongues, silver bells having golden tongues, lapis lazuli bells having crystal tongues, and crystal bells having lapis lazuli tongues.
"Ānanda! Once that great hall of justice had been fully completed, eighty-four thousand minor kings constructed a great lotus pond not far from the hall."
Ānanda! That great lotus pond is one yojana in length and one yojana in width. Ānanda!

That great lotus pond was lined with bricks made of the four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and its bottom was strewn with sands of the four kinds of jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Ānanda! That great lotus pond has stairways made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with gold steps and silver treads, silver steps and gold treads, lapis lazuli steps and crystal treads, and crystal steps and lapis lazuli treads.

"Ānanda! That great lotus pond is encircled on all sides by railings made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with gold railings having silver hooks, silver railings having gold hooks, lapis lazuli railings having crystal hooks, and crystal railings having lapis lazuli hooks."

Ānanda! That great flower pond is covered with a network of nets, and bells are suspended within them. Those bells are made of four treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden bells have silver tongues; the silver bells have golden tongues; the lapis lazuli bells have crystal tongues; and the crystal bells have lapis lazuli tongues.

“Ānanda! Within that great lotus pond there are various kinds of water flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, and white lotuses—which are ever-present in both water and bloom; it has a guardian who does not allow anyone to pass through.”

Ānanda! On the banks of that great lotus pond there are various kinds of terrestrial flowers: sumana flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mahāsugandhika flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pārijātaka flowers.
“Ānanda! When this great palace and the great lotus pond had been fully completed, eighty-four thousand minor kings established Tāla groves not far from the palace.”
Ānanda! That Tāla Grove is one yojana in length and one yojana in width. Ānanda!

Within the Tālavana grove, eighty-four thousand tāla trees were planted, made of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden tāla trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of silver; the silver tāla trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of gold; the lapis lazuli tāla trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of crystal; and the crystal tāla trees had leaves, flowers, and fruits of lapis lazuli.

Ānanda! That Tāla Grove is surrounded on all sides by railings made of four precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden railings having silver hooks, silver railings having golden hooks, lapis lazuli railings having crystal hooks, and crystal railings having lapis lazuli hooks.

Ānanda! That Tāla Grove is covered with a network of nets, with bells suspended among them. Those bells are made of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with golden bells having silver tongues, silver bells having golden tongues, lapis lazuli bells having crystal tongues, and crystal bells having lapis lazuli tongues.
“Ānanda! When this great palace, the lotus pond, and the Tāla Grove were thus fully completed, the eighty-four thousand minor kings went together to King Mahāsudassana and said to him:
‘O Heavenly King!’”
"You should know that the great palace, the lotus pond, and the Tāla Grove have all been fully completed; we only pray that the Heavenly King may enjoy them as he desires. Ānanda!
At that time, King Mahāsudarśana then had this thought:

"I ought not to ascend this great hall first. If there are senior śramaṇas or brahmins residing in this royal city of Kuśinagara, I would rather invite them all to assemble and sit in this great hall; I shall provide them with the finest flavors and most exquisite delicacies, an abundance of various foods to chew, eat, and digest, serving them with my own hands until they are all fully satisfied. Once they have finished eating, I will collect the vessels, provide water for washing, and then bid them farewell to return."

“Ānanda! After King Mahāsudassana had formed this thought, he immediately invited the most venerable śramaṇas and brahmins residing in that royal city of Kuśinagara; they all assembled and ascended the Great Righteous Palace. Once they were all seated together, the king personally provided water for washing, and then served with his own hands exquisite, most delicious delicacies—a variety of abundant foods to be chewed, swallowed, and digested—until everyone was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished, the vessels were cleared away, the water for washing was offered, and after receiving their blessings, he dismissed them to return home.”
"Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana again had this thought:
'Now, I ought not to indulge in sensual desires within the Great Palace Hall; it would be better for me to ascend and dwell alone in the Great Palace with only a single attendant.'"

"Ānanda! Later on, King Mahāsudassana, taking a single attendant with him, ascended the Great Palace and entered the Golden Chamber. There he sat upon a silver royal couch, spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and muslins, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and adorned with Kāliṅga-bāhulā and Pāṭaliputtaka spreads. Having sat down, free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, filled with joy and happiness, he attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna."

Emerging from the golden pavilion, he next entered the silver pavilion and sat upon a golden royal couch, which was spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine silks and gauzes, provided with a body-cushion, and furnished with pillows at both ends, as well as *kāliṅga-pāvāra* and *pāṭali-santānaka* covers. Having sat down, free from sensual desires and free from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna.

Emerging from the silver pavilion, he entered the lapis lazuli pavilion and sat upon a crystal throne. It was spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with brocades, silks, and fine gauzes, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and adorned with *kāliṅga-paveṇī* and *paccattharaṇa* cloths. Having sat down, free from sensual desires and free from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attained and dwelt in the first *dhyāna*.

Emerging from the beryl pavilion, he entered the crystal pavilion and sat upon a beryl throne spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauze, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and draped with Kalinga and Pārasīka woolen cloths. Having sat down, free from sensual desires and free from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, born of seclusion, filled with joy and happiness, he attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna.

“Ānanda! At that time, the eighty-four thousand ladies and the precious woman had not seen King Mahāsudassana for a long while; each harbored a sense of longing and, thirsting with a yearning desire, wished to see him.”
Thereupon, eighty-four thousand ladies went together to the Woman-Jewel and said to her:
"O Queen! You should know that we have all not beheld the Heavenly King for a long time."
"O Queen!
We now wish to go together to see the Heavenly King.
Having heard this, the Woman-Jewel addressed the Minister of the Army:
"You should know this now!
We have all not beheld the Heavenly King for a long time; we wish to go and see him.

Upon hearing this, the Minister of War immediately escorted eighty-four thousand ladies and the Woman-Jewel to the Great Hall of Justice. He also accompanied eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand foot soldiers, and eighty-four thousand minor kings to the Great Hall of Justice. As they were departing, the sound was so great that its resonance shook the earth.
When King Mahāsudassana heard that sound, which was loud and its resonance shook the air, he asked his attendants:
"Whose voice is this, so loud and its resonance so shaking?"
The attendant replied, "O Heavenly King!

These eighty-four thousand ladies and the Jewel of Women have now all come together to the Great Hall of Justice. Furthermore, eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantrymen, and eighty-four thousand minor kings have likewise all come together to the Great Hall of Justice."
"Therefore, its sound is loud and its resonance shakes the earth.
Having heard this, King Mahāsudassana said to his attendant:
"Go quickly down from the palace; prepare a golden couch in the open air at once, and upon completion, return and inform me."
The attendant, having received these instructions, immediately followed the prince from the palace steps; he quickly spread the golden couch upon the open ground and returned to report:
"I have already spread the golden couch upon the open ground for the Heavenly King; it is now as the Heavenly King intends."
"Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana then descended from the palace together with his attendants, ascended the golden couch, and sat down cross-legged. Ānanda!"
At that time, the eighty-four thousand ladies and the woman-treasure all went forward together to approach King Mahāsudassana.
Ānanda, when King Mahāsudassana saw the eighty-four thousand ladies and the woman-treasure from afar, as soon as he saw them, he closed his sense faculties.
Thereupon, when the eighty-four thousand ladies and the jewel of a woman saw that the King had closed off his sense faculties, they thought to themselves:
"The Heavenly King will certainly have no further need of us."
"Why is this? Because as soon as the Heavenly King saw us, he immediately closed off his sense faculties.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said].
Thereupon, the Woman-Jewel went to King Mahāsudassana; having arrived, she said to him:

"Your Majesty, please know that those eighty-four thousand wives and this Woman-Jewel are all Your Majesty’s possession. I only pray that Your Majesty will always keep us in mind until the end of our lives."

There are eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantrymen, and eighty-four thousand minor kings—all of whom belong to the Heavenly King. We only pray that the Heavenly King will constantly keep us in mind until the end of our lives.
At that time, having heard these words, King Mahāsudarśana said to the Jewel-Woman:
"Sister! For a long night you have taught me to do evil and prevented me from practicing loving-kindness."
"Sisters!
From this day forward, you must teach me to practice loving-kindness and not allow me to do evil. Ānanda!
The eighty-four thousand ladies and the woman-treasure withdrew to one side; shedding tears and weeping with grief, they spoke these words:
"We are not the sisters of the Heavenly King, yet now the Heavenly King addresses us as sisters."
"Ānanda! Those eighty-four thousand ladies and the woman-treasure each wiped away their tears with their robes and went again to visit King Mahāsudassana. Having arrived, they said to him:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"How then, sisters, shall we teach the Heavenly King to practice loving-kindness and not do evil?
King Mahāsudarśana replied: "Sisters!..."
"For my sake, you should speak thus:
'Does the Heavenly King know?
Human life is short and fleeting; one must depart for the next world, and therefore one should practice the holy life (brahmacarya).'"
"O Heavenly King! There is no birth that does not end.
You should know that this phenomenon will inevitably come; it is not to be cherished nor is it to be rejoiced in, for it destroys all worlds. It is called death."

Therefore, regarding the eighty-four thousand wives and the woman-treasure, if Your Majesty has thoughts of or desires for them, I only pray that Your Majesty will completely sever and abandon them, never thinking of them again until the end of your life.

Regarding the eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantrymen, and eighty-four thousand minor kings—if the Heavenly King has any desire for or thought of them, we only pray that the Heavenly King will completely sever, abandon, and from this point forward never think of them again.
“Sisters, you have thus instructed me to practice loving-kindness and not to do evil. Ānanda,
those eighty-four thousand wives and the woman-jewel said:
"O Heavenly King!
From this day forward, we shall teach the Heavenly King to practice loving-kindness and not allow him to commit evil.
O Heavenly King!"
Human life is short and fleeting, and one must depart for the next world; that dharma will inevitably come, which is neither desirable nor pleasing, destroying all worlds—this is called death.

Therefore, regarding the eighty-four thousand wives and the woman-treasure, if Your Majesty has thoughts of or desires for them, we only pray that Your Majesty will completely sever and abandon them, and never think of them again until the end of your life.

Regarding these eighty-four thousand elephants, eighty-four thousand horses, eighty-four thousand chariots, eighty-four thousand infantrymen, and eighty-four thousand minor kings—if the Heavenly King has any desire for or thought regarding them, we only pray that the Heavenly King will completely sever and renounce them, never thinking of them again until the end.

"Ānanda! King Mahāsudassana taught the Dharma to those eighty-four thousand queens and the woman-jewel, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and establishing them in joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to teach them the Dharma, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and establishing them in joy, he dismissed them and sent them back."
“Ānanda! When those eighty-four thousand ladies and the Woman-Jewel knew that King Mahāsudassana had sent them away, they each bowed in farewell and returned. Ānanda!”

Not long after those eighty-four thousand ladies and the Woman-Jewel had departed, King Mahāsudassana returned with his attendant to ascend the great palace. He entered the golden chamber and sat upon the silver throne, which was spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with a body-cushion, and furnished with pillows at both ends, including Kalinga-bāhulā and paccattharaṇa. Having sat down, he reflected thus:

"This is my final limit; thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of harm, strife, mutual hatred, flattery, hypocrisy, deception, and false speech—these immeasurable evil and unwholesome states are my final limit."
With a mind imbued with loving-kindness, he dwells having pervaded one direction, accomplished and abiding therein.

Likewise the second, third, and fourth directions; the four intermediate points, above and below; everywhere and in all respects, he dwells having pervaded the entire world—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, exceedingly vast and sublime, immeasurable and well-cultivated.

“Emerging from the golden pavilion, he next entered the silver pavilion and sat upon a golden royal couch. It was spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and draped with *kāliṅgaprāvāra* and *pārāsītika* blankets. Having sat down, he reflected thus:

‘This is my final existence; thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of cruelty, strife, mutual hatred, flattery, hypocrisy, deception, and false speech—all these immeasurable evil and unwholesome states are now at their end.’”
With a mind imbued with compassion, he dwells having pervaded one direction, accomplished and perfected.

In this same way, he dwells having pervaded the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, all around and everywhere; free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world, accomplished and perfected.

Emerging from the silver pavilion, he entered the lapis lazuli pavilion and sat upon a crystal throne. It was spread with woolen carpets (*kūrma*) and rugs (*tūla*), covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with under-linens and pillows at both ends, and adorned with *kāliṅga-paśvara* and *pāṭala-sītalana* cushions. Having sat down, he made this reflection:

"This is my final state; thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill-will, thoughts of harm, strife, mutual hatred, flattery, hypocrisy, deception, and false speech—these immeasurable evil and unwholesome states are now at their end."
With a mind imbued with joy, he dwells having pervaded one direction;

likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below, encompassing all everywhere—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.

“Emerging from the beryl pavilion, he enters the crystal pavilion and sits upon a beryl throne spread with woolen carpets and rugs, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and draped with *kāliṅgaprāvāra* and *pārāśarīna* cloths. Having sat down, he reflects thus:

‘This is my final limit; thoughts of desire, thoughts of ill will, thoughts of cruelty, strife, mutual hatred, flattery, hypocrisy, deceit, and false speech—these immeasurable evil and unwholesome states are my final limit.’”
With a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells having pervaded one direction;

likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below, encompassing all everywhere—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.

“Ānanda! When King Mahāsudassana was at the end of his life, he experienced a slight sensation of death-pain, just as a householder or a householder’s son might experience a slight discomfort after eating an exquisite meal.”
Ānanda! When King Mahāsudassana was at the end of his life, the subtle sensation of death-pain that arose was likewise like this. Ānanda!
"At that time, King Mahāsudarśana cultivated the four brahmavihāras; having abandoned desire through mindfulness, he passed away from there and was reborn among the Brahmā devas. Ānanda!"
In times past, during a different era, as for that King Mahāsudarśana, do you think he was someone else?
Do not conceive such a thought; you should know that he was none other than myself, Ānanda!

At that time, for my own benefit and for the benefit of others, for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world, I sought what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and sought their peace, security, and happiness.
At that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate conclusion; it was not ultimately pure, nor was the holy life (brahmacarya) brought to its ultimate conclusion.
At that time, one was not yet free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had one yet attained liberation from all suffering.

“Ānanda! I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One.

I now act for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others; I benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
I have now taught the Dharma that reaches the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life; I have brought the holy life to its final consummation.
I have now escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.

“Ānanda! From the city of Kuśinagara, from the Śāla grove of the Mallas of Upavattana, from the Nairañjanā River, from the Kakutthā River, from the Devakula monastery, and from the place where my bed was prepared for me—in all these locations, I have relinquished my body seven times. On six of those occasions, I was a wheel-turning monarch; now, on this seventh occasion, I am a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
“Ānanda! Among gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins—from the heavens down to humans—I no longer see anyone who, having cast off this body, could again do so; such a thing is impossible.”
Ānanda! This is now my final birth, my final existence, my final body, my final form; having attained this final self, I declare this to be the end of suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Mahāsudassana Sutta, the fourth, ends here, totaling 4,615 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 14, totaling 9,354 characters; recited in the second section on the Small Earth Fort (Kṣullakāgrasūtra).
Madhyama Āgama, Volume Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
69. Sūtra on the Thirty Similes (69). Madhyama Āgama, Chapter on Kings, Sūtra on the Thirty Similes, Number Five.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Sanctuary, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, observing the rains retreat.

At that time, on the fifteenth day, when it was the occasion for reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, the World-Honored One arranged his seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. Having sat, he entered a state of meditative concentration and observed the minds of the bhikṣus.

Then the Blessed One saw that the assembly of bhikṣus was sitting in silence, in profound silence, free from sleep because they had removed the hindrances; the assembly of bhikṣus sat in a state that was deep, most deep, tranquil, most tranquil, and sublime, most sublime.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also present in the assembly.
Then, the Blessed One addressed him, saying: "Śāriputra!"

The community of bhikṣus sat in silence, in profound silence; they were without sleep, for they had removed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). The community of bhikṣus sat in deep absorption, in most profound absorption; they were tranquil, in extreme tranquility; sublime, in extreme sublimity.
“Śāriputra! Who is able to revere and serve the community of bhikṣus?
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Thus this assembly of bhikṣus sits in silence, in profound silence; they are without sleep because they have removed the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). This assembly of bhikṣus sits in profundity, in extreme profundity; they are at peace, in extreme peace; they are sublime, in extreme sublimity.”
“World-Honored One!

There is no one capable of reverently honoring and serving the community of bhikṣus; only the World-Honored One is able to reverently honor and serve the Dharma, the community of bhikṣus, the precepts, heedfulness, generosity, and meditative concentration—it is only the World-Honored One who is able to reverently honor and serve.”
The World-Honored One said:
“Sāriputta! It is so, it is so.”

There is no one capable of honoring and serving the community of bhikṣus; only the World-Honored One is able to honor and serve the Dharma, the community of bhikṣus, the precepts, heedfulness, generosity, and meditative concentration—only the World-Honored One is able to honor and serve these.

Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister possessed various kinds of ornaments: silks, brocades, and woolens; finger-rings, armlets, and bracelets; necklaces and throat-ornaments; and strings of beads of natural colors.
Śāriputra! In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take the virtue of the precepts as their ornament. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes the virtue of the precepts as their ornament, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra!

It is just as a king or a great minister has five insignia—the sword, the parasol, the celestial crown, the fly-whisk with a jeweled handle, and the decorated sandals—which guard their person and ensure their security and well-being.
Śāriputra! In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs guard their holy life by maintaining the precepts. Śāriputra!
“Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī fulfills the prohibitive precepts as a safeguard for the holy life, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.”
"Just as a king or a great minister has a gatekeeper, Śāriputra,
so too do monks and nuns have the guarding of the six sense faculties as their gatekeepers."
Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes the guarding of the six sense faculties as their gatekeepers, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a gatekeeper who was intelligent, wise, discerning, and fully understanding. Śāriputra!
In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take right mindfulness as their gatekeeper. Śāriputra!
If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are accomplished in right mindfulness as their gatekeeper, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a great minister had a fine bathing pool, filled with clear, pure water. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns take their own minds as the bathing pool and spring. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns accomplish taking their own minds as the bathing pool and spring, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a bath-attendant who was constantly employed to bathe them. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns take a virtuous friend as their bath-attendant. Śāriputra!
If monks and nuns are accomplished in taking a virtuous friend as their bath-attendant, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
“Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister had body-unguents such as tagara, aloeswood, agallochum, sandalwood, storax, clove, and douliang.”
Śāriputra! In this way, monks and nuns take the virtue of the precepts as their unguent. Śāriputra!
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī achieves the fragrance of moral virtue, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra!
It is just as if a king or a great minister possessed fine garments, such as kṣauma cloth, silk brocade, white cotton cloth, and kāliṅga-pāvaṭa cloth.
Śāriputra! It is so.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take shame and remorse as their clothing.
Śāriputra! If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs achieve the robes of shame and remorse, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a great minister had a fine couch that was exceedingly broad and high. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns take the four dhyānas as their bed and seat. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns accomplish the four dhyānas as their bed and seat, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
“Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a skilled barber whom they constantly employ for bathing. Sāriputta!”
In this way, monks and nuns take right mindfulness as their barber. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns achieve right mindfulness as their barber, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as when a king or a great minister has various kinds of delicacies and fine foods with diverse flavors. Śāriputra!
In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take joy as their sustenance.
Śāriputra! If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are accomplished in taking joy as their sustenance, they are able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if a king or a great minister had various kinds of drinks: mango drinks, jambu drinks, sugarcane drinks, grape drinks, and mṛdvīkā drinks.
Śāriputra! In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take the flavor of the Dharma as their drink. Śāriputra!
“Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī achieves the flavor of the Dharma as their drink, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.”

It is just as if a king or a great minister possessed exquisite flower garlands—garlands of blue lotuses, garlands of campaka flowers, garlands of sumana jasmine, garlands of vārṣika jasmine, and garlands of atimuktaka flowers.
Śāriputra! In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take the three concentrations—emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness—as their floral garlands. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī achieves the three concentrations as their flower garland, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra!
"Just as a king or a great minister has various dwellings— pavilions, halls, and towers—
so too, Śāriputra,
do monks and nuns have three dwellings as their abodes: the celestial abode, the Brahma abode, and the noble abode."
Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes the three abodes as their dwelling, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as a king or a high minister has an official in charge of their affairs, namely, a chamberlain. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns take wisdom as their guardian of the dwelling. Śāriputra!
If monks and nuns achieve wisdom as their guardian of the dwelling, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

“Śāriputra! It is just as when a king or a high minister has four kinds of taxes from various kingdoms and towns: one portion is provided for the king and given to the queen and the ladies of the palace;
two portions are supplied to the crown prince and the ministers.”
"Śāriputra, one-third shall be provided for all the people of the kingdom;
one-fourth shall be supplied to śramaṇas and brahmins."
In this way, monks and nuns take the four foundations of mindfulness as their tax. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns accomplish the four foundations of mindfulness as their tax, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as a king or a great minister has four kinds of armies: the elephant army, the cavalry, the chariot army, and the infantry. Śāriputra!
In this way, monks and nuns take the four right endeavors as their fourfold army. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns are accomplished in the four right endeavors as their fourfold army, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as kings and great ministers have various kinds of litters: elephant litters, horse litters, carriage litters, and palanquins. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns take the four bases of psychic power as a palanquin. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns achieve the four bases of psychic power and make them their palanquin, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

“Śāriputra! It is just as when a king or a high minister possesses various types of chariots adorned with many fine skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, woven together in various colors and decorated with diverse ornaments.”
Śāriputra! In this way, monks and nuns take serenity and insight as their vehicle. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes serenity and insight as their vehicle, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
"Just as a king or a high minister has a driver— that is, a charioteer—
so too, Śāriputra,
do monks and nuns take right mindfulness as their driver."
Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī achieves right mindfulness as their charioteer, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if a king or a great minister possessed an exceedingly high banner. Śāriputra!
In this way, monks and nuns take their own minds as a high banner. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns achieve the state of taking their own minds as a high banner, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
“Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a fine road, level and smooth, leading only toward his pleasure gardens. Sāriputta!”
In this way, Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs take the Noble Eightfold Path as their road—level, straight, and smooth—which leads only toward Nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!

If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes the Noble Eightfold Path as their way—level, straight, and direct, leading only toward Nirvāṇa—they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a commander-in-chief who was intelligent, wise, discerning, and fully understanding. Śāriputra!
In this way, monks and nuns take wisdom as their chief minister. Śāriputra!
If monks and nuns are accomplished in taking wisdom as their chief minister, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a great hall that was extremely vast, lofty, and spacious. Sāriputta!
In this way, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs take wisdom as their great hall of justice. Śāriputra!
If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs achieve wisdom as their great hall of justice, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
“Sāriputta! It is just as when a king or a high minister ascends a lofty palace and observes the people below coming and going, running and leaping, standing, sitting, and lying down.”
Śāriputra! In this way, monks and nuns ascend the lofty palace of unsurpassed wisdom to observe their own minds, making them upright and supple, and joyfully remaining detached from worldly things.

Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes the lofty palace of unsurpassed wisdom and, for the purpose of observing their own minds, makes them upright and supple, and with joy remains detached, they will then be able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if a king or a high minister had a chief minister of the clan who was thoroughly versed in the family lineage. Śāriputra!
In this way, monks and nuns take the four noble lineages as their ministers of justice. Śāriputra,
if monks and nuns are accomplished in the four noble lineages as their ministers of justice, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Śāriputra! It is just as if there were a king or a high minister who had a renowned and skilled physician capable of curing all manner of diseases. Śāriputra!
In this way, monks and nuns take right mindfulness as their skilled physician. Śāriputra!
If monks and nuns are accomplished in right mindfulness as their skilled physician, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.

“Sāriputta! It is just as if a king or a great minister had a royal couch, spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades, silks, and gauzes, provided with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and adorned with Kalinga, Pausnara, and Paṭṭasuttarāna cloths.”
Śāriputra! In this way, monks and nuns take the concentration of non-obstruction as their royal couch. Śāriputra!
Śāriputra, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī accomplishes unimpeded concentration as their proper seat, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome. Śāriputra!
"Just as a king or a great minister possesses a famous jewel of precious quality,
Śāriputra, in the same way,
a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī takes the liberation of the immovable mind as their famous jewel of precious quality."
Śāriputra! If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī achieves the jewel-like liberation of the immovable mind, they are then able to abandon evil and cultivate what is wholesome.
Sāriputta! It is just as when a king or a high minister has bathed thoroughly with pure water, anointed his body with fine perfumes, and his person is thus utterly purified. Sāriputta!
In this way, monks and nuns regard their own minds as the supreme purity of the body. Śāriputra,

if monks and nuns are accomplished in regarding their own minds as the purity of the body, they will then be able to revere, honor, and serve the Blessed One, the Dharma, the Saṅgha of monks, the precepts, heedfulness, generosity, and meditative concentration.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Sāriputta and the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifth discourse, the *Sattatiṃsa-upama-sutta*, ends here, totaling 2,388 characters. 70. The Discourse on the Wheel-Turning King (70). Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on Kings, the sixth discourse, the *Cakkavatti-sīhanāda-sutta*. Second Sub-section: Recitation of the Small Earth Fort. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Malla Kṣatriyas, staying on the bank of the river Aciravatī in the Mango Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!"
Take the Dharma as your own lamp; take refuge in your own Dharma. Do not take other lamps as your light; do not take other Dharmas as your refuge. Monks!

If you take the Dharma as your own lamp, take refuge in your own Dharma, and do not take other lamps as your light or other Dharmas as your refuge, you will be able to seek and learn for your benefit, attaining immeasurable merit.

Why is that? Monks! In the past there was a king named Dṛḍhadhyāyi, a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), intelligent and wise. He possessed a fourfold army to govern the world, ruling with sovereign mastery as a righteous Dharma-king. He had accomplished the seven treasures and attained the four kinds of human supernormal powers.
How does one accomplish the seven treasures and attain the four kinds of human sovereign powers?
It is as previously explained: by accomplishing the seven treasures, one attains the four kinds of human sovereign powers.
"Then, at a later time, King Dṛḍhadhyāna’s divine wheel-treasure shifted and suddenly left its original place.
Someone who saw this went to King Dṛḍhadhyāna and said:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"You should know that the divine wheel-treasure has shifted from its original place.
Having heard this, King Dṛḍhacintin said:
"Crown Prince!..."
"O Prince, my divine Wheel-Treasure has shifted from its original place.

I have heard this from the ancients: if the divine Wheel-Treasure of a Wheel-turning King shifts from its original place, that king will certainly not remain long; his life will not endure for much longer."
"Prince! I have already obtained the desires of the human world; now I shall seek the desires of the heavens.
Prince, I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave my home for the homeless life to study the Way."

"Prince! I now entrust these four continents to you; you should govern and transform them according to the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma. Do not allow various evil deeds or those who do not practice the holy life to exist within the kingdom."

"Prince! If you later see that the divine wheel-treasure has shifted from its original place, you should likewise entrust the administration of this kingdom to your crown prince and instruct him well."

Once you have entrusted the kingdom to the crown prince, you too shall shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for the homeless state to study the Way here.

King Dṛḍhadhyāna entrusted the kingdom to the crown prince; having given him these excellent instructions, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and with deep faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path.

"At that time, seven days after King Dṛḍhadhyāyi had left the household life to study the Way, that divine wheel-treasure suddenly vanished and was no longer seen. Having lost the divine wheel-treasure, the Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja King became greatly distressed and sorrowful, finding no joy; he then went to where his father, the seer King Dṛḍhadhyāyi, was staying."
Having arrived, he said:
"O Heavenly King!
You should know that seven days after the Heavenly King began his study of the Way, that celestial wheel-treasure (cakraratna) vanished and was no longer seen."
The seer King Dṛḍhadhyāyi said to his son, the Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja:
"Do not harbor grief or distress because you have lost the divine wheel-treasure."
"Why is that? You did not receive this divine wheel from your father.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja then addressed his father again, saying:
"O Heavenly King! What should I do now?
His father, the seer King Dṛḍhamati, said to his son:

"You should train in the dharma of succession. If you train in the dharma of succession, then on the fifteenth day, when the *prātimokṣa* is recited, after you have bathed and washed and ascended to the main hall, that divine wheel-treasure will surely come from the east; it shall have a thousand spokes, complete in every respect, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, with a color like a flame, its brilliance shining forth."
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja again addressed his father, saying:
"O Heavenly King!
What is the method of succession that you wish me to learn?"

Once I had completed my training, on the fifteenth day during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, after I had bathed, washed, and ascended the main hall, that divine Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*) came from the east. The wheel had a thousand spokes, all complete, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, its color like a flame, radiating brilliant light.
The seer King Dṛḍhadhyāyi again addressed his son, saying: "You should contemplate the Dharma according to the Dharma and practice the Dharma according to the Dharma.

You should, for the sake of the crown prince, the queen, the court ladies, as well as the ministers, the citizens, the śramaṇas, and the brahmins—even down to the insects—uphold the Dharma-fast (dharma-upavāsa). On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, you should practice generosity, bestowing upon those who are destitute: śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar; providing them with food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mats, woolen rugs, fine cushions, attendants, and bright lamps."
If there are in your country venerable ones, men of renown and virtue—whether śramaṇas or brahmins—you should go to them from time to time, inquire about the Dharma, and receive the Dharma, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
What are wholesome dharmas?
What are unwholesome dharmas?
What constitutes an offense?
What constitutes merit?
What is sublime?
And what is not sublime?
What constitutes the dark?
What constitutes the bright?
From what do the phenomena of darkness and brightness arise?
What is the meaning of the present life?
What is the meaning of future lives?
How does one act so as to experience what is wholesome and not what is unwholesome?
Having heard this from him, act according to what was said.
If there are those who are poor within your kingdom, you should provide wealth and goods to relieve them.
"Son! This is called the dharma of succession; you should learn it well.

Once you have learned it well, on the fifteenth day when the *prātimokṣa* is recited, after you have bathed and washed and ascended to the main hall, that divine Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*) will surely come from the east. The wheel has a thousand spokes, all complete, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, its color like a flame, its radiance brilliant and dazzling."

"Then, at a later time, King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja contemplated the Dharma according to the Dharma and practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma. He observed the Dharma-fast (dharma-uposatha) for the sake of the crown prince, the queen, the concubines, the ministers and citizens, the śramaṇas and brahmins, and even down to the insects. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, he practiced giving, bestowing upon those who were destitute—śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar—food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, couches and mattresses, woolen rugs, fine carpets, servants, and bright lamps."

If there are in that country venerable ones, men of renown and virtue—whether śramaṇas or brahmins—he would go to them at the appropriate time and inquire about the Dharma and receive the Dharma, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
What are wholesome dharmas?
What are unwholesome dharmas?
And what constitutes an offense?
What constitutes merit?
What is sublime?
And what is not sublime?
What constitutes the black?
What constitutes the white?
From what do the phenomena of black and white arise?
What is the meaning of the present life?
What is the meaning of future lives?
How does one act so as to experience what is wholesome and not what is unwholesome?
Having heard this from him, he acted according to what was taught.
If there were those who were poor within his kingdom, he would immediately provide wealth and goods to assist and relieve them at all times.

When King Kṣatriya Mūrdhāta, on the fifteenth day of the latter fortnight during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, had bathed and washed himself and ascended the main hall, that divine wheel-treasure came from the east. The wheel had a thousand spokes, was complete in every respect, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, its color like a blazing fire, and its radiance dazzlingly bright. He too became a Wheel-turning Monarch, achieved the seven treasures, and attained the four kinds of human sovereign virtues.
"How does he achieve the possession of the seven treasures and the four kinds of human supernormal powers?
It is as previously described.
At a later time, that wheel-turning king’s celestial wheel-treasure shifts and suddenly departs from its original place."
Someone who saw this went to the Wheel-Turning King and said:
"O Heavenly King!
You should know that the divine Wheel-Treasure has moved away from its original place."
Having heard this, the Wheel-Turning King said:
"Prince! My divine wheel-treasure has shifted from its original place."
"Prince! I once heard this from my father, the seer King Dṛḍhadhyāna:
'If the divine wheel-treasure of a Wheel-turning King moves away from its original place, that king will certainly not remain long; his life will not endure.'"
"Prince! I have already obtained the desires of the human realm; now I shall seek the desires of the heavens. Prince!"
"I wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path.

Prince! I now entrust these four continents to you; you should govern and transform them according to the Dharma, not by what is contrary to the Dharma, and ensure that there are no evil deeds or those who do not practice the holy life within the kingdom."

"Prince! If you later see the precious wheel-treasure of the devas move away from its original place, you too shall entrust the administration of this kingdom to your crown prince and instruct him well."

Once you have handed over the kingdom to the crown prince, you too shall shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path here.

The Wheel-turning King, having invested his crown prince with the kingdom and given him excellent instructions, then shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path.

"Seven days after that Wheel-turning King had renounced the world to study the Path, the celestial Wheel-treasure vanished and was no longer seen. Having lost the celestial wheel, the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja felt no sorrow or distress; rather, he became stained by desire, attached to desire, greedy for desire without satiety, bound by desire, touched by desire, and driven by desire. Failing to see the peril and failing to know the way out, he began to govern the kingdom according to his own whims. Because he governed the kingdom according to his own whims, the nation subsequently declined and no longer flourished, unlike in former times when the successive Wheel-turning Kings studied the traditional laws, causing the land and its people to increase and prosper without decline."

The Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja was likewise; he governed the kingdom according to his own whims, and because he governed the kingdom according to his own whims, the kingdom subsequently declined and no longer flourished.
Thereupon, the brahmin state preceptor traveled throughout the realm and saw that the people of the kingdom were increasingly declining and no longer flourishing.

He then thought to himself: "King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja governs the country according to his own whims; because he governs by his own whims, the territory and its people are increasingly declining and no longer flourishing. This is unlike the former wheel-turning kings who followed the laws of succession; under them, the territory and its people grew ever more prosperous and never declined."

This Kṣatriya King Mahāsammata was also like this: he governed the kingdom according to his own whims. Because he governed the kingdom according to his own whims, the realm and its people gradually declined and were no longer able to prosper.
The brahmin state preceptor then went together with him to visit King Mūrdhaja of the Kṣatriya caste and said to him:
"O Heavenly King!

You should know that you have been governing the kingdom according to your own whims. Because you govern the kingdom according to your own whims, the realm and its people are increasingly declining and no longer prospering. This is unlike the former Universal Monarchs (Cakravartin kings) who followed the laws of succession; under them, the realm and its people flourished and grew ever more prosperous, without any decline."

Today, the Heavenly King is likewise; he governs the kingdom according to his own whims. Because he governs the kingdom according to his own whims, the land and its people continue to decline and no longer flourish.
Having heard this, King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja said:
"Brahmin! What should I do?"
The state preceptor, the brahmin, replied:
"O Heavenly King!

There are people in the kingdom who are intelligent and wise, clearly understanding calculation; there are ministers and their retinues in the kingdom who study and master the scriptures, reciting, practicing, and upholding the successive methods of transmission, just as all our own retinues do."
"O Heavenly King!
You should train in the dharma of succession.

Having trained in the dharma of succession, on the fifteenth day when the *prātimokṣa* is recited, after you have bathed and ascended to the main hall, that divine wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) will surely come from the east. It has a thousand spokes, is complete in all its parts, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands, with a color like the flame of a fire, and radiating brilliant light."
The Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja asked again:
"Brahmin! What is this method of succession that you wish for me to learn?"

Once I have completed my training, on the fifteenth day when the *prātimokṣa* is recited, having bathed and purified myself and ascended to the main hall, that divine Wheel-Treasure will surely come from the east. The wheel has a thousand spokes, complete in every respect, pure and spontaneous, not made by human hands; its color is like a flame, radiating brilliant light.
The state preceptor, the brahmin, replied:
“O Great King!

You should contemplate the Dharma as Dharma and practice the Dharma as Dharma. For the sake of the crown prince, the queen consort, the court ladies, as well as the ministers, the people, the śramaṇas, the brahmins, and even down to the insects, you should observe the Dharma-fast. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of each month, you should practice generosity by giving to those who are destitute—śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar—providing them with food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, scented ointments, dwellings, mattresses, woolen rugs, fine carpets, servants, and bright lamps.”
If there are in the kingdom venerable ones, renowned and virtuous śramaṇas or brahmins, you should go to them at the appropriate time and inquire about the Dharma and receive the Dharma, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
What are wholesome dharmas?
What are unwholesome dharmas?
What constitutes an offense?
What constitutes merit?
What is sublime?
And what is not sublime?
What constitutes the black?
What constitutes the white?
From what do the phenomena of black and white arise?
What is the meaning of the present life?
What is the meaning of future lives?
How does one practice so as to experience what is wholesome and not what is unwholesome?
Having heard this from him, one should act according to what was said.
If there are those who are poor within the kingdom, one should provide wealth and goods to relieve them.
"O Great King!
This is called the Dharma of succession, which you should properly take up and learn.

Having properly taken it up and learned it, on the fifteenth day at the time of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, after you have bathed and washed yourself and ascended to the main hall, that divine Wheel-Treasure will surely come from the east. The wheel has a thousand spokes, complete in every respect, pure and natural, not made by human hands, its color like a blazing fire, radiating brilliant light."

"Later on, King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja observed the Dharma according to the Dharma and practiced the Dharma according to the Dharma. He maintained the observance of the Dharma-fast (dharma-uposatha) for his crown prince, the queen consort, the court ladies, as well as for his ministers, subjects, śramaṇas, and brahmins, even down to the insects. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, he practiced generosity, bestowing upon destitute śramaṇas, brahmins, the poor, the solitary, and beggars from afar: food and drink, clothing and bedding, vehicles, flower garlands, scattered flowers, fragrant ointments, dwellings, couches, mattresses, woolen rugs, fine carpets, servants, and bright lamps."
If there are in that country venerable and renowned śramaṇas or brahmins, he would go to them at the appropriate time and inquire about the Dharma and receive the Dharma, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
What are wholesome dharmas?
What are unwholesome dharmas?
What constitutes an offense?
What constitutes merit?
What is sublime?
And what is not sublime?
What constitutes the black?
What constitutes the white?
From what do the phenomena of black and white arise?
What is the meaning of the present life?
What is the meaning of future lives?
How does one practice so as to experience what is wholesome and not what is unwholesome?
Having heard this from him, he acted according to what was said.

However, among the people in the kingdom there were those who were poor and unable to provide goods for relief; thus, those who were destitute and lacked wealth could not be supported. Consequently, the people became increasingly impoverished. Because of their poverty, they began to steal the property of others.
Because of their theft, the owners would track them down, arrest them, and bring them before King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja, saying:
“O Great King!
This man has stolen my property; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked that man:
"Is it true that you have stolen?
The man replied,
"O Great King!"
"I have indeed committed theft. Why is this so?
O Heavenly King!"
"Because of our poverty, if we do not steal, we will have no means to sustain ourselves.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja immediately brought forth wealth and gave it to them, saying to the thieves:
"Return now; do not do this again in the future."
Thereupon, the people of the kingdom heard that if there was anyone among them who committed theft, King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja would simply provide them with wealth and goods from his own treasury.
Because of this, people thought to themselves:
"We too should steal the property of others.
Thereupon, the people of the country each vied with one another to commit theft of others' property.
This is why those who are impoverished and lack wealth cannot provide relief or succor;
consequently, people fall further into destitution, and because of this destitution, theft becomes increasingly prevalent.
Because theft became so prevalent, the lifespan of those people further decreased, and their physical appearance further deteriorated. Bhikṣus,
once their lifespan had decreased and their appearance had deteriorated,
the father’s lifespan was eighty thousand years, while the son’s lifespan was forty thousand years.

"Monks! When the lifespan of those people was forty thousand years, there was a man who stole another's property. The owner caught him, bound him, and brought him before King Mahāsaṃmata, the Kṣatriya born from the crown of the head, saying:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"This man has stolen my property; I pray that Your Majesty, the Heavenly King, will punish him.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked the man:
"Did you truly steal it?"
That person replied:
"O Great King!
I have indeed committed theft."
"Why is this? Because of our poverty;
if we do not steal, we will have no means to sustain ourselves.
Upon hearing this, King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja thought to himself:

"If there are those in my kingdom who steal the property of others and then further provide wealth to compensate them entirely, in this way the state treasury will be pointlessly exhausted, and theft will consequently flourish."
"I shall now rather make an extremely sharp blade; if there is anyone in my kingdom who commits theft, I will immediately arrest them, place them beneath a high stake, and behead them."
Thereupon, the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja subsequently issued an edict to have extremely sharp swords made:
"If there is anyone in the kingdom who steals the property of others, they shall immediately be arrested, seated beneath a high standard, and their heads shall be severed."

When the people of the kingdom heard that King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja had ordered the forging of sharp swords, they would immediately seize anyone in the country who stole another's property, place them beneath a high stake, and behead them.
"I would rather fashion myself into a sharp sword and go about plundering goods; if I encounter one who has plundered goods, I shall seize that owner and cut off his head."
Thereupon, at a later time, that man fashioned a sharp sword, went out to plunder goods, seized the owner of those goods, and cut off his head.
This is because those who are impoverished and lack material wealth cannot be provided for or relieved;
consequently, people become increasingly destitute. Due to this destitution, theft increases;
and because theft increases, killing with weapons increases.
Because of the increase in killing with weapons, the lifespan of those people decreases further, and their physical form deteriorates further.
Once their lifespan has decreased and their form has deteriorated, O Bhikṣus!
The father’s lifespan was forty thousand years, and the son’s lifespan was twenty thousand years. “Monks!

When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there was a man who stole another’s property. The owner caught him, bound him, and brought him before King Mahāsaṃmata, the Kṣatriya born from the crest, saying:”
"O Great King!
This man has stolen my wealth; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked that man:
"Is it true that you have stolen?
At that time, the thief thought to himself:

"If King Mahāsammata, the Kṣatriya born from the crown of the head, were to know the truth, he might bind and whip me, or cast me out, or banish me, or fine me with wealth, or subject me to various forms of torture, or impale me on a stake, or decapitate me. Would it not be better for me to deceive King Mahāsammata, the Kṣatriya born from the crown of the head, with a lie?"
Having reflected thus, he said:
"O Great King!
I have not committed theft; it was because I am destitute and lacked wealth that I was unable to provide for or relieve [the needy]."
As people became increasingly impoverished, because of that poverty, theft increased;
because theft increased, violence and murder increased;
and because violence and murder increased, false speech and divisive talk increased.
Monks, because false speech and divisive speech increase, the lifespan of those people decreases and their physical form deteriorates.
Once their lifespan has decreased and their form has deteriorated, monks—
The father’s lifespan was twenty thousand years, and the son’s lifespan was ten thousand years. “Monks!

When the human lifespan is ten thousand years, among the people there are those with virtue and those without virtue. As for those without virtue, they give rise to feelings of jealousy toward those with virtue and violate their wives.”
This is because those who are impoverished and lack material wealth cannot be provided for or relieved; consequently, people become increasingly destitute.
Due to this destitution, theft increases further;
and due to the increase of theft, lethal violence increases further.
Because the killing with knives increases, false speech and divisive speech increase;
because false speech and divisive speech increase, envy and sexual misconduct increase.
Because of the increase in envy and sexual misconduct, the lifespan of those people further diminishes and their physical form further deteriorates.
Once their lifespan has diminished and their form has deteriorated, O Bhikṣus!
The father’s lifespan is ten thousand years, and the son’s lifespan is five thousand years. “Monks!
When the human lifespan is five thousand years, three things increase: unrighteousness, sensual desire, evil greed, and false teachings.”
Monks, because these three factors increase, the lifespan of those people diminishes and their physical form deteriorates.
Once their lifespan has diminished and their form has deteriorated, monks—
The father’s lifespan was five thousand years, and the son’s lifespan was two thousand five hundred years. Monks!
When the human lifespan is two thousand five hundred years, three further qualities increase: divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Monks, because these three factors increase, the lifespan of those people diminishes further, and their physical form deteriorates further.
Once their lifespan has diminished and their form has deteriorated, monks—
The father’s lifespan was two thousand five hundred years, and the son’s lifespan was one thousand years. Monks!
When the human lifespan is one thousand years, one thing increases further: namely, wrong view.
Because of the increase of this one dharma, the lifespan of those people further diminishes, and their physical form further deteriorates.
Once their lifespan has diminished and their form has deteriorated, O bhikṣus!
"The father lives for a thousand years, while the son lives for five hundred years. 'Monks!

When the human lifespan is five hundred years, those people throughout their entire lives are unfilial toward their parents; they cannot revere śramaṇas or brahmins, do not practice compliant conduct, do not perform meritorious deeds, and do not perceive the consequences of sin in future lives.'"

Because he was unfilial toward his parents, failed to revere śramaṇas and brahmins, did not practice compliant conduct, did not perform meritorious deeds, and did not perceive the consequences of sin in future lives—monks!
The father’s lifespan was five hundred years, while the son’s lifespan was either two hundred and fifty or two hundred years.
Monks! Now, if there is one who is long-lived, their lifespan may be a hundred years or even more than that.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
“Monks! In the distant future, when the lifespan of humans is ten years.”
"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, girls marry as soon as they are five months old. Monks!"

When the human lifespan is ten years, there will be a grain called foxtail millet (*priyaṅgu*) which will be considered the finest delicacy, just as polished rice is the supreme dish for people today. Monks!
When the human lifespan is ten years, there will be a grain called *priyaṅgu* which will be considered the finest delicacy. Monks!
When the human lifespan is ten years, all the delicious foods existing today—clarified butter, salt, honey, sugarcane, and sugar—all these will have completely vanished.

"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, those who practice the ten paths of unwholesome action will be respected by others, just as those who practice the ten paths of wholesome action are respected by others today."
"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, it is likewise so: those who practice the ten paths of unwholesome action will be respected and honored by others."
"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, there is no longer even the name of 'wholesome,' let alone the practice of the ten paths of wholesome action. Monks!"
When the human lifespan is ten years, there will be those called "Punishers" who travel everywhere, visiting every household to inflict punishment. Monks!

When the human lifespan is ten years, a mother harbors an extreme intent to harm her son, and the son likewise harbors an extreme intent to harm his mother. Fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen will turn toward one another with murderous intent, just as a hunter, having sighted a deer, harbors an extreme intent to kill it.

"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, it is likewise so: the mother harbors an extremely harmful intent toward her son, and the son likewise harbors an extremely harmful intent toward his mother; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen, as they face one another in turn, harbor intentions of thievery and malice."

"Monks! When the human lifespan is ten years, there shall be a seven-day period of the calamity of weapons. There, if one seizes a blade of grass, it immediately transforms into a weapon; if one seizes a piece of firewood, it likewise transforms into a weapon. With these weapons, they will kill one another. After those seven days of the calamity of weapons have passed, it shall cease."

"At that time, there will also be those who feel shame and remorse, who loathe and do not love [the violence]. During those seven days of the kalpa of weapons, they will enter the mountains and wilds to hide in secluded places. Once the seven days have passed, they will emerge from their hiding places in the mountains and wilds; seeing one another again, they will give rise to hearts of compassion and will cherish each other with the utmost affection."

It is like a compassionate mother who has only one son; after being separated for a long time, he returns from afar and safely arrives home. Upon seeing one another, they rejoice; she gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, cherishing him with the utmost affection.

After seven days had passed in this manner, those people emerged from their secluded places in the mountains and wilderness; seeing one another, they gave rise to hearts of compassion and felt intense mutual affection. Having met together, they spoke these words:
"O Worthy Ones!..."

Now that we have met, we have attained peace and security; because we previously gave rise to unwholesome states, we now encounter this situation where our kinsmen have all died. We should surely practice wholesome dharmas together.
"How shall we together practice the wholesome Dharma?
We are all people who take life; it would now be better for us to collectively abstain from killing and sever the taking of life, for we ought to practice this wholesome Dharma together."
They then practiced such wholesome dharmas together.
Having practiced these wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical appearance became more excellent.
Once their lifespan had increased and their appearance had become more excellent, monks!
"Monks! Those who live for ten years give birth to children who live for twenty.
Then, monks, those who live for twenty years think thus:"
"If those who seek to practice virtue find their lifespan increasing and their physical form becoming more beautiful, we should together further increase our practice of virtue.
How shall we together further increase our practice of virtue?"
"We have already collectively abstained from killing and abandoned killing; yet we still collectively practice taking what is not given.
