We should rather abstain from taking what is not given and abandon taking what is not given; we ought to collectively practice this wholesome dharma."
They then practiced such wholesome dharmas together.
Having practiced these wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical appearance became more beautiful.
Once their lifespan had increased and their appearance had become more beautiful, O bhikṣus!
When people have a lifespan of twenty years, they give birth to children who live for forty years.
"Monks! Those with a lifespan of forty years also think thus:"
"If those who seek to cultivate virtue find their lifespan increasing and their physical appearance becoming more excellent, we should together further increase our practice of virtue.
How shall we together further increase our practice of virtue?"
"We have already abandoned killing and severed killing; we have abandoned taking what is not given and severed taking what is not given; yet we still engage in sexual misconduct.
We should rather abandon sexual misconduct and sever sexual misconduct; we ought to practice this wholesome dharma together."
They then practiced these wholesome dharmas together.
Having practiced these wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical appearance became more excellent.
Once their lifespan had increased and their appearance had become more excellent, O bhikṣus!
A person with a lifespan of forty years gives birth to a child who lives for eighty years. "Monks!
A person with a lifespan of eighty years also thinks thus:"
"If those who seek to practice virtue find that their lifespan increases and their physical appearance becomes more excellent, we should together further increase our practice of virtue.
How shall we together further increase our practice of virtue?"

"We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing; we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; yet we still practice false speech."
‘We would rather abstain from false speech and sever false speech; we should practice this wholesome dharma together.
They then practiced such wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increases and their physical form becomes more beautiful.
When their lifespan has increased and their form has become more beautiful, monks,
a person with an eighty-year lifespan gives birth to a child with a lifespan of one hundred and sixty years.
“Monks! Those whose lifespan was one hundred and sixty years also thought:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we further increase our practice of wholesome deeds?

We have already abstained from killing and have abandoned killing; we have abstained from taking what is not given and have abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and have abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and have abandoned false speech; yet we still engage in divisive speech."
‘We would rather abstain from divisive speech and sever divisive speech; we should practice this wholesome dharma together.
They then proceeded to practice such wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical form became more beautiful.
Once their lifespan had increased and their form had become more beautiful, monks,
a person with a lifespan of one hundred and sixty years would give birth to a child with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years.
“Monks! Those people with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years also thought:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How shall we together further increase our practice of wholesome deeds? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; yet we still engage in harsh speech."
‘We would rather leave harsh speech behind and sever harsh speech; we should together practice this wholesome dharma.
They then proceeded to practice such a wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical form became more beautiful.
When their lifespan had increased and their form had become more beautiful, monks,
a person with a lifespan of three hundred and twenty years gave birth to a child with a lifespan of six hundred and forty years.
“Bhikkhus! Those whose lifespan is six hundred and forty years also think thus:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we together further increase our practice of virtue? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; we have abstained from harsh speech and abandoned harsh speech; yet, we still engage in frivolous speech."
‘We would rather leave frivolous speech behind and sever frivolous speech; we should together practice this wholesome dharma.
They then proceeded to practice such a wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical appearance became more excellent.

Bhikṣus! When their lifespan had increased and their appearance had become more excellent, those who lived for six hundred and forty years gave birth to children who lived for two thousand five hundred years.
“Bhikṣus! Those whose lifespan was two thousand five hundred years also thought:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we together further increase our practice of wholesome deeds? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; we have abstained from harsh speech and abandoned harsh speech; we have abstained from frivolous chatter and abandoned frivolous chatter. Yet, we still practice greed and envy."
‘We would rather abandon greed and envy and sever greed and envy; we should practice this wholesome dharma together.
They then proceeded to practice such wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical form became more beautiful.
When their lifespan had increased and their form had become more beautiful, monks,
those who lived for two thousand five hundred years gave birth to children who lived for five thousand years.
“Bhikkhus! Those whose lifespan was five thousand years also thought:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we further increase our practice of the wholesome? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; we have abstained from harsh speech and abandoned harsh speech; we have abstained from frivolous speech and abandoned frivolous speech; we have abstained from covetousness and abandoned covetousness; yet we still practice ill will."
‘We would rather abandon ill will and sever ill will; we should practice this wholesome dharma together.
They then proceeded to practice such a wholesome dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical appearance became more excellent.
Bhikṣus! Once their lifespan had increased and their appearance had become more excellent, those who lived for five thousand years gave birth to children who lived for ten thousand years.
“Monks! When people have a lifespan of ten thousand years, they also think:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, their lifespan increases and their physical appearance improves; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we further increase our practice of wholesome deeds? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; we have abstained from harsh speech and abandoned harsh speech; we have abstained from frivolous speech and abandoned frivolous speech; we have abstained from covetousness and abandoned covetousness; we have abstained from ill will and abandoned ill will; yet we still practice wrong view."
"We would rather abandon wrong views and sever wrong views; we should practice this wholesome Dharma together.
They then practiced such wholesome Dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increases and their physical form becomes more beautiful.
Once their lifespan has increased and their form has become more beautiful, monks,
the sons born to those who lived for ten thousand years will live for twenty thousand years.
“Monks! Those whose lifespan was twenty thousand years also thought:
‘If one seeks to practice what is wholesome, one’s lifespan increases and one’s physical form becomes more beautiful; we should together further increase our practice of the wholesome.’”
"How might we further increase our practice of the wholesome? We have already abstained from killing and abandoned killing;

we have abstained from taking what is not given and abandoned taking what is not given; we have abstained from sexual misconduct and abandoned sexual misconduct; we have abstained from false speech and abandoned false speech; we have abstained from divisive speech and abandoned divisive speech; we have abstained from harsh speech and abandoned harsh speech; we have abstained from frivolous speech and abandoned frivolous speech; we have abstained from covetousness and abandoned covetousness; we have abstained from ill will and abandoned ill will; we have abstained from wrong view and abandoned wrong view. Yet, there still exist unrighteousness, evil desires, greedy conduct, and deviant dharmas."
"We would rather leave these three unwholesome, evil states and abandon these three unwholesome, evil states; we should practice this wholesome Dharma together.
They then practiced such wholesome Dharma together.
Having practiced wholesome dharmas, their lifespan increased and their physical form became more beautiful.
Once their lifespan had increased and their form had become more beautiful, monks,
those people with a lifespan of twenty thousand years gave birth to children with a lifespan of forty thousand years.

“Bhikkhus! When the human lifespan is forty thousand years, people are filial and obedient toward their parents; they honor and respect śramaṇas and brahmins, carry out their duties with compliance, cultivate meritorious deeds, and perceive the retribution for sins in future lives.”

"Because he was filial toward his parents, respected and honored recluses and brahmins, performed services with compliance, cultivated meritorious deeds, and saw the transgressions of future lives, bhikkhus!"
When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, those born had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Monks!

When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa was extremely prosperous and joyful, with a vast population where villages were so close together that a cock could fly from one to another.
"Monks! When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, girls shall not marry until they are five hundred years old. Monks!"

When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there are only these afflictions: cold and heat, excrement and urine, desire, lack of appetite, and old age; there are no other ailments besides these.

“Bhikṣus! When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, there was a king named Śaṅkha who was a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin). He was intelligent and wise; possessing the fourfold army, he governed the world, exercising sovereign mastery over it.”

The Dharma King who acts in accordance with the Dharma accomplishes the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure; these are called the seven.

Endowed with a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, brave and fearless, and capable of subduing all opposing hosts, he will surely govern this entire earth, even unto the great ocean; not by means of the sword or staff, but through the teaching of the Dharma, he will bring about peace and happiness.

“Monks! When the Kṣatriya King born from the crown of the head becomes a lord of men and governs the world, he exercises his own domain as inherited from his father. Because he exercises his own domain as inherited from his father, his lifespan does not diminish, his physical form does not deteriorate, he never loses his happiness, and his strength does not decline.”
"O bhikṣus!

You too should likewise shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to train in the Path. You should practice within your own domain, that which was obtained from your father."
"O bhikṣus!

Because you practice within your own domain, which was inherited from your father, your lifespan does not diminish, your physical form does not become unsightly, you have never lost your happiness, and your strength does not decline."
"How does a bhikkhu practice within his own domain as received from his father?

This bhikkhu contemplates the internal body as body; he contemplates internal feelings, mind, and phenomena as feelings, mind, and phenomena. This is called a bhikkhu practicing within his own domain as received from his father."
What is the life-span of a bhikkhu?

It is when this bhikkhu cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through desire, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment;

he cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through energy, the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through mind, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through investigation, each based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment. This is called the life-span of a bhikkhu.
What is the form of a bhikṣu?

This bhikṣu cultivates the prohibitive precepts and guards the liberation through them; furthermore, he properly maintains dignified conduct and decorum, regards even the slightest transgression with constant fear, and undertakes and upholds the training rules—this is called the form of a bhikṣu.
"What is the happiness of a bhikṣu?

This bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; this is called the happiness of a bhikṣu."
What is the power of a bhikkhu?

It is when this bhikkhu has exhausted all taints (āsrava), attained the taintless state, and through liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, dwells having realized, awakened to, and personally witnessed for himself in this very life: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is. This is called the power of a bhikkhu.
“Bhikkhus! I do not see any power that is so irresistible as the power of Māra the King; yet a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted can overcome it by means of the power of unsurpassed noble wisdom.”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The sixth discourse, the *Cakkavatti-sīhanāda Sutta*, ends here, totaling 6,313 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, scroll 15, totals 8,721 characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 16, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. 71.
Pāyāsi Sutta (71). Madhyama Āgama, Chapter on Kings, Pāyāsi Sutta, Number Seven.

Thus have I heard: At one time, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was traveling through the country of Kosala with a large community of bhikkhus. He arrived at Setavyā and stayed in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of that village.

At that time, there was a king in Sāvatthī named Pāyāsi, who possessed extreme wealth and prosperity; his resources were immeasurable, his livestock and industries beyond counting, and he was fully endowed with various fiefs and manors. All the springs, ponds, grasses, and trees of the city of Sāvatthī belonged to the king, having been granted to him by King Pasenadi of Kosala.

Thereupon, the brahmins and householders of Setavyā heard that there was a śramaṇa named Kumāra Kassapa who was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala with a large community of bhikṣus, and had arrived here at Setavyā, staying in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of that village.

That śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa possesses great renown that is heard throughout the ten directions; Kumāra Kāśyapa is unimpeded in his eloquence and skillful speech, and what he teaches is subtle and profound—he is a learned Arhat.
"If there is anyone who sees this Arhat and pays him respectful homage, they will swiftly obtain great benefit; we should go and see that śramaṇa Kumāra-Kāśyapa."
The brahmins and householders of Setavyā, each accompanied by their own peers, departed from Setavyā together toward the north and arrived at the Siṃsapā Grove.

At that time, King Pāyāsi was in his main hall when he saw from afar the brahmins and householders of Setavyā, each accompanied by their own peers, departing together from Setavyā toward the north and proceeding to the Śiṃśapā Grove.
Having seen this, King Pāyāsi said to his attendants:
"For what reason have these brahmins and householders of Setavyā today gone out from Setavyā together with their respective peers toward the north, proceeding as far as the Siṃsapā Grove?"
The attendant replied,
"Your Majesty!

Those brahmins and householders of Setavyā have heard that the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa, traveling through the kingdom of Kosala with a large community of bhikkhus, has arrived here at Setavyā and is staying in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of that village."
"O Heavenly King!

That śramaṇa Kumāra-Kāśyapa possesses great renown that is heard throughout the ten directions. Kumāra-Kāśyapa’s eloquence is unimpeded and his teachings are subtle and profound; he is a learned Arhat."
"If there are those who see this Arhat and pay him respectful homage, they will swiftly obtain great benefit; we should go to see that śramaṇa Kumāra-Kāśyapa."
"O Great King!
For this reason, these brahmins and householders of Sāvatthī, each accompanied by their own kind, have departed together from Sāvatthī toward the north, reaching the Siṃsapā Grove."
Having heard this, King Pāyāsi said to his attendant:
"Go to those brahmins and householders of Setavyā and say to them:
'King Pāyāsi addresses you, the brahmins and householders of Setavyā:'"
“Virtuous ones, you may stay; I shall go with you to see that ascetic Kumāra Kassapa.
You are foolish!
Do not be deceived by him into thinking that there is a future life and that beings are reborn.”
"I see it thus and I declare it thus: there is no future world, and no beings are reborn.
The attendant, having received these instructions, immediately went to where the brahmins and householders of Setavyā were and said to them:
"King Pāyāsi has told the brahmins and householders of Setavyā:"
"Virtuous ones, you may stay; I shall go with you to see that śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa.
You are deluded!
Do not be deceived by him into thinking that there is a future life and that beings are reborn."
"I see it thus and I declare it thus:
there is no future world, and no beings are reborn.
Having heard this teaching, the brahmins and householders of Setavyā replied to their attendant, saying:
“As you command, Your Majesty,” the attendant replied, returning to announce the King’s decree:
“The brahmins and householders of Setavyā are waiting for the Great King; may the Great King know that the time has come.”
Then King Pāyāsi immediately commanded his charioteer:
"Prepare the carriage quickly; I wish to depart now.
Having received these instructions, the charioteer quickly finished preparing the carriage and returned to inform the king.
"The carriage is prepared; it is as the Great King intends.
Thereupon, King Pāyāsi mounted his chariot and set out for the place where the brahmins and householders of Setavyā were, traveling north with them to the Śiṃśapā Grove.

At that time, King Pāyāsi saw from afar the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa among the groves of trees; he immediately alighted from his chariot and proceeded on foot to where the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side, asking:
"Kassapa!..."
"I now wish to ask a question; would you deign to grant me leave?
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied, "Pāyāsi!"
"If you wish to ask anything, you may do so; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
Then King Pāyāsi asked: "Kāśyapa!..."
"I see it thus and I declare it thus: there is no future world, and no beings are reborn.
Śramaṇa Kumāra-Kāśyapa, what do you think?"
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
"Pāyāsi! I shall now question Your Majesty; answer as you see fit."
"What do you think, Great King?
Are these present sun and moon of this life, or of a future life?
Pāyāsi replied:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra-Kāśyapa speaks thus, I see it in this way and declare it in this way: there is no future world, and no beings are reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there yet another evil that exceeds this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
I had a close relative who was gravely ill; I went to where he was, and having arrived, I said to him:
"You should know, O kinsmen, that I hold such a view and speak thus:
'There is no future world; no beings are reborn.'"
There are recluses and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is a future world; there are beings reborn.
I have always lacked faith in what they say.
He further spoke these words:

"If there are men or women who commit evil deeds, who lack diligence, who are indolent, lazy, envious, and stingy; who do not open their hands in generosity, who have no aspiration, and who are excessively attached to wealth—by reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up and their lives end, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell."

"If what those śramaṇas and brahmins have said is true, and if you—my own kinsmen—have committed evil deeds, being unenergetic, indolent, lazy, envious, and greedy; if you have not opened your hands, have no aspiration, and are excessively attached to wealth and property, such that upon the dissolution of the body after death you will surely go to a miserable destination and be born in hell, then you may return and say to me:
'Pāyāsi!'"
"In that hell, there is such and such suffering.
If it were truly so, I would have seen it for myself.
Having heard my words and received my instruction, not one of them came back to tell me: [that it was as I said].
“Pāyāsi! In those hells, such and such are the sufferings. “Kāśyapa! [said Pāyāsi.]
"For this reason, I have come to the thought:
'There is no future world; there are no beings reborn.
" Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied:
“Pāyāsi! I shall ask the King further; answer as you see fit.
Suppose there were royal officers who arrested a criminal and brought him before the King, saying:”
"O Heavenly King!
This man has committed an offense; Your Majesty should punish him.
The King said to him:

"Take him away and bind both his hands behind his back; make him ride a donkey with a broken drum tied to it that sounds like a donkey's bray. After you have proclaimed this throughout the city, exit through the southern gate, place him beneath a high marker, and cut off his head."

Having received these instructions, he immediately bound the criminal’s hands behind his back, made him mount a donkey, and broke a worn-out drum that sounded like the braying of a donkey. After proclaiming the order throughout the city, they exited through the southern gate and sat beneath a high stake, intending to execute him by beheading.
As this person was about to die, he said to the executioner:
"Please wait a moment; I wish to see my parents, wife, children, slaves, and servants. Allow me to go for a short while."
"What do you think, Great King?
Would that executioner ever release this criminal and allow him to go for even a moment?
Pāyāsi replied:
"No, Kāśyapa," the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa replied.

“Pāyāsi! It is the same for the king’s kinsmen and relatives: if they commit evil deeds, lack diligence, are indolent, lazy, envious, stingy, and greedy; if they do not open their hands, do not aspire [to virtue], and are excessively attached to wealth—due to these causes and conditions, when their bodies break up at the end of life, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.”
When the hell-wardens seized him and were tormenting him with extreme suffering, he said to the wardens:
"O hell-wardens! Wait a moment;
do not torment me so severely. I wish to go for a short while to visit King Pāyāsi and say this to him:"
"He makes him see for himself the various kinds of suffering within that hell.
What do you think, O King?
"Would those hell-wardens ever release the King’s kinsmen and allow them to come here even for a moment?
Pāyāsi replied, "No."
“Kāśyapa! the Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa replied, “Pāyāsi!”
"You should contemplate the future life in this manner; do not rely on what is seen by the physical eye. Pāyāsi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill will; and who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, passing away from or proceeding to happy or unhappy states—and they see this according to reality, in accordance with the karma performed by those beings."
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, I see it in this way and declare:
there is no future world, and no beings are reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: “Pāyāsi!
Is there anything more evil than this?”
Pāyāsi replied: "It is so, Kāśyapa!"
Furthermore, there is yet another evil thing, Kāśyapa!
I had a close relative who was gravely ill; I went to where he was, and having arrived, I said to him:
"O kinsmen, you should know that I hold such a view and speak thus:
'There is no future world; no beings are reborn.'"
There are recluses and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is a future world; there are beings reborn.
I have always lacked faith in what they say.
He further spoke these words:

"If there are men or women who practice sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort, who are free from envy and lack of stinginess or greed, who open their hands, are hopeful, and with an open mind relinquish all, providing for the orphaned and the destitute, always delighting in giving and not being attached to wealth and goods—by reason of these causes and conditions, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be reborn in the heavens."

“If what those śramaṇas and brahmins have said is true, and if you, my kinsmen, practice sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort, being free from envy and without stinginess or greed; if you open your hands, extend yourself, and cultivate a generous mind, giving to the orphaned and the poor, always delighting in charity, unattached to wealth and possessions, then when your bodies perish and your lives end, you will surely ascend to a good destination and be reborn in the heavens. In that case, you may return and say to me:
‘Pāyāsi! ...’”
"The heavens are thus and so blissful.
If that were indeed the case, I would have seen it for myself.
Having heard my words and received my instruction, none of them ever came back to tell me:
"Pāyāsi! Such and such is the pleasure in the heavens.
"Kāśyapa! [he replied.]
For this reason, I have formed this thought:
"There is no future world; there are no beings reborn.
Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied:
"Pāyāsi! Listen as I speak a parable; for the wise, upon hearing a parable, understand its meaning. Pāyāsi!"
Suppose there were a public latrine outside a village or town, deep enough to submerge a person's head and filled with excrement, and a man had fallen into it and sunk to the bottom.

If another person, out of compassion for him, seeking his welfare and benefit, seeking his peace and happiness, were to slowly pull him out from atop the latrine, scrape him with bamboo splinters, wipe him with tree leaves, and wash him with warm water.
At a later time, having bathed himself thoroughly and anointed his body with fragrances, he ascended the main hall and enjoyed himself with the five objects of desire.
What do you think, O King?
"Would that person ever again remember his former latrine with joy and praise,
or desire to see it again? Pāyāsi replied, "No."
Kāśyapa!

If there were another person who, recollecting that latrine, would joyfully praise it and desire to see it, I would not love that person; how much less so one who themselves recollects their former latrine and joyfully praises it?
"Furthermore, it is not possible for one who wishes to see [the results of such deeds] again in this very place.

"Reṣi! Suppose a king has a kinsman who practices sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort; who is free from envy and lack of greed; who extends his hand in generosity, is open-minded and relinquishing, provides for the orphaned and the destitute, always delights in giving, and is unattached to material wealth. Because of these causes and conditions, when his body breaks up at the end of life, he will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in a heavenly realm. Having been born in a heavenly realm, he will enjoy himself amidst the five celestial sensual pleasures."
"What do you think, O King?
Would that son of a deva ever abandon those five celestial sensual pleasures to dwell upon these five human sensual pleasures with longing and praise, desiring to see them again?"
Pāyāsi replied, “No, Kāśyapa.”
Why is this? The five desires of the human realm are a foul and impure place; they are utterly loathsome, undesirable, unworthy of affection, coarse, and unclean.
Kāśyapa!
Compared to the five desires of the human realm, the celestial desires are supreme, most excellent, most wonderful, and most superior.

If those sons of the gods were to abandon the five celestial desires and instead recall the five desires of the human realm with joy and praise, wishing to see them once more, such a thing would not be possible.
“Pāyāsi! You should contemplate the world beyond in this manner; do not rely on what is seen by the physical eye. Pāyāsi!”

If there are recluses or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill will; and who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—then, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, they see these beings as they die and are reborn: beautiful or ugly, sublime or not sublime, passing away from or being born into good or bad destinations, exactly as it truly is, according to the karma performed by those beings.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I see it in this way and declare:
there is no future world, and no beings are reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there yet another evil that exceeds this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “So it is, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
I had a close relative who was gravely ill; I went to his side, and having arrived, I said to him:
"O kinsmen, you should know that I hold this view and speak thus:
'There is no future world; no beings are reborn.'"
There are recluses and brahmins who hold such a view and speak thus:
"There is a future world; there are beings reborn.
I have always lacked faith in what they say.
He further spoke these words:

"If there are men or women who practice sublime conduct with diligence, exerting themselves without slackening, free from envy and without stinginess or greed; who open their hands, are hopeful, and with an expansive mind let go of all, providing for the orphaned and the destitute, always delighting in giving and not being attached to wealth—by reason of this, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will surely ascend to a good destination and be born in the heavens."

"If what those śramaṇas and brahmins have said is true, and if you, my kinsmen, practice sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort, being free from envy and without stinginess or greed; if you open your hands, are generous, expansive in mind, and relinquish your wealth; if you provide for the orphaned and the destitute, always delighting in giving and remaining unattached to material things—then when your bodies perish at the end of life and you surely ascend to a good destination and are reborn in the heavens, you may return and say to me: 'Pāyāsi!'"
"The heavenly realms are thus and thus blissful.
If you, while in the heavens, should think:
"If I were to return, what would I obtain?"
"The royal house of Pāyāsi possesses much wealth; I shall give it to you.
Having heard my words and received my instruction, he did not come at all to say to me:
"Pāyāsi!..."
"The heavens are thus and thus blissful.
Kāśyapa! For this reason, I have formed this thought:
"There is no future world; there are no beings reborn.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied, "Pāyāsi!"
The lifespan in the heavens is long, while human life is short.

One hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night for the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*). Calculating thirty such days as a month and twelve such months as a year, the celestial lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one thousand years.
What do you think, O King?

Suppose you have kinsmen who practice sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort, who are free from envy and lack of stinginess, who open their hands, are generous, expansive in mind, and relinquishing; who provide for the orphaned and the destitute, always delighting in giving, unattached to material wealth, and because of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they surely ascend to a happy destination and are reborn in the heavens. Having been reborn in the heavens, they then think:

‘We should first enjoy ourselves for one day and night with the five celestial sensual pleasures, or for two, three, four, up to six or seven days, enjoying ourselves with the five celestial sensual pleasures.’
Thereafter, you should go and say to King Pāyāsi:
"The joys in heaven are such and such," so as to enable him to see it for himself.
"What do you think, O King? Will you ever actually obtain that much livelihood?
Pāyāsi asked: "Kāśyapa!"
"Who has come from the future world to speak these words, O Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa?

Long is the lifespan in the heavens, while short is the life in the human realm; one hundred years in the human world constitutes a single day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa devas. With such a day and night, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; the celestial lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa devas is one thousand such years."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
"Pāyāsi! Listen as I speak a parable; for the wise, upon hearing a parable, understand its meaning."

"Pāyāsi! It is just as if there were a blind man who were to say: 'There are no colors of black or white, nor is there anyone who sees colors of black or white; there are no colors of long or short, nor is there anyone who sees colors of long or short; there are no colors of near or far, nor is there anyone who sees colors of near or far; there are no colors of coarse or fine, nor is there anyone who sees colors of coarse or fine.'"
Why is this? Because I have never seen or known it from the beginning, therefore form does not exist.
When that blind man speaks in this way, is he speaking the truth?
Pāyāsi replied, "No, Kāśyapa!"
Why is this so? Kāśyapa!

There are black and white forms, and there is also the seeing of black and white forms; there are long and short forms, and there is also the seeing of long and short forms; there are near and far forms, and there is also the seeing of near and far forms; there are coarse and subtle forms, and there is also the seeing of coarse and subtle forms.
"If a blind person were to say, 'I do not see and I do not know;
therefore, form does not exist,' what he says would not be true.
Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
“King Pāyāsi is also like one who is blind. If the King were to say this:
‘Who has come from the world beyond to speak, O Śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa?’”

The lifespan in the heavens is long, while the life span in the human realm is short; one hundred years in the human realm constitutes a single day and night for the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). Calculating thirty such days as a month and twelve such months as a year, the celestial lifespan in the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one thousand years.
King Pāyāsi said:
"Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa!
This is highly improper; you should not speak in this way."
Why is this so? Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa!
Your diligence is like that of a blind man compared to mine, Kāśyapa!

If one knows that I, or my kinsmen, have practiced sublime conduct with diligence and tireless effort, being free from envy and without stinginess or greed; if we have opened our hands, been liberal, and with an open mind have renounced all to provide for the orphaned and the destitute, always delighting in giving and remaining unattached to wealth—then by virtue of these causes and conditions, upon the dissolution of the body after death, such a person will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens.
Kāśyapa!

I should now immediately practice giving, cultivate various meritorious deeds, observe the fasts and maintain the precepts, and then take my own life by means of a blade, or by ingesting poison, or by throwing myself into a pit or a well, or by hanging myself.
"Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa!
You should not compare your own diligence to that of a blind man.
Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa replied:
"Pāyāsi! Listen further as I speak a parable; for the wise understand its meaning upon hearing a parable. Pāyāsi!"

It is just as if there were a brahmin who had a young wife who had only recently become pregnant, while his former wife already had a son; then that brahmin suddenly passed away, and after his death, the former wife’s son said to his stepmother:
"Stepmother!..."
"You should know that all the wealth and property currently in this house now belong entirely to me; I see no one else with whom it should be shared.
The stepmother replied, "I am currently pregnant; if I give birth to a son, you should share it with him."
"If a daughter is born, all property shall belong to you.
Then the son of the former wife spoke again and yet again to his stepmother:
"Now, whatever wealth and goods there are in this house should all belong to me; I see nothing else that ought to be divided."
The stepmother also replied twice and thrice:
"I am now pregnant; if I give birth to a son, you should share [the property] with him;
if I give birth to a daughter, the goods shall belong entirely to you."

Thereupon, the stepmother—foolish, lacking understanding, unskilled in discernment, and devoid of wisdom—desiring to preserve her own life, instead brought about her own ruin. She entered the room, took a sharp blade, and slit open her own belly to see whether it was a boy or a girl.
That fool was ignorant and lacked understanding; he possessed no wisdom and, while seeking to preserve his own life, instead brought harm upon himself and the child within his womb.
You should know that Pāyāsi is likewise thus: ignorant and lacking understanding, possessing no wisdom, yet desiring to preserve his life, he instead thinks:
"Kāśyapa!..."

"If I knew that my kinsmen and relatives, through their sublime conduct and diligent effort, were persevering without slackening, free from envy and without stinginess or greed, open-handed, generous, liberal in mind, giving to the orphaned and the poor, always delighting in charity, and unattached to wealth—that by reason of this they would, at the breaking up of the body after death, surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in heaven—then I should immediately practice giving, cultivate meritorious deeds, observe the fast and keep the precepts, and then take my own life with a blade, or consume poison, or throw myself into a pit or well, or hang myself."
"O Śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa!
You should not compare my diligence to that of a blind man.
"Pāyāsi! [he replied.]
If a person who is diligent in effort attains long life, they will obtain great merit;
if they obtain great merit, they will attain rebirth in heaven and long life. Pāyāsi!
"You should contemplate the future life in this manner, and not as it is seen by the physical eye. Pāyāsi!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill-will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill-will; who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye that surpasses that of humans, see these beings at the time of death and at the time of birth: whether they are beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, and whether they go to good or bad destinations. They see them truly, according to the karma performed by those beings."
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, I see it in this way and declare it thus:
there is no future world, and no beings are reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there anything more evil than this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
I had a close relative who was gravely ill; I went to his place to comfort and look after him, and he likewise comforted and looked after me.

If he were to pass away, I would again go to him to offer my condolences and look upon him, yet he would no longer offer his condolences or look upon me, nor would I offer my condolences or look upon him.
Kāśyapa! For this reason, I have formed this thought:
no sentient beings are born.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
“Pāyāsi! Listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning through a parable.”
"Pāyāsi!

It is just as if there were a man skilled at blowing the conch shell who, having never heard the sound of a conch in a certain region, went to that place and, in the darkness of night, climbed a high mountain and blew the conch with all his might."
Those many people had never before heard the sound of a conch shell; having heard it, they thought:
"What kind of sound is this?
It is so exquisite, so extraordinary, truly delightful, beautiful to behold and listen to, and brings such joy to the heart."
Then, those people went together to where the skilled conch-blower was; having arrived, they asked:
"What is this sound?
It is so exquisite, so extraordinary, truly delightful, beautiful to behold and hear, and makes the heart rejoice."
The skilled conch-blower set the conch upon the ground and said to the crowd,
"Gentlemen! You should know that this is the very sound of the conch."
Thereupon, the people kicked the conch shell with their feet and spoke these words:
"O conch, let out a sound! O conch, let out a sound!
But there was no sound at all.
The skilled conch-blower then thought to himself:
"These people here are foolish and ignorant; they lack discernment and possess no wisdom."
"Why is this? It is because one seeks sound from an insentient object.
At that time, the skilled conch-blower took back the conch, rinsed it thoroughly with water, held it to his mouth, and blew it with all his might.
At that time, having heard this, the people thought to themselves:
"The conch is truly marvelous. Why is this so?"
"It means that by means of the hands, by means of water, and by means of the breath from the mouth, a pleasant sound is produced that fills the four quarters.
"In this way, Pāyāsi!
If a person’s life remains, they are able to speak and offer mutual comfort; but once their life has ended, they can no longer speak or offer mutual comfort."
Pāyāsi! You should observe the arising of sentient beings in this manner, and not as it is seen by the fleshly eye. Pāyāsi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill will; and who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye that surpasses that of humans, see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, passing away from or proceeding to fortunate or unfortunate realms—and they see this truly, according to the karma performed by those beings.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa speaks thus, I see it in this way and declare:
no living being is reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there anything more evil than this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
I have a chief magistrate who arrests a criminal and brings him to me; having arrived, he says to me:
"O Heavenly King!
This man has committed an offense; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him. I said to him:
"Take this criminal and weigh him while he is alive; having weighed him while alive, place him back on the ground and strangle him with a rope; once he is dead, weigh him again."
"I wish to know at what time this man was most light and soft, and his complexion so radiant and fine:
was it when he was dead, or when he was alive?
Following my instructions, they took that criminal; having weighed him while alive, they laid him back on the ground, strangled him with a rope, and after killing him, weighed him again.
While that sinner was alive, his body was extremely light, soft, and supple, and its complexion was radiant and fine;
once he has died, his skin becomes heavy and thick, hard rather than soft, and its complexion lacks radiance.
Kāśyapa!
For this reason, I have this thought:
no sentient beings are born.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
"Pāyāsi! Listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning through a parable."

Pāyāsi! It is just as if an iron ball or an iron plowshare were scorched by fire all day long; at that time, it would be extremely light and soft, its color bright and lustrous. But once the fire has been extinguished, as it gradually cools, it becomes increasingly solid and heavy, turning hard and no longer soft, and its color ceases to be bright and lustrous.
In this way, Pāyāsi!
When a person is alive, their body is extremely light, soft, and supple, and its complexion is bright and radiant;
once they have died, it becomes heavy and thick, hard and no longer supple, and the complexion loses its radiance.
Pāyāsi! You should observe the arising of sentient beings in this manner, and not as it is seen by the fleshly eye. Pāyāsi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill will; and who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see beings as they die and are reborn: beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, passing away from or proceeding to happy or unhappy destinations, according to the karma performed by those beings, seeing it as it truly is.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I see it in this way and declare:
no sentient being is born."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there yet another evil that exceeds this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
My right-hand officers arrest criminals and bring them to me; having arrived, they say:
"O Heavenly King!
This man has committed a transgression; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him. I said to him:

"Take this sinner and place him upside down in an iron cauldron, or perhaps in a copper cauldron; seal its mouth tightly and kindle a fire beneath it. Once the fire is lit, observe the sentient being as they enter and exit, coming and going, circling about."

Following my instructions, they took these offenders and placed them upside down in iron cauldrons, or sometimes in copper cauldrons; they sealed the openings tightly and lit fires beneath them. Once the fires were lit, they watched as the sentient beings entered and emerged, moving back and forth and circling within.
Kāśyapa! By means of such skillful methods, I do not perceive the birth of sentient beings. Kāśyapa!
"For this reason, I have formed this thought:
'No sentient beings are born.
Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa replied:
“Pāyāsi! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?

If you were to eat excellent, most delicious, and superior delicacies, and sleep by day upon a couch, would you ever recall seeing in a dream gardens, groves, bathing pools, trees with flowers and fruits, and clear springs flowing in long streams, where you might play to your heart's content, wandering and coming and going?
Pāyāsi replied,
“I do recall having done so.
Kāśyapa asked again:
"If you were to eat excellent, most delicious, and superior food, and then sleep by day upon a couch, would there at that time be any attendants standing by?
He replied, "There would be."
Kāśyapa asked again:

"If you were eating excellent, most delicious, and superior delicacies and were sleeping by day upon a couch, at such a time, would there be any attendants standing nearby who saw you entering or exiting, moving about, or coming and going?"
Pāyāsi replied:
"Even an extraordinary person could not see it, much less those who serve as his attendants. "Pāyāsi!..."
"You should observe the arising of sentient beings in this way; do not view them as the physical eye perceives. Pāyāsi!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire, inclining toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill-will, inclining toward the abandonment of ill-will; who have severed and abandoned delusion, inclining toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye that surpasses that of humans, see these sentient beings at the time of death and at the time of birth—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, whether excellent or inferior, and whether they go to good or bad destinations. They see them truly, according to the karma performed by those sentient beings."
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I see it in this way and I declare:
no living being is reborn."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said: "Pāyāsi!
Is there yet another evil that exceeds this?"
Pāyāsi replied, “It is so, Kāśyapa!”
There is yet another evil, Kāśyapa!
I have a chief magistrate who arrests criminals and brings them to me; having arrived, he says to me:
"O Heavenly King!
This man has committed a transgression; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him. I said to him:
"Take this sinner, flay his skin, cut away his flesh, sever his tendons, break his bones, and even reach his marrow, seeking therein the birth of a sentient being.

He, having received my instruction, took this sinner, flayed his skin, cut away his flesh, severed his tendons, broke his bones, and even reached his marrow, seeking therein the birth of a sentient being.
“Kāśyapa!
I employ such skillful means to seek the birth of sentient beings, yet in the end, I do not see the birth of any sentient being.
Kāśyapa!”
"For this reason, I have formed this thought:
'No sentient beings are born.
Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa replied:
“Pāyāsi! Listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning upon hearing a parable. Pāyāsi!”
It was as if there were a fire-worshipping matted-hair brahmin living near the side of a road; not far from him, some merchants had stayed overnight.
When the merchants departed in haste at dawn after the night had passed, they forgot a young child behind them.
Thereupon, the fire-worshipping matted-hair brahmin rose early in the morning to inspect the merchants' lodgings. Seeing a small boy staying alone without a guardian, he thought to himself:
"This child now has no one to rely upon; if I do not nourish him, he will surely die."
He then took him up and carried him away, returning to his own place to raise and nurture him.
As the boy grew older, his faculties matured.
At that time, the fire-worshipping matted-hair Brahmin had some minor business to attend to among the people. Thereupon, the fire-worshipping matted-hair Brahmin instructed the youth, saying:
"I have a small matter to attend to and shall depart for the human world for a short time; you should maintain this fire and take care not to let it go out.
If the fire should be extinguished, you may seek it by taking these fire-drills."

At that time, after the fire-worshipping brahmin with matted hair had given his instructions, he departed for the human world; subsequently, while the youth went out to play, the fire was completely extinguished.
He went back to seek fire; taking a fire-drill, he struck it against the ground and spoke these words:
"Fire! Fire! But no fire emerged.
He then struck it with even greater force upon a stone:
"Fire! Fire! Fire! he cried, yet no fire emerged.
Since no fire emerged, he broke the fire-drill into ten pieces and then a hundred pieces, cast them aside, sat upon the ground, and spoke in grief and distress:
"If we cannot obtain fire, what shall we do?
At that time, the fire-worshipping matted-hair brahmin, having finished his business among men, returned to his own place. Upon arrival, he asked:
"Young man! What is this?"
"Do you not play about while watching the seeds catch fire, so as not to let them go out?
The youth replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
I went out to play, and after I returned, the fire had gone out.
I sought for fire and took my fire-drill, striking it against the ground while saying these words: "Fire! Fire!"
The fire still did not emerge.
He struck the stone again with even greater force, crying out:
"Fire! Come forth! Fire! Come forth!"
"Yet the fire still did not emerge.
Since the fire would not emerge, he broke the fire-drill into ten pieces and then a hundred pieces, cast them aside, and sat down on the ground,
Venerable Sir!"
"I have sought fire in this manner, yet I cannot obtain it; what shall I do?
At that time, the fire-worshipping matted-hair brahmin thought to himself:
"This youth is extremely foolish and lacks understanding; he is not well-versed in the teachings and possesses no wisdom."
"Why is that? Do you seek fire by using the fire-drill from ignorance?

Thereupon, the fire-worshipping matted-hair brahmin took dry fire-drills and a fire-board, placed them on the ground, and drilled them; immediately fire emerged, growing increasingly intense. He said to the young man:
"Young man!

The method for seeking fire should be like this; it should not be as you have done out of folly and lack of understanding, being devoid of wisdom and seeking fire from an ignorant fire-drill with such a mindset."

"You should know that Pāyāsi is likewise so: foolish and lacking penetration, unskilled in understanding, and devoid of wisdom, he seeks the arising of a living being within dead flesh—even down to the marrow—within which there is no consciousness."
Pāyāsi! You should observe the arising of sentient beings in this manner, and not as it is seen by the physical eye. Pāyāsi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who have severed and abandoned desire and are inclined toward the abandonment of desire; who have severed and abandoned ill will and are inclined toward the abandonment of ill will; who have severed and abandoned delusion and are inclined toward the abandonment of delusion—they, with the purified divine eye surpassing that of humans, see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, sublime or unrefined—as they pass to good destinations or bad destinations, seeing them exactly as they are according to the karma these beings have performed.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:

"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I cannot ultimately abandon this view of mine—the grasping through desire, the grasping through hatred, the grasping through fear, and the grasping through delusion."
Why is this? If people from other countries were to hear of this, they would say:
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long time, yet he has been subdued, disciplined, and made to abandon it by the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa."
"Kāśyapa! Therefore, these views of mine—grasping through desire, grasping through anger, grasping through fear, and grasping through delusion—I can never abandon.
The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa replied:
"Pāyāsi! Listen as I speak a parable, for the wise understand the meaning upon hearing a parable. Pāyāsi!"
It is like two friends who leave their homes to pursue a livelihood. While traveling on the road, they first see a great deal of unowned flax. Upon seeing it, one says to his companion:
"You should know that there is now this great deal of unowned flax; I wish to take some with you, carry it back carefully, and we shall have the means for our use."
He then took up his heavy burden.
Along the road, he again saw a great quantity of cotton thread and cotton cloth, very abundant and without an owner;
he also saw much silver, likewise without an owner.
One man, having seen this, abandoned his load of hemp and took the silver to carry on his own person.
Later, while on the road, he saw a large heap of gold with no owner.
At that time, the man carrying the silver said to the man carrying the hemp:

"You should know this now: this gold is exceedingly abundant and has no owner. You may set aside your sesame, and I shall set aside my silver burden; I wish to take this gold together with you, carry it back on our shoulders, and thereby obtain its use."
The man carrying the hemp spoke to the man carrying the silver:

"This load of hemp of mine is already well-prepared; it has been packed and bound firmly. I have carried it from afar and cannot abandon it. You may take care of your own affairs; do not worry about me."
Thereupon, the man carrying silver forcibly seized the load of hemp, threw it to the ground, and crushed it.
The man carrying the hemp said to the man carrying the silver:

"You have already thus crushed my load; however, this load of hemp of mine was bound very tightly and I have come from a great distance. I wish to carry this hemp back myself and will certainly not abandon it. You may take care of your own business; do not worry about me."
The man carrying silver immediately set down his silver burden and took up a heavy load of gold himself to return.
As the man carrying gold was returning, his parents saw him from afar coming home with the gold;
having seen him, they exclaimed: "Welcome, worthy son!"
Come quickly, worthy son!

By means of this gold, you shall swiftly obtain a livelihood; you may support your parents, provide for your wife, children, slaves, and servants, and furthermore, you may give alms to śramaṇas and brahmins, perform meritorious deeds, ascend to higher realms, and through wholesome fruits and rewards, be reborn in heaven with long life.
The hemp-carrier returned to his home. His parents saw him from afar returning with the hemp; having seen him, they reviled him, saying:

"You sinner has come! You man of no virtue has come! Because of this hemp, you will not be able to support yourself, provide for your parents, or supply your wife, children, slaves, or servants. Furthermore, you will not be able to give alms to śramaṇas and brahmins, perform meritorious deeds to ascend to higher realms, or attain the good fruits and rewards of rebirth in heaven and long life."

"You should know, Pāyāsi, that it is just the same for you: if you do not abandon this view—this grasping out of desire, this grasping out of hatred, this grasping out of fear, and this grasping out of delusion—you will surely undergo immeasurable evil and be further reviled by the multitude."
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I cannot abandon this view of mine—this grasping through desire, grasping through hatred, grasping through fear, and grasping through delusion."
Why is this? If people from other countries were to hear of this, they would say:
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long night, yet he has been subdued, disciplined, and caused to abandon it by the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa."
"Kāśyapa! For this reason, I cannot ultimately relinquish these views of mine: the grasping of desire, the grasping of hatred, the grasping of fear, and the grasping of delusion.
The Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa replied:
“Pāyāsi, listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning through parables.
Pāyāsi, it is just as if a merchant, together with a great multitude, were traveling along a road plagued by famine and scarcity with a thousand wagons.”
Within this great assembly there were two leaders, who thought to themselves:
"By what cause shall we be delivered from this peril?
They further thought:
"I should divide this great assembly into two groups, with five hundred in each.
Thereupon, that caravan of merchants was divided into two groups, with five hundred in each.

Thereupon, a merchant leader was traveling with five hundred wagons toward the road of famine. That merchant leader, always leading the way in front, saw a man coming from a side path; his clothes were completely soaked, his body was black and his head yellow, his two eyes were extremely red, he wore a garland of *bālaka* flowers, and he rode a donkey-cart with mud clinging to both its wheels. Upon seeing him, the merchant leader asked:
"Has it rained on the road of famine?"
"Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?
The man replied,
"Because of the great rain that fell along this road during the famine, there is very fresh water and an abundance of firewood and grass."
"Virtuous ones!
You should discard your old water, firewood, and grass so that your mounts do not suffer from lack; before long, you shall obtain fresh water and excellent firewood and grass."
Having heard this, the leader of the merchants immediately returned and went to the other merchants, telling them:

"As I was traveling in front, I saw a man coming from a side path; his clothes were entirely wet, his body was black and his head yellow, his two eyes were extremely red, he wore a garland of *hingu* flowers, and he was riding a donkey-cart with mud clinging to both its poles."
I asked him: "In this path of famine, does it rain?
Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass?"
He replied to me, saying:
"In the midst of this famine, a great rain has fallen from the heavens; there is now plenty of fresh water, as well as abundant firewood and grass.
O worthy ones!"
"You should discard your old water, firewood, and grass so as not to let your mounts suffer from lack; before long, you shall obtain fresh water and excellent firewood and grass."
"O merchants!
We should discard our old water, firewood, and grass; before long we shall obtain fresh water, firewood, and grass, so do not let our transport be exhausted."

Those merchants immediately abandoned their old water, firewood, and grass; however, traveling for one day, they could not find fresh water, firewood, or grass. After two days, three days, and even up to seven days of travel, they still failed to obtain fresh water, firewood, or grass. Once the seven days had passed, they were killed by man-eating spirits.
The second merchant leader then thought to himself:
"The first merchant leader has already passed through the perilous difficulties; by what means shall we now likewise escape this danger?"
After the second caravan leader had formed this thought, he proceeded together with five hundred carts toward the road of famine.

The second caravan leader led the way himself and saw a man coming from a side path; his clothes were completely soaked, his body was black and his head yellow, his two eyes were extremely red, he wore a garland of *hing* flowers, and he was riding a donkey cart with mud clinging to both its wheels. Upon seeing him, the second caravan leader asked:
"Has it rained in the road of famine?"
"Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass there?
The man replied, "Due to the great drought on this road, it has rained heavily from the heavens; there is indeed very fresh water, as well as an abundance of firewood and grass."
"Venerable friends!
You should discard your old water, firewood, and grass so that your carriage does not run short; before long, you shall obtain fresh water and fine firewood and grass."
"Having heard this, the second merchant leader immediately returned and went to the other merchants, telling them:

'As I was traveling ahead, I saw a man coming from a side path. His clothes were completely soaked; his body was black and his head yellow; his two eyes were extremely red; he wore a garland of *bālaka* flowers and rode in a donkey cart, with mud clinging to both its wheels.'"
I asked him: "In this path of famine, does it rain?
Is there fresh water, firewood, and grass?"
He replied to me:
"On this road through the famine-stricken land, it has just rained heavily; there is very fresh water and plenty of firewood and grass.
O worthy ones!"
"You should discard your old water, firewood, and grass so as not to let your mounts suffer from exhaustion; before long, you shall obtain fresh water and excellent firewood and grass."
“O merchants!
We must not yet discard our old water, firewood, and grass; only when we have obtained new water, firewood, and grass shall we then cast them away.”

Because he did not discard his old water, firewood, and grass, he traveled for one day without obtaining new water, firewood, or grass; he traveled for two days, three days, and even up to seven days, yet still failed to obtain new water, firewood, or grass.

As the second merchant leader was traveling ahead, he saw that the first merchant leader and the other merchants had been killed by man-eating demons. Having seen this, the second merchant leader said to the merchants:
"Look at how the first merchant leader was foolish and ignorant, lacking discernment and wisdom; having brought about his own death, he has likewise caused the deaths of all these people."
"O merchants, if you wish to take the goods of the previous merchants, take them as you please.
You should know that Pāyāsi is just like this.

If you persist in this view—grasping it out of desire, grasping it out of hatred, grasping it out of fear, or grasping it out of delusion—and never relinquish it, you will then incur immeasurable evil and be detested by the multitude, just like the first merchant leader and his merchants.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:

“Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa has spoken thus, I still cannot abandon this view of mine—this grasping out of desire, grasping out of hatred, grasping out of fear, and grasping out of delusion.”
Why is this? If people from other countries were to hear of this, they would say:
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long time, yet he has been subdued, disciplined, and made to abandon it by the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa."
"Kāśyapa! For this reason, these views of mine—clinging through desire, clinging through anger, clinging through fear, and clinging through delusion—I can never abandon.
Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said:
“Pāyāsi! Listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning upon hearing a parable. Pāyāsi!”

It is like two people who have agreed to play a game of dice. While playing, the first player secretly eats the stakes; he eats one, two, three, or even many. The second player then thinks to himself:
"I am playing with this man, yet he repeatedly deceives me by stealing and eating the stakes—whether one, two, three, or even many."
Having seen this, he said to his companion, "I wish to rest now; we shall play again later.
Thereupon, the second player left that spot, smeared poison on his dice, and having done so, returned and said to his companion:
"Come and play with me.
He immediately came and played with him.
The first player again stole the beans—perhaps one, two, or three, or even many—and having eaten the beans, he immediately rolled his eyes, spat foam, and was on the verge of death.
Thereupon, the second player spoke this verse to the first player:
"This [ball] is smeared with poison; you greedily ate it without realizing it.
Because you deceived me by sitting here, you will surely suffer great affliction later."

"You should know, Pāyāsi, that it is just the same for you: if you persist in this view—clinging to it out of desire, clinging to it out of hatred, clinging to it out of fear, or clinging to it out of delusion—and never abandon it, you will then incur immeasurable evil and be detested by all people, just as a performer who deceives others with a trick ends up suffering the calamity himself."
King Pāyāsi spoke again:
"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I cannot ultimately abandon this view of mine—the grasping of desire, the grasping of anger, the grasping of fear, and the grasping of delusion."
Why is this? If people from other countries were to hear of this, they would say:
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long night, yet he was subdued, disciplined, and made to abandon it by the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa."
"Kāśyapa! For this reason, I cannot ultimately relinquish these views of mine: grasping through desire, grasping through anger, grasping through fear, and grasping through delusion.
Venerable Kumāra Kāśyapa said:
"Pāyāsi! Listen further to a parable I shall speak; for the wise understand the meaning through parables. Pāyāsi!"
It is like a pig-herder who, while traveling on a road, sees a great deal of manure that has no owner. He then thinks to himself:
"This manure can nourish many pigs; I had better take it with me. He then takes it and continues on his way.

He immediately took it up and carried it away. On the way, he encountered a heavy rain; the liquid manure flowed and overflowed, drenching and defiling his body. Nevertheless, he continued to carry it and never abandoned it; thus, he himself incurred immeasurable evil and was loathed by all people.

You should know, Pāyāsi, that it is just the same for you: if you do not ultimately relinquish this view—whether it be a grasping out of desire, a grasping out of hatred, a grasping out of fear, or a grasping out of delusion—you will then incur immeasurable evil and be loathed by the multitude, just like a swineherd.
King Pāyāsi spoke again:

"Although the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa has spoken thus, I cannot ultimately abandon this view of mine—this grasping out of desire, grasping out of hatred, grasping out of fear, and grasping out of delusion."
Why is this? If people from other countries were to hear of this, they would say:
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long night, yet he was subdued, disciplined, and made to abandon it by the ascetic Kumāra Kassapa."
"Kāśyapa! For this reason, these views of mine—grasping through desire, grasping through anger, grasping through fear, and grasping through delusion—I can never abandon.
Venerable Kumāra-Kāśyapa said:
“Pāyāsi! Listen further to my final parable; if you understand it, that is well;
if you do not understand it, I shall no longer speak the Dharma.”
"Pāyāsi! It is just as if a great boar were the leader of five hundred boars traveling along a perilous path.
On the way, he encountered a tiger. Upon seeing the tiger, the boar thought to himself:"
"If I fight with him, the tiger will surely kill me;
yet if I flee out of fear, my kinsmen will look down upon me with contempt.
I do not know by what skillful means I may now escape this peril."
Having formed this thought, he said to the tiger:
"If you wish to fight, we may fight together;
if not, lend me your path to pass."
Having heard this, the tiger spoke to the pig, saying:
"I grant you leave to fight me, but you shall not have the way.
The pig spoke again, saying:
"Tiger! Wait a moment; wait while I put on my grandfather's armor, and then we shall fight together.
Having heard this, the tiger thought to himself:
"He is not my enemy, much less my grandfather's armor," he said,
and then addressed the boar: "Do as you wish."
The pig immediately returned to its original latrine, wallowed in the excrement until it had smeared itself up to its eyes, and then went to where the tiger was, saying:
"If you wish to fight, then let us fight;
if not, lend me a path to pass."
When the tiger saw the pig, he thought again:
"I do not usually eat small insects because I cherish my teeth; how much less would I ever approach this foul-smelling pig?"
Having thought this, the tiger said to the pig:
"I grant you passage; I will not fight with you.
Once the pig had passed through, he turned back toward the tiger and spoke this verse:
“Tiger, you have four feet, and I too have four feet;
come and fight with me—why do you flee in fear?”
When the tiger had heard this, he also spoke in verse, replying to the pig:
“Your bristles stand on end in dense rows; Of all animals, you are the lowest of the low.
Pig, you should depart at once; The stench of your excrement is unbearable.”
Then the boar, boasting of himself, spoke again in verse:
"When the two kingdoms of Magadha and Aṅga hear that I am fighting with you, they will come to join me in battle; why do you flee in fear?"
Upon hearing this, the tiger spoke again in verse:
"Your entire body is stained with filth; you pig, your stench overwhelms me.
You fight only because you seek victory; I shall now grant you victory."
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:
"Pāyāsi! It is the same for me:

if you do not abandon this view of yours—this grasping out of desire, hatred, fear, or delusion—you will surely incur immeasurable evil for yourself and be loathed by all people, just as that tiger was surpassed by the pig."
Having heard this, King Pāyāsi said:
"Venerable sir!

When you first spoke the parable of the sun and moon, I understood it upon hearing it and accepted it with joy. However, I wished to seek from the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa an even higher and more sublime teaching of wisdom; for that reason, I asked you again and again."
"I now take refuge in the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied: "Pāyāsi!"
"Do not take refuge in me; I have taken refuge in the Buddha, and you too should take refuge in him.
King Pāyāsi replied, "Venerable sir!"

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. May the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa accept me as a lay follower of the Buddha; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
"Venerable Kumāra Kassapa!
From this day forward, I shall practice giving and cultivate merit.
Venerable Kumāra Kassapa asked:
“Pāyāsi! You wish to practice giving and cultivate merit; to how many people do you give, and for how long can you continue?”
King Pāyāsi replied,
"I give to a hundred people, or even up to a thousand, for one day, two days, or even up to seven days.
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa said:

"If King Pāyāsi practices giving and cultivates merit, bestowing gifts upon a hundred or even a thousand people for one day, two days, or up to seven days, the śramaṇas and brahmins of all quarters will hear:
'King Pāyāsi possesses views that have been held for a long night; he has been subdued, disciplined, and caused to abandon them by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa.'"
"Once those from all directions have heard of this, they will all come from afar; within seven days, they will not be able to receive the King's offerings.
If they do not obtain food through the King’s act of faith, the King will lack merit and shall not enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
"King Pāyāsi!
It is just as if there were a seed that is neither crushed nor damaged, neither split nor torn, not harmed by wind or sun, nor injured by water, and was well-stored during the autumn season."

Suppose that householder plows his fertile field deeply and prepares the ground thoroughly, sowing the seed at the proper time; yet, if the rainfall is unsuitable, what do you think, Bhāradvāja? Would those seeds be able to sprout and grow?
He replied, "No. Venerable Kumārajīva said:
“Pāyāsi! You are just like this.

If you practice giving and cultivate merit by bestowing gifts upon a hundred or even a thousand people for one day, two days, or up to seven days, the śramaṇas and brahmins of all directions will hear of it:”
"King Pāyāsi held a long-standing view, but he has been subdued, disciplined, and caused to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa."
"When people from all directions hear of this, they will all come from afar; within seven days, they will not have time to receive the King's offerings.
If they do not obtain food through the King’s gift of faith, the King will have no merit and shall not enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
