King Pāyāsi asked again:
"Venerable sir!
What should I do?"
The Venerable Kumāra Kassapa replied:
“Pāyāsi! You should practice giving to cultivate merit and constantly observe the long fast.”
If King Pāyāsi practices giving and cultivates merit, constantly observing the long fast, then śramaṇas and brahmins from all directions will hear:
"King Pāyāsi held a view that has been maintained for a long night; he has now been subdued, disciplined, and made to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kassapa."

"Once those from all directions have heard this, they will all come from afar; they shall all be able to receive the King’s offerings of faith, whereby the King will possess merit and obtain long-lasting peace and happiness."

Pāyāsi! It is just as if there were a seed that is neither crushed nor destroyed, neither split nor torn apart, not damaged by wind or sun, nor harmed by water, and is well-stored during the autumn season.

If that householder were to plow a fertile field deeply, thoroughly prepare the ground, sow the seeds at the proper time, and the rainfalls were timely, what do you think, Bhāradvāja? Would those seeds be able to sprout and grow?
He replied, "It was born.
The Venerable Kumārajīva said:

“Pāyāsi! You are just like this; if you were to practice giving and cultivate merit by constantly providing for those who observe the long fast, then śramaṇas and brahmins from all directions would hear of it:”
"King Pāyāsi held a view for a long night, but he has been subdued, disciplined, and caused to abandon it by the śramaṇa Kumāra Kāśyapa."

"Once those from all directions have heard this, they will all come from afar; they shall all be able to receive the King’s offerings of faith, whereby the King will possess merit and enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
Thereupon, King Pāyāsi said:
"Venerable Sir!
From this day forward, I shall practice giving to cultivate merit and constantly observe the long fast."

At that time, the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa taught the Dharma to King Pāyāsi and the brahmins and householders of Setavyā, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and establishing them in joy. Having used countless skillful means to teach them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and establishing them in joy, he remained silent.

Thereupon, King Pāyāsi, along with the brahmins and householders of Setavyā, having been taught the Dharma by the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, inspired with aspiration, filled with longing, and established in joy, rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Although King Pāyāsi practiced giving and cultivated merit, it was extremely coarse and inferior: he gave only bean soup and vegetables with a single slice of ginger, and furthermore, he gave coarse, worn-out cloth garments.

At that time, the superintendent of the kitchen was named Uttara. While he was performing acts of giving and cultivating merit, he offered a formal blessing to the Elder on behalf of King Pāyāsi, saying:
"If there is any karmic fruit of this gift, may it not fall upon King Pāyāsi in this life or in future lives."
When King Pāyāsi heard that while Udāyin was practicing giving and cultivating merit, he would always entrust the Elder to offer this blessing:
"If there is any karmic reward for this gift, may it not be experienced by King Pāyāsi in this life or in future lives."
Having heard this, he immediately called him and asked:
"Uttara! When you were practicing generosity and cultivating merit, did you entrust me with a request for the Elder to offer a blessing?"
"If this gift were to have a karmic reward, may King Pāyāsi not receive it in this life or in future lives.
Is that what you say? Udāyin replied:
"It is indeed so, Great King! Why is this?
For what reason?"
"Although the Heavenly King practices giving and cultivates merit, his offerings are extremely coarse and poor—bean soup and leafy vegetables with only a single slice of ginger.
O Heavenly King!
This food cannot even be touched by hand, much less eaten by oneself!"
The Heavenly King gave me this coarse and worn-out cloth garment.
O Heavenly King!
This garment is such that one cannot even step upon it with one's feet, much less wear it oneself?
"I revere the Heavenly King, but I do not value the gift bestowed;
therefore, Heavenly King, I do not wish for you to receive the karmic reward of this inferior gift.
Having heard this, King Pāyāsi said:
“Uttara! From this day forward, you should provide food just as I eat it, and you should give gifts just as I wear my robes.”
Thereupon, from that time forward, Uttara ate the same food as the king and gave away in alms the same clothing as the king wore.
At that time, because Udāyin had supervised the practice of giving for King Pāyāsi, when his body broke up and his life ended, he was reborn among the Four Great Kings.
Because King Pāyāsi had practiced giving without a sincere heart, when his body broke up and his life ended, he was reborn in an empty palace within the Śiṃśapā forest.
The Venerable Kātyāyana frequently went to wander through that empty palace in the Śiṃśapā grove. Seeing King Pāyāsi from afar, the Venerable Kātyāyana asked him: "Who are you?"
King Pāyāsi replied: "Venerable Kevaḍḍha!
Have you heard that there is a king named Pāyāsi in the land of Jambudvīpa?"
The Venerable Kātyāyana replied,
"I have heard that in Jambudvīpa, in the city of Sāvatthī, there is a king named Pāyāsi. King Pāyāsi said:
“Venerable Kevaddha, I am that very person; my original name was King Pāyāsi.
Venerable Kevaddha then asked again:
“King Pāyāsi held such a view and spoke thus:”
"There is no future world, and there are no beings reborn.
By what means, then, could they have been born here, dwelling in the empty palaces within the small *śirīṣa* grove of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven?
King Pāyāsi replied:
"Venerable Pūraṇa Kāśyapa!
I indeed formerly held this view, but I have been subdued, disciplined, and caused to abandon it by the venerable ascetic Kumāra Kāśyapa."
If the Venerable Kapphiṇa returns to Jambudvīpa, I pray that you will announce throughout the people of Jambudvīpa:

"When practicing giving and cultivating merit, one should give with a sincere heart, give with one's own hand, go in person to give, give with deep faith, and give with the knowledge that there is karma and the retribution of karma."
Why is this? It is so that you do not receive the retribution for your almsgiving in such a manner as King Śreṇika Bimbisāra of Vaḍḍha.
King Śreṇika was a master of almsgiving, yet because he practiced giving without a sincere heart, he was reborn in an empty palace within the Small Nyagrodha Grove of the Four Great Kings Heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Kapphiṇa accepted [the invitation] in silence.
Thereupon, whenever the Venerable Kapphiṇa came down to Jambudvīpa, he would proclaim throughout the people of Jambudvīpa:
"Give with a devoted heart; give with your own hands; give by going in person; give with deep faith; give knowing that there is karma and the retribution of karma."
Why is this? It is so that you do not receive the retribution for your giving in the same manner as King Śreṇiya Bimbisāra of Vaiśālī.
King Śreṇiya was a master of giving, yet because he practiced generosity without a sincere heart, he was reborn in an empty palace within the Small Jambu Grove of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Thus spoke the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa.
King Pāyāsi, the brahmins and householders of Setavyā, and the bhikkhus, having heard what the Venerable Kumāra Kassapa had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Pāyāsi Sutta*, the seventh, ends here, totaling 10,367 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 16, totaling 10,367 characters, concludes here with the first section, the "Chapter on Kings," totaling 35,621 characters.

Within the second recitation section, the "Minor Earth-City" (*Kṣudrakapattana*), the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 17, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Chapter on King Dīrghāyu (Dīghāvu-vagga) of the Madhyama Āgama. This chapter contains fifteen sūtras.
Recited in the second section, the Minor Earth-Castle (Kṣudrakapṛthivīpura). [The sūtras include:
Dīrghāyu, Deva, Aṣṭānu-smṛti, Śuddha, Acyuta, Mārga, Uruvilvākāśyapa, and Sākya-tri-gotra.
The Brahmā who invited the Buddha, the Victorious Deva, Kāṭhina,
and the Mindfulness of the Body; Cīramati, the Most Venerable Elder, Anīgha, and the True Man—
these are the teachers of the places, listed in order from last to first.
72. The Discourse on the Previous Life of King Dīrghāyu (72). Majjhima Nikāya, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, The Discourse on the Previous Life of King Dīrghāyu, First. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Kuśāmbakas and staying at the Ghoṣitārāma monastery.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were frequently quarreling with one another.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, saying:
"Bhikṣus!..."
"You all must not engage in mutual strife. Why is this?
'If one seeks to stop strife with strife, strife will never come to an end.'"
"Only patience can bring an end to strife; this is the dharma that is worthy of honor. Why is this so?
Long ago in the past, there was a king of the Kośala, named Dīghāvu, and there was also a king of the Kāsī, named Brahmadatta; those two kings were constantly at war with one another."
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī mobilized the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.
Having mobilized these four divisions, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī personally led his forces forth, intending to engage in battle with King Dīghāvu of Kosala.

King Dīghāvu of Kosala heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāsi had mobilized the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—and having mobilized these four divisions, was coming to wage war against him.
Upon hearing this, King Dīrghāyu of Kośala also mobilized the fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.

Having mobilized these four divisions, King Dīrghāyu of Kośala personally led his forces out to the border, where they drew up their battle lines and fought; [the other king] was then utterly defeated.

Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru of the Kośala kingdom completely seized all four divisions of King Brahmadatta’s army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—and furthermore captured King Brahmadatta of Kāśī alive. Having taken him, he immediately released him and said to him:
"You who are now in such dire straits, I now grant you amnesty; do not commit such acts again in the future."
"King Brahmadatta of Kāsī again raised fourfold armies—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—three times more."
Having mobilized his fourfold army, he then personally led his troops to engage in battle with King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom.

When King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom heard that King Brahmadatta of Kāśi had again mobilized his fourfold army—consisting of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and having mobilized these fourfold forces, was coming to fight him, [he prepared his own defenses].
When King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom heard this, he thought to himself:
"I have already conquered him; why need I conquer him again?
I have already subdued him; why is it necessary to subdue him further?"
"I have already struck him down; why should I strike him again?
An empty bow is sufficient to subdue him.

Having thought this, King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom remained calm and did not mobilize his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—nor did he go there himself.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāśi came and defeated him, seizing all four divisions of the long-lived King of Kośala’s army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry.

"Then, King Jīvaka of the Kośala kingdom, hearing that King Brahmadatta of Kāśī had come and completely seized his fourfold army—the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—thought to himself:
'A battle would be most extraordinary!'"
Fighting is extremely evil! Why is this so?
For one who strikes shall strike again;
one who subdues shall be subdued again; and one who harms shall be harmed again.
"I would rather take only one wife and, traveling together in a single chariot, flee to Vārāṇasī.
Thereupon, King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom took only his wife, and together they traveled in a single chariot, fleeing to Vārāṇasī.
King Dīrghāyu of Kośala further thought to himself:
"I should now travel from village to village and town to town to receive instruction and gain extensive learning.

Having had this thought, King Dīrghāyu of Kośala immediately went from village to village and town to town to receive instruction and gain extensive learning; because of his extensive learning, he was thereafter known by the name Dīrghāyu Paṇḍita.
The Venerable Āyuṣmān further thought to himself:

"That which was to be learned, I have now attained. I should go into the city of Vārāṇasī and stay in the streets and alleys, performing music with a joyful countenance and exquisite sounds. When the noble and wealthy clansmen of Vārāṇasī hear this, they will be filled with great joy and find their own delight."

Having formed this thought, the Doctor Jīvaka went into the city of Vārāṇasī and stood at every street and alleyway, performing exquisite music with a joyful countenance. When the noble and wealthy clansmen of Vārāṇasī heard him, they were filled with great delight and amused themselves.
Thereupon, when King Brahmadatta’s outer retinue heard of the general amnesty, his middle retinue, inner retinue, and the brahmin state preceptor heard of it in succession.
When the brahmin state preceptor heard this, he summoned him to see him.

Thereupon, the physician Jīvaka went to the brahmin state preceptor’s residence and stood before him; with a joyful countenance, he performed exquisite musical arts. Having heard them, the brahmin state preceptor was filled with great joy and amused himself.
Thereupon, the brahmin state preceptor said to the doctor Jīvaka, "From this day forward, you may stay with me; I shall provide for your needs.
The doctor Jīvaka replied:
"Venerable One! I have a wife; what should I do with her?
The brahmin state preceptor replied:
“Doctor! You may bring her here to live with my household, and I shall provide for her.
Thereupon, the Doctor Jīvaka brought his wife to live with the house of the Brahmin State Preceptor, and the Brahmin State Preceptor immediately provided for them.
Later, at that time, the wife of the long-lived physician, harboring a sense of grief and melancholy, thought to herself:

"I wish for the fourfold army to march in procession with drawn, gleaming blades, passing by slowly; I desire to observe them all, and I also wish to obtain the water used for sharpening the swords to drink."
Having had this thought, the wife of the physician Jīvaka said to him:
"My heart is filled with grief, and I have had this thought:

'I wish for the fourfold army to draw up its ceremonial procession, with bright white blades drawn, and pass by slowly; I wish to observe it all, and I also wish to obtain the water used for sharpening swords to drink.'"
The Venerable Āyusmān then said to his wife:
"Do not harbor such thoughts. Why is this?"

"We have now been defeated by King Brahmadatta; by what means will you be able to see the fourfold army drawn up in ceremonial procession, with polished white blades drawn, passing by slowly and steadily? We wish to behold it all, and we also wish to obtain the water used for sharpening the swords to drink."
The wife spoke again, saying:
"If you, my lord, can obtain it, I have hope for life; if you cannot, I shall surely die, there is no doubt.

Thereupon, the physician Jīvaka went to the brahmin state preceptor, stood before him with a sorrowful and haggard countenance, and performed various musical performances with a harsh, faint voice; having heard this, the brahmin state preceptor could find no joy.
Thereupon, the brahmin state preceptor asked: "Doctor!
Previously you stood before me, performing exquisite music with a joyful countenance; having heard it, I was filled with the greatest delight and found my own entertainment."
Why do you now stand before me with such a sorrowful and haggard countenance, performing various musical performances with such a wretched and faint voice?
Having heard this, I find no joy.
“Venerable Doctor Jīvaka!
Is your body free from ailment, and is your mind free from sorrow and distress?
The Doctor Jīvaka replied:
"Venerable sir!
My body is free from ailment; it is only my mind that is burdened with sorrow.
"Venerable sir! [he continued].
My wife, harboring grief and sorrow, thought to herself:

"I wish to see the fourfold army drawn up in ceremonial procession, with bright, unsheathed blades drawn, passing by slowly; I wish to observe it all, and I also wish to drink the water used for sharpening the swords."
I then replied to my wife, saying:
"Do not harbor such thoughts. Why is this?

As I am now, by what means could you have fourfold military arrays with ceremonial processions, drawing polished white blades, passing by slowly and steadily, so that I might observe them all around, or even desire to drink the water used for sharpening swords?"
My wife spoke to me again, saying:
"Venerable sir, if you can obtain it, I have hope for life; if you cannot, my death is certain.
Venerable sir!
"If my wife is not whole, I too have no reason [to live].
The Brahmin National Preceptor asked, "Doctor!..."
"Can you see your wife?
He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"You shall indeed see it.
Thereupon, the brahmin state preceptor led the physician Jīvaka to his wife's quarters.

At that time, the physician Jīvaka’s wife was pregnant with a son of noble merit. Because the brahmin state preceptor saw that the physician Jīvaka’s wife was pregnant with a son of noble merit, he knelt upon the ground with his right knee, joined his palms toward the physician Jīvaka’s wife, and addressed her three times:
"King Jīvaka Śākyarāja! King Jīvaka Śākyarāja!
he commanded his attendants, saying:
"Do not let anyone know," the brahmin state preceptor told him, "O Doctor!"

"Do not be distressed; I can cause your wife to see four types of military arrays in ceremonial procession, with bright, drawn blades held aloft as they pass by slowly and deliberately, and I can also cause her to drink the water used for sharpening their swords."
"Then, the brahmin state preceptor went to King Brahmadatta of Kāsī; having arrived, he said to him:
'O Great King!'"

"Know that a virtuous star has appeared; we pray that Your Majesty will array the fourfold army, marshal the ceremonial procession, draw your gleaming white blades, and lead the way with measured steps to display the majesty of your forces. We pray that Your Majesty will personally go forth to observe them as they sharpen their swords at the water-mill."
"O Heavenly King!
If one acts in this way, there will surely be an auspicious response.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī immediately commanded his minister of war:

"Minister! You should know now that a virtuous star has appeared. You ought to quickly prepare the fourfold army, arrange the ceremonial procession, and draw forth the gleaming white blades. Lead them out with slow and dignified steps to display the majesty of our military might; we shall sharpen our swords at the water-mill, and I myself will go out to observe. If you act in this manner, there will surely be auspicious omens."

At that time, the commander-in-chief received the king’s command, arrayed the fourfold army, and set forth the ceremonial procession. Drawing their gleaming white blades, they marched forward slowly and deliberately to display the majesty of the military forces; as they whetted their swords upon water-grinders, Brahmadatta himself went out to observe them.

"Because of this, the wife of the physician Jīvaka was able to witness the fourfold army drawn up in ceremonial procession, with gleaming white blades drawn and led forward slowly and deliberately, displaying their martial majesty; furthermore, she also obtained the water used for sharpening their swords to drink."

Having drunk the water from the whetted blade, his grief was immediately dispelled. Soon, a virtuous son was born, for whom they performed the naming ceremony and gave him the name *Dīrghāyu* (Long-Life) Boy. He was entrusted to others to be raised in secret;

as he gradually grew up, the boy Dīrghāyu became like a Kṣatriya born from the crown of the head, governing the world and possessing a great kingdom. Regarding various arts and skills—riding elephants, riding horses, training and galloping, archery, wrestling, casting nets, casting hooks, driving chariots, and sitting in palanquins—he became thoroughly proficient in all such diverse and wondrous arts. In many kinds of marvelous practical matters, he was exceptionally superior, fierce and courageous beyond the world, brilliant and outstanding, with no field of knowledge, however subtle, hidden, or remote, that he did not master.
Thereupon, when Brahmadatta heard that King Jīvaka of Kosala had become a physician and was residing in this city of Vārāṇasī under that name, Brahmadatta immediately commanded his attendants:
"Go quickly and arrest King Jīvaka of Kosala; bind his two hands behind his back, force him to ride a donkey, and break a broken drum so that its sound is like the braying of a donkey."
Having issued the proclamation everywhere, he departed through the southern gate of the city and sat beneath a high post to interrogate him regarding his words.

His attendants, having received these instructions, immediately went to arrest King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom; they bound his two hands behind his back, made him ride a donkey with a broken, beaten drum sounding like the bray of a donkey, and after proclaiming the edict everywhere, they departed through the southern gate of the city and sat beneath a high post to interrogate him regarding his words.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka followed behind his father, or remained at his side, and said to him:
"O Heavenly King, do not fear!
O Heavenly King, do not fear!"
"In this very place, I shall surely be able to rescue you; I shall surely be able to rescue you.
King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala addressed him, saying:
"Young man, you must endure!"
"Child, you must endure!
Do not give rise to resentment, but simply practice loving-kindness.
When the people heard King Dīrghāyu speak these words, they questioned the king:
"What do you mean by this?
The king replied to the crowd, "This youth is intelligent; he will surely understand my words."
"At that time, the youth Jīvaka exhorted the noble and wealthy clansmen of the city of Vārāṇasī: 'Gentlemen!

Practice generosity and cultivate merit, offering prayers for the long life of the King of Kośala. By means of this merit from giving, may the King of Kośala live long, remain secure and at peace, and attain liberation.'"

Thereupon, the various noble and eminent clansmen of the city of Vārāṇasī, exhorted by the youth Jīvaka, practiced giving and cultivated merit, and offered this blessing for the longevity of King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom:
"By the merit of this giving, may King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom live long and be secure, and may he attain liberation."
When King Brahmadatta of Kāśi heard that the noble clansmen of Vārāṇasī were practicing generosity and cultivating merit, he offered this blessing for the longevity of King Dīrghāyu of Kośala:
"By the merit of this giving, may King Dīrghāyu of Kośala live long, be secure, and attain liberation."
Upon hearing this, he was seized with great terror and his hair stood on end:
"Could it be that the noble and wealthy clans within this city of Vārāṇasī have turned against me?
Setting aside those other matters for now, I must urgently deal with this matter first."
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī commanded his attendants:
"Go quickly and kill the King of Kosala, Jīvaka, and cut him into seven pieces."
The attendants received these instructions and immediately went in haste to kill King Jīvaka, cutting him into seven pieces.
Thereupon, the youth Jīvaka addressed the noble and influential clans of the city of Vārāṇasī, saying: "Gentlemen, look at this!

King Brahmadatta of Kāśi is cruel, violent, and unrighteous. He seized my father, King Jīvaka of the Kośala kingdom—a man without fault—and having plundered his kingdom, its granaries, and its wealth, he has executed him with merciless cruelty, cutting him into seven pieces."

"Gentlemen, you may go; wrap my father in new silk cloths, take seven portions of his remains, pile up all kinds of incense and fragrant wood, and cremate him. Then, establish a shrine for him and write a letter to me from it, saying:
'O Prince Jīvaka, King of the Kośala!'"
"He spoke these words: 'Are you not afraid that later you will bring suffering upon your descendants?

Thereupon, the noble clansmen of Vārāṇasī, having been exhorted by the youth Jīvaka, immediately went to collect [the remains] with new silk cloths. They took those seven pieces of the corpse, piled up all kinds of perfumes and fragrant wood, and cremated them. They erected a shrine hall for him and also wrote a letter to Brahmadatta, saying:
"Prince Jīvaka of the King of the Kośala!..."
"He spoke these words: 'Do you not fear that later on, this will bring calamity upon your descendants?
Then, the wife of King Jīvaṃdhara said to the youth Jīvaka:

'You should know that this King Brahmadatta of the Kāsī kingdom is cruel, violent, and unrighteous. He seized your father, King Jīvaṃdhara of the Kośala kingdom—a man who was innocent—and having plundered his kingdom, its granaries, and its wealth, he executed him with malicious cruelty, cutting him into seven pieces.'"
"Come, child!
Let us mount one chariot and flee from Vārāṇasī; if you do not go, disaster will surely befall you.
Thereupon, the wife of King Dīrghāyu mounted a single chariot with the youth Jīvaka and departed from Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka thought to himself:
"I would rather go from village to village and town to town to study and acquire extensive learning.

Having had this thought, the youth Jīvaka went from village to village and town to town to study and acquire extensive learning; because of his extensive learning, he was thereafter called Jīvaka the Doctor.
The Doctor Jīvaka further thought to himself:

"That which was to be learned, I have now attained. I should go to the city of Vārāṇasī and stay in the streets and alleys, performing exquisite music with a joyful countenance. When the noble and wealthy clansmen of Vārāṇasī hear this, they will be greatly delighted and enjoy themselves."

After the physician Jīvaka had formed this thought, he went into the city of Vārāṇasī and stayed at every street and alleyway, playing exquisite music with a joyful countenance. When the various noble and wealthy clans of Vārāṇasī heard this, they were filled with great joy and amused themselves.

Then, when the outer retinue of King Bandhula the Madda heard [the news], it passed through the middle retinue, the inner retinue, and the brahmin state preceptor, until finally King Bandhula the Madda himself heard it; he then summoned them to see him.

Thereupon, Dr. Jīvaka went to King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha, stood before him, and with a joyful countenance performed exquisite musical entertainments; having heard this, King Bimbisāra of Rājagṛha was filled with great delight and enjoyed himself.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta, having granted a general amnesty, said: "Doctor!
From this day forward, you may dwell with me; I shall provide for all your needs."

Thereupon, the physician Jīvaka took up residence there; King Brahmadatta of Aḍḍhāla provided him with all necessities. Subsequently, the king came to trust him and entrusted everything to him, even handing over his own personal sword for self-defense to the physician Jīvaka.
"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī commanded his charioteer:
'Prepare the carriage; I wish to go hunting.
Having received these instructions, the charioteer immediately finished preparing the carriage and returned to report: "
"The carriage is prepared; it is as the Great King intends.
Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī set out together with the physician Jīvaka in a chariot. As they went, the physician Jīvaka thought to himself:

"This King Brahmadatta of Kāsī is cruel, violent, and unrighteous. He seized my father, the King of Kosala, who was long-lived and innocent of any fault; he plundered his kingdom, its granaries, and its treasures, and then, out of malice and cruelty, unjustly put him to death by cutting him into seven pieces."
"I would rather now drive the chariot so that the fourfold army is separated and each part is placed in a different location.
Having formed this thought, the physician Jīvaka immediately drove the chariot away from the fourfold army, placing them each in a separate location.

"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī, having traveled along the road and being oppressed by wind and heat, became distressed, parched with thirst, and utterly exhausted; wishing to lie down, he immediately alighted from his chariot and fell asleep, using the knees of the physician Jīvaka as a pillow."
Thereupon, Dr. Jīvaka again had this thought:

"This King Brahmadatta of Rājagṛha is cruel, violent, and unrighteous; he seized my father, who was innocent, plundered his kingdom, its granaries, and its wealth, and out of malicious resentment, unjustly put him to death by cutting him into seven pieces."
"But today he is already in my hands; I must simply take my revenge.
Having thought this, Dr. Jīvaka immediately drew a sharp sword, placed it upon the neck of King Brahmadatta of Kāśī, and spoke these words:
"I shall kill you now!"
"I shall kill you now!
The physician Jīvaka then thought to himself:
"I have done wrong."
Why is this? I recall that when my father was beneath the banner tree in days past, as he approached his death, he said to me:
"Child, you must endure!"
"Young man, you must endure!
Do not give rise to resentment; you should simply practice loving-kindness.
Having remembered this, he raised his sword and returned it to its scabbard.
"At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī saw in a dream the youth Jīvaka, the son of King Ajātaśatru of Kośala, drawing a sharp sword with his hand and placing it upon my neck, saying these words:
'I shall kill you now!'"
"I shall kill you now!
Having seen this, he was terrified and his hair stood on end; he then quickly woke up in alarm and rose to say to the physician Jīvaka:
"You should know that in my dream, I saw the prince Jīvaka, the son of King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom, who drew a sharp sword with his hand, placed it upon my neck, and spoke these words:"
"I will kill you now! I will kill you now!
Having heard this, the physician Jīvaka replied:
“O Heavenly King, do not fear!
O Heavenly King, do not fear! Why is this?
"O Heavenly King! That son of King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom, the youth Jīvaka, was none other than myself.
At that time, I thought to myself:"

“King Brahmadatta of Kāsī is cruel, violent, and unrighteous; he seized my father, who was innocent, plundered his kingdom, its granaries, and its treasures, and then, out of malice and cruelty, unjustly executed him by cutting him into seven pieces.”
"But today it is already in my hands; I shall simply take revenge.
"O Heavenly King!
I drew a sharp sword, placed it upon the King's neck, and spoke these words:"
"I shall kill you now! I shall kill you now! O Deva!
I further had this thought:
"I am at fault. Why is that? Because—"
I recall how, in the past, when my father was beneath the banner tree, he spoke to me at the time of his death:
"Child, you must endure! Child, you must endure!"
"Do not give rise to bonds of enmity; you should simply practice loving-kindness.
Having remembered this, he raised his sword and returned it to its scabbard. King Brahmadatta of Kāsī said:
"O youth! You have made this statement:
'Young man, you should endure!'"
"Young man, you should be patient!
I have already understood this meaning.
The young man spoke again:
"What is the meaning of the statement: 'Do not give rise to bonds of enmity, but practice only loving-kindness'?
The youth Jīvaka replied: "O Great King! [The meaning is as follows...]"
"Do not give rise to bonds of enmity; you should simply practice loving-kindness"—this is what he meant.
Upon hearing this, King Brahmadatta of Kasi said, "Young man!..."
"From this day forward, I shall bestow my entire realm upon you, and I shall restore your father’s original kingdom to you.
Why is this? What you have done is most difficult; you have granted me my very life."
Having heard this, the youth Jīvaka replied, "Your Majesty, your own kingdom belongs to Your Majesty; however, please restore to me my father's original kingdom."
"Then King Brahmadatta of Kāsī, having returned together with the youth Jīvaka, entered the city of Vārāṇasī. Seated upon the main throne, he addressed his ministers, saying:
'If you were to see the youth Jīvaka, the son of King Dīrghāyu of Kosala, what would you do?'"
When the ministers heard this, some said:
"O Heavenly King!
If you see him, you should cut off his hands."
Or again, they might say these words:
"O Great King!
If you see him, you should cut off his feet."
Or again, some might say:
"One should take his life.
Then King Brahmadatta, having granted a pardon, addressed his ministers, saying:
"O you, those who wish to see the son of King Dīrghāyu of the Kośala kingdom, the youth Jīvaka—it is he right here.
Do not give rise to evil intentions toward this youth."
"Why is this? This youth has performed a most difficult deed; he has bestowed life upon me.

Thereupon, King Brahmadatta of Kāsī bathed the youth Jīvaka with royal bathing water, anointed him with royal perfumes, clothed him in royal garments, seated him upon the golden throne, gave him his daughter as a wife, and sent him back to his own country.
“Monks! Those kings, the Kṣatriya Mūrdhāta, being great lords of nations who governed the world, personally practiced patience and further praised patience;
they personally practiced loving-kindness and further praised loving-kindness.”
"One practices kindness oneself and further praises kindness. Monks!
You too should likewise, having attained faith, leave the home life for the homeless state to train in the Path; you should practice patience and further praise patience."
"One practices the mind of loving-kindness oneself and further praises loving-kindness;
one practices beneficence oneself and further praises beneficence.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, some of the bhikṣus spoke as follows:
“The World-Honored One, Lord of the Dharma, please remain for now. He guides and instructs me; how could I not guide and instruct him?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, being displeased with the deportment, etiquette, training, and practice of the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī, rose from his seat and spoke these verses:
“With various words, They cause dissension within the most venerable assembly.”
When the noble Saṃgha is being destroyed, there is no one able to rebuke or stop it;
even if their bodies are crushed or their lives are cut short, or if they are robbed of elephants, oxen, horses, and wealth,
and their kingdoms are broken and utterly annihilated, they would still seek reconciliation.
How much more so for you, who with petty words of abuse cannot restrain those in harmony;
if you do not contemplate the true meaning, how can the bonds of enmity ever cease?
If one could restrain those in harmony through insults and reproaches, [then such things would be effective].
If one contemplates the true meaning, the bonds of enmity will surely cease.
If one seeks to stop strife with strife, strife will never come to an end;
only through patience can strife be stilled—this is the dharma that is most noble.
He harbors anger toward the wise and true person, speaking words of base insolence;
he slanders the Sage, the Muni—this is the conduct of the lowly and the unwise.
When others do not understand the meaning, he thinks, "I alone am able to know it."
If one can understand the meaning, that anger will surely cease.
If one finds a companion established in concentration, and the wise practice virtue together,
they will abandon their former attachments and always follow one another with joy.

If one does not find a companion for meditative concentration, the wise person should practice virtue alone, like a king governing his kingdom with discipline, or like an elephant wandering alone in the wilderness.
Walking alone, do no evil; like an elephant wandering alone in the wilderness.
It is better to walk alone in virtue than to dwell with the wicked.
If one cannot find a virtuous friend who is one's equal,
one should remain firm in resolve and dwell alone, rather than associate with the evil.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One immediately ascended into the air by means of his supernormal power and traveled to the village of Bālakaloṇakāra.

Now, in the village of Bālakaloṇakāra, there was the Venerable Bhaddiya, son of the Śākya clan, who did not sleep day or night, diligently practicing the Path, with his mind always settled in meditative concentration, abiding in the factors of enlightenment.

Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the Venerable Son of the Śākyas went out to meet him, took his robe and bowl, prepared a seat for the Buddha, and drew water to wash his feet. After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat upon the seat of the Venerable Son of the Śākyas, Bhaṇḍu.
Having sat down, the Buddha addressed him, saying: "Bhikṣu Bhaṇḍu!"
“Are you always at peace and free from want?
The Venerable Bhagu, son of the Śākyas, replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"I am always at peace and secure, lacking for nothing.
The World-Honored One asked again:
"Bhikṣu Vāgīśa!"
"How is it that you are at peace and free from want?
The Venerable Bāhuna replied:
"World-Honored One!"
Day and night I do not sleep, but practice the Way with diligent effort; my will and conduct are always settled, and I abide in the factors of enlightenment.
World-Honored One!
Thus I am constantly at peace and secure, lacking for nothing.
The Blessed One thought again:
"This son of good family is traveling in peace and happiness; I should now preach the Dharma for him.

Having had this thought, he preached the Dharma to the Venerable Bāhuna, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having used countless skillful means to preach the Dharma to him, and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed, proceeding to the Ārāmavatī Forest.
He entered the Ghoṣitārāma forest, went to the foot of a tree, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down cross-legged.
The World-Honored One further reflected:

"I have already escaped from those monks of Kauśāmbī, who were constantly quarreling, disputing, contending with one another, hating one another, and angrily brawling. I do not take pleasure in thinking of that region, namely the place where the monks of Kauśāmbī reside."
At that time, there was a great elephant who was the king of a herd of elephants; having separated himself from the herd, he wandered alone and also arrived at the Protected Forest.
He entered the Guhasīvana forest, reached the Sāla tree named Bhadda, and stood leaning against that Bhadda Sāla tree.
At that time, the great elephant had this thought:

"I have now escaped from that herd of elephants—the females, the males, and the young elephants of all sizes. That herd of elephants was always walking in front; they trampled the grass and muddied the water. At those times, I ate that trampled grass and drank that turbid water. Now, however, I eat fresh grass and drink clear water."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, knowing with his mind-made mind the thoughts in that great elephant’s heart, spoke this verse:
“As one elephant is equal to another elephant, With bodies fully formed and tusks complete;
So too is one mind equal to another mind, If one delights in dwelling alone in the forest.”
Thereupon, the Blessed One gathered his robes and took up his bowl from the Ārāmadanda forest and proceeded to the Paṇḍavapabbata forest.

At that time, three sons of noble family were residing together in the Paṇḍavapabbata forest: the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila; such was the conduct of those venerable ones.

If any of those alms-collectors returned first, they would prepare the bedding, fetch water, bring out the foot-washing basin, and set out the footstool, a cloth for wiping the feet, a water jar, and a rinsing pitcher.
If the alms-food obtained is sufficient for him to eat it all, he eats it entirely;
if there is a remainder, he places it in a vessel, covers it, and sets it aside.
Having finished eating, he puts away his bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his *niṣīdana* over his shoulder, and enters a room to sit in meditation.

If there are other alms-seekers who return later and are able to finish the food, they may also eat it all; if it is not sufficient, they should take the remaining food from the previous meal to supplement it and eat.

If there is any remainder, he pours it onto clean ground or into water free of insects. Having taken that food vessel, washed and wiped it clean, he sets it aside. He folds away the bedding and mats, puts away the footstool for washing, gathers and wipes the foot-towels, and lifts up the foot-washing stand, along with the water jar and the rinsing pitcher. Having swept and sprinkled the dining hall and cleared it of waste until it is clean, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and enters a room to sit in meditation.

When those venerable ones reached the time of late afternoon, if any among them rose first from their meditation, they would see that the water jar and the wash-basin were empty and devoid of water. They would then take them to fetch water; if they were able to lift them, they would carry them back and set them down to one side.
If they could not lift them, they would beckon another bhikṣu with their hand, and the two of them would lift them together and place them to one side, neither speaking to nor questioning the other.
Those venerable ones gathered once every five days, either discussing the Dharma together or maintaining noble silence.
Then, the forest guardian saw the Blessed One approaching from afar and called out to stop him, saying:
"Sramana! [Stop!]"
"Śramaṇa!
Do not enter this forest. Why is that?"
"In this grove there are three sons of noble family—the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila. Should they see you, some misfortune might occur."
The Blessed One said:
"O forest-guardian!
If he were to see me, it would certainly be possible; there would be no impossibility."
Then, the Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One approaching from afar and immediately rebuked him, saying:
"You forest-guardian!
Do not address the Blessed One as 'Great One'."
"You, forest-guardian!
Do not stop the Sugata. Why is that? Because—"
"Our Honored One has come! Our Sugata has come!
Venerable Anuruddha went out to meet the Blessed One, took his robe and bowl, Venerable Nandiya prepared a seat for the Buddha, and Venerable Kimbila fetched water for the Buddha.

"Are you always at peace and free from want?
Venerable Anuruddha replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I am always at peace and secure, lacking for nothing.
The World-Honored One asked Āniruddha again:
"In what way are you at peace and secure, lacking for nothing?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied,
"World-Honored One,
I had this thought:"
“World-Honored One! I possess a wholesome benefit and great merit, namely, that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.
World-Honored One!

I constantly direct the bodily action of loving-kindness toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction; I direct the verbal action of loving-kindness and the mental action of loving-kindness toward them, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction.”
"Bhagavān! I had this thought:
'I would now rather abandon my own mind and follow the minds of those worthy ones.'"
"World-Honored One!
I then set aside my own mind and followed the minds of those worthy ones.
World-Honored One!"
"I have never had even a single thought of dissatisfaction,
World-Honored One!
Thus I am always at peace and secure, lacking for nothing."
He questioned the Venerable Nandiya, and his answer was likewise.
He then asked the Venerable Kimbila:
"Are you always at ease and free from want?"
The Venerable Kimbila replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am always at peace and secure; I lack for nothing.”
He asked, "Kimbila! Are you at peace, and do you lack for nothing?"
The Venerable Kimbila addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have had this thought:"
“World-Honored One! I possess a wholesome benefit and great merit, namely, that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.
World-Honored One!

I constantly direct the bodily action of loving-kindness toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction; I direct the verbal action of loving-kindness and the mental action of loving-kindness toward them, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction.”
"Bhagavān! I had this thought:
'I would rather now abandon my own mind and follow the minds of those worthy ones.'"
"World-Honored One!
I then set aside my own mind and followed the minds of those worthy ones.
World-Honored One!"
"I have never had a single unwholesome thought,
World-Honored One!
Thus I am always peaceful and secure, lacking for nothing."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Ānanda! In this way, you all constantly dwell in harmony, living in peace and free from contention, with one mind and one teacher, blending like water and milk; have you attained any of the superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma) and dwelt therein in peaceful comfort?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“World-Honored One!

In this way, we always dwell in harmony, living in peace and free from dispute; with one mind and one teacher, we are as blended as water and milk, having attained the superhuman states with their various gradations, and we abide in happiness.”
“World-Honored One!
When we obtain light, we then see forms; yet that light by which we see forms soon thereafter ceases.
The World-Honored One told them:
“Anuruddha! You have not mastered this characteristic;
you think that one who perceives forms by means of the attainment of light will continue to see forms once that light has vanished. However, the light for seeing forms soon thereafter ceases.”
Ānanda! Before I had yet attained the awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, I also perceived forms through light, but that light by which I saw those forms soon vanished again.
"Anuruddha! I had this thought:

'What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I previously saw forms—the very light for seeing those forms—suddenly vanishes?'"
"Ānanda! I practiced with diligence and without indolence;
my body remained settled, possessed of right mindfulness and clear comprehension, free from delusion, and attained one-pointed concentration."
Ānanda! I had this thought: "I practice with diligence and without indolence;

my body is stilled, I possess right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, I am free from delusion, and I have attained one-pointed concentration. If there were no path in the world, could I see or know that [the state beyond]?"

"This doubt arose within my mind; because of this doubt, I lost my concentration and my vision vanished. Once my vision had vanished, the radiance by which I previously saw forms also immediately disappeared."
Ānanda! I shall now resolve to think thus:
"No affliction of doubt shall arise within my mind."

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I previously saw forms also perishes immediately?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'The affliction of non-attention has arisen in my mind;

because of this affliction of non-attention, I have lost my concentration and my vision has been extinguished. Once my vision is extinguished, the light by which I formerly perceived forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve to think thus:
'In my mind, I shall not give rise to the affliction of doubt, nor shall I give rise to the affliction of non-attention.'"

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Anuruddha! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the radiance by which I formerly saw forms also perishes.’”
"Ānuruddha! I further had this thought:

'A perception of bodily illness has arisen in my mind. Because of this perception of bodily illness, I have lost my concentration and my vision has vanished. Once my vision has vanished, the light by which I previously saw forms has also immediately disappeared.'"
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve to think thus:
'In my mind, I will not give rise to the affliction of doubt, nor the affliction of lack of mindfulness, nor the affliction of the perception of bodily illness.'"

“Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again.”
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I previously saw forms also perishes immediately?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'The affliction of drowsiness has arisen in my mind;
because of this affliction of drowsiness, I have lost my concentration and my vision has ceased. Once my vision has ceased, the light by which I previously saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve:
'In my mind, I shall not give rise to the affliction of doubt, nor the affliction of lack of mindfulness, nor the affliction of thoughts of physical illness, nor the affliction of drowsiness.'"

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I previously saw forms also perishes immediately?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'An excess of over-exertion has arisen in my mind;

because of this excess of over-exertion, I have lost my concentration and my vision has perished. Once my vision has perished, the light by which I previously saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! It is just as if a strong man were to seize a fly too tightly; the fly would immediately die.
In the same way, Ānanda!"

In my mind, there arose the fault of over-exertion; because of this fault of over-exertion, I lost my concentration and my vision was extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the radiance by which I previously saw forms also vanished.
Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this thought: "In my mind, I shall not give rise to the affliction of doubt;

I shall not give rise to the affliction of lack of mindfulness; I shall not give rise to the affliction of perceptions of physical illness; I shall not give rise to the affliction of drowsiness; nor shall I give rise to the affliction of excessive diligence."
"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort."

Because he dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, he attained radiance and saw forms; however, the radiance by which he saw those forms soon vanished again.
"Anuruddha! I further had this thought:
'What affliction is there in my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I formerly saw forms also perishes immediately? "
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'In my mind, the affliction of excessive indolence has arisen;

because of this affliction of excessive indolence, I have lost my concentration and my vision has perished. Once my vision has perished, the radiance by which I previously saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! It is just as if a strong man were to catch a fly too loosely;
the fly would simply fly away. Ānanda!"

In my mind, the affliction of excessive indolence arose; because of this affliction of excessive indolence, I lost my concentration and my vision was extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the light by which I had previously seen forms also vanished. As soon as that light for seeing forms disappeared, it ceased to be.
Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this thought: "In my mind, may no affliction of doubt arise;

may no affliction of lack of mindfulness arise; may no affliction of the perception of physical illness arise; may no affliction of drowsiness arise; may no affliction of excessive diligence arise; and may no affliction of excessive indolence arise."

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Anuruddha! I further had this thought:

‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose concentration and lose my vision; and once vision is lost, why does the radiance by which I formerly saw forms also immediately vanish?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought:

'A state of fear and affliction has arisen in my mind; because of this fear and affliction, I have lost my concentration and my vision has ceased. Once my vision has ceased, the radiance by which I previously saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"

"Ānanda! It is just as if a person were traveling on a road when enemies and bandits came from the four directions; upon seeing them, that person would become fearful and terrified, and the hair on his entire body would stand on end."
In this way, Āniruddha!

A state of fear and distress arose within my mind; because of that fear and distress, I lost my concentration and my vision was extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the light by which I previously saw forms also vanished.
Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this mindfulness: "In my mind, may no affliction of doubt arise;

may no affliction of lack of mindfulness arise; may no affliction of the perception of bodily illness arise; may no affliction of drowsiness arise; may no affliction of excessive exertion arise; may no affliction of excessive indolence arise; and may no affliction of fear arise."

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Anuruddha! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once vision is lost, the radiance by which I previously saw forms also immediately perishes.’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought:

'The joy that arose in my mind became a source of affliction; because of this affliction of joy, I lost my concentration and my vision was extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the light by which I previously saw forms also vanished.'"
"Ānanda! It is just as if a person, originally seeking one treasure trove, were suddenly to obtain four treasure troves; upon seeing them, he would feel great joy and delight."
In this way, Ānanda, a malady of joy arose within my mind;
because of that malady of joy, I lost my concentration and my vision was extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the radiance by which I formerly saw forms also vanished.
Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this mindfulness:

"In my mind, may no affliction of doubt arise; may no affliction of lack of mindfulness arise; may no affliction of the perception of physical illness arise; may no affliction of drowsiness arise; may no affliction of excessive exertion arise; may no affliction of excessive indolence arise; may no affliction of fear arise; and may no affliction of over-exuberance arise."

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, my mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, my mind free from negligence, and practiced with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:

‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, why does the radiance by which I formerly saw forms also vanish immediately?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'The affliction of self-exaltation has arisen in my mind.

Because of this affliction of self-exaltation, I have lost my concentration and my vision has been extinguished. Once my vision was extinguished, the light by which I previously saw forms also vanished. "
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this thought:

'In my mind, may no affliction of doubt arise; may no affliction of lack of mindfulness arise; may no affliction of the perception of bodily illness arise; may no affliction of drowsiness arise; may no affliction of excessive exertion arise; may no affliction of excessive indolence arise; may no affliction of fear arise; may no affliction of elation arise; and may no affliction of self-exaltation arise.'"

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose my concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the light by which I previously saw forms also perishes immediately?’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'Various afflictions of perception have arisen in my mind;

because of these various afflictions of perception, I have lost my concentration and my vision has ceased. Once my vision has ceased, the radiance by which I previously saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this thought: 'In my mind, I shall not give rise to the affliction of doubt;

I shall not give rise to the affliction of lack of mindfulness; I shall not give rise to the affliction of the perception of bodily illness; I shall not give rise to the affliction of drowsiness; I shall not give rise to the affliction of excessive exertion; I shall not give rise to the affliction of excessive laxity; I shall not give rise to the affliction of fear; I shall not give rise to the affliction of elation; I shall not give rise to the affliction of self-exaltation; nor shall I give rise to the affliction of various discursive thoughts.'"

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms; yet that radiance for seeing forms soon vanished again."
“Ānanda! I further had this thought:
‘What affliction is there within my mind that causes me to lose concentration and lose my vision? Once my vision is lost, the radiance by which I previously saw forms also immediately perishes.’”
"Ānanda! I further had this thought: 'A fault of not observing forms has arisen in my mind.

Because of this fault of not observing forms, I have lost my concentration and my vision has ceased. Once my vision has ceased, the radiance by which I formerly saw forms has also immediately vanished.'"
"Ānanda! I shall now resolve to maintain this thought: 'In my mind, I will not give rise to the affliction of doubt;

I will not give rise to the affliction of lack of mindfulness; I will not give rise to the affliction of thoughts of physical illness; I will not give rise to the affliction of drowsiness; I will not give rise to the affliction of excessive exertion; I will not give rise to the affliction of excessive indolence; I will not give rise to the affliction of fear; I will not give rise to the affliction of elation; I will not give rise to the affliction of self-exaltation; I will not give rise to the affliction of various perceptions; nor will I give rise to the affliction of non-contemplation of forms.'"

"Ānanda! Desiring not to give rise to this affliction, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence. Because I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I attained radiance and saw forms."

Ānanda! If a doubt arises in my mind, he attains purity of mind; he is free from the mental affliction of discursive thought, the perception of bodily illness, drowsiness, excessive exertion, excessive indolence, fear, exhilaration, arrogance, the arising of various perceptions, and the failure to contemplate the afflictions of form and mind; thus he attains purity of mind.
“Ānanda! I further had this thought: ‘I shall train in three concentrations:

I shall train in the concentration with directed thought and evaluation; I shall train in the concentration without directed thought and with limited evaluation; I shall train in the concentration without directed thought and without evaluation.’”

"Ānanda! I then practiced and trained in the three concentrations: I practiced and trained in the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation; I practiced and trained in the concentration without directed thought and with sustained evaluation; and I practiced and trained in the concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation.

Whenever I practiced and trained in the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, my mind would naturally incline toward the concentration without directed thought and with sustained evaluation; in this way, I certainly did not lose this knowledge and vision."
Ānanda! Having known this thus, I spent the day, the night, and the entire day and night training in the concentration accompanied by directed thought and evaluation.

Ānanda! At that time, while practicing this mode of abiding, if I were training in the concentration with directed thought and evaluation, my mind would incline toward the concentration without directed thought and evaluation; in this way, I certainly did not lose this knowledge and vision.

Ānanda! Having known this thus, I practiced throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the entire day and night, cultivating the concentration accompanied by directed thought and evaluation.
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Ānanda!

If I were to practice the concentration of non-discursive thought with minimal observation, my mind would instead incline toward the concentration of discursive thought and observation; thus, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision.
Ānanda! Having known this thus, I spent the entire day, the entire night, and the entire day and night training in the concentration of non-ideation and minimal observation.
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of abiding;

if I cultivated and trained in the concentration of non-discursive thought with limited observation, my mind would naturally incline toward the concentration of neither discursive thought nor observation, and thus I certainly did not lose this knowledge and vision.
Ānanda! Having known this thus, I spent the day, the night, and the entire day and night training in the concentration of non-ideation and limited observation.
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Ānanda!

If I were to practice the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought, my mind would incline toward the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought; in this way, I would certainly not lose this knowledge and vision.
Ānanda! Having known this thus, I practiced the concentration of neither-vitarka-nor-vicāra throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the entire day and night.
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling;

if I cultivated and trained in the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought, my mind would incline toward the concentration with sustained thought and minimal directed thought, and thus I did not lose this knowledge and vision.
Ānanda! Having known this thus, I spent the entire day, the entire night, and the whole day and night training in the concentration of neither directed thought nor sustained evaluation.
"Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Anuruddha!"
At times, Ānanda, I perceived light but did not see forms. Then,
Ānanda, I thought to myself:
"For what cause and for what reason does one perceive light yet not see forms? Āniruddha!
I further thought to myself:
"If I attend to the mark of light and do not attend to the mark of form, at that time I know the light but do not see forms. Āniruddha!
Having known this thus, Ānanda, throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the day and night, I perceived light but did not see forms. Ānanda!
At that time, Ānanda, I was practicing this mode of dwelling.
There were occasions when I saw forms but did not perceive the light.
Ānanda! I had this thought:
"For what cause and for what reason do I see forms but do not perceive the light?"
"Ānanda! I further had this thought:
'If I were to attend to the mark of form but not to the mark of light, at that time I would know the form but not the light.'"
"Ānanda! Thus, having known this, throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the day and night, I perceived forms but did not perceive light."
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Ānanda!
"At times, Ānanda, I had a slight perception of light and also saw forms slightly. Then,
Ānanda, I thought to myself:"
"For what cause and for what condition do I have little knowledge of light and also see little form?
Āniruddha! I further had this thought:

"If I enter meditative concentration slightly, because of entering concentration slightly, my eye becomes slightly purified; because my eye is slightly purified, I know light slightly and also see forms slightly."
"Ānanda! Having known this thus, throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the day and night, I possessed but little knowledge of light and saw but little of forms."
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Ānanda!
At times, Ānanda, I knew light extensively and saw forms extensively. Then,
Ānanda, I had this thought:
"For what cause and for what reason do I extensively know light and also extensively see forms?
Āniruddha! I further thought this:

"If I enter into a broad meditative absorption, because of this broad absorption, my eye becomes broadly purified; because my eye is broadly purified, I broadly know light and also broadly see forms."
"Ānanda! Having known this thus, throughout the day, throughout the night, and throughout the day and night, I extensively perceived light and also extensively saw forms."
Ānanda! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling. Ānanda!

If there arise within my mind such afflictions as doubt, lack of mental purity, discursive thought, the perception of physical illness, drowsiness, excessive exertion, excessive indolence, fear, elation, or arrogance, and if various perceptions arise such that one does not contemplate the afflictions of form and mind—[then this is the case].

Having attained purity of mind, he trains and thoroughly trains in concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation; he trains and thoroughly trains in concentration without directed thought and with diminished sustained evaluation; he trains and thoroughly trains in concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation; he trains and thoroughly trains in exclusively focused concentration; he trains and thoroughly trains in mixed concentration; he trains and thoroughly trains in limited concentration; and he trains and thoroughly trains in vast and immeasurable concentration.

My knowledge and vision born of self-mastery are extremely clear and pure; they incline toward and abide in concentration. Through diligent cultivation of the factors of the path, birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is.
"Anuruddha! At that time, I practiced this mode of dwelling.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first chapter of the *Cūḷa-kammavibhaṅga Sutta* (The Short Discourse on the Analysis of Karma), consisting of nine thousand two hundred and eighteen characters, is hereby concluded. *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume Seventeen, nine thousand two hundred and eighteen characters.
