Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
73. The Discourse on Devas (73). The Second Discourse on Devas from the Chapter of King Dīrghāyu, in the Madhyama Āgama.
Recited in the Second Section on Small Earth Forts. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the land of Ceti and stayed in the Jātiyā Grove by the riverbank.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Before I had attained the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, I had this thought:"
"I might be able to produce that radiance, and by means of that radiance, see forms and colors;
thus, my knowledge and vision would become exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.
Because I dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I have attained radiance and can thus perceive forms and colors.
However, I had not yet gathered together with those devas, nor had we exchanged greetings, nor engaged in conversation, nor offered mutual responses.
Then I thought to myself:

"I should rather produce a radiance so that, by means of that radiance, I may see forms and colors, and gather together with those devas, exchange greetings, engage in conversation, and offer mutual responses."
"Thus my knowledge and vision have become exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I have attained radiance and can see forms and colors; furthermore, I assemble together with those devas, mutually offering greetings, engaging in discourse, and exchanging responses.
However, I did not know that deva’s clan, his name, or his birth.
Then I thought to myself:

"I should rather produce a radiance, so that by means of that radiance I may see his form and color, and gather together with that deva to exchange greetings, engage in conversation, and respond to one another."
"I also know that those devas have such a clan, such a name, and such a birth.
Thus my knowledge and vision are exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making this knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I immediately attained radiance and was able to see forms and colors. I also gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in conversation, and offered responses;
furthermore, I knew the lineage, the name, and the birth of those devas.
However, I did not know how those devas eat, nor how they experience pleasure and pain.
Then I thought to myself:

"I would rather produce a radiance so that, by means of that radiance, I might see their forms and colors, and join with those devas in assembly, greeting one another, engaging in discourse, and exchanging responses."
He also knows that those devas have such a clan, such a name, and such a birth;
he also knows that those devas eat such food and experience such suffering and pleasure.
"Thus my knowledge and vision became exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I immediately attained radiance and was able to see forms and colors. I gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in conversation, and responded to one another;
I also knew the family name, the personal name, and the birth of those devas, as well as what they ate and how they experienced pleasure and pain.
However, I did not know that those devas were so long-lived, so long-abiding, and so long-lived until their span was exhausted. I further thought:

"I would rather be able to produce light, and by means of that light see forms and colors, and gather together with those devas to comfort one another, to engage in discourse, and to provide answers."
He also knows that those devas have such surnames, such names, and such births;

he also knows that those devas eat such food and experience such suffering and pleasure; he also knows that those devas have such long lifespans, abide for such a duration, and their lives end in such a manner.
"Such is my knowledge and vision, which is exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making this knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligent effort, I have attained radiance and can see forms and colors; I have gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in conversation, and responded to one another;
I also know the family name, the personal name, and the birth of those devas;
and I also know what those devas eat and how they experience pleasure and pain.
I also know that those devas have such long lifespans, abide for such a duration, and their lives end in such a manner.
However, I do not know by what specific actions those devas, having performed such and such karma, die here and are reborn there.
"I further had this thought:

'I wish that I might produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance see forms and colors, and gather together with those devas to comfort one another, to engage in discourse, and to exchange responses;
and may I also know those devas' lineage, their names, and their birth.'"
He also knows how those devas eat, and how they experience pleasure and pain;
he also knows how those devas have such long lifespans, dwell for such a duration, and reach the end of their lives;
and he also knows that after those devas have performed such and such karma, they die here and are reborn there.
"In this way, my knowledge and vision have become exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making my knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I have attained radiance and can perceive forms and colors. I have gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in conversation, and offered responses;
I also know the family name, the personal name, and the birth of those devas, as well as what they eat and the kind of pleasure and pain they experience.
He also knows that those devas have such a long life span, abide for such a duration, and their lives end in such a manner;
he also knows that after those devas have performed such and such karma, they die here and are reborn there.
However, I did not know which heaven or which specific heavens those [beings] belonged to.
Then I thought to myself:

"I shall instead produce a radiance, and by means of that radiance, see their forms and colors; and may I assemble together with those devas, mutually console one another, engage in discourse, and exchange responses."
He also knows that those devas have such a clan, such a name, and such a birth;
he also knows that those devas eat such food and experience such suffering and pleasure;
he also knows that those devas have such a long life, abide for such a duration, and their lifespan ends in such a manner.
I also know that those devas, having performed such and such karma, die here and are born there;
I also know them in this or that particular heaven.
Thus, my knowledge and vision are exceedingly vast, bright, and pure.
"For the sake of attaining supreme clarity and purity of knowledge and vision, I dwelt in seclusion alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence.

Because I dwelt in seclusion alone, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, I immediately attained radiance and beheld forms and colors; I gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in conversation, and responded to their inquiries;
I also knew those devas' surnames, their names, and their origins."
He also knows how those devas eat, and how they experience pleasure and pain;
he also knows how those devas have such long lifespans, stay for such a duration, and reach the end of their lives;
and he also knows that after those devas have performed such and such karma, they die here and are reborn there.
I also knew those devas and which specific heavens they belonged to;
yet I did not know within those heavenly realms whether I had previously been born there or had never been born there.
Then I further thought:
"May I be able to produce light, and by means of that light see forms and colors, and gather together with those devas to greet one another, engage in discourse, and exchange responses;
may I also know that those devas have such a clan, such a name, and such a birth;
and may I also know what those devas eat, and how they experience pleasure and pain."
He also knows that those devas have such long lifespans, abide for such a duration, and have their lives ending in such a manner;
he also knows that after those devas have performed such and such karma, they die here and are reborn there;
and he also knows those devas within each respective celestial realm.
"I also know of that heavenly realm whether I was born there in the past or not.
Thus, my knowledge and vision are exceedingly bright and pure.
For the sake of making this knowledge and vision exceedingly bright and pure, I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because I dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, I immediately attained radiance and beheld forms and colors; I also gathered together with those devas, exchanged greetings, engaged in discourse, and offered responses;
furthermore, I knew the lineage, the name, and the birth of those devas, as well as what they ate and how they experienced pleasure and pain.
He also knows that those devas have such a long life, such a duration of stay, and such an end to their lifespan;
he also knows that after those devas have performed such and such karma, they die here and are reborn there;
and he also knows those devas within this or that particular celestial realm.
I also know whether I have previously been born among those heavenly beings or have not yet been born there.

"If I had not correctly known these eight modes of conduct, I could not have declared with certainty that I had attained them, nor would I have known that I had awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path;
nor would I have been able to transcend this world—including its gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins."
I have not yet attained liberation through various modes of liberation;

nor have I yet abandoned all perversions, nor do I yet know according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
If I have attained these eight modes of conduct with full awareness, I may declare them as such; I also know that I have awakened to the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path.
I have transcended this world with its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins.

I have attained various liberations; my mind is already free from all perversions. Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second discourse on the Deva-sūtra ends here, totaling one thousand seven hundred and seventy-four characters. 74. The Discourse on the Eight Recollections (74), from the Chapter of King Dīrghāyu in the Madhyama Āgama. The third discourse, the Discourse on the Eight Recollections, in the second sub-section of the Small Earth-City Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Pañcasala and staying at the Deer Park in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest on Mount Kālaparvata.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was staying in the Jātiya Forest on the banks of the river in Ceti.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was sitting in meditation in a secluded place, reflecting and thinking to himself:
"The Path arises from desirelessness; it is not attained through desire."
The Path proceeds from contentment; it is not attained through lack of satiety.
The Path proceeds from seclusion; it is not attained by delighting in assemblies, nor by dwelling in assemblies, nor by joining in assemblies.
The Path is attained through diligence, not through indolence;
it is attained through right mindfulness, not through wrong mindfulness;
it is attained through a concentrated mind, not through a distracted mind.
"The Path proceeds from wisdom; it is not attained through folly.
Thereupon, with his knowledge of the minds of others, the World-Honored One knew what the Venerable Anuruddha was thinking, reflecting upon, and practicing within his mind.

The Blessed One, having known this, immediately entered the concentration corresponding to that [form]. Just as a strong man might flex or extend his arm, in such a moment, the Blessed One suddenly vanished from the Deer Park in the Bhaya Forest on Mount Paṅkadhā in Vāraṇasī and appeared before the Venerable Anuruddha in the Jātiśroṇa Waterbank Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from his meditative concentration and praised the Venerable Anuruddha,
saying: “Excellent, excellent, Anuruddha!”
It means that while you were sitting in meditation in a quiet place, this thought arose in your mind:
"The Path comes from non-desire; it is not obtained through desire.
The Path comes from contentment; it is not obtained through lack of satiety."
The Path is attained through seclusion, not through delighting in social gatherings, nor by dwelling in social gatherings, nor by joining in social gatherings.
The Path is attained through diligence, not through indolence.
The Way is attained through right mindfulness, not through wrong mindfulness;
it is attained through a concentrated mind, not through a distracted mind;
it is attained through wisdom, not through ignorance.
“Ānanda! You have received from the Tathāgata this eighth recollection of a great man.

Having received it, you should then contemplate that the Path is attained through non-diversion, delighting in non-diversion, and practicing non-diversion; it is not attained through diversion, nor delighting in diversion, nor practicing diversion.”

Ānanda! If you accomplish these eight recollections of a great person, you will certainly be able to leave behind sensual desires and unwholesome states, and reach the attainment of the fourth dhyāna, dwelling in its accomplishment.

Ānanda! If you, having accomplished the eight recollections of a great man, further attain these four higher states of mind that dwell in happiness in the present life—attaining them easily and without difficulty—it will be like a king or a royal minister who possesses a fine chest filled with various garments. If he wishes to wear one before midday, he takes it and wears it; at midday or after midday, if he wishes to wear a garment, he takes it and wears it, according to his own will and ease.
Ānanda! You are just like this:
you have obtained rag-robes as your foremost garment; with a mind free from desire, you practice this way of dwelling.

“Ānanda! If you were to accomplish the eight recollections of a great man and further attain these four higher mental states—which provide a pleasant dwelling in the present life and are easily attained without difficulty—it would be like a king or a royal minister having an excellent chef who prepares various kinds of pure, exquisite, sweet, and delicious delicacies.”
Ānanda! You too are like this:
you always practice alms-gathering as your primary meal; with a mind free from desire, you practice this mode of dwelling.

“Ānanda! If you were to accomplish the eight recollections of a great man and further attain these four higher states of mind, which provide a pleasant dwelling in the present life and are easily obtained without difficulty, it would be like a king or a royal minister possessing fine houses, or even multi-storied pavilions and palaces.”
Ānanda! You are just like this:
dwelling under a tree is your foremost abode; with a mind free from desire, you practice this mode of dwelling.

“Ānanda! If you, having accomplished the eight recollections of a great man, further attain these four higher mental states that dwell in happiness in the present life—attaining them easily and without difficulty—it will be as if a king or a royal minister has a fine couch spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with brocades and fine silks, provided with a soft inner coverlet and pillows at both ends, including those of Kalinga and Pārasamudraka.”
Ānanda! You are just like this:
among grass seats and leaf seats, you regard them as the foremost seat; your mind is free from desire, and you practice this mode of dwelling.

“Ānanda! If you, having accomplished the eight recollections of a great man, further attain these four states of higher mind that dwell in happiness in the present life—attaining them easily and without difficulty—then if you travel to the east, you will surely find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction;
if you travel to the south, the west, or the north, you will likewise surely find peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction.”

“Ānanda! If you, Āniruddha, were to accomplish the eight recollections of a great man and further attain these four higher mental states—dwelling in happiness in this very life—which are easily obtained and not difficult to find, I would still not say that your wholesome qualities are stationary, much less that they are declining.”
"You should simply increase wholesome qualities day and night and not let them decline. Ānanda!

If you accomplish these eight recollections of a great man and further attain these four states of higher mind—which provide a pleasant dwelling in the present life and are easily attained without difficulty—you will surely obtain one of two fruits: either you will attain final knowledge in this very life, or else you will become a non-returner."

“Ānanda! You should first accomplish these eight recollections of a great man and likewise attain these four higher mental states, dwelling in happiness in this very life—attaining them with ease and without difficulty—and only then enter the rains retreat at the Śiṃśapā Forest on the banks of the Vaggumudā River.”

At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the Venerable Anuruddha, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and bringing him to the fulfillment of joy; by means of countless skillful methods, he taught him the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him with longing.

Having achieved this state of joy, he entered the concentration of the "as-it-is" (yathābhūta). By means of that concentration, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, the Blessed One suddenly vanished from the Śrīparvata forest on the banks of the Śiprā River and appeared in the Deer Park at the Bhairava Forest on Mount Pañcaśaila in Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the Blessed One arose from his meditative absorption and, turning back, addressed him, saying: “Ānanda!”

"If there are bhikṣus wandering in the Khadiraka Grove on Mount Ajañña in the Deer Park, cause them all to assemble in the lecture hall; once they have assembled in the lecture hall, return and inform me."
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, the Venerable Ānanda prostrated at his feet and immediately went to issue the command:
"To all bhikṣus who are traveling in the Deer Park within the Bhayaṇḍa Forest on Mount Kālapabbata, let them all assemble in the lecture hall."
Having gathered in the lecture hall, he returned to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

All the bhikṣus who were traveling in the Deer Park within the Forest of Fear on Mount Tāḍa have been ordered to assemble in the lecture hall; I only wish that the World-Honored One would know the proper time.”

Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda and went to the lecture hall; he spread out a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down. Having sat down, he addressed them, saying: "Bhikṣus!
"I shall now explain to you the eight recollections of a Great Man; listen attentively and reflect upon them well.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"The eight recollections of a great man are as follows: the Way arises from non-desire, not from desire;
the Way arises from contentment, not from insatiability."
The Path is attained through seclusion; it is not attained by delighting in social gatherings, nor by dwelling in social gatherings, nor by associating with social gatherings.
The Path is attained through diligence; it is not attained through indolence.
The Way is attained through right mindfulness, not through wrong mindfulness;
it is attained through a concentrated mind, not through a distracted mind;
it is attained through wisdom, not through folly.

The Path is attained through non-diversion, delighting in non-diversion, and practicing non-diversion; it is not attained through diversion, nor through delighting in diversion, nor through practicing diversion.
"How is it that the Path proceeds from desirelessness and is not attained through desire?"

It means that a bhikṣu attains freedom from desire and knows for himself that he has attained freedom from desire, yet he does not cause others to know that he is free from desire. He attains contentment, seclusion, diligence, right mindfulness, concentration of mind, wisdom, and non-diversion;

he knows for himself that he has attained non-diversion, and he does not wish for others to know that he is free from desire. This is called the Path arising from freedom from desire, not from having desire.
"How is it that the Path arises from contentment and not from lack of satiety?

It means that a bhikṣu practices contentment: he takes clothing only to cover his body and food only to fill his belly. This is what is meant by 'the Path arises from contentment and not from lack of satiety.'"
"How is it that the path is attained through seclusion, and not through delighting in company, nor dwelling in company, nor associating with company?

It is this: when a bhikkhu practices seclusion and accomplishes the two kinds of seclusion—both bodily and mental seclusion—it is called attaining the path through seclusion, and not through delighting in company, nor dwelling in company, nor associating with company."
"What is it that the path is attained through diligence and not through indolence?

It means that a bhikṣu constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he always rouses his own mind, remaining single-minded and firm, never relinquishing skillful means for the sake of the roots of all goodness. This is what is meant by the path being attained through diligence and not through indolence."
"How is it that the path is attained through right mindfulness and not through wrong mindfulness?

It means that a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body, and contemplates feelings, mind, and phenomena internally as feelings, mind, and phenomena; this is called the path being attained through right mindfulness and not through wrong mindfulness."
"How is it that the path is attained from a concentrated mind, not from a distracted mind?

It means that a bhikṣu, detached from desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; this is called the path being attained from a concentrated mind, not from a distracted mind."
"What is the path that proceeds from wisdom and is not attained through delusion?

It means that a bhikṣu practices wisdom, contemplates the law of arising and passing away, and attains such knowledge—noble, penetrating, clear, and discerning—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering. This is called the path that proceeds from wisdom and is not attained through delusion."

"How is it that the path is attained through non-diversion (*anidāna*), delighting in non-diversion, and practicing non-diversion—not through diversion, not through delighting in diversion, and not through practicing diversion?

It is when a bhikṣu constantly extinguishes diversion in his mind, delights in dwelling in *nirvāṇa* without remainder, and his mind always dwells in joy and liberation; this is called attaining the path through non-diversion, delighting in non-diversion, and practicing non-diversion—not through diversion, not through delighting in diversion, and not through practicing diversion."
"Monks, after the bhikkhu Anuruddha had accomplished these eight recollections of a great man, he then entered the rains retreat at the branch-stūpa on the bank of the Sappinī River in the forest."
I instruct him thus: "Dwell alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence.

Having dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, that son of noble family—for whom the shaving of hair and beard, the donning of the saffron robes, and the departure from home out of deep faith to lead the homeless life are for the sake of training—brings the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion. In this very life, he knows it for himself, realizes it for himself, and attains realization through his own experience, dwelling in the knowledge: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha had attained arhatship with a mind of right liberation; having become a senior elder, he then spoke these verses:
"The unsurpassed Teacher of the world, knowing my thoughts from afar, With body and mind upright, entered meditative concentration, And suddenly arrived here, traveling through the air."
Beyond what my mind can conceive, you have taught even more;
the Buddhas delight in non-diversion, being far removed from all diversion.
Having understood the Dharma from them, they joyfully abide within the True Dharma.
Having attained mastery in samādhi, I have fulfilled my task in the Buddha’s Dharma.
I do not delight in death, nor do I wish for birth;
I remain at ease with whatever comes, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
"In Vaiśālī, at the Bamboo Grove, my life will come to an end;
beneath that very bamboo grove, I shall attain parinirvāṇa without remainder.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the Venerable Anuruddha and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Discourse on the Eight Recollections, the third, ends here with one thousand nine hundred and fifty-four characters. 75. The Discourse on the Path of Purity and Imperturbability (75), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, the Discourse on the Path of Purity and Imperturbability, the fourth;
recited in the second section of the Minor Earth-City. Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Kurus, staying at the Kuru town of Khānumata.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Sensual desire is impermanent, hollow, and false; it is a dharma of falsehood, which is illusory, deceptive, and delusive.”

Whether it be sensual desires of the present life or of future lives, or forms of the present life or of future lives—all these are the realm of Māra and are the bait of Māra. Because of them, the mind gives rise to immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, such as covetousness, ill will, and strife; these act as obstacles for a noble disciple while training.

The learned noble disciple reflects in this way: "That which the Blessed One has spoken of as sensual desire is impermanent, hollow, false, and deceptive by nature; it is an illusion, a fraud, and a delusion."

Whether it be sensual pleasures of the present life or of future lives, or forms of the present life or of future lives—all these are the realm of Māra and are the bait of Māra. Because of them, the mind gives rise to immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, such as covetousness, ill will, and strife; these act as obstacles for a noble disciple while training.
He reflects thus: "I can attain the accomplishment of a great mind and dwell therein, overwhelming the world and maintaining control over my mind.

If I attain the accomplishment of a great mind and dwell therein, overwhelming the world and maintaining control over my mind, then such immeasurable evil and unwholesome states as covetousness, ill will, and strife—which act as obstacles for a noble disciple while training—will not arise."
"By practicing in this way and training in this way, cultivating it thus and spreading it widely, he attains purity of mind regarding that state (*sthāna*).
Having attained purity of mind regarding that state, the bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable (*āniñjya*) therein, or he attains liberation through wisdom."
At a later time, when his body has broken up and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the Unshakable Realm (*āniñjya*).
This is called the first teaching on the pure path to the Unshakable Realm.

"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple reflects in this way: 'Whatever exists as form, all that consists of the four great elements and what is derived from the four great elements. These four great elements are impermanent phenomena; they are suffering and subject to cessation.'"
Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and spreading this practice extensively, he attains purity of mind regarding the bases (*sthāna*).
Having attained purity of mind regarding the bases, that bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable (*āniñjya*) therein or achieves liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*).
At a later time, when his body has disintegrated and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the Unshakable.
This is called the second teaching on the pure path to the Unshakable.

"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple contemplates in this way: 'Whether it be sensual desires of the present life or of future lives, or forms of the present life or of future lives, or perceptions of sensual desire in the present life or of future lives, or perceptions of form in the present life or of future lives—all such perceptions are impermanent phenomena, they are suffering, and they are subject to cessation. At that time, he necessarily attains the perception of immovability."

Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and extensively spreading this practice, he attains purity of mind regarding the spheres of experience. Having attained purity of mind regarding the spheres of experience, that bhikṣu either enters the imperturbable (āniñjya) therein, or attains liberation through wisdom.
At a later time, when his body has broken up and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the Unshakable.
This is called the third teaching on the pure path to the Unshakable.
"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple contemplates in this way: 'Whether it be perceptions of sensual desire in the present life or perceptions of sensual desire in future lives;

whether it be perceptions of form in the present life or perceptions of form in future lives, as well as perceptions of the immovable—all such perceptions are impermanent phenomena, they are suffering, and they are subject to cessation. At that time, he attains the perception of the sphere of nothingness."

Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and expanding upon this practice, he attains purity of mind regarding the bases of power (*sthāna*). Having attained purity of mind regarding these bases, a bhikṣu either enters the unshakable state (*akopya*) therein, or else achieves liberation through wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*).
At a later time, when his body breaks up and his life ends, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the Unshakable Realm (*āniñjya*).
This is called the first teaching on the path to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) that is pure.

"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple contemplates in this way: 'This world is empty; it is empty of a self and of what belongs to a self; it is empty of permanence, empty of constancy, empty of eternity, and empty of unchangingness.'"

Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and spreading this practice extensively, he attains purity of mind regarding the sphere [of nothingness]. Having attained purity of mind regarding that sphere, a bhikṣu either enters the sphere of nothingness or achieves liberation through wisdom.
At a later time, when his body has broken up and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of nothingness.
This is called the second teaching on the path to the pure sphere of nothingness.
"Furthermore, the learned noble disciple reflects in this way: 'I do not act for the sake of another, nor do I act for my own sake. "

Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and spreading this practice extensively, he attains purity of mind regarding that sphere. Having attained purity of mind regarding that sphere, the bhikṣu either enters the sphere of nothingness or attains liberation through wisdom.
At a later time, when his body has broken up and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of nothingness.
This is called the third teaching on the path to the pure sphere of nothingness.

"Furthermore, the well-versed noble disciple contemplates in this way: 'Whether it be sensual desires of the present life or future lives, forms of the present life or future lives, perceptions of sensual desire in the present life or future lives, perceptions of form in the present life or future lives, as well as the perception of the immovable and the perception of the sphere of nothingness—all such perceptions are impermanent phenomena, they are suffering, and they are subject to cessation. At that time, he attains the state of non-perception."

Practicing in this way, training in this way, and cultivating and spreading this practice extensively, he attains purity of mind regarding the sphere. Having attained purity of mind regarding the sphere, that bhikṣu either enters the state of non-perception therein or achieves liberation through wisdom.
"At a later time, when his body has broken up and his life has ended, because of that original intention, he will certainly reach the sphere of non-perception.
This is what is called explaining the pure path of non-perception.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu who practices in this way—without 'I' and without 'mine,' such that 'I' shall not exist and 'mine' shall not exist, and whatever previously existed is entirely relinquished—[then he is one who has attained liberation]."
“World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu practices in this way, will he reach the end [of suffering] and attain parinirvāṇa?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! This matter is not fixed; some may attain it, while others may not.
Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
how does a bhikṣu practice so as not to attain parinirvāṇa?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Ānanda! If a bhikkhu practices in this way—without a self and without what belongs to a self, thinking ‘I shall not exist’ and ‘what belongs to me shall not exist,’ and whatever previously existed, he completely relinquishes it.”
"Ānanda! If a bhikṣu delights in that equanimity, clings to that equanimity, and dwells in that equanimity, Ānanda!
A bhikṣu who practices in such a manner will certainly not attain parinirvāṇa."
The Venerable Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One,
if a bhikṣu still has something to grasp, can he not attain parinirvāṇa?”
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda! If a bhikkhu has anything to grasp, he will certainly not attain parinibbāna.”
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One,
what has that bhikṣu received?”
The Blessed One said:

“Ānanda! There remains a further state within existence, namely the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is the foremost among states of existence; that is what those bhikṣus experience.”
The Venerable Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One,
does that bhikṣu undergo further practice?”
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda, it is in this way that a bhikkhu undertakes other practices.”
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how must a bhikṣu practice so that he will certainly attain parinirvāṇa?”
The Blessed One said: “Ānanda!

If a bhikkhu practices in this way—without ‘I’ and without ‘mine,’ such that ‘I shall not be’ and ‘mine shall not be,’ and whatever was previously present is entirely relinquished—then he is liberated.”
Ānanda! If a bhikṣu does not delight in that equanimity, does not cling to that equanimity, and does not dwell in that equanimity, Ānanda!
A bhikṣu who practices in this way will certainly attain parinirvāṇa.
Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
if a bhikkhu has nothing further to attain, will he necessarily realize parinirvāṇa?"
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda! If a bhikkhu has nothing further to grasp, he will certainly attain parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:

“The World-honored One has already taught the path of pure non-agitation, has already taught the path of pure nothingness, has already taught the path of pure non-perception, and has already taught nirvana without remainder.”
“World-Honored One!
What is noble liberation?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Ānanda! A learned noble disciple contemplates in this way: whether it be sensual desires of the present life or of future lives, forms of the present life or of future lives, perceptions of sensual desire in the present life or of future lives, perceptions of form in the present life or of future lives, as well as the perception of the imperturbable, the perception of the sphere of nothingness, and the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—all such perceptions are impermanent phenomena, they are suffering, and they are subject to cessation; this is what is called ‘one’s own self.’”
If one possesses these, they are birth, they are old age, they are sickness, and they are death. Ānanda!
If these phenomena were all extinguished without remainder and no longer existed, then there would be no birth, no old age, no sickness, and no death.

The Noble One observes thus: "If there is anything that exists, it must be the Dharma of liberation; if there is anything that is nirvana without remainder, it is called the Deathless. Observing in this way and seeing in this way, he will certainly attain liberation of the mind from the outflow of sensual desire, and liberation of the mind from the outflows of existence and ignorance.

Having attained liberation, he knows he is liberated; he knows, in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

“Ānanda! I have now for your sake taught the path of pure imperturbability, taught the path of pure nothingness, taught the path of non-perception, taught nirvana without remainder, and taught noble liberation.”

"Just as a venerable teacher acts toward his disciples with great loving-kindness and compassion, out of pity and concern, seeking their welfare and benefit, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness—this I have now done for you.

You yourselves must now do likewise: go to secluded places, to the foot of trees, or to empty, quiet, and peaceful spots, and sit in meditation and reflection. Do not be negligent; apply yourselves with diligence and vigor, lest you later regret it."
"This is my instruction; this is my admonition.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Sūtra on the Path of Purity and Immovability, the fourth, ends here, totaling one thousand seven hundred and eighty-seven characters. 76. The Ukkacelā Sūtra (76), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, the fifth sūtra, recited in the second sub-section on the Small Earthen City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Ukkacelā and stayed by the bank of the Gaṅgā River.
At that time, a certain bhikkhu rose from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I only pray that you will briefly explain the Dharma for me.
Having heard it from the World-Honored One, I shall dwell in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence.

Because he dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, this son of noble family—who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Way—has reached the culmination of the unsurpassed holy life. In this very life, he has known it for himself, awakened to it for himself, and realized it through his own direct experience, dwelling in its attainment: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
The Blessed One said:
“Monks, you should train yourselves thus:

to cause the mind to abide, remaining inwardly unshakable and immeasurably well-cultivated; furthermore, observing the internal body as body, practicing with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governing the mind so that it is free from stinginess and greed, and ensuring the mind is without sorrow or distress.”

Furthermore, he contemplates the external body as a body, practicing with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governing his own mind so that it is free from stinginess and greed, and his heart is without sorrow or distress.

Furthermore, he contemplates the internal and external body as a body, practicing with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governing his own mind, causing it to be free from stinginess and greed, and ensuring that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

"Monks! This concentration should be well-cultivated while going and while coming; it should also be cultivated while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while sleeping, while waking, and while both sleeping and waking."

Furthermore, one should also cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation (savitarka-savicāra), the concentration without directed thought and with limited sustained evaluation (avitarka-avicāra-mātra), and the concentration without directed thought or sustained evaluation (avitarka-avicāra). One should also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy (prīti-sahagata), the concentration accompanied by bliss (sukha-sahagata), the concentration accompanied by equanimity (upekṣā-sahagata), and the concentration accompanied by relinquishment (tyāga-sahagata).
“Bhikkhus! If one cultivates this concentration and cultivates it thoroughly, bhikkhus,

one should further cultivate the contemplation of internal feelings as feelings, practicing with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governing the mind, and causing it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that the mind is without sorrow or distress.”

Furthermore, observing external sensations as one observes internal ones, he practices with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension; skillfully governing his own mind, he causes it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

Furthermore, observing both the internal and external, he perceives awareness as awareness; he practices with extreme diligence, establishes right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governs his own mind, and causes it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

"Monks! This concentration should be well-cultivated while going and while coming; it should also be cultivated while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while sleeping, while waking, and while both sleeping and waking."

Furthermore, one should also cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*), the concentration without directed thought and with limited sustained evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra-mātra*), and the concentration without directed thought or sustained evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*). One should also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy (*prīti-sahagata*), the concentration accompanied by bliss (*sukha-sahagata*), the concentration accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā-sahagata*), and the concentration accompanied by relinquishment (*tyāga-sahagata*).
“Monks! If one cultivates this concentration and cultivates it thoroughly, monks, one should further cultivate the contemplation of the internal mind as mind.

Practicing with extreme diligence, establishing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, one should skillfully restrain the mind, causing it to be free from stinginess and greed, and ensuring that the mind is without sorrow or distress.”

Furthermore, he contemplates the external mind as being like the internal mind; he practices with extreme diligence, establishes right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governs his own mind, and causes it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

Furthermore, he contemplates the internal and external mind as being like the mind itself; practicing with extreme diligence, he establishes right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governing his own mind so that it is freed from stinginess and greed, and his heart is without sorrow or distress.

"Monks! This concentration should be well-cultivated while going and while coming; it should also be cultivated while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while sleeping, while waking, and while both sleeping and waking."

Furthermore, one should also cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, the concentration without directed thought and with limited sustained evaluation, and the concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation; one should also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by equanimity, and the concentration accompanied by relinquishment.
“Monks! If one has cultivated this concentration and cultivated it thoroughly, monks, one should further cultivate the contemplation of internal phenomena according to the Dharma.

One should practice with extreme diligence, establish right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and skillfully restrain the mind so that it is free from stinginess and greed, and the heart is without sorrow or distress.”

Furthermore, he contemplates external phenomena as they truly are; he practices with supreme diligence, establishes right mindfulness and right situational awareness, skillfully governs his own mind, and causes it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

Furthermore, he contemplates internal and external phenomena as they truly are; he practices with extreme diligence, establishes right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, skillfully governs his own mind, and causes it to be free from stinginess and greed, so that his heart is without sorrow or distress.

"Monks! This concentration should be well-cultivated while going and while coming; it should also be cultivated while standing, while sitting, while lying down, while sleeping, while waking, and while both sleeping and waking."

Furthermore, one should also cultivate the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, the concentration without directed thought and with diminished sustained evaluation, and the concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation; one should also cultivate the concentration accompanied by joy, the concentration accompanied by bliss, the concentration accompanied by equanimity, and the concentration accompanied by relinquishment.

“Monks! If one cultivates this concentration and cultivates it thoroughly, then, monks, the mind should be accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervading one direction, dwelling in its accomplishment;

likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below—pervading everywhere, all around, the mind accompanied by loving-kindness, free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, free from contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, well-cultivated, pervading the entire world, dwelling in its accomplishment.”

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world and achieved mastery therein.
“Monks! If you cultivate this concentration and cultivate it thoroughly, then whether you travel to the east, you will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction;
and whether you travel to the south, the west, or the north, you will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction.”
“Monks! If you cultivate this concentration and have cultivated it thoroughly, I would not even say that your wholesome qualities remain, much less that they decline;
rather, they shall increase day and night and never diminish.”

"Monks! If you cultivate this concentration and perfect its cultivation, you will surely attain one of two fruits: either you will realize ultimate knowledge in this very life, or else, with something remaining, you will become a non-returner."

Thereupon, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu received and retained it well; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. Retaining the Buddha’s teaching, he dwelt alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Because he dwells in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, this son of noble family—having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Way—has brought the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion. In this very life, he has known it for himself, awakened to it for himself, and having realized it through his own direct experience, he dwells therein; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
That venerable one, having realized the Dharma, attained arhatship.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Ukkacelā Sutta*, the fifth, ends here. (1,206 characters). 77. The *Sāketā-tayo-putta Sutta* (77), from the *Dīghāvu-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Sāketā-tayo-putta Sutta*, the sixth; recited in the second section on Small Earthly Cities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Sāketa and staying in the Blue Grove.

At that time, there were three sons of noble family from Sāketa—Venerable Aniruddha, Venerable Nandiya, and Venerable Kimbila—who were all young and had recently gone forth to study; they had all entered this True Dharma together not long ago.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus:

"These three sons of noble family are all young and have newly gone forth to study; they have not long since entered this True Dharma together. Do these three sons of noble family delight in practicing the holy life within this True Dharma and Vinaya?"
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.
The World-Honored One again asked the bhikṣus a second and a third time:

"These three sons of good family are all young and have newly gone forth to study; they have only recently entered this True Dharma together. Do these three sons of good family delight in practicing the holy life within this True Dharma and Vinaya?"
At that time, the bhikṣus likewise remained silent and did not answer for a second and a third time.
Thereupon, the Blessed One questioned the three sons of noble family himself and addressed the Venerable Anuruddha:
"Anuruddha, you three sons of noble family are all young and have newly gone forth to study; it has not been long since you all together entered this True Dharma."
"Do you take pleasure in practicing the holy life within this True Dharma and Discipline?
Venerable Anuruddha replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"So it is. We delight in this True Dharma and practice the holy life.
The World-Honored One asked:

“Anuruddha! When you were young children, with pure black hair and bodies in the prime of youth, you delighted in play, enjoyed frequent bathing, and cherished your physical appearance. Later, your kinsmen and your parents, all filled with affection and longing for you, wept and wailed in sorrow, not wishing for you to leave the household life to study the Path.”
It is because of this, Ānuruddha, that you have been able to shave off your hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to train in the path.

You have set out to practice the path not out of fear of kings, nor out of fear of bandits, nor out of fear of debt, nor out of fear of terror, nor out of fear of poverty and the inability to survive; rather, you have done so because you are weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and suffering, or because you desire to reach the end of this great mass of suffering.
“Ānanda! Did you not go forth to train in the path because of such a mind?
They replied:
"So it is, Ānanda!
If a son of noble family leaves the household life to train in the path with such a mind, does he know its source and thereby attain immeasurable wholesome dharmas?"
The Venerable Anuruddha addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
Ānuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.
The Blessed One said to them: “Ānuruddha!

If one is overwhelmed by desire and entangled by unwholesome states, one cannot relinquish pleasure or attain unsurpassed cessation. Such a person’s mind gives rise to increased discursive thought, ill will, and sloth; the mind becomes discontented, the body experiences restlessness and stretching, and the mind is distressed by overeating.

That bhikṣu is unable to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, or the harassment of mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, wind, and sun. He cannot endure harsh sounds or the blows of sticks and staves. When his body encounters various diseases that cause extreme pain, even to the point where life is about to cease, he is unable to withstand all such unpleasantness.
Why is this so? Because they are shrouded by desire and entangled by unwholesome dharmas, they are unable to relinquish pleasure and attain unsurpassed cessation.

If one is free from desire and not entangled by unwholesome dharmas, one will certainly attain the relinquishing of pleasure and unsurpassed cessation; in such a person, the mind does not give rise to covetousness, ill will, or sloth-and-torpor; the mind does not experience dissatisfaction; the body does not experience yawning or stretching; nor does one eat excessively, and the mind is free from grief and anxiety.

That bhikṣu is then able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the afflictions of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh words and the striking of staffs. When his body encounters various illnesses that cause extreme suffering, even to the point where life is about to cease, he is able to withstand all such unpleasant conditions.
Why is this? Because they are not overwhelmed by desire, nor are they entangled by unwholesome dharmas; furthermore, they have attained the bliss of equanimity and unsurpassed cessation.
The Blessed One asked:
"Anuruddha! For what reason does the Tathāgata [do so]?"
“Is there anything that should be removed, anything that should be employed, anything that should be endured, anything that should be ceased, or anything that should be rejected?
Āniruddha addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma proceeds from the Blessed One. We pray only that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
“Ānanda, listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall analyze its meaning for you.”
Ānuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.
The Blessed One said to them: “Ānuruddha!

The various outflows (āsrava) and defilements are the root of future existence, resulting in the retribution of feverish suffering, and are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death. It is not that the Tathāgata has not exhausted them, nor that he does not know them; rather, there are some which he eliminates, some which he employs, some which he endures, some which he ceases, and some which he vomits forth.

Ānanda! It is only because of this body, because of the six sense bases, and because of life that the Tathāgata may have something to eliminate, something to employ, something to endure, something to cease, or something to relinquish.
Ānanda! For this reason, the Tathāgata may eliminate something, employ something, endure something, cease something, or relinquish something.
The Blessed One asked: “Ānanda,

for what purpose does the Tathāgata dwell in secluded places, in mountain forests and at the foot of trees, delighting in dwelling on high cliffs that are silent, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma?”
The Venerable Anuruddha addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may fully understand its meaning."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Ānanda, listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
Ānuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.
The World-Honored One addressed them, saying: “Ānuruddha!

It is not because the Tathāgata has not yet attained what he wishes to attain, nor has yet acquired what he wishes to acquire, nor has yet realized what he wishes to realize, that he dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in dwelling upon high cliffs, in silence and stillness, remote, free from evil, and devoid of human beings, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.

Ānanda! It is for two reasons that the Tathāgata dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in dwelling on high cliffs, in silence and stillness, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma:
first, so as to personally experience dwelling in the bliss of the present Dharma; second, out of compassion for future generations.

There may be people born later who emulate the Tathāgata by dwelling in secluded places—among mountain forests and beneath trees—delighting in high cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.

Ānanda! For this reason, the Tathāgata dwells in secluded places, in mountain forests and beneath trees; he delights in dwelling on high cliffs, in silence and stillness, far removed from evil, devoid of people, practicing meditative sitting in accordance with the Dharma.
The Blessed One asked: “Ānanda,

for what reason does the Tathāgata, when a disciple has passed away, declare that such-and-such a person is born in such-and-such a place, or that such-and-such a person is born in such-and-such a place?”
The Venerable Anuruddha addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
“Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall analyze its meaning for you.”
Ānuruddha and the others received the instruction and listened.
The Blessed One said to them: “Ānuruddha!

The Tathāgata does not speak for the sake of seeking followers, nor does he deceive people, nor does he desire to win the pleasure of others; yet, when his disciples pass away, he predicts that such-and-such a person will be born in such-and-such a place, and such-and-such a person will be born in such-and-such a place.

Ānanda! The Tathāgata speaks of the rebirth of certain disciples—stating that such-and-such a person is born in such-and-such a place, or such-and-such a person is born in such-and-such a place—only for the sake of those clansmen and clanswomen of pure faith who possess supreme confidence, supreme love, and supreme joy, and who, having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, wish to emulate it in such and such ways. Thus, after their lives have ended, he makes these declarations regarding them.

If a bhikkhu hears that a certain venerable one has passed away at a certain place, and that he was prophesied by the Buddha as one who has attained ultimate knowledge, for whom birth is exhausted, whose holy life is established, who has done what was to be done, and who knows according to reality that there is no further state of existence.

Either he has seen that venerable one for himself, or he has heard of him repeatedly from others, that the venerable one possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recollects that the Venerable One possesses faith, observes the precepts, is widely learned, is generous, and possesses wisdom; having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, his mind may form the aspiration to emulate him in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, a bhikṣu will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Ānanda!"

Furthermore, a bhikkhu hears that a certain venerable one has passed away at a certain place; he was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose five lower fetters have been exhausted, who has been reborn in that intermediate state to attain parinirvāṇa, having attained the dharma of non-retrogression and not returning to this world.

Either he has seen that venerable one for himself, or he has heard of him repeatedly from others, that the venerable one possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recollects that the Venerable One possesses faith, observance of the precepts, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom; and having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may form the aspiration to emulate him in such and such ways.
Ānanda! In this way, a bhikkhu will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Ānanda!

Furthermore, a bhikṣu hears that a certain venerable one has passed away at a certain place; he was prophesied by the Buddha as one for whom the three fetters are exhausted and lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, who attains the state of a once-returner to the heavens and the human realm, and having returned once more, will put an end to suffering.

Either one has seen that venerable one for oneself, or has repeatedly heard it from others, that "that venerable one possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recalls that the venerable one possesses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom; and having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may aspire to emulate him in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, a bhikkhu will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

Furthermore, a bhikkhu hears that a certain venerable one has passed away at a certain place; he was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose three fetters are exhausted, who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, who is destined for full awakening, and who will undergo at most seven more existences, having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human world before reaching the end of suffering.

Either he has personally seen that venerable one, or he has repeatedly heard of him from others, saying: "That venerable one possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recollects that the Venerable One possesses faith, observes the precepts, is widely learned, is generous, and possesses wisdom; and having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may aspire to emulate him in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, a bhikkhu will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

If a bhikṣuṇī hears that a certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away at a certain place, and that she was prophesied by the Buddha as having attained ultimate knowledge—realizing for herself according to truth: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Either he sees that bhikṣuṇī for himself, or he hears of her repeatedly from others, that she possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls that the bhikṣuṇī possesses faith, maintains the precepts, is widely learned, practices generosity, and possesses wisdom; having heard this true Dharma and Vinaya, they may wish in their heart to emulate her in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, that bhikṣuṇī will surely attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
"Ānanda! [he said].

Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī hears that a certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away at a certain place; she was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni) have been exhausted, who has been reborn in that intermediate state to attain parinirvāṇa, who has attained the dharma of non-retrogression, and will not return to this life.

Either he has seen that bhikṣuṇī for himself, or he has heard of her repeatedly from others, that she possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls that the bhikṣuṇī possesses faith, maintains the precepts, is learned, is generous, and possesses wisdom; having heard this Dharma and Vinaya, their mind may aspire to emulate her in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, that bhikṣuṇī will surely attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Ānanda!"

Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī hears that a certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away at a certain place; she was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose three fetters are exhausted, whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, and who will attain the state of a once-returner to the heavens and the human realm, and having returned once more, will reach the end of suffering.

Either he has seen that bhikṣuṇī for himself, or he has heard of her repeatedly from others, that she possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls that the bhikṣuṇī possesses faith, maintains the precepts, is widely learned, practices generosity, and possesses wisdom; having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may wish to emulate her in such and such ways.
"Anuruddha! In this way, that bhikkhunī will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Anuruddha!"

Furthermore, a bhikṣuṇī hears that a certain bhikṣuṇī has passed away at a certain place; she was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose three fetters are exhausted, who has attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna), who will not fall into states of woe, who is destined for perfect awakening, and who, after experiencing at most seven more existences—having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human realm—will reach the end of suffering.

Either he has personally seen that bhikṣuṇī, or he has repeatedly heard it from others, that "that bhikṣuṇī possesses such faith, observes such precepts, has such extensive learning, practices such generosity, and possesses such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recalls that the bhikṣuṇī possesses faith, maintains the precepts, is widely learned, practices generosity, and possesses wisdom; and having heard this Dharma and Vinaya, their mind may form the aspiration to emulate her in such and such ways.
"Anuruddha! Thus, this bhikkhunī will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Anuruddha!"

If a lay follower hears that a certain lay follower has passed away in a certain village, and that he was prophesied by the Buddha as one for whom the five lower fetters have been exhausted, who will be reborn in that realm and there attain parinirvāṇa, having attained the state of non-retrogression and not returning to this world; [he too would rejoice].

Either he has seen that upāsaka for himself, or he has repeatedly heard of him from others, that "that upāsaka possesses such faith, observes such ethical discipline, possesses such extensive learning, practices such generosity, and possesses such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recalls that the upāsaka possessed faith, observed the precepts, was learned, practiced generosity, and possessed wisdom; having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may form the aspiration to emulate him in such and such ways.
"Anuruddha! In this way, such a lay follower will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Anuruddha!"

Furthermore, a lay follower hears that a certain lay follower has passed away in a certain village; he was prophesied by the Buddha as one for whom the three fetters are exhausted, whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, and who will attain the state of a "once-returner" between heaven and earth, and having returned once more, will reach the end of suffering.

Either he sees that upāsaka for himself, or he hears of him repeatedly from others, that "that upāsaka possesses such faith, observes such ethical discipline, possesses such extensive learning, practices such generosity, and possesses such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recalls that the upāsaka possessed faith, observed the precepts, was learned, practiced generosity, and possessed wisdom; having heard this Dharma and Vinaya, his mind may form the aspiration to emulate him in such and such ways.
Ānanda! In this way, that upāsaka will certainly attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness. Ānanda!

Furthermore, a lay follower hears that a certain lay follower has passed away in a certain village; he was prophesied by the Buddha as one for whom the three fetters have been exhausted, who has attained the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), who will not fall into states of woe, who is destined for full awakening, and who will undergo at most seven more existences, having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human realm before reaching the end of suffering.

Either he sees that upāsaka for himself, or he hears of him repeatedly from others, that "that upāsaka possesses such faith, observes such precepts, has such extensive learning, practices such generosity, and possesses such wisdom."

Having heard this, that person recalls that the upāsaka possessed faith, observed the precepts, was learned, practiced generosity, and possessed wisdom; having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, he may form the aspiration in his heart to emulate him in such and such ways.
"Anuruddha! A lay follower such as this will certainly attain relief from illness and dwell in peace and happiness. Anuruddha!"

If a laywoman hears that a certain laywoman has passed away in a certain village, and that she was prophesied by the Buddha: "Her five lower fetters have been exhausted; she has been reborn in that intermediate state and will there attain parinirvāṇa, having attained the state of non-retrogression and not returning to this world."

Either he sees that female lay follower for himself, or he repeatedly hears from others that this female lay follower possesses such faith, observes such precepts, possesses such extensive learning, practices such generosity, and possesses such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls that the lay follower possesses faith, observes the precepts, is widely learned, is generous, and possesses wisdom; and having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may wish to emulate her in such and such ways.
“Ānanda! In this way, the female lay follower will surely attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
“Ānanda! [he said.]

Furthermore, a female lay follower hears that another female lay follower has passed away in a certain village; she was prophesied by the Buddha as one for whom the three fetters have been exhausted, whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, and who will attain the state of "once-returning" between the heavens and the human world, and having returned once more, will reach the end of suffering.

Either he sees that female lay follower for himself, or he hears of her repeatedly from others, that she possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls that the lay follower possessed faith, observed the precepts, was widely learned, practiced generosity, and possessed wisdom; having heard this true Dharma and Vinaya, their mind may aspire to emulate such qualities in various ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, the upāsikā will surely attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
"Ānanda! [he said.]

Furthermore, a female lay follower hears that a certain female lay follower has passed away in a certain village; she was prophesied by the Buddha as one whose three fetters have been exhausted, who has attained the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), who will not fall into the miserable realms, who is destined for full awakening, and who shall undergo at most seven more existences, having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human world before reaching the end of suffering.

Either he has seen that female lay follower for himself, or he has heard of her repeatedly from others, that she possesses such faith, such ethical discipline, such extensive learning, such generosity, and such wisdom.

Having heard this, that person recalls how that lay follower possessed faith, observed the precepts, was learned, practiced generosity, and had wisdom; and having heard this True Dharma and Discipline, their mind may wish to emulate them in such and such ways.
"Ānanda! In this way, the female lay follower will surely attain relief and dwell in peace and happiness.
"Ānanda! [he said].
"For this reason, the Tathāgata, when his disciples pass away, declares: 'A certain one is born in such-and-such a place; another is born in such-and-such a place.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Anuruddha and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth discourse, "The Discourse on the Three Sons of Noble Family from Sāketa," ends here, totaling three thousand four hundred and six characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume XVIII, totaling ten thousand one hundred and twenty-seven characters.

The Discourse on the Brahmā’s Invitation to the Buddha (78) From the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, Discourse on the Brahmā’s Invitation to the Buddha, Number Seven, Recited at the Second Small Earth-City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a Brahmā dwelling in the Brahma-heaven who conceived such a wrong view:

"This place is permanent; this place is eternal; this place endures; this place is essential; this place is not subject to cessation; this is the escape from suffering; and beyond this escape, there is no further escape that is superior, more excellent, or more sublime."

Thereupon, the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that Brahmā with his knowledge of others' minds, immediately entered a concentration corresponding to that state. By means of this concentration, as swiftly as a strong man might extend or contract his arm, he suddenly vanished from the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park at Śrāvastī, and went to the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, seeing the World-Honored One approaching, that Brahmā deity immediately invited him, saying:
"Welcome, Great Seer! Herein is the eternal;
