herein is the constant; herein is the enduring; herein is the essential; herein is the deathless Dharma; herein is the way of escape. Beyond this way of escape, there is no other way of escape that surpasses it—none that is superior, more sublime, or most excellent."
Thereupon, the Blessed One said: “Brahmā!

You describe the impermanent as permanent, the non-eternal as eternal, the non-abiding as abiding, the non-essential as essential, and what is subject to termination as what is not subject to termination. You describe what is not the way out as the way out, claiming that there is no other way out superior to this one, which is more excellent, sublime, and supreme.”
Brahmā! You possess this ignorance. Brahmā!
"You possess this ignorance.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was present in that assembly.
Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Monks! Do not contradict what this Brahmā has spoken; do not oppose what this Brahmā has spoken. Monks!”
If you were to oppose what this Brahmā has said, or act contrary to what this Brahmā has said, it would be like a person who, when auspicious matters arrive, pushes them away and rejects them.
What the bhikṣu has said is likewise so. Therefore, bhikṣu! I tell you:
do not contradict what this Brahmā has said; do not oppose what this Brahmā has said.
"Monks! If you were to oppose what this Brahmā has said, or act contrary to what this Brahmā has said, it would be, monks,
just like a person falling from a mountain peak who, though reaching out into the air with hands and feet, finds nothing to grasp."
What the bhikṣu has said is likewise so. Therefore, bhikṣu! I tell you:
do not contradict what this Brahmā has said; do not oppose what this Brahmā has said.
"Monks! If you were to oppose what this Brahmā has said, or act in contradiction to what this Brahmā has said, it would be, monks, just as if a person were to fall from a tree;
though they might reach out with their hands and feet to grasp at branches and leaves, they would find nothing."
What the bhikṣu has said is likewise so. Therefore, bhikṣu! I tell you:
do not contradict what this Brahmā has said; do not oppose what this Brahmā has said.

Why is this so? This Brahmā is the Brahmā, the blessed one, the powerful transformer, the most venerable, the maker, the creator, and the father. All sentient beings—those who have existed and those who will exist—are born from him; he knows all that is to be known and sees all that is to be seen.
“Great Seer!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who hate the earth and revile the earth, when their bodies break up at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn among other lowly, vulgar deities of music. Likewise, those who hate the water, fire, wind, devas, and Prajāpati, or who hate Brahmā and revile Brahmā, when their bodies break up at the end of life, will certainly be reborn among other lowly, vulgar deities of music.”
"O Great Seer!

If there are recluses or brahmins who delight in earth and praise earth, when their bodies break up at the end of life, they will certainly be reborn among the most supreme and venerable Brahmā gods. Likewise, those who delight in water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, or Prajāpati, and who praise Brahmā, when their bodies break up at the end of life, will certainly be reborn among the most supreme and venerable Brahmā gods."
"Great Seer!
Do you not see this Great Assembly of Brahmā sitting here like us?
That Māra Pāpīyān was neither Brahmā nor a member of Brahmā’s retinue; yet he claimed for himself, "I am Brahmā."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This Māra Pāpīyas is not Brahmā, nor is he a member of Brahmā’s retinue; yet he claims for himself, 'I am Brahmā.
If one speaks of Māra Pāpīyas, this is indeed Māra Pāpīyas."
The World-Honored One, having known this, addressed him, saying:
"Māra Pāpīyas! You are not Brahmā, nor are you a member of Brahmā’s retinue; yet you claim for yourself that I am Brahmā."
"If it is said that there is a Māra Pāpīyān, you yourself are that Māra Pāpīyān. Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyān thought:
"The World-Honored One knows me; the Sugata sees me."
Having understood this, he became sorrowful and suddenly vanished from that place.
Then, that Brahmā requested the World-Honored One a second and even a third time:
"Welcome, Great Seer!"

"In this place there is permanence; in this place there is constancy; in this place there is endurance; in this place there is the essential; in this place there is the non-terminating dharma; in this place there is the definitive escape. Beyond this escape, there is no other escape superior to it—nothing more excellent, nothing more sublime, and nothing more supreme."
The Blessed One also spoke to him a second and a third time: “Brahmā!

You describe the impermanent as permanent, the non-eternal as eternal, the non-abiding as abiding, the non-essential as essential, and what is subject to cessation as what is not subject to cessation. You describe what is not the way out as the way out, claiming that there is no other way out superior to this one, which is more excellent, sublime, and supreme.”
Brahmā! You possess this ignorance. Brahmā!
"You possess this ignorance.
Thereupon, the Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Great Seer!
"In the past, there were śramaṇas and brahmins whose lifespans were extremely long and who remained for an exceedingly long time.
Great Seer! Your life is very short;
it does not equal even a single moment of solitary meditation (*ekāsanika*) by those śramaṇas and brahmins."

Why is this so? Because he has fully known all that is to be known and fully seen all that is to be seen. If there were any other way of deliverance superior to it—more excellent, more sublime, or most supreme—he would know it;

and if there were no such way of deliverance superior to it—more excellent, more sublime, or most supreme—he would likewise know that. Thus, he knows that there is no other way of deliverance superior to it, none more excellent, none more sublime, and none most supreme.
"O Great Seer!

You conceive the thought of non-deliverance regarding that which is deliverance, and the thought of deliverance regarding that which is not deliverance. Thus, you do not attain deliverance and become utterly deluded."
Why is this? Because there are no objective realms. Great Seer!
If there are recluses or brahmins who love the earth and praise the earth, they are under my control, they follow my will, and they act according to my commands.
In this way, water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and Prajāpati—those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā—are subject to my sovereignty, follow my will, and act according to my commands.
"O Great Seer!
If you love the earth and praise the earth, you shall likewise be under my authority, follow my will, and carry out my commands."

In this way, water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and Prajāpati—whoever loves and delights in Brahmā and praises Brahmā—are likewise subject to my sovereignty, must follow my desires, and must obey my commands.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said:
“Brahmā! It is as you have said; these are the truths spoken by Brahmā.”
"If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who love the earth and praise the earth, they shall be subject to your will, follow your desires, and act according to your commands."

In this way, water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and Prajāpati—those who delight in the Brahmā world and praise the Brahmā world—are subject to your mastery, they follow your desires, and they act according to your commands.
"O Brahmā! If I were to delight in the earth and praise the earth, I would likewise be subject to your sovereignty, acting according to your desires and following your commands."

In this same way, whether it be water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, or Prajāpati—those who delight in Brahmā and praise Brahmā—I too am at your disposal, acting according to your wishes and following your commands.
“Brahmā! If these eight matters are those that I personally delight in and praise, they are likewise so for them as well, Brahmā.”
I know the place from which you have come, the place to which you will go, where you dwell, where you will pass away, and where you will be reborn.
There are Brahmās who possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.
Thereupon, the Brahmā addressed the Blessed One, saying: “Great Seer!
How is it that you know what I know and see what I see?”
How do you know me?

Like the sun, which exercises sovereign power and illuminates all directions—this constitutes a thousandfold world-system—is it within this thousandfold world-system that you have attained sovereignty?
"Do you know, Brahmā, that in such-and-such places there is neither day nor night, and that the Great Seer has previously traversed them and repeatedly experienced them?
The Blessed One replied, "Brahmā!"

Just as the sun exercises sovereign power, illuminating all directions across this thousandfold world-system, so too do I attain mastery within that thousandfold world-system, and I also know that in various places therein there is neither day nor night.
Brahmā! I have traversed those regions; I have repeatedly experienced them. Brahmā!
"There are three kinds of devas: the Ābhassara (Radiant) devas, the Parittābha (Limited Radiance) devas, and the Appamāṇābha (Immeasurable Radiance) devas.
Brahmin! Whatever knowledge and vision those three kinds of devas possess, I too possess that same knowledge and vision."
"Brahmā! If those three kinds of devas lack knowledge and vision, I myself possess knowledge and vision. Brahmā!"
Brahmā! If those three classes of devas and their retinues possess knowledge and vision, I likewise possess that knowledge and vision. Brahmā!
If those three classes of devas and their retinues lack knowledge and vision, I likewise possess my own knowledge and vision.
"Brahmā! If you possess knowledge and vision, I too possess this knowledge and vision. Brahmā!"
If you have no knowledge and no vision, I likewise possess knowledge and vision. Brahmā!
If you and your retinue possess knowledge and vision, I too possess such knowledge and vision.
"Brahmā! If you and your retinue lack knowledge and vision, I myself possess knowledge and vision. Brahmā!"
"You do not grant me everything equally, nor do you grant me all things exhaustively; rather, it is I who am the most excellent and supreme among you.
Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Great Seer!..."
By what means do you claim that those three kinds of gods possess knowledge and vision? If those three kinds of gods possess knowledge and vision, then you likewise possess that knowledge and vision;
if those three kinds of gods lack knowledge and vision, then you likewise possess your own knowledge and vision.

If those three kinds of gods and their retinues possess knowledge and vision, then you likewise possess that knowledge and vision; if those three kinds of gods and their retinues lack knowledge and vision, then you likewise possess your own knowledge and vision.
If I have knowledge and vision, you likewise possess this knowledge and vision;
if I lack knowledge and vision, you likewise possess knowledge and vision of your own;
if I and my retinue have knowledge and vision, you likewise possess this knowledge and vision.
"If I and my retinue were without knowledge and without vision, you yourself would possess knowledge and vision,
Great Seer! Is this not a statement of affection?"
Having asked this, they do not know how to increase their wisdom, but rather increase their delusion.

Why is this? Because consciousness has immeasurable objects; there are immeasurable cognitions, immeasurable views, and immeasurable distinctions, such that I know each one individually: "This is the earth, I know the earth"; water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, and Prajāpati—I know them as such; and Brahmā—I know Brahmā as Brahmā.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said: “Brahmā!
If there are recluses or brahmins who, regarding earth, have the perception of earth, thinking: ‘Earth is mine; earth belongs to me; I belong to earth’;”
Having reckoned earth to be the self, he no longer knows earth.

Likewise, regarding water, fire, wind, the spirit (īśvara), the celestial lord (deva), the Lord of Beings (prajāpati), Brahmā, the Untroubled (anabhraka), and the Heatless (atapa): where there is purity, he perceives it as pure; he thinks, "Purity is the self," "Purity is mine," and "I am in purity.
Having reckoned purity to be the self, he no longer knows purity.
Brahmā! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who understand earth as earth, [realizing] "earth is not my self, earth is not mine, and I am not in earth";
having no longer reckoned earth as their self, they then truly know earth.

In this way, regarding water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Heaven of No Affliction, and the Heaven of No Heat—if they are pure, one knows them as pure; yet purity is not the self, purity is not what belongs to the self, and the self does not exist within purity.
When one no longer conceives of purity as being the self, one then truly knows purity.
Brahmā! Regarding earth, I know earth as earth; earth is not my self, earth is not mine, and I am not possessed by earth.
Since I do not conceive of earth as being my self, I then know earth.

In this way, regarding water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, the Heaven of No Affliction (Avṛha), and the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa)—if they are pure, one knows them as pure; yet purity is not the self, purity is not mine, and the self is not within purity.
Once I no longer conceive of purity as being the self, I then know purity [for what it is].
Thereupon, Brahmā addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Great Seer!
These sentient beings love existence, delight in existence, and practice for existence; you have already uprooted the very foundation of existence.”
Why is this so? Because he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Then he spoke in verse:
"One who sees fear in existence and sees no fear in non-existence, therefore should not delight in existence;
for what is there in existence that cannot be severed?
O Great Sage!"
"I now wish to conceal my own form.
The World-Honored One said, "Brahmā!"
“If you wish to conceal your form, do so as you please.
Thereupon, the Brahmā immediately concealed his form according to his desire.
The World-Honored One then knew: “Brahmā!”
"You are there, you are here, you are in between.
Thereupon, the Brahmā manifested his powers to the full; yet, wishing to conceal his own form, he was unable to do so, and returned to abide within the Brahma realm.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said: "Brahmā!
I, too, now wish to conceal my own form."
Brahmā addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Great Seer! If you wish to conceal your form, do so as you desire."
Thereupon, the Blessed One thought to himself:

"I shall now manifest a psychic power (*ṛddhi*) corresponding to my intention, emitting a most sublime radiance that illuminates all the Brahmā heavens while remaining hidden myself, so that the Brahmās and their retinues may hear my voice but not see my form."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately manifested the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) corresponding to his form, emitting an exceedingly wondrous radiance that illuminated all the Brahmā heavens; he then withdrew himself, causing all the Brahmās and their retinues to hear his voice alone without seeing his physical form.
Thereupon, Brahmā and his retinue each thought to themselves:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary!"
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this?
Because he emits most exquisite light that illuminates all the Brahmā heavens while remaining hidden; thus we and our retinues hear his voice but do not see his form.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again thought to himself:
"I have already transformed this Brahmā and his retinue; I should now rather withdraw my supernormal power."
The World-Honored One then withdrew his supernormal power and returned to abide among the Brahmā gods.
Thereupon, Māra the Evil One went before that assembly a second and even a third time.
At that moment, Māra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Great Seer Sudarśana is well-seeing, well-knowing, and well-attained; yet he does not instruct, admonish, or rebuke his disciples, nor does he preach the Dharma for them, nor does he become attached to his disciples.
Because he is not attached to his disciples, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will not be reborn among the lowly and base celestial musicians.”
One practices the unconditioned and experiences peace and happiness in the present life.
Why is this so? O Great Seer!
"O Great Seer, this is merely a source of weariness for the Tathāgata.

In the past, there were śramaṇas and brahmins who instructed their disciples, admonished their disciples, preached the Dharma to their disciples, and took delight in being attached to their disciples."
Because he was attached to his disciples, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn among the lowly musicians and entertainers.
Great Seer! Therefore I say to you:
do not instruct or reprimand disciples, do not preach the Dharma for the sake of disciples, and do not be attached to disciples.
Do not, for the sake of your disciples, undergo the destruction of the body and the end of life only to be reborn among the lowly and base musicians and celestial musicians;
practice the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and you shall experience peace and happiness in this present life.
Why is this? Great Seer!
You are needlessly troubling yourself.
Thereupon, the Blessed One said: "Māra Pāpīyān!
You do not speak for the sake of seeking my welfare; it is not for my benefit, nor for my happiness, nor for my peace and security."

"Do not instruct or admonish disciples; do not preach the Dharma for disciples; do not become attached to disciples. Because of such attachment to disciples, at the breaking up of the body after death, you will be reborn among the lowly and base deities of music and dance."
Practicing the unconditioned, one experiences peace and happiness in the present life.
Why is this so? Great Seer!
"You have needlessly exhausted yourself. Māra Pāpīyān!
You have formed this thought:
"This śramaṇa Gautama teaches the Dharma to his disciples; having heard the Dharma, those disciples will depart from my realm.
Māra Pāpīyān! For this reason, you now say this to me:
"Do not instruct, admonish, or rebuke disciples; do not preach the Dharma for disciples; do not become attached to disciples.
Do not, because of attachment to disciples, at the breaking up of the body after death, be reborn among the lowly and base deities of music and song."
Practicing the unconditioned, one experiences peace and happiness in the present life.
Why is this so? O Great Seer!
"You are needlessly wearying yourself. "Māra Pāpīyān!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who instruct their disciples, admonish their disciples, teach the Dharma to their disciples, and take pleasure in being attached to their disciples; [then they are truly teachers]."
Because of his attachment to disciples, at the dissolution of the body after death, he was reborn among the lowly and base deities of music and song.

Those recluses and brahmins are not recluses though they claim to be recluses; they are not brahmins though they claim to be brahmins; they are not arhats though they claim to be arhats; they are not perfectly awakened ones though they claim to be perfectly awakened ones.
Māra Pāpīyān!

I am truly a śramaṇa and claim to be a śramaṇa; I am truly a brahmin and claim to be a brahmin; I am truly an arhat and claim to be an arhat; I am truly a samyaksaṃbuddha and claim to be a samyaksaṃbuddha.
Māra Pāpīyān!
Whether I teach the Dharma to my disciples or do not teach it, you may depart for now; I myself know now when it is appropriate to teach the Dharma to my disciples and when it is not.

This was the request made by Brahmā, while Māra Pāpīyān acted in opposition; yet the World-Honored One spoke in accordance with it. For this reason, this sutra is titled "The Buddha’s Response to the Request of Brahmā.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
The Brahmā and his retinue, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Sūtra on the Brahmā’s Invitation*, the seventh, ends here; three thousand and ninety characters. 79. *The Sūtra on the Deva Viśeṣacintin* (79). *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, *The Sūtra on the Deva Viśeṣacintin*, the eighth. Recited in the second sub-section of the Small Earth-City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thereupon, the householder Seṭṭhi Sāleyyaka addressed a messenger:

"Go to the Buddha and, on my behalf, prostrate yourself, pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One, and inquire after the World-Honored One’s health: whether his body is robust and free from ailment, whether he is at ease and free from disease, and whether his daily activities are light and convenient and his strength is as usual?"
He spoke these words:

"The householder Śeṣavatī bows his head at the feet of the Buddha and inquires after the World-Honored One’s health, asking if your holy body is robust and strong, free from ailment and at ease, and whether your daily activities are light and convenient and your strength remains as usual."

"Once you have delivered my greetings to the Buddha, go to the Venerable Anuruddha, prostrate at his feet on my behalf, and inquire after the Venerable’s health: whether he is strong and well, free from illness, comfortable in his daily life, and whether his physical strength remains as usual."
He spoke these words:

"The householder Sessu has bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha and inquires after the Venerable One’s health—whether he is strong, well, free from illness, and whether his daily activities are light and easy, and his strength as usual?"
The householder Sese invited the Venerable Anuruddha and three others to share a meal tomorrow.
If they accept the invitation, they should further say:
"Venerable Anuruddha!..."

The householder Seniya is very busy and has much to do; he must attend to the various affairs of the king and act as a counselor to adjudicate matters. Therefore, I pray that the Venerable Anuruddha, out of compassion, will come to the house of the householder Seniya tomorrow morning accompanied by four others.

Thereupon, having received the instructions from the seer’s son regarding the remaining wealth, the messenger went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The householder Śeṣavatī bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquired after the World-Honored One: "Is your holy body robust and strong? Are you at ease, free from illness, and light in your movements? Is your vigor as it was before?"
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the messenger:
"May the master of the household, Śeṣavat, be at peace and happy; may gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings be at peace and happy."

Thereupon, the messenger, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and retained it well; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Venerable Anuruddha was, prostrated at his feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“Venerable Anuruddha! [...]”

The householder Seta bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha and inquired after the Venerable’s health, asking: "Is your holy body strong and robust? Are you well and free from illness? Is your daily life easy and comfortable? And is your physical strength as it usually is?"
"The householder Seta invites the Venerable Anuruddha and three others to share a meal tomorrow.
At that time, the Venerable Pukkusāti was seated in meditation not far from the Venerable Anuruddha.
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Worthy Kaccāyana!
What I said just now—that tomorrow we shall enter the city of Sāvatthī for the sake of alms—was precisely this."
"Now the householder Sāleyyaka has sent someone to invite us four to provide a meal for tomorrow.
Venerable Tissa Moggalliputta immediately said:
"Venerable Anuruddha, please accept this invitation in silence for the sake of that man."
"Tomorrow we shall emerge from this Dark Forest and enter the city of Śrāvastī for the sake of alms.
For the sake of those people, the Venerable Aniruddha accepted their request by remaining silent.
Thereupon, knowing that the Venerable Anuruddha had accepted by remaining silent, the messenger further addressed him, saying:
"The householder Sela reports to the Venerable Anuruddha!"

The householder Seniya is very busy and has much to do; he serves as a minister to adjudicate the various affairs of the king. May the Venerable Anuruddha, out of compassion, come tomorrow morning accompanied by four others to the house of the householder Seniya.
The Venerable Anuruddha said to the messenger, "Return at once;
I myself shall know the proper time.
Thereupon, the messenger rose from his seat, prostrated himself in salutation, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Then, when the night had passed and at dawn, the Venerable Anuruddha dressed, took his bowl, and together with three others, went to the house of the householder Senānī.
At that time, the householder Senānī was surrounded by his female attendants and stood at the middle gate, waiting for the Venerable Anuruddha.
When Senānī saw the Venerable Anuruddha approaching from afar, he joined his palms toward the Venerable Anuruddha and said in praise:
"Welcome, Venerable Anuruddha!"
"Venerable Anuruddha has not come here for a long time.
Thereupon, the householder Seniya respectfully supported and embraced the Venerable Anuruddha, leading him into his home, where he prepared a fine seat and invited him to sit.
Venerable Anuruddha then sat upon that bed. Sekhasutta, the son of a banker, prostrated at the feet of Venerable Anuruddha, withdrew to sit at one side, and having sat down, he said:
"Venerable Anuruddha!..."
"I wish to ask something; I only pray that you will grant me your attention.
Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Wealth-Owner!"
"I shall reflect upon what I have heard according to your questions.
Then the householder Sela asked the Venerable Anuruddha:
"There are some recluses and brahmins who come to me and say to me:"
“Householder!
You should cultivate the liberation of the great mind.
Thus spoke the Venerable Anuruddha.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brahmins who come to me and say to me:
"O Master of Wealth!
You should cultivate the liberation of the immeasurable mind."
"Venerable Anuruddha!
Regarding these two liberations—the liberation of the great mind and the liberation of the immeasurable mind—are they different in both phrasing and meaning?"
"Is it for the sake of one meaning with different phrasing?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Dhanika!"
“You previously asked about this matter; you should answer it first, and I shall answer afterwards.
The householder Sūciśresthin replied, “Venerable Anuruddha!

The liberation of the great mind and the liberation of the immeasurable mind—these two liberations are identical in meaning though different in expression; Śreṇika Vatsagotra was unable to answer this matter.
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Dhananjani!
Listen as I explain to you the liberation of the great mind and the liberation of the immeasurable mind."

Regarding the "liberation of the great mind": if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin dwelling in a secluded place, or having gone to the foot of a tree, an empty and quiet location, who dwells having attained the pervasive accomplishment of the liberation of the great mind through the mental resolve based on a single tree—his liberation of mind is limited to this and does not exceed it.

If one does not rely on a single tree, one should rely on two or three trees; having attained the great liberation of mind through mental resolve, one dwells pervading it with complete accomplishment, yet that limit of his liberation of mind does not exceed this.

If one does not rely on two or three trees, one should rely on a single grove; if one does not rely on a single grove, one should rely on two or three groves; if one does not rely on two or three groves, one should rely on a single village; if one does not rely on a single village, one should rely on two or three villages; if one does not rely on two or three villages, one should rely on a single country; if one does not rely on a single country, one should rely on two or three countries; if one does not rely on two or three countries, one should rely on this great earth, extending even to the great ocean.

One dwells having attained the pervasive liberation of the great mind through intentional understanding; that which constitutes its limit does not exceed this liberation of mind—this is called the liberation of the great mind.
“Householder! What is the immeasurable liberation of mind?

If a śramaṇa or brahmin dwells in a secluded place, or goes to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet, and peaceful location, his mind is imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and he dwells having perfected its pervasion of one direction. Likewise, he dwells having perfected its pervasion of the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, encompassing all everywhere. With a mind imbued with loving-kindness—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having perfected its pervasion of the entire world.”

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—one dwells having pervaded the entire world; this is called the liberation of the immeasurable mind.
"Householder!

Regarding the liberation of the great mind and the liberation of the immeasurable mind—do these two liberations differ in both meaning and phrasing, or do they have the same meaning but differ in phrasing?"
The householder Isidatta said to the Venerable Anuruddha:
"As I have understood the meaning from what I heard from the Venerable One, these two types of liberation differ both in their meaning and in their phrasing."
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Gahapati, there are three kinds of devas: the Ābhassara (Radiant) devas, the Parittābha (Limited Radiance) devas, and the Appamāṇābha (Immeasurable Radiance) devas."
Among them, as for the Ābhāsvara devas, they are born in a single place and do not form such thoughts as: "This is mine," or "That is mine.
Rather, wherever the Ābhāsvara devas go, they find joy therein.
"O Householder!
It is just as a fly on a piece of meat does not form the thought: 'This is mine; that is mine.'"
"However, as soon as the fly follows the piece of meat away, it finds delight therein.
In the same way, those gods of Radiance do not form such thoughts: 'This is mine; that is mine.'"
"However, wherever the Ābhāsvara devas go, they find joy therein.
At times, when the Ābhāsvara devas gather in one place, although their bodies differ, their radiance does not differ."
"O Householder!
It is just as when someone lights countless lamps and places them within a single room; although those lamps are distinct, their light is not different.
In the same way, those gods of Radiance gather in one place; although their bodies are distinct, their radiance is not different."
At times, the Ābhāsvara devas disperse individually; when they disperse, their bodies become distinct and their radiance also becomes distinct. O Gṛhapati!
It is just as if a person were to take many lamps from a single room and distribute them to various rooms; those lamps then become distinct and their radiance also becomes distinct.
In this way, those devas of Radiance each dispersed; as they dispersed, their bodies were different and their radiance was also different.
Thereupon, the Venerable Tissa Moggalliputta said: “Venerable Anuruddha!
"When those devas born of light are gathered in one place, can it be known that some are superior and others inferior,
or that some are more excellent and others less so? Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Worthy Kaccāyana!"
"One might say that those born among the Ābhāsvara devas dwell in a single place, yet one knows there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, and of excellence and lack thereof.
The Venerable Tissa Moggalliputta further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha!"
“Venerable Kaccāyana, by what cause and by what condition do those devas born in that same place come to know of superiority and inferiority, or of the exquisite and the non-exquisite?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“Worthy Kaccāyana, [it is so].”

If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who dwells in a secluded place, or goes to the foot of a tree or an empty, quiet location, and relying on a single tree, achieves and dwells in the mental liberation of the perception of light, with the mind’s perception of light becoming exceedingly intense, his mental liberation is limited to that and does not go beyond it.

If he does not rely on one tree, but relies on two or three trees, he dwells having attained mastery through the mental perception of light; his mind’s perception of light becomes exceedingly intense, and the limit of that liberation of mind does not exceed this.
“Worthy Kaccāyana!
Of these two liberations of mind, which liberation is superior, more excellent, more sublime, and most supreme?
The Venerable Kaccāyana replied:
“Venerable Anuruddha!

If there are recluses or brahmins who do not rely on a single tree, but rather rely on two or three trees, and who dwell having attained mastery through the mental perception of light, with the mind’s perception of light reaching its full intensity, their liberation of mind is limited to that and does not go beyond it.”
"Venerable Anuruddha!
Of these two liberations, this liberation is superior, excellent, sublime, and foremost.
Venerable Anuruddha asked again:
“Wise Kaccāyana! If one does not rely on two or three trees, one might rely on a single grove;

if one does not rely on a single grove, one might rely on two or three groves; if one does not rely on two or three groves, one might rely on a single village; if one does not rely on a single village, one might rely on two or three villages; if one does not rely on two or three villages, one might rely on a single country; if one does not rely on a single country, one might rely on two or three countries; and if one does not rely on two or three countries, one might rely upon this great earth, even unto the great ocean.”

He dwells having attained mastery through the mental resolve of the perception of light; his mind’s perception of light is so exceedingly intense that his liberation of mind does not extend beyond this limit.
Worthy Kātyāyana!
"Of these two liberations, which liberation is superior, more excellent, more sublime, and most supreme?
The Venerable Kaccāyana replied: "Venerable Anuruddha!"

If there are recluses or brahmins who do not rely on two or three trees, they may rely on a single grove; if they do not rely on a single grove, they may rely on two or three groves; if they do not rely on two or three groves, they may rely on a single village; if they do not rely on a single village, they may rely on two or three villages; if they do not rely on two or three villages, they may rely on a single country; if they do not rely on a single country, they may rely on two or three countries; and if they do not rely on two or three countries, they may rely upon this great earth, even unto the great ocean.

He dwells having attained mastery through the mental resolve of the perception of light; his mind’s perception of light is so exceedingly intense that his liberation of mind does not exceed this limit, Venerable Ānanda.
"Between these two liberations, this liberation is superior, excellent, sublime,
and supreme. Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Kaccāyana!"

Due to these causes and conditions, those born among the Ābhāsvara devas dwell together in one place, yet they know there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, excellence and lack thereof. Why is this?

Because the minds of people differ in their degree of excellence, their cultivation becomes either refined or coarse; because their cultivation is refined or coarse, the persons resulting from it possess degrees of superiority and inferiority.
"Venerable Kaccāyana!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus: 'There are superior and inferior persons among human beings.
The Venerable Tissa Kaccāyana asked again:
“Venerable Anuruddha!
When those born in the Heaven of Pure Radiance (Sudassa) dwell in one place, can it be known that there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, or excellence and lack thereof?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“Venerable Kaccāyana!

One may say that those born in the realm of the devas of Pure Radiance (Sudassa) exist in a single place, yet they know there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, and of excellence and lack thereof.
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana asked again:
"Venerable Anuruddha!

Those devas born in the Heaven of Pure Radiance dwell in one place; for what cause and by what condition do they know that some are superior while others are inferior, or that some are excellent while others are not?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kaccāyana!

Suppose there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who, dwelling in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty, quiet, and peaceful location, attains mastery in the sphere of the Ābhāsvara devas (the gods of pure radiance) and dwells having pervaded it. Yet, he does not cultivate, practice, or expand that concentration, nor does he bring it to ultimate perfection."
At a later time, when his body broke up and his life ended, he was reborn among the Śubhakṛtsna devas.
Having been born there, he did not attain ultimate cessation, nor did he attain ultimate tranquility, nor did he reach the end of his lifespan.
Worthy Kaccāyana!

It is just as with blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses—born in water and grown in water—which, while still at the bottom of the water, have their roots, stalks, leaves, and flowers all saturated, drenched, and moistened by the water, such that there is no part of them not soaked.
Worthy Kaccāyana!

Suppose there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who dwells in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty, quiet, and peaceful location, and whose mind attains mastery over the Ābhāsvara Heaven (the Heaven of Radiant Purity), pervading it and dwelling therein in accomplishment; yet he does not cultivate, practice, expand, or fully perfect that concentration. When his body breaks up and his life ends, he is reborn among the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
"Once born, he does not attain ultimate stillness, does not attain ultimate tranquility, nor does he reach the end of his lifespan.
Worthy Kātyāyana!"

Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who, having attained mastery of mind, dwell having achieved the pervasion of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; they repeatedly cultivate, repeatedly practice, and repeatedly expand that meditative concentration until it is perfectly accomplished. When their bodies break up at the end of life, they are reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas.
Once he was born, he attained supreme tranquility, attained supreme peace, and his life came to its natural end.
Venerable Kaccāyana!
It is just as when blue, red, or white lotuses grow in the water and rise above the water, remaining there unsullied by the water.
Worthy Kaccāyana!

Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who dwell in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty and quiet location; they resolve their minds upon the Ābhāsvara Heaven, pervading it and dwelling in its accomplishment. They repeatedly cultivate, repeatedly practice, and repeatedly expand that meditative concentration until it is fully perfected. When their bodies break up and their lives end, they are reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas.
"Once born there, they attain supreme tranquility, supreme stillness, and also reach the end of their lifespan. Worthy Kātyāyana!
For this reason and by these conditions, those born among the Śubhakṛtsna devas in a single place know that there are distinctions of superiority and inferiority, excellence and lack thereof."

Why is this so? Because the minds of people vary in their degree of excellence, their cultivation necessarily becomes refined or coarse; and because cultivation varies in its refinement or coarseness, those who attain it likewise differ in their degree of excellence.
"Venerable Kaccāyana!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus: 'There are superior and inferior persons among human beings.
The Venerable Tissa Kaccāyana asked again:
"Venerable Anuruddha!
When those born in the realm of the Ābhāsvara devas dwell together in one place, can it be known that there are differences among them—superior and inferior, excellent and not excellent?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kaccāyana!

One may say that those devas born in the realm of Universal Purity and Radiance are born in one place, yet they know there are some who are superior and others who are not, some who are excellent and others who are not."
The Venerable Tissa Moggaliputta further asked: "Venerable Anuruddha!

Those devas born in the realm of the Universal Radiance (Subhakinhā) dwell in a single place; by what cause and by what condition do they know that there are some who are superior and others who are inferior, or that some are excellent and others are not?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Worthy Kaccāyana!

If there are recluses or brahmins who dwell in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty, quiet, and peaceful location, and who, having resolved their minds upon the Ābhāsvara Heaven, dwell having attained pervasion of it."
He did not completely cease his sleep, nor did he skillfully pacify his remorse; consequently, after his body dissolved and his life ended, he was reborn among the Subhakṛtsna devas.
Having been reborn there, his radiance was not perfectly pure.
Venerable Kaccāyana!
It is just as when a lamp is lit, depending on the conditions of oil and a wick; if the oil contains dregs and the wick is impure, because of these, the light produced will not be bright or clear.
Worthy Kaccāyana!

Thus, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who dwells in a secluded place, or goes to the foot of a tree, or to an empty and quiet location, and with a mind liberated by the sphere of universal purity, dwells having fully accomplished its pervasion; yet he does not excessively cease sleep, nor does he properly still his remorse and agitation—then, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn among the gods of the sphere of universal purity.
Once he has been born there, his radiance is not exceedingly pure.
"Venerable Kātyāyana!

Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who dwell in secluded places, or at the foot of a tree, or in empty and quiet locations, who attain and abide in the mastery of pervading the Ābhāsvara Heaven with a mind of universal purity."
Having completely stilled sleep and well-regulated his breathing and remorse, at the breaking up of the body after death, he was reborn among the Subhakṛtsna Ābhāsvara devas.
Having been reborn there, his radiance was exceedingly bright and pure.
Worthy Kātyāyana!

It is just as when a lamp is lit, depending on the conditions of oil and a wick; if the oil is free of dregs and the wick is perfectly clean, the light produced by these conditions will be exceedingly bright and pure.

“Wise Kaccāyana! Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who, dwelling in a secluded place, or at the foot of a tree, or in an empty, quiet, and peaceful location, attain and dwell in the mastery of the universal pervasion of the Ābhāsvara (Luminous) devas through mental resolve.”
Having thoroughly stilled sleep and well-calmed remorse through proper breathing, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn among the Subhakṛtsna Radiant Devas.
Once reborn there, his radiance is exceedingly bright and pure.

“Wise Kaccāyana! For this reason and by this condition, those devas born in the realm of Universal Purity and Radiance, though dwelling in one place, know that there are those who are superior and those who are not, and those who are excellent and those who are not.”

Why is this so? Because the minds of people vary in their degree of excellence, their cultivation consequently becomes either refined or coarse; and because cultivation varies in its refinement or coarseness, those who attain it likewise vary in their degree of excellence.
"Venerable Kaccāyana!
The Blessed One has also spoken thus: 'There are superior and inferior persons among men.
Thereupon, the Venerable Tissa Kaccāyana addressed the householder Citta Gahapati:
“Excellent! Excellent,
Dhanapati!”
"You have brought us great benefit. Why is that?

Previously, when we asked the Venerable Anuruddha about the *abhyudayika* devas, we had never heard such a teaching from the Venerable Anuruddha as this: 'There are those devas; there exist those devas; such are those devas.'"
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha said: "Worthy Kaccāyana!

There are many such devas who say that these suns and moons possess such great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual authority, yet their light does not reach [the light of] those [devas]. They gather with me, comfort one another, engage in discussion, and exchange replies; however, I do not speak of them in this way, saying 'those devas,' 'there are those devas,' or 'such are those devas.'"

At that time, having understood that the Venerable One had finished speaking, the householder Revata rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and with his own hands served a variety of most pure, exquisite, and abundant foods—both solid and soft—to ensure he was fully satisfied.
When the meal was finished, the vessels were put away, and after the water for washing had been served, [the householder] took a small seat and sat apart to listen to the Dharma.

Once the householder Sela was seated, the Venerable Anuruddha preached the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having used countless skillful means to preach the Dharma to him, and having exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and departed.
This is what the Venerable Anuruddha said.
Having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken, the householder Seniya and the bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Jyotiṣka-sūtra*, the eighth, ends here, totaling three thousand five hundred and ninety-nine characters. 80. The *Kathina-sūtra* (80), from the *Dīrghāyu-rāja-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the ninth sūtra. Recited in the second section on the Small Earth City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was also staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, dwelling among the Sālaṭa mountain crags.
Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the Venerable Anuruddha put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for food.
The Venerable Ānanda likewise, at dawn, dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī for alms.
Seeing that the Venerable Ānanda was also going for alms, the Venerable Anuruddha said to him: "Worthy Ānanda!"
"You should know, Venerable One, that my three robes of coarse cotton have worn out.
You may now request some bhikṣus to make robes for me."
The Venerable Ānanda silently consented to the request of the Venerable Anuruddha.

Thereupon, having finished his alms-round in Śrāvastī and eaten his meal, the Venerable Ānanda put away his robes and bowl after midday, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, took the keys in his hand, and went from room to room. Seeing the bhikṣus there, he addressed them, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Now let us go to Mount Sālavatika to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.
Then, having heard the words of the Venerable Ānanda, all those bhikṣus went to Mount Sālavatika to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.
Then, the Blessed One saw the Venerable Ānanda holding the keys in his hand, going from room to room; having seen him, he asked: “Ānanda!
"For what purpose do you carry a key in your hand and go from room to room?
Venerable Ānanda replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"I have now requested the bhikṣus to make robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.
The World-Honored One said, "Ānanda!"
"Why did you not invite the Tathāgata to make robes for the bhikṣu Aniruddha?
Thereupon, Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will go to Mount Sālāra to make robes for Venerable Aniruddha."
The Blessed One gave his silent assent to the Venerable Ānanda.
Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda and went before the community of bhikkhus at Sālāṭaviya Rock Mountain, where he spread out a seat and sat down.
At that time, eight hundred bhikkhus together with the Blessed One were gathered and seated in the Sālarāhagiri cave, making robes for the Venerable Anuruddha.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed him, saying:
"Maudgalyāyana!"
"I am able to stretch out the cloth for Āniruddha, cut it into pieces, join them together, and sew them.
Then, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will stretch out the cloth for the worthy Āniruddha; the bhikṣus shall then jointly cut, join, and sew it together."

Thereupon, the Blessed One spread out his robe and cut it to size; the bhikṣus then joined together to slice and join the pieces, and on that very same day, they completed the three robes for the Venerable Aniruddha.
At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that the Venerable Anuruddha had finished making his three robes, addressed him, saying: "Anuruddha!
Preach the *kaṭhina* rules to the bhikṣus; I now have a backache and wish to rest for a while."
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: “Indeed,
World-Honored One.”

Thereupon, the Blessed One folded his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) in four layers and spread it upon the bed; he folded his outer robe (saṃghāṭī) to serve as a pillow and lay down on his right side, with one foot resting upon the other, maintaining the perception of light, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and constantly bearing in mind the thought of rising.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous friends!
Before I had gone forth to study the Path, I was weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, weeping, lamentation, sorrow, and grief; I desired to bring an end to this great mass of suffering."
"Venerable friends!
Having become weary [of worldly life], I have formed this reflection:
'The household life is extremely narrow and a place of defilement; going forth to study the Path is open and vast.'"

"I am now bound at home by fetters; I cannot practice the holy life for as long as life lasts. It would be better for me to renounce both small and great wealth, and to renounce both few and many kinsmen, shaving off my hair and beard, donning the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, leaving the household life for homelessness to study the Path."
"Venerable friends!

At a later time, having relinquished both small and great wealth, and having relinquished both few and many kinsmen, I shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the path."
"Venerable friends!

Having left the household life to study the Path and having renounced my clan, I have received the training of a bhikṣu. I practice the prohibitive precepts and guard the code of liberation; furthermore, I properly maintain dignified deportment and etiquette. Seeing even the slightest fault, I always harbor fear and dread, and I uphold the training rules."
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from killing and have severed the act of killing. Having laid aside the sword and staff, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and possessing a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, I benefit all beings down to the smallest insects; thus, I purify my mind regarding the taking of life."

"Venerable friends! I abstain from taking what is not given; I have abandoned taking what is not given. I take only what is given, delighting in giving and receiving; I am ever fond of generosity, rejoicing without stinginess, and do not look for reward. Thus, I have purified my mind regarding taking what is not given."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from unchaste conduct and severed unchaste conduct; I diligently cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), exerting myself in sublime practice, pure and stainless, free from desire and having abandoned sexual intercourse. Regarding unchaste conduct, I have purified my mind."
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from false speech and have abandoned false speech. I speak the truth, delight in the truth, abide in the truth, and am unshakable. I am entirely trustworthy and do not deceive the world; I have purified my mind regarding false speech."

"Venerable friends! I am free from divisive speech; I have abandoned divisive speech and practice non-divisive speech. I do not cause dissension among others, nor do I report what I have heard here to those over there with the intent to divide these people, nor do I report what I have heard there to those over here with the intent to divide those people. I seek to reconcile those who are divided and I rejoice in the harmony of those who are united. I do not form factions, I do not delight in factions, and I do not praise factions; I have purified my mind of divisive speech."

"Venerable friends! I am free from harsh speech and have abandoned harsh speech. If there is anything I say, it is not coarse or violent in tone, nor is it foul-sounding or grating to the ear; it is not something disliked by the multitude, nor is it unloved by the multitude. It does not cause others distress and does not prevent them from attaining concentration; such speech I have abandoned."

Whatever I say is pure, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; it is pleasing to the ear and enters the heart, being delightful and lovely, bringing peace and happiness to others. My speech is articulate and complete, causing no fear, and enabling others to attain concentration. Speaking such words, I purify my mind of coarse speech.
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from frivolous speech and have severed frivolous speech. I speak at the proper time, speak what is true, speak on the Dharma, speak on the meaning, speak of tranquility, and speak with delight in tranquility. My words are timely, appropriate, well-instructive, and well-reproving; I have purified my mind of frivolous speech."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from trade and livelihood; I have abandoned trade and livelihood. I have discarded scales and measures, I do not accept goods for profit, I do not bind others in servitude, I do not hope for short-measures when weighing or measuring, and I do not deceive others with small profits. Regarding trade and livelihood, I have purified my mind."
"Venerable friends!
I abstain from accepting widows or young girls; I have severed the acceptance of widows or young girls, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of widows or young girls."
"Venerable friends!
I have abstained from accepting slaves and servants; I have severed the acceptance of slaves and servants, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of slaves and servants.
Venerable friends!"

I abstain from accepting elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; I have severed the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
"Venerable friends!
I have abstained from accepting chickens and pigs; I have severed the acceptance of chickens and pigs, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of chickens and pigs.
Venerable friends!"

I have abstained from accepting fields, estates, and shops; I have severed the acceptance of fields, estates, and shops; I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of fields, estates, and shops.
"Venerable friends!
I have abstained from receiving rice, wheat, and beans; I have severed the practice of receiving rice, wheat, and beans; I have purified my mind regarding the receiving of rice, wheat, and beans."
"Venerable friends!
I abstain from intoxicants, I have severed intoxicants; I have purified my mind regarding the drinking of intoxicants.
Venerable friends!"
"Venerable friends! I abstain from high and wide beds; I have renounced high and wide beds, and I have purified my mind regarding high and wide beds.
Venerable friends!
I abstain from garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents; I have renounced garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents, and I have purified my mind regarding garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from singing, dancing, and visiting performances; I have abandoned singing, dancing, and visiting performances, and I have purified my mind regarding singing, dancing, and visiting performances."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from the acceptance of precious objects of form and appearance; I have severed the acceptance of precious objects of form and appearance; I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of precious objects of form and appearance."
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from eating at improper times and have severed the habit of eating at improper times; I eat but one meal a day, do not eat at night, and train myself to eat only during the proper time. Regarding eating at improper times, I have purified my mind."
“Venerable friends!

I have already accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue; now I shall further train in extreme contentment: taking only enough clothing to cover the body and enough food to sustain the frame, wherever I travel, I shall go with only my robes and bowl, moving without attachment or longing, just as a hawk flies through the sky with its two wings.”
Venerable friends!
I am also like this: wherever I travel, I go with only my robes and bowl, proceeding without attachment or lingering regret.
Venerable friends!

I have already accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue and extreme contentment; I shall further train in guarding the sense faculties, constantly mindful of closing them off, mindful of clarity and penetration, achieving success through guarding mindfulness, and always maintaining clear comprehension.
If the eye sees forms, yet one does not grasp at their signs nor relish them—because of [the danger of] anger and contention—one guards the faculty of the eye.
Because covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states do not arise in the mind directed toward them, one guards the faculty of the eye.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and when the mind cognizes mental phenomena, one does not grasp at their characteristics nor does one relish those phenomena, because of [the presence of] anger and contention.

One guards the faculty of the mind so that covetousness, sorrow, dejection, and evil, unwholesome states do not arise within the mind; because one is intent upon that [goal], one guards the faculty of the mind.
“Venerable friends!

Having accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue and supreme contentment, and having guarded my sense faculties, I shall further train in clear comprehension regarding going out and coming in; in looking ahead and looking aside; in bending and stretching, lowering and raising [the limbs]; in maintaining dignified deportment; in properly wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and other robes and carrying the alms bowl; and in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent—all of these I shall practice with clear comprehension.”
"Venerable friends!

Having accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue and supreme contentment, and having guarded my sense faculties and maintained clear comprehension in going out and coming in, I shall further train in dwelling alone in seclusion—staying in a remote place, or at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet location, in a mountain cleft, a stone cave, an open space, or a haystack; or staying in a forest grove, or among the burial mounds."
"Venerable friends!

Having gone to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet, and peaceful spot, I spread out my sitting mat, sit down cross-legged, straighten my body and set my intention, with mindfulness directed inward and not outward, having abandoned covetousness."

My mind is free from contention; seeing the wealth and various articles of livelihood belonging to others, I do not give rise to covetousness or the desire to acquire them for myself; I purify my mind of such covetousness.

In this way, having abandoned ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and having severed doubt and crossed over confusion, I am without hesitation regarding all wholesome dharmas; I have purified my mind of doubt and perplexity.
Venerable friends!

I have abandoned these five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and being secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, I have attained and abide in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration—purified, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and possessing an unshakable mind—I have realized through direct experience the supernormal power of the knowledge of the bases of psychic power."
"Venerable friends!

I have attained immeasurable bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): namely, dividing one into many and combining many into one; remaining as one when alone; possessing knowledge and vision that are unimpeded by stone walls, as if moving through space;
sinking into the earth as if it were water, walking upon water as if it were earth, and sitting cross-legged, ascending into the void like a soaring bird."
Now these sun and moon possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; with their hands they can reach as far as the Brahma-heaven.
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration—purified, stainless, and untroubled; supple, well-established, and possessing an immovable mind—I have cultivated the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear to realize it for myself."
"Venerable friends!
With my divine ear, I hear the voices of humans and non-humans, whether they are near or far, and whether they are sublime or not.
"Venerable friends!"

Having attained such concentration of mind—purified, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and unshakable—I have cultivated and realized the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.

"Venerable friends! I am mindful of, contemplate, attend to, and observe other beings; with the knowledge of others' minds, I know their minds as they truly are: when there is a mind with desire, I know it as a mind with desire as it truly is; when there is a mind without desire, I know it as a mind without desire as it truly is. Likewise, I know a mind with ill will and one without ill will; a mind with delusion and one without delusion; a mind with impurity and one without impurity; a mind that is concentrated and one that is scattered; a mind that is lofty and one that is low; a mind that is small and one that is great; a mind that is cultivated and one that is uncultivated; a mind that is concentrated and one that is unconcentrated; a mind that is not liberated, I know as a mind that is not liberated as it truly is; and a mind that is liberated, I know as a mind that is liberated as it truly is."
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration—purified, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and immovable—I have realized the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives through training."
Venerable friends!

Possessing practice and possessing characteristics, he recollects his immeasurable past experiences: namely, one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births; aeons of formation, aeons of destruction, and immeasurable aeons of both formation and destruction. He recalls: "Those beings had such-and-such names; they underwent such-and-such experiences in the past. I was born there with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such a lifespan until its end. Dying here, I was born there; dying there, I was born here. I was born here with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such a lifespan until its end."
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration, my mind is purified, free from defilement and affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable; I have cultivated and realized the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of death and rebirth."
"Venerable friends!

With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I see these beings as they die and are reborn—of beautiful or ugly appearance, noble or ignoble, and as they pass away from or are reborn in good or bad destinations—seeing them exactly as they truly are according to the karma these beings have performed."

If these sentient beings accomplish misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind; if they do not revile the noble ones, possess right view, and accomplish the karma of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens.
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration—purified, free from defilement and affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable—I have trained to realize the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows."
"Venerable friends!

I know this suffering as it truly is; I know the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. I know these taints, the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are."

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence and ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Venerable friends!

If there is a bhikkhu who has transgressed the precepts, broken the precepts, failed in the precepts, perforated the precepts, defiled the precepts, or whose precepts are dark, yet wishes to rely on the precepts to establish the precepts, using the precepts as a ladder to ascend to the Hall of Unsurpassed Wisdom and the Pavilion of the True Dharma—such a thing is simply impossible."
"Venerable friends!

Suppose there were a multi-storied pavilion not far from a village, within which a ladder was installed with either ten rungs or twelve rungs. If someone were to come seeking to ascend that pavilion, it would be impossible for them to reach the second rung without first climbing onto the first rung;
likewise, it would be impossible for them to reach the third or fourth rung, or to ascend to the pavilion itself, without first climbing onto the second rung."
"Virtuous ones!

In this way, if there is a bhikṣu who has transgressed the precepts, broken the precepts, impaired the precepts, perforated the precepts, defiled the precepts, or whose precepts are black, and yet wishes to rely on the precepts to establish the precepts, using the precepts as a ladder to ascend to the hall of unsurpassed wisdom and the pavilion of the True Dharma—such a thing is simply impossible."
"Venerable friends!

If there is a bhikkhu who has not transgressed the precepts, nor broken them, nor made them deficient, nor torn them, nor defiled them, nor blackened them, and who wishes to rely on the precepts to establish the precepts, taking the precepts as a ladder to ascend to the Hall of Unsurpassed Wisdom and the Pavilion of the True Dharma—this is certainly possible."
"Venerable friends!

Suppose not far from a village there is a multi-storied pavilion with upper chambers and galleries, in which a ladder has been set up with either ten rungs or twelve rungs. If someone were to come seeking to ascend that pavilion and gallery, and having climbed the first rung of this ladder, wished to climb to the second rung—this would certainly be possible;
and having climbed the second rung, wishing to climb the third and fourth, until finally ascending the pavilion and gallery—this would certainly be possible."
Venerable friends!

Thus, if there is a bhikṣu who has not violated, broken, defiled, pierced, sullied, or blackened the precepts, and who desires to rely upon the precepts to establish his conduct, using the precepts as a ladder to ascend to the hall of unsurpassed wisdom and the pavilion of the True Dharma—this is certainly possible.
"Venerable friends!

I rely upon the precepts to establish my conduct; taking the precepts as a ladder, I ascend the hall of unsurpassed wisdom and the pavilion of the True Dharma, and by means of a small skillful means, I behold a thousand worlds."
"Venerable friends!
It is just as if a person with sight were standing on a high tower and, by means of a small device, were to look down upon the open ground below and see a thousand earthen trenches.
Venerable friends!"

I am also like this: relying on the precepts and establishing myself in the precepts, I take the precepts as a ladder to ascend to the hall of unsurpassed wisdom and the pavilion of the True Dharma, where, by means of a small expedient, I observe the thousandfold world system.
Venerable friends!
If a king’s great elephant possesses either the seven treasures or fewer than eight, and covers them with tāla leaves, it is just as I have concealed these six supernormal powers.
“Venerable friends!
If you have any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal knowledge of the power of psychic potency (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), you should ask me; I shall answer you.
Venerable friends!”
If anyone has any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal power of the divine ear, they should ask me, and I shall answer them.
Venerable friends!
If anyone has any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, they should ask me, and I shall answer them.
"Venerable friends!
If you have any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, you should ask me, and I shall answer you.
Venerable friends!"
If anyone has any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal power of knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, they should question me, and I shall answer them.
Venerable friends!
If anyone has any doubt regarding my realization of the supernormal power of knowledge of the destruction of the taints, they should question me, and I shall answer them.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda said: "Venerable Anuruddha!

Now eight hundred bhikkhus, together with the Blessed One, are seated here at Sālāṭaviya Rock; they are making robes for the Venerable Anuruddha. Should anyone have any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal power of the knowledge of psychic potency (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), let them question him, and the Venerable Anuruddha shall answer."
If anyone has any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal power of the divine ear, they should question him; the Venerable Anuruddha will answer.
If anyone has any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, they should question him; the Venerable Anuruddha will answer.
If anyone has any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, they should question him; the Venerable Anuruddha will answer.

If anyone has any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, they should question him; the Venerable Anuruddha will answer.

If anyone has any doubt regarding the Venerable Anuruddha’s realization of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, they should ask him, and the Venerable Anuruddha will answer.

But for a long night we have known the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha with our own minds; like the Venerable Anuruddha, he possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.
Thereupon, the Blessed One’s ailment having subsided and he having attained well-being, he immediately rose and sat down cross-legged.
Once seated, the Blessed One praised the Venerable Anuruddha, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent! Āniruddha,
most excellent!
Ānanda! It was you who expounded the *kaṭhina* rules to the bhikṣus. Ānanda!
"You should further explain the *kaṭhina* rules to the bhikṣus.
Āniruddha! You should repeatedly explain the *kaṭhina* rules to the bhikṣus."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus!
You should receive the kaṭhina rite, recite and study the kaṭhina rite, and properly maintain the kaṭhina rite.”
Why is this? The Kāṭhina rite is in accordance with the Dharma; it is the foundation of the holy life, leading to penetration and awakening, and also leading to Nirvāṇa.

If a son of good family shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and out of supreme faith leaves home for the homeless life to study the Path, he should receive the Kāṭhina rite with a sincere heart, properly receiving and properly maintaining the Kāṭhina rite.
Why is this? I do not see any bhikṣus of the past making robes in such a manner as the bhikṣu Aniruddha;
nor do I see any bhikṣus of the future or the present making robes in such a manner as the bhikṣu Aniruddha.

Why is this? Because now, eight hundred bhikkhus and the Blessed One are seated together here on Mount Sālarāja, and for the sake of the bhikkhu Anuruddha, they are making robes. Such is the bhikkhu Anuruddha: he possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Anuruddha and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The ninth chapter, the Kāṭhina Sūtra, ends here. [3,780 characters]. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 19, [10,469 characters]. The Second Recitation Section: The Small Earth Fort.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 20, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. 81.
The Discourse on Mindfulness of the Body (81). Madhyama Āgama, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, The Tenth Discourse on Mindfulness of the Body, Part Two.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅga together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, and proceeded to the Aṭaṇḍaka monastery where the Jñātiputras resided.
At that time, when the night had passed and at dawn, the World-Honored One dressed in his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Āṭaṇā to beg for food.

Having finished eating, after midday he put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and went to a certain grove. Entering that grove, he approached the foot of a tree, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, after the midday meal, a great number of bhikṣus gathered and sat together in the lecture hall, discussing this matter:
"Venerable friends!
The World-Honored One is truly marvelous!"
How extraordinary!

One cultivates mindfulness of the body, analyzing and disseminating it, knowing it thoroughly, contemplating it thoroughly, practicing it thoroughly, and mastering it through purification; being well-equipped and well-practiced, one dwells with a unified mind. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body yields great fruit and reward: one gains vision and, possessing eyes, perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting in meditative seclusion; with his pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, he heard the bhikṣus, after their midday meal, assembled and seated in the lecture hall, discussing this matter together.
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One is truly marvelous!
He is truly extraordinary!"

One cultivates mindfulness of the body, analyzing and expanding it, knowing it thoroughly, observing it thoroughly, cultivating it thoroughly, and purifying it thoroughly; being well-equipped and practicing well, one dwells with a unified mind. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body yields great fruit and reward: one attains the eye and, possessing vision, beholds the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Having heard this, the Blessed One rose from his meditation in the late afternoon and went to the lecture hall before the assembly of bhikṣus, where he sat upon the prepared seat.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What was it that you were discussing just now?"
"For what reason have you gathered and sat in the lecture hall?
Then, the bhikṣus replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"Venerable friends! After our midday meal, we gathered and sat together in the lecture hall to discuss this matter.
It is truly marvelous, Venerable friends, how extraordinary the Blessed One is!"
How extraordinary!

One cultivates mindfulness of the body, analyzing and disseminating it, knowing it thoroughly, observing it thoroughly, practicing it thoroughly, and purifying it thoroughly; being well-equipped and well-practiced, one abides in a state of single-mindedness. The Buddha has said that mindfulness of the body yields great fruit and reward: one attains vision and, with eyes, beholds the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
“World-Honored One!
We were just now discussing this very matter together; for this reason, we have gathered here in the lecture hall.
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus again, saying:
