"How is it that I have taught the cultivation of mindfulness of the body, its analytical exposition, and its wide dissemination, which yield great fruit and reward?
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Blessed One, saying:

"The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma proceeds from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may fully understand its meaning."
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall explain its meaning for you.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: "How does a bhikṣu practice the mindfulness of the body?

A bhikṣu, when walking, knows that he is walking; when standing, knows that he is standing; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; when lying down, knows that he is lying down; when sleeping, knows that he is sleeping; when awake, knows that he is awake; and when both sleeping and waking, knows that he is both sleeping and waking."
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows it as it truly is.
This is called a bhikkhu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu practices mindfulness of the body: he is clearly aware when going out and coming in; he observes and discerns well when bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, and maintains a composed and dignified demeanor; he is careful in wearing his saṃghāṭī robe and other robes and carrying his bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he is clearly aware of it all.
In this way, as the bhikkhu follows the movements of his body, he knows them truly as they are.

If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikkhu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, when a bhikkhu practices mindfulness of the body, if unwholesome and unskillful thoughts arise, he treats, cuts off, destroys, and stills them with mindfulness of wholesome states. It is just as a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice who, holding a marking line, uses it to mark the wood and then chops and trims it with a sharp axe until it is straight.
In this way, when a bhikṣu gives rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts, he treats, cuts off, destroys, and stops them with thoughts of wholesome dharmas.
In this way, as the bhikṣu follows the movements of his body, he knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [realities] as they truly are.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: the bhikṣu keeps his teeth pressed together, his tongue pressed against the upper palate, and with the mind he governs the mind, governing it so that it is severed, extinguished, and stilled.

It is like two strong men seizing a weak man, twisting him about everywhere and beating and forging him at will; in this way, the bhikṣu brings his teeth together, presses his tongue against the upper palate, and with the mind governs the mind, subduing, severing, extinguishing, and stilling it.
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows it as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body, when breathing in, knows he is breathing in; when breathing out, knows he is breathing out. When breathing in long, he knows he is breathing in long; when breathing out long, he knows he is breathing out long. When breathing in short, he knows he is breathing in short; when breathing out short, he knows he is breathing out short.

He trains himself to be aware of the entire body while breathing in; he trains himself to be aware of the entire body while breathing out. He trains himself to calm the bodily formations while breathing in; he trains himself to calm the verbal formations while breathing out.
In this way, a bhikkhu, following his bodily formations, knows them as they truly are.

If he thus dwells in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind to attain a concentrated mind, then, having attained a concentrated mind, he knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: the bhikṣu, with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, drenches, saturates, and thoroughly suffuses this body; there is no part of his body that is not pervaded by the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

It is just as when a bath-attendant places bathing powder in a vessel, mixes it with water to form a paste, and soaks it until it is moist and supple, pervading everywhere without leaving any part untouched.

In the same way, the monk’s joy and happiness born of seclusion drenches and moistens his body, pervading this entire body completely; there is no part of his body that is not suffused with the joy and happiness born of seclusion.
In this way, a bhikkhu, following his bodily conduct, knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows it as it truly is. This is called a bhikkhu’s cultivation of mindfulness of the body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu cultivates mindfulness of the body. The bhikṣu’s joy and happiness born of concentration drench, saturate, and thoroughly pervade this body; there is no part of the body that is not permeated by the joy and happiness born of concentration."

It is like a mountain spring that is utterly pure and clear, full and overflowing. Although water comes from the four directions, there is no way for it to enter; rather, from the very bottom of that spring, water gushes forth of its own accord, flowing out and soaking the mountain, moistening it, and filling it everywhere until there is no place it does not pervade.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s rapture and bliss born of concentration drench, saturate, and thoroughly pervade his entire body; there is no part of his body that is not permeated by the rapture and bliss born of concentration.
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, he cuts off all afflictions of the mind and attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows it as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: the joy born of the absence of rapture produces a bliss that drenches, moistens, and thoroughly suffuses this entire body; there is no part of the body that is not pervaded by this joy-born bliss.

It is like the blue lotus, the red, the crimson, and the white lotuses, which grow in water and are nurtured by water; from their roots, stems, flowers, and leaves, they are all thoroughly moistened and saturated, pervading everywhere without any part remaining untouched.

In this way, the bhikṣu experiences pleasure born of the absence of joy; it drenches and moistens his body, pervading and filling it entirely, such that there is no part of his body not permeated by this pleasure born of the absence of joy.
In this way, a bhikkhu, following his bodily conduct, knows it as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows it as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing the mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices the mindfulness of the body: within this very body, he dwells having attained a pervasive suffusion with a pure mind through understanding; within this very body, there is no place not pervaded by his pure mind.
It is as if there were a person wearing a robe of seven or eight cubits that covers this body from head to foot, leaving no part of the body uncovered.
In the same way, a bhikkhu dwells having attained and suffused his entire body with a pure mind, such that there is no part of this body not pervaded by the pure mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing the mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practicing the mindfulness of the body maintains the perception of light; he properly receives it, properly retains it, and properly attends to it with his mind. As it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before; as it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day; as it is below, so it is above; as it is above, so it is below. Thus, being free from inversion and without mental entanglement, he cultivates a luminous mind, and his mind is never again shrouded by darkness.
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body by observing signs, receiving them well, retaining them well, and attending to them with a well-directed mind.
Just as someone sitting might observe a person lying down, or someone lying down might observe a person sitting,
so too does a bhikkhu observe the signs, having properly received them, properly retained them, and properly attended to them with his mind.
In this way, a bhikṣu, by following his bodily conduct, comes to know things as they truly are above.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows things as they truly are above.
This is called a bhikkhu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu practicing mindfulness of the body dwells observing this very body, according to its position and according to its state—whether beautiful or ugly—from the head down to the feet, seeing it as full of various impurities: that is to say, within this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain and its membranes, tears, sweat, snot, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, spittle, bile, and urine.

It is like a person with sight who clearly sees all the various seeds contained within a vessel—namely, rice, millet, barley, wheat, large and small sesame, mung beans, rape, mustard, and mustard seeds.

In this way, a bhikṣu dwells observing this body as it is, according to its appearance and its condition, from the head down to the feet, seeing it as filled with various kinds of impurities: namely, that within this body there are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, excrement, brain and its membranes, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, spittle, bile, and urine.
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows things as they truly are above.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows things as they truly are above.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body by observing the various elements of the body, thinking: "In this body of mine there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element."
Just as a butcher slaughters an ox, flays its hide, spreads it upon the ground, and divides it into six portions;

so too does a bhikṣu contemplate the various elements of the body: "Within this body of mine are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element."
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body observes a corpse—one, two, up to six or seven days old—pecked at by crows and vultures, devoured by jackals and dogs, burned by fire, or buried in the earth, all of which have become putrid and decayed. Having seen this, he compares himself to it: "Now this body of mine is also like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it."
In this way, a bhikṣu, by following his bodily conduct, knows things as they truly are above.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, severing all afflictions of the mind and attaining a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows things as they truly are above.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: as he previously saw bones on a charnel ground, bluish-black, decayed, half-eaten by scavengers, and lying on the ground as a skeleton, having seen this, he compares himself to it: "Now, this body of mine is also like this; it possesses this same nature and shall ultimately not escape it."
In this way, a bhikṣu, following the movements of his body, comes to know the higher [truth] as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, severing all afflictions of the mind and attaining a concentrated mind—having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: a bhikṣu sees, as before, a discarded path where the skin, flesh, and blood have been removed and only the sinews remain connected; having seen this, he compares himself to it, thinking: "Now, this body of mine is also like this; it possesses the same nature and, in the end, cannot escape it."
In this way, a bhikṣu, by following his bodily conduct, knows things as they truly are above.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, and having severed all afflictions of the mind, he attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows things as they truly are above.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body sees, as before, the bones and joints of a charnel ground scattered in all directions—the foot-bones, shin-bones, thigh-bones, hip-bones, vertebrae, shoulder-bones, neck-bones, and skull—each lying in a different place. Having seen this, he compares himself [to it], thinking: "Now, this body of mine is also like this; it possesses the same nature and can never escape it."
In this way, a bhikṣu, by following his bodily conduct, knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, he cuts off all afflictions of the mind and attains a concentrated mind; having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows the higher [truth] as it truly is.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices mindfulness of the body: as he previously saw bones on a charnel ground—white like conch shells, blue like the color of a pigeon, red as if smeared with blood, or decayed and reduced to powder—he compares himself to them, thinking: "Now this body of mine is also like this; it possesses the same nature and shall ultimately not escape it."
In this way, a bhikṣu, following his bodily conduct, comes to know things as they truly are above.

If he thus dwells alone in seclusion, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence, severing all afflictions of the mind and attaining a concentrated mind—having attained a concentrated mind, he then knows things as they truly are above.
This is called a bhikṣu practicing mindfulness of the body.
If one practices mindfulness of the body in this way and develops it extensively, all wholesome dharmas are contained therein—namely, the factors of the path.
If one possesses a mind whose resolve is all-pervasive, like the great ocean in which all small rivers are contained,
then for one who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extensively diffuses it, all wholesome dharmas are contained therein— namely, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).

“If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who do not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and who wander with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity against them and will surely succeed.”

Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins are empty and lack mindfulness of the body, it is just like a jar that is empty and contains no water, set upright upon the ground. If someone were to bring water and pour it into the jar, what do you think, bhikṣus?
“Would that jar, being thus, receive water?
The bhikṣu replied, “It would.”
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Because that emptiness contains no water and is firmly settled upon the ground; therefore, it must receive [the rain].

"In this way, if there are śramaṇas or brahmins who do not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and who wander with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity against them and will certainly succeed in finding it."
Why is this? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins are empty of mindfulness of the body.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who correctly establish mindfulness of the body and wander with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān may watch for an opportunity to find them, but he will ultimately be unable to do so.

Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins are not empty of mindfulness of the body, it is just like a jar filled with water, standing securely on the ground. If someone were to bring water and pour it into that jar, what do you think, bhikkhus? Would it overflow?”
“Would that jar, being thus, be able to receive water again?
The bhikṣu replied, “No.”
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Because that vessel is filled with water and is placed upright on the ground; for this reason, it does not receive [the rain].

"In this way, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who maintains right mindfulness of the body and dwells with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān may watch for an opportunity to find him a weakness, but he will ultimately never succeed."
Why is that? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins do not maintain mindfulness of the body with emptiness.

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who do not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and wander with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyas will watch for an opportunity against them and will certainly succeed in finding it.
Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins lack mindfulness of the body, it is just as if a strong man were to throw a large, heavy stone into soft mud. What do you think, bhikṣu?
“Would you accept mud?
The bhikṣu replied, “I would.”
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Because the mud is deep and the stones are heavy, one must necessarily undergo [the consequences].

"In this way, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who does not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and wanders with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity against him and will certainly succeed."
Why is this? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins lack mindfulness of the body.

If there were any śramaṇas or brahmins who correctly established mindfulness of the body and wandered with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān would seek an opportunity against them, but he would ultimately never succeed.

Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins are not devoid of mindfulness of the body. It is just as if a strong man were to throw a light tuft of wool against a flat door-panel. What do you think, bhikkhus? [Would it move?]
“Would he accept it?
The bhikṣu replied, “No.”
World-Honored One! Why is this?
Because the hair-ball is light and the door-panel stands level, it does not receive [the blow].

"In this way, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who correctly establishes mindfulness of the body and dwells with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān may watch for an opportunity to find him, but he will ultimately never succeed."
Why is that? Because those ascetics and brahmins do not possess the mindfulness of the body in a non-empty manner.

If there are ascetics or brahmins who do not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and wander with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyān will watch for an opportunity against them and will certainly succeed in finding one.

Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins are empty and devoid of mindfulness of the body, it is like a person seeking fire who uses dry wood as the source and drills with a dry drill—what do you think, bhikṣu?
“Would that person, acting in this way, obtain fire?
The bhikṣu replied, “He would.”
World-Honored One!
Why is this? Because he uses a dry drill to bore into dry wood; for this reason, he will certainly succeed.

"In this way, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who does not correctly establish mindfulness of the body and wanders with a narrow mind, Māra Pāpīyān will seek an opportunity against him and will certainly succeed in finding it."
Why is this? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins lack mindfulness of the body.

If there were any śramaṇas or brahmins who correctly established mindfulness of the body and wandered with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān would seek to find an opportunity against them, but he would ultimately never succeed.

Why is that? Because those recluses and brahmins do not possess the mindfulness of the body in a non-empty manner. It is as if a person seeking fire were to take wet wood as the source and use a wet drill to bore it—what do you think, bhikṣu?
“Would that person, in such a manner, obtain fire?
The bhikṣu replied, “No.”
World-Honored One!
Why is this so? Because he uses a damp drill to bore into damp wood; for this reason, he does not succeed.

"In this way, if there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who correctly establishes mindfulness of the body and wanders with an immeasurable mind, Māra Pāpīyān may watch for an opportunity to find him a weakness, but he will ultimately never succeed."
Why is that? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins are not empty of mindfulness of the body.
One who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus develops it extensively should be known to possess eighteen virtues.
What are the eighteen?

A bhikṣu is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the afflictions of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh words and the blows of sticks and staves. When his body encounters various illnesses that cause extreme pain, even to the point where life is about to cease, he is able to withstand all such unpleasantness. Thus practicing the mindfulness of the body and thus extensively disseminating it—this is called the first virtue.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is able to endure dissatisfaction; if dissatisfaction arises, his mind ultimately does not cling to it. One who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extensively disseminates it—this is called the second virtue."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu is able to endure fear; even if fear arises, his mind never becomes attached to it. One who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extensively disseminates it—this is called the third quality."
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu may give rise to three unwholesome thoughts:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.

If, when these three unwholesome thoughts arise, his mind is ultimately not attached to them—thus practicing the mindfulness of the body and thus extending it widely—this is called the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh virtue."

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; one who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extends it—this is called the eighth quality."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu whose three fetters have been exhausted attains the stage of *srotāpanna*; he is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, is certain to proceed toward perfect enlightenment, and will undergo at most seven more existences among gods and humans. Having gone back and forth once, he shall reach the end of suffering. For one who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extensively disseminates it, this is called the ninth virtue."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu whose three fetters have been exhausted and whose lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated, attains the state of a 'once-returner' to the heavens and the human realm; having returned once more, he realizes the end of suffering. One who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extensively disseminates it—this is called the tenth virtue."

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu who has exhausted the five lower fetters is reborn in that realm and attains parinibbāna there; having attained the state of non-retrogression, he does not return to this world. For one who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extends it extensively—this is called the eleventh virtue."

"Furthermore, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu possesses liberation through the cessation of the breath, attains the formless by departing from form, and dwells having personally realized and accomplished such a concentration, yet through wisdom observes and knows the taints and abandons the taints—one who thus cultivates mindfulness of the body and thus extends it widely—this is called the twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, and seventeenth quality."

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu possesses the bases of psychic power, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; his taints are exhausted, and he attains the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, he knows it for himself, realizes it for himself, and dwells having personally witnessed its fulfillment: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."
To practice mindfulness of the body in this way and to cultivate it extensively—this is called the eighteenth virtue.
One should know that for one who practices mindfulness of the body in this way and cultivates it extensively, these eighteen virtues will arise.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Kāyagatāsati Sūtra*, the tenth, ends here, totaling 4,225 characters. Regarding the eighteen virtues, those numbered six, seven, eight, and thirteen through seventeen should actually be included within the fifth and the eighteenth virtues.
In the Southern Text, this sutra is included among the fourth and twelfth [sections], and its underlying principle remains difficult to comprehend.

82. The Cūḷa-māluṅkya Sutta (82), the eleventh sutra in the Chapter on King Dīghāvu of the Madhyama Āgama, recited in the second sub-section of the Minor Earth-City (Kṣudrakapattana). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time, after the midday meal and having attended to some minor business, a great number of bhikṣus gathered and sat in the lecture hall, desiring to settle a dispute by discussing this Dharma and Vinaya, this teaching of the Buddha.
At that time, the bhikkhu Citta the Elephant-Cub was also present in the assembly.

While the many bhikkhus were discussing this Dhamma and this Vinaya, this teaching of the Buddha, the bhikkhu Citta the Elephant-Cub vied with them to speak in the midst of their discourse; he did not wait for the bhikkhus to finish their exposition, nor did he question the venerable elder bhikkhus with respect or with careful consideration.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila was present in that assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila addressed the bhikṣu Citto Hatthārohaputto, saying: "Friend!

"You should know that when many bhikṣus are expounding this Dharma and Vinaya, the teaching of the Buddha, you must not compete to speak within it; rather, you may speak only after the bhikṣus have finished their discourse."
You should question the venerable elder bhikṣus with reverence and with careful observation; do not question the venerable elder bhikṣus without reverence or without careful observation.
At that time, the kinsmen and friends of the bhikṣu Ciñcā-Māṇava were all present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the kinsmen and friends of the bhikṣu Ciñcā-Māṇava addressed the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila, saying: "Worthy Mahākoṭṭhila!..."
Do not reprimand or reproach the bhikṣu Citra-hastin excessively. Why is this?
The bhikṣu Citra-hastin possesses great virtue in his precepts and extensive learning; although he may appear to be indolent, he is not conceited.
“Worthy Mahākoṭṭhita! The bhikkhu Cittalapabbatavāsī is able to assist the bhikkhus whenever they have need.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita spoke to the friends and relatives of the bhikkhu Cittalapabbatavāsī:
"Venerable friends!
One who does not know the minds of others must not rashly speak of what is pleasing or displeasing. Why is that?

Suppose there is a person who, while in the presence of the Blessed One, and in the presence of those elders and seniors of long-standing spiritual practice who are conscientious, modest, lovable, and venerable, maintains himself well and guards his conduct well;

yet later, when he is away from the presence of the Blessed One and away from those elders and seniors of long-standing spiritual practice who are conscientious, modest, lovable, and venerable, he frequently associates with householders, engaging in joking, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter.
Having frequently associated with householders and engaged in joking, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that thought of desire has arisen, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
Venerable friends!
"It is just like a cow that enters another's field; the field-guard catches it, either tying it with a rope or confining it in a pen.
Venerable friends, if someone were to say, 'This cow will never again enter another's field,' would he be speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."

That is to say, as for that ox, though it may break or untie the rope with which it is bound, or breach or leap over the enclosure that restrains it, it enters another's field no differently than before.
"Venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who, while in the presence of the Blessed One and before those elders of long-standing seniority who practice the holy life (brahmacarya)—those who are modest, conscientious, lovely, and venerable—maintains himself well and guards himself well;

yet later, when he is away from the presence of the Blessed One and away from those practitioners of the holy life who are modest, conscientious, lovely, and venerable, he frequently associates with householders, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter."
He frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter; having done so, desire arises in his mind.
Once desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
Once his body and mind were thus heated with distress, he abandoned the precepts and withdrew from the holy life.
Venerable friends!
This is what is called "one person."
"Furthermore, worthy sirs!

Suppose there is a person who attains the first dhyāna. Having attained the first dhyāna, he then abides therein himself, no longer seeking what has not yet been attained, nor wishing to acquire what has not yet been acquired, nor wishing to realize what has not yet been realized."
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having thus frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind are thus feverish, he abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
O virtuous ones!

It is just as when, during a great rain, the lakes and ponds in the countryside become filled with water; whatever sand, stones, grass, wood, insects, fish, turtles, frogs, and other aquatic creatures were previously seen there—whether moving away or coming toward, running or staying still—all of them can no longer be seen once the waters have completely filled them.
"Venerable friends!

Suppose someone were to say this: 'In that lake, one will never again see sand, stones, grass, trees, insects with shells, fish, turtles, frogs, or any other aquatic creatures, whether they are going or coming, running or standing. Would such a person be speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."

The waters of that lake may be drunk by elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, pigs, deer, or water buffaloes; or they may be taken for use by humans, or blown upon by the wind and scorched by the sun.

While it was full, one might not have seen the sand, stones, grass, wood, insects, fish, turtles, frogs, or other aquatic creatures as they went and came, ran and stayed. But once the water has receded, these things are seen again just as before.
“In this way, worthy one!

Suppose there is a person who attains the first dhyāna. Having attained that first dhyāna, he dwells securely in it and no longer seeks what has not yet been obtained, nor strives to acquire what has not yet been acquired, nor endeavors to realize what has not yet been realized.
Later, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter.”
He frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of clamorous talk; having done so, desire arises in his mind.
Once desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
"Once his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and ceases his practice of the Way.
O Worthy Ones!
This is what is called 'one person.'"
"Furthermore, worthy friends!

Suppose there is a person who attains the second dhyāna. Having attained the second dhyāna, he abides therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, does not seek to acquire what has not yet been acquired, and does not seek to realize what has not yet been realized."
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in joking, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having frequently associated with laypeople and engaged in joking, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that thought of desire has arisen in him, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind are thus feverish, he abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
Worthies!
"Just as when it rains heavily, the dust in the middle of the four-way intersection is extinguished and turned into mud.
Venerable friends!
If someone were to say, 'This mud in the four-way intersection will never dry up and will never turn back into dust,' would he be speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."

On this crossroads, whether elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, pigs, deer, water buffaloes, or people pass by, the mud on that crossroads, having been dried up by the wind and scorched by the sun, turns back into dust once again.
“In this way, venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who attains the second dhyāna. Having attained the second dhyāna, he dwells securely therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, nor desires to obtain what has not yet been obtained, nor desires to realize what has not yet been realized.”
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having thus frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
O Venerable Ones!
This is called one person.
Furthermore, venerable friends, there may be a person who attains the third dhyāna.

Having attained the third dhyāna, he then abides therein himself, no longer seeking what has not yet been obtained, desiring to obtain it; no longer seeking what has not yet been acquired, desiring to acquire it; no longer seeking what has not yet been realized, desiring to realize it.
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having thus frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
Venerable friends!
"It is like a mountain spring or a lake, clear and level at its banks, settled and unmoving, with no waves.
Venerable friends!
If someone were to say that this mountain spring or lake will never again move, nor will it have waves—is that person speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."
Or suppose a great wind suddenly arises from the east and blows upon that lake, causing its waves to surge;
likewise, great winds may suddenly arise from the south, the west, or the north and blow upon that lake, causing its waves to surge.
“In this way, worthy friends!

Suppose there is a person who attains the third dhyāna; having attained the third dhyāna, he dwells securely therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, nor strives to obtain what has not yet been obtained, nor endeavors to realize what has not yet been realized.”
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having frequently associated with laypeople and engaged in such jesting, arrogance, and idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
Once his body and mind have become feverish, he abandons the precepts and deserts the holy life. Worthies!
This is called the first kind of person.
Furthermore, venerable friends, there may be a person who attains the fourth dhyāna;

having attained the fourth dhyāna, he dwells securely therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, nor strives to obtain what has not yet been obtained, nor strives to realize what has not yet been realized.
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having thus frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
When his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and deserts the holy life.
O virtuous ones!
It is just as when a householder or a householder’s son, having eaten exquisite food until they are fully satiated, no longer has any desire for that which they previously wished to eat.
"Venerable friends!
If someone were to say this: 'Those householders and sons of householders will never again desire to obtain food'—would he be speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."
“After that householder or householder’s son has passed the night in hunger, he may wish to obtain again those very foods he previously did not desire.
Thus it is, venerable sirs!”

Suppose there is a person who attains the fourth dhyāna; having attained the fourth dhyāna, he abides therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, does not strive to obtain what has not yet been obtained, and does not seek to realize what has not yet been realized.
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
Once his body and mind have become feverish, he then abandons the precepts and deserts the holy life.
Venerable friends!
This is called one kind of person.

Furthermore, venerable friends, there may be a person who attains the concentration of non-perception. Having attained that concentration of non-perception, he dwells securely therein and no longer seeks what has not yet been obtained, nor strives to obtain what has not yet been acquired, nor strives to realize what has not yet been realized.
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having thus frequently associated with laypeople, engaged in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once that desire has arisen in his mind, his body becomes feverish and his mind becomes feverish.
Once both his body and mind have become feverish, he abandons the precepts and deserts the path.
Venerable friends!

It is just as if, in a certain secluded place, one hears the sound of the *cīrī-miri* insects; yet in that secluded place, there may be a king or a royal minister staying overnight, and there are the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, and footfalls, the sounds of conch shells, drums, *mṛdaṅga* lutes, and *paṇava* drums, the sounds of dancing, singing, and stringed instruments, and the sounds of eating and drinking—if he has previously heard the sound of the *cīrī-miri* insects, he no longer hears those other sounds.
"Venerable friends!
If someone were to say this: 'In that secluded place, one will never again hear the sound of the chirli-miri insect,' would he be speaking correctly?"
He replied: "No. Why is that? Because..."

When that king and his ministers, having passed the night, returned to their respective dwellings at dawn, they no longer heard the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, or foot-soldiers; nor did they hear the sounds of conch shells, drums, *mṛdaṅga* lutes, *kumbha-tūṇava* drums, dancing, singing, or the sound of stringed instruments, nor the sound of eating and drinking. Yet, once they had departed, they heard those sounds just as before.
"In this way, worthy friends!

Having attained the concentration of the mind of non-perception, and having attained it, one dwells in self-composure; one no longer seeks what has not yet been attained, nor strives to obtain what has not yet been obtained, nor endeavors to realize what has not yet been realized."
At a later time, he frequently associates with laypeople, engaging in jesting, arrogance, and various kinds of idle chatter;
having frequently associated with laypeople and engaged in such jesting, arrogance, and idle chatter, desire arises in his mind.
Once desire has arisen in the mind, there is bodily fever and mental fever.
When one’s body and mind are thus feverish, one then abandons the precepts and deserts the holy life.
O worthy ones!
"This is what is called 'there being one person.

At that time, the bhikṣu Citra-hastin immediately thereafter renounced the precepts and abandoned the path. When Citra-hastin’s kinsmen and friends heard that the bhikṣu Citra-hastin had renounced the precepts and abandoned the path, they went to the place where the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila was, and having arrived, they said to him:
"Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila!"
Did he know the mind of the bhikṣu Citta-hastinī-putra, or did he know it because of some other matter?
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Citta-hastinī-putra has now abandoned the precepts and ceased his practice as a monk.
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita said to those friends:
"Virtuous ones! This matter is indeed as it should be."
Why is this? Because they do not know things as they truly are, and they do not see things as they truly are. Why is this?
"Because they do not know things as they truly are, and do not see things as they truly are.
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila.
Having heard what the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Cīramālikasūtra*, the eleventh, ends here, totaling two thousand four hundred and forty-seven characters. 83. The Discourse on the Elder’s Sleep (83) *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, The Twelfth Discourse on the Elder’s Sleep, Recited in the Second Minor Earth-City Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Vajjī country, staying at the Deer Park in the Bhayaṇḍa Forest on Mount Isigili.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and was staying in the village of Sājīva.
There, while the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was sitting in meditation alone in a quiet place, reflecting, he fell asleep.

The Blessed One, perceiving from afar that the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was sitting in solitary seclusion, meditating in quietude, yet had fallen asleep, knew this and immediately entered a corresponding state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

By means of that concentration, as swiftly as a strong man might extend or contract his arm, he vanished from the Deer Park in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest on Mount Isigili in Pāveyyaka and appeared before the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna at the village of Sājñika in the kingdom of Magadha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One arose from his meditative absorption and said:
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
You are addicted to sleep."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
You are overcome by sleep.
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Regarding the sign by which you are attached to sleep: do not cultivate that sign, nor spread it abroad; in this way, sleep shall be extinguished.”
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if your sleep does not cease because of this, you should follow the Dharma as you have heard it from the beginning;
by receiving, upholding, widely disseminating, and reciting it accordingly, your sleep shall be extinguished."

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If your sleep does not cease because of this, you should follow the Dharma as you have heard it from the beginning, receive and uphold it accordingly, and explain it extensively to others; in this way, your sleep may be extinguished."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If your sleep does not cease because of this, you should follow the Dharma as you have heard it from the beginning;
by receiving and upholding it, reflecting upon it with the mind, and contemplating it with the intellect, your sleep will thus be able to cease."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If you do not cease from sleep because of it, you should rub your ears with both hands; in this way, your sleep may be brought to an end."
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if your sleep does not cease because of this, you should wash your face and eyes with cold water and sprinkle it over your body; in this way, your sleep shall be extinguished.”

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If your sleep does not cease because of this, you should go out from the room, look toward the four directions, and gaze upon the stars; in this way, your sleep may be brought to an end."

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If you do not extinguish this sleep because of it, you should go out from the room and walk up and down on the open ground at the edge of the house, guarding your sense faculties and keeping the mind settled within; by attending to the perception of what lies ahead, you will be able to extinguish this sleep."

"Mahāmaudgalyāyana! If you do not extinguish this sleep because of it, you should leave the walking path and go to the end of the walking path; there, spread out your sitting mat, sit down cross-legged, and in this way, your sleep may be extinguished."
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana, if you do not cease [your practice] because of sleepiness, you should return to your room, fold your upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) in four layers and spread it upon the bed;

fold your outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*) to make a pillow, lie on your right side with one foot placed upon the other, maintaining the perception of light, established in right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and constantly intending to arise."
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Do not calculate the pleasure of the couch or the comfort of lying down; do not covet wealth and profit;
do not be attached to fame. Why is this?
I say that all dharmas are beyond conjunction, yet I also speak of conjunction.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
What dharma do I say is beyond conjunction?
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If the monastic and the lay followers were to assemble together in this manner, I say that such a gathering of the Dharma is not possible.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

If monastics and laypeople gather together, there will be much that is said; if there is much that is said, there will be frivolous chatter; if there is frivolous chatter, the mind will not find rest.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If the mind does not rest, then the mind is separated from concentration.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
Therefore, I say that one cannot meet with them.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
What dharma, I ask, can one meet with?
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!

In those secluded places, I say this Dharma may be practiced together: in mountain forests, under trees, in empty and tranquil spots, on high cliffs, in stone caves, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people—therein one should dwell in accordance with meditative seclusion.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
I say that this Dharma may be practiced in communal assembly.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"

If you enter a village to wander for alms, you should cultivate a sense of revulsion toward gain; you should cultivate revulsion toward offerings and honor. Once you have developed a mind of revulsion toward gain, offerings, and honor, you may then enter the village to beg for food.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Do not enter the village for alms with such a lofty and haughty mind. Why is that?
In the households of various elders, such things occurred: when a bhikṣu came to beg for alms, he caused the elder to lose his composure, and the bhikṣu then thought to himself:
"Who is ruining this elder's household?"
"Why is this? When I enter the householder's home, the householder does not pay attention to me.

Because of this, anxiety arises; because of anxiety, agitation arises; because of agitation, the mind does not find rest; because the mind does not find rest, the mind then departs from concentration.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana! When you preach the Dharma, do not do so with contentious speech. If you speak with contention, you will have much to say; because of this excessive speaking, agitation will arise; because agitation arises, the mind will not find rest; and because the mind does not find rest, it will depart from meditative concentration.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
When you preach the Dharma, do not be forceful; preach the Dharma like a lion.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
When you preach the Dharma, do so with a humble mind; relinquish power, extinguish power, and destroy power. You should not be forceful, but preach the Dharma like a lion.
"Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
You should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the Venerable Mahā-Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“Bhagavān, how does a bhikṣu attain the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life?
The Bhagavān replied:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

If a bhikṣu experiences pleasure, experiences pain, or experiences neither-pain-nor-pleasure, he contemplates those perceptions as impermanent, contemplates their arising and passing away, contemplates their cessation, contemplates dispassion toward them, contemplates their extinction, and contemplates relinquishment.”

Having contemplated the impermanence of both internal and external mental formations, having contemplated their arising and passing away, their cessation, their dispassion, their fading away, and their relinquishment, one does not cling to this world.
Because of this non-clinging to the world, one does not become weary;

because of this lack of weariness, one attains parinirvāṇa, knowing according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Mahā-Maudgalyāyana!
In this way, a bhikṣu attains the ultimate; he reaches the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and brings the holy life to its final completion.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twelfth discourse, "The Discourse on the Elder’s Sleep," ends here; it contains 1,137 characters. This concludes the twenty-seventh fascicle of the Madhyama Āgama, containing 8,009 characters. [Recited in] the second *Kṣullakagrāmaka* section.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 21.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
84. The Sūtra on Being Thornless (84). The Thirteenth Sūtra in the Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, entitled "The Sūtra on Being Thornless."
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Vaiśālī and stayed at the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Monkey River.

There were several renowned and virtuous elder senior great disciples, namely Cāraka, Upacāraka, Bhadrika, Bhaddaji, Aniruddha, and Yaśas; these and other such renowned and virtuous elder senior great disciples were also traveling through Vaiśālī and staying at the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Monkey River, all dwelling near the Buddha’s leaf hut.
When the Licchavis of Vaiśālī heard that the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī by the Monkey River near the High Staircase Pavilion, they thought to themselves:

"We should surely manifest great supernormal power and royal majesty, proclaiming our arrival with a loud voice, as we depart from Vaiśālī to go to where the Buddha is, in order to make offerings and pay him homage."

At that time, the renowned and virtuous elders, the senior and most venerable great disciples, having heard that the Licchavis of Vaiśālī had performed great *ṛddhi* (supernatural powers), assumed royal majesty, and were proclaiming aloud as they departed Vaiśālī to come to the Buddha’s dwelling to make offerings and pay their respects, thought to themselves:

"Meditation has sound as its thorn; the World-Honored One has also said that meditation has sound as its thorn. We would rather go to the Goatherd’s Grotto in the Sāla Grove, where we may dwell in solitude, free from distraction, living apart in a secluded and quiet place, sitting in meditative composure and reflecting."

Thereupon, those renowned and virtuous ones—the elders, the senior monks, and the great disciples—went to the Goatherd’s Grotto in the Sāla Grove; there they dwelt without distraction, living in seclusion and solitude, staying in quiet retreats, sitting in meditation and reflecting.

At that time, a great multitude of Licchavis from Vaiśālī, manifesting great supernormal powers and assuming royal majesty, proclaimed aloud as they departed from Vaiśālī and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was to make offerings and pay him homage.

Some Licchavis of Vaiśālī bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat down to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side; and some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down in silence.

At that time, when the many Licchavis of Vaiśālī were each seated in their places, the Blessed One taught them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; having taught them the Dharma through countless skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, he remained silent.

Thereupon, the many Licchavis of Vaiśālī, having had the Dharma taught to them by the Blessed One, having been inspired with longing and established in joy, rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Not long after the Licchavis of Vaiśālī had departed,
the Blessed One asked the bhikṣus:
"Where have the elders, the senior disciples, and the great disciples gone?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“World-Honored One! When the elders,

the senior disciples, and the great disciples heard that the Licchavis of Vaiśālī had performed great *ṛddhi* (supernatural powers) and displayed royal majesty, proclaiming it with loud voices as they departed from Vaiśālī to come to the Buddha’s presence to make offerings and pay their respects, they thought thus:”
"Meditation has sound as its thorn; the World-Honored One has also said that meditation has sound as its thorn.

We should rather go to the Goatherd’s Grotto at the Sāla Grove, where we may dwell without distraction, living apart, in solitude, in a secluded and quiet place, sitting in meditation and reflecting."
“World-Honored One!
Let the elders, the senior disciples, and the great disciples go together to him.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One sighed and said:
“Excellent! Excellent!
It is fitting that the elders, the most venerable ones, and the great disciples should speak thus.”
“Meditation has sound as its thorn; the World-Honored One has also said that meditation has sound as its thorn.

Why is this so? It is because I have indeed spoken thus: for one in meditation, there is a thorn; for one who upholds the precepts, breaking the precepts is a thorn; for one who guards the sense faculties, adorning the body is a thorn; for one who cultivates the contemplation of impurity, the perception of beauty is a thorn; for one who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, anger is a thorn; for one who abstains from alcohol, drinking alcohol is a thorn; and for one who leads the holy life, beholding women is a thorn.

For one who enters the first dhyāna, sound is a thorn; for one who enters the second dhyāna, applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) are thorns; for one who enters the third dhyāna, joy (*prīti*) is a thorn; for one who enters the fourth dhyāna, inhalation and exhalation are thorns; for one who enters the sphere of infinite space, the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is a thorn; for one who enters the sphere of infinite consciousness, the perception of the sphere of infinite space is a thorn; for one who enters the sphere of nothingness, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is a thorn; for one who enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is a thorn; and for one who enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling themselves are thorns.
"Furthermore, there are three thorns:
the thorn of sensual desire, the thorn of ill will, and the thorn of delusion.

These three thorns have been abandoned and fully understood by the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted; their roots have been uprooted, they are extinguished and will not arise again. Thus, the Arhat is without thorns, the Arhat is free from thorns, the Arhat is without thorns and free from thorns."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Thirteenth Discourse on the Thornless concludes, totaling eight hundred and thirty-five characters. 85. The Discourse on the True Person (85). Middle Āgama, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, The Fourteenth Discourse on the True Person. Recited in the Second Section on the Small Earth City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now teach you the Dharma of the true person and the Dharma of the untrue person. Listen closely, listen closely, and reflect upon it well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"What is the non-Dharma of a true person?"

Suppose there is a person who has gone forth from a noble and wealthy family to study the Path, while others have not; because of that noble and wealthy lineage, he regards himself as superior and others as inferior. This is called the way of one who is not a true person.
The Dharma of the True Person is to contemplate in this way: "I do not abandon lust, anger, and delusion because I belong to a noble and wealthy clan.

There may be another person who is not from a noble or wealthy family but has left the household life to study the Path; he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Because of this, he receives offerings and respect. One who thus proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of Truth neither esteems himself nor disparages others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, there may be a person who is handsome and attractive, while others are not. Because of that handsomeness and attractiveness, he esteems himself and disparages others; this is called the way of those who are not true persons."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"I do not practice the abandonment of lust, anger, and delusion because of this physical beauty and attractiveness.

There may be a person who is neither beautiful nor attractive, yet they practice the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforming to the Dharma, following the Dharma in its successive stages; because of this, they receive offerings and respect. One who thus proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of Truth does not hold themselves dear nor disparage others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, there may be one person who is eloquent and skilled in discourse, while others are not. Because of this eloquence and skill in discourse, he esteems himself and disparages others; this is called the practice of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"I do not sever lust, anger, and delusion because of my eloquence and skill in speech.

There may be another person who lacks eloquence and skill in speech, yet he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma and its successive stages; because of this, he receives offerings and respect. Thus, one who proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of True Reality neither exalts himself nor disparages others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, there may be a certain person who is an elder, recognized by the king and known by the multitude, and possesses great merit, whereas others do not. Because he is such an elder—recognized by the king and known by the multitude, and possessing great merit—he holds himself in high esteem and looks down upon others. This is called the practice of one who is not a true man."
The Dharma of the True Person involves making this observation:
"It is not because I am an elder, recognized by kings and known to the masses, and possessed of great merit, that I have severed lust, anger, and delusion."

"Suppose there is a person who is not an elder, neither recognized by kings nor known by the multitude, and who possesses no great merit; yet he practices according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma. Because of this, he receives offerings and respect. One who thus proceeds toward the attainment of the True Dharma does not exalt himself nor disparage others; this is called the Dharma of a true person."

"Furthermore, there may be a person who recites the Sūtras, upholds the Vinaya, studies the Abhidharma, is well-versed in the Āgamas, and has extensively studied many scriptures, whereas others do not. Because he is well-versed in the Āgamas and has extensively studied many scriptures, he esteems himself and disparages others; this is called the way of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"It is not because of my familiarity with the Āgamas or my extensive study of scriptures that I have severed lust, anger, and delusion."

"Furthermore, there may be a person who is not well-versed in the Āgamas and has not studied many scriptures, yet he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma and its successive stages. Because of this, he receives offerings and respect. One who thus proceeds toward the attainment of the True Dharma does not exalt himself nor disparage others; this is called the Dharma of a true person."

"Furthermore, suppose there is a person who wears rag-robes, maintains the three dharma-robes, and possesses the 'unconceited' robe, while others do not. Because he possesses this unconceited robe, he holds himself in high esteem and looks down upon others; this is called the practice of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"I do not sever lust, anger, and delusion because I wear these robes of non-arrogance.

There may be another person who does not wear the robes of non-arrogance, yet he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, accords with the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma and its successive stages; because of this, he receives offerings and respect. Thus, one who proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of True Reality neither exalts himself nor disparages others—this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, there may be a person who constantly practices begging for alms, limiting his rice to five sheng and restricting himself to food from seven houses, or perhaps eating only once a day, abstaining from even water after midday; yet others do not do so. Because he abstains from water after midday, he esteems himself and disparages others. This is called the way of those who are not true persons."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this kind of contemplation:
"It is not because of my abstaining from drinking liquids after midday that I have severed lust, anger, and delusion.

There may be another person who does not abstain from drinking liquids after midday, yet he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; because of this, he receives offerings and respect. Thus, one who proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of Truth neither esteems himself nor disparages others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, there may be a person who dwells in a secluded place, beneath the trees of a mountain forest, or stays upon a high cliff, or halts in the open air, or resides among burial mounds; whereas others do not. Because of this knowledge of the proper time, he esteems himself and disparages others. This is called the practice of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"It is not because of my knowledge of the proper time that I have abandoned lust, anger, and delusion.

There may be another person who does not know the proper time, yet he practices the Dharma according to the Dharma, conforms to the Dharma, and proceeds toward the Dharma and its successive stages; because of this, he receives offerings and respect. Thus, one who proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of True Reality neither exalts himself nor disparages others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

"Furthermore, suppose there is a person who attains the first dhyāna; because he has attained the first dhyāna, he esteems himself and disparages others. This is called the practice of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Person involves this contemplation:
"Regarding the first dhyāna, the World-Honored One has taught it in immeasurable ways; if one forms a conceptual attachment to it, that is called craving."

Because of this, he receives offerings and respect; one who thus proceeds toward attaining the Dharma of True Reality does not exalt himself nor disparage others—this is called the Dharma of a True Person.

"Furthermore, suppose there is a person who attains the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, while others do not. Because he has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he esteems himself and disparages others; this is called the practice of one who is not a true person."
The Dharma of the True Persons involves this contemplation:
"Regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the World-Honored One has taught it in immeasurable ways; if one calculates or conceptualizes it, that is called craving."

Because of this, he receives offerings and respect. One who thus proceeds toward the attainment of the Dharma of True Reality neither esteems himself nor disparages others; this is called the Dharma of the True Person.

“Monks! These are called the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person. You should know the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person; having known the qualities of a true person and the qualities of one who is not a true person, you should abandon the qualities of one who is not a true person and train in the qualities of a true person. You should train yourselves in this way.”
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
[The section on] the Noble and Distinguished, the Handsome, the Eloquent, the Elder, and the Reciters of the Sūtras.
Robes, food, non-action, and meditation; the four formless [attainments] follow at the end.

Thus ends the Fourteenth Sūtra of the *Mahāpuruṣa*, totaling one thousand two hundred and ninety-three characters. 86. Sūtra on the Places of Teaching (86). Long Discourses, Chapter on King Dīrghāyu, Sūtra on the Places of Teaching, Number Fifteen. Recited in the Second Minor Town Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation and, accompanied by several young bhikṣus, went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side; the young bhikṣus also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
how should I instruct and admonish these young bhikṣus?"
"How does one provide instruction?
How does one preach the Dharma for their sake?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! You should explain the foundations and teach the foundations to the young bhikṣus.

If you explain the foundations and teach the foundations to the young bhikṣus, they will attain security, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish with distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.”
Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One,
now is precisely the right time.”
"O Sugata!
Now is precisely the right time.

If the World-Honored One were to explain the stations and the teaching on the stations for the sake of these young bhikṣus, I and the young bhikṣus, having heard them from the World-Honored One, shall properly receive and uphold them."
The World-Honored One said:
"Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect upon this well."
"I shall explain this in detail for you and for the young bhikṣus.
The Venerable Ānanda and the others received the instruction and listened.
The Blessed One said:

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Ānanda!”

"These five aggregates of clinging, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five aggregates of clinging to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six internal sense bases: the eye base, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases. Ānanda!”

"These six internal sense bases, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these six internal sense bases to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be tormented by fever, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six external bases: the base of forms, and the bases of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. Ānanda!”

"These six external bases, you should explain to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct these six external bases to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the duration of their lives."

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six groups of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these six classes of consciousness to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these six classes of consciousness to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be distressed by feverish heat, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six bases of contact: the contact of the eye, the contact of the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, and the contact of the mind.”

Ānanda! Regarding these six bases of contact, you should explain them to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these six bases of contact to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six bodies of sensation: visual sensation, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental sensation. Ānanda!”

"These six bodies of awakening, you should explain them to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct these six bodies of awakening to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six groups of perception: the perception of the eye, and the perceptions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Ānanda!”

"These six groups of perception, you should explain to the young bhikṣus and teach them. If you explain and teach these six groups of perception to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six groups of volition: volition regarding the eye, and volition regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these six groups of volition to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these six groups of volition to the young bhikṣus, they will attain tranquility, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by fever, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six bases of craving: craving for the eye, and craving for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Ānanda!”

"These six bases of craving, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus.
