If you explain and teach these six bases of craving to the young bhikṣus, they will attain security, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by fever, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the six elements: the earth element, the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these six elements to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus regarding these six elements, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the phenomena produced by dependent origination:
‘When this exists, that exists; when this does not exist, that does not exist. When this arises, that arises; when this ceases, that ceases.’”

Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; conditioned by birth are old age and death.

If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if volitional formations cease, then consciousness ceases; if consciousness ceases, then name-and-form cease; if name-and-form cease, then the six sense bases cease; if the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases; if contact ceases, then feeling ceases; if feeling ceases, then craving ceases; if craving ceases, then clinging ceases; if clinging ceases, then existence ceases; if existence ceases, then birth ceases; and if birth ceases, then aging and death cease.

Ānanda! This dependent origination and the phenomena produced by dependent origination—you should explain this to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in this dependent origination and the phenomena produced by dependent origination, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four foundations of mindfulness: contemplating the body as body, and contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these four foundations of mindfulness to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these four foundations of mindfulness to the young bhikṣus, they will attain security, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four right endeavors: a bhikkhu, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, arouses desire, seeks after means, exerts effort, and applies himself with uplifted mind to their abandonment.”
For the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, he generates desire, seeks means, exerts effort, applies energy, uplifts the mind, and strives.
For the sake of bringing about arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, seeks means, exerts effort, applies energy, uplifts the mind, and strives.

For the sake of maintaining, not forgetting, not regressing, further increasing, extensively spreading, and bringing to full completion the wholesome states that have already arisen, one arouses desire, seeks after skillful means, and practices with diligence, uplifting the mind and exerting effort.

Ānanda! You should explain these four right endeavors to the young bhikṣus and instruct them in them. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in these four right endeavors, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). A bhikṣu, having accomplished the concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*), burns away all formations (*saṃskāra*) by cultivating the base of psychic power, relying on dispassion, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, aspiring for the unsurpassed state. Likewise, he accomplishes the concentration of energy (*vīrya-samādhi*), the concentration of mind (*citta-samādhi*), and the concentration of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-samādhi*), burning away all formations.”
One cultivates the bases of psychic power, relying on dispassion, relying on detachment, and relying on cessation, with the aspiration for the state beyond categories. Ānanda!

You should explain these four bases of psychic power to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct these four bases of psychic power to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four dhyānas: a bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.”

Ānanda! You should explain these four dhyānas to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and teach these four dhyānas to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the Four Noble Truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these Four Noble Truths to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in these Four Noble Truths, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish with affliction, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you four perceptions: that a bhikṣu has a small perception, a great perception, an immeasurable perception, and a perception of nothingness.”

Ānanda! You should explain these four perceptions to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and teach these four perceptions to the young bhikṣus, they will attain tranquility, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four immeasurables: a bhikkhu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, dwells having pervaded one direction, accomplished and suffused with it.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated.

Likewise, one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated.

Ānanda! You should explain these four immeasurables to the young bhikṣus and instruct them in them. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in these four immeasurables, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four formless states: a bhikkhu, having abandoned all perceptions of form, even attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

Ānanda! You should explain these four formless attainments to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct these four formless attainments to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish with distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four noble lineages: that monks and nuns, obtaining coarse and plain robes, know contentment and do not seek to fulfill their desires for the sake of clothing.”
If he does not obtain robes, he is not distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not become deluded;
if he obtains robes, he is not stained by them nor attached to them, having no desire for them, no greed for them, no contact with them, and no calculation regarding them.

Seeing the peril and knowing the way out, one uses robes; for one who thus understands the benefit of such matters and remains diligent and clearly comprehending, this is called a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī dwelling rightly in the ancient noble lineage.

Regarding such food and dwellings, one desires to abandon what is to be abandoned and desires to cultivate what is to be cultivated. Because of this desire to abandon what is to be abandoned and to cultivate what is to be cultivated, one does not hold oneself in high esteem nor disparage others. One who is thus diligent, untiring, and possesses right knowledge regarding these matters is said to be a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī dwelling correctly in the ancient noble lineage.

Ānanda! You should explain these four noble lineages to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and instruct these four noble lineages to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be troubled by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the four fruits of the śramaṇa: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the supreme fruit of arhatship.”

Ānanda! You should explain these four fruits of asceticism to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and teach these four fruits of asceticism to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five perceptions of mature liberation: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of the impurity of foul secretions, and the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in.”

Ānanda! These five perceptions of liberation through ripening, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five perceptions of liberation through ripening to the young bhikṣus, they will attain security, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five bases of liberation; by means of these, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has not yet attained liberation of mind, they may attain liberation of mind; if their outflows have not yet been exhausted, they may exhaust them without remainder; if they have not yet attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa, they may attain unsurpassed nirvāṇa.”
What are these five? Ānanda!
The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; those wise fellow practitioners of the holy life also teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.

Ānanda! If the Blessed One teaches the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, and those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life also teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, they, having heard the Dharma, will understand it and comprehend its meaning;
because they understand the Dharma and comprehend its meaning, they will attain joy.
Because of joy, one attains rapture;
because of rapture, one attains tranquility of body;
because of tranquility of body, one attains the experience of bliss.
Because of the experience of joy, one attains concentration of mind. Ānanda!
Because of the concentration of mind, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī attains vision according to reality and knowledge according to truth.
Because one sees things as they truly are and knows them as they really are, one attains disenchantment;
because of disenchantment, one attains dispassion;
because of dispassion, one attains liberation.

Because of liberation, one knows that one is liberated; one knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

Ānanda! This is called the first station of liberation. Because of this, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs whose minds were not yet liberated attain liberation; those who had not exhausted all outflows attain their exhaustion without remainder; and those who had not attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa attain unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

The World-Honored One does not preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, nor do those wise practitioners of the holy life preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; rather, they merely read extensively the teachings as they have previously heard and recited them."
If one does not extensively read those teachings as they were originally heard and recited, but merely explains them extensively to others according to what was originally heard and recited;

or if one does not explain those teachings as they were originally heard and recited to others extensively, but merely reflects upon and discriminates them with the mind according to what was originally heard and recited.
If one does not mentally reflect upon or discriminate the teachings previously heard or recited, but merely skillfully upholds the characteristics of the various samādhis—

Ānanda, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī skillfully upholds the characteristics of the various samādhis, they will then know the Dharma and understand its meaning; because they know the Dharma and understand its meaning, they will attain joy.
Because of joy, one attains gladness;
because of gladness, one attains tranquility of body;
because of tranquility of body, one attains the experience of bliss.
Because of the experience of joy, one attains concentration of mind. Ānanda!
Because of the concentration of mind, a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī attains vision according to reality and knowledge according to truth.
Because one sees things as they truly are and knows them as they really are, one attains disenchantment;
because of disenchantment, one attains dispassion;
because of dispassion, one attains liberation.

Because of liberation, one comes to know liberation: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—one knows this as it truly is.

Ānanda! This is called the fifth station of liberation. By means of this, monks and nuns who have not yet attained liberation of mind attain liberation; who have not yet exhausted all outflows attain their exhaustion without remainder; and who have not yet attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* attain unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.

Ānanda! These five bases of liberation you should explain to the young bhikṣus to instruct them. If you explain and teach these five bases of liberation to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be troubled by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. Ānanda!”

"You should explain these five faculties to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these five faculties to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be troubled by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Ānanda!”

"These five powers, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus. If you explain and teach these five powers to the young bhikṣus, they will attain security, gain power and happiness, their bodies and minds will be free from feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the five elements of renunciation.
What are these five?

Ānanda! A well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and deeply contemplates sensual desire. Because he thoroughly and deeply contemplates sensual desire, his mind does not incline toward it, does not delight in it, does not approach it, and does not have faith-understanding in it.

If a thought of sensual desire arises, it immediately melts away and shrivels up; it turns back and cannot expand, and he abandons it, dwelling no longer in desire, loathing and wearying of sensual desire.
Ānanda! It is just as when chicken feathers and sinews are placed in a fire; they immediately melt away and shrivel up, and once transformed, they can no longer be stretched out. Ānanda!

The well-learned noble disciple is also like this, observing desire with extreme gravity. Because he observes desire with such extreme gravity, his mind does not incline toward desire, does not delight in desire, does not draw near to desire, and does not have faith-understanding in desire.

If a thought of desire arises, it immediately dissolves and shrivels away; it turns back and cannot expand, as he abandons and does not dwell upon desire, feeling revulsion and weariness toward desire.

Contemplating desirelessness, the mind inclines toward desirelessness, delights in desirelessness, draws near to desirelessness, and gains faith and understanding in desirelessness; the mind becomes unobstructed and unturbid, attaining happiness and being able to bring about happiness, remaining far removed from all desires and the various outflows, fevers, and sorrows born of desire.

One understands that, one is liberated from that, and one is further liberated from that; one no longer experiences such a perception, namely, the perception that arises with desire as its cause—this, Ānanda, is the escape from desire.
This is called the first realm of the definitive escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a learned noble disciple thoroughly and deeply contemplates ill will; because he thoroughly and deeply contemplates ill will, his mind does not incline toward ill will, does not delight in ill will, does not draw near to ill will, and does not place faith in or resolve upon ill will."

If a mind of anger arises, it is immediately melted away and shriveled up; it turns back so that it cannot expand. One abandons and does not dwell in anger, feeling revulsion and weariness toward anger as something foul and evil.
Ānanda! It is just as when chicken feathers and sinews are placed in fire: they immediately melt away and shrivel up, so that they can no longer be stretched out again. Ānanda!

The well-learned noble disciple is likewise in this regard: he observes hatred with extreme gravity. Because he observes hatred with such extreme gravity, his mind does not incline toward hatred, does not delight in hatred, does not approach hatred, and does not find faith or conviction in hatred.

If a thought of hatred arises, it is immediately dissolved, consumed, and shriveled; it turns back and cannot expand, being abandoned and not remaining, as he finds hatred foul, loathsome, and wearying.

He contemplates non-ill will, inclines his mind toward non-ill will, delights in non-ill will, draws near to non-ill will, and resolves with faith in non-ill will. His mind is unobstructed and unturbid; he attains happiness and is able to bring about happiness. He remains far removed from all ill will, as well as from the outflows, fevers, and sorrows that arise because of ill will.

One understands that, one is liberated from that, and one is further liberated from that; one no longer experiences this perception, namely, the perception born of anger. Such, Ānanda, is the escape from anger.
This is called the second realm of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and deeply contemplates harm; because he thoroughly and deeply contemplates harm, his mind does not incline toward harm, does not delight in harm, does not draw near to harm, and does not have faith-understanding in harm."
If a mind of malice arises, it immediately melts away and shrivels up; it turns back and cannot expand, abandoning and not dwelling in malice, detesting and wearying of that foul and evil malice.
Ānanda! It is just as when chicken feathers or sinews are placed in a fire; they immediately melt away and shrivel up, so that they can no longer be stretched out again. Ānanda!

The well-versed noble disciple is likewise thus: he observes harm with extreme gravity. Because he observes harm with extreme gravity, his mind does not incline toward harm, does not delight in harm, does not draw near to harm, and does not have faith-understanding in harm.

If a thought of harm arises, it immediately dissolves and shrivels away; it turns back and cannot expand, and having abandoned it, he does not dwell in harm, but finds it foul, loathsome, and wearying.

He contemplates harmlessness; his mind inclines toward harmlessness; he delights in harmlessness; he draws near to harmlessness; he has faith and understanding in harmlessness; his mind is unobstructed, his mind is unturbid, and his mind attains happiness. He is able to bring about happiness, remaining far removed from all harm and from the outflows, fevers, and sorrows born of harm.

He understands that, he is liberated from that, and he is further liberated from that; he no longer experiences this perception, namely, the perception born of harm. Such is the escape from harm. Ānanda!
This is called the third element of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple thoroughly and deeply contemplates form. Because he thoroughly and deeply contemplates form, his mind does not incline toward form, does not delight in form, does not draw near to form, and does not place faith in or resolve upon form."

If a thought of form arises, it immediately dissolves and shrivels away; it cannot be extended or expanded once it has turned back. One abandons and does not dwell upon form, feeling revulsion and weariness toward form.
Ānanda! It is just as when chicken feathers and sinews are placed in a fire; they immediately melt away and shrivel up, becoming so transformed that they can no longer be stretched out. Ānanda!

The well-learned noble disciple is also like this: he observes form with extreme thoroughness. Because he observes form with such extreme thoroughness, his mind does not incline toward form, does not delight in form, does not draw near to form, and does not find faith or understanding in form.

If a thought of form arises, it immediately dissolves and shrivels away; it turns back and cannot expand, being abandoned and no longer dwelling upon form, as he finds form foul, loathsome, and wearying.

Contemplating the formless, the mind inclines toward the formless, delights in the formless, and draws near to the formless; one gains faith and understanding in the formless, the mind becomes unobstructed and free from turbidity, attains happiness, and is able to bring about bliss, remaining far removed from all forms and the outflows, fevers, and sorrows born of form.

One understands that, one is liberated from that, and one is further liberated from that; one no longer experiences this perception, namely, the perception arising with form as its cause. Such, Ānanda, is the escape from form.
This is called the fourth realm of escape.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, a well-learned noble disciple observes his own body with extreme care. Because he observes his own body with extreme care, his mind does not incline toward his body, does not delight in his body, does not draw near to his body, and does not place faith in or understand his body."

If one's own body and mind arise, they immediately melt away and shrivel; they turn back and cannot be extended, abandoning their own bodies so that they do not dwell within them, feeling revulsion and weariness toward their own bodies as something foul and loathsome.
Ānanda! It is just as when chicken feathers or sinews are placed in a fire; they immediately melt away and shrivel up, so that they can never again be stretched out. Ānanda!

The learned noble disciple is likewise in this way: he observes his own body with extreme gravity. Because he observes his own body with such extreme gravity, his mind does not incline toward his body, does not delight in his body, does not draw near to his body, and does not have faith-understanding in his body.

If a thought of self arises in his mind, it immediately dissolves and shrivels away; it cannot expand or spread out again. He abandons and does not dwell upon his body, feeling revulsion and weariness toward his body.

One contemplates the absence of a self-body, directs the mind toward the absence of a self-body, delights in the absence of a self-body, draws near to the absence of a self-body, and gains faith and understanding in the absence of a self-body. Thus, the mind becomes unobstructed, the mind becomes unturbid, the mind attains happiness, and one is able to bring about happiness, remaining far removed from all notions of a self-body and the various outflows, fevers, and sorrows born of a self-body.

He understands them, he is liberated from them, and he is further emancipated from them; he no longer experiences these perceptions, namely, those perceptions that arise with his own body as their cause. In this way, there is an escape from his own body.
Ānanda! This is called the fifth element of the outlet. "Ānanda!"

"These five elements of escape, you should explain and teach to the young bhikṣus; if you explain and teach these five elements of escape to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by fever, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."
“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the seven riches: the riches of faith, ethical discipline, shame, dread of wrongdoing, learning, generosity, and wisdom. Ānanda!”

"These seven treasures, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus; if you explain and teach these seven treasures to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the seven powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. Ānanda!”

"These seven powers, you should explain and teach them to the young bhikṣus; if you explain and teach these seven powers to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain power, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish with distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the seven factors of enlightenment: the factor of mindfulness, the factor of investigation of phenomena, the factor of energy, the factor of rapture, the factor of tranquility, the factor of concentration, and the factor of equanimity.”

Ānanda! You should explain these seven factors of enlightenment to the young bhikṣus and instruct them. If you explain and instruct these seven factors of enlightenment to the young bhikṣus, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by feverish distress, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.

“Ānanda! I have previously taught you the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; these are the eight.”

Ānanda! You should explain this Noble Eightfold Path to the young bhikṣus and instruct them in it. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in this Noble Eightfold Path, they will attain tranquility, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be feverish with affliction, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!”
"How extraordinary!
The Blessed One has taught the stations and the instruction on the stations for the sake of the young bhikṣus.
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda! So it is, so it is.
How extraordinary!
"How extraordinary!
I have taught the stations and the instruction on the stations for the young bhikṣus, Ānanda!"
"If you were to ask the Tathāgata further about the summit-dharmas and the falling away from the summit-dharmas, you would then have the utmost faith and joy in the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!"
Now is precisely the right time, Sugata!
Now is precisely the right time!

If the Blessed One were to explain the summit-dharma (*mūrdha-dharma*) and the falling away from the summit-dharma to the young bhikṣus, as well as provide instruction thereon, then I and the young bhikṣus, having heard it from the Blessed One, would properly receive and uphold it.
The Blessed One said: "Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall explain to you and to the young bhikṣus the summit-dharma (mūrdha-dharma) and the falling away from the summit-dharma."
The Venerable Ānanda and the others received the instruction and listened.
The World-Honored One said to them: “Ānanda!

The learned noble disciple, with a mind directed toward reality, reflects, weighs, and skillfully contemplates and analyzes impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. As he thus reflects, thus weighs, and thus skillfully contemplates and analyzes, there arises in him patience, joy, and desire; he desires to hear, desires to reflect, and desires to contemplate. Ānanda!
This is called the stage of the summit (mūrdhan). Ānanda!
If one attains this stage of the summit and yet loses it and declines, failing to cultivate its protection and failing to practice with diligence—Ānanda!
This is called falling back from the stage of the summit.
In this same way, Ānanda, there is the arising of internal and external consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, elements, and dependent origination.

The well-learned noble disciple contemplates, weighs, and skillfully examines this dependent origination and the phenomena of dependent origination as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. As he thus contemplates, thus weighs, and thus skillfully examines and distinguishes them, there arises in him patience, joy, and aspiration; he desires to hear, desires to reflect, and desires to contemplate.
Ānanda! This is called the dharma of the summit. Ānanda!
Ānanda, if one has attained this state of the summit (mūrdha-dharma) but then loses it and declines, failing to practice its protection and failing to cultivate diligence—
this, Ānanda, is called falling away from the state of the summit. Ānanda!

"You should explain this Summit Dharma (*mūrdhāna*) and the falling away from the Summit Dharma to the young bhikṣus and instruct them in it. If you explain and instruct the young bhikṣus in this Summit Dharma and the falling away from the Summit Dharma, they will attain peace, attain strength, and attain happiness; their bodies and minds will not be afflicted by fever, and they will practice the holy life for the rest of their lives."

“Ānanda! For your sake, I have taught you the stations and the instructions on the stations, as well as the summit-dharma and the falling away from the summit-dharma. Just as a teacher who has great compassion, pity, and sympathy for his disciples, seeking their welfare, benefit, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness, I have now done so.

"You yourselves must likewise do so: go to a secluded place, to the mountains, forests, or the foot of a tree, to an empty and quiet spot, and sit in meditation with contemplation. Do not be negligent; apply yourselves with diligent effort, lest you later have cause for regret."
"This is my instruction; this is my admonition.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the young bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The aggregates, the internal and external, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, volition, craving, the elements,
dependent origination, mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the meditations, the truths,
the perceptions, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, the lineages, the fruits of recluseship, and liberation.
The *Āyatana-sutta*, the *Indriya-sutta*, the *Bala-sutta*, the *Nissaraṇa-sutta*, the *Dhana-sutta*, the *Bala-sutta*, the *Bojjhaṅga-sutta*, the *Magga-sutta*, and the *Sīsapā-vanopama-sutta*:

thus ends the fifteenth discourse, the *Āyatana-sutta*. [Total: 5,197 characters]. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Fascicle 21: [Total: 7,324 characters]. The second section, the *Dīghāvu-rāja-vagga*, is complete:

Chapter Three: The Chapter on Defilement (Kleśavarga). This chapter contains ten sūtras. Recited at the Second Small Earth-City (Dvitiya-kṣudra-pāṭaliputra). 1. Defilement (Kleśa) 2. Seeking (Paryeṣaṇā) 3.
The Bhikṣu’s Request (Bhikṣuparipṛcchā) 4. Wisdom (Jñāna) 5. Cunda’s Questions on Views (Cundaparipṛcchādṛṣṭi)
The Metaphor of the Flower, the Purity of Water, and Brahmā; Black, Abiding, and Non-existence follow last.
(87) The Sūtra on the Chapter of Defilements (87), the First Sūtra of the Chapter of Defilements in the Madhyama Āgama. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Pañcasala, staying at the Deer Park in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest on Mount Kālaparvata.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
There are four kinds of persons in the world."
What are the four?
There may be a person who internally possesses impurity but does not know it; he does not know, as it truly is, that he has internal impurity.
Or there may be a person who internally possesses impurity and knows it; he knows, as it truly is, that he has internal impurity.
There may be a person who is inwardly truly free from defilement but does not know it, and being inwardly free from defilement, does not know it as it truly is;
or there may be a person who is inwardly truly free from defilement and knows it, and being inwardly free from defilement, knows it as it truly is.
"Venerable friends!
If there is a person who is inwardly truly defiled yet does not know it, and who does not know his inner defilement as it really is, this person is the most base among all people."

If there is a person who truly possesses internal impurity within and knows it as it really is—knowing that they have internal impurity as it truly is—that person is the most excellent among all people.
If there is a person who is inwardly truly defiled yet does not know it, and who does not know, as it truly is, that they are inwardly defiled, this person is the most base among all people.
If there is a person who truly has no impurity within and knows it for himself, knowing it as it really is—that person is the most excellent among all people.
Then, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Sāriputta, and said to him:
“Venerable Sāriputta! ”
For what cause and for what reason are the former two said to both possess defilement and have defiled minds, yet one is base and the other is supreme?
Furthermore, for what cause and for what reason are the latter two said to both be without defilement and have undefiled minds, yet one is base and the other is supreme?
Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta replied to that bhikkhu: "Worthy one!

If there is a person who is inwardly defiled yet does not know it, and who does not know as it truly is that he is inwardly defiled, you should know that such a person does not desire to abandon his defilements, does not seek the means [thereof], and does not train with diligence; thus, being possessed of defilements, he passes away with a mind defiled by those impurities."
Because he dies with a defiled mind due to the presence of impurities, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unfavorable destination. Why is this?
Because he dies with a defiled mind due to the presence of impurities.
"O Wise One!

It is just as if someone were to buy a copper plate from a market stall or a copper smith’s workshop that was already defiled by dust and grime. Having brought it home, they do not wash away the dust repeatedly, nor do they scrub it repeatedly, nor do they dry it in the sun; furthermore, they place it in a dusty location. In this way, the copper plate would only take on more dust and grime."
"O Worthy One!

Thus, if there is a person who internally possesses defilements yet does not know them—who does not know, as it truly is, that they have internal defilements—it should be known that such a person does not desire to abandon those defilements, does not seek the means [for their abandonment], and does not train with diligence.

Being possessed of defilements, they pass away with a defiled mind; because they pass away with a defiled mind due to possessing defilements, they die an ignoble death and are reborn in an unfavorable destination."
Why is that? Because he has passed away with a mind defiled by impurities.
"Worthy one!..."

If there is a person who knows, as it truly is, that "there is impurity within me; this impurity truly exists within me," one should know that such a person desires to abandon this impurity, seeks the means for its removal, and trains with diligence. He then becomes free from impurity and passes away with a mind undefiled by impurity.
Because he passes away with a mind free from impurity and undefiled by impurity, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a happy destination.
Why is that? Because he has died with a mind free from defilement and untainted by impurities,
O worthy one!

It is just as if someone were to buy a copper plate from a marketplace or a copper smith’s workshop; though it is defiled by dust and grime, once they have brought it home, they wash away the dust repeatedly, polish it repeatedly, and dry it repeatedly in the sun, keeping it away from dusty places, so that the copper plate becomes utterly pure and clean.
"O Wise One!

Thus, if there is a person who knows as it truly is: 'I have impurity within; this impurity truly exists within me,' one should know that such a person, desiring to abandon this impurity, seeks the means and trains with diligence. He then becomes free from impurity, and he passes away with a mind unstained by impurity.
Because he passes away with a mind unstained by impurity, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a happy destination."
Why is that? Because he has died with a mind free from defilement and untainted by impurities.
"Venerable one!..."

If there is a person who is internally free from impurity, yet does not know as it truly is that they are indeed free from this impurity within, you should know that such a person does not guard against those phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because they do not guard against those phenomena known through the eye and ear, they become entangled by a mind of desire;

thus, possessing desire and impurity, they pass away with a defiled mind. Because they pass away with a mind possessed of desire and impurity, they die an ignoble death and are reborn in an unfavorable destination.
Why is that? Because, O worthy one, he passes away with a mind defiled by desire and impurity.
Worthy one!

It is just as if a person were to buy a copper plate from a market stall or from a copper smith’s workshop; it is stainless and pure. Having brought it home, if they do not wash away the dust repeatedly, do not polish it repeatedly, and do not dry it repeatedly in the sun, but place it where there is much dust, that copper plate will inevitably become covered with grime and dirt.
"O Wise One!

Thus, if there is a person who has no impurity within himself, yet does not know as it truly is that he has no such impurity within, you should know that this person does not guard against those things known by the eye and the ear. Because he does not guard against those things known by the eye and the ear, he becomes entangled by a mind of desire; he thus possesses desire and impurity, and with a defiled mind, he passes away.
Because he passes away with a defiled mind possessed by desire and impurity, he dies an ignoble death and is reborn in an unfavorable realm."
Why is that? Because he has passed away with a mind defiled by desire and impurity,
O worthy one.

If there is a person who knows as it truly is: "I have no impurity within; indeed, there is no such impurity within me," you should know that this person guards against those phenomena known through the eye and ear. Because he guards against those phenomena known through the eye and ear, he is not entangled by a mind of desire. Thus, being without desire and without impurity, he passes away with an undefiled mind.
Because he passes away with an undefiled mind, free from desire and impurity, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a good destination.
Why is that? Because, O worthy one, he has passed away with a mind free from desire, free from defilement, and unstained by impurity.
O worthy one!

It is just as if someone were to buy a copper plate from a marketplace or from a copper smith; it would be stainless and pure. Having brought it back, they would wash and polish it repeatedly, scrub and wipe it repeatedly, and dry it repeatedly in the sun, keeping it away from dusty places; in this way, the copper plate would become exceedingly clean and pure.

"O Wise One! Thus, if there is a person who knows as it truly is: 'I have no internal corruption; I truly have no such corruption within,' you should know that this person guards against those things known through the eye and the ear. Because he guards against those things known through the eye and the ear, his mind is not entangled by desire. Being thus without desire and without corruption, he passes away with a mind unpolluted.
Because he passes away with a mind unpolluted, being without desire and without corruption, he dies a noble death and is reborn in a good destination."
Why is that? Because he has passed away with a mind free from desire, free from corruption, and undefiled by impurity,
O Worthy One.
For these reasons and by this condition, it is said that the first two persons both possess defilement and a defiled mind, yet one is base and the other is supreme.
For these reasons and by this condition, it is said that the latter two persons both lack defilement and a defiled mind, yet one is base and the other is supreme.
Then, another bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Sāriputta, and said:
"Venerable Sāriputta!..."
"Regarding what was said about 'defilement,' what constitutes defilement?
Venerable Sāriputta replied to the bhikkhus:
"Venerable friends!"
Immeasurable evil and unwholesome states arise from desire; this is called "defilement.
Why is this so? Because there may be a person whose mind gives rise to such a desire:
"I have transgressed the precepts; let no one else know that I have transgressed.

O Worthy One! There may be others who do know of his transgression, and because they know he has transgressed, evil thoughts arise in him. If such evil thoughts or desires arise in his mind, both are unwholesome.
"O Wise One! There may be a person who gives rise to such a desire:
'As for the precepts I have transgressed, let others reprove me in private; do not let them reprove me for my transgression in the midst of the assembly.'"
"O Worthy One!

Suppose another person rebukes one in the midst of a crowd, not in private. Because of that person rebuking one in the midst of a crowd, not in private, an evil thought arises in one's mind. If that thought of evil arises, or if a thought of desire arises, both are unwholesome."
"Venerable sir!
There may be a person who gives rise to this desire in their mind:
'May the transgression of the precepts that I have committed be censured by those superior to me, and not be censured for my transgression of the precepts by those who are inferior.'"
"O Worthy One!

There may be an inferior person who rebukes one who has broken the precepts; such a person is not a superior one. Because that rebuke comes from an inferior person rather than a superior one, the mind of the accused immediately gives rise to ill-will. Whether it be the arising of ill-will in the mind or the arising of desire in the mind, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person whose mind gives rise to such a desire:

‘May I sit before the Buddha and question the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus; let no other bhikṣu sit before the Buddha to question the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu sitting before the Buddha who questions the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma, and the World-Honored One explains it for the sake of the bhikkhus. Because of that other bhikkhu sitting before the Buddha, questioning the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma and being taught by him for the sake of the bhikkhus, a mind of ill will arises in [the first bhikkhu]. If that mind of ill will arises, or if a mind of desire arises, both are unwholesome."
"O Worthy One!
There may be a person who conceives such a desire in their mind:

'When the bhikkhus enter the inner quarters, may I be the very first among them; may the bhikkhus follow and attend upon me as I enter the inner quarters; let no other bhikkhu be the very first among the bhikkhus when they enter the inner quarters, nor let the bhikkhus follow and attend upon him as he enters.'"
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, when the bhikkhus enter the inner quarters, goes at their very head, and the bhikkhus follow him as he leads them inside. Because that bhikkhu goes at the head of the bhikkhus when they enter the inner quarters and leads them inside while they follow him, an evil thought arises in his mind. If such an evil thought arises in his mind, or if a lustful thought arises, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who conceives such a desire in their mind:

‘When the bhikkhus have entered the inner hall, may I be the foremost among them, receiving the first seat, the first water for washing, and the first food; let no other bhikkhu be the foremost among the bhikkhus when they have entered the inner hall, nor receive the first seat, the first water for washing, and the first food.’”
"O Worthy One!
Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, when the other bhikkhus have already entered the inner hall, takes the highest seat, receives the first water for washing, and receives the first food.

Because he has taken the highest seat, received the first water for washing, and received the first food while the other bhikkhus have already entered, evil thoughts arise in his mind. If such evil thoughts arise in his mind, or if thoughts of desire arise, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who gives rise to this desire:
‘When the bhikṣus have finished eating, gathered up their bowls, and the water for washing has been served, may I preach the Dharma to these laypeople, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them;’”

Do not allow other bhikṣus to do so; rather, after the bhikṣus have finished eating, the food vessels have been collected, and the water for washing has been distributed, you should preach the Dharma to the lay devotees, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, after the bhikkhus have finished their meal, the bowls have been cleared away, and the water for washing has been served, teaches the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting them, inspiring them, and bringing them to a state of joy.

Because that other bhikkhu—after the bhikkhus have finished their meal, the bowls have been cleared away, and the water for washing has been served—teaches the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting them, inspiring them, and bringing them to a state of joy, an evil thought arises in [the first bhikkhu's] mind. Whether that mind gives rise to evil or gives rise to desire, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who conceives such a desire in their mind:

‘When laypeople go to the park, let me meet with them, assemble with them, sit with them, and converse with them; do not let other bhikkhus meet with those laypeople when they go to the park, nor assemble with them, nor sit with them, nor converse with them.’”
“O Worthy One!

Suppose there are other bhikṣus with whom laypeople go to the monastery park, where they meet together, assemble together, sit together, and converse together. Because of this—due to those other bhikṣus with whom the laypeople go to the monastery park, meet, assemble, sit, and converse—their minds may give rise to ill will. If their minds give rise to ill will or if their minds give rise to desire, both are unwholesome.”
“Wise one! There may be a person who conceives such a desire in his mind:

‘May I be recognized by the king, as well as by the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country; may I be known and esteemed by them. May no other bhikkhu be recognized by the king, nor be known and esteemed by the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who is known and esteemed by a king, as well as by the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country. Because that other bhikkhu is known and esteemed by the king, the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country, [this bhikkhu] conceives an evil thought. Whether he conceives an evil thought or a lustful thought, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who gives rise to such a desire in their mind:
‘May I be respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; may no other bhikṣu be respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.’”
"Venerable one!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who is respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. Because that other bhikkhu is respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, evil thoughts arise in [the first bhikkhu’s] mind. If such evil thoughts arise in his mind, or if thoughts of desire arise, both are unwholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who gives rise to such a desire in their mind:

‘May I obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all the necessities of life, but let no other bhikṣu obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all the necessities of life.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikṣu who obtains robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various articles of livelihood. Because that other bhikṣu obtains robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and various articles of livelihood, evil thoughts arise in [the first bhikṣu's] mind. If such evil thoughts or covetous thoughts arise in his mind, both are unwholesome."

“Wise one! Thus, if those wise fellow practitioners of the holy life do not know that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable evil and unwholesome thoughts of desire, then he is not a śramaṇa yet is perceived as a śramaṇa; he is not a wise śramaṇa yet is perceived as a wise śramaṇa; he does not possess right knowledge yet is perceived as possessing right knowledge; he does not possess right mindfulness yet is perceived as possessing right mindfulness; he is not pure yet is perceived as being pure.”
"O Worthy One!

Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who know that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable evil and unwholesome thoughts and desires, they will regard him as not being a śramaṇa and will perceive him as not being a śramaṇa; they will regard him as not being a wise śramaṇa and will perceive him as not being a wise śramaṇa; they will regard him as not possessing right knowledge and will perceive him as not possessing right knowledge; they will regard him as not possessing right mindfulness and will perceive him as not possessing right mindfulness; they will regard him as not being pure and will perceive him as not being pure."

“Wise one! It is just as if someone were to buy a copper vessel or bowl from a marketplace or a copper smith’s workshop, fill it with excrement, cover it over, and carry it away. As he passes by shops and approaches a crowd of people, those who see him all desire to eat from it; their minds are filled with great delight and they feel no aversion, conceiving instead a notion of purity.

Once he has carried it away and stops at a certain place to open it up and show its contents, when the people see it, none of them wish to eat from it; they have no sense of delight and feel intense loathing, conceiving a notion of impurity.”
"If one does not even use it when wishing to eat, how much less so when one has no desire to eat from the start? 'Worthy one!

Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who do not know that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable evil, unwholesome, and lustful thoughts, then he is not a śramaṇa yet conceives himself as a śramaṇa; he is not a wise śramaṇa yet conceives himself as a wise śramaṇa; he does not possess right knowledge yet conceives himself as possessing right knowledge; he does not possess right mindfulness yet conceives himself as possessing right mindfulness; he is not pure yet conceives himself as pure.'"
"O Wise One!

Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who know that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable evil, unwholesome thoughts and desires, they will regard him as not being a śramaṇa and will perceive him as not being a śramaṇa; they will regard him as not being a wise śramaṇa and will perceive him as not being a wise śramaṇa; they will regard him as not possessing right knowledge and will perceive him as not possessing right knowledge; they will regard him as not possessing right mindfulness and will perceive him as not possessing right mindfulness; they will regard him as not being pure and will perceive him as not being pure."
"O Worthy One!
You should know that such a person must not be associated with, nor should they be honored, revered, or served.

If a bhikkhu associates with one whom he should not associate with, or honors, reveres, and serves one whom he should not honor, revere, or serve, then for a long night he will obtain neither profit nor benefit; he will not be aided, nor will he find peace, happiness, or the end of suffering and grief."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:
‘May others not know that I have transgressed the precepts.’”
"O Worthy One!
Suppose another person knows that he has transgressed the precepts; because others know of his transgression, no evil arises in his mind.
If no evil arises in his mind and no desire arises in his mind, then both of these are wholesome."
"O Wise One! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:
'May others reprove me for my transgression of the precepts in private; do not let them reprove me for my transgression of the precepts in public.'"
"O Worthy One!
Suppose another person rebukes one in the midst of an assembly, not in private. Because that rebuke occurs in the midst of an assembly and not in private, no ill will arises in the mind;
if the mind is without ill will and no desire arises in the mind, then both are wholesome."
"O Worthy One!
There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:
'May the transgression of my precepts be censured by superior persons, and not be censured for the transgression of my precepts by those who are inferior.'"
"O Worthy One!

There may be an inferior person who rebukes one for breaking the precepts; this is not a superior person. Because the rebuke comes from an inferior person and not a superior one, no ill will arises in the mind.
If there is no ill will in the mind and no desire arises, both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘May I sit before the Buddha and question the World-Honored One about the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus, and may no other bhikṣu sit before the Buddha to question the World-Honored One about the Dharma for the sake of the bhikṣus.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu sitting before the Buddha who questions the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma, and the World-Honored One explains it for the sake of the bhikkhus. Because of that other bhikkhu sitting before the Buddha, questioning the World-Honored One regarding the Dharma and having it explained for the sake of the bhikkhus, no ill will arises in his mind.
If his mind is free from ill will and no desire arises in his mind, then both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘When the bhikkhus enter the inner quarters, let me be the very first among them; let the bhikkhus follow and attend upon me as I enter the inner quarters; do not let another bhikkhu be the very first among the bhikkhus when they enter the inner quarters, nor let the bhikkhus follow and attend upon him as he enters.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, when the bhikkhus enter the inner quarters, goes foremost before them, and the bhikkhus follow him as he leads them inside. Because that bhikkhu goes foremost before the other bhikkhus when they enter the inner quarters and the bhikkhus follow him as he leads them inside, no ill will arises in his mind.
If his mind is free from ill will and no sensual desire arises in his mind, then both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘When the bhikkhus have entered within, may I be the one seated at the highest place, receive the first seat, the first water for washing, and the first food; let no other bhikkhu, when the bhikkhus have entered within, be the one seated at the highest place, receive the first seat, the first water for washing, and the first food.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, when the other bhikkhus have already entered the inner hall, takes the highest seat, receives the first water for washing, and receives the first food. Because he takes the highest seat, receives the first water for washing, and receives the first food while the other bhikkhus have already entered, no ill will arises in his mind.
If his mind is free from ill will and no desire arises in his mind, both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘After the bhikkhus have finished eating, put away their bowls, and performed the ritual washing of the hands, I shall teach the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, so that no other bhikkhu, after the bhikkhus have finished eating, put away their bowls, and performed the ritual washing of the hands, shall teach the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who, after the bhikkhus have finished their meal, the bowls have been cleared away, and the water for washing has been served, teaches the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Because that other bhikkhu, after the bhikkhus have finished their meal, the bowls have been cleared away, and the water for washing has been served, teaches the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, no evil arises in his mind.
If his mind is free from evil and no desire arises in his mind, both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘When the householders go to the park, let it be me with whom they meet, assemble, sit together, and converse; let it not be some other bhikkhu with whom the householders go to the park to meet, assemble, sit together, and converse.’”
"O Worthy One!

When other bhikkhus go to visit the assembly groves of laypeople, they may meet with them, gather with them, sit together with them, and engage in discussion with them. Because of meeting, gathering, sitting, and discussing with those other bhikkhus who visit the assembly groves of laypeople, their minds do not give rise to ill will.
If their minds are free from ill will and no desire arises in their minds, then both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘May I be recognized by the king, as well as by the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the land; may I be known and respected, while other bhikkhus are not recognized by the king, nor known and respected by the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the land.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who is well-known to a king, as well as to the king’s ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country; because that other bhikkhu is well-known and held in high esteem by the king, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and the people of the country, his mind does not give rise to ill will.
If his mind is free from ill will and no desire arises in his mind, both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘May I be honored and respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; let no other bhikṣu be honored and respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.’”
"Venerable sir!

Suppose there is another bhikkhu who is respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; because that other bhikkhu is respected by the fourfold assembly of bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, his mind does not give rise to ill will.
If his mind is free from ill will and no desire arises in his mind, both of these are wholesome."
“Wise one! There may be a person who does not give rise to such a desire:

‘May I obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all the necessities of life, but let no other bhikṣu obtain robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all the necessities of life.’”
"O Worthy One!

Suppose another bhikkhu obtains robes, alms-food, bedding, medicinal requisites, and other articles for the necessities of life; because that [first] bhikkhu has obtained these robes, alms-food, bedding, medicinal requisites, and articles for the necessities of life from the other bhikkhu, no ill will arises in his mind.
If his mind is free from ill will and no desire arises in his mind, then both are virtuous."

“Wise one! Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who do not know that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable wholesome mental aspirations, they will perceive that ascetic as not being an ascetic, perceive a wise ascetic as not being wise, perceive right knowledge as not being right knowledge, perceive right mindfulness as not being right mindfulness, and perceive purity as not being pure.”
"O Worthy One!

Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who know that such a person has given rise to such immeasurable wholesome thoughts and desires, they will regard him as a true ascetic, perceiving him as a true ascetic; they will perceive him with wisdom as one possessing wisdom, perceive him with right knowledge as one possessing right knowledge, perceive him with right mindfulness as one possessing right mindfulness, and perceive him as pure as one who is pure."

“Wise one! It is just as if someone were to buy a copper vessel or bowl from a market stall or a copper smith’s workshop, fill it with various kinds of pure and delicious food and drink, cover it over, and carry it away. As they pass by shops and approach a crowd of people, that crowd, having seen it, would all have no desire to eat; they would feel no affection for it, but rather loathe it intensely, perceiving it as impure, and would say:
‘Away with that filth! Away with that filth!’”

Having taken it away, he stays in one place and opens it up for display. When the people see it, they all desire to eat it; their minds are filled with great affection and delight, and they feel no aversion, but instead conceive pure thoughts toward it.
"If that person originally had no desire for food, yet upon seeing it wishes to eat, how much more so would they do so if they originally desired to obtain food?

"Worthy one! In this way, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who do not recognize that such a person has given rise to these immeasurable wholesome desires and intentions, then those ascetics will perceive what is not an ascetic as an ascetic; they will perceive what is not a wise ascetic as a wise ascetic; they will perceive what is not right knowledge as right knowledge; they will perceive what is not right mindfulness as right mindfulness; and they will perceive what is not pure as pure."
"Venerable!

Thus, if there are wise fellow practitioners of the holy life who know that such a person has given rise to such immeasurable wholesome intentions and desires, they will regard him as a recluse, with the perception of a recluse; they will regard him as one possessing wisdom, with the perception of one possessing wisdom; they will regard him as possessing right knowledge, with the perception of right knowledge; they will regard him as possessing right mindfulness, with the perception of right mindfulness; and they will regard him as pure, with the perception of purity."
"O Wise One!
You should know that such persons as these ought to be approached, honored, and served;
if a bhikṣu is one who should be approached, he should approach them; if they are ones who should be honored and served, he should honor and serve them."
In this way, he will for a long night gain profit and benefit; he will obtain abundance, peace, and happiness, and shall also be free from suffering, sorrow, and grief.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was present in that assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
"I now wish to speak a simile regarding this matter; will you listen as I speak?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied, "Worthy Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
"If you wish to speak a simile, you may do so.
Then the Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sāriputta!"

I recall that on one occasion, while traveling through Rājagṛha, I was staying among the mountain crags. At that time, having passed the night, at dawn, I put on my robes, took my bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for alms, going to the house of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the former chariot-maker and naked ascetic.
At that time, there was another wheelwright in that village who was fashioning and repairing a chariot axle. Then, the elder wheelwright, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, went to that house.
Upon seeing him fashioning the axle, the elder wheelwright, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, thought to himself:
"If this wheelwright were to take his axe and fashion the axle by cutting away all its imperfections, then this axle would become truly excellent."

Then, that chariot-maker, acting exactly according to what the former chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūraṇa, had thought in his mind, took up an axe and hacked away at those various unsightly parts.
Thereupon, the former chariot-maker, the naked ascetic Pūraṇa, was filled with great joy and said this:
"O son of a chariot-maker!..."
If your mind is thus, you will know my mind.
Why is this? Because you took up an axe to hew and repair the axle of the chariot at its various defective points, exactly according to my intention.
"In this way, Venerable Śāriputra!

If one is flatterer, deceitful, envious, lacks faith, is indolent, lacks right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, lacks concentration and wisdom, has a deluded mind, does not guard the sense faculties, does not cultivate the life of a śramaṇa, and lacks discernment."
Venerable Sāriputta!
It is for the sake of knowing that mind by means of this mind that this Dharma is taught.
Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a person who is neither sycophantic nor deceitful, free from envy, possessed of faith, diligent and without indolence, endowed with right mindfulness and right wisdom, cultivating concentration and wisdom, whose mind is not deranged or deluded, who guards the sense faculties, and who extensively practices the life of a śramaṇa with skillful discernment.
“Venerable Sāriputta, those who hear the Dharma taught by you are like those who, being hungry, desire food, or being thirsty, desire drink— both with their mouths and with their minds.”

It is like a daughter of a Kṣatriya, or a daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman, who is beautiful and lovely; having bathed thoroughly until she is utterly pure, she anoints her body with fragrances, puts on bright, clean garments, and adorns her countenance with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.

Suppose there were someone who, out of longing for that woman, seeking her profit and welfare, seeking her peace and happiness, [offered her] a garland of blue lotuses, or a garland of campaka flowers;
or a garland of sumana flowers, or a garland of vārṣika flowers.
Or he might give her a garland of atimuktaka flowers;
she would receive it with both hands in joy and use it to adorn her head.
Venerable Śāriputra!

Thus, if there is a person who is not flatterous, not deceitful, free from envy, endowed with faith, diligent and without indolence, possessed of right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, practicing concentration and wisdom, whose mind is not deranged or deluded, who guards the sense faculties, and who extensively cultivates the life of a recluse with skillful discernment—when such a person hears the Dharma taught by the Venerable Śāriputra, they will be like one hungry desiring food or thirsty desiring a drink, both in body and in mind.
"How extraordinary, Venerable Sāriputta!
How marvelous!
Venerable Sāriputta constantly rescues fellow practitioners of the holy life, leading them away from what is unwholesome and establishing them in what is wholesome."
Thus these two venerable ones addressed one another and rose from their seats to depart.
This is what the Venerable Śāriputra said.
Having heard what the Venerable Śāriputra had said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Pāpaka-sutta*, the first, ends here with five thousand one hundred and ninety-six characters. 88. The *Dhamma-paryeṣaṇa-sutta* (88), the second in the *Pāpaka-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Recited by the Second Minor Earth-City [School]. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of the Kośalas together with a great assembly of bhikṣus. He proceeded to the Śiṃśapā Grove north of the village of Pañcasālā, accompanied by renowned and virtuous elders, senior disciples, and great followers, namely: the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, and other such renowned and virtuous elders, senior disciples, and great followers. They all resided near the Buddha’s leaf-hut in the vicinity of Pañcasālā.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should practice seeking the Dharma; do not practice seeking food and drink. Why is this?"
Out of my compassion for you, my disciples, I wish to have you practice the seeking of the Dharma, rather than the seeking of food and drink.
If you were to seek food and drink instead of seeking the Dharma, you would not only be at fault yourselves, but I too would lack a good reputation.
"If you all practice seeking the Dharma and do not practice seeking food and drink, then you will be excellent yourselves and I too shall have a good reputation.
Why is it that these disciples rely on the Buddha for the sake of seeking food and drink, rather than for the sake of seeking the Dharma?"
Having finished my meal and concluded my eating, there was still some food remaining. Later, two bhikṣus arrived, their strength weakened by hunger and thirst.
I said to them: "I have finished my meal and concluded my eating; there is still some food remaining. If you wish to eat, take it."
"If you do not take it, I shall take it and pour it onto clean ground, or else pour it into water free of insects.
Then the first of those two bhikṣus thought to himself: "The World-honored One has finished eating;

the meal is completed, yet there is still leftover food. If I do not take it, the World-honored One will surely take it and pour it onto clean ground, or else pour it into water free of insects. I had better take it and eat it myself."
He then took the food.
Although that bhikṣu enjoyed peace and stability for one day and one night after taking this food, because he had taken this food, it was not to the Buddha’s liking.

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu, by reason of taking such food, fails to achieve fewness of desires, does not know contentment, does not achieve ease of maintenance, does not achieve ease of satisfaction, does not know the proper time, does not know moderation, does not achieve diligence, does not achieve sitting in meditation, does not achieve pure conduct, does not achieve seclusion, does not achieve single-mindedness, does not achieve energetic application, and furthermore, does not attain nirvāṇa.
Therefore, because that bhikṣu took this food for such reasons, he did not act in accordance with the Buddha’s intention.
This is called a disciple practicing in reliance on the Buddha for the sake of seeking food and drink, rather than for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
"How do the disciples practice seeking the Dharma rather than seeking food and drink?
Regarding those two bhikṣus, the second bhikṣu thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has finished his meal and the meal is complete, yet there is still leftover food. If I do not take it, the World-Honored One will surely pour it onto clean ground or perhaps pour it into water free of insects."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said that the lowest and most inferior among foods is leftover food; therefore, I would rather not accept this food.
Having formed this thought, he immediately did not take it.

"Although that bhikṣu may suffer and find no peace for a single day and night because he does not accept this food, it is precisely because he does not accept this food that he acts in accordance with the Buddha’s intention."

Why is this? Because that bhikṣu, by virtue of not taking this food, attains fewness of desires, contentment, ease of maintenance, ease of satisfaction, knowledge of the proper time, moderation, diligence, seclusion, one-pointedness of mind, energetic application, and also attains nirvāṇa.
Therefore, because that bhikṣu did not accept this food, he attained what was pleasing to the Buddha’s mind.
This is called the disciples practicing in reliance upon the Buddha for the sake of seeking the Dharma, and not for the sake of seeking food and drink.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed his disciples:

"If there is a Dhamma and Discipline in which the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dhamma and Discipline does not benefit many people, nor does it bring happiness to many; it is not for the sake of compassion for the world, nor for the sake of seeking the goal, benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for gods and humans."

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the middle and lower disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people, nor do many people find happiness therein; it is not for the sake of compassion for the world, nor for the sake of seeking the goal, benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for gods and humans.

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people and brings happiness to many; it is for the sake of compassion for the world, and for the sake of seeking the goal, benefit, welfare, peace, and happiness for both gods and humans.

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and lower disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people and brings happiness to many; it is for the sake of compassion for the world, and seeks the welfare, benefit, meaning, peace, and happiness of both gods and humans.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also present in the assembly.
Then, the Blessed One addressed him, saying: "Śāriputra!"
"You should teach the Dharma to the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma; I suffer from back pain and wish now to rest for a while.
Venerable Śāriputra then accepted the Buddha’s instruction, saying, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!

Thereupon, the World-Honored One folded his uttarāsaṅga fourfold and spread it upon the bed; he rolled up his saṃghāṭī to serve as a pillow and lay down on his right side, with one foot resting upon the other, maintaining the perception of light, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, constantly mindful of rising.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
