You should know that the Blessed One has just now spoken the Dharma in brief."

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya whose teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, that Dharma and Vinaya does not benefit many people; many people do not obtain happiness; it does not bring compassion to the world, nor does it seek the goal, benefit, welfare, peace, or happiness for gods and humans.

If there is a Dharma and Discipline in which the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the middle and lower disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Discipline does not benefit many people, nor do many people obtain happiness; it does not bring compassion to the world, nor does it seek the goal, benefit, welfare, peace, or happiness for gods and humans.

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people and brings happiness to many; it is for the sake of compassion for the world, and seeks the welfare, benefit, well-being, and happiness of both devas and humans.

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and lower disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then that Dharma and Vinaya benefits many people and brings happiness to many; it is for the sake of compassion for the world, and seeks the welfare, benefit, meaning, and happiness of both devas and humans.
"However, the Blessed One has taught this Dharma in an extremely concise manner; how do you understand its meaning?
How do you analyze it in detail?
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu in the assembly who spoke as follows:
“Venerable Sāriputta!
If those elders and seniors should declare of themselves:

‘I have attained final knowledge; my births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I know as it truly is that there will be no further existence.’”
"When fellow practitioners of the holy life hear that monk say of himself, 'I have attained ultimate knowledge,' they will be filled with joy.
Furthermore, another monk spoke thus:
"Venerable Sāriputta!..."
If middle or lower disciples aspire for the unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, fellow practitioners of the holy life, upon seeing their conduct, will become joyful.
It is in this way that the bhikkhu explains this matter, which does not accord with the intention of the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Śāriputra addressed those bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!
Listen as I speak for your sake."
"Venerable friends!

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the senior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, those senior disciples may be censured for three reasons."
What are the three?
The teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the senior disciple does not train in renunciation; for this reason, the senior disciple may be censured.
If the teacher speaks of dharmas that should be abandoned, yet the senior disciple does not abandon those dharmas; for this reason, the senior disciple may be censured.
Regarding that which is to be realized through direct knowledge, if a senior disciple abandons skillful means, the senior disciple may be censured on this account.

Furthermore, if there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the senior disciple does not delight in dwelling in seclusion, the senior disciple may be censured for these three matters.
"Venerable friends!

If there is a Dhamma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the middle and junior disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, those middle and junior disciples may be censured for three reasons."
What are the three?
The teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the middle and lower disciples do not train in renunciation; for this reason, the middle and lower disciples may be censured.
If the Venerable Teacher teaches a dharma that is to be abandoned, yet the middle and lower disciples do not abandon that dharma, the middle and lower disciples may thereby be censured.
Regarding what is to be realized through direct knowledge, if the middle and lower disciples abandon the means [for its attainment], the middle and lower disciples may thereby be censured.

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya where the teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, yet the middle and lower disciples do not delight in dwelling in seclusion, then those middle and lower disciples possess these three grounds for censure.
"Venerable friends!

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then those senior disciples possess three qualities worthy of praise."
What are the three?
The teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciple likewise trains in renunciation; by this, the senior disciple may be praised.
If the teacher speaks of dharmas that should be abandoned, the senior disciple then abandons those dharmas; by this, the senior disciple may be praised.

Regarding that which is to be realized through direct knowledge: if a senior disciple is diligent and studies with effort, not abandoning skillful means, then by these qualities the senior disciple may be praised.
Venerable friends!

If there is a Dhamma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the senior disciple also delights in dwelling in seclusion, then by these three matters the senior disciple may be praised.
"Venerable friends!

If there is a Dharma and Vinaya in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then those middle and junior disciples possess three qualities worthy of praise."
What are the three?
The teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion; the middle and lower disciples also train in renunciation. It is on account of this that the middle and lower disciples may be so praised.
If the Venerable Teacher speaks of dharmas that can be abandoned, the middle and lower disciples then abandon those dharmas; by this, the middle and lower disciples may be praised.

Regarding what is to be realized through direct knowledge, the middle and lower disciples study with diligence and vigor, not relinquishing their skillful means; by this, the middle and lower disciples may be praised.
Venerable friends!

If there is a Dhamma and Discipline in which the Teacher delights in dwelling in seclusion, and the middle and junior disciples also delight in dwelling in seclusion, then these middle and junior disciples possess these three qualities worthy of praise.
The Venerable Śāriputra again addressed the bhikṣus: "Virtuous ones!

There is a middle way that enables the mind to abide, attains concentration and bliss, accords with the Dharma and follows the sequence of the Dharma, brings about supernormal powers and awakening, and also leads to nirvāṇa."
Venerable friends!

What is the Middle Way that enables the mind to become settled, attains concentration and bliss, accords with the Dharma and follows the sequence of the Dharma, achieves the superknowledges and awakening, and also attains Nirvana?
"Venerable friends!
Sensual desire is evil, and the thought of sensual desire is also evil. One should abandon the thought of sensual desire and also abandon the thought of evil sensual desire.

It is the same for ill will, enmity, stinginess and jealousy, deceit and fraud, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, conceit, extreme conceit, arrogance, heedlessness, pride, and contentiousness."
"Venerable friends!
Greed is evil, and attachment is also evil; one should abandon greed and also abandon attachment.
Venerable friends!"

"This is called the Middle Way, which enables the mind to abide, attains concentration and bliss, accords with the Dharma and its sequence, achieves the superknowledges and enlightenment, and also attains Nirvana.
O Venerable Ones!"

Furthermore, there is a Middle Way that enables the mind to abide, attains concentration and bliss, accords with the Dharma and follows the sequence of the Dharma, achieves the superknowledges and awakening, and also attains Nirvana.
O virtuous ones!

What, moreover, is this middle way by which one can attain stability of mind, attain concentration and bliss, accord with the Dharma and its sequence, attain the superknowledges and awakening, and also attain nirvana?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path: right view up to right concentration; these are the eight.

Venerable friends, this is called the Middle Way that enables the mind to abide, to attain concentration and happiness, to accord with the Dharma and follow the sequence of the Dharma, to attain supernormal powers and awakening, and also to attain Nirvana.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One’s ailment was immediately dispelled and he attained peace and comfort. Rising from his reclining position, he sat cross-legged and praised the Venerable Śāriputra:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent!
Śāriputra, you have taught the Dharma to the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma. Śāriputra!
"You should further preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma.
Śāriputra! You should repeatedly preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should all together receive the Dharma according to the Dharma, recite it, practice it, and uphold it. Why is this so?

This Dharma is in accordance with the Dharma; it possesses both principle and meaning, serving as the foundation for the holy life (*brahmacarya*), leading to supernormal powers and awakening, and also to *nirvāṇa*.

For those sons of good family who have shaved off their hair and beards, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith have left the home life for homelessness to study the Way—this Dharma is in accordance with the Dharma and should be properly received and upheld.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Sāriputta and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The second *Dharmaparyeṣaṇa-sūtra* ends here, totaling 2,286 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 22, totals 7,482 characters. [Recited in] the second minor *Kṣudrakasūtra* section.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 23.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kapiśī during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. 89.
Bhikṣu-praśna-sūtra (89). Chapter on Defilements. Bhikṣu-praśna-sūtra, the third [sūtra], recited in the second section of the Minor Earth-City Collection.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, observing the rains retreat.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones! If a bhikṣu should invite other bhikṣus, saying: 'Venerable sirs, please speak to me, instruct me, and admonish me; do not spare me.'"
Why is that? Venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who speaks harshly and is established in the practice of speaking harshly; because he is established in the practice of speaking harshly, his fellow practitioners of the holy life do not speak with him, nor do they instruct or reprove him, but rather find fault with that person.
Venerable friends!
What is the factor of harsh speech?
If one is possessed of the factor of harsh speech, those who live the holy life will not speak with that person; they will not instruct, reprove, or even address them.
Venerable friends!
There may be a person who has evil desires and thoughts of desire.
Venerable friends!
If there are those who harbor evil desires and dwell upon such desires, this is called the dharma of perverse speech.

Thus, they engage in defiled conduct and remain bound by the fetter of silence; they are deceitful, sycophantic, stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous; they lack shame and dread of blame; they possess malice and wicked intent; they speak words of anger; they revile bhikṣus, treat bhikṣus with contempt, and expose the faults of bhikṣus; they avoid one another and speak only of external affairs; they are mute, full of anger, and their hatred and envy are intense; they have evil friends and evil companions; they are ungrateful and fail to recognize kindness.
"Venerable friends!
If there is someone who is ungrateful and does not recognize kindness, this is called the dharma of perverse speech.
Venerable friends!"
This is called the quality of contentious speech.

If there is one who possesses the quality of contentious speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life will not speak to him; they will not instruct him, nor reprove him, but will find fault with that person, O worthy ones!
"A bhikkhu should reflect within himself:
'Venerable friends!
If there is anyone who has evil desires and thoughts of desire, I do not love them.'"
"If I harbor evil desires and dwell upon them, they too will not love me.
A bhikkhu who observes in this way should train himself thus: "I shall not act upon evil desires, nor shall I dwell upon them."

Thus, they engage in defiled conduct and remain bound by the fetter of silence; they are deceitful, sycophantic, stingy, greedy, and envious; they lack shame and dread of blame; they are malicious and harbor evil intentions; they speak words of hatred and revile the bhikṣus, treating them with contempt and exposing their faults; they avoid one another and speak only of external matters; they are silent, full of anger, and their malice and envy burn intensely; they keep evil friends and evil companions; they are ungrateful and fail to recognize kindness.
"Venerable friends!
If there is one who is ungrateful and does not recognize kindness, I do not love him;
and if I were ungrateful and did not recognize kindness, he would likewise not love me."
When a bhikkhu observes in this way, he should train himself thus:
"Venerable sirs, if a bhikkhu does not invite other bhikkhus [to his meals], he is practicing ingratitude and being ungrateful. Venerable friends! [He should train himself thus.]
"Speak to me, instruct me, and admonish me; do not find fault with me.
Why is that? O worthy ones!"

Suppose there is a person who is skilled in speech and accomplished in the qualities of skillful speech; because he is accomplished in the qualities of skillful speech, his fellow practitioners of the holy life speak well to him, instruct him well, and reprove him well, without finding fault with him.
Venerable friends!
What is the quality of being easy to speak with?

If one is endowed with the quality of being easy to speak with, fellow practitioners of the holy life will speak well to them, instruct them well, and reprove them well, without finding fault with that person.
"Venerable friends!
There may be a person who has no evil desire and does not dwell upon desire.
Venerable friends!"

If there is a person who does not harbor evil desires and does not dwell upon them, this is called the Dharma of virtuous speech. Thus, one is unstained while acting amidst stains; one does not speak with fetters or attachments;

one is not deceitful or flattering; one is not stingy, greedy, or envious; one is not shameless or lacking in moral dread; one harbors no ill will or malicious intent; one does not utter words of anger; one does not revile a bhikṣu for his reviling, nor revile a bhikṣu for his arrogance, nor revile a bhikṣu for his confession of faults; one does not avoid one another to discuss external matters; one does not fail to speak, nor is one consumed by anger, hatred, or envy; one does not associate with evil friends or evil companions; and one is neither ungrateful nor unappreciative of kindness.
"Venerable friends!
If there is someone who is not ungrateful and recognizes kindness, this is called a well-spoken Dharma teaching,
venerable friends!"
These are called the qualities of good speech.

If one is endowed with these qualities of good speech, fellow practitioners of the holy life will speak well of them, and they will be well-instructed and well-rebuked without being made difficult by others.
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu should reflect within himself:
'Venerable friends!'"
If there is someone who does not harbor evil desire and does not dwell upon desire, I love that person;
if I do not harbor evil desire and do not dwell upon desire, they also love me.
A bhikṣu who observes in this way should train thus: he shall not act upon evil desires nor dwell on them;

he shall not practice defilement while remaining undefiled; he shall not abide in the fetter of silence; he shall not be deceitful or flattering; he shall not be stingy, greedy, or envious; he shall not be shameless or lacking in moral dread; he shall not harbor malice or ill will; he shall not utter words of hatred; he shall not revile a bhikṣu for his reviling, nor revile a bhikṣu for his contempt, nor revile a bhikṣu for his confession; he shall not avoid one another and speak of external affairs; he shall not be characterized by silence, anger, or the blazing of hatred and envy; he shall not have evil friends or evil companions; and he shall not be ungrateful or unappreciative.
"Venerable friends!
If there is one who is not ungrateful and does not fail to recognize kindness, I love that person;
and if I am not ungrateful and do not fail to recognize kindness, they too will love me."
When a bhikkhu contemplates in this way, he should train himself thus: "Venerable friends, if a bhikkhu contemplates in this manner, it will surely be of great benefit:
'Am I one who has evil desires and thoughts of desire, or am I one who does not have evil desires and thoughts of desire?'"
"Venerable friends!
If a bhikkhu, when reflecting, knows: 'I am one who has evil desires and thoughts of desire,' he does not take delight in them, but seeks their abandonment."
"Venerable friends!

If, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows: 'I have no evil desires and do not dwell upon them,' he becomes joyful, thinking: 'I am pure; I seek to train in the Noble Dharma. For this reason, he is joyful."
Venerable friends!
It is just as when a person with sight looks at themselves in a mirror and sees whether their face is clean or unclean.
Venerable friends!
Venerable friends, if a person with sight sees that their face is stained with impurities, they are not pleased and immediately seek to wash it. Venerable friends,
if a person with sight sees that their face is free of impurities, they are immediately pleased, thinking, "My face is pure," and for that reason they are pleased.
"Venerable friends!
If, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows: 'I am practicing evil desires and dwelling upon sensual thoughts,' he does not take delight in them, but seeks their abandonment."
"Venerable friends!

If, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows: 'I do not engage in evil desires, nor do I dwell upon them,' he then becomes joyful, thinking: 'I am pure; I seek to train in the noble Dhamma. For this reason, he is joyful."
In this way, I am stained by defiled conduct and stained by undefiled conduct;
I abide in the fetter of silence and do not abide in the fetter of non-silence;
I am characterized by deception, flattery, and sycophancy, and I am not characterized by deception, flattery, and sycophancy.
For the sake of stinginess, greed, and envy; for the sake of being without stinginess, greed, and envy;
for the sake of shamelessness and lack of remorse; for the sake of being without shamelessness and lack of remorse;
for the sake of anger and malicious intent; for the sake of being without anger and malicious intent.
Speaking with anger because of anger; speaking with anger though not out of anger;
censuring a bhikṣu because of censure; censuring a bhikṣu though not out of censure;
showing contempt for a bhikṣu because of contempt; showing contempt for a bhikṣu though not out of contempt.
Confessing for the sake of one who has rebuked a bhikṣu, or confessing for the sake of one who has not rebuked a bhikṣu;
for the sake of mutual avoidance, or for the sake of not mutually avoiding;
for the sake of speaking of external matters, or for the sake of not speaking of external matters.
Is it that you are prone to idle talk, anger, and intense envy, rather than being free from idle talk, anger, and intense envy?
Is it that you have evil friends and evil companions, rather than having no evil friends or evil companions?
Is it that you are ungrateful and unappreciative, rather than not being ungrateful or unappreciative?
"Venerable friends!
If, when reflecting, a bhikkhu knows: 'I am ungrateful and do not recognize kindness,' he will not be glad, and he will seek to abandon that state."

"Venerable friends! When a bhikkhu reflects, he knows: 'I am not ungrateful nor unappreciative. He then becomes joyful, thinking: 'I am myself pure; I seek to train in the Noble Dhamma. For this reason, he is joyful."
Venerable friends!
It is just as when a person with eyes looks at themselves in a mirror, they see whether their face is clean or unclean.
Venerable friends!
Venerable friends, if a person with sight sees that their face has impurities, they are not pleased and immediately seek to wash it. Venerable friends,
if a person with sight sees that their face is free of impurities, they are immediately pleased, thinking, "My face is pure," and for that reason they are pleased.
"Venerable friends!
When a bhikkhu reflects in this way, if he knows himself to be ungrateful and unappreciative, he will not find joy and will seek to abandon that state."
"Venerable friends!

When a bhikkhu reflects at such a time, he knows: 'I am not ungrateful nor unappreciative. He then becomes joyful, thinking, 'I am pure; I seek to train in the sublime Dhamma,' and for this reason he is joyful."
Because of joy, one attains rapture.
Because of rapture, one attains tranquility of body.
Because of tranquility of body, one experiences pleasure.
Because of the experience of joy, one attains a concentrated mind.
Venerable friends!
Because of a concentrated mind, the learned noble disciple sees things as they truly are and knows them as they really are.
Because one sees things as they truly are and knows them as they really are, one attains disenchantment.
Because of disenchantment, one attains dispassion.
Because of dispassion, one attains liberation.

Because of liberation, one knows that one is liberated; one knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Having heard what the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third discourse on the Bhikkhu-invitation is finished, totaling one thousand five hundred and sixty-three characters. 90. The Discourse on Knowing the Dhamma (90). Middle Āgama, Chapter on the Defiled, The Discourse on Knowing the Dhamma, the fourth; recited in the second section on the Small Earthen City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
At that time, the Venerable Cunda addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
'I know all phenomena and those things that can be known, yet I have no pursuit of gain.'"

Yet that worthy one dwells with a mind characterized by the increase of ill will; likewise, he dwells with strife, contention, resentment, malice, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, and lack of dread;
and he dwells with a mind characterized by evil desires and evil views. That worthy one dwells with a mind characterized by evil desires and evil views.

Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that this worthy one does not know those phenomena which ought to be known regarding the phenomena that can be known, yet he is without the pursuit of gain (*āśā*). Why is that?

Because this worthy one dwells with a mind characterized by the pursuit of gain; likewise, he possesses strife, contention, resentment, malice, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desires, and evil views.
Why is that? Because those venerable ones dwell with minds characterized by evil desires and evil views.
"Venerable friends!..."

It is like a person who is not wealthy yet claims to be wealthy; who has no fief from a state yet claims to have one; and who has no livestock yet claims to have them. When he wishes to use his wealth, he possesses no gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, or amber; he has no livestock or grain, nor does he have any servants or slaves.
His relatives and friends went to him and spoke thus:

"You are truly not wealthy, yet you claim to be wealthy; you have no fiefdom, yet you say you have one; you have no livestock, yet you say you have them. However, when it is time to use them, you have no gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, or amber; you have no livestock or grain, nor do you have any servants."
"In this way, friends!
If there is a bhikkhu who speaks thus:"
"I know that regarding all phenomena which are objects of knowledge, there is no increase of malice.

Yet, that worthy one dwells with a mind in which malice has increased; likewise with strife, contention, resentment, hatred, the fetter of ill-will, the bond of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desire, and evil views;
yet that worthy one dwells with a mind in which evil desire and evil views have arisen.
Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that this worthy one does not know those things that ought to be known regarding all phenomena, yet he harbors no malice. Why is this?

Because the mind of this worthy one does not incline toward malice, but is directed toward the exhaustion of it and toward *nirvāṇa* without remainder; likewise, he is free from contention, strife, resentment, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desires, and evil views.
Why is that? Because that worthy one’s mind does not incline toward unwholesome views, having attained the extinction of the remainderless nirvana.
"Worthy ones!..."
There may be a bhikkhu who does not say:
"I know those things that can be known regarding all phenomena, yet I have no malicious intent.

Nevertheless, that worthy one dwells with a mind in which no malicious intent arises; likewise, he dwells with a mind in which no dispute, resentment, anger, obsession, the bond of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of remorse, evil desire, or evil views arise. That worthy one dwells with a mind in which no evil desire or evil view arises.
Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that this worthy one truly knows those phenomena that ought to be known, and is without malice. Why is this?

Because this worthy one dwells with a mind that does not give rise to evil malice; likewise, he is free from contention, strife, resentment, hatred, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desires, and evil views.
Why is that? Because those worthy ones dwell with minds free from evil desires and evil views.
"Worthy ones!..."

It is like a person who is very wealthy but says he is not wealthy; who possesses a fief yet says he has no fief; or who possesses livestock yet says he has no livestock. Yet when he wishes to use his resources, there are gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, and amber; there are livestock and grain; and there are also servants and slaves.
His relatives and friends went to him and spoke thus:

"You are truly very wealthy, yet you say you are not; you possess fiefdoms, yet you say you have none; you possess livestock, yet you say you have none. However, when you wish to use them, there are gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, crystal, and amber; there are livestock, rice, and grain; and there are also slaves and servants."
"In this way,
worthy friends!
If there is a bhikṣu who does not speak thus:"
"I know that among all phenomena, there are no phenomena to be known that involve malicious intent.

Thus, that worthy one dwells with a mind free from the arising of malicious intent; likewise, he dwells with a mind free from disputes, resentment, hatred, obsession, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of remorse, evil desires, and evil views. Indeed, that worthy one dwells with a mind in which evil desires and evil views do not arise.
Fellow practitioners of the holy life know that this worthy one understands those phenomena that are to be known, yet he harbors no malice. Why is this?

Because for this worthy one, the mind is directed toward the exhaustion of malice and toward nirvana without remainder; likewise, he is free from contention, strife, resentment, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desires, and evil views.
"Why is this? Because for that worthy one, the mind has turned away from unwholesome views, and he has attained parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Thus spoke the Venerable Cunda.
Having heard what the Venerable Cunda had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fourth discourse, "The Discourse on Knowing the Dhamma," ends here; it contains eight hundred and eighty-one words. 91. The Discourse on Cunda’s Question Concerning Views (91). The Middle Length Discourses, Chapter on the Defiled, Fifth Discourse: Cunda’s Question Concerning Views. Recited in the Second Sub-section of the Small Earth-City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Kosambī in the Ghosita Park.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Mahācunda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
Among the various views that arise in the world, there are those who conceive of a self, who conceive of a sentient being, who conceive of a person, a life-span, a soul, or a world.
World-Honored One!
By what means of knowing and by what means of seeing can this view be extinguished and abandoned, so that other views do not continue and are not accepted?
At that time, the Blessed One said:

"Cunda! Various views arise and continue to arise in the world, namely: the view that there is a self, the view that there is a sentient being, that there is a person, that there is a life-span, that there is a soul, and that there is a world."

Cunda! If all phenomena are to be extinguished without remainder, one should know thus and see thus, so that this view may be extinguished and abandoned, and other views may not continue or be accepted; in this way, you should train in gradual reduction.
"Cunda! Within the Noble Dharma and Discipline, what is gradual decline?
A bhikkhu, having become detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; he then forms this thought:"
"I am gradually declining. Cunda!

In the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, it is not only a matter of gradual decline; there are four higher mental states for dwelling in happiness in the present life, from which the practitioner may emerge and then return again, thinking thus:
"I am gradually declining. Cunda!

In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, it is not only a matter of gradual decline that a bhikkhu, having transcended all perceptions of form, attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he then forms this thought:
"I am gradually declining. Cunda!

In the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, it is not only a matter of gradual decline; there are four stages of liberation through cessation, wherein one transcends form to attain the formless. A practitioner who has arisen from these states should explain them to others, and they will think thus:
"I am gradually declining.
"Cunda! Within the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, it is not only a matter of gradual decline.
"Cunda! Others have evil desires and thoughts of desire, whereas I have no evil desires or thoughts of desire; you should train yourself to gradually diminish them. Cunda!"
"He harbors malice and anger, whereas I harbor no malice or anger; I should train myself to gradually diminish [these]. Cunda!
He engages in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct, whereas I engage in no unchaste conduct; I should train myself to gradually diminish [these]."

"Cunda! He has increased latent tendencies, contentious thoughts, is entangled by drowsiness, is restless and arrogant, and possesses doubt; whereas I am without doubt, I should train in gradual reduction."
"Cunda! He possesses the fetter of hatred, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of dread; whereas I possess shame and dread—I should train myself to gradually diminish these."
"Cunda! He has conceit, whereas I have none; you should train yourself to gradually diminish it, Cunda!"
"He possesses overweening pride, whereas I am free from overweening pride; I should train myself to gradually diminish it. Cunda!
He is of little learning, whereas I am of great learning; I should train myself to gradually diminish it."
"Cunda! He does not contemplate wholesome states, whereas I do contemplate wholesome states; therefore, you should train yourself to gradually diminish [unwholesome states]. Cunda!
"He practices unrighteous and evil conduct, whereas I practice this righteous and sublime conduct; I shall train myself to gradually diminish [the former]. Cunda!
He has false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and evil precepts, whereas I have no evil precepts; I shall train myself to gradually diminish [these]."
"Cunda! Others may lack faith, be indolent, lack mindfulness, lack concentration, and possess corrupt wisdom; I do not possess corrupt wisdom, and I shall train in its gradual reduction."
"Cunda! If merely by generating the thought and aspiring to learn all wholesome dharmas one brings about much benefit, how much more so when one practices wholesome dharmas through body and speech?"
"Cunda! He has evil desires and thoughts of desire, whereas I have no evil desires or thoughts of desire; thus should you resolve your mind. Cunda!"
"He harbors malice and anger, whereas I harbor no malice or anger; thus should one resolve to arouse the mind. Cunda!
He engages in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct, whereas I engage in no unchaste conduct; thus should one resolve to arouse the mind."

"Cunda! He has increased discursive thought, a contentious mind, is entangled in drowsiness, is arrogant and conceited, and possesses doubt; whereas I am without doubt—thus should you resolve your mind."

"Cunda! He possesses the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of remorse; whereas I possess shame and remorse. You should resolve your mind [to cultivate these qualities], Cunda!"
"He has pride, but I am without pride; thus should one resolve to attain enlightenment. Cunda!
He has increased pride, but I am without increased pride; thus should one resolve to attain enlightenment."
"Cunda! He is of little learning, whereas I am of much learning; you should resolve your mind [to practice] accordingly, Cunda!"
"He does not contemplate wholesome qualities, whereas I do contemplate wholesome qualities; I shall arouse the mind [of awakening]. Cunda!
He practices what is contrary to the Dharma and unwholesome conduct, whereas I practice this Dharma and sublime conduct; I shall arouse the mind."
"Cunda! He has false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and evil precepts; I have no evil precepts—I should resolve my mind thus, Cunda!"
"He has lack of faith, indolence, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and possesses wrong wisdom; I shall not possess wrong wisdom, but shall instead resolve my mind [to attain right wisdom].
“Cunda! [The Buddha said.]
Just as the evil path is opposed to the right path, and just as a bad crossing is opposed to a good crossing,
so too, Cunda, those with evil desires are opposed to those without evil desires.
Malicious intent and anger are the opposites of non-malicious intent and non-anger.
Killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct are the opposites of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
Excessive scrutiny, contentiousness, sloth, restlessness and pride, and doubt are the opposites of freedom from doubt.
The fetter of aversion, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of dread stand in opposition to shame and dread.
Pride stands in opposition to non-pride.
Excessive pride stands in opposition to the absence of excessive pride.
The one who has heard little stands in opposition to the one who has heard much;
the one who does not contemplate wholesome dharmas stands in opposition to the one who contemplates wholesome dharmas;
the one who practices what is unrighteous and evil stands in opposition to the one who practices this Dharma and sublime conduct.
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—these unwholesome precepts are the opposites of wholesome precepts.
Lack of faith, laziness, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and unwholesome wisdom are the opposites of wholesome wisdom.
"Cunda! There are some phenomena that are dark, with dark retribution, leading to an evil destination.
There are some phenomena that are bright, with bright retribution, resulting in an upward ascent."
In this way, Cunda!
Those with evil desires attain transcendence by means of being free from evil desires.
Those with harmful intentions and malice attain transcendence by means of being free from harmful intentions and malice.
Those who engage in killing, taking what is not given, and unchaste conduct, take the practice of celibacy as their excellence.
Those who harbor ill will, contentious intent, sloth and torpor, restlessness and arrogance, and doubt, take the absence of doubt as their excellence.
For those bound by ill will, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of dread, the means of transcendence is shame and dread.
For the conceited, the means of transcendence is the absence of conceit.
For those with increased pride, the means of ascending is the absence of increased pride.
For those who have not heard much, the means of ascending is extensive learning.
For those who do not contemplate all wholesome dharmas, the means of ascending is the contemplation of all wholesome dharmas.
Those who practice unrighteous and evil conduct ascend by means of practicing this sublime Dharma-conduct;
those who engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and immoral discipline ascend by means of virtuous discipline.
For those who lack faith, are indolent, lack mindfulness, lack concentration, and possess poor wisdom, it is by means of wholesome wisdom that they ascend. "Cunda!
It is impossible for one who is not self-disciplined to discipline another who is not disciplined."
It is impossible that one who is themselves submerged and drowning could ever pull out another who is submerged and drowning.
It is impossible that one who has not attained parinirvāṇa themselves could cause another who has not attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa.
Cunda! If one who has disciplined themselves wishes to discipline others who have not yet been disciplined, such a thing is certainly possible.
If one who has not themselves sunk into the depths wishes to pull out others who have sunk, such a thing is certainly possible.
It is indeed possible, Cunda, that one who has attained parinirvāṇa may cause others who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa to attain it.
It is so. Cunda!
Those with evil desires regard the absence of evil desire as parinirvāṇa;
those with harmful intent and anger regard the absence of harmful intent and anger as parinirvāṇa;
those who kill, take what is not given, or engage in unchaste conduct regard pure conduct (brahmacarya) as parinirvāṇa.
For those who possess increased scrutiny, contentious intent, drowsiness, restlessness and pride, and doubt, parinirvāṇa is attained through the absence of doubt.
For those who possess the fetter of anger, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of remorse, parinirvāṇa is attained through shame and remorse.
For those who are conceited, non-conceit is parinirvāṇa.
For those who increase their conceit, the non-increase of conceit is parinirvāṇa.
For those who have not heard much, extensive learning is parinirvāṇa.
Those who do not contemplate the various wholesome dharmas take the contemplation of those wholesome dharmas as parinirvāṇa;
those who practice unrighteous and evil conduct take the practice of these sublime dharmas as parinirvāṇa.
For those who engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, as well as those with unwholesome precepts, they take wholesome precepts as parinirvāṇa.
For those who lack faith, are indolent, lack mindfulness, lack concentration, and possess unwholesome wisdom, they take wholesome wisdom as parinirvāṇa.
“Thus it is, Cunda!
I have already taught you the Dharma of gradual reduction, the Dharma of generating the mind of awakening, the Dharma of counteraction, the Dharma of ascending, and the Dharma of parinirvāṇa.”

Just as a venerable teacher acts toward his disciples by giving rise to great loving-kindness, compassion, pity, and sympathy, seeking their welfare and benefit, and seeking their peace and happiness, so have I now done.

"You yourselves must also likewise act: go to a secluded place, such as a mountain forest, the foot of a tree, or an empty, quiet location; sit in meditation and contemplate, do not be negligent, apply yourselves with diligent effort, and do not let yourselves have cause for regret."
"This is my instruction; this is my admonition.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Mahācunda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Cunda-paṭipadā-sutta*, the fifth, ends here with one thousand five hundred and seventy-five characters. 92. The *Uppala-sutta* (92), the sixth sutta in the *Vejayanta-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Recited in the second section on Small Earthly Cities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are certain dharmas that are extinguished through the body but not through the mouth;
there are certain dharmas that are extinguished through the mouth but not through the body."
There are some phenomena that are not extinguished through body or speech, but are extinguished only through the vision of wisdom.
What are the phenomena that are extinguished through the body and not through speech?
A monk may be filled with unwholesome bodily conduct, fully possessing and adhering to it. When the other monks see this, they rebuke that monk:
"Venerable sir!
When unwholesome bodily conduct is fulfilled and fully maintained, why do you remain attached to the body?
Venerable sir!"
"One should abandon unwholesome bodily conduct and cultivate wholesome bodily conduct.
Later, he abandons unwholesome bodily conduct and cultivates wholesome bodily conduct; this is called a phenomenon that ceases through the body, not through speech.
"What is it that causes a phenomenon to cease through the mouth, rather than through the body?
A bhikṣu may be filled with unwholesome verbal conduct, fully embracing and adhering to it through his speech. When the other bhikṣus see this, they rebuke that bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable one!'"
If unwholesome verbal conduct is abundant and fully maintained, why be attached to speech?
Worthy one!
You should abandon unwholesome verbal conduct and cultivate wholesome verbal conduct.
At a later time, he abandons unwholesome verbal conduct and cultivates wholesome verbal conduct; this is called the Dharma perishing from speech, not perishing from the body.
"How is it that certain phenomena are not extinguished through body or speech, but are extinguished only through the vision of wisdom?

The increase of vitarka is not extinguished through body or speech, but is extinguished only through the vision of wisdom. Likewise, contention, malice, resentment, the fetter of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desires, and evil views are not extinguished through body or speech, but are extinguished only through the vision of wisdom."
This is called the Dharma not being extinguished through body or speech, but rather extinguished through the vision of wisdom.

"The Tathāgata may have an observation wherein he observes the minds of others and knows that this person has not cultivated the body, cultivated morality, cultivated the mind, or cultivated wisdom in such a way that—just as by cultivating the body, morality, mind, and wisdom—one attains the extinction of increased discursive thought."

Why is this so? Because these people dwell with minds giving rise to and increasing ill will and harmful intent; yet, they are able to extinguish such disputes, resentment, hatred, the fetters of anger, the knot of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, and lack of remorse, as well as evil desires and evil views.
Why is this? Because this person dwells with the arising of evil desires and evil views.

Knowing that this person thus cultivates the body, cultivates morality, cultivates the mind, and cultivates wisdom—just as they cultivate the body, so too do they cultivate morality, the mind, and wisdom—they attain the cessation of increased discursive thought.

Why is this? Because such a person dwells with a mind that does not give rise to ill will or covetousness; thus, they attain the cessation of disputes, quarrels, resentment, malice, the fetter of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, envy, deceit, flattery, lack of shame, and lack of dread. They also attain the cessation of evil desires and evil views.
Why is this? Because these people dwell with minds that give rise neither to evil desires nor evil views.
They are like blue lotuses, red, pink, or white lotuses—born in the water, grown in the water, yet rising above the water, unsoiled by it.
In this way, the Tathāgata is born in the world and grows in the world, yet he practices the supramundane way and does not cling to worldly dharmas. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has transcended all worlds.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!”
"What shall this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied:
“Ānanda! This sutra is titled ‘The Simile of the Blue and White Lotus’; you should receive, uphold, and recite it well in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You all should together receive this Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, reciting, practicing, and upholding it. Why is this?

This Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus is in accordance with the Dharma and possesses meaning; it is the foundation of the holy life (brahmacarya), leading to penetration, leading to awakening, and also leading to Nirvāṇa."

If a son of good family, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, out of supreme faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, he should receive this Sūtra of the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus and skillfully recite and uphold it.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Sūtra on the Simile of the Blue and White Lotus, the sixth, ends here with seven hundred and three characters. 93. The Sūtra on the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇī (93). Majjhima Nikāya, Chapter on the Defiled, The Sūtra on the Brahmin Jāṇussoṇī, the seventh; recited in the second sub-section of Khuddakapāṭha. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering along the banks of the Nerañjarā River at Uruvelā, staying beneath the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree, having just attained the Way.
Then, a certain brahmin named Jāṇussoṇī, wandering about after the midday meal, approached the place where the Buddha was.
Seeing the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī coming from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus on account of him:
"If there are those whose minds are defiled by twenty-one impurities, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell."

What are the twenty-one defilements? They are: the defilement of a mind of wrong view; the defilement of a mind of unrighteous desire; the defilement of a mind of evil greed; the defilement of a mind of false dharma; the defilement of a mind of craving; the defilement of a mind of ill will; the defilement of a mind of sloth and torpor; the defilement of a mind of restlessness and remorse; the defilement of a mind of doubt; the defilement of a mind bound by anger; the defilement of a mind fettered by silence; the defilement of a mind of stinginess; the defilement of a mind of envy; the defilement of a mind of deceit and fraud; the defilement of a mind of flattery and guile; the defilement of a mind lacking shame; the defilement of a mind lacking dread of blame; the defilement of a mind of pride; the defilement of a mind of great pride; the defilement of a mind of arrogance; and the defilement of a mind of negligence.
If one possesses these twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

It is like a garment stained with grease and grime being given to a dyer; once the dyer receives it, he may wash it thoroughly with strong lye, or with soap powder, or by soaking it in earth, thereby cleansing this stained and greasy garment.
Although dyers may treat them by washing them thoroughly with caustic ash, soap powder, or earth-water, these soiled garments still retain their stained colors.
In this way, if one has twenty-one defilements in the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.
What are the twenty-one defilements?

The defilement of the mind through wrong view; the defilement of the mind through unrighteous desire; the defilement of the mind through evil greed; the defilement of the mind through false doctrine; the defilement of the mind through lust; the defilement of the mind through ill will; the defilement of the mind through sloth and torpor; the defilement of the mind through restlessness and remorse; the defilement of the mind through doubt; the defilement of the mind through the fetter of anger; the defilement of the mind through the knot of silence; the defilement of the mind through stinginess; the defilement of the mind through envy; the defilement of the mind through deceit; the defilement of the mind through flattery; the defilement of the mind through lack of shame; the defilement of the mind through lack of dread; the defilement of the mind through conceit; the defilement of the mind through great conceit; the defilement of the mind through arrogance; and the defilement of the mind through negligence.
"If one possesses these twenty-one defilements that pollute the mind, one will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.
If one possesses these twenty-one defilements but they do not pollute the mind, one will certainly go to a good destination and be born in the heavens."

What are the twenty-one defilements? They are: the defilement of a mind of wrong view; the defilement of a mind of unrighteous desire; the defilement of a mind of evil greed; the defilement of a mind of false dharma; the defilement of a mind of craving; the defilement of a mind of anger; the defilement of a mind of sloth and torpor; the defilement of a mind of restlessness and remorse; the defilement of a mind of doubt; the defilement of a mind bound by malice; the defilement of a mind of silence (mūka-citta); the defilement of a mind of stinginess; the defilement of a mind of envy; the defilement of a mind of deceit; the defilement of a mind of flattery; the defilement of a mind lacking shame; the defilement of a mind lacking dread of blame; the defilement of a mind of pride; the defilement of a mind of great pride; the defilement of a mind of arrogance; and the defilement of a mind of negligence.
If there is one whose mind is not defiled by these twenty-one impurities, they will certainly go to a good destination and be born in the heavens.

It is just as when a pure, white cloth from Vārāṇasī is given to a dyer: once the dyer receives it, he may wash it thoroughly with strong lye, or with soap powder, or with earth until it is completely clean.

Although this pure, white cloth from Vārāṇasī is treated by the dyer and washed thoroughly with strong lye, or with soap powder, or with earth until it is completely clean, this pure, white cloth from Vārāṇasī was already pure to begin with, and is now pure once more.
Thus, if one whose mind is not defiled by the twenty-one impurities will certainly reach a good destination and be reborn in the heavens.
What are the twenty-one impurities?

The defilement of a mind of wrong view; the defilement of a mind of unrighteous desire; the defilement of a mind of evil greed; the defilement of a mind of false dharma; the defilement of a mind of craving; the defilement of a mind of ill will; the defilement of a mind of sloth and torpor; the defilement of a mind of restlessness and remorse; the defilement of a mind of doubt; the defilement of a mind bound by anger; the defilement of a mind fettered by silence; the defilement of a mind of stinginess; the defilement of a mind of envy; the defilement of a mind of deceit and fraud; the defilement of a mind of flattery and guile; the defilement of a mind lacking shame; the defilement of a mind lacking dread of blame; the defilement of a mind of conceit; the defilement of a mind of great conceit; the defilement of a mind of arrogance; and the defilement of a mind of heedlessness.
If there is one whose mind is not defiled by these twenty-one impurities, they will certainly reach a good destination and be born in the heavens.
If one knows that wrong view is an impurity of the mind, having known it, one should then abandon it.

In this way, there are the defilements of the mind: the defilement of unrighteous desire, the defilement of evil greed, the defilement of false views, the defilement of covetousness, the defilement of ill will, the defilement of sloth and torpor, the defilement of restlessness and remorse, the defilement of doubt, the defilement of the obsession of anger, the defilement of the fetter of resentment, the defilement of stinginess, the defilement of envy, the defilement of deceit, the defilement of flattery, the defilement of shamelessness, the defilement of lack of dread, the defilement of conceit, the defilement of arrogance, and the defilement of haughtiness. If one knows that negligence is a defilement of the mind, having known it, one abandons it; then that mind, accompanied by loving-kindness, dwells pervading the ten directions, having attained fulfillment.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one abides, having accomplished this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, joy, and equanimity—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
“Brahmin!
This is called bathing the inner mind, not bathing the outer body.
At that time, the brahmin said to the World-Honored One:
“Gautama! You may go to the Bahuka River to bathe.
The World-Honored One asked:
“Brahmin! If one goes to a river with abundant water to bathe, what does he obtain?
The Brahmin replied:
"Gautama! That river with its abundant waters is a sign of worldly purity, a sign of crossing over, and a sign of merit,
Gautama!"
"If one goes to a river with abundant water to bathe, he shall purify himself of all evils.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for that brahmin:
"O brahmin of beautiful head, If you enter a river with abundant water..."
These fools constantly indulge in play, unable to purify their dark karma.
O handsome one, where are you going to the spring? What is the purpose of the river with its many waters?
When a person has committed unwholesome deeds, what benefit is there in clear water?
The pure one is free from defilement; the pure one constantly recites the precepts;
the pure one possesses pure and white karma, and always attains pure conduct.
If you do not kill living beings, and never take what is not given,
Truthful and not speaking falsely, always with right mindfulness and clear comprehension—when a brahmin trains thus, all sentient beings find peace.
Why would a brahmin return home? The spring within the home is never pure.
"Brahmin, you should train yourself to cleanse with the Dharma;
what need is there for foul water? Simply remove the impurities of the body.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I too have had this thought: to purify oneself with the wholesome Dharma, what need is there for foul and evil water?
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the brahmin was filled with great joy in his heart;
he immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The brahmin said:
"World-Honored One!
I have understood."
"Sugata! I have understood.

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Sunetta and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh discourse, the Sunetta Sutta, ends here; it contains one thousand two hundred and ten characters. 94. The Discourse on the Black Bhikṣu (94) The Middle Āgama, Chapter on Defilements, The Black Bhikṣu Sutta, the eighth. Recited in the Second Minor Earth-City Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and was staying at the Eastern Garden in the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kāla and his mother, the bhikṣuṇī Mṛgāramātṛ, who were constantly fond of quarreling, went to where the Buddha was.
The World-Honored One saw the bhikṣu Kāla approaching from afar, and on account of Kāla, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"There may be a person who constantly delights in quarreling and does not approve of the settling of disputes."

If there is a person who always delights in strife and does not approve of the cessation of strife, this teaching is not pleasant, not lovely, not delightful, cannot inspire affection, cannot inspire reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to nirvāṇa.
“There may be a person who has evil desires and does not praise the cessation of evil desires.

If there is a person who has evil desires and does not praise the cessation of evil desires, this state is not pleasant, not lovely, not delightful; it cannot inspire affection, cannot inspire reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.”

“Suppose there is a person who violates the precepts, transgresses the precepts, is deficient in the precepts, has holes in the precepts, and defiles the precepts, such that he is not called one who upholds the precepts.

If there is such a person who violates, transgresses, is deficient in, has holes in, and defiles the precepts, and is not called one who upholds the precepts, this state is not pleasant, not lovely, and not delightful; it cannot inspire affection, cannot inspire reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.”

“Suppose there is a person who is bound by the fetter of anger, possessed of the knot of silence, possessed of stinginess and envy, possessed of flattery, deceit, and hypocrisy, and lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame, not being one who values shame and dread of blame.

If there is a person who is bound by the fetter of anger, possessed of the knot of silence, possessed of stinginess and envy, possessed of flattery, deceit, and hypocrisy, and lacking a sense of shame and dread of blame—one who does not possess shame and dread of blame—then these qualities are not pleasant, not lovely, not delightful; they cannot cause one to feel affection, cannot cause one to feel reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to nirvāṇa.
"There may be a person who does not associate with fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) and does not praise such association.

If there is a person who does not associate with fellow practitioners of the holy life and does not praise such association, this dharma is not delightful, not lovely, not pleasing; it cannot inspire affection, cannot inspire reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the state of a *śramaṇa*, cannot lead to one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to *nirvāṇa*."
"There may be a person who does not contemplate all phenomena and does not praise the contemplation of all phenomena.

If there is a person who does not contemplate all phenomena and does not praise the contemplation of all phenomena, this dharma is not delightful, not lovable, and cannot inspire affection, cannot inspire reverence, cannot lead to cultivation, cannot lead to mastery, cannot lead to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa."
"There may be a person who does not sit in meditation and does not praise sitting in meditation.

If there is such a person who does not sit in meditation and does not praise sitting in meditation, this dharma is not pleasant, not lovely, and not delightful; it cannot cause one to feel affection for it, cannot cause one to revere it, cannot lead to its cultivation, cannot lead to its mastery, cannot lead to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, cannot lead to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, and cannot lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa."
Although this person thinks:
"May all fellow practitioners of the holy life provide me with offerings, respect,
and service," yet those fellow practitioners do not offer him offerings, respect, or service.

Why is this so? Because that person possesses these immeasurable unwholesome qualities; and because he possesses these immeasurable unwholesome qualities, it causes his fellow practitioners of the holy life not to offer him support, respect, or service.
It is just like a wicked horse tied to its stall and fed; though it thinks to itself:
"May people tie me up in a secure place, give me good food and drink, and look after me well."
"Yet people do not tether him in a secure place, nor do they give him good food, nor do they look after him with care. Why is this?

Because that horse possesses evil qualities—namely, being extremely coarse and wicked, and lacking gentleness—which causes people not to tether him in a secure place, nor to give him good food, nor to look after him with care."
In this way, although this person thinks:
"May all fellow practitioners of the holy life honor, respect,
and serve me," yet those fellow practitioners do not honor, respect, or serve him.

Why is this? Because that person possesses these immeasurable unwholesome qualities; and because they possess these immeasurable unwholesome qualities, it causes fellow practitioners of the holy life not to offer them support, respect, or service.
"Suppose there is a person who does not delight in quarreling and praises the cessation of quarreling.

If there is such a person who does not delight in quarreling and praises the cessation of quarreling, this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it can inspire affection, inspire reverence, inspire cultivation, and inspire upholding; it can lead to the state of a śramaṇa, lead to one-pointedness of mind, and lead to the attainment of Nirvāṇa."
“There may be a person who is free from evil desires and praises the cessation of evil desires.

If there is such a person who is free from evil desires and praises the cessation of evil desires, this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it can inspire affection, inspire reverence, inspire cultivation, and inspire upholding; it can lead to the state of a śramaṇa, lead to one-pointedness of mind, and lead to nirvāṇa.”

"Suppose there is a person who does not violate the precepts, does not transgress the precepts, does not break the precepts, does not pierce the precepts, and does not defile the precepts, and who praises the observance of the precepts."

If there is a person who does not violate the precepts, does not transgress the precepts, does not break the precepts, does not pierce the precepts, and does not defile the precepts, and who praises those who uphold the precepts—this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it can inspire affection, inspire reverence, inspire cultivation, and inspire maintenance; it can lead to the state of a śramaṇa, lead to one-pointedness of mind, and lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.

"There may be a person who is free from the fetter of anger, free from the knot of silence, free from stinginess and envy, free from flattery, deceit, and fraud, and free from shamelessness and lack of dread, while praising both shame and dread."

If there is a person who is free from the fetter of anger, free from the bond of silence, free from stinginess and envy, free from flattery, hypocrisy, and deception, and free from shamelessness and lack of moral dread—one who praises those possessing shame and moral dread—this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it can cause one to feel affection, it can cause one to feel reverence, it can lead to its cultivation, it can lead to its maintenance, it can lead to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, it can lead to the attainment of single-mindedness, and it can lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.
"There may be a person who has practiced the holy life and praises the practice of the holy life.

If there is such a person who has practiced the holy life and praises the practice of the holy life, this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it inspires affection, inspires reverence, inspires cultivation, inspires upholding, leads to the state of a śramaṇa, leads to one-pointedness of mind, and leads to nirvāṇa."
"There may be a person who contemplates all phenomena and praises the contemplation of all phenomena.

If there is such a person who contemplates all phenomena and praises the contemplation of all phenomena, this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and joyful; it can inspire affection, inspire reverence, inspire cultivation, and inspire upholding; it can lead to the state of a śramaṇa, lead to one-pointedness of mind, and lead to the attainment of Nirvāṇa."
“Suppose there is a person who sits in meditative seclusion and praises sitting in meditative seclusion.

If there is such a person who sits in meditative seclusion and praises sitting in meditative seclusion, this Dharma is delightful, lovely, and pleasing; it can inspire affection, inspire reverence, inspire cultivation, and inspire upholding; it can lead to the state of a śramaṇa, lead to one-pointedness of mind, and lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa.”
Although this person does not harbor the thought,
"May fellow practitioners of the holy life honor, revere, and attend upon me," nevertheless,
those fellow practitioners of the holy life do honor, revere, and attend upon him.

Why is this? Because that person possesses these immeasurable wholesome qualities; and because they possess these immeasurable wholesome qualities, it causes fellow practitioners of the holy life to provide them with offerings, respect, and service.
It is just as when a fine horse is tied to its stall and fed;
although it does not think, "May people tie me in a secure place, give me good food and drink, and look after me well."
"Yet people tie that horse to a secure place, provide it with good food and drink, and look after it well.

Why is this? Because that horse possesses wholesome qualities—namely, that it is well-trained and exceedingly gentle—which causes people to tie it to a secure place, provide it with good food and drink, and look after it well."
In this way, although this person does not harbor the thought,
"May fellow practitioners of the holy life honor, revere, and attend upon me," nevertheless,
those fellow practitioners of the holy life do honor, revere, and attend upon him.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The eighth discourse, the Kāḷaka-bhikṣu Sūtra, ends here; it contains one thousand five hundred and twenty-seven characters. 95. Dharmasthiti Sūtra (95), Middle Āgama, Chapter on Defilements, the ninth discourse, the Dharmasthiti Sūtra, recited in the second sub-section of the Small Earth-City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I say that the decline of wholesome qualities does not abide and does not increase; I say that the abiding of wholesome qualities does not decline and does not increase; I say that the increase of wholesome qualities does not decline and does not abide.”
What is meant by "retreating from wholesome qualities, neither abiding in nor increasing them"?

It is this: suppose a bhikṣu possesses faithful conviction, moral discipline, extensive learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence, as well as the teachings (āgama) and their realizations. If that person retreats from these qualities, neither abiding in nor increasing them, this is called "retreating from wholesome qualities, neither abiding in nor increasing them."
What is meant by dwelling in wholesome qualities without decline or increase?

A bhikkhu may possess profound faith, observance of the precepts, extensive learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, the *āgama*s, and their attainments; yet he dwells in these qualities without either declining or increasing. This is called dwelling in wholesome qualities without decline or increase.
What is meant by "increasing wholesome qualities without falling back or remaining stationary"?

A bhikṣu may possess profound faith, observance of the precepts, extensive learning, generosity, wisdom, eloquence, the Āgamas, and their realizations; such a person increases these qualities within this Dharma without falling back or remaining stationary—this is called increasing wholesome qualities without falling back or remaining stationary.
"A bhikkhu should reflect in this way, which will surely be of great benefit:
'Do I frequently practice with increased伺 (vitarka), or do I frequently practice without increased 伺?'"
"Am I one who frequently practices a mind of ill-will, or am I one who frequently practices a mind free from ill-will?
Am I one who frequently practices the fetter of sloth-and-torpor, or am I one who frequently practices freedom from the fetter of sloth-and-torpor?"
Do I frequently practice arrogance, or do I frequently practice the absence of arrogance?
Do I frequently practice doubt, or do I frequently practice the absence of doubt?
Do I frequently engage in bodily strife, or do I frequently refrain from bodily strife?
Do I frequently harbor a defiled mind, or do I frequently maintain a mind free from defilement?
Do I practice faith more frequently, or do I practice lack of faith more frequently?
Do I practice diligence more frequently, or do I practice indolence more frequently?
Do I practice mindfulness more frequently, or do I practice lack of mindfulness more frequently?
‘Do I practice much concentration, or do I practice much lack of concentration?
Do I practice much unwholesome wisdom, or do I practice much wholesome wisdom?

If, when a bhikkhu examines himself, he knows: ‘I practice much covetousness, ill will, the fetter of sloth and torpor, restlessness and haughtiness, doubt, bodily agitation, a defiled mind, lack of faith, laziness, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and I practice much unwholesome wisdom,’ then that bhikkhu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, quickly seeks out the means, trains with extreme diligence, maintains right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endures without falling back.
Just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire would urgently seek means to save their head or clothing,

so too a bhikṣu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, quickly seeks means to train with extreme diligence, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, enduring them so as not to let them regress.

“If, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows: ‘I frequently practice without covetousness, without ill will, without the entanglement of sloth, without restlessness and haughtiness, without doubt, without bodily strife, and without a defiled mind; I possess faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and frequently practice without unwholesome wisdom’—then that bhikkhu, desiring to abide in these wholesome qualities so as not to forget them, not to fall back from them, but to cultivate and spread them, should quickly seek the means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and clear comprehension, and endure without allowing them to decline.”
It is just as when a person’s head or clothing is set on fire, they urgently seek means to save their head and save their clothing.

In the same way, a bhikṣu who wishes to abide in this wholesome dharma—so that it is not forgotten, does not decline, but is practiced and widely disseminated—should swiftly seek means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endure so as not to let it regress.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The ninth discourse, *The Discourse on Abiding in the Dharma*, ends here, totaling six hundred and thirty-one characters. 96. The Discourse on Non-existence (No. 96) The tenth discourse in the *Chapter on Defilements* (*Vyasana-varga*) of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Recited in the second section on the Small Earthen City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!..."

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have not heard the Dharma, they do not hear it; those who have already heard the Dharma forget it. Furthermore, regarding the teachings they originally practiced, widely disseminated, recited, and mastered through wisdom—their understanding of them—they no longer remember them, knowing them yet as if they did not know.
"Venerable friends!
This is called the decline of the pure qualities of a bhikkhu or a bhikkhunī.
"Venerable friends!"

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have not yet heard the Dharma, they shall hear it; those who have already heard the Dharma shall not forget it. Furthermore, regarding the teachings that were originally practiced, widely disseminated, recited, and mastered, and which were understood through wisdom—they shall constantly remember them, knowing them and knowing them ever more deeply.
This is called the further increase of the pure qualities of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī.
"Virtuous ones!
A bhikṣu should practice contemplation in this way:
"Am I possessed of thoughts of ill will, or am I free from thoughts of ill will?
Am I possessed of a mind of malice, or am I free from a mind of malice?
Am I entangled by sloth and torpor, or am I free from being entangled by sloth and torpor?"
Am I one who possesses pride that needs taming, or am I one who lacks such pride?
Am I one who possesses doubt, or am I one who lacks doubt?
Am I one who possesses internal strife, or am I one who lacks internal strife?
"Do I have a defiled mind, or am I free from a defiled mind?
Do I have faith, or am I without faith?
Do I have diligence, or am I without diligence?"
Do I possess mindfulness or am I without mindfulness?
Do I possess concentration or am I without concentration?
Do I possess unwholesome wisdom or am I without unwholesome wisdom?
"Venerable friends!

When a bhikkhu examines himself, he knows: 'I have covetousness, a mind of ill will, the fetter of sloth and torpor, restlessness and haughtiness, doubt, bodily strife, and a defiled mind; I lack faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and possess unwholesome wisdom.'"
"Venerable friends!

Because that bhikṣu desires to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, he quickly seeks skillful means, trains with extreme diligence, maintains right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endures them without allowing them to cause him to regress."
Venerable friends!
It is just as if a person whose head was on fire or whose clothes were on fire would urgently seek means to extinguish that fire on their head and extinguish that fire on their clothes.
Venerable friends!

In this way, because that bhikṣu desires to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, he quickly seeks skillful means, training with extreme diligence, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, enduring them so as not to let them persist.
"Venerable friends!

If, when examining himself, a bhikkhu knows: 'I have no covetousness, no mind of ill will, no entanglement of sloth and torpor, no restlessness and haughtiness, no doubt, no bodily strife, and no defiled mind; I possess faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and am free from unwholesome wisdom,' then that bhikkhu, desiring to abide in these wholesome qualities—so as not to forget them, not to fall back from them, but to cultivate and spread them—should quickly seek the means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endure so as not to let them decline."
Just as when a person’s head or clothing is on fire, they urgently seek means to save their head or clothing;
