so too, O worthy ones, a bhikkhu who wishes to abide in this wholesome Dharma— so that it is not forgotten and does not decline, but is practiced and widely disseminated— should quickly seek means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endure so as not to let it regress.
Thus spoke the Venerable Sāriputta. Having heard what the Venerable Sāriputta had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The tenth sutta [of this section] ends here; it contains five hundred and sixty-eight characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, scroll twenty-three, contains eight thousand six hundred and fifty-eight characters. The third section, the "Chapter on Defilements" (*Saṃkilesavagga*), ends here; it contains sixteen thousand one hundred and forty characters.
This concludes scroll twenty-four of the *Madhyama Āgama*, recited at the Lesser Earthen City (*Kṣudrakapattana*).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Causes (Hetuvarga). This chapter contains ten sūtras. Recited at the Second Small Earth-City.
Causes, Bases, and the Two Aggregates of Suffering; Higher Mind and Mindfulness.
Siṃhanāda, Udumbara, Praṇidhāna, and Saṃjñā are the last [nine].
(97) The Mahānidāna Sūtra (97), First in the Nidāna Vagga of the Madhyama Āgama. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Kośala and staying at the Kośalan town of Kalmāṣadamya.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling in solitude, sitting in meditation and reflecting, when this thought arose in his mind:
"This dependent origination is most wonderful, exceedingly profound, and its illumination is also exceedingly profound; yet, as I observe it, it appears to me as something extremely shallow."
Thereupon, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Now, as I dwell in seclusion and solitude, sitting in quiet meditation and reflecting, this thought arose in my mind:

"This dependent origination is most wonderful, exceedingly profound, and its illumination is also exceedingly profound; yet, as I contemplate it, I see it as being extremely shallow, even to the point of extreme shallowness."
The World-Honored One said:
"Ānanda! Do not harbor such a thought; this dependent origination is most shallow, indeed most shallow."
Why is that? This dependent origination is extremely profound, and its elucidation is also extremely profound, Ānanda!

Because they do not know this dependent origination as it truly is, do not see it as it really is, and have neither awakened to nor mastered it, those beings—like the interlocking parts of a loom, like creeping vines—suffer great agitation and turmoil. Hastening and clamorous, they pass from this world to that world and from that world back to this one; coming and going, they are unable to transcend birth and death.
"Ānanda! Therefore, know that this dependent origination is extremely profound, and its clarification is also extremely profound. Ānanda!"
If someone should ask,
"Is there a condition for old age and death?
one should answer thus:
"Old age and death have a condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the condition for old age and death?"
"You should answer thus:
'It is conditioned by birth. Ānanda!"
If someone should ask:
"Is birth conditioned?
one should answer thus:
"Birth also has a condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the condition for birth?"
One should answer thus:
"It is conditioned by existence (bhava). Ānanda!
If someone should ask,
"Is there a condition for existence?
one should answer thus:
"Existence also has a condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the condition for existence?"
"You should answer thus:
'It is conditioned by feeling. Ānanda!"
If someone should ask,
"Is feeling conditioned?
one should answer thus:
"Feeling also has a condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the condition for feeling?"
"You should answer thus:
'It is conditioned by craving. Ānanda!"

Thus, with craving as condition there is feeling; with feeling as condition there is becoming; with becoming as condition there is birth; with birth as condition there is aging and death; with aging and death as condition there is sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—all these arise with aging and death as their condition. In this way, this entire mass of suffering, which is purely of a painful nature, comes into being.

"Ānanda! 'Conditioned by birth, there is old age and death'—this is said to mean that conditioned by birth, there is old age and death; you should understand this as what is called 'conditioned by birth, there is old age and death. Ānanda!"

If there were no arising, Ānanda, there would be no fish and the species of fish; no birds and the species of birds; no mosquitoes and the species of mosquitoes; no nāgas and the species of nāgas; no devas and the species of devas; no ghosts and the species of ghosts; no gods and the species of gods; and no humans and the species of humans. Ānanda!

If, for those various sentient beings in their respective places, there were no birth—that is, if each were individually without birth—then even if one were separated from birth, would there still be aging and death?
He replied, "There is none. "Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

Therefore, one should know that the cause of old age and death, the origin of old age and death, the root of old age and death, and the condition for old age and death is this very birth. Why is this so?
Because of arising, there is aging and death. "Ānanda!
Conditioned by existence, there is birth; this is called 'conditioned by existence, there is birth,' and it should be understood as such."

Ānanda! If there were no fish, nor the species of fish; no birds, nor the species of birds; no mosquitoes, nor the species of mosquitoes; no nāgas, nor the species of nāgas; no spirits, nor the species of spirits; no ghosts, nor the species of ghosts; no devas, nor the species of devas; and no humans, nor the species of humans.
Ānanda! Regarding those various sentient beings who, in their respective places, do not exist and are each non-existent—if they were to be separated from existence, would there be birth?
He replied, “There is none. “Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
Therefore, one should know that what constitutes the cause of birth, the accumulation of birth, the root of birth, and the condition for birth is this "existence" (bhava). Why is this so?
Because with existence as a condition, there is birth.

“Ānanda! As for the statement, ‘With feeling as condition, there is existence,’ this refers to the fact that with feeling as condition there is existence; you should understand that this is what is meant by ‘with feeling as condition, there is existence. Ānanda!”
"If there is no feeling, and each [condition] is without feeling, then even if one were to be separated from feeling, would there still be 'existence' (bhava),
or could 'existence' be established? He replied, "No."
“Ānanda! For this reason, you should know that what has a cause, a condition, a root, and a source is this very feeling. Why is that?
With feeling as condition, there is becoming. Ānanda!

Regarding "with craving as condition, there is feeling," this is said to mean that with craving as condition, there is feeling; one should know that what is meant by "with craving as condition, there is feeling" is precisely this.
"Ānanda!
If there were no craving, and each person were without craving, even if one were to be separated from craving, would there still be feeling established upon feeling?
He replied:
“No, [it is not]. “Ānanda!
Therefore, you should know that this craving is the cause of feeling, the origin of feeling, the root of feeling, and the condition for feeling.”
Why is that? Because with craving as condition, there is feeling. "Ānanda!

Thus, conditioned by craving, there is seeking; conditioned by seeking, there is gain; conditioned by gain, there is decision-making; conditioned by decision-making, there is lustful desire; conditioned by lustful desire, there is attachment; conditioned by attachment, there is possessiveness; conditioned by possessiveness, there is the household; and conditioned by the household, there is guarding.

Ānanda! Conditioned by guarding, there arise swords and staves, strife, contention, flattery, deceit, false speech, and double-tongued talk; thus incalculable evil and unwholesome states arise, and such a complete mass of great suffering is produced.

Ānanda! If there were no guarding, and each person lacked guarding—if one were to be devoid of guarding—would there still arise swords and staves, strife and contention, flattery, deception, false speech, and double-tongued talk, as well as immeasurable evil and unwholesome states?
He replied, "No, Ānanda. "Ānanda! [he continued.]
Therefore, one should know that these weapons, staves, quarrels, disputes, flattery, deception, false speech, and double-tonguedness give rise to immeasurable evil and unwholesome states.
That which has this as its habituation, this as its basis, and this as its condition is called this "guarding. Why is that?

Because with guarding as a condition, there arise swords and staves, strife and contention, flattery, deception, false speech, and double-tongued talk; thus, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states arise, and in this way, a complete mass of great suffering is fully produced.
“Ānanda! Because there is guarding regarding the home, this is called ‘guarding regarding the home. You should know what is meant by ‘guarding regarding the home. Ānanda!”
"If there is no home, and each person is without a home, even if one were to leave the home,
would there be anything to guard? He replied, "No."
"Ānanda! For this reason, you should know that what is the cause of guarding, the practice of guarding, the root of guarding, and the condition for guarding is this household. Why is that?
“With the household as condition, there is guarding. Ānanda!

‘With stinginess as condition, there is the household’—this is said to mean that with stinginess as condition, there is the household; you should know what is meant by ‘with stinginess as condition, there is the household.’”
"Ānanda!
If there were no stinginess, and each person were without stinginess—if one were free from stinginess—would there still be households?
He replied:
"No. "Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that the cause of this household, its accumulation, its root, and its condition is this very stinginess."
Why is this? Because of stinginess, there is a household. "Ānanda!

"Conditioned by attachment, there is stinginess; this is what is called being conditioned by attachment to stinginess. You should know that this is what is meant by 'conditioned by attachment to stinginess. Ānanda!
If there were no attachment, and each person were without attachment—if one were free from attachment—would stinginess still exist?"
He replied, “No, Ānanda. “Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
Therefore, one should know that the cause of stinginess, the habituation of stinginess, the root of stinginess, and the condition of stinginess is this very attachment.
Why is this so? Because with attachment as a condition, stinginess arises.

“Ānanda! Regarding the statement, ‘With craving as condition, there is attachment,’ this refers to the statement, ‘With craving as condition, there is attachment. You should know that what is meant by ‘with craving as condition, there is attachment’ is precisely this. Ānanda!
"If there is no desire, and each individual is without desire, then if one were to be free from desire,
would there still be attachment? He replied, "No."

“Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that this which is the cause of attachment, the accumulation of attachment, the root of attachment, and the condition for attachment is this very desire. Why is that?
"Because of desire, there is attachment. Ānanda!

Regarding the statement that 'conditioned by the factors of existence (bhava), there is lustful desire,' one should understand that this refers to what is called 'conditioned by the factors of existence, there is lustful desire.'"
"Ānanda!
If there were no parts, and each thing were without parts, even if one were to separate them, would there still be lustful desire?
He replied:
"No. "Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that this portion is the cause of sensual desire, the accumulation of sensual desire, the root of sensual desire, and the condition for sensual desire."
Why is this so? Because of conditions and factors, there is defiled desire. "Ānanda!
Regarding "having a portion based on benefit," this refers to having a portion based on benefit; one should understand that this is what is called "having a portion based on benefit.
Ānanda! If there were no benefit, and each individual had no benefit—if one were separated from benefit, would there still be a portion?
He replied, "There is none, Ānanda. "Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]
Therefore, one should know that what constitutes its cause, its practice, its root, and its condition is this gain.
Why is this so? Because it is conditioned by gain that there is division.
“Ānanda! That which is conditioned by the pursuit of gain is called ‘conditioned by the pursuit of gain’; this is what should be understood as ‘conditioned by the pursuit of gain. Ānanda!”
"If there is no seeking, and each person is without seeking, would there be any benefit if one were to be free from seeking? He replied, "No."
“Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that what constitutes the cause of benefit, the condition for benefit, the root of benefit, and the basis for benefit is this very seeking. Why is that?
Because of seeking, there is a distinct gain. "Ānanda!
'Conditioned by craving, there is seeking'—this is said to mean that conditioned by craving, there is seeking; one should know this as what is meant by 'conditioned by craving, there is seeking.'"
"Ānanda!
If there were no craving, and each individual were without craving, even if one were to be separated from craving, would there still be seeking?
He replied:
“No. “Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that this which is sought as a cause, sought as an accumulation, sought as a root, and sought as a condition is this very craving.”
Why is this? Because craving is the condition for seeking. "Ānanda!
Craving for sensual pleasure and craving for existence—these two factors arise through the conditions of awakening and the objects of awakening.
Ānanda! If someone were to ask:
"Does feeling have a condition?
One should answer thus:
"Feeling also has a condition."
If someone were to ask,
"What is the condition for awakening?
one should answer thus:
"It is conditioned by contact.
One should know that what is called "conditioned by contact" possesses feeling. Ānanda!

If there were no eye-contact, and if for each [person] there were no eye-contact, then even if one were separated from eye-contact, would there still arise, conditioned by eye-contact, feelings of pleasure, feelings of pain, or feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant?
He replied, “No, Ānanda. “Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
If there were no contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind— each being devoid of mental contact—
and if one were to be separated from mental contact, would there still arise, conditioned by that mental contact, feelings of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure?
He replied, "No, Ānanda.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]
Therefore, one should know that what constitutes the cause of feeling, the accumulation of feeling, the root of feeling, and the condition for feeling is this contact. Why is this so?
Because conditioned by contact, there is feeling.
"Ānanda! If someone were to ask:
'Is contact conditioned?'"
One should answer thus:
"Contact has a condition.
If there should be one who asks:
"What is the condition for contact?
One should answer thus:
"It is conditioned by name-and-form."
"You should know that what is called 'contact' (phassa) has name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its condition. Ānanda!
Is there contact involving resistance (sappaṭigha-phassa) apart from these activities and apart from this object, which consists of the group of names (nāmakāya)?"
He replied, "No, Ānanda.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]
"If there is a physical body that acts and has objects of perception, apart from this action and apart from these objects,
would there be any further contact associated with verbal designation? He replied, "No."
“If one were to be separated from the name-body and the form-body, could there still be the designation of ‘contact’ and the experience of contact? He replied, “No.”
“Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that this contact-pleasure (phassa) has name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as its cause, its origin, its root, and its condition.”
Why is that? Because with name-and-form as condition, there is contact. "Ānanda!
If someone should ask,
"Is name-and-form conditioned?
one should answer thus:
"Name-and-form has a condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the condition for name-and-form?"
One should answer thus:
"It is conditioned by consciousness.
One should know that what is called "conditioned by consciousness" is name-and-form.
"Ānanda! If consciousness were not to enter the mother’s womb, would there be name-and-form to constitute this body?
He replied:
"No. "Ānanda! If consciousness were to enter the womb and immediately depart, would name-and-form (nāmarūpa) then coalesce with the vital essence?"
He replied, "I do not understand. "Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
“If the consciousness of a young boy or girl were to be severed, destroyed, and cease to exist at its very inception, would name-and-form continue to grow and develop? He replied, “No.”
“Ānanda! Therefore, you should know that what is the cause of name-and-form, the origin of name-and-form, the root of name-and-form, and the condition for name-and-form is this consciousness.”
Why is this? Because conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form.
"Ānanda!..."
If someone asks,
"Does consciousness have an object-condition?
one should answer thus:
"Consciousness also has an object-condition.
If someone were to ask:
"What is the object-condition of consciousness?"
One should answer thus:
"It is conditioned by name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
One should know that what is called "consciousness (vijñāna) exists conditioned by name-and-form."

Ānanda! If consciousness were not to obtain name-and-form, and if consciousness were neither established upon nor dependent on name-and-form, would that consciousness then have birth, aging, illness, death, or suffering?
He replied, "No, Ānanda.
"Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]

Therefore, one should know that the cause of consciousness, the condition for the arising of consciousness, the source of consciousness, and the basis of consciousness is this very name-and-form (nāmarūpa). Why is this so?
Because with name-and-form as a condition, consciousness comes to be.

Ānanda! This is how, conditioned by name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there is consciousness (vijñāna); and conditioned by consciousness, there is also name-and-form. By means of this designation, through the transmission of designations, and through the transmission of teachings, it can be conventionally established that consciousness and name-and-form exist together.
“Ānanda! How is it that there is one who holds the view that there is a self?
Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

There may be one who perceives that consciousness is the self; or again, there may be one who does not perceive that consciousness is the self, yet perceives that the self can perceive, and that the nature of the self is capable of perceiving.

Or again, there may be one who neither perceives that consciousness is the self nor perceives that the self can perceive, yet perceives that the nature of the self is capable of perceiving, while seeing only that the self has nothing to perceive.
Ānanda! If there is one who perceives a certain feeling as the self, you should ask him:
"You have three feelings: [pleasant, painful, and neutral]."
"There are the feeling of pleasure, the feeling of pain, and the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure. Of these three feelings, which one do you perceive as the self?
"Ānanda! [the Buddha asked.]
One should further say to him:
"If there is one who experiences a pleasant feeling, at that time two feelings cease—
the painful feeling and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling— and at that time he experiences only the pleasant feeling."
The pleasant feeling is a phenomenon that is impermanent, a phenomenon that is suffering, and a phenomenon that is subject to cessation.
If the pleasant feeling has ceased, one does not think: "Has the self been extinguished?"
"Ānanda! If, moreover, there is one who perceives a painful feeling, at that time two feelings cease:
the pleasant feeling and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time, he perceives only the painful feeling."
The perception of suffering is a phenomenon that is impermanent, a phenomenon that is suffering, and a phenomenon that is subject to cessation.
When the perception of suffering has ceased, one does not think: "Has the self (ātman) been extinguished?"
Ānanda! If there is another who experiences a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, at that time two feelings have ceased—
the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling— and at that time he experiences only the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant.
The sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant is a phenomenon that is impermanent, a phenomenon that is suffering, and a phenomenon that is subject to cessation.
If that sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure has ceased, would one not think: "Has the self been extinguished?"
"Ānanda!
Since such impermanent phenomena are merely devoid of suffering and pleasure, would one still perceive and recognize them as the self?
He replied:
"No. "Ānanda! For this reason, regarding such impermanent phenomena that are merely free from suffering and pleasure, one should not further perceive or cognize them as a self."
Ānanda! Suppose there is another person who does not see that consciousness is the self, but rather sees that the self can perceive and that the nature of the self is capable of perceiving.
To such a person, one should say: "If you were without perception, perception could not be found; therefore, it should not be said to belong to me."

"Ānanda! One might thus see that consciousness is not the self, yet [one might think] the self is capable of conscious awareness; would one then see that the nature of the self is capable of conscious awareness?
He replied:
"No, Ānanda. Therefore, one should not view it thus:
that consciousness is not the self, but the self is able to cognize; rather, one should view it as the nature of the self that is able to cognize."

Ānanda! Suppose there is another person who does not see that awakening is the self, nor that the self is capable of awakening, but rather sees that it is the nature of the self to awaken, yet sees the self as being without any act of awakening. You should say to him:
"If you have no awakening at all and it is entirely unattainable, then if the self were separate from awakening, the self would not be pure."

"Ānanda! Will he then further perceive that awakening is not the self, nor perceive that the self is capable of awakening, nor that the qualities of the self (dharma) are capable of awakening, but rather perceive only that the self has nothing to awaken?"
He replied, “No, Ānanda.
“Ānanda! [the Buddha continued.]

Therefore, one should not view it thus: that consciousness is not the self, nor that the self can perceive, nor that the qualities of the self can perceive; rather, one sees that the self has nothing to perceive. This is called the first view: that there exists a self which possesses perception.
"Ānanda! How is it that there are some who do not see the existence of a self?
Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: “Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze its meaning for you.”
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

There may be one who does not perceive the conscious self as the soul, nor perceives that the soul is capable of consciousness; yet they do not perceive that the nature of the soul is capable of consciousness, nor do they perceive that the soul is devoid of consciousness.

Having thus not seen [them], he does not grasp at this world; having not grasped it, he does not become weary; being without weariness, he attains parinirvāṇa, knowing according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

Ānanda! This is called a designation; it is spoken as a designation, transmitted as a transmission, and can be conventionally established as existing. One who knows this has nothing to be grasped. Ānanda!

If a bhikṣu is thus rightly liberated, he no longer holds the view that the Tathāgata exists after death, nor that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, nor that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, nor that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this is called "one who does not see a self."
"Ānanda! How is it that there is one who designates a designation of a self?
Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!
Some designate the self as having limited form;
others designate the self as not having limited form, but rather as having immeasurable form.
Furthermore, there is one who designates the self as having limited form, yet does not designate it as having infinite form, but rather designates the self as having limited formlessness.

Furthermore, there is one who designates the self as neither finite form nor infinite form, nor does he designate the self as finite formlessness, but rather designates the self as infinite formlessness.

“Ānanda! If there were one who designated a limited amount of form as the self, and so designated it, then now that he has designated a limited amount of form as the self, at the breaking up of the body after death, he would likewise speak and likewise hold this view: ‘If the self should depart from this limited amount of form, it would think in such and such a way,’ and he would form such a thought.”

Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates a certain limited form as the self, and thus designates it; in this way, there is one who views a certain limited form as the self and becomes attached to it.

“Ānanda! Suppose there is another who designates the self as being neither of limited form nor of infinite form. He now designates the self as being of infinite form; yet, when his body breaks up at the end of life, he speaks thus and holds such a view: ‘When the self departs from infinite form, it thinks in such and such a way,’ and he forms this thought.”
Ānanda! Thus, there is one who designates an immeasurable form as the self, and thus he becomes attached to an immeasurable form by viewing it as the self.

“Ānanda! Suppose there is another who does not designate the self as having limited form, nor does he designate it as having infinite form, but designates the self as having limited formlessness. He now designates the self as having limited formlessness; when his body breaks up at the end of life, he speaks thus and holds such a view: ‘If the self were to depart from limited formlessness, it would think in such and such a way,’ and he forms this thought.”
Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates a certain limited formless state as the self; in this way, there is one who clings to a certain limited formless state as the self.

“Ānanda! Suppose there is another who does not designate the self as having limited form, nor designate it as having infinite form, nor designate it as having limited formlessness, but designates the self as having infinite formlessness. Now, while designating the self as having infinite formlessness, at the breaking up of the body after death, he likewise speaks and likewise views [the self] as existing; and when the self is separated from infinite formlessness, he likewise and thus reflects, forming such a thought.”

Ānanda! Thus, there is one who, being infinite and formless, designates a self through such designation; thus, there is one who, being infinite and formless, clings to a self through such clinging. This is called "there is one who designates a self through such designation."
“Ānanda! How is it that there is one who designates a designation for a selfless provision?
Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze its meaning for you."
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

There is one who does not designate the self as having limited form, nor designate it as having infinite form, nor designate it as having limited formlessness, nor designate it as having infinite formlessness.

Ānanda! If there were someone who designated the self as being "not limited by form," he would not now designate the self as being "not limited by form"; even after the breakup of the body at the end of life, he would neither speak nor hold such a view. Furthermore, when the self is separated from what is not limited by form, he would neither think in such a way nor form such a thought.

Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates the self as being neither a small amount of form; and in this way, there is one who, not seeing attachment to the self as being neither a small amount of form, nevertheless becomes attached to it.

“Ānanda! Suppose there were another who, regarding that which is not infinite form, designates it as the self; he does not designate that which is not infinite form as the self now, nor will he speak thus or hold such a view after the breakup of the body at the end of life. Furthermore, when the self is separated from infinite form, he would not think in such a way, nor would he form such a conception.”

Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates the self as being "not of infinite form," yet designates it so; and in this way, there is one who does not see attachment to the self as being "not of infinite form," yet becomes attached to it.

"Ānanda! Suppose there is another who designates the self as being neither finite nor infinite in form; he does not designate the self as being neither finite nor infinite in form now, nor will he speak thus or hold such a view after the breakup of the body at the end of life. Furthermore, when the self is separated from the state of being neither finite nor infinite in form, he would not think in such a way, nor would he form such a thought."

Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates the self as being "not merely a portion of the formless"; in this way, there is one who, though not seeing attachment to the self as being "not merely a portion of the formless," nevertheless becomes attached to it.

“Ānanda! If there were another who, regarding the ‘Infinite Formless’ as the self, were to designate it as such, he would not be designating the ‘Infinite Formless’ as the self now; and at the breaking up of the body, after death, he would neither speak nor hold the view that when the self departs from the Infinite Formless, it thinks in such and such a way or forms such and such a thought.”

Ānanda! In this way, there is one who designates the self as being "not infinite formless," and thus designates it; in this way, there is one who, though not seeing attachment to the self as "not infinite formless," nevertheless becomes attached to it.
"Ānanda! This is called the designation of 'one who has no self' where there is no self to be designated.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"
There are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and two bases (*āyatana*).
What are the seven stations of consciousness?
Sentient beings with form who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions—namely, humans and the gods of the desire realm—this is called the first station of consciousness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are beings with form who have diverse bodies but a single perception—namely, the Brahmā gods at the time of their first birth, who are not subject to untimely death. This is called the second station of consciousness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, there are beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions; these are the Ābhāsvara devas. This is called the third station of consciousness.
Furthermore, Ānanda...
There are beings with form who possess a single body and a single perception; these are the gods of the Universal Purity (Subhakṛtsna). This is called the fourth station of consciousness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are formless beings who have transcended all perceptions of form, ceased perceptions of sensory resistance, and do not attend to perceptions of diversity; they dwell having attained the sphere of infinite space, namely the gods of Infinite Space. This is called the fifth station of consciousness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are formless beings who have transcended the sphere of infinite space and dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; these are the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is called the sixth station of consciousness.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are formless beings who have transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell having attained the sphere of nothingness; these are the gods of the sphere of nothingness. This is called the seventh station of consciousness.
“Ānanda! What are the two places where there are beings with form who are without perception and without thought? They are the Heaven of No-Perception; this is called the first place.

Furthermore, Ānanda, there are formless beings who have transcended the sphere of nothingness and dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; these are the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called the second station.
“Ānanda! Regarding the first station of consciousness: there are sentient beings with form who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions—namely, human beings and the gods of the desire realm.

If a bhikṣu understands that station of consciousness, understands its origin, understands its cessation, understands its gratification, understands its peril, and understands the escape from it as they truly are;”
"Ānanda! Would this bhikṣu find delight in that station of consciousness, or would he become attached to and dwell upon that station of consciousness?
He replied:

"No. "Ānanda! The second station of consciousness consists of sentient beings who possess form, being diverse in body but uniform in perception; this refers to the Brahmā gods at the beginning of their existence, before their lifespan has ended."

If there is a bhikṣu who knows that consciousness-abiding, knows the arising of consciousness-abiding, and knows its cessation, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it as they truly are— Ānanda!
“Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness,
or would he become attached to and dwell upon them? He replied, “No.”
“Ānanda! The third station of consciousness consists of sentient beings with form who have a single body but diverse perceptions; these are the Ābhāsvara devas.

If a bhikṣu knows that station of consciousness, knows the origin of that station of consciousness, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its peril, and knows the escape from it as they truly are—”
"Ānanda! Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness, or would he become attached to and dwell upon them?
He replied:
"No, [it is not so]. Ānanda!
The fourth station of consciousness consists of sentient beings who possess form, being uniform in body and uniform in perception—namely, the gods of the Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) heaven."

If there is a bhikṣu who knows that consciousness-abiding, knows the arising of consciousness-abiding, and knows its cessation, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it as they truly are— Ānanda!
"Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness,
or would he become attached to and dwell upon them? He replied, "No."

“Ānanda! The fifth station of consciousness is that of formless beings who have transcended all perceptions of form, extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and do not attend to perceptions of diversity; they dwell having attained the sphere of infinite space—namely, the gods of the sphere of infinite space.”

If there is a bhikṣu who knows that station of consciousness, knows the origin of the station of consciousness, and knows its cessation, its gratification, its peril, and the escape from it as they truly are— Ānanda!
"Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness,
or would he become attached to and dwell upon them? He replied, "No."

“Ānanda! As for the sixth station of consciousness: formless beings who have transcended the entire sphere of infinite space and dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness—namely, the gods of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

If there is a bhikṣu who knows that abode of consciousness, knows the origin of the abode of consciousness, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its peril, and knows the escape from it as they truly are— Ānanda!
“Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness,
or would he become attached to and dwell within them? He replied, “No.”

“Ānanda! As for the seventh station of consciousness: there are formless beings who have transcended the entire sphere of infinite consciousness and dwell having attained the sphere of nothingness; these are the gods of the sphere of nothingness.”

If there is a bhikṣu who knows that consciousness-abiding, knows the origin of consciousness-abiding, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its peril, and knows the escape from it as they truly are— Ānanda!
"Would this bhikṣu find delight in those stations of consciousness, or would he become attached to and dwell upon those stations of consciousness? He replied, "No."
“Ānanda! As for the first station:
there are beings with form who are without perception and without thought; this refers to the Heaven of Non-perception.
If a bhikṣu knows that station, knows the origin of that station, knows its cessation, knows its gratification, knows its peril, and knows the escape from it as they truly are—”
"Ānanda! Would this bhikṣu find delight in that place, or would he become attached to and dwell upon it?
He replied:
"No, [it is not]. "Ānanda! As for the second place:

those beings who are formless, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; that is, the devas of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
If there is a bhikkhu who knows that place as it really is— knowing its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its danger,
and the escape from it— Ānanda!
"Would this bhikṣu find delight in that place, or would he be attached to and dwell upon it? He replied, "No."

“Ānanda! If there is a bhikkhu who knows those seven stations of consciousness and two abodes as they truly are, and whose mind is not defiled or attached, having attained liberation—he is called a bhikkhu who is an Arhat, known as one liberated by wisdom.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda,
there are eight liberations.
What are the eight?
Perceiving forms while contemplating forms—this is called the first liberation.
Furthermore, with the internal perception of formlessness, one contemplates external forms—this is called the second liberation.
Furthermore, having personally realized and attained the pure liberation, one dwells therein—this is called the third liberation.

Furthermore, by transcending all perceptions of form, by extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is called the fourth liberation.
Furthermore, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the fifth liberation.
Furthermore, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, one dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness; this is called the sixth liberation.
Furthermore, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, one dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh liberation.

Furthermore, having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having personally realized the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling; and by means of wisdom, one perceives the knowledge of the exhaustion of all taints—this is called the eighth liberation.

Ānanda! If there is a bhikkhu who knows those seven stations of consciousness and two bases as they truly are, whose mind is not stained by attachment and has attained liberation; and who, having realized these eight liberations through direct experience in both forward and reverse order, dwells having accomplished them, and who also possesses the wisdom that perceives the exhaustion of all taints—he is called an Arahant bhikkhu, and is named "liberated in both ways."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Mahānidāna Sūtra* ends here, totaling five thousand four hundred and seventy-two characters. 98. *Smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* (98), Middle Āgama, Section on Causes, *Smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, the second [sūtra], recited at the minor town of Kṣudrakagrāmaka. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Kuru country and stayed at the Kuru town of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"There is a single path for purifying sentient beings, for crossing over sorrow and fear, for extinguishing suffering and affliction, for ending lamentation, and for attaining the True Dharma; it is called the four foundations of mindfulness."

If there were any Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past who had completely severed the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—who established their minds in right abiding through the four foundations of mindfulness, cultivated the seven factors of enlightenment, and attained the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening of enlightenment.

If there are future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have completely severed the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—who establish their minds in right abiding within the four foundations of mindfulness, cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, and attain the unsurpassed, perfectly complete awakening of enlightenment.

I am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I too have abandoned the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and established my mind in right dwelling upon the four foundations of mindfulness, cultivating the seven factors of awakening, thereby attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
“What are the four?
They are the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body, and likewise contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
What is the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the body as body?”

A bhikṣu, when walking, knows that he is walking; when standing, knows that he is standing; when sitting, knows that he is sitting; when lying down, knows that he is lying down; when sleeping, knows that he is sleeping; when awake, knows that he is awake; and when both sleeping and waking, he knows that he is both sleeping and waking.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body: the bhikṣu is clearly aware of his going out and coming in; he observes and discerns well when bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, and maintains a dignified and composed deportment; he properly wears the saṃghāṭī and other robes and carries the bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or whether sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he is clearly aware of it all.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu contemplates the body as body. When unwholesome and unskillful thoughts arise in the bhikkhu, he subdues, eliminates, and stills them by means of skillful mental states. It is just as a carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice who takes a marking line and applies it to the wood, then uses a sharp axe to hew and straighten it."
In this way, when a bhikṣu gives rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts, he treats, cuts off, extinguishes, and stops them with thoughts of wholesome dharmas.

Thus, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body: the bhikṣu keeps his teeth together, presses his tongue against the upper palate, and with the mind governs the mind, governing it to bring about its cessation, abandonment, and stilling.
It is like two strong men seizing a weak man, twisting him about in every direction and beating and forging him at will.
In this same way, the bhikṣu presses his teeth together, touches his tongue to the upper palate, and with his mind governs the mind, subduing, severing, extinguishing, and stilling it.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body: a bhikṣu, when mindful of inhaling, knows he is mindful of inhaling; when mindful of exhaling, knows he is mindful of exhaling. When inhaling long, he knows he is inhaling long; when exhaling long, he knows he is exhaling long. When inhaling short, he knows he is inhaling short; when exhaling short, he knows he is exhaling short.

He experiences the whole body while inhaling; he experiences the whole body while exhaling. He experiences the calming of bodily formations while inhaling; he experiences the calming of verbal formations while exhaling."

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu, with the joy and bliss born of seclusion, drenches, saturates, and thoroughly suffuses this body; there is no part of his body that is not pervaded by the joy and bliss born of seclusion."

It is just as when a skilled bath-attendant places bathing powder in a vessel, mixes it with water to form a paste, and soaks it until it is moist and supple, pervading everywhere without leaving any part untouched.

In the same way, the rapture and bliss born of seclusion drenches and suffuses this body, pervading it entirely; there is no part of this body that is not permeated by the rapture and bliss born of seclusion.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu’s rapture and bliss born of concentration drench, saturate, and completely fill this body; there is no part of his body that is not pervaded by the rapture and bliss born of concentration."

It is like a mountain spring, pure and unturbid, full and overflowing; though waters come from the four directions, they have no means of entering it. Rather, from the very bottom of that spring, water wells up spontaneously, flowing and overflowing outward, soaking the mountain and moistening the earth, pervasively filling everywhere until there is nowhere it does not reach.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s rapture and bliss born of concentration drench, saturate, and thoroughly pervade his entire body; there is no part of his body that is not suffused with the rapture and bliss born of concentration.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu experiences joyless bliss which drenches, saturates, and completely fills this body; there is no part of the body that is not pervaded by this joyless bliss."

It is like blue lotuses, red, crimson, or white lotuses, born in water and growing in water, remaining at the bottom of the water; their roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves are all drenched and moistened, thoroughly saturated and pervading everywhere without exception.
In this way, the bhikṣu experiences joyless bliss; it saturates and moistens his body, pervading and filling it entirely, such that there is no part of his body not permeated by this joyless bliss.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu contemplates the body as body. In this body, the bhikkhu dwells having attained and suffused it with a pure mind, such that there is no part of this body not pervaded by his pure mind."
It is as if there were a person wearing a robe of seven or eight cubits that covers them from head to foot, leaving no part of their body uncovered;
in this same way, the bhikṣu, with a pure mind, pervades every part of this body without exception.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. This bhikṣu maintains the perception of light, properly receiving and properly upholding it, and properly recollecting what has been recollected: as it was before, so it is after; as it is after, so it was before; as it is by day, so it is by night; as it is by night, so it is by day; as it is below, so it is above; as it is above, so it is below."
Thus, being without inversion and with a mind free from entanglements, he cultivates a luminous mind that is never again shrouded by darkness.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; establishing mindfulness upon the body, he possesses knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. This bhikṣu properly grasps the signs of contemplation and properly recollects what is being attended to, just as a person sitting might observe someone lying down, or someone lying down might observe someone sitting."
In this way, a bhikṣu properly receives the signs for contemplation and properly recollects what he has attended to.

Thus, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. A bhikṣu, remaining with this body just as it is, according to its state—whether in good or bad condition—contemplates from head to foot that it is filled with various kinds of impurities:

'In this body of mine there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, undigested food, excrement, brain and its membranes, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, spittle, bile, and urine. "
It is just as when various seeds are placed in a vessel, and a person with sight clearly perceives them all—namely, rice, millet, radishes, and mustard seeds.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells with this body according to its state, whether in favorable or unfavorable conditions; from head to foot, he contemplates it as filled with various impurities:

"Within this body of mine there are head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, thin skin, flesh, sinews, bones, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, stomach, undigested food, excrement, brain and its membranes, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, spittle, bile, and urine."

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body: the bhikṣu contemplates the various elements of the body, [perceiving], 'In this body of mine there are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.'"
It is just as a butcher slaughters an ox, flays its hide and spreads it upon the ground, and divides the carcass into six portions.

In the same way, a bhikṣu contemplates the various elements of the body: "Within this body of mine are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element."

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu contemplates a corpse that has been dead for one or two days, up to six or seven days—pecked by crows and vultures, devoured by jackals and wolves, burned by fire, or buried in the earth until it is completely putrid and decayed. Having seen this, he compares himself to it:
'Now this body of mine is also like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.'"

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. A bhikṣu sees, as he did before, bones on a charnel ground—bluish, rotting, half-eaten by scavengers, and skeletal fragments lying upon the earth. Having seen this, he compares himself to it:
'Now this body of mine is also like this; it shares this same nature and can never escape it.'"

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu, as before, sees a charnel ground where skin, flesh, and blood have departed, leaving only sinews connecting the bones; having seen this, he compares himself to it:
"Now this body of mine is also like this; it possesses this same nature and shall ultimately not escape it."

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body."

"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. A bhikṣu, as before, sees the bones and joints of a charnel ground scattered in all directions—the foot bones, shin bones, thigh bones, hip bones, vertebrae, shoulder blades, neck bones, and skull—each lying in a different place. Having seen this, he compares himself [to that]:
'Now this body of mine is also like this; it possesses this same nature and can never escape it.'"

"In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as body. The bhikṣu sees, as before, bones on a charnel ground—white like conch shells, blue like the color of a pigeon, red as if smeared with blood, or decayed and reduced to powder. Having seen this, he compares himself [to them], thinking:
"This body of mine is also like this; it shares this same nature and can never escape it."

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and contemplates the external body as body; he establishes mindfulness upon the body, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating the body as body.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī contemplates the body as the body in this way, even to a small degree, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating the body as the body.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating feelings as feelings?
When a bhikkhu experiences a pleasant feeling, he knows, "I experience a pleasant feeling.
When he experiences a painful feeling, he knows, "I experience a painful feeling.
When he experiences a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "I experience a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
He discerns the body as pleasant, the body as painful, and the body as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
the mind as pleasant, the mind as painful, and the mind as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
and nutriment as pleasant, nutriment as painful, and nutriment as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
There is nutriment for pleasure, nutriment for pain, and nutriment for neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
there is desire for pleasure, desire for pain, and desire for neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
When one is experiencing pleasure without desire, pain without desire, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure without desire, one then knows: "I am experiencing neither-pain-nor-pleasure without desire."

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates internal feelings as feelings, contemplates external feelings as feelings, and establishes mindfulness upon feelings; he possesses knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration—this is called a bhikṣu contemplating feelings as feelings.
If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī thus contemplates feelings as feelings to a small degree, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating feelings as feelings.
What is the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating the mind as the mind?

A bhikkhu, when his mind is possessed by desire, knows as it truly is that his mind is possessed by desire; when his mind is free from desire, he knows as it truly is that his mind is free from desire. When there is ill will, he knows it as it truly is; when there is no ill will, he knows it as it truly is. When there is delusion, he knows it as it truly is; when there is no delusion, he knows it as it truly is. When there is defilement, he knows it as it truly is; when there is no defilement, he knows it as it truly is.

There is conjunction and there is separation; there is the low and there is the high; there is the small and there is the great; there is the cultivated and there is the uncultivated; there is the concentrated and there is the unconcentrated; there is the mind that is not liberated, which one knows as "not liberated" according to reality, and there is the mind that is liberated, which one knows as "liberated" according to reality.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the internal mind as mind, contemplates the external mind as mind, establishes mindfulness upon the mind, and possesses knowledge, vision, clarity, and penetration; this is called a bhikṣu contemplating the mind as mind.
If there is a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who thus contemplates the mind as mind in this way, even to a small degree, this is called the application of mindfulness to the mind as mind.
What is the application of mindfulness to phenomena as phenomena?

Visual consciousness arises conditioned by forms, giving rise to internal fetters. A bhikkhu, when there is actually an internal fetter within him, knows as it truly is that there is an internal fetter; when there is actually no internal fetter within him, he knows as it truly is that there is no internal fetter; if an unarisen internal fetter arises, he knows as it truly is that it has arisen; and if an arisen internal fetter is abandoned and does not arise again, he knows as it truly is that it has been abandoned.

It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: mental consciousness arises conditioned by mental phenomena, giving rise to internal fetters. A bhikkhu, when there is actually an internal fetter within him, knows as it truly is that there is an internal fetter; when there is actually no internal fetter within him, he knows as it truly is that there is no internal fetter; if an unarisen internal fetter arises, he knows as it truly is that it has arisen; and if an arisen internal fetter is abandoned and does not arise again, he knows as it truly is that it has been abandoned.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates internal phenomena as phenomena and contemplates external phenomena as phenomena; he establishes mindfulness upon phenomena, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating phenomena as phenomena, namely, the six internal bases.
"Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena as phenomena.

A bhikṣu truly knows when there is desire within him as 'there is desire'; he truly knows when there is no desire within him as 'there is no desire. He truly knows when unarisen desire arises; he truly knows when arisen desire is extinguished and does not arise again. It is the same with ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, and restlessness-and-regret."

When there is doubt within, one knows as it truly is that there is doubt within; when there is no doubt within, one knows as it truly is that there is no doubt within; if doubt that has not yet arisen arises, one knows as it truly is that it has arisen; if doubt that has already arisen ceases and does not arise again, one knows as it truly is that it has ceased.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates internal phenomena as phenomena and contemplates external phenomena as phenomena; he establishes mindfulness upon phenomena, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikṣu contemplating phenomena as phenomena, namely, the five hindrances.

"Furthermore, a bhikkhu contemplates phenomena as phenomena. A bhikkhu truly knows that when the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is present within him, 'The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is present';

he truly knows that when the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is not present within him, 'The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is absent. He truly knows how the unarisen factor of enlightenment of mindfulness arises; he truly knows how the arisen factor of enlightenment of mindfulness becomes stabilized, is not forgotten, does not decline, and is further cultivated, developed, and expanded. It is the same for the factors of enlightenment of energy, rapture, tranquility, and concentration."

A bhikkhu, when the factor of enlightenment of equanimity truly exists within him, knows as it really is that the factor of enlightenment of equanimity exists; when the factor of enlightenment of equanimity does not truly exist within him, he knows as it really is that the factor of enlightenment of equanimity does not exist. If the factor of enlightenment of equanimity has not yet arisen, he knows as it really is how it arises; if the factor of enlightenment of equanimity has already arisen, he knows as it really is how it remains, is not forgotten, does not decline, and is further cultivated, developed, and expanded.

In this way, a bhikkhu contemplates internal phenomena as phenomena and contemplates external phenomena as phenomena; he establishes mindfulness upon phenomena, possessing knowledge and vision, clarity and penetration. This is called a bhikkhu contemplating phenomena as phenomena, namely, the seven factors of enlightenment.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who thus contemplate phenomena according to the Dharma even for a short time, this is called the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates phenomena according to the Dharma.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who establish their minds and dwell correctly in the four foundations of mindfulness for seven years, they will certainly attain one of two fruits: either they will realize ultimate knowledge in this very life, or they will become non-returners with remainder. This applies not only to seven years, but also to six, five, four, three, two, or one year.

If there be a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who, for seven months, establishes the mind and dwells correctly in the four foundations of mindfulness, they will certainly attain one of two fruits: either they will attain ultimate knowledge in this very life, or they will become a non-returner with remainder. This applies not only to seven months, but also to six, five, four, three, two, or one month.

If there is a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī who, for seven days and seven nights, establishes their mind and dwells correctly in the four foundations of mindfulness, they will certainly attain one of two fruits: either they will realize ultimate knowledge in this very life, or they will become a non-returner with remainder. This applies not only to seven days and seven nights, but also to six, five, four, three, two, or even one day and one night.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who, for even a brief moment, establish their minds and dwell correctly in the four foundations of mindfulness, then by practicing thus in the morning, they will surely attain progress by evening; and by practicing thus in the evening, they will surely attain progress by morning.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta*, the second [sūtra], ends here, totaling 3,137 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 24, contains 8,609 characters. This concludes the second recitation section, the "Minor Earth-Castle" (*Kṣudrakapṛthivīkoṭṭaka*).
Madhyama Āgama, Scroll Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
99. The Discourse on the Aggregate of Suffering (99). Chapter on Causes: The Third Discourse on the Aggregate of Suffering. Recited in the Second Minor Earth-City Section.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after the midday meal, when the monks had a little business to attend to, they gathered and sat together in the lecture hall.

Thereupon, many followers of other teachings, having wandered about in the afternoon, went to where the bhikṣus were; after exchanging greetings with one another, they sat down to one side and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."

"Venerable friends! The śramaṇa Gautama teaches the knowledge of the abandonment of desire, teaches the knowledge of the abandonment of form, and teaches the knowledge of the abandonment of perception.
We too, venerable friends, teach the knowledge of the abandonment of desire, teach the knowledge of the abandonment of form, and teach the knowledge of the abandonment of perception."
“Between the śramaṇa Gautama and ourselves, both of whom know these two things and have abandoned these two things, what is the superiority?
What is the distinction?
Then, having heard what those many followers of other teachings had said, the bhikṣus neither approved nor disapproved; they rose and departed in silence, thinking to themselves:
"Regarding what has been thus spoken, we shall learn it from the Blessed One.

Having said this, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and sat down to one side; they then related to the Buddha, in its entirety, the discussion they had shared with the many followers of other teachings.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should immediately ask the many followers of other teachings as follows:
'Venerable sirs!'"
What is the gratification of sensual desires?
What is the danger of sensual desires?
What is the escape from sensual desires?
What is the gratification of form?
What is the danger of form?
What is the escape from form?
What is the gratification of perception? What is its danger?
What is the escape from it?

"O monks! If you were to ask such questions, they, having heard them, would instead engage in mutual debate and discuss other external matters; their anger and contention would increase further, and they would certainly rise from their seats and withdraw in silence."

Why is this? Because I do not see anyone in this world—whether among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or any other assembly—who can understand and explain this meaning, except for the Tathāgata, his disciples, or those who have heard it from them.
The Buddha said:
"What is the flavor of desire?

It refers to the pleasure and joy that arise because of the merits of the five sensual desires; this is the ultimate flavor of desire, beyond which there is nothing superior, yet its afflictions are exceedingly many."
"What is the peril of desire?

A son of noble family sustains himself by means of various crafts: he may engage in agriculture, or practice trade, or study writing, or master arithmetic, or understand engineering, or excel at engraving seals, or compose literary works, or produce calligraphy, or be learned in the scriptures, or serve as a brave general, or attend upon a king."

In cold weather they suffer from the cold; in hot weather they suffer from the heat; they are afflicted by hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the bites of mosquitoes and gadflies; performing such deeds, they seek to acquire wealth.

When that son of good family employs such skillful means, practices such conduct, and makes such a quest, yet fails to obtain wealth and resources, he gives rise to sorrow, suffering, grief, and distress; his mind then becomes deluded, and he speaks thus:
"All my efforts were in vain; all my hardships were in vain; what I sought has yielded no fruit."
That son of good family, employing such skillful means and practicing in this way, seeks in this manner; if he should obtain wealth, he then cherishes it, guarding and concealing it in secret.
Why is this? [He thinks:

"May these possessions of mine not be seized by the king, plundered by thieves, burned by fire, rotted away, or lost; may they not yield no profit when spent, or may the various undertakings I perform not fail to succeed."

Thus he guards and conceals [the treasure] in secret; yet if it is seized by a king, plundered by bandits, consumed by fire, rotted away, or lost, he gives rise to sorrow, suffering, grief, and distress, and his mind becomes deluded, saying:
"That which I have cherished for so long has now been lost."
"This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

Furthermore, because sentient beings have desire as their cause, desire as their condition, and desire as their root, mother quarrels with child, child quarrels with mother; father and son, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen all quarrel with one another."

Once they have thus engaged in mutual strife and contention, the mother speaks ill of the son and the son speaks ill of the mother; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen speak ill of one another—how much more so, then, toward others?
This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

Furthermore, because sentient beings have desire as their cause, desire as their condition, and desire as their root, kings quarrel with kings, brahmins quarrel with brahmins, householders quarrel with householders, commoners quarrel with commoners, and nations quarrel with nations. Because they fight and harbor mutual hatred, they inflict harm upon one another using various weapons—whether by punching, throwing stones, striking with clubs, or hacking with swords. During such combat, they either die or are terrified, undergoing extreme suffering. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

"Furthermore, sentient beings, conditioned by desire and with desire as their basis, don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields to enter the ranks of battle; they fight with elephants, or horses, or chariots, or infantry, or even with men and women."

At the time of that battle, they may die or be terrified, experiencing extreme suffering; this is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

"Furthermore, because sentient beings are caused by desire and conditioned by desire, taking desire as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields to go and seize other kingdoms, besiege cities, and break down fortifications. They engage in mutual combat, beating drums and blowing horns, shouting and crying out at the top of their voices. Some strike with mallets, some with halberds and lances, some with sharp wheels, some with arrows, some by raining down stones in confusion, some with great crossbows, and some by sprinkling molten copper beads upon them."

When they are engaged in battle, they may die or be terrified, undergoing extreme suffering; this is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

"Furthermore, because sentient beings are caused by desire, conditioned by desire, and take desire as their root, they don armor and robes, carry spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields to enter villages, towns, countries, and cities; they break through walls and open up treasuries, plundering wealth and property, cutting off royal roads, or going into other alleys to destroy villages, harm towns, annihilate countries, and raze cities."
Among them, some may be seized by the king’s men and subjected to various forms of torture and punishment:
having their hands cut off, their feet cut off, or both hands and feet cut off; having their ears cut off, their noses cut off, or both ears and noses cut off;
or being cut into pieces, having their beards plucked out, their hair plucked out, or both beard and hair plucked out; or being placed in a cage, wrapped in cloth, and burned with fire, or...
Buried in sand, entangled in grass, or scorched by fire; or placed within the belly of an iron donkey, or thrust into the mouth of an iron pig, or cast into the mouth of an iron tiger to be burned;
or set in a copper cauldron, or boiled in an iron cauldron;
or cut into pieces, or pierced with sharp forks, or hooked with iron hooks, or laid upon an iron bed.
They are doused with boiling oil while lying on beds; or they sit upon iron mortars and are pounded with iron pestles;
or they are stung by dragons and snakes; or they are whipped with whips, struck with canes, or beaten with clubs;
or they are impaled alive upon high stakes, or their heads are decapitated.

Remaining therein, one either dies or is terrified, experiencing extremely heavy suffering; this is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

"Furthermore, because sentient beings are conditioned by desire and have desire as their root, they engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind. Later, when they are afflicted by illness and confined to their beds, or sitting or lying on the ground, suffering oppresses their bodies and they experience extremely heavy, unpleasant, and disagreeable pain."

If that person has committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, these will manifest before them at the time of death to obscure their vision, just as when the sun is about to set behind a great mountain ridge, its shadow covers the earth.
In this way, if one has committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind that stand as obstructions before them, they will think:
"My former evil deeds stand before me and obscure me; I did not perform meritorious actions in the past, but instead committed many evil deeds."
