If there were someone who committed evil and acted with violence solely for the sake of sin, who performed no merit and practiced no goodness, being without fear, without refuge, and without a place of return—wherever such a person might be reborn, I would certainly be born there as well.

From this there arises remorse; one who regrets dies unwholesomely and passes away without merit. This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

"Furthermore, beings, with desire as the cause and desire as the condition, taking desire as their root, engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. Because of these misconducts of body, speech, and mind, and conditioned by them, at the breaking up of the body after death, they inevitably go to a state of woe and are reborn in hell. This is called the mass of suffering in future lives, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root; this is called the peril of desire."
"What is the escape from sensual desire?
If one cuts off sensual desire, abandons sensual desire, extinguishes sensual desire so that it is exhausted, and transcends sensual desire—this is called the escape from sensual desire."

If there are recluses or brahmins who do not know, as it truly is, the gratification of sensual desires, the peril of sensual desires, and the escape from sensual desires, they will ultimately be unable to sever their own desires; how much less could they possibly sever the desires of others?

If there are recluses or brahmins who wish to know, as it truly is, the gratification of sensual desires, the peril of sensual desires, and the escape from sensual desires, they are able both to remove them for themselves and to sever them in others.
"What is the gratification of form?
When a daughter of the kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or artisans is fourteen or fifteen years old, at that time her beauty is most exquisite."

If, because of that beautiful form and conditioned by that beautiful form, one gives rise to pleasure and joy, this is the ultimate savoring of that form; there is nothing beyond it, yet the afflictions resulting from it are exceedingly many.
"What is the peril of form?

If one sees someone who was once beautiful, yet later becomes extremely aged—hair white, teeth fallen out, back bent, feet crooked, walking with a staff, the prime of youth having faded, the end of life approaching, the body trembling, and the faculties decayed and withered—what do you think about this?"
"If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, "It is so."

“Furthermore, if you were to see that beautiful woman afflicted by illness, lying upon her bed or sitting or lying on the ground, her body oppressed by suffering and undergoing extreme agony—what do you think?”
"If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, "It is so."

"Furthermore, if one were to see that beautiful woman dead for one or two days, up to six or seven days—pecked at by crows and vultures, devoured by jackals and wolves, burned by fire, or buried in the ground, until she has completely rotted and decayed—what do you think?"
"If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, "It is so."

"Furthermore, if you were to see that same beautiful woman on the charnel ground, her bones bluish-black, decayed and putrid, half-eaten and reduced to fragments scattered upon the earth—what do you think?"
“If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, “It is so.”
"Furthermore, if you were to see that same beautiful woman on a charnel ground, stripped of skin, flesh, and blood, with only the tendons connecting the bones—what do you think?
If she originally possessed such beauty, would its destruction not give rise to distress?"
He replied, “It is so. He continued, “Furthermore,

if you were to see that same beautiful woman’s charnel ground, with her bones and joints disarticulated and scattered in all directions— the foot bone, the shin bone, the thigh bone, the hip bone, the vertebrae, the shoulder blade, the neck bone, and the skull bone each lying in a different place— what would you think?”
"If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, "It is so."

"Furthermore, if one were to see that same beautiful corpse on the charnel ground—its bones white as a conch shell, blue like the color of a pigeon, red as if smeared with blood, or rotted and crumbled into dust—what do you think about this?"
"If there was originally beautiful form, does its cessation give rise to affliction?
He replied, "It is so."
"This is called the peril of form.
What is the escape from form?
If one cuts off form, relinquishes form, extinguishes form so that form is exhausted, and transcends form to reach the escape—this is called the escape from form."

If there are recluses or brahmins who do not know, as it truly is, the gratification in form, the danger in form, and the escape from form, they will ultimately be unable to sever their own attachment to form; how much less could they sever that of others?

If there are recluses or brahmins who know, as it truly is, the gratification of form, the peril of form, and the escape from form, they are able to remove it for themselves and can also cause others to sever their attachment to form.
“What is the gratification of the awakening factor?

Here, a bhikkhu, detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; at that time, he does not think of harming himself, nor does he think of harming others. This absence of thoughts of harm is called the gratification of the awakening factor.”
Why is this so? Because one who does not harbor thoughts of harm accomplishes this happiness; this is called the gratification of the awakening-factor.
What is the danger of the awakening-factor?
Vitality is an impermanent phenomenon, a phenomenon of suffering, and a phenomenon subject to cessation;
this is called the peril of vitality.

"What is the escape from vitality? If one cuts off vitality, relinquishes vitality, extinguishes vitality so that vitality is exhausted, and transcends vitality—this is called the escape from vitality."

If there are recluses or brahmins who do not know, as it truly is, the gratification of feelings, the danger of feelings, and the escape from feelings, they will ultimately be unable to sever their own feelings; how much less could they possibly sever the feelings of others?

If there are recluses or brahmins who truly know, as it really is, the gratification of feeling, the danger of feeling, and the escape from feeling, they are able both to remove it themselves and to sever the feelings of others.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Dukkha-khandha Sutta*, the third, ends here, totaling two thousand one hundred and sixty-five characters. 100. *Dukkha-khandha Sutta* (100), *Madhyama Āgama*, *Nidāna-varga*, *Dukkha-khandha Sutta*, the fourth; recited in the second sub-section of *Kṣudrakagrāma*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas and was staying at Anupiya in the Nyagrodha Park of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Śākya Mahānāma, having wandered about in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Thus do I understand the Dharma of the Blessed One, which has caused the three defilements within my mind—
the defilement of lustful intent, the defilement of hateful intent, and the defilement of deluded intent—
to be extinguished. World-Honored One!
"I understood this Dharma in such a way, yet within my mind, there still arose states of passion, hatred, and delusion.
World-Honored One!
I had this thought:"
"What dharma do I possess that has not been extinguished,
such that it causes defiled states, states of hatred, and states of delusion to arise again within my mind?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Mahānāma! There is one thing that you have not extinguished: namely, that you remain living at home, having not reached full faith, left the household life, become homeless, and trained in the path.”
Mahānāma! If you were to eliminate this one dharma, you would certainly not remain at home, but would surely go forth with faith, leaving the household life for homelessness to train in the path.
“Because you do not extinguish even a single dharma, you remain at home; you have not reached the state of faith, left the household life, become homeless, and studied the Path.
Thereupon, Mahānāma the Śākya rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for me, so that my mind may be purified, my doubts removed, and I may attain the Path.”
The Blessed One said:
“Mahānāma! There are five strands of sensual pleasure that are lovely, desirable, delightful, associated with desire, and which cause one to rejoice.”
What are these five? They are:

the eye cognizing forms, the ear cognizing sounds, the nose cognizing odors, the tongue cognizing tastes, and the body cognizing tangibles; by means of these, the king and his retinue obtain peace, happiness, and joy.
"Mahānāma! This is the ultimate flavor of sensual desire; there is nothing beyond it, yet its afflictions are exceedingly many. Mahānāma!"
What is the peril of sensual desire? Mahānāma!

A son of noble family, according to his craft, maintains himself by means of it—whether by farming, or by trade, or by learning to write, or by proficiency in arithmetic, or by knowledge of craftsmanship, or by skill in engraving seals, or by composing literary works, or by calligraphy, or by understanding the scriptures, or by serving as a brave general, or by attending upon a king.

In cold weather they feel cold, and in hot weather they feel hot; tormented by hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the bites of mosquitoes and gadflies, they perform such deeds as these in their pursuit of wealth.

Mahānāman! When this son of good family employs such means, practices such conduct, and makes such a quest, yet fails to obtain wealth and property, he gives rise to sorrow, suffering, grief, and distress; his mind then becomes deluded, and he speaks thus:
"All was done in vain, all was done in vain; the result of my quest is fruitless."
“Mahānāma! When that son of good family employs such skillful means, practices such conduct, and makes such a quest, if he acquires wealth, he then cherishes, guards, and conceals it in secret.”
Why is this? [I think:

"May these possessions of mine not be seized by the king, plundered by thieves, burned by fire, rotted away, or lost; may they not yield no profit when brought forth, or may the various undertakings I perform not fail to succeed."

Thus he guards his secret store; yet if a king should seize it, or thieves rob it, or fire burn it, or it should decay or be lost, he then gives rise to sorrow, suffering, grief, and distress, and delusion arises in his mind, whereby he speaks thus:
"Whatever I have cherished for a long night, that has now been lost."
“Mahānāma! Thus, this mass of suffering in the present life has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!”

Furthermore, sentient beings, because they are caused by desire and conditioned by desire, and because desire is their root, mothers quarrel with their sons and sons quarrel with their mothers; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen likewise quarrel with one another in succession.

Once they have thus engaged in mutual strife, the mother speaks ill of the son and the son speaks ill of the mother; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen speak ill of one another—how much more so regarding others?
Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!

Furthermore, because sentient beings are conditioned by desire and take desire as their root, kings contend with kings, brahmins with brahmins, householders with householders, commoners with commoners, and nations with nations. Due to this mutual hatred arising from contention, they inflict harm upon one another using various weapons—whether by striking with fists or throwing stones, or by beating with clubs or hacking with swords. During such battles, they either die or are struck with terror, undergoing extreme suffering.
Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!

Furthermore, because sentient beings are conditioned by desire, have desire as their object, and take desire as their root, they don armor and robes, carry spears, bows, and arrows, or take up swords and shields to enter the ranks of an army; or they fight with elephants, or horses, or chariots, or infantry; or they fight with men and women. At the time of such combat, they may die or be terrified, undergoing extreme suffering.
"Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!"

Furthermore, sentient beings, conditioned by desire and with desire as their root, don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields to invade other kingdoms. They besiege cities and destroy fortresses, engaging in mutual combat. They beat drums and blow horns, shouting at the top of their voices; they strike with mallets, or use halberds and lances, or sharp wheels, or shoot with arrows, or rain down stones in confusion, or use great crossbows, or sprinkle molten copper beads upon one another. At the time of such battle, they either die or are terrified, undergoing extreme suffering.
Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!

Furthermore, because sentient beings are caused by desire and conditioned by desire, taking desire as their root, they don armor and robes, take up spears, bows, and arrows, or grasp swords and shields to enter villages, towns, countries, and cities. They breach walls and open treasuries, plundering wealth and property; they block royal roads or go into other lanes, destroying villages, harming towns, exterminating countries, and razing cities.
Therein, some may be seized by royal officials and subjected to various forms of torture and punishment:
having their hands cut off, their feet cut off, or both hands and feet cut off; having their ears cut off, their noses cut off, or both ears and noses cut off;
or being cut into pieces, having their whiskers plucked out, their hair plucked out, or both whiskers and hair plucked out; or being placed in a cage, wrapped in cloth, and burned with fire, or...
Buried in sand, entangled in grass, or scorched by fire; or cast into the belly of an iron donkey, or placed within the mouth of an iron pig, or burned inside the mouth of an iron tiger;
or set in a copper cauldron, or boiled in an iron cauldron;
or cut into pieces, or pierced with sharp spears, or hooked with iron hooks, or laid upon an iron [bed].
They are doused with boiling oil while lying on a bed; or they sit upon iron mortars and are pounded with iron pestles;
or they are stung by dragons and snakes; or they are whipped with whips, beaten with canes, or struck with clubs;
or they are impaled alive upon high stakes, or their heads are decapitated.
Within that, they may die or be terrified, experiencing extreme suffering. Mahānāma!
This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root.

“Mahānāma! Furthermore, because sentient beings are conditioned by desire, have desire as their cause, and take desire as their basis, they engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind. Later on, when they fall ill and are confined to bed, or sit or lie upon the ground, their bodies are oppressed by suffering and they experience extremely heavy, unpleasant, and disagreeable pain.”

If that person has committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, these will manifest before them at the time of death, obscuring their vision, just as when the sun is about to set, its shadow is cast over the earth by the side of a great mountain ridge.
Thus, if one has committed evil conduct of body, speech, and mind that stands as an obstruction before them, they think: "Evil conduct of my past stands before me to obscure me;

I have not performed meritorious deeds in the past but have committed much evil karma. If there should be a place where those who commit wicked and violent acts, who do only what is sinful, who perform no merit and practice no goodness, who are without fear, without refuge, and without resort, are reborn—there I shall certainly be born."
"From this there arises remorse; one who regrets dies unwholesomely and passes away without merit.
Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in the present life, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root."

"Mahānāma! Furthermore, because sentient beings are conditioned by desire, have desire as their causal condition, and take desire as their basis, they engage in misconduct of body, and misconduct of speech and mind."

Because of those evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, and by reason of them and conditioned by them, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.
Mahānāma! This is called the mass of suffering in future lives, which has desire as its cause, desire as its condition, and desire as its root. Mahānāma!
Therefore, one should know that sensual desire is exclusively without pleasure and consists of immeasurable suffering and affliction.
A well-versed noble disciple who does not see this as it truly is, being overwhelmed by sensual desire, fails to attain the joy of renunciation and unsurpassed peace.
Mahānāma! In this way, that learned noble disciple may regress because of desire. Mahānāma!
“Mahānāma, I know that sensual desires bring no pleasure, but immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Having known this as it truly is, I am neither overwhelmed by sensual desires nor entangled by evil; thus, I have attained the bliss of equanimity and unsurpassed peace.”
"Mahānāma! For this reason, I do not regress because of desire. Mahānāma!"
At one time, Mahānāma, I was traveling through Rājagṛha and staying at the Seven-Leaf Hut of the seers on Mount Vaideha.

In the afternoon, having risen from my meditation, I went to the Vulture Peak Mountain. There, I saw many Nirgranthas practicing the "non-sitting" discipline, constantly standing and never sitting, undergoing extreme suffering.
I went to them and asked:
"O Nirgranthas!
For what reason do you practice this 'practice of not sitting,' constantly standing and never sitting, undergoing such suffering?"
He spoke thus: "Gautama!
I have a venerable teacher named Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta; he taught me and made this statement:..."
"O Nigaṇṭhas! If you have unwholesome karma from past lives, it shall surely be exhausted by means of this asceticism;
if you now guard your conduct with the body and guard your conduct with speech and mind, then by virtue of these causes and conditions, you will no longer commit evil or unwholesome deeds."
"Mahānāma! I asked them again: 'O Nigaṇṭhas!'"
"Do you all have faith in the Venerable Teacher without any doubt?
They replied to me once more: "It is so."
"Gautama!
We have faith in the Venerable Teacher and have no doubts.
"Mahānāma! [the Buddha replied.]
I asked again: "Nigaṇṭhas!

If that is so, then your venerable teacher Nigaṇṭha Naṭaputta must have previously committed grave evil and unwholesome karmas. Having originally been a Nigaṇṭha who died, he has now been born among humans and has gone forth as a Nigaṇṭha, practicing the 'no-sitting' observance—standing constantly without sitting—and undergoing such suffering just like you and your disciples."
He further said to me: "Gautama!
Pleasure does not arise from pleasure; it must be attained through suffering. For example, the pleasure of King Bimbisāra is such that the śramaṇa Gautama cannot equal it."
I spoke again, saying:
"You are deluded and frantic; what you have said is meaningless. Why is this so?
"You are unskilled and lack understanding; you do not know the proper time when you say that the pleasure of King Bimbisāra is superior to that of the śramaṇa Gautama."
Nigaṇṭhas!
You should have originally asked this:
"Who possesses the superior happiness?"
"Is it King Bimbisāra,
or is it the śramaṇa Gautama,
Nigaṇṭhas?"
"Nigaṇṭhas! If I were to say that my happiness is superior and that King Bimbisāra’s is not, you might well say:
'As for the happiness of King Bimbisāra, the śramaṇa Gautama is not his equal.'"
Those Nigaṇṭhas then spoke thus:
"Gautama! We now ask the Śramaṇa Gautama: [our question]"
Who is the victor whose excellence is to be rejoiced in? Is it King Bimbisāra,
or is it the śramaṇa Gautama?
I spoke again, saying: "Nigaṇṭhas!
I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
"Nigaṇṭhas, what do you think?
Could King Bimbisāra, by remaining silent and speechless as he desired, thereby obtain joy and happiness for seven days and seven nights?"
The Nirgrantha replied: "No, Gautama!"
“Would one obtain joy and happiness for six, five, four, three, two, or even one day and night?
The Nirgrantha replied, “No.”
"Gautama!
he replied. He asked again: "Nigaṇṭha!"
"Could I attain such joyful happiness by remaining silent and speechless for one day and one night?
The Nirgrantha replied, "It is so."
"Gautama!
Is one able to obtain joy and happiness for two, three, four, five, or six days and nights, or even for seven days and seven nights?
The Nirgrantha replied:
"So it is, Gautama. I then asked him again:
"O Nirgranthas! What do you think?
Who possesses the superior happiness?"
"Is it King Bimbisāra, or is it I?
The Nirgrantha replied:
"Gautama! According to our understanding of what the śramaṇa Gautama has said, Gautama excels in excellence, while King Bimbisāra does not."
“Mahānāma! For this reason you should know that desire has no pleasure, but possesses immeasurable suffering and affliction.

If a learned noble disciple does not see things as they truly are, he will be overwhelmed by desire and entangled by evil and unwholesome states, and thus fail to attain the relinquishment of pleasure and supreme tranquility.”
Mahānāma! In this way, that learned noble disciple is one who desires to regress. Mahānāma!
I know that sensual desires bring no pleasure, but rather immeasurable suffering and affliction.
Having known this as it truly is, I am not overwhelmed by desire, nor am I entangled by evil and unwholesome states; thus, I have attained the bliss of equanimity and unsurpassed peace.
"Mahānāma! For this reason, I do not regress because of desire.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Mahānāma and the monks, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Dukkhandha Sutta*, the fourth, ends here; 2,254 characters. 101. The *Adhicitta Sutta* (101), from the *Nidāna-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Adhicitta Sutta*, the fifth, for recitation in the second minor section of *Kaccāyanagotta*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate five signs."

Having repeatedly contemplated these five signs, unwholesome thoughts that arise are immediately extinguished; once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind abides constantly, resting within and attaining concentration with one-pointedness.
“What are the five?

A bhikkhu attends to a sign that is associated with the wholesome; if unwholesome thoughts arise, he attends to another sign associated with the wholesome by means of that [original] sign, so as not to give rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts.”

By means of this mark, he further attends to another mark associated with the wholesome; once unwholesome thoughts that have already arisen are extinguished, and those evil thoughts having been extinguished, the mind becomes stable, abiding within, stilled, one-pointed, and attains concentration.
It is like a master carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice who takes a marking line and applies it to the wood, then uses a sharp axe to hew and shape it until it is straight.
In this way, bhikṣus!
By means of this sign, one further contemplates another sign that is associated with the wholesome, so as not to give rise to unwholesome and evil thoughts.

Having contemplated another sign associated with the wholesome by means of that sign, any unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are immediately extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains constantly settled, abiding in internal tranquility, and attains concentration through single-mindedness.

If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind, he should repeatedly contemplate this foremost sign. Once he has contemplated this sign, unwholesome thoughts that arise will immediately be extinguished. When evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains constantly settled, stilled within, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu! One should maintain mindfulness associated with wholesome signs.

If unwholesome thoughts arise, one should contemplate those thoughts as being evil and fraught with calamity: 'This thought is unwholesome; this thought is evil; this thought is loathed by the wise; if this thought is fully developed, one will not attain penetration, will not attain awakening to the Path, and will not attain Nirvāṇa, because it gives rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts.'"

As he thus contemplates evil, any unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are immediately extinguished. Once these evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, abiding in internal stillness, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.

It is like a young man, handsome and lovely, who has bathed and washed himself, put on bright and clean clothes, anointed his body with fragrance, and groomed his beard and hair until they are perfectly pure and clean; yet someone ties a dead snake, a dead dog, or a half-eaten corpse—bluish in color, bloated, foul-smelling, rotting, and oozing impurities—to his neck, whereupon he becomes disgusted by the filth and finds it neither pleasing nor delightful.
In this way, bhikṣus, he contemplates this thought:

"This thought is fraught with danger; this thought is unwholesome; this thought is evil; this thought is loathed by the wise. If this thought is fully developed, one will not attain penetration, will not awaken to the path, and will not attain nirvāṇa, because it gives rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts."

When he thus contemplates evil, any unwholesome thoughts that have arisen are immediately extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind abides constantly, attains rest within, and achieves concentration with one-pointedness.

If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind (*adhicitta*), he should repeatedly contemplate this second mark. By contemplating this mark, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen will immediately be extinguished. Once evil thoughts are extinguished, the mind abides constantly, attains internal stillness, and achieves concentration with one-pointedness.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

When one is attending to a sign associated with the wholesome, if unwholesome thoughts arise; or when one is contemplating the defects of the unwholesome, if unwholesome thoughts again arise—that bhikṣu should not attend to those thoughts, lest they give rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts."

He does not attend to those thoughts; as soon as unwholesome thoughts have arisen, they are immediately extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, stilled within, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.
Suppose there is a person with sight, and forms are present in the light, yet they do not see them—either because they close their eyes or move their body away.
What do you think?
"If form exists within radiance, can that person perceive the characteristics of form? He replied, "No."

“In this way, bhikṣus, one should not entertain such thoughts, lest they give rise to evil and unwholesome thoughts. By not entertaining such thoughts, any unwholesome thoughts that have already arisen will be extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, attains internal stillness, and achieves concentration with a single-pointed intent.”

If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind (*adhicitta*), he should repeatedly contemplate this third mark. Having contemplated this mark, unwholesome thoughts that arise will immediately be extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains constantly settled, stilled within, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.
"Furthermore, bhikṣu!

When unwholesome thoughts arise while you are attending to wholesome signs, or when unwholesome thoughts arise while you are contemplating the defects of those thoughts, or when unwholesome thoughts arise even when you are not attending to them at all—in such cases, that bhikṣu, for the sake of those thoughts, should gradually diminish them through the practice of reflection, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise."

With this reflection, he should gradually diminish his thoughts through intentional application; as soon as unwholesome thoughts have arisen, they are extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, abiding in internal stillness, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.
It is like a person walking on a path who proceeds with great speed and thinks to himself:
"Why am I going so fast? I should now rather walk slowly."
He then walked slowly.
Again he thought:
"Why am I walking slowly?"
"Is it better to remain here? He then remained.
Again, he had this thought:
"What am I standing for?
It would be better to sit. He then sat down.
Again, he thought to himself: "Why am I sitting?
It would be better to lie down."
He then lies down.
In this way, that person gradually stills the coarse activities of the body.

You should know that it is the same for a bhikṣu: he forms this thought that he shall gradually diminish his mental activity through volitional effort, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise.

With this reflection, he should gradually diminish his thoughts through mental application; as soon as unwholesome thoughts have arisen, they are extinguished. Once evil thoughts are extinguished, the mind abides steadily, resting within, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.

If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind (*adhicitta*), he should repeatedly contemplate this fourth mark. By contemplating this mark, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen will immediately be extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains constantly settled, resting within, and attains concentration with one-pointedness.
"Furthermore, monks!

When unwholesome thoughts arise while one is mindful of wholesome mental objects; when unwholesome thoughts arise while one is contemplating the defects of unwholesome thoughts; when unwholesome thoughts arise even when one is not being mindful; and when unwholesome thoughts continue to arise even as one gradually diminishes mindfulness through the practice of reflection—that monk should contemplate in this way."

When a bhikṣu, because of such thoughts, gives rise to unwholesome thoughts, that bhikṣu should clench his teeth together, press his tongue against the upper palate, and with the mind cultivate the mind—receiving, maintaining, and subduing it so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise.

He cultivates the mind with the mind, upholding and subduing it; as soon as unwholesome thoughts arise, they are extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, resting within and attaining concentration through one-pointedness.
"Just as two strong men might seize a weak man and hold him down to subdue him,

so too, bhikkhu, with teeth clenched against teeth and tongue pressed against the upper palate, you should train the mind with the mind, holding it fast and subduing it, so that evil and unwholesome thoughts do not arise."

He cultivates the mind with the mind, upholding and subduing it; as soon as unwholesome thoughts arise, they are extinguished. Once evil thoughts have been extinguished, the mind abides constantly, ceasing within, and attains concentration in one-pointedness.

If a bhikṣu wishes to attain the higher mind (*adhicitta*), he should repeatedly attend to this fifth characteristic. By attending to this characteristic, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen will immediately be extinguished. Once evil thoughts are extinguished, the mind remains constantly settled, resting within, and attains one-pointed concentration.
“If a bhikkhu wishes to attain the higher mind (*adhicitta*), he should repeatedly bring these five signs to mind.

By repeatedly bringing these five signs to mind, unwholesome thoughts that have arisen will be extinguished; once evil thoughts are extinguished, the mind remains steadfast, attains internal tranquility, and achieves one-pointed concentration.”

If, when a bhikṣu contemplates signs associated with the wholesome, no unwholesome thoughts arise; when he contemplates the faults of the unwholesome, no unwholesome thoughts arise; when he does not engage in such contemplation, no unwholesome thoughts arise; and when he gradually diminishes his contemplation through the practice of reflection, no unwholesome thoughts arise; and when he cultivates the mind with the mind, upholding and subduing it, no unwholesome thoughts arise—then he attains mastery, such that he can direct his thoughts as he wishes and refrain from directing them as he wishes.

If a bhikṣu contemplates what he wishes to contemplate and does not contemplate what he does not wish to contemplate, this is called a bhikṣu who is master of his thoughts and possesses mastery over the tracks of thought.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Adhicitta Sūtra*, the fifth, ends here, totaling 1,456 characters. 102. *Sati Sūtra* (102), the sixth in the *Nidāna-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, recited in the second sub-section of *Kṣudrakagrāma*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Before I had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I had this thought:”

"I should divide these various thoughts into two parts: thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness shall constitute one part; thoughts free from sensual desire, thoughts free from ill will, and thoughts free from harmfulness shall constitute another part."

At a later time, I then distinguished these thoughts into two categories: thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and harmfulness as one category, and thoughts free from sensual desire, free from ill will, and free from harmfulness as another category.

Practicing in this way, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, if a thought of sensual desire arises, I immediately recognize the arising of that thought of sensual desire:
"It harms oneself, it harms others, and it harms both; it destroys wisdom, brings much vexation, and prevents the attainment of Nirvana."
I perceived that [anger] harms oneself, harms others, and harms both; it destroys wisdom, brings much affliction, and prevents the attainment of Nirvana, and thus it quickly subsided.

Furthermore, thoughts of anger and thoughts of harm arose within me. I immediately perceived that these thoughts of anger and harm arise to harm oneself, harm others, and harm both; they destroy wisdom, bring much affliction, and prevent the attainment of Nirvana.
"Perceiving that [these thoughts] harm oneself, harm others, and harm both; that they destroy wisdom, cause much affliction, and prevent the attainment of Nirvana, one should quickly extinguish them.

'I have given rise to sensual thoughts—I do not accept them, I sever them, I eliminate them, I cast them out. I have given rise to thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm—I do not accept them, I sever them, I eliminate them, I cast them out.'"
Why is this? Because from such views, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states will inevitably arise.

It is just as in the month after spring, when fields have been sown, the pasture lands are not extensive; if a cowherd boy lets his cattle graze in a marshy field and they enter another's field, the cowherd boy immediately takes up his staff and goes to stop them.
Why is this? Because the cowherd knows that as a consequence, there will inevitably be verbal abuse, beating, binding, and transgression.
For this reason, the cowherd takes up his staff and goes to prevent it.

I am also like this: when thoughts of sensual desire arise, I do not accept them, but cut them off, eliminate them, and cast them out; when thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harm arise, I do not accept them, but cut them off, eliminate them, and cast them out.
Why is that? Because through this view of mine, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states will inevitably arise.
A bhikkhu, according to what he contemplates and according to what he attends to, his mind finds delight therein.
If a bhikṣu frequently dwells on thoughts of sensual desire, he abandons thoughts free from sensual desire; because he frequently dwells on thoughts of sensual desire, his mind finds delight therein.

If a bhikṣu frequently dwells on thoughts of ill will or thoughts of harm, he abandons thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm; because he frequently dwells on thoughts of ill will and harm, his mind finds delight therein.

In this way, monks, one who is not free from thoughts of sensual desire, not free from thoughts of ill will, and not free from thoughts of harmfulness, cannot escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and weeping; nor can they be free from all suffering.
Practicing in this way, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligence, a thought of non-desire arises within me.
As soon as that thought of non-desire arises, I am aware of it; it harms neither myself nor others, nor does it harm both. Cultivating wisdom without weariness, one attains Nirvana.

Realizing that this does not harm oneself, does not harm others, nor harms both, and that through the cultivation of wisdom one attains nirvana without toil, one should then swiftly cultivate and widely disseminate it.

Furthermore, he gives rise to thoughts of non-ill will and thoughts of non-harming. He then reflects: "I have awakened to the arising of thoughts of non-ill will and thoughts of non-harming; these do not harm oneself, do not harm others, nor do they harm both. By cultivating wisdom, one attains nirvana without toil."

One realizes that this does not harm oneself, does not harm others, nor does it harm both; it cultivates wisdom, is free from weariness, and leads to the attainment of Nirvana. Thus, one should swiftly cultivate and widely disseminate it.

“I gave rise to thoughts free from desire and cultivated many such reflections; I gave rise to thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harmfulness, and cultivated many such reflections. I further thought:

‘One who cultivates many reflections becomes forgetful due to physical agitation, which then harms the mind. It would be better for me to discipline the inner mind, remaining constantly in internal stillness, attaining concentration with one-pointedness, so as not to harm the mind.’”
At a later time, I then disciplined my inner mind, dwelling constantly in internal tranquility; with a single-pointed mind, I attained concentration without harming the mind.
Having given rise to thoughts free from desire, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma;
having given rise to thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harm, I further gave rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Why is that? Because I do not see any immeasurable evil or unwholesome states arising from this.
It is just as when, after the autumn harvest has gathered all the grain, a cowherd releases his cattle into the wild fields and thinks to himself:
"My ox is among the herd. Why is this?
Because if the cowherd were not to see it, he would consequently be subject to abuse, beating, and binding; thus, there would be fault. For this reason, he thinks: [as stated above].
"My oxen are among the herd.
In the same way, once I have given rise to thoughts free from desire, I further give rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma and the successive stages of the Dharma;
once I have given rise to thoughts free from ill will and thoughts free from harmfulness, I further give rise to thoughts directed toward the Dharma and the successive stages of the Dharma.
Why is that? Because I do not see how this could give rise to immeasurable evil and unwholesome states.
A bhikkhu, according to what he contemplates and what he reflects upon, finds his mind delighting therein.
If a bhikṣu frequently dwells upon thoughts of non-desire, he abandons thoughts of desire; because he frequently dwells upon thoughts of non-desire, his mind finds joy therein.

If a bhikṣu frequently dwells upon thoughts of non-ill will and thoughts of non-harming, he abandons thoughts of ill will and thoughts of harming; because he frequently dwells upon thoughts of non-ill will and thoughts of non-harming, his mind finds joy therein.

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is inward tranquility and mental unification, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness. Thus he attains and dwells in the perfection of the third dhyāna.

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

“When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, stainless, free from affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable, he inclines toward the realization of the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of the outflows. He then knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are.
He also knows these outflows as they truly are; he knows the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as they truly are.”

Having known thus and seen thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

When this bhikṣu is free from thoughts of desire, free from thoughts of ill will, and free from thoughts of harm, he attains liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, and all suffering.
It is as if there were a great spring in a secluded wilderness where a herd of deer lived and roamed.

A man came there who did not seek their welfare, benefit, peace, or happiness; instead, he blocked the level and straight path, opened a treacherous road, dug a great pit and trench, and stationed men to guard it.
In this way, all the deer died out.

Then another person came, seeking their welfare, benefit, peace, and happiness; he opened up a level and upright path, blocked off the evil ways, and drove away the hunters, so that the deer were all able to attain safety and relief.
“Monks! You should know that I have spoken this parable for the purpose of making the meaning known; for the wise, upon hearing a parable, understand its underlying intent.
This teaching has a specific meaning: the ‘great spring’ refers to the love, longing, and delight in the five sensual pleasures.”
What are the five? They are:

the eye cognizing forms, the ear cognizing sounds, the nose cognizing odors, the tongue cognizing tastes, and the body cognizing tangibles. You should know that the "great spring of water" refers to these five desires.
You should know that the great herd of deer represents the śramaṇas and brahmins.
You should know that the single person who comes and does not seek for them meaning and benefit, nor seek for their peace, security, and happiness, is Māra Pāpīyān.
To block the straight path and open a single evil road refers to these three unwholesome and unvirtuous thoughts:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.
One should know that the "evil road" refers to these three unwholesome and unvirtuous thoughts.
Furthermore, there are other evil paths, namely the Eightfold Wrong Path: wrong view through to wrong concentration; these constitute the eight.
One should know that those who create great pits and moats are ignorance itself.
One should know that those who act as guardians are the retinue of Māra Pāpīyān.

Furthermore, if another person comes who seeks for them meaning and benefit, and seeks their peace, security, and happiness, one should know that this is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
To block off the evil paths and open the level and upright path refers to these three wholesome thoughts:
the thought of non-desire, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harming.
One should know that the Path consists of these three wholesome thoughts.
Furthermore, there is another path, namely the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, and so on, up to right concentration—these are the eight. “Monks!
For your sake, I have opened the level and upright path, closed off the evil paths, filled in the pits and moats, and removed the guardians.”

Just as a venerable teacher acts toward his disciples by giving rise to great loving-kindness, feeling compassion, pity, and sympathy, seeking their welfare and benefit, and seeking their peace and happiness—this I have now done.

"You yourselves must likewise act accordingly; go to secluded places—among the mountains, forests, at the foot of trees, or in empty, quiet, and peaceful locations—and sit in meditation with contemplation. Do not be negligent; apply yourselves with diligent vigor so that you shall have no cause for regret later."
"This is my instruction; this is my admonition.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth section on Mindfulness ends, totaling one thousand five hundred and ninety-three characters. *Madhyama Āgama*, Fascicle Twenty-five, totaling seven thousand four hundred and sixty-eight characters.
*Madhyama Āgama*, Fascicle Twenty-six, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
103. Siṃhanāda Sūtra (103), Chapter on Causes, Siṃhanāda Sūtra, Seventh, Second Recitation of the Minor Earth-City Section.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering through the Kuru country and stayed at the Kuru town of Kalmāṣadamya.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this world, there are the first śramaṇa, the second, the third, and the fourth śramaṇas; beyond these, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins. All other paths are entirely empty of śramaṇas and brahmins."
Wherever you may be among the assembly, make such a true lion’s roar.
Monks! There may be followers of other teachings who come to question you:
"Venerable sirs!
What practice do you possess, what power do you possess, and what wisdom do you possess, that you make such a declaration as this:
'There is a first śramaṇa, a second, a third, and a fourth; beyond these there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins; all other paths are empty, devoid of śramaṇas and brahmins'?"
"Wherever you may be among the assembly, you should let out such a true lion's roar.
"Bhikkhus! You should answer the followers of other teachings in this way:"
"Venerable friends! Our Blessed One possesses knowledge and vision; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taught four dharmas. Because of these four dharmas, we speak thus:

'Herein are the first śramaṇa, the second, the third, and the fourth śramaṇa. Beyond these, there are no other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; all other paths are empty of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. Thus, wherever we are among the assemblies, we utter this true lion’s roar."
"What are the four?
Venerable friends!

We have faith in the Teacher, faith in the Dharma, and faith in those endowed with the virtues of the precepts; we love and respect our fellow practitioners, and we serve them with reverence and diligence."
"Venerable friends! Our Blessed One possesses knowledge and vision; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught these four dharmas. Because of these four dharmas, we speak thus:

'There is this first śramaṇa, the second, the third, and the fourth śramaṇa. Beyond these, there are no other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas; all other paths are empty of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. It is with reference to this that we, wherever we may be among the assemblies, utter this true lion’s roar."
“Monks! A follower of another school might further say this:
‘O worthy ones!...’”
We also have faith in the Venerable Teacher, saying, "He is our Teacher.
We have faith in the Dharma, saying, "It is our Dharma.
Our moral virtue is complete, saying, "It is our precepts."
We love and respect those who follow the same path, serving them with reverence and diligence—namely, those of our own path, whether they have gone forth or remain at home.
Venerable friends!
Between the two kinds of teachings—the teaching of the ascetic Gautama and our own—what is superior, what is the intended meaning, and what is the distinction?
"Monks! You should question the followers of other teachings in this way:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Is there one ultimate goal, or are there many ultimate goals?
Monks! If a follower of another school answers in this way:
"Venerable friends!
There is one ultimate goal; there is no plurality of ultimate goals.
Thus spoke the Bhikkhu.
"You should further ask those of other schools:
'Venerable sirs!
Is it for one who possesses desire that ultimate perfection is attained?'"
"Is it for one who is free from desire that ultimate certainty is attained?
Monks! If a follower of another school answers in this way:
"It is for those without desire that the ultimate goal is attained; it is not for those with desire that the ultimate goal is attained.
Monks! You should further ask the followers of other teachings:
"Venerable friends!
Is it one who harbors ill will who attains the ultimate goal?
Or is it one who is free from ill will who attains the ultimate goal?"
"Monks! If a follower of another school answers thus:
'It is for one free from anger that the ultimate goal is attained, not for one possessed by anger.'"
"Monks! You should further ask the followers of other teachings:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Is it for one who possesses delusion that the ultimate goal is attained?
Or is it for one who is free from delusion that the ultimate goal is attained?
Monks, if a follower of another teaching should answer in this way:
"Venerable friends!
It is for one free from delusion that the ultimate goal is attained, not for one possessed by delusion. "Bhikkhus!"
"You should further ask those of other schools:
'Venerable sirs!
Is it the case that one who possesses craving and possesses clinging attains the ultimate goal?'"
"Is it for one who is without craving and without feeling that ultimate perfection is attained?
Monks! If a follower of another school answers in this way:
"Venerable friends!
It is for one who is without craving and without grasping that the ultimate goal is attained; it is not for one who has craving and grasping that the ultimate goal is attained.
Thus spoke the Bhikṣu.
"You should further ask those heterodox teachers:
'Venerable sirs,
is it for one who lacks wisdom and does not speak of wisdom that ultimate perfection is attained?'"
"Is it the case that those who possess wisdom and who teach wisdom attain the ultimate goal?
Bhikṣus! If a follower of another school were to answer in this way:
"Venerable friends!
It is those who possess wisdom and speak of wisdom who attain the ultimate goal, not those who lack wisdom and do not speak of wisdom.
Thus spoke the Bhikṣu.
"You should further ask those heterodox teachers:
'Venerable sirs!
Is it for one who possesses hatred and contention that ultimate perfection is attained?'"
"Is it for one who is without hatred and without contention that ultimate certainty is attained? Monks!
If a follower of another school answers thus:
“Venerable friends!
It is for one who is without hatred and without contention that the ultimate goal is attained; it is not for one who has hatred and contention that the ultimate goal is attained. “Monks!”
"You, as followers of other teachings, should speak thus:
'Venerable sirs!
It is as you say that there is one ultimate truth, and not many ultimate truths;'"
Those who are free from desire attain the ultimate goal; those with desire do not attain the ultimate goal.
Those who are free from hatred attain the ultimate goal; those with hatred do not attain the ultimate goal.
Those who are free from delusion attain the ultimate goal; those with delusion do not attain the ultimate goal.
Those who are without craving and without grasping attain the ultimate; those with craving and grasping do not attain the ultimate.
Those who possess wisdom and teach wisdom attain the ultimate; those without wisdom and who do not teach wisdom do not attain the ultimate.
Those who are without hatred and without contention attain the ultimate; those with hatred and contention do not attain the ultimate.
If there are recluses or brahmins who rely on immeasurable views, they all rely upon two views: the view of existence and the view of non-existence.

Those who rely on the view of existence become attached to the view of existence; relying upon and dwelling in the view of existence, they harbor hostility toward and dispute with the view of non-existence.

If one relies on the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*), one becomes attached to that view of non-existence; relying upon and dwelling in that view of non-existence, one harbors hatred and contention toward the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*).

"Should there be any ascetics or brahmins who do not know, as it truly is, the cause, the origin, the cessation, the exhaustion, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding [the aggregates], they all possess desire, anger, delusion, craving, and clinging; they lack wisdom and do not speak with wisdom; they harbor hatred and contention. Such persons are not freed from birth, aging, sickness, and death, nor can they transcend sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; they do not attain the end of suffering."

If there are recluses or brahmins who, regarding these two views, know their cause, their origin, their cessation, their exhaustion, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them as they truly are, then all of them—being free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, free from craving, and free from clinging, possessing wisdom, proclaiming wisdom, without malice, and without contention—shall attain liberation from birth, old age, disease, and death; they shall also be able to transcend sorrow, lamentation, weeping, pain, and despair, and thus reach the end of suffering.

“Or there may be certain recluses and brahmins who posit the abandonment of feeling, yet do not posit the abandonment of all feelings; they posit the abandonment of the feeling of sensual desire, but do not posit the abandonment of the feeling of rules and observances, the feeling of views, or the feeling of self.”
Why is this? Because those recluses and brahmins do not know the three bases as they truly are.
Therefore, although they may posit the abandonment of feeling, they do not posit the abandonment of all feelings.

Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who posit the abandonment of feeling, yet they do not posit the abandonment of all feelings; they posit the abandonment of the feeling of sensual desire and the feeling of precepts, but they do not posit the abandonment of the feeling of views and the feeling of self.

Why is this? Because those śramaṇas and brahmins do not know these two points as they truly are; therefore, although they establish the abandonment of feeling, they do not establish the abandonment of all feelings.

Furthermore, there are recluses and brahmins who posit the abandonment of feeling, yet they do not posit the abandonment of all feelings; they posit the abandonment of the feeling of sensual desire, the feeling of precepts and vows, and the feeling of views, but they do not posit the abandonment of the feeling of self. Why is this so?
Those śramaṇas and brahmins do not know that single point as it truly is; therefore, although they propose the abandonment of feeling, they do not propose the abandonment of all feelings.

In such a Dharma and Vinaya, if one places faith in the honored teacher, that is neither correct nor supreme; if one places faith in the Dharma, that too is neither correct nor supreme; if one is endowed with the virtue of the precepts, that too is neither correct nor supreme; and if one loves and respects one's fellow practitioners and serves them with reverence and diligence, that too is neither correct nor supreme.

"If there is a Tathāgata who appears in the world—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—he establishes the relinquishing of clinging; in this very life he establishes the relinquishing of all clinging, establishing the relinquishing of clinging to sensual desire, clinging to precepts and vows, clinging to views, and clinging to a self."
What is the cause and condition of these four feelings? From what do they arise, and what is their root?
These four feelings have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their condition; they arise from ignorance, and ignorance is their root.

If there is a bhikkhu for whom ignorance has been exhausted and true knowledge has arisen, he will no longer, from that point on, undergo the acquisition of sensual desire, the acquisition of precepts and vows, the acquisition of views, or the acquisition of a self. Having not undergone these acquisitions, he is without fear; being without fear, he severs the causal conditions and will certainly attain parinirvāṇa. He knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

In this True Dharma and Discipline, if one has faith in the Honored Teacher, that is correct and foremost; if one has faith in the Dharma, that is correct and foremost; if one is fully endowed with the virtue of precepts, that is correct and foremost; if one loves and respects one’s fellow practitioners and serves them with reverence and diligence, that is correct and foremost.

"Venerable friends! We possess such conduct, such power, and such wisdom; for this reason, we speak thus: 'There is the first śramaṇa, the second, the third, and the fourth śramaṇa. Beyond these, there are no other śramaṇas or brahmins; all other paths are empty of śramaṇas and brahmins.'"
"For this reason, wherever we may be among the assembly, we utter such a true lion’s roar.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, the seventh, ends here, totaling one thousand six hundred and ninety characters. 104. The *Udumbara Sūtra* (104), the eighth in the *Nidāna-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, recited in the second section on Small Earth Forts. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.
At that time, there was a householder named Śāṭha who, at dawn, departed from Rājagṛha intending to go to the Buddha to make offerings and pay him homage.
Thereupon, the householder Sāḷha thought to himself:

"Let alone going to the Buddha; perhaps the World-Honored One and the venerable bhikṣus are sitting in meditation. I would rather go to the Udumbarikā forest to visit the park of the heterodox teachers."
Thereupon, the householder Bhūtamati went to the Udumbarikā forest and approached the park of the heterodox teachers.

At that time, in the Udumbarikā forest park, there was a certain heterodox teacher named Aśoka, who was the preeminent leader among those heterodox teachers, honored by the multitude, and one who had subdued many. He was the one to whom five hundred heterodox teachers looked for guidance; he was agitating the assembly with a loud voice, discoursing on various matters such as talk of birds, talk of speech, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of strife, talk of food and drink, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of maidens, talk of courtesans, talk of worldly affairs, talk of what is not the Path, and talk of the ocean and of nations—discoursing thus on various matters such as talk of birds, all of them gathered together and seated there.
Then, seeing from afar that the householder Saccaka was approaching, the heterodox teacher Acelaka Kāśyapa immediately commanded his own assembly, making them all silent:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak; remain silent, delighting in silence, and each of you compose yourselves."
Why is this? This householder Saccaka has come; he is a disciple of the ascetic Gautama.

If there were any disciples of the ascetic Gautama whose name and virtue were so far-reaching and esteemed that they were worthy of veneration, yet who lived as householders residing in Rājagaha, he would be the foremost among them; he does not speak, delights in silence, and keeps himself restrained.
"If they know that this assembly remains silent, they might perhaps come.
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Aśoka caused the assembly to remain silent, and he himself remained silent as well.
Thereupon, the householder Bhūtamati went to where the ascetic Akkosaka-Bhāradvāja was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. Seated there, the householder Bhūtamati said:
"Akossaka!..."

When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwells in a secluded place among mountains, forests, or beneath trees, or stays upon a high cliff, silent and without sound, far removed from evil and devoid of people, he sits in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, being of such a nature, dwells in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees, or staying on high cliffs—in silence and stillness, far removed from noise, free from evil, and devoid of people, sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.

Dwelling in seclusion, he always delights in sitting in meditation, abiding in peace and happiness; that Buddha, the World-Honored One, has never once for a single day or night held a gathering with his assembly as you do today with your followers.
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Aśvatthāman said:
"Householder! Stop!"
Stop! On what basis do you know that the ascetic Gautama possesses liberation through empty wisdom?

This is not worth discussing—whether it be consistent or inconsistent, favorable or unfavorable; for that ascetic Gautama goes from extreme to extreme, delights in extremes, and dwells among extremes.
Just as a blind ox in a remote region eats, walking from edge to edge, delighting in the edges, and staying at the edges, so too is that ascetic Gautama.
"Householder!

If that śramaṇa Gautama were to come to this assembly, I would extinguish him with a single discourse as easily as one plays with an empty jar; I would also recount to him the parable of the blind ox."
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Aśoka addressed his own assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs!

Should the śramaṇa Gautama happen to come to this assembly, and if he should certainly arrive, you must not show him respect by rising from your seats or joining your palms toward him; do not invite him to sit, but reserve a single seat for him in advance. Once he has arrived here, speak to him as follows:"
“‘Gautama! There is a seat; sit as you please.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was sitting in meditation, he heard with his purified divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, the conversation between the householder Sūṣaddhika and the wanderer Aśvatthīputra. Having heard this, he rose from his meditation in the late afternoon and proceeded to the Wanderers’ Park at the Udumbarikā Grove.”
Seeing the World-Honored One approaching from afar, the wanderer Aśoka rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him, saying:
"Welcome, Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"It has been a long time since you last came here; please, sit upon this seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This foolish man has acted contrary to his own vow."
The Blessed One, having understood this, sat upon the bed. The wanderer Acela then exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
The Blessed One asked him: "Acela!..."
"What was the subject of your discussion just now with the householder Sāti?
For what reason have you gathered here and are seated thus?
The wanderer Acelaka Kassapa replied:
“Gautama! We have had this thought:
‘What kind of Dharma does the śramaṇa Gautama possess, by which he instructs his disciples?’”
"Once my disciples have received this instruction, they shall attain peace and security; for the rest of their lives, they shall purely cultivate the holy life and explain it to others.
"Gautama! [the king said.]
"Just now, I was discussing this very matter with the householder Sāti; for that reason, we have gathered here and are seated together.
When the householder Sāti heard those words, he thought to himself:
"This ascetic Akkosaka-Bhāradvāja is indeed speaking falsely."
"Why is that? Because he has deceived the World-Honored One in the very presence of the Buddha.
Having known this, the World-Honored One said:
“O Aśvatthāman!
My Dharma is profound!
It is most marvelous!”
How extraordinary!
It is difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to see, and difficult to attain—this which I call teaching and training my disciples.
Once the disciples have received this teaching and training, they practice the pure holy life (brahmacarya) for the duration of their lives and also explain it to others.
"O Aśvatthāman!

If there are points regarding the practices you detest that your own teacher’s school has failed to understand, you may question me about them; I shall certainly be able to answer so as to satisfy your mind."
Thereupon, the assembly of heterodox practitioners, agitated and confused, raised their voices in unison and cried out in a loud voice:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary!"
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this?
Because he is able to set aside his own school of thought and follow the doctrines of others in response to whatever questions are asked.
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Aśvatthāman commanded his own assembly to remain silent, and having done so, he asked:
"Gautama, what is the practice that leads to being uncomprehending and loathsome?"
"How is it that one attains fulfillment?
How is it that one does not attain fulfillment?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied:

“Anīgha! There are some recluses and brahmins who go naked and wear no clothes; some use their hands as clothing, some use leaves as clothing, and some use beads as clothing. Some do not fetch water with a jar, and some do not fetch water with a vessel. They do not eat food obtained by force of weapons or plunder, nor do they eat food obtained by deception. They do not go themselves, nor do they send a messenger; they do not request what is honored, nor what is well-honored, nor what is highly honored.”
If there are two people eating together, one should not eat with them; one should not eat at the home of a woman who is pregnant, nor at the home of one who keeps dogs;
even if flies carrying filth fly into the house, one should not eat;
one should not consume fish, nor eat meat, nor drink alcohol, nor drink foul water, or perhaps abstain from drinking altogether—thus training in non-attachment.
Regarding the practice of moderation in drinking and eating: one may take a single mouthful and consider that sufficient;
or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, considering seven mouthfuls sufficient; or one morsel of food and consider that sufficient;
or two, three, four, up to seven morsels, considering seven morsels sufficient.
Some eat once a day, taking that single meal as sufficient; others eat once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once every half-month or month, taking that single meal as sufficient.
"Or they eat leafy vegetables, or they eat millet, or they eat wild rice, or they eat various husks,
or they eat *tutthula* food, or they eat coarse food; or they go to secluded places and dwell in seclusion,
or they eat roots, or they eat fruits, or they eat fruits that have fallen naturally, or they carry..."
Some wear garments made of joined pieces; some wear garments of wool; some wear garments of head-hair;
some wear garments of both wool and head-hair; some wear whole skins; some wear perforated skins; some wear garments of whole and perforated skins;
some wear disheveled hair; some wear braided hair; some wear hair both disheveled and braided; or some have shaved their heads. Or...
Some shave their beards; some shave both beard and hair; some pluck out their hair; some pluck out their beards;
some pluck out both beard and hair; some remain standing while others sit; some practice squatting;
some lie upon thorns, using thorns as a bed; some lie upon fruits, using fruits as a bed; and some devote themselves to water.
Day and night they draw water with their hands; some serve the sacrificial fire, keeping it burning throughout the entire night;
others serve the sun and moon or worship great virtuous deities, joining their palms toward them.
In such ways as these, they undergo immeasurable suffering and practice the conduct of feverish affliction.
"O Aśoka! What do you think?
Is it complete when one does not clearly understand such conduct that is loathsome?"
"Is it not complete?
The wanderer Aśoka replied, "Gautama!"
"In this way, one is fully possessed of such unwholesome and loathsome conduct; it is not that one is not so possessed.
The Blessed One spoke again, saying:
"Aṅgulimāla!"
"I have explained to you that this unwholesome, loathsome, and complete course of action is defiled by immeasurable impurities.
The wanderer Acelaka asked:
"Gautama, how is it that you have explained to me that this unwholesome, loathsome, and complete course of action is defiled by immeasurable impurities?"
The Blessed One replied: “Aṅgulimāla,
there may be one who practices austerities as a practitioner of asceticism, yet because of those austerities, he harbors evil desires and thoughts of desire.”
"Without ill will!

If there is one who practices austerities as a practitioner of asceticism, yet because of those austerities as a practitioner of asceticism harbors evil desires and thoughts of desire—this, without ill will, is what is called [the first kind of person]."
"O Acelaka, the practice of asceticism is defiled.
Furthermore, O Acelaka, there is one who practices the asceticism of pure austerity; because of this practice of pure austerity, he gazes upward at the sun and inhales the solar essence."
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is one who practices the asceticism of a pure and austere practitioner; because of this practice of pure and austere asceticism, he gazes upward at the sun and inhales the solar essence. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is what is called [such a practitioner]."
The practice of asceticism is a defilement.
Furthermore, O Unwrathful One!

There may be someone who practices asceticism through self-mortification; because of this practice of asceticism through self-mortification, he becomes arrogant, and having attained this practice of asceticism through self-mortification, his mind becomes bound and attached to it.

"Anīgha! Suppose there is a practitioner of asceticism who, because of that practice of asceticism, becomes conceited; having attained that practice of asceticism, his mind becomes bound and attached to it. This, Anīgha, is what is called [the first kind of ascetic]."
"Practicing asceticism is a defilement.
Furthermore, Unenvious One!
There may be someone who practices pure asceticism, and because of that practice of pure asceticism, he holds himself in high esteem and looks down upon others."
"O Aṅgīrasa!

If there is one who practices austerities as a practitioner of asceticism, and because of those austerities as a practitioner of asceticism, holds himself in high esteem and looks down upon others—this, O Aṅgīrasa, is called..."
The practice of asceticism is a defilement.
Furthermore, O Aṅgirasa, there may be one who practices the asceticism of purification; because of this asceticism of purification, he goes from house to house and proclaims himself thus:
"I practice austerities; my practice is extremely difficult. O Aṅgirasa!
Suppose there were one who practices a life of austerity and performs asceticism, and because of that austere practice and asceticism, goes from house to house and proclaims of himself:
"To say, 'I practice austerity; my practice is extremely difficult,' O Aṅgulimāla,
is called the defilement of one who practices asceticism."
"Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a certain practitioner of asceticism who performs austerities. Because of these ascetic practices, if he sees a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is respected, honored, and venerated by others, he immediately gives rise to jealousy and says:
'Why do they respect, honor, and venerate that śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa?'"
"You should revere, make offerings to, and serve me.
Why is this? Because I practice asceticism."
"Without anger!

Suppose there is a practitioner of austerities who practices a life of asceticism, and because of this practice of austerities, he sees a certain śramaṇa or brahmin being honored, supported, and venerated by others. He then gives rise to jealousy and says:
'Why do they honor, support, and venerate that śramaṇa or brahmin?'"
"You should revere, make offerings to, and serve me.
Why is this? Because I practice asceticism."
This, O Aṅgulimāla, is called the defilement of one who practices asceticism.
Furthermore, O Aṅgulimāla:

There may be one who practices austerities and asceticism; because of these austerities and asceticism, if he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is honored, supported, and reverently served by others, he then rebukes that śramaṇa or brahmin face-to-face, saying:
"Why do you honor, support, and reverently serve them?"
You have many desires and many cravings, and you constantly eat; you eat five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, tree-seeds, fruit-seeds, joint-seeds, and seed-seeds.
"Just as a torrential rain causes great harm to the seeds of the five grains and disturbs both domestic animals and the people,
so too it is with those recluses and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others."
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a practitioner of asceticism who practices a life of austerity, and because of this practice of austerity, he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and served by others, and he then openly rebukes that śramaṇa or brahmin, saying:
'Why do you respect, honor, and serve him?'"
You have many desires and many cravings, and you constantly eat food consisting of five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, fruit-seeds, joint-seeds, and seed-seeds.
"Just as a torrential rain causes much damage to the seeds of the five grains and disturbs both livestock and people," so it is, Unenvious One!
When those śramaṇas and brahmins frequently enter the homes of others, it is likewise thus. This is what is meant. Unenvious One!
“Practicing asceticism is a defilement. Furthermore, Unenvious One!

There may be someone who practices the asceticism of painful austerity; because of this practice of painful austerity, there arise sorrow, delusion, and terror; secret conduct out of fear; apprehension regarding loss of reputation; and increased covetousness and negligence.”

"Anīgha! Suppose there is a practitioner of austerities who practices a life of asceticism, yet because of that practice of austerities, he experiences sorrow, delusion, and fear; he acts with secret dread, suspects the loss of his reputation, and increases his watchfulness and negligence. This, Anīgha, is what is meant by [the first kind of ascetic]."
“Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla, there is one who practices asceticism with impurity.

Again, Aṅgulimāla, there may be someone who practices asceticism through pure austerities; yet because of those pure austerities, he gives rise to the view of a self, extreme views, wrong views, and clinging to views, becoming difficult to deal with and lacking restraint in mind. Thus, regarding matters that are accessible to other recluses and brahmins, he remains inaccessible.”
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is one who practices the ascetic life of self-mortification, and because of that practice of the ascetic life of self-mortification, he gives rise to the view of a self, the view of extremes, wrong views, and dogmatic clinging to views; he is difficult to deal with and lacks restraint in his mind, regarding as permissible for śramaṇas and brahmins those things that should not be permitted. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is called [the first]."
The practice of asceticism is a defilement.
Furthermore, Unchagging One!
