There may be someone who practices the asceticism of pure austerity, yet because of that practice of pure austerity, he harbors anger, entanglements, the fetter of silence, stinginess, envy, flattery, deceit, hypocrisy, lack of shame, and lack of dread of blame.

"Anīgha! Suppose there is one who practices austerities as an ascetic, and because of those austerities as an ascetic, he is possessed by the fetters of anger, the bond of silence, stinginess, envy, flattery, deceit, hypocrisy, lack of shame, and lack of dread. This, Anīgha, is called [the first kind of ascetic]."
“Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla, there is one who practices the asceticism of self-mortification;
yet because of this asceticism of self-mortification, he engages in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter, and is possessed of evil conduct.”
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a practitioner of austerities who, because of those austerities, engages in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter, and is possessed of evil precepts. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is what is called..."
“Furthermore, Unenvious One! There may be someone who practices the asceticism of painful austerities,
yet because of that practice of painful austerities, he lacks faith, is indolent, lacks right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and possesses corrupted wisdom.”
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a practitioner of asceticism who practices austerities, yet because of those ascetic practices, he lacks faith, is indolent, lacks right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and possesses corrupt wisdom. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is what is meant [by that]."
"O practitioner of austerities, you are defiled.
You are not free from ill will. Have I not told you that this practice, which is incomplete, loathsome, and fully possessed of defilements, is stained by immeasurable impurities?"
The wanderer Aśoka replied: "It is so, Gautama;
for my sake you have explained this practice that is incomprehensible, loathsome, and complete, defiled by immeasurable impurities."
“Anavatapta! I shall further explain to you this practice that is incomprehensible and loathsome, yet which is not defiled by immeasurable impurities.
The heterodox teacher Anavatapta asked again:
“How is it, Gautama? Please explain to me how one can possess such a practice that is incomprehensible and loathsome, yet not defiled by immeasurable impurities?
The Blessed One replied:
“Aṅgulimāla! [It is so.]”
There may be one who practices the ascetic practice of austerity; because of this practice of austerity, he does not harbor ill will toward sensual desires nor does he dwell upon them. Anīgha!

If there is one who practices the ascetic practice of austerity and, because of this practice of austerity, does not harbor ill will toward sensual desires nor dwell upon them, this, Anīgha, is called [the first kind of ascetic].
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement.
Furthermore, O Aṅgirasa, there may be one who practices pure asceticism; because of this practice of pure asceticism, he does not look upon the sun nor does he inhale its heat.
"O Aṅgulimāla!
Suppose there is a practitioner of asceticism who, by virtue of that practice of asceticism, does not look upon the sunlight nor consume its heat; this, O Aṅgulimāla, is called [the first]."
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. "Furthermore, Anīgha!

There may be one who practices asceticism through the practice of purification; because of this practice of purification, he does not become arrogant, and having attained the practice of purification, his mind is not bound by attachment."
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is one who practices the ascetic practice of austerity, and because of this ascetic practice of austerity he does not become conceited; having attained the ascetic practice of austerity, his mind is not bound or attached to it. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is called [the true practitioner]."
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement.
"Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!
There may be one who practices pure asceticism; because of this practice of pure asceticism, he does not exalt himself nor disparage others."
"Without ill will!
If one practices austerities as an ascetic, and because of those austerities does not exalt oneself nor disparage others—this, without ill will, is called [the practice of austerities]."
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. "Furthermore, Anīgha!
Suppose there is one who practices a pure and ascetic practice; because of this pure and ascetic practice, he does not go from house to house and proclaim himself, saying: [I am an ascetic...]"
"I practice a life of purity and austerity; my practice is extremely difficult.
O Aṅgirasa! If there were one who practiced a life of purity and austerity, yet because of that practice of purity and austerity, did not go from house to house to proclaim it for himself:
"‘I practice pure and ascetic conduct; my practice is extremely difficult’—
this, O Aṅgirasa, is called the absence of impurity in one who practices asceticism."
"Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a certain practitioner of asceticism who practices a life of austerity. Because of this practice of asceticism, if he sees a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is respected, honored, and venerated by others, he does not give rise to jealousy, saying:
'Why do they respect, honor, and venerate that śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa?'"
"You should revere, make offerings to, and serve me.
Why is that? Because I practice asceticism."
"Without ill will!

Suppose there is one who practices a life of austerity and asceticism; because of that practice of austerity and asceticism, if he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is honored, supported, and venerated by others, he does not give rise to jealousy, saying:
'Why do they honor, support, and venerate that śramaṇa or brahmin?'"
"You should revere, make offerings to, and serve me.
Why is this? Because I practice asceticism."
This, Anīgha, is called the absence of defilement for one who practices asceticism. Furthermore, Anīgha:

Suppose there is one who practices austerities with a life of purity; because of these austerities, if he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and served by others, he does not confront that śramaṇa or brahmin and say:
"Why do you respect, honor, and serve them?"
You have many desires and many cravings, and you constantly eat; your food consists of five types of seeds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, fruit-seeds, joint-seeds, and seed-seeds.
"Just as a torrential rain causes much damage to the seeds of the five grains and disturbs both livestock and people,
so too it is with those recluses and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others."
"O Ahiṃsaka!

Suppose there is a practitioner of asceticism who practices a life of austerity, and because of this practice of austerity, he sees a śramaṇa or brahmin who is respected, honored, and venerated by others, yet he does not confront that śramaṇa or brahmin and say:
'Why do you respect, honor, and venerate him?'"
You have many desires and many cravings, and you constantly eat; your food consists of five types of seeds: root-seeds, stem-seeds, fruit-seeds, joint-seeds, and seed-seeds.

"Just as a torrential rain causes much damage to the seeds of the five grains and disturbs both livestock and people, so too it is with those recluses and brahmins who frequently enter the homes of others. Thus it is said, O Aṅgīrasa!
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. "Furthermore, Anīgha!

There may be one who practices the asceticism of a pure and austere practitioner; because of this practice of pure and austere asceticism, he does not experience sorrow, delusion, or terror; he does not engage in secret conduct out of fear; he does not doubt or fear the loss of his reputation; and he does not increase his pursuit of gain or negligence."
"O Aṅgulimāla!

If there is one who practices austerities as a practitioner of asceticism, and because of these austerities does not become distressed, deluded, or terrified; does not engage in secret conduct out of fear; does not doubt or fear the loss of reputation; and does not increase his pursuit of sensory objects or negligence—this, O Aṅgulimāla, is called [true austerity]."
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. "Furthermore, Anīgha!

There may be one who practices the ascetic practice of purification; because of this ascetic practice of purification, he does not give rise to the view of a self, the view of extremes, wrong views, or dogmatic clinging to views, nor does he find it difficult to act. His mind is without limitation, and he masters those teachings that are accessible to other recluses and brahmins.
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a practitioner of pure asceticism who, by virtue of that practice of pure asceticism, does not give rise to the view of a self, the view of extremes, wrong views, or adherence to views; who does not find it difficult to practice, whose mind is without limitation, and who masters those teachings that are accessible to other recluses and brahmins—this, O Aṅgulimāla, is what is called [true asceticism]."
One who practices asceticism is free from impurity.

Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla, there may be one who practices the ascetic practice of purification; because of this ascetic practice of purification, he is free from the obsession of anger, the fetter of resentment, stinginess, envy, flattery, deceit, guile, lack of shame, and lack of dread of wrongdoing.
"O Aṅgulimāla!

Suppose there is a practitioner of pure asceticism who, by means of that practice of pure asceticism, is free from anger, obsession, the fetter of silence, stinginess, envy, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, and lack of dread of blame. This, O Aṅgulimāla, is what is called [the true practitioner]."
One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. "Furthermore, Anīgha!

There may be someone who practices pure asceticism; by virtue of that pure ascetic practice, they do not engage in false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, or frivolous chatter, nor do they possess immoral conduct."
"Anavatapta!

Suppose there is one who practices the ascetic life of a practitioner of austerities, and because of this practice of the ascetic life of a practitioner of austerities, he does not engage in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or frivolous speech, yet does not possess the precepts of evil conduct—this, Anavatapta, is what is called [the first]."
"One who practices asceticism is free from defilement. Furthermore, Anīgha!

There may be one who practices the ascetic practice of purification; because of this ascetic practice of purification, he is without lack of faith or indolence, possesses right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and is without evil wisdom."
"O Aṅgīrasa!

If there is one who practices the ascetic practice of austerity, and because of this ascetic practice of austerity, he is without lack of faith or indolence, possesses right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and is without evil wisdom—this, O Aṅgīrasa, is what is called [the true practitioner]."
One who practices asceticism is without defilement and without ill will!
Have I not taught you that this practice, which is incomplete and loathsome, is not defiled by immeasurable impurities?
The wanderer Aśoka replied, “It is so.
Gautama, you have explained to me this practice that is complete yet not fully understood and is loathsome, which is nevertheless not defiled by immeasurable impurities.”
The wanderer Aśoka asked: “Gautama!
Is this practice of incomprehensible and loathsome conduct the attainment of the foremost, the attainment of the truth?”
The Blessed One replied:
“Aṅgulimāla! This practice of the uncomprehending and the loathsome does not attain the foremost, nor does it attain the truth.”
"However, there are two kinds: those who have attained the skin and those who have attained the joints.
The heterodox teacher Aśvatthāman asked again: "Gautama!"
"How is it, Unchāṭa, that one who practices what is disagreeable and unpleasant attains the outer bark?
The Blessed One replied: "Unchāṭa!"

In this regard, there may be a certain śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four courses of conduct: he does not kill, does not incite others to kill, and does not approve of killing; he does not steal, does not incite others to steal, and does not approve of stealing; he does not take another’s wife, does not incite others to take another’s wife, and does not approve of taking another’s wife; he does not speak falsely, does not incite others to speak falsely, and does not approve of false speech.

Practicing these four modes of conduct, he dwells having attained the state of being joyful yet not progressing further; his mind, accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervades one direction and dwells there having achieved it.

Likewise, he dwells having achieved it as he pervades the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir—everywhere all around, his mind accompanied by loving-kindness, free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention; extremely vast, exceedingly great, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, it pervades the entire world and dwells there having achieved it.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, joy, and equanimity—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
"O Aṅgulimāla! What do you think?
Can such an uncomprehending and loathsome conduct obtain even the outer bark?"
Ametta replied: “Gautama!
In this way, one who practices such incomprehensible and loathsome conduct obtains only the outer bark.”
"Gautama!
How can this uncomprehending and loathsome conduct attain moderation?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Without ill will! There may be a certain śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four courses of conduct: he does not kill, does not incite others to kill, and does not approve of killing; he does not steal, does not incite others to steal, and does not approve of stealing; he does not take another’s wife, does not incite others to take another’s wife, and does not approve of taking another’s wife; he does not speak falsely, does not incite others to speak falsely, and does not approve of speaking falsely.”

Practicing these four modes of conduct, he delights in them and does not progress further; yet, possessing such practice and its characteristics, he recollects his immeasurable past experiences—whether one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births, an eon of formation, an eon of destruction, or immeasurable eons of both formation and destruction.

"Those beings were named so-and-so; I have previously experienced them, having been born there with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of stay, and such a lifespan until its end. From here I died and was reborn there; from there I died and was reborn here. I am now born here with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of stay, and such a lifespan until its end."
"O Aśvatthāman! What do you think?
Can such an uncomprehending and loathsome conduct ever reach its limit?"
Aṅgulimāla replied: “Gautama,
it is thus that this practice of the loathsome, when not fully understood, attains its limit.”
"Gautama!
How can this incomprehensible and loathsome practice attain the foremost state and attain reality?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Without ill will! There may be a certain śramaṇa or brahmin who practices four courses of conduct: he does not kill living beings, does not incite others to kill, and does not participate in killing; he does not steal, does not incite others to steal, and does not participate in stealing; he does not take another’s wife, does not incite others to take another’s wife, and does not participate in taking another’s wife; he does not speak falsely, does not incite others to speak falsely, and does not participate in false speech.”
Practicing these four modes of conduct, he delights in them and does not progress further.

With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he sees beings as they die and are reborn—of beautiful or ugly appearance, excellent or inferior, passing away from or being born into good or bad destinations—seeing, according to reality, how these beings fare in accordance with their own karma.

If these sentient beings accomplish evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; revile the noble ones; hold wrong views and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and possess right view and perform deeds of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
"O Aśvattha! What do you think?
Can such an incomprehensible and loathsome practice attain the foremost state or the truth?"
Araṇemi replied: “Gautama!
In this way, this uncomprehending and loathsome practice attains the foremost and the true.”
"Gautama!

Why is it that, because they have not realized and witnessed this practice which is uncomprehended and loathsome, do the disciples of the ascetic Gautama rely on the ascetic life to practice the holy life?
The Blessed One replied:
“Ānanda! It is not because of the realization of the practice of the ‘unrepulsive’ that my disciples practice the holy life under me. Ānanda!”
"Furthermore, there is something else that is most supreme, most wonderful, and most excellent; for the sake of realizing that, my disciples practice the holy life under me.
Thereupon, the groups of heterodox wanderers, agitated and confused, raised a great clamor:
"So it is, so it is! For the sake of realizing that very thing, the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama."
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Aśvatthāman commanded his own assembly to be silent, and having done so, he addressed [the Buddha], saying:

“Gautama! What else is there that is more distinct, most supreme, most wonderful, and most excellent, for the sake of which the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama rely upon the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the holy life?”
Thereupon, the Blessed One replied: “Aṅgīrasa!

When a Tathāgata—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One—appears in the world, he abandons the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and, free from desire and free from evil, unwholesome states, he attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.”

Having thus attained such concentration of mind—purified, stainless, and untroubled; supple, well-established, and immovable—he proceeds toward the realization of the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows.

He knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. He also knows these taints, the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Anuruddha!
This is called something further, more excellent, more sublime, and more supreme; for the sake of realizing that, my disciples practice the holy life in dependence upon me."
Thereupon, the householder Saccaka said: "Aṅgulimāla!
The Blessed One is here;
you may now silence him with a single argument, like one emptying an empty jar, or like speaking to a blind ox grazing in a remote land."
Having heard this, the Blessed One said to the wanderer Acelaka Akkosaka:
"Is it true that you speak thus?
The wanderer Acelaka Akkosaka replied:
"It is indeed so, Gautama!
The Blessed One asked again:
"Aṅgulimāla!"

Have you ever heard from elder teachers of the past that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, when staying in secluded places such as mountain forests, at the foot of trees, or on high cliffs—silent and soundless, remote and free from evil, devoid of human habitation—would dwell there in accordance with the practice of meditative seclusion?

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwell in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and trees, or on high cliffs—in silence and stillness, far removed from noise, free from evil, and devoid of people, sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.
Dwelling in seclusion, he always delights in sitting in meditation, peaceful and happy; he has never for even a single day or night gathered in assembly like you today with your retinue.
The wanderer Acelaka replied: “Gautama! I have heard this from the elders of my own ancient school:

‘In the past, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha was in a secluded place—whether in the mountains, forests, or at the foot of a tree, or perhaps on a high cliff, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people—he would dwell there in accordance with the practice of meditative seclusion.’”

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, dwell in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees, or staying on high cliffs—in silence and stillness, far removed from noise, free from evil, and devoid of people, sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.
Dwelling in seclusion, he always delights in sitting in meditation, living in peace and happiness; he has never for even a single day or night gathered in assembly like I do today with my retinue.

“Anīgha! You do not entertain such thoughts as those of the Blessed One when he stays in a secluded place, in the mountains and forests, or beneath trees, or dwells upon high crags—silent, free from noise, remote, without evil, and uninhabited by people—sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma.”
"Does that ascetic Gautama, who dwells in seclusion and always delights in sitting in meditation, living in peace and happiness, study the path to perfect enlightenment?
The heterodox teacher Aśvajit replied, "Gautama!"

If I had known this, on what basis would I have made such statements as: "The doctrine is extinguished in a single debate, like handling an empty jar," or "The blind ox is grazing in the borderlands"?
The Blessed One said: "Aṅgirimā!
I now possess a Dharma that is well-accorded with what is wholesome; I am able to realize various phrases of liberation. On account of this, the Tathāgata declares himself to be fearless."

"O bhikṣus, when my disciples come to me, they are free from flattery and deceit; they are upright and sincere, without falsehood. Once I have instructed and taught them accordingly, they will surely attain ultimate knowledge."
"Without ill will!
If you should think:
'The ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma out of attachment to his teacher.'"
"Do not think thus; I shall return the teacher to you and preach the Dharma for you.
Without anger!
If you think thus:"
"Do not harbor such a thought as: 'The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma out of greed for disciples. Return your disciples to me; I shall preach the Dharma for you."
"O Aśvatthāman! If you should think:
'The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma for the sake of seeking offerings.'"
"Do not think thus; I shall return your offerings to you and will instead preach the Dharma for you.
Without anger!
If you should think thus:"
"Do not harbor such a thought as: 'The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma for the sake of seeking praise.
Let praise return to you; I shall preach the Dharma for your sake."
"Without ill will!
If you should think thus:
'If I possess a doctrine that is well-aligned with what is wholesome, and if I am able to realize various points of liberation, then that ascetic Gautama would be one who robs me and destroys me.'"
"Do not harbor such thoughts; I shall restore the Dharma to you and preach the Dharma for you.
Thereupon, the great assembly remained silent.
Why is that? Because he was held under the control of the Māra King.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the householder Sārthavāha, saying:
"Behold this great assembly standing in silence. Why is this?
It is because they have been constrained by the King of Māra."
He ensured that not a single member of the assembly of heterodox teachers would think:
"I shall test my practice of the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama.

Having understood this, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the householder Saccaka, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Using countless skillful means, he taught the Dharma to him until he was exhorted, inspired, and filled with joy. Then, rising from his seat, he took the householder Saccaka by the arm and, soaring through the air by means of his supernormal power, departed.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the householder Sāti rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The eighth *Udumbarasīha-sutta* ends here, totaling five thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight characters. 105. *Praṇidhāna-sutta* (105), *Madhyama Āgama*, Section on Causes (*Nidāna-varga*), the ninth *Praṇidhāna-sutta*. Recited in the second sub-section of the Small Earth-City (*Kṣudrakagrāma*). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, dwelling in seclusion and solitude, living in a quiet place, sat in meditation and reflection, and this thought arose in his mind:

“The World-Honored One has consoled me with conversation and taught me the Dharma; I have obtained full ordination without abandoning meditation, and I have accomplished the practice of contemplation in this empty and quiet place.”
Thereupon, having formed this thought, the bhikṣu rose from his meditation in the late afternoon and went to where the Buddha was.
Seeing that bhikṣu coming from afar, the World-Honored One, on account of him, addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should wish that the World-Honored One might greet me with kind words, preach the Dharma for me, and enable me to receive full ordination without abandoning my meditative concentration, so that I may accomplish the practice of contemplation in a secluded and quiet place."
"Monks! You should wish:

'May I have kinsmen who, because of me, upon the dissolution of the body after death, shall surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens; may they receive the full precepts without abandoning meditation, and achieve contemplative practice in empty and quiet places.'"

"Monks! You should make this aspiration: 'May all those who give me robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the various requisites for life, find great merit and great radiance in their giving, obtain a great reward, and, having attained the full precepts, not neglect meditation, but achieve contemplative practice in empty and quiet places.'"
“Monks! You should resolve:

‘May I be able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the afflictions of wind and sun; may I also endure harsh words and the striking of sticks and staves. When my body encounters various illnesses that cause extreme pain, even to the point where life is about to cease, may I be able to withstand all such unpleasant things. Having attained the full precepts, may I not abandon meditation, but achieve contemplative practice in empty and quiet places.’”
"Monks! You should aspire thus:

'May I be able to endure what is unpleasant; if the unpleasant arises, may my mind never be attached to it; having attained the full precepts, may I not abandon meditation, and may I accomplish the practice of contemplation in empty and quiet places.'"
"Monks! You should resolve:

'May I be able to endure fear; if fear should arise, may my mind never be attached to it; may I attain the full precepts without abandoning meditation, and may I accomplish the practice of contemplation in empty and quiet places.'"
"Monks! You should resolve:

'If I should give rise to the three evil and unwholesome thoughts—thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness—may my mind never become attached to these three evil and unwholesome thoughts; may I be fully endowed with the precepts, not abandon meditative concentration, and achieve the practice of contemplation in a secluded and quiet place.'"
“Monks! You should aspire thus:

‘May I be free from sensual desires and free from evil, unwholesome states, up to attaining and dwelling in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; may I possess the full precepts without abandoning dhyāna, and may I achieve the practice of contemplation in a secluded and quiet place.’”
"Monks! You should resolve:

'May my three fetters be exhausted, and may I attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), no longer falling into states of woe, destined for full awakening, and experiencing at most seven more existences; having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human world, may I then reach the end of suffering. May I obtain the complete precepts without abandoning meditation, and may I achieve the practice of insight in empty and quiet places.'"

"Monks! You should wish: 'May my three fetters be exhausted; may lust, anger, and delusion be attenuated; may I attain the state of a once-returner to the heavens and the human realm; having returned once more, may I then reach the end of suffering; may I possess the full precepts without abandoning meditation, and may I accomplish the practice of contemplation in empty and quiet places.'"
"Monks! You should wish:

'May my five lower fetters be exhausted; may I be born in that realm and there attain parinirvāṇa, attaining the state of non-retrogression and not returning to this world, having received full ordination without abandoning meditation, and accomplishing contemplative practice in empty and quiet places.'"

“Monks! You should wish: ‘May I be at peace and liberated; having transcended form, may I attain the formless; may I dwell having realized with my own body the meditative attainment corresponding to that state; and through wisdom, may I contemplate and sever the taints, knowing the taints. Thus, having attained the complete precepts, you should not neglect meditation, but should accomplish the practice of contemplation in empty and quiet places.”
"Monks! You should aspire:

'May I attain the power of psychic transformation, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; may my taints be exhausted so that I attain the taintless state, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing and realizing for myself in this very life, attaining through personal experience and dwelling therein: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is; may I obtain full ordination without abandoning meditation, and achieve contemplative practice in a secluded and quiet place.'"

Thereupon, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu received and retained it well; he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Having received this instruction from the Buddha, that bhikṣu dwelt in seclusion and quietude, sat in meditation and reflection, practiced with diligence, and was without negligence of mind.

Because he dwelt in seclusion and quietude, sat in meditation and reflection, practiced with diligence, and was without negligence of mind, he—like a son of noble family who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Way—brought the unsurpassed holy life to its conclusion. In this very life, he knew it for himself, realized it for himself, and attained realization through his own effort, dwelling therein: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
Having understood the Dharma, that venerable one attained the state of an Arhat.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Praṇidhāna-sūtra*, the ninety-sixth, ends here; it contains eight hundred and sixty-five characters. 106. The *Saṃjñā-sūtra* (106), the tenth discourse in the *Hetu-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, recited in the second section on the Small Earth City (*Kṣudrakagrāmaka*). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who perceive earth as earth, and think: 'Earth is the self; the self is in earth; the self is in the earth,' and having thus reckoned that earth is the self, they do not truly know earth."
Likewise regarding water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, Avṛha, and Atapa. They perceive purity as pure;

purity is the self (*ātman*), purity is what belongs to the self, and the self is what belongs to purity. Having reckoned that purity is the self, they do not know purity—the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; nor do they know the one, the distinct, the manifold, what is seen, heard, sensed, and known, or the attainment of observing what the mind intends and what the mind contemplates.

From this world to that world, and from that world to this world, he conceives of everything as being everything; everything is the self (*ātman*), everything is the domain of the self, and the self is the domain of everything. Having reckoned that everything is the self, he does not know everything.

“If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who, regarding the earth, knows the earth as it is: ‘The earth is not the self; the earth is not the locus of the self; the self is not the locus of the earth. Having ceased to reckon that the earth is the self, he then knows the earth.”
In this same way, regarding water, fire, wind, the spirits, the devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, Avṛha, and Atapa:
one knows that what is pure is pure; yet purity is not the self, purity does not belong to the self, and the self does not belong to purity.

Having no longer reckoned that purity is the self, he then knows purity: the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; as one, as distinct, as manifold; as seen, heard, sensed, and known; and he attains contemplation of what the mind intends and what the mind thinks.

From this world to that world, and from that world to this world, he knows everything regarding all things. Nothing is the self; nothing belongs to the self; the self does not belong to anything. Having ceased to reckon that "everything is the self," he then knows everything.
“I know earth as earth: earth is not the self, earth is not the locus of the self, and the self is not the locus of earth. Having no longer reckoned that earth is the self, I then know earth.”
In this same way, regarding water, fire, wind, spirits, devas, Prajāpati, Brahmā, Avṛha, and Atapa:
when it is pure, I know it as pure; yet purity is not the self, purity does not belong to the self, and the self does not belong to purity.

I do not reckon that purity itself is the self; rather, having known purity, I then know the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—whether singular, distinct, manifold, seen, heard, cognized, or known—and I attain the contemplation of what the mind intends and what the mind contemplates.

From this world to that world, and from that world to this world, I know all regarding everything; nothing is the self, nothing belongs to the self, and the self does not belong to anything. Having realized that "everything is the self" is not the case, I have come to know all things.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The tenth *Saṃjñā-sūtra* ends here, totaling five hundred and twenty-six characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 26, totaling eight thousand nine hundred and seventy-nine characters; the fourth chapter, the "Nidāna-varga," ends here, totaling twenty-five thousand five hundred and fifty-six characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 27.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Section 5: The Forest Chapter (Vana-varga). This fifth chapter contains ten sūtras; it belongs to the second recitation section, the Minor Earth-City (Kṣudra-kṣudraka).
Two Forests, Contemplating the Mind (2) Datta, Nūpura, Dharmapāla, Udāyin, Madhupindika, Gautamī at the end.
107 The Forest Discourse (107), Saṃyukta Āgama, Forest Chapter, First: The Forest Discourse. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus, there is a certain grove where a bhikṣu dwells; I too dwell in this grove.

Therein, if one lacks right mindfulness, one regains right mindfulness; if the mind is undisciplined, one attains concentration; if one is not yet liberated, one attains liberation; if the outflows are not yet exhausted, one attains the exhaustion of outflows; and if one has not yet attained the unsurpassed peace of Nirvāṇa, one attains Nirvāṇa."

Whatever requisites for one practicing the Path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these can be sought out and obtained with ease, without difficulty.

That bhikṣu dwells depending on this forest; having dwelt depending on this forest, if he lacks right mindfulness, he does not attain right mindfulness; if his mind is undisciplined, he does not attain a disciplined mind; if he is not liberated, he does not attain liberation; if his outflows are not exhausted, he does not attain the exhaustion of outflows; and if he has not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa*, he does not attain *nirvāṇa*.

However, whatever requisites for one training on the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these he seeks and obtains easily, without difficulty.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I have left the household life to study the Path not for the sake of clothing, nor for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites, nor for the sake of any other articles of livelihood."

However, while I dwell in this forest, if I am without right mindfulness and do not attain right mindfulness; if my mind is undisciplined and do not attain a concentrated mind; if I am not liberated and do not attain liberation; if my taints are not exhausted and do not attain the exhaustion of taints;

and if I do not attain unsurpassed, secure Nirvana, yet fail to attain Nirvana—nevertheless, whatever requisites for one training on the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of life—I seek them all and obtain them easily, without difficulty.
“Having observed this, that bhikṣu may abandon this forest and depart.

A bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a certain forest; I dwell in dependence upon this forest. There, one who lacks right mindfulness attains right mindfulness; one whose mind is undisciplined attains a concentrated mind; one who is not yet liberated attains liberation; one whose outflows are not yet exhausted attains the exhaustion of outflows; and one who has not attained the unsurpassed peace of Nirvāṇa attains Nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for the life of a seeker of the Way are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these are sought and obtained with ease and without difficulty.”

That bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon this forest. Having dwelt in dependence upon this forest, he who lacked right mindfulness regains right mindfulness; his mind, which was undisciplined, attains concentration; if he had not attained liberation, he now attains liberation; his outflows, which were not yet exhausted, become exhausted; and if he had not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa*, he now attains *nirvāṇa*.

However, whatever requisites for the life of a seeker of the path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and other articles of daily life—he seeks them all, they are very difficult to obtain.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I have left the household life to study the Path not for the sake of clothing, nor for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites, nor even for the sake of various articles of daily life."

Yet, while dwelling in this forest, those who lack right mindfulness attain it; those whose minds are undisciplined attain concentration; those who are not yet liberated attain liberation; those whose taints are not yet exhausted attain the exhaustion of taints; and those who have not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa* attain *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for a seeker of the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these are extremely difficult to obtain when sought after here.
"Having observed this, that bhikṣu may dwell in this forest. A bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a certain forest; I too dwell in dependence upon this forest.

There, one who lacks right mindfulness attains right mindfulness; one whose mind is undisciplined attains a concentrated mind; one who is not liberated attains liberation; one whose taints are not exhausted attains the exhaustion of taints; and one who has not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa* attains *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for the life of a seeker of the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all other articles of daily life—all these can be sought and obtained there without difficulty."

That bhikṣu dwells relying upon this forest; having dwelt relying upon this forest, he may lack right mindfulness and fail to attain right mindfulness, his mind may be undisciplined and fail to attain concentration, he may be unliberated and fail to attain liberation, his taints may not be exhausted and fail to reach their exhaustion, and he may not attain unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa.
Yet they do not attain nirvāṇa;

and as for the robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all other articles of daily life required by those who study the Path, it is extremely difficult to obtain them all through seeking.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way: "I dwell in dependence upon this forest;

yet, lacking right mindfulness, I do not attain right mindfulness; with a mind that is undisciplined, I do not attain concentration; being unliberated, I do not attain liberation; with outflows that are not exhausted, I do not attain the exhaustion of outflows; and I do not attain unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, the requisites for one training on the path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—that I seek after them all are extremely difficult to obtain."
“Having observed this, that bhikṣu immediately leaves that grove and departs at midnight, without taking leave of them.

‘A bhikṣu dwells in dependence on a certain grove; I dwell in dependence on this grove. There, one who lacks right mindfulness regains right mindfulness; one whose mind is undisciplined attains a concentrated mind; one who is not yet liberated attains liberation; one whose outflows are not yet exhausted attains the exhaustion of outflows; and one who has not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa* attains *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for a seeker of the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these can be sought and obtained there easily and without difficulty.’”

That bhikṣu dwells relying upon this forest; having dwelt relying upon this forest, he who lacked right mindfulness attains right mindfulness, his unconcentrated mind attains concentration, and if he was not yet liberated, he attains liberation. His outflows that were not yet exhausted become exhausted, and if he had not attained the unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa*, he attains *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for the life of a seeker of the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these he seeks and obtains easily and without difficulty.
That bhikṣu should reflect thus: "I dwell in dependence upon this forest;

if my mindfulness is absent, I shall regain it; if my mind is undisciplined, I shall attain concentration; if I am not liberated, I shall attain liberation; if my outflows are not exhausted, I shall attain the exhaustion of outflows; and if I have not attained the unsurpassed peace of Nirvāṇa, I shall attain it.

Furthermore, whatever requisites for the life of a seeker of the Way are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these can be sought and obtained with ease and without difficulty."

Having observed in this way, that bhikṣu dwells relying upon this forest, remaining there for his entire life until the end of his natural span. Just as he dwells relying upon the forest, so too does he dwell relying upon cemeteries, villages, towns, or people.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first *Vana Sūtra* ends here, totaling one thousand one hundred and sixty-five characters. 108. *Vana Sūtra* (108), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Forests, *Vana Sūtra*, Second [in this section], Recited at the Lesser Earth City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Bhikṣus, there is a certain grove where a bhikṣu dwells; I too dwell in this grove. Whatever it is for which one has gone forth to train in the Way—desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa—that goal has been attained by me. Furthermore, whatever requisites for life a practitioner of the Way requires—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these are sought after and obtained without difficulty.”

That bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon this forest. Having dwelt in dependence upon this forest, he does not attain that goal for which he has gone forth and studied the path—the state of a śramaṇa—and yet all the requisites for one who studies the path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for use in sickness, and other articles of daily life—are easily obtained by him without difficulty.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I have left the household life to study the Path not for the sake of clothing, nor for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites, nor even for the sake of any other articles of livelihood."

Yet, although I dwell in this forest for the sake of having gone forth to study the Way and desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa, I have not attained that goal. As for the requisites required by one who studies the Way—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of daily life—all these are sought and obtained with ease and without difficulty.
“Having observed this, that bhikṣu may abandon this forest and depart.

‘A bhikṣu dwells in dependence on a certain forest; I dwell in dependence on this forest. Whatever it was for which I went forth and studied the Path—desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa—that goal has been attained by me. Furthermore, the requisites required by one who studies the Path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these are sought after and obtained without difficulty.’”

That bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon this forest; having so dwelt, that which he has set out for by going forth and training in the way—the attainment of the goal of a śramaṇa—that goal is attained by him. Yet, whatever requisites for life a seeker of the way requires—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for the sick, and all such articles—he finds it very difficult to obtain them all through seeking.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I have left the household life to study the Path not for the sake of clothing, nor for the sake of food and drink, bedding, or medicinal requisites, nor even for the sake of any other articles of livelihood."

However, it is for this forest that I dwell, having gone forth to train in the path and desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa; yet this goal has not been attained by me. Furthermore, whatever requisites for one training in the path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine for illness, and all other articles of daily life—all these are extremely difficult to obtain when sought after.
“Having observed this, that bhikkhu may dwell in this forest. A bhikkhu dwells in dependence on a certain forest;

I too dwell in dependence on this forest. Whatever purpose for which one goes forth and trains in the path—desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa—that goal has been attained by me. Furthermore, the requisites required by one who trains in the path—robes, almsfood, bedding, medicinal requisites for use in sickness, and all other articles of daily life—all these are sought out and easily obtained without difficulty.”

That bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon this forest; having so dwelt, he fails to attain that goal for which he went forth and studied the path—the state of a śramaṇa—and all the requisites required by one who studies the path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and various articles of daily life—all these he seeks in vain and finds very difficult to obtain.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I dwell in reliance upon this forest for the purpose of going forth and training in the path, desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa; yet I have not attained this goal. Furthermore, the requisites required by one who trains in the path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all such articles of livelihood—all these I seek with great difficulty and find hard to obtain."
“Having observed this, that bhikṣu immediately leaves that forest and departs at midnight without taking leave of anyone. A bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a certain forest, thinking:

‘I dwell in dependence upon this forest; whatever it was for which I went forth and studied the Path—desiring to attain the state of a śramaṇa—that goal has been attained by me. Furthermore, the requisites required by one who studies the Path—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these are sought out and obtained with ease, without difficulty.’”

That bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon this forest; having so dwelt, he attains that goal for which he went forth and trained in the holy life—the state of a śramaṇa—and he obtains all the requisites for the life of one who trains: robes, almsfood, bedding, medicinal requisites for use in sickness, and all other articles of daily life, seeking them out with ease and without difficulty.
That bhikṣu should reflect in this way:

"I dwell in dependence upon this forest; for the sake of that for which I have gone forth and studied the Path—desiring to attain the goal of a śramaṇa—that goal has been attained by me. Whatever requisites for the life of one who studies the Path are required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all other articles of livelihood—all these can be sought after and obtained without difficulty."

Having made this observation, that bhikṣu dwells relying upon this forest, remaining there for the rest of his life until his end. Just as it is with dwelling in reliance on a forest, so it is likewise with dwelling among cemeteries, in villages, or in reliance upon human habitation.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The second discourse of the *Vana-vagga*, the *Vana-sutta*, ends here, totaling eight hundred and thirty-one characters. 109. The Discourse on Observing One’s Own Mind (109) The Third Discourse of the *Vana-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, recited in the Second Minor Earth-City Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is unable to skillfully observe the minds of others, he should skillfully observe his own mind; in this way, he should train."
How does a bhikṣu skillfully observe his own mind?
A bhikṣu who possesses this reflection will certainly find great benefit:
"Have I attained internal tranquility, yet failed to attain the supreme dharma of insight?"
Is it that because I have not attained the dharma of supreme insight (vipaśyanā), I cannot attain internal tranquility (śamatha)?
Or is it that because I have not attained internal tranquility, I also cannot attain the dharma of supreme insight?
"Have I attained internal tranquility, and have I also attained the supreme method of insight (vipaśyanā)?

If, after examining himself, a bhikṣu knows, "I have attained internal tranquility, but I have not attained the supreme method of insight," then that bhikṣu, having attained internal tranquility, should seek the supreme method of insight. At a later time, he will attain both internal tranquility and the supreme method of insight.

If a bhikkhu, having investigated, knows: "I have attained the supreme dharma of insight (vipassanā), but I have not attained internal tranquility (samatha)," then that bhikkhu, having established himself in the supreme dharma of insight, should seek internal tranquility; at a later time, he will attain both the supreme dharma of insight and internal tranquility.

If a bhikṣu, having observed this, knows: "I have not attained internal tranquility, nor have I attained the supreme insight into the Dharma," then that bhikṣu, failing to attain these wholesome qualities, desires to obtain them; he therefore swiftly seeks skillful means, trains with extreme diligence, maintains right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endures without allowing himself to regress.
It is just as if a person whose head or clothing were on fire would urgently seek means to save their head or clothing.

In the same way, a bhikkhu who has not yet attained these wholesome qualities, desiring to attain them, quickly seeks means to do so; he trains with extreme diligence, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, enduring without allowing himself to regress. At a later time, he attains internal tranquility and also attains the supreme method of insight through wisdom.

If a bhikṣu, having observed thus, knows: "I have attained internal tranquility and have also attained the supreme method of insight through wisdom," then that bhikṣu, established in these wholesome qualities, should seek to realize the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Why is this? I say that one may not possess all types of robes, yet I also say that one may possess all types of robes.
What kind of robes do I say one may not possess?
If the possession of robes leads to the increase of unwholesome and non-virtuous states and the decline of wholesome states, such robes I say one must not possess.
What kind of robes do I say one may possess?
If by keeping a robe one increases wholesome qualities and causes unwholesome, evil qualities to decline, such a robe I say may be kept.
As it is with robes, so it is with food and drink, beds and seats, and villages and towns; I say that one should not associate with all people, yet I also say that one may associate with all people.
Who is the person whom I say one should not associate with?
If associating with a person causes unwholesome and evil states to increase and wholesome states to decline, such a person I say one should not associate with.
Who is the person with whom I say one may associate?
If, by associating with a person, one increases wholesome qualities and causes unwholesome and evil qualities to decline, such a person is one with whom I say one may associate.
“He understands, as they truly are, the dharmas that should be practiced and the dharmas that should not be practiced.

Having understood, as they truly are, the dharmas that should be practiced and those that should not be practiced, he does not practice those dharmas that should not be practiced, and he practices those dharmas that should be practiced. Once he has ceased practicing what should not be practiced and is practicing what should be practiced, wholesome dharmas increase and unwholesome, evil dharmas decline.”
"This is what is meant by a bhikṣu who skillfully observes his own mind, skillfully knows his own mind, and skillfully adopts and abandons.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Third Discourse on Contemplating the Mind, totaling six hundred and thirty-five characters, ends here. 110. The Discourse on Contemplating the Mind (110), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on the Forest (*Vana-vagga*), the Fourth Discourse on Contemplating the Mind, recited by the Second Small Earth-City School. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who cannot skillfully observe the minds of others, he should skillfully observe his own mind; he ought to train himself in this way."
How does a bhikṣu skillfully observe his own mind?
A bhikṣu who possesses this reflection will certainly find much benefit:
"Do I frequently practice with increased covetousness, or do I frequently practice without increased covetousness?"
Do I frequently practice a mind of ill will, or do I frequently practice a mind free from ill will?
Do I frequently practice the entanglement of sloth and torpor, or do I frequently practice freedom from the entanglement of sloth and torpor?
Do I frequently practice arrogance, or do I frequently practice the absence of arrogance?
Do I frequently practice doubt, or do I frequently practice the absence of doubt?
Do I frequently engage in bodily strife, or do I frequently refrain from bodily strife?
Do I frequently engage in a defiled mind, or do I frequently engage in an undefiled mind?
"Do I practice faith more frequently, or do I practice lack of faith more frequently?
Do I practice diligence more frequently, or do I practice indolence more frequently?
Do I practice mindfulness more frequently, or do I practice lack of mindfulness more frequently?"
"Do I practice much concentration, or do I practice much lack of concentration?
Do I practice much unwholesome wisdom, or do I practice much wholesome wisdom?

When a bhikkhu examines himself in this way, if he knows: "I practice much covetousness, ill will, the fetter of sloth and torpor, restlessness and haughtiness, doubt, bodily agitation, a defiled mind, lack of faith, laziness, lack of mindfulness, lack of concentration, and I practice much unwholesome wisdom," then that bhikkhu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, quickly seeks out the means, trains with extreme diligence, maintains right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endures without retreating.
It is just as when a person’s head or clothing is set on fire, they urgently seek means to save their head or clothing.

In the same way, a bhikkhu, desiring to extinguish these evil and unwholesome states, quickly seeks means and trains with extreme diligence, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, enduring so as not to let them persist.

If, when a bhikkhu examines himself, he knows: "I frequently practice without covetousness, without a mind of ill will, without the fetter of sloth and torpor, without restlessness and haughtiness, without doubt, without bodily strife, and without a defiled mind; I possess faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and I frequently practice without unwholesome wisdom."
Once that bhikṣu has established himself in these wholesome dharmas, he should seek to realize the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows. Why is this?
Because I have said that one must not possess any robes at all, yet I have also said that one may possess any robes.
What kind of robe do I say one must not possess?
If possessing a robe leads to the increase of evil and unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states, such a robe I say one must not possess.
What kind of robe do I say may be kept?
If by keeping a robe one increases wholesome qualities and causes unwholesome, evil qualities to decline, such a robe I say may be kept.

As it is with clothing, so it is with food and drink, beds and seats, and villages and towns; I say that one should not associate with all people, yet I also say that one may associate with all people.
Who is that person whom I say one should not associate with?
If associating with a person causes unwholesome and evil states to increase and wholesome states to decline, such a person I say one should not associate with.
Who is the person with whom I say one may associate?
If, by associating with a person, one increases wholesome qualities and causes unwholesome, evil qualities to decline—such a person is one with whom I say one may associate.
“He knows, as it truly is, the dharmas that should be cultivated and the dharmas that should not be cultivated.

Having known, as they truly are, the dharmas that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated, he does not cultivate the dharmas that should not be cultivated, and he cultivates the dharmas that should be cultivated. Having ceased to cultivate the dharmas that should not be cultivated and having cultivated the dharmas that should be cultivated, he increases wholesome dharmas and causes unwholesome, evil dharmas to decline.”
"This is called a bhikṣu who skillfully observes his own mind, skillfully knows his own mind, and skillfully adopts and abandons.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Sūtra on Self-Observation of the Mind, the Fourth, ends here with six hundred and sixty characters. 111. The Sūtra on Attaining the Holy Life (111), Madhyama Āgama, Forest Chapter, The Sūtra on Attaining the Holy Life, the Fifth; Recited by the Second Small Earth-City School. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Kurus, staying at the Kuru town of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall preach the Dharma for you—excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both phrasing and meaning, complete and pure, revealing the holy life (brahmacarya). This is called the Dharma that leads to the holy life, which is able to exhaust all outflows (āsrava)."
"Listen attentively, all of you, and reflect well upon it.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The World-Honored One said:

"You should know the taints; you should know the cause from which the taints arise; you should know the retribution of the taints; you should know the excellence of the taints; you should know the cessation of the taints; and you should know the path leading to the cessation of the taints."

You should know feeling, know the cause from which feeling arises, know that feeling has a result, know the excellence of feeling, know the cessation of feeling, and know the path leading to the cessation of feeling.

You should know perception, know the cause from which perception arises, know that perception has a result, know the excellence of perception, know the cessation of perception, and know the path leading to the cessation of perception.

You should know desire; you should know the cause from which desire arises; you should know that desire has a result; you should know the excellence of desire; you should know the cessation of desire; and you should know the path leading to the cessation of desire.

You should all know karma; know the causes from which karma arises; know that karma has its retribution; know the distinctions among karmas; know the cessation of karma; and know the path to the cessation of karma.

You should know suffering; you should know the cause from which suffering arises; you should know that suffering has a retribution; you should know the excellence of suffering; you should know the cessation of suffering; and you should know the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
"How does one know the outflows?
It is said that there are three outflows:
the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance; this is called knowing the outflows."
How does one know the cause from which the outflows arise?
It is ignorance. Because of ignorance, there are outflows; this is called knowing the cause from which the outflows arise.
How does one know that the outflows (āsrava) have retribution?

It is said that for one who is entangled by ignorance (avidyā), being drenched by the various outflows, they consequently receive retribution—either attaining a favorable state or an unfavorable state. This is called knowing that the outflows have retribution.
What is the knowledge of the relative superiority of the outflows (*āsrava*)?

It means that some outflows lead to birth in the hells, some lead to birth among animals, some lead to birth among hungry ghosts, some lead to birth in the heavens, and some lead to birth among humans; this is called the knowledge of the relative superiority of the outflows.
How does one know the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava*)?
It is said that with the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), the outflows cease; this is called knowing the cessation of the outflows.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of the outflows?
This refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration;

this is called knowing the path to the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava*). If a bhikṣu thus knows the outflows, knows the cause by which they arise, knows the retribution received from them, knows their relative superiority, knows their total cessation, and knows the path to their cessation, he is said to have mastered the holy life and is able to exhaust all outflows.
"What is the knowledge of feeling?
It means there are three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; this is called the knowledge of feeling."
How does one know the cause from which perception arises?
It is contact (*sparśa*).
Because of contact, perception then exists; this is what is meant by knowing the cause from which perception arises.
How is it known that feeling has a retribution? It is craving.
Craving is the retribution for feeling; this is what is meant by knowing that feeling has a retribution.

What is the excellence of the knowledge of feelings? It is this: when a bhikṣu feels a pleasant feeling, he knows he feels a pleasant feeling; when he feels a painful feeling, he knows he feels a painful feeling; when he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. He knows a pleasant bodily feeling, a painful bodily feeling, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant bodily feeling; a pleasant mental feeling, a painful mental feeling, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant mental feeling; a pleasant feeling of food, a painful feeling of food, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of food; a pleasant feeling of non-food, a painful feeling of non-food, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of non-food; a pleasant feeling of desire, a painful feeling of desire, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of desire; and when he feels a pleasant feeling of non-desire, a painful feeling of non-desire, or a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of non-desire, he knows he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of non-desire. This is called the excellence of the knowledge of feelings.
How does one know the cessation of feeling?
It is said that with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of feeling.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called the knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of perception.

If a bhikṣu thus knows perception, knows the cause from which perception arises, knows the result of perception, knows the excellence of perception, knows the total cessation of perception, and knows the path leading to the cessation of perception, he is said to have attained the holy life and is able to exhaust all perceptions.
"How does one know perceptions?
It is said that there are four perceptions.

A bhikṣu knows the perception of the small, knows the perception of the great, knows the perception of the immeasurable, and knows the perception of the sphere of nothingness; this is called knowing perceptions."
How does one know the cause from which perception arises?
It is contact (*sparśa*).
Because of contact, there is perception; this is called knowing the cause from which perception arises.
How does one know that perception has a retribution?
It is by means of speech.
One speaks in accordance with that perception; this is called knowing that perception has a retribution.
What is the knowledge of the excellence of perceptions?

It means that there may be a perception that perceives forms, or a perception that perceives sounds, or a perception that perceives odors, or a perception that perceives tastes, or a perception that perceives tangibles; this is called the knowledge of the excellence of perceptions.
How does one know the cessation of perception?
It is said that when contact ceases, perception ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of perception.
How does one know the path to the cessation of perception?
This refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path to the cessation of perception.

If a bhikkhu thus knows perception, knows the cause by which perception arises, knows that perception has a result, knows the excellence of perception, knows the total cessation of perception, and knows the path to the cessation of perception, he is said to have attained the holy life and is able to exhaust all perceptions.
"How does one know desire?
It refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*), which are lovely, delightful, beautiful in form, associated with longing, and exceedingly pleasant."
What are the five?
The eye cognizes forms, the ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes odors, the tongue cognizes tastes, and the body cognizes tangibles; these are called the cognitions of desire.
How does one know the cause from which desire arises?
It is contact (*sparśa*).
Because of contact, there is desire; this is called knowing the cause from which desire arises.
How does one know that sensual desire has a retribution?

It means that according to the seeds of desire, one dwells in attachment and delight; because of this, one receives retribution in the realms of merit, the realms of non-merit, and the immovable realms. This is called knowing that sensual desire has a retribution.
What is the knowledge of the excellence of desire?

It means that there may be a desire for visible forms, or a desire for sounds, or a desire for odors, or a desire for tastes, or a desire for tangibles; this is called the knowledge of the excellence of desire.
How does one know the cessation of desire?
It is said that when contact (*sparśa*) ceases, desire ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of desire.
How does one know the path to the cessation of desire?
This refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view up to right concentration; this is called knowing the path to the cessation of desire.

If a bhikṣu thus knows desire, knows the cause from which desire arises, knows the retribution experienced by desire, knows the excellence of desire, knows the total extinction of desire, and knows the path to the extinction of desire, he is said to have mastered the holy life and is able to exhaust all desires.
"How does one know karma?
It is said that there are two types of karma:
volitional karma (*cetanā*) and karma after having willed (*cetayitvā*); this is what is meant by knowing karma."
How does one know that karma arises from its cause?
It is through contact (*sparśa*).
Because of contact, there is karma; this is called knowing that karma arises from its cause.
How does one know that karma has its retribution? It is said:

there is karma that is black with black retribution; there is karma that is white with white retribution; there is karma that is both black and white with both black and white retribution; and there is karma that is neither black nor white, which is without retribution, whereby all karmas are exhausted. This is called knowing that karma has its retribution.
What is meant by knowing the relative superiority of karma?

It means that there is karma that leads to birth in the hells, or karma that leads to birth among animals, or karma that leads to birth among hungry ghosts, or karma that leads to birth in the heavens, or karma that leads to birth among humans; this is called knowing the relative superiority of karma.
How does one know the cessation of karma?
It means that when contact (*phassa*) ceases, karma ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of karma.
How does one know the path to the cessation of karma?
This refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration; this is called knowing the path to the cessation of karma.

If a bhikṣu thus knows karma, knows the cause from which karma arises, knows that karma has retribution, knows the relative superiority of karmas, knows the total exhaustion of karma, and knows the path to the cessation of karma, he is said to have attained the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and is able to exhaust all karma.
"How does one know suffering?

It is said that birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the beloved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering—this is called knowing suffering."
How does one know the cause from which suffering arises?
It is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Suffering arises because of craving; this is called knowing the cause from which suffering arises.
How does one know that suffering has a retribution?

It is said that some sufferings are subtle and perish slowly; some sufferings are subtle and perish quickly; some sufferings are intense and perish slowly; and some sufferings are intense and perish quickly. When such suffering and its associated pain are exhausted, this is called knowing that suffering has a retribution.
What is the superior understanding of suffering?

It refers to the unlearned, deluded worldling who does not encounter a virtuous friend and does not practice the noble Dharma; when such a person experiences an intense and extremely heavy pain arising in the body, and their life is about to end, they emerge from this state and seek it elsewhere.

There may be certain śramaṇas or brahmins who maintain a single-spelled incantation, or two, three, four, or many-spelled incantations, or they maintain a hundred-spelled incantation; they treat my suffering, thinking: "Thus, suffering arises conditioned by seeking, and suffering arises conditioned by clinging; [now] suffering is extinguished. This is called knowing the excellence regarding suffering.
How does one know the cessation of suffering?
It means that with the cessation of craving, suffering ceases; this is called knowing the cessation of suffering.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
That is to say, the Noble Eightfold Path—consisting of right view through to right concentration as its eight factors—is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
If a bhikṣu thus knows suffering, knows the cause from which suffering arises, knows the retribution of suffering, knows the excellence of suffering, and knows the complete cessation of suffering.
"One who knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering is said to have attained the holy life (brahmacarya) and is able to bring all suffering to an end.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Dharmapada-sūtra*, the fifth, ends here; one thousand six hundred and forty-two characters. 112. The *Anupā-sūtra* (112). *Madhyama Āgama*, Forest Chapter, the *Anupā-sūtra*, the sixth; recited in the second section on Small Earthly Cities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Vajjian country, staying at Anupā, a town of the Vajjis.
At that time, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One rose from his meditation, descended from the hall, and said: "Ānanda,
let us go together to the river Ajiravatī to bathe."
The Venerable Ānanda replied, “So be it.

Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda and went to the river Aciravatī; he removed his robes on the bank, entered the water to bathe, and having bathed, came back out, dried his body, and put on his robes.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was fanning the Buddha with a fan.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One turned his gaze toward him and said: “Ānanda!”
