Because of his negligence, Devadatta has fallen into extreme suffering and hardship; he will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell, where he shall remain for an entire kalpa beyond all rescue.

Ānanda! Have you not heard from the bhikṣus that I have declared categorically that Tiṣya will certainly go to an evil destination, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa without possibility of rescue?
"Very well," the Venerable Ānanda replied.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu said to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Did the Blessed One, by knowing the mind of Dīghāvu with his own mind of others' thoughts, declare categorically that Dīghāvu would certainly go to a state of misery, be born in hell, and remain there for a full aeon without possibility of rescue?"
The World-Honored One said:
“Ānanda! That bhikṣu may be small, medium, or great; or he may be young and unaware of himself.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already given a definitive prediction regarding them, there is doubt. Ānanda!
I do not see anyone in this world—among gods, Māras, Brahmās, ascetics, or brahmins, from humans up to the gods—who could claim that I have given a categorical declaration as Tissa Mātanga has done.
Why is that? Ānanda! I have declared with certainty that Tiṣya will certainly go to an evil destination, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa, beyond all possibility of rescue.

Ānanda! If I had seen even a hair’s breadth of pure, white dharma in Tiṣya-datta, I would not have declared categorically that Tiṣya-datta will certainly go to an evil destination, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa without possibility of rescue.

Ānanda! Since I do not see even a hair’s breadth of pure, white dharma in Tiṣya, I have declared categorically that Tiṣya will certainly go to a state of misery, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa, beyond all possibility of rescue.
“Ānanda! Suppose there were a large, deep latrine not far from a village, and a person had fallen into it and sunk to the bottom.

If someone were to come, moved by great compassion, pitying and taking pity on that person, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace, security, and happiness, and having arrived, were to look around and say this:”
"Can this person find even a single spot the size of a hair's breadth that is not defiled by excrement, so that I may seize him and pull him out?
He searched everywhere but did not see a single pure place the size of a hair's breadth that was not defiled by excrement, from which he could seize him with his hand and pull him out.
In this way, Ānanda!

If I had seen even a single hair’s breadth of pure, white dharma in Tiṣya, I would not have declared categorically that Tiṣya will certainly go to an evil destination, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa without possibility of rescue.

Ānanda! Because I do not see even a hair’s breadth of pure, white dharma in Tiṣya, I have declared categorically that Tiṣya will certainly go to an evil destination, be born in hell, and remain there for an entire kalpa without possibility of rescue.

The eye leaks as it views forms; the ear leaks as it hears sounds; the nose leaks as it smells odors; the tongue leaks as it tastes flavors; the body leaks as it feels tangibles; the mind leaks as it cognizes all phenomena—this is called the abscess of all outflows.

“Monks! I have already taught you the boil and the root of the boil. That which a teacher does for his disciples—arousing great compassion, pitying and sympathizing with them, seeking their welfare and benefit, and seeking their peace and happiness—that I have now done.

The Udāra Sūtra, the eighth, ends here with five hundred and fourteen characters. 115. The Honey Ball Simile Sūtra (115), Madhyama Āgama, Forest Chapter, The Ninth Honey Ball Simile Sūtra, recited in the second sub-section of the Small Earth-City. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas and was staying at Kapilavastu.
At that time, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered Kapilavastu for the purpose of begging for food.

Having finished eating, after midday, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, and went to the Śākya Monastery in the Bamboo Grove. Entering that great forest, he approached a certain tree, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.

Thereupon, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi set aside his staff and proceeded; wandering about after midday, he went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, and stood before the Buddha leaning on his staff, asking the World-Honored One:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"What constitutes its fundamental principle?
What Dharma do you teach?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Śāriputra!

If all the world—including gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans up to the heavens—could be made free from strife, practicing the pure brahma-faring of one who has abandoned desire, relinquishing crookedness, removing regret, and being without attachment to existence or non-existence, nor even with conceptualization;
this is the foundation of my doctrine, and my teaching is likewise."
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi neither approved nor disapproved; he merely shook his head and departed.

Not long after the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi had left, the World-Honored One rose from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon, went to the lecture hall, sat upon a seat prepared before the assembly of bhikṣus, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"This morning, having dressed and taken my bowl for the sake of alms, I entered Kapilavastu."

Having finished his meal, after midday he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, and went to the Śākyas’ Bamboo Grove Monastery. Entering that great forest, he went beneath a tree, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.

Thereupon, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi set aside his staff and walked on; after midday, while wandering about, he came to where I was. After exchanging greetings with one another, he stood before me leaning on his staff and asked me:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!..."
"What is its fundamental principle?
What Dharma does it teach? I replied:
"Śāriputra!

If all those in the world—gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans up to the gods—could be made to cease quarreling, to practice the pure life of a brahmin free from desire, to abandon crookedness and deceit, to eliminate remorse, and to neither cling to existence nor non-existence, nor even to ideation;
this is the foundation of my doctrine, and my teaching is likewise."
“Having heard what I said, that Yaññadatta the Śākya neither approved nor disapproved, but shook his head and departed.
Thereupon, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One! ”
How can all the world—including gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, from humans up to the devas—be made free from strife?
How does one practice the renunciation of desire and attain the purity of a brāhmaṇa?
"How does one abandon crookedness and deceit, eliminate remorse, and neither cling to existence nor non-existence, while remaining free from conceptualization?
The World-Honored One replied, "Monk!..."

If a person, for whatever reason, has gone forth to train in the path, and regarding past, future, and present phenomena, they do not crave, delight in, cling to, or dwell upon them through their reflection and cultivation—this is called the end of suffering. It is the end of the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, the underlying tendency toward ill will, the underlying tendency toward existence, the underlying tendency toward conceit, the underlying tendency toward ignorance, the underlying tendency toward views, the underlying tendency toward doubt; it is the end of strife, contention, malice, envy, flattery, deception, false speech, double-tongued speech, and immeasurable other evil and unwholesome states. This is called the end of suffering.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, he rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in private meditation.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Venerable friends!..."
"You should know that the Blessed One has briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis, and then rose from his seat, entered his room, and sat in quiet meditation:

'If a person, regarding that for which they have left the household life to train in the path—the thoughts and practices, as well as all phenomena of the past, future, and present—does not crave them, does not delight in them, does not cling to them, and does not dwell upon them, this is called the end of suffering.'"

The underlying tendency to sensual desire, the underlying tendency to ill will, the underlying tendency to existence, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to ignorance, the underlying tendency to views, and the underlying tendency to doubt; as well as strife, contention, malice, envy, flattery, deceit, fraud, false speech, and double-tongued speech—along with immeasurable other evil and unwholesome states: this is called the end of suffering.
Then he further thought:
"Venerable friends!
Who among you is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated?"
He further thought to himself:

"The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One and by wise fellow-practitioners; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated."
"Venerable friends!
Let us go together to the Venerable Mahākaccāyana and request him to explain this matter;
if the Venerable Mahākaccāyana analyzes it for us, we shall properly receive and uphold it."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:
"Venerable Mahākātyāyana!"
"You should know that the Blessed One has briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis;
he has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling to sit in private meditation. 'Monks!'"

If a person, for whatever reason they have set out from home to train in the path, contemplates and practices with regard to past, future, and present phenomena, without craving, delighting in, clinging to, or dwelling upon them—this is called the end of suffering.

The underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of existence, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt; as well as strife, contention, malice, envy, flattery, deceit, fraud, false speech, and double-tongued speech, along with immeasurable evil and unwholesome states—this is called the end of suffering.
We then thought to ourselves:
"Venerable friends!
Who among us is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly explained?"
We further thought to ourselves:

"The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One and by wise fellow practitioners of the holy life; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated."
"I only pray that the Venerable Mahākaccāyana will explain this in detail out of compassion.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana addressed them, saying:
"O noble ones!"
Listen to a parable, for the wise understand the meaning upon hearing a parable.
Venerable friends!

Suppose there is a person who desires to seek the heartwood; for the sake of seeking that heartwood, he takes an axe and enters a forest. There he sees a great tree composed of roots, trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit. That person does not touch the roots, the trunk, the joints, or the fruit, but touches only the branches and leaves.
It is just as you have said, worthy ones; while the World-Honored One was present, he left him and came to me to ask about this matter.
Why is that? Worthy ones!

One should know that the Blessed One is the eye, is wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma, is the Lord of Dharma, and is the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of ultimate truth, and it is from him, the Blessed One, that all meanings are revealed.
Virtuous ones, you should go to the Blessed One and inquire about this matter:
"Blessed One, what is this?"
"What is the meaning of this?
As the Blessed One has spoken it, you venerable ones should receive and uphold it well.
Then, the bhikṣus said:
“Certainly, Venerable Mahākaccāna!

The Blessed One is the eye, he is wisdom, he is the meaning, he is the Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, and the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of the truths, and all meanings are manifested by that Blessed One. We should go to where the Blessed One is and ask him about this matter:”
“World-Honored One!
What is this? What is the meaning of this?”
“As the Blessed One has spoken it, we shall properly receive and uphold it.

However, Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One as well as by wise fellow-practitioners; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has briefly stated. We only pray that the Venerable Mahākaccāna will, out of compassion, explain it in detail.”
The Venerable Mahākaccāyana addressed the bhikkhus:
"Virtuous friends, listen together to what I shall say.
Virtuous friends!..."

Conditioned by the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises; the coming together of these three factors constitutes contact. Conditioned by contact, there is feeling; what is felt is perceived as an ideation; what is ideated is intended; what is intended is remembered; and what is remembered is discriminated.

A bhikkhu, for this reason, goes forth to train in the path; through reflection and cultivation, he does not crave, does not delight in, does not cling to, and does not dwell upon any phenomena—past, future, or present. This is called the end of suffering.

The underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of existence, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt; as well as strife, contention, malice, envy, flattery, deceit, fraud, false speech, and double-tonguedness—along with immeasurable other evil and unwholesome states: this is called the end of suffering.

In the same way, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental objects as conditions, mental consciousness arises; the coming together of these three factors constitutes contact. Conditioned by contact, there is feeling; what is felt is perceived; what is perceived is intended; what is intended is thought about; what is thought about is reflected upon; and what is reflected upon is discriminated.

A bhikkhu, for this reason, goes forth to train in the path; through reflection and cultivation, he does not crave, does not delight in, does not cling to, and does not dwell upon past, future, or present phenomena herein—this is called the end of suffering.

The underlying tendency of sensual desire, the underlying tendency of ill will, the underlying tendency of existence, the underlying tendency of conceit, the underlying tendency of ignorance, the underlying tendency of views, and the underlying tendency of doubt; as well as strife, contention, envy, malice, flattery, deceit, false speech, and double-tongued speech, along with immeasurable other evil and unwholesome states—this is called the end of suffering.
"Venerable friends!
For a bhikkhu, apart from the eye, apart from forms, and apart from eye-consciousness, for there to be contact or for the designation 'contact' to exist—that is impossible.
If one does not designate contact, yet designates feeling as existing, this is impossible.
If one does not designate feeling, yet designates mindfulness, renunciation and training in the path, reflection, and cultivation as existing, this is impossible.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, and body—apart from the mind, apart from mental objects, and apart from mental consciousness—it is impossible that there could be contact or the designation of contact. This is not the case.
If one does not designate contact, yet designates feeling as existing, this is impossible.
If one does not designate feeling, yet designates mindfulness, renunciation and training in the path, reflection, and cultivation as existing, this is impossible.
"Venerable friends!

For a bhikkhu, conditioned by the eye, conditioned by forms, and conditioned by eye-consciousness, there is the occurrence of contact; for the designation of 'contact' to occur, this condition must necessarily exist."
Based on the designation of further contact, there must be a basis for the designation of feeling;
based on the designation of feeling, there must be a basis for the designation of mindfulness, the life of renunciation and training in the path, and the cultivation of reflection.

In the same way, for the ear, nose, tongue, and body, conditioned by the mind, conditioned by mental objects, and conditioned by mind-consciousness, there is the occurrence of contact; where there is contact, there must necessarily be this basis.
Based on the designation of renewed contact, there must be a basis for the designation of feeling;
based on the designation of feeling, there must be a basis for the designation of mindfulness, the life of renunciation and training in the path, and the cultivation of reflection.
"Venerable friends!
The Blessed One, having briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling to sit in meditation, saying: 'Monks!'"

If a person, for whatever reason they have set out to leave the household life to study the Path, contemplates and cultivates the phenomena of the past, future, and present without craving, delighting in, clinging to, or dwelling upon them—this is called the end of suffering.

The underlying tendencies of sensual desire, ill will, existence, conceit, ignorance, views, and doubt; as well as strife, contention, envy, malice, flattery, deceit, false speech, and double-tonguedness—along with immeasurable other evil and unwholesome states—these are said to be the end of suffering.
"This was the Blessed One’s brief statement, without detailed analysis of its meaning; I have explained it extensively according to these phrases and this text.
Venerable friends!
You may go before the Buddha and present it in full. If the meaning is indeed as the Blessed One has spoken, then you, venerable friends, may accept and uphold it."

Then, having heard what the Venerable Mahākaccāna had said, those bhikkhus received and recited it well; they rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Mahākaccāna three times, and departed for the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they prostrated themselves in salutation, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
Having briefly explained this meaning to the Blessed One without detailed analysis, he rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in meditation;
the Venerable Mahākātyāyana then expounded it at length using these very phrases and these very words.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Among my disciples, there are those who possess vision, wisdom, the Dharma, and its meaning. Why is this?
It is because when the Teacher has briefly explained this meaning to his disciples without extensive analysis, those disciples elaborate upon it through these very phrases and these very words.
As the bhikṣu Kātyāyana has spoken, you should receive and uphold it in this way. Why is that?
Because he has explained the meaning of contemplation, and it should be so.

"Monks! It is just as if a person, while wandering in a secluded place, a mountain forest, or among the trees, were suddenly to find a ball of honey; whatever part he tasted would yield its flavor. In the same way, a son of noble family, within this Dharma and Vinaya of mine, gains its flavor according to what he contemplates: he gains its flavor by contemplating the eye, and he gains its flavor by contemplating the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
“World-Honored One!
"What is the name of this Dharma?
How should I receive and uphold it?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Ānanda! This teaching is called 'The Simile of the Honey Ball'; you should receive and uphold it.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Monks, you should receive, recite, and study this Dharma taught through the parable of the honey ball.
Why is that? Monks!"
This parable of the honey-ball possesses both the letter and the meaning; it is the foundation of the holy life, leading to penetration, leading to awakening, and leading to Nirvana.

If a son of good family, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the Way, he should properly receive and uphold this parable of the honey-ball.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The ninth Sūtra on the Simile of the Honey Ball ends here, totaling two thousand two hundred seventy-two characters. 116. The Sūtra on Gautamī (116) The Tenth Sūtra in the Forest Chapter of the Madhyama Āgama, recited in the Second Minor Section on Small Earthly Cities. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas and was staying at the Nyagrodha Grove in Kapilavastu, observing the rains retreat together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!
Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of asceticism?
For this reason, can a woman, out of faith, go forth from the home into homelessness to train in this true Dharma and Vinaya?
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Gotamī! Do not harbor this thought:
'May women, out of deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to train in this True Dharma and Discipline.'"
“Gautamī! Thus, you shall shave off your hair, don the saffron robes, and for the remainder of your life, purely cultivate the holy life.
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been thus enjoined by the Buddha, bowed her head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, the bhikṣus were mending robes for the Buddha. Before long, the World-Honored One, having completed his summer retreat at Śrāvastī and finished repairing his robes, and after the three months had passed, took up his robes and bowl and was about to travel among the people.

When Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī heard that the bhikṣus were mending robes for the Buddha, she thought: "Before long, after the World-Honored One has completed his summer retreat at Śrāvastī and finished repairing his robes, and once the three months have passed, he will take up his robes and bowl and set out to wander among the people."
Having heard this, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went again to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!
Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of asceticism?
For this reason, can a woman, out of faith, go forth from the home into homelessness to train in this true Dharma and Vinaya?
The World-Honored One also spoke a second time, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
Gautamī! Do not harbor this thought:
"May women, within this True Dharma and Vinaya, out of faith, leave the home life for homelessness and train in the Path."
“Gautamī! Thus, you shall shave off your hair, don the saffron robes, and for the remainder of your life, purely cultivate the holy life.
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been again enjoined by the Buddha, bowed her head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, having completed the summer retreat at Śrāvastī and finished mending his robes, the World-Honored One, after the three months had passed, took up his robes and bowl and set out to wander among the people.

Having heard that the World-Honored One, after completing his summer retreat at Śrāvastī and finishing the mending of his robes, had passed the three months and was now taking up his robes and bowl to wander among the people, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī [heard this].

Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with the elder Śākya women, followed behind the Buddha and proceeded by stages until they reached Nādikā, where they stayed at the Kalandaka Nivāpa Monastery in Nādikā.
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went again to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!
Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of the ascetic life?
For this reason, can a woman, out of faith, go forth from the home into homelessness to train in this true Dharma and Vinaya?
The World-Honored One repeated this three times, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
Gautamī! Do not harbor this thought:
"May women, within this true Dharma and Vinaya, out of faith, leave the home life for homelessness and train in the path."
"Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī!
Thus, you shall shave off your hair, don the saffron robes, and for as long as life lasts, purely cultivate the holy life."
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having been thus restrained three times by the Blessed One, bowed her head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī stood outside the gate, her bare feet stained with mud, her body covered in dust, utterly exhausted and weeping in sorrow.

The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī standing outside the gate, her bare feet smeared with ointment and stained with dust, her body covered in grime, utterly exhausted and weeping in sorrow. Having seen her, he asked:
“Gautamī! Why are you standing here?”
"For what reason do you stand outside the gate with feet smeared by mud, body covered in dust,
utterly exhausted, and weeping? Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī replied,
"Venerable Ānanda!"
"A woman cannot, within this true Dharma and Discipline, out of faith go forth from the home into homelessness to study the Path.
The Venerable Ānanda said: "Gautamī!"
"Stay here for now; I shall go to the Buddha and report this matter.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī replied, "So be it."
"Venerable Ānanda!
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
Can a woman attain the fourth fruit of asceticism?
For this reason, can a woman, out of faith, go forth from the home into homelessness to train in this true Dharma and Vinaya?
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop! Stop!"
Ānanda! Do not harbor this thought:
"Can women, within this true Dharma and Vinaya, attain full confidence, leave the household life, become homeless, and train in the path?"
"Ānanda! If women were to go forth from the home into homelessness out of faith to train in this true Dhamma and Discipline, this holy life would not endure for long."
“Ānanda! Suppose there were a household with many women and few men; would that household be able to prosper and flourish?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
"No, World-Honored One. "It is so, Ānanda!"
"If women were to obtain this true Dharma and Vinaya, and with faith go forth from home into homelessness to practice the path, this holy life would not endure for long."
Ānanda! Just as when weeds grow within a field of rice or a field of wheat, they inevitably ruin that field; even so, Ānanda!
If women were to obtain this True Dharma and Discipline, and with faith go forth from the household life into homelessness to practice the path, this holy life would not endure for long.
The Venerable Ānanda spoke again, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to the World-Honored One."
"Why is that? After the Blessed One’s mother passed away, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī nurtured and raised the Blessed One.
The Blessed One replied:
"So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda!
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has been of great benefit to me; after her mother passed away, she raised and nurtured me."
Ānanda! I have also greatly benefited Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī. Why is that?

Ānanda! Because of me, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī has taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; she is free from doubt regarding the Triple Gem and regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; she has perfected faith, upholds the prohibitive precepts, cultivates extensive learning, achieves generosity, and attains wisdom; she has abandoned killing and severed the practice of killing, abandoned taking what is not given and severed the practice of taking what is not given, abandoned sexual misconduct and severed the practice of sexual misconduct, abandoned false speech and severed the practice of false speech, and abandoned intoxicants and severed the practice of intoxicants.

Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who, because of another person, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; who has no doubt regarding the Triple Gem, nor regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; who has perfected faith, upholds the prohibitive precepts, cultivates extensive learning, perfects generosity, and attains wisdom; who abstains from killing and has abandoned killing, abstains from taking what is not given and has abandoned taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct and has abandoned sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech and has abandoned false speech, and abstains from intoxicants and has abandoned intoxicants—Ānanda!

Even if this person were to provide that other person with clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites for illness, and all other necessities of life until the end of their lifetime, they would still be unable to repay their kindness.
“Ānanda! I now establish for women eight rules of respect, which women must not transgress and which they shall uphold for as long as they live.”
Ānanda! It is just as a fisherman or a fisherman’s apprentice constructs a dam in deep water to guard the water, so that it does not flow out.
In this same way, Ānanda!
I now proclaim for women the eight rules of respect for teachers, which women must not transgress and which they shall uphold for as long as they live.
What are these eight?
Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī should seek to receive full ordination from a bhikṣu. Ānanda!
I have established this first rule for female disciples: that women must not transgress it, and they shall uphold it for as long as their lives endure.
“Ānanda! Every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī shall go to the bhikṣus to receive instruction. Ānanda!”
I have established this second rule for the veneration of teachers for women; that is to say, women must not violate it, but shall uphold it for as long as they live.
“Ānanda! If there is no bhikṣu at the place where one resides, a bhikṣuṇī may not undertake the summer retreat. Ānanda!”
I have established this third rule for the veneration of the Teacher for women: that women must not transgress it, but shall uphold it for as long as they live.
“Ānanda! When a bhikṣuṇī has completed her summer retreat, she should request three matters before both assemblies: seeking [clarification on what she has] seen, heard, or suspected.”
Ānanda! For women, I have established this fourth rule of respect for the Teacher, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as they live.

“Ānanda! If a bhikṣu does not permit a bhikṣuṇī to question him, then the bhikṣuṇī may not question the bhikṣu regarding the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma; however, if he permits her to question him, the bhikṣuṇī may question him regarding the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.”
Ānanda! For women, I have established this fifth rule of respect for teachers, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as their lives last.
“Ānanda! A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu may speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī. Ānanda!”
I have established this sixth rule for the veneration of teachers for women; that is to say, women must not violate it, but shall uphold it throughout their entire lives.
“Ānanda! If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo the mānatva penance for fifteen days before both assemblies. Ānanda!”
I have established this seventh rule for female disciples; that is to say, women must not transgress it, but shall uphold it for as long as they live.

“Ānanda! Although a bhikṣuṇī may have been ordained for a hundred years, she must nevertheless show the utmost humility toward a bhikṣu who has only just received full ordination; she should prostrate herself in salutation, serve him with reverence, and join her palms in greeting.”
Ānanda! For women, I have established this eighth rule of respect for teachers, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as life lasts.
“Ānanda! For women, I have established these eight rules of respect for teachers, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as they live.”

Ānanda! If Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī upholds these eight rules of respect for her teacher, she may go forth to study the path within this True Dharma and Discipline, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī.

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and retained it well; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was and said to her: “Gautamī!
"Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, women may, out of faith, go forth from the home into homelessness to train in this True Dharma and Discipline.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Blessed One has established these eight rules of respect for women; they must not be transgressed by women, but shall be observed by them for as long as life lasts."
What are the eight? Gautamī!
A bhikṣuṇī shall seek to receive full ordination from a bhikṣu.
"Gotamī! The Blessed One has established this first rule of respect for women, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as their life lasts."
“Gautamī! A bhikṣuṇī must go every half-month to receive instruction from the bhikṣus. Gautamī!
This is the second rule of respect established by the Blessed One for women; it must not be transgressed by women, who shall uphold it for as long as they live.”
"Gotamī! If there are no bhikṣus residing at a place of stay, a bhikṣuṇī may not undertake the summer retreat there. Gotamī!"
The Blessed One has established this third rule for the Teacher for women, which states that women must not transgress it, but shall uphold it for as long as they live.
“Gautamī! When a bhikṣuṇī has completed her summer retreat, she should request three matters before both assemblies: what she has seen, heard, or suspected.”
"Gautamī! The Blessed One has established this fourth rule of respect for women, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as life lasts."

“Gautamī! If a bhikṣu does not permit a bhikṣuṇī to question him, the bhikṣuṇī may not question the bhikṣu regarding the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma; if he permits her to question him, the bhikṣuṇī may question him regarding the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma.”
"Gotamī! The Blessed One has established this fifth rule of respect for women, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as life lasts."
“Gautamī! A bhikṣuṇī must not speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu may speak of an offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī. Gautamī!”
The Blessed One has established this sixth rule for the Teacher for women, which states that women must not transgress it, but shall uphold it for as long as they live.
"Gotamī! If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must perform the mānatva penance for fifteen days before both assemblies."
Gautamī! The Blessed One has established this seventh rule for the Teacher for women, which must not be transgressed by women and which they shall uphold for as long as life lasts.

"Gotamī! Although a bhikṣuṇī may have been ordained for a hundred years, she must nevertheless show the utmost humility toward a bhikṣu who has only just received full ordination; she should prostrate herself in salutation, serve him with reverence, and inquire after his well-being with palms joined."

Gautamī! The Blessed One has established this eighth rule for the veneration of teachers for women; that is to say, women must not transgress it, and women shall uphold it for as long as their lives last.
“Gautamī! The Blessed One has established these eight rules of respect for women; they must not be transgressed by women, who shall uphold them for as long as life lasts.”
"Gautamī! Thus has the Blessed One spoken:

'If Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī upholds these eight rules of respect for the teacher, she may go forth into homelessness to study the Path within this True Dharma and Vinaya, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī.'"
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī said to him:
"Venerable Ānanda, please allow me to speak a parable;
for the wise, upon hearing a parable, understand its meaning."
Venerable Ānanda!

It is just as if there were a daughter of a Kṣatriya, or a daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman, who was beautiful and lovely; having bathed thoroughly and anointed her body with perfumes, she put on bright, clean clothes and adorned her appearance with various kinds of necklaces and ornaments.

Furthermore, suppose there is someone who, out of affection for that woman, seeking her profit and welfare, and seeking her peace and happiness, takes the filaments of a blue lotus, or a garland of campaka flowers, or the filaments of a sumana flower, or the filaments of a vārṣika flower, or the filaments of an atimuktaka flower, and presents them to her.
She rejoiced and received them with both hands, using them to adorn her head.
"In this way, Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One has established these eight rules of respect for women; I shall receive and uphold them upon the crown of my head for as long as I live."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went forth from the household life to study the path within the True Dharma and Vinaya; she received full ordination and became a bhikṣuṇī.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī later became the leader of a great community of bhikṣuṇīs; together with the elder and senior bhikṣuṇīs who were known by the king, who had long practiced the holy life, she went to the place where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated herself in salutation, stood to one side, and said:
"Venerable Ānanda!..."
"You should know that these elder bhikṣuṇīs are highly esteemed by the king, having long cultivated the holy life;
whereas those bhikṣus are young and newly trained, having left the household life late in their lives and having only recently entered this True Dharma and Vinaya."
I pray that these bhikṣus will, according to their seniority, bow their heads in salutation to the bhikṣuṇīs, serve them with reverence, and inquire after their well-being with palms joined.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda said:
"Gotamī, stay here for now; I shall go to the Buddha and report this matter."
Gautamī Mahāprajāpatī replied, “Indeed,
Venerable Ānanda!”
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. With palms joined toward the Buddha, he said to him:
“World-Honored One!

Today, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, together with the elder bhikṣuṇīs who are senior, venerable, and known to kings, having long practiced the holy life, all came to where I was; they prostrated at my feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined, addressed me, saying:
"Venerable Ānanda!..."
"These elder bhikṣuṇīs are highly venerable and well-known to the king; they have long cultivated the holy life.
Those bhikṣus, however, are young and newly trained, having left the home life late in life and having only recently entered this True Dharma and Vinaya."
I pray that these bhikṣus may, according to their seniority, bow their heads in salutation to the bhikṣuṇīs, serve them with reverence, and inquire after their well-being with palms joined.
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop! Stop!"
Ānanda! Guard these words; be careful not to speak thus. Ānanda!

If you were to know as I know, you would not utter even a single word, much less speak in such a manner. Ānanda! If women had not been permitted to go forth from the home into homelessness out of faith to train in this True Dharma and Discipline, the brahmins and householders would have spread their robes upon the ground and said: [The remainder of the passage follows: "Let the Blessed One accept these robes; let the Sugata accept them for the sake of the world, for the benefit of the many, out of compassion for the multitude, for the welfare and happiness of devas and humans. "A diligent śramaṇa may proceed upon the higher path; a diligent śramaṇa practices what is difficult to practice, so that I may long enjoy benefit, profit, peace, and happiness."

"Ānanda! If women were not permitted to go forth from the home into homelessness out of faith to train in this true Dhamma and Discipline, then brahmins and householders would have offered their hair as a gift and said:
'May the diligent śramaṇas walk upon the higher path; may the diligent śramaṇas practice what is difficult to practice, so that we may long enjoy benefit, profit, peace, and happiness.'"

“Ānanda! If women had not, within this True Dharma and Discipline, out of faith gone forth from the home into homelessness to practice the path, then whenever the brahmins and householders saw a recluse, they would have offered various kinds of food and drink with their own hands, standing by the roadside waiting and saying:
‘Venerable sirs!’”
"Receive this food; take it with you and use it as you please, so that I may obtain long-lasting benefit, profit, peace, and happiness. Ānanda!

If women were not permitted to go forth from the home into homelessness out of faith to train in this true Dharma and Discipline, then those faithful brahmins, upon seeing an energetic śramaṇa, would respectfully support and embrace him, lead him inside, and present him with various kinds of wealth, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"This feeling is graspable and portable; it can be used as one wishes, bringing me long-lasting benefit, profit, peace, and happiness.
Thus spoke Ānanda.

If women were not able, within this true Dharma and Discipline, to go forth from the home into homelessness out of faith to train in the path, then these sun and moon—though they possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority—would still not equal the spiritual power and majesty of a diligent śramaṇa; how much less so, then, could the emaciated heterodox practitioners?

Ānanda! If women had not, within this true Dharma and Discipline, out of faith, gone forth from the home into homelessness to practice the path, the true Dharma would have remained for a thousand years; now five hundred years have been lost, and five hundred years remain.

Ānanda! You should know that women are incapable of performing five things: if a woman were to become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; or a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin); or Śakra, Lord of the Devas; or Māra, the King of the Demons; or Mahābrahmā—it is absolutely impossible for such a thing to occur.

It should be known that there are five things a man may accomplish: if a man becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; or a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin); or Śakra, Lord of the Devas; or Māra, the King of the Demons; or Mahābrahmā—these are certainly possible.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Softness Discourse (117), the first in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"Since I first left home to study the Way, I have lived in leisure, composure, and ease, with extreme gentleness. When I was in the house of my father, King Śuddhodana, he constructed various palaces for me—palaces for spring, summer, and winter—for the sake of my pleasure in play."
Not far from the palace, he further constructed various kinds of lotus ponds: blue lotus ponds, red lotus ponds, crimson lotus ponds, and white lotus ponds.

In that pond, various kinds of water flowers—blue lotuses, red lotuses, pink lotuses, and white lotuses—were planted; it was always filled with water and always blooming with flowers. He appointed guards to protect it and did not allow anyone access, for the sake of his own pleasure in sporting there.

On the banks of that pond, various kinds of terrestrial flowers were planted—sumana flowers, vārṣika flowers, campaka flowers, sugandhika flowers, mahāsugandhika flowers, atimuktaka flowers, and pāṭala flowers—for the sake of my pleasant pastimes.

Furthermore, you shall have four men bathe me; once I have been bathed, they shall anoint my body with red sandalwood incense; having anointed my body, they shall clothe me in new silk garments—new on the outside and inside, on the top and bottom, and throughout the surface and lining—and day and night they shall constantly cover me with a parasol, so that the Prince is not drenched by the dew at night nor scorched by the sun during the day.

Just as in other families coarse grain, barley rice, bean soup, and gingered vegetables are considered the finest food, so too in my father King Śuddhodana’s household, the lowest servant has fine rice and delicacies as his finest food.

"Furthermore, if there are wild animals of the fields, the most excellent of wild animals—such as the *tittira*, *vartaka*, *kapinjala*, *kapiñjala*, *kapiñjala*, *nīca*, *heḷi*, *niśa*, and *miśraśilami*—these wild animals, the most excellent of wild animals, shall constantly provide such food for me."

"I recall that in the past, when my father Suddhodana was at home during the four months of the summer retreat, he would ascend to the upper terrace of the main palace; there were no men present, only female musicians with whom he amused himself, never once descending below. When I wished to go out to the gardens for an excursion, thirty elite riders were selected for the finest mounts, with a ceremonial procession of guards in front and behind to escort me—how much more so for others?"
"I possess this supernormal power (ṛddhipāda), which is most supple.

Furthermore, I recall that in the past, while observing laborers resting upon a field, I went beneath a jambu tree, sat down cross-legged, and—detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states—with directed thought and evaluation, born of detachment, joy and happiness, attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna."
I had this thought:

"The unlearned, foolish worldling is himself subject to the nature of illness and cannot escape it; yet when he sees another who is ill, he feels aversion, contempt, and disdain, neither loving nor rejoicing in it, while failing to examine himself."
I further thought: "I myself am subject to the nature of illness and cannot escape it.
If I were to see the illness of others and feel aversion, contempt, or disdain for it, failing to love or rejoice in it, that would not be fitting for me, for I too possess this same nature."
Having observed this, any arrogance arising from the thought that one is not subject to illness is immediately extinguished.
I further reflected:

"The unlearned, foolish worldling is himself subject to the law of aging and cannot escape it; yet, seeing others grow old, he feels aversion, contempt, and disdain, neither loving nor rejoicing in it, while failing to observe his own condition."
I further thought: "I myself am subject to the law of aging and cannot escape it.
If I were to see others grow old and feel hatred, contempt, lack of affection, or aversion toward them, that would not be fitting for me, for I too am subject to this same law."
Having observed in this way, if one gives rise to arrogance because of life, that arrogance is immediately extinguished of its own accord.

The unlearned, foolish worldling, through the arrogance of being free from illness and the pride of noble status, becomes heedless; due to desire, he gives rise to delusion and does not practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
The unlearned, foolish worldling, being arrogant due to youth, wealth, and nobility, gives rise to delusion because of sensual desire and does not practice the holy life.
The unlearned, foolish worldling, being arrogant due to longevity, wealth, and nobility, gives rise to delusion because of sensual desire and does not practice the holy life.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The nature of sickness, the nature of old age, And the nature of death—these are inherent in all things; Yet the worldling views them with aversion."
If I were to harbor hatred and fail to cross over this Dharma, it would not be fitting for me; yet such a Dharma exists.
Practicing in this way, one knows the Dharma that transcends birth.
Free from illness and in the prime of youth, one becomes arrogant regarding longevity;
by severing all such arrogance, one perceives the peace of desirelessness.
One who awakens thus has no fear of desires.
"Attaining the state of being without conceptualization, one practices the pure holy life.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the Migāramātupāsāda.
At that time, in the late afternoon, the World-Honored One rose from his meditation, descended from the hall, and said: "Udāyin,
let us go together to the Eastern River to bathe."
"Very well," the Venerable Udāyin replied.

Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Udāyin and went to the Eastern River; he removed his robes on the bank, entered the water to bathe, and having finished bathing, came back out, dried himself, and put on his clothes.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a noble elephant named Smṛti, who performed all kinds of musical displays as he crossed the eastern river.
When the people saw this, they said:
"This is a dragon among dragons; he must be a great Dragon King. Who is he?"
Venerable Udāyin joined his palms toward the Buddha and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
An elephant possesses a massive body; when the multitude sees it, they say this:”
"This is a dragon among dragons, a great nāga king;
who might he be? The World-Honored One replied, "It is so."
"It is so, Udāyin! It is so, Udāyin!"
The elephant received a massive body; when the multitude saw it, they said:
"This is a dragon among dragons! Is he a great dragon king, or who is he?"
"Udāyi! Horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, serpents, humans, and trees grow into large forms.
Udāyi! When people see them, they say this:"
“Who is this dragon among dragons, this great dragon king?
Who is he? Udāyin!

If there is anyone in the world—whether among devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brahmins, from humans up to the gods—who does not harm others by way of body, speech, or mind, I declare that such a person is a dragon.

Udāyin! In this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods—the Tathāgata does not harm others by means of body, speech, or mind. Therefore, I am called a Nāga.
Thereupon, the Venerable Udāyin joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!

I pray that the World-Honored One will bestow his power upon me; Sugata, may you bestow your power upon me, so that I may stand before the Buddha and praise the World-Honored One with verses corresponding to the nāgas."
The Blessed One said,
"Do as you wish. Thereupon,
the Venerable Udāyin, standing before the Buddha, praised the Blessed One with verses appropriate to a nāga:
“The Fully Awakened One has been born among humans; having mastered right concentration for himself, he cultivates and practices the Brahma-faring.
With his mind stilled, he is able to dwell in self-bliss.
He is revered by all people, transcending all phenomena.”
He is also revered by the devas, an unattached True Person (Arhat).
Having transcended all fetters, he has departed from the forest to leave the forest behind;
having abandoned sensual pleasure for desirelessness, he is like pure gold extracted from stone.
The Perfectly Awakened One is heard everywhere, like the sun rising in the void;
he stands supreme among all dragons, like Mount Tai among the many mountains.
He is praised as a Great Dragon, yet he causes no harm.
The supreme dragon among all dragons, the unsurpassed dragon of ultimate truth;
gentle and free from harm—these two are the feet of the dragon.
Asceticism and the holy life (brahmacarya)—this is called the dragon’s way of conduct.
Great Faith is his trunk; the two virtues are his tusks;
Mindfulness is his neck and Wisdom his head; he discerns and analyzes the Dharma.
Upholding all teachings is his belly; delighting in seclusion are his two arms.
Abiding in the proper regulation of inhalation and exhalation, with the inner mind reaching supreme concentration;
whether moving or stationary, the Naga is concentrated; sitting concentrated, even lying down he is concentrated.
The Naga is concentrated at all times—this is called the constant law of the Naga.
One accepts food from a household free of impurity; if there is impurity, one does not accept it.
Having obtained foul and unclean food, one abandons it like a lion.
Whatever offerings are received, they are accepted out of compassion for others.
The dragon consumes the offerings of others, sustaining his life without attachment.
Having severed both great and small fetters, he is liberated from all bonds;
wherever he wanders, his mind remains free of attachment.
Just as the white lotus flower, born in water and nurtured by water,
is unsullied by mud and water, possessing a wondrous fragrance and a lovely color;
even so is the Supreme Awakened One, born in the world and moving through the world.
Not stained by desire, like a lotus unsullied by water;
just as when a fire blazes fiercely, it ceases if no more fuel is added—
without fuel the fire does not continue, and this fire is said to be extinguished.
The wise have spoken this parable to cause its meaning to be understood;
it is that which is known by the Nāgas, as taught by the Nāga among Nāgas.
Far removed from lust and hatred, having severed delusion and attained the outflow-free state.
"The dragon has abandoned its body; this dragon is said to have attained extinction.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Udāyin rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Nāga Elephant Sūtra, the second, ends here with seven hundred and thirty characters. 119. The Sūtra on the Places of Discourse (119), the third sūtra in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are these three grounds for speaking, not four nor five.
If a bhikṣu, having seen something, speaks on its account, saying 'I have seen,' 'I have heard,' 'I have cognized,' or 'I have known,' then what the bhikṣu says is that this is what he knows."
What are the three?
Bhikṣus, based on the past, one speaks thus: "In the past, there was [a self]. Bhikṣus!
Because of speaking in reference to the future world, it is said that there is such a thing as the time of the future world;
bhikkhus!
Because of speaking in reference to the present world, it is said that there is such a thing as the time of the present world.
These are called the three grounds for speaking; there is neither a fourth nor a fifth.

If a bhikkhu, having seen something, speaks on its account, saying, "I have seen, heard, sensed, or known," and the bhikkhu speaks thus, claiming, "This is what I know," he acquires meaning through the wholesome practice of what was spoken, and does not acquire meaning through the unwholesome practice of what was not spoken.

“The noble disciple listens to the Dharma with both ears and with a single-minded focus. Having listened to the Dharma with both ears and a single-minded focus, he abandons one dharma, cultivates one dharma, and realizes one dharma. Having abandoned one dharma, cultivated one dharma, and realized one dharma, he attains right concentration.”
Once the noble disciple has attained right concentration of mind, he then abandons all lust, anger, and delusion; thus the noble disciple attains liberation of mind.

Having attained liberation, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

Because there are four bases according to what he has said, one should examine the person: "Is this worthy one one with whom it is appropriate to speak, or one with whom it is not appropriate to speak?

If this worthy one engages in unilateral discourse but does not answer unilaterally; engages in analytical discourse but does not answer analytically; engages in interrogative discourse but does not answer by interrogation; or engages in restrictive discourse but does not answer restrictively—then such a worthy one is one with whom one should not speak, nor with whom one should engage in discourse."

If this worthy one were to engage in categorical discourse and provide categorical answers, analytical discourse and provide analytical answers, interrogative discourse and provide interrogative answers, or dialectical discourse and provide dialectical answers, then this worthy one could engage in conversation with me and could also debate with me.

"Furthermore, based on what has been said, there are four further points by which one should observe a person: 'Is this worthy person one with whom it is appropriate to speak, or one with whom it is not appropriate to speak?'"

If this worthy one does not abide in what is possible or what is impossible, does not abide in that which is known, does not abide in metaphors, and does not abide in the tracks of the path—then it is impossible to speak with this worthy one, nor is it possible to debate with him.

If this worthy one abides in what is possible and what is impossible, abides in that which is known, abides in that which is illustrated by analogy, and abides in the tracks of the path—then it is possible to converse with this worthy one, and it is also possible to debate with him.

When speaking, one should cease verbal activity, relinquish what has been seen, abandon thoughts of enmity, and abandon desire, hatred, delusion, pride, silence, stinginess, jealousy, the seeking of victory, and the subduing of others; one should not cling to what is lost, but speak of the meaning and the Dharma.

Having explained the meaning and the Dharma, he instructs and further enjoins others; he rejoices himself and causes others to rejoice. Thus he explains the meaning and thus he explains the matter: this is the noble explanation of meaning, this is the noble explanation of matter, namely, the ultimate exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Then, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“If there is contentious debate, With minds muddled and harboring pride,
The un-Aryan ones disparage virtue, Each seeking the other's weakness.”
Merely seeking out the faults of others, with the intent to subdue them,
and vying with one another for victory— this is not what the Noble One teaches.
If you wish to engage in debate, the wise should know the proper time.
There are phenomena and there are meanings; such is the teaching of the noble treatises.
The wise speak thus: they are without contention and without arrogance;
their minds are never satiated, yet they are free from fetters and without outflows.
In accordance with reality and without inversion, one speaks with correct knowledge;
what is well-spoken is thus acceptable, and one never speaks what is evil.
One does not engage in contentious debate, nor does one accept the disputes of others.
Knowing the proper occasion and knowing how to speak—this is what they discuss.
Thus the Noble One has taught: the wise attain both meanings;
they find happiness in the present life and security in the world to come.
"You should know that the wise do not speak of inversion or permanence.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Discourse on the Bases, the third, ends here with seven hundred and twenty-three characters. 120. The Discourse on Impermanence (120), Madhyama Āgama, Great Division, the fourth discourse in the section on the Discourse on Impermanence, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Form is impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not the self.
Sensation is also impermanent; what is impermanent is suffering; what is suffering is not the self."
Perception is also impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not a self.
Volitional formations are also impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not a self.
Consciousness, too, is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not the self.
Thus, form is impermanent, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is not the self.

The learned noble disciple contemplates in this way and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment; with unimpeded right reflection and right mindfulness, he thus knows and thus sees, and his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, and his mind is liberated from the taints of existence and ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.

If there are sentient beings and the nine abodes of sentient beings, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the remaining Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), among these, the Arhat in the world is foremost, greatest, most excellent, supreme, most venerable, and most sublime.
"Why is this? Because among those in the world, the Arhat attains peace and happiness.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Non-attachment is the foremost bliss; having severed desire and being free from craving, one forever abandons the conceit of 'I am' and tears asunder the net of ignorance.
Such a person attains immovability, for their mind is free from defilement."
Untainted by the world, having attained the stainless Brahma-faring,
Thoroughly understanding the five aggregates and the seven wholesome qualities of the objective realm,
The Great Hero wanders through his domain, free from all fear.
Having accomplished the jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment, Possessing the training in the three trainings,
Wondrously praised as a supreme friend, The Buddha’s most excellent true son.
Accomplishing the tenfold path, A great nāga with a mind of ultimate concentration.
This is the foremost in the world; therein, there is no craving.
Unshakable amidst all affairs, one is liberated from future existence;
having severed birth, old age, sickness, and death, what was to be done is accomplished and the outflows are extinguished.
Having aroused the knowledge of one beyond training, having attained the final body,
and being fully endowed with the supreme holy life, his mind is not dependent on others.
Whether above, below, or in any direction, he has no attachment or delight.
He is able to roar the lion’s roar, the unsurpassed awakening in the world.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Discourse on Impermanence, Chapter Four, ends here with four hundred and thirteen characters. 121. The Discourse on Entreaty (121), Middle Collection, Great Division, The Discourse on Entreaty, Fifth, Part One. [The character "請" (qǐng) is pronounced *cí* and *jǐng* in the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all observing the rains retreat.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the World-Honored One was reciting the *Prātimokṣa* at the time of invitation, he sat upon a seat spread before the assembly of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I am a brahmin who has attained final extinction; I am the unsurpassed King of Physicians. This present body of mine is my very last."
"I am a brahmin who has attained final extinction; I am the unsurpassed King of Physicians. This body I now receive is my very last.
You, my followers, are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed by the Dharma."
"I declare that you all are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed by the Dharma; you should now teach and transform others, and instruct and admonish one another.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
As I have previously declared:
"I am a brahmin who has attained final extinction; I am the unsurpassed King of Physicians. This present body I receive is the very last."
"I am a brahmin who has attained final extinction; I am the unsurpassed King of Physicians. This body I now receive is my very last.
You, my followers, are my true sons, born from my mouth and transformed by the Dharma."
"I say to you all: you are my true sons, born from my mouth, transformed by the Dharma. You should teach and transform one another, and admonish one another.
World-Honored One!

He causes those who are undisciplined to become disciplined; he causes those who have not found rest to find rest; he causes those who have not crossed over to cross over; he causes those who are not liberated to attain liberation; he causes those who have not reached final extinction to reach final extinction; he causes those who have not attained the Path to attain the Path; and he causes those for whom the holy life has not been established to establish the holy life.

Knowing the path, awakening to the path, recognizing the path, and explaining the path, the disciples of the Blessed One subsequently attain the Dharma; having received instruction and reproof, and having received such instruction and reproof, they follow the words of the Blessed One and proceed accordingly, attaining their goal as intended and gaining excellent knowledge of the True Dharma.
"Indeed, World-Honored One, do you not find fault with my conduct of body, speech, and mind?
At that time, the World-Honored One said: "Sāriputta!"
I do not find fault with your conduct of body, speech,
and mind. Why is this so, Śāriputra?

You possess keen intelligence, great intelligence, swift intelligence, nimble intelligence, sharp intelligence, expansive intelligence, profound intelligence, liberating intelligence, and penetrating intelligence.
Sāriputta! You have accomplished true wisdom. Sāriputta!
It is just as when a Wheel-Turning King has a crown prince who, without transgressing the instructions, receives the investiture transmitted by his father-king and is able to transmit it in turn.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
“Śāriputra, you are able to turn the wheel of Dharma that I have turned.
Therefore, I do not find fault with your conduct of body, speech, or mind.”
Venerable Sāriputta again joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One, you do not find fault with my conduct of body, speech, and mind;..."
“Does the Blessed One not find fault with the bodily, verbal, and mental conduct of these five hundred bhikṣus?
The Blessed One replied: “Śāriputra!”
I do not find fault with the conduct of body, speech, and mind of these five hundred bhikṣus.
Why is that? Śāriputra!

These five hundred bhikṣus have all attained non-attachment; their taints are exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, the heavy burden is laid down, and the fetters of existence are ended, having attained the noble goal, right knowledge, and right liberation.

With the exception of one bhikkhu, I have also previously declared that he has attained ultimate knowledge in this very life: birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—knowing this as it truly is.
"Śāriputra! For this reason, I do not find fault with the bodily, verbal, and mental conduct of these five hundred bhikṣus.
A second time, the Venerable Śāriputra joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"Yes, indeed.
World-Honored One, you do not find fault with my conduct of body, speech, and mind;
nor do you find fault with the conduct of body, speech, and mind of these five hundred bhikṣus."
World-Honored One!
Among these five hundred bhikṣus, how many have attained the penetration of the three knowledges (trividyā),
and how many have attained both-fold liberation (ubhayatobhāgavimukti)?
"How many bhikṣus have attained liberation through wisdom?
The World-Honored One replied, "Śāriputra!"

Of these five hundred bhikṣus, ninety bhikṣus attained the mastery of the three clear knowledges (traividyā), ninety bhikṣus attained both-fold liberation (ubhayatobhāgavimukti), and the remaining bhikṣus attained liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti).
"Śāriputra! This assembly is without branches and without leaves, and it is also without knots or crookedness; it is pure and true, having attained right abiding.
At that time, the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāniputta was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Puṇṇa rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"Indeed, sir."
May the Blessed One empower me with his majesty; may the Sugata empower me with his majesty, so that I may offer praise in accordance with the meaning before the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus.
The Blessed One said:
"Vāsiṣṭha, do as you wish."
Thereupon, the Venerable Puṇṇa Kassapa, standing before the Buddha and the assembly of bhikkhus, praised him with verses appropriate to the meaning:
“Today is the day of the fifteenth, when the assembly of five hundred has gathered;
having severed all fetters and bonds, you are the unimpeded Sage who has reached the end of existence.”
Pure and radiant light shines forth; liberated from all existence, birth, old age, sickness, and death are exhausted. The outflows are extinguished and what was to be done is accomplished.
The fetters of remorse and doubt are subdued, and conceit along with the outflows of existence are utterly ended.
Having uprooted the thorns of the fetters of craving, there is no higher physician to be found.
Valiant as a lion, he has removed all fear;
having crossed over birth and death, all outflows have been extinguished.
Just as a wheel-turning monarch, surrounded by his ministers,
rules over all lands as far as the great ocean;
so too does this valiant one, the unsurpassed leader of merchants, subdue all.
The disciples delight in reverence; with the threefold knowledge, they are free from the fear of death.
All are children of the Buddha; having forever removed the branches, leaves, and joints, they turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. I prostrate to the Supreme Honored One.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifth sūtra, the *Yācanā-sutta*, ends here, totaling one thousand and thirteen characters. 122. The Campā Sūtra (122), the sixth sūtra in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Campā and stayed by the side of the Gaṅgā pool.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the month, when the *Prātimokṣa* was being recited, the World-Honored One prepared a seat and sat down before the assembly of bhikṣus.

Once the World-Honored One was seated, he immediately entered meditative concentration and observed the minds of the assembly with his knowledge of others' minds; having observed their minds, he sat in silence until the end of the first watch of the night.
Thereupon, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, pressed his palms together toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!
The first watch of the night has passed; the Buddha and the assembly of bhikkhus have been sitting together for a long time. We only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again sat in silence until midnight.
That one bhikṣu rose from his seat once more, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed and the middle watch is drawing to a close. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been sitting together for a long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*.”
The Blessed One remained silent and did not answer for a second time.
Thereupon, the Blessed One again sat in silence until the end of the night.
That one bhikkhu rose from his seat three times, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has concluded, and the last watch is nearly over; it is approaching dawn, and before long the light will break. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for a very long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those bhikṣus:
"In this assembly, there is one bhikṣu who has already become impure.
At that moment, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"For which bhikṣu did the Blessed One say that there is one bhikṣu among this assembly who has already become impure?"

"I should enter the concentration corresponding to the object (*tathatā-vimokṣa-samādhi*), and by means of the knowledge of others' minds within that concentration, observe the minds of this assembly.

Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then entered the concentration corresponding to the object, and by means of the knowledge of others' minds within that concentration, he observed the minds of the assembly. Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then knew that among the monks for whom the World-Honored One had spoken, there was one monk who had already become impure.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana arose from his meditative absorption, went before that bhikṣu, took him by the arm, led him out, opened the door, and placed him outside, saying:
"Foolish man, go far away! Do not remain here. You shall no longer be able to join the assembly of bhikṣus; from this moment forth, you are no longer a bhikṣu."
He closed the door, locked it from within, and returned to where the Buddha was. Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit at one side and said:
“World-Honored One, regarding that which you said concerning a bhikṣu in this assembly who has already become impure—I have already expelled him.”
"World-Honored One!

The first watch of the night has passed, the middle watch has concluded, and the last watch is drawing to a close; it is about to dawn, and before long the light will appear. The Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus have been seated together for a very long time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will speak on the *prātimokṣa*."
The Blessed One said:
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
That foolish person shall incur a great offense for having provoked and disturbed the Blessed One and the community of bhikṣus.”
Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If the Tathāgata were to preach "liberation through knowledge" to an impure assembly, that person’s head would immediately split into seven pieces.
Therefore, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
From this day forward, you all shall speak of liberation through understanding; the Tathāgata will no longer speak of liberation through [external] means.
Why is this? It is thus, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

There may be a deluded person who is fully aware of his coming and going, who observes and discerns well, who is composed in his movements—bending and stretching, looking down and looking up—and who properly wears the saṃghāṭī and other robes and carries the bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he is fully aware of it all, appearing as if he were a true practitioner of the holy life. When he approaches those who are true practitioners of the holy life, they may not recognize him for what he is.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If those who know the Brahmās were to perceive this, they would think:
'This śramaṇa is defiled; this śramaṇa is an insult; this śramaṇa is hateful; this śramaṇa is a thorn.'"
Once they have recognized this, they should expel him together.
Why is that? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

It is just as if a householder had a fine field of paddy or a field of wheat, where a weed called *śyāmāka* grew; its roots were similar, and its stalks, nodes, leaves, and flowers were all like those of wheat. Once the grain had ripened, the householder saw it and thought:
'This wheat is defiled; this wheat is loathsome and thorny.'"
Having recognized this, he immediately pulled it out and cast it away outside. Why was this?
So that it would not defile the other fine, excellent barley.
In this way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
