There may be a foolish person who is fully aware of his going out and coming in, who observes and discerns well, who is composed in his movements—bending and stretching, looking down and looking up—and who properly wears the saṃghāṭī robe and other garments, as well as his bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he is fully aware of all these actions. He appears like one of true brahmacarya, yet when he approaches those who are truly practitioners of brahmacarya, they may not recognize him for what he is.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If those Brahmās who possess knowledge should form this thought:
'This śramaṇa is a defiler; this śramaṇa is a disgrace; this śramaṇa is hateful; this śramaṇa is a thorn.'"
Once this is known, you should expel them together.
Why is this? So that they do not defile those who practice the holy life.
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

It is just as when a householder winnows grain in the autumn: among the heap of grain, that which is fully ripened remains when winnowed, while that which is unripened or consists of chaff and husks is carried away by the wind. Having seen this, the householder takes up a broom and sweeps it clean.”
Why is that? So as not to allow them to defile and mix with other pure, fine rice.
Thus it is, Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

There may be a deluded person who is fully aware of his coming and going, who observes and discerns well his bending and stretching, his looking down and looking up, and whose deportment is dignified and orderly; who wears the saṃghāṭī and other robes and carries the bowl with skill; and who is fully aware of all his actions—walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent—such that he appears to be a true practitioner of the holy life (brahmacarya). When he approaches other true practitioners of the holy life, they may not recognize him as such.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If those who know the Brahmās were to perceive this, they would think:
'This śramaṇa is defiled; this śramaṇa is disgraced; this śramaṇa is hateful; this śramaṇa is a thorn.'"
Once this is known, you should expel him together [with the others].
Why is that? So as not to allow him to defile those who practice the holy life.
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana!

It is just as when a householder, wishing to divert the flow of a spring, constructs a water channel and enters the forest with an axe to strike at the trees. If a tree is solid and firm, its sound is faint; if it is hollow, its sound is loud. Having recognized this, the householder cuts and trims the joints to fashion the water channel.”

In this way, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, there may be a deluded person who is fully aware of his going out and coming in, who observes and discerns well, who is composed in his movements—bending and stretching, looking down and looking up—and who properly wears his saṃghāṭī robe and other robes and carries his bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, he is fully aware of all these actions, appearing as if he were one of true brahmacarya. When he approaches those who are truly practitioners of brahmacarya, they may not recognize him for what he is.
"Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
If those who know the Brahmās should think thus:
'This ascetic is defiled; this ascetic is an insult; this ascetic is hateful; this ascetic is a thorn.'"
"Once you have recognized this, you should expel him together.
Why is that? So that he does not defile those who practice the holy life."
Then, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Know that when they gather together, there are those with evil desires, hatred, and envy;
those who harbor resentment and stinginess; and those who are jealous, deceitful, and fraudulent."
Among the multitude, they falsely claim to have ceased [evil], yet in private they call themselves śramaṇas;
secretly they perform various evil deeds, and their evil views remain unguarded.
Deceiving others with false speech—thus should one know them.
Do not gather with those who have come together; cast them out and do not dwell with them.
They are full of deceit and false speech; they claim to have attained peace when they have not.
Know the proper time and possess pure conduct; cast them out and remain far removed from them.
"Pure and together with the pure, one should always remain in harmony;
through harmony one attains peace, and thus one reaches the end of suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Cāpāla Sūtra*, the sixth, ends here; it contains one thousand three hundred and fifty-one characters. 123. The Sāmaññaphala Sutta (Sāmaññaphala-sūtra) *Madhyama Āgama*, Great Division (*Mahāvarga*), The Seventh Recitation: The Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra (Śramaṇa Viṃśatikoṭi) was also traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying in the Andhavana forest. During the early and late watches of the night, he remained awake in study, dwelling with diligent application, and cultivating the factors of enlightenment.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāriputra Mahākoṭṭhita dwelt in peace and solitude, sitting in meditation and reflecting, his mind forming this thought:
"Among the disciples of the Blessed One who diligently train in the True Dharma and the Vinaya, I am the foremost; yet my mind has not attained liberation from the outflows."

"My parents' family is extremely wealthy and prosperous, possessing vast amounts of money and property; would it not be better for me now to abandon the precepts and cease my monastic practice, so that I may practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing with his knowledge of others' minds the thoughts in the mind of the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśākha, addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to him and summon the Śramaṇa Viśākha here."
Thereupon, a certain bhikṣu replied, “So be it.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśākha was and said to him:
“The World-Honored One calls for you!
Hearing the bhikṣu’s words, the Venerable Śāriputra went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One said:
"O śramaṇa!
It is true that you dwell in quietude alone, sitting in meditation and reflecting, with this thought arising in your mind:..."
"If there were disciples of the Blessed One who diligently train in the True Dharma and the Discipline, I would be foremost among them; yet my mind has not attained liberation from the outflows."

"My parents' family is extremely wealthy and prosperous, possessing vast riches; would it not be better for me now to abandon the precepts and cease my practice as a seeker, so that I may practice giving and cultivate various meritorious deeds?"
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, son of the twenty crores, was ashamed and abashed, and he was no longer fearless, thinking:
"The Blessed One knows the thoughts in my mind."
With palms joined toward the Buddha, he said,
"It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One told him:
“Śramaṇa! I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
What do you think?”
"When you were living at home, you were skilled at playing the lute; did the lute follow the melody of the song, or did the song follow the melody of the lute?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied: "It was so."
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One asked again:
"What do you think?"
“If the strings of a lute are too tight, will there be a harmonious sound that is lovely and pleasant?
The śramaṇa replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One asked again:
“What do you think?”
"If the strings of a lute are too loose, would there be any harmonious sound that is pleasant and delightful?
The śramaṇa replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One asked again:
“What do you think?”
"If one plays the lute with the strings tuned neither too tight nor too loose, but exactly in the middle, would there not be a harmonious sound that is lovely and pleasant?
The śramaṇa replied, "It would be so."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied, “It is so.”
"O Śramaṇa!
Excessive diligence causes the mind to become agitated;
a lack of diligence causes the mind to become indolent."
"Therefore, you should distinguish these times and observe these signs; do not be negligent.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra (Saṃpūṣa), having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and upheld it well. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction through the parable of playing the lute, he dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.

Having thus dwelt in seclusion and solitude, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, that son of noble family—having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Way—brought the unsurpassed holy life to its completion. In this very life, he knew it for himself and realized it for himself; having personally attained realization, he lived in fulfillment: birth was exhausted, the holy life was established, what was to be done had been accomplished, and there would be no further existence, knowing this as it truly is.
Having realized the Dharma, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśākha attained arhatship.
At that time, having attained arhatship, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśākha thought to himself:
"Now is the right time; I should go to the Blessed One and declare that I have attained ultimate knowledge."
Thereupon, the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśvabhū went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikkhu who has attained non-attachment, whose taints are exhausted, whose holy life is established, who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, severed the fetters of existence, attained the true goal through his own effort, and is liberated through right knowledge and right wisdom—then at that time, he delights in these six bases: he delights in dispassion, delights in seclusion, delights in non-contention, delights in the exhaustion of craving, delights in the exhaustion of clinging, and delights in the immovability of the mind.
"Bhagavān! There may be a person who thinks:
'This worthy one, by relying on faith, delights in the absence of desire.'"
"One should not view it in such a way; rather, the exhaustion of desire, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion—this is the bliss of being without desire.
World-Honored One!
There may be a person who thinks thus:"
"One should not view it thus: 'This worthy one, because he seeks offerings through greed for profit and reputation, delights in seclusion.
Rather, it is the exhaustion of lust, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion that constitutes delighting in seclusion."
"Bhagavān!
Suppose there is a person who thinks:
'This worthy one, by relying upon the precepts, delights in non-contention.'"

"One should not contemplate in such a way; rather, it is the exhaustion of desire, the exhaustion of hatred, and the exhaustion of delusion that constitutes delight in non-contention, delight in the extinction of craving, delight in the extinction of sensation, and delight in the immovability of the mind."
"Bhagavān!

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained non-attachment, whose taints are exhausted, whose holy life is established, who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, who has untied the fetters of existence, who has attained the noble goal for himself, and who is liberated through right knowledge and right liberation—he at that time delights in these six bases."

“Bhagavān! If there is a bhikṣu who has not yet attained mastery in his training but seeks the unsurpassed, peaceful, and secure nirvāṇa, at that time he accomplishes the faculty of training and the precepts of training.”

At a later time, his taints were exhausted and he attained the state of being without taints; with mind liberated and wisdom liberated, he came to know and realize for himself in this very life, attaining and dwelling in personal realization: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.
At that time, he accomplishes the faculties of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) and the precepts of one beyond training.
World-Honored One!

Just as a young child, at that time he accomplishes minor faculties and minor precepts; later, when he becomes fully endowed with the faculties of one in training (śaikṣa), at that time he accomplishes the faculties of one in training and the precepts of one in training.
"So it is, World-Honored One!

If there is a bhikṣu who has not yet attained mastery in his training, but seeks and aspires for unsurpassed, secure nirvāṇa, at that time he accomplishes the faculty of training and the precepts of training."

At a later time, when his taints have been exhausted and he has attained the state of being without outflows—having achieved liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom—he knows and realizes for himself in this very life, attaining and dwelling in personal realization: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence"—knowing this as it truly is. At that time, he is endowed with the faculties of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and the precepts of one beyond training.

If there are forms known by the eye that come into contact with the eye, they cannot cause him to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; his mind dwells within, well-restrained and maintained, as he contemplates the nature of arising and passing away.

If there are sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, flavors known by the tongue, tangibles known by the body, or mental phenomena known by the mind that encounter the mind, they cannot cause one to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; rather, the mind dwells within, well-restrained and maintained, contemplating the law of arising and passing away.
“World-Honored One!

Suppose there were a great mountain of stone not far from a village—unbroken, unimpaired, and not brittle; firm, stable, solid, and unified. If a great wind and rain were to come from the east, they could not cause it to shake, nor could they move or shift it.
Nor would the wind from the east move it to the south. If a great wind and rain were to come from the south, they could not cause it to shake, nor could they move or shift it.”
Nor does the wind from the south move to the west; even if a great wind and rain come from the west, they cannot cause it to shake, nor can they move or displace it.
Nor does the wind from the west move to the north; even if a great wind and rain come from the north, they cannot cause it to shake, nor can they move or displace it.
Nor does the wind from the north move to other directions.

In this way, even if there are forms cognizable by the eye that come before the eye, they cannot cause one to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; the mind dwells within, well-restrained and maintained, contemplating the nature of arising and passing away.

If there are sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, flavors known by the tongue, tangibles known by the body, or mental objects known by the mind that encounter the mind, they cannot cause one to lose this liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; rather, the mind dwells within, well-restrained and guarded, contemplating the phenomena of arising and passing away.
Then, the Venerable Śāṇavāsa spoke these verses: "Delighting in desirelessness,
with a mind set on seclusion, rejoicing in non-contention,
one experiences the joy of the exhaustion of sensation."
Furthermore, delighting in the exhaustion of sensations, the mind remains unshaken;
knowing things as they truly are, one attains liberation of mind from this.
Having attained liberation of mind, the bhikṣu brings his faculties to rest.
Having acted, one does not dwell upon it; there is nothing further to seek or do.
Like a mountain of stone, which the wind cannot move, so too are form, sound, smell, taste, and bodily touch.
"Neither pleasant nor unpleasant phenomena can move my mind.

Having thus spoken before the Buddha regarding his attainment of ultimate knowledge, the Venerable Śramaṇa Veṭhadīpa rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, not long after the Venerable Śramaṇa Viśākha had departed, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Sons of good family!

You should come before me and speak of having attained ultimate knowledge in this manner, just as the Śramaṇa Viśākha came before me and spoke of having attained ultimate knowledge—without praising himself, without disparaging others, and explaining the meaning according to the various circumstances of the present life."

Do not let them be like those obsessed with deluded overweening pride, who come before me claiming to have attained ultimate wisdom; they do not attain the true meaning, but only undergo great weariness and toil.

The śramaṇa Veṭaḍīpa has come before me and declared that he has attained ultimate knowledge; he does not praise himself nor disparage others, and he explains the meaning according to the various circumstances of this present life.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh discourse, the Sāmaññaphala-sutta (The Discourse on the Fruits of the Ascetic Life), ends here, totaling one thousand seven hundred and thirty-nine characters. 124. The Discourse on the Eight Difficulties (Aṭṭha-dukkhakkhandha-sutta), the eighth discourse in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When a person practices the holy life, there are eight obstacles and eight inopportune times."
What are these eight?

It is when a Tathāgata—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—appears in the world and teaches the Dharma that leads toward cessation, leads toward final extinction, and leads toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One.
At that time, that person is born into hell.
This is called the first difficulty for a person practicing the holy life, the first untimely [occasion].

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfected in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—appears in the world and teaches the Dharma, which leads toward cessation, leads toward final extinction, and leads toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Sugata.

At that time, such a person will be born among animals, or among hungry ghosts, or in the long-lived heavens, or in the borderlands among barbarians; they will lack faith and gratitude, and will be devoid of reciprocity, being far removed from monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
This is called the fifth difficulty for a person practicing the holy life, the fifth inopportune moment.

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfected in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader, trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One, appears in the world and teaches the Dharma that leads toward cessation, leads toward final extinction, and leads toward the path of awakening—this being the teaching proclaimed by the Sugata.

Although that person was born at that time in a central land, they were deaf and mute like a sheep bleating; they always communicated by hand gestures and were unable to understand or explain the meaning of good and evil.
This is called the sixth difficulty and the sixth inopportune time for a person practicing the holy life.

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—appears in the world and teaches the Dharma that leads toward cessation, leads toward final extinction, and leads toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Sugata.

At that time, although such a person is born in a central land, they are not deaf, not mute, and do not bleat like a sheep; they do not communicate by hand gestures, and they are able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil. Nevertheless, they hold wrong views and inverted views, maintaining such views and speaking thus:

"There is no giving, no sacrifice, and no offering of incantations; there is no karma of good or evil, nor is there any retribution for good or evil deeds; there is no this world and no other world; there is no father and no mother; and in this world there is no true person who has reached the good destination, who has gone well, who has fared rightly—one who, having personally known and realized this world and the other world, dwells having attained realization through their own direct experience."
"This is called the seventh difficulty and the seventh inopportune time for a person practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, when a Tathāgata—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfected in knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader, trainer of persons, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One—does not appear in the world and does not teach the Dharma that leads to cessation, leads to extinction, and leads to the path of awakening, as expounded by the Sugata."

At that time, that person will be born in a central land; they will not be deaf, nor mute, nor will they bleat like a sheep, nor will they communicate by hand gestures. Furthermore, they will be able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil, possessing right view and no inverted views, and will see and speak thus:
"There is giving and there is fasting, as well as the recitation of incantations;
there are good and evil karmas, and there are the retributions for good and evil karmas."
There is this world and the other world; there is father and mother.

There are in the world true persons who have fared on to the good destination, who have fared well and are headed for the good, who know, realize, and personally witness for themselves this world and the other world, and dwell having achieved that realization.
"This is called the eighth difficulty and the eighth inopportune time for a person practicing the holy life (brahmacarya).
There is one non-difficulty and one opportune time for a person practicing the holy life."
What is the one thing that is not difficult for a person practicing the holy life, and what is the one right occasion?

It is when a Tathāgata—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, called the Buddha, the Blessed One—appears in the world and teaches the Dharma that leads toward cessation, leads toward final extinction, and leads toward the path of awakening, as proclaimed by the Well-Gone One.

At that time, that person will be born in a central land; they will not be deaf, nor mute, nor will they bleat like a sheep, nor will they communicate by hand gestures. Furthermore, they will be able to understand and explain the meaning of good and evil, possessing right view and no inverted views, seeing thus and speaking thus:
"There is giving and there is fasting, as well as the recitation of mantras;
there are good and evil karmas, and there are the retributions for good and evil karmas."
There is this world and the other world; there is father and mother.

There are in the world true persons who have fared on to the good destination, who have fared well and are heading for the good, who know, realize, and personally witness for themselves this world and the other world, and dwell having attained their accomplishment.
"This is what is meant by saying that for a person practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), there is one thing that is not difficult and one that is the right time.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If one has obtained a human body, And the most subtle and wondrous Dharma is preached,"
If one does not attain the fruit, it is because one has certainly failed to meet its proper time.
It is often said that the holy life (brahmacarya) is difficult;
for a person in a future life, to encounter such a time is exceedingly rare in this world.
If you wish to regain a human body and hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma,
you should study with diligent effort for the sake of compassion for yourself.
When discussing or hearing the wholesome Dharma, do not let its proper time pass by.
If one loses this opportunity, one will surely grieve over falling into hell.
If one does not encounter that time, one will not hear the teaching of the wholesome Dharma;
like a merchant who has lost his wealth, one will undergo immeasurable birth and death.
If one attains a human body, hears the teaching of the true and wholesome Dharma,
and reverently follows the instruction of the World-Honored One, one will surely encounter such a time.
If one encounters such a time, one is capable of practicing the true holy life (brahmacarya).
Having attained the unsurpassed eye, as taught by the Kinsman of the Sun;
he constantly guards himself, advances while free from the latent tendencies,
severs all fetters, and subdues Māra and his retinue.
"He has transcended the world; it is said that he has attained the exhaustion of all outflows.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Eighth Discourse on the Eight Difficulties ends here, totaling one thousand thirty-three words. 125. The Discourse on Poverty (125), the Ninth Discourse in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the Third Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Is it a great suffering for a person in this world who possesses desire and is impoverished?
The bhikṣus replied: [Yes, World-Honored One.]
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus again, saying:
"If there is a person who, being poor and desirous, borrows wealth from another's house; in this world, is borrowing wealth from another's house a great suffering?
The bhikṣus replied, "It is so."
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Suppose there is a person who borrows wealth or goods but is unable to repay it at the appointed time, and says: [as follows]"
"A long-drawn breath.
"Is a long-drawn breath in this world considered a great suffering?
The bhikṣus replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus again, saying:
“If there is a person who borrows money and does not repay it for a long time, and the creditor demands it back— would the creditor’s demand for repayment in this world be a great suffering?
The bhikṣus replied, “It would be so.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“Suppose there is a person who owes a creditor money, but is unable to repay it. The creditor repeatedly goes to that person’s place to demand payment. Is it a great suffering in this world for the creditor to repeatedly go to that person’s place to demand payment?”
The bhikṣus replied,
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
The Blessed One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Suppose there is a person who owes money, and the creditor goes repeatedly to him to demand repayment, but he intentionally does not return it; consequently, he is seized and bound by the creditor. Is being seized and bound by a creditor in this world a great suffering?"
The bhikṣus replied,
“It is so, World-Honored One!”

"This is what constitutes the great suffering for those with desire in the world: that those with desire in the world are impoverished is a great suffering; that those with desire in the world borrow goods and wealth is a great suffering; that those with desire in the world incur long-term interest on their loans is a great suffering; that those with desire in the world are pursued and demanded by creditors is a great suffering; that those with desire in the world are repeatedly visited at home by creditors seeking repayment is a great suffering; and that those with desire in the world are bound and imprisoned by creditors is a great suffering."

Thus, if there is one who, within this noble Dharma, lacks faith in wholesome qualities, lacks restraint, lacks extensive learning, lacks generosity, and lacks wisdom regarding wholesome qualities—even if they possess much gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mani-jewels, white conch, shell-discs, coral, amber, agate, tortoise-shell, carnelian, beryl, red stone, and jade beads—they are nonetheless poor and lack power and influence; this, I declare in my noble Dharma, is the poverty of unwholesomeness.
"Those evil deeds of body, speech, and mind are, in my noble Dharma, called 'unwholesome borrowing.

When one desires to conceal those evil deeds of body and does not reveal them, does not wish to speak of them, does not wish for others to censure them, and does not seek to rectify them; when one likewise desires to conceal those evil deeds of speech and mind and does not reveal them, does not wish to speak of them, does not wish for others to censure them, and does not seek to rectify them—this, in my noble Dharma, is called 'unwholesome long-term interest.'"
Whether he is walking through a village or outside a village, those fellow practitioners of the holy life who see him will say:
"Venerable sirs!
This person acts in such a way, behaves in such a way, is so evil, and is so impure; he is a thorn to this village."
He spoke thus: "Venerable friends!

I do not act in such a way, I do not practice in such a way, I am not so evil, and I am not so impure; nor am I a thorn to the village or town. This is what is called 'the reproach of the unwholesome' as taught within our Noble Dharma."
"Whether he is in a secluded place, or in a mountain forest under a tree, or dwelling in a quiet retreat, he entertains three unwholesome thoughts:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness. In my noble Dharma, these are called the unwholesome states that one frequently seeks out."

He engages in misconduct of body, speech, and mind; having engaged in such misconduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will certainly go to a state of misery and be born in hell. This, in my noble Dharma, is called the unwholesome bond.
I do not see any other bondage that is more painful, more heavy, more coarse, or more unpleasant than the bondage of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
"These three bonds of suffering have been known and extinguished by the Arhat bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted; he has uprooted them so that there will never again be a future birth.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke this verse:
"The suffering of poverty in the world, Borrowing money and wealth from others..."
Having lent money and wealth, one suffers the distress of being pursued by others.
When the creditor goes to demand repayment, one is consequently seized and bound;
this bondage is a most grievous suffering, yet people in the world delight in sensual desires.
It is the same regarding the noble Dharma: if one lacks right faith, and is without shame or dread of blame, one will commit evil and unwholesome deeds.
One performs unwholesome actions with the body, and likewise with speech and mind.
Concealing [one's faults] and being unwilling to speak of them, one does not delight in the correction of the True Teaching.
If one repeatedly engages in such conduct, the mind will be afflicted by suffering;
whether in a village or in a secluded place, this will inevitably lead to remorse.
Through bodily and verbal habitual practices, as well as the thoughts of the mind, evil karma increases ever more;
one acts and acts again repeatedly.
That evil karma lacks wisdom; having performed many unwholesome deeds, [it leads to suffering].
Once one has completed whatever [deeds] have arisen, one will inevitably go to be bound in hell.
This bondage is most grievous suffering; it is that from which the heroic and powerful are free.
By acquiring wealth and profit in accordance with the Dharma, one attains peace and security without being burdened by debt.
Giving brings joy, and both parties obtain benefit;
thus, for such householders, merit increases through giving.
In this same way, within the Noble Dharma, if there is one who possesses sincere faith, [they shall likewise find great increase].
Fully endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, may one be free from stinginess and greed.
Having abandoned the five hindrances, always delighting in the practice of diligence,
and having accomplished the various meditative concentrations, may one remain ever content while renouncing worldly pleasures.
Having attained the bliss of non-nutriment, Pure as one bathed in water, With an unshakable mind liberated, All fetters of existence are exhausted.
Health is Nirvana; It is called the unsurpassed lamp.
"Free from sorrow, free from dust, and at peace—this is called immovability.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Dāridrya Sūtra*, the ninth, ends here; one thousand ten characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Scroll Twenty-nine; eight thousand eight hundred three characters.
The *Madhyama Āgama*, Scroll Thirty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
126. The Discourse on Sexual Conduct (126). Chapter on the Great Practices, Discourse on Sexual Conduct, Number Ten, Third Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"How many people in the world, householder, engage in sensual desire?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Householder!"
In this world, there are ten types of people who engage in sensual desire. What are these ten?

Householder, there is one type of person who engages in sensual desire who seeks wealth through unlawful and unrighteous means. Having sought wealth through unlawful and unrighteous means, he does not provide for his own well-being and security, nor for his parents, wife, children, slaves, or servants; nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life.
Thus, there is one person who pursues sensual desires. Furthermore, householder, there is another person who pursues sensual desires who seeks wealth through unrighteous and immoral means.

Having sought wealth through unrighteous and immoral means, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and servants; yet he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and receive the karmic reward of rebirth in heaven with long life.
Thus there is one person who practices sensual desire. Furthermore, householder, there is another person who practices sensual desire who seeks wealth through unrighteous and immoral means.

Having sought wealth through unrighteous and immoral means, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers; he also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with it, receive the fruit of bliss, and be reborn in heaven with long life.
Thus there is one person who pursues sensual desires.
"Furthermore, householder, there is another person who pursues sensual desires;

he seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, he does not provide for his own well-being and security, nor for his parents, wife, children, slaves, or laborers; nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life."
Thus there is one person who indulges in sensual desires. Furthermore, householder, there is another person who indulges in sensual desires;

he seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth by lawful and unlawful means, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers, yet he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, receive the fruit of bliss, and be reborn in heaven with long life.
Thus there is one person who pursues sensual desires.
Furthermore, householder, there is another person who pursues sensual desires;

he seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through both lawful and unlawful means, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers. He also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life.
"Thus there is one person who pursues sensual desires.
Furthermore, householder, there is another person who pursues sensual desires;

he seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path. Having sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path, he does not provide for his own well-being and security, nor for his parents, wife, children, servants, or laborers; nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life."

Thus there is one person who pursues sensual pleasures. Furthermore, householder, there is another person who pursues sensual pleasures who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path;

having sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers, yet he does not make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and receive the karmic reward of rebirth in heaven with long life.
"Thus, there is one who is a person practicing sensual desire.

Furthermore, householder, there is another person practicing sensual desire who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path; having sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path, he is able to provide for his own security and well-being, as well as for his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers, and also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and receive the karmic fruit of rebirth in heaven with long life."
Having acquired wealth and possessions, one becomes attached to them; being bound by attachment, one fails to see their dangers and, unaware of the way of escape, uses them.
Such is the person who pursues sensual desires.

Furthermore, householder, there is a person of sensual desire who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path. Having sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path, he is able to provide for his own well-being and security, as well as for his parents, wife, children, servants, and laborers; he also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life.

Having acquired wealth and goods, one is neither stained nor attached to them; one is neither bound nor entangled by them; being unentangled and unstained, one perceives their peril and disadvantage and employs them with knowledge of the way of escape.
"Thus there is one who is a person of sensual indulgence.
'Householder!

If there is a person of sensual indulgence who seeks wealth through unrighteousness and lack of moral conduct, and having sought wealth through unrighteousness and lack of moral conduct, does not provide for his own well-being and security, nor for his parents, wife, children, slaves, or laborers; nor does he make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins so that they may ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life—this person of sensual indulgence is the lowest among all persons of sensual indulgence.'"
"Householder!

Suppose there is a person driven by sensual desire who seeks wealth through both lawful and unlawful means. Having sought wealth through lawful and unlawful means, he maintains himself in comfort, as well as his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers; he also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, and be reborn in heaven with long life. Such a person driven by sensual desire is the most excellent among all those driven by sensual desire."
“Householder!

Suppose there is a person of desire who seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path; having sought wealth in accordance with the Dharma and by the right path, he maintains himself in security, as well as his parents, wife, children, slaves, and laborers, and also makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins, causing them to ascend to higher realms, experience happiness together with joy, receive the fruit of happiness, and be reborn in heaven with long life.”

Having obtained wealth and property, one who is neither stained nor attached, neither bound nor entangled, and who—being unentangled—is free from defilement and attachment, seeing its peril and knowing the way of escape while using it: such a person among those who desire conditioned phenomena is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most venerable, and the most sublime among all who desire conditioned phenomena.

It is just as there is milk because of the cow; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the essence of butter. This essence of butter is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most venerable, and the most sublime of all.
In this way, householder,
among those who desire conditioned phenomena, one who practices this path is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most venerable, and the most sublime.
Then, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If one seeks wealth through what is not Dharma, Or through both Dharma and non-Dharma,
One neither makes offerings nor uses it oneself, Nor bestows it as a gift for the sake of merit."
Both possess evil, and among those who indulge in sensual desires, they are the lowest.
If one seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma, obtaining it through one's own diligent effort,
and uses it for the sake of others as well as oneself, one also creates merit through such giving.
Both possess virtue, yet they are supreme among those who indulge in sensual desires.
If one attains the wisdom of liberation, even while indulging in desires as a householder,
seeing their perils and practicing contentment, using wealth with moderation—
"He has attained wisdom that transcends desire; among those who practice desire, he is supreme.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Kāmasutta*, the tenth, ends here, totaling one thousand two hundred and fifty-three characters. 127. *Puññābhisandasutta* (127), the eleventh discourse in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
“How many kinds of persons who are fields of merit exist in the world?
The World-Honored One replied,
“Householder!”
In the world, there are generally two kinds of persons who are fields of merit.
What are these two?
First, those in training (śaikṣa); second, those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
There are eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Householder!
What are the eighteen types of those in training?

The one who practices through faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the one who practices through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the one liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the one attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), the one realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), the one who goes from family to family (*kulaṃkula*), the one with only one interval remaining (*ekavīcika*), the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattipratipannaka*), the one who has attained stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka*), the one who has attained once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmipratipannaka*), the one who has attained non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and the one who flows upward to the Akaniṣṭha heaven (*ūrdhvasrotas akaniṣṭhaparama*): these are called the eighteen persons in training (*śaikṣa*).
"Householder!
What are the nine persons beyond training? They are:

the one who contemplates the Dharma, the one who advances in the Dharma, the one of immovable nature, the one of a nature prone to fall back, the one of a nature not prone to fall back, the one who guards the Dharma—falling back if they do not guard it and not falling back if they do guard it—the one who dwells in reality, the one liberated by wisdom, and the one doubly liberated. These are called the nine persons beyond training."
Then, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“Those in the world who are in training and those beyond training, Who are worthy of honor and reverence—
They are able to rectify their bodies, And likewise their speech and minds.”
"The lay devotee is a fertile field; by giving to him, one obtains great merit.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the lay devotee Anāthapiṇḍada and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Kṣetra-guṇa Sūtra*, the eleventh, ends here with two hundred and sixty-seven characters. 128. The *Upāsaka Sūtra* (128), the twelfth in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, together with a great assembly of five hundred upāsakas, went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was, prostrated himself in salutation, and withdrew to sit to one side; the five hundred upāsakas likewise prostrated themselves in salutation and withdrew to sit to one side.

Once the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and the five hundred upāsakas were seated to one side, the Venerable Śāriputra taught them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; he taught them the Dharma through countless skillful means.
Having inspired them with longing and brought them to a state of joy, he rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Not long after the Venerable Sāriputta had departed, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and five hundred lay followers also went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side.
When the Venerable Sāriputta and the assembly had taken their seats, the Blessed One addressed him, saying: "Sāriputta,

if you know that a noble disciple who is a lay follower well guards his practice of the five dharmas and attains the four higher mental states, he dwells in happiness in this very life, and these are easily attained without difficulty."

"Śāriputra! You should declare that for the noble disciple, the hells are exhausted; the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and all other evil destinations are also exhausted. Having attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), he does not fall into evil states, is destined for perfect enlightenment, and will undergo at most seven more existences; after seven往返 (returns and goings) between the heavens and the human world, he shall reach the end of suffering."

“Sāriputta! How does a noble lay disciple properly guard his practice of the five dharmas? A noble lay disciple abstains from killing and abandons killing; he discards the sword and staff, possesses a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing, and possesses a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, seeking the welfare of all beings down to the smallest insects.”
"He purifies his mind regarding the taking of life; this noble disciple in white robes practices with careful protection—this is the first dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The noble disciple clad in white leaves taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, delights in giving and taking, is always fond of generosity, rejoices without stinginess, does not look for reward, is not obscured by theft, and constantly protects himself.
"He purifies his mind regarding taking what is not given; this is the second dharma by which a noble disciple who is a white-robed lay follower practices well-guarded conduct.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The noble disciple clad in white avoids sexual misconduct and abandons sexual misconduct. Whether she is protected by her father, or protected by her mother, or protected by both parents; whether she is protected by her brothers, or protected by her sisters, or protected by her husband’s parents; whether she is protected by her relatives, or protected by those of the same clan; or whether she is another man’s wife, subject to the fear of flogging and punishment, or even one who has been formally betrothed with a garland—such women he does not violate.
"He purifies his mind regarding sexual misconduct; this noble disciple in white robes practices with proper restraint—this is the third quality.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The noble disciple clad in white leaves false speech and abandons false speech; he speaks the truth, delights in the truth, abides in the truth unshakably, is entirely trustworthy, and does not deceive the world.
"He purifies his mind regarding false speech; this is the fourth quality of a noble disciple who is well-guarded in conduct, Śāriputra.
Furthermore, Śāriputra:"
The noble disciple clad in white abstains from liquor and abandons liquor.
He purifies his mind regarding the drinking of liquor; this, for the noble disciple clad in white who practices well-guarded conduct, is the fifth quality.
“Sāriputta! How does a noble disciple who is a layperson attain the four states of higher mind that dwell in happiness in the present life, which are easy to obtain and not difficult?

A noble disciple who is a layperson recollects the Tathāgata: ‘That Tathāgata is the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader, the Trainer of persons, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’”

Having thus recollected the Tathāgata, any evil desires that may exist are immediately extinguished; furthermore, whatever unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts exist within the mind are likewise extinguished.
When a noble disciple clad in white takes the Tathāgata as their object of focus, the mind becomes tranquil and attains joy.
If there are evil desires, they are immediately extinguished; likewise, whatever unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing states exist within the mind are also extinguished.
"The white-robed noble disciple attains the foremost state of higher mind, dwelling in happiness in this very life; it is easily attained and not difficult to obtain.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

The noble disciple clad in white recollects the Dharma: "The Dharma well-expounded by the Blessed One leads inevitably to the ultimate goal; it is free from affliction and feverish distress, and is eternally constant and unchanging."

Having thus observed, thus awakened, thus known, and thus reflected upon the Dharma, any evil desires that may exist are immediately extinguished; likewise, whatever unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing states exist within the mind are also extinguished.
When a noble disciple who is a lay follower takes the Dharma as an object of focus, their mind becomes tranquil and attains joy.
Any evil desires that may arise are immediately extinguished, and whatever unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing states exist within the mind are likewise extinguished.
The noble disciple in white robes attains this second higher mind.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the noble disciple in white robes recollects the Saṅgha:

"The noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata is well-directed and rightly directed; it proceeds toward the Dharma and follows the Dharma in due order; that Saṅgha truly possesses the four pairs and the eight classes of noble ones—the Arhats and those practicing for Arhatship, the Anāgāmins and those practicing for Anāgāminship, the Sakṛdāgāmins and those practicing for Sakṛdāgāminship, and the Srotāpannas and those practicing for Srotāpanna-ship. This is called the four pairs and eight classes.

That is to say, the assembly of Tathāgatas has accomplished ethical discipline (*śīla*), accomplished meditative concentration (*samādhi*), accomplished wisdom (*prajñā*), accomplished liberation (*vimukti*), and accomplished the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśana*); they are worthy of reverence and respect, worthy of honor and offerings, and are the excellent field of merit for the world.

As he thus recollects the assembly of the Tathāgata, any evil desires that may arise are immediately extinguished; likewise, any unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts within his mind are also extinguished.

When a noble disciple who is a layperson takes the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata as their object of focus, their mind becomes tranquil and attains joy; if there are evil desires, they are immediately extinguished, and whatever unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing states exist within the mind are likewise extinguished.
“Śāriputra, this noble disciple clad in white robes is said to have attained the third higher mind, an abiding in happiness in the present life, which is easily obtained and not difficult to attain.
Furthermore, Śāriputra...”

The noble disciple clad in white reflects upon his own precepts (*śīla*): "These precepts of mine are unbroken and unperforated; they are untainted and unpolluted; they stand firm like the earth, are not false, are praised by the noble ones, and are fully and properly undertaken."

As he thus reflects upon himself, any evil desires that arise are immediately extinguished; likewise, any unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing thoughts within his mind are also extinguished.

When a noble disciple who is a lay follower takes the *śīla* (precepts) as his object of focus, his mind becomes tranquil and attains joy; if any evil desires arise, they are immediately extinguished, and any unwholesome, defiled, sorrowful, or distressing states within his mind are likewise extinguished.
“Śāriputra, this noble disciple in white robes is said to have attained the fourth higher mind, dwelling in happiness in the present life, which is easy to attain and not difficult. Śāriputra,

if you know that a noble disciple in white robes who well guards and practices these five dharmas attains these four higher minds and dwells in happiness in the present life, which is easy to attain and not difficult— then, Śāriputra!”

I declare that for you, a noble disciple living as a layperson, hell is exhausted; the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and all other evil states are also exhausted. You have attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, are no longer subject to falling into lower realms, and are destined for perfect enlightenment. At most, you will undergo seven more existences; after seven往返 (rounds) between the heavens and the human world, you shall reach the end of suffering.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The wise person dwelling at home, Seeing the terrors of hell,
By upholding the noble Dharma, Eliminates all evil."
Do not harm living beings; knowing this, be able to renounce such acts.
Speak no falsehoods regarding the truth, and do not steal the wealth of others.
Be content with your own wife and take no pleasure in the wives of others.
Abandoning and renouncing the drinking of intoxicants— the root of mental confusion and madness—
one should always be mindful of the Perfectly Awakened One, contemplate all wholesome dharmas,
and maintain mindfulness of the Sangha while observing the impurity of the body; from this, one shall obtain joy.
One who wishes to practice giving should do so with the hope of its blessings;
first give to those whose minds are stilled, and in this way one will achieve the fruit of retribution.
I shall now speak of those whose minds are stilled; Śāriputra, you should listen well.
Whether black or white, red or yellow,
brindled or of lovely hue— be they oxen or various pigeons—
wherever they may be born, a skilled driver keeps them before him.
With physical strength fully perfected, moving swiftly and with ease, one should adopt whatever is beneficial;
do not consider outward form to be wrong.
Thus, in this human world, wherever one may be born, [one should act accordingly].
Whether they be kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or craftsmen—
wherever such elders dwell, maintaining pure precepts,
and who are unattached to the world, the Sugatas— to give to them brings great fruit.
Foolish and ignorant, lacking wisdom and learning, one who gives to such a person obtains little fruit; they possess no light and shed no radiance.
But if there is light that sheds radiance, it belongs to the wise disciples of the Buddha.
Those who place faith in the Sugata have roots that grow and are firmly established.
They are born in auspicious realms and enter the homes of noble families at will;
finally attaining nirvana, they each possess their own specific conditions.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the Venerable Śāriputra, the monks, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, and the five hundred upāsakas rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Upāsaka Sūtra, Chapter Twelve, ends here; 1,549 characters. 129. The Enemy Sūtra (129), Middle Āgama, Great Division, The Enemy Sūtra, Chapter Thirteen, Third Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are seven ways of acting as an enemy that constitute being an enemy; these occur when men and women are overcome by anger."
What are the seven?
An enemy does not wish for an enemy to possess a beautiful appearance. Why is that?

Regarding an enemy: one does not delight in an enemy possessing a beautiful complexion. When a person harbors ill will, is habituated to ill will, is overwhelmed by ill will, and their mind does not relinquish ill will, then even though they may bathe well and anoint their body with famous perfumes, their complexion remains ugly.
Why is this? Because one is shrouded by ill will and the mind does not relinquish it.
This is called the first dharma of an enemy that acts as an enemy: namely, when states of ill will arise in men and women.
"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for an enemy to sleep in peace. Why is this?
Because an enemy does not delight in an enemy sleeping in peace; when a person is full of hatred, habituated to hatred, and enveloped by hatred, their mind does not relinquish that hatred."

Although he lies upon a couch spread with woolen rugs and fine carpets, covered with brocades, silks, and gauzes, with a body-cushion and pillows at both ends, and with *kāliṅga-paṭalikā* and *pārāśvatara-nīla* blankets, he nevertheless sleeps in sorrow and distress.
Why is this? Because they are shrouded by ill will and their minds do not relinquish it.
This is called the second dharma of an enemy that acts as an enemy: namely, when men and women are overcome by ill will.
"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for an enemy to obtain great benefit. Why is this?
An enemy does not delight in an enemy obtaining great benefit; when a person harbors ill will, habituates to ill will, is overwhelmed by ill will, and their mind does not relinquish ill will."
That which ought to gain profit fails to gain it, while that which ought not to gain profit gains it.
These two conditions contradict one another, resulting in a great lack of benefit.
Why is this? Because one is shrouded by ill will and the mind does not relinquish that ill will.
This is called the third dharma of an enemy that acts as an enemy, namely: when men and women are overcome by ill will.
"Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for his enemy to have friends. Why is this?
Because an enemy does not delight in his enemy having friends; when a person is full of hatred, habituated to hatred, and overwhelmed by hatred, their mind does not relinquish that hatred."
If he has relatives or friends, they will abandon him and avoid him. Why is this?
Because he is shrouded by anger and his mind does not relinquish that anger.
This is called the fourth way an enemy acts as an enemy: when men and women come to him while they are full of anger.
Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for the enemy to have a good reputation.
Why is this? An enemy does not delight in an enemy having a good reputation; when a person harbors hatred, practices hatred, is overwhelmed by hatred, and their mind does not relinquish hatred.
That evil reputation and ugliness will spread its fame in all directions. Why is this?
Because he is shrouded by hatred and his mind does not relinquish hatred.
This is called the fifth way an enemy acts as an enemy: when men and women come upon one while they are filled with anger.
Furthermore, an enemy does not wish for their enemy to be exceedingly wealthy.

Why is that? An enemy does not delight in the extreme wealth of an enemy; when a person is possessed by anger, habituated to anger, and overwhelmed by anger, their mind does not relinquish that anger.
He engages in such conduct of body, speech, and mind that he causes himself to lose great wealth. Why is this?
Because he is shrouded by anger and his mind does not relinquish its anger.
This is called the sixth way in which an enemy acts as an enemy: when men and women are overcome by anger.
Furthermore, an enemy does not desire that his enemy’s body be destroyed and his life end, nor does he wish for him to surely reach a good destination and be reborn in heaven.

Why is this so? An enemy does not wish for an enemy to go to a good destination. When a person is full of hatred, habituates to hatred, is overwhelmed by hatred, and does not relinquish hatred from the mind, they engage in misconduct of body, speech, and mind. Having committed such misconduct of body, speech, and mind, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will inevitably go to a bad destination and be reborn in hell.
Why is this? Because one is shrouded by ill will and the mind does not relinquish it.
This is called the seventh dharma of an enemy that acts as an enemy: namely, when men and women are overcome by ill will.
"These seven types of enemies act as enemies; they are those among men and women who come when one is filled with anger.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The angry person acquires an ugly complexion, And sleeps in painful unrest."
One who ought to obtain great wealth instead obtains only misfortune;
though surrounded by kinsmen and good friends, he remains far removed from those who are free of anger.
By repeatedly practicing anger, his ill repute spreads in all directions.
Through anger one performs deeds of body and speech; through the fetter of resentment one carries out mental karma.
When a person is overwhelmed by resentment, they lose all their wealth and possessions.
Anger gives rise to disadvantage; anger gives rise to mental defilement.
Fear arises within, yet people do not perceive it.
The angry person does not know the meaning; the angry person does not understand the Dharma.
Sightless, blind, and obscured by darkness—such is one who delights in anger.
When anger first arises, it manifests as an ugly countenance, just as smoke begins to rise when fire is first kindled.
From this, hatred and envy are born, and because of this, people become resentful.
Whatever one who is angry does— whether it be a virtuous deed or an unwholesome one—[it is all tainted by that state].
When anger has subsequently ceased, the feverish heat burns like fire.
Regarding this so-called feverish heat of karma, and those various phenomena by which one is entangled—I shall now speak of each of them; listen with attentive minds.
The one who harbors hatred may even kill his father, as well as his brothers, and likewise slay his sisters;
the hater commits many acts of destruction.
Those whom he has begotten and nurtured— only through such a person does this world come to be seen.
Because of him she was able to remain alive, yet this mother, out of anger, would have harmed her.
Lacking shame and a sense of propriety, bound by wrath, there is nothing one will not say;
when a person is overwhelmed by hatred, there is no word they will not utter.
Committing the transgression of delusion, one brings about one's own premature death;
unaware at the time of doing so, one gives rise to terror through anger.
Bound and attached to one’s own body, one’s craving and delight become boundless.
Though one may cherish one's own body, the angry person brings harm upon themselves:
they may pierce themselves with a blade, throw themselves from a cliff,
hang themselves with a rope, or consume various poisonous drugs.
Such as this is anger; death has its basis in anger.
When all such things are severed, one is able to awaken through wisdom.
Even minor unwholesome karmas, the wise are able to eliminate through their understanding.
One should endure this practice, desiring that there be no foul appearance;
being without anger and without sorrow, removing the smoke and being free from arrogance;
taming oneself to sever ill-will, one extinguishes all outflows until none remain.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The thirteenth discourse, “The Enemy,” ends here, totaling one thousand one hundred and fifteen characters. 130. The Discourse Teaching Udāyin (130) The Great Chapter of the Madhyama Āgama, the fourteenth discourse, “Teaching Udāyin,” for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta served as the overseer of the monastery for the elders of his native village; he was honored by the people, yet he was violent, hasty, and cruel, being exceedingly coarse and harsh. He reviled and rebuked the bhikṣus, and because of this, the bhikṣus from his native village all abandoned him and departed, finding no pleasure in staying there.
Thereupon, the upāsakas of Sāvatthī, seeing that all the bhikkhus of Sāvatthī had departed and did not wish to remain there, thought to themselves:
"For what reason have all these bhikkhus of Sāvatthī abandoned us and departed, no longer wishing to dwell here?"

When the lay followers (*upāsaka*) of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka heard that the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka—the elder of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka who served as the master of the monastery (*vihārasvāmin*) and was honored by all—had become violent, impetuous, and wicked, being exceedingly coarse and harsh, reviling and rebuking the monks, for this reason the monks of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka all abandoned him and departed, finding no pleasure in staying there.

When the lay followers (upāsaka) of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka heard this, they immediately went together to the place where the Venerable Dharmika was staying, drove him out, and compelled him to leave all the monasteries of Sthūlakoṣṭhaka.

Thereupon, the Venerable Dāmali, having been driven out by the lay followers of his native land and compelled to leave the monasteries of that region, gathered his robes and took up his bowl to wander forth. Traveling on, he eventually reached Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thereupon, the Venerable Dabba approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!

Among the lay followers (*upāsaka*) of my birthplace, I have committed no offense, made no improper statement, and committed no transgression; yet those lay followers of my birthplace have unjustly driven me out, ordering me to leave the monasteries of my birthplace."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Stop, stop, Dāmi!
Why is it necessary to speak of this?"
The Venerable Dāmali joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed him a second time, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Regarding the lay followers (*upāsaka*) of my native land, I have defiled nothing, said nothing, nor committed any offense against them; yet the lay followers of my native land have unjustly driven me out, forcing me to leave the monasteries of my native land.”
The Blessed One also spoke a second time:

"Dāmali! In the past, there were merchants in this Jambudvīpa who boarded a ship and entered the ocean, taking a shore-scouting hawk with them. Once they had not traveled far into the great ocean, they released the shore-scouting hawk; if the shore-scouting hawk reached the edge of the great ocean, it would never return to the ship."
"Just as a hawk watching the shore, if it cannot reach the great ocean, returns to the ship;
even so, Tāmī, because you were driven out by the upāsakas born in that land and forced to leave the various monasteries of that land, you have returned to my presence."
"Stop, stop, Dāman!
Why must you speak further of this?
The Venerable Dāman replied for a third time:

“World-Honored One, regarding the lay followers (*upāsaka*) of my native land, I have defiled none, spoken ill of none, nor committed any offense against them; yet the lay followers of my native land have unjustly driven me out, forcing me to leave the monasteries of my native land.”
The Blessed One also addressed him three times, saying:
"Dhammika! Do you abide in the way of the śramaṇas, yet are you being driven out by the upāsakas of your native land, so that you must leave the monasteries of your native land?"
Thereupon, the Venerable Dāmali rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One,
how does a śramaṇa abide in the dharma of a śramaṇa?”
The Blessed One said:
"Dāmali! In the past, there were people whose lifespan was eighty thousand years."

"Dammi! When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, this Jambudvīpa will be exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a vast population; the villages and towns will be so close together that a cock could fly from one to another."
"Daṃmī! When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, girls marry at the age of five hundred. Daṃmī!"
When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be such diseases as excrement, urine, desire, lack of appetite, and old age. Tāmi!

When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, there will be a king named Gārava, intelligent and wise, who will be a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) possessing a fourfold army; he will rule the world righteously as a Dharma-king, endowed with the seven treasures.

Those seven treasures are the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the minister-of-war treasure; these are the seven.

He will possess a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, courageous and fearless, capable of subduing all opposing hosts. He will surely rule over this entire earth as far as the great ocean, not by means of the sword or staff, but through the Dharma, bringing about peace and security.
“Tāmra, King Kāla has a tree named Supatiṭṭha-nigrodharāja. Tāmra!”
The King of Nyagrodha Trees was firmly established and possessed five branches: the first branch provided food for the king and the queen;
the second branch provided food for the crown prince and the ministers.
The third branch is the food of the people of the country.
The fourth branch is the food of recluses and brahmins.
The fifth branch is the food of birds and beasts.
"Tammi! The fruits of the well-established king of trees, the nyagrodha, are as large as two-sheng jars and have a flavor like pure honey balls. Tammi!"
The fruits of the king of trees, the well-established Nyagrodha, have no owner and there is no mutual stealing among them.

A certain person came, extremely emaciated by hunger and thirst and with a haggard complexion; desiring to eat the fruit, he went to the place where the king of trees, the well-established Nyagrodha, stood. Having eaten his fill of the fruit, he broke off its branches and departed carrying the fruit with him.
A certain deva dwelt in dependence upon the king of trees, the Nyagrodha, and he thought:
"How strange are the people of Jambudvīpa!
They are ungrateful and lack any sense of reciprocity."

Why is this? Because after one has eaten one's fill of the fruit from the well-established king of nyagrodha trees and then breaks off its branches to carry the fruit away, it would rather cause the well-established king of nyagrodha trees to become fruitless and cease producing fruit.
"The *Nyagrodha* king tree, Sthira, has no fruit and does not produce fruit.

Then another person came, extremely emaciated from hunger and thirst, his complexion haggard, desiring to eat fruit. He went to where the *Nyagrodha* king tree, Sthira, was located; seeing that the *Nyagrodha* king tree, Sthira, had no fruit and did not produce fruit, he immediately went to King Kāla and said:
"O Heavenly King!..."
"You should know that the well-established King of Nyagrodha Trees bears no fruit, nor does it produce fruit.

Having heard this, King Gālava—like a strong man extending or contracting his arm—vanished from Kośala and appeared before Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Standing before Śakra, he said: "Kauśika! [The Blessed One has said: 'You should know that the well-established King of Nyagrodha Trees bears no fruit, nor does it produce fruit.'"
"You should know that the well-established King of Nyagrodha Trees bears no fruit, nor does it produce fruit.
Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and King Gālava vanished from among the Thirty-three Gods and arrived at Kurūsu in the space of time it takes for a strong man to flex or extend his arm.

Not far from where the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Sālavatī, stood, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, exercised his psychic power of transformation to create a great torrent of water and a violent storm. Having created this great torrent of water and violent storm, he uprooted the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Sālavatī, and cast it down, standing it on its roots.

Thereupon, the tree deity who dwells in the king of nyagrodha trees, Sthira, became distressed, sorrowful, and despondent because of this; weeping with tears streaming down his face, he stood before Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, asked: "O Deva!
For what reason do you stand before me, distressed by sorrow and grief, weeping and shedding tears?"
That deva replied: "Kauśika!
You should know that even when great waters and violent storms arise, the king of trees, the well-established Nyagrodha, remains with its roots pulled up and stands upright."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said to that tree deity: "O Deva!
You who abide by the dharma of tree deities—did the great waters and violent winds and rains uproot and overturn the King of Trees, the Nyagrodha, while you remained well-established within it?"
The tree deity replied:
"Kauśika! How does a tree deity abide in the dharma of a tree deity?"
The Lord Śakra replied: "O Deva!

If a person wishes to take the root of a tree and carries the root away, or wishes to take the trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits of the tree and carries them away, the tree-deva should not become angry, should not feel hatred or envy, and should harbor no resentment in his heart."
"The tree deity abandons its intention and dwells as a tree deity; thus does the tree deity abide in the dharma of a tree deity.
The deva spoke again, saying: "Kauśika!"

"I, the tree deity, did not abide by the dharma of tree deities; from this day forward, I shall abide by the dharma of tree deities. May the Nyagrodha tree king, the sovereign of trees, be restored to its original state."

Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested his supernormal power (ṛddhi) accordingly; having manifested that supernormal power, he further conjured a great flood and a violent storm. Once the great flood and the violent storm had been conjured, the King of Nyagrodha Trees, Supratiṣṭhita, was restored to its former state.
In this way, Dāmali!
If there is a bhikṣu who does not revile one who reviles him, does not become angry at one who is angry, does not break [the harmony] with one who breaks it, and does not strike one who strikes him.
"In this way, Dāmali,
a śramaṇa dwells in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
