Thereupon, the Venerable Dāmali rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and with tears streaming down his face, said weeping:
“World-Honored One!
I am not a śramaṇa dwelling in the dharma of a śramaṇa; from this day forward, I shall be a śramaṇa dwelling in the dharma of a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Tāmra! In the past there was a Great Teacher named Sunetra, who was revered as a master by the non-Buddhist seers; he had abandoned sensual desire and attained the bases of psychic power.”
"Taṃmī! The Great Teacher Sunetra has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. Taṃmī!"
The Great Teacher Sunetra taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world to his disciples. Tāmra!

When the Great Teacher Sunetra taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world, among those disciples there were some who did not fully practice the Dharma; after their lives ended, they were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

"Taṃmī! When the Great Teacher Sunetra teaches the Dharma of the Brahma-world, if among his disciples there are those who fully practice the Dharma, they cultivate the four brahmavihāras and abandon sensual desire; at the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the Brahma-heaven."
"Tammi! At that time, the Great Teacher Sunetra had this thought:

'I should not go to the next world and be born in the same place as my disciples. It would be better for me now to further cultivate superior loving-kindness; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of my life, I shall attain birth among the Ābhāsvara devas.'"

"Tammi! At that time, the Great Teacher Sunetra further cultivated superior loving-kindness; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of his life, he was reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas."

"Taṃmī! The Great Teacher Sunetra and his disciples have not practiced the path in vain; they have attained great fruits. Just as it was with the Great Teacher Sunetra, so it was with Mūlika Pāṭimātṛputra, the Brahmin Araṇemi, Ghoṭamukha, Hatthaka Āḷavaka, Cūḷa-Māluṅkyaputta, and Satyabhūti."
“Dāmi! The seven teachers, including Purāṇa Kāśyapa, also each had immeasurable hundreds of thousands of disciples. Dāmi!”
The teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world to his disciples.

When the teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa taught the Dharma of the Brahma-world, among those disciples there were some who did not fully practice the Dharma; after their lives ended, they were reborn either in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, or in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, or in the Yāma Heaven, or in the Tuṣita Heaven, or in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

When the teacher Pūraṇa Kāśyapa teaches the Dharma of the Brahma-world, if there are disciples who fully practice the teaching, they cultivate the four Brahma-abodes and abandon desire; at the end of their lives, they attain rebirth in the Brahma-heaven.
"Dammi! The seven teachers, the Pūraṇas, had this thought:

'I should not go to the next world and be born in the same place as my disciples. It would be better for me now to further cultivate superior loving-kindness; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of my life, I shall attain birth among the Ābhāsvara gods.'"

"Dammi! At that time, those seven Pūraṇa Kāśyapa teachers later further cultivated superior loving-kindness; having cultivated superior loving-kindness, at the end of their lives they were reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas."
"Tammi! The seven Purāṇa Kassapas, along with their disciples, have practiced the path not in vain and have attained great fruits. Tammi!"

If one reviles those seven teachers along with their immeasurable hundreds of thousands of retinues, striking them, inciting anger, and reproaching them, one will certainly undergo immeasurable suffering.

If there is a bhikṣu who is a disciple of the Buddha established in right view and has attained a minor fruit, and one reviles, strikes, incites anger toward, and reproaches him, the suffering one undergoes for this is even greater than that.
Therefore, Dhammika!
You should each take turns protecting one another. Why is that?
"Once one is free from these faults, there is no further loss.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Sujāta, Mūlapaṇṇaka, Āḷavaka the brahmin, Gotamīśataka, Hatthidipa the māṇava, Cūḷa-Māluṅkyaputta, Saccabandhu."
"In a past age, there were seven teachers of renown and virtue;
free from the bonds of craving, they delighted in compassion, and their fetters of desire were exhausted in the past.
They had disciples numbering in the hundreds of thousands."
Even if they have abandoned the fetters of desire, yet for a moment do not reach the ultimate;
if those external seers, while well-guarded in their practice of asceticism,
harbor hatred and jealousy in their hearts, the one who reviles them will suffer much retribution.
If one who has attained right view, A son of the Buddha dwelling in the lesser fruit,
Is reviled, censured, beaten, or struck, The transgression incurred is greater than that.
Therefore, you, Dharmika, Should each protect one another.
Thus they protect one another; there is no crime more grave than this.
Such extremely heavy suffering is also loathed by the Noble Ones;
one will inevitably receive an ugly form and take up a place of false views.
This is the lowest of persons, as taught in the Noble Dharma:
one who has not yet abandoned sensual desire, yet has attained the five subtle faculties—
faith, energy, mindfulness, right concentration, and right insight.
Thus one encounters this suffering, the retribution for what was previously committed.
Having first suffered that retribution oneself, one subsequently harms others.
If one can protect oneself, one is thereby able to protect others.
"Therefore, one should guard oneself; for the wise, there is boundless joy.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Dharmika and the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Tāṇḍyasūtra*, the fourteenth, ends here; 2,424 characters. 131. The *Māravijaya-sūtra* (131), the fifteenth discourse in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Pāveyya, staying at the Deer Park in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest on Mount Ajjhuna.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was instructing [his disciples] and building a meditation hut for the Buddha; he was walking back and forth upon the open ground.
At that moment, Māra transformed himself into a minute form and entered the belly of the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"My belly now feels as if it were filled with beans; I should enter a concentration corresponding to this state, and by means of that concentration, observe my own belly."

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to the head of his walking path, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), sat down cross-legged, and entered a state of meditative concentration (samādhi) corresponding to the object. Using this concentration, he observed his own abdomen; thus, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana knew that the Māra was within his belly.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately arose from his meditative absorption and said to Māra the King:
"Come out, Pāpīyan! Come out, Pāpīyan!"

Do not harass the Tathāgata, nor harass the disciples of the Tathāgata; do not bring about what is meaningless and unbeneficial for a long night, lest you be born in an evil realm and undergo immeasurable suffering.
At that time, Māra the Evil One thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa speaks thus without seeing or knowing:
'You, Pāpīyan, come forth!'"
"Go forth, Pāpīyan!

Do not harass the Tathāgata, nor do you harass the disciples of the Tathāgata. Do not bring about what is meaningless and unbeneficial for a long night; you will surely be reborn in an evil realm and undergo immeasurable suffering."

"Your venerable teacher possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; yet even he was unable to know or see quickly—how much less could his disciples know or see?"
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke again to Māra:
“I also know your thought; you think thus:
‘This śramaṇa speaks these words without knowing or seeing.’”
“Come out, Pāpīyan! Come out, Pāpīyan!

Do not harass the Tathāgata, nor harass the disciples of the Tathāgata. Do not bring about harm and disadvantage for a long night; you will surely be reborn in an evil destination and undergo immeasurable suffering.”

Your venerable teacher possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; yet even he could not thus know and see so swiftly—how much less could his disciples know and see?
Then Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa speaks thus only because he knows and perceives me.
Thereupon, Māra Pāpīyas transformed himself into a minute form, emerged from his mouth, and stood before the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana said: "Pāpīyan!
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Kakusandha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One. At that time, I was Māra, named Pāpa, and I had a sister named Kālī; you are her son."
Pāpīyan! For this reason, you are my nephew. Pāpīyan!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Saṃjñeya had two great disciples: one named Ghoṣa and the other named Saṃjñā.
Pāpīyān! For what reason is the Venerable One named Svara? Pāpīyān!
The Venerable Ghosila dwells in the Brahma Heaven; with his constant voice, he fills a thousand worlds, such that no other disciple’s voice is his equal, his peer, or his superior.
Pāpīyan! For this reason, the Venerable One’s name is Ghoṣa. "Pāpīyan!"
Furthermore, for what reason, Pāpiman, is the Venerable One called "The One of Perception"?

It is because, based upon that perception, when the Venerable One wanders through villages and towns, at dawn after the night has passed, he puts on his robes, takes up his bowl, and enters the village for alms, well-guarding his body, well-restraining his sense faculties, and established in right mindfulness.

Having finished his alms-round and concluded his meal, he put away his robes and bowl after midday, washed his hands and feet, and placing his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, went to a secluded place—whether to a mountain forest, beneath a tree, or to a quiet, solitary dwelling—where he spread out his sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, and swiftly entered the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

At that time, if there were cowherds, shepherds, wood-gatherers, grass-cutters, or travelers who entered that mountain forest, and seeing him, perceived that he had entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they would think:
"Now this śramaṇa has passed away while sitting in this secluded place; we should gather dry wood and grass, pile them over his body, and cremate him."
He immediately gathered firewood and grass, piled them over his body, and set them ablaze; then he departed.

When the night had passed and it was dawn, that venerable one arose from his meditative absorption, shook out his robes, and set out to wander through the village where he resided. As usual, he put on his garments, took up his alms bowl, and entered the village for alms, well-guarding his body, well-restraining his sense faculties, and established in right mindfulness.
Those who tend cattle and sheep, those who gather firewood and grass, or travelers on the road—whoever among those entering that mountain forest had seen him previously, would think:
"This śramaṇa sat in this secluded place and passed away; yesterday we gathered dry wood and grass, piled them over his body, cremated him with fire, and have now departed."
"Yet this worthy one further conceives of perceptions.
Pāpīyan! For this reason, the Venerable One’s 'perception' is called 'perception.'"
“Pāpīyaṇ! At that time, the evil Māra thought to himself:

‘This shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has cut off his lineage and has no offspring. He practices meditation, watching, increasing his watching, and watching repeatedly—just like a donkey that, having carried a heavy load all day and being tethered to a manger without receiving any barley, watches, increases his watching, and watches repeatedly for the sake of that barley.’”

In this way, this shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has cut off his lineage and has no offspring. Though he practices meditation, he spies, intensifies his spying, and spies again and again—just as a kitten stays by the edge of a mouse hole, spying, intensifying its spying, and spying again and again, because it wishes to catch a mouse.

In this way, this shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has severed his lineage and is without offspring. Though he practices meditation, he spies, intensifies his spying, and spies again and again—just as an owl or a fox stays among a dry pile of firewood, spying, intensifying its spying, and spying again and again for the sake of catching mice.

In this way, this shaven-headed ascetic is bound by darkness; having cut off his lineage so that there is no offspring, he practices meditation, observing, observing intensely, and observing repeatedly—just like a heron on the edge of a water’s bank, observing, observing intensely, and observing repeatedly for the sake of catching fish.
In this way, this shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; having cut off his lineage so as to be childless, he practices meditation, observing, observing intensely, and observing repeatedly.
What does he observe?
For what purpose does he investigate?
What is it that he seeks to investigate?
He is agitated, deranged, frantic, and ruined; I do not know from where he has come.
I do not know where he has gone, nor where he dwells;
I do not know his death or his birth. I should rather instruct the brahmins and householders: "Come together and revile this diligent śramaṇa, beat him, and reprimand him."
Why is this? Because when one is being reviled, struck, or rebuked, they might perhaps give rise to an evil mind, thinking, 'May I find an opportunity against him. O Pāpīyān!
At that time, Māra instructed the brahmins and householders; those brahmins and householders reviled the energetic śramaṇas, striking them and rebuking them.

Those brahmins and householders would strike him with wood, pelt him with stones, or lash him with staves; they would wound the heads of the diligent śramaṇas, tear their robes, or break their alms-bowls.

At that time, if any brahmins or householders should die, on account of this and by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.
Having been born there, he thinks:
"I must endure this suffering, and I shall further endure even more extreme suffering than this. Why is that?"
"Because we have committed evil deeds against the diligent śramaṇas. "Pāpīyan!

The disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairaṭyaghoṣa, having wounded their heads, torn their robes, and broken their alms-bowls, went to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vairaṭyaghoṣa was staying."
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin was surrounded by an immeasurable hundred thousand followers as he preached the Dharma.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Saṃjīva saw from afar his disciple approaching with a wounded head, torn robes, and a broken bowl; having seen him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see him?"
The Māra instructed the brahmins and householders:
"Come, all of you together, revile the diligent śramaṇas; break them and scold them. Why is this so?..."
"When they are being reviled, beaten, or rebuked, should they give rise to an evil thought, thinking, 'May I find an opportunity to harm them,' bhikkhus!
You should dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, having achieved its fulfillment."

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world, so that the Evil Māra, seeking an opportunity, finds no such opportunity.

"O Pāpīyān! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha Bakkula taught his disciples with this instruction: they, having received the teaching, dwell having suffused one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, and thus achieve mastery over it."

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, joy, and equanimity—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
For this reason, that evil Māra sought an opportunity but could not find one. "Pāpīyan!
At that time, the evil Māra again thought to himself:"
"I have sought an opportunity against these diligent śramaṇas through this means, yet I have been unable to find one.

I should instead command the brahmins and householders: 'Come, all of you together, honor, support, and serve the diligent śramaṇas; perhaps by honoring, supporting, and serving the diligent śramaṇas, they will give rise to evil thoughts, thereby allowing me to gain an advantage.'"

“Pāpīyan! Once those brahmins and householders have been instructed by the Evil Māra, they will together revere, honor, support, and serve the energetic śramaṇas. They will spread their robes upon the ground and say:

‘May the energetic śramaṇas walk upon this; may the energetic śramaṇas perform what is difficult to perform, so that we may obtain benefit and great advantage, and experience peace, security, and happiness for a long night.’”
The brahmins and householders spread their hair upon the ground and spoke thus:

"May the diligent śramaṇas walk upon this; may the diligent śramaṇas perform what is difficult to perform, so that we may obtain long-lasting benefit and profit, and enjoy peace, security, and happiness."
The brahmins and householders, holding various kinds of food and drink in their hands, stood by the roadside waiting and spoke thus:
"O diligent śramaṇas, please accept this food; take it with you and use it as you wish, so that we may obtain long-lasting benefit, profit, peace, and happiness."

When the faithful brahmins and householders saw the energetic śramaṇa, they respectfully supported and embraced him, leading him inside. They presented him with various kinds of wealth and spoke thus:
"Accept this, use this; take this and go; use it as you please."

At that time, if any brahmins or householders were to die, by virtue of this and on account of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they would certainly go to a good destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
Having been born there, he thinks:
"I should experience this pleasure, but I shall further experience a supreme bliss even more excellent than this. Why is that?"
"Because we have practiced wholesome conduct toward the diligent śramaṇa. "Pāpīyan!

Having received the honor, offerings, and service of the disciples of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kakusandha, they went to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kakusandha was staying."
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin was surrounded by an immeasurable hundred thousand followers as he preached the Dharma for them.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bakkula saw from afar his disciples coming to pay their respects, make offerings, and perform services; having seen them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you see them?"
The Māra instructed the brahmins and householders:

"Come together and pay homage to, make offerings to, and serve the diligent śramaṇas; or, by paying homage to, making offerings to, and serving the diligent śramaṇas, perhaps they will give rise to evil thoughts, thereby allowing me to gain an advantage."

“Monks! You should contemplate the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena; contemplate the law of arising and passing away; contemplate desirelessness; contemplate relinquishment; contemplate cessation; contemplate abandonment. In this way, you will cause the evil Māra to seek an opportunity, yet find none.”

“Pāpīyan! When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Buddha Bakkula teaches his disciples with this instruction, they receive the teaching and contemplate all conditioned phenomena as impermanent, contemplate the law of arising and passing away, contemplate desirelessness, contemplate relinquishment, contemplate cessation, and contemplate eradication; thus, the evil Māra seeks an opportunity but cannot find it.”
“Pāpīyan! At that time, the evil Māra again thought to himself:
‘I sought an opportunity against this ascetic of diligent effort through these means, yet I could not find one.’”

"I would rather transform myself into the form of a youth, take a large staff in my hand, stand by the side of the road, and strike the head of the Venerable Ghosila until it is shattered and the blood stains his face."

“Pāpīyaṇ! After the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vebhāra, while wandering through the villages and towns he relied upon, dressed in the morning and took his bowl, entering the village for alms, with the Venerable Ghosa following behind as his attendant.”

Pāpīyān! At that time, the evil Māra transformed himself into the form of a youth, holding a large staff in his hand; standing by the side of the road, he struck the head of the Venerable Ghosaka, breaking it so that blood flowed and stained his face.
Pāpīyan! After the Venerable Ghosila had his head split open and blood flowed from it, he followed behind the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Saṅkhaśaṅkha like a shadow that never leaves him.

“Pāpīyan! When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kakusandha arrived at the village, he exerted the full power of his body and turned his gaze to the right with a majestic look, like the gaze of a dragon; without fear, without dread, and without alarm or terror, he surveyed all directions.”

"Pāpīyan! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kakusandha saw the Venerable Ghosila with his face smeared by blood from a broken head, following behind the Buddha like a shadow never leaving him, and he spoke thus:
'This evil Māra is fierce and violent, possessing great power; this evil Māra knows no satiety.'"
"O Pāpīyan! Before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin had finished speaking these words, at that moment, the evil Māra’s body fell right there into the Avīci Great Hell."
Pāpīyān! This great hell has four names: first, the Defectless; second, the Hundred Nails; third, the Reverse Thorns; and fourth, the Six Contacts.
Within that great hell, there are wardens who go to the place where the evil demons reside and say to them:
"You should now know this: if [the nails] such as these are driven together, you should know that it shall be for a full hundred years."

Thereupon, when Māra Pāpīyas heard these words, his heart immediately trembled; struck with terror and dread, the hair on his body stood on end. He addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana in verse, saying:
"How was it that in those hells, The evil Māra once dwelt within them?
How did he harass the Buddha’s holy life, And how did he offend those bhikṣus?"
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately replied to Māra Pāpīyas with a verse:
“In the hell named Avīci, The evil Māra once dwelt,
Harassing the Buddha’s holy life And violating those bhikṣus.”
Those iron nails number one hundred, each with its prongs turned upward;
this hell is named Unblemished (Anavilā), where Māra the Evil One once dwelt.
If there are those who do not know—those bhikṣus who are disciples of the Buddha—[let them beware].
One must inevitably undergo such suffering, receiving the retribution for black karma.
With various kinds of gardens and groves, people dwell upon the earth;
they eat naturally grown non-glutinous rice and reside in the Northern Continent.
The rocky peaks of Mount Sumeru are perfumed by those who practice well;
having cultivated liberation, they maintain their final body.
Standing firm upon the great springs, they dwell in palaces until the end of the kalpa.
Golden in color and lovely to behold, shining like the flickering flames of fire,
he performed various kinds of music and went to the abode of Śakra;
this was because he had originally offered a single house with a mind of excellent awakening and understanding as his gift.
If Śakra goes before him and they ascend the Vaijayanta Palace,
seeing Śakra, he is filled with great joy and the celestial maidens each dance.
But if he sees a bhikṣu approaching, he turns back in shame and modesty.
If in the Vaijayanta Palace, one sees a bhikṣu questioning about the meaning:
“Great Sage, are you able to know that through the exhaustion of craving one attains liberation?
The bhikṣu then answers him according to the meaning of his question.
"Kauśika, I know this: through the exhaustion of craving, one attains liberation.
Hearing his reply, Śakra attained joy and happiness.
"The bhikṣu has brought great benefit; what he has spoken is in accordance with the truth."
Regarding the Vaijayanta Palace, one asks Śakra, the King of Devas:
"What is the name of this palace? You, Śakra, who uphold the city?
Śakra replies to the Great Seer: "Its name is Vaijayanta."
This is called the thousandfold world-system; within this thousandfold world-system,
there is no palace superior to this Vaijayanta, where the Heavenly King Śakra,
the Lord of Devas, dwells at his own will as he traverses it.
Nanda, who delights in wandering, manifested as a hundred figures in a single row.
Within the Vaijayanta Palace, Śakra wanders with sovereign ease;
from within that great Vaijayanta Hall, he can cause it to tremble with a single toe.
That which the celestial kings behold with their eyes, where Śakra wanders with sovereign ease—
such as the Hall of Mṛgāramātṛ, whose foundations are so deep and firm that it is difficult to move and impossible to shake—
even this he can cause to tremble by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).
There lies a ground of lapis lazuli, trodden by the Noble Ones;
it is smooth, pleasant to the touch, and spread with soft cotton mattresses.
With loving speech and mutual harmony, the Heavenly King is ever joyful.
They were skilled at performing music, their melodies and rhythms perfectly harmonious;
they said that the devas had gathered for this assembly to discourse on the stage of *srotāpanna*.
There were many thousands, even hundreds of millions (*koṭi*), of such beings.
Reaching the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the one with the eye of wisdom preached the Dharma;
hearing the Dharma he preached, they rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
"I too possess this Dharma, just as the seer has taught."
Having ascended to the Brahma Heaven, he questioned that Brahmā regarding his state; because of this, Brahmā held this view:
"In the past I existed, and I remain here eternally, constantly and unchanging."
Brahmā answered him: "O Great Sage, I have no such view;
I claim that there was a 'self' in the past, eternal and unchanging.
I perceive this realm wherein all Brahmās have passed away."
By what means can I now explain that which is eternally unchanging?
I behold this world as taught by the Perfectly Awakened One:
it arises according to causes and conditions, and wherever it goes, it returns.
Fire has no thought, "I shall burn the foolish person";
yet if a fool touches a blazing fire, he will inevitably be burned by it.
So it is with you, Pāpīyan: you have provoked and harassed the Tathāgata.
Having long engaged in unwholesome deeds, you shall likewise experience their retribution for a long time.
O Māra, do not loathe the Buddha; do not harass or harm the bhikṣu.
A single bhikṣu has subdued you, dwelling now within the Forest of Fear.
That ghost, filled with grief and sorrow at being rebuked by Maudgalyāyana, was terrified and lacked wisdom; he immediately vanished from that place.
Thus spoke the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
Having heard what the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had spoken, Māra Pāpīyas rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifteenth discourse, "The Subduing of Māra," ends here, totaling three thousand two hundred and seventy-four characters. The thirty-ninth fascicle of the Madhyama Āgama ends here, totaling five thousand one hundred and fifteen characters.
[End of] Fascicle Thirty-one of the Madhyama Āgama.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
132. The Sūtra of Rāṣṭrapāla (132) The Sixteenth Sūtra of the Great Section, The Sūtra of Rāṣṭrapāla, for the Third Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Kurū with a great assembly of bhikṣus; he went to Thullakoṭṭhita and stayed in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhita.
At that time, the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita heard:

"The ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who has left the Śākya clan to go forth and study the Way, is traveling through the Kuru country together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and has arrived here at Thullakoṭṭhita, staying in the Siṃsapā Grove north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhita."

That śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown that is heard throughout the ten directions; the śramaṇa Gautama is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.

In this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans up to the devas, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized [this] for himself.

If he preaches the Dharma, it is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it possesses both meaning and phrasing, is complete and pure, and clearly reveals the holy life (brahmacarya).
"If one sees the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and honors, prostrates to, makes offerings to, and serves him, one will swiftly obtain great benefit.
We should go together to see the śramaṇa Gautama, to pay our respects and make offerings."

Having heard this, the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita, each accompanied by their respective circles of kinsmen, departed from Thullakoṭṭhita and traveled north to the Sīsapā Grove, desiring to see the Blessed One, pay him homage, and make offerings to him.

Having approached the Buddha, those brahmins and householders of Toraṇavatī either bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side, or exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat down to one side, or joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat down to one side, or, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down in silence.

At that time, when the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had each taken their seats, the Buddha taught them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Having taught them the Dharma through countless skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, he remained silent.

At that time, the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita, having been exhorted by the Buddha through his teaching of the Dharma, inspired with longing, and established in joy, each rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the householder’s son Ratahara remained seated and did not rise.

Then, not long after the brahmin Todeyya and the householder had departed, the householder’s son Ratahara rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, pressed his palms together toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I were to remain at home, I would be bound by fetters and unable to practice the holy life with purity for as long as I live.
“World-Honored One!
May I receive ordination from the World-Honored One to study the Path and attain full admission, so that I may become a bhikṣu and purely cultivate the holy life.
The World-Honored One asked:
“Householder’s son!
Have your parents given you permission to go forth from the home into homelessness with deep faith in this True Dharma and Discipline to practice the path?
The householder’s son Ratahāra replied:
“World-Honored One!
My parents have not yet granted me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness with right faith within this True Dharma and Discipline to study the Path.
The World-Honored One said:
“Son of a householder!

If your parents do not permit you to go forth with right faith from home into homelessness to train in the True Dharma and Discipline, I cannot ordain you for the homeless life to train in the Way, nor can I grant you full ordination.”
The householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla said:
“World-Honored One!

I shall employ skillful means to petition my parents, so that they will certainly grant me permission to, with right faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path within the True Dharma and Vinaya.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Son of a householder!
Do as you wish."

Thereupon, the householder’s son Ratahāra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received it well and retained it well; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned home.
He said: "Venerable Sirs!

As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I were to remain at home, I would be bound by fetters and unable to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) purely for as long as life lasts. I only pray that you two will grant me permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness with full faith within this True Dharma and Discipline, to train in the Path."
Ratthapāla’s parents said to him: “Ratthapāla!
We have only you, our one son;

we hold you in extreme love and affection, our hearts are always delighted by you, and we never tire of seeing you. Even if you were to die, we would not wish to abandon you, much less endure the separation of being parted from you while still alive.”
The householder’s son Ratahula repeated his request a second and a third time, saying:
“Venerable sirs!

As I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, if I remain at home, I shall be bound by fetters and unable to practice the holy life with purity for as long as I live. I pray that you both will grant me permission to go forth from the household life into homelessness within this True Dharma and Discipline, out of faith, to train in the Way.”
The householder’s son Rāṭṭhapāla’s parents also spoke to him a second and a third time, saying:
“Rāṭṭhapāla! We have only you, our one son;

we hold you in extreme love and affection, our hearts are always delighted by you, and we never tire of seeing you. Even if you were to die, we would not wish to abandon you, much less endure being separated from you in life and no longer seeing you.”
Thereupon, the householder’s son Ratahāra immediately lay down on the ground, saying:

“From this moment forth, I shall not rise; I shall neither drink nor eat, until my parents grant me permission to go forth from the home into homelessness within the True Dharma and Discipline to train in the Path.”
Thereupon, the householder’s son Ratahāra did not eat for one day; he went on to two, three, four, and many days without eating.
Then the parents of the householder’s son Ratahāra went to where their son was and said to him: “Ratahāra!...”
"You are exceedingly delicate and your body is most refined; you have always sat and slept upon fine beds. Do you not know suffering now, Ratahara?
You should rise quickly, practice giving, and joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds."
Why is that? Ratahara!
The domain of the World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult, and leaving the household life to study the Path is likewise exceedingly difficult.
At that time, the householder’s son Ratahāra remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the parents of the householder’s son Ratahāra went to the place where Ratahāra’s kinsmen and ministers were and spoke these words:
“Come all together to where Ratahāra is and urge him to rise from the ground.”
The kinsmen and ministers of the householder’s son Ratahara then went together to where Ratahara was and said to him: “Ratahara!”
"You are exceedingly delicate and your body is most refined; you have always sat and slept upon fine beds. Do you not now know suffering? Ratahula!
You should rise quickly, practice giving, and joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds."
"Why is this? The domain of the World-Honored One is exceedingly difficult, and to leave the household life to study the Path is likewise exceedingly difficult.
At that time, the householder’s son Ratakhara remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the parents of the householder’s son Ratahara went to where his good friends, companions, and associates were, and spoke these words:
“Come all together to where Ratahara is, and urge him to rise from the ground.”
Thereupon, the householder’s son Ratthapāla’s good friends, companions, and associates went together to where the householder’s son Ratthapāla was and spoke these words: “Ratthapāla!
"You are exceedingly delicate; your body is most excellent, and you have always sat and slept upon fine beds.
Do you not now know suffering, Ratahara?
You should rise quickly, practice giving, and joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds."
Why is that? Rāṭṭhapāla!
The domain of the Blessed One is exceedingly difficult, and leaving the household life to train in the path is likewise exceedingly difficult.
At that time, the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla remained silent and did not answer.
Then, Rāṣṭrapāla’s good friends, companions, and associates went to where the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla were and spoke to them as follows:

“Please allow Rāṣṭrapāla to go forth from the home into homelessness with firm faith in the True Dharma and Discipline to practice the holy life; if he so desires, you may still see him in this very life.”
"If he does not find delight [in this], he will surely return of his own accord to his parents' home.
If you do not grant him permission now, he will certainly die without a doubt; what benefit would that bring?
Thereupon, having heard this, the parents of the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla spoke to Rāṣṭrapāla’s good friends, companions, and peers, saying:

"I now permit Ratakhara to go forth from the home life into homelessness within this True Dharma and Discipline with full faith to study the Path; if he returns after having studied the Path, he may certainly be seen."
Then the householder’s son Ratthapāla’s good friends, companions, and peers went together to where Ratthapāla was and spoke to him thus:
“Householder’s son!...”

"Parents, if you permit me to go forth from the home into homelessness with full faith within this True Dharma and Discipline to study the Path, once I have completed my training on the Path, I shall return to see you."

Having heard these words, the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla was greatly delighted; love and joy arose within him. He rose from the ground and gradually restored his body. Once his body had recovered, he departed from Toraṇavatī and went to where the Buddha was. Bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he said: “World-Honored One!...”
"Father and mother, please grant me permission to go forth from the home life into homelessness with full faith in the True Dharma and Discipline, to train in the path.
I only pray, World-Honored One, that you will allow me to leave the household life under the World-Honored One to train in the path and receive full ordination, so that I may become a bhikṣu."

Thereupon, the Blessed One ordained the householder’s son Rāṣṭrapāla to follow the path of training and conferred upon him full ordination. Having conferred full ordination, he remained for some time in Thullakoṭṭhita; thereafter, having adjusted his robes and taken up his bowl, he traveled by stages until he arrived at Sāvatthī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.

The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla went forth to train in the path; having received full ordination, he dwelt alone in seclusion, his mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort. Having thus dwelt alone in seclusion, his mind free from negligence, and practiced with diligent effort, he—

For a son of good family who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of supreme faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path—this is solely for the sake of reaching the unsurpassed holy life, wherein in this very life he knows it himself, realizes it himself, and attains realization through personal experience, dwelling with the knowledge: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.
Having realized the Dharma, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla attained the state of an Arhat.
Then, nine or ten years after the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had become an Arhat, he thought to himself:
"I previously promised that once I had gone forth to study the Path, I would return to see my parents; I should now go back to fulfill that original commitment."
Thereupon, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I originally had a vow: once I have left the household life to study the Way, I shall return to see my parents.
World-Honored One!
I now take my leave to go and see my parents, to fulfill that original vow."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"As for this son of the Laṭṭha clan, it is simply impossible that he would ever renounce the precepts, abandon the path, and return to sensual desires as before."
The World-Honored One, having known this, said: "Go!
Deliver those who have not yet been delivered; bring liberation to those who have not yet attained liberation; bring final extinction to those who have not yet attained final extinction."
"Ratthapāla! Now, do as you wish.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ratthapāla received and retained it well; he then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Having returned to his own quarters, he gathered up his bedding, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and traveling by stages, he went to Thullakoṭṭhita and stayed in the Sīsapā Grove to the north of the village of Thullakoṭṭhita.
Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the Venerable Ratakhara dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered Toraṇa to beg for alms.
The Venerable Ratakhara thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One praises systematic begging for alms; I should now go about Toraṇa begging for alms in systematic order.”
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla then went on his alms-round through Toraṇavatthu, proceeding from house to house until he reached his own home.

At that time, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father was standing at the middle gate, grooming his beard and hair. Seeing the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father spoke these words:
“This bald ascetic, bound by darkness, who has cut off our lineage and left us childless, has brought ruin upon my family.”

"I have an only son whom I cherish and love deeply; my heart is always patient and joyful toward him, and I never tire of seeing him. Since he is being taken away to undergo asceticism, you must not give him food."
The Venerable Ratahara did not receive any alms from his own father’s household; instead, he received only this jeering:
“This shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has cut off our lineage so that there are no descendants, and he has ruined our family.”
"I have an only son whom I cherish and dote upon; my heart always delights in him, and I never tire of seeing him. Since he is being taken away to undergo his ordination, you must not give him food."
Having understood this, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla quickly went out.
At that time, a maidservant from the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father’s household was carrying stinking, rotten food in a winnowing basket, intending to discard it in a heap of refuse.
When the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla saw his father’s female servant carrying foul, putrid food in a winnowing basket, intending to discard it in a midden, he spoke these words:
"Sister!..."
"If this food and drink, though rotten and unfit for consumption according to the rules, may be placed in my bowl, I shall eat it.
At that time, a female servant from the house of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father poured the stinking, rotten food from a winnowing basket into his bowl.

As he was pouring [the water] into his bowl, he observed two signs: he recognized the sound of his voice and the appearance of his hands and feet. Having noted these two signs, he went at once to where the Venerable Rāṭṭhapāla’s father was and spoke these words:
"Venerable sir, you should know this: your son Rāṭṭhapāla has returned here to Thullakoṭṭhita; you may go and see him."

Having heard this, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father was filled with great joy and exultation; he adjusted his robe with his left hand, rubbed and smoothed his beard and hair with his right hand, and hurried to where the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was.
At that time, the Venerable Ratahara was eating this putrid, rotten food while facing a wall.
Seeing the Venerable Ratahara eating this putrid, rotten food while facing a wall, his father said to him:
"Ratahara! You, Ratahara!"
"You are so delicate and your body is so excellent; you have always eaten fine food, Ratahara!
How can you possibly eat such foul, putrid food?"
"Ratthapāla! For what reason have you come here to Thullakoṭṭhita instead of returning to your parents' home?
Venerable Ratthapāla replied:
“Householder!
When I entered my father’s house, I received no alms, but only this sneer:
‘This shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has cut off our lineage and left us childless, ruining our family.’”

"I have but one son, whom I hold most dear and cherish; my heart is ever filled with love for him, and I never tire of beholding him. Since he is going away to be ordained, you must not give him food."
"Having heard this, I immediately went out.
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s father then apologized, saying,
"May Rāṣṭrapāla forgive me!"
"Ratthapāla, it is well that you have endured this!
I truly did not know that Ratthapāla would return to his father’s house.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ratthapāla’s father respectfully supported the Venerable Ratthapāla and led him inside; he prepared a seat for him to sit upon, and the Venerable Ratthapāla sat down.
Then, having seen that the Venerable Ratakhara was seated, his father went to where his wife was and spoke these words:
"You should know now that the noble son Ratakhara has returned home; you must quickly prepare food and drink."
Upon hearing this, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother was filled with great joy and exultation; she quickly prepared food and drink.

Having prepared the food and drink, she swiftly brought out money and piled it upon the ground in the middle of the courtyard, forming a great heap. That massive pile of coins was such that those standing on one side could not see those sitting on the other.
Having accumulated a great quantity of coins, he went to where the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was and spoke these words: "Rāṣṭrapāla!
This is the wealth that belonged to your maternal portion;
your father’s wealth is immeasurable, numbering hundreds of thousands beyond calculation, and I now entrust it all to you."
"Ratthapāla!
You should abandon the precepts and cease the life of a renunciant; engage in sensual pleasures, practice giving, and joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds. Why is this so?"
"The domain of the World-Honored One is extremely difficult to fathom; to leave the household life and train in the Path is likewise extremely difficult.
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said to his mother, "I wish now to say something; would you grant me your attention?"
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother said:
“Son of a householder!
Listen to what you have to say.”
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said to his mother:
"One should have a new cloth bag made, fill it with coins, carry it on a cart to the Ganges River, and pour them into its depths."
"Why is that? Because of this money, it causes people grief, suffering, sorrow, and lamentation, so that they find no happiness.
Thereupon, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother had this thought:
"By this means I shall not be able to cause my son Ratahara to abandon his precepts and cease his practice; I had better go to his former wife and speak these words:
'O daughters-in-law!'"

"You may first adorn your bodies with the necklaces you previously wore—those which the son of the Licchavis, Ratahāra, held most dear when he was still living at home. Having quickly adorned yourselves with these necklaces, all of you go together to where the son of the Licchavis, Ratahāra, is, and each embrace one of his feet, saying:
'We do not know, noble sir, what heavenly maiden is superior to us that would cause you to abandon us to practice the holy life for her sake?'"
"Then her mother went to the former wife of the Venerable Rāṭṭhapāla and spoke to her as follows:
'O daughters-in-law!'"

"You may first adorn your bodies with the necklaces you previously wore—those which the son of the Licchavi clan, Ratahāra, held most dear when he was still living at home. Having quickly adorned yourselves with these necklaces, you all go together to where the son of the Licchavi clan, Ratahāra, is, and each embrace one of his feet, saying:
'We do not know, noble sir, what goddess is superior to us that would cause you, noble sir, to abandon us and practice the holy life for her sake?'"

At that time, the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s former wives each adorned their bodies with the very same necklaces and ornaments they had previously worn—those which the venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had cherished most deeply when he was still living at home.
Having adorned their bodies with these necklaces, they went to where the Venerable Rāṭṭhapāla was, each embracing one of his feet and saying:
"We wonder, noble sir, what heavenly maiden is superior to us that you have caused us to abandon you and practice the holy life for her sake?"
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said to his former wife:
"Sisters, you should know that I do not practice the holy life for the sake of celestial nymphs."
"The purpose for which one practices the holy life has been attained; what was to be done according to the Buddha’s teaching is now accomplished.
Standing to one side, the wives of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla wept with tears falling as they spoke these words:
"We are not sisters to our noble brother, yet our noble brother calls us sisters."
Thereupon, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla turned back and looked at them, saying to his parents:
"Householder!
If you would give food, give it at the proper time; why do you trouble me?"

At that time, the parents rose from their seats, personally provided water for washing, and served various kinds of abundant, exquisite delicacies—both solid foods and those requiring mastication—personally pouring them out until he was thoroughly satiated.
When the meal was finished, the vessels were collected, and the water for washing had been served, [the Venerable] took a small seat and sat apart to listen to the Dharma.

The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla preached the Dharma to his parents, exhorting them to aspire with longing, bringing them to a state of joy. Having used countless skillful means to preach the Dharma to them, exhorting them to aspire with longing and bringing them to a state of joy, he rose from his seat and spoke these verses:
"Behold this adorned form, With its precious jewels and necklaces; [Yet it is subject to decay and dissolution. The body is like a jar of clay, A vessel filled with various impurities."
With hair coiled to the right and eyebrows painted with dark blue pigment—
this deceives the foolish and ignorant, yet does not delude those who have crossed to the other shore;
for with various beautiful colors, they adorn a body that is foul and putrid.
This deceives the foolish, but does not deceive those who have crossed to the other shore;
with various perfumes smeared over their bodies, and yellow orpiment coloring their feet.
This deceives the foolish, but does not deceive those who have crossed to the other shore.
Clad in pure and exquisite robes, adorned as if by illusion—
this deceives the foolish, yet does not delude those who have crossed to the further shore,
who have severed the leather thongs and straps, and demolished the gates of the deer-park.
"I have abandoned the bait and departed; who would delight in the bonds of a deer?

Having spoken this verse, the Venerable Ratahara rose into the air by means of his psychic power and went to the Tālapuṭa forest. Entering that grove, he spread out his sitting mat beneath a Vibhītaka tree and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, King Koravya, surrounded by his ministers in front and behind, sat in the main hall and praised the Venerable Ratahara, saying:
"If I had heard that the clansman Ratahara had come here to Thullakotthita, I would certainly have gone to see him."
Thereupon, King Kaurava said to the hunter, "Go and inspect the Tāla forest; I wish to go hunting.
Having received these instructions, the hunter immediately went to inspect the Tāla forest.

Thereupon, the hunter went about inspecting the Tinduka forest and saw the Venerable Ratakhara sitting beneath a Vibhitaka tree with his *niṣīdana* spread out, seated in the full lotus posture. He then thought to himself:
"The one whom King Kaurava and his ministers used to sit with in the royal hall, praising and extolling him, is here now."
At that time, having finished inspecting the Tosalī forest, the hunter returned to King Koravya and said:
"Great King,
you should know that I have completed the inspection of the Tosalī forest according to Your Majesty’s wishes."
"Great King, it was your former practice, while seated in the main hall with your ministers, to sigh with admiration and praise the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
'If I hear that the clansman Rāṣṭrapāla has come here to Thullakoṭṭhita, I shall certainly go to see him.'"
"The venerable son of the Laṭṭhaka clan is now in the Tālapuṭa grove, beneath a bhallātakī tree, having spread out his sitting mat and sat down cross-legged."
"Great King, if you wish to see him, you may go at once.
Having heard this, King Kūlāva told his charioteer:
"Prepare the carriage quickly; I now wish to go and see Ratahara."
The charioteer, having received these instructions, immediately prepared the carriage with haste; when it was ready, he returned and reported, "Great King,
you should know that the carriage is prepared and awaits Your Majesty’s pleasure."

Thereupon, King Kūṭadanta mounted his carriage and set out, proceeding to the Tālapuṭa grove. From afar he saw the Venerable Rataḥvara; immediately alighting from his carriage, he advanced on foot toward the Venerable Rataḥvara.
When the Venerable Ratahara saw King Kūlāva approaching, he said this:
"Great King,
have you come now wishing to sit yourself?"
King Kaurava said:
"Although I have now reached my own territory, it is my wish that the clansman Ratahāra should invite me to sit."
The Venerable Ratahara then invited King Koravya, saying, "There is a separate seat; Great King, please be seated.
Thereupon, King Koravya exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ratahara, withdrew to sit at one side, and said to Ratahara:
“Is it because your family has declined that you have gone forth to study the Way?
Or is it because you lack wealth that you practice the Way? Ratahara!

The house of the Kaurava kings possesses great wealth; I shall provide you with wealth, Ratahara, and urge you to abandon your precepts and cease your practice of the Way, so that you may indulge in desires, practice giving, and joyfully cultivate meritorious deeds.”
Why is that? Ratahara!
It is extremely difficult to follow a teacher’s instruction, and it is likewise extremely difficult to leave the household life to study the Path.
Having heard this, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said:
"Great King, you now invite me with what is impure; it is not a pure invitation."
Having heard this, King Koravya asked:
"How should I invite Ratahara with pure intentions, and not with impure ones?"
The Venerable Ratthapāla said: "Great King,
you should speak thus:"
"Ratthapāla! The people of my kingdom are peaceful and happy;

they are without fear and without strife, and there are no thorns or forced labor. Grain is abundant and alms are easily obtained. Since you, Ratthapāla, dwell within my kingdom, I shall protect you in accordance with the Dhamma."
"Great King!
Thus it is that you have invited me with purity, not with impurity.
Having heard this, King Kūlāva said:
"I now invite Ratahara with purity, not with impurity. The people of my kingdom are peaceful and happy;

they are without fear and without strife, and there are no thorns or burdensome corvée labor. Grain is abundant and alms are easy to obtain. Since Ratahara dwells within my kingdom, I shall protect him in accordance with the Dharma."
"Furthermore, Rāṣṭrapāla! There are four kinds of decline;
because of these declines, one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path."
What are the four?
They are the decline of illness, the decline of old age, the decline of wealth, and the decline of kinsmen. Rāṭṭhapāla!
What is decline due to illness?
Suppose there is a person who suffers from a chronic disease, one that is extremely grave and painful. He thinks to himself:

"I suffer from a chronic disease, one that is extremely grave and painful. Although I truly have desire, I am unable to pursue it. I would now rather shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to train in the Way."

Later, due to the decline caused by illness, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of deep faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path; this is what is meant by "decline through illness."
"Ratthapāla! What is the decay of old age?
There may be a person who is aged, whose faculties have matured, and whose lifespan is nearly exhausted; he thinks to himself: [as follows]"

"I am advanced in years and my faculties have matured; my life span is nearly at its end. Although I truly have desire, I am unable to indulge in it. I should now shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to practice the Way."

At a later time, due to the decline of old age, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path; this is called the decline of old age.
"Ratthapāla! What is the decline of wealth?
Suppose there is a person who is poor and powerless; he thinks to himself: "
"I am poor and powerless; I would now rather shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path."

Later, due to the decline of his wealth, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path; this is called the decline of wealth.
“Ratthapāla! What is the decline of one’s kin?
Suppose there is a person whose relatives have been cut off at their root, having died out and perished; he then thinks:”
"My kinsmen have been cut off; they have died and perished. I should now shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path."

Later, due to the decline of his relatives, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path; this is called the decline of relatives.

"Formerly, Rāṣṭrapāla was free from illness and possessed of well-being; his digestive process was balanced, being neither cold nor hot, but even, peaceful, and harmonious. Because of this, whatever he ate, chewed, or swallowed was digested with ease and comfort."
Ratthapāla did not shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path because of physical decline due to illness.

“In former times, when Raṭṭhapāla was a young boy with pure black hair and a robust physique, he made his living as a musician, finding great delight in it; he adorned his body and constantly enjoyed playing.”

At that time, all your kinsmen did not wish for you to study the Way; your parents wept and wailed, filled with grief and distress, and would not permit your renunciation of the household life to study the Way.
Yet you have shaved off your hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of supreme faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path.
Ratahula did not shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path because of old age and decay.
“Ratthapāla! This is the foremost house, the greatest house, the most excellent house, the highest house among those of Toraṇavatthu—namely, in terms of wealth.”
Ratthapāla!
It is not because of the decline of wealth that one shaves off hair and beard, puts on the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path.

"Ratthapāla! In this Todeyya grove, your great and wealthy kinsmen and relatives all still exist; yet, Ratthapāla, it was not because of the decline of your kin that you shaved off your hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Path."

"Ratthapāla, regarding these four kinds of decline, there may be one who, having experienced such decline, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path."

I see that Ratahara is entirely free from such decline; he could certainly shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path.
Ratthapāla!

What have you known and seen, and what have you heard, that you have shaved off your hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the path?
The Venerable Rāṭṭhapāla replied: “Great King! The Blessed One knows and sees;

the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has taught four matters for which I have found acceptance and delight. I know, see, and have heard these things; therefore, having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, out of deep faith I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness to study the Path.”
What are these four?
Great King!

This world is without protection and without anyone upon whom one can rely; this world is subject to the law of aging; this world is impermanent and must inevitably be abandoned; this world is never full and knows no satisfaction, for it is driven about by craving.
King Kūṭadanta asked:
"Ratthapāla! Regarding what you have just said:..."
"Great King!
This world is without protection; there is nothing upon which one can rely.
Thus spoke Ratahara.

I have sons, grandsons, brothers, and kinsmen; I have elephant troops, chariot troops, cavalry, and infantry—all skilled in archery and horsemanship, stern, resolute, and courageous. I have princes and wrestlers, as well as Pālakr̥tin and Mahānagna, who possess the ability to read physiognomy, strategic planning, calculation, literacy, and eloquence. I have ministers and retainers who maintain mantras and know their application; wherever they travel, they are able to suppress any fear or danger that may arise.
As Ratahara has said: "Great King!
This world is without protection; there is nothing upon which one can rely."
"Ratthapāla! What is the meaning of what you have just said?
The Venerable Ratthapāla replied:
“Great King!
I now ask you a question; answer it as you see fit.
Great King!”
"Does this body have any illness?
King Koravya replied, "Ratthapāla!"
"Now this body of mine is constantly afflicted with wind-disorders.
The Venerable Ratahara asked:
"Great King!"

"Great King, when a wind disorder arises and produces extreme and intense suffering, could one at that time say to his sons, grandsons, brothers, elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry—all of whom are skilled in archery and horsemanship, stern, courageous, and fierce;

to the princes, wrestlers, Yodhājīvas, and Mahānagnas; to those who read physiognomy, deliberate, calculate, know scripts, and are eloquent in debate; to the ministers, courtiers, and kinsmen; or to those who maintain mantras and know incantations: 'Come all of you together and temporarily take upon yourselves this extreme and intense suffering for me, so that I may be free from illness and attain peace and happiness'?"
King Koravya replied, "No. Why is that? Because—"
"I have performed these actions myself; through the conditions and causes of my own karma, I alone must undergo extreme suffering—most grievous suffering.
The Venerable Ratahara said, "Great King!
For this reason, the World-Honored One has said that this world is without protection and without anyone upon whom one can rely.

I desire to accept and delight in this; I know, see, and have heard this. Therefore, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path.
King Koravya said: "If Ratahara says:
'Great King!'"
"In this world there is no protection, nothing upon which one can rely. Rāṣṭrapāla!
I too wish for this and would find joy in it.
"Why is that? Because in this world there is truly no protection and nothing upon which one can rely.
King Kūṭadanta asked again:
"If, as Ratahara has said: 'Great King!
All in this world are subject to the law of aging.'"
“What is the meaning of what the Venerable Ratahara has just said?
The Venerable Ratahara replied:
“Great King!”
I now ask the King; answer as you see fit.
If the Great King were twenty-four or twenty-five years of age, what would you think?
"At that time, how was your speed compared to now?
At that time, how were your physical strength, your body, and your complexion compared to now?
King Kūlāva replied:
"Ratthapāla! When I was twenty-four or twenty-five years old, I recall that at that time, in terms of speed, physical strength, bodily form, and complexion, there was no one who surpassed me."
Ratthapāla! I am now extremely old;
my faculties have fully matured in decay, my life span is nearly exhausted, and having reached eighty years of age, I can no longer rise up.
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: "Great King,
for this reason the Blessed One has said that everything in this world is subject to the law of aging."

"I desire to endure and find joy in this; I know, see, and have heard this. For this reason, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and with deep faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path."
King Kūṭadanta said: "If Ratahāra says:
'Great King!'"
"All that exists in this world tends toward the nature of aging.
This is what I also wish to accept and find pleasure in. Why is that?
"In this world, everything truly tends toward the nature of aging.
King Koravya asked again: "If, as Ratahara has said:"
"Great King!
This world is impermanent; one must inevitably depart from it.
What is the meaning of what Raṭṭhapāla has just said?
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said: “Great King!
I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"Great King!
Is there the kingdom of Aṅga, with its abundant palace and abundant storehouses?
King Krauḷāva replied:
"So it is," [the King replied]. Then the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla asked again:
"Great King!..."

There may be one who possesses a prosperous kingdom, a prosperous harem, and abundant storehouses; yet when the time comes that the Dharma arrives and cannot be relied upon, they will tolerate and delight in destruction—for there is no one in all the world who does not return to death.
"At that time, could the abundance of the kingdom of Koṭigāma, the abundance of the royal palace,
and the abundance of the storehouses be carried from this world into the next? King Koravya replied, "No."
"Why is that? Because I am alone and without a second, and I have no companion as I pass from this world to the next.
Thus spoke the Venerable Ratakhara.
"Great King!
For this reason, the World-Honored One has taught that this world is impermanent and must inevitably be abandoned.

I desire to accept and rejoice in this; I know, see, and have heard this. Therefore, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, left my home for the homeless life to study the Way."
King Koravya said: "If Ratahara says:
'Great King!'"
As for the statement, "This world is impermanent;
one must inevitably leave it behind," I too wish to accept and delight in this. Why is that?
"This world is truly impermanent; one must inevitably depart from it.
King Koravya asked again: "What does Ratahāra say?"
"Great King!
This world is never full; there is no satiety, for one is driven about by craving.
What is the meaning of what Raṭṭhapāla has just said?
The Venerable Raṭṭhapāla replied:
“Great King, I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"Great King!
Does the kingdom of Aṅga have abundant villages, abundant palaces, and abundant storehouses?
King Koravya replied:
"So it is," replied the Venerable Ratahara. Then he asked again:
"Great King!"

Suppose there is a kingdom called Abhaya, with abundant palaces and abundant storehouses. If a person were to come from the east—one who is trustworthy, reliable, and does not deceive the world—and say to the king:
"I have come from the east and have seen that kingdom to be exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a great multitude of people."
"Great King!
Would you be able to obtain all the wealth, the people, and the labor of that country, desiring to govern that country?
King Kaurava replied:
"Ratthapāla! If I knew of such a wealthy kingdom, with its vast wealth, its people, and its laborers, and if I could bring those people under my command and governance, I would certainly take it."

“In the same way, suppose someone were to come from the further shore of the great ocean in the south, the west, or the north—someone trustworthy and reliable, who does not deceive the world—and say to the king:
‘I have come from the further shore of the great ocean; I saw that land to be exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a vast population.’”
"Great King!
Would you obtain all the wealth, people, and labor of that country, desiring to govern that kingdom?
King Kaurava replied:
"Ratthapāla! If I knew of such a wealthy kingdom, with its vast wealth, people, and laborers, and if I could bring those people under my control and governance, I would certainly take it."
The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla said: "Great King!
For this reason, the Blessed One has said that this world is never filled and knows no satiety; it is driven about by craving."

I desire to endure and delight in this; I know, see, and have heard this. For this reason, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and with deep faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Path.
King Koravya said: "If what the Licchavi Ratahara has spoken—'Great King! [is true, then...]
"In this world there is no fulfillment; there is no satiety, for one is driven about by craving.
This is what I also desire to accept and delight in. Why is that?
"In this world, there is truly no fulfillment; there is no satiety, for one is driven about by craving.
The Venerable Ratahara said:
"Great King!"

The World-Honored One knows and sees; the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught these four matters to me. I know, accept, and delight in them; I know, see, and hear them. For this reason, I have shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith, left home for the homeless life to study the Path.
Then, the Venerable Rāṭṭhapāla spoke this verse:
“I see people in the world who, though possessing wealth, are deluded and do not give;
having acquired riches, they seek more still, greedily amassing possessions out of stinginess.”
When a king has gained the world, he governs it according to his power;
yet, never satisfied with what is within the seas, he seeks further beyond the oceans.
Both the king and his people, before they have escaped desire, reach the end of their lives.
With disheveled hair, wife and children weep; alas, how difficult it is to endure!
Clad in shrouds, they are buried, or else piled upon wood and consumed by fire.
Driven by karma, one proceeds to the next world; once burned, there is no more mindful awareness.
After death, wealth does not follow; neither wife nor children, nor servants.
This is common to both the poor and the rich, and likewise for the foolish and the wise.
The wise harbor no grief; only the foolish embrace sorrow and dejection.
Therefore, wisdom is supreme, for it leads to the attainment of the path of perfect enlightenment.
Those who are deeply attached to existence and its continuations, being deluded, commit evil deeds;
they act according to what is not the Dharma and forcibly seize from others by means of their strength.
Those of little wisdom follow the example of others; the foolish commit many evil deeds.
They enter the womb and proceed to future lives, undergoing birth and death again and again.
Having already been born into this world, they alone perform all manner of evil acts.
Just as a thief, bound by others, is harmed by his own evil deeds,
so too these sentient beings, having reached the next world,
are harmed by their own evil deeds committed for themselves.
If the mature fall by themselves, the young and old are likewise so.
Desiring to adorn and cherish what is pleasant, the mind pursues beautiful and foul forms.
Bound and harmed by desire, fear arises because of desire.
"O King, having perceived this realization, I know him to be a wondrous śramaṇa.
Thus spoke the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla.
Having heard what the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had said, King Koravya rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Ratthapāla Sutta*, the sixteenth, ends here. Total: 6,777 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 31.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
133. Upāli Sūtra (133). Chapter on the Great Discourses, Upāli Sūtra, the seventeenth, for the third recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Nālandā, in the Pāvāla Mango Grove.
At that time, the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, having wandered about in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was staying. They exchanged greetings and sat down to one side.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked:
"Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, how many practices do you prescribe so that one does not engage in evil deeds and does not commit evil deeds?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied: “Gautama!
Our venerable teacher, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, does not prescribe for us a course of conduct that would prevent us from engaging in evil deeds or committing evil deeds.”
"However, he has established punishments for us so that we do not engage in unwholesome actions and do not commit unwholesome deeds.
The Blessed One asked again:
"Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the son of Nigaṇṭha, establishes how many punishments to ensure that one does not engage in unwholesome actions and does not commit unwholesome deeds?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied: "Gautama!
Our venerable teacher, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, has prescribed three types of punishment for us, so that we do not commit evil deeds and do not perform evil deeds."
"What are the three?
They are bodily transgression, verbal transgression, and mental transgression.
The World-Honored One asked again:
“Ascetic! In what way are bodily punishment, verbal punishment, and mental punishment distinct?
The ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra replied:
“Gautama! Our bodily retributions are distinct, our verbal retributions are distinct, and our mental retributions are distinct.
The World-Honored One then asked again:

“Ascetic! These three types of punishment are similar; which punishment does the son of the Nigaṇṭhas prescribe as the most severe, so that one would not commit evil deeds and would not perform evil deeds?”
"Is it through bodily punishment, verbal punishment, or mental punishment?
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha of Long Asceticism replied, "Gautama!"

These three punishments are similar in this way; my venerable teacher, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, has prescribed the punishment of the body as the most severe, so that one does not engage in unwholesome actions and does not commit unwholesome deeds.
"Verbal punishment is not so; mental punishment is the most base, for it does not reach the body, whereas physical punishment is extremely great and very heavy.
The World-Honored One asked again: "Ascetic!"
"Do you say that corporal punishment is the most severe?
The ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra replied, "Gautama!"
"Physical punishment is the most severe.
The World-Honored One asked again, a second and third time: "Ascetic!"
"Do you say that corporal punishment is the most severe?
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha of Long Austerities also replied a second and a third time: "Gautama!"
"Physical punishment is the most severe.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having ascertained this matter with the long-practicing Nigaṇṭha three times, remained silent.
The Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapasvin asked:
"How many punishments does the ascetic Gautama prescribe so that people do not practice evil deeds and do not commit evil deeds?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:
“O ascetic! I do not prescribe punishment to prevent one from performing evil deeds or committing evil deeds.
I simply prescribe karma to prevent one from performing evil deeds or committing evil deeds.”
The long-practicing ascetic Nigaṇṭha asked:
“Gautama, how many kinds of karma do you prescribe so that one does not engage in unwholesome karma and does not perform unwholesome karma?
The Blessed One replied again:
