“O ascetic! I have established three courses of action so that one does not engage in unwholesome karma and does not perform unwholesome karma.
What are these three?
"Namely, bodily action, verbal action, and mental action.
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha asked: "Gautama!"
"Are bodily action, verbal action, and mental action different from one another?
The World-Honored One replied once more:
"O Ascetic!"
"My bodily actions are different, my verbal actions are different, and my mental actions are different.
The ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra asked:
"Gautama!..."
Since these three types of action are thus similar, which one should be designated as the most grave so that one does not commit evil actions and does not perform evil deeds?
Is it bodily action, verbal action, or mental action?
The Blessed One replied again:
“O ascetic!
These three types of action are thus comparable; yet I designate mental action as the most weighty, so that one does not engage in unwholesome action and does not perform unwholesome action.”
"Physical and verbal actions are not like that.
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha asked, "Gautama!"
"Is the mental action that is designated as the most weighty?
The World-Honored One replied once more:
"O Ascetic!"
"I designate mental action as the most serious.
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha asked a second and a third time:
"Gautama!..."
"Is mental action considered the most weighty?
To this, the World-Honored One also replied a second and a third time:
"O ascetic!"
"I declare that mental action is the most weighty.

Thereupon, after the ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra had repeatedly confirmed this matter with the Blessed One, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed, going to where the son of the Nirgranthas was.
When Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta saw the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha approaching from afar, he immediately asked him: "Ascetic!
From where have you come?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied:
"Venerable sir,
I have come from the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama at the Pāvārika-ambavana in Nālandā."
The son of the Nigaṇṭhas asked:
"Ascetic! Have you had any discussion with the śramaṇa Gautama?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied,
"Let us debate.
Then Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said:
“Ascetic! If you have any discussion with the śramaṇa Gautama, tell it all to me; perhaps I may understand what he has discussed.
Thereupon, the ascetic Dīrgha Nirgrantha told him everything that had been discussed with the Blessed One. Upon hearing this, the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent, ascetic!

It is well that you, as a disciple, practice the dharma toward your teacher; that your actions are characterized by wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness; that you have attained security and fearlessness, achieving mastery over yourself; that you have reached great eloquence and obtained the banner of the Deathless, dwelling in the realm of the Deathless through personal realization."

Why is that? Because you previously attributed the infliction of corporal punishment to the śramaṇa Gautama as the most severe means for preventing the commission of evil deeds and ensuring that one does not perform evil deeds.
"Verbal punishment is not so; mental punishment is the lowest, as it does not reach the body, whereas physical punishment is the greatest and most severe.
At that time, the lay follower Upāli was present among the assembly with five hundred other lay followers, and they all joined their palms toward the son of Nigaṇṭha.
Thereupon, the householder Upāli said to the long-practicing ascetic Nigaṇṭha:
"Has the Venerable One already ascertained this matter concerning the śramaṇa Gautama on three occasions?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied:
"Householder!
I have already ascertained this matter concerning the śramaṇa Gautama two or three times."
The householder Upāli said to the long-practicing ascetic Nirgrantha:
"I too am able to go up to three times to verify such matters regarding the śramaṇa Gautama, and then follow accordingly, whether it be to lead him forward or pull him back."
"Just as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram and pull it in whatever direction he wishes,
so too am I able to pull the Śramaṇa Gautama toward this matter two or three times until the matter is thoroughly settled, pulling him in whatever direction I wish."
"Just as a strong man might take a fine fur garment in his hand and shake it to remove the dust,
so too have I been able to examine these matters with the ascetic Gautama up to three times, pulling and dragging them as they were led."
It is just as when a wine-seller or his apprentice takes a wine-straining bag, places it in deep water, and then pulls or drags it about according to their will and desire.
I am likewise able to go as many as three times to verify such matters with the śramaṇa Gautama, and then follow wherever he leads me.

It is like a king of nāga-elephants sixty years of age, possessing great pride, endowed with tusks, feet, and body, and with vigorous strength; when a strong man takes him away to wash his thighs, his back, his flanks, his belly, his tusks, and his head with water, and to play in the water.
I am likewise able to go as many as three times to verify such matters with the śramaṇa Gautama, and then return according to what he has clarified.
I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is, engage in discussion with him, and return only after having defeated him.
The son of the Nigaṇṭhas said to the householder Upāli:
"I can subdue the śramaṇa Gautama; you can as well, and the Nigaṇṭha of Long Asceticism can too."
Thereupon, the ascetic Nirgrantha Dīrgha addressed the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, saying:
"I do not wish for the householder Upāli to go to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is."

Why is this? The śramaṇa Gautama knows the spells of illusion and transformation; he can use these spells to create disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and we fear that the householder Upāli will be transformed by the śramaṇa Gautama and turned into his disciple.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: “O ascetic!
It is simply impossible that the householder Upāli would become a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama through his magical transformations.”
"If the śramaṇa Gautama accepts the householder Upāli as his disciple through a transformation, such a thing would certainly be possible.
The householder Upāli said this a second and a third time to the son of Nigaṇṭha:
"I shall now go to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is, engage in discussion with him, and return only after having defeated him."
The son of Nigaṇṭha also replied a second and third time:
"You should go quickly!
I can subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, and you can as well, as can the ascetic Nigaṇṭha of Long Practice."
The long-practicing ascetic Nigaṇṭha spoke again and yet again, saying:
"I do not wish for the householder Upāli to go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is."

Why is this? The śramaṇa Gautama knows the spells of illusion and transformation; he can use these spells to create disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and we fear that the householder Upāli will be transformed by the śramaṇa Gautama and turned into his disciple.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: "O ascetic!
It is simply impossible that the householder Upāli would become a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama through his magical transformations."
"If the śramaṇa Gautama were to accept the householder Upāli as his disciple through a transformation, such a thing would certainly be possible.
Householder Upāli! Go as you please."

Thereupon, the householder Upāli bowed his head at the feet of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and asked:
"Gautama!..."
"Has the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Pāṭikaputta come here today?
The World-Honored One replied, "He has."
“Householder!
the householder Upāli asked, “Gautama! What is it?”
"Did you have any discussion with the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta?
The Blessed One replied, "I did."
The householder Upāli said: “Gotama!
If you have any discussion with the ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra regarding long-term austerities, tell it all to me; having heard it, I may perhaps understand it.”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One recounted in full everything he had discussed with the ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra.
At that time, the householder Upāli heard this and exclaimed in praise: "Excellent!"
"O ascetic!

This means that toward one's teacher, one practices the dharma of a disciple; one’s actions are characterized by wisdom, eloquence, intelligence, and decisiveness; one is secure and fearless, having achieved self-mastery; one attains great eloquence and gains the banner of the Deathless, personally realizing and dwelling in the realm of the Deathless."

Why is this? It is because the ascetic Gautama has prescribed that corporal punishment is the most severe, intended to prevent one from committing evil deeds and to ensure that one does not perform evil deeds.
Verbal punishment is not so [severe], and mental punishment is the lowest; it does not equal the extreme greatness and extreme severity of corporal punishment.
At that time, the Blessed One said:
"Householder!
I wish to discuss this matter with you; if you abide in the ultimate truth, answer with the ultimate truth."
The householder Upāli replied,
“Gautama! I abide in the ultimate truth and answer by means of the ultimate truth.”
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
You should simply engage me in discussion on this matter.
The Blessed One asked:
“Householder!
What do you think?

Suppose there were a Nirgrantha who delights in giving, takes pleasure in practicing generosity, is free from frivolity and delights in being free from frivolity, is utterly pure, and practices incantations to the utmost degree.”
"When they come and go, they kill many insects, both large and small.
What do you think, householder?
Does the son of Nigaṇṭha prescribe retribution for this killing of living beings?"
The householder Upāli replied: “Gautama!
If there is volition, there is great demerit; if there is no volition, there is no great demerit.”
The Blessed One asked:
“Householder,
what do you say intention is?”
The householder Upāli replied: “Gautama,
it is mental action.”
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder,
you should reflect carefully before you answer."
What you have said is contradictory: the former contradicts the latter, and the latter contradicts the former; thus it is inconsistent.
Householder!
You yourself declared here in this assembly:
"Gautama! I abide in ultimate truth and answer with ultimate truth.
Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"However, you should discuss this matter with me.
"Householder!
What do you think?"
If there is a Nirgrantha who comes to drink hot broth and abstains from cold water, and when he has no hot broth he wishes to drink cold water but cannot obtain it, he then passes away.
"Householder!
How can it be said that the son of Nigaṇṭha has been reborn?
The householder Upāli replied:
“Gautama! There is a heaven named Manopadosika; when that Nigaṇṭha passes away—if he dies with a corrupted mind—he will certainly be reborn there.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Householder!
You should reflect before you answer.
What you have said contradicts what came before, and what comes after contradicts what came before; thus, it is inconsistent.”
"You declared here in this assembly: 'Gautama!
I abide in the ultimate truth; I answer by means of the ultimate truth.'"
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
You should simply engage me in discussion on this matter.
"Householder! [the Buddha replied.]
What do you think?
Suppose someone were to come carrying a sharp sword and say this:
‘Within this Lake Nanda, I shall, in a single day, hack, mince, cut, split, tear, and slice all sentient beings, making them into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh.’”
"Householder!
What do you think?

Would that person be able, within a single day, to hack, mince, cut, tear, split, and slice all sentient beings within this Nanda Lake, making them into a single mass of flesh and a single heap of flesh?"
The householder Upāli replied:
“No, sir. And why is that? Because:”
This Nanda is internally extremely wealthy and prosperous, and it has a great many inhabitants.

Therefore, that person would certainly be unable, within a single day, to hack, chop, cut, tear, split, and slice all the sentient beings within this Nanda into a single mass of flesh or a single heap of flesh.
"Gautama!
That person has exerted himself in vain. "Householder!"
What do you think?
Suppose a śramaṇa or brahmin were to come who possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, having attained mastery over the mind, and were to say:
"By giving rise to a single thought of anger, I shall cause all these Nanda-nandas to burn from within and be reduced to ashes."
"Householder!
What do you think?
Could those śramaṇas and brahmins truly cause this entire Nanda to be burned up and reduced to ashes from within?"
The householder Upāli replied: “Gautama,
how could it be only one Nanda?”
"Not only two, three, or four, Gautama!

Those śramaṇas and brahmins possess great supernormal power (ṛddhi), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; their minds have attained mastery. If they were to give rise to a single thought of anger, they could burn all the people in every kingdom until they were reduced to ashes—how much more so a single Nanda?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder,
you should reflect before you answer."
What you have said is contradictory; the former contradicts the latter, and the latter contradicts the former, thus it is inconsistent.
In this very assembly, you yourself declared:
"Gautama!..."
"I abide in the ultimate truth and answer according to the ultimate truth,
Śramaṇa Gautama!
You should simply engage me in discussion regarding this matter."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Householder!

Have you ever heard that the great marsh is without affairs, the qilin is without affairs, the deer is without affairs, the profound stillness is without affairs, the empty wilderness is without affairs, and that 'without affairs' is itself without affairs?"
The householder Upāli replied:
“Gautama, I have heard that there is.”
“Householder! What do you think?

For whom is that great marsh a place of non-action; for whom is it a place where the qilin roam, where the elk and deer roam, where there is tranquil stillness, where there is the empty wilderness—where non-action is itself non-action?”
The householder Upāli remained silent and did not answer.
The World-Honored One said to him,
“Householder!”
Answer quickly!
Householder!
Answer quickly!
"Now is not the time for silence.
Householder, you yourself have declared here before this assembly: 'Gautama!'"
"I abide in the ultimate truth and answer with the ultimate truth,
Śramaṇa Gautama!
You should simply engage me in discussion on this matter."
Thereupon, after remaining silent for a moment, the householder Upāli said:
“Gautama, it was not that I was silent; I was merely reflecting upon this matter.”
"Gautama!

Those foolish Nigaṇṭhas lack skillful understanding and are unable to discern; they do not recognize the fertile field and fail to examine themselves. For a long night they have deceived me, and being led astray by them, I maintained that among the bodily punishments prescribed for the śramaṇa Gautama, the most severe is that which prevents one from committing evil deeds and causes one not to perform evil deeds, whereas verbal and mental punishments are not equal to it."

According to the meaning I understand from what was said by the śramaṇa Gautama, when a seer gives rise to a single thought of anger, it can cause the great marsh to become desolate, the qilin to become desolate, the elk and deer to become desolate, the tranquility to become desolate, and the wilderness to become desolate; once desolate, it is truly desolate.
"Bhagavān!
I have understood. Sugata!"
I have understood.

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder!
You should act in silence; do not proclaim this aloud. Such superior persons practice virtue in silence."
The householder Upāli said:
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I feel even greater joy toward the World-Honored One.”
Why is that? Because the Blessed One has spoken thus:
"Householder!..."
“Go in silence; do not proclaim this. Such superior persons perform good deeds in silence.
“World-Honored One!

If I were to become a disciple of other śramaṇas or brahmins, they would immediately carry banners, streamers, and parasols, traveling everywhere throughout Nālandā to proclaim: ‘[Such-and-such] has become a disciple of [so-and-so].’”
"The householder Upāli has become my disciple; the householder Upāli has become my disciple.
Yet, the Blessed One has said:
'Householder!'"
"Go silently; do not proclaim it. Such superior persons perform good deeds in silence.
The householder Upāli said:
"World-Honored One!"

"From this day forward, I do not permit any of the Nirgranthas to enter my house; I allow only the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One’s disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—to enter."
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder!
Those Nigaṇṭhas whom you have long revered as your family’s teachers—if they should come, you ought to provide for them with offerings according to your means."
Upāli said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One!
For this reason, I feel even greater joy toward the Blessed One.”
Why is this? It is because the Blessed One has spoken thus:
"Householder!..."
“Those Nirgranthas, whom your family has long revered and honored—if they should come, you ought to provide them with offerings according to your means.
“World-Honored One! [he replied.]
I have previously heard the World-Honored One speak thus:
"One should give to me, and not to another;
one should give to my disciples, and not to the disciples of others."
If one gives to me, one shall obtain great merit; if one gives to another, one shall not obtain great merit.
If one gives to my disciples, one shall obtain great merit; if one gives to the disciples of others, one shall not obtain great merit.
The World-Honored One said:
"Householder!
I do not speak in such a manner."
"You should give to me, not to another;
you should give to my disciples, not to the disciples of others.
If you give to me, you shall obtain great merit; if you give to another, you shall not obtain great merit."
"If one gives to my disciples, one shall obtain great merit; if one gives to the disciples of others, one shall not obtain great merit.
"Householder!

Although I speak thus, one should give to all with a joyful heart according to one's inclination; yet, if one gives to those who are not diligent, one shall not obtain great merit, whereas if one gives to those who are diligent, one shall obtain great merit."
The householder Upāli said:
“World-Honored One!
May you please not do so.”
"I myself know when I give to the Nirgranthas and when I do not give to the Nirgranthas.
World-Honored One!

I now once again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, until my very end, I take refuge."

Thereupon, the Blessed One taught the Dharma to the householder Upāli, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and establishing him in joy; by means of countless skillful methods, he taught him the Dharma, exhorting and inspiring him with longing.

Having brought about joy, he taught the Dharma of the fundamentals as is the custom of all Buddhas, so that those who heard it would be delighted—namely, he spoke on generosity, on ethical discipline, and on the way to rebirth in heaven; he censured sensual desire as a calamity and birth-and-death as a defilement, while praising the excellence of dispassion and the purity of the factors of the path.

When the Blessed One had taught this Dharma to him, the Buddha knew that he possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a supple mind, a patient mind, an uplifted mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free from doubt, and a mind free from hindrances; that he was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma—that is, the essential method as taught by all Buddhas.
The Blessed One then taught him suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
There and then, while seated, the householder Upāli perceived the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—just as a piece of white cloth is easily dyed with color.
Thus, while seated, the householder Upāli realized the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Thereupon, the householder Upāli saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he awakened to the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, transcended uncertainty, and recognized no other teacher as supreme. No longer depending on others and free from hesitation, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit and attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the Blessed One.
He immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!

I now take refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live."
Thereupon, the householder Upāli, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, received and retained it well. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and returned home.

He then commanded his gatekeepers: "You should know this: from this day forward, I am now a disciple of the World-Honored One. When any of the Nirgranthas come, do not allow them to enter the gate; only allow the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One’s disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter."
If any Nirgranthas come, you should say to them:
"Venerable sirs!

The householder Upāli has now been transformed by the Buddha and has become his disciple; he therefore does not permit any Nirgranthas to enter the gate, but permits only the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One’s disciples—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter."
"If you require food, you may stay here; we shall bring out food for you.

Thereupon, when the ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra heard that the householder Upāli had been converted by the śramaṇa Gautama and become his disciple, he no longer permitted the Nirgranthas to enter his gate, but permitted only the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter.
Having heard this, the long-practicing Nigaṇṭha went to the son of the Nigaṇṭhas and said to him:
"Venerable sir!
This is what I originally taught."
The son of Nigaṇṭha asked:
"Ascetic! What was it that you originally asserted?"
The ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas replied:
"Venerable sir!
What I said originally was that I did not wish for the householder Upāli to go to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama."

Why is this? The śramaṇa Gautama knows the spells of illusion and transformation; he can use these spells to create disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. We fear that the householder Upāli will be transformed by the śramaṇa Gautama and created as his disciple.
"Venerable Sir!
The householder Upāli has now been converted by the śramaṇa Gautama.
Having become his disciple, he no longer permits the Nirgranthas to enter his gate, but allows only the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter."
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: "O ascetic!
It is impossible that the householder Upāli would ever become a disciple through being converted by the śramaṇa Gautama."
"If the śramaṇa Gautama were to accept the householder Upāli as his disciple through a supernatural transformation, such a thing would certainly be possible.
The long-practicing Nirgrantha spoke again, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"If you do not believe what I have said, you may go yourself, or you may send a messenger.
Thereupon, the son of Nigaṇṭha said: "O Ascetic!"

"You should go there yourself and observe: has the householder Upāli been converted into a disciple by the śramaṇa Gautama, or has the śramaṇa Gautama been converted into a disciple by the householder Upāli?"
Having received the instruction from Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas went to the house of the lay follower Upāli.
Seeing the ascetic Nigaṇṭha Dīrgha-tapas approaching from afar, the gatekeeper said this:
"Venerable sir!"

The lay follower Upāli has now received the Buddha’s transformation and become a disciple; he will not allow any of the Nirgranthas to enter the gate, but will only allow the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter.
"If you wish to obtain food, you may stay here; we shall bring forth food and give it to you.
The ascetic Nirgrantha Dīrgha replied, "Gatekeeper!..."
"I do not require food.
Having learned of this matter, the ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra shook his head and departed, going to where the Nirgrantha son was and said to him:
"Venerable sir!..."
"This is exactly as I have previously taught.
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked: "Ascetic!"
"What was it that you originally asserted?
The ascetic Nirgrantha Jñātiputra replied:
"Venerable sir!"
What I originally intended to say was that I did not wish for the householder Upāli to go to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama. Why is this?

Because the śramaṇa Gautama knows the spells of illusion and transformation; he is able to use spells to transform and create disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and I feared that the householder Upāli would be transformed by the śramaṇa Gautama and turned into a disciple.
Venerable Sir!

The householder Upāli has now been converted by the śramaṇa Gautama; having become his disciple, he no longer permits the Nirgranthas to enter his gate, but allows only the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to enter.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: "O ascetic!
It is simply impossible that the householder Upāli would become a disciple through being converted by the śramaṇa Gautama."
"If the ascetic Gautama were to accept the householder Upāli as a disciple, it would certainly be possible.
The long-practicing Nigaṇṭha said,
"Venerable sir!"
"If you do not believe what I have said, I pray that the Venerable One will go there himself.
Thereupon, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a great assembly of five hundred Nigaṇṭhas, went to the house of the householder Upāli.
Seeing from afar the son of the Nigaṇṭhas arriving together with a great assembly of five hundred Nigaṇṭhas, the gatekeeper said:
"Venerable sir!

The householder Upāli has now been converted by the Buddha and has become his disciple; he no longer permits the Nigaṇṭhas to enter the gate, but allows only the fourfold assembly of the World-Honored One’s disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—to enter."
"If you wish to obtain food, you may stay here; we shall bring out food and give it to you.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: "Gatekeeper!"
"I have no need for food; I only wish to see the householder Upāli.
The gatekeeper said, "May the Venerable One remain here while I enter now to inform the householder Upāli."
The gatekeeper immediately went in and announced:
"Householder,
you should know that Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, together with a great assembly of five hundred Nigaṇṭhas, is standing outside the gate, saying these words:"
"I wish to see the householder Upāli.
The householder Upāli told the gatekeeper:
"Go to the middle gate, prepare a seat, and once it is finished, return and inform me."
The gatekeeper, having received these instructions, went to the middle gate; having finished arranging the seats, he returned and reported:
"Householder, you should know that the seats have been arranged; I pray only that you yourself will know the proper time."

The householder Upāli took the gatekeeper and went to the middle gate. There was a couch there that was exceedingly high and vast, and most beautifully spread with fine coverings—the very one upon which the householder Upāli had previously seated the son of Nigaṇṭha when he brought him in his arms.
The householder Upāli sat upon it, assuming the full lotus posture, and addressed the gatekeeper:
"Go out to where the son of Nigaṇṭha is and speak these words:
'Venerable sir!'"
The householder Upāli said,
"Venerable sir, if you wish to enter, you may do as you please.
Having received these instructions, the gatekeeper went out to where Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta was and spoke to him thus:
“Venerable sir!
The householder Upāli says:
‘Venerable sir, if you wish to enter, you may do as you please.’”
Thereupon, the son of Nigaṇṭha entered through the middle gate together with a great assembly of five hundred Nigaṇṭhas.
Seeing from afar the son of Nigaṇṭha entering with the great assembly of five hundred Nigaṇṭhas, the householder Upāli spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!"
"There is a seat; sit as you please.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said:
"Householder!"
"Is this how you should act?
Ascend the high seat, sit cross-legged, and converse with others just as one who has left the household life to study the Path does—no different at all.
The householder Upāli said:
“Venerable sir!
I have my own property; I may give it away as I wish, or I may not give it away. This seat is mine, therefore I say:
‘There is a seat; sit as you please.’”
The son of Nigaṇṭha spread his seat and sat down, saying:
"Householder!
For what reason is this so?"
"Seeking to subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, you have instead been subdued by him yourself.
It is just as if someone seeking eyes went into the forest and returned having lost his own eyes.
In this way, householder, you set out to subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, but you have instead been subdued by the śramaṇa Gautama."
It is just as if someone, entering a pool because of thirst, were to return thirsty once more.
So it is with the householder: desiring to go and subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, he has instead returned having been subdued himself.
“Householder!
Why is that so? The householder Upāli replied:
"Venerable sir!
Listen as I speak a parable; for the wise, upon hearing a parable, understand its meaning.
Venerable sir!"
For example, there was a certain brahmin who had a young wife.
While she was pregnant, she said to her husband, "I am now pregnant; go to the market and buy fine toys for the child."
Then, that brahmin said to his wife:
"Once you have given birth in safety and peace, why worry about having nothing?
If a son is born, I shall buy male playthings for you; if a daughter is born, I shall likewise buy female playthings for you."
The wife spoke to her husband two or three times, saying:
"I am now pregnant; when you go to the market, quickly buy fine toys for the child and bring them back."
The brahmin also spoke to his wife two or three times, saying:
"Once you have given birth in safety and peace, why worry about having nothing?
If a boy is born, I shall buy toys for boys to bring back; if a girl is born, I shall likewise buy toys for girls to bring back."
That brahmin felt such deep compassion for his wife that he immediately asked her,
"What kind of toy do you wish to buy for your son?
His wife replied to him:
"Go and buy a monkey for the child as a fine plaything.
Having heard this, the brahmin went to the marketplace and purchased a monkey and playthings.
He brought it back and said to his wife,
"I have bought this monkey toy for our child and have returned.
When his wife saw it, she disliked its poor color and immediately said to her husband:
"You may take this monkey toy to a dyer's house, have it dyed yellow, make it extremely lovely, and pound it until it becomes lustrous.
Having heard this, the brahmin immediately took the monkey toy, went to a dyer's house, and said to him:
"Dye this monkey toy for me in a fine yellow, making it extremely lovely and pounding it until it becomes lustrous."
At that time, the dyer said to the brahmin:
"It is permissible to dye the monkey toy yellow to make it extremely attractive; however, it must not be pounded to produce a gloss."
Thereupon, the dyers spoke this verse:
"The monkey endures the dye, but cannot endure being pounded;
if pounded, its life would end. It can never be beaten."
"This is a foul and filthy sack, filled with impurities like a monkey. "Venerable sir!

You should know that the teachings of the Nirgranthas are likewise; they are unable to endure the challenging questions of others, nor can they withstand reflection and investigation. They are stained only by delusion, not by wisdom."
"Venerable sir!

Listen further: suppose there were a clean cloth from Vārāṇasī, and its owner took it to a dyer's house and said to him, 'Please dye this cloth so that it becomes an exquisite color, one that is truly lovely.'"
"It shall also be thoroughly pounded so that a luster arises.
Then, the dyer said to the owner of the cloth:
"This cloth may be dyed to produce an excellent color, making it lovely."
"It may also be pounded thoroughly so that a luster arises.
Thereupon, the dyers spoke this verse:
"Just as a garment from Vārāṇasī, White and pure, receives the dye,"
"Once ground, it becomes soft and its luster and color are enhanced. "Venerable sir!

You should know that the teachings of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas are likewise; they are perfectly able to withstand the difficult questions of others, and they can be readily contemplated and investigated."
"It is only that his wisdom is defiled, not his ignorance.
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said:
"The householder has been transformed by the magical incantations of the śramaṇa Gautama."
The householder Upāli said: "Venerable sir!
It is a well-performed feat of illusion, a most excellent feat of illusion."
Venerable sir!

This illusion-transforming spell causes my parents to obtain benefit and profit for a long night, and brings them peace, security, and happiness; as does it for my wife, children, slaves, servants, and laborers, as well as for King Nanda, and for all the world—including devas, Māras, and Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins—from humans up to the heavens, causing them to obtain benefit and profit for a long night, and bringing them peace, security, and happiness.
The son of Nigaṇṭha said: "Householder!
When Naṭa-bhaṭika declared that the householder Upāli was a disciple of the Nigaṇṭhas, who is he now actually the disciple of?"
Thereupon, the householder Upāli rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and—as if there were a Buddha present—joined his palms toward that direction and said:
"Venerable sir!..."
Listen to what I say:
"The heroic one, free from folly, has severed defilements and brought himself under control;
possessing peerless and subtle reflection, he trains in the precepts, meditation, and wisdom."
Tranquil and free from defilement, the Buddha’s disciple Upāli,
having practiced under the Great Sage, attained virtue and mastery in speech;
with wholesome mindfulness and sublime right contemplation, he is neither elated nor dejected.
Immovable and eternally sovereign, the Buddha’s disciple Upāli;
Without crookedness and always content, having abandoned stinginess he attained fulfillment;
Having become a śramaṇa, he perfected awakening; in his final body, he was a venerable mahāsattva.
Peerless and free from defilement, the Buddha’s disciple Upāli;
Free from illness and immeasurable, he has attained the profound state of a Muni.
Ever peaceful and courageous, he dwells in the subtle contemplation of the Dharma.
The Tamer is ever free from play; the Buddha’s disciple Upāli is a great dragon who delights in dwelling on high.
With all fetters exhausted, he has attained liberation;
his eloquence is pure, and through the arising of wisdom, he is free from sorrow and grief.
There is no returning for Śākyamuni; the Buddha’s disciple Upāli rightly proceeds in meditative reflection. There is no defilement of his purity;
he always smiles without anger. Delighting in seclusion, he has attained the foremost state.
Fearless and ever-diligent is the Buddha’s disciple Upāli;

among the seven seers there is none his equal. Having attained the threefold knowledge and reached the state of Brahma, he is like a bright lamp after a pure bath; having found rest, he has severed the knots of enmity.
Brave and utterly pure is the Buddha’s disciple Upāli;
Having attained the wisdom of tranquility like the earth, his great wisdom removes the world’s greed.
Worthy of worship is the Unsurpassed Eye; this Supreme Being has no equal.
The charioteer is free from anger; he is Vāri, the disciple of the Buddha.
Having severed all craving, he is unsurpassed and virtuous; he is a well-trained, peerless driver.
He is ever joyful and unsurpassed, free from doubt and possessed of radiance.
Having severed pride, the Unsurpassed Awakened One; the Buddha’s disciple Vappa has severed craving.
The Peerless Awakened One is smokeless and without flame;
having departed thus, he is the Well-Gone One—peerless and beyond compare.
His fame has already reached perfection; he is the Buddha’s disciple Vāri.
This is the Buddha of a hundred hardships, whom he had never before contemplated.
What Upāli has spoken, there the devas have come to him.
"May you kindly grant me eloquence, according to the Dharma and according to the person;
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asks the disciple of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta asked:
“Householder!
With what intention do you praise the śramaṇa Gautama?
The householder Upāli replied:
“Venerable sir!
Listen as I speak a parable, for the wise understand the meaning through parables.
It is like a skilled garland-maker or his apprentice, who gathers various flowers and binds them together with long threads to create diverse garlands.”
Thus it is, O Venerable One!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses immeasurable praise; he is my own object of veneration, and for that reason I offer this praise.
When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Upāli became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him;
however, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta immediately vomited hot blood and, upon reaching the country of Pāvā, passed away shortly thereafter due to this affliction.
The Buddha spoke thus.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the lay follower Upāli rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The seventeenth discourse, "Upāli," ends here; it contains six thousand two hundred and sixty-three characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume Thirty-two.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 33.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
134. Śivaka-praśna Sūtra (134). Great Section, Śivaka-praśna Sūtra, Number Eighteen. Third Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and was staying at the Indrasailaguhā on Mount Vaibhāra, north of the village of Naḍika, east of the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, heard that the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and was staying at the Indrasailaguhā on Mount Vebhāra, north of the village of Āmrapālī, east of Rājagṛha.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, addressed Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharva:

"I have heard that the World-Honored One is traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and is currently staying at the Indrasailaguhā on Mount Vaidehaka, north of the village of Nyagrodhika, east of the city of Rājagṛha."
"Pañcasikha!
Come, let us go together to see the Buddha.
Pañcasikha the musician replied:

“Very well. Thereupon, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, carrying his vīṇā lute made of beryl, followed along with Śakra, the Lord of Devas. Hearing that Śakra, the Lord of Devas, held such profound reverence as to wish to go and see the Buddha, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven likewise followed as attendants upon Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

Then, Śakra, King of Devas, together with the gods of the Thirty-three and the Pañcaśikha Gandharva, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, suddenly vanished from the Heaven of the Thirty-three and appeared at Mount Vebhāra, not far from the stone cave, to the north of the village of Āmrapālī and east of Rājagṛha, the capital of the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, Mount Vepulla was brilliantly illuminated, its radiance like a blazing flame. When the residents living on the slopes of the mountain saw this, they thought to themselves:
"Mount Vepulla is engulfed in a great conflagration!"
Then, having stationed himself in one place, Śakra, the King of Devas, said: "Pañcaśikha!

Thus does the Blessed One dwell in remote forest retreats, beneath trees in the mountains and woods; he delights in dwelling on high crags, in solitude and silence, secluded, free from evil, and devoid of people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma."
They possess great majesty and dwell together with the devas; they delight in seclusion, abide in peaceful meditation, and wander in happiness.
We have not yet gained their attention; we should not proceed forward.
“Pañcasikha!
You go on ahead; we shall follow after you.
Pañcasikha the musician replied:
“Very well. Then, having received the instruction from Śakra, King of Gods, Pañcaśikha took up his vīṇā of lapis lazuli and went first to the Indra Cave, where he thought to himself:
“I know this place is neither too near nor too far from the Buddha; let the Buddha know me and hear my voice.”
Having settled there, he tuned his lapis lazuli lute and sang these verses corresponding to desire, corresponding to the nāgas, corresponding to the śramaṇas, and corresponding to the arhats:
“O Worthy One, I pay homage to your parents, Candra and Tamburu;
I say that because you were born so exceptionally sublime, you have caused my heart to rejoice.”
As one tormented by heat seeks a cool breeze, And as one parched with thirst longs to drink cold water,
So do I love you, Just as Rāhula loves the Dharma.
Just as it is extremely difficult to draw up water, So too is it with attachment to desire.
Having gathered together through immeasurable births, They give as if they were unattached.
The pond water is clear and cool, With golden sand at its bottom;
Like nāgas and elephants oppressed by heat, They enter this pond water to bathe.
Just as a hook draws in an elephant, my mind has been subdued by you;
though you do not perceive my conduct, I have not yet captured you.
My mind is utterly attached to you, and this grievous distress burns my heart.
Therefore, I find no joy, like a man who has entered a tiger’s mouth.
Like a son of the Śākyas contemplating dhyāna, I always delight in solitude;
like a Muni who has attained awakening, may I attain your wondrous, pure tranquility.
Just as the Muni delights in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, so do I delight in this;
I constantly seek to obtain you. As one who is ill desires medicine, as one who is hungry desires food.
Worthy one, you have stilled my mind, Just as water extinguishes fire.
Whatever merit I have created By making offerings to those who are unattached— May all that be pure and sublime; I shall share its fruit with you.
I vow that I shall end my life together with you, never to be parted and left alone;
I would rather die with you than live apart from you.
O Śakra, grant me this wish, O Honored One of the Thirty-three Heavens!
O Supreme Honored One among men, you are the firmest object of my aspiration.
Therefore, I pay homage to the Great Hero; bowing my head, I revere the Highest among men, who has severed the thorns of all craving—I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and praised Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Pañcasikha!

Your singing voice accords with the sound of the lute, and the sound of the lute accords with your singing voice; your singing voice does not issue forth outside the sound of the lute, nor does the sound of the lute issue forth outside your singing voice."
"Pañcasikha!
Do you perhaps recall having sung in the past these verses associated with sensual desire, verses associated with nāgas, verses associated with recluses, and verses associated with arhats?"
The son of Pañcaśikha replied, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Only the Great Seer himself should know this."
"Great Seer!
In the past, when the World-Honored One had first attained enlightenment, he was dwelling at the foot of the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree on the banks of the Nerañjarā River in Uruvelā."
At that time, there was a daughter of King Dandabhu, a master of music, named Bhadrayaśā.
There was a deity named Ghaṭa, the charioteer of Māndhātṛ, who sought to obtain her as his wife.
"O Great Seer!
When he sought to desire her, I likewise sought to obtain her.
However, O Great Seer!"

When I sought her, I was ultimately unable to obtain her; at that time, I stood behind her and sang these verses associated with desire, verses associated with nāgas, verses associated with śramaṇas, and verses associated with arhats.
"O Great Seer!
While I was reciting this verse, that woman turned her gaze toward me and, with a serene smile, spoke to me, saying:
'Pañcasikha!'"

I have never seen that Buddha, the World-Honored One; however, I have heard from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven of that World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat.
"Pañcasikha!
If you can praise the World-Honored One in such a way, you may join me in serving the Great Seer.
We met only once; since then, I have not seen him again.
Then, Śakra, the King of Devas, had this thought:
"Since Pañcaśikha has already caused the Blessed One to arise from his meditative absorption, he has acted as my intermediary with the Sugata."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, said: "Pañcaśikha!

Go there at once and, on my behalf, prostrate at the Buddha's feet and inquire after the World-Honored One: Is his holy body robust and healthy? Is he free from illness and living in comfort? Is his daily life easy and his strength as usual?"
He spoke these words: "O Great Seer!

Śakra, the Heavenly King, bows his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquires after the World-Honored One: Is your holy body robust and strong? Are you at ease, free from illness, and light in your movements? Is your vigor as it was before?"
"O Great Seer!
Śakra, the King of Devas, and the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens wish to see the World-Honored One.
Pañcaśikha the musician replied:
“Indeed, sir.
Thereupon, Pañcaśikha the musician set aside his lapis lazuli lute, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"O Great Seer!

Śakra, the King of Devas, bows his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquires after the World-Honored One’s holy body: Is it robust and strong? Are you at ease and free from illness? Is your daily life light and convenient? Is your vigor as it was before?"
"Great Seer!
Śakra, the King of Devas, and the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three wish to see the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Five knots!
Today, King Śakra is at peace and happy, as are all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and various other beings who are at peace and happy."
"Pañcasikha!
If King Śakra wishes to see me, let it be according to his desire.

Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, Pañcasikha received and retained it well; he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed for the abode of King Śakra, where he addressed him, saying:
“O Deva-king!
I have already informed the Blessed One; the Blessed One now awaits the Deva-king. May the Deva-king himself know the proper time.
Thereupon, Śakra, the Deva-king, together with the gods of the Thirty-three and the Pañcaśikha Gandharvas, went to where the Buddha was.
Then Śakra, King of the Devas, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and, repeating himself three times, announced his name and lineage, saying:
“O Great Seer! I am Śakra, King of the Devas; I am Śakra, King of the Devas.”
The World-Honored One said: "So it is. So it is."
"Kauśika! You are Śakra, the King of Devas.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, repeatedly announced his own name and lineage, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Pañcaśikha Gandharvas also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then Śakra, the King of Gods, said: “O Great Seer!
"Am I sitting near or far from the World-Honored One?
The World-Honored One replied, "Sit near me."
"Why is this? Because you have a great retinue of celestial deities.

Thereupon, Śakra, King of the Gods, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side; the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Pañcaśikha Gandharva youths likewise bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the Indra Cave suddenly became vast and spacious.
Why was this? It was due to the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha and the majestic virtue of the various devas.
Then, having sat down, Śakra, King of the Devas, addressed him, saying: "O Great Seer!
For a long night I have desired to see the World-Honored One and to inquire about the Dharma."
"Great Seer!
Once in the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and was staying within a stone cave, Great Seer!
at that time, for my own sake and for the sake of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, I mounted a chariot drawn by a thousand elephants and went to the house of King Viśvantara."

At that time, King Vessavaṇa had a concubine named Pañcasatā. At that moment, the World-Honored One had entered meditative absorption in profound stillness; the concubine joined her palms and paid homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.
"O Great Seer!
I said to her: 'Sister!'"

"It is not the time for me to go and see the World-Honored One now, as the World-Honored One has entered meditative concentration. If the World-Honored One awakens from his concentration, sister, you should prostrate at the Buddha’s feet on my behalf and inquire after the World-Honored One: Is your holy body healthy and strong? Are you at ease, free from illness, light in your movements, and as vigorous as usual?"
He spoke thus: "O Great Seer!

Śakra, the King of Devas, bows his head at the feet of the Buddha and inquires after the World-Honored One’s holy body: Is it healthy and strong? Are you at ease and free from illness? Are your daily activities light and convenient? Is your physical strength as it was before?"
"Great Seer! That sister of mine bows her head at the Buddha’s feet and inquires after the World-Honored One’s welfare: does the World-Honored One remember her?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Kauśika! That sister of yours has prostrated at my feet, fully conveyed your message, and inquired after my welfare; I, too, remember her, Kauśika!"
"When you depart, upon hearing this sound, you will awaken from your meditative absorption. "Great Seer!

In the past, I have heard that when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader, trainer of persons, teacher of devas and humans—known as Buddha, the Blessed One—appears in the world, the hosts of devas increase and the asuras decrease."
"Great Seer!

With my own eyes I have seen disciples of the World-Honored One, bhikṣus who practiced the holy life under the World-Honored One, abandoning desire and becoming free from desire; at the breaking up of the body after death, they attained a good destination and were reborn among the devas."
"Great Seer!

Gopikā, the daughter of the Śākyas, is a disciple of the Blessed One and has likewise practiced the holy life under the Blessed One. Loathing this female body and longing for a male form, she has transformed her woman's body and received a man's form. Having abandoned desire and become free from passion, at the breaking up of the body after death, she has attained rebirth in a sublime place, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, as my son."
Once he was born, all the devas knew that the devaputra Gopa possessed great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.
"Great Seer!

I have further seen three other disciples of the Blessed One who likewise practiced the holy life under the Blessed One; yet, without having abandoned desire, at the breaking up of the body after death, they were reborn in the lowly palaces of musicians."
Once she was born, she came daily to the Heaven of the Thirty-three to serve the devas and attend upon the Devaputra Gopa.
When the Devaputra saw her, he spoke this verse:
"O Upāsikā with beautiful eyes, my name is Gopī;..."
I revere the Buddha and the Dharma, And with a pure mind, I make offerings to the Saṅgha.
Having received the grace of the Buddha, The great benefactor among the sons of Śākya, He was born wondrously in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; He is known as the Devaputra Āyuṣmān.
Seeing that former bhikṣu, now born as a celestial musician deity, standing before me with palms joined, Gopa spoke this verse for him:
"This was formerly a son of Gautama; when I was once a human being..."
They come to my home, where they are provided with excellent food and drink.
Originally equal to the Sages, they practiced the unsurpassed Brahma-faring;
now, driven by others, they come daily to serve the gods.
I formerly served you and heard the holy and well-spoken Dharma;
having attained faith and perfected the precepts, I was born as a wondrous being among the Thirty-three Gods.
You, who were formerly honored with service, have practiced the unsurpassed Brahma-faring.
Now compelled by others, you come daily to serve the gods.
With what face can you do this? Having received and upheld the Buddha-dharma, you turn your back on it and do not face the Dharma; this is the eye that awakens to the well-spoken teaching.
In the past I saw you all, now born into lowly families of musicians and performers;
having practiced unrighteous conduct yourselves, you have given birth to unrighteousness within yourselves.
When I was formerly a householder, I observed my own superior virtues today.
"Transforming women into sons of heaven, they enjoy the pleasures of the five desires at will.
Having heard this, those who reviled Gautama became weary of their own ways and praised Gautama, saying:
"We shall now proceed to practice what the Son of Heaven has truly spoken."
"Exerting oneself toward those [teachings] and recollecting the Dharma and Vinaya of Gautama,
one knows that sensual desire brings calamity and danger, and thus immediately abandons that desire.
Though bound by the fetters of desire, one attains its relinquishment and seclusion."
Like an elephant breaking its tether, he transcends the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Indra, Brahmā, and all others gather there;
he ascends their very seats, a hero who has abandoned worldly desires.
Having seen this, Śakra, the supreme deva, the god among gods, felt weary [of worldly existence] and said:
"He was originally born into a lowly station, yet he has transcended the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Having become weary [of the world], Miao Xi spoke;
later, Gu-po said:
“In the human realm there is a supreme Buddha, Śākyamuni who understands desire.”
Among those sons, one loses mindfulness; though I rebuke him, he regains it.
Among the three [types of sons], one is born among musicians and performers.
Another accomplishes the equal and right path, abiding in the bliss of the heavenly faculties of meditative concentration.
When you preach such a Dharma, your disciples will be free from delusion;
they will cross over the outflows, sever wrong views and doubt, and pay homage to the Buddha who has conquered the sense-faculties.
If they awaken to all phenomena, they shall attain the two stages of advancement.
"Having attained advancement, he was reborn among the Brahmā gods;
we know his Dharma, and thus the Great Seer has come here.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"This spirit has long been free from flattery and deceit, without guile, but straightforward and honest.

If there is one who asks, it is because they desire full knowledge; they do not wish to cause disturbance. Their questioning is likewise so; therefore, I shall indeed explain the profound Abhidharma."
The World-Honored One, having understood this, spoke these verses for the sake of Śakra, King of Devas:
"For the sake of happiness in the present life, And also for happiness in future lives, Kauśika, ask whatever you wish; Ask according to what your heart desires."
Whatever questions they may ask, I shall resolve them all for them.
Having already granted his permission, the World-Honored One, the Sun-like One who seeks the meaning of the Dharma,
was questioned by the virtuous Vāsava in the kingdom of Magadha.
Thereupon, Śakra, King of the Devas, addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“World-Honored One!
Among devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and other various kinds of beings, how many fetters (saṃyojana) does each possess?”
Having heard this, the World-Honored One replied:
"Kauśika! Devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and various other beings each have two fetters: stinginess and envy."
Each of them formed this thought:
"May I be without staff, without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, without strife, without quarrel, and without suffering, so that I may wander in peace and happiness."
"Although he forms this thought, he nevertheless still possesses the staff, the fetters, enmity, ill will, strife, contention, and suffering; he does not dwell in peace and happiness."
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"So be it, Great Seer! Gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings each have two fetters."
He forms this thought:
"May I be without staff, without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, without contention, without strife, and without suffering, so that I may dwell in peace and happiness."

"Although he has this thought, he nevertheless still possesses the staff, possesses fetters, possesses enmity, possesses ill will, possesses strife, possesses quarreling, and possesses suffering; he does not dwell in peace and happiness."
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
"I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and transcended delusion, and I am free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer!
As for stinginess and envy, what is their cause, what is their condition, from what do they arise, and by what do they exist?"
"Furthermore, by what cause are there no stinginess or envy?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One replied: "Kauśika!"
Avarice and envy arise because of love and non-love; they are conditioned by love and non-love; they are born from love and non-love; they exist through love and non-love.
"If there were neither love nor non-love, then there would be no stinginess or envy.
Having heard this, Śakra, King of the Devas, replied:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"Yes indeed, Sugata! Yes indeed, Great Sage!
Stinginess and envy arise because of love and non-love; they are conditioned by love and non-love; they are born from love and non-love; they exist through love and non-love."
If there were neither love nor non-love, then there would be no stinginess or envy.
So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!
"So be it, Great Seer!
I fully understand all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and transcended my delusions, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer!..."
Regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant: by what cause and by what condition do they arise? From what do they originate, and through what do they exist?
Furthermore, by what cause and by what condition are there no pleasant or unpleasant things?
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: "Kauśika!
That which is pleasant and that which is unpleasant arise because of desire, conditioned by desire, born from desire, and exist by virtue of desire."
"If there is no desire, then there is neither love nor non-love.
Having heard this, Śakra, King of the Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
"Yes indeed, Sugata! Yes indeed, Great Sage!
Like and dislike arise because of desire, conditioned by desire, born from desire, and exist by virtue of desire. If there were no desire, then there would be no like or dislike."
"So be it, World-Honored One!
So be it, Sugata! So be it, Great Sage!"
"I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer! As for desire, what is its cause, what is its condition, from what does it arise, and by what does it exist?"
"Furthermore, by what cause is there an absence of desire?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One replied: "Kauśika!"
“Desire arises from thought and is conditioned by thought; it is born of thought and exists because of thought.
If there were no thought, then desire would not exist.
When King Śakra heard this, he said:
"Yes indeed, World-Honored One!
Yes indeed, Sugata!
Yes indeed, Great Sage!"
Desire arises from thought and is conditioned by thought; it is born from thought and exists because of thought. If there were no thought, then there would be no desire.
Indeed, World-Honored One!
"So be it, Sugata! So be it, Great Sage!
I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; having heard what the Buddha has spoken, I have severed my doubts, transcended my delusions, and am free from all hesitation."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"O Great Seer!
“What is the cause, what is the condition, from what does mindfulness arise, and by what does it exist?
Furthermore, by what cause is there an absence of mindfulness?
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied:

“Kauśika! Mindfulness arises because of volition; it is conditioned by volition, born from volition, and exists because of volition. If there were no volition, then mindfulness would not exist. Because of mindfulness, desire arises; because of desire, there arise likes and dislikes. Because of likes and dislikes, there arise stinginess and envy. Because of stinginess and envy, there arise swords and staves, strife, contention, malice, flattery, deception, false speech, and double-tongued talk. Thus, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states arise within the mind, and in this way, this entire mass of suffering comes into being.”

If there is no volition, then there is no mindfulness; if there is no mindfulness, then there is no desire; if there is no desire, then there is neither love nor hatred; if there is neither love nor hatred, then there is no stinginess or envy; if there is no stinginess or envy, then there is no sword or staff, no strife, no malice, no flattery, no deception, no false speech, and no double-tonguedness. Within the mind, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states do not arise. In this way, this entire mass of suffering ceases.
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
“Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
"Yes, indeed, Sugata! Yes, indeed, Great Sage! Mindfulness arises because of volition, conditioned by volition;

it is born from volition and exists because of volition. If there were no volition, then mindfulness would not exist. Because of mindfulness, desire arises; because of desire, there arise the pleasant and the unpleasant. Because of the pleasant and the unpleasant, there arise stinginess and envy; because of stinginess and envy, there arise weapons and staves, strife, contention, malice, flattery, deception, lying, and double-tongued speech. Thus, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states arise within the mind, and in this way, this entire mass of suffering comes into being."

If there is no volition, then there is no mindfulness; if there is no mindfulness, then there is no desire; if there is no desire, then there is neither love nor hatred; if there is neither love nor hatred, then there is no stinginess or envy; if there is no stinginess or envy, then there is no use of weapons or staves, no strife, no malice, no flattery, no deception, no false speech, and no double-tongued talk; and in the mind, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states do not arise. In this way, this entire mass of suffering ceases.
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
“I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, for I am free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, Śakra, King of the Devas, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer! What is the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation?"
"Bhikkhu, what practice leads toward the path of cessation of conceptual proliferation?
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied:
"Kosiya!..."

The path to the cessation of conceptual proliferation consists of the Noble Eightfold Path—namely, right view through to right concentration as the eight factors, Kauśika; this is called the path to the cessation of conceptual proliferation.
"A bhikkhu, by practicing this, follows the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation.
When the deva-king Śakra had heard this, he said:
"Indeed, Blessed One!"
"Yes indeed, Sugata!
Yes indeed, Great Sage!
That which is the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation is the Noble Eightfold Path, consisting of the eight factors from right view through to right concentration."
"Great Seer! This is the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation.
A bhikṣu who practices this proceeds toward the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation."
So it is, World-Honored One! So it is, Sugata!
"Indeed, Great Seer!

Regarding the Dharma as taught by the Buddha, I have understood it all; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has taught."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"O Great Seer!
“Bhikkhu, one who is treading the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation—how many things does he abandon, and how many things does he practice?
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied:
“Kosiya!...”
A bhikṣu who follows the path leading toward the cessation of conceptual proliferation abandons three things and cultivates three things.
What are these three?
First is mindfulness, second is speech, and third is seeking.
"Kauśika! Regarding mindfulness, I say there are two kinds: that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.

If it is a mindfulness that is not to be practiced, I immediately sever it; if it is a mindfulness that is to be practiced, I know the proper time for it. Possessing both mindfulness and wisdom, I act so as to bring that mindfulness to fulfillment."
The same applies to speech. Kauśika!
Regarding those who seek, I say there are also two kinds: that which is practicable and that which is impracticable.

If they seek that which is impossible to accomplish, I immediately reject it; if they seek that which is possible to accomplish, I act for them with awareness and wisdom at the proper time, so as to fulfill their quest.
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"Yes indeed, Great Seer!
A bhikkhu who is treading the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation abandons three things and cultivates three things.
What are these three?"
The first is mindfulness, the second is speech, and the third is seeking.
The Great Seer has taught that there are two kinds of mindfulness: that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.

If a thought increases unwholesome and evil states and diminishes wholesome states, the Great Seer abandons it; if a thought diminishes unwholesome and evil states and increases wholesome states, he cultivates it.
The Great Sage knows the proper time for them; he possesses mindfulness and wisdom because he has perfected that mindfulness, and his speech is likewise.
The Great Sage teaches that there are two kinds of seeking: that which is practicable and that which is impracticable.
If one seeks to increase unwholesome and evil states and diminish wholesome states, the Great Seer cuts them off.

If one seeks to diminish unwholesome and evil states and increase wholesome states, the Great Seer knows the proper time for that person, possessing mindfulness and wisdom, so as to fulfill that aspiration.
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
"I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and transcended delusion, and I am free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
Then, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:

"Great Seer! How many qualities does a bhikkhu possess who is progressing toward the path that leads to the cessation of proliferation, and how many qualities does he protect as he practices for liberation?"
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: "Kauśika!
For a bhikṣu, there are six qualities that lead toward the path of the cessation of conceptual proliferation, and six qualities for protecting one's practice of liberation."
What are the six? The eye perceives forms;
the ear hears sounds; the nose smells odors; the tongue tastes flavors; the body feels tangibles; and the mind cognizes phenomena. Kausika!
Regarding the eye seeing forms, I say there are two kinds: those that may be practiced and those that may not be practiced.

If the eye seeing forms is such that it should not be practiced, I immediately sever it; if the eye seeing forms is such that it may be practiced, I act for its sake with mindfulness and wisdom, so as to bring it to fulfillment.

In the same way, regarding the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling odors, the tongue tasting flavors, the body feeling tangibles, and the mind cognizing mental phenomena, I say that there are likewise two kinds: those that are to be practiced and those that are not to be practiced.

If the mind perceives a phenomenon that is unwholesome, I immediately abandon it; if the mind perceives a phenomenon that is wholesome, I maintain mindfulness and wisdom at the time of knowing it, so as to accomplish it.
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One! Indeed, Sugata!”
"Indeed, Great Seer!

For a bhikkhu who is progressing toward the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation, there are six qualities; he should guard himself by practicing these six qualities that lead to liberation."
What are the six?
The eye sees forms, the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body feels tangibles, and the mind cognizes phenomena.
Regarding the Great Seer’s statement that "the eye sees forms," there are two kinds: those that may be practiced and those that may not be practiced.
If, when the eye perceives forms, unwholesome and evil states increase and wholesome states diminish, the Great Seer immediately abandons them.

If, when the eye perceives forms, unwholesome and evil states diminish and wholesome states increase, the Great Seer knows the proper time for that, being mindful and wise, in order to bring it to fulfillment.

In the same way, when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, and the body perceives tangibles, the Great Seer has taught that the mind’s cognition of mental objects likewise has two types: those that are to be practiced and those that are not to be practiced.

If, when the mind cognizes mental phenomena, it increases unwholesome and evil states and diminishes wholesome states, the Great Seer immediately abandons them; but if, when the mind cognizes mental phenomena, it diminishes unwholesome and evil states and increases wholesome states, [he does not abandon them].
The Great Seer knows the proper time for them; he possesses mindfulness and wisdom, having accomplished their welfare.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"Indeed, Great Seer!
As the Dharma taught by the Buddha, I have understood it all; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has taught."
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer!..."

“Bhikkhu, for one who is treading the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation, while his life lasts for even a single moment, how many factors does he further abandon, and how many factors does he practice?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One replied: “Kauśika!

A bhikkhu who is progressing toward the path that leads to the cessation of conceptual proliferation, while his life lasts for even a single moment, further abandons three things and practices three things.
What are these three?
The first is joy, the second is sorrow, and the third is equanimity.
Kauśika! Regarding joy, I say there are two kinds: that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.
If joy is unwholesome, I shall immediately abandon it; if joy is wholesome, I shall know the proper time for it, possessing mindfulness and wisdom, in order to accomplish it.
It is the same with sorrow.
"Kauśika! Regarding relinquishment, I say there are likewise two kinds: that which may be practiced and that which may not be practiced.

If it is a relinquishment that should not be practiced, I shall immediately sever it; if it is a relinquishment that may be practiced, I shall know the proper time for it, possessing mindfulness and wisdom, so as to bring it to fulfillment."
Then, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"Indeed, Great Seer!

A bhikṣu who is progressing toward the path leading to the cessation of conceptual proliferation, while his life yet endures for even a single moment, abandons three things and practices three things."
What are the three?
First is joy, second is sorrow, and third is equanimity.
Regarding joy, the Great Seer has taught that there are two kinds: that which is to be practiced and that which is not to be practiced.

If joy increases unwholesome and evil states and diminishes wholesome states, the Great Seer immediately abandons it; if joy diminishes unwholesome and evil states and increases wholesome states, the Great Seer recognizes the proper time for it, possessing mindfulness and wisdom, because he has accomplished that state.
It is the same with grief.
The Great Seer taught that renunciation is also of two kinds: that which is practicable and that which is impracticable.
If a form of renunciation increases unwholesome and evil states and diminishes wholesome states, the Great Seer immediately abandons it.

If one abandons and diminishes unwholesome and evil states while increasing wholesome states, the Great Seer knows the proper time for that person, possessing mindfulness and wisdom, because he has accomplished that end.
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
"I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and transcended delusion, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer! Do all śramaṇas and brahmins have the same teaching, the same desire, the same affection, the same pleasure, and the same intention?"
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: “Kauśika!
Not all śramaṇas and brahmins share the same doctrine, the same desire, the same affection, the same pleasure, or the same intention.”
Then, Śakra, the King of Devas, asked again: "Great Seer!
For what reason do all śramaṇas and brahmins not speak with one voice, nor have one desire, one love, one pleasure, and one intention?"
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: “Kauśika!

In this world there are various kinds of realms and immeasurable realms. According to the realm each knows, that very realm—according to its own power and according to its own skillful means—declares exclusively: ‘This alone is the truth; all else is false.’”
Kauśika! For this reason, all śramaṇas and brahmins do not share the same doctrine, the same desire, the same affection, the same pleasure, or the same intention.
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"Indeed, Great Seer!

In this world there are various kinds of realms and immeasurable realms. Each, according to the realm they know, proclaims that very realm as the sole truth by means of its own power and its own skillful methods, asserting that all else is false."
"Great Seer!
For this reason, all śramaṇas and brahmins do not share the same teaching, the same desire, the same affection, the same pleasure, or the same intention."
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
"I have understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, being free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, Śakra, King of the Devas, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Great Seer! Have all śramaṇas and brahmins attained the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life?"
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: “Kauśika!
It is not necessarily the case that all śramaṇas and brahmins have attained the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life.”
Then, Śakra, the King of Devas, asked again:
"Great Seer! For what reason?"
Is it not the case that not all śramaṇas and brahmins have attained the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life?
Having heard this, the Blessed One replied: "Kauśika!
