If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who have attained the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, yet whose minds are not rightly and well liberated, they do not reach the ultimate; they do not reach the ultimate purity; they do not reach the ultimate holy life; they do not bring the holy life to its ultimate conclusion."

Kauśika! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, have attained liberation through a mind that is upright and wholesome, they have reached the ultimate, the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and have brought the holy life to its final completion.
At that time, having heard this, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata!"
"Indeed, Great Seer!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who have reached the unsurpassed destruction of craving, yet their minds are not rightly and well liberated, they do not reach the ultimate; they do not reach the ultimate purity, they do not reach the ultimate holy life, and they do not bring the holy life to its final consummation."
"O Great Seer!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding the unsurpassed extinction of craving, have attained liberation through right and wholesome mind, they have reached the ultimate; they have reached the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and have brought the holy life to its final completion."
So it is, World-Honored One!
So it is, Sugata! So it is, Great Sage!
"I have fully understood all that the Buddha has taught; I have severed my doubts and crossed over my delusions, and I am free from hesitation because I have heard what the Buddha has spoken.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, Śakra, the King of Devas, received it well and retained it well, and said:
"O Great Seer!..."
For a long night I have been pierced by the thorn of doubt, which the World-Honored One has extracted today. Why is this?
Because you are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Blessed One asked:
“Kauśika! Do you recall ever having asked other śramaṇas or brahmins such a question in the past?”
Then Śakra, King of Gods, replied:
"World-Honored One!
Only the Great Seer himself shall know this."
"O Great Seer!

The gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three have assembled in the Hall of Dharma; each harbors grief and sorrow, repeatedly sighing and saying: 'If we were to encounter a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, we would certainly go to see him.'"
"O Great Seer!
However, having failed to encounter a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, we have instead pursued the fulfillment of the five qualities of sensual pleasure."
"O Great Seer! We were heedless;
having acted with heedlessness, the devaputras of great majesty have passed away from their most exquisite abodes. O Great Seer!"

When I saw the Great Majestic Virtue Deva-son in that most exquisite place, at the very moment of his death, I felt immediate and profound revulsion; my hair stood on end, and I thought: "May I not die quickly in this place."
“Great Seer!

Because of this disenchantment and because of this sorrow and distress, whenever I see other śramaṇas or brahmins dwelling in secluded places—among the mountain forests and beneath trees, delighting in high cliffs, silent and still, remote, free from evil, and devoid of people—sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma, they delight in seclusion, sitting in meditation in peace and security, wandering in happiness.”
Having seen him, I thought, "This is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha," and I immediately went to pay my respects.
He did not recognize me and asked me, "Who are you?"
I then replied to him: "Great Seer!
I am Śakra, the Heavenly King."
"O Great Seer!
I am Śakra, the King of the Devas.
He then asked me again:
"I have seen the Śākyas, and I have also seen those of the Śākya clan.
For what reason are they called 'Śākyas,' and for what reason are they of the 'Śākya clan'?
I then answered him:
"O Great Seer!
If anyone comes to ask me about my affairs, I answer them according to my ability and according to my strength.
For this reason, I am called 'Śākya'."
He spoke thus:

"If we were to question the Śākyan according to his matters, the Śākyan would likewise answer me according to my matters; he would ask about my affairs while I would not ask about his, and he would take refuge in me while I would not take refuge in him."
"O Great Seer!
From that śramaṇa or brahmin, I did not even obtain instruction on the rules of dignified conduct (īryāpatha), much less such a question.
Then, Śakra, King of the Devas, spoke in verse:
“Having explained [the past] and having finished explaining [the past], Śāriputra now speaks these words:
‘He has distanced himself from all mental conceptions and eliminated all doubts and hesitations.
Having wandered through the world for a long time, he sought and investigated for the Tathāgata.’”
Seeing a śramaṇa or a brahmin sitting in seclusion in a remote place,
one thinks, "This is one who has attained perfect enlightenment," and goes to pay him homage and serve him.
How can one achieve progress?
Thus I questioned him;
having been questioned, he could not know the Noble Path and the tracks of the Path.
Now, O Blessed One, regarding whatever doubts I may have, [please explain them for me].
Whatever you have contemplated and reflected upon, and the course of your mind’s activity;
knowing the hidden and the manifest within the heart, O Wise One, speak for me.
The Honored Buddha is my teacher; the Honored One, the Unattached Muni, is my teacher.
The Honored One has severed all fetters; having crossed over himself, he delivers sentient beings.
The Awakened One is the foremost of the awakened; the Driver is the supreme of drivers.
The One at Rest is the most sublime of those at rest; the Great Sage has delivered himself and delivers others.
"Therefore, I pay homage to the World-Honored One;
I bow my head to the Supreme among Men, who has severed all thorns of craving. I pay homage to the Kinsman of the Sun.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One asked:
"Kauśika! Do you perhaps recall a time in the past when you attained such detachment and such joy, namely, the joy of Dharma regarding me?
At that time, Śakra, the King of Devas, replied:
“World-Honored One!
Only the Great Seer himself should know this.
O Great Seer!”
Once, on one occasion, the devas and the asuras were engaged in battle.
Great Seer!
While the devas and the asuras were fighting together, I had this thought:
"May the devas be victorious and defeat the asuras; may the food of both the devas and the asuras be entirely provided for the consumption of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
O Great Seer!

When the devas and asuras were engaged in battle, the devas prevailed and defeated the asuras; they caused all the food of the devas and the food of the asuras to become the food of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
"O Great Seer!

At that time, there was detachment from existence accompanied by joy, yet it was mixed with weapons, enmity, strife, and malice; one could not attain supernormal powers, nor the path of awakening, nor Nirvana."
"Great Seer!
Today I have attained liberation and joy; free from weapons and staves, enmity, strife, and malice, I have attained penetration and awakening, and have also attained Nirvana."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Kauśika! By what cause do you attain detachment and attain joy?"
"Do you feel joy in the Dharma regarding this attainment of self?
Then, Śakra, King of the Devas, replied:
"O Great Seer!"
I had this thought:

"When I pass away from this life, I shall be reborn among humans. Among them, there are certain clans that are exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable assets, with livestock and industries beyond counting, and fully endowed with various fiefs and manors—namely, the clans of Kṣatriya elders, Brāhmaṇa elders, householder elders, and other clans that are exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable assets, with livestock and industries beyond counting, and fully endowed with various fiefs and manors."
Having been born into such a clan and having perfected the faculties, one gains faith in the Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata.
Having gained faith, one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep conviction leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path and cultivate wisdom.
Having trained in knowledge, if one attains knowledge, one then attains ultimate knowledge and reaches the ultimate limit.
Having trained in knowledge, having so trained, if one attains knowledge but does not attain ultimate knowledge.

If there are devas who possess great merit and blessings, whose physical forms are majestic, whose radiance is brilliant and resplendent, who have immense power, and who dwell in peace and happiness, long abiding in their palaces and born into the highest state—I would be born among them.
Then, Śakra, King of Devas, spoke in verse:
"Having relinquished my celestial body, I have descended to be born among humans;
Entering the womb without delusion, In accordance with the inclinations of my own mind."
Having attained the perfection of the body, one reaches the upright and direct path;
practicing the perfection of the holy life, one always delights in alms-gathering.

Having trained in knowledge, once one has trained in knowledge, if one attains knowledge, one then attains ultimate knowledge and reaches the ultimate limit. Having trained in knowledge, if after training in knowledge one attains knowledge but does not attain ultimate knowledge, one shall become a supreme and wondrous deva; when the names of all devas hear it, one will be reborn among them in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
"O Great Seer!
May I attain the state of an Anāgāmin.
O Great Seer!"
"I have now certainly attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The World-Honored One asked, "Kauśika!"
"For what reason have you attained such an excellent, lofty, and vast distinction, that you claim for yourself the attainment of the stage of *srotāpanna*?
Then, Śakra, King of the Devas, replied with a verse:
"There is no other venerable one; it is solely the domain of the World-Honored One."
I have attained the most supreme descent [of grace], never before has such a place existed.
O Great Sage, as I sit here, within this very celestial body, I further obtain an increase in my lifespan; thus I see it with my own eyes.

When this Dharma was taught, Śakra, King of the Devas, became free from dust and removed of defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him; likewise, eighty thousand devas also became free from dust and removed of defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.

Thereupon, Śakra, King of the Gods, saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he realized the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, and crossed beyond delusion. Having no other superior, no longer relying on others, and free from hesitation, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit and attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the World-Honored One.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live.”
Thereupon, Śakra, the King of Devas, praised Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharvas, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have brought me great benefit through your five fetters. Why is this?

It is because of you that the Buddha has awakened from his meditative absorption; since you first caused the World-Honored One to awaken from his concentration, we were subsequently able to see the Buddha."
"Pañcaka!

When I return from here, I shall give you my daughter, the princess Kalyāṇī Candraprabhā, as your wife; and I shall appoint her father, King Bandhumat, as your king over his own kingdom of musicians."
Thereupon, Śakra, King of the Devas, addressed the gods of the Thirty-three, saying:
"Come, all of you!

If we were formerly the Brahmā Kings dwelling in the Brahma-heaven and used to pay homage and serve him with reverence two or three times, now they all pay homage and serve the World-Honored One with reverence."
Why is this so? World-Honored One, Brahmā is the creator;

he is the most honored among those who give birth to sentient beings. Regarding those sentient beings who exist and those who are yet to exist, he knows them all that can be known and sees them all that can be seen.

Thereupon, Śakra, King of the Devas, along with the gods of the Thirty-three and the Pañcaśikha Gandharvas—who had formerly been Brahmās dwelling in the Brahma-heaven and had thrice paid reverent homage—now all paid reverent homage to the Blessed One, bowing their heads to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Thereupon, Śakra, the King of Devas, together with the Trāyastriṃśa gods and the Pañcaśikha Gandharva, once again paid reverent homage to the World-Honored One; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and then suddenly vanished from that place without a trace.

At that time, the Brahmā deity, his form majestic and his radiance brilliant, approached the Buddha as night was turning toward dawn. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and immediately addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“For the sake of great benefit and meaning, One who perceives what is beneficial and meaningful is called a deva.
The Worthy One dwells in the kingdom of Magadha; Vāsava asks about this matter.”

When the Great Seer taught this Dharma, Śakra, King of Devas, became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him; likewise, eighty thousand devas also became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahmā, saying:
"So it is, so it is. That which has been spoken by the Brahmā is thus."
“For the sake of great benefit and meaning, seeing the advantage of the goal, he is called a Deva;
the Worthy One dwelling in the kingdom of Magadha was questioned by Vāseṭṭha.”

“Brahmā! When I taught the Dharma, Śakra, King of Devas, was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him; likewise, eighty thousand devas were also distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
At that time, Śakra, King of the Devas, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Pañcaśikha Gandharva, and Mahābrahmā, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Śreṇika-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the eighteenth, ends here, totaling seven thousand three hundred and sixty-eight characters. 135. The *Sujāta-sūtra* (135), the nineteenth in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Abalambavana (the Forest Abounding in Frogs).

At that time, when his father was approaching death, the householder’s son Sujāta, for the sake of the six directions, left him a final instruction, teaching and admonishing him well, saying: "Sujāta!..."
"After my life has ended, you should join your palms and pay homage toward the six directions, saying:
'If there are sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall fully revere, make offerings to, and serve them.'"
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, as for any sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, or the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them all.
‘Once I have fully paid them respect, made offerings, and performed services for them, they too shall pay me respect, make offerings, and perform services for me.
Having heard his father’s instruction, the householder’s son Sujāta said to his father: “Yes.”
“As you have commanded.

Thereupon, after his father had passed away, the householder’s son Susīma bathed at dawn, put on new linen garments, and holding fresh kuśa grass in his hand, went to the water’s edge. With palms joined, he paid homage toward the six directions, saying:
“If there are any sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall honor, support, and serve them all with the utmost respect.”
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, regarding all sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them.
"Once I have fully honored, made offerings to, and served him, he too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Then, at the end of the night, when dawn had broken, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms.

When the World-Honored One was entering the city of Rājagṛha for alms, he saw from afar the householder’s son Sujāta at early dawn, having bathed and dressed in new linen garments, holding fresh kuśa grass in his hand, proceeding to the water’s edge, and with palms joined, paying homage to the six directions:
“If there be any sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall revere, support, and serve them all.”
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, as for any sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them all.
"Once I have fully honored, made offerings to, and served him, he too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Having seen this, the Blessed One went to where the householder’s son Bhadraka was and asked:
"Householder’s son!"

Under the instruction of which śramaṇa or brahmin have you been taught to show respect, make offerings, and perform services? At dawn, having bathed and put on new kṣauma garments, holding fresh kuśa leaves in your hands, you go to the water’s edge and, with palms joined, pay homage to the six directions, saying:
"If there be any sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall fully respect, make offerings to, and serve them."
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, regarding any sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them all.
"Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served him, will he in turn honor, make offerings to, and serve me?
The householder’s son Sujāta replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"I do not accept the teachings of other śramaṇas or brahmins,
World-Honored One!
When my father was approaching the end of his life, he gave me a final instruction regarding the six directions, instructing and admonishing me well, saying:"
“Sujāta! After my life has ended, you should join your palms and pay homage toward the six directions, saying:
‘If there are sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall fully revere, make offerings to, and serve them.’”
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, as for any sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them all.
"Once I have fully honored, made offerings to, and served him, he too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
World-Honored One!

Having received my father’s final instructions, out of reverence, service, and worship, I bathed at dawn, put on new kṣauma garments, and holding fresh kuśa leaves in my hand, went to the water’s edge. With palms joined, I paid homage to the six directions, saying:
"If there are sentient beings in the eastern direction, I shall honor, serve, and worship them all."
Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served them, they too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Likewise, regarding any sentient beings in the south, the west, the north, the nadir, or the zenith, I shall fully honor, make offerings to, and serve them all.
‘Having fully honored, made offerings to, and served him, he too shall honor, make offerings to, and serve me.
Having heard this, the Blessed One said:
“Householder’s son!
I say that there are six directions; I do not say they do not exist.
Son of a householder!

If there is a person who skillfully distinguishes these six directions and is free from the defilement of the four types of evil and unwholesome karma, he will be worthy of honor and respect in this present life; at the breaking up of the body after death, he will certainly go to a good destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
"Householder’s son!
Sentient beings have four kinds of karma and four kinds of defilements.
What are these four?"
"Son of a householder!
Taking life is a seed of karma for sentient beings, a seed of defilement; taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech are seeds of karma for sentient beings, seeds of defilement."
Then, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“Killing, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct with another’s wife,
and speech that is not truthful— the wise do not praise these.”
“Householder’s son!
There are four causes by which a person incurs much demerit. What are the four?
"One acts out of desire, acts out of hatred, acts out of fear, and acts out of delusion.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Desire, hatred, fear, and delusion— One who acts thus commits evil and unrighteous conduct."
"He will surely see his reputation perish, like the moon waning toward its disappearance.
Householder’s son!
A person gains great merit through four causes."
"What are the four?
Not acting out of desire, not acting out of anger, not acting out of fear, and not acting out of delusion.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Having severed desire, free from anger and fear, practicing the Dharma without delusion—
his fame will spread far and wide, like the moon gradually waxing full.
Householder’s son!”
Those who seek wealth and property should know that there are six unrighteous ways. What are these six?
The first is said to be seeking wealth and property through various forms of gambling; this is an unrighteous way.
The second is that seeking wealth by traveling at improper times is an unrighteous path.
The third is that seeking wealth through drinking alcohol and indulgence is an unrighteous path.
The fourth is that seeking wealth by associating with evil associates is an unrighteous path.
Fifth, it is said that constantly delighting in music and seeking wealth and goods is an unrighteous path.
Sixth, it is said that seeking wealth and goods through laziness is an unrighteous path.
"O Son of a Householder!
If a person engages in various forms of gambling, one should know that there are six calamities and afflictions. What are these six?
First, if one loses, resentment arises.
Second, failure brings shame;
third, defeat leads to restless sleep;
fourth, it causes one's enemies to rejoice.
Fifth, it causes one's kinsmen to harbor anxiety.
Sixth, when one speaks among the assembly, people do not place trust in what is said.
Son of a householder!

Those who gamble do not attend to their work; when they do not attend to their work, their undertakings will not succeed. They cannot acquire wealth they have not yet obtained, and the wealth they already possess will steadily diminish.
“Householder’s son, one who wanders at improper times should know that there are six calamities.
What are the six?
First, one does not protect oneself.”
Second, one does not protect one's wealth and property;
third, one does not protect one's wife and children;
fourth, one is suspected by others.
Fifth, one will experience much suffering and affliction throughout many lifetimes;
sixth, one will be slandered by others.
Son of a householder!

A person who acts at improper times does not attend to their affairs; when one does not attend to their affairs, their undertakings will not succeed. Wealth not yet acquired cannot be obtained, and wealth already possessed will gradually diminish and be consumed.
"Householder’s son!
If a person drinks alcohol and becomes negligent, you should know that there are six calamities.
The first is the loss of present wealth and property."
Second, there will be many illnesses;
third, various conflicts and disputes will increase;
fourth, that which should be concealed will be revealed.
Fifth, they do not praise or protect [the Dharma].
Sixth, their wisdom is extinguished and delusion arises.
Son of a householder!

When people drink alcohol and become dissolute, they do not attend to their affairs; when they do not attend to their affairs, their undertakings fail to succeed. Thus, wealth not yet acquired cannot be obtained, and wealth already possessed is gradually consumed and diminished.
“Householder’s son!
If a person associates with evil friends, you should know that there are six calamities.
What are these six?
First, associating with thieves;
second, associating with those who practice deception;
third, associating with those who are crazed or intoxicated.
Fourth, associating with those who are self-indulgent;
fifth, pursuing assemblies for amusement and play;
sixth, regarding such people as one's close friends and companions.
"Son of a householder!

If a person associates with evil friends, they will not attend to their affairs; when one does not attend to their affairs, their undertakings will not succeed. What wealth has not yet been acquired cannot be obtained, and the wealth already possessed will gradually diminish."
“Householder’s son!
If a person delights in music and performance, you should know that there are six calamities and afflictions. What are these six?
First, they delight in hearing songs;
second, they delight in watching dances;
third, they delight in going to provide musical entertainment.
Fourth, they delight in playing with bells;
fifth, they delight in clapping their hands;
sixth, they delight in large gatherings.
"Son of a householder!

If a person delights in music and performance, they will not attend to their work. When one does not attend to their work, their undertakings will not succeed; they will fail to acquire wealth they have not yet obtained, and the wealth they already possess will gradually diminish."
“Householder’s son!
If there is one who is indolent, you should know that there are six calamities and afflictions. What are these six?
First, one does not perform work when it is too early;
second, one does not perform work when it is too late;
third, one does not perform work when it is too cold.
Fourth, one does not engage in work when excessively hot;
fifth, one does not engage in work when excessively full;
sixth, one does not engage in work when excessively hungry.
"Householder's son!

If a person is indolent, they do not engage in business; if they do not engage in business, their undertakings will not succeed. They will not acquire wealth they have not yet obtained, and the wealth they already possess will gradually diminish."
Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Engaging in various diversions for the sake of form, addicted to wine and delighting in music,
associating with evil companions, and being indolent, failing to perform one's work— ”
Lax and failing to guard oneself, one is ruined in this very place.
Moving about without restraint, one commits sexual misconduct with another’s wife;
with constant enmity in the heart, one's prayers bring no benefit.
Drinking alcohol and dwelling on the beauty of women— these things ruin a person here.
Committing repeated unwholesome deeds, being obstinate and refusing instruction,
reviling śramaṇas and brahmins, and holding perverted, false views.
Committing violent acts and black deeds, such a person brings ruin to this place.
Lacking resources and destitute of wealth, drinking alcohol and losing their clothing and bedding,
with debts flowing like a spring, they will surely destroy their own family and clan.
Frequently going to taverns and associating with evil friends, one fails to obtain the wealth one ought to have; such companionship is for pleasure.
Abounding in evil friends and constantly following unwholesome associates, [one falls into ruin].
In both this life and the next, both will meet with ruin.
When people practice evil, it diminishes; when they practice good, it flourishes.
As one practices what is superior, that excellence increases; therefore, one should practice what is superior.
If one practices ascent, one shall attain ascent;
constantly reaching the ascent of wisdom, one further acquires pure precepts and the most sublime excellence.
By day they delight in sleep, and by night they prefer to wander.
The heedless who constantly drink alcohol cannot establish a household;
even amidst great cold and great heat, such as the person who is indolent,
they ultimately fail to accomplish their work and shall never obtain wealth or profit.
Whether it be cold or great heat, one regards them as no more than grass.
If a person performs such deeds, they shall never lose their happiness.
"O son of a householder!
There are four who are not kin but resemble kin. What are the four?
First, one who knows affairs is not a kin but resembles a kin.
Second, those who speak endearing words to one's face though they are not kin, appearing as if they were kin;
third, those whose speech is not that of kin, yet appear as if they were kin;
fourth, companions for the miserable realms who are not kin, yet appear as if they were kin.
"Householder's son!
For four reasons, one knows that a matter is not a true relative, though it appears to be like a relative.
What are these four?"
First, seizing wealth by means of official authority;
second, taking much from what is little;
third, acting through intimidation.
"Fourth, one may associate with others for the sake of profit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"People take knowledge as their task, And their speech is exceedingly gentle;..."
"Fearing intimacy for the sake of profit, one should know that those who are not kin act as if they were;
one should always distance oneself from them, just as one would avoid a place on the road where there is danger.
Householder’s son!"
For four reasons, affectionate words spoken to one's face are not from a true friend, though they appear as such.
What are these four?
First, the restriction of excellent matters.
Second, inciting others to commit evil;
third, praising them to their face;
and fourth, speaking ill of them behind their back.
Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If one restrains [others] from excellent and wholesome dharmas, And instructs them to commit evil and unwholesome deeds;
If one praises them to their face, But speaks ill of them behind their back."
If one knows the subtle and the coarse, and likewise awakens to both these teachings—
that what is near is not to be relied upon— one who knows a person thus should always keep them at a distance, as one would a road beset by terrors.
“Householder’s son!
For four reasons, speech is not from a true friend, though it resembles that of a friend.
What are these four?
First, identifying with past events;
second, necessarily deliberating on future events;
third, speaking falsely and untruthfully.
"Fourth, regarding present phenomena that must perish, one should recognize and speak of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"To recognize faults and the future, And to engage in empty discourse on present perishing phenomena,"

"One should speak of what ought not to be done; one should recognize those who are not kin as if they were kin, yet always keep them at a distance, just as one would avoid a path where there is danger.
Householder’s son!"
Due to four reasons, the companions of the evil realms are not kin, yet they appear as if they were kin.
What are these four?
First, they teach various forms of play.
Second, teaching unseasonable conduct;
third, teaching to drink alcohol;
fourth, teaching to associate with evil friends.
Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Teaching various kinds of games, drinking liquor, violating another's wife,
practicing what is base and not practicing what is superior— such a person perishes like the waning moon."
One should always keep far from them, as if there were danger on the road.
"Son of a householder!
You should know that there are four kinds of virtuous friends."
What are the four?
First, one who shares in both suffering and happiness should be known as a virtuous kinsman.
Second, one who feels compassion and concern should be known as a virtuous kinsman.
Third, one who seeks your welfare should be known as a good friend.
Fourth, one who provides benefit should be known as a good friend.
Son of a householder!
One should know that those who share one's suffering and joy for four reasons are true virtuous friends.
What are these four?
First, they sacrifice themselves for the sake of others.
Second, for the sake of relinquishing wealth;
third, for the sake of relinquishing wife and children;
fourth, that which is spoken of as forbearance.
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Having renounced wealth, wife, and children, capable of enduring what has been taught,
and knowing those who share one's joys and sorrows— the wise should associate with such as these."
“Householder’s son!
You should know that one who shows compassion for four reasons is a virtuous kinsman.
What are these four?
First, teaching the sublime Dharma;
second, restraining unwholesome dharmas;
third, speaking praise in one's presence.
"Fourth, one repels enemies.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Instructing others in what is wondrously good and restraining evil, One faces them with praise and repels their enmity."
One who knows well and feels compassion—such a wise person should associate with.
"Son of a householder!
One should know that a true friend seeks profit for four reasons."
What are the four?
First, the disclosure of secret matters;
second, not concealing secrets.
"Third, one rejoices when gaining profit.
Fourth, one does not grieve when failing to gain profit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"One who reveals secrets without concealment, who shares in joy and does not harbor grief,
and who knows how to seek benefit from virtuous friends— such a person a wise one should associate with.
Son of a householder!"
One should know that a person who provides benefit through four matters is a virtuous friend.
What are these four?
First, they know when one's wealth and possessions are exhausted.
Second, knowing that one's wealth and goods are exhausted, they provide them with material things.
Third, seeing those who are negligent, they instruct and reprimand them.
Fourth, they always regard them with compassion.
Thereupon the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"One who knows when one's wealth is exhausted and gives material goods, who teaches against negligence with compassionate concern,
and who knows how to benefit a virtuous friend— the wise should associate with such a person."
“Son of a householder!
Within the Noble Dharma and Discipline there are six directions: the east, the south, the west, the north, the nadir, and the zenith.”
"Householder’s son!
Just as it is with the eastern direction, so should you, my son, regard your parents; you should honor, respect, and provide for your parents with five things.
What are these five?..."
First, increasing wealth and goods;
second, preparing for all matters;
third, providing whatever is desired.
Fourth, they do not act contrary to their parents' wishes when permitted to act as they please.
Fifth, they offer all their private possessions to them.

When a child honors, reveres, and makes offerings to their parents with these five matters, the parents likewise regard their child with these five matters of wholesome mindfulness. What are these five?
First, they cherish their children;
second, they provide for them without deficiency;
third, they ensure that their children do not incur debt.
Fourth, they arrange marriages that are appropriate;
fifth, they entrust all their wealth and possessions to their sons according to their wishes.
By these five matters, the parents hold their sons in favorable regard.
Householder’s son!
Thus, both are distinguished in the eastern direction.
Householder’s son!
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, "the eastern direction" refers to one's children and parents.
Householder’s son!
If one is compassionate and filial toward one's parents, there will surely be increase and no decline.
“Householder’s son!
Just as it is with the south, so too should a disciple regard his teacher; a disciple should honor and provide for his teacher with five things.”
What are the five?
First, being well-disciplined and compliant;
second, being well-attentive in service.
Third, they rise quickly.
Fourth, the actions they perform are wholesome.
Fifth, they are able to honor and respect their teachers.
The disciple honors and makes offerings to the teacher with these five matters, and the teacher likewise regards the disciple with wholesome thoughts through five matters.
What are these five?
The first is teaching technical skills.
Second, teaching with speed;
third, teaching the entirety of what one knows;
fourth, establishing [the student] in wholesome methods.
Fifth is entrusting [the disciple] to a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Master, you should mindfully attend to your disciples through these five matters,
son of a householder!
In this way, both are distinguished in the South.
Son of a householder!
In the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, "the South" refers to the disciple and the teacher.
"Householder’s son!
If a person is compassionate and obedient toward their teacher, there will certainly be increase and no decline.
Householder’s son!"
Just as it is with those in the West, so it is when a husband contemplates his wife and children: the husband should love, respect, and provide for his wife and children with five matters.
What are these five?
First, he should cherish and care for them.
Second, not being contemptuous;
third, serving as an ornament and embellishment;
fourth, attaining mastery within one's household.
Fifth, he is mindful of his wife and kinsmen.
When a husband loves, respects, and provides for his wife with these five matters, the wife should honor and comply with her husband through thirteen matters. What are these thirteen?
First, she cherishes and respects her husband;
second, she reverently makes offerings to her husband;
third, she maintains virtuous thoughts toward her husband.
Fourth, the undertaking of activities;
fifth, the skillful gathering of followers;
sixth, previously providing attentive service.
Seventh, he subsequently acts with loving-kindness.
Eighth, his speech is truthful.
Ninth, he does not restrict the gates [of the senses].
Tenth, seeing him approach, one offers praise.
Eleventh, one prepares and sets out a seat to wait for him.
Twelfth, one provides pure, exquisite, and abundant food and drink.
Thirteenth, she honors śramaṇas and brahmins.
Wife, by these thirteen matters, she respectfully serves and complies with her husband.
Son of a householder!
In this way, both [terms] in the western direction are distinguished.
Son of a householder!
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, "the western direction" refers to husband, wife, and children.
"Son of a householder!
If a person treats their wife and children with loving-kindness and compassion, there will certainly be increase and no decline.
Son of a householder!"
Just as with those in the north, so too should a master regard his slaves and servants; the master should compassionately care for and provide for his slaves and servants by means of five matters.
What are the five?
First, performing work according to one's strength;
second, eating at the proper time.
Third, drink it according to the proper time.
Fourth, take rest during the day.
Fifth, provide medicinal decoctions when ill.
If the masters compassionately care for and provide for their slaves and laborers with these five matters, the slaves and laborers should serve their masters well by means of nine matters.
What are these nine?
First, performing tasks according to the occasion;
second, performing tasks with single-minded concentration;
third, performing all tasks.
Fourth, one serves them beforehand;
fifth, one acts with affection afterward;
sixth, one speaks with sincerity.
Seventh, not being separated [from them] in times of urgency;
eighth, praising [them] when traveling to other regions;
ninth, extolling the virtues of the master and his household.
"Servants, laborers, and messengers shall serve their masters well by means of these nine matters.
Son of a householder!
Thus, in the north, both [master and servant] are distinguished."
"Son of a householder!
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, 'the north' refers to the masters, as well as the slaves and servants.
Son of a householder!"
"If there is anyone who shows compassion toward their slaves and laborers, they will certainly experience increase and never suffer decline.
Son of a householder!
Just as one treats inferiors, so should a friend regard his friends and ministers; a friend should love, respect, and provide for his friends and ministers with five things."
What are the five?
First, affection and respect;
second, not being contemptuous.
Third, not to deceive or mislead;
fourth, to bestow precious treasures;
fifth, to provide for and care for one's relatives, friends, and ministers.
A friend honors, respects, and provides for a friend’s minister with these five things; the friend’s minister likewise regards the friend with wholesome mindfulness. What are these five?
First, knowing when wealth and goods are exhausted;
second, providing wealth and goods once they have been exhausted;
third, seeing negligence and admonishing it.
Fourth is affection;
fifth is being a refuge in times of urgency.
A friend and minister regards a friend with these five qualities of wholesome mindfulness.
"Son of a householder!
In this way, both [realms] below are distinguished.
Son of a householder!"
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, those who are "lower" are one's friends and the ministers of one's friends.
Householder’s son!
If a person treats the ministers of their friends with loving-kindness and compassion, there will certainly be increase and no decline.
“Householder’s son!
Just as with the zenith, so too should a donor regard śramaṇas and brahmins; a donor should honor and make offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins with five things.”
What are the five?
First, not exercising restraint.
Second, seeing those who come, praising them as virtuous.
Third, to prepare and provide beds for them;
fourth, to provide pure, exquisite, and abundant food and drink;
fifth, to protect them in accordance with the Dharma.
When a donor honors and makes offerings to śramaṇas and brahmins with these five things, the śramaṇas and brahmins likewise maintain wholesome thoughts toward the donor with five things.
What are these five?
First, teaching faith, practice, and belief;
second, teaching the prohibitions and precepts;
third, teaching extensive learning.
Fourth, they teach generosity.
Fifth, they teach wisdom, establish wisdom, and cause wisdom to arise.
By means of these five matters, the śramaṇas and brahmins mindfully attend to the benefactor.
"Householder’s son!
In this way, both are distinguished in the zenith.
Householder’s son!"
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, those who are superior are the donors, the śramaṇas, and the brahmins.
Son of a householder!
If a person honors and reveres the śramaṇas and brahmins, there will certainly be increase and no decline.
“Householder’s son, there are four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*). What are the four?
First is giving (*dāna*);
second is pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*).”
"Third is beneficial conduct;
fourth is impartial benefit.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Generosity and kind speech, always acting for the benefit of others,
and bringing equal benefit to all sentient beings— such that one's fame reaches far and wide—
these are what sustain the world, just like a charioteer."
If there were no one to sustain them,
a mother would not receive offerings and respect because of her son, nor would a father likewise because of his son; yet,
if there is this dharma of sustenance, one thereby obtains great merit and blessings.
Illuminating afar like the light of the sun, Swift benefit is translated as "quickness";
One who does not speak crudely is called "intelligent," And thus one gains a good reputation.
One certainly attains high merit without toil; Swift benefit is translated as "quickness."
Having accomplished faith and morality, one thus gains a good reputation;
always rising without indolence and delighting in giving food and drink to others,
leading them with disciplined and upright conduct, one thus gains a good reputation.
Relatives and ministers share in one's sorrows; their affection and joy have their limits.
Those who are reckoned among one's kin are as excellent and sublime as lions.
First, one should learn the arts and crafts; thereafter, one should seek wealth and goods.
After seeking wealth and property, he divided it into four portions:
one portion for food and drink, one portion for agricultural enterprises,
and one portion set aside in storage to meet urgent needs.
One part for cultivation and trade, one part for interest on loans,
the fifth for taking a wife, and the sixth for building a house;
if a household possesses these six matters, it will not fail to quickly attain happiness.
He will surely possess abundant wealth, flowing like the waters of the ocean.
Seeking wealth in this manner, just as a bee gathers from flowers,
he who seeks riches through the long night shall enjoy happiness for himself.
When disbursing wealth, do not let it go too far, nor let it be dissipated everywhere;
one must not give wealth to the violent or the powerful.
The east is for one's parents; the south is for one's teachers and elders.
The west represents wife and children; the north, servants and slaves;
the lower direction, kinsmen, friends, and ministers; and the upper direction, śramaṇas and brahmins.
May you pay homage to these directions, and both shall attain great renown.
"Having paid homage to these various directions, the donor shall be reborn in heaven.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the householder’s son Sujāta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
