136. The Discourse on the Merchant Seeking Wealth (136). Chapter Twenty: The Great Section. Third Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, various merchants in Jambudvīpa gathered together in a merchant's hall and had this thought:
'We would rather equip ships for the sea, enter the great ocean to fetch treasures, and bring them back to provide for our households.'"
Again, they thought:

"Virtuous ones, when entering the ocean, it is impossible to know in advance whether one will be safe or unsafe. We would do well each to prepare equipment for floating across the sea, namely, goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts made of bound wood."
At a later time, they each prepared their own equipment for crossing the sea—goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts—and entered the great ocean.

In the midst of the sea, their ship was wrecked by a king of makara fish; those merchants each took up their own means of floating upon the ocean—goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts made of bundled wood—and drifted toward various directions.

"At that time, a great wind suddenly arose from the eastern sea, blowing the merchants to the western shore of the ocean. There they encountered a group of women who were exceedingly beautiful and upright, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament."
Having seen them, she spoke these words:
"Welcome, worthy sirs!
You have come well, worthy sirs!"

"This most wondrous and excellent place of Sukhāvatī, with its gardens, groves, bathing pools, places for sitting and reclining, and lush, verdant forests—abounding in wealth such as gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch, giant clam shells, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *cakra* pearls—is entirely yours, O worthy ones. You should enjoy it together with us; do not let the merchants of Jambudvīpa even dream of traveling southward."
Those merchants all took pleasure together with their wives.
Through these unions with their wives, those merchants fathered sons or daughters.
At a later time, there was a wise merchant in Jambudvīpa who, dwelling alone in a secluded place, had this thought:
"For what reason?"
"Are these women restraining us and preventing us from traveling south?
I shall rather wait for the women with whom I live; once I know they have fallen asleep, I will rise slowly and quietly and go south in secret."
"Then that wise merchant of Jambudvīpa, later on, waited for his co-resident woman; once he knew she was asleep, he rose slowly and quietly and stole away toward the south."

Once that wise merchant of Jambudvīpa had traveled south, he heard from afar a great sound of loud wailing and lamentation, the voices of many people crying out in distress, calling for their fathers and mothers, and summoning their wives, children, and all their beloved kin and friends, saying, "We shall no longer see the beautiful Jambudvīpa, its peace and happiness!"
Having heard this, that merchant was seized with extreme terror; his hair stood on end as he thought, "May neither humans nor non-humans disturb or harass me!
Thereupon, the wise merchant of Jambudvīpa restrained his fear and continued traveling southward.

After that wise merchant of Jambudvīpa had traveled southward, he suddenly saw a great iron city to the east; having seen it, he looked all around but could not find its gate, nor even a place large enough for a kitten to pass through.

"Thereupon, a wise merchant of Jambudvīpa, seeing a great grove of trees to the north of the Iron City, went to that grove; having reached it, he climbed up slowly and steadily, and once atop, he asked the great assembly of people:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"Why do you weep and lament so bitterly, calling out for your fathers and mothers, and crying for your wives, children, and all those dear relatives and friends?
Is it because you shall no longer behold the beautiful Jambudvīpa, so peaceful and blissful?"
Then the great assembly replied to him, saying: "Worthy one!
We are merchants from Jambudvīpa who have all gathered together in the merchant's hall and formed this thought:"
“Venerable sir! We thought to ourselves: ‘We would rather board a sea-going vessel and enter the great ocean to fetch treasures for our household needs.
Venerable sir!
This was what we further reflected upon.”
"Venerable friends!

When we enter the ocean, it cannot be known in advance whether it will be safe or unsafe; therefore, we should each prepare equipment for floating across the sea, namely, goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts."
"O Wise One!
At a later time, each of us prepared our own means for crossing the sea—namely, goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts—and we entered the great ocean."
"Venerable sir!
While we were at sea, our ship was wrecked by a king of makara fish.
Venerable sir!"
We merchants each mounted our respective sea-faring vessels—goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts—and drifted toward various directions.

At that time, a great wind suddenly arose from the east of the ocean, blowing us merchants onto the western shore of the sea. There we encountered a group of women who were exceedingly beautiful and upright, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament.
Having seen them, she spoke these words:
"Welcome, worthy sirs!
You have come well, worthy sirs!"

"This most wondrous and excellent realm of Sukhāvatī, with its gardens, groves, bathing pools, places for sitting and reclining, and lush, verdant forests; and its abundance of wealth—gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, *maṇi* gems, pearls, emeralds, white conch, *śaṅkha-śilā*, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *bhrūmaka* gems—all this we shall give to you, O worthy ones. You should enjoy it together with us; do not even let the merchants of Jambudvīpa who travel south know of it, even in their dreams."
“‘Wise one! We have enjoyed ourselves together with that woman.
Because of our union with her, we have fathered sons or daughters.’”
"O Wise One!
If those women had not heard that other merchants from Jambudvīpa were in the midst of the ocean with their ships destroyed by the king of makaras, they would have been sporting together with us."
"Venerable sir!
If those women were to hear that there are merchants from Jambudvīpa in the ocean whose ships have been wrecked by the king of makaras, they would devour us, subjecting us to extreme oppression."
When they eat humans, if there are any remaining hairs, body hair, nails, or teeth, those women take them all and eat them.
When they eat humans, if drops of blood fall upon the ground, those women then use their hands and claws to dig four inches deep into the earth, taking that [blood] and eating it.
"O Worthy One!

You should know that we merchants of Jambudvīpa originally numbered five hundred; of those, two hundred and fifty have already been devoured, while the remaining two hundred and fifty are all now here within this great iron city."
“Wise man!
Do not believe the words of that woman; she is no true person, but merely a rākṣasī.

Thereupon, the wise merchant from Jambudvīpa, having descended slowly and calmly from the great grove, returned by the same path to the place where he had previously lived with the woman. Knowing that the woman was still asleep and had not yet woken, that wise merchant from Jambudvīpa went quickly during that very night to where the other merchants from Jambudvīpa were and spoke these words:
"Come, all of you!
We shall go to a secluded place; each of you should go alone, do not bring your children with you, for we shall gather there together to discuss a matter in secret."
Then those merchants from Jambudvīpa went together to a secluded place; each departed alone, leaving their children behind.
Thereupon, one wise merchant among them spoke, saying: "Merchants!..."
I then dwelt alone in a quiet place and had this thought:
"For what reason do these women restrain us and not allow us to go south?"
"I would rather wait for my wife who lives with me; once I know she has fallen asleep, I shall rise quietly and slowly, and go south in secret.
Thereupon, I waited for my wife who lived with me; knowing she had fallen asleep, I rose quietly and slowly, and went south in secret.

Having traveled south, I heard from afar a great sound of loud wailing and many voices crying out in grief and distress, calling for fathers and mothers, and summoning wives, children, and all beloved kinsmen and friends, lamenting that they would no longer behold the safety and happiness of the beautiful Jambudvīpa.
Having heard this, I was seized with extreme terror; my hair stood on end, and I thought, "May neither humans nor non-humans come to harass me.

Thereupon, I suppressed my fear and continued traveling south. Having traveled further south, I suddenly saw a great iron city to the east. Upon seeing it, I looked all around but could not find a gate, nor even a space large enough for a kitten to pass through.
"I further saw a great grove of trees to the north of the Great Iron City; I went to that grove and climbed up slowly and steadily. Having ascended, I asked those people in the crowd:
'O worthy ones!'"
"Why do you weep and lament so bitterly, calling out for your fathers and mothers, and crying for your wives, children, and all those dear relatives and friends?
Is it because you shall no longer behold the beautiful Jambudvīpa, which is so peaceful and blissful?"
That great assembly replied to me, saying:
"Venerable sir!
We are merchants from Jambudvīpa who have all gathered together in the merchant hall and formed this thought:"
“‘We should rather board a sea-going vessel and enter the great ocean to fetch treasures to provide for our household needs.
Wise one! This was the thought we further conceived.”
"Venerable friends!

When we enter the sea, it cannot be known in advance whether it will be safe or unsafe. We would do well to each prepare equipment for floating across the sea—namely, goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts made of bound wood."
"O Worthy One!
At a later time, each of us prepared our own equipment for crossing the sea—namely, goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts made of bound logs—and then entered the great ocean."
"Venerable sir!
While we were at sea, our ship was destroyed by a king of makara fish.
"Venerable sir! [he continued.]
"We merchants each mounted our own sea-faring vessels—goat-skin bags, large gourds, and rafts—and drifted toward various directions.

At that time, a great wind suddenly arose from the east of the ocean and blew us merchants onto the western shore of the sea. There we encountered a group of women who were exceedingly beautiful and well-proportioned, their bodies adorned with every kind of ornament. Upon seeing us, those women spoke these words:
'Welcome, worthy sirs!'"
Come quickly, worthy sirs! Herein lies the most excellent and wondrous place of supreme bliss:

gardens, groves, bathing pools, places for sitting and reclining, and lush, verdant forests. There is an abundance of wealth—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, emeralds, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and swirled gems. All of this is given to you; you should enjoy it together with us, so that the merchants of Jambudvīpa do not even dream of traveling south.
"O Worthy One! We took pleasure together with that woman.
Because we united with her, we fathered sons or daughters."
"O Wise One!
Had that woman not heard that there were other merchants in the ocean in Jambudvīpa whose ships had been wrecked by the king of makaras, she would have enjoyed herself with us."
"O Worthy One!
If that woman hears that there are other merchants from Jambudvīpa in the ocean whose ships have been wrecked by the king of makaras, she will devour us, and we shall suffer extreme oppression."
When they eat a person, if there are remaining hairs, body hair, nails, or teeth, those women take them all and eat them.
When they eat a person, if drops of blood fall upon the ground, those women then dig the earth with their hands and claws to a depth of four inches and take that to eat.
"O Worthy One!

You should know that we merchants of Jambudvīpa originally numbered five hundred; of these, two hundred and fifty have already been devoured, while the remaining two hundred and fifty are all now here within this great iron city."
“Wise one!
Do not believe the words of that woman; she is no true person, but merely a rākṣasī demon.
Thereupon, the merchants of Jambudvīpa asked that wise merchant of Jambudvīpa:
"Venerable one!
You did not ask that great assembly, 'Venerable ones!
Is there any means by which we and you may cross safely from here to Jambudvīpa?'"
The wise merchant of Jambudvīpa replied:
"Venerable sirs!
At that time, I did not ask in such a manner."
Thereupon, the merchants of Jambudvīpa said:
"Venerable one!
Once you have returned to the place where you formerly lived with your wife, wait until she is asleep; then, rising slowly and quietly, go south again in secret."
He went again to where that great assembly was and asked them:
"Venerable sirs!
Is there any skillful means by which we and you may safely cross from here and reach Jambudvīpa?"
Thereupon, the wise merchant of Jambudvīpa silently accepted the proposal for the sake of the merchants.

At that time, the wise merchant of Jambudvīpa returned to the place where his cohabiting wife was; waiting until she had fallen asleep, he rose slowly and quietly, then stole away toward the south and went back to where the great assembly of people was, asking:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Is there perhaps some skillful means by which we, as well as you, might safely cross from here and reach Jambudvīpa?
Those people of the great multitude replied,
"Venerable sir!"
"There is no other means by which we might safely cross from here to Jambudvīpa.
Venerable sir!
This is what I thought:"
"We shall join together to break down and dig through this wall and return to our original place.
As soon as they had formed this thought, the wall rose even higher than it was before.
"Venerable sir!
This is called the means by which we were prevented from crossing safely from here to Jambudvīpa.
Venerable sir!"
"There may be another means by which you might safely cross from here to Jambudvīpa, but we have no such means at all.
Venerable sirs!
We heard a voice in the sky proclaiming:"
“The merchants of Jambudvīpa are foolish and unstable, and they lack discernment. Why is this?

They were unable to set out toward the south at the time when the *pātimokkha* was recited on the fifteenth day. There, the horse-king Bhadra feeds on naturally grown non-glutinous rice; he is secure and happy, his faculties are fully satisfied, and he has thrice proclaimed:”
"Who wishes to cross to the other shore? Who wishes to cause me to be liberated? Who wishes to lead me from here safely across to Jambudvīpa?
You all should go together to the horse-king Bhalluka and speak these words:
"We wish to reach the other shore; we pray that you will liberate us, and we pray that you will lead us from here safely across to Jambudvīpa."
"O wise ones! This is called the skillful means by which I shall lead you safely from here across to Jambudvīpa.
O merchants, come!"
"You may go to where that horse-king Balaha is and speak these words:
'We wish to cross over to the other shore; we pray you deliver us, and we pray you lead us safely from here to Jambudvīpa.'"
"Then, a wise merchant from Jambudvīpa said: 'Merchants!
Go now to the presence of the horse-king Balāha and speak these words:'"
“We wish to cross over to the other shore; we pray that you deliver us, and we pray that you lead us safely from here to Jambudvīpa.

Following the will of the devas, when it was the time for the merchants to recite the *pātimokkha* on the fifteenth day, the horse-king Bhalluka ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice; he was peaceful and happy, his faculties fully satisfied, and he cried out again and again:
“Who wishes to cross to the other shore? Who wishes to be delivered by me? Who wishes that I lead them safely from here to Jambudvīpa?”
At that time, we immediately went to that place and spoke these words:
"We wish to cross over to the other shore; we pray that you will deliver us, and we pray that you will lead us safely from here to Jambudvīpa."

"Then, on the fifteenth day, when the horse-king Bālāha was reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, having eaten naturally grown rice, he was at peace and happy, his faculties fully satisfied. He cried out three times:
'Who wishes to cross to the further shore?'"
"I shall deliver them; I shall lead them from here across in safety to Jambudvīpa.
Then, having heard this, the merchants of Jambudvīpa went to the place where the horse-king Bhalluka was and spoke these words:
"We wish to cross over to the other shore; we pray that you will deliver us, and we pray that you will lead us from here across in safety to Jambudvīpa."
Then the horse-king Balaha said: "Merchants!
Those women will surely come bringing their children with them and speak these words:"
"Venerable sirs! Welcome back here.

This place is a place of supreme bliss and exquisite beauty, with gardens, groves, bathing pools, and places for sitting and reclining; the forests are lush and verdant. There is an abundance of wealth—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, mother-of-pearl, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *cakra* beads—all of which we give to you. You should enjoy them together with us; even if you do not accept me, you should at least take pity on our son."
If those merchants should think thus: "I have sons and daughters;

I have supreme bliss and most excellent dwellings, with gardens, groves, bathing pools, places for sitting and reclining, and lush, verdant forests; I possess abundant wealth—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, emerald, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and spiral-patterned gems."
"Even though he may mount my very back, he will surely fall headlong into the water and be devoured by that woman; he shall suffer great torment."
When they eat a person, if there are any remaining strands of hair, body hair, nails, or teeth, those women will take them all and eat them.
Furthermore, when they eat a person, if there are drops of blood on the ground, those women will dig the earth with their hands and claws to a depth of four inches and eat it.
If that merchant does not form such thoughts as:

"I have sons and daughters; I have places of supreme joy and most wonderful excellence—gardens, groves, bathing pools, and places for sitting and reclining where the trees and forests are lush and verdant; I possess abundant wealth, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, *śaṅkha-śilā*, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *cakra-maṇi*."
"...that woman, though she were to hold but a single hair from my body, would surely reach the continent of Jambudvīpa in safety.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those women came carrying their sons and spoke these words:"
"Virtuous ones! Welcome back here.

This place is a most excellent and wondrously blissful realm, with gardens, groves, bathing pools, and places for sitting and reclining; the forests are lush and verdant. There is an abundance of wealth—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and *āvarta* pearls—all of which we give to you virtuous ones. You shall enjoy them together with us."
If that merchant should think to himself: "I have sons and daughters;

I have a most delightful and excellent place, with gardens, groves, bathing pools, and places for sitting and reclining, where the trees and forests are lush and verdant; I possess abundant wealth—gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and spiral-jade."

"Even if he were to mount the king of horses, Kālāśva, with his back positioned directly upon the horse's spine, he would surely fall headlong into the water and be devoured by those women, suffering their oppression."
When they eat a person, if there remain any hair, body hair, nails, or teeth, those women take them all and eat them.
Furthermore, when they eat that person, if drops of blood fall upon the ground, those women then dig the earth with their hands and claws to a depth of four inches and take that up to eat.
If that merchant does not entertain such thoughts as:

"I have sons and daughters; I possess most delightful and exquisite places, including gardens, groves, bathing pools, and sites for sitting and reclining, with lush, verdant forests; I have abundant wealth, gold, silver, crystal, beryl, mani-jewels, pearls, green jade, white conch, musaragalva, coral, amber, agate, tortoise shell, red stone, and spiral-patterned gems."
"Those who hold even a single hair from the horse-king Bālāha will surely reach the continent of Jambudvīpa in safety.

"Monks, I have told this parable so that you may understand its meaning. This is what it signifies: my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively spread, well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float; it has been widely distributed and pervades everything, even unto gods and humans."

Thus, this Dharma of mine is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively proclaimed, well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float; it is spread abroad and pervades everywhere, even unto gods and humans.
"If there is a bhikṣu who thinks thus:
'The eye is mine; I have eyes. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are mine; I have a mind. "
"Those [who say this] will surely be harmed, just as merchants are devoured by rākṣasas.

My Dharma is well-expounded, fully disclosed and extremely extensive, well-guarded and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and widely distributed, reaching even to gods and humans."

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively detailed, well-guarded, and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and widely disseminated, even unto gods and humans.
If a bhikṣu should think thus: "The eye is not mine;
I do not possess the eye. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are not mine; I do not possess the mind."
"Thus, that bhikṣu shall depart in peace and security, just as a merchant riding a well-bred horse king crosses safely over [a river].
My Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed and extensive, well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float; it is spread abroad and pervades everywhere, even unto gods and humans."

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively proclaimed, well-guarded, and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and pervasively disseminated, even unto gods and humans.
"If there is a bhikṣu who thinks thus:
'Form is my self; I possess form; sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are my self; I possess mental phenomena.'"
"Such a person," he said, "will surely meet with harm, just as a merchant is devoured by a rākṣasa.
My Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, and well-guarded without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and widely disseminated, even unto gods and humans."

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively detailed, well-guarded, and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it has spread far and wide, reaching even unto gods and humans.
If a bhikṣu should think thus: "Form is not my self;
I do not possess form. Sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena are not my self; I do not possess mental phenomena."
Thus, that bhikṣu may depart in peace, just as a merchant riding a well-bred horse king crosses over safely.
My Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively spread, well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float; it is widely distributed and reaches even unto devas and humans.

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively proclaimed, well-guarded, and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it has spread everywhere, even unto devas and humans.
"If there is a bhikṣu who thinks thus:

'The aggregate of form is my self; I possess the aggregate of form. Perception, conception, mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are my self; I possess the aggregate of consciousness.'"
"Thus it shall be," [I say], "that bhikṣu will surely be destroyed, just as a merchant is devoured by a rākṣasa.

My Dharma is well-expounded, its disclosure is most extensive, and it is well-guarded without any deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and widely disseminated, reaching even unto gods and humans."

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively detailed, well-guarded, and without deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and pervasively distributed, reaching even unto gods and humans.
If a bhikṣu should think thus: "The aggregate of form is not my self;
I do not possess the aggregate of form. The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not my self; I do not possess the aggregate of consciousness."
Thus, that bhikṣu shall go in peace and security, just as a merchant riding a well-bred horse king crosses over in safety.
My Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, and extensively spread; it is well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float, pervading and circulating even unto gods and humans.

Thus, this Dharma of mine is well-expounded, fully revealed, and extensively proclaimed; it is well-guarded and without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float, pervasively spread even unto gods and humans.
"If there is a bhikṣu who thinks thus:
'The earth is my self; I possess the earth. Water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are my self; I possess consciousness.'"
"Those [who speak thus] will surely be harmed, just as merchants are devoured by rākṣasas.

My Dharma is well-expounded, its disclosure is most extensive, and it is well-guarded without any deficiency; like a bridge, a raft, or a float, it is spread abroad and widely distributed, reaching even unto gods and humans."

In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, fully revealed, extensively proclaimed, well-guarded without deficiency, like a bridge, a raft, or a float; it has spread everywhere, reaching even unto gods and humans.
If a bhikṣu should think thus:
"The earth is not my self; I do not possess the earth. Water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are not my self; I do not possess consciousness."
Thus, that bhikṣu shall depart in safety, just as a merchant riding a well-bred horse-king safely crosses over.
Then the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"If there is one who does not have faith in the true Dharma and Vinaya spoken by the Buddha..."
That person will surely be harmed, as if being devoured by a rākṣasa.
If a person has faith in the True Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Buddha,
they shall cross over in safety, like one riding the king of tawny horses.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twentieth chapter, "The Merchant Seeking Wealth," ends here, totaling 4,273 characters. 137. The Discourse on the World (Lokasutta), the twenty-first discourse in the Great Section of the Madhyama Āgama, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“The Tathāgata has personally awakened to the world and also speaks of it for others; the Tathāgata knows the world.”
The Tathāgata has personally awakened to the worldly habituations and has also taught them to others; the Tathāgata has abandoned the worldly habituations.
The Tathāgata has personally awakened to the cessation of the world and has also taught it to others; the Tathāgata has realized the cessation of the world through direct experience.
The Tathāgata has personally realized the path of the world and has also taught it to others; the Tathāgata has cultivated the path of the world.
If there is anything whatsoever that is entirely universal and correct, all of that is known, seen, and realized by the Tathāgata.

Why is this? From the night the Tathāgata awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until this very night, he shall attain final extinction in the realm of nirvana without remainder.

In the meantime, whatever the Tathāgata may speak with his own mouth, or whatever he may respond to, all of it is the ultimate truth; it is not false, it does not deviate from suchness, nor is it inverted. It is the ultimate truth, examined and real. If one speaks of a lion, one should do so as one speaks of the Tathāgata.

Why is this so? When the Tathāgata speaks among the assembly, it is called the Lion’s Roar. To all the world—including gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans up to the heavens—the Tathāgata is one who possesses the state of Brahmā; the Tathāgata has attained the state of ultimate coolness; he is without affliction and without fever; he possesses the true reality that is not false.
Thereupon, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Knowing all the world, Transcending all the world, Teaching all the world, He knows all worlds as they truly are."
That most supreme and honored Hero, Able to untie all bonds,
Having attained the exhaustion of all karma, Is fully liberated from birth and death.
Whether they be devas or humans, If there are those who take refuge in the Buddha,
I bow my head in worship to the Tathāgata, the profoundly deep and vast great ocean.
Having known this, I also offer reverence;
the devas, gandharvas, and kinnaras likewise bow their heads in worship—those who follow the deceased.
I bow my head in homage to the wise one, I take refuge in the supreme among men,
Free from sorrow, detached from dust, at peace, And possessing unimpeded liberation.
Therefore, one should delight in dhyāna, Abiding in seclusion and supreme concentration.
"One should make for oneself a lamp of wisdom; if one lacks this, one will surely lose the opportune moment.
To lose the opportune moment brings sorrow and grief, namely, falling into the hells.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twenty-first discourse, “The World,” ends here, totaling three hundred and ninety-six characters. 138. Discourse on Merit (138), Great Chapter of the Madhyama Āgama, Discourse on Merit, the Twenty-second, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not fear merit; cherish what the mind intends. Why is this so?
"Merit" is a term for happiness.
To fear merit is to have a mind that does not delight in what it contemplates. Why is this so?
Non-merit is said to be suffering. Why is this?
I recall that in the long night of the past, I performed meritorious deeds and for a long night received their retribution, which was cherished and desired by my mind.

In the past, I practiced loving-kindness for seven years; during seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction, I did not return to this world. When the world was being destroyed, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when the world was being formed, I descended to be born within an empty Brahmā palace. There, among the Brahmās, I became a Great Brahmā; in other places, I became the King of the Gods (Śakra) thirty-six times, and I became a Kṣatriya King Born from the Crown of the Head countless times.

“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand great elephants, equipped with fine trappings, adorned with various precious jewels, and covered with white pearl nets, headed by the elephant king Uposatha.”

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand horses, well-equipped with fine trappings, adorned with various jewels, and interlaced with gold and silver, with the horse-king Valāha as their leader."

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand chariots, adorned with four kinds of ornaments and decorated with various beauties; they were woven with the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, variegated in color, and embellished with diverse decorations, headed by those called 'Chariots of Delightful Sound' which were exceedingly swift."

“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand great cities, exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with vast populations, of which the royal city of Kusāvatī was the foremost.”

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand palaces made of four kinds of jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—with the Palace of Righteous Dharma as the foremost."

“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand state thrones made of four kinds of precious substances—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with embroidered silks and fine gauze, provided with body-cushions and pillows at both ends, and adorned with Kaśmīra-paṭṭa and pāṭaliputra-dukūla fabrics.”
"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand pairs of garments: there were kṣauma garments, brocade garments, cotton garments, and kāliṅgapravāra garments."

"Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, I had eighty-four thousand women whose bodies were radiant and pure, their beauty surpassing that of humans and falling only slightly short of that of the devas; they were of upright countenance, bringing joy to all who beheld them, and were fully adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments—all of them being of the Kṣatriya caste, with immeasurable others from other clans."
“Monks! When I was the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, there were eighty-four thousand varieties of food, constantly provided day and night, prepared for my sake with the desire that I might eat them.”
"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand kinds of food, there is one kind of food that is most exquisite, pure, and possesses immeasurable flavors; this is what I constantly eat."
"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand women, there was one Kṣatriya woman who was most upright, beautiful, and exquisite, and she constantly attended upon me. Monks!"

Among those eighty-four thousand pairs of garments, there was one pair—whether it were a garment of kṣauma silk, or a brocade garment, or a garment of cotton, or a garment of kāliṅgapravāraka—that was what I habitually wore.

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand thrones, there was one throne made of gold, or silver, or beryl, or crystal, spread with woolen rugs and carpets, covered with fine brocades and silken gauzes, provided with a mattress for the body and pillows at both ends, and upholstered with Kalingabāhula and Pāṭaliputtaka cloth; this was where I used to lie down."

“Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand palatial towers, there is one tower made either of gold, or silver, or beryl, or crystal, named the Hall of the True Dharma (Saddharmaprāsāda), which is where I constantly reside.”
“Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand great cities, there was one city that was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, with a vast population, named Kuśāvatī; this was my constant dwelling place.”

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand chariots, there was one chariot adorned with every excellence, its sides woven with variegated colors from the skins of lions, tigers, and leopards, decorated with all manner of ornaments, swift and exceedingly fast, known as the 'Chariot of Delightful Sound. This was the one I constantly rode to visit the Udena Grove."

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand horses, there was one horse with a body of deep blue-black color and a head like that of a crow, named the King of Horses, Kanthaka. He was the one I constantly rode when I went to visit the Udena Park."

"Monks! Among those eighty-four thousand great elephants, there was one elephant whose entire body was pure white and whose seven limbs were perfectly aligned; it was named the Elephant King Uposatha, whom I constantly rode when going to the Udena Park for recreation."
“Monks! I had this thought:

‘What is the fruit of this karma, what is the retribution of this karma, that causes me today to possess such great supernormal power, such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual authority?’”
"Monks! I further had this thought:

'These are the fruits of the three types of action, the results of the three types of action, which have caused me today to possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority.'"
"First is giving, second is self-mastery, and third is protection.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Behold this retribution of merit, Sublime, virtuous, and bringing great benefit."
Monks, in the past, I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years.
Through seven cycles of cosmic formation and destruction, I did not return to this world.
When the world was being destroyed, I was reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When the world was being formed, he was born among the Brahmā gods; as a Brahmā, he was Mahābrahmā,
and he was born thirty-six times as a lord of the Śakras and as an infinite hundred times as a wheel-turning monarch.
The Kṣatriya King born from the crown of the head was the most honored among men.
Governing the world according to the Dharma and not by sword or staff, he did not inflict injustice; he taught with true peace and happiness.
Transmitted from one to another according to the Dharma, it pervades the entire earth;
born into such a clan, possessing great wealth and abundant riches,
with grain and treasures in full abundance, one achieves the seven precious jewels.
Therefore, by virtue of this great merit, he attains mastery wherever he is born.
The Buddhas who guide the world—what those Buddhas have taught is known to be most extraordinary;
those who witness his supernormal powers are not few.
Whoever knows yet does not believe will thus be born into darkness;
therefore, one should act for oneself.
If you desire great blessings, you should revere the Dharma and constantly mind the Buddha’s discipline and law.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Puṇya-sūtra*, the twenty-second, ends here, totaling one thousand one hundred and fifty-four characters. 139. *Śāntivarga-sūtra* (139), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Great Section (*Mahāvagga*), *Śāntivarga-sūtra*, the twenty-third, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“Young bhikṣus who have newly accomplished the precepts should frequently go to the path of cessation and contemplate the signs: the sign of bones, the sign of blueness, the sign of festering, the sign of being devoured, and the sign of a skeleton.”

Having properly received and mastered these signs, he returns to his dwelling, washes his hands and feet, spreads out his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and sits cross-legged upon the bed. He then contemplates these signs: the sign of bones, the blue sign, the putrefying sign, the sign of being devoured, and the sign of the skeleton.
Why is this so? If that bhikṣu cultivates this sign, he will swiftly eliminate the diseases of desire and ill-will within his mind.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a young bhikṣu has not yet awakened to the higher mind,
he should resort to the path of cessation in order to eliminate his sensual desire.
With no anger or strife in his heart, he should feel compassion for all living beings."
Pervading all directions, one should go and observe all bodies.
One should contemplate the sign of blueness, as well as their putrefaction and decay;
one should observe them being devoured by birds and insects, with each bone connected to the next in the joints.
Cultivating such signs, one returns to one's original place;
having washed one's hands and feet, one spreads a mat and sits upright.
One should contemplate reality within the internal body and the external body.
Filled with excrement and urine, with the heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, and so forth—
if you wish to go on almsround among villages and towns,
you should always maintain right mindfulness before you, as if wearing armor wrapped around your body.
If one sees a form that is lovely, pure, and associated with desire, having seen it, one contemplates it as it truly is:
one rightly recollects the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya.
Within this, there is no bone or sinew; there is no flesh, nor is there blood.
There are no kidneys, heart, liver, or lungs; there are no tears, saliva, or brain.
All earth is empty, and the water element is likewise so;
all fire elements are empty, and the wind element is likewise empty.
Whatever thoughts there may be that are associated with pure desire,
all of them cease when observed with wisdom as it truly is.
Thus practicing with diligence, one should constantly maintain the perception of impurity.
"Having forever severed lust, anger, and delusion, and having eliminated all ignorance, one gives rise to pure clarity; such a bhikṣu has reached the end of suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twenty-third discourse, *The Discourse on the Path of Cessation*, ends here; it consists of three hundred and seventy-two characters. 140. *The Discourse on Reaching the Limit* (140). The Great Chapter of the Madhyama Āgama, the twenty-fourth discourse, *The Discourse on Reaching the Limit*, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Among the various modes of livelihood, the lowest and most extreme is that of begging for food.
It is a great reproach in the world to go about with a shaven head, carrying an alms bowl in one's hands; yet that son of noble family accepts it for the sake of the Dharma."

Why is this? Is it not because you have become weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, grief, and despair, and have sought the end of this entire mass of suffering—this pure and complete heap of misery—that you have gone forth from home to train in the path with such a mind?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “So it is.
The Blessed One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

“Those foolish people leave the household life to study the Path with such a mind, yet they practice with a pursuit of sensual desire that is extremely heavy and deeply attached; turbidity and entanglements fill their hearts, they are full of malice and envy and lack faith; they are indolent and lose right mindfulness, lacking right concentration; their wisdom is corrupt and their minds are deranged; their faculties are restless and distracted; their observance of the precepts is exceedingly lax; they do not cultivate the life of a śramaṇa, nor do they increase or broaden their practice.”
It is like using ink to wash away ink-stains, blood to remove blood, filth to remove filth, turbidity to remove turbidity, or a latrine to remove a latrine—it only increases the impurity.
"From darkness they enter further darkness; from obscurity they enter deeper obscurity. I say that such foolish people who observe the precepts of a recluse are just like this.

That is to say, those people harbor desires so heavy with defilement that they entangle their minds in turbidity; they are full of envy and lack faith; they are indolent and have lost right mindfulness; they lack right concentration and possess evil wisdom; their minds are deranged and their faculties are disordered; their observance of the precepts is extremely lax; they do not cultivate the life of a recluse, nor do they expand their practice."

It is like wood from a person’s funeral pyre at a deserted site: the ashes of that fire are of no use to those in the wilderness, nor are they of use to those in villages or towns. I say that such foolish people who maintain the precepts of a śramaṇa are just like this.

It means that such a person’s conduct is characterized by extremely heavy attachment to sensual desires; their mind is clouded and entangled; they are malicious, envious, and lack faith; they are indolent and have lost right mindfulness; they lack right concentration; their wisdom is corrupted and their mind is deranged; their faculties are restless and agitated; their observance of precepts is exceedingly lax; they do not cultivate the life of a śramaṇa, nor do they increase or broaden their practice.
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The fool loses sensual pleasure, And further loses the goal of the ascetic life;
Having lost both ends alike, He is like a smoldering ember."
Just as in a deserted place, where the embers of a fire that once consumed people remain,
and the village is abandoned;
so it is with those attached to desire— they are like the lingering embers of a burnt-out fire, having lost both ends alike.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twenty-fourth sutra, *Pārāyana*, ends here, totaling four hundred and twenty-two characters. 141. *Upama Sutta* (141), Middle Discourses, Great Chapter, *Upama Sutta*, the twenty-fifth, third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there are immeasurable wholesome dharmas to be attained, they all have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their practice, arise from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost.”
Heedfulness is the foremost among all wholesome qualities.
Just as when one engages in agricultural work, it is entirely because of the earth, by depending on the earth, and established upon the earth that one is able to perform such work.

Thus, if there are immeasurable wholesome dharmas to be attained, they all have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their practice, arise from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost;
for heedfulness is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas.

Just as in a village of seeds and a village of spirits, the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees grow and flourish; all of them grow and flourish because they depend on the earth, rely on the earth, and are established upon the earth.

"In this way, whatever immeasurable wholesome dharmas may be attained, they all have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their practice, arise from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their precursor;
indeed, among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the foremost."
Just as among all root-fragrances, aloeswood is foremost;
just as among all tree-fragrances, red sandalwood is foremost;
just as among all water-blooming flowers, the blue lotus is foremost.
Just as among all land flowers, the sumana flower is the foremost;

just as among all animal tracks, they are all contained within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint encompasses them all—thus that elephant’s footprint is the most supreme because it is vast.

Thus, if there are immeasurable wholesome dharmas to be attained, they all have non-heedlessness as their root, non-heedlessness as their practice, arise from non-heedlessness, and have non-heedlessness as their foremost;
for non-heedlessness is the most preeminent among all wholesome dharmas.
Just as among all beasts, that lion king is the foremost;
just as when arrayed in battle for combat, it is the solemn vow alone that is the most essential.

It is like the rafters of a multi-storied pavilion; they all depend upon the rafters-beams for their support, and the rafters-beams sustain them all. Among these rafters-beams, the primary ones are considered the most supreme, because they support everything.

"In this way, if there are immeasurable wholesome dharmas to be attained, they all have heedfulness as their root, heedfulness as their practice, arise from heedfulness, and have heedfulness as their foremost;
for among all wholesome dharmas, heedfulness is the most supreme."
Just as among all mountains, Sumeru, the king of mountains, is the foremost;
just as among all springs, the great ocean that gathers the waters is the foremost;
and just as among all those with massive bodies, the Asura King is the foremost.
Just as among all those who serve and attend, Māra is foremost;
just as among all those who practice desire, King Mandhātṛ is foremost;
and just as among all minor kings, the Wheel-Turning King is foremost.
Just as among all the stars in the void, the lunar palace is foremost;
just as among all dyed garments, white silk is foremost;
just as among all lights, the light of wisdom is foremost.
Just as among all assemblies, the assembly of the Tathāgata’s disciples is foremost;
and just as among all phenomena, whether conditioned or unconditioned, the exhaustion of craving, the absence of desire, cessation, and nirvāṇa are foremost.

Just as among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; with perception, without perception, or even neither with nor without perception—the Tathāgata is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most venerable, and the most sublime among them.

It is just as there is milk because of the cow; from milk comes curd; from curd comes fresh butter; from fresh butter comes clarified butter; and from clarified butter comes the essence of ghee. This essence of ghee is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most venerable, and the most sublime.

Thus, among all sentient beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether with form or formless; whether with perception, without perception, or even neither with nor without perception—the Tathāgata is the foremost, the greatest, the highest, the most excellent, the most honored, and the most sublime among them.
Then the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"If one seeks wealth and property, It will increase exceedingly;
Praise belongs to the heedful, Who speak with wisdom regarding both worldly affairs and the state beyond."
Those who are not heedless will surely attain both goals:
they shall gain them in this very life and likewise in the world beyond.
The heroic one who contemplates these goals—the wise one—will certainly be liberated.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The twenty-fifth discourse, the *Upamā-sūtra*, ends here, totaling seven hundred and seventy-one characters. The thirty-fourth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* ends here, totaling seven thousand three hundred and eighty-eight characters. The first section, the *Mahāvarga*, of the *Madhyama Āgama* ends here, totaling fifty thousand three hundred and sixty-nine characters.
