Brāhmaṇa-varga (The Chapter on Brahmins). This second chapter contains ten sūtras. Recitation Section 3.
Vassakāra, Kala, Saṅkha; Ghoṭamukha, Hatthipadopama, Sutasoma, Kimsuka, Icchānaṅgala, Assapura.
(142) The Vassakāra Sutta, the first in the Brahmajāla-vagga of the Majjhima Nikāya. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha harbored enmity toward the Vṛjis; he often said among his retinue:

"The people of the Vṛji possess great supernormal powers, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. I shall exterminate the Vṛji race, destroy the Vṛji, and cause the people of the Vṛji to encounter immeasurable calamities."
Thereupon, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha, hearing that the Blessed One was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain while wandering in Rājagṛha, addressed his minister Vassakāra, saying:
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is staying at Vulture Peak Mountain while wandering in Rājagṛha."
"Vassakāra!
Go to where the ascetic Gotama is, and in my name inquire after his health, asking whether he is at ease, free from illness, and whether his strength remains as usual."
One should speak these words: "Gautama!
Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra, the King of Magadha, inquires after your holy body—whether you are at ease, free from illness, and whether your strength remains as usual?"
"Gautama!
King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha harbors enmity toward the Vṛjis; he constantly says among his retinue:

'The people of the Vṛji country possess great psychic power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. I shall annihilate the Vṛji race, destroy the Vṛjis, and cause the people of the Vṛjis to encounter immeasurable calamities.'"
"What will the śramaṇa Gautama say? "Vassakāra!
Whatever the śramaṇa Gautama says, you should receive and uphold it well."
"Why is that? Because such a person would never speak falsely.

Having received the King's command, the minister Vassakāra mounted his finest carriage and, accompanied by five hundred carriages, departed from Rājagaha and proceeded directly to the Vulture Peak Mountain.

Ascending Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot to where the Buddha was staying. Having exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, he withdrew to sit at one side and said: "Gautama!
"Does King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha inquire after your holy health, asking if you are at ease, free from illness, and as strong as usual, Gautama? Gautama!
King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha harbors hatred toward the Vṛjis and frequently says among his retinue:"

"The people of the Vṛji possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; I shall exterminate the Vṛji race, destroy the Vṛji, and cause the people of the Vṛji to encounter immeasurable calamities."
"What will the śramaṇa Gautama say?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One said: "Vassakāra!
In the past, I once traveled to the country of the Vajjis. In that country, there was a monastery named Khānumata. Vassakāra!
At that time, I taught the seven principles of non-decline to the people of the Vajjis, and the people of the Vajjis were able to accept and practice those seven principles of non-decline.
"Vassakāra!
If the people of the Vajjī country practice the seven principles of non-decline and do not transgress them, the Vajjīs will surely prevail and shall remain undecayed.
The minister Vassakāra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The ascetic Gautama has briefly explained this matter without detailed analysis; we are unable to understand its meaning. We pray that the ascetic Gautama will explain it in detail so that we may come to know its meaning.”
The Blessed One said: “Vassakāra!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain this matter to you in detail.”
The minister Vassakāra accepted the instruction and listened.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Blessed One, holding a fly-whisk; the Blessed One turned his head and asked him: “Ānanda!”
"Have you heard that the Bhaggas frequently assemble and gather in great numbers?
Venerable Ānanda replied,
"World-Honored One, I have."
"I have heard that the Vajjis hold frequent assemblies and gather in great numbers.
The World-Honored One then addressed the minister Vassakāra:
"If those Vajjis hold frequent assemblies and gather in great numbers, the Vajjis will surely prevail and shall not decline."
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Have you heard that the Bhaggas assemble together, perform the affairs of the Bhaggas together, and rise up together?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"World-Honored One!
I have heard that the Bhaggas assemble together, perform the affairs of the Bhaggas together, and rise up together."
The Blessed One further addressed the minister Vassakāra:
“If those Licchavis assemble together, perform the affairs of the Licchavis together, and rise up together, the Licchavis will surely prevail and shall not decline.”
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Have you heard that the Vajjis do not enact what was not previously enacted, do not alter what was originally enacted, and properly practice the ancient Vajjian traditions?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that the Vṛjis do not establish what was not previously established, nor do they alter what was originally established; they practice the ancient laws of the Vṛjis with excellence.”
The Blessed One further addressed the minister Vassakāra:

"If those things not previously established by the Vajjis are not newly established, and those things already established are not altered, and if they properly uphold and practice the ancient laws of the Vajjis, then the Vajjis will surely prevail and shall not decline."
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Have you heard that the Vṛjis do not violate the wives or daughters of others by means of force?
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!
I have heard that among the Vṛjis, one does not violate the wives or daughters of others by means of force.
The World-Honored One again addressed the minister Vassakāra:
“If the Licchavis do not violate the wives or daughters of others by means of force or power, then the Licchavis will surely prevail and shall not decline.
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:

“Have you heard that there are those among the Licchavis who are renowned for their virtue and respected, whom the Licchavis all honor, revere, serve, and support, and from whom they receive instruction when they hear it?”
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"World-Honored One!

I have heard that among the Bhaggas there are those of renowned virtue and great respect whom the Bhaggas all honor, revere, serve, and support; they receive the teachings when they hear them from such persons."
The Blessed One again addressed the minister Vassakāra:

"If those among the Vajjis who are renowned, virtuous, and respected are honored, revered, and supported by all the Vajjis together, and if they accept the instructions they hear from them, then the Vajjis will surely prevail and not decline."
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:

“Have you heard that all the old monasteries belonging to the Bhaggas are collectively maintained, refurbished, honored, venerated, and served by them; that their original endowments are constantly provided without interruption, and that their original practices are not diminished?”
The Venerable Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard that regarding all the ancient monasteries in Bhṛgukaccha, the people of Bhṛgukaccha collectively maintain, repair, revere, support, and pay homage to them; they continue the original offerings without ceasing, and they do not diminish the original endowments.”
The Blessed One again addressed the minister Vassakāra:

“If all the old monasteries belonging to the Vajjis are collectively repaired by the Vajjīs, and if they continue to honor, support, and pay homage to them, and if what was originally bestowed is maintained without neglect, and what was originally established is not diminished, then the Vajjīs will surely prevail and shall not decline.”
The Blessed One again asked the Venerable Ānanda:

“Have you heard that the Bhaggas all together protect the Arhats with great love and respect, always wishing that future Arhats might come, and that those who have already arrived may dwell here long; and that they always ensure they do not lack robes, alms-food, bedding, medicine for illness, or any other requisites for life?”
Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard that the Vajjis all together protect the Arhats with great love and respect; they constantly wish for future Arhats to come, and for those who have already arrived, they desire that they dwell long and always ensure they do not lack robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, or any other necessities of life.”
The Blessed One further addressed the minister Vassakāra:

"If the Vajjis all together protect the Arhats with great love and respect, constantly wishing that those who have not yet become Arhats might come, and that those who have already arrived might dwell there long, and if they ensure that the Arhats never lack robes, alms-food, bedding, medicinal requisites, or any other articles for living, then the Vajjis will surely prevail and shall not decline."
Vassakāra!
If the Licchavis practice these seven principles of non-decline, and those who uphold these seven principles of non-decline prevail among the Licchavis, they will indeed remain undecaying.
Thereupon, the minister Vassakāra rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"Gotama!..."
If that Vṛji were to possess even one of these seven qualities of non-decline, King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha would not be able to subdue him; how much less so when he possesses all seven?
"Gautama!
I have many affairs of state; please withdraw and return home.
The World-Honored One replied:
"You may go as you please.
Then, having heard what the Buddha had said, the minister Vassakāra received it well, rose, circumambulated the World-Honored One three times, and departed.
Not long after the minister Vassakāra had departed,
the Blessed One turned back and addressed him, saying:
"Ānanda!..."
"If there are bhikṣus dwelling in various places on Vulture Peak Mountain, let them all be summoned to assemble in the lecture hall; once they have all assembled, let them come and inform me."
Venerable Ānanda then accepted the Buddha’s instruction,
saying: “So be it,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda issued a proclamation:
"To all bhikṣus who reside in various places on Vulture Peak Mountain, I now command you all to assemble in the lecture hall."
When everyone had assembled, they returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves in salutation, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!
We have already issued the proclamation: "
"If there are bhikṣus dwelling in various places on Vulture Peak Mountain, let them all assemble in the lecture hall.
Now they have all assembled; we only pray that the World-Honored One will know the proper time.
Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda and went to the lecture hall; having spread out a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus, he sat down and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now teach you the seven principles of non-decline. Listen closely and reflect upon them well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “So be it.
The Buddha said:
“What are the seven?
If bhikṣus assemble frequently and gather in great numbers, the bhikṣus will surely prevail, and the Dharma will not decline.
If bhikṣus assemble together in unison, perform communal affairs together, and rise together as a body, the bhikṣus will surely prevail, and the Dharma will not decline.”

If a bhikṣu does not establish what has not yet been established, does not alter what has already been established, and faithfully observes the precepts as I have taught them, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.

If a bhikṣu does not follow along with the arising of this craving for future existence—which is accompanied by delight and desire, and which delights in various things—that bhikṣu will surely be victorious, and the Dharma will not decline.

If there are elder and senior bhikṣus with whom one practices the holy life together, and if the bhikṣus all revere, honor, and provide offerings to them, and receive their instructions when they hear them, then those bhikṣus will surely excel and the Dharma will not decline.

If a bhikṣu dwells in a secluded place—a mountain forest, a high crag, a quiet retreat, silent and free from noise, remote, without evil, and uninhabited by people—and sits in meditation accordingly, delighting in that dwelling without departing, then that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.

If monks collectively protect all fellow practitioners of the holy life with the utmost reverence and affection, always wishing that future practitioners of the holy life would come, and once they have arrived, desiring that they dwell there long and happily, and ensuring they never lack robes, alms-food, bedding, medicinal requisites, and other necessities for living—then these monks will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
"If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas for non-decline and maintains them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall further explain to you seven more dharmas for non-decline; listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, "So be it.
The Buddha said:
“What are the seven?
If a bhikkhu honors his teacher, reveres him, regards him with extreme weight, makes offerings to him, and serves him, that bhikkhu will surely excel, and the Dhamma will not decline.

If a bhikṣu reveres, honors with the utmost respect, and serves the Dharma, the Saṅgha, the precepts, heedfulness, the requisites, and meditative concentration, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
“If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas for non-decline and upholds them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“I shall further explain to you seven more dharmas for non-decline; listen attentively and reflect upon them well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, "So be it.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?
If a bhikkhu does not engage in action, does not delight in action, and does not practice action, that bhikkhu will surely prevail, and the Dharma will not decline."
One who does not engage in frivolous talk, does not delight in frivolous talk, and does not practice frivolous talk;
one who does not engage in social gatherings, does not delight in social gatherings, and does not practice social gatherings;
one who does not engage in worldly entanglements, does not delight in worldly entanglements, and does not practice worldly entanglements.
One who does not indulge in sleep, does not delight in sleep, and does not habituate themselves to sleep;
one who practices the holy life (brahmacarya) not for the sake of gain, nor for fame, nor for others;
one who does not practice it merely for a moment, nor for the sake of surpassing others in virtue, but rather abandons such efforts midway so as to cause others to surpass them in virtue.
The bhikṣus will surely be victorious, and the Dharma will not decline.
If bhikṣus practice these seven principles for the non-decline of the Dharma, upholding them without transgression, the bhikṣus will surely be victorious, and the Dharma will not decline.
The Blessed One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall further explain to you seven principles for non-decline; listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, "So be it.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?

If a bhikṣu is endowed with the wealth of faith, the wealth of precepts, the wealth of shame, the wealth of remorse, the wealth of extensive learning, the wealth of generosity, and the wealth of wisdom, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline."
“If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas that prevent decline and maintains them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“I shall further explain to you seven more dharmas that prevent decline; listen attentively and reflect upon them well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “So be it.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?

If a bhikṣu is endowed with the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and is endowed with the power of wisdom, that bhikṣu will surely prevail, and the Dharma will not decline."
“If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas that prevent decline and maintains them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“I shall further explain to you seven more dharmas that prevent decline. Listen attentively and reflect upon them well.”
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “So be it.
The Buddha said:
"What are the seven?

If a bhikkhu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, depending on seclusion, depending on dispassion, depending on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment; and if he cultivates the awakening factors of discrimination of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration;

and if he cultivates the awakening factor of equanimity, depending on seclusion, depending on dispassion, depending on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment—then that bhikkhu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline."
"If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas for non-decline and maintains them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall further explain to you seven more dharmas for non-decline; listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
At that time, the bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed, we shall.
The Buddha said:

“What are the seven? If a bhikṣu should grant face-to-face resolution where face-to-face resolution is appropriate; should grant resolution through recollection where resolution through recollection is appropriate; should grant resolution for one not insane where resolution for one not insane is appropriate; should grant self-confession where self-confession is appropriate; should grant suspension where suspension is appropriate; should grant mutual reconciliation where mutual reconciliation is appropriate; and when a dispute arises within the Saṃgha, should settle it by means of the method for settling disputes known as ‘discarding like refuse’—then the bhikṣus will surely prevail, and the Dharma will not decline.”
"If a bhikṣu practices these seven dharmas for non-decline and maintains them without transgression, that bhikṣu will surely excel, and the Dharma will not decline.
The World-Honored One further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I shall now explain to you six dharmas of consolation; listen attentively and reflect upon them well."
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, "So be it.
The Buddha said:

"What are the six? By means of a compassionate bodily action directed toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, this is a dharma that consoles, a dharma of love, a dharma of joy; it causes them to feel affection and respect, to offer service and reverence, to practice and to gather [virtue]; thereby one attains the state of a śramaṇa, attains single-mindedness, attains diligence, and attains nirvāṇa."
Such are the compassionate verbal actions and compassionate mental actions.

If there is any gain of Dharma, or if one gains profit in accordance with the Dharma—even down to the food one eats oneself that remains in the alms bowl—one should share such portions of gain with fellow practitioners of the holy life; this is the practice of providing comfort.

One who loves the Dharma and delights in the Dharma will cause [the Dharma] to be loved and held in high esteem, will cause it to be honored and revered, will cause it to be cultivated and embraced; such a person attains the state of a śramaṇa, attains single-mindedness, attains diligence, and attains nirvāṇa.

If one possesses morality that is unbroken, untorn, unstained, and unblemished; like the earth, it does not depend on others; it is praised by the noble ones, and is fully and rightly undertaken—such a portion of morality, when shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life, is a source of consolation.

One who loves the Dharma and delights in the Dharma will cause [the Dharma] to be loved and held dear, to be honored and revered, to be practiced and embraced; such a person attains the state of a śramaṇa, attains one-pointedness of mind, attains diligence, and attains nirvāṇa.

If one perceives this as the noble way of escape, clearly understanding and penetrating it so as to rightly bring an end to suffering—such a portion of vision, when shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life, is a source of consolation.

One who loves the Dharma and delights in the Dharma will cause [the Dharma] to be cherished and held in high esteem, will cause it to be honored and revered, will cause it to be cultivated and embraced; such a person attains the state of a śramaṇa, attains one-pointedness of mind, attains diligence, and attains nirvāṇa.
"The six methods of consolation that I have spoken of were taught for this very reason.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Vassakāra Sutta*, the first [sutta] of the [chapter], completed; three thousand seven characters. 143. The *Vassakāra Sutta* (143), from the *Brahmañña Vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The second and third recitations. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Sangārava was wandering about after the midday meal when he went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side and said:
"Gotama!..."
"I wish to ask something; if you grant me leave, I shall venture to speak.
The World-Honored One replied, "Māṇava!"
"If there be any doubt, ask whatever you wish.
The Māṇava Sañjaya then asked:
"Gautama!..."
"Brahmin, one who practices begging for wealth according to the Dharma may either perform a fast oneself or instruct others to perform a fast. Gautama!
Whether one performs a fast oneself or instructs others to do so, all such actions constitute immeasurable tracks of merit, because they are caused by the fast."

The disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama shave off their hair and beards according to their clans, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path; they discipline themselves, bring themselves to rest, and bring themselves to cessation.
"In this way, the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice a single path of merit according to their clans, rather than practicing immeasurable paths of merit, for the sake of training in the Way.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was attending the Buddha, holding a fly-whisk.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda asked: "Māṇava!
Of these two paths, which is the most supreme, the most wonderful, and the most excellent?"
The Māṇava Saṅgārava said:
“Ānanda! I revere, respect, and make offerings to both the ascetic Gotama and Ānanda.”
The Venerable Ānanda spoke again, saying:
"Māṇava! I am not asking you whom you revere, respect, and worship."
"I merely ask you this: between these two paths, which is the most supreme, the most wonderful, and the most excellent?
The Venerable Ānanda asked this a second and even a third time: "Māṇava!"
"Of these two paths, which is the most supreme, the most wonderful, and the most excellent?
The Māṇava Saṃjaya also spoke a second and a third time, saying: "Ānanda!"
"I revere, respect, and honor both the śramaṇa Gautama and Ānanda.
The Venerable Ānanda spoke again, saying: "Māṇava!"
I do not ask you whom you revere, respect, and worship;
I simply ask you regarding these two paths: which one is the most supreme, the most wonderful, and the most excellent?
Thereupon, the Blessed One thought to himself:
"This Māṇava Sañjaya has been defeated by Ānanda; I should indeed rescue him."
The Blessed One, having understood this, asked:
"Māṇava! What was it that the king and his ministers gathered together in a great assembly were discussing yesterday?"
"For what reason have we gathered together?
The Māṇava Saṃjaya replied, "Gautama!"
In the past, the king and his ministers assembled in a great gathering and discussed this matter together:
"By what cause and by what condition did the śramaṇa Gautama establish few precepts, yet so many bhikṣus attained the Path?"
"For what cause and for what reason do you now prescribe so many precepts, yet the bhikṣus attain the Path in such small numbers? "Gautama!
Formerly, the king and his ministers gathered in a great assembly and discussed this very matter; it was for this reason that we met together."
At that time, the World-Honored One said:
"Māṇava! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit."
What do you think?

If there were a śramaṇa or brahmin who practiced such a path and followed such a track, and having practiced this path and followed this track, his taints would be exhausted, he would attain the taintless state, and through liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he would know for himself, realize for himself, and dwell having personally realized: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence," knowing it as it truly is.

He speaks thus to others: "I myself have practiced this path, this track; having practiced this path, having followed this track, all taints have been exhausted, I have attained the taintless, and through liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, I have known it for myself, realized it for myself, and attained realization for myself, dwelling in that accomplishment: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."

Come together with me, and you too shall personally practice this path and this track. Having practiced this path and followed this track, all taints will be exhausted; you will attain the taintless state, liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. You will know it for yourselves, realize it for yourselves, and dwell having attained realization for yourselves: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.

He himself also practiced this path and followed this track; having practiced this path and followed this track, his taints were exhausted, he attained the taintless, and his mind was liberated and his wisdom was liberated. Knowing and realizing it for himself, he dwelt having personally realized and accomplished it: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
He teaches it to another, and that other teaches it to yet another; in this way, it is passed on through countless hundreds of thousands.
What do you think, Māṇava?

Is it because of their practice of the path that my disciples—having shaved off their hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of faith left the home life for homelessness—practice only a single track of merit and not immeasurable tracks of merit?
The Māṇava Saṅgārava replied: "Gautama!

As I understand the meaning of what the ascetic Gautama has said, those disciples of the ascetic Gautama shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to train in the path; they practice immeasurable bases of merit and do not practice even a single base of merit because of their training in the path."
The Blessed One again addressed Saṃgārava, saying:
"There are three kinds of manifestation:
the manifestation of the bases of psychic power, the manifestation of telepathic recollection, and the manifestation of instruction."
“Māṇava! How does one manifest the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

There is a certain ascetic or brahmin who possesses great psychic power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; having attained mastery over the mind regarding the bases of psychic power, he practices the immeasurable virtues of psychic power: namely, dividing one into many and combining many into one; remaining as one while being one; possessing knowledge and vision such that he is not obstructed by walls or rocks, moving through them as if through open space.”
He sinks into the earth as if it were water, and treads upon the water as if it were solid ground; he sits cross-legged and ascends into the void like a bird in flight.

Now, these sun and moon possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; with his hand he touches them, and his body reaches as far as the Brahma-heaven.
Māṇava! This is called the manifestation of the bases of psychic power. Māṇava!
What is the manifestation of divining thoughts?

There is a certain śramaṇa or brahmin who divines another’s mind by means of external signs, knowing: "He has such a thought; he has this kind of thought; he truly has this thought. His countless divinations are not few, and all of them are true and without falsehood.

He does not discern the thoughts of others through external signs; rather, he discerns the thoughts of others solely by hearing the voices of devas and non-human beings. He knows: "Such is their thought, such is their thought; they truly possess this thought. His countless and inexhaustible discernments are all in accordance with ultimate truth and are without falsehood.

He does not discern another's thoughts by means of external signs, nor does he discern another's thoughts by hearing the voices of devas or non-humans; rather, having heard their internal reflections, their thoughts, and their speech, he discerns another's thoughts, thinking: "They have such a thought, they have this kind of thought, they truly have this thought. His countless and manifold discernments are all true and without falsehood.

One does not discern another's intention by means of external signs, nor does one discern another's intention by hearing the voices of devas or non-human beings, nor by their thoughts, reflections, or speech. Having heard their voice, one does not discern their intention; rather, having seen another enter the meditative concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*asaṃjñāsaṃjñāsamādhi*), and having seen this, one forms this thought:
"This worthy one does not think or reflect, yet he acts according to his wish."
That worthy one, having awakened from this concentration, reflects in this way.

As he awakens from this concentration, he reflects in such and such a manner; he discerns the past, he discerns the future, and he discerns the present. He discerns what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, as well as states of tranquility and abiding in tranquility, and he discerns the mind and the mental factors associated with the mind.
“Māṇava! This is called the manifestation through the recollection of portents. Māṇava!”
What is the demonstration of instruction?

There is a certain ascetic or brahmin who practices such a path and follows such a track; having practiced this path and followed this track, his taints are exhausted, he attains the taintless state, and his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated. He knows and realizes for himself, attaining realization through his own effort, dwelling in that attainment: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
He says to others:

"I have practiced this path, this track; having practiced this path, having followed this track, my taints have been exhausted, I have attained the taintless, and through liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, I have known it for myself, realized it for myself, and having witnessed it for myself, I dwell in its accomplishment: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."

Come, all of you, and likewise practice this path and this track yourselves. Having practiced this path and this track, with the destruction of the outflows, you will attain the state free from outflows; with mind liberated and wisdom liberated, you will know it for yourselves, realize it for yourselves, and dwell having achieved realization for yourselves: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—knowing this as it truly is.

He himself also practiced such a path and such a track; having practiced this path and this track, his taints were exhausted, and he attained the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Knowing and realizing it for himself, he dwelt having personally realized it: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knew this as it truly is.
He teaches it to others, and they teach it to others; in this way, it is transmitted in succession to immeasurable hundreds of thousands. Māṇava!
This is called the manifestation of instruction.
"Among these three manifestations, which one is the most supreme, the most exquisite,
and the most excellent? The Māṇava Saṃjaya replied, "Gautama!"

"O Gautama! If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who possess great supernormal power (ṛddhi), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; who have attained mastery over the mind regarding supernormal power, and who can even extend their bodies as far as the Brahma-heaven—"
"This was done by oneself and exists by oneself; one receives its retribution by oneself.
Gautama! Among all manifestations, this is the manifestation of the Great Dharma."
"Gautama! If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who, by means of external signs, divine another's intention, and even divine their mind and mental factors— Gautama!"
"This too is self-made and self-existent; one receives its retribution oneself.
Gautama! Among all manifestations, this too is a manifestation of the Great Dharma."
"Gautama!

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who practice such a path and follow such a track, and having practiced this path and followed this track, their taints are exhausted, they attain the taintless state, and through the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, they know for themselves, realize for themselves, and dwell having attained realization for themselves: ‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,’ knowing this as it truly is."
He teaches it to others, and they teach it to others; in this way, it is transmitted in succession to immeasurable hundreds of thousands. Gautama!
Among the three kinds of demonstrations, this demonstration is the most supreme, the most exquisite, and the most excellent.
The Blessed One again asked Saṅgārava:
"Among the three manifestations, which manifestation do you praise?
The renunciant Saṅgārava replied:
"Gautama! On account of three demonstrations, I proclaim the ascetic Gautama as such. Why is that? Because—"
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great *ṛddhi*, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual power; his mind has attained mastery, such that his body reaches as far as the Brahma-heaven.
The śramaṇa Gautama discerns the minds of others by means of their external signs, even discerning the mind and its mental concomitants. The śramaṇa Gautama demonstrates such a path and such a track;

having practiced this path and followed this track, his taints have been exhausted, he has attained the taintless state, and his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated. Having known and realized this for himself, he dwells having achieved personal realization: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
The śramaṇa Gautama teaches it to others, and they teach it to others; in this way, it is transmitted successively to immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
Gautama! For this reason, regarding these three demonstrations, I praise the śramaṇa Gautama!
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said:
"Māṇava, you have mastered this discourse well."

Why is this? I possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority; having attained mastery over the mind through supernormal power, my body can even reach the Brahma Heaven.
"Mañava! By means of external signs, I discern the intentions of others, and even discern their minds and mental factors. Mañava!"

I have personally practiced this path and followed this track; having practiced this path and followed this track, all taints have been exhausted, and I have attained the taintless state, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Having known it for myself and awakened to it, I dwell having realized it through my own direct experience: birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is.
I have taught it to others, and they have taught it to others; in this way, it has been transmitted in succession to immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
Māṇava! Therefore, you must thoroughly master this discourse; you should receive and uphold it well in this manner.
"Why is that? This meaning which has been explained should be understood in this way.
Thereupon, the Māṇava Saṃjaya addressed [the Blessed One], saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have understood. Sugata!”
"I have understood, World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Māṇava Sangārava, the Venerable Ānanda, and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Sangāravasutta*, the second [sutta], ends here, totaling two thousand two hundred and fifty-two characters. 144. The *Saṅkhāra-Moggallānasutta* (144), from the *Brāhmaṇavagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The third recitation of the *Saṅkhāra-Moggallānasutta*, the third [sutta]. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the Migāramātupāsāda.
At that time, the brahmin Gaṇaka-Maudgalyāyana, having wandered about in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side and said:
"Gotama!..."
"I wish to ask something; if you will grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth.
The World-Honored One said, "Maudgalyāyana! [Ask whatever you wish]."
"Ask whatever you wish; do not hesitate or doubt.
Then Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana asked: "Gautama!
This Sāḷha’s Mother’s Hall was constructed gradually, step by step, until finally it was completed. Gautama!
As for this Sāḷha’s Mother’s Hall, when ascending the ladder, one first climbs one step, and subsequently the second, third, and fourth.
"Gotama! In this way, the Sālaguha Hall gradually ascends step by step. Gotama!"
Gautama, this elephant trainer also gradually and sequentially completes the training of the elephant; that is, by means of the hook.
Gautama, this horse trainer also gradually and sequentially completes the training of the horse; that is, by means of the bit.
"Gautama!
This kṣatriya also gradually proceeds through the stages until he reaches completion, namely because of his mastery of the bow and arrow.
Gautama!"
These brahmins also gradually proceed through the stages until they reach completion, that is to say, by virtue of studying the scriptures.
Gautama! We study arithmetic and subsist by means of arithmetic; we too gradually proceed through the stages until we reach completion.
If there are disciples, whether male or female, whom one first teaches to count one by one—two, two; three, three; ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand—in successive order up to the highest number.
"Gautama!
This is how we study arithmetic; we sustain our lives by means of arithmetic, gradually progressing through the stages until completion.
Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, how does one proceed through the gradual stages until completion?
The Blessed One replied,
"Maudgalyāyana!"
"If there is a correct exposition that proceeds through successive stages until completion—
Maudgalyāyana! This,
in my Dharma and Vinaya, is called a correct exposition."
Why is that? Moggallāna!
I have gradually brought this Dhamma and Vinaya to completion through successive stages.
"Maugandalyāyana!
If a young bhikṣu has newly come to study the Path and has just entered the Dharma and Vinaya, the Tathāgata first instructs him: 'Bhikṣu!'"
"Come, you shall be pure in the protection of life through body, and pure in the protection of life through speech and mind. Maudgalyāyana!
If a bhikṣu is pure in the protection of life through body, and pure in the protection of life through speech and mind, the Tathāgata further instructs him:
"Monks! Come, observe the body internally as body, and likewise observe feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena.
Thus spoke Maudgalyāyana.
If a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena, the Tathāgata further instructs him:
"Bhikṣu!..."

Come, observe the internal body as body; do not dwell on thoughts associated with desire. Continue until you observe feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena; do not dwell on thoughts associated with what is contrary to the Dharma.

“Maudgalyāyana! If a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body and does not attend to thoughts associated with desire, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena and not attending to thoughts associated with what is contrary to the Dharma, the Tathāgata further instructs him: ‘Bhikṣu!’”

Come, guard your sense faculties; constantly mind their closure, and mind clarity and penetration. By guarding the mindful mind, you will achieve success. Always maintain clear comprehension (*saṃprajānan*): when the eye sees forms, do not grasp at their signs (*nimitta*), nor savor the forms, lest there be quarrels and disputes; thus, guard the faculty of the eye.
In his mind, he does not give rise to covetousness, ill will, or unwholesome and evil states; because he is intent upon that [state], he guards the faculty of the eye.

Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If the mind cognizes mental phenomena, he neither grasps at their signs nor relishes them—namely, out of fear of quarrels—he guards the faculty of the mind.
"Because no covetousness, sorrow, or unwholesome, evil states arise within his mind, he guards the faculty of the mind by inclining toward that [state].
"Maudgalyāyana!"

If a bhikṣu guards his sense faculties, constantly mindful of closing them off, mindful of clarity and penetration, and achieves success by guarding his mindfulness and mind, always maintaining clear comprehension: when the eye sees forms, he does not grasp at their signs nor relish the forms, because of [the danger of] anger and strife; thus he guards the eye faculty.
In his mind, he does not give rise to covetousness, ill will, sorrow, or unwholesome states; because he is intent upon that [liberation], he guards the faculty of the eye.

Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If the mind cognizes mental phenomena, he does not grasp at their signs nor relish those phenomena—namely, out of fear of quarrels and disputes—he guards the faculty of the mind.
"When no covetousness, grief, or unwholesome, evil states arise in the mind, and because one is thus inclined toward that state, one guards the faculty of the mind," the Tathāgata further instructs:
"Bhikkhu!..."

Come, you shall be fully aware of going out and coming in; you shall clearly observe and discern your bending and stretching, your lowering and raising, and your dignified deportment; you shall properly wear the saṃghāṭī and other robes along with the alms bowl; and whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent, you shall maintain full awareness of them all.

"Maughulayana! If a bhikṣu is fully aware when going out and coming in; is skillful in observing and discerning when bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, and in his dignified deportment; is skillful in wearing the saṃghāṭī and other robes and carrying the bowl; and is fully aware in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent—then the Tathāgata further instructs him: 'Bhikṣu!'"

Come, dwell alone in seclusion, in a place free from affairs—whether at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet spot, in a mountain cave or rock chamber, in an open field or a heap of straw, or in a forest grove, or dwelling among the burial mounds.

Having gone to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet, and peaceful spot, you should spread out your sitting mat, sit down cross-legged, straighten your body and set your intention, and maintain mindfulness without distraction; abandon covetousness and ensure that your mind is free from contention.
Seeing the wealth and various articles of livelihood belonging to others, do not give rise to covetousness or the desire to obtain them for yourself; you must purify your mind of such covetousness.

Likewise, regarding ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt, and perplexity—being free from hesitation concerning all wholesome qualities—you must purify your mind of such doubt and perplexity.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—you, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, shall attain and dwell in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
"Maugalyāyana! If a bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna—Maugalyāyana!"
The Tathāgata brings great benefit to young bhikṣus through instruction and admonition.
Maudgalyāyana!
If there are bhikṣus who are elders, seniors, or long-practiced in the holy life, the Tathāgata further instructs them with the teaching that culminates in the exhaustion of all outflows.
The monk Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana then asked again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
When all disciples have been thus instructed and thus admonished, do they all attain ultimate knowledge and necessarily enter Nirvāṇa?"
The Blessed One replied: “Moggallāna!
It is not the case that one always succeeds; there are those who succeed and those who do not.”
The monk Saṅkhyā-Maudgalyāyana asked again:
"Gautama! For what cause and for what reason is there nirvāṇa, and is there a path to nirvāṇa?"
The Śramaṇa Gautama is the present guide; when a bhikṣu receives such instruction and such admonition, does he attain ultimate nirvāṇa, or does he not?
The Blessed One said:
"Moggallāna! I shall question you in return; answer as you see fit."
"Maugalyāyana! What do you think?
Do you know the location of Rājagṛha and are you familiar with the way there?"
The elder Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana replied, “Indeed.
I know the location of Rājagṛha and I am also familiar with the path there.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Moggallāna! Suppose someone were to come wishing to see that king and arrive at Rājagaha."
That person asked you:

"I wish to see the King; having arrived at the city of Rājagṛha, could you, who are skilled in calculation and know the location of Rājagṛha and are familiar with its paths, point them out and tell me how to get there?"
"You should say to that person:
'From here, travel eastward to such-and-such village; from that village, you shall go to such-and-such town, proceeding in this manner by successive stages until you reach Rājagṛha.'"

If there are fine gardens outside the city of Rājagṛha, with level ground, multi-storied pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, long flowing rivers, and clear springs, he sees them all and knows them all.
Having heard your words and received your instruction, that person will travel east from here; but before long, he will abandon the right path and return by way of a wrong path.

If there were fine gardens outside the city of Rājagṛha, with level ground, watchtowers, bathing pools, various flowering trees, long flowing rivers, and clear springs, they would see none of these, nor would they even know of them.
"Furthermore, suppose another person comes wishing to see that king and arrives at the city of Rājagṛha.
That person asks you:
'I wish to see the king; I have come to the city of Rājagṛha.'"
"Can you tell me the way, showing me how the arhat Maudgalyāyana knows the location of Rājagṛha and is familiar with its paths?
You should say to that person:
"From here, travel eastward to such-and-such a village; from that village, you shall go to such-and-such a town, proceeding in this manner by stages until you reach Rājagṛha."

If there are fine gardens outside the city of Rājagṛha, with level ground, multi-storied pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, long flowing rivers, and clear springs, he sees them all and knows them all.

Having heard your words and received your instructions, that person immediately departed from here toward the east, traveling to such-and-such a village; from that village, he proceeded to such-and-such a town, and thus moving on by stages, he reached the city of Rājagṛha.

If there are fine gardens outside the city of Rājagṛha, with level ground, multi-storied pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, long flowing rivers, and clear springs, he sees them all and knows them all.
“Maudgalyāyana! For what cause and for what reason is it that, although there is this city of Rājagṛha and the road to Rājagṛha,
you who are currently our guide, the very first person to receive your instruction will, before long, abandon the level and correct path and return by a wicked road?”

If there were fine gardens outside the city of Rājagṛha, with level ground, multi-storied pavilions, bathing pools, various flowering trees, a long flowing river, and clear springs—if one did not see any of these, would one not know them either?

Suppose that second person follows your instructions and, traveling along the level and correct road, eventually reaches Rājagṛha. If there are fine gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, watchtowers, bathing pools, various flowering trees, a long flowing river, and clear springs—would he see and know them all?
The monk Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana replied:
“Gautama! I have no business at all;
there is that city of Rājagṛha, and there is the road to Rājagṛha.”

I am now the Teacher; yet that foremost person does not follow my instruction, but abandons the level and right path to return to an evil path. If there were a fine park outside the city of Rājagṛha—its ground level and even, with watchtowers, bathing pools, various flowering trees, flanking a long-flowing river, and further possessing clear springs—would he not see any of it at all, or would he not know of it?

That second person followed my instructions and, proceeding along the level and correct path, eventually reached Rājagṛha. If there were fine gardens outside Rājagṛha, with level ground, watchtowers, bathing ponds, various flowering trees, long flowing rivers, and clear springs—would he not see and know them all?
The Blessed One said: "It is so,
Maudgalyāyana!"
I, too, have no further task; there is that Nirvāṇa and there is the path to Nirvāṇa.
As a teacher, I thus instruct and thus admonish the bhikṣus so that they may attain ultimate Nirvāṇa, though some may not.
"Maugandalyāyana!
Each bhikṣu shall simply follow his own practice.
At that time, the World-Honored One will then certify their practice, meaning that they have reached the ultimate exhaustion of the outflows."
The monk Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana replied,
“Gautama, I have understood.”
"Gautama! I have understood. Gautama!"

It is like a fertile field where there is a grove of *sāla* trees, and within it is a keeper of the *sāla* grove who is wise, capable, and diligent; he weeds the roots of the *sāla* trees at the proper time, levels the high ground and fills the low ground, and fertilizes and irrigates them without missing the right season.
If there are weeds of filth and evil growing at its edges, he pulls them all out and discards them;
if there are branches that are crooked or not straight, he trims and corrects them all;

if there is an exceptionally fine tree with a straight trunk, he protects it temporarily, weeding and digging around it at the proper times, enriching it with manure and irrigating it without missing the right season.
In this way, O Gautama, that excellent grove of *sāla* trees becomes increasingly lush and beautiful.

Likewise, there are some people who are flatterers, deceivers, utterly unworthy, lacking faith, indolent, lacking mindfulness, lacking concentration, possessed of evil wisdom, deranged in mind, with restless faculties, lax in their observance of the precepts, and who do not extensively cultivate the life of a *śramaṇa*.
"Gautama! Such a person cannot work together with me. Why is that?"
"Gotama! Such a person defiles the holy life. Gotama!"

Furthermore, if there is another person who is neither flatterer nor deceiver, who possesses a degree of faith, is diligent and untiring, endowed with mindfulness and concentration, as well as wisdom, who holds the precepts with the utmost reverence, and extensively cultivates the life of a śramaṇa.
"Gotama! Such a person as this can work together with me. Why is that? Because..."
"Gotama! Such a person as this leads the pure holy life. Gotama!"
"Just as among all fragrant roots, aloeswood is the foremost.
Why is that, Gautama?"
"Venerable Gautama, that aloeswood is the most supreme among all root-fragrances.
Just as, among all *sāla* trees, red sandalwood is the foremost."
Why is that? Gautama!
Because red sandalwood is the most excellent among all the fragrances of the *sāla* trees.
"Gotama! Just as among all water-born flowers, the blue lotus is the foremost. Why is that?"
Gautama! This is because the blue lotus is the most excellent among all water flowers. Gautama!
"Just as among all land flowers, the sumana flower is the foremost.
Why is that, Gautama?"
"O Gautama, because the sumana flower is the most excellent among all land flowers,
just as the śramaṇa Gautama is the foremost among all the debaters in the world."
Why is this so? Because the śramaṇa Gautama, as a master of debate, is able to subdue all non-Buddhist heterodox teachers.
World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The third discourse, the Saṅkhyā Maudgalyāyana Sūtra, ends here with 2,354 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 35, contains 7,613 characters. This concludes the third recitation section.
Madhyama Āgama, Scroll Thirty-Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. 145.
The Discourse on Ghaṭīkāra Maudgalyāyana (145). Chapter on the Brahmins. The Discourse on Ghaṭīkāra Maudgalyāyana, Fourth [Discourse], Third Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, not long after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda was traveling in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, Varṣākāra, the minister of Magadha, was governing the city of Rājagṛha for the purpose of defending it against the Vṛjis.
Thereupon, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, dispatched the laborers Kumbhakāra and Moggallāna to the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka-nivāpa.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having passed the night, dressed in the early morning and took his bowl and robe, entering the city of Rājagaha for alms.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"Let alone begging for alms in Rājagṛha; I would rather go to where Ghoṭamukha Kalandaka is working in the fields."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda went to where the brahmin Ghoṭamukha, a farm laborer, was.
Seeing the Venerable Ānanda approaching from afar, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Venerable Ānanda, and said:
"Welcome, Ānanda!"
"It has been a long time since you last came here; please sit upon this seat.
Venerable Ānanda then sat upon that seat.
The brahmin Ghoṭamukha and Venerable Ānanda exchanged greetings with one another, and having sat down to one side, the brahmin said:
“Ānanda! I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Maudgalyāyana!
You may ask; having heard it, I shall consider it. He then asked:
“Ānanda! Is there perhaps even one bhikkhu who is equal to the śramaṇa Gotama?

While the Venerable Ānanda was discussing this matter with the brahmin Kumāra Kassapa, at that time the Magadhan minister Vassakāra, while consoling the laborers on the fields, went to where the brahmin Kumāra Kassapa was among the field workers.

The Magadhan minister Vassakāra saw from afar the Venerable Ānanda sitting among the Brahmin Koṭṭhita Moggallāna’s laborers in the fields; he approached the Venerable Ānanda, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and asked:
“Ānanda!...”
"With what matter did you discuss things with the brahmin Ghoṭamukha, and for what reason have you come together here?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Vassakāra!..."
The brahmin Kumāra-Kassapa asked me:
"Ānanda! Is there perhaps even one bhikkhu who is equal to the śramaṇa Gotama?"
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
“Ānanda, how did you answer him?”
The Venerable Ānanda replied: “Vassakāra!
There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the Blessed One.”
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
"Indeed, Ānanda!
There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the Blessed One."
"Is there perhaps any bhikkhu who was appointed by the ascetic Gotama while he was still alive, such that after my parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu would be the one upon whom you all should rely?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra!

There is not a single bhikkhu known and seen by the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—whom he established during his lifetime as one upon whom the bhikkhus should rely after my parinirvāṇa, such that we now rely upon him."
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
“Indeed, Ānanda.”
There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the śramaṇa Gautama;

nor is there a single bhikkhu whom the śramaṇa Gautama established while he was still alive, saying, "After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu shall be the reliance for all bhikkhus," such as the one upon whom you now rely.

"Is there perhaps a single bhikkhu who was unanimously elected by the assembly, such that after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One, he might be relied upon by the bhikkhus—meaning, would you now rely upon him?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied: “Vassakāra!

There is not even a single bhikkhu who has been unanimously honored by the assembly as one upon whom the bhikkhus may rely after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One—such that we might say, ‘He is the one upon whom we now rely.’”
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
“Indeed, Ānanda.”
There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the śramaṇa Gautama;

nor is there a single bhikkhu whom the śramaṇa Gautama established during his lifetime, saying, "After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu shall be the reliance for all bhikkhus," such that you now rely upon him;

nor is there a single bhikkhu whom the community has collectively honored and appointed, saying, "After the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu shall be the reliance for all bhikkhus," such that you now rely upon him.

Ānanda! If that were so, would you have no one to rely upon, yet remain united, without dispute, in peace, following the same teaching, blending as one like water and milk, and dwelling happily, just as when the Śramaṇa Gautama was alive?
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Vassakāra! Do not speak thus, saying that we have no support."
"Why is that? It is because we have something upon which we rely.
Thus spoke Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha.
“Ānanda! Why are what you have said previously and what you have said now inconsistent?
Ānanda, you have just now spoken thus:”
"There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the Blessed One;

nor is there a single bhikkhu known and seen by the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One—whom he established during his lifetime, saying: 'After my parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu shall be the resort for the bhikkhus, as I am now the resort for you.

Nor is there a single bhikkhu whom the community has collectively assembled and honored, saying: 'After the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa, this bhikkhu shall be the resort for the bhikkhus, as we are now the resort.'"
"Ānanda! For what cause and for what reason do you now say that I have something upon which I rely?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Vassakāra! We do not rely on persons; we rely on the Dhamma.
Vassakāra!"
Whenever we travel through villages or towns and gather together in one place on the fifteenth day for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*,
if there is a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, we request that bhikṣu to teach us the Dharma.
If that assembly is pure, we shall all joyfully practice what that bhikṣu has taught.
If that assembly is not pure, we shall instruct them to act according to what is taught by the Dharma.
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda! It was not you who taught this to be done;
rather, it is the Dharma that teaches this to be done."

Ānanda! Such few or many teachings as can be made to endure for a long time—such as when Ānanda and others live in harmony, without dispute, in peace and security, following the same single teaching, blending like water and milk, and dwelling happily, just as they did when the Śramaṇa Gautama was alive.
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
"Ānanda, are there any who are worthy of veneration?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Vassakāra, there is one who is worthy of veneration."
Vassakāra said:
"Ānanda! Why are the earlier and later statements inconsistent?"
Ānanda spoke thus:
"There is not a single bhikkhu who is equal to the Blessed One;
nor is there a single bhikkhu whom the Blessed One, while he was still present, established as one upon whom the bhikkhus should rely after my parinibbāna—such as the one upon whom we now rely."

Nor was there a single bhikkhu who, together with the assembly, rose in unison to honor him, saying: "This bhikkhu shall be our reliance after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One; he is the one upon whom we may rely now."
“Ānanda! For what cause and for what reason do you now say that there is one who is worthy of veneration?
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Vassakāra! The Blessed One knows and sees;

the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has declared that there are ten qualities by which one may be honored. If we see a bhikkhu who possesses these ten qualities, we shall together love, revere, respect, support, honor, and pay homage to that bhikkhu.”
What are the ten? Vassakāra!

A bhikkhu cultivates the precepts, guards the code of liberation, and further maintains excellent deportment and decorum; seeing even the slightest fault as a cause for fear, he undertakes and trains in the rules of training.
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who practices the higher training in virtue to the utmost degree, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu."
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu is widely learned and of great erudition; he retains what he has heard without forgetting and accumulates vast learning.
That which is called the Dharma is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, perfectly pure, and reveals the holy life."
Having thus extensively studied these dharmas, having heard them much and recited them up to a thousand times, one examines them with the mind and sees clearly into their profound depths.
Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who is extremely learned, we then together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu.
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu acts as a good friend, acts as a good companion, and acts as a good associate.
Vassakāra!"
If we see a bhikṣu who is a supreme spiritual friend, we shall together love, revere, respect, honor, venerate, and serve that bhikṣu.
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu delights in dwelling in seclusion, having accomplished two kinds of seclusion: that of the body and that of the mind.
Vassakāra!"
If we see a bhikṣu who dwells in extreme joy and seclusion, we shall together love, revere, respect, honor, and venerate that bhikṣu, and pay him homage.
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu delights in solitary meditation; he practices internal tranquility, does not abandon investigation, achieves insight, and increases the practice of emptiness."
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who delights in solitary meditation, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu."
"Furthermore, Vassakāra! A bhikkhu is contented;
he takes robes only to cover his body and food only to sustain his life. Wherever he travels, he goes with only his robes and bowl, moving without attachment or longing."
Just as a hawk flies through the air with its two wings, so too is a bhikṣu contented:
he takes clothing only to cover his body and food only to sustain his frame; wherever he travels, he goes with only his robes and bowl, moving without attachment or longing.
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who is extremely contented, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and worship that bhikkhu."
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu constantly practices mindfulness, achieves right mindfulness, and always remembers without forgetting what was practiced long ago and heard long ago."
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who possesses supreme right mindfulness, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu."
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!

A bhikkhu constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas. He always rouses his own mind, remaining single-minded and firm, establishing the roots of all that is good and never relinquishing skillful means."
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who is exceedingly diligent, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu."
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu practices wisdom, contemplating the law of arising and passing away; he attains such knowledge, noble insight, clarity, and discernment, whereby he rightly brings an end to suffering."
Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu who practices with supreme wisdom, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu.
"Furthermore, Vassakāra!

A bhikkhu whose taints have been exhausted attains the state free from taints; with mind liberated and wisdom liberated, he dwells having realized for himself through direct knowledge, having understood and attained it: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."
"Vassakāra!
If we see a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, we shall together love, revere, honor, support, and pay homage to that bhikkhu."
“Vassakāra!
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, through his knowledge and vision, has declared these ten qualities as worthy of veneration.
Vassakāra!”
If we see a bhikṣu practicing these ten dharmas, we shall together love, revere, respect, support, honor, and pay homage to that bhikṣu.
Thereupon, that great assembly raised a loud cry: "The straight path can indeed be cultivated;

it is not the case that it cannot be cultivated. If the straight path can be cultivated and is not uncultivable, then one should follow the Arhats of the world by loving them, honoring them, respecting them, making offerings to them, and serving them."
If those venerable ones are capable of cultivating the straight path and do so cultivate it, for this reason they are loved, revered, honored, supported, and served by the world as Arhats.
Thereupon, Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, together with his retinue, asked: “Ānanda,
where are you traveling now?”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"I am currently wandering here in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, in this city of Rājagaha.
"Ānanda! [the King said.]

The Bamboo Grove Kalandaka Garden is exceedingly lovely and delightful; it is perfectly pleasing, not noisy by day and tranquil at night, free from mosquitoes and gadflies, as well as flies and fleas, and neither cold nor hot.
“Ānanda, do you dwell happily in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
"So it is, Vassakāra! So it is!"
"Vassakāra!

The Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, is exceedingly delightful and truly enchanting; it is not noisy by day and is tranquil at night; there are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor are there flies or fleas; it is neither cold nor hot."
"Vassakāra!
I delight in dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden. Why is that?"
"Because of the World-Honored One's protection.
At that time, the great general Pāṇḍaka was among that assembly.
The great general Pāṇḍaka addressed [the Buddha], saying:
"So it is, Vassakāra! So it is!"
"Vassakāra!

The Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, is exceedingly delightful and truly enchanting; it is not noisy by day and is tranquil at night; there are no mosquitoes or gadflies, nor are there flies or fleas; it is neither cold nor hot. That venerable one would find pleasure in dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden."
"Why is that? Because this venerable one practices vitarka and delights in vitarka.
Having heard this, Vassakāra, the minister of Magadha, said:
“General Pāṭali! In the past,
while the śramaṇa Gautama was wandering through the Kevaddha Grove, General Pāṭali,
I went there several times and saw the śramaṇa Gautama.”
"Why is that? Because the ascetic Gautama practices vitarka, delights in vitarka, and praises all forms of vitarka.
Having heard this, the Venerable Ānanda said to him:
"Vassakāra! Do not speak thus;
the ascetic Gotama does not proclaim all types of investigation (*vitarka*). Why is that? [Because]..."
"The Blessed One sometimes mentions investigation (*vitarka*) and sometimes does not.
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again: "Ānanda!"
“The ascetic Gautama does not praise attention; what kind of attention does he not praise?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Vassakāra!...”

There may be one who, being entangled by sensual desire, gives rise to sensual desire and does not know, as it truly is, the escape from it; because he is obstructed by sensual desire, he harbors thoughts of it, increases those thoughts, and dwells intensely upon them.
Vassakāra!
This is called the first investigation that the Blessed One did not praise.
Furthermore, Vassakāra!

There may be one who, being缠缚 (bound) by ill will, gives rise to ill will and does not know, as it truly is, the way out of it; because he is obstructed by ill will, he harbors thoughts of resentment, increases those thoughts of resentment, and dwells deeply upon them.
Vassakāra!
This is called the second kind of investigation that the Blessed One did not praise.
Furthermore, Vassakāra!

Enveloped by sleep, one gives rise to drowsiness and does not know, as it truly is, the means of escape from it; because one is obstructed by that sleep, one reflects, reflects further, and reflects intensely.
Vassakāra!
This is called the third reflection, which the Blessed One did not praise.
Furthermore, Vassakāra!
Enshrouded by doubt, one gives rise to doubt and does not know, as it truly is, the way out; because one is obstructed by doubt, one reflects, reflects further, and reflects repeatedly.
Vassakāra!
This is called the fourth vitarka, which the Blessed One did not praise.
Vassakāra!
"The Blessed One does not praise these four modes of attention.
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra said: "Ānanda!"
These four types of vitarka are subject to increase and are grounds for increase; yet the śramaṇa Gautama does not praise them.
Why is this? Because he is one who has attained perfect enlightenment.
The Magadhan minister Vassakāra asked again:
“Ānanda, what is it that the ascetic Gotama frequently speaks of?”
Venerable Ānanda replied: "Vassakāra!
A bhikkhu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna."
"Vassakāra!
The Blessed One has praised these four modes of attention.
Thus spoke Vassakāra, the minister of Magadha.
“Ānanda! These four modes of reflection are worthy of praise, worthy of being praised; they are what the śramaṇa Gautama praises. Why is that? Because—”
"Because of my perfect enlightenment, Ānanda!
My affairs are many and pressing; I request that you withdraw and return home."
The Venerable Ānanda replied, “You may return as you wish.

Thereupon, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the Magadhan minister Vassakāra received and retained it well; he then rose from his seat, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda three times, and departed.

Venerable Ānanda replied, "Moggallāna!"

If there is the liberation of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as the liberation through wisdom and the liberation of an Arhat—what is the distinction between these three types of liberation?
"What excellence do they possess?
Venerable Ānanda replied, "Moggallāna!"

If the liberation of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as well as the liberation through wisdom and the liberation of the Arhat—these three liberations are without distinction, nor is there any superiority among them.
The brahmin Gotama Moggallāna said: "Ānanda!

Knowing that he had accepted through his silence, the brahmin Ghoṭamukha rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and with his own hands served an abundance of most excellent, pure, and exquisite foods—both solid and soft—to ensure he was fully satiated. Venerable Ānanda taught the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having used immeasurable skillful means to teach the Dharma to him, he exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him.
