Having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, Vassakāra the Magadhan minister, along with his retinue and the brahmin Ghoṭamukha, were delighted and respectfully practiced it.

The *Gomayapindika-maudgalyāyana Sūtra*, the fourth, ends here, totaling three thousand one hundred and forty-three characters. 146. The *Hastipadopama Sūtra* (146), from the *Brahmaṇavarga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*. The fifth sūtra, for the third recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the heterodox teacher Pūraṇa rose from his dwelling in Śrāvastī at dawn, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in greeting, and sat down to one side.

The Buddha taught the Dharma for him, exhorting him to aspire with longing, inspiring joy, and bringing it to fulfillment; having taught him the Dharma through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting him to aspire with longing, and inspiring joy, he remained silent.

The heterodox teacher Bīraṇa, having been exhorted by the Buddha with a discourse on the Dharma that inspired longing and brought about joy, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa mounted an excellent white carriage and, together with five hundred disciples, departed from Śrāvastī at dawn and proceeded to a secluded place, intending to instruct his disciples in the recitation of the scriptures.
When the brahmin Jātiśroṇa saw the heterodox teacher Pilindavatsa approaching from afar, he asked:
"Vatsa! Where have you come from this morning?"
The heterodox teacher Bīra replied: “Brahmin!
I have come to pay homage to and make offerings to the World-Honored One.”
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked:
"Vatsa! Do you know whether the ascetic Gautama practices wisdom in a secluded and tranquil place?"
The heterodox teacher Bīra replied: "Brahmin!
What kind of person can be said to know the Blessed One’s practice of wisdom in empty and tranquil places?"
Brahmin!
If one knows that the World-Honored One trains in wisdom in empty and tranquil places, one should likewise do so.
However, Brahmin!

The teachings I have studied contain four propositions; because of these four propositions, I am firmly convinced that the Blessed One is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, and a Samyaksaṃbuddha; that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent; and that the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed.
"Brahmin!

It is as if a skilled elephant trainer, wandering in a secluded place, were to see the tracks of a great elephant among the trees and groves; having seen them, he would certainly believe that the elephant must be immense for such tracks to exist."
"Brahmin! It is the same for me.

There is a fourfold meaning in the verses I have studied; because of this fourfold meaning, I am firmly convinced that the Blessed One is a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent; and that the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."
“What is the meaning of the four propositions?
O Brahmin!

There are wise Kṣatriya scholars who are learned and resolute; they can subdue the people of the world and claim to know all things. Thus, based on their various views, they compose literary works and circulate them throughout the world.”
He thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such and such questions; if he can answer them, I shall ask again, but if he cannot answer, I will submit and depart."

Upon hearing that the Blessed One was traveling through a certain village, he went to that place; yet, having seen the Blessed One, he did not even dare to question him, much less could he subdue him.
"Brāhmaṇa!

From the study of the scriptures, I have derived this meaning of the first sentence; by virtue of this meaning, I shall certainly place my faith in the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent; and that the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."

"In this way, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise śramaṇas—learned, resolute, and capable of subduing the world, knowing all things without exception—compose treatises based on various views and circulate them throughout the world."
He thought to himself:
"I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such-and-such questions; if he can answer them, I shall ask again, but if he cannot answer, I shall submit and depart."

Upon hearing that the World-Honored One was traveling through a certain village or town, he went to that place; yet, having seen the World-Honored One, he did not even dare to question him, much less could he subdue him.
"O Brahmin!

Having understood the meaning of this fourth line through my study of the scriptures, and by virtue of this meaning, I have gained firm faith in the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; I have faith that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent, and that the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."
"O Brahmin!

The texts I have studied contain these four statements. Because of these four statements, I certainly have faith in the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One; that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent; and that the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said: “Vāseṭṭha!
You have made a great offering to the ascetic Gotama; for whatever reason and on whatever basis, you have joyfully carried it out.”
The heterodox teacher Bīra replied: “Brahmin! So it is, so it is.”
"I have made the utmost offerings to that Blessed One and have praised him most highly; all the world should likewise make offerings to him.

At that time, having heard this meaning, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa immediately descended from his vehicle, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Veṇuvana Anāthapiṇḍika Park, paid homage three times, saying:

Jātiśroṇa the brahmin related to the Buddha in full detail the matter of his discussion with the heterodox teacher Pilindavatsa; having heard this, the World-Honored One said to him:
"Brahmin!..."

The heterodox teacher Bīla’s discourse on the simile of the elephant’s footprint was neither well-executed nor complete. Now, I shall explain to you the simile of the elephant’s footprint as it is well-executed and complete; listen well to it.
"Brahmin!

It is as if a skilled elephant trainer, wandering in a secluded place, were to see the tracks of a great elephant among the trees and groves; having seen them, he would certainly believe that the elephant is immense, for such are its tracks."
"O Brahmin!
Even if that skilled elephant trainer is not a believer, there is another female elephant in this forest named Kaliṇī, who is extremely large in stature; those tracks belong to her."
He immediately followed this track and saw the footprint of a great elephant; having seen it, he was certain that the elephant must be immense to have such a footprint. "Brahmin!

That skilled elephant trainer may not yet believe it, for in this forest there is another female elephant named Karālī, whose body is exceedingly large and tall, and she is the one who made these tracks."
Following this track, he then saw the tracks of a great elephant; having seen them, he was certain that the elephant must be immense to leave such tracks.
"Brahmin!
That skilled elephant trainer may not yet believe it, for in this forest there is another female elephant named Bhadrā, whose body is exceedingly large and tall, and she left these tracks."
He then follows this track and again sees the tracks of a great elephant. Having seen them, he is certain that the elephant must be immense for such tracks to exist.

Following these tracks, he sees the tracks of a great elephant; the tracks of the great elephant are exceedingly long and wide, extending everywhere around, pressed deep into the ground. He also sees the elephant itself—whether it is going or coming, standing still or running, standing upright or lying down.
Having seen the elephant, he then reflects: "If there are such tracks, there must certainly be a great elephant."
“Brahmin! It is so.

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—appears in the world, he, in this world with its devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans to gods, knows for himself, awakens to it himself, and dwells having realized it through his own direct experience: ‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,’ knowing this as it truly is.”

He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, complete and pure, and clearly reveals the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
When householders or the sons of householders hear the Dharma he teaches, they gain faith. Having gained faith in the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and Discipline (*vinaya*), they then think:
"The household life is extremely narrow and a place of defilement; going forth to study the Path is open and vast."

"I am now at home, bound by fetters, and unable to practice the pure holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as life lasts. It would be better for me to renounce both small and great wealth, and to renounce both few and many kinsmen; having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, I shall go forth from the household life with deep faith to become a homeless seeker of the Way."

"At a later time, he renounces both small and great wealth, and renounces both few and many kinsmen; shaving off his hair and beard and donning the saffron robes, with deep faith he leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the Way."
Having gone forth, he abandoned the marks of kinship and received the essential precepts of a bhikṣu; he cultivated the prohibitive precepts and guarded the code of liberation.
Furthermore, he skillfully maintained dignified conduct and decorum; seeing even the slightest fault as a mote of dust, he was constantly filled with dread and upheld the training rules.

"He abstains from killing and has abandoned killing; he lays aside the sword and staff, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he benefits all beings, even down to the smallest insects; thus, regarding the taking of life, he purifies his mind."

He abstains from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, delights in giving, is always fond of generosity, rejoices without stinginess, and does not look for reward; thus, he purifies his mind regarding taking what is not given.

He abstains from unchaste conduct and abandons unchaste conduct; he diligently cultivates the holy life, exerts himself in sublime practice, remains pure and stainless, and being free from desire and having severed lust, he purifies his mind of unchaste conduct.

"He abstains from false speech and abandons false speech; he speaks the truth, delights in the truth, abides in the truth, and is unwavering; he is entirely trustworthy and does not deceive the world; thus, he purifies his mind regarding false speech."

He abstains from divisive speech and has severed divisive speech; he practices non-divisive speech, does not cause dissension among others, does not hear something here to report it there with the intent to divide those people, nor does he hear something there to report it here with the intent to divide these people. He seeks to reconcile those who are divided and delights in the harmony of those who are united. He does not form factions, does not take pleasure in factions, and does not praise the affairs of factions; thus, he purifies his mind regarding divisive speech.
He abstains from harsh speech and has abandoned harsh speech.

Whatever he says is free from words that are coarse, rough, offensive to the ear, unpleasant to the multitude, unloved by the multitude, which cause others distress and prevent them from attaining concentration; such speech he has abandoned.

Whatever he says is pure, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; it is pleasing to the ear and enters the heart, delightful and lovely, bringing peace and security to others. His speech is articulate and clear, not causing fear, and it enables others to attain concentration. Speaking in such a manner, he purifies his mind of harsh speech.

He abstains from frivolous speech and has abandoned frivolous speech; he speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks in accordance with the Dharma, speaks meaningfully, speaks for the sake of tranquility, and speaks delighting in tranquility. His words are appropriate to the occasion, and he is skilled in instructing and admonishing. Thus, he purifies his mind of frivolous speech.

"He abstains from trade, has abandoned trade, and has discarded scales and measures; he does not accept goods on commission, does not bind others in servitude, does not hope for a reduction in measures, and does not deceive others with small profits—he thus purifies his mind regarding trade."
He abstains from taking widows or maidens; he has severed the practice of taking widows or maidens.
He purifies his mind regarding the taking of widows or maidens.
He abstains from accepting male and female slaves and has renounced the acceptance of male and female slaves; he purifies his mind regarding the acceptance of male and female slaves.

He abstains from accepting elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep and has renounced the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; he purifies his mind regarding the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
He abstains from accepting chickens and pigs, he has renounced accepting chickens and pigs, and he purifies his mind regarding the acceptance of chickens and pigs.
He abstains from accepting fields and shops, he has renounced accepting fields and shops, and he purifies his mind regarding the acceptance of fields and shops.

He abstains from taking rice, wheat, and beans that have been cultivated for consumption; he has severed the practice of taking rice, wheat, and beans that have been cultivated for consumption; he purifies his mind regarding the taking of rice, wheat, and beans that have been cultivated for consumption.
“He abstains from intoxicants and has abandoned intoxicants; he purifies his mind regarding the drinking of intoxicants.
He abstains from high and wide beds and has abandoned high and wide beds; he purifies his mind regarding high and wide beds.”
He abstains from garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and unguents; he has renounced garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and unguents; he purifies his mind regarding garlands, necklaces, perfumes, and unguents.

He abstains from singing, dancing, and visiting performances; he has severed singing, dancing, and visiting performances, and he purifies his mind regarding singing, dancing, and visiting performances.
He abstains from the treasure of the physical form of rebirth, renounces the treasure of the physical form of rebirth, and purifies his mind regarding the treasure of the physical form of rebirth.

He abstains from eating at improper times, renounces eating at improper times, eats but one meal a day, does not eat at night, and observes the practice of eating only during the prescribed time; he purifies his mind regarding eating at improper times.

"Having already accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue, he further practices extreme contentment: taking only enough clothing to cover his body and food to fill his belly, wherever he travels, he is accompanied only by his robes and bowl; he moves without attachment or longing, just as a hawk flies through the air with its two wings."

Having already accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue (*śīlaskandha*) and being thoroughly contented, he further guards his sense faculties, constantly mindful of their closure; mindful of clarity and penetration, he achieves success by guarding his mindfulness and heart, always maintaining clear comprehension (*samprajanya*).
If the eye sees forms, yet one does not grasp at perceptions nor relish those forms—because of anger and contention—one guards the faculty of the eye.
Because no covetousness, anxiety, grief, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind directed toward them, one guards the faculty of the eye.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and when the mind cognizes mental objects (*dharma*), one does not grasp at perceptions nor relish those objects; rather, because of [the potential for] anger and contention, one guards the faculty of the mind (*manendriya*).
No covetousness, grief, or unwholesome, evil states arise in his mind; because he is intent upon that [state], he guards the faculty of the mind.

Having thus accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue, as well as perfect contentment and the guarding of the sense faculties, he further maintains clear comprehension in going out and coming in; he clearly discerns and reflects upon his movements—bending and stretching, looking down and looking up—and his deportment is composed and dignified. He is mindful and clearly comprehending whether wearing the saṃghāṭī robe and other robes or carrying the alms bowl; whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether sleeping or waking; whether speaking or remaining silent, he is in every case clearly comprehending.

Having already accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue, as well as being extremely contented, guarding the sense faculties, and possessing clear comprehension in going out and coming in, he further dwells alone in seclusion, in a place free from affairs—whether at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet spot, in a mountain cleft, a stone cave, or a heap of straw in the open air; or he goes to a forest grove, or stays among the tombs.

Having gone to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet, and peaceful spot, he spreads his sitting mat, sits down cross-legged, and with body erect and mind resolved, he turns his mindfulness inward and does not look outward. He abandons covetousness and harbors no contention in his heart. Seeing the wealth and various articles of daily life belonging to others, he does not give rise to covetousness, desiring to obtain them for himself; thus, he purifies his mind of covetousness.

"In this way, having abandoned ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and having cut off doubt and overcome delusion, one has no hesitation regarding wholesome qualities; thus, one purifies the mind of doubt."

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and being secluded from sensual desires and secluded from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness.
"Brahmin!
This is what the Tathāgata has mastered, this is what the Tathāgata practices, and this is what the Tathāgata has mastered.

Yet he does not consider this to be the end; for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has well-expounded the Dharma, and the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples has entered upon the good path."

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is inward tranquility and mental unification, free from applied and sustained thought, born of concentration, and characterized by joy and bliss.
"O Brahmin!
This is what the Tathāgata has mastered, this is what the Tathāgata practices, and this is what the Tathāgata has mastered.

Yet he does not consider this to be the end; for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent, and the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."

“With the fading away of joy and desire, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; he experiences happiness with the body, which the Noble Ones describe as ‘equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness. Thus he attains and abides in the third dhyāna.”
"Brahmin!
This is what the Tathāgata has mastered, this is what the Tathāgata practices, and this is what the Tathāgata has mastered.

Yet he does not consider this to be the end; for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent, and the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
"O Brahmin!
This is what the Tathāgata has mastered, this is what the Tathāgata practices, and this is what the Tathāgata has mastered.

Yet he does not consider this to be the end; for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent, and the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is well-directed."

“Having attained such a concentrated mind—purified, stainless, free from affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable—he proceeds toward the realization of the superknowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows.”
He knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are.
He knows these taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Brahmin!
This is what the Tathāgata has mastered, this is what the Tathāgata practices, and this is what the Tathāgata has internalized.
He considers this to be the end, World-Honored One."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is excellent; the noble Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is excellent.
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Is this parable of the elephant's footprint well-composed and complete?"
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī replied:
“Indeed it is so, Gautama!”
"In this way, the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint is well-expounded and complete.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī said:
"World-Honored One!"
I have understood,
Sugata! I have comprehended.
"Bhagavān!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the Bhagavān accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi and the heterodox ascetic Pāṭikāputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Elephant’s Footprint Simile*, the fifth [sūtra], ends here; it contains 2,988 characters. 147. *The Discourse on the Virtue of Hearing* (147), the sixth discourse in the *Brahmaṇa-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Janavasabha was wandering about in the afternoon when he went to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side and said:
“Gautama!...”
"I wish to ask a question; if you grant me leave, I shall venture to state it.
The World-Honored One replied, "Brāhmaṇa!"
"Ask whatever you wish.
Upon hearing this, the Brahmin Jāti asked:
"Among the disciples of the Śramaṇa Gautama, some remain at home while others leave home to study the Path. For what purpose do they extensively learn and recite the teachings?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"Brahmin! Among my disciples, there are some who remain at home and others who have left the household life to study the Path. They extensively learn and recite [the teachings] because they desire to discipline themselves, to bring themselves to rest, and to seek their own final cessation."
“Brahmin!
Whether my disciples are householders or have gone forth to study the Path, it is for this reason that they cultivate extensive learning through recitation.
The Brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
"Gautama! Is there a distinction between extensive learning and recitation?
Is there merit in extensive learning and recitation?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Brahmin, there is a distinction in extensive learning and recitation; indeed, extensive learning and recitation possess merit.
The Brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
"Gautama! What is the distinction, what is the merit, in extensive learning, recitation, and practice?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Brahmin! When a learned noble disciple works during the day desiring to obtain profit from it, if that work fails and is not accomplished, he does not become sorrowful, distressed, or weeping; he does not beat his breast in anguish, nor does he become delirious.
"Brāhmaṇa!

If a learned noble disciple performs work during the day desiring to gain profit from it, and that work he has performed fails and is not accomplished, then, having failed and not accomplished that work, he does not become sorrowful, distressed, or weeping; he does not beat his breast in anguish, nor does he become deluded or frantic. Brāhmaṇa!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has mastered the recitation [of the teachings],
and one who possesses these qualities. "Furthermore, brahmin,

when a well-learned noble disciple encounters whatever objects of affection he may have— which are now different, no longer present, no longer associated, and already separated from him— he does not grieve, lament, weep, beat his breast in distress, nor does he become delirious with madness."
"Brāhmaṇa!

If a learned noble disciple possesses affection for someone, yet that affection becomes otherwise, dissolves, no longer corresponds, and they have already parted from one another, and yet he does not become sorrowful or distressed, does not weep, does not beat his breast in anguish, nor does he become deluded or mad—Brāhmaṇa!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and one who merely recites and practices;
such is this merit. "Furthermore, brahmin, the well-learned noble disciple knows that all material wealth is impermanent, and thus he reflects upon leaving the household life to study the Path."
"Brahmin!
If a learned noble disciple knows that all material wealth is impermanent and reflects upon leaving the household life to study the Path, Brahmin!
This is what is meant by the distinction between one who has heard much and recited the teachings, and it possesses this merit."
Furthermore, brahmin,

having realized that all wealth and possessions are impermanent, the learned noble disciple shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the path.

Brahmin, when a learned noble disciple, having understood that all wealth and possessions are entirely impermanent, shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the Path—Brahmin!
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has mastered the recitation [of the teachings], and it possesses these virtues.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas; he can also endure being oppressed by wind and sun, as well as harsh words and the striking of sticks. When his body encounters various illnesses that are extremely painful, even to the point where life is about to cease, he is able to withstand all that is unpleasant."
"Brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and fleas; if he can endure being oppressed by wind and sun, as well as harsh words and the striking of sticks; and if, when his body encounters various illnesses that cause extreme pain until life itself is about to cease, he is able to withstand all that is unpleasant—then, Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between extensive learning through recitation and practice; such is this merit.
"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple is able to endure dissatisfaction; once dissatisfaction has arisen, his mind never becomes attached to it."
"Brāhmaṇa!

If a learned noble disciple is able to endure displeasure, and once displeasure has arisen, his mind never becomes attached to it—Brāhmaṇa, this is called the distinction in extensive learning and recitation; this is its merit."
"Furthermore, brahmin!
A well-learned noble disciple is able to endure fear; once fear has arisen, his mind never becomes attached to it.
Brahmin!"

“Brahmin, if a well-learned noble disciple is able to endure fear, and having experienced fear, his mind never becomes attached to it—this, Brahmin, is called the distinction of extensive learning and recitation; this is its merit.”
"Furthermore, brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple gives rise to the three unwholesome and evil thoughts—thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty—even after these three unwholesome and evil thoughts have arisen, his mind ultimately does not become attached to them."
"Brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple should give rise to the three unwholesome and evil thoughts—thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty—and yet, having given rise to these three unwholesome and evil thoughts, his mind never becomes attached to them, then, Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has mastered the recitation [of the teachings],
and one who possesses these qualities. "Furthermore, brahmin,
a well-learned noble disciple, having departed from sensual desires and departed from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna."
"Brahmin!
If a learned noble disciple, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna—Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has mastered the recitation [of the teachings], and one who possesses this merit.

"Furthermore, brahmin, the well-learned noble disciple, having exhausted the three fetters, attains stream-entry; he is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms and is destined for full awakening. Having undergone at most seven more existences—seven rounds of coming and going between the heavens and the human world—he shall then reach the end of suffering."
"Brāhmaṇa!

If a learned noble disciple has exhausted the three fetters and attained the stage of stream-entry (srotāpanna), not falling into states of woe and certain of proceeding toward perfect awakening, experiencing at most seven more existences—having gone back and forth seven times between the heavens and the human realm—he shall then reach the end of suffering. Brāhmaṇa!"
This is called being extensively learned and having practiced recitation with distinction; such is this merit.

"Furthermore, brahmin, when a well-learned noble disciple has exhausted the three fetters and has attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, he attains the state of 'once-returner. Having returned once more to the realms of gods and humans, he then reaches the end of suffering."
"Brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple has exhausted the three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, such that they attain the state of 'once-returning'—having returned once more to the heavens and the human realm, they shall then reach the end of suffering. Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between one who has heard much and practiced recitation and one who possesses these qualities.

"Furthermore, brahmin, when a well-heard noble disciple has exhausted the five lower fetters, having been born in that realm, he attains parinirvāṇa there; he attains the state of non-retrogression and does not return to this world."
"Brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple has exhausted the five lower fetters, having been reborn in that realm, they attain parinirvāṇa right there, attaining the state of non-retrogression and not returning to this world. Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has practiced recitation, and one who possesses this merit.

"Furthermore, brahmin, a well-learned noble disciple attains the liberation of cessation; having transcended form, he enters and dwells in the formless attainments as they truly are, realizing them with his own body and accomplishing them through practice. Through the observation of wisdom, he abandons the taints and knows the taints."
"Brahmin!

If a learned noble disciple possesses the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling, attains the formless attainments as they truly are, dwells having personally realized them through the body, and through the observation of wisdom cuts off the taints and knows the taints—Brahmin!"
This is called the distinction between one who is widely learned and has practiced recitation; such is this merit.

"Furthermore, brahmin, the well-learned noble disciple possesses the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhipāda*), the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of birth and death. With all taints exhausted, he attains the taintless state, achieving liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, he knows and realizes for himself, having personally witnessed and accomplished his goal, dwelling in the realization: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is."
"Brāhmaṇa!

If a learned noble disciple possesses the power of the bases of psychic potency, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of past lives, and knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings; if his taints are exhausted, he has attained the taintless state, and through liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he dwells having realized for himself in this very life, having directly known and awakened to it, having achieved his own realization: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,' knowing this as it truly is—then, Brāhmaṇa!"
"This is what is called the distinction and the merit found in extensive learning, recitation, and practice.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī again asked the Blessed One:

"Regarding this extensive learning, recitation, and practice that possesses such distinctions and such merit, is there perhaps another distinction, another merit that is more supreme, more sublime, and more excellent?"
The Blessed One replied: “Brahmin!

This extensive learning and recitation has its distinctions and its merits, but there is nothing further distinguished, nothing further meritorious, that is most supreme, most sublime, and most excellent.”
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said:
“World-Honored One!
I have understood.”
“Sugata! I have understood.
World-Honored One!”

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth discourse, the *Sutasoma Sutta*, ends here; it consists of one thousand six hundred and nine characters. 148. The Discourse on What is Suffering (*Kiṃdukkha Sutta*), the seventh in the Brahmin Chapter of the Madhyama Āgama, the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa was wandering about in the afternoon when he went to where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side and said: “Gautama!
"I wish to ask a question; if you grant me leave, I shall venture to state it.
The World-Honored One replied, "Brahmin!"
"Ask whatever you wish.
Upon hearing this, the brahmin Jāti asked:
"Gautama!..."
"What are the sufferings of those who live as householders?
And what are the sufferings of those who have gone forth to study the Path?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Brahmin! For one living at home, lack of autonomy is suffering; for one who has gone forth to study the Path, autonomy is suffering.
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
“Gautama! For one living at home, why is lack of mastery considered suffering?
And for one who has left the home life to study the Way, why is mastery considered suffering?”
The World-Honored One replied: “Brahmin!

If one who lives at home finds that their money does not increase, and their gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, and crystal do not increase; and if their livestock, grain, and male and female servants and laborers also do not increase—at such a time, the householder experiences sorrow, suffering, grief, and distress.”
For this reason, those who live as householders have much sorrow and suffering, and harbor much grief and lamentation.
O Brahmin!

If one who has left the home life to study the Way acts according to desire, or acts according to hatred and delusion, then that one who has left the home life to study the Way experiences sorrow, suffering, grief, and lamentation.
For this reason, those who have left the household life to study the Way often experience much sorrow and suffering, and harbor much grief and distress.
O Brahmin!
Thus, for one living at home, lack of autonomy is suffering; for one who has left the household life to study the Way, autonomy is suffering.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked again:
“Gautama, what is the pleasure for one who lives at home?”
"What joy is there for one who has gone forth to study the Way?
The World-Honored One replied, "Brahmin!"
"The householder finds joy in autonomy, while the one who has gone forth to study the Way finds joy in non-autonomy.
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again: "Gautama!"
“Householders, in what way do they find pleasure in autonomy?
And those who have left the home life to study the Path, in what way do they find pleasure in non-autonomy?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Brahmin! If a householder’s money increases, and his gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, and crystal all increase; if his livestock, grain, and male and female slaves and servants also increase—at that time, the householder is happy and joyful.”
For this reason, those who live as householders have much happiness and joy.
O Brahmin!

When those who have gone forth to study the Way act without following desire, and act without following hatred or delusion, at that time, those who have gone forth to study the Way possess happiness and joy.
For this reason, those who have left the household life to study the Path possess much happiness and joy.
O Brahmin!
Thus, while those living at home take sovereignty as their pleasure, those who have left the household life to study the Path take non-sovereignty as their pleasure.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked again:
“Gotama, for what reason do gods and humans certainly lack benefit and meaning?”
"For what reason will it bring certain benefit and meaning to gods and humans?
The World-Honored One replied, "Brahmin!"

"If gods and humans contend with one another, there will certainly be no benefit or righteous purpose; if gods and humans do not contend with one another, there will certainly be benefit and righteous purpose.
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again: "Gautama!"
"How is it that when devas and humans contend with one another, there is necessarily no benefit or righteous purpose?
And how is it that when devas and humans do not contend, there is necessarily benefit and righteous purpose?
The Blessed One replied:

“Brahmin! When gods and humans engage in strife, contention, and mutual hatred, at that time the gods and humans are afflicted by sorrow, suffering, and grief. It is because of this that gods and humans experience much sorrow and suffering, and harbor much grief.”
"O Brahmin!

When gods and humans do not quarrel and do not harbor enmity or hatred, at that time gods and humans are joyful and delighted; for this reason, gods and humans experience much happiness and much delight."
“Brahmin!

Thus, when gods and humans contend with one another, there will certainly be no benefit or righteous purpose; when gods and humans do not contend, there will certainly be benefit and righteous purpose.
The Brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
"Gautama! For what reason do gods and humans inevitably fail to obtain benefit and inevitably encounter suffering?
For what reason do gods and humans inevitably obtain benefit and inevitably encounter happiness?"
The Blessed One replied: "Brahmin!
If gods and humans practice what is contrary to the Dharma and perform evil deeds, they will certainly not obtain benefit, but will certainly encounter suffering."
"If gods and humans can practice in accordance with the Dharma and do not commit evil, they will certainly obtain benefit and certainly attain happiness.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked again: "Gautama!"
How is it that gods and humans who practice what is contrary to the Dharma and commit evil will certainly gain no benefit and will certainly encounter suffering?
How is it that gods and humans who practice in accordance with the Dharma and do not commit evil will certainly obtain great benefit and will certainly attain happiness?
The Blessed One replied: "Brahmin!

When gods and humans practice unrighteousness and evil through their bodily actions, and practice unrighteousness and evil through their speech and mental actions, at that time, gods and humans will surely decline, while the asuras will surely flourish."
"O Brahmin!

If gods and humans act in accordance with the Dharma through their bodily conduct and guard their bodies, and act in accordance with the Dharma through their verbal and mental conduct and guard their speech and minds, then at that time, gods and humans will surely flourish, while the asuras will surely decline."
"Brahmin!
Thus, those gods and humans who practice what is contrary to the Dharma and commit evil will certainly obtain no benefit and will certainly encounter suffering.
Brahmin!"
"In this way, those gods and humans who act in accordance with the Dharma and do not commit evil will certainly obtain benefit and certainly attain happiness.
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
"Gautama!..."
"How does one contemplate an evil friend?
The World-Honored One replied: "Brahmin!"
"One should contemplate an evil friend as being like the moon.
When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked again:
"Gotama!..."
"How, then, should one contemplate an evil friend as being like the moon?
The World-Honored One replied, "Brahmin!"
Just as the moon at its waning diminishes day by day, so too do his palaces diminish, his radiance diminish, and his form and color diminish, vanishing away day after day.
"O brāhmaṇa!
There is a time when the moon even reaches its waning until it is no longer seen at all.
O brāhmaṇa!"

An evil companion may also gain faith in the True Dharma and Discipline of the Tathāgata; yet once they have gained that faith, at a later time they become neither filial nor respectful, their conduct becomes contrary, they do not establish right knowledge, and they do not incline toward the Dhamma and the sequence of the Dhamma. Consequently, they lose their faith, and they likewise lose their virtue, learning, aspiration, and wisdom.
"O brāhmaṇa!
There are times when this evil friend teaches the destruction of wholesome dharmas, just like the waning of the moon.
O brāhmaṇa!"
"In this way, one should regard an evil friend as being like the moon.
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked again:
"Gotama!..."
“How does one contemplate a spiritual friend?
The Blessed One replied, “Brahmin!”
"One should regard a spiritual friend as being like the moon.
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa asked again:
"Gautama!..."
"How, then, should one contemplate a spiritual friend as being like the moon?
The World-Honored One replied: "Brahmin!"
It is just as when the moon first appears, young, bright, and pure, increasing day by day.
O Brahmin!
At times, on the fifteenth day, its orb becomes full.
"Brāhmaṇa!

In this way, a good spiritual friend gains faith in the True Dharma and Discipline of the Tathāgata. Having gained that faith, they subsequently become filial and respectful, acting in accordance with it, establishing themselves in right knowledge, and progressing toward the Dhamma that follows the Dhamma. Their faith increases, and their virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom likewise increase."
"Brāhmaṇa!
There are times when that spiritual friend is fully endowed with wholesome qualities, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
Brāhmaṇa!"
"In this way, one should contemplate a spiritual friend as being like the moon.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as the moon, free from defilement, Traverses the realm of space,"
Just as all the stars in the world are eclipsed by their radiance,
so too is faith in extensive learning likely to be free from stinginess and greed;
for all the stinginess of the world eclipses the radiance of generosity.
Just as there is a great dragon that raises clouds, thunder, and lightning,
and lets fall rain most profusely, filling all the earth; so too,
one who has faith and extensive learning, may perhaps be free from stinginess and greed.
Abundant food and drink are given; joyfully one is urged to increase and expand such giving.
Like the most intense peals of thunder, like the falling rain from heaven, so vast is that rain of merit, showered by the donor.
"With abundant wealth and great renown, one will be born in a favorable realm;
such a person shall enjoy blessings, and after death, be reborn in the heavens.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh discourse, *The Discourse on Suffering*, ends here, totaling one thousand four hundred and twenty-five characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume Thirty-six, ending with nine thousand one hundred and sixty-five characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume Thirty-seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kaśmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Sūtra 149: On What One Desires (Brahmacarya-varga, Sūtra 8, Third Recitation) Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Janavasabha was wandering about after the midday meal when he went to where the Buddha was staying. Having exchanged greetings with him, he sat down to one side and said:
“Gautama!...”
"I wish to ask something; if you grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth.
The World-Honored One replied, "Ask whatever you wish."
The brahmin then asked: “Gautama!
What does a kṣatriya desire, what does he practice, what does he establish himself upon, what does he rely upon, and what is his end?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"A kṣatriya seeks to obtain wealth and property; he practices wisdom, establishes himself by means of the sword, relies upon the people, and finds his fulfillment in sovereignty."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked: “Gautama,
what does the householder desire, what does he practice, what does he establish, what does he rely upon, and in what does he find his conclusion?”
The Blessed One replied:
“A householder, desiring to acquire wealth, practices wisdom, establishes himself in technical skills, and relies upon manual labor; he considers his work finished only when that labor is completed.”
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked:
“Gotama, what does a woman desire, what does she practice, what does she establish, what does she rely upon, and what is her end?”
The Blessed One replied:
"A woman desires a man; she practices adornment, establishes herself through her sons, relies on being peerless, and finds her fulfillment in sovereignty."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked:
“Gautama, what does theft desire, what is its practice, what is its foundation, what is its support, and what is its cessation?”
The Blessed One replied:
"A thief is one who intends to take what is not given, goes to a hidden place, stands there with a weapon, relies upon darkness, and completes the act by means of invisibility."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇī asked: "Gautama!
What does a brahmin desire, what does he practice, what does he establish, what does he rely upon, and what is his culmination?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"A brahmin seeks to obtain wealth, practices wisdom, establishes himself through the scriptures, and relies upon fasting and precepts, taking the Brahma Heaven as his ultimate goal."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi asked:
"Gotama! What does the ascetic desire, what does he practice, what does he establish, what does he rely upon, and what is his culmination?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"A śramaṇa desires to attain the ultimate truth, practices wisdom, establishes himself in the precepts, relies on non-abiding, and takes nirvāṇa as his final goal."
The brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said:
“World-Honored One!
I have understood.”
"Sugata! I have understood.
World-Honored One!"

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The eighth discourse, the *Kāmavagga*, ends here, totaling four hundred and twenty-two characters. 150. The Discourse to Uggāhamāna (150) The Middle Length Discourses, Chapter on Brahmins, The Discourse to Uggāhamāna, the Ninth; Third Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Sanctuary.

At that time, the brahmin Usūyārañña was wandering about after his midday meal when he approached the place where the Buddha was. They exchanged greetings, and having sat down to one side, he said to him:
“Gotama!...”
"I wish to ask something; if you will grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth.
The World-Honored One replied, "Ask whatever you wish."
The brahmin Ussoṇḍī then asked: "Gautama!

For the four castes, the brahmins have established four types of service: they have established service for the brahmins, and they have established service for the kshatriyas, the householders, and the artisans."
"Gautama!
A brahmin establishes the service due to a brahmin; a brahmin should serve a brahmin, and kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans should also serve a brahmin."
"Gotama! These four castes should serve the brahmins. Gotama!"
The brahmins establish the service for the kṣatriyas; the kṣatriyas should serve the kṣatriyas, and the householders and artisans should also serve the kṣatriyas.
"Gautama!
These three castes should serve the kṣatriya.
Gautama!"
"Brahmins establish services for householders; householders should serve householders, and craftsmen should also serve householders, Gautama!"
"These two castes, O Gautama, should serve the householder.
A brahmin provides service for the artisan; the artisan should serve the artisan. Who else is so lowly as to provide service for the artisan? Only the artisan serves the artisan."
The Blessed One asked:

"Brahmin! Do the brahmins themselves know that they have established four types of service for the four castes—service established for the brahmins, and service established for the kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans?"
The brahmin Ussoṇaka replied:
"I do not know, Gautama."

However, these brahmins themselves make this claim: "In this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation of recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods—the brahmin does not know himself as one who establishes four types of service for the four castes; he establishes service only for the brahmin, and establishes service for the kṣatriya, the householder, and the artisan."
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin! It is just as if someone were to forcibly give meat to another and say this:"
"A man may eat, but he must pay me the price.
Brahmin! Your preaching to the other brahmins is just like this.

Why is this so? Because the brahmin does not know that he has established four types of service for the four castes: he establishes service for the brahmin, and he establishes service for the kṣatriya, the householder, and the artisan.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Brahmin! How do you serve?"
If there is service, and because of that service one remains as they were without becoming superior, is this true service?
If there is service, and because of that service one becomes superior and no longer remains as they were, is this true service?
"Brahmin! If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service there is only equality and no superiority, is that true service?
If one serves a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, and because of that service there is only equality and no superiority, is that true service?"
"Brahmin! If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service there is one who excels and none who is equal, is that true service?
If one serves a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, and because of that service there is one who excels and none who is equal, is that true service?"
The brahmin Ussoṅgala replied: “Gautama!
If, by serving someone, there were only what is equal and no excellence, I should not serve them.”
"If, by serving someone, one becomes superior through that service rather than remaining as one was before, I should serve them.
Gautama! If, by serving a brahmin, one remains as they were through that service rather than becoming superior, I should not serve them."
"O Gotama, if in serving kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, there is only equality and no superiority resulting from that service, I should not serve them."
If, by serving a brahmin, one becomes superior through that service and no longer remains equal, I should serve him.
If, by serving a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, one becomes superior through that service and no longer remains equal, I should serve him.
The Blessed One said:

“Brahmin! If another brahmin were to come who is neither foolish nor deluded, who is not inverted and whose mind is free from inversion, being independent and self-possessed, I would ask that brahmin:”
"What do you think?
If there is service, and because of that service one remains as they are without excelling, is that true service?
Or if there is service, and because of that service one excels and does not remain as they are, is that true service?"
"Brahmin! If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service there is equality but no superiority, is that true service?
If one serves a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, and because of that service there is equality but no superiority, is that true service?"
"Brahmin! If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service there is one who excels and none who is equal, is that true service?
If one serves a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, and because of that service there is one who excels and none who is equal, is that true service?"
“O Brahmin! That Brahmin was neither foolish nor deluded, nor was he perverted; his mind was free from perversion, and being self-possessed and autonomous, he replied to me:
‘Gautama!’”
If, by serving someone, as a result of that service, there is equality but no superiority, I should not serve them.
If, by serving someone, as a result of that service, there is superiority but no equality, I should serve them.
"Gautama!
If, by serving a brahmin, there were only equality and no superiority resulting from that service, I would not serve him.
If, by serving a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, there were only equality and no superiority resulting from that service, I would not serve them."
"Gautama!
If there are brahmins whom I should serve, and because of serving them I would become superior and not inferior, then I should serve them.
If there are kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen whom I should serve, and because of serving them I would become superior and not inferior, then I should serve them."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"
If, by means of such service, one loses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom, can that be considered true service?
If there is service, and because of that service one increases in faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom—is this considered true service?
"Brahmin!
If, by serving a brahmin, one loses faith, precepts, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, would that be considered true service?"
If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, and because of that service loses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, noble aspiration, and wisdom—is that truly considered service?
"Brahmin!
If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service, one’s faith, precepts, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom increase—is this truly 'serving'?"

When one serves a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, and through that service increases one's faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom—is this truly considered "service"?
The brahmin Ujjaya replied: "Gautama!
If, by serving someone, one's faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom would decline because of that service, I should not serve them."
If, by serving someone, my faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom increase as a result of that service, then I should serve them.
"Gautama!
If, by serving a brahmin, one loses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, I should not serve him."
If, by serving kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, one loses faith, virtue, learning, aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, I should not serve them.
"Gautama!
If by serving a brahmin, through that service, one increases in faith, precepts, learning, aspiration, and wisdom, then I should serve him."
If, by serving a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, one increases in faith, virtue, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom because of that service, I should serve them.
The World-Honored One said:

"Brahmin! If another brahmin were to come who is neither foolish nor deluded, who is not inverted and whose mind is free from inversion, being autonomous and self-possessed—I would ask that brahmin: "
"What do you think?
If there is service such that, because of that service, one loses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom—is that truly service?"
If there is service, and because of that service one increases in faith, precepts, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom—is that considered true service?
"Brahmin!
If, by serving a brahmin, one loses faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, noble aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, is that true service?"
If one serves kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, and because of that service loses faith, virtue, learning, aspiration, and wisdom—is this truly called service?
"Brahmin!
If one serves a brahmin, and because of that service, one’s faith, precepts, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom increase—is this true service?"
When one serves kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, if through that service one increases in faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom—is this considered true service?
"O Brahmin! That Brahmin was neither foolish nor deluded, nor was he inverted; his mind was free from inversion, and being autonomous and at ease, he answered me in this way:
'Gautama!'"
If, by serving him, I were to lose my faith, virtue, learning, aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, then I should not serve him.
If, by attending upon someone, my faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom increase as a result of that service, I should attend upon them.
"Gautama!
If, by serving a brahmin, one loses faith, virtue, learning, aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, I should not serve him."
If, by serving kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, one loses faith, virtuous conduct, extensive learning, noble aspiration, and wisdom because of that service, I should not serve them.
"Gautama!
If by serving a brahmin, through that service, one increases in faith, precepts, extensive learning, aspiration, and wisdom, then I should serve him."
If, by serving a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman, one’s faith, ethical discipline, extensive learning, generosity, and wisdom increase because of that service, I should serve them.
The brahmin Ussoṇḍī addressed him, saying: “Gautama!

For the four castes, a brahmin establishes four kinds of personal property; he establishes personal property for the brahmins, and he establishes personal property for the kṣatriyas, the householders, and the artisans.”
"Gautama! When a brahmin establishes for himself the possession of his own wealth as a brahmin, Gautama!

A brahmin establishes for himself the possession of his own wealth through begging. If a brahmin treats begging with contempt, he then treats his own wealth with contempt; having treated his own wealth with contempt, he then suffers loss."
"Just as a cowherd who cannot look after his cattle will suffer loss, so it is, Gautama!

When a brahmin provides for himself by means of begging for his own property, if that brahmin treats those whom he begs from with contempt, he treats his own property with contempt; and having treated his own property with contempt, he suffers loss."
“Gautama! When a brahmin designates weapons and arrows as his own property for a kṣatriya, Gautama!
If that kṣatriya treats those weapons and arrows with contempt, he is treating his own property with contempt; having treated his own property with contempt, he then suffers loss.”
"Just as a cowherd who cannot look after his cattle will suffer loss, so it is, Gautama!

A brahmin provides a kṣatriya with bows and arrows as his own property; if the kṣatriya treats those bows and arrows with contempt, he treats his own property with contempt, and having treated his own property with contempt, he suffers loss."
"Gautama! When a brahmin provides for a householder by means of his own property, Gautama!

when a brahmin provides for a householder through agricultural work as his own property, if the householder treats that agricultural work with contempt, he then treats his own property with contempt; having treated his own property with contempt, he then suffers loss."
"Just as a cowherd who cannot look after his cattle will suffer loss, so it is, Gautama!

When a brahmin provides a householder with the means for farming and his own wealth, if that householder treats the farming with contempt, he treats his own wealth with contempt; having treated his own wealth with contempt, he then suffers loss."
"Gautama! When a brahmin craftsman prepares his own materials, Gautama!

when a brahmin craftsman prepares sesame as his own material, if that craftsman treats the sesame with contempt, he then treats his own materials with contempt; having treated his own materials with contempt, he then suffers loss."
"Just as a cowherd who cannot look after his cattle will suffer loss, so it is, Gautama!

When a brahmin craftsman prepares oil-seeds as his own property, if he treats those seeds with contempt, he treats his own property with contempt; having treated his own property with contempt, he suffers loss."
The Blessed One asked:

"Brahmin! Do the brahmins themselves know that they have established four kinds of property for the four castes—property established for the brahmins, and property established for the kṣatriyas, the householders, and the artisans?"
The brahmin Ussoṇḍī replied:
“I do not know, Gautama.”

However, the brahmins themselves declare: "In this world, among gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans up to the gods, I do not know of anyone who establishes four kinds of personal property for the four castes, but rather establishes personal property for the brahmins, and establishes personal property for the kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans."
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin! It is just as if someone were to forcibly give meat to another and say this:"
"A man may eat, provided he receives his wages.
O Brahmin! Your teaching to the other brahmins is also just like this.

Why is that? Because the brahmin does not know that he has established four kinds of personal property for the four castes: he has established personal property for the brahmin, and he has established personal property for the kṣatriya, the householder, and the artisan.
In this way, brahmin!

Having well understood and well known all phenomena for myself, I establish for others the dharma of cessation, the dharma of final extinction, the dharma of the path to awakening, and the dharma of the happy realms; I establish them as their own property.
The Blessed One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"
Is it not the case that there are brahmins who, in this empty space, are unattached, unbound, untouched, and unimpeded, while kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans are not so?
The brahmin Ussoṇḍī replied: “Gautama!
Just as a brahmin is not attached to, bound by, touched by, or obstructed by this space, so it is with a kshatriya, a householder, and a craftsman.”

“Brahmin! I myself have well understood and well known all phenomena; for the sake of others, I have established the teaching of cessation, the teaching of final extinction, the teaching of the path to awakening, and the teaching of the happy realms, as well as the teaching of one’s own possessions.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"

Is it possible that there are brahmins who are able to practice a mind of loving-kindness—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—while this is not the case for kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen?
The brahmin Ussoṇaka replied: “Gautama!
A brahmin can practice a mind of loving-kindness—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—and the same is true for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans.”

“Brahmin! I myself have well understood and well known all phenomena; for the sake of others, I have established the dharma of cessation, the dharma of final extinction, the dharma of the path to awakening, and the dharma of the happy realms, as well as the establishment of one’s own possessions.”
The World-Honored One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"
Suppose a hundred people were to come, and one among them were to say to them:
"Come all together!
If there are any born into the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste, only they can take bathing powder to the water and bathe, thereby removing impurities and becoming utterly pure."
"O Brahmin! What do you think?
Would those of the Kṣatriya caste or the Brahmin caste, by taking bath-powder to the water and bathing, be able to remove their impurities and become utterly pure?"
Is it that those belonging to the class of householders or the class of artisans are unable to take soap powder to the water to bathe and remove impurities for the sake of extreme purity?
Or is it that all people of the hundredfold classes are able to take soap powder to the water to bathe and remove impurities for the sake of extreme purity?
The brahmin Ussoṇḍī replied: “Gautama!
All those hundred kinds of people are able to take soap powder to the water to bathe, removing impurities until they are utterly pure.”
“Thus it is, brahmin!

Having myself well understood and well known all phenomena, I establish for others the teaching of cessation, the teaching of final extinction, the teaching of the path to awakening, and the teaching of the happy realms; I establish the possession of one's own wealth.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"
Suppose a hundred people were to come, and one among them were to say to them:
"Come all together!
Only those born of the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste are able to use extremely dry sāla or candana wood as fire-kindlers and, by drilling with a fire-drill, produce and nurture fire."
"Brahmin! What do you think?
Can those of the Kṣatriya caste or the Brahmin caste take extremely dry sāla or sandalwood as the fire-drill base and, by drilling with a fire-stick, produce and nurture a fire?"

If one belongs to the class of householders or the class of artisans, would they produce fire and nurture it by using a dry pigsty or dog trough, or *eranda* wood, or other inferior timber as the fire-drill base, and then drilling with a fire-stick?
"Could all these hundred kinds of people take various types of wood as fire-sticks and, by drilling them,
produce and nurture a fire? The brahmin Ujjaya replied, "Gautama!"
"All those hundred kinds of people are able to use various types of wood as fire-drills; by boring with them, they produce fire and nurture it. "It is so."
"Brahmin!

Having myself well understood and well known all phenomena, I establish for others the dharma of cessation, the dharma of final extinction, the dharma of the path to awakening, and the dharma of the happy realms; I establish them as my own possessions."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"

If those hundred people were all to use various kinds of wood as fire-drills and produce fire by drilling them, nurturing it until it grows, would all those fires have flames, color, heat, and light, and would they all be able to perform the functions of fire? Or is it that only one of those fires has flames, color, heat, and light, and is able to perform the functions of fire?
Is it that this particular fire alone has no flame, no color, no heat, and no light, and thus cannot perform the functions of fire?
Or is it that all fires possess flames, color, heat, and light, and are all capable of performing the functions of fire?
The brahmin Ujjaya replied: "Gautama!

If a hundred kinds of people were all to take various types of wood as fire-drills and, by drilling them, produce and nurture fire, all those fires would possess flames, color, heat, and light, and all would be capable of performing the functions of fire."
If that fire were to exist alone, possessing only flame, color, heat, and light, yet still be able to perform the functions of fire, such a thing is impossible.
If that fire were to exist alone, lacking flame, color, heat, and light, and thus unable to perform the functions of fire, such a thing is likewise impossible.
"But, Gautama!
All those fires possess flames, have color, have heat, and have light; all are capable of performing the functions of fire. "It is so."
"Brāhmaṇa!

Having well understood and well known all phenomena for myself, I establish for others the dharma of cessation, the dharma of final extinction, the dharma of the path to awakening, and the dharma of happy rebirths; I establish [the teaching of] one's own possessions."
The World-Honored One asked:
"Brahmin, what do you think?"

Suppose those hundred people all take various kinds of wood as fire-drills and produce fire by drilling them, nurturing that fire. If someone were to place dry grass and wood into that fire, it would produce flames, color, heat, and smoke. Would there be any distinction among those flames, colors, heats, and smokes? Or would the flames, colors, heats, and smokes differ from one another?
The brahmin Ussoḍhaka replied: "Gautama!

Suppose those hundred kinds of people all use various types of wood as fire-drills and, by boring with them, produce and nurture fire. If someone were to place dry grass and wood into that fire, it would produce flames, color, heat, and smoke. Regarding those flames, color, heat, and smoke, I cannot designate any distinction between one flame, color, heat, and smoke and another flame, color, heat, and smoke."
The Blessed One said: "Brahmin!

Such is the fire I have attained, such is the fire of non-negligence that can extinguish negligence and arrogance. Regarding this fire, even fire itself cannot be said to possess any distinction from it."
The brahmin Ussoḍhaka replied:
“World-Honored One,
I have understood.”
"Sugata! I have understood.
World-Honored One!"

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Usūyāla rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The ninth discourse, the *Usūyāla Sutta*, ends here, totaling three thousand five hundred and eighty-five characters. 151. The *Assalāyana Sutta* (151), the tenth discourse in the *Brahmaṇa-vagga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of brahmins were gathered in a schoolhouse in Kosala, discussing this matter together:
“The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.”
"The Brahmin caste is white, while all others are black;
the Brahmin attains purity, whereas the non-Brahmin does not attain purity;
the Brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā himself. Yet the ascetic Gautama proclaims that all four castes are equally pure, establishing and demonstrating this."
He thought to himself:
"Venerable sirs!
Who has the power to go to the presence of the ascetic Gautama and, regarding this matter, challenge him with questions in accordance with the Dharma?"
He further thought: "The Māṇava Acelakālāyana is of noble parentage and pure birth;

his lineage of parents extends back through seven generations without interruption, and he has been free from evil throughout his lives. He is widely learned and possesses a retentive memory, having mastered the four Vedas and deeply penetrated the five modes of exposition: cause, condition, rightness, phrasing, and stylistic embellishment."
"The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta has the power and ability to go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama and to challenge him with this matter according to the Dharma.
O virtuous ones!"
"Let us go together to the brahmin Āḷāra Kālāma and speak this matter to him; we shall accept whatever the brahmin Āḷāra Kālāma says."
Thereupon, many brahmins of Kosala went to where the young brahmin Aṭṭhaka Āḷavaka was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:
"Young brahmin!..."
"Many of us brahmins have gathered here in the Kosalas at the debating hall and discussed this matter together:
'The brahmin caste is superior, while others are not;
the brahmin caste is pure, while others are all dark.'"
"Brahmins attain purity, while non-Brahmins do not attain purity;

Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā and fashioned by Brahmā. Yet the śramaṇa Gautama proclaims that all four castes are entirely pure, establishing and demonstrating this."
We thought to ourselves:
"Venerable sirs!
Who has the power to go to the presence of the ascetic Gautama and thus challenge him with this matter according to the Dharma?"

We further thought to ourselves: "The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta was raised by his parents and his birth was pure; even through seven generations of ancestors, his lineage remained unbroken. In every life he has been free from evil, widely learned, and possessed of a retentive memory. He has recited the four Vedas and has deeply mastered the five types of exposition: those concerning causes, conditions, correctness, phrasing, and wordplay."
The Māṇava Acela-Roññāyana has the power to go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama and, regarding this matter, challenge him with questions in accordance with the Dhamma.
I wish that the Māṇava Acela-Roññāyana would go to the presence of the ascetic Gotama and, regarding this matter, challenge him with questions in accordance with the Dhamma.
The Mānaṣaka Acela-Rāmadatta said to the brahmins:
"Venerable sirs!
The ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; and one who teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma cannot be challenged or censured."
The many brahmins of Kosala said, "Māṇava!
You have not yet been defeated; you must not submit prematurely."

Why is this so? Because the Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta was raised by his parents and born in purity; his lineage of ancestors has remained unbroken for seven generations, and throughout those births he has been free from evil. He is widely learned and possesses total retention (*dhāraṇī*); he has recited the four Vedas and has deeply mastered the five modes of exposition: cause, condition, rightness, phrasing, and etymological play.
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta has the power and ability to go to the presence of the ascetic Gautama and to challenge him on this matter according to the Dharma.
I wish that the Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta would go to the presence of the ascetic Gautama and challenge him on this matter according to the Dharma.
The young brahmin Aṭṭhaka, son of Rohaṇa, accepted the proposal of the many brahmins of Kosala in silence.

Thereupon, the young brahmin Aṭṭhaka, son of Rohaṇa, together with those many brahmins of Kosala, went to where the Buddha was staying. Having exchanged greetings with him, they sat down to one side and said:
“Gotama, [we have come].”
"I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
The World-Honored One replied, "Māṇava!"
"Ask whatever you wish.
Then Assalāyana asked: "Gotama!..."
The various brahmins speak thus:
"The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is white; all others are black."
The brahmin attains purity; the non-brahmin does not attain purity.
The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, and is Brahmā himself.
“I do not yet know how the śramaṇa Gautama will explain this.
The World-Honored One said:
“I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"Mañjuśrī!
Have you heard that in the countries of Vṛji and Kāśī there are two castes—the masters and the slaves—and that masters become slaves and slaves become masters?"
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta replied: “Gautama!
I have heard that in the countries of Ujjenī and Kaṃpilla there are two castes, the masters and the slaves; there, masters become slaves and slaves become masters.”
“Thus it is, Māṇava!
