If a brahmin is one who has set out correctly, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma.”
“Whether they be kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, if they proceed correctly, they too will attain good understanding and know for themselves in accordance with the Dharma.
The Māṇava Aśvajit Bālakāśyapa said:
“Gautama! [Is this so?]”
"How marvelous!
How extraordinary!
You have so skillfully spoken this parable."
However, the brahmins make such claims as these:
"The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is white; all others are black."
A brahmin attains purity; one who is not a brahmin does not attain purity.
A brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, and is Brahmā himself.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"
Is it only the brahmin who is unattached and unbound in this empty space, untouched and unimpeded;
while the kṣatriya, the householder, and the craftsman are not so?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta replied: “Gautama!
In this space, the brahmin is neither attached nor bound; he is neither touched nor obstructed.”
"It is the same for kṣatriyas, householders,
and craftsmen. "In this way, māṇava,
if a brahmin is rightly directed, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma."
“Kṣatriyas, householders, and craftsmen who proceed correctly will also attain good understanding and know for themselves that they are in accordance with the Dharma.
The Mānaṣaka Aśvajit Rāmagrāmīya said:
“Gautama! [Is this so?]”
How marvelous!
How extraordinary!
You have so skillfully spoken this parable.
However, the brahmins make such claims as these:
"The brahmin caste is superior, while others are inferior;
the brahmin caste is pure, while all others are dark."
A brahmin attains purity, whereas one who is not a brahmin does not attain purity;
the brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, and is Brahmā himself.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"
Is it only the brahmins who are able to practice a mind of loving-kindness— free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—
or is it not also the case for the kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmaṇa replied: “Gautama,
a brahmin is able to practice a mind of loving-kindness, free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention.”
"It is the same for kṣatriyas, householders, and artisans.
"So it is, māṇava!"
If a brahmin is one who has entered the right path, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma;
if a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman is one who has entered the right path, they too attain thorough understanding and know for themselves in accordance with the Dharma.
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta said:
“Gautama, it is most wonderful!
"How extraordinary!
You have spoken this parable most excellently.
However, the various brahmins speak thus:"
“The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is white; others are all black.
The brahmin attains purity; those who are not brahmins do not attain purity.”
“The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth; he is created by Brahmā.
The World-Honored One asked: “Māṇava!
What do you think?
Suppose a hundred people were to come, and one person among them were to say to them:
"Come together!"
"If one is born into the Kṣatriya caste or the Brahmin caste, only they can take soap powder to the water to bathe, removing impurities and becoming utterly pure.
Thus he spoke, O Māṇava!
What do you think?
Can those of the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste take bath powder to the water and bathe, thereby removing impurities and becoming utterly pure?
Is it that those belonging to the class of householders or the class of artisans are unable to take soap powder to the water to bathe and remove impurities for the sake of extreme purity?
Or is it that all people of the hundredfold classes are able to take soap powder to the water to bathe and remove impurities for the sake of extreme purity?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta replied: “Gautama!
All those hundred kinds of people are able to take soap powder to the water and bathe, removing dirt until they are utterly pure.”
"Thus it is, Māṇava!
If a brahmin is one who has set out correctly, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma."
“Whether they be kṣatriyas, householders, or craftsmen, if they proceed correctly, they too will attain good understanding and know for themselves according to the Dharma.
The Mānaṣaka Aśvajit Rāmaputra replied, “Gautama! [Is this so?]”
"How marvelous!
How extraordinary!
It is wonderful that you have spoken this parable."
However, the brahmins make such claims as these:
"The brahmin caste is superior, while others are inferior;
the brahmin caste is pure white, while all others are black."
A brahmin attains purity, whereas one who is not a brahmin does not attain purity;
the brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, and is Brahmā himself.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"
Suppose a hundred people were to come, and one among them were to say to them:
"Come all together!

Only those born into the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste are able to use extremely dry sāla or candana wood as the fire-drill base and, by drilling with a fire-stick, produce and nurture a fire."
"Mañava! What do you think?
Can those of the Kṣatriya caste or the Brāhmaṇa caste take extremely dry sāla or sandalwood as the fire-drill base and, by drilling with it, produce and nurture a fire?"

If they belong to the class of householders or the class of artisans, would they produce fire and nurture it by using a dry trough for pigs or dogs, or *eranda* wood, or other inferior wood as the fire-drill base, and then drilling with a drill?
"Could all these hundred kinds of people take various types of wood as fire-drills, bore into them with a fire-stick, and thereby produce and nurture fire?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta replied:
"Gautama, [they could]."
"All those hundred kinds of people are able to take various types of wood as fire-drills, and by drilling with them, they produce fire and nurture it. "It is so."
"Mañjuśrī! If a brahmin proceeds rightly, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma;
if a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman proceeds rightly, they too attain thorough understanding and know for themselves in accordance with the Dharma."
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta said:
"Gautama, it is most wonderful!
"How extraordinary!
You have eloquently spoken this parable.
Yet, the various brahmins speak thus:"
“The Brahmin caste is superior, while others are not equal to it;
the Brahmin caste is white, while others are all black;
the Brahmin attains purity, whereas one who is not a Brahmin does not attain purity.”
"The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā.
The World-Honored One asked: "Māṇava!..."
What do you think?
If those hundred people were all to take various kinds of wood as fire-drills and, by drilling them, produce and nurture fire;
All those fires possess flames, color, heat, and light, and all are capable of performing the functions of fire.
Is it that only those specific fires possess flames, color, heat, and light, and are capable of performing the functions of fire?
Is it that this particular fire alone lacks flame, lacks color, lacks heat, and lacks light, such that it cannot perform the functions of fire?
Or is it that all fires possess flame, possess color, possess heat, and possess light, and are all capable of performing the functions of fire?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta said: “Gautama!
Suppose those hundred kinds of people all take various types of wood as fire-drills and, by drilling them with a fire-stick, produce and nurture fire.”
All those fires possess flames, color, heat, and light, and all are capable of performing the functions of fire.
It is absolutely impossible that a fire could perform the functions of fire while possessing only flames, color, heat, and light individually.
If that fire were alone without flame, without color, without heat, and without light, such that it could not perform the function of fire, that would be impossible, Gautama!
"But all those fires have flames, have color, have heat, and have light; they are all capable of performing the functions of fire.
"It is so, Māṇava!"
If a brahmin is one who has entered the right path, he attains thorough understanding and knows for himself in accordance with the Dharma;
if a kṣatriya, a householder, or a craftsman is one who has entered the right path, they too attain thorough understanding and know for themselves in accordance with the Dharma.
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta said:
"Gautama, it is most wonderful! "
"How extraordinary!
You have skillfully spoken this parable.
However, the various brahmins speak in this way:"
“The Brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The Brahmin caste is white; others are all black.
The Brahmin attains purity; one who is not a Brahmin does not attain purity.”
"The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth; he is created by Brahmā, the very essence of Brahmā.
The World-Honored One said: "Māṇava!"
If this body follows whatever birth it takes, it is counted among that very class:
if born into the brahmin caste, it is counted among the brahmin caste;
if born into the kṣatriya, householder, or artisan castes, it is counted among the artisan caste.
Māṇava! It is just as with fire: it is reckoned according to what it arises from;
if it arises because of wood, it is reckoned as wood-fire.
If it arises from grass, dung, or wood, it is reckoned as wood-fire.
In the same way, Māṇava,
this body is reckoned according to whatever it is born from.
If one is born into the brahmin caste, one is counted among the brahmins;
if one is born into the kṣatriya, householder, or artisan castes, one is counted among the artisans.
The Blessed One asked:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"

If a Kṣatriya woman unites with a Brahmin man, and as a result of that union they later give birth to a son—whether he resembles the father, resembles the mother, or resembles neither—how would you explain this?
“Is he a kṣatriya or a brahmin?
The Mānaṇa Acela-Rāmadatta replied:
“Gautama! [He is a kṣatriya.]”

When a Kṣatriya woman unites with a Brāhmaṇa man, from that union a son is subsequently born; he may resemble his father, or resemble his mother, or resemble neither parent. I do not call him a Kṣatriya, nor do I call him a Brāhmaṇa.
"Gautama!
I speak only of that other body. "So it is."
"O Māṇava! This body belongs to whichever class it is born into.
If it is born into the Brahmin caste, it belongs to the number of the Brahmin caste."
"If one is born into the kṣatriya, householder, or artisan class, one is then counted among the artisans.
The Blessed One asked: "Māṇava!

If a brahmin woman were to unite with a kṣatriya man, and as a result of that union they later gave birth to a son who resembles the father, or resembles the mother, or resembles neither parent—how would you explain this?
"Was he a brahmin, or was he a kṣatriya?
The māṇava Aśvajit Rāmagrāmīya replied: "Gautama!"

When a brahmin woman and a kṣatriya man come together, from that union they subsequently give birth to a son who may resemble his father, or resemble his mother, or resemble neither; I do not call him a brahmin, nor do I call him a kṣatriya.
"Gautama!
I speak only of that other body. "So it is, Māṇava!"
This body follows its place of birth and is counted among that very class.
If one is born into the brahmin caste, one is counted among the brahmin caste;
if one is born into the kṣatriya, householder, or artisan castes, one is counted among the artisan caste.
The Blessed One asked:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"

Suppose a man has many mares, and he lets out one male donkey; among them, one mare mates with the male donkey, and as a result of that mating, she subsequently gives birth to a foal. How would you explain this?
“Was he a donkey or a horse?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta replied, “Gautama! [He was neither.]”
"If a horse and a donkey were to mate together, and as a result of that mating a foal were subsequently born, I would not call it a donkey, nor would I call it a horse, O Gotama!"
"I was merely speaking of that mule.
"In this same way, Māṇava, whatever this body is born as, it is reckoned among those very things."
If one is born into the brahmin caste, one is counted among the brahmins;
if one is born into the kṣatriya, householder, or artisan castes, one is counted among the artisans.
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava! In times past, there were many seers living together in a secluded place, free from worldly affairs, who conceived such an evil view:..."
"The Brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The Brahmin caste is white; others are all black.
The Brahmin attains purity; those who are not Brahmins do not attain purity."
"The Brahmā is the son of Brahmā; he was born from his mouth; he was created by Brahmā.

Then, having heard that many seers were dwelling together in a secluded, high place, and having conceived such an evil view, the seer Asita Devala put on saffron robes, wrapped his head in a saffron cloth, took up a staff and a parasol, disguised himself in white garments, and instead of entering through the gate, went directly to the hermitage where the seers dwelt and paced back and forth in their quiet chamber.

At that time, there was a seer dwelling in a secluded place on high ground who saw the seer Asita Devala wearing a saffron robe, his head wrapped in a saffron cloth, leaning on a staff and holding a parasol, disguised in white garments and not entering through the gate, as he walked up and down in the quiet chamber where the seers resided.
Having seen this, he went to where many sages were dwelling together in a secluded, high place, and spoke these words:
"Venerable ones!

There is now a man wearing saffron robes, with his head wrapped in a saffron cloth, leaning on a staff and holding a parasol; disguised in white garments, he has entered not through the gate but has come to the hermitage to walk in meditation within the quiet chamber. We should surely go together and cast a spell upon him."
“‘Do you become ashes? Do you become ashes?
Thereupon, the many seers who lived together in a secluded high place went to where the seer Asita Devala was; having arrived, they chanted together:
‘Become ashes! Become ashes!’”
"Chanting the incantation according to the ritual method, [he said], 'Become ash! Become ash! As he did so, her radiant countenance became even more beautiful, and her body grew supple and lustrous."
Those many seers then thought to themselves:
"When we previously cast spells upon you, saying 'Become ashes! Become ashes!', you indeed became ashes.
Now, when we cast spells upon this man, saying 'Become ashes! Become ashes!', this man's countenance becomes even more radiant and his body more lustrous than before. We should surely question him."
He then asked him:
"Who are you? The seer Asita Devala replied:
"Venerable sirs!
Have you heard of the seer Asita Devala?
They replied:
"I have heard that there is an ascetic named Asita Devala. He replied again, "I am he."
Those many seers then collectively took their leave of the seer Asita Devala, saying:
"We pray that you will grant us your forgiveness; we did not know that you were the seer Asita Devala."
Then the seer Asita Tisyamata addressed the other seers, saying: "I have already forgiven you.
You have indeed given rise to wrong views: [that the world is eternal, that it is finite, that the soul and the body are identical, and that a Tathāgata exists after death]."
“The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is white; all others are black.
Brahmins attain purity; non-brahmins do not attain purity.”
"The brahmin is the son of Brahmā; he was born from his mouth, created by Brahmā.
Those seers replied, "So it is."
Asita then asked the seers:
"Do you yourselves know your own fathers?
Those seers replied:
"I know it.

That brahmin takes a brahmin wife, not one who is not a brahmin; his father was likewise a brahmin, and so on back through seven generations of fathers—thus that brahmin takes a brahmin wife, not one who is not a brahmin."
Asita then asked the seers:
"Do you know your own mothers?
Those seers replied:
"I know it.

That brahmin takes a husband from among brahmins, not from non-brahmins; his mother was likewise a mother, and so on back through seven generations of mothers—his ancestors were all brahmins, and he takes a husband from among brahmins, not from non-brahmins."
Asita then asked the sages:
"Do you yourselves know how you were conceived in the womb?
Those sages replied:
"I know it.

Through the convergence of three factors, conception occurs: the union of the parents, the mother’s season being favorable and she being capable of conceiving, and the gandharva having arrived. Āsīla!"
"At such a gathering of circumstances, one enters the mother's womb.
Āsīta then asked the sages:
"Do you know whether the one being born will be male?"
Are you a woman?
Do you know where you have come from?
Have you come from the Kṣatriya clan?
"Have brahmins, householders, or craftsmen come?
Or have they come from the east, the south, the west, or the north?
Those seers replied:
"I do not know.
Asita then spoke again to those sages, saying,
"Virtuous ones!..."
Not seeing and not knowing this, you do not understand conception: from where does one come?
Is it a male or a female?
Does one come from the kṣatriya caste?
"Have these brahmins, householders, and artisans come?
Have they come from the east, the south, the west, or the north?
And yet, he speaks thus:
"The Brahmin caste is superior, while others are not equal;
the Brahmin caste is white, while others are all black;
the Brahmin attains purity, whereas one who is not a Brahmin does not attain purity."
"The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā. "Māṇava!

Even when those many seers dwelling in the secluded heights were thus well-instructed and well-rebuked by the seer Asita Devala, they were unable to establish what constitutes a pure brahmin; how much less so can you and your teachers, who wear garments of skin and grass?"

Thereupon, the Māṇava Acela-Roja, having been rebuked and censured face-to-face by the Blessed One, felt inward grief; with his head bowed and silent, he was deprived of his eloquence and remained speechless.
Then, having rebuked and censured the young brahmin Āḷavaka face-to-face, the Blessed One, having caused him to rejoice, addressed him, saying:
"Young brahmin!..."
There was a brahmin who prepared a sacrificial feast and practiced giving. He had four sons: two were fond of study, while the other two were not.
What do you think, Māṇava?
"To whom did that brahmin first offer the foremost seat, the foremost water for washing, and the foremost food?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāyana-dona replied: "Gautama!"
If that brahmin has two sons who are fond of learning, he will invariably offer them the first seat, the first water for washing, and the first meal.
The Blessed One asked again:

"Māṇava, suppose there is another brahmin who prepares a sacrificial feast and practices giving. He has four sons: two are fond of learning but are not diligent, taking pleasure in practicing unwholesome dharmas; the other two do not study, yet they are diligent and take pleasure in practicing sublime dharmas."
"What do you think, Māṇava?
To whom did those brahmins first offer the foremost seat, the foremost water for washing, and the foremost food?
The Māṇava Acela-Rāyana answered:

"Gautama! If that brahmin has two sons who, though unlearned, are diligent and delight in practicing the sublime Dharma, he would surely first offer them the foremost seat, the foremost water for washing, and the foremost food."
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava! You first praised learning, and afterwards you praised the observance of the precepts."
“Māṇava! I teach that all four castes are entirely pure, establishing and proclaiming this; you also teach that all four castes are entirely pure, establishing and proclaiming this.”
Thereupon, the Māṇava Acela-Rāmadatta rose from his seat, intending to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
At that moment, the great assembly raised a loud cry:
“How extraordinary is the Śramaṇa Gautama!”
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?
Just as the śramaṇa Gautama has taught and demonstrated that all four castes are entirely pure, so too has Aśvalāyanamāṇava taught that all four castes are entirely pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of that great assembly, addressed them, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Āḷavaka! Since you are content in mind, you may return to your seat; I shall preach the Dharma for you.

The young brahmin Āḷavaka bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. Having used immeasurable skillful means to preach the Dharma for him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, the World-Honored One remained silent.

Then, after the Buddha had taught the Dharma to the Māṇava Acelasutāyana, exhorting him, inspiring him with longing, and bringing him to a state of joy, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, not far away, many brahmins of Kosala were returning when they rebuked Assalāyana with various words, saying:
"What do you intend to do?"
Desiring to subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, he was instead defeated and returned by the śramaṇa Gautama.
It is just like a man who enters a forest for the sake of his eyes, yet returns having lost those very eyes.
Āḷavaka! You are just like this:
desiring to subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, you have instead been defeated and turned back by the śramaṇa Gautama.
It is just as if a person were to enter a pond to drink, only to return thirsty.
Ācemanadaṇḍa! You are just like this:
wishing to subdue the śramaṇa Gautama, you have instead been subdued by the śramaṇa Gautama and returned.
"Acela Rāmaputta! What do you wish to do?
Thereupon, the young brahmin Acela Rāmaputta spoke to the many brahmins of Kosala:
“Venerable friends!
I have already said before:
‘The ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma; one who teaches the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma cannot be challenged or censured.’”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Māṇava Acela-Rāyana rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The tenth discourse, the Acela Sutta, ends here with 4,413 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 37, totaling 8,420 characters, concludes here; the second section, the Brāhmaṇa Vagga, ends with 25,198 characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 38.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Recitation Section on Analysis (Vibhaṅga-bhāṇavāra), Chapter 1: Brāhmaṇa-varga. This chapter contains ten sūtras. Fourth Daily Recitation: Named "Analysis" (Nidāna).
Śuka, Śūrpāraka, Bharukaccha, Vaidiśa, Sāketā, and Vārāṇasī; Pīlukavana,
Thūna, Āgamahāna, Āpaṇa, and Brahmā.
152. The Śuka Sūtra (152). Middle Discourses, Chapter on Brahmins, The Śuka Sūtra, First, Third Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
At that time, the young brahmin student Śuka Todeyyaputta had some business to attend to and went to Rājagaha, where he stayed as a guest in the house of a householder.
Thereupon, the young brahmin student Śuka Todeyyaputta asked the householder in whose home he was staying:

"Is there any recluse or brahmin who is a leader among teachers, who presides over a great assembly, and who is honored by others—someone whom I might visit at the proper time to pay my respects and honor him, and perhaps, through such respectful service, find joy?"
The householder replied:
"There is, dear friend!"

The śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, having renounced his Śākya lineage, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and with deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path, has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Beloved of the Gods!
You may go to see him at any time and pay your respects; perhaps, through this act of veneration, your heart will find joy.
The parrot youth then asked again:
“Where is the śramaṇa Gautama now?
I wish to see him.
The householder replied:
“The ascetic Gotama is staying here in Rājagaha at the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary; you should go and see him.
Thereupon, the young brahmin Śuka left the householder’s home where he was lodging and went to the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary.

From afar, the young brahmin Śuka saw the World-Honored One amidst the grove of trees, upright, handsome, and beautiful, like the moon among the stars, radiant and brilliant, shining like a mountain of gold; endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, his majestic power was sublime, his faculties were tranquil and settled, free from all obscuration or hindrance, perfected in self-mastery, with a mind at rest in silent stillness.
Having seen him, he went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, and sat down to one side. He said:
"Gautama, I wish to ask a question; may I venture to state it if you will grant me leave?"
The Blessed One said,
"Ask whatever you wish.
The young brahmin Śuka asked:

“Gautama! According to what I have heard, if one who remains at home attains a good understanding, they will know what is in accordance with the Dharma; however, this is not the case for one who has gone forth to study the Path.”
"I ask the Gautama: what is this matter?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This matter is not fixed."
The parrot mona addressed him, saying:
"Gautama! I pray that you will now analyze this matter for me."
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava, listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in full detail."
The parrot-monk (śuka-māṇava) received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Māṇava!
If there are those, whether householders or those who have gone forth, who study the path yet practice it erroneously, I do not praise them. Why is this?

Because if there are householders or those who have gone forth who study the path yet practice it erroneously, they will not attain skillful understanding and will not know what is in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, Māṇava, if there are those,
whether householders or those who have gone forth, who study the path yet practice in a deviant manner,
I do not praise them, Māṇava.
If there are those, whether householders or those who have gone forth, who train in the path and practice right conduct, I praise them. Why is this?

Because if there are those, whether householders or those who have gone forth, who train in the path and practice right conduct, they will certainly attain skillful understanding and thus know what is in accordance with the Dharma.
Therefore, Māṇava!
If there are those, whether householders or those who have gone forth, who train in the path and practice right conduct, of them I speak highly. Māṇava!
I have spoken thus; I have explained these two dharmas, analyzed them in this way, and demonstrated them in this manner.

Should there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who possess firm and steadfast power, who penetrate deeply, and who are single-mindedly attached, saying, "This alone is the truth, and all else is false," [they do so regarding these two].
The young brahmin Śuka replied, “Gautama!
According to what I have heard, one who remains at home possesses great benefit and great merit; this is not the case for one who leaves the home life to study the Path.”
"I ask the Gautama, how is this matter?
The World-Honored One replied,
"This matter is not fixed."
The young brahmin Śuka said:
“Gautama! I pray that you will further analyze this matter for me.”
The World-Honored One said:
“Māṇava! Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in full detail.”
The parrot youth received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Young man!
If one who lives as a householder encounters great calamities, great strife, or great animosity, and practices wrong conduct, they will not attain great fruits nor possess great merit.

It is just like agricultural work: where there are great calamities, great strife, and great enmity, one who practices in a deviant manner will not obtain a great fruit, nor will there be great merit.
In this way, māṇava!
It is likewise for one who lives at home. Māṇava!

For those who have left the household life to study the Way, there are few calamities and afflictions, few disputes, and few enmities; yet those who practice deviant paths shall not attain great fruits nor possess great merit.
It is just as in the case of a livelihood: if there is little misfortune, little strife, and little enmity, yet one practices what is wrong, one will not obtain great fruit, nor possess great merit.
In this way, māṇava!
It is likewise for one who has gone forth to study the Path. "Māṇava!..."
If a householder encounters great calamities, great strife, or great enmity, by practicing right conduct, they will obtain a great reward and possess great merit.

It is just as in the case of agricultural work: even when there are great calamities, great strife, and great enmity, one who practices the right path will obtain a great fruit and possess great merit.
In this way, māṇava!
It is likewise for one who lives at home. Māṇava!

For one who has left the household life to study the Way, there will be few calamities and afflictions, few quarrels and disputes, and few enmities and hatreds; practicing with rectitude, one attains great karmic fruition and possesses great merit.
It is just as in the case of managing a livelihood: if there is little misfortune, little strife, and little enmity, one who practices right conduct will obtain great rewards and possess great merit.
In this way, māṇava,
it is also thus for one who has gone forth to study the Path. Māṇava!
I speak thus, teaching these two dharmas, analyzing them in this way, and elucidating them in this manner.
If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who possess firm and steadfast power, who penetrate deeply, and who are single-mindedly attached, declaring, "This alone is the truth; all else is false."
The young brahmin Śuka replied: “Gautama!
Those brahmins prescribe five dharmas that yield great rewards, possess great merit, and bring about blessings and goodness.”
The World-Honored One said:
"If the brahmins establish five dharmas that yield great fruit and reward, possess great merit, and bring about blessings and goodness."
“Can you speak now among this assembly?
The parrot youth replied, “Gautama! [I can.]”
"I have no objection. Why is that?
Gautama!"
"Now he is sitting here before this assembly.
The World-Honored One said,
"You may speak now."
The young brahmin Śuka replied:
“Listen well, Gautama!
"Gautama!
The Brahmin establishes the first true dharma as having great fruit and reward, great merit, and resulting in the performance of merit and the attainment of goodness;
the second is recitation and study, the third is fervent practice, and the fourth is asceticism."
"Gautama!
The brahmin establishes a fifth holy life (brahmacariya) which has great fruit, great merit, and brings about the making of merit and the attainment of the wholesome.
The Blessed One replied:
"If there are brahmins who establish five dharmas that yield great fruit, possess great merit, and result in the performance of merit and the attainment of goodness—
among those brahmins, is there even one brahmin who speaks thus:
'Having personally known, personally realized, and personally witnessed these five dharmas for myself in this very life, do I establish their fruit?'"
The young brahmin Śuka replied to the Blessed One,
“No, Gautama.”
The Blessed One said:
"Is there any teacher or lineage of teachers, even back to the seventh generation of ancestors, who has made such a claim:
'Having personally known, personally realized, and personally witnessed these five dharmas within this very life, I establish the fruit [of my attainment]'?"
The young brahmin Śuka replied to the Blessed One,
“No, Gautama.”
At that time, the World-Honored One asked:

"Māṇava! Suppose there were a brahmin in the past who, at the end of his life and upon passing away, had recited and mastered the scriptures, propagated the scriptures, and studied the canonical texts."
First is Nyatṭha; second is Vāma; third is Vāmadeva; fourth is Viśvāmitra; fifth is Yajñadattā; sixth is Aṅgīrasa; seventh is Vasiṣṭha; eighth is Kāśyapa; ninth is Bharadvāja; tenth is Bhṛgu.
That is to say: regarding those brahmins who are currently fully versed in the scriptures, having studied, recited, mastered, and learned them—do they ever speak thus:
"Having directly known, directly awakened to, and personally realized these five dharmas within this very life, do I establish their fruit?"
The young brahmin Śuka replied to the Blessed One,
“No, Gautama.”
"However, it is merely because the brahmins have accepted and maintained it out of faith.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If, among all those brahmins, not even a single brahmin were to speak thus:"
"Regarding these five dharmas of mine, having known them for myself, awakened to them for myself, and realized them for myself within this present life, I proclaim their fruit and retribution.
Furthermore, I have no teacher or lineage master, nor even my parents back through seven generations, who could say:

"Regarding these five dharmas of mine, having known them for yourself, awakened to them for yourself, and realized them for yourself within this present life, you should proclaim their fruit and retribution."
"In the past, there was a brahmin who, at the end of his life and upon passing away, had recited and maintained the scriptures, disseminated the scriptures, and mastered the sacred texts:
first, Yājñavalkya; second, Vāmadeva; third, Vāmadevya; fourth, Viśvāmitra; fifth, Nārada Kaṇiṇa; sixth, Aṅgiras; seventh, Bṛhaspati; eighth, Kāśyapa; ninth, Bhāradvāja; and tenth, Vasiṣṭha."
That is to say, these present-day brahmins—who are fully versed in the scriptures, having studied, recited, mastered, and learned them—do not make this claim:
"Having personally known, personally realized, and personally witnessed these five dharmas within the present life, I establish their fruit and retribution."
“Māṇava! Is it not because of this that those brahmins lack a foundation for their faith and inclination?
Śuka Māṇava replied:
"Gautama! Truly there is no root; it is merely that the brahmins have heard it and accepted it as such.
The World-Honored One said:
"It is like a group of blind men supporting one another: he who is in front cannot see those behind him, nor can he see those in the middle;
he who is in the middle cannot see those in front of him, nor can he see those behind him."
Those who are behind do not see what is in the middle, nor do they see what is in front. Māṇava!
It is just the same with those brahmins of whom you speak.
“Māṇava! You first spoke of faith, and then you spoke again of learning.
Māṇava Śuka became angry with the Blessed One; resentful, envious, and displeased, he reviled the Blessed One, censured the Blessed One, and insulted the Blessed One.
"One should revile Gautama!
One should point a finger at Gautama!
One should bring about Gautama's downfall!"
He said to the Blessed One:
"There is a brahmin named Vassakāra, of the lineage of the Ujjñeyyas; he speaks thus:
'If there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who has knowledge and vision regarding the states that transcend the human, and who declares, "I have attained them in this very life. "
Having heard this, I laughed aloud; my mind did not approve, for it was false and unreal, and moreover, contrary to the Dharma.
How can one born among humans claim to have attained the Dharma that transcends humanity?
"If one were to say regarding a human being that 'I know and I see the Dharma,' this would not be the case.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The young brahmin Śuka, son of Todeyya, is angry with me; he hates, envies, and is displeased with me; he slanders me, points his finger at me, and reviles me."
"One should revile you, Gautama!
One should point a finger at you, Gautama!
One should cast you down, Gautama!"
And he said to me: “Gautama!
There is a brahmin named Vāseṭṭha, of the lineage of the Pure Rectifiers; he speaks thus:”

"If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins who claim to have knowledge and vision regarding the states superior to the human realm, asserting that they have realized them for themselves—having heard this, I laugh at them;
my mind does not approve, for it is false and unreal, and moreover, it is not in accordance with the Dharma."
How can one born among humans claim to have attained the Dharma that transcends humanity?
If one speaks of the Dharma that transcends humanity, saying "I know it" or "I see it," this is not possible.
The World-Honored One, having understood this, addressed him, saying:
“Māṇava! The brahmin Vokkāṇa Sāṇavāsī, of the lineage of Ujjñā, has purified his transformation; he knows the thoughts in the minds of all śramaṇas and brahmins, and only then does he speak thus.”
"If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who claim to have knowledge and vision regarding the superhuman states, asserting, 'I have realized this for myself,' upon hearing this, I laugh at them heartily;
I do not approve of their intent, for it is false and unreal, and moreover, it is not in accordance with the Dharma."
How can one born among humans claim to have attained the Dharma that transcends humanity?
If one speaks of the Dharma that transcends humanity, saying "I know it" or "I see it," is this not impossible?
The young brahmin Śuka replied: “Gautama!

The brahmin Vakkali Sāṇavāsī, whose lineage is pure and upright, has a maidservant named Bhaṇḍu who cannot even know what is passing through his master’s mind; how much less could he know the thoughts in the minds of all śramaṇas and brahmins?”
"If one were to claim that [a blind person] knows, such a thing is simply impossible.
The World-Honored One said:
"It is like a man born blind who makes this statement:"
"There are no colors of black or white, nor is there anyone who sees colors of black or white.
There are no beautiful or ugly colors, nor is there anyone who sees beautiful or ugly colors.
There are no long or short colors, nor is there anyone who sees long or short colors."
There are no forms that are near or far, nor is there any seeing of forms that are near or far.
There are no forms that are coarse or subtle, nor is there any seeing of forms that are coarse or subtle.
From the beginning, I have neither seen nor known them; therefore, form does not exist.
“Was what that man blind from birth said true?
The parrot-monk (Śuka-māṇava) replied to the Blessed One: “No, [it was not].”
"Gautama! Why is this so?
There are black and white colors, and there are also those who see black and white colors."
There are beautiful and ugly forms, and there is also the seeing of beautiful and ugly forms.
There are long and short forms, and there is also the seeing of long and short forms.
There are near and distant forms, and there is also the seeing of near and distant forms.
There are coarse and subtle forms, as well as visible coarse and subtle forms.
If one were to say, "I did not see or know them from the beginning;
therefore, form does not exist," such a statement made by one born blind would be untrue.
“Māṇava! Is not what the brahmin Vokkāṇa Sāṇavāsī—whose lineage is upright and pure—says like that of one who is born blind and sightless?”
The parrot-ascetic Māṇava replied to the Blessed One:
“Like one who is blind,
Gautama!”
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"

If there were brahmins in the past who, at the end of their lives and after passing away, had recited and upheld the scriptures, disseminated the scriptures, and studied the canonical texts—such as the brahmin Saṅgārava, the brahmin Janussoni, the brahmin Vāseṭṭha, and your father Todeyya—was there anything among what they said that was acceptable or unacceptable, true or untrue, superior or inferior?
The parrot youth Māṇava replied to the Blessed One:

“If there were brahmins of the past who, at the end of their lives and after passing away, had recited and mastered the scriptures, disseminated the scriptures, and studied the canonical texts—namely, the brahmin Saṅga, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa, the brahmin Vokkāṇa, and my father Todeyya.”
Regarding what he has said, it is my intention that it be made acceptable and not unacceptable, made true and not untrue, and made exalted and not base.
At that time, the Blessed One asked:
"Māṇava! Regarding what was said by the brahmin Vokkāṇa Sāṇavāsī, whose lineage is pure and upright—is it not the case that what he has spoken is unacceptable and that there is nothing acceptable?"
"Is it not that there is nothing untrue and nothing true?
Is it not that there is nothing low and nothing high?
The parrot youth (Śuka-māṇava) replied to the World-Honored One:
"It is indeed so,
Gautama! Furthermore, Māṇava!"
There are five things that act as obstacles, as coverings, and as blindness; they can extinguish wisdom, cause one to exhaust oneself in vain, and prevent the attainment of Nirvana.
"What are the five? Māṇava!

Sensual desire is the foremost dharma that acts as an obstacle, a covering, and a blindness that leaves one sightless; it can extinguish wisdom, leading only to fruitless exhaustion, and prevents the attainment of Nirvāṇa."

Māṇava! Anger, the view of a self-identity, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt as the fifth factor—these constitute obstacles, coverings, and causes of blindness; they destroy wisdom and lead to fruitless exhaustion, so that one does not attain nirvāṇa.
"Mañjuśrī! What do you think?

If one is obstructed, covered, and entangled by these five qualities, it is simply impossible that they could—whether desiring to contemplate their own welfare, the welfare of others, or the welfare of both, or to know the thoughts in the minds of all śramaṇas and brahmins—ever achieve such things."

"Mañava! The brahmin Puṣkarasādi, though his lineage was upright and pure, was defiled by desire, stained by desire, touched by desire, dependent on desire, attached to desire, and immersed in desire; he practiced desire without seeing its peril and without knowing the way of escape."

Hindered, covered, and shrouded by these five qualities, it is simply impossible that he would be able to contemplate his own welfare, the welfare of others, or the welfare of both, nor to know the thoughts in the minds of all recluses and brahmins.
"Furthermore, Māṇava!
There are five strands of sensual pleasure, which are cherished and desired; they are associated with passion for lovely forms and are exceedingly delightful."
"What are the five?
The eye cognizes forms; the ear cognizes sounds; the nose cognizes odors; the tongue cognizes tastes; the body cognizes tangibles. Māṇava!"
"What do you think?
Is it not the case that because sentient beings give rise to pleasure and joy on account of these five strands of sensual desire, they do not transcend them?
Śuka Māṇava replied to the Blessed One:
"So it is, Gautama. Thus did the Blessed One ask.
“Māṇava! What do you think?
If one kindles a fire by means of grass and wood, and another kindles a fire apart from grass and wood, which of these flames is the most excellent, the most sublime, and the most supreme?”
The parrot-ascetic Māṇava replied: “Gautama!
It is impossible for fire to burn apart from grass and wood; such a thing can only occur through the power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhipāda*).”
"Gautama!
If one were to kindle a fire apart from grass and wood, its radiance would be supreme, most exquisite, and most excellent.
The World-Honored One replied:
"So it is, so it is, Māṇava!
It is simply impossible that fire could burn apart from grass and wood; there is no such possibility, except by the power of psychic mastery (ṛddhipāda)."
Māṇava, if one were to kindle a fire apart from grass and wood, its flame would be supreme, most wonderful, and most excellent; this is what I am speaking of metaphorically now.

Māṇava, just as it is with a fire kindled by means of grass and wood, so too is the pleasure and joy produced by sentient beings—namely, that which arises because of sensual desires and evil, unwholesome states—and they do not attain the abandonment of pleasure or its cessation.

Māṇava! Just as fire burns when separated from grass and wood, so too do sentient beings experience the pleasure of equanimity that arises; that is to say, due to the separation from desire, they obtain the pleasure of equanimity and cessation through various wholesome dharmas.
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava, what do you think?"
There was a brahmin who prepared a sacrificial feast and practiced giving. From the east, a kṣatriya youth arrived and said to him:
"I shall receive the foremost seat, the foremost water for washing, and the foremost food and drink therein."
If he does not receive the first seat, the first water for washing, or the first food and drink among them, he immediately gives rise to resentment and harbors hatred and envy.
Or suppose a young brahmin comes from the south and says:
"I obtained pure and exquisite food there.
Although he did not obtain pure and exquisite food there, he nevertheless gives rise to resentment and harbors malice and envy.
Or suppose a householder’s son comes from the west and says:
"I obtained abundant food there.
Although he did not obtain abundant food there, he conceives resentment and harbors malice and envy.
Or suppose a young artisan comes from the north and says:
"I obtained abundant food there.
Although he did not obtain abundant food there, he nevertheless gives rise to resentment and harbors hatred and jealousy.
“Māṇava! When those brahmins practice such giving, what kind of fruit do they establish?
The Māṇava Śuka replied:
"Gautama! A brahmin does not practice giving with such a state of mind as to cause others to give rise to resentment or harbor hatred and jealousy.
Gautama!"
"You should know, brahmin, that one practices giving with a heart of compassion; having practiced giving with a heart of compassion, one then attains great merit.
The World-Honored One said, "Māṇava!"
"Brahmin, is it not the case that there is a sixth practice established which brings great fruit, great merit, and leads to the performance of merit and the attainment of goodness?
The young brahmin Śuka replied to the Blessed One: "It is so."
"Gautama!
the World-Honored One asked, "Māṇava!"

If there are five dharmas established by a brahmin that yield great fruit, possess great merit, and bring about the performance of merit and the attainment of goodness—where do you see these dharmas mostly residing: among householders or among renunciants?
"Have you gone forth to study the Path?
The young brahmin Śuka replied, "Gautama!"

If there are five dharmas established by a brahmin that yield great fruit and reward, possess great merit, and result in the performance of merit and the attainment of goodness, I see that these dharmas mostly pertain to those who have left the household life to study the Path, rather than to those who remain at home.
Why is this? Those who live at home have many affairs, many activities, much resentment, and much hatred and contention; they are unable to maintain the protection of truth.
"Gotama!

Those who have left the household life to study the Path have few concerns, little to do, few fetters of resentment, and little hatred or contention; they will surely be able to maintain their truthfulness."
"Gautama!
As for those who possess truthfulness, I observe that they mostly dwell among those who have left the household life to study the Way, rather than those who remain at home. Why is this so?"

Householders have many affairs, much to do, many grudges, and much hatred and contention; they are unable to practice giving, unable to recite and study, unable to practice austerities, and unable to practice the holy life.
"Gautama!

Those who have left the household life to study the Way have few concerns, little to do, little cause for resentment, and little cause for hatred or contention; thus they are able to practice giving, able to recite and study, able to practice asceticism, and able to practice the holy life."
"Gautama!
As for those who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*), I see that this dharma is mostly found among those who have gone forth to study the Way, not among those who remain at home.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Māṇava! If there are brahmins who establish five dharmas that yield great fruit, possess great merit, and result in the performance of wholesome merit, I say these arise from the mind.”
"What is meant by 'the mind'?
It is the mind that is without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; it is for the sake of cultivating that, O Māṇava!"
"What do you think?
If there is a bhikṣu who guards his truthfulness, because he guards his truthfulness, he attains joy and gladness, Māṇava."
If there is joy and gladness that are wholesome and associated with what is wholesome, I say that these arise from the mind. What is the mind?

It is the mind that is without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; for the sake of cultivating that mind, one is able to practice giving, practice recitation and study, practice asceticism, and practice the holy life.
Because he practices the holy life for that cause, he attains joy and rapture.
Māṇava! If there is joy and rapture, which are associated with what is wholesome, I say that they arise from the mind.
What is meant by "the mind"?
It is when the mind is without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention; that mind, accompanied by loving-kindness, pervades one direction, achieving and dwelling therein.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters, enmity, ill will, and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters, free from enmity, free from ill will, and free from contention—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, he dwells having pervaded the entire world.

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Sūkhāntika rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: “Gautama!
I now have the utmost faith in the śramaṇa Gautama!
I only pray that Gautama will skillfully expound the Dharma for me, so that I may come to know: "This is freedom from illness; this is nirvāṇa."
The Blessed One said: “Kṣemaka!
If your noble eye of wisdom is not yet purified, even if I were to speak to you of health and nirvāṇa, you would ultimately be unable to understand it; it would merely be a vain weariness to me.”
"Kṣemaka! It is just as if a man born blind were told by another who had been there:
'You should know this: this is blue, yellow, red, or white.'"
“Sūkhāntika! Would that man born blind, by relying on the words of others, know what is blue, yellow, red, or white?
He replied to the World-Honored One:
"No, Gautama! It is so."

"Kṣemaka! If your noble eye of wisdom is not yet purified, you will never be able to understand my teaching on illness-free Nirvāṇa, even if I were to speak of it for you; it would merely be a vain exhaustion to me."
Kṣemaka! I shall explain to you the sublime medicine according to its likeness, which brings about the purification of the noble eye of wisdom that has not yet been purified. Kṣemaka!
If your noble eye of wisdom becomes purified, you will know for yourself: "This is freedom from disease;
this is Nirvāṇa. Sūkhāntika!

It is just as if there were a man born blind, for whom his kinsmen, out of compassion, seeking his welfare, benefit, security, and happiness, sought a physician for his eyes. That physician administered various treatments: inducing vomiting, administering purgatives, applying nasal drops, or administering enemas, or piercing his veins, or inducing tears.
"Kṣemaka! If such a state exists, one may attain purity of both eyes. Kṣemaka!"
If his two eyes were to become clear and pure, he would then see for himself that this was blue, yellow, red, or white; seeing those soiled and impure garments, he would think:
"That is my enemy; for a long night, he has deceived me with these soiled and impure garments."
"Then he will harbor a mind of hatred. Kṣemaka!
Such a person might even go so far as to kill him."
In this way, Kūṭadanta!
I have taught you the medicine that corresponds to its description, which brings about the purification of the noble eye of wisdom that has not yet been purified. Kūṭadanta!
"If your noble eye of wisdom becomes purified, you will then know for yourself: 'This is freedom from illness;
this is Nirvana. Kṣemaka!
There are four things by which the unpurified noble eye of wisdom attains purification."
What are the four? They are:
associating with virtuous friends, honoring and serving them, hearing the sublime Dharma, and reflecting well upon it, thereby proceeding toward the Dharma that follows the Dharma.
"Khemaka! You should train yourself in this way:
draw near to virtuous friends, honor and serve them, hear the sublime Dharma, reflect upon it well, and proceed toward the Dharma that follows the Dharma."
Uttara! You should train yourself in this way. Uttara!

Having approached a spiritual friend and having served them with reverence, you will hear the sublime Dharma. Having heard the sublime Dharma, you will reflect upon it well. Having reflected upon it well, you will proceed toward the Dhamma that follows the Dhamma. Having proceeded toward the Dhamma that follows the Dhamma, you will know this suffering as it truly is; you will know the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are.
"How does one know suffering as it truly is?

It is said that birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the beloved is suffering, not obtaining what one seeks is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. Thus one knows suffering as it truly is."
How does one know the origin of suffering as it truly is?
It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; thus one knows the origin of suffering as it truly is.
What is knowing the cessation of suffering as it really is?

It is this: regarding this craving which leads to future existence and is accompanied by delight and lust, one desires the cessation of this and that existence—its remainderless abandonment, relinquishment, vomiting out, exhaustion, dispassion, disappearance, and cessation; thus one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is.
How does one know the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is?
It refers to the Noble Eightfold Path: right view, up to and including right concentration—these are the eight. In this way, one knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is.
When this Dharma had been taught, the heterodox practitioner Assaji was distanced from dust and free from defilement; the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.

Thereupon, the heterodox practitioner Assaji saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he realized the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, transcended confusion, and held no other as supreme. No longer following others, free from hesitation, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit and attained fearlessness in the Dharma of the World-Honored One.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you allow me to leave the household life to study the Way, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu.”
The World-Honored One said:
“Welcome, bhikṣu!
Practice the holy life.”
The heterodox practitioner Sañjikāputta immediately left the household life to study the Path, received full ordination, and became a bhikṣu.
Having left the household life to study the Path, received full ordination, and mastered the Dharma, Sañjikāputta attained the state of an Arhat.
The Buddha spoke thus.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Venerable Soṇadaṇḍa rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The second *Soṇadaṇḍa-sūtra* ends here, totaling 4,121 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 38, totals 8,662 characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 39.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
154. Pāṭaligāma Sūtra (154). Chapter on the Brahmins. Pāṭaligāma Sūtra, Third and Fourth Divisions.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Park, at the Hall of Migāra’s Mother.

At that time, there were two men, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, belonging to the brahmin caste, who had shaved off their hair and beards, donned saffron robes, and out of faith had gone forth from the home life into homelessness to practice the path.
When the brahmins saw this, they rebuked and censured him most severely and harshly, saying to him:
"The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is pure; all others are black."
The brahmin attains purity; the non-brahmin does not attain purity.
The brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth; he is created by Brahmā, the progenitor of Brahmā.

"You have abandoned what is superior for what is inferior; you have abandoned the white for the black. That shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by darkness; he has cut off his lineage and is without offspring.
Therefore, what you have done is a great evil, a most grievous transgression."

At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, descended from the hall, and walked back and forth on the open ground in the shadow of the hall, preaching the profound and subtle Dharma for the bhikṣus.

Seeing the Blessed One from afar, the Venerable Vāsiṣṭha rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, descended from the hall, and began to walk up and down in the open air within the shadow of the hall, preaching the profound and subtle Dharma to the bhikṣus.
Having seen this, the Venerable Vāsiṣṭha said: "Worthy Bālapa!

You should know that the Blessed One has arisen from his meditation in the late afternoon, descended from the hall, and is walking up and down in the open air within the shadow of the hall, teaching the profound and subtle Dharma to the bhikṣus."
"Worthy Bālapa! Let us go together to the Buddha; perhaps we may hear the Dharma from him because of this.
Thereupon, Vāseṭṭha and Bālapa went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and followed behind him as he walked up and down.
The Blessed One turned back and addressed those two men: "Vāseṭṭha!

When you two brahmins, having renounced the brahmin caste, shaved off your hair and beards, donned saffron robes, and with deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the path—did the other brahmins not reprimand you severely upon seeing you?"
He replied: "Indeed,
World-Honored One!"
When the brahmins saw him, they rebuked and censured him most severely, with great urgency and harshness.
The World-Honored One asked: “Vāseṭṭha!
“World-Honored One, when those brahmins see [this], why do they rebuke and reproach him so excessively, with such urgency and severity?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!”
When the various brahmins saw us, they said:
"The brahmin caste is superior; others are not equal to it.
The brahmin caste is white; all others are black."
A brahmin attains purity; one who is not a brahmin does not attain purity.
A brahmin is the son of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, and is Brahmā himself.
"You have abandoned the superior for the inferior, and abandoned the white for the black. That shaven-headed śramaṇa is bound by the black; he has severed his lineage and is without offspring.
Therefore, what you have done is a great evil, and you have committed a most grievous transgression."
"World-Honored One!
When the various brahmins see us, they rebuke and reproach us in this manner with such extreme urgency and severity.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Vāsiṭṭha! What those brahmins have said is utterly wicked and extremely base. Why is that?
It refers to those who are deluded and lack discernment; failing to recognize a fertile field and unable to know themselves, they speak thus:
"We brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā."
Why is this so? Vāsiṭṭha!
This unsurpassed clarity, practice, and realization of mine does not speak of birth as superior, nor does it speak of lineage, nor does it speak of pride.
"He approves of my views and does not approve of my views; it is because of his sitting, because of his water, and because of the scriptures he has studied.
Vāseṭṭha! If there were those engaged in marriage, they would have to speak of birth, they would have to speak of lineage, and they would have to speak of pride:
"He approves of my views and disapproves of my views; he is attached to sitting, to water, and to the scriptures he has studied.
Vāseṭṭha! If there are those who calculate by birth, calculate by clan, or calculate with pride, they are utterly far removed from my unsurpassed clarity, practice, and realization.
Vāseṭṭha! To speak of birth, to speak of lineage, to speak of pride—saying, "He agrees with my views, he does not agree with my views;
it is because of his sitting, because of his water, or because of the scriptures he has studied"—these have no distinction from my unsurpassed clear knowledge, conduct, and realization.
Furthermore, Vāseṭṭha!

There are three kinds of things that cause all people to dispute with one another, which are a mixture of wholesome and unwholesome qualities; these are then either praised or not praised by the noble ones.
What are the three?
They are the kṣatriya caste, the brāhmaṇa caste, and the householder caste. Vāsiṣṭha!
What do you think? If a kṣatriya kills living beings,
takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and so on up to holding wrong views— and if a householder does the same—
is he not likewise a non-Brahmin?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Kṣatriyas may likewise kill living beings, take what is not given, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, and even hold wrong views; the same is true for brahmins and householders.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Vāseṭṭha, what do you think?"

"Brahmins abstain from killing, renounce killing, refrain from taking what is not given, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from false speech, and so on, up to abstaining from wrong views and attaining right view;
is it not the same for kṣatriyas and householders?"
He replied:
“World-Honored One!

A brahmin may likewise abstain from killing, sever killing, refrain from taking what is not given, refrain from sexual misconduct, and refrain from false speech, up to and including abstaining from wrong views and attaining right view.”
"It is the same for the kṣatriyas and the householders.
The World-Honored One asked: "Vāseṭṭha!"
What do you think?
Are there not immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas practiced by kṣatriyas and householders,
but not by brahmins?
"If there are immeasurable wholesome dharmas, are these practiced by the brahmins,
and not by the kṣatriyas or householders?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
If there are immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas, those kṣatriyas and householders may practice them as well, and the brahmins are likewise so.”
“If there are immeasurable wholesome qualities, those brahmins may practice them as well; it is the same for kṣatriyas and householders too.
“Vāsiṣṭha! [he said.]
There may be immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas that are practiced exclusively by kṣatriyas and householders, but not by brahmins.
There may be immeasurable wholesome dharmas that are practiced exclusively by brahmins, but not by kṣatriyas and householders.
Those brahmins may indeed say:
"We brahmins are the sons of Brahmā; we were born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, the progenitor. Why is this so?

Vāseṭṭha! One sees a brahmin woman at the time of her first marriage; after the marriage, one sees her when she is pregnant; after she has become pregnant, one sees her when she gives birth—either a boy or a girl.
Vāseṭṭha! These brahmins are likewise subject to the laws of the world; they too are born from the birth canal. Yet, they speak falsely and slanderfully regarding Brahmā, making this claim:
"We brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, born from his mouth, created by Brahmā."

“Vāseṭṭha! Whether a son of good family, or one of various clans, or one of various names, having abandoned various families, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the path under me—he should speak thus:
‘We brahmins are the sons of Brahmā; we were born from his mouth; we are created by Brahmā, the Great Brahmā.’”
"And why is that? Vāsiṭṭha!

Because that son of good family has entered my True Dharma and Discipline, received my True Dharma and Discipline, and reached the further shore; having severed doubt and crossed over delusion, he is free from hesitation and has attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the World-Honored One."
Therefore, they should say this:
"We brahmins are the sons of Brahmā; we were born from his mouth, created by Brahmā, the Great Brahmā. Vāseṭṭha!

That Brahmā is said to be the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. "Brahmā" refers to the Tathāgata; "coolness" refers to the Tathāgata; being without affliction and without fever, and not departing from suchness—this is the Tathāgata.
Vāsiṣṭha! What do you think?
Do the Śākyas humble themselves, out of love, respect, and profound veneration, to provide offerings and serve King Prasenajit of Kośala?
He replied: “It is so,
World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Vāseṭṭha, what do you think?"

If the Śākyas direct their minds toward me with love, respect, and the utmost reverence, making offerings and serving me, would King Prasenajit of Kosala likewise direct his mind toward my person with love, respect, and the utmost reverence, making offerings and serving me?
He replied to the Blessed One:
"That the Śākyas humble themselves with profound affection and reverence, making offerings and serving King Prasenajit of Kośala, is nothing extraordinary."

"It is truly extraordinary that King Prasenajit of Kosala, having lowered his mind with such deep affection, reverence, and great respect, makes offerings and serves the World-Honored One," [the King said].
The World-Honored One replied, "Vāsiṣṭha!"
King Prasenajit of Kosala did not think in such a manner; rather, he felt deep affection and reverence for my person, honoring and serving me with the utmost gravity, thinking:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama is of an exceedingly high lineage, while my own lineage is low."
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses vast wealth and treasures, whereas my wealth and treasures are meager.
The śramaṇa Gautama’s physical form is most exquisite, whereas my form is not exquisite.
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great majestic power, whereas my majestic power is slight.
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses wholesome wisdom, whereas I possess unwholesome wisdom. "Vāsiṣṭha!

It is simply because King Prasenajit of Kosala loves and respects the Dharma, and out of his profound reverence and service toward it, that he directs his humble mind toward me with love and respect, and offers me profound reverence, worship, and service."
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Vāsiṣṭha! There comes a time when this world is completely destroyed.”

When this world is destroyed, if there are beings born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, they there possess exquisite forms born of mind; all their limbs and sense faculties are complete; they take joy as food, possess self-radiance, ascend into the void, and dwell for a long time in pure form.

Vāseṭṭha! At times this great earth is filled with water; upon that great mass of water, stirred by the wind, it coagulates into essence, gathering and combining together, just as when milk is churned, it coagulates into essence, gathering and combining together.
In this way, Vāseṭṭha!

At one time, this great earth was filled with water. Upon that great body of water, stirred by the wind, it condensed into essence; through its gathering and combination, from this the "taste of earth" (pṛthivī-rasa) arose, possessing color, fragrance, and flavor.
What is its color?
It is like the color of fresh butter or refined butter.
What is its taste?
"It is like the taste of a honey ball.
Vāseṭṭha! There comes a time when this world is once again formed.

If there are beings born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven who, when their lifespan, karma, merit, and life have all come to an end, pass away and are reborn here as humans; having been born in this world, they possess a wondrous form born of mind, with all limbs and sense faculties complete; they feed on joy, their bodies emit radiance, they ascend into the sky, and their pure form abides for a long time."
Vāsiṣṭha! At that time, there were no sun or moon in the world, nor were there the constellations; there was no day or night, no month or fortnight, and no seasons or years.

Vāsiṣṭha! At that time, there will be no fathers and no mothers, no males and no females; furthermore, there will be no great families, nor will there be slaves or servants—there will be only equal sentient beings.
Then, there was a sentient being who was gluttonous and lacked integrity, and he thought to himself:
"What is this 'earth-flavor'?
I should perhaps take some of this earth-flavor with my finger and taste it."
At that time, sentient beings then took some of this essence of the earth with their fingers and tasted it.
Thus, once sentient beings had come to know the essence of the earth, they desired to eat it further.
At that time, sentient beings again had this thought:
"Why do we eat this essence of the earth with our fingers, thereby exhausting ourselves?
It would be better for us now to take handfuls of this essence of the earth and eat it."
At that time, those beings began to take handfuls of this earth-flavor and eat it.
Among those beings, there were others who, seeing those beings each taking handfuls of this earth-flavor and eating it, thought to themselves:
"This is truly good; this is truly pleasant. We too should take handfuls of this earth-flavor and eat it."
At that time, those beings took handfuls of this essence of the earth with their hands and ate it.
As they did so, their bodies became increasingly thick, heavy, and solid; whatever pure radiance they had previously possessed vanished, and darkness naturally arose.

"Vāsiṣṭha! According to the natural law of the world, such things occur spontaneously: when darkness arises, the sun and moon necessarily arise; once the sun and moon have arisen, the constellations arise; once the constellations have arisen, day and night are formed; once day and night have been formed, there are months, half-months, seasons, and years."
They ate the essence of the earth and dwelt for a very long time.

"Vāsiṭṭha! Among those beings, those who ate much of the essence of the earth developed an unattractive appearance, while those who ate little of the essence of the earth developed a beautiful appearance. From this, it was known that there were superior and inferior appearances; and because of these superior and inferior appearances, beings began to disparage one another, saying: [...]"
"I am superior in physical form; your form is inferior.
Because they gave rise to arrogance and unwholesome states due to such superiority and inferiority regarding their forms, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) then vanished.
Once the essence of the earth had vanished, those beings gathered together and, weeping most piteously, spoke these words:
"What is this 'earth-flavor'?
What is this 'earth-flavor'?

It is like a person today who chews a delicious substance and does not speak its original name; although they possess it, they do not know its meaning. This explanation of the meaning of contemplation is also like this.
Vāsiṭṭha! After the disappearance of the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa), those beings produced the "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), which possessed color, fragrance, and flavor.
What was its color?
It is like the color of fresh butter or refined butter.
What is its taste?
It is like the taste of a honey pill.
They consumed the essence of this earth and remained in the world for a very long time.

"Vāsiṣṭha! Among those beings, those who consumed much of the earth's essence developed an unattractive appearance, while those who consumed little of the earth's essence developed a beautiful appearance. From this, it was known that there were degrees of superiority and inferiority in appearance; because of these differences in appearance, beings began to disparage one another, saying: [...]"
"I am superior in physical form; your form is inferior.
Because of this superiority and inferiority regarding their forms, they gave rise to arrogance and unwholesome states, and consequently, the earth-fertility perished.
Once the earth-fertility had perished, those beings gathered together and, weeping most piteously, spoke these words:
"How is it that the ground is fertile?
How is it that the ground is fertile?

This is like people today who, when criticized by others, do not speak of their original name; though they uphold [the teachings], they do not know their meaning. This explanation of contemplating the meaning is also like this.
"Vāsiṭṭha! After the essence of the earth had perished, those beings were born upon the *bala* plants, which possessed color, fragrance, and flavor.
What was their color?"
Its color is like that of the *utpala* flower.
What is its taste?
It is like the taste of a ball of thick honey.
"By eating this *pāla*, they dwelt in the world for a very long time.

'Vāsiṭṭha! If there were beings who ate much *pāla*, they would develop an unattractive complexion; those who ate little *pāla* would have a beautiful complexion. From this, it was known that there were degrees of excellence and inferiority in complexion. Because of these differences in complexion, beings began to disparage one another, saying:'"
"I am superior in physical form; your form is not as good as mine.
Because of this superiority and inferiority regarding physical form, they gave rise to arrogance and unwholesome states, and thus the *brahma* vanished.
Once the *brahma* had vanished, those sentient beings gathered together and, weeping most piteously, spoke these words:
"How is it, Vaira? How is it, Vaira?

This is like people today who, when touched by suffering phenomena, do not speak the original words; though they receive and uphold them, they do not know their meaning. This explanation of contemplating the meaning is also like this.

“Vāsiṣṭha! After the Brahmasahambhas had passed away, those beings were born with naturally grown non-glutinous rice that was pure white and without husks or chaff; it was four inches long, growing back in the evening if harvested in the morning, and growing back in the morning if harvested in the evening. When ripe, it had a salty flavor and lacked any sign of decay.”

The sentient beings eat this naturally grown non-glutinous rice; after those sentient beings have eaten this naturally grown non-glutinous rice, various forms arise among them: some sentient beings take on male forms, while others take on female forms.
If those beings are born with the forms of males or females, upon seeing one another, they speak thus:
"Evil beings have been born! Evil beings have been born!"
“Vāsiṣṭha! Those beings who are born as ‘evil’ are said to be women.

If those beings are born with male or female forms, they then watch one another; having watched one another, they gaze at one another with their eyes; having gazed at one another, they become impassioned; having become impassioned, they experience feverish distress; having experienced feverish distress, they become attached to one another; and having become attached, they engage in sexual desire.”
If they see someone engaging in sexual desire, they immediately strike or pelt them with wood, stones, staffs, or clods of earth, saying:
"Ho! You wretched and evil being, you are committing an unrighteous act!"
"How do sentient beings collectively perform this?
It is just as when people nowadays welcome a new bride, scattering flower bundles or hanging flower garlands, and saying these words:
'May the new bride be at peace; may the new bride be at peace.'"
"What was formerly detestable is now beloved. Vāsiṭṭha!

If there are sentient beings who find the unwholesome and impure dharmas loathsome, who feel aversion and shame, and who possess a sense of moral dread, they will then separate themselves from the crowd for one day, two days, up to six or seven days, half a month, a month, or even a year."
"Vāsiṣṭha! If there are sentient beings who wish to practice this impure conduct, they establish a household and say:
'One commits evil here; one commits evil here.'"

"Vāseṭṭha! This is called the first cause and the first condition for the worldly practice of establishing households; it is the ancient, foremost wisdom, which is in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma—the wisdom honored by those who follow the Dharma."
Among them, there was a certain indolent being who thought to himself:
"Why do I take the naturally grown rice day after day? I would rather take enough for one day's meal all at once."
He then took the rice for one day’s meal all at once.
Thereupon, another being said to that being: “O being!...”
"Come, let us go together to fetch rice.
He replied, "I have already fetched it all; you may take it yourself."
Having heard this, those beings thought to themselves:
"This is truly good; this is truly excellent. Might I not also take the rice intended for tomorrow's meal?"
He then took the rice for the next day as well.
Furthermore, another sentient being said to that sentient being:
"Sentient being!..."
"Come, let us go together to fetch rice.
He replied, "I have already brought enough rice for tomorrow as well; you may take it yourself."
Having heard this, those beings thought to themselves:
"This is truly good; this is truly excellent. Would it not be better for me to take seven days' worth of rice all at once?"
Then, those beings immediately gathered seven days' worth of rice at once.
