As those beings took such a great quantity of naturally grown non-glutinous rice and accumulated it, the previously harvested rice began to sprout husks; even that harvested seven days prior began to sprout husks, and wherever it was cut, it no longer grew again.
Thereupon, those beings gathered together and wept most piteously, saying these words:
"We have given rise to evil and unwholesome states, namely that we have stored up last year's rice."

Why is this? We originally possessed a wondrous form born of mind, with all our limbs and sense faculties complete; we took joy as our food, our bodies were self-luminous, we ascended into the void, and our pure form endured for a long time. From that place where we were born, there was the "taste of the earth," which possessed color, fragrance, and flavor.
What is its color?
It is like the color of fresh butter or refined butter.
What is its taste?
It was like the taste of a honey ball.
We lived for a very long time subsisting on the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*).

Among us, those who ate too much of the essence of the earth developed an unattractive complexion, while those who ate little possessed a beautiful complexion. From this, it became known that there were distinctions of superiority and inferiority in complexion. Because of these differences in complexion, we began to disparage one another, saying: [The original Chinese text continues with the disparagement.]
"Your complexion is inferior to mine.

Because of such thoughts of superiority regarding their complexions, and because of the resulting arrogance and unwholesome states, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) vanished. After the essence of the earth had vanished, the "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) appeared for us, possessing color, fragrance, and flavor.
What is its color?
It is like the color of fresh butter or clarified butter.
What is its taste?
It was like the taste of a honey ball.
We sustained ourselves for a long time by eating this earth-fat (*pṛthivī-rasa*).

Among us, those who ate much of the earth-fat developed an unattractive complexion, while those who ate little of the earth-fat possessed a beautiful complexion. From this, it became known that there were differences of superiority and inferiority in complexion; because of these differences in complexion, we began to disparage one another, saying: [...]* *Note: The original text fragment ends with "言" (saying), indicating the beginning of the verbal exchange of contempt.*
"I am superior in physical form; your form is inferior.
Because of this superiority and inferiority regarding physical form, contempt and unwholesome states arose, and consequently, the earth-fat vanished.
After the earth-fat had vanished, we were born as *pāla* [vegetation], possessing color, fragrance, and flavor.
What is its color?
It is like the color of the kunda flower.
What is its taste?
"It is like the taste of a ball of thick honey.
We eat *pāra* and dwell in this world for a very long time.

If we eat much *pāra*, our complexion becomes foul; if we eat little *pāra*, our complexion becomes excellent. From this, we know that there are degrees of excellence and inferiority in complexion. Because of these differences in complexion, we began to disparage one another, saying:"

"I am superior in physical form; your form is inferior. Because of such thoughts of superiority and inferiority regarding physical form, arrogance and unwholesome states arose, and thus the *pāla* vanished. After the *pāla* had vanished, we were born with naturally occurring *śāli* rice—pure white, without husks, and without red powder.

It was four inches long; if harvested in the morning, it grew by evening, and if harvested in the evening, it grew by morning. When ripe, it had a salty flavor and lacked any sign of decay. We ate that naturally occurring *śāli* rice. As we took more than our share and hoarded it, the overnight *śāli* rice developed husks and red powder. By the time it was harvested for the seventh day, it too had developed husks and red powder. Wherever it was harvested, it no longer grew back. "What if we were to cultivate fields and establish boundary markers? they said.
"Then, the sentient beings began to cultivate fields and established boundary markers.
Among them was one being who possessed his own rice but entered another's field to steal that person's rice. When the owner saw this, he spoke these words: 'Hey!'"
"Shame! You wretched and evil being, why have you done this?
You possess your own rice, yet you enter another's field to steal that man's rice."
"You may go now; do not do this again.

However, that being stole another's rice a second and even a third time. When the owner had likewise seen him do so a second and a third time, he struck him with his fist, led him to the assembly, and said to the assembly:
"This being has his own rice, yet he enters my field and steals my rice."
Then that one being also said to the assembly:
"This one being struck me with his fist and dragged me here to the assembly.
Thereupon, all those beings gathered together and, weeping most piteously, spoke these words:
“We have given rise to evil and unwholesome states, namely, the guarding of fields.
Why is this? Because of the guarding of fields, we engage in disputes and litigation; there is loss and exhaustion, there is mutual slander, and there is the striking of fists.”

"We would rather select from among this multitude one who is handsome in appearance, most excellent and foremost, and establish him as the Lord of the Fields (Kṣetrapati). If there is anyone who should be censured, let him censure them; if there is anyone who should be expelled, let him expel them. And whatever rice we obtain, we shall deliver it to him in accordance with the Dharma."

Thereupon, among those beings, whoever was handsome in form and appearance, most exquisite and foremost, the multitude together raised him up and established him as the Lord of the Fields (*kṣetrapati*). If there was anyone who deserved reprimand, they would reprimand him; if there was anyone who deserved expulsion, they would expel him. And if there were rice, they would deliver it to that Lord of the Fields according to the law.

The master of this field is called a *kṣatriya*; he who causes sentient beings to dwell in happiness according to the Dharma and who guards and practices the precepts is a king; such a king is truly called a king.

Vāseṭṭha! This is called the first cause and the first condition by which, in this world, those of the kṣatriya caste are traditionally regarded as the foremost in wisdom, acting according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma, and being honored by people for their accordance with the Dharma.

"Thereupon, those other beings regarded guarding as a disease, guarding as an abscess, and guarding as a piercing arrow; they abandoned guarding, relied upon non-action, built huts of grass and leaves, and practiced meditation."
From that state of non-action, every morning at dawn, he enters villages, towns, and royal cities to beg for alms. When many beings see him, they give to him with reverence and respect, saying:

"This extraordinary being regards guarding as a disease, guarding as an abscess, and guarding as a piercing arrow; he has thus abandoned guarding and, relying on non-action, dwells in a hut of grass and leaves to practice meditation."
"These venerable ones who have abandoned harm and unwholesome, evil states are brahmins; it is because they are brahmins that they are called 'brahmins.

Those beings, having studied meditation but not attaining meditation, having studied asceticism but not attaining asceticism, having studied seclusion but not attaining seclusion, having studied one-pointedness of mind but not attaining one-pointedness of mind, and having studied diligence but not attaining diligence, then abandoned their secluded life and returned to villages, towns, and royal cities, where they built four-pillared houses and composed scriptures.
When many sentient beings have seen this, they no longer offer gifts, nor do they show him honor or respect, but instead say:

"This other being originally took guarding as his illness, took guarding as his abscess, and took guarding as his thorn; he then abandoned guarding and relied on seclusion, building a hut of grass and leaves to practice meditation but failing to attain it, practicing asceticism but failing to achieve it, practicing solitude but failing to attain it, practicing one-pointedness of mind but failing to attain it, and practicing diligence but failing to achieve it. He has now abandoned seclusion and returned to villages and royal cities, building four-pillared houses and composing scriptures."
"These venerable ones further study and become widely learned; they no longer study meditation, for this wide learning is what is called 'wide learning.
Thus spoke Vāseṭṭha.

This is called the first cause and the first condition by which there exists in the world the brahmin caste, possessing ancient and supreme knowledge, acting according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma, and being honored by people for their accordance with the Dharma.
"Then, those other beings each went to various directions to engage in agricultural work; because they each engaged in agricultural work in various directions, they were called *vessa*."

Vāsiṭṭha! This is called the first cause and the first condition by which there exist in the world the Vaiśya caste, who possess the ancient, foremost wisdom, who act according to the Dharma and not contrary to the Dharma, and whom people revere for their accordance with the Dharma.
“Vāseṭṭha, once these three castes have arisen in the world, one then knows there is a fourth, the caste of recluses.
How is it that, when these three castes exist in the world, one then knows there is a fourth, the caste of recluses?

Among the kṣatriya caste, a son of good family is able to reproach himself for evil and unwholesome states, and feels personal revulsion toward evil and unwholesome states; having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, he goes forth from home into homelessness out of deep faith to study the Path, thinking:
"I shall become a śramaṇa and practice the holy life."
He then becomes a śramaṇa and practices the holy life (brahmacarya).

In this same way, sons of noble families from the Brahmin caste or the Vaiśya caste also censure within themselves evil and unwholesome states, and out of self-loathing and aversion for evil and unwholesome states, they shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to study the Path.
They also think: "I shall become a śramaṇa and practice the holy life."
"Then one becomes a śramaṇa and practices the holy life (brahmacarya). Vāseṭṭha!
Thus, once these three castes have arisen in the world, one then knows that there is a fourth, the caste of śramaṇas."
“Vāsiṭṭha! I shall now explain these three castes in detail.
In what way do these three castes exist in such abundance?”
A son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste who practices unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, experience nothing but suffering.

In this way, sons of noble families from the Brahmin caste or the Vaiśya caste who practice unwholesome deeds of body, and unwholesome deeds of speech and mind, will experience nothing but suffering when their bodies perish at the end of life.

Vāseṭṭha! A son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste who practices wholesome conduct with his body and wholesome conduct with his speech and mind, upon the dissolution of the body after death, experiences exclusively happiness.

In this way, sons of noble families from the Brahmin caste or the Vaiśya caste who practice wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, experience exclusively happiness.

Vāseṭṭha! A son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste, who practices two courses of action by way of body as well as restraint, and two courses of action by way of speech and mind as well as restraint—when his body breaks up at the end of life, he experiences both suffering and pleasure.

In this way, sons of noble family from the Brahmin caste or the Vaiśya caste who practice two kinds of conduct regarding the body along with protective conduct, and two kinds of conduct regarding speech and mind along with protective conduct, will experience both suffering and pleasure upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life.

“Vāseṭṭha! A son of noble family from the Kṣatriya caste, practicing the factors of awakening, reflecting well and contemplating well, comes to know thus and see thus: his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence and ignorance. Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this he knows as it truly is.”

In this way, sons of noble family from the Brahmin caste or the Vaiśya caste who cultivate the factors of awakening and practice them with right reflection and right contemplation come to know thus and see thus: their minds are liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, and their minds are liberated from the outflows of existence and ignorance. Being liberated, they know they are liberated; they know truly: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Vāsiṣṭha! Thus these three types have been extensively analyzed.
The Brahmā Lord of Devas spoke this verse:
“The Kṣatriya is the most honored among bipeds;
being of noble lineage, he seeks to train in knowledge and conduct, and thus he is praised by gods and humans.”
"Vāseṭṭha! The Lord of the Brahmā Heaven has well spoken this verse; it is not ill-spoken.
He has well sung and recited it; it is not ill-sung."
His speech is well-recited and not ill-spoken.
He speaks thus:
"The Kṣatriya is the most honored among bipeds; he is said to possess a noble lineage."
"One who seeks learning, clarity, and practice is praised by gods and humans. Why is this so?
For I also speak thus:
“The Kṣatriya is the most honored among bipeds;
being of noble lineage, he seeks to train in knowledge and conduct, and thus he is praised by devas and humans.”
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the Venerable Vāsiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and the other bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Bālapaṇḍita Sūtra, the third, ends here; five thousand and sixty-eight characters. 155. The Sudatta Sūtra (155), Middle Āgama, Chapter on Brahmins, Sudatta Sūtra, the fourth; the third recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the householder Sudatta went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in greeting, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The World-Honored One asked him:
"Householder, does your family practice giving?"
The householder Sudatta replied:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"The almsgiving practiced at home is merely coarse and cannot be considered excellent;
it consists of rice with the husks, hemp soup, and a single slice of ginger and vegetables.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Householder!
Whether one gives coarse food or exquisite food, both yield their respective fruits.
Householder!”

If one practices coarse giving—giving without faith, without intentionality, not with one's own hands, not going in person to give, without reflection, not out of conviction, and without regard for the karmic fruits and retributions—one should contemplate that such is the retribution one will receive.

The mind does not desire a fine home, does not desire fine vehicles, does not desire fine clothing and bedding, does not desire fine food and drink, and does not desire the excellence of the five sensual pleasures.
Why is this? It is because they practice giving without a sincere heart.
Householder!
One should know that the retribution received is like this,

householder! If one practices coarse giving— giving with faith, intentional giving, giving with one's own hand, giving by going in person, giving with reflection, giving out of conviction, or giving while contemplating the karmic results of action— one should contemplate the reception of such retribution in this way.

The mind desires to obtain a good home, desires to obtain good vehicles, desires to obtain fine clothing and bedding, desires to obtain excellent food and drink, and desires to obtain the merits of the five objects of sensual pleasure.
Why is this? It is because one practices giving with a most sincere mind.
Householder!
"You should know that the retribution received is thus. Householder!

If one practices a sublime gift, yet gives without faith, gives without intentionality, does not give with one's own hand, does not go in person to give, does not give with reflection, does not give out of trust, and does not give while contemplating the karmic results of action—then you should observe that such is the retribution received."

The mind does not desire a fine home, does not desire fine vehicles, does not desire fine clothing and bedding, does not desire fine food and drink, and does not desire the excellence of the five objects of sensual pleasure.
Why is this? It is because they practice giving without a sincere heart.
Householder!
One should know that the experience of retribution is thus.
Householder!

If one practices sublime giving—giving with faith, intentional giving, giving with one's own hand, going in person to give, giving with reflection, giving out of conviction, and giving while contemplating the ripening of karmic results—one should contemplate the experience of such retribution.
The mind desires a good family, desires fine vehicles, desires excellent clothing and bedding, desires superior food and drink, and desires the excellence of the five objects of sensual pleasure.
Why is this? It is because one practices giving with a sincere heart,
householder!
"You should know that the retribution received is like this. Householder!

In the past, there was a brahmin great householder named Sūlambha, who was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable assets. He held many fiefdoms and estates filled with various treasures, and his livestock and industries were beyond calculation."

His practice of giving was of such a nature: he performed great acts of charity by offering eighty-four thousand golden bowls filled with crushed silver, and he performed great acts of charity by offering eighty-four thousand silver bowls filled with crushed gold.
He performed such great acts of giving as these: he offered eighty-four thousand golden bowls filled with gold dust, and he performed such great acts of giving as these:
he offered eighty-four thousand silver bowls filled with silver dust.
He performed such a great act of giving as this: eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned and magnificently decorated, with white trappings covering their backs;
he performed such a great act of giving as this: eighty-four thousand horses, adorned and magnificently decorated, with white trappings and golden *piṇa* ornaments.

He performed such great acts of giving as these: eighty-four thousand cows, covered with cloth and ropes, each yielded one *sheng* of milk when milked; he likewise performed such great acts of giving as these:
eighty-four thousand women, of upright and beautiful countenance, who brought joy to all who beheld them, fully adorned with various precious necklaces and ornaments.
"How much more so for other foods that are chewed, swallowed, and digested?

Householder, if a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and if another were to give food sufficient to satisfy all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, this latter gift would be far superior to that former one."
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa, yet another person were to give a meal to even a single *srotāpanna*, the latter gift would be far superior to that former one."
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for a hundred stream-enterers (srotāpanna), yet another were to provide food for even a single once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin)—this latter gift would be superior to that former one."
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, providing food to all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, and providing food to one hundred stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and one hundred once-returners (sakṛdāgāmin), yet another person were to provide food to even a single non-returner (anāgāmin)—this latter gift would be superior to that former sacrifice."
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for one hundred stream-enterers, one hundred once-returners, and one hundred non-returners—yet if there were another who were to provide food for even a single arhat, this latter gift would be superior to that former one."
“Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, providing food for all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, and providing food for one hundred stream-enterers, one hundred once-returners, one hundred non-returners, and one hundred arhats; yet if there were another who were to provide food for even a single pratyekabuddha, this latter gift would be superior to that former one.”
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for a hundred stream-enterers, a hundred once-returners, a hundred non-returners, a hundred arhats, and a hundred pratyekabuddhas; yet if there were another who were to provide food for even one Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—this latter gift would be far superior to that former gift."
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for a hundred stream-enterers, a hundred once-returners, a hundred non-returners, a hundred arhats, and a hundred pratyekabuddhas; yet if someone were to build a dwelling and offer it to the community of bhikṣus from the four quarters, this would be far superior to that gift."
“Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great giving, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary persons throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for a hundred stream-enterers, a hundred once-returners, a hundred non-returners, a hundred arhats, and a hundred pratyekabuddhas, and build dwellings to give to the community of bhikṣus from the four directions—yet if there were someone who, with a joyful heart, takes refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and receives the precepts, this would be far superior to that giving.”
"Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, providing food for all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, and providing food for a hundred srotāpannas, a hundred sakṛdāgāmins, a hundred anāgāmins, a hundred arhats, and a hundred pratyekabuddhas; and if he were to build dwellings and offer them to the community of bhikṣus from the four directions, and with a joyful mind take refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and receive the precepts; yet if there were someone who practiced loving-kindness toward all those sentient beings for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, this would be far superior to that gift."
“Householder!

If a brahmin such as Sūlambha were to perform such a great sacrifice, and furthermore provide food for all the ordinary people throughout Jambudvīpa, and provide food for a hundred stream-enterers, a hundred once-returners, a hundred non-returners, a hundred arhats, and a hundred pratyekabuddhas; and if he were to build dwellings and offer them to the community of bhikṣus from the four directions, and with a joyful mind take refuge in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—and receive the precepts, and practice loving-kindness toward all sentient beings for even as long as it takes to milk a cow; yet if there were someone who could contemplate all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, this latter person’s practice would be far superior to that sacrifice.”
"What do you think, householder?
Was that brahmin great householder named Sūlambha someone else in the past?
Do not think so."
Why is this? You should know that he was none other than myself.
In the past, I was a brahmin great householder named Sūlana.
"Householder!

At that time, for my own benefit, as well as for the benefit of others, for the benefit of many people, out of compassion for the world, I sought what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, seeking their peace, security, and happiness."

At that time, the teaching of the Dharma did not reach its ultimate conclusion; it was not the ultimate purification, not the ultimate holy life, and the holy life was not brought to its final completion.
At that time, one was not yet free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow, nor had one yet attained liberation from all suffering.
"Householder!

I have now appeared in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat."

I now benefit myself and also benefit others; I benefit many people, out of compassion for the world, seeking what is meaningful and beneficial for gods and humans, and seeking their peace, security, and happiness.
I have now attained the ultimate in teaching the Dharma; it is the ultimate purity, the ultimate holy life, and the completion of the holy life.
I am now free from birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, and sorrow; I have now attained liberation from all suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the householder Sudatta and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Sudatta Sūtra*, the fourth, ends here, totaling one thousand five hundred and eighty-nine characters. 156. The *Brahmāyusūtra* (156), the fifth in the *Brāhmaṇa-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the fifth in the Fourth Sectioned Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, many brahmins of the Kośala country were wandering about in the afternoon when they went to where the Buddha was staying. Having exchanged greetings with one another, they sat down to one side and said to him: “Gotama!
"I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
The World-Honored One replied, "Ask whatever you wish."
Then, the brahmins asked: "Gautama!
Are there now any brahmins who study the ancient brahminical dharma, or have they transcended the ancient brahminical dharma?"
The Blessed One replied:
"Now there are no brahmins who study the ancient brahminical dharma; long ago, the brahmins already transcended the ancient brahminical dharma.
At that time, the brahmins asked:
"Gautama! Why is it that there are now no brahmins who study the ancient brahminical dharma? For how long have these brahmins transgressed the ancient brahminical dharma and come [to this state]?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Regarding those who existed in the past, Who disciplined themselves through arduous practice,
Renounced the fivefold qualities of sensual desire, And lived the pure holy life."
The holy life and the practice of precepts lead to a nature that is thoroughly gentle;
with a mind of forgiveness, clarity, and harmlessness, one maintains patience to guard the mind.
In ancient times there was this Dharma, yet the brahmins did not protect it.
The brahmin does not guard his wealth and grain;
he recites and studies [the texts on] wealth and grain. This is the treasury the brahmin guards:
clothing of various colors, houses, and couches.
In Fengcheng and in all other lands, the brahmins study in this manner;
let these brahmins not be harmed, for they uphold and protect all dharmas.
When they go to the gates of others, no one shall restrain them.
Having left his home to seek the Dharma, he arrived at the time of the meal.
While living as a brahmin in the household, those who saw him desired to give alms;
for forty-eight years, he practiced the pure holy life.
Seeking the perfection of clear conduct, one should practice as the brahmins did of old:
they did not steal others' property, nor did they harbor fear.
Bound by the bond of love, one should dwell in harmonious union with them.
Not for the sake of afflictions, one should not associate with those who consort with lust.
Among all those who are brahmins, none are able to practice in such a way;
if there were such a supreme practice, a brahmin would seek it with the utmost firmness.
Those who do not engage in any sexual practices even in their dreams,
and because of this practice of the holy life (brahmacarya), declare themselves to be "Brahmā, I am Brahmā";
knowing that they possess such conduct, the wise should understand them as such.
The bedding is thin and the clothing extremely sparse; life is sustained by consuming ghee and milk.
All begging is performed according to the Dharma; one observes the fast and practices giving.
During the time of the fast, there is no improper begging; one seeks only from oneself.
When establishing his altar and practicing generosity, he does not slaughter oxen;
he regards them as his parents, brothers, and other kinsmen.
People and oxen are likewise [to be treated]; through this, he gives rise to happiness.
When food and drink provide strength to the body, the rider enjoys peace and security.
Knowing this principle, do not take pleasure in killing oxen;
their bodies are soft and vast, and they possess a brilliant luster and renown.
Diligently seeking one's own benefit was the practice of the brahmins of old;
for the sake of their own welfare, they were devoted exclusively to what is beneficial and what is not.
Such a person, coming to this world, will surely cross over and be liberated from this world.
That moon passes beyond the moon; one beholds its intention directed toward that [realm].
It sports in the night, with adorned women surrounding it, led by auspicious oxen—women of supreme beauty.
The subtle desires of humans are the constant aspiration of the brahmin;
possessing a full set of vehicles and being skilled at tailoring and fine work are the constant aspirations of the brahmin.
Dwelling in a household and contracting marriages are the constant aspirations of the brahmin.
He created this bondage, and from him we have come.
O Great King, when practicing the fast and giving alms, do not lose its profit;
may you abound in wealth, goods, and grain, and whatever surplus money you possess.
The Great King associated with this: the Brahmin, the chariot, the elephant-fast, and the horse-fast; the horse-fast does not block the gate.
Gathering together to perform the fast and giving, he bestowed wealth and goods upon the Brahmins.
He gains profit from this, cherishing and begrudging his wealth.
Because he gives rise to desire, his craving increases again and again,
like the water of a vast pond and immeasurable material possessions.
Such people possess cattle; regarding the necessities of life, they create these bonds from which we have come.
O Great King, when you observe the fast and practice giving, do not lose the profit of your wealth.
Abounding in wealth, grain, and rice, and possessing many cattle— if you, Great King,
correspond to this description; if you, O Brahmin,
possess hundreds of thousands of countless oxen and carriages, yet slaughter them for the sake of a sacrificial feast.
His horns were not harmed; though he was once equal to an ox or a pig, he went and seized the ox by the horn, took a sharp blade, and killed it.
He called out to the ox and its owner—a *rākṣasa* named Gandha.
When he cried out "Unlawful! as he was stabbing the ox with a knife, this practice of the Dharma was observed during the fast;
having transcended [the world], he stood foremost, killing without cause and remaining far removed from the laws of decline.
In former times there were three diseases:
those who would not eat out of desire, and those who gave rise to ninety-eight diseases because of their hatred and envy toward cattle.
Thus, this increase of strife is for that reason loathed by the wise.
If one sees such things as these, who would not feel aversion?
Such conduct in this world is the mark of the most base and ignorant;
each acts out of desire for hatred, like a wife slandering her husband.
Whether a Kṣatriya woman or a Brāhmaṇa woman, even one who guards her lineage,
if she violates the laws of birth, she becomes subject to desire through her own will. "It is so."
“Brahmin! Now that there are no more Brahmins who study the Brahmin dharma, it has been this long since a Brahmin has transcended the Brahmin dharma.
Thereupon, many Brahmins from the Kosalā country said:
“World-Honored One!
I have understood. Sugata!”
"I have understood, World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the many brahmins and bhikṣus of the Kośala country rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Brahmāyusūtra, the fifth, ends here; nine hundred and fifty-nine characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume Thirty-nine; ten thousand six hundred and ninety characters.
Within the fourth *Vibhaṅga-bhāṇaka*, the Madhyama Āgama, Volume Forty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kapiśī during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
157. The Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Grove (157). Chapter on the Brahmins. The Sixth Sūtra on the Yellow Reed Grove.
Fourth Recitation Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Veḷuvana and staying in the Yellow Reed Grove.
At that time, the brahmin Vairaṇyā was aged and advanced in years; his life was drawing to a close and his end was near. At one hundred and twenty years of age, he walked leaning upon a staff.
After midday, while wandering about, he went to where the Buddha was staying. Having exchanged greetings with one another, he stood leaning on his staff before the Buddha and said: "Gautama!
"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama is extremely young and has only recently gone forth to study.

When śramaṇas or brahmins of renown and virtue come to visit him in person, he does not pay them homage, nor does he show them respect; he does not rise from his seat for them, nor does he invite them to sit."
"Gautama!
This matter is truly most unacceptable.
The World-Honored One replied:

“Brahmin! From among gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins—from humans up to the heavens—I have never yet seen anyone come before me who could cause the Tathāgata to pay homage, show respect, rise from his seat, and invite him to sit.”
"Brahmin!

If anyone should come to me wishing to have the Tathāgata pay them homage and show them respect, and should rise from their seat to invite the Tathāgata to sit, that person's head shall surely split into seven pieces."
The brahmin spoke again:
"Gautama, there is no flavor.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Brahmin! There is a matter that makes me tasteless, yet it is not as you say.

If there were tastes of forms, tastes of sounds, tastes of odors, tastes of flavors, or tastes of tangibles—the Tathāgata has severed them with knowledge, extinguished them, uprooted them, so that they shall never arise again. This is the matter that makes me tasteless, yet it is not as you say.”
The brahmin spoke again:
"Gautama, you have no fear.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Brahmin! There is a matter that makes me free from fear, yet it is not as you say.

If there were fear regarding form, or fear regarding sound, smell, taste, or touch, the Tathāgata has severed, extinguished, and uprooted them through his knowledge so that they shall never arise again; this is the matter that makes me free from fear, yet it is not as you say.”
The brahmin spoke again:
"Gautama, you do not enter a womb.
The World-Honored One replied:
“Brahmin! There is a reason why I do not enter a womb, yet it is not as you say.

If there be any śramaṇa or brahmin who, regarding the future bed of the womb, has severed knowledge [of craving], brought it to cessation, uprooted it so that it shall never arise again—I say that such a person does not enter a womb. The Tathāgata, regarding the future bed of the womb, has severed knowledge, brought it to cessation, uprooted it so that it shall never arise again; for this reason, I do not enter a womb.”
"This is what is meant by having a condition that prevents me from entering a womb, yet it is not as you say. O Brahmin!

Regarding these sentient beings who have come through ignorance, who delight in ignorance, who are shrouded by ignorance, and who are wrapped in the egg of ignorance—I first contemplated the Dharma, and among these sentient beings, I am the foremost."
It is like a hen that has laid ten or twelve eggs, which she attends to at the proper time, covers at the proper time, warms at the proper time, and protects at the proper time.

Later on, if the hen becomes negligent, there may be one among those chicks who, with its beak or its claws, pecks through the eggshell and emerges safely; that chick would be the foremost among them.

I am also like this: regarding these sentient beings who have come from ignorance, who delight in ignorance, who are shrouded by ignorance, and who are wrapped within the egg of ignorance—I first contemplate the Dharma, and I am the foremost among these sentient beings.

“Brahmin! I took bundles of *kuśa* grass and went to the Bodhi tree; I spread the grass beneath the tree, laid out my sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), and sat down cross-legged. Without breaking this formal posture, I resolved that I would not rise until the outflows were exhausted. I did not break this formal posture until the outflows were exhausted.”

Once I was seated, having become detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, filled with joy and happiness, I attained and dwelt in the first dhyāna. This, I say, was the first attainment of the higher mind that I achieved at that time; it was a dwelling in happiness in this very life, easily obtained and not difficult to attain, a joyful abode free from fear, secure and blissful, leading to the realization of Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, with internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, I attained and dwelt in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and happiness. This is what I call my attainment at that time of the second higher state of mind; it was a dwelling in peace and happiness in this very life, easily obtained and not with difficulty, a happy abode free from fear, secure and blissful, leading to the realization of Nirvana."
"Furthermore, brahmin!

With the fading away of joy, I dwelt in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; this is what the Noble Ones describe as 'equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness,' attaining and abiding in the third dhyāna. This, I say, was the third attainment of higher mind that I achieved at that time, whereby I attained a state of ease in this very life—attained without difficulty, dwelling in happiness free from fear, secure and blissful, leading to the ascent of Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, brahmin!

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, I entered and dwelt in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity. This, I say, was when I attained the fourth higher state of mind; I obtained a dwelling in happiness in this very life, easily and without difficulty, abiding in bliss without fear, secure and joyful, leading to the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

Having attained such a state of meditative concentration—pure, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and possessing an unshakable mind—I have realized and witnessed the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives."
I possess the practice and the characteristics [of this knowledge], recollecting my immeasurable past experiences— namely, one birth, two births, a hundred births,
a thousand births; aeons of formation, aeons of dissolution, and immeasurable aeons of both formation and dissolution—
in which those beings were named so-and-so, and as they passed through those times, I was born there with such a clan name.
With such a name, born in such a way, eating such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain,
having such a long life, abiding for such a duration, and at the end of such a lifespan— dying here and being reborn there,
dying there and being reborn here— I was born in this place, with such a clan, such a name, and such [a lineage].
"Such was my birth, such was my food and drink, such was the suffering and pleasure I experienced, such was my longevity,
such was my duration of stay, and such was the end of my life; this is what I call the first clear vision attained by me during the first watch of the night."

Because he was fundamentally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligent effort, it is said that ignorance was extinguished and wisdom arose, darkness was destroyed and light was established, and nescience was extinguished and knowledge arose; thus, through the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, he attained realization and clear penetration as his witness.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

Having attained such a state of concentration—purified, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and possessing an unshakable mind—I have cultivated and realized the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of death and rebirth. With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I see these beings as they die and are reborn—of beautiful or ugly appearance, excellent or inferior, passing away from or being born into good or bad destinations—and I see them exactly as they are, according to the karma these beings have performed."

If these sentient beings accomplish misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; possess right view and accomplish the karma of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavens.
This is called my attainment of this second clear knowledge during the middle watch of the night.

Because I was fundamentally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligence, ignorance ceased and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light was established; nescience ceased and wisdom arose—namely, the clear knowledge that bears witness to the understanding of birth and death.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

Having attained such a state of concentration—pure, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and unshakable—I have trained to realize the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I know this suffering as it truly is; I know the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are."
One knows these taints as they truly are; one knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, and my mind is liberated from the taint of existence and the taint of ignorance. Being liberated, I know I am liberated; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is.
This is what I call the third clear knowledge attained by me during the last watch of the night.

Because I was fundamentally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligence, ignorance was extinguished and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light was established; nescience was extinguished and wisdom arose—namely, the clear knowledge that realizes the destruction of the outflows.
"Furthermore, brahmin!

If there is one who speaks correctly, speaking the Dharma that is not delusive, and who, among all beings born into the world, is the most supreme and is not overwhelmed by suffering or pleasure—know that this one who speaks correctly is none other than myself."
Why is this? I speak of the dharma of non-delusion;
when sentient beings are born into the world, those who possess it are the most excellent of all sentient beings, for they are not obscured by suffering or pleasure.
Thereupon, the brahmin Vairaṇyāya immediately cast aside his staff, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The World-Honored One is foremost; the World-Honored One is great; the World-Honored One is supreme; the World-Honored One is victorious; the World-Honored One is equal; the World-Honored One is unequaled; the World-Honored One has no equal; the World-Honored One is without obstruction; the World-Honored One is one who has no obstructor.”
"Bhagavān!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the Bhagavān accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Vairaṭṭha and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth *Huanglu yuan jing* (The Sūtra of the Yellow Reed Grove) ends here, totaling 1,602 characters. 158. The *Tou na jing* (Sūtra of Tuṇḍa), the seventh in the *Brahma-varga* of the *Madhyama Āgama*, the fourth section of the Recitation Collection. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the brahmin Dhona, wandering about after the midday meal, went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side. The World-Honored One asked him: “Dhona!
"If anyone asks you, 'Are you a brahmin?
Do you declare yourself to be a brahmin?
how would you answer? The brahmin Thona replied:

“Gautama! If there is one who is rightly called a brahmin, he is one who is honored by his parents, whose birth is pure, and whose lineage of parents remains unbroken for seven generations; who has been free from evil life after life; who is widely learned and possesses total retention; who has recited the four Vedas and has deeply mastered the five modes of exposition: cause, condition, rightness, phrasing, and embellishment.”
"Gautama!
It is I who am truly called a brahmin. Why is that? Because..."

I was raised by my parents and born into purity; even through seven generations of ancestors, my lineage has remained unbroken. In every birth I have been free from evil. I am widely learned and possess total retention (*dhāraṇī*); I have recited the four Vedas and deeply mastered the five modes of exposition: cause, condition, directness, phrasing, and playful expression.
The Blessed One said:
“Tona! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit.”
"O Ṭhāna! What do you think?

If there were brahmins in the past who, at the end of their lives and the passing away of their term, had recited and mastered the scriptures, propagated the scriptures, and studied the sacred texts—namely, those called Yājñavalkya, Vāmadeva, Vāmadevya, Viśvāmitra, Nārada, Kāśyapa, Bhṛgu, Parāśara, Gautama, Ātreya, and Vasiṣṭha—it was said that these established five kinds of brahmins: a brahmin like Brahmā, a brahmin resembling a deva, a brahmin who does not transcend the boundary, a brahmin who transcends the boundary, and a fifth, the caṇḍāla brahmin."
"Thona! Of these five kinds of brahmins, to whom do you resemble? Thona replied:
“Gautama, you have briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis; I am unable to understand it.
I only pray that the Śramaṇa Gautama will explain it well so that I may understand its meaning.”
The World-Honored One said:
“Thona! Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in detail.”
Headanā replied:
"Indeed it is so, Gautama!"
The brahmin Ṭhāna accepted the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ṭhāna!
In what way is a brahmin like Brahmā?

Suppose there is a brahmin who is of noble birth by both his father and mother, pure in his origin, and whose lineage remains unbroken for seven generations back, with no evil conduct in each successive birth. For forty-eight years he practices the celibate life of a youth (*kumāra-brahmacarya*), desiring to acquire the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts.

Having obtained the scriptures and mastered the study of the canonical texts, he sought wealth and goods to make offerings to his teacher; this was done in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to it.
What would constitute being contrary to the Dharma?

It is not agriculture, nor the pursuit of livelihood; it is not writing, nor calculation, nor mathematics, nor sealing, nor calligraphy, nor composition, nor the study of scriptures, nor poetry; it is not by means of the sword or staff, nor is it the business of kings.

Seeking through lawful means, he seeks wealth and material goods to offer as support to his teacher; having given these gifts, his mind is imbued with loving-kindness, and he dwells having accomplished the pervasion of one direction.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
"Thona! In this way, the brahmin is just like Brahmā. Thona!"
In what way is a brahmin like a deva?
If there is a brahmin who is of noble birth by both parents, whose lineage is pure, and whose ancestral line remains unbroken for seven generations, being free from evil life after life.

For forty-eight years he practiced the celibate life of a youth, desiring to obtain scriptures and to study and recite the canonical texts. Having obtained those scriptures and completed his study and recitation of the canonical texts, he sought wealth and goods for the sake of making offerings to his teacher, doing so in accordance with the Dharma and not contrary to it.
What is that which is not in accordance with the Dharma?
It is not agriculture, nor trade, nor writing, nor calculation, nor arithmetic, nor sealing, nor calligraphy, nor composition, nor scripture, nor poetry, nor the use of weapons, nor royal service.

Seeking and begging in accordance with the Dharma, one seeks material goods to make offerings to the teacher. Having bestowed these material gifts, one practices sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind. Having practiced sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.
"Thona! Such a brahmin is like a deva.
"Thona! [he said.]
What is meant by a brahmin who does not transgress the boundaries?

If there is a brahmin who is of noble birth by both his father and mother, pure in origin, and whose lineage remains unbroken for seven generations back, with no evil deeds committed in each successive birth; if he practices the celibate life of a youth for forty-eight years, desiring to acquire the scriptures and to study and recite the canonical texts.

Having obtained the scriptures and mastered the study of the canonical texts, he sought wealth and goods to make offerings to his teacher; this was done in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to it.
What would constitute being contrary to the Dharma?

It is not agriculture, nor the pursuit of livelihood; it is not writing, nor calculation, nor mathematics, nor sealing, nor calligraphy, nor composition, nor the study of scriptures, nor poetry; it is not by means of the sword or staff, nor is it the business of kings.

He seeks and begs for wealth in accordance with the Dharma to provide offerings for his teacher; having given away that wealth as an offering, he then seeks a wife for himself in accordance with the Dharma, and not contrary to the Dharma.
What is it that is contrary to the Dharma?

It is not so for a brahmin: he does not set his mind upon a brahmin woman with the intent to cause mutual passion, to bind her to himself, and to unite with her; nor does he approach a woman who is not a brahmin, nor one who is not of the kṣatriya caste, nor one who is pregnant, nor one who is giving birth.
"O Headman!
For what reason do the brahmins not approach for conception?
Lest those men and women be called impure through sexual intercourse; therefore, the brahmins do not approach for conception."
"Thona! For what reason do the brahmins not engage in procreation?
Lest the names 'man' and 'woman' become associated with impurity and anger; for this reason, the brahmins do not engage in procreation."
Headman! That which he pursues is not for the sake of wealth, nor for pride, nor for adornment, nor for decoration; it is solely for the sake of his son.

Headana! Once that son has been born, if there are established boundaries, oaths, or ritual enclosures belonging to the ancient brahmins, he remains within them, adheres to them, and does not transgress them.
"In this way, Brahmin, one does not transcend the realm.
'Tona! How, then, does a Brahmin transcend the realm?"

If there is a brahmin who is well-born by both parents, pure in birth, such that his lineage remains unbroken for seven generations back, and who has been free from evil throughout each successive life; if he practices the celibate conduct of a youth for forty-eight years, desiring to acquire the scriptures and to recite and study the sacred texts.

Having obtained the scriptures and mastered the study of the canonical texts, he sought wealth and goods to make offerings to his teacher; this was done in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to it.
What would constitute acting contrary to the Dharma?

It is not agriculture, nor the pursuit of livelihood; it is not writing, nor calculation, nor arithmetic, nor sealing, nor calligraphy, nor composition, nor the study of scriptures, nor poetry; it is not by means of the sword or staff, nor is it the business of kingship.

He seeks and begs for wealth in accordance with the Dharma to provide offerings for his teacher; having bestowed that wealth as a gift, he seeks a wife for himself in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to the Dharma.
What is contrary to the Dharma?

A brahmin does not act in such a way as to direct his intentions toward a brahmin woman so that they may love one another, be united, and come together; he approaches a woman who is not a non-brahmin, nor a kṣatriya woman, one who is not pregnant, and one who has not given birth.
"Thona! For what reason do the brahmins not approach those who are pregnant?
Lest the names 'impure' and 'sexual intercourse' be applied to that man and woman; for this reason, the brahmins do not approach those who are pregnant."
"O Ṭhāna! For what reason do the brahmins not engage in sexual intercourse?
Lest the names 'man' and 'woman' become associated with impurity and anger; for this reason, the brahmins do not engage in sexual intercourse."
"Headman! That which he pursues is not for the sake of wealth, nor for pride, nor for adornment, nor for decoration; it is solely for the sake of his son."
Once he has fathered a son, if there are any former sites of vows by brahmins, or boundaries, or enclosures, he does not dwell therein, does not maintain them, and thus transcends them.
"Thona! In this way, a brahmin is said to have transcended the realms. Thona!"
What is a brahmin who is a *caṇḍāla* among brahmins?

Suppose there is a brahmin who is acknowledged by his parents, whose birth is pure, and whose lineage remains unbroken for seven generations of ancestors, with no evil conduct throughout those lives; he practices the celibate life of a student for forty-eight years, desiring to acquire the scriptures and to recite and study the canonical texts.

Having obtained the scriptures and mastered the study of the canonical texts, he sought wealth and goods to make offerings to his teacher; this was done in accordance with the Dharma, not contrary to it.
What would constitute being contrary to the Dharma?

It is not agriculture, nor the pursuit of livelihood; it is not writing, nor calculation, nor mathematics, nor sealing, nor calligraphy, nor composition, nor the study of scriptures, nor poetry; it is not by means of the sword or staff, nor is it the business of kings.

He seeks and begs for wealth in accordance with the Dharma to provide offerings for his teacher; having given that wealth as an offering, he then seeks a wife for himself in accordance with the Dharma, and not contrary to the Dharma.
What is it that is not in accordance with the Dharma?

A brahmin does not act in this way: he does not set his heart upon a brahmin woman so as to cause mutual affection, mutual attraction, and union; he does not approach a woman who is not a brahmin, nor one who is a kṣatriya, nor one who is pregnant, nor one who has recently given birth.
"O Ṭhāna! For what reason do the brahmins not approach a woman who is pregnant?
It is so that neither the man nor the woman shall be called by the name of 'impure sexual intercourse'; for this reason, the brahmins do not approach a pregnant woman."
"O Headman!
For what reason do the brahmins not engage in procreation?
Lest the names 'man' and 'woman' become associated with impurity and anger; for this reason, the brahmins do not engage in procreation."
"Headman! That which he pursues is not for the sake of wealth, nor for pride, nor for adornment, nor for ornamentation; it is solely for the sake of his son."
After he has fathered sons, he performs deeds appropriate for a king, deeds appropriate for a thief, and deeds appropriate for those on a wrong path, and speaks thus:
"A brahmin should perform all kinds of deeds; a brahmin is neither defiled nor stained by them, just as fire burns both the pure and the impure."
"A brahmin should not perform any actions; a brahmin is neither stained by them nor defiled by them.
Thus, Tona, such a brahmin is a "brahmin-cāṇḍāla."
"Thona! Of these five kinds of brahmins, to whom do you resemble? Thona replied:
"Gautama! Even I am not equal to this last of the brahmins, the outcaste; how much less so anyone else?
World-Honored One!"
"I have understood,
Sugata! I have comprehended."
"Bhagavān!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the Bhagavān accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, for as long as I live, until the end of my life, I take refuge."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the brahmin Thona rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh discourse, the *Thona Sutta*, ends here; it consists of one thousand eight hundred and fifty characters. 159. The *Aggañña Sutta* (159), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Brahmins, the eighth discourse in the fourth sub-section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the brahmin Aggahana, having wandered about in the afternoon, went to where the Buddha was. They exchanged greetings, and he sat down to one side and said:
"Gotama!..."
"I wish to ask something; if you would grant me leave, I shall venture to set it forth.
The World-Honored One replied, "Ask whatever you wish."
The brahmin then asked: "Gautama!
Upon what do the brahmin scriptures rely?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"The brahminical scriptures depend upon persons.
The brahmin then asked again:
“Gautama! Upon what does a person depend and abide?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Human beings subsist on rice and wheat.
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama!..."
"On what do rice and wheat depend for their dwelling?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Rice and wheat depend on the earth for their dwelling."
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what does the earth rest?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"The earth rests upon water.
The brahmin then asked again:
“Gautama! Upon what does water depend for its existence?
The Blessed One replied:
“Water rests upon wind.
The brahmin then asked again: “Gautama!
"On what does wind depend for its abiding?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Wind abides depending on space."
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what does emptiness depend for its abiding?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Space has no basis; it exists only because of the sun and the moon.
The brahmin then asked again:
“Gautama! Upon what do the sun and moon rely for their abiding?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The sun and moon abide supported by the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
The brahmin then asked again: “Gautama!
"On what do the gods of the Four Great Kings rely for their dwelling?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The gods of the Four Great Kings dwell relying upon the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what do the Thirty-three Gods rely for their dwelling?"
The Blessed One replied,
“The Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell depending upon the Yāma heaven.
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! On what does the Ābhāsvara Heaven depend for its abode?
The World-Honored One replied:
“The Ābhāsvara devas dwell depending on the Ābhāsvara devas.
The brahmin then asked again:
“Gautama!...”
"On what do the Tuṣita devas rely for their dwelling?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The Tuṣita devas dwell relying upon the Nirmāṇarati devas."
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what do the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven rely for their dwelling?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"The gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven dwell depending upon the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
The brahmin then asked again:
“Gautama! Upon what do the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others’ Emanations depend for their dwelling?
The Blessed One replied:
"The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven resides upon the Brahma-world.
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama!..."
"On what does the Brahma-world depend for its abiding?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The Brahma-world depends on Great Brahmā for its abiding."
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what does Mahābrahmā rely for his dwelling?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"Great Brahmā abides in reliance upon patience and gentleness.
The brahmin then asked again:
"Gautama! Upon what does patience and gentleness depend?

In this world, among its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among recluses and brahmins, from humans to gods, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and realized through his own direct experience; he teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life.
"Furthermore, Udāyin! 'That ascetic Gautama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.

Having heard this, the young brahmin Uttara prostrated at the feet of the brahmin Brahmāyu, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and observed the thirty-two marks on the body of the World-Honored One.
He saw thirty of the marks on the Blessed One’s body, yet he harbored doubts regarding two marks: the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue.
The Blessed One thought to himself:
"This Udāra is observing the thirty-two marks on my body; he sees thirty marks, yet he harbors doubts regarding two: the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue."
"I should now resolve his doubts.

Knowing this, the World-Honored One immediately manifested a supernatural feat (*ṛddhipāda*) according to his will; having manifested that supernatural feat, he caused the young brahmin Uttara to see the horse-like organ between his thighs and his broad, long tongue.

Thereupon, the Blessed One performed a feat of psychic power just as he had described; having performed that feat of psychic power, the young brahmin Uttara beheld the Blessed One’s private organ concealed within a sheath and his broad, long tongue.
As for the mark of the broad and long tongue: he extends his tongue from his mouth until it completely covers his face.
Having seen this, the young brahmin Uttara thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has accomplished the thirty-two marks of a great man. For one who has accomplished these marks of a great man, there must be two possible destinies that are true and not false."

If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a universal monarch (cakravartin), intelligent and wise, possessing a fourfold army to govern the world with sovereign mastery; as a righteous Dharma-king, he will be endowed with the seven treasures.

The young brahmin Uttara then thought to himself:
"I shall observe his deportment and etiquette most closely, as well as the direction in which he travels.
Thereupon, the young brahmin Uttara followed after the Buddha, observing his deportment and etiquette, as well as the direction in which he traveled, throughout the four months of the summer retreat.

After the four months of the summer retreat had passed, the young brahmin Uttara, having been delighted by the Blessed One’s deportment and etiquette, and having observed the direction of his travels, addressed him, saying:
“Gotama! [...]”
"I have some business now and wish to take my leave to return.
The World-Honored One said, "Uttara!"
"You may go as you please.

Having heard what the Blessed One had said, the young brahmin Uttara received it well and retained it well; he then rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed for the presence of the brahmin Brahmāyu.
He bowed his head at the feet of the brahmin Brahmāyu and sat down to one side.
The brahmin Brahmāyu asked: "Uttara!..."
"Is it truly as we have heard—that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown that has spread throughout the ten directions; is it so, or is it not so?
Does he truly possess the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?"
The young brahmin Uttara replied:
"Indeed it is so,
Venerable Sir."

It is exactly as we have heard: the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown that has spread throughout the ten directions; the śramaṇa Gautama is indeed such as he is said to be, and not otherwise, for he truly possesses the thirty-two marks.
"Venerable sir!
The śramaṇa Gautama stands with his feet level and firm. Venerable sir, this is called the mark of a great person, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the śramaṇa Gautama."
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
on the soles of the feet of the śramaṇa Gautama there are wheels with a thousand spokes, all fully complete. This, Venerable Sir,
is called the mark of a great man, the mark of a mahāpuruṣa, of the śramaṇa Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
the fingers and toes of the Śramaṇa Gautama are slender and long; this, Venerable Sir,
is called a mark of a great man, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the Śramaṇa Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
the feet of the ascetic Gautama are well-placed and straight; this, Venerable Sir,
is called a mark of a Great Man, a mark of a Mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the ascetic Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
the heels and the areas behind the ankles of the śramaṇa Gautama are both flat and full on both sides; this, Venerable Sir,
is called a mark of a great man, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the śramaṇa Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the feet of the ascetic Gautama have ankles that are even;
this, Venerable Sir, is called a mark of a great man, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the ascetic Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
the hairs on the body of the śramaṇa Gautama point upward; this, Venerable Sir,
is called the mark of a great person, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, belonging to the śramaṇa Gautama.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir,
the śramaṇa Gautama has webbed fingers and toes like those of a king of geese; this, Venerable Sir,
is called a mark of a great man, a mark of a mahāpuruṣa, of the śramaṇa Gautama.
"Furthermore, Venerable Sir!
The hands and feet of the Śramaṇa Gautama are exceedingly wonderful, supple and soft, like *tūla* cotton; this, Venerable Sir, is called..."
"Venerable sir, the ascetic Gautama possesses the marks of a great man and a superior being.
Furthermore, venerable sir, the ascetic Gautama’s skin is soft and delicate, such that dust and water do not adhere to it. This, venerable sir, is called..."
The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a Great Man. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, for the Śramaṇa Gautama, each hair grows individually;
that is to say, from each single pore of his body a single hair grows, which is deep blue-black in color and curls to the right like a conch shell. This, Venerable Sir, is called [the mark].
The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a great man and a supreme being.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the Śramaṇa Gautama has calves like those of an antelope, just like a king of deer; this, Venerable Sir, is called [the mark].
The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a Great Man and a Superior Being.
Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the Śramaṇa Gautama has the private organ concealed within a sheath, like that of a noble horse-king; this, Venerable Sir, is called [the mark].
The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a Great Man and a Superior Being.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the body of the Śramaṇa Gautama is perfectly rounded and beautiful, like a nyagrodha tree, with its upper and lower parts in harmonious proportion. This, Venerable Sir, is called [the mark].

Furthermore, venerable sir, the ascetic Gautama’s body is not crooked; because his body is not crooked, when he stands upright with his arms extended, he can touch his knees. This, venerable sir, is called..."

The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a great man and a superior being.

The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses the marks of a Great Man and a Supreme Being.

a mahāpuruṣa. Venerable sir,

"Furthermore, Venerable Sir! I have seen the ascetic Gautama putting on his robes, having already put them on; donning his outer cloak, having already donned it; leaving his cell, having already left it; leaving the monastery grounds, having already left them; walking along the path toward a village, having already set out; entering the village, having already entered it; being in the street, having already reached it; entering a house, having already entered it; arranging his seat, having already arranged it; sitting down, having already sat down; washing his hands, having already washed them; receiving food and drink, having already received it; eating, having already eaten; washing his hands and reciting the blessing, rising from his seat, leaving the house, having already left it; being in the street, leaving the village, having already left it; entering the monastery grounds, having already entered them; and entering his cell, having already entered it."
"Venerable One!
The śramaṇa Gautama wears his robes with perfect composure—neither too high nor too low; the robes do not cling to his body, yet the wind cannot cause them to move away from his person."
"Venerable One!
The śramaṇa Gautama wears his robe with perfect composure—neither too high nor too low; the robe does not cling to his body, yet the wind cannot cause it to move away from his person."
"Venerable One!

The ascetic Gautama always wears new cloth that conforms to the noble ones; he cuts it with a knife and dyes it an unattractive color. Thus, when those noble ones dye their cloth an unattractive color, they do not do so for the sake of wealth, nor for pride, nor for self-adornment, nor for decoration. Rather, it is only to shield themselves from the touch of mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, and sun, and out of a sense of shame to cover their bodies."
"When he leaves his room, his body is neither bent nor tilted. Venerable sir!
When the ascetic Gautama leaves his room, he never bends his body. Venerable sir!
When the ascetic Gautama wishes to walk, he first lifts his right foot; he lifts it correctly and sets it down correctly. His gait is unhurried and undisturbed, and there is no agitation."
When walking, his two ankles never clash; Venerable Sir!
When the śramaṇa Gautama walks, he is not besmeared by dust. Why is this?
"Because of his past virtuous conduct, when he leaves the park, his body is neither slumped nor held too high.
Venerable sir!

When the ascetic Gautama leaves the park, he never slumps his body as he proceeds toward the village; his body is turned slightly to the right, and he observes like a dragon, looking all around with full awareness. He is neither afraid nor terrified, nor does he feel any dread, as he surveys the various directions."
Why is this? Because he is a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; when he enters a village, his body neither bends nor inclines.
Venerable sir!

When the śramaṇa Gautama enters a village, he never lowers his body; while in the streets and alleys, he does not look down nor look up, but gazes straight ahead, such that what is known and seen therein is unobstructed.
“Venerable sir!
The faculties of the śramaṇa Gautama are constantly composed. Why is this so? Because—”
Because of his past virtuous conduct, when he enters a house, his body does not bend or lean.
Venerable sir!
When the śramaṇa Gautama enters a house, he never bends his body.
"Venerable One!

The ascetic Gautama turns his body to the right and sits upright upon the bed; he does not sit upon the bed with excessive physical force, nor does he sit pressing his hands against his thighs. Having sat upon the bed, he is neither dejected, nor distressed, nor yet does he feel pleasure."

When receiving water for washing, one should take neither too much nor too little, neither too high nor too low; likewise, when receiving food and drink, one should take neither too much nor too little, neither too high nor too low.
"Venerable sir!
The śramaṇa Gautama accepts food with his bowl level, eating the soup and the solid food equally.
Venerable sir!"

The śramaṇa Gautama takes his food in mouthfuls, placing them evenly and slowly into his mouth. Before a mouthful has arrived, he does not open his mouth prematurely; once it is in his mouth, he chews it three times before swallowing. He does not break up the rice or the soup, and while some remains in his mouth, he places another mouthful inside.
“Venerable One!

The śramaṇa Gautama, through three kinds of purity, desires to obtain the flavor of food, yet he does not desire to be stained by that food. He does not do so for the sake of wealth, nor for the sake of pride, nor for self-adornment, nor for embellishment; he only desires to maintain the body, to dwell long without affliction, to suppress existing ailments, to prevent new diseases from arising, and to preserve his life without distress, possessing strength and happiness.”
When the meal was finished, he received water for washing his hands; it was neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little.
He received water for rinsing his bowl; it was neither too high nor too low, neither too much nor too little.

Having washed his hands until they were clean, he also cleansed his bowl; having washed the bowl until it was clean, he also cleansed his hands. Having wiped his hands, he then wiped the bowl; having wiped the bowl, he then wiped his hands. Once he had washed and wiped the bowl, he set it aside at one side, neither too close nor too far, without looking at the bowl repeatedly, nor being preoccupied with the bowl.
He did not disparage this food, nor did he praise that food; he simply remained silent with a sense of shame.

He then taught the Dharma to the laypeople, exhorting them, inspiring them with longing, and bringing them to a state of joy. Having used immeasurable skillful means to teach them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and bringing them to joy, he rose from his seat and withdrew to depart. When he went forth, his body was neither bowed nor held aloft.
“Venerable sir!
When the ascetic Gautama went forth, he never lowered his body.
In the streets and alleys, he did not look down nor did he look up; he only gazed straight ahead, and therein there was no obstruction to what he knew or saw.”
"Venerable One!
The faculties of the śramaṇa Gautama are constantly settled. Why is this so?"
Because of his past virtuous conduct, when he leaves the village, his body is neither bent nor held aloft.
Venerable sir!
When the ascetic Gautama leaves the village, he never bends his body; when he enters the park, his body is neither bent nor held aloft.
"Venerable One!
When the śramaṇa Gautama enters the park, he never lowers his body.
After his midday meal there, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting mat (niṣīdana) upon his shoulder, and enters his room to sit in meditation."
"Venerable sir!
For the benefit of the world, the ascetic Gautama has entered his chamber to sit in meditation.
Venerable sir!"
The śramaṇa Gautama rose from his meditative seclusion in the late afternoon with a radiant complexion. Why was this?
Because he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
