“Venerable Sir! The śramaṇa Gautama utters eight kinds of vocal tones: first, the profound; second, the *vimālapa*; third, that which enters the heart; fourth, the lovely; fifth, the perfectly full; sixth, the *ghoṣavat*; seventh, the distinct; and eighth, the wise.”
"Beloved by many, cherished by many, and remembered by many, he brings peace of mind to them.
Venerable sir!

The ascetic Gautama teaches the Dharma according to the assembly; his voice does not carry beyond the assembly, but remains within it as he teaches the Dharma to them, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them. Having taught the Dharma to them through immeasurable skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, he immediately rises from his seat and returns to his own quarters."
"Venerable sir!
Such is the appearance of the śramaṇa Gautama; yet he possesses even more excellence than this.
Venerable sir!"
"I wish to go to that śramaṇa Gautama and train in the holy life under him.
The brahmin Brahmāyu replied,
"Do as you please."

Thereupon, the young brahmin Uttara prostrated at the feet of the brahmin Brahmā, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to study the path under the World-Honored One and receive full ordination, to become a bhikṣu, and to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) under the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One ordained the young brahmin Uttara, causing him to study the path and receive full ordination.

Having delivered the young brahmin Uttara, having caused him to train in the Path and receive full ordination, he traveled through the Videha country together with a great assembly of bhikṣus; proceeding by stages, he arrived at Mithilā and stayed in the Mahādeva Mango Grove at Mithilā.

The brahmins and householders of Vesālī heard that the ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who had left the Śākya clan to go forth and study the Way, was traveling through the Vajji country with a large community of bhikṣus and had arrived here at Vesālī, staying in the Mahāvana mango grove.

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown that is heard throughout the ten directions; the śramaṇa Gautama is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.

In this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans up to the devas, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and realized through his own direct experience.

He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, complete and pure, and clearly reveals the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

If there are those who see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and pay him respect, prostrate before him, make offerings to him, and serve him, they will swiftly obtain great benefit. We should surely go together to see that śramaṇa Gautama!
Having paid homage and made offerings,

those brahmins and householders of Mithilā, each accompanied by their respective circles of kinsmen, departed from Mithilā and traveled north to the Mahādeva mango grove, desiring to see the Blessed One, pay him homage, and make offerings to him.

Having approached the Buddha, some of the brahmins and householders of Mithilā bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Buddha and sat to one side; some joined their palms toward the Buddha and sat to one side; and some, having seen the Buddha from afar, sat down in silence.

When those brahmins and householders of Vesālī had each taken their seats, the Buddha taught them the Dharma, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them; having taught them the Dharma through countless skillful means, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, he remained silent.

The brahmin Brahmāyu heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, had renounced his kin and lineage to leave the household life and study the Path; he was wandering through the country of Vedehī accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus, and having traveled by stages, he had arrived at this country of Mithilā and was staying in the Mahāvana mango grove.

That śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown, which is heard throughout the ten directions. That śramaṇa Gautama is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One.

In this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, ascetics, and brahmins, from humans up to the gods, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and realized for himself through direct experience.

He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, complete and pure, and clearly reveals the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

If there are those who see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and pay him respect, prostrate before him, and serve him with offerings, they will swiftly obtain great benefit. I should surely go to see the śramaṇa Gautama!
Having paid homage and made offerings,
the brahmin Brahmāyu said to his charioteer:
"Quickly prepare the carriage!"
"I now wish to go and visit the śramaṇa Gautama!
The charioteer received his instructions and immediately hurriedly prepared the carriage; having finished, he returned and reported, "The carriage is ready;
Your Honor may know the time [to depart] yourself."

Thereupon, Brahmayu mounted his most excellent and wonderful chariot and departed from Mithilā, traveling north to the Great Nyagrodha Grove, desiring to see the World-Honored One to pay him homage and make offerings.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable assembly as he taught the Dharma. From afar, the brahmin Brahmā saw the World-Honored One surrounded by an immeasurable assembly as he taught the Dharma; having seen this, he was struck with fear.
Thereupon, Brahmayu stepped aside onto the path and stood beneath a tree, addressing a young brahmin student:

"Go to that ascetic Gautama and inquire on my behalf whether his holy body is robust and healthy, whether he is at ease and free from illness, whether his daily activities are light and convenient, and whether his strength remains as usual."
He spoke these words:

"Gautama! My teacher Brahmā inquires after your holy body—whether it is robust and healthy, at ease and free from illness, whether your daily activities are light and convenient, and whether your physical strength remains as usual?"
"Gautama! My teacher Brahmā wishes to come and see the ascetic Gautama.
Thereupon, the young brahmin (māṇava) immediately accepted the instruction and went to where the Buddha was. Having exchanged greetings with him, he sat down to one side and said:
"Gautama! My teacher Brahmā inquires after your holy body—whether it is robust, at ease, free from illness, light in its movements, and whether your physical strength remains as usual?"
"Gautama! My teacher Brahmā wishes to come and see the ascetic Gautama!
The World-Honored One replied:
“Māṇava! May the brahmin Brahmā be at peace and happy; may gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and all other various beings be at peace and happy.”
“Māṇava! The brahmin Brahmā wishes to come as he pleases.

Thereupon, having heard what the Buddha had said, the Māṇava received and retained it well; he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed. He returned to where the brahmin Brahmā was and said to him:
"Venerable Sir!
I have already informed the śramaṇa Gautama; that śramaṇa Gautama is now waiting for you. May the Venerable Sir know the proper time.
The brahmin Brahmā then descended from his chariot and proceeded on foot to where the Buddha was.
When that assembly saw the brahmin Brahmāyu approaching from afar, they immediately rose from their seats, opening a path to make way for him.
Why was this? Because he possessed renown, virtue, and great learning.
The brahmin Brahmāyu addressed that assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs, each of you sit down again; I wish to go straight to see the śramaṇa Gautama."
Thereupon, Brahmayu went to where the Buddha was staying; having exchanged greetings with him, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, Brahmayu did not lose his two faculties: the faculty of sight and the faculty of hearing.

Once the brahmin Brahmā was seated, he scrutinized the Buddha’s body for the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; he perceived thirty of them, yet he harbored doubt regarding two: the male organ concealed within a sheath and the broad, long tongue.
The brahmin Brahmā immediately addressed the World-Honored One in verse, saying:
“As I have heard in the past, there are thirty-two marks of a Great Man;
yet when I seek them within you, I do not see two of them upon the body of the Venerable Śramaṇa Gautama.”
Do you possess the mark of the concealed organ like a horse?
You are the most honored among all people and profoundly secret; why is it that you, the supreme among men, do not reveal your wondrous tongue for us to see?
If the Honored One possesses a broad and long tongue, I pray that I may behold it;
for now I truly have a mind of doubt, and I beseech the Tamer to resolve my uncertainty.
The Blessed One thought to himself:

"This brahmin Brahmā seeks to find the thirty-two marks upon my body; he has seen thirty of them, yet he harbors doubt regarding two—the sheathed male organ and the broad, long tongue. I should now dispel his uncertainty."

The Blessed One, having understood this, performed a feat of psychic power (*ṛddhi*) such that it appeared as he willed. Having performed such a feat of psychic power, the brahmin Brahmayu beheld the Blessed One’s body with its male organ concealed within a sheath (*kośagatavastiguhya*) and his broad, long tongue. Regarding that broad, long tongue: the tongue issued from his mouth and completely covered his face.
Having stilled his supernormal powers, the Blessed One spoke these verses to the brahmin Brahmāyu:
"The thirty-two marks of a Great Man, which you have heard of in the past—
all of them are present upon my body, perfectly complete, supreme, and correct."
The Tamer has severed my doubts; the Brahmin has given rise to sublime faith.
Most difficult to see or hear is the Supreme, Perfectly Awakened One.
"To transcend the world is exceedingly difficult; it is the supreme, perfectly complete awakening.
O Brahmin, I am the perfectly awakened one, the unsurpassed King of the True Dharma.
Having heard this, the Brahmin Brahmā thought to himself:

"This ascetic Gautama is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man; for one who is endowed with these marks of a great man, there are necessarily two possible destinies, which are true and not false."
If he remains a householder, he will certainly become a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), intelligent and wise, possessing a fourfold army to govern the world.

As a righteous Dharma-king, he will possess the seven treasures. Those seven treasures are: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the minister-treasure who is a military commander; these are called the seven.

He will be endowed with a full thousand sons, handsome in appearance, courageous and fearless, capable of subduing all other hosts. He will surely rule over this entire earth as far as the great ocean, not by means of the sword or staff, but through the teaching of the Dharma, bringing about peace and security.

If one shaves off hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and with deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path, one will certainly attain the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame shall spread far and wide, heard throughout the ten directions.
Thereupon, the Blessed One thought to himself:

"This brahmin Brahmā has for a long time been free from flattery and free from deceit. Whatever he wishes to ask, he desires to know it all; it is not for the sake of causing annoyance. It is even so with him; I should indeed explain to him the profound Abhidharma."
The World-Honored One, having understood this, spoke in verse for the sake of the brahmin Brahmā:
"Because of delighting in the Dharma in the present life, And for the benefit of future lives,
O brahmin, regarding the matter you ask, I shall answer according to what you have contemplated in your mind."
Regarding each of those various matters, I shall sever your doubts for you.
Since the World-Honored One has granted permission to ask, the brahmin Brahmā,
following what was in his original mind, then questioned the World-Honored One about these matters.
“What constitutes a brahmin? What is the meaning of the threefold knowledge?
On what basis is one called ‘unattached,’ and what is ‘perfectly awakened enlightenment’?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Having extinguished evil and unwholesome states, established in the discernment of the holy life,
and cultivated the rectitude of a brahmin— one is a brahmin by this.
One who has clear understanding of the past, and sees both happiness and the miserable realms,"
Having attained the teaching on the exhaustion of ignorance, he is known as one who establishes the state of a Muni.
Thoroughly knowing the pure mind, he is completely liberated from lust, anger, and delusion;
having accomplished the three types of higher knowledge, these constitute his threefold penetration.
Far removed from unwholesome states, dwelling correctly in the ultimate truth,
honored by the world as foremost, one is thereby unattached.
Bringing benefit to gods and humans, providing the eye that destroys all strife.
"Knowing and seeing all things universally and exhaustively, he has thereby attained perfect enlightenment.
Thereupon, Brahmayu rose from his seat, wishing to prostrate at the Buddha's feet; at that moment, the great assembly simultaneously raised a loud clamor, crying out:
"How extraordinary is the Śramaṇa Gautama!"
How extraordinary!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this so?
Among all the brahmins and householders in this kingdom of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost, by virtue of his noble birth. The brahmin Brahmāyu has been honored by his parents;

he is pure in his conception and birth, and his lineage remains unbroken through seven generations of ancestors, with no evil ever arising in his family line. Yet, he has lowered himself before the śramaṇa Gautama, paying him respect and prostrating before him, making offerings and serving him.
"How extraordinary! How remarkable!
The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power (ṛddhi), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority!"
Why is this? Among all the brahmins and householders in this country of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost, specifically because of his mastery of the sacred texts.

The brahmin Brahmāyu was widely learned and possessed a comprehensive mastery; he had recited the four Vedas and deeply penetrated the five modes of exposition: causal analysis, conditional analysis, philological analysis, textual analysis, and etymological analysis.
"He has lowered his mind with the utmost reverence to pay homage to the śramaṇa Gautama, making offerings and serving him.
'The śramaṇa Gautama is truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary! "
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. Why is this?
Among all the brahmins and householders in the kingdom of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost in terms of wealth.

The brahmin Brahmāyu was extremely wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable assets and livestock and property beyond calculation. He was fully endowed with various fiefs and food-grant villages, and his sustenance was abundant, including grass, wood, and water in Mithilā. It is said that King Ajātaśatru Vaidehīputra of Magadha had specifically granted him these as a brahminical endowment; yet he has directed his mind toward the śramaṇa Gautama with the utmost humility, paying him respect, bowing before him, and serving him with offerings.
"How extraordinary! How remarkable is the śramaṇa Gautama!
He possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority."
Why is this so? Among all the brahmins and householders in this kingdom of Mithilā, the brahmin Brahmāyu is the foremost, in terms of his lifespan.

The brahmin Brahmāyu is a most venerable elder, endowed with a full lifespan of one hundred and twenty-six years; he has directed his mind with the utmost humility toward the śramaṇa Gautama, paying him homage, making offerings, and serving him.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing with his mind the thoughts in the minds of that great assembly, and having known them, addressed the brahmin Brahmāyu: "Stop!
"Stop, brahmin!
Be content simply with what is in your mind; you may return to your seat, and I shall teach the Dharma to you."

The brahmin Brahmā bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him until he was filled with joy.

Employing immeasurable skillful means, he taught the Dharma to them, exhorting them to aspire with longing and bringing them to a state of joy. Then, according to the practice of all Buddhas, he first spoke on the principles of upright conduct, which brought delight to those who heard it; namely, he spoke of generosity, spoke of ethical discipline, and spoke of the dharma for rebirth in the heavens. He censured sensual desires as calamities and the cycle of birth and death as defilement, while praising the excellence of desirelessness and the pure whiteness of the factors of the path.

Having spoken thus, the Buddha knew that he possessed a joyful mind, a fulfilled mind, a supple mind, a patient mind, an uplifted mind, a one-pointed mind, a mind free from doubt, and a mind free from hindrances; that he was capable and empowered to receive the True Dharma of the Buddhas—that is, the essential method as taught by all Buddhas—and so the World-Honored One fully explained to him suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that very seat, the brahmin Brahmā saw the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—just as a piece of white cloth is easily dyed with color.
Thus, while seated, Brahmā saw the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Thereupon, Brahmā saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he realized the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, transcended delusion, and recognized no other teacher. No longer dependent on another and free from hesitation, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit and attained fearlessness in the Dharma of the World-Honored One. He then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said: “World-Honored One!...”

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
Then the brahmin Brahmāyaṇa joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that you will deign to accept my invitation for tomorrow, together with the community of bhikṣus."
The Blessed One accepted the Brahmin Brahmā’s request by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Blessed One had accepted by his silence, the Brahmin Brahmā bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed to return to his home.

That very night, he prepared exquisite and superior delicacies, as well as various abundant foods for chewing, sucking, and swallowing; having finished the preparations, at dawn he spread out the seats and, when the time arrived, announced:
"World-Honored One! [The meal is ready]."
"The meal is prepared; may the Blessed One know the time.

Thereupon, at dawn after the night had passed, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl, and with the bhikṣus following as attendants and the Blessed One leading the way, went to the home of the brahmin Brahmāyu. He sat down on a seat prepared before the assembly of bhikṣus.

When the brahmin Brahmāyu knew that the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus were seated, he personally provided water for washing and served various kinds of exquisite dishes and abundant foods, both solid and soft, pouring them with his own hands until they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and the vessels had been cleared away, and the water for washing had been offered, he took a small seat and sat down to receive the words of blessing.
Once the brahmin Brahmā was seated, the World-Honored One recited this benediction for him:
"The sacrificial fire is foremost among offerings; The universal sound is the root of all sounds.
The king is the most honored among men; The ocean is the longest of all rivers."
The moon is the most luminous among the stars, and in its radiant illumination, none surpasses the sun;
yet throughout the upper and lower regions and all directions,
including the entire world from humans up to the heavens, the Buddha alone is the foremost.

Then, having pronounced a blessing for the brahmin Brahmāyu, the Blessed One rose from his seat and departed. After staying in the kingdom of Mithilā for several days, he adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and set out on his journey toward Sāvatthī. Traveling by stages, he arrived at Sāvatthī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then, while many bhikṣus were begging for alms in Śrāvastī, they heard that the brahmin Vāmaka of Miśrikā had asked the Buddha about his affairs in verse and had subsequently passed away.

Having heard this, the bhikṣus finished their meal; after midday, they put away their robes and bowls, washed their hands and feet, placed their sitting mats (niṣīdana) over their shoulders, and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves in salutation, withdrew to stand to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."

"Many of us bhikṣus, having dressed in the early morning and taken our bowls, entered Śrāvastī for alms, when we heard that the brahmin Vāmaka of Mithilā had questioned the Buddha on certain matters in verse, and that he subsequently passed away."
“World-Honored One!
Where has he gone? To what place has he been born? What will become of him in future lives?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Monks! The brahmin Brahmā has gained a great benefit; he has understood the Dharma at the very end, and for the sake of the Dharma, he has not troubled me. Monks!”
“The brahmin Brahmāyu has exhausted the five lower fetters; having been reborn there, he will attain parinirvāṇa, having attained the state of non-retrogression and not returning to this world.
At that time, the World-Honored One declared that Brahmāyu had attained the stage of *anāgāmin*.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the brahmin Brahmāyu and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The tenth sūtra, the *Brahmāyu Sūtra*, ends here, totaling six thousand seven hundred and seventy-six characters. The forty-first fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* ends here, totaling six thousand seven hundred and seventy-six characters. The first section, the *Brāhmaṇa Varga*, of the *Madhyama Āgama* concludes here, totaling thirty thousand four hundred and fifty-four characters.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 42.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
2. The Second Chapter: Fundamental Analysis (*Mūlapariyāya-vagga*). This chapter contains ten sūtras; it belongs to the Fourth Recitation Section on Analysis.
The Analysis of the Six Elements and Bases;
The Discourse on Contemplating Phenomena, the Hot Springs, the Forest, and the Honored One in the Meditation Cell;
Ānanda’s Teaching, Mental Activity, Kuru, and the Absence of Dispute; The Parrot and the Analysis of Karma.
162. The Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Elements (162). The First Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Elements, from the Fundamental Analysis Section of the Madhyama Āgama. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha and went to the city of Rājagaha to stay for the night.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One went to the potter’s workshop and said, “Potter!
I wish to stay one night in your workshop; would you grant me permission?”
The potter replied:
"I have committed no offense.
However, a certain bhikṣu has already been staying there; if he permits it, you may stay as you please."
At that time, the Venerable Pukkusāti was already staying there in the potter’s hut.
Then the Blessed One went out from the potter’s house, entered the hut, and said to the Venerable Pukkusāti: “Bhikkhu!”
"I now wish to stay one night in your pottery shed;
would you grant me leave? Venerable Pukkusa replied, "Sir!"
"I have no objection.
Furthermore, this grass seat has already been spread in the potter's hut; if you wish to stay, you may do as you please.

At that time, the World-Honored One went out from the potter's hut to wash his feet, then returned inside, spread a *niṣīdana* upon the grass seat, and sat cross-legged. Throughout the night, he remained silent, sitting in stillness with a concentrated mind. The Venerable Pukkusa Mallaputta likewise remained silent throughout the night, sitting in stillness with a concentrated mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous! That this bhikṣu dwells in such profound stillness and tranquility!"
"I should now rather ask that bhikṣu:
'Who is your teacher?
Upon whom do you rely to leave the household life, study the Path, and receive the Dharma?'"
Having reflected thus, the World-Honored One asked:
"Bhikṣu, who is your teacher?"
"Under whom did you go forth, study the Path, and receive the Dharma?
The Venerable Pukkusāti replied:
"Worthy one!"

"There is a śramaṇa, Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who has renounced his Śākya clan, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left his home for the homeless life to study the Path. He has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; he is my teacher, and it is in reliance upon him that I have gone forth to study the Path and receive the Dharma."
The World-Honored One then asked again:
"Bhikkhu, have you ever seen your teacher?"
The Venerable Pukkusāti replied,
“I do not see it.
The Blessed One asked:
"If one sees the teacher, is it recognized?
Venerable Pukkusāti replied,
"It is not recognized."
However, worthy one!

I have heard that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Perfectly Accomplished in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Trainer of Beings, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the Fortunate One—he is my teacher; relying upon him, I have gone forth to study the Path and receive the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"This son of good family has left the household life to study the Way under me and receive the Dharma; should I now preach the Dharma for him?"
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Pukkusāti:

“Monk, I shall teach you the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; it possesses both meaning and phrasing, is perfectly pure, and reveals the holy life. It is called ‘The Analysis of the Six Elements. Listen closely and attend well to what I shall say.”
The Venerable Pukkusāti replied,
“Indeed. The Buddha said to him:
“Monks! A person consists of six groups of elements, six bases of contact, eighteen mental explorations, and four abodes.
If one dwells in these, and does not hear of matters that cause distress, having not heard of such matters, the mind will not feel aversion, sorrow, or weariness, nor will it be terrified.”
Thus, one should be instructed, practice heedfulness and wisdom, guard the true reality, and cultivate generosity.
Monks! You should train in the supreme, you should train in ultimate tranquility, and analyze the six elements.
Thus it is, bhikkhus!
A person consists of a collection of six elements. For what reason is this said?
Namely: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
"Monks! When it is said that 'a person consists of a collection of six elements,' it is for this reason that it is so stated. Monks!"
A person has six bases of contact; for what reason is this said?

It is because, monks, the eye-base contacts forms, the ear-base hears sounds, the nose-base smells odors, the tongue-base tastes flavors, the body-base feels tangibles, and the mind-base cognizes mental phenomena.
"Monks! It is because a person has six bases of contact that this is said. Monks!"
There are eighteen modes of mental activity for persons; what is the reason for this statement?

It is said that when a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye, he dwells observing forms with joy, he dwells observing forms with displeasure, or he dwells observing forms with equanimity. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognizes dharmas, he dwells observing dharmas with joy, he dwells observing dharmas with displeasure, or he dwells observing dharmas with equanimity.
"Monks! These six contemplations of joy, six contemplations of grief, and six contemplations of equanimity, when combined, constitute eighteen modes of practice. Monks!"
Regarding the statement that "a person has eighteen modes of mental activity," it is for this reason that it is said:
"Bhikkhus! A person has four stations. For what reason is this said?"
That is to say: the dwelling place of true reality, the dwelling place of wisdom, the dwelling place of generosity, and the dwelling place of tranquility.
Bhikṣus, it is because a person possesses these four dwelling places that this is said.
What is the wisdom of heedfulness of a bhikṣu?
If there is a bhikṣu who analyzes the element of the body, thinking: "In this present body of mine, there is an internal earth element that has undergone birth; what is this?"
That is to say: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, coarse and fine skin, skin, flesh, bones, tendons, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, spleen, large intestine, small intestine, and feces.

Whatever else of this kind exists within this body, internal and comprised of the internal, which is solid, possesses the nature of solidity, and is situated internally as part of one's birth-endowment—this, monks, is called the internal earth element.
"Monks! Whatever constitutes the internal earth element and the external earth element—all that is collectively called the earth element. All that is not mine, I am not that, and it is not my self."
Observing with such wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become stained or attached to this earth element; this is called the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, there is the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu analyzes the body element, he considers: "What is this internal water element that exists within my present body and is subject to birth?

It refers to the brain membrane, tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, spittle, lymph, and urine—such as these and whatever else remains within the body, comprised internally, which is watery in nature, moistens the interior, and is received at birth; this, bhikṣu, is called the internal water element."
"Monks! Whether it be the internal water element or the external water element, all of it is collectively called the 'water element. All of that is not mine, I am not that, and it is not my self."
Observing with such wisdom, he knows it as it truly is; his mind is not stained by or attached to this water element. This is called the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, there is the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu analyzes this body-element, he considers: "Now, within this body of mine, there exists an internal fire-element that has been received at birth; what is this?

It refers to the heat of the body, the warmth of the body, the feverishness of the body, and the temperature that sustains the body—namely, that which digests food and drink. Such as these, whatever else remains within the body, comprised internally, having the nature of fire and being hot within, which has been received at birth: this, bhikṣu, is called the internal fire-element."
“Monks! Whether there is the internal fire element or the external fire element, all of it is collectively called the fire element. All of that is not mine; I am not that; nor is it my self.”
Observing with such wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become defiled or attached to this fire element; this is called the wisdom of heedfulness of a bhikṣu.
"Furthermore, there is the wisdom of heedfulness of a bhikṣu."
If there is a bhikṣu who analyzes the body element, he considers: "Within this present body of mine, there exists an internal wind element that has arisen;
what is this? It is known as: upward-moving wind, downward-moving wind, lateral wind, contracting wind, distending wind, non-path wind, joint-by-joint wind, out-breath wind, and in-breath wind."

In this manner, whatever else exists internally within this body, comprised of the internal wind and possessing the nature of wind that moves within, and which has been acquired at birth—this, monks, is called the internal wind element.
"Monks! Whether there is the internal wind element or the external wind element, all of it is collectively called the wind element. All of that is not mine; I am not that; nor is it my self."
Observing with such wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become stained or attached to this wind element; this is called the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu.
"Furthermore, there is the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu."
If there is a bhikṣu who analyzes the element of the body, he considers: "Now, within this body of mine, there is the internal element of space which undergoes birth; what is this?

It refers to the emptiness of the eye, the emptiness of the ear, the emptiness of the nose, the emptiness of the mouth, and the movement of the throat—namely, the swallowing, chewing, savoring, and digesting of food, its gradual descent, its passage, and its exit."

In this manner, whatever else remains within this body, which is internal and comprised of the internal, and which exists as space not covered by flesh, skin, bone, or sinew—this, O bhikṣu, is called the internal space element.
"Monks! Whether there is the internal space-element or the external space-element, all of it is collectively called the space-element. All of that is not mine, I am not that, and it is not my self."
Observing with such wisdom and knowing it as it truly is, the mind does not become defiled or attached to this element of space; this is called the heedful wisdom of a bhikṣu. “Bhikṣus!

If there is a bhikṣu who knows these five elements as they truly are, and having known them as they truly are, his mind is not defiled by them and is liberated—what remains is only residual consciousness; what kind of consciousness is this?
There is the consciousness of pleasure, the consciousness of pain, the consciousness of joy, the consciousness of grief, and the consciousness of equanimity. Monks!

Due to the contact of pleasant sensation, a feeling of pleasure arises; one perceives that feeling of pleasure, and having perceived that feeling of pleasure, one knows, "I perceive a feeling of pleasure."

If a bhikṣu extinguishes this pleasant contact and that pleasant contact, and having extinguished this pleasant contact and that pleasant contact, whatever pleasant feeling arises from that pleasant contact and that pleasant contact is also extinguished, stilled, and ceased; having known this, he is cooled.
"Monks! Because of contact with a painful object, a painful feeling arises. One feels that painful feeling, and having felt that painful feeling, one knows: 'I feel a painful feeling.

If a monk were to extinguish this contact with a painful object, and having extinguished this contact with a painful object, any painful feeling that arose from that contact with a painful object would also be extinguished, stilled, and ceased; he would know: 'It has become cool.'"
“Monks! Due to the contact of joy, the perception of joy arises; one perceives that perception of joy, and having perceived that perception of joy, one knows, ‘I perceive the perception of joy.

If a monk should extinguish this contact of joy, and having extinguished this contact of joy, whatever perception of joy arose from that contact of joy is likewise extinguished, stilled, and ceased, and he knows it has become cool.”

“Monks! Due to the contact of mental grief (*daurmanasya-sparśa*), a feeling of grief arises. One feels that feeling of grief; having felt that feeling of grief, one knows: ‘I feel a feeling of grief.

If a monk were to extinguish this contact of mental grief, and having extinguished this contact of mental grief, any feeling of grief arising from that contact of mental grief would likewise be extinguished, stilled, and ceased; he would know it has become cooled.”

"Monks! Through the feeling of equanimity born of contact, the perception of equanimity arises. Having perceived that perception of equanimity, and having fully understood the perception of equanimity, one knows: 'I perceive the perception of equanimity.

If a monk extinguishes this feeling of equanimity born of contact, and having extinguished it, whatever perception of equanimity arose from that feeling of equanimity is likewise extinguished, stilled, and ceased; he knows: 'It is cooled.'"

"Monks! Through various contacts (*phassa*), various feelings (*vedanā*) arise; when those various contacts cease, those various feelings also cease. He knows that this feeling has contact as its source, contact as its origin, contact as its condition, is born from contact, has contact as its primary cause, and proceeds dependent upon contact."
“Monks! Just as fire is produced from a fire-drill due to the friction caused by drilling and the application of human effort and heat,
so it is, monks!”

When those various numerous trees are separated and dispersed, if fire were to arise from them, that fire would be heated for as many times as it arose; yet when they are all extinguished and stilled, the firewood becomes cold.
In this way, bhikṣus!

Through various contacts (sparśa), various perceptions (saṃjñā) arise; through the cessation of those various contacts, those various perceptions also cease. He knows that these perceptions originate from contact, have contact as their root, have contact as their source, are born from contact, have contact as their primary cause, and proceed in dependence upon contact.
If a bhikkhu is liberated without being stained by these three perceptions, that bhikkhu abides solely in equanimity, which is utterly pure.
Bhikkhus! That bhikkhu reflects thus:
"I direct this pure equanimity into the sphere of infinite space; I cultivate such a mind, relying upon it, dwelling in it, establishing it, taking it as its object, and being bound to it."

I take this same purified equanimity and transfer it into the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I cultivate such a mind, relying upon them, dwelling in them, establishing myself in them, taking them as an object, and being bound to them.

“Monks! It is just as a skilled and masterful goldsmith heats gold with fire, forging it until it is extremely thin, and then repeatedly tests it with fire, refining it thoroughly until it is pure, exceedingly supple, and radiant.”

"Monks! This gold, when repeatedly refined by a goldsmith through heating until it is purified, made extremely pliable and radiant, can then be fashioned by that goldsmith into whatever he intends—whether as fine silken cloths, ornate new garments, finger-rings, armlets, necklaces, or jeweled wreaths—exactly according to his will."
In this way, bhikṣus! That bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I transfer this pure equanimity into the sphere of infinite space; I cultivate such a mind, relying upon it, dwelling in it, establishing it, taking it as an object, and being bound to it."

Having transferred this pure equanimity of mine into the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I cultivate such a mind, relying upon it, dwelling in it, establishing it, taking it as an object, and being bound to it.
That bhikṣu further reflects:
"This pure equanimity of mine, which relies on the sphere of infinite space, is therefore conditioned.
That which is conditioned is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering."
If it were suffering, one would know it as suffering; having known it as suffering, one would abandon both this and that and no longer enter the sphere of infinite space.
This pure equanimity of mine—which relies upon the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—is therefore conditioned.
If something is conditioned, it is impermanent; if it is impermanent, it is suffering. If it is suffering, one knows it as suffering.

Having known it as suffering, one relinquishes both this and that, and no longer migrates into the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

"Monks! If a monk observes these four stations with wisdom and knows them as they truly are, yet his mind does not find fulfillment therein and does not settle into them; [he is one who has transcended them]."

At that time, he no longer engages in conditioned activity nor entertains any thoughts of existence or non-existence. He perceives the final sensation of the body and knows it as the final sensation of the body; he perceives the final sensation of life and knows it as the final sensation of life. When the body breaks up and life ends, when the lifespan has reached its conclusion, everything he perceived ceases and subsides; he knows that he has attained the state of coolness.

“Monks! It is as if, for example, a lamp were lit, depending on oil and a wick. If no one were to further add oil, nor continue the wick, then that which was previously extinguished would not be continued thereafter, and nothing more would be received.”

In this way, bhikṣus! When one experiences the final sensation of the body, one knows: "I experience the final sensation of the body"; when one experiences the final sensation of life, one knows: "I experience the final sensation of life. With the breaking up of the body and the end of life, when the lifespan has been exhausted, everything that was being experienced ceases, subsides, and comes to an end; one knows that it has reached total coolness.
"Monks! This is called a monk’s first right wisdom—that which leads to ultimate cessation. A monk whose taints are exhausted accomplishes this; he accomplishes the ground of the first right wisdom."
"Monks! This liberation abides in the ultimate truth and is unshakable. 'Ultimate truth' refers to things as they truly are; 'false speech' refers to illusory phenomena."
“Monks! One who has accomplished that first noble truth is established therein. Monks!”

Monks, when that bhikṣu gives a gift and speaks of giving, if there should be an enemy from the past, at that moment he relinquishes it, casts it off, becomes liberated from it, and brings it to an end. Monks!

This is called the bhikṣu’s foremost gift of true wisdom: namely, the relinquishing of all worldly exhaustion, being without desire, cessation, calming, and stilling. When a bhikṣu accomplishes this, he accomplishes the foremost ground for giving.
"Monks! That monk’s mind is defiled by desire, hatred, and delusion; he does not attain liberation. Monks!"
When all this lust, anger, and delusion are exhausted—without desire, extinguished, stilled, and ceased—one attains the foremost tranquility.
Monks! One who accomplishes that accomplishes the state of foremost tranquility.

“Monks! To say ‘I am’ is an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall be’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall neither be nor not be’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall have form’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall be formless’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall be neither with form nor without form’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall have perception’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall be without perception’ is also an inflation of the self; to say ‘I shall be neither with perception nor without perception’ is also an inflation of the self.”
"O bhikṣus! This is arrogance, this is haughtiness, this is heedlessness.
If one were free from all such self-exaltation, arrogance, haughtiness, and heedlessness, the mind would be said to be at rest."
"Monks! If the mind is at peace, one does not feel hatred, sorrow, weariness, or fear. Why is that? Because..."
Because that bhikṣu has accomplished the Dharma, there is no longer anyone who can speak of him with hatred.

If he is not hated, he does not grieve; if he does not grieve, he does not suffer; if he does not suffer, he does not become weary; if he is not weary, he does not fear. Because he is not afraid, he shall attain parinirvāṇa: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
When this Dharma had been taught, the Venerable Pukkusāti became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.

Thereupon, the Venerable Pukkusāti saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he realized the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, transcended uncertainty, and no longer relied on others. Being without further dependence and free from hesitation, he dwelt in the realization of the fruit and attained fearlessness in the Dharma of the Blessed One. He then rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, and said:
"Blessed One!"
I repent my transgression,
O Sugata! I confess it.
They are like fools, like the deluded, like those who are unstable, like those who lack discernment; they do not recognize a fertile field and cannot know themselves.
Why is this? Because I have been called by them the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as their sovereign.
"I only pray that the Blessed One will grant me absolution for my transgression; having confessed my transgression, I shall not commit it again.
The Blessed One said, "Monk!"
"You are truly foolish; you are truly unstable; you do not understand well, in that you claim the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, to be your sovereign."

“Monks! If you are able to repent of your own transgressions, having seen them, disclose them, and guard against committing them again—monks, in this way you will benefit and not harm yourselves within the Noble Dharma and Discipline; that is to say, being able to repent of your own transgressions, having seen them, disclosing them, and guarding against committing them again.”
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Pukkusāti rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first discourse, "The Analysis of the Six Elements," ends here, totaling three thousand one hundred and thirty-one characters. 163. The Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Bases (163), Middle Length Discourses, Fundamental Section on Analysis, Second Sub-section on Analysis. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall teach you the Dharma, which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it possesses both meaning and phrasing, is complete and pure, and reveals the holy life—namely, the Sūtra on the Analysis of the Six Sense Bases.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
"World-Honored One!"
"We shall surely receive your instruction. The Buddha said: "You should know the six internal bases;

you should know the six internal bases of contact; you should know the eighteen internal mental activities; you should know the thirty-six internal 'swords'; within these, you should sever that which is to be severed and accomplish that which is to be accomplished; you should know the immeasurable internal teachings of the Dharma; and the three internal foundations of mindfulness, which are practiced by the noble ones."

When the Noble One has completed his training, he is able to instruct the multitude; as the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men, he tames those who follow all paths—this is called the section on the Discourse on the Analysis of the Six Bases.
Regarding the statement, “The six sense bases should be known as internal,” for what reason is this said?
It refers to the eye base, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases; it is for this reason that it is said, “The six sense bases should be known as internal.”
Regarding the statement, "The six bases of contact should be known as internal":

for what reason is this said? It is because visual contact is for the purpose of seeing forms; auditory contact is for the purpose of hearing sounds; olfactory contact is for the purpose of smelling odors; gustatory contact is for the purpose of tasting flavors; tactile contact is for the purpose of feeling tangibles; and mental contact is for the purpose of cognizing phenomena. It is for this reason that it is said, "The six bases of contact should be known as internal."
"Regarding the eighteen mental explorations (*aṣṭādaśa-manopavicārāḥ*) that should be known as internal: for what reason is this said?

A monk, having seen a form with the eye, dwells exploring the form with joy, dwells exploring the form with sorrow, or dwells exploring the form with equanimity. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. Having cognized a phenomenon (*dharma*) with the mind, he dwells exploring the phenomenon with joy, dwells exploring the phenomenon with sorrow, or dwells exploring the phenomenon with equanimity. These are called the six explorations of joy, the six explorations of sorrow, and the six explorations of equanimity; collectively they are termed the eighteen mental explorations. It is for this reason that it is said: 'The eighteen mental explorations should be known as internal.'"
"Regarding the 'thirty-six knives,' one should know that as internal; for what reason is this said?

There are six kinds of joy based on attachment, six kinds of joy based on non-attachment; six kinds of grief based on attachment, six kinds of grief based on non-attachment; and six kinds of equanimity based on attachment, six kinds of equanimity based on non-attachment."
"What are the six bases of attachment for joy?
What are the six bases of non-attachment for joy?
Having seen a form with the eye, joy arises; one should know that there are two kinds: either based on attachment or based on non-attachment."
What is attachment based on joy?

When the eye perceives a form that is pleasing, which the mind attends to, desires, and finds delight in, one wishes to obtain what has not yet been obtained, and having obtained it, one recollects it and gives rise to joy. Such joy is called attachment based on joy.
What is the joy based on dispassion?

It is knowing that form is impermanent, subject to change, exhausted, dispassionate, ceased, and stilled; that all past and present forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation. Having recollected this, joy arises. Such joy is called joy based on dispassion.

In the same way, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have cognized their respective objects and give rise to joy, one should know that there are two kinds: either based on attachment or based on non-desire.
What is attachment based on joy?

It is when the mind cognizes a dharma that is delightful; one attends to it with the mind, loves the dharma, and experiences pleasure associated with desire. One desires to obtain what has not yet been obtained, and having obtained it, one recollects it and gives rise to joy. Such joy is called attachment based on joy.
What is the basis of joy upon non-desire?

It is knowing that phenomena are impermanent, subject to change, exhaustion, non-desire, cessation, and subsiding; recollecting that all phenomena, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation, one gives rise to joy. Such joy is called the basis of joy upon non-desire.
"What are the six kinds of sorrow based on attachment?
What are the six kinds of sorrow based on non-desire?
When one sees a form with the eye and sorrow arises, it should be known that there are two types: either based on attachment or based on non-desire."
What is sorrow based on attachment?

When the eye perceives a form that is pleasing, agreeable, lovely, and associated with desire, if one who has not yet obtained it does not obtain it, or if one who has already obtained it finds it pass away, disintegrate, cease, and change, sorrow arises. Such sorrow is called sorrow based on attachment.
How does sorrow depend on dispassion?

One knows that form is impermanent, subject to change, exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, and subsiding; one recollects that all forms, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation, and having recollected this, one reflects:
"When shall I dwell, having attained perfection in that state, namely:..."
"The noble ones dwell having accomplished their practice.
This is called the supreme equipment for contact with the aspiration to fear [suffering], knowing that suffering and birth give rise to sorrow.
Such sorrow is said to be the basis for sorrow through non-desire.

In the same way, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have cognized mental phenomena and sorrow arises, one should know that it is of two kinds: either based on attachment or based on non-desire.
What is sorrow based on attachment?

It is when the mind cognizes a dharma that is pleasing, and one attends to it, loves it, and experiences pleasure associated with desire; yet, that which has not been obtained is not obtained, and that which has been obtained passes away, disperses, perishes, changes, and transforms, giving rise to sorrow. Such sorrow is called sorrow based on attachment.
How does sorrow depend on dispassion?

One knows that phenomena are impermanent, subject to change, exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, and stilling; that all phenomena—past and present—are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation. Having reflected thus, one forms this thought:
"When shall I dwell having attained that state?"
That is to say:
"One dwells having attained the practice of the noble ones.
This is called the supreme equipment for contact with aspirations and terrors, wherein one knows suffering and the arising of sorrow.
Such sorrow is called sorrow based on non-desire.
What are the six kinds of equanimity based on attachment?
What are the six kinds of equanimity based on non-desire?
When one has seen a form with the eye and gives rise to equanimity (*upekṣā*), it should be known that there are two kinds: either based on attachment or based on non-desire.
What is equanimity based on attachment?

When the eye cognizes a form and equanimity arises, if that person is unlearned, lacks wisdom, and is foolish, deluded, and an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana*), they possess equanimity toward forms but do not depart from forms; this is called equanimity based on attachment.
What is equanimity based on dispassion?

Knowing that form is impermanent, subject to change, exhausted, dispassionate, ceased, and stilled—recalling that all forms, past and present, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation—one dwells having abandoned them.

If one cultivates equanimity with a sincere intention, this is called equanimity based on non-attachment; likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and when the mind has cognized dharmas and equanimity arises, it should be known that there are two kinds: either based on attachment or based on non-attachment.
What is equanimity based on attachment?

When the mind cognizes phenomena and equanimity arises, yet one is not learned, lacks wisdom, and is foolish, deluded, and an ordinary person—one maintains equanimity toward phenomena without being free from them; this is called equanimity based on attachment.
How does one dwell in equanimity based on dispassion?

One knows with the mind that phenomena are impermanent, subject to change, exhausted, dispassionate, ceased, and stilled; having recollected that all phenomena—past and present—are impermanent, suffering, and subject to cessation, one dwells in equanimity.
If one cultivates equanimity with a resolute intention, this is called "equanimity based on non-desire.

These are the six types of joy based on attachment and the six types of joy based on non-desire; the six types of grief based on attachment and the six types of grief based on non-desire; and the six types of equanimity based on attachment and the six types of equanimity based on non-desire. Taken together, these are said to be the thirty-six "blades. One should know that the "internal" refers to what is spoken of by reason of these.
Regarding the statement, "In this regard, one who abandons those [fetters] accomplishes this," for what reason is it so stated?
It is because these six types of joy depend upon dispassion (*vairāgya*); they take hold of it, rely upon it, and abide in it.
That is to say, these six types of joy depend on attachment; by extinguishing them, removing them, and vomiting them out, one thus abandons them.
These six types of sorrow depend on non-desire; they grasp this, rely on this, and abide in this.
This means that these six types of sorrow rely on attachment; by extinguishing them, removing them, and vomiting them out, one thus abandons them.
This means that these six types of equanimity rely on dispassion, taking this as their basis, relying on this, and abiding in this.
This means that these six types of equanimity rely on attachment; they are the cessation of that, the removal of that, the vomiting out of that—it is thus the abandonment of that.
This means that these six types of grief rely on non-desire; they grasp at this, rely on this, and abide in this.
That is to say, these six types of joy rely on dispassion; they extinguish that, eliminate that, and vomit out that—thus they sever that.
That is to say, these six types of equanimity rely on dispassion; they grasp this, rely on this, and abide in this.
That is to say, these six types of grief rely upon desirelessness; they are extinguished by it, removed by it, vomited out by it—in this way, they are abandoned by it.
"There is equanimity with manifold contacts and manifold feelings, and there is equanimity with a single contact and no manifold feelings."
What is the equanimity that has immeasurable contact and manifold contact?
If equanimity is directed toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, this equanimity has immeasurable contact and manifold contact.
What is the abandonment of a single mode of contact (*ekābhisaṃskāra*) without a manifold mode of contact?

It means that one abandons [the desire for sensation] by relying on either the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, or the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the abandonment of a single mode of contact without a manifold mode of contact; that is, this abandonment possesses one mode of contact, not a manifold mode of contact.
One grasps this, relies on this, and dwells in this; that is to say, this relinquishing involves immeasurable contacts and various contacts.
One extinguishes them, removes them, and vomits them out; in this way, one abandons them.

It takes up the immeasurable, relies on the immeasurable, and abides in the immeasurable; that is to say, this equanimity has a single further experience (*anubhava*), not manifold further experiences—it takes up this, relies on this, and abides in this.
It is said that this equanimity has immeasurable further experiences, manifold further experiences.
"To extinguish that, to remove that, to vomit that out—thus is it abandoned. Regarding this, it is said: "One who abandons that within achieves this.
For what reason is it said, "One should know that immeasurable teaching is internal"?

The Tathāgata has four disciples: one of superior conduct, one of superior intention, one of superior mindfulness, and one of superior wisdom; there is also one who possesses eloquence and has achieved the foremost eloquence, living for a hundred years. For a full hundred years, the Tathāgata taught the Dharma to him—excepting the times for eating and drinking, for defecation and urination, for sleep and rest, and for assemblies—and regarding the words and phrases of the Dharma taught by that Tathāgata, he contemplated their meaning with wisdom, swiftly discerning the meaning so that he no longer had to ask the Tathāgata about the Dharma again.

Why is this so? Because the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is without limit and is an inexhaustible Dharma; its phrases and dharma-words are for the contemplation of meaning. Even until the end of the lives of the four disciples, it is like four skilled archers who draw their strong bows and release them together; being well-trained, well-informed, and possessing skillful means, they pierce through to the past with speed.

In this way, World-Honored One, you have four disciples: one with superior conduct, one with superior resolve, one with superior mindfulness, and one with superior wisdom; there is also one who has attained eloquence and possesses the foremost eloquence, living for a hundred years. For a full hundred years, the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma to them, except during times for eating and drinking, times for defecation and urination, times for sleep and rest, and times for assemblies.

Regarding the Dharma taught by that Tathāgata, he contemplates the meaning of its words and phrases; through wisdom, he swiftly contemplates their meaning and no longer needs to ask the Tathāgata about the Dharma again.
Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is infinite and inexhaustible; one should know that the immeasurable teaching of the Dharma is internal. For this reason it is said:
"The three foundations of mindfulness are those practiced by the noble ones; having practiced them, the noble ones are able to instruct the multitudes."
For what reason is this said?

If the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples out of compassion and pity, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace and happiness, and giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion—this is for their benefit, this is for their happiness, and this is for their benefit and happiness.

If those disciples are disrespectful, do not practice accordingly, do not establish themselves in wisdom, their minds do not incline toward the Dharma or the secondary Dharma (anudharma), they do not receive the true Dharma, they contravene the teachings of the World-Honored One, and are unable to attain meditative concentration, the World-Honored One does not feel sorrow or distress on account of this.

But the Blessed One, being detached and having nothing to do, possesses constant mindfulness and constant wisdom; this is called the first station of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna). It is that which is practiced by the noble ones (ārya); once the noble ones have practiced it, the multitude can be instructed.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples out of compassion and pity, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace and happiness; he gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, thinking: 'This is for their benefit, this is for their happiness, this is for their benefit and happiness.'"

If those disciples are respectful and compliant in their conduct and established in wisdom, yet their minds incline toward the Dharma and the secondary Dharma (anudharma), upholding the true Dharma and not contradicting the teaching of the World-Honored One, and are able to attain meditative concentration—yet even so, the World-Honored One does not consider this alone to be cause for rejoicing.

But the Blessed One, having relinquished all that is to be done, possesses constant mindfulness and constant wisdom; this is called the second application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), which is practiced by the noble ones (ārya). Having practiced it, the noble ones are able to instruct the multitude.

"Furthermore, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to his disciples out of compassion and pity, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace and happiness; he gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, thinking: 'This is for their benefit, this is for their happiness, this is for their benefit and happiness.'"

There may be disciples who are disrespectful and do not practice accordingly; they do not establish themselves in wisdom, their minds do not incline toward the Dharma or the secondary Dharma (anudharma), they do not receive the true Dharma, they contravene the teachings of the World-Honored One, and they are unable to attain meditative concentration.

There may be disciples who, practicing with reverence and compliance, are established in wisdom; their minds are directed toward and inclined toward the Dharma and the secondary Dharma (anudharma); they uphold the true Dharma, do not contravene the teachings of the World-Honored One, and are able to attain meditative concentration.

The World-Honored One does not feel sorrow on account of this, nor does he feel joy; rather, the World-Honored One dwells in equanimity, free from purposeful striving, with constant mindfulness and constant awareness. This is called the third application of mindfulness.
This refers to that which is practiced by the noble ones; having practiced it, the multitude may be instructed. The three foundations of mindfulness are what is practiced by the noble ones.
It is because they have practiced these that the multitude may be instructed; it is for this reason that it is so stated.
“The Unsurpassed Tamer of Men is the Tamer of Men who proceeds toward all directions.
For what reason is this said?
A Tamer of Men is one who tames men by proceeding toward a single direction—whether east, south, west, or north.”
One who trains an elephant directs the elephant toward one direction—whether east, south, west, or north;
one who trains a horse directs the horse toward one direction—whether east, south, west, or north;
and one who trains an ox directs the ox toward one direction—whether east, south, west, or north.

The Unsurpassed Tamer of Men tames those who proceed toward all directions. Among these, one who internally possesses the perception of form observes forms externally; this is called the first direction.
One who is internally without the perception of form observes forms externally; this is called the second direction.
One dwells having attained and touched with the body the liberation of the beautiful; this is called the third direction.

Transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one dwells having attained and touched the sphere of infinite space, which is "infinite space"; this is called the fourth direction.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the fifth direction.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness; this is called the sixth direction.
Having transcended the sphere of nothingness, one dwells having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh direction.

Having transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells having attained the bodily contact of the cessation of perception and feeling; with wisdom one observes the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows—this is called the eighth direction.
"The Unsurpassed Tamer of Men, the Tamer of Men who proceeds toward all directions—it is for this reason that it is so called.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Vibhaṅga-Ṣaḍāyatana-sūtra*, Second, ends here; two thousand five hundred and twelve characters. 164. The *Vibhaṅgadhamma-vipassanā-sūtra* (164), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Fundamental Vibhaṅga Section, *Vibhaṅgadhamma-vipassanā-sūtra*, Third, Fourth Recitation Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I shall preach the Dharma for you—excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; possessing both meaning and phrasing, complete and pure, revealing the holy life. It is called the Sūtra on the Discernment and Contemplation of Dharmas.”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!"
"I shall surely receive your instruction.
The Buddha said, "Bhikṣu!"
"Observe in this way, in this way. Having observed thus, bhikkhu, the mind goes outward and scatters;
the mind does not abide within, and it is ungrasping yet fearful."
"Monks! Observe in this way, observe thus. Monks! Having observed in this manner, the mind does not go outward nor is it scattered;
the mind dwells within, is without grasping and without fear. In this way, there is no further birth, aging, sickness, or death—this is called the end of suffering."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, he rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in private meditation.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Venerable friends!..."
"You should know that the Blessed One has briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis, and then rose from his seat, entered his room, and sat in meditation:
'Monks! Contemplate in such and such a way; having contemplated thus, monks! "
The mind wanders outward and scatters; the mind does not abide within, and it is terrified by what it does not grasp.
Bhikṣu! Observe in this way, in this manner. Having observed thus, bhikṣu!

The mind does not go outward nor is it scattered; the mind abides within, neither grasping nor fearing. In this way, one is no longer subject to birth, aging, illness, and death—this is called the end of suffering.
They further thought:
"Venerable friends!
Who among us is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just spoken in brief?"
He further thought to himself:

"The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One as well as by wise fellow-practitioners; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly explained."
"Venerable friends!
Let us go together to the Venerable Mahākaccāna and request him to explain this matter; if the Venerable Mahākaccāna analyzes it for us, we shall properly receive and uphold it."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Mahākātyāyana was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:
"Venerable Mahākātyāyana!"
"You should know that the Blessed One spoke this meaning in brief without detailed analysis, then rose from his seat, entered his room, and sat in meditative seclusion, saying:
'Monks! Contemplate in such and such a way; having contemplated thus, monks! "
The mind wanders outward and scatters; the mind does not abide within, and it is terrified without receiving anything.
Monks! Observe in this way, in this manner. Having observed thus, monks!

The mind does not go outward nor is it scattered; the mind abides within, neither grasping nor fearing. In this way, birth, old age, sickness, and death no longer arise; this is called the end of suffering.
We then thought to ourselves:
"Venerable friends!
Who among us is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated?"
We further thought to ourselves:

"The Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One and by wise fellow-practitioners; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated."
"I only pray that the Venerable Mahākaccāna will explain this in detail out of compassion.
Then, the Venerable Mahākaccāna said to them, "Virtuous ones!..."
Listen to my parable, for the wise understand its meaning upon hearing it.
Venerable sirs!

It is just as if there were a man seeking wood, who, for the sake of obtaining wood, took an axe and entered a forest. There he saw a great tree with roots, trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit; yet that man did not touch the roots, the trunk, the joints, or the fruit, but touched only the branches and leaves.
It is just as you have said, worthy ones. While the Blessed One is present, he has left him to come to me and ask about this matter.
Why is that? Worthy ones!

One should know that the Blessed One is the eye, is wisdom, is the meaning, is the Dharma, is the Lord of Dharma, and is the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of the ultimate truth and manifests all meanings—by means of that Blessed One.
"Venerable friends!
You should go to the Blessed One and ask him about this matter:
'Blessed One!'"
"What does this mean?
What is the significance of this?
As the Blessed One has spoken it, you venerable ones should receive and uphold it well.
Then the bhikṣus replied,
“Indeed it is so,
Venerable Mahākātyāyana!”

The Blessed One is the eye, he is wisdom, he is the meaning, he is the Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, and the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of the ultimate truth and manifests all meanings. Therefore, we should go to where the Blessed One is and ask him about this matter:
"Blessed One!..."
"What does this mean?
What is the significance of this?
We shall properly receive and uphold it just as the Blessed One has spoken.

However, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is constantly praised by the Blessed One and by wise fellow practitioners of the holy life; the Venerable Mahākaccāna is able to extensively analyze the meaning of what the Blessed One has briefly explained.
“I only wish that the Venerable Mahākaccāna would explain this in detail out of compassion.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed the bhikkhus:
“O worthy ones!...”
Listen together to what I say,
worthy ones!
How is it that a bhikkhu’s mind goes outward and scatters?

"Venerable friends! When a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, consciousness consumes the characteristic of the form; consciousness clings to the characteristic of the pleasure in the form; consciousness is bound by the characteristic of the pleasure in the form. That mind, fettered by the attachment to the taste of that characteristic of the form, flows outward and scatters.

It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. When the mind cognizes a mental phenomenon, consciousness consumes the characteristic of the phenomenon; consciousness clings to the characteristic of the pleasure in the phenomenon; consciousness is bound by the characteristic of the pleasure in the phenomenon. That mind, fettered by the attachment to the taste of that characteristic of the phenomenon, flows outward and scatters."
Venerable friends!
In this way, a bhikkhu’s mind goes outward and scatters abroad.
Venerable friends!
"How is it, venerable friends, that a bhikkhu’s mind does not go outward in distraction?

Here, venerable friends, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, his consciousness does not feast upon the sign of the form; his consciousness does not cling to the pleasure-sign of the form; his consciousness is not bound by the pleasure-sign of the form. That sign of the form and its gratification do not fetter his mind, so it does not go outward in distraction."

In the same way, with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind cognizing mental phenomena (*dharma*), consciousness does not consume the characteristic of mental phenomena; consciousness does not cling to the characteristic of the pleasure of mental phenomena; consciousness is not bound by the characteristic of the pleasure of mental phenomena. That flavor of the characteristic of mental phenomena does not fetter the mind, nor does it issue forth and scatter outwardly.
"Venerable friends!
In this way, the mind of a bhikṣu does not go outward to scatter abroad.
Venerable friends!"
"How is it that a bhikkhu’s mind does not abide within?
Venerable friends!

A bhikkhu, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna."
That consciousness is attached to and relishes seclusion; it depends on it, dwells in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound by it, so that the consciousness does not abide within.

Furthermore, venerable friends, when a bhikkhu has stilled directed thought and evaluation, with internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by rapture and happiness.
That consciousness becomes attached to the flavor of concentration; it relies upon it, dwells in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound by it, such that the consciousness does not abide within.

Furthermore, venerable friends, a bhikkhu, detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, "He who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells happily"—attaining and abiding in the third dhyāna.
That consciousness is attached to the flavor of non-joy; it relies upon it, dwells in it, is conditioned by it, and is bound by it, such that the consciousness does not abide within.

Furthermore, venerable friends, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

That consciousness becomes attached to the flavor of equanimity and the purity of mindfulness; it depends upon that, dwells in that, is bound by that as its object, and thus the consciousness does not abide within.
"Furthermore, worthy ones!

A bhikkhu, having transcended all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, attains and dwells in the base of infinite space.
