Sūtra on the Mind (172), Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on the Mind, Sūtra on the Mind, Number One. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu was sitting in meditation in a secluded and tranquil place, reflecting with this thought in his mind:
"Who leads the world away?"
"Who is it that becomes stained and attached?
Who is it that exercises mastery?
Then, at the hour of late afternoon, the bhikkhu rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, sat down to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Just now, while I was sitting in meditation in a solitary and tranquil place, this thought arose in my mind:
‘Who leads the world away?’”
"Who is it that becomes stained and attached?
Who is it that gives rise to mastery?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One sighed and said:
“Excellent! Excellent, bhikṣu!”
This means there is a noble path and a noble contemplation, with supreme eloquence and skillful reflection:
"Who leads the world away?
Who is subject to defiled attachment?"
"Who gives rise to sovereignty?
"Bhikṣu! Is this what you asked?"
The bhikkhu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣus! The mind leads the world; the mind is its point of attachment; the mind exercises mastery over it."
Monks! He leads the world away; he is attached to it; he exercises mastery over it. Monks!
The well-versed noble disciple is not led away by the mind, nor is he defiled by the mind, nor does he fall under the sway of the mind.
Monks! The well-versed noble disciple does not follow the dictates of the mind; rather, it is the mind that follows the well-versed noble disciple.
The bhikṣu said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked:
"World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu who is learned is called a 'bhikṣu who is learned. "
"Bhagavān!
What is a bhikṣu who is learned?
How is a bhikṣu who is learned designated?"
Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Monks! There is a noble path and a noble vision, with most excellent eloquence and skillful reflection. [He says:
'World-Honored One!'"
"A bhikkhu of much learning, a bhikkhu of much learning," [you] say,
World-Honored One.
In what way is one a bhikkhu of much learning?
"How is a bhikṣu of great learning designated? "Bhikṣu,
is that what you have asked?"
The bhikṣu replied: “It is so,
World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One said: “Monks, what I have taught is very extensive:

namely, the discourses (sutta), songs (geyya), prophecies (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), causal narratives (udāna), recorded sayings (itivuttaka), legends (jātaka), birth stories (abbhutadhamma), analytical expositions (vedalla), marvelous events (adbhutadharma), and explanations of the meaning (upadeśa).”

"Monks! If there is a son of good family who understands the meaning and the Dharma of even a four-line verse spoken by me, who proceeds toward the Dharma and inclines toward the Dharma, he proceeds in accordance with the holy life."
"Monks! There is no description of a learned monk that surpasses this. Monks!"
"In this way, a bhikkhu is one of great learning; it is in this manner that the Tathāgata designates a bhikkhu of great learning.
The bhikkhus said: "Excellent!"
Excellent!
Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked:
“World-Honored One!
"A bhikṣu who is learned possesses penetrating wisdom; a bhikṣu who is learned possesses penetrating wisdom," [you] say, World-Honored One.
In what way does a learned bhikṣu possess penetrating wisdom?
"How does one designate a learned bhikṣu as one who possesses clear and penetrating wisdom?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, bhikṣu!
To possess a noble path and a noble contemplation, with most sublime eloquence and skillful reflection— this is indeed excellent.
“World-Honored One!
A bhikṣu who is learned possesses clear and penetrating wisdom; World-Honored One, one speaks of a bhikṣu who is learned as possessing clear and penetrating wisdom.”
"What is the wise and discerning wisdom of a learned bhikṣu?
How is the wise and discerning wisdom of a learned bhikṣu established? "Bhikṣus! [The Buddha said: "It is as follows."
“Is it as you have asked?
The bhikṣu replied, “It is so.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied: “Bhikṣu!”

If a bhikkhu, having heard of this suffering, further perceives suffering as it truly is with wisdom; and having heard of the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering, further perceives the path leading to the cessation of suffering as it truly is with wisdom—then, bhikkhu!
"In this way, a bhikkhu who is learned possesses clear and penetrating wisdom; it is in this manner that the Tathāgata designates a bhikkhu who is learned as possessing clear and penetrating wisdom.
The bhikkhu said: "Excellent!"
Excellent!
Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!
At that time, the bhikṣu, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked:
"World-Honored One!"
“Bhagavān, regarding the ‘intelligent bhikṣu of keen wisdom and vast wisdom,’ who is said to be an intelligent bhikṣu of keen wisdom and vast wisdom?
Bhagavān, in what way is a bhikṣu intelligent, of keen wisdom, and of vast wisdom?”
"How does one designate a bhikṣu as being clever, wise, and possessed of broad wisdom?
Having heard this, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent, bhikṣu!
You who possess the noble path and noble insight, with most sublime eloquence and virtuous reflection, [you say]:
'World-Honored One!'"
"What is meant by a wise bhikṣu possessing keen wisdom and broad wisdom?
How is it that a wise bhikṣu is designated as possessing keen wisdom and broad wisdom?
"Bhikṣus! [the Buddha said.]
"Is it as you have asked?
The bhikṣu replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:

“If a bhikṣu does not think of harming himself, does not think of harming others, nor does he think of harming both; rather, the bhikṣu thinks only of benefiting himself and benefiting others, benefiting many people, having compassion for the world, and seeking what is meaningful, beneficial, secure, and happy for gods and humans.”
“Monks! Thus is a wise monk, one of keen and broad intelligence; thus does the Tathāgata designate a wise monk as one of keen and broad intelligence.
The monks said to him:
“Excellent! Excellent!
Indeed it is so.”
"World-Honored One!

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣu received it well, retained it well, and mastered it through recitation; he then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, having heard the instruction of the Blessed One, a bhikkhu dwelt alone in seclusion, his mind free from negligence, practicing with diligence.

Having dwelt alone in seclusion, his mind free from negligence, and practicing with diligence, he—having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith as a son of noble family who has shaved off hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, training for the sake of the unsurpassed holy life—realized for himself in this very life, through his own direct knowledge and realization, that he had attained the goal: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence," knowing this as it truly is.
Having understood the Dharma, that venerable one attained even the state of an Arhat.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Citta Sutta, the first, ends here; it contains one thousand fifty-four words. 173. The Pūmī Sutta (173). Majjhima Nikāya, Citta Vagga, Pūmī Sutta, the second; the fourth section for recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
At that time, the Venerable Bhumija was also staying in the secluded meditation hall at Rājagṛha.

Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the Venerable Bhumija put on his robes, took his bowl, and intended to enter Rājagṛha to go on almsround. The Venerable Bhumija then thought to himself:
"Let me set aside going into Rājagṛha for alms; I shall instead go to the house of the young prince Jīvaka Śreṇyaputra."
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhumija went to the residence of the young prince Jīvaka Śyāmaputra.

Seeing the Venerable Bhumija approaching from afar, the young prince Jīvaka Śyāmaputra rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, and with palms joined toward the Venerable Bhumija, spoke thus:
"Welcome, Venerable Bhumija!"
"The Venerable Bhumija has not come here for a long time; please sit upon this seat.
The Venerable Bhumija then took his seat.
Prince Jīvaka Komārabhacca bowed his head at the feet of the Venerable Bhumija, withdrew to sit on one side, and said:
“Venerable Pūriya!
I wish to ask you something; will you allow me to ask?
Venerable Pūriya replied:
“O Prince! Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
Thereupon, the Prince questioned the Venerable Bhumija:
“Or there may come to me certain recluses and brahmins who say to me:

‘Prince, if someone practices the holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly attain its fruit; or if they practice it without an aspiration; or if they practice it with both aspiration and no aspiration; or if they practice it with neither aspiration nor no aspiration, they will certainly attain its fruit.’”
"Venerable Pūtimāṃsa!
With what intention and for what reason did the Teacher say this?
Venerable Pūtimāṃsa replied:
“Prince! I have not heard this directly from the Blessed One, nor have I heard it from those of holy life. Prince!”
The Blessed One has spoken thus:

"Whether a person practices the holy life with a vow, or without a vow, or with both a vow and no vow, or neither with a vow nor without a vow, if they practice the holy life correctly, they will certainly attain the fruit."
The youth Rājakumāra said:

"If the Venerable Teacher Pūraṇa holds such a view and speaks thus, then among the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its śramaṇas and brahmins, from humans up to the gods, he stands at the very pinnacle."
"Venerable Bhumija,
please eat here.
Venerable Bhumija accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Venerable Bhūmī had accepted by remaining silent, the royal youth rose from his seat, personally provided water for washing, and with his own hands served a variety of most excellent, pure, and exquisite foods—both solid and soft—in great abundance until he was fully satisfied. When the meal was finished, the vessels were cleared away, and after the water for washing had been offered, the youth took a small seat and sat apart to listen to the Dharma.

The Venerable Bhūmi taught the Dharma to him, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; by means of countless skillful methods, he taught the Dharma to him, exhorting and inspiring him with longing faith.

Having attained joy, he rose from his seat and departed for the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and related to the Buddha everything that had been discussed with the royal youth.
Having heard this, the Blessed One said:
"Bhūmī! For what reason have you not explained the four similes to Prince Rājakumāra?"
The Venerable Bhumija asked:
“World-Honored One!
What are the four similes?”
The Blessed One replied: “Bhūmi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a false holy life with the intention of attaining a result, they will certainly not obtain that result. Whether they practice a false holy life without an intention, with an intention and no intention, or with neither an intention nor no intention, they will certainly not obtain a result.”
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Path. Pūmi!

It is just as if there were someone who, desiring to obtain milk, were to milk a cow by its horns; they would certainly not obtain milk. Whether one has no aspiration, or has both aspiration and non-aspiration, or neither aspiration nor non-aspiration—if such a person desires to obtain milk and milks a cow by its horns, they will certainly not obtain milk.
Why is that? Because he seeks milk through wrong means, namely by milking a cow's horn.
It is thus, Bhumija!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit; nor will they attain its fruit if they practice a wrong holy life without an aspiration, with both aspiration and no aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor no aspiration.
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Path. "Pūrṇa!

If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who possesses right view and concentration of right view, and he practices the holy life with a vow, he will certainly attain the fruit; or if he practices the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or neither with a vow nor without a vow, he will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "the Path," Bhumija!

It is just as if there were a person who desired milk: by feeding the cow until it is full and then milking it, he will certainly obtain milk. Whether one has no wish, or a wish, or neither a wish nor no wish, if a person who desires milk feeds the cow until it is full and then milks it, he will certainly obtain milk.
Why is that? Because one seeks milk correctly, namely by milking the cow.
It is thus, Bhumija!

If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who possesses right view and concentration of right view, and who practices the holy life with a vow, he will certainly attain its fruit; or if he practices the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or with neither a vow nor no vow, he will certainly attain its fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the correct means is what is called "having the path.
"Pūmi! [This is so]."

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit; nor will they attain its fruit if they practice a wrong holy life without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
Why is this so? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Path. Pūrṇa!

It is just as if there were someone who, desiring to obtain ghee, filled a vessel with water and churned it; they would certainly not obtain ghee. Whether one has no aspiration, or has both aspiration and non-aspiration, or neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, if such a person, desiring to obtain ghee, fills a vessel with water and churns it, they will certainly not obtain ghee.
Why is this? Because one who seeks ghee through wrong means is like one who churns water.
Thus it is, Bhūmi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with the aspiration for results, they will certainly not attain the fruit. Whether they practice a wrong holy life without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, they will certainly not attain the fruit.
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Way. "Pūrṇa!..."

If there are recluses or brahmins who possess right view and concentration of right view, and they practice the holy life with a vow, they will certainly attain the fruit; or if they practice the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or with neither a vow nor no vow, they will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "the existence of the Path. Pūmi!

It is just as if there were a person desiring to obtain ghee who, taking a vessel and filling it with curd, churns it; he will certainly obtain the ghee. Whether one has no aspiration, or has an aspiration, or has neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, if a person desiring to obtain ghee takes a vessel and fills it with curd and churns it, he will certainly obtain the ghee.
Why is that? Because one seeks butter through the correct method, which is to churn the curd.
Thus it is, Bhumija!

If there are recluses or brahmins who possess right view and concentration of right view, and they practice the holy life with a vow, they will certainly attain the fruit; or if they practice the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or with neither a vow nor no vow, they will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "having the path.
"Pūmi! [This is what it means]."

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit; nor will they attain its fruit if they practice a wrong holy life without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is what is called the absence of the Path. Pūmi!

It is just as if there were someone who, desiring to obtain oil, were to place sand in a press and soak it with cold water before pressing it; they would certainly not obtain oil. Likewise, for one who has no aspiration, or who has both aspiration and non-aspiration, or who has neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, and yet desires to obtain oil by placing sand in a press and soaking it with cold water before pressing it—they will certainly not obtain oil.
Why is this? Because seeking oil through wrong means is like pressing sand.
Thus it is, Bhūmi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit; nor will they attain its fruit if they practice a wrong holy life without an aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration.
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is called "the absence of the Path. "Pūrṇa!

If there are recluses or brahmins who possess right view and concentration of right view, and they practice the holy life with a vow, they will certainly attain the fruit; or if they practice the holy life without a vow, with both vow and no-vow, or with neither vow nor no-vow, they will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "the path.

It is just as if there were a person who wished to obtain oil: he takes sesame seeds, places them in a press, soaks them in warm water, and presses them; he will certainly obtain oil. Whether one has no aspiration, or has an aspiration, or has neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, if a person wishing to obtain oil takes sesame seeds, places them in a press, soaks them in warm water, and presses them, he will certainly obtain oil.
Why is that? Because one seeks oil correctly, which means by pressing sesame seeds.
Thus it is, Bhumija!

If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who possesses right view and concentration of right view, and he practices the holy life with a vow, he will certainly attain the fruit; or if he practices the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or with neither a vow nor no vow, he will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "the path. "Pumila!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a false holy life with a specific aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit; whether they practice a false holy life without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, they will certainly not attain its fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Way. Pūrṇa!

It is just as if someone wishing to obtain fire were to use wet wood as the fire-drill base and drill with a wet pivot; they would certainly not obtain fire. Whether one has no aspiration, or has both aspiration and non-aspiration, or neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, if a person wishing to obtain fire uses wet wood as the fire-drill base and drills with a wet pivot, they will certainly not obtain fire.
Why is that? Because seeking fire through wrong means is like drilling into wet wood.
Thus it is, Pūmi!

If there are recluses or brahmins who hold wrong views and are fixed in wrong views, and they practice a wrong holy life with the aspiration for results, they will certainly not attain the fruit. Whether they practice a wrong holy life without aspiration, with both aspiration and non-aspiration, or with neither aspiration nor non-aspiration, they will certainly not attain the fruit.
Why is this? Because seeking results through wrong means is called the absence of the Path. "Pūrṇa!..."

If there are recluses or brahmins who possess right view and concentration of right view, and they practice the holy life with a vow, they will certainly attain the fruit; or if they practice the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or with neither a vow nor no vow, they will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit through the right means is what is called "the path. Pūmi!

It is just as if there were someone who desired fire: by using dry wood as the fire-drill base and drilling with a dry drill, he would certainly obtain fire. Whether one has no aspiration, or has an aspiration, or has neither an aspiration nor a non-aspiration, if one uses dry wood as the fire-drill base and drills with a dry drill, one will certainly obtain fire.
Why is that? Because one seeks fire correctly by means of drilling dry wood.
It is thus, Bhūmi!

If there is a śramaṇa or brahmin who possesses right view and concentration of right view, and he practices the holy life with a vow, he will certainly attain the fruit; or if he practices the holy life without a vow, with both a vow and no vow, or neither with a vow nor without a vow, he will certainly attain the fruit.
Why is this so? Because seeking the fruit correctly is what is called "having the path. "Pūrṇa!

If you were to explain these four similes to Prince Rājakumāra, upon hearing them, the prince would surely be greatly delighted and would provide for you for as long as he lives—namely, clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various other necessities of life.
The Venerable Bhumī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have never before heard these four similes; by what means could I have spoken them?”
"Only now have I heard this from the Blessed One.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Bhūmī and the monks rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Pūrima-sutta*, the second, ends here; two thousand eighty-three characters. 174. *Dhamma-sutta* (174), *Madhyama Āgama*, *Citta-varga*, the third and fourth recitations of the *Dhamma-sutta*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the world, there are four kinds of dharmas of feeling that are real. What are the four?

There are some dharmas of experience that are pleasant in the present but result in suffering in the future; there are some dharmas of experience that are painful in the present but result in pleasure in the future; there are some dharmas of experience that are painful in the present and also result in suffering in the future; and there are some dharmas of experience that are pleasant in the present and also result in pleasure in the future.
"What is the teaching that brings happiness in the present but results in the experience of suffering as its future retribution?
There may be certain śramaṇas or brahmins who enjoy themselves with beautifully adorned women and say to them:

'What terror do these śramaṇas and brahmins see in the future regarding sensual desires, and what calamity do they perceive, such that they sever desire and establish the practice of renouncing desire?'"
"This is a delightful adornment; the body of this woman is pleasant to touch and brings further pleasure.

He enjoys himself with this woman, playing and sporting with her. Having fully indulged in these practices, when his body breaks up and his life ends, he goes to an evil destination and is reborn in hell. Only then does he think:
"That ascetic or brahmin, seeing this future terror and seeing this calamity regarding sensual desires, abandoned desire and established the abandonment of desire."
"It is because of desire, through the strife of desire, and conditioned by desire that we undergo such extreme suffering and most grievous pain.
"It was as if, in the last month of spring when the midday sun was at its peak heat, there were seeds of a kudzu vine; scorched by the sun, they burst open and fell beneath a śāla tree."

At that time, the tree deity became terrified because of this. Then, the neighboring seed-village deities, the village deities of the hundred grains and medicinal herbs, and the kinsmen and friends among the tree deities—seeing that the seed deity would face fear and calamity in the future—went to where that tree deity was and consoled him, saying:
"O tree deity, do not be afraid!"
"O tree deity, do not fear!
This seed may now be eaten by deer, or eaten by peacocks, or blown away by the wind, or burned by a village fire, or burned by a wild fire, or it may be ruined and fail to become a seed."
Thus it is, tree spirit!
You shall find peace and security.

If this seed is not eaten by deer, nor eaten by peacocks; if it is not carried away by the wind, nor burned by village fire, nor burned by wild fire; and if it is not spoiled or rendered unfit to be a seed—this seed being neither deficient nor perforated, nor split open, and not damaged by wind, rain, or sun—it will quickly sprout upon being saturated by heavy rain.
Then that tree deity thought: "For what reason?
What future terror does that neighboring seed-spirit, the village deity, the deity of the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees, and his kinsmen and friends see in these seeds?"
"What calamity has occurred that you have come to comfort me, saying:
'O tree spirit, do not fear!'"
"O tree deity, do not fear!
O tree deity!

This seed may have been eaten by deer, or eaten by peacocks; it may have been carried away by the wind, or burned by a village fire, or burned by a forest fire; or it may have become rotten and ceased to be a viable seed."
Thus it is, tree spirit! You shall find peace and security.

If this seed is not eaten by deer, nor eaten by peacocks; if it is not carried away by the wind, nor burned by village fire, nor burned by wild fire; and if it is not spoiled or rendered unfit to be a seed; if this seed is neither deficient nor perforated, nor split asunder, and is not damaged by wind, rain, or sun; and if it receives the soaking of heavy rain, it will then quickly sprout.

"The stalk, branches, and leaves become supple and knotted; touching them brings joy to the body. This stalk, branches, and leaves are supple and knotted; touching them brings joy to the body, a pleasant contact that is further delightful."
This dependent tree grows large branches, nodes, and leaves, entwining that tree and covering it from above.
Once it has covered it from above, the deity of that tree then thinks:

"Those neighboring seed-village deities, the village deities of the hundred grains, medicinal herbs, and trees, as well as my kinsmen and friends, saw this future terror regarding the seed and, seeing this calamity, have come to console me, saying:"
“Tree spirit, do not fear!
Tree spirit, do not fear!

This seed may have been eaten by deer, or eaten by peacocks; it may have been blown away by the wind, or burned by a village fire, or burned by a forest fire; or it may have rotted and failed to become a seed.”
Thus it is, tree spirit!
You shall find peace and security.

If this seed is not eaten by deer, nor eaten by peacocks; if it is not carried away by the wind, nor burned by village fire, nor burned by wild fire; and if it is not spoiled or rendered unfit to be a seed—this seed being neither deficient nor pierced, nor split asunder, and not damaged by wind, rain, or sun—it will quickly sprout when drenched by heavy rain.
‘It is because of seeds, with seeds as a condition, that I experience this extreme suffering, this most heavy suffering.
In this way, there may be certain recluses or brahmins who enjoy themselves with beautifully adorned women and say:

‘What fear do these recluses and brahmins see regarding the future in relation to sensual desires, and what calamity do they perceive, that they abandon sensual desires and establish the abandonment of sensual desires?’”
"This delightful adornment brings pleasure and pleasant contact to the woman's body.

He enjoys himself with that woman, playing and sporting with her; having fully indulged in this practice, when his body breaks up and his life ends, he goes to a miserable destination and is reborn in hell, where he then reflects:
"That ascetic or brahmin, seeing this future terror and seeing this calamity regarding sensual desire, abandoned desire and established the relinquishing of desire."
"Because of desire, because of contention over desire, and because of the conditions of desire, we have experienced such extreme suffering and most grievous pain.
This is called the practice that yields happiness in the present but results in the experience of suffering as its retribution in the future.
"What is the phenomenon that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution in the future?

There may be one who possesses naturally heavy and turbid desire, heavy and turbid hatred, and heavy and turbid delusion; he frequently follows his desirous mind and experiences suffering and distress, and he frequently follows his hateful and deluded minds and experiences suffering and distress."

He undergoes suffering and distress for as long as his life lasts while practicing the holy life, even to the point of weeping and shedding tears; yet, having received this teaching and brought it to full completion, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn among the devas. This is called a teaching that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant reward in the future.
"What is the dharma that is painful in the present and will also result in painful retribution in the future?

There are certain śramaṇas and brahmins who go naked and without clothing; some use their hands as clothing, some use leaves as clothing, and some use beads as clothing. They do not take water from a jar, nor do they take water from a well. They do not eat food obtained by force, by weapons, or by robbery; they do not eat food obtained through deception or falsehood. They do not go in person, nor do they send a messenger; they do not accept invitations to come, nor accept invitations to go, nor accept invitations to stay."

If there are two people eating together, he does not eat among them; he does not eat at the home of a pregnant woman, nor at the home of one who keeps dogs; if flies carrying filth fly into the house, he does not eat; he does not consume fish, nor eat meat, nor drink alcohol, nor drink foul water, or perhaps drinks nothing at all, training in the practice of non-drinking.
Or he may eat one mouthful, taking that single mouthful as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven mouthfuls, taking those seven mouthfuls as sufficient.
Or he may eat one morsel, taking that single morsel as sufficient; or two, three, four, up to seven morsels, taking those seven morsels as sufficient.
Some eat once a day, taking that single meal as sufficient; others eat once every two, three, four, five, six, or seven days, or once every half-month or month, taking that single meal as sufficient.
Some eat leafy vegetables, some eat millet, some eat wild rice, some eat mixed grains, some eat *tuttula* food, and some eat coarse food.
Or they go to a secluded place and dwell in seclusion; they may eat roots, or fruits, or fruits that have fallen of their own accord.

They may wear garments made of joined pieces, or woolen garments, or *śīrṣaka* (head-covering) garments, or garments made of both wool and *śīrṣaka*, or garments made of whole hides, or garments made of perforated hides, or garments made of both whole and perforated hides.

Some wear their hair loose; some wear it braided; some wear it both loose and braided; some have shaved their heads; some have shaved their beards; some have shaved both beard and hair; some have plucked out their hair; some have plucked out their beards; and some have plucked out both beard and hair.
Some remain standing or sit while fasting; some practice the squatting gait; some lie upon thorns, using thorns as their bed; others lie upon grass, using grass as their bed.
Some serve water, drawing it with their hands day and night;
some serve fire, keeping it burning throughout the night;
others serve the sun, the moon, or venerable and noble deities, joining their palms and facing toward them.

In this manner, they undergo immeasurable suffering and practice with feverish agitation; having fully acquired these teachings, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell. This is called a teaching that is painful in the present and brings a painful retribution in the future.
"What is the Dharma that brings happiness in the present and will also yield a pleasant retribution in the future?

There may be one who is naturally not burdened by heavy desire, not burdened by heavy hatred, and not burdened by heavy delusion; he does not repeatedly follow a mind of desire and thereby experience suffering and distress, nor does he repeatedly follow a mind of hatred or a mind of delusion and thereby experience suffering and distress. With joy and gladness, he practices the holy life for as long as his lifespan lasts, even unto a state of rapturous delight."

Having received and fully mastered this Dharma, he exhausts the five lower fetters; he is reborn there by transformation and attains parinirvāṇa, reaching the state of non-retrogression and no longer returning to this world.
This is called the practice of receiving dharma that brings happiness in the present and will also bring the retribution of happiness in the future.
It is because there truly exist these four kinds of practices for receiving dharma in the world that this is said.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third discourse, *The Discourse on Receiving the Dharma*, ends here, totaling one thousand five hundred eighty-three characters. 175. *The Discourse on Receiving the Dharma* (175), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Chapter on the Mind, the fourth discourse in the fourth section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Kuru people at the Kuru capital of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this world, such desires, such hopes, such cravings, such pleasures, and such intentions cause the unwholesome states—which are neither delightful nor desirable—to cease, and give rise to the wholesome states which are delightful and desirable."
Although he has such desires, such hopes, such cravings, such pleasures, and such intentions, yet unwholesome phenomena arise and wholesome phenomena cease; this is a state of delusion.
My Dharma is profound, difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, and difficult to penetrate.

Such is my Dharma—profound, difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, and difficult to penetrate—that with the cessation of what is not pleasing, not beloved, and not agreeable, there arises what is pleasing, beloved, and agreeable; this is the state of non-delusion.
“In the world, there are four kinds of dharmas that are experienced. What are these four?

There are some dharmas that are pleasant in the present but result in suffering in the future; some dharmas that are painful in the present but result in happiness in the future; some dharmas that are painful in the present and also result in suffering in the future; and some dharmas that are pleasant in the present and also result in happiness in the future.”
"What is the practice that brings happiness in the present but results in suffering as its retribution in the future?

There is one who personally delights in and rejoices in killing; because of killing, he experiences pleasure and rejoices. He personally delights in and rejoices in taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view; because of wrong view, he experiences pleasure and rejoices."

Such bodily pleasure and mental pleasure, which are unwholesome in their origin and unwholesome in their arising, do not lead toward wisdom, do not lead toward awakening, and do not lead toward nirvāṇa; this is called the experience of a dharma that brings happiness in the present but results in suffering as its retribution in the future.
"What is the dharma that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution in the future?

There is one who personally undergoes suffering and personally experiences grief by abandoning killing; because of abandoning killing, suffering and grief arise. He personally undergoes suffering and personally experiences grief by abandoning taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to abandoning wrong view; because of abandoning wrong view, suffering and grief arise."

Such bodily and mental suffering that is wholesome, well-undertaken, and well-arisen—which leads toward wisdom, leads toward awakening, and leads toward Nirvana—is called "a dharma that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution in the future."
"What is the dharma that is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future?

There may be someone who, out of self-inflicted suffering and self-inflicted grief, takes life; because of taking life, they give rise to suffering and grief. That person, out of self-inflicted suffering and self-inflicted grief, likewise engages in taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to wrong view; because of wrong view, they give rise to suffering and grief."

Such bodily suffering and mental suffering, which arise from the unwholesome and are born of the unwholesome, do not lead to wisdom, do not lead to awakening, and do not lead to nirvāṇa; this is called a phenomenon that brings suffering in the present and will also bring the retribution of suffering in the future.
"What is the practice of the Dharma that brings happiness in the present and results in a happy retribution in the future?

There may be one who personally delights in and rejoices in abandoning killing; because of abandoning killing, he experiences happiness and joy. He personally delights in and rejoices in abandoning taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and so on, up to abandoning wrong view; because of abandoning wrong view, he experiences happiness and joy."

Such bodily pleasure and mental pleasure, which are wholesome in their origin and wholesome in their arising, lead toward wisdom, lead toward awakening, and lead toward Nirvana; this is called the teaching that is pleasant in the present and will also yield a pleasant result in the future.

"If there is a feeling that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering as its future retribution, that deluded person does not know it as it truly is—that this feeling is pleasant in the present but results in suffering as its future retribution. Not knowing it as it truly is, they continue to practice it without abandoning it; having practiced it without abandoning it, qualities that are unpleasant, unlovely, and disagreeable arise, while qualities that are pleasant, lovely, and agreeable cease."

It is like the amani medicine, which possesses excellent color, fragrance, and flavor in a single portion, yet is mixed with poison. Should someone take it for the sake of an illness, at the time of ingestion its color, fragrance, and flavor are pleasant, agreeable to the palate, and do not harm the throat; however, once ingested and within the abdomen, it no longer functions as medicine.

Thus, regarding this feeling that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering as its retribution in the future, the deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing this feeling as it truly is, they continue to practice and do not abandon it. Having continued to practice without abandoning it, phenomena that are unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable arise, while pleasant, lovely, and desirable phenomena cease; this is called the phenomenon of delusion.

"If there is a feeling that is painful in the present but will result in a pleasant ripening in the future, a deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing this feeling as it truly is—that it is painful in the present but will result in a pleasant ripening in the future—they do not cultivate its practice but instead abandon it. Having abandoned it through non-cultivation, what is disagreeable, unlovely, and undesirable arises, while what is agreeable, lovely, and desirable ceases; this is called a deluded state."

“If there is a feeling that is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future, that deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing this feeling as it truly is—that it is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future—they continue to practice it and do not abandon it. Having practiced it and not abandoned it, then what is unpleasant, unlovely, and disagreeable arises, while what is pleasant, lovely, and agreeable ceases.”

It is like excrement and urine mixed with poison; though someone might take it for the sake of a disease, at the time of ingestion it is foul in color, malodorous, and tasteless—unpalatable and irritating to the throat—and once it has entered the stomach, it no longer functions as medicine.

Thus, this feeling is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future; yet that deluded person does not know it as it truly is. Not knowing it as it truly is—that this feeling is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future—they continue to practice it without ceasing. Having practiced it without ceasing, there arise things that are unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable, while things that are pleasant, lovely, and desirable perish. This is called the nature of delusion.

"If there is a feeling that is pleasant in the present and will also result in a pleasant retribution in the future, yet that deluded person does not know it as it truly is—that this feeling is pleasant in the present and will also result in a pleasant retribution in the future—having failed to know it as it truly is, they do not cultivate it but instead abandon it. Having abandoned it through non-cultivation, things that are unpleasant, unlovely, and undesirable arise, while things that are pleasant, lovely, and desirable cease. This is called a deluded state."

One does not know the practiced dharma as it truly is, nor does one know the unpracticed dharma as it truly is; having failed to know the practiced dharma and the unpracticed dharma as they truly are, one practices what should not be practiced and fails to practice what should be practiced. Having practiced what should not be practiced and failed to practice what should be practiced, there arises that which is not delightful, not dear, and undesirable, and that which is delightful, dear, and desirable ceases. This is called the dharma of delusion.

“If there is a feeling that is pleasant in the present but results in suffering as its future retribution, the wise one knows it as it truly is: ‘This feeling is pleasant in the present but will result in suffering as its future retribution. Having known it as it truly is, he does not practice it but abandons it. Once he has abandoned it through non-practice, then states that are joyful, lovely, and agreeable arise, while states that are not joyful, not lovely, and disagreeable cease. This is called the quality of wisdom.”

If there is a feeling that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution in the future, the wise person knows it as it truly is: "This feeling is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution in the future. Having known it as it truly is, they practice and do not abandon it. Having practiced it without abandoning it, joy, delight, and agreeable states arise, while lack of joy, lack of delight, and disagreeable states cease.

It is like a mixture of feces and urine combined with various medicinal herbs; if someone takes it for the sake of an illness, at the time of ingestion it is foul in color, malodorous, and tasteless—unpalatable and irritating to the throat—but once ingested and in the stomach, it becomes medicine.

Thus, regarding this dharma of feeling that is painful in the present but brings a pleasant result in the future, the wise one knows it as it truly is. Having known it as it truly is—that this dharma of feeling is painful in the present but brings a pleasant result in the future—he practices it without interruption. Having practiced it without interruption, joy, love, and agreeable states arise, while lack of joy, lack of love, and disagreeable states cease. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

"If there is a feeling that is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future, the wise one knows it as it truly is: 'This feeling is painful in the present and will also result in a painful retribution in the future. Having known it as it truly is, he does not practice it and abandons it. Once he has abandoned it through non-practice, then qualities that are joyful, lovely, and agreeable arise, while qualities that are not joyful, not lovely, and not agreeable cease. This is called the quality of wisdom."

If there is a feeling that is pleasant in the present and will also yield a pleasant result in the future, the wise one knows it as it truly is: "This feeling is pleasant in the present and will also yield a pleasant result in the future. Having known it as it truly is, he practices it without interruption. Having practiced it without interruption, joy, affection, and agreeable states arise, while lack of joy, lack of affection, and disagreeable states cease.

It is like ghee and honey mixed with various medicinal herbs; if someone takes them for the sake of an illness, at the time of ingestion they possess fine color, fragrance, and flavor, being pleasant to the palate and not irritating the throat, yet once ingested into the stomach, they immediately become medicine.

Thus, this dharma of feeling is pleasant in the present and will also yield a pleasant result in the future; the wise one knows this as it truly is. Having known it as it truly is—that this dharma of feeling is pleasant in the present and will also yield a pleasant result in the future—he practices it continuously and does not abandon it. Having practiced it continuously and not abandoned it, joy, affection, and agreeable states arise, while lack of joy, lack of affection, and disagreeable states cease. This is called the dharma of wisdom.

One knows the dharmas to be practiced as they truly are, and one knows the dharmas not to be practiced as they truly are. Having known the dharmas to be practiced as they truly are and the dharmas not to be practiced as they truly are, one practices those dharmas that are to be practiced and does not practice those dharmas that are not to be practiced. Having practiced those dharmas to be practiced and refrained from practicing those not to be practiced, there arises what is joyful, lovely, and agreeable, and what is not joyful, not lovely, and disagreeable ceases. This is called the dharma of wisdom.
"In the world, there truly are these four kinds of ways of experiencing [feelings] (vedanā-dharma);
it is for this reason that I have spoken thus.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

176. The Discourse on the Practice of Meditation (176). Chapter Five of the Section on the Mind: The Fourth Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this world, there are four types of practitioners of dhyāna who are truly real.
What are the four?

There may be one practicing meditation who, though flourishing, considers himself declining; or one practicing meditation who, though declining, considers himself flourishing; or one practicing meditation who, when declining, knows his decline as it truly is; or one practicing meditation who, when flourishing, knows his flourishing as it truly is.
"How is it that a practitioner of meditation who is flourishing is said to be declining?

That practitioner of meditation, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna."
As that mind cultivates right reflection, it proceeds from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the first dhyāna and the concentration has ceased."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection and attained joy and tranquility; thus, I have passed from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing it as it truly is, he regresses from suchness; his mind then loses its concentration, and thus a practitioner of meditation who was flourishing comes to believe he is declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, with directed thought and evaluation stilled, becomes inwardly tranquil and one-pointed; without directed thought or evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss."
Cultivating right reflection with that mind, he proceeds from the second dhyāna to the third dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the second dhyāna and my meditative absorption has ceased."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection, and through joy and tranquility, I have passed from the second dhyāna to the third dhyāna; this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing it as it truly is, he regresses from reality and his mind loses its concentration; thus, this practitioner of meditation, though flourishing, claims to be declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity and seeks nothing; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, 'He who has equanimity and mindfulness dwells in happiness'—and thus attains and abides in the third dhyāna.
Cultivating right reflection with that mind, he proceeds from the third dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the third dhyāna and my meditative absorption has ceased."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection, attaining joy and tranquility; as I proceed from the third dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing it as it truly is, he regresses from suchness and his mind loses its concentration; thus, a practitioner of meditation who is actually flourishing considers himself to be declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, with the fading away of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity. Cultivating right reflection with that mind, he proceeds from the fourth dhyāna to the sphere of infinite space; this is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of dhyāna then reflects:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the fourth dhyāna and the concentration of cessation."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection and attained blissful tranquility; by proceeding from the fourth dhyāna to the sphere of infinite space, this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing it as it truly is, he regresses from reality and his mind loses its concentration; thus, a practitioner of meditation who is actually flourishing mistakenly believes he is declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attends to perceptions of diversity; he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space, thinking 'space is infinite. As he cultivates right reflection with that mind, he proceeds from the sphere of infinite space to the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of meditation then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the sphere of infinite space and the meditative absorption."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection, which is blissful and tranquil; having passed from the sphere of infinite space, I am proceeding toward the sphere of infinite consciousness—this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing it as it truly is, he regresses from reality and his mind loses its concentration; thus, a practitioner of meditation who is actually flourishing mistakenly thinks he is declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, having transcended the sphere of infinite space, dwells having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness. As he cultivates right reflection with that mind, he proceeds from the sphere of infinite consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness; this is a more excellent tranquility and peace."
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another realm; I have lost the sphere of infinite consciousness and have fallen away from the meditative attainment of cessation."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection, becoming blissful and tranquil; having proceeded from the sphere of infinite consciousness to the sphere of nothingness, this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he regresses from suchness and his mind loses its concentration; thus, a practitioner of meditation who is actually flourishing mistakenly believes he is declining.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation transcends the base of infinite consciousness; being without anything, he dwells having attained the base of nothingness. He cultivates right reflection with that mind, proceeding from the base of nothingness toward the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another realm; I have lost the sphere of nothingness and the meditative absorption of cessation."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "My mind has cultivated right reflection and attained joyful tranquility; by proceeding from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is a superior tranquility."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he regresses from reality; his mind then loses its concentration, and thus the practitioner of meditation, though flourishing, claims to be declining.
"What is it that causes a practitioner of meditation to decline yet believe they are flourishing?

It is when that practitioner of meditation, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna."
He abandons other minor perceptions and cultivates the path to the second dhyāna. That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind has cultivated right reflection; it is blissful and tranquil. Thus, I have passed from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna; this is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the first dhyāna, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions and entering the second dhyāna."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to recognize that mind and thereby loses his concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is actually declining thinks he is flourishing.

Furthermore, when the practitioner of meditation has stilled directed thought (*vitarka*) and evaluation (*vicāra*), and through internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, becomes free from directed thought and evaluation, attaining the joy and bliss born of concentration, he dwells having achieved the second dhyāna.
He abandons other minor perceptions and cultivates the path to the third dhyāna. That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind has cultivated right reflection; it is blissful and tranquil, having progressed from the second dhyāna to the third dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the second dhyāna, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions to enter the third dhyāna."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to perceive that mind and consequently loses his concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is actually declining claims to be flourishing.

Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, free from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity and seeks nothing, possessing right mindfulness and right clear comprehension while experiencing pleasure with the body.
That is to say, he dwells having attained the third dhyāna, which is described by the Noble Ones as "the state of equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss, free from pleasure.
While he is contemplating other minor perceptions and cultivating the path to the fourth dhyāna, that practitioner of meditation reflects:
"My mind has cultivated right reflection; it is blissful and tranquil. As I proceed from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna, this is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the third dhyāna, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions and entering the fourth dhyāna."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to recognize that mind and consequently loses his concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is declining believes himself to be flourishing.

Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, with the fading away of pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.
He abandons other minor perceptions and cultivates the path to the sphere of infinite space. That practitioner of dhyāna then reflects: "My mind has cultivated right reflection;
it is blissful and tranquil. From the fourth dhyāna, I am proceeding toward the sphere of infinite space, which is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the fourth dhyāna, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions and entering the sphere of infinite space."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he does not perceive that mind and consequently loses his concentration; thus, while practicing meditation, one who is actually declining claims to be flourishing.

Furthermore, a practitioner of meditation transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attends to perceptions of diversity; with the thought "space is infinite," he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space.
He abandons other minor perceptions and cultivates the path of the base of infinite consciousness; that practitioner of dhyāna then reflects:
"My mind has cultivated right reflection, which is blissful and tranquil; having moved from the base of infinite space to the base of infinite consciousness, this is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the base of infinite space, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions and entering the base of infinite consciousness."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to recognize that mind and consequently loses his concentration; thus, this practitioner of meditation, though declining, believes himself to be flourishing.
Furthermore, a practitioner of meditation transcends the base of infinite space and attains the base of infinite consciousness, dwelling having achieved this base of infinite consciousness.
He conceives other minor thoughts and cultivates the path to the sphere of nothingness. That practitioner of meditation then reflects: "My mind has cultivated right reflection;
it is blissful and tranquil. Having proceeded from the sphere of infinite consciousness to the sphere of nothingness, this is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the sphere of infinite consciousness, rather than contemplating other minor perceptions and entering the sphere of nothingness."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to perceive that mind and thereby loses his concentration; thus, while practicing meditation, he declines yet believes he is flourishing.
Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation transcends the sphere of infinite consciousness and, being without anything whatsoever, dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness.

He attends to other minor perceptions and cultivates the path to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That practitioner of meditation then reflects: "My mind has cultivated right reflection;
it is blissful and tranquil. Having passed from the sphere of nothingness to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is a superior tranquility."

That practitioner of meditation does not know it as it truly is: "It would be better to contemplate a perception associated with disenchantment and enter the sphere of nothingness, rather than contemplating some other minor perception and entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Not knowing this as it truly is, he fails to perceive his own mind and thereby loses his concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is actually declining claims to be flourishing.
How does a practitioner of meditation who is declining know his decline as it truly is?

That practitioner of meditation, by his practice, his characteristic, and his sign, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the accomplishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Not receiving this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the mental formations associated with the sphere of nothingness as a basis for regression; that practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the attainment of cessation."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is declining knows that he is declining as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner of meditation who practices with a certain conduct, characteristic, and sign, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, there is nothing whatsoever; he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness.

Not accepting this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the recollections and perceptions associated with the sphere of infinite consciousness that were his previous domain.
That practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original sign and moved toward another place; I have lost the sphere of nothingness and the meditative absorption."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is declining knows his decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner of meditation who practices, whose signs are such, and whose marks are such: having transcended the sphere of infinite space, he dwells, having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness, with the thought, 'Infinite is consciousness. "

Not receiving this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the mental formations associated with the base of infinite space—the very factors of regression—and that practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original sign and moved toward another state; I have lost the base of infinite consciousness; my meditative absorption has ceased."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, the practitioner of meditation who is declining knows his decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner of meditation who dwells with the practice, the characteristic, and the sign: transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory impact, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, he attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space, [perceiving] 'space is infinite. "

Not receiving this practice, not recollecting this sign or its mark, he practices only the recollection and perception associated with the delight in form—the very basis for falling back. That practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from the original sign and moved toward another place; I have lost the sphere of infinite space and the meditative absorption."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness, his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, when a practitioner of meditation experiences decline, he knows that decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation dwells having attained and accomplished the fourth dhyāna, which is characterized by the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and sorrow, it is neither painful nor pleasant, but is pure equanimity and mindfulness."

Not receiving this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the recollections and perceptions associated with the third dhyāna—the very factors of his original regression. That practitioner of meditation then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the fourth dhyāna and the meditative absorption."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation experiences decline, he knows that decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner of meditation who dwells with the practice, the characteristic, and the sign: having become detached from joy and desire, he dwells in equanimity, free from seeking; mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences pleasure with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, 'He dwells in equanimity, mindful, and happy,' thus attaining and abiding in the third dhyāna.

Not receiving this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the mental applications associated with the second dhyāna—the very factors for falling back from it. That practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original sign and moved toward another state; I have lost the third dhyāna and the cessation of concentration."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation experiences decline, he knows that decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as the practitioner of meditation practices what is practiced, what is characterized, and what is marked—wherein initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) have ceased, and there is internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, being without initial application and without sustained application, and possessing the joy and happiness born of concentration—he attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the second dhyāna.

Not receiving this practice, not attending to these signs or marks, he practices only the mental formations associated with the first dhyāna that lead to falling back; that practitioner of meditation then thinks:
"My mind has departed from its original state and moved toward another place; I have lost the second dhyāna and my meditative absorption has ceased."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation experiences decline, he knows that decline as it truly is.

"Furthermore, as for the practitioner of meditation, his practice, his characteristic, and his sign consist in this: detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, born of detachment, he attains and dwells in the fulfillment of the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by joy and pleasure."

Not receiving this practice, not recollecting this sign or its mark, he practices only those thoughts and perceptions associated with sensual pleasure—the very factors for regression—and that practitioner of dhyāna then thinks:
"My mind has departed from the original sign and moved toward another place; I have lost the first dhyāna and the state of meditative absorption."

Having known this as it truly is, he does not regress from suchness and his mind does not lose its concentration; thus, when a practitioner of meditation declines, he knows that decline as it truly is.
“How does a practitioner of meditation who is flourishing truly know that he is flourishing?

That practitioner of meditation, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
When that mind cultivates right reflection and becomes blissful and tranquil, it proceeds from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna; this is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind cultivates right reflection and has become blissful and tranquil, proceeding from the first dhyāna to the second dhyāna; this is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.

"Furthermore, when the practitioner of meditation has stilled initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), and with internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, is without initial application and without sustained application, attaining the joy and bliss born of concentration, he dwells having attained the second dhyāna; his mind cultivates right reflection, which is blissful and tranquil. He proceeds from the second dhyāna to the third dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of meditation then reflects: "My mind has cultivated right contemplation;
it is blissful and tranquil. From the second dhyāna, I shall proceed to the third dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of dhyāna, detached from joy and desire, dwells in equanimity and seeks nothing; with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he experiences happiness with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, 'He who has equanimity and is mindful dwells in happiness'—and thus attains and abides in the third dhyāna."
With that mind, he cultivates right reflection, which is blissful and tranquil; he proceeds from the third dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then forms this thought:
"My mind cultivates right reflection, which is blissful and tranquil; I have proceeded from the third dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna, which is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity."
Cultivating that mind with right reflection, he experiences happiness and tranquility as he proceeds from the fourth dhyāna to the sphere of infinite space; this is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"I have cultivated my mind with right reflection, experiencing happiness and tranquility as I proceeded from the fourth dhyāna to the sphere of infinite space; this is indeed a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.

"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attends to perceptions of diversity; [perceiving] 'space is infinite,' he dwells having attained the sphere of infinite space.
That mind, having cultivated right reflection, is blissful and tranquil; it proceeds from the sphere of infinite space to the sphere of infinite consciousness, which is a superior tranquility.
That practitioner of meditation then reflects:
"My mind, having cultivated right reflection, is blissful and tranquil; it has proceeded from the sphere of infinite space to the sphere of infinite consciousness, which is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation, having transcended the entire sphere of infinite space, attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Cultivating right reflection with his mind, he experiences joy and tranquility; from the sphere of infinite consciousness, he proceeds to the sphere of nothingness, which is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of meditation then reflects: "My mind has cultivated right reflection;
it is blissful and tranquil. Moving from the sphere of infinite consciousness toward the sphere of nothingness, this is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then becomes aware of that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.
"Furthermore, the practitioner of meditation transcends the entire sphere of infinite consciousness; there being nothing whatsoever, he dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness.

His mind cultivates right reflection, becoming blissful and tranquil. From the sphere of nothingness, he proceeds to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is a superior tranquility."
That practitioner of meditation then reflects thus: "My mind has cultivated right reflection;
it is blissful and tranquil. Moving from the sphere of nothingness toward the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is a superior tranquility."

Having known this as it truly is, he then perceives that mind without losing his concentration; thus, when the practitioner of meditation is flourishing, he knows that he is flourishing as it truly is.
"In the world, there are indeed these four types of practitioners of meditation;
it is for this reason that I have spoken thus.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, those bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

That bhikṣu should understand it in this way:
