Chapter Four: The Section on Pairs (Yamaka-vagga) The Section on Pairs consists of five sūtras; originally there were ten sūtras, but the latter five have been assigned to the fifth recitation (bhāṇavāra), hence it is called the Fourth Section on Pairs.
1. The Horse-Rider and the Horse-Rider (*Assakhaḷuṅka*) 2. The Goatherd and the Goatherd (*Ajapāla-nigrodha*) 3.
The Cowherd and the Cowherd (*Gopālaka*) 4. The Peacock and the Peacock (*Moranivāpa*) 5. Seeking Liberation (*Muttaka*)—this is the last.
182. The Sūtra on Māpīya (182). Middle Discourses, Chapter on Pairs, The First Sūtra on Māpīya. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅga with a large community of bhikṣus; he arrived at Māpīya and stayed there at the Horse-wood Monastery together with the assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"When people see you śramaṇas, they recognize you as śramaṇas; when people ask you whether you are śramaṇas, do you yourself claim to be śramaṇas?"
The bhikṣus replied:
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"Therefore, you all must, by means of this, train yourselves as true śramaṇas and as true brahmins; having trained yourselves as true śramaṇas and as true brahmins, you shall indeed be genuine śramaṇas, not false śramaṇas."

If one receives robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine for illness, and various kinds of requisites for living, the one who provides them gains great merit, attains great fruit, acquires great virtue, and receives a vast reward; you all should train yourselves in this way.
"What is it like to be in accordance with the Dharma of a śramaṇa and the Dharma of a brahmin?

One’s bodily conduct is pure; one looks upward and confesses openly, guarding oneself well without flaw. Because of this purity, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others; being without defilement or turbidity, one is praised by wise fellow practitioners of the holy life."
If you should think thus: "My bodily conduct is pure;
what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall no longer train; I have already achieved virtue and righteousness; there is nothing further to be done."
“Monks! I shall speak to you so that those who seek the goal of a śramaṇa do not lose the goal of a śramaṇa.
If one wishes to be a superior practitioner, monks, if the body is already pure, what further should one do?”
One should train in the purity of verbal conduct, looking upward with confession, well-guarded and without flaw.
Because of this purity of verbal conduct, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others; being free from defilement and turbidity, one is praised by the wise who lead the holy life.
"If you should think: 'My conduct of body and speech is pure;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there is nothing further to be learned; I have already achieved virtue and righteousness; there is no further practice to be undertaken.'"
"Monks! I shall speak for you so that those who seek the goal of a śramaṇa do not lose the goal of a śramaṇa.
If one wishes to be a superior practitioner, monks, when body and speech are already pure, what else should one further do?"
One should train in the purity of mental conduct, looking upward with full disclosure, guarding it well without flaw.
Because of this purity of mental conduct, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others; being free from defilement and turbidity, one is praised by wise fellow practitioners of the holy life.
If you should think: "My conduct of body, speech, and mind is pure;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there is nothing further to learn; I have already achieved virtue and righteousness; there is no further task to be performed."
"Monks! I shall speak to you so that those who seek the goal of a śramaṇa do not lose the goal of a śramaṇa.
If one wishes to be a superior practitioner, monks, if one’s conduct of body, speech, and mind is pure, what else should one do?"
One should train in the purity of livelihood, looking upward with confession, well-guarded and without flaw.
Because of this purity of livelihood, one does not exalt oneself nor disparage others; being free from defilement and turbidity, one is praised by wise fellow practitioners of the holy life.
"If you should think thus:

'My conduct of body, speech, mind, and livelihood is pure; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is nothing further to be learned; I have already achieved virtue and righteousness; there is no further practice to be undertaken.'"
"Monks! I shall speak to you so that those who seek the goal of a śramaṇa do not lose the goal of a śramaṇa.
If one wishes to be a superior practitioner, monks, and if one’s bodily, verbal, and mental livelihood-conduct is pure, what else should one further do?"

A bhikṣu should train in guarding the sense faculties, constantly mindful of closing them off, mindful of clarity and penetration, and achieving success through guarding the mind of mindfulness. Always intending to apply his attention, if he sees forms with the eye, he does not grasp at their signs nor does he relish the forms, because of the danger of contention; thus he guards the faculty of the eye.
In his mind, he does not give rise to covetousness, ill will, sorrow, or unwholesome and evil states; because he is intent upon that [liberation], he guards the faculty of the eye.

Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. If the mind cognizes mental phenomena, he neither grasps their signs nor relishes them—namely, to avoid quarrels and disputes—and thus he guards the faculty of the mind.
If no covetousness, grief, or unwholesome, evil states arise in the mind, one approaches that state by guarding the faculty of the mind. If you should think:

"My conduct of body, speech, and mind, and my livelihood are pure; I have guarded the sense faculties; what was to be done has been accomplished; I have nothing further to learn; I have achieved virtue and meaning; there is nothing more to be done."
"Monks! I shall speak to you so that you do not seek the goal of a śramaṇa and yet lose the goal of a śramaṇa.
If one who desires to be a superior practitioner wishes to purify their conduct of body, speech, mind, and livelihood, and to guard the sense faculties, what else should they further do?"

A bhikṣu should train himself to be clearly aware when going out and coming in; he should be well-observant and discerning in bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, and in his dignified deportment; he should be skilled in wearing the saṃghāṭī and other robes and carrying the alms bowl; and in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, he should in all cases maintain clear awareness.
"If you should think thus: 'My conduct of body, speech, mind, and livelihood is pure;

I guard my sense faculties; I am mindful and clearly conscious in going out and coming in; I have done what was to be done; there is nothing further to learn; I have attained virtue and righteousness; there is no further work to be done. "
"Monks! I shall speak to you so that you do not seek the goal of a recluse and yet lose the goal of a recluse.

If one who desires to train in the higher training wishes to be pure in bodily, verbal, mental, and livelihood conduct, guarding the sense faculties and being clearly aware in coming and going, what further should he do?"

A bhikṣu should train to dwell alone in seclusion, staying in a place free from affairs—whether at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet spot, in a mountain cave or stone chamber, on open ground amidst straw heaps, in a forest grove, or among burial mounds.

Having gone to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty, quiet, and peaceful spot, he spreads his sitting mat, sits down cross-legged, straightens his body and sets his intention, and with mindfulness directed inward, he abandons covetousness. His mind is free from contention; seeing the wealth and various belongings of others, he does not give rise to covetousness, desiring for himself to obtain them. Thus, he purifies his mind of covetousness.

In this way, having abandoned ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, and restlessness-and-regret, and having cut off doubt and crossed over perplexity, he has no hesitation regarding wholesome states; thus, he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.

Having attained such concentration of mind—purified, stainless, and free from affliction; supple, well-established, and unshakable—he inclines toward the realization of the superknowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
He then knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are.
He also knows these taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Having known thus and seen thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
This is called being a śramaṇa, being a brahmin, being noble, and being one who has performed the ritual purification. What is a śramaṇa?

It refers to one who has stilled and ceased all evil and unwholesome states, all outflows and defilements that serve as the basis for future existence, which result in the retribution of feverish distress and suffering, and which are the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is called a śramaṇa.
What is a brahmin?

It is one who has distanced himself from all evil and unwholesome states, from the taints and corruptions that are the root of future existence, the cause of feverish suffering and retribution, and the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death; such a person is called a brahmin.
What is meant by "noble"?

It refers to being far removed from all evil and unwholesome states, from the taints and defilements that serve as the basis for future existence, which result in the retribution of feverish suffering, and which are the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is what is called "noble."
What is meant by "purifying bath"?

It refers to purifying all evil and unwholesome states, as well as the taints and defilements that serve as the basis for future existence, resulting in the retribution of feverish suffering, and acting as the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is called the purifying bath.
"This is what is called a śramaṇa; this is what is called a brahmin; this is what is called a noble one; this is what is called one who has performed the ritual bath.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Mādhura Sūtra*, Chapter One, ends here; one thousand three hundred and forty-seven characters. 183. *Mādhura Sūtra* (183), Middle Discourses, Twin Section, *Mādhura Sūtra*, Second, Fourth Recitation. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅguttara with a large community of bhikṣus. He arrived at Mādhura and stayed at the Horse Park Monastery (*Aśvavana*) together with the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“When people see you śramaṇas, they recognize you as śramaṇas; when people ask you if you are śramaṇas, do you yourselves claim to be śramaṇas?”
The bhikṣus replied:
“It is so, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Therefore, you all, by means of this and for the sake of being true śramaṇas, must train yourselves in the path of the śramaṇa so as not to be non-śramaṇas.

Having trained in the path of the śramaṇa, you must be śramaṇas in truth and not in vain. If you receive robes, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and various other requisites for life, those who provide these will obtain great merit, great fruit, great virtue, and a vast reward; you all should train yourselves in this way."
"What is it that is neither the path of a recluse nor a recluse? If one has covetousness and does not abandon covetousness;

if one has ill will and does not abandon ill will; if one has malice and does not abandon malice; if one has stubborn silence and does not abandon stubborn silence; if one has fetters and does not abandon fetters; if one has stinginess and does not abandon stinginess; if one has envy and does not abandon envy; if one has flattery and deceit and does not abandon flattery and deceit; if one has fraudulence and does not abandon fraudulence; if one has lack of shame and does not abandon lack of shame; if one has lack of dread of blame and does not abandon lack of dread of blame; if one has evil desires and does not abandon evil desires; if one has wrong view and does not abandon wrong view—these are the stains of a recluse, the flattery of a recluse, the hypocrisy of a recluse, and the crookedness of a recluse. Having gone toward an evil destination and not yet reached its end, one trains in what is not the path of a recluse and is thus not a recluse."
"Just as a newly forged battle-axe is extremely sharp, possessing both head and blade, yet wrapped within a *saṃghāṭī* robe—I say that such a foolish student of the śramaṇa path is just like this."

That is to say: one who has covetousness and does not cease covetousness; one who has ill will and does not cease ill will; one who has malice and does not cease malice; one who is silent [in resentment] and does not cease such silence; one who has fetters and does not cease fetters; one who is stingy and does not cease stinginess; one who is envious and does not cease envy; one who is sycophantic and deceitful and does not cease such sycophancy and deceit; one who is shameless and does not cease shamelessness; one who is reckless and does not cease recklessness; one who has evil desires and does not cease evil desires; and one who has wrong views and does not cease wrong views—even if such a person carries the saṃghāṭī robe, I do not call him a śramaṇa.

If one who wears the saṃghāṭī has covetousness but has stilled covetousness, has ill will but has stilled ill will, has malice but has stilled malice, has silence [of resentment] but has stilled silence, has fetters but has stilled fetters, has stinginess but has stilled stinginess, has envy but has stilled envy, has flattery but has stilled flattery, has lack of shame but has stilled lack of shame, has lack of dread but has stilled lack of dread, has evil desires but has stilled evil desires, and has wrong views but has stilled wrong views—then his kinsmen and friends will go to him and say:
"O worthy man!"
"You should train in wearing the saṃghāṭī robe. O worthy one, by training in wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, there is the cessation of covetousness where covetousness was;

the cessation of ill will where ill will was; the cessation of malice where malice was; the cessation of silence [of resentment] where silence was; the cessation of fetters where fetters were; the cessation of stinginess where stinginess was; the cessation of envy where envy was; the cessation of flattery where flattery was; the cessation of shamelessness where shamelessness was; the cessation of lack of dread where lack of dread was; the cessation of evil desire where evil desire was; and the cessation of wrong view where wrong view was."

"If one wears the saṃghāṭī while harboring the view of a self, or possesses covetousness, ill will, hatred, resentment, fetters, stinginess, envy, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, lack of remorse, evil desires, and wrong views—then it is for this reason that one wears the saṃghāṭī."
I say that such a person is not a śramaṇa.

Likewise, one who is naked, one with matted hair, one who does not sit, one who eats only once a day, one who constantly splashes water, or one who carries water—I say that such a person who carries water is not a śramaṇa.

If one holds water, there may be covetousness, yet one ceases covetousness; there may be ill will, yet one ceases ill will; there may be hatred, yet one ceases hatred; there may be silence [out of resentment], yet one ceases such silence; there may be fetters, yet one ceases fetters; there may be stinginess, yet one ceases stinginess; there may be envy, yet one ceases envy; there may be flattery and deceit, yet one ceases flattery and deceit; there may be lack of shame, yet one ceases lack of shame; there may be lack of dread, yet one ceases lack of dread; there may be evil desires, yet one ceases evil desires; there may be wrong views, yet one ceases wrong views. Then his kinsmen and friends approach him and say: "O worthy one!..."
"You should hold water.

Having held water, there will be the cessation of covetousness, the cessation of ill-will, the cessation of malice, the cessation of silence [out of resentment], the cessation of fetters, the cessation of stinginess, the cessation of envy, the cessation of flattery and deceit, the cessation of lack of shame, the cessation of lack of dread, the cessation of evil desires, and the cessation of wrong views."

If one carries water while maintaining the view of self, or harboring covetousness, malice, hatred, silence born of resentment, fetters, stinginess, envy, flattery and deceit, lack of shame, lack of remorse, evil desires, and wrong views—then, because they carry water with such qualities, I say that person is not a śramaṇa.
This is called not being on the path of a śramaṇa, and not being a śramaṇa. What is the path of a śramaṇa, such that one is not a non-śramaṇa? If there is covetousness, one quiets covetousness;

if there is ill will, one quiets ill will; if there is malice, one quiets malice; if there is harsh speech, one quiets harsh speech; if there are fetters, one quiets the fetters; if there is stinginess, one quiets stinginess; if there is envy, one quiets envy; if there is flattery and deceit, one quiets flattery and deceit; if there is lack of shame, one quiets lack of shame; if there is lack of dread of blame, one quiets lack of dread of blame; if there are evil desires, one quiets evil desires; if there are wrong views, one quiets wrong views. Having completely eliminated the jealousy of a śramaṇa, the flattery of a śramaṇa, the hypocrisy of a śramaṇa, and the crookedness of a śramaṇa—which lead to an evil destination—one trains in the path of a śramaṇa; thus, one is not a non-śramaṇa.
This is called the path of the recluse; one is not a non-recluse.

Having thus accomplished virtue, he is pure in body, pure in speech and mind. He is free from covetousness, has no ill will in his heart, is without sloth, and is free from restlessness, pride, and arrogance. Having severed doubt and crossed over delusion, he possesses right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, being without folly. His mind, accompanied by loving-kindness, dwells pervading one direction, having accomplished it.

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
He forms this thought:
"There is the coarse, there is the sublime, and there is perception; I have come to this superior way of escape, knowing it as it truly is.

Having thus known and thus seen, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsava*) and ignorance (*avijjā-āsava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows as it truly is: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacariya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence to be undergone."
"It is like this: not far from a village, there is a fine bathing pool, filled with clear, flowing water, its banks covered with lush green grass and surrounded on all sides by flowering trees.

Suppose a person were to come from the east, utterly exhausted by hunger, thirst, and fatigue; he would take off his clothes on the bank, enter the pool to bathe refreshingly, thereby removing dirt and heat, as well as his thirst and exhaustion."

In the same way, suppose a person comes from the south, the west, or the north, exhausted by hunger and thirst. He takes off his clothes on the bank, enters the pool to bathe with delight, and thereby removes impurities, dispels heat, and also relieves his thirst and fatigue.

In this way, a son of noble kṣatriya lineage shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path. He practices internal tranquility and attains internal tranquility. One who possesses internal tranquility, I call a śramaṇa, I call a brāhmaṇa, I call a noble one, and I call one who is purified by bathing.

In this way, when sons of noble families—whether brahmins, householders, or craftsmen—shave off their hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leave the home life for homelessness to train in the path, they practice internal tranquility and attain internal tranquility. One who possesses internal tranquility, I call a śramaṇa, I call a brāhmaṇa, I call a noble one, and I call one who has been purified by bathing.
"What is a śramaṇa?

It is one who has stilled and brought to rest all evil and unwholesome states, as well as the outflows (āsrava) and defilements that are the root of future existence, which result in feverish suffering and are the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is called a śramaṇa."
What is a brahmin?

It refers to one who has distanced himself from all evil and unwholesome states, from the taints and corruptions that are the basis for future existence, which result in feverish suffering and are the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death; such a person is called a brahmin.
What is meant by "noble"?

It refers to being far removed from all evil and unwholesome states, from the taints and corruptions that serve as the basis for future existence, which result in feverish suffering and are the causes of birth, old age, sickness, and death; this is what is called "noble."
What is meant by "cleansing bath"?

It refers to cleansing oneself of all evil and unwholesome dharmas, as well as the taints and impurities that serve as the basis for future existence, resulting in the retribution of feverish distress, and acting as the cause of birth, old age, sickness, and death—this is called the cleansing bath.
"This is what is called a śramaṇa; this is what is called a brahmin; this is what is called a noble one; this is what is called one who has performed the ritual bath.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Māyā-sūtra*, Part Two, ends here; one thousand four hundred and sixty characters. 184. The *Gośṛṅga-śāla-vana-sūtra* (184), Middle Āgama, Paired Section, *Gośṛṅga-śāla-vana-sūtra*, Third and Fourth Recitations. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Bhṛgukacchas, staying in the Gośṛṅga-śāla grove together with many learned, venerable bhikṣus who were great disciples.

The Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Ānanda—these many learned elder bhikkhus and great disciples likewise traveled through the Bāhika country of Śrāvastī and stayed together near the Buddha’s leaf-hut in the Gosiṅga Sāla Grove.

Then, at the end of the night, when dawn had broken, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, and the Venerable Aniruddha went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was staying.
When the Venerable Ānanda saw from afar that those venerable ones had departed, he said: "Friend Revata,
you should know that these venerable ones— Mahāmoggallāna, Mahākassapa, Mahākaccāyana, and Anuruddha— having passed the night, went early this morning to the place where the Venerable Sāriputta was."
"Venerable Revata!
We should now go together with these venerable ones to visit the Venerable Sāriputta; perhaps we may, through him, hear a little or much of the Dharma from the Venerable Sāriputta."

Then, at the end of the night, when dawn had broken, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Śāriputra was staying.
When the Venerable Sāriputta saw those venerable ones approaching from afar, he addressed them on account of those venerable ones, saying:
"Welcome, worthy Ānanda!"
Welcome, Ānanda! Welcome, Ānanda!
You are the attendant of the Blessed One who understands the Blessed One’s intention, and you are constantly praised by the Blessed One as well as by wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
I now ask the Venerable Ānanda: this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all the sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance, just like celestial flowers.
“Venerable Ānanda!
What kind of bhikkhu causes the Sāla grove of Goatherd’s Peak to shine?
Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who has studied extensively and heard much, who maintains it without forgetting, and who has accumulated vast learning—namely, that Dhamma which is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; which is meaningful and well-phrased; which is perfectly pure and reveals the holy life.”

Having thus extensively studied and heard these various dharmas, practicing them until they reach a thousandfold, he contemplates them with his mind, seeing them clearly and penetrating them deeply; the teachings he expounds are concise, swift, and in accord with the truth, intended to sever all fetters.
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu brings radiance to the Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn.
Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Worthy Revata! The worthy monk Ānanda has already spoken according to his knowledge.
Now, I ask you again, worthy Revata: this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all the sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance, like celestial flowers.”
"Venerable Revata!
What kind of bhikkhu would cause this Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Revata replied:
“Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who delights in solitary meditation, practices internal tranquility, does not neglect sitting in dhyāna, achieves insight (vipassanā), always prefers dwelling in seclusion, and rejoices in quiet places—Venerable Sāriputta!”
"In this way, the bhikṣu has caused the Sāla grove of Gośṛṅga to be set ablaze.
Venerable Śāriputra asked again: "Worthy Āniruddha!"
The venerable Bhikkhu Līḷhaka has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, I shall further question the venerable Anuruddha: This Sāla Grove of the Deer Park is most delightful; the moon shines brightly at night, and all the sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance like celestial flowers.
“Venerable Anuruddha!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
If there is a bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye and perfected the divine eye, he can see, with little effort, all within a thousand worlds in a mere moment."
Venerable Sāriputta!
It is as if a person with sight were standing atop a high building and could, with little effort, see in an instant the thousand bricks lying on the open ground below.
Venerable Sāriputta!

In this way, if there is a bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye and perfected the divine eye, he can, by means of slight effort, see the entirety of a thousandfold world-system in an instant, Venerable Sāriputta!
"In this way, the bhikṣu has inspired the Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn.
The Venerable Śāriputra asked again: "Worthy Kaccāyana!"
The venerable bhikkhu Anuruddha has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, I shall further question the venerable Kaccāyana. This Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is most delightful; at night there is a bright moon, and all the sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance like that of celestial flowers.
“Venerable Kaccāyana!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Sāla Grove of the Goatherd’s Banyan to shine?
Venerable Mahākaccāyana replied:
“Venerable Sāriputta!

It is as if two bhikkhus who are Dharma-teachers were discussing the profound Abhidhamma; they understand and fully know the matters asked about, their answers are unimpeded, and their eloquence in expounding the Dharma is swift.”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sāl Grove of the Deer Park.
Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
“Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
The worthy bhikṣu Kātyāyana has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now I shall further question the venerable Mahākāśyapa. This Gośīrṣa Sāla Grove is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all the sāla trees are emitting exquisite fragrances like celestial flowers.”
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
What kind of bhikṣu causes the Sālavana of Gośṛṅga to flourish?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa replied:

“Worthy Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who, being himself free from worldly concerns, speaks of being free from worldly concerns; who, being himself of few desires, speaks of having few desires; who, being himself content, speaks of being content; who, being himself devoted to dwelling in seclusion and solitude, speaks of being devoted to dwelling in seclusion and solitude; who, being himself diligent in practice, speaks of being diligent in practice; who, being himself established in right mindfulness and clear comprehension, speaks of being established in right mindfulness and clear comprehension; who, being himself attained to concentration, speaks of being attained to concentration; who, being himself possessed of wisdom, speaks of possessing wisdom; who, being himself with all taints exhausted, speaks of having all taints exhausted; and who, being himself inciting others toward aspiration and accomplishing joy, speaks of inciting others toward aspiration and accomplishing joy—Worthy Śāriputra! [Such a one is indeed a true disciple.]”
"In this way, the bhikkhu has inspired the Sāla Grove of the Deer Park.
The Venerable Sāriputta asked again:
"Friend Moggallāna!"
The Venerable Mahākāśyapa has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now I shall further question the worthy Maudgalyāyana: This Sāla Grove of the Cow’s Horns is exceedingly delightful; with the bright moon at night, all the sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance, like celestial flowers.
“Worthy Maudgalyāyana!
What kind of bhikṣu can cause the Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn to flourish?
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana replied:
“Venerable Sāriputta!
If there is a bhikkhu who possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual potency, with immeasurable mastery over supernormal powers;”

He practices the immeasurable bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): transforming one into many and combining many into one; remaining as one when alone; possessing knowledge and vision that penetrate through stone walls without obstruction, as if through empty space; entering and emerging from the earth as if it were water; walking upon water as if on land without sinking; ascending into the sky and sitting cross-legged like a bird; and even reaching out with his hand to touch the sun and moon—which possess great psychic power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority—and traveling as far as the Brahma world.
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn.
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna asked:
“Venerable Sāriputta!
I and the other venerable ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge.
I now ask the venerable Sāriputta: this Goatherd’s Sal Forest is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all the sal trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance like celestial flowers.”
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Grove of Sāl Trees at the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Sāriputta replied:
“Wise Maudgalyāyana!

If there is a bhikṣu who follows mastery over his mind rather than being controlled by his mind, and he wishes to go on a journey during the forenoon while staying in a certain place, he will go on that very journey during the forenoon while staying in that very place.”
If he wishes to go for a stroll at midday or in the late afternoon while staying in a particular place, he goes for a stroll at midday or in the late afternoon right there where he is staying.
Worthy Maudgalyāyana!

It is just as when a king or a royal minister possesses a great many garments of various kinds and exquisite colors; if he wishes to wear one before midday, he takes it and wears it; if he wishes to wear one at noon or in the afternoon, he takes it and wears it.
Worthy Maudgalyāyana! It is so.

If there is a bhikṣu who follows the mastery of his own mind rather than being followed by his mind, and if he wishes to dwell and wander during the forenoon at whatever place he chooses, he will dwell and wander during the forenoon at that very place.
Venerable Maudgalyāyana! If he wishes to dwell wherever he may stay and wander during the midday or the afternoon, he will dwell right there and wander during the midday or the afternoon.
"In this way, bhikkhu, you have inspired the Sāla grove of Igboḷa.
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"Worthy Moggallāna!"
"I and all of you venerable ones have each spoken according to our own understanding. Venerable Moggallāna!
We should now go together with those venerable ones to the presence of the Buddha and discuss this matter there, so that we may know who among us has spoken most excellently."

Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Venerable Mahākaccāyana, the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Buddha was. Those venerable ones bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side; the Venerable Ānanda also bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"World-Honored One!

Today, at dawn after the night had passed, the Worthy Mahāmoggallāna, the Venerable Mahākassapa, the Worthy Kaccāyana, the Worthy Anuruddha, the Worthy Lakkhaṇa, and the Worthy Ānanda came to my dwelling. Having seen those worthies approaching from afar, I spoke concerning them:..."

If there is a bhikṣu who has studied extensively and is widely learned, who maintains what he has learned without forgetting and accumulates vast erudition—namely, the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; which possesses both meaning and phrasing, is complete and pure, and reveals the holy life.

Having thus extensively studied and heard these various dharmas, practicing them until they reach a thousandfold, he contemplates them with his mind, seeing them clearly and penetrating them deeply; the teachings he expounds are concise, swift, and in accord with the truth, intended to sever all fetters.
“Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sālavana of the Ox-Horn.
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
It is indeed as the bhikṣu Ānanda has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Ānanda is accomplished in extensive learning (bahuśruta).
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
“World-Honored One!
After the worthy Ānanda had spoken thus, I further asked him:”
"Venerable Revata! The venerable bhikkhu Ānanda has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, Venerable Revata, I shall ask you further: this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is exceedingly delightful; with the bright moon at night, all these sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance, like celestial flowers."
"Venerable Revata!
What kind of bhikkhu would cause this Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Revata then replied to me:
"Venerable Sāriputta!

If there is a bhikkhu who delights in solitary meditation, practices internal tranquility, does not neglect sitting in dhyāna, achieves insight (vipassanā), and always prefers living in seclusion, taking joy in quiet and peaceful places—Venerable Sāriputta!"
"In this way, bhikṣus, you cause the Sāla Grove of the Horns of the Deer to flourish.
The World-Honored One praised them, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent,
Śāriputra! It is just as the bhikṣu Revata has spoken.
"Why is that? Because the bhikṣu Līl̥avata always delights in sitting in meditation.
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
After the venerable Revata had spoken thus, I asked him further:
‘Venerable Anuruddha!’”
The venerable Bhikkhu Līḷhaka has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, I shall further question the venerable Anuruddha: This Sāla Grove of the Deer Park is most delightful; at night, under the bright moon, all the sāla trees emit a wondrous fragrance like celestial flowers.
“Venerable Anuruddha!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Anuruddha then replied to me:
"Venerable Sāriputta!
If there is a bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye and perfected the divine eye, he can, by means of slight effort, see all within a thousand worlds in an instant."
Venerable Sāriputta!

It is just as if a person with sight were standing atop a high building and, looking down at a cleared space below where there were a thousand clay bricks, could see them all completely in an instant through a slight application of skillful means.
"Venerable Sāriputta! It is so.

If there is a bhikkhu who has attained the divine eye and perfected the divine eye, he can, through even a slight application of skillful means, see the entirety of a thousandfold world system in an instant."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sālavana of the Ox-Horn.
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
As the bhikṣu Aniruddha has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Aniruddha has perfected the divine eye.
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"World-Honored One!
After the worthy Anuruddha had spoken thus, I asked him further:"
“Venerable Kaccāna! The venerable Bhikkhu Anuruddha has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, Venerable Kaccāna, I shall ask you further: this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all these sāla trees are emitting exquisite fragrances like celestial flowers.”
“Venerable Kaccāyana!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to shine?
Venerable Kaccāyana then replied to me:
"Venerable Sāriputta!

It is as if two bhikṣus who are Dharma-teachers were discussing the profound Abhidharma; they thoroughly understand and know the matters asked about, their answers are unhindered, and their eloquence in expounding the Dharma is swift."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sālavana of the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree.
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
As the bhikṣu Kātyāyana has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Kātyāyana is a master of analytical exposition.
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"World-Honored One!
After the worthy Kaccāyana had spoken thus, I questioned him further, saying:"
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
The worthy Bhikṣu Kātyāyana has already spoken according to his understanding.

Now, I shall further question the Venerable Mahākāśyapa. This Gośīrṣa Sāla Grove is most delightful; at night, under the bright moon, all the sāla trees emit a wondrous fragrance like celestial flowers."
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa!
What kind of bhikṣu can cause the Sāla Grove of the Deer Park to radiate its splendor?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa then replied to me:

“Worthy Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who himself has no worldly concerns and speaks of having no worldly concerns; who himself has few desires and speaks of having few desires; who himself is content and speaks of being content; who himself delights in seclusion and solitude and speaks of delighting in seclusion and solitude; who himself practices with diligence and speaks of practicing with diligence; who himself establishes right mindfulness and right situational awareness and speaks of establishing right mindfulness and right situational awareness; who himself attains concentration and speaks of attaining concentration; who himself possesses wisdom and speaks of possessing wisdom; who himself has exhausted all outflows and speaks of having exhausted all outflows; and who himself encourages others toward aspiration and achieves joy, and speaks of encouraging others toward aspiration and achieving joy.”
"O worthy Śāriputra!
In this way, a bhikṣu inspires the Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn.
Thus the Blessed One praised him.
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
As the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa constantly practices non-action.
The Venerable Sāriputta said:
"World-Honored One!
After the Venerable Mahākassapa had spoken thus, I further asked him:”
"Venerable Moggallāna! The Venerable Mahākassapa has already spoken according to his knowledge.

Now, Venerable Moggallāna, I ask you further: this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn is most delightful; with the bright moon at night, all these sāla trees are emitting a wondrous fragrance, like celestial flowers."
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
What kind of bhikṣu can cause this Sāla Grove of the Ox-Horn to blaze forth?
Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana then replied to me:

"Venerable Sāriputta! Suppose there were a bhikkhu possessed of great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, with mastery over immeasurable supernormal powers. He would exercise those immeasurable supernormal powers, transforming one into many and combining many into one; remaining as one, he would be conscious and perceptive, passing unhindered through solid rock as if through empty space; entering and emerging from the earth as if it were water; walking upon water as if on land without sinking; ascending into the sky while sitting cross-legged like a bird; and even reaching out his hand to touch the sun and moon, which possess great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, and traveling as far as the Brahma-world."
"Venerable Sāriputta!
In this way, a bhikkhu inspires the Sāl Grove at Igāṇi.
The Blessed One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, Śāriputra!”
As the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana possesses great supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
Thereupon, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
After I and the other venerable ones had spoken thus,
we addressed the Venerable Sāriputta, saying:
"Venerable Sāriputta!..."

I and the other venerable ones have each spoken according to our own knowledge. Now I ask the Venerable Śāriputra: this Sāla Grove of the Cow’s Horns is most delightful; with the bright moon shining at night, all the sāla trees are emitting exquisite fragrances like celestial flowers.
"Venerable Sāriputta!
What kind of bhikkhu causes this Sāl Grove at Igālika to shine forth?
Venerable Sāriputta then replied to me:
“Worthy Maudgalyāyana!

If there is a bhikṣu who follows the mastery of his mind rather than being followed by his mind, and if he wishes to go wandering before midday at whatever place he may be staying, then he goes wandering before midday at that very place where he is staying.”
If he wishes to dwell wherever he may stay and wander during the midday or the afternoon, he shall dwell there and wander during the midday or the afternoon.
Worthy Maudgalyāyana!

It is just as when a king or a royal minister possesses a great many garments of various kinds and exquisite colors; if he wishes to wear one before midday, he takes it up and wears it; if he wishes to wear one at noon or in the afternoon, he takes it up and wears it.
Worthy Maudgalyāyana! It is so.

If there is a bhikṣu who follows the mastery of his mind rather than being followed by his mind, and if he wishes to go wandering during the forenoon at whatever place he may be staying, he will go wandering during the forenoon at that very place where he is staying.
If he wishes to dwell wherever he may stay and wander during the midday or the afternoon, he shall dwell there and wander during the midday or the afternoon.
"Venerable Maudgalyāyana!
In this way, such a bhikṣu causes the Sāla grove of Gośīrṣa to arise.
Thus the Blessed One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent,
Maudgalyāyana!”
As the bhikṣu Śāriputra has said.
Why is this? Because the bhikṣu Śāriputra exercises mastery over his mind according to his will.
Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
After I and the other worthy ones had spoken thus, we said:
"Worthy Maudgalyāyana!
We and the other worthy ones have each spoken according to what we know."
"Worthy Maudgalyāyana!
We should rather go together with those worthy ones to the presence of the Buddha and discuss this matter there, so that we may know who among us has spoken most excellently."
“World-Honored One!
Among us, who has spoken well?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Śāriputra! Everything is excellent. Why is that? Because—”
"All these dharmas have been fully taught by me, Śāriputra!
Listen to what I say: it is such a bhikṣu who causes this Grove of Sāl Trees at Gośṛṅga to flourish."

Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who, in whatever city, town, or village he dwells, rises at dawn after the night has passed, puts on his robes and takes up his bowl to enter the village for alms, guarding his body well, restraining his sense faculties well, and establishing mindfulness well.

Having finished his almsround, after midday has passed, he puts away his robes and bowl, washes his hands and feet, and placing his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, he goes either to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty and quiet spot. There he spreads his sitting mat and sits cross-legged. Without breaking that cross-legged posture until the outflows (*āsrava*) are exhausted, he remains seated cross-legged until the outflows are exhausted.
"Śāriputra! In this way, a bhikṣu brings glory to the Grove of Horned Śāla Trees.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

This concludes the third discourse, the Go-vat-sāla-vana Sūtra, totaling three thousand seven hundred and eighty-five characters. 185. The Go-vat-sāla-vana Sūtra (185), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, the "Paired Discourses" (*Yamaka-varga*), the fourth discourse in the fourth section of the recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the land of Namadī and was staying at the Ghaṭīkāra Monastery.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, dressed in the early morning and took his bowl, entering Nādikā to beg for food. Having finished eating after midday, he proceeded to the Gośṛṅga Sāla Grove.
At that time, there were three sons of noble family dwelling together in the Goatherd’s Banyan Grove: the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila.

The Venerable Ones conducted themselves in this manner: if any among those who had gone for alms returned first, they would prepare a seat, fetch water, bring out the foot-washing vessel, set out a footstool, a towel for drying the feet, a water jar, and a rinsing pitcher.
If the alms-food obtained is sufficient for him to eat entirely, he eats it all.

If there is a remainder, he places it in a vessel, covers it, and sets it aside. Having finished eating, he puts away his bowl, washes his hands and feet, places his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and enters a room to sit in quiet meditation.

If there are other alms-seekers who return later and are able to finish the food, they may eat it all; if it is not sufficient, one should take the remaining food from the previous meal to supplement it and eat; if there is still a surplus, one should pour it out onto clean ground or into water free of insects.

Having taken those eating vessels, washed and wiped them clean, and set them aside to one side; having folded away the bedding and mats, gathered and washed the footstool, and put away and wiped the foot-towels; having lifted up the foot-washing stand along with the water-jar and the rinsing-pitcher; having swept and sprinkled the dining hall and cleared it of refuse until it was clean; having gathered and put away his robes and bowl, and washed his hands and feet; and having placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, he entered the room for quiet meditation.

When those venerable ones reached the hour of late afternoon, if any among them had previously arisen from meditative seclusion and saw that the water jar or the wash-basin was empty and devoid of water, they would take it up to fetch more. If they were able to lift it, they would carry it back and set it down to one side; if they could not lift it, they would beckon another bhikṣu with their hand, and the two of them would lift it together and set it down to one side, without speaking to one another or questioning one another.
Those venerable ones gathered once every five days, either to discourse on the Dharma together or to maintain noble silence.
Then, the forest guardian saw the Blessed One approaching from afar and went out to scold him, saying, "Ascetic! [Stop!]"
"Śramaṇa!
Do not enter this forest. Why is that?"
"In this grove there are three sons of noble family: the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila. Should they see you, it may not be well."
The Blessed One said:
"O forest-guardian!
If he were to see me, it would certainly be possible; there would be no impossibility."
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha saw the Blessed One approaching from afar and immediately rebuked that forest-guardian, saying:
"You forest-guardian!
Do not rebuke the Blessed One!"
"You, forest-guardian!
Do not revile the Sugata!
For what reason? Because—"
"Our Honored One has come! Our Sugata has come!
Venerable Anuruddha went out to meet the Blessed One and took his robe and bowl; Venerable Nandi took up a seat for the Buddha, and Venerable Kimbila fetched water for him.
At that time, the Blessed One, having washed his hands and feet, sat upon the seat prepared by that venerable one. Having sat down, he asked:
"Ānanda, are you always at ease and free from want?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am always at peace and secure; I lack for nothing.”
The Blessed One asked again:
“Ānanda, how are you at ease? Are you free from lack?”
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"World-Honored One!
I had this thought:"
“World-Honored One! I possess a wholesome benefit and great merit, namely that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.
World-Honored One!

I constantly direct acts of loving-kindness through my body toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction; I direct acts of loving-kindness through my speech and acts of loving-kindness through my mind, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction.”
"Bhagavān! I had this thought:
'I would now rather abandon my own mind and follow the minds of those worthy ones.'"
"I then set aside my own mind and followed the minds of those worthy ones; I never once harbored a single thought of dissent.
World-Honored One!
Thus I have always been peaceful and secure, lacking for nothing."
He questioned the Venerable Nandiya, and his answer was likewise.
He then asked the Venerable Kimbila:
"Are you always at peace and free from want?"
The Venerable Kimbila replied:
“World-Honored One, I am always at peace and secure; I lack for nothing.”
He asked, "Kimbila! Are you at peace, and do you lack for nothing?"
The Venerable Kimbila addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I had this thought:”
“World-Honored One! I have gained a great benefit and possess great merit, namely that I practice the holy life together with such fellow practitioners of the holy life.
World-Honored One!

I constantly direct the bodily action of loving-kindness toward those fellow practitioners of the holy life, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction; I direct the verbal action of loving-kindness and the mental action of loving-kindness toward them, whether they see me or not, remaining equal and without distinction.”
"Bhagavān! I had this thought:
'I would now rather abandon my own mind and follow the minds of those worthy ones.'"
"I then set aside my own mind and followed the minds of those virtuous ones; I never once harbored an unwholesome thought.
World-Honored One!
Thus I have always been peaceful and secure, lacking for nothing."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Āniruddha! Is it so that you all constantly dwell in harmony, peaceful and without dispute, with one mind and one teacher, blending together like water and milk, and have attained some portion of the superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma) for dwelling in peace and happiness?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“World-Honored One!

In this way, we always dwell in harmony, peaceful and without dispute, with one mind and one teacher, blending as one like water and milk. Having attained the Dharma that transcends the human, we abide in a state of well-being with its various stages of excellence.”
"World-Honored One!
We have become detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, and have attained and dwell in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
World-Honored One!"

In this way, we shall always remain in harmonious union, peaceful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single teacher; blending together like water and milk, we shall attain the Dharma supreme among men and abide in a state of well-being, each according to our respective levels of attainment.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Ānanda! Setting aside this dwelling and transcending it, is there perhaps any other superior human state that one might attain, wherein there is a graduated peace and a blissful dwelling?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
“World-Honored One!
Apart from this dwelling, transcending it and going beyond it, there is yet another superior human state, characterized by degrees of excellence and peaceful abiding.”
"World-Honored One!
My mind is accompanied by loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and I dwell having pervaded one direction, having achieved it.

In this same way, I dwell having pervaded the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, encompassing all everywhere; my mind is accompanied by loving-kindness, free from fetters and free from enmity, free from ill will and free from contention—vast, exceedingly great, immeasurable, well-cultivated, pervading the entire world, having achieved it."

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
"World-Honored One!

Apart from this dwelling, transcending this and passing beyond this, is there yet another superior human state (uttarimanussadhamma) wherein one may abide in peace and happiness with further distinctions?"
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Ānanda! Setting aside this dwelling and transcending it, is there perhaps any other superior human state that one might attain, wherein there is a distinction of gradations and a peaceful dwelling?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"World-Honored One!
Apart from this dwelling, surpassing it and going beyond it, there is yet another superior human state that possesses degrees of distinction and provides a peaceful dwelling."
"Blessed One!
We have transcended all perceptions of form and attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where we dwell having achieved its mastery.
Blessed One!"
Having relinquished this dwelling and having transcended it, one thinks: "There is yet another superior human state beyond this, characterized by degrees of distinction and peaceful abiding."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"Ānanda! Setting aside this dwelling and transcending it, is there perhaps some other superior human state that one might attain, wherein there is a graduated distinction of peaceful and happy abiding?"
The Venerable Anuruddha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Apart from this dwelling, transcending it and going beyond it, there is yet another superior human state that possesses degrees of distinction and provides a peaceful dwelling.”
“World-Honored One!

We have attained the bases of psychic power, the knowledge of the divine ear, the knowledge of others’ minds, the knowledge of past lives, and the knowledge of birth and death. Our taints are exhausted; we have attained the state beyond taints, with liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, we have known it for ourselves, realized it for ourselves, and having witnessed it through our own realization, we dwell in its accomplishment. Birth has been ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and we know truly that there will be no further existence.”
"Bhagavān!
Setting aside this dwelling and surpassing it, is there some other further human state of attainment wherein one dwells in peace and security with distinct degrees of excellence?"
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Ānanda! Setting aside this dwelling and surpassing it, is there perhaps any other superior human state that one might attain, wherein there is a graduated peace and a blissful dwelling?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"World-Honored One!
Apart from this dwelling, beyond this, and transcending this, there is no other superior human state that can provide a distinct and peaceful abiding."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"This son of noble family wanders about in peace, security, and happiness; I should now preach the Dharma for him."

Having had this thought, the Blessed One then taught the Dharma to the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila; he inspired them, incited their longing, and established them in joy. Having taught them the Dharma through countless skillful means, inspiring them, inciting their longing, and establishing them in joy, he rose from his seat and departed.
Thereupon, the Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila escorted the World-Honored One; having followed him for as far as was appropriate, they returned to their respective dwellings.
The Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimbila praised the Venerable Anuruddha, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Anuruddha!

Previously we had never heard the Venerable Anuruddha speak such a meaning as this: that we possess such great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual power; yet the Venerable Anuruddha has praised us most highly before the Blessed One."
The Venerable Anuruddha praised the Venerables Nandiya and Kimbila, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable sir!
I have never before heard from these worthy ones that the Venerable One possesses such great supernormal power, such great majesty, such great merit, and such great spiritual authority."

However, for a long time I have known the Venerable One’s mind with my own mind; the Venerable One possesses great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority. For this reason, I spoke to the World-Honored One in such and such a manner.

Thereupon, the celestial being Dīrgha, whose physical form was exceedingly sublime and whose radiance was magnificent, approached the Buddha as night was turning toward dawn. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“O Great Seer!

The people of the Vṛjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that there currently dwell among them the World-Honored One and three sons of noble family: the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimbila.
Having heard these words from the Deva of the Long Ghosts, the Earth Deity let out a great sound, crying: "O Great Seer!

The people of the Vajjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that there currently dwell here the World-Honored One and three sons of noble family: the Venerable Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila."

Having heard this sound from the earth spirits, it was instantly transmitted through the gods of the space, the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Gods, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, until it reached the Brahma Heaven:
"O Great Seer!..."
The Vṛjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that the World-Honored One currently resides among them, along with three sons of noble family: the Venerable Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.
The World-Honored One said:
"So it is, so it is, Dīrgha Devaputra!"

The Vṛjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that the World-Honored One is currently present among them, as are these three sons of noble family: the Venerable Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.
"O Dīrgha Ghost-Deva!
Upon hearing your voice, the Earth Deity let forth a loud and majestic sound, crying out:
'Great Seer!'"
The Vajjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that the World-Honored One currently resides among them, along with three sons of noble family: the Venerable Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.

Having heard this sound from the earth deity, it was instantly transmitted through the deities of the space realm, the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, reaching as far as the Brahmā Heaven:
"O Great Seer!..."

The people of the Vajjis have gained a great and excellent benefit, in that there currently dwell among them the World-Honored One and three sons of noble family: the Venerable Aniruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila.
"Long-lived devas!

If those three families have a son of such a lineage who shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to study the Path—then those three families, by recollecting the cause and the practice of that son of noble lineage, will also for a long night obtain great and wholesome benefit, peace, and happiness."

If those in that village or town—including devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, from humans up to the gods—who remember the causes and the practices of these three sons of noble family, they too will for a long night obtain benefit and advantage, peace, and happiness.
"Long-ghost Deva!
These three sons of noble family possess such great supernormal power, great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, these three sons of noble family and the deva Dīrgha were filled with joy and practiced accordingly.

The Fourth Sūtra of the Gośṛṅga Sāla Forest, totaling two thousand three hundred and eight characters, is finished. 186. The Sūtra on Seeking Liberation (186), Middle Āgama, Paired Section, The Fifth Sūtra on Seeking Liberation, the Fourth Recitation Division. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Kuru people at the Kuru capital of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikkhus:
"If, based on his own mind, one does not know another's mind as it truly is, then that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, cannot be known; how then can one seek to understand the Tathāgata?"
Then, the bhikṣus addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Bhikṣu, listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in full detail."
Then, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The World-Honored One told them:

"For one who, based on that mind, does not know the minds of others as they truly are, one should seek to understand the Tathāgata through two matters: first, the eye’s cognition of forms; second, the ear’s hearing of sounds."
If there are defiled phenomena known by the eye and ear, does that venerable one possess them or not?
When one investigates, it is known that whatever defiled phenomena are known by the eye and ear, those the venerable one does not possess.
If this is not so, one should further inquire: if there are dharmas known by the eye and ear that are mixed [with other faculties], do those exist for that Venerable One, or do they not?
When searching, one realizes that whatever mixed phenomena known by the eye and ear exist, those do not belong to that venerable one.
If these are absent, one should search further: as for those pure phenomena known by the eye and ear, does that venerable one possess them or not?
When investigating, one knows that whatever pure and bright qualities of eye and ear he possesses, those the Venerable One has.
If he has these, one should further investigate: does the Venerable One practice this dharma for a long night, or does he practice it only temporarily?
If one investigates, one will know that this venerable one has practiced this dharma for a long night and has not practiced it only briefly.
If he is one who practices constantly, one should further investigate: does this venerable one enter this meditative concentration for the sake of fame, or for the sake of profit and gain?
"Is he not entering this dhyāna for the sake of fame, nor for the sake of profit or worldly gain?
If one seeks [the reason], one will know that the Venerable One has entered this dhyāna not because of calamity or affliction."
"If someone were to say:
'That venerable one delights in non-frightfulness, is free from desire and does not practice desire;
his desires are exhausted,' one should then ask him: "
"Venerable sir!

By what practice, by what power, and by what wisdom do you, having rightly observed this for yourself, speak thus: 'That venerable one delights in non-fearfulness, is free from desire and does not act out of desire; has his craving been exhausted?'"
If he should answer thus:
"Venerable sir!
I do not know that person's mind, nor do I know it through any other means; however, that venerable one may dwell alone, or in a group, or in an assembly."

Whether it be a Sugata or one transformed by a Sugata acting as my master, through food I may see that worthy one; yet I do not know for myself. I have heard this from that venerable one, having received it directly from him in his presence: "I delight in practice without fear; being free from desire, I do not engage in desire; desire is exhausted."
"Worthy one!

I possess such conduct, such power, and such wisdom that I can rightly observe for myself and declare: 'That venerable one delights in practice, is without fear, is free from desire and does not act out of desire; his craving has been exhausted.'"
"Furthermore, one should inquire of that Tathāgata regarding the Dharma:
'If there are phenomena known by the defiled eye or ear, is there a place where these phenomena are extinguished without remainder?'"
If there are phenomena known by the eye and ear that are mixed, there is a place where those phenomena are extinguished without remainder.
If there are phenomena that are pure and bright, there is a place where those phenomena are extinguished without remainder; it is regarding this that the Tathāgata gives his answer.
If there are dharmas known by the eye or ear that are defiled, there is a place where these dharmas are extinguished without remainder.
If there are dharmas known by the eye or ear that are mixed, there is a place where these dharmas are extinguished without remainder.
If there are dharmas known by the eye or ear that are defiled, the Tathāgata has extinguished and severed them, uprooting them from their very foundation so that they shall never arise again.
If there are dharmas known by the eye or ear that are mixed, the Tathāgata has extinguished and severed them, uprooting them from their very foundation so that they shall never arise again.
If there is a pure and bright quality, such am I—pure and bright; such is my sphere of experience, such am I as a śramaṇa; thus have I accomplished this True Dharma and Discipline.

A faithful disciple goes to see the Tathāgata and attends upon him; from the Tathāgata he hears the Dharma, which the Tathāgata preaches for him—ever more exalted and ever more sublime, skillfully removing both the dark and the bright.

The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for them—ever higher and ever more sublime, ever more wondrous and ever more excellent—for those who skillfully eliminate both black and white [deeds]. Having heard it thus and thus, they know how to abandon one dharma and attain the ultimate realization regarding all dharmas; they develop serene faith in the World-Honored One, thinking: "That World-Honored One is truly and perfectly awakened."
Furthermore, one should ask him:
"Venerable sir,
by what practice, by what power, and by what wisdom do you know how to abandon one dharma and thereby attain the ultimate goal regarding all dharmas?"
"I have serene faith in the Blessed One; is that Blessed One truly a Perfectly Awakened One?
He replied thus:
"Venerable sir!"

I do not know the mind of the Blessed One, nor do I know it through any other means; rather, it is because of my such serene confidence in the Blessed One that he teaches me the Dharma—ever more exalted, ever more sublime, and effectively removing both the dark and the light.
"Venerable sir!

Just as the Blessed One has taught the Dharma to me, so have I heard it; the Tathāgata has taught the Dharma to me—ever higher than the high, ever more sublime than the sublime, excellently removing both black and white."

Having heard this thus, I know that by abandoning one dharma, one attains the ultimate realization regarding all dharmas; I have serene faith in the World-Honored One, for that World-Honored One is perfectly and fully awakened.
"Venerable sir!

I possess such practice, such power, and such wisdom that I have known and abandoned one dharma, and I have attained the ultimate realization regarding all dharmas; I have gained serene confidence in the Blessed One, that the Blessed One is a Truly Perfected Buddha."

If one possesses such conduct and such power, being deeply attached to the Tathāgata with the faculty of faith firmly established, this is called the wisdom associated with the indestructible root of faith and vision. No śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can take it away; thus one seeks the Tathāgata and thus correctly knows the Tathāgata.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifth chapter, "Seeking the Meaning of the Sūtra," ends here, totaling one thousand eighteen characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 48, totaling nine thousand nine hundred nineteen characters, concludes the fourth section, the "Paired Section" (*Yamaka-varga*), totaling nine thousand nine hundred nineteen characters. The fourth "Recitation for Analysis" (*Vibhaṅga-bhāṇaka*) is finished.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 49.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.

Recitation for the Afternoon (Paścādbhāṣita), Part 1: The Chapter on Pairs (Yamaka-varga). This first chapter contains five sūtras. The fifth daily recitation is called the Recitation for the Afternoon; it consists of three and a half chapters, totaling thirty-six sūtras.

The Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga Sutta) [The titles of the preceding suttas are: The Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga), The Discourse to Kūṭadanta, The Discourse on the Noble Path (Ariyapariyesanā), The Discourse at the Eastern Park (Pubbārāma), The Discourse on the Small Void (Cūḷasuññata), And the Great Void (Mahāsuññata) is last.

Discourse on Knowledge (Ñāṇavibhaṅga Sutta), No. 187, from the Middle Length Discourses (Majjhima Nikāya), Chapter Two: The Pairs. First: The Discourse on Knowledge. Thus have I heard: [At one time the Blessed One was staying at...]
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“If there should come a bhikṣu who says to you, ‘I have attained the knowledge that my births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I know truly that there will be no further existence,’ when you hear this, you should approve it well and joyfully practice accordingly.”
Having approved and rejoiced in what was said, one should then further question that bhikṣu as follows:
"Venerable sir!
The World-honored One has spoken of the five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
"Venerable sir!
How does one know, how does one see these five aggregates of clinging, so as to attain the knowledge of non-appropriation and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of the taints?
A monk whose taints are exhausted, having attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established, should answer the questioner thus:
"Venerable friends!
The form-aggregate (rūpa-skandha) is not a fruit, it is empty, undesirable, impermanent, unreliable, and subject to change; such I know it to be."

If one has desire, passion, attachment, bondage, and the impulse of clinging toward the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), then through its exhaustion, the absence of desire, its cessation, stilling, and stopping, one attains the knowledge of non-appropriation; with the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), the mind is liberated.

In this same way, I know that the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not a fruit, are empty, hollow, undesirable, impermanent, unreliable, and subject to change.

If one has desire for, attachment to, clinging to, bondage by, and is bound and driven by the aggregate of consciousness, then through the exhaustion of that, the absence of desire, its cessation, calming, and stopping, one comes to know non-appropriation; with the exhaustion of the taints, the mind is liberated.
"Venerable friends!
Having known and seen these five aggregates of clinging in this way, I have attained the knowledge of having nothing further to grasp; my taints are exhausted, and my mind is liberated.
A monk whose taints are exhausted, knowing that the holy life has been established, should answer the Dharma in this manner.
“Having heard this, you should all approve it well and joyfully practice it.
Having approved it well and joyfully practiced it, you should further question that bhikṣu in this way:
‘Venerable friend!...’”
The World-Honored One has taught that there are four nutriments by which sentient beings subsist and are nourished.
What are these four?
First is edible food, whether coarse or subtle; second is contact; third is mental volition; and fourth is consciousness.
“Venerable sir!
How does one know, how does one see these four nutriments, so as to attain the knowledge of non-clinging and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of the taints?
A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, having attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established, should answer the questioner thus:

"Venerable friends! Regarding edible food, my mind is neither elated nor depressed; it is not dependent, not bound, not defiled, and not attached. I have attained liberation, I have attained release, and I have attained complete liberation. My mind is free from perversion; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this I know as it truly is."

In this way, regarding the nutriment of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, he is neither elated nor depressed; he does not lean upon them, is not bound by them, is not defiled by them, and does not cling to them. Having attained liberation and deliverance, having fully attained liberation, his mind is free from inversion. Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows, as it truly is, that there will be no further existence.
"Venerable friends!
Knowing thus and seeing thus these four nutriments, I have attained the knowledge of non-clinging and the liberation of the mind through the destruction of the taints.
A monk whose taints are destroyed, having known that the holy life has been established, should answer the Dharma in this way.
“Having heard this, you should all approve it well and joyfully practice it.
Having approved it well and joyfully practiced it, you should further question that bhikṣu in this way:
‘Venerable sir!...’”
The World-Honored One speaks of four kinds of discourse. What are these four?

First is the discourse on what is seen as seen; second is the discourse on what is heard as heard; third is the discourse on what is cognized as cognized; and fourth is the discourse on what is known as known.
“Venerable sir!
How does one know, how does one see these four declarations so as to attain the knowledge of non-appropriation and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of the taints?
A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, having attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established, should answer the questioner thus:
"Venerable friends!
