Regarding the view of views, I speak of it as neither high nor low, neither leaning nor bound, neither stained nor attached; having attained liberation and release, I have attained complete liberation. My mind is free from inversion; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and I know according to reality that there will be no further existence."

Thus, having heard what was to be heard, cognized what was to be cognized, and known what was to be known, one speaks neither with elation nor depression; one is neither dependent nor bound, neither defiled nor attached. Having attained liberation and deliverance, having attained complete liberation, the mind is free from inversion. Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and one knows, as it truly is: "There is no further state of existence."
"Venerable friends!
Having known and seen these four declarations in this way, I have attained knowledge of non-clinging, and my mind is liberated through the destruction of the taints.
A monk whose taints are destroyed, having known that the holy life has been established, should answer the Dharma in this manner.
“Having heard this, you should all approve it well and joyfully practice it.
Having approved it well and joyfully practiced it, you should further question that bhikṣu in this way:
‘Venerable sir!...’”
The Blessed One has spoken of the six internal sense bases: the eye base, and the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases.
Venerable sir!
How should one know, how should one see these six internal sense bases, so that one attains the knowledge of non-appropriation and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of the taints?
“When a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted has realized that the holy life has been established, a person who knows the Dharma should answer thus:
‘Venerable friends!
Regarding the eye and eye-consciousness, I know both the eye-consciousness and the phenomena known by eye-consciousness; having known these two things, I have known them.’”
Venerable friends!

If the eye and eye-consciousness, and the phenomena known by eye-consciousness, have their pleasure exhausted—having attained that exhaustion, dispassion, cessation, calming, and stopping—one knows the state of non-appropriation; with the exhaustion of the taints, the mind is liberated. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as mind-consciousness: when mind-consciousness and the phenomena known by it both know these two things, having known them, [one attains liberation].
Venerable friends!

If the mind and mental consciousness cognize mental phenomena, and that pleasure has been exhausted—having reached its exhaustion, being without desire, ceased, stilled, and brought to an end—one knows through realization that there is nothing further to be grasped, and the mind is liberated through the destruction of the taints.
"Venerable friends!
When I know and see these six internal sense bases in this way, I attain the knowledge of non-appropriation, and my mind is liberated through the exhaustion of the taints.
A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, having attained the knowledge that the holy life has been established, should answer the Dharma in this manner.
“Having heard this, you should all approve it well and joyfully practice it.
Having approved it well and joyfully practiced it, you should further question that bhikṣu in this way:
‘Venerable one!...’”
The Blessed One has taught the six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

Venerable sir, how should one know and how should one see these six elements so that one attains the knowledge of non-appropriation and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of the taints?
“When a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted has realized that the holy life has been established, a questioner should answer him thus:

‘Venerable friends! I do not regard the earth element as mine; I am not of the earth element; the earth element is not my self. Yet, I say that the three types of feeling abide dependent upon the earth element, where consciousness and the underlying tendencies adhere. When these are exhausted, devoid of desire, ceased, stilled, and brought to an end, one realizes there is nothing further to be grasped, and the mind is liberated through the exhaustion of the taints.’”

In this way, the elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are not mine; I do not belong to the element of consciousness, nor does the element of consciousness belong to a self. Yet, it is said that the three types of feeling abide dependent upon the element of consciousness, and one is attached by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) toward consciousness. When these are exhausted, devoid of desire, ceased, stilled, and brought to an end, one attains the knowledge of having nothing further to grasp, and the mind is liberated through the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
"Venerable friends!
Having known and seen these six elements in this way, I have attained the knowledge of non-appropriation; my taints are exhausted and my mind is liberated.
A monk whose taints are exhausted, having known that the holy life has been established, should answer the questioner in this manner regarding the Dharma.
“Having heard this, you should all approve it well and joyfully practice it.
Having approved it well and joyfully practiced it, you should then further question that bhikṣu in this way:
‘Venerable friend!’”

How does one know, how does one see, so that this internal body together with consciousness and all external signs—the entire notion of "self," "my making," and the underlying tendencies of pride—are fully understood and their roots are utterly severed, so that they never arise again?
“When a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted has realized that the holy life has been established, one who knows the Dharma should answer thus:
‘Venerable friends!
Before I went forth to train in the path, I was weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; I desired to sever this great mass of suffering.’”
"Venerable friends!
Having become weary [of worldly life], I have formed this view: living as a householder is extremely narrow and a place of defilement; leaving home to study the Path is open and vast."

"I am now at home, bound by fetters, unable to practice the pure holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as life lasts. It would be better for me to renounce both small and great wealth, and to renounce both few and many kinsmen; having shaved off my hair and beard and donned the saffron robes, I shall go forth from the household life into homelessness out of deep faith to train in the Way."
"Venerable friends!

At a later time, having renounced both small and great wealth, and having renounced both few and many kinsmen, I shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the path."
"Venerable friends!

Having gone forth to study the Path and abandoned the marks of my clan, I have received the essential precepts of a bhikṣu. I cultivate the prohibitions and restraints, guard the Prātimokṣa, and further maintain proper deportment and decorum. Seeing even the slightest fault, I always harbor fear and dread, upholding and practicing the essential points of training."
“‘Venerable friends!

I abstain from killing and have severed the act of killing. Having laid aside the sword and staff, possessing a sense of shame and dread of blame, and endowed with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, I seek the welfare of all beings, even down to the smallest insects. Thus, I purify my mind regarding the taking of life.’”

I abstain from taking what is not given; I have abandoned taking what is not given. I take only what is given, I delight in giving, I am always fond of practicing generosity, and I rejoice without stinginess, not looking for reward. Thus, I purify my mind regarding taking what is not given.
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from unchaste conduct and severed unchaste conduct; I diligently cultivate the holy life, exerting myself in sublime practice, pure and stainless, free from desire and having abandoned lust. Regarding unchaste conduct, I have purified my mind."

"Venerable friends! I abstain from false speech; I have abandoned false speech. I speak the truth, delight in the truth, abide in the truth, and am unshakable. I am entirely trustworthy and do not deceive the world; I have purified my mind regarding false speech."

"Venerable friends! I am free from divisive speech; I have abandoned divisive speech. I practice non-divisiveness and do not cause dissension. I do not repeat here what I have heard there with the intent to divide these people, nor do I repeat there what I have heard here with the intent to divide those people. I reconcile those who are divided and rejoice in the reconciliation of those who are united. I do not form factions, do not delight in factions, and do not praise factions. Thus, I purify my mind of divisive speech."
“Venerable friends!
I am abstinent from harsh speech; I have abandoned harsh speech.

Whatever words I may utter that are coarse and rough, foul-sounding and grating to the ear, unpleasant to the multitude, unloved by the multitude, causing others distress, and preventing them from attaining concentration—such speech I have abandoned.

Whatever I say is pure, harmonious, gentle, and smooth; it is pleasing to the ear and enters the heart, being delightful and lovely, bringing peace and happiness to others. My speech is articulate and clear, not causing fear, and enables others to attain concentration. Speaking such words, I purify my mind of coarse speech.

"Venerable friends! I am free from frivolous speech; I have abandoned frivolous speech. I speak at the proper time, speak what is true, speak according to the Dharma, speak according to the meaning, and speak for the sake of tranquility. I delight in the cessation of disputes; I am timely and appropriate in my words, and I am skilled in instruction and reproof. Thus, I purify my mind of frivolous speech."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from trade and livelihood, having abandoned trade and livelihood; I have discarded scales and measures, as well as receiving goods; I do not bind others in service, I do not hope for short-measures or over-weighing, nor do I deceive others with small profits. Thus, I have purified my mind regarding trade and livelihood."
“‘Venerable friends!
I abstain from accepting widows and young girls; I have severed the practice of accepting widows and young girls, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of widows and young girls.’”
"Venerable friends!
I have abstained from accepting male and female slaves; I have severed the acceptance of male and female slaves; I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of male and female slaves.
Venerable friends!"

I abstain from accepting elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; I have severed the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
"Venerable friends!
I abstain from accepting chickens and pigs; I have severed the acceptance of chickens and pigs, and I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of chickens and pigs, venerable friends!"
I have abstained from accepting fields, lands, and shops; I have severed the acceptance of fields, lands, and shops; I have purified my mind regarding the acceptance of fields, lands, and shops.
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans; I have severed the practice of receiving raw rice, wheat, and beans; I have purified my mind regarding the receiving of raw rice, wheat, and beans."
"Venerable friends!
I am abstinent from liquor, having abandoned liquor; I have purified my mind regarding the drinking of intoxicants.
Venerable friends!"
"Venerable friends! I abstain from high and wide beds; I have renounced high and wide beds, and I purify my mind regarding high and wide beds.
Venerable friends!
I abstain from garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents; I have renounced garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents, and I purify my mind regarding garlands, jewelry, perfumes, and unguents."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to see or hear them; I have abandoned singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to see or hear them. Regarding singing, dancing, theatrical performances, and going to see or hear them, I have purified my mind."
"Venerable friends!

I have abstained from the enjoyment of precious forms and images, I have severed the enjoyment of precious forms and images, and I have purified my mind regarding the enjoyment of precious forms and images."
"Venerable friends!

I abstain from eating at improper times and have severed the practice of eating at improper times; I eat but one meal a day, do not eat at night, and observe the practice of eating only during the proper time. Regarding eating at improper times, I have purified my mind."
"Venerable friends!

I have accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue and further practice contentment: I take clothing only to cover the body and food only to sustain the frame. Wherever I go, my robes and bowl follow me of their own accord, and I am free from any lingering attachment."
"Just as a goose flies through the air with both wings, so too am I, venerable friends!

I have accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue (*ārya-śīlaskandha*) and perfect contentment; furthermore, I guard my sense faculties, constantly mindful of their restraint, mindful of clarity and penetration, and having achieved the guarding of mindfulness, I always intend to arouse [wholesome] thoughts."
If the eye sees forms, yet one does not grasp at their signs nor relish them—because of [the desire to avoid] anger and contention—one guards the faculty of the eye.
Because no covetousness, sorrow, or evil unwholesome states arise in the mind directed toward them, one guards the faculty of the eye.

In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, and body, if the mind cognizes mental phenomena, it does not grasp their signs nor does it relish those phenomena; rather, because of [the potential for] anger and contention, one guards the faculty of the mind.
"No covetousness, grief, or unwholesome, evil states arise in my mind; because I am intent upon that [state], I guard the faculty of the mind.
Venerable friends!

I have accomplished this noble aggregate of virtue and extreme contentment, the noble guarding of the sense faculties, and right mindfulness in going out and coming in. I am well-observing and discerning in bending and stretching, looking down and looking up, and in my deportment—whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent—I maintain right mindfulness in all things."
"Venerable friends!

I have accomplished this noble aggregate of ethical discipline and perfect contentment; I have also accomplished the noble guarding of the sense faculties, attained right mindfulness in going out and coming in, and dwell alone in seclusion in a place devoid of affairs—whether at the foot of a tree, in an empty and quiet spot, in a mountain cleft, a stone cave, an open space, or a heap of straw; or I go into the forest, or stay among the charnel grounds."
"Venerable friends!

I have already gone to a secluded place, or to the foot of a tree, or to a vacant and tranquil spot, where I spread my sitting mat and sit cross-legged, with body erect and mind focused, maintaining mindfulness and not turning away from it; I have eliminated covetousness and my mind is free from contention."
Seeing the wealth and various articles of livelihood belonging to others, I do not give rise to covetousness or the desire to acquire them for myself; thus, I purify my mind of covetousness.
Likewise, regarding ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, I sever doubt and transcend confusion, having no hesitation concerning wholesome qualities; thus, I purify my mind of doubt.
"Venerable friends!

I have abandoned these five hindrances—corruptions of the mind and weakness of wisdom—and, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, I have attained and abide in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna."
"Venerable friends!

Having attained such a state of concentration where the mind is purified, free from defilement and affliction, supple, well-established, and immovable, I have directed it toward the realization of the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows."
“‘Venerable friends!

I know this suffering as it truly is; I know the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. I know these taints, the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.’”

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"Venerable friends!

Thus do I know and thus do I see: regarding the consciousness within my own body and all external signs, every sense of 'I,' every 'mine-ness,' and the underlying tendencies of conceit have been abandoned through full knowledge; their root has been utterly uprooted, so that they shall never arise again."
The bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, having realized that the holy life has been established, should answer the Dharma in this way:
"When you hear this, you should well approve it, rejoice, and practice it accordingly."
Having approved and rejoiced in what was said, one should then speak thus to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!

We have already approved and rejoiced in your initial statement; however, we wish to go from excellence to further excellence, seeking wise responses and eloquence. For this reason, we ask you again and again."
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first discourse, the *Jñāna-sūtra*, ends here, totaling 2,846 characters. 188. The Āyāraṇa Sutta (188), Middle Discourses, Twin Section, the second discourse in the fifth sub-section of the recitation: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and was staying at the Eastern Park in the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall.

Then, at the hour of late afternoon, the World-Honored One rose from his meditative seclusion, descended from the hall, and walked back and forth upon the open ground in the shadow of the hall, extensively expounding the profound and subtle Dharma for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the heterodox teacher Ajita, a disciple of the śramaṇa Māṭhara, saw from afar the World-Honored One rising from his meditative seclusion and descending from the hall to walk up and down upon the open ground within the shadow of the hall, extensively expounding the profound and subtle Dharma for the bhikṣus.
The heterodox teacher Āyana, a disciple of the śramaṇa Māṭhara, went to where the Buddha was staying; after exchanging greetings with him, he followed the Buddha as he walked up and down.
The World-Honored One turned back and asked, "Āyana!"
The śramaṇa Mantu truly reflected five hundred times:

"If there be any other śramaṇas or brahmins who are all-knowing and all-seeing, and who claim of themselves, 'I know all without remainder; I see all without remainder,' yet perceive faults in him and acknowledge their own faults."
The wanderer Ajita, a disciple of the śramaṇa Māluṅkyāputra, replied:
“Gautama! The śramaṇa Māluṅkyāputra truly contemplated five hundred thoughts.”

If there were any other ascetics or brahmins who claim to know all and see all, and who declare, "I have known everything without remainder and seen everything without remainder," yet who find fault in others while claiming fault in themselves.
The Blessed One asked again:
"Āyana! How does the ascetic Māluṅkyaputta contemplate five hundred thoughts?"

If there were any other recluses or brahmins who knew all and saw all, and who claimed, "I know without remainder and see without remainder," would they acknowledge their own faults upon seeing those [other teachers'] faults?
The heterodox teacher Ajita, a disciple of the śramaṇa Makkhali, replied:
“Gautama! The śramaṇa Makkhali speaks thus:”
Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, sleeping, or waking, whether by day or by night, his knowledge and vision are always unimpeded.

At times he may encounter rogue elephants, runaway horses, runaway chariots, rebel soldiers, fleeing men, or fleeing women; or while traveling such paths, he may encounter vicious elephants, vicious horses, vicious oxen, or vicious dogs; or he may come upon a swarm of snakes, or be pelted with clods of earth, or struck with sticks; or he may fall into ditches or drains, or fall into a latrine; or he may ride a recumbent ox, or fall into a deep pit, or enter among thorns; or seeing a village or town, he may ask for its name or the way to it; or seeing men or women, he may ask their clan or names; or he may observe empty houses, or enter such clans in this manner.
Once he had entered, he asked me:
"Venerable sir, from where have you come?
I replied to him:
"Venerable ones!
I am heading toward an evil destination," [said] Gautama.
The śramaṇa Māṭhara reflected in this manner for five hundred thoughts:

"If there be any other śramaṇas or brahmins who are all-knowing and all-seeing, and who claim of themselves, 'I have known everything without remainder; I have seen everything without remainder,' I shall find fault with them."
Thereupon, the Blessed One ceased his walking meditation, went to the head of the walkway, spread out a sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, and asked the bhikṣus:
"Do you all receive and uphold the teachings on wisdom that I have spoken?"
Those bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.
The World-Honored One then asked them a second and a third time: "Bhikṣus!"
"Do you accept and uphold the matters of wisdom that I have taught?
The bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer, even after being asked a second and a third time.
At that moment, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time. Sugata!”
Now is the very time.
If the Blessed One were to speak to the bhikṣus concerning the matter of wisdom, the bhikṣus, having heard it from the Blessed One, would properly receive and uphold it.
The World-Honored One said:
"Bhikṣus! Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in full detail."
Then, the bhikṣus replied:
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction and listen."
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"There are generally two kinds of assemblies: the first is called the assembly of the Dharma, and the second is called the assembly of non-Dharma.
What is the assembly of non-Dharma?"

Suppose there is one who practices what is contrary to the Dharma and speaks what is contrary to the Dharma, and his assembly likewise practices what is contrary to the Dharma and speaks what is contrary to the Dharma. This person who acts contrary to the Dharma stands before an assembly that acts contrary to the Dharma; based on what he himself knows, he utters false and deceptive words rather than the truth. He displays conceptual distinctions, establishes his own conduct, and disseminates the sequential teaching of the Dharma, desiring to sever the malice in the minds of others—a difficult challenge that cannot be easily refuted.

Within the True Dharma and Discipline, one must not establish what one knows for oneself. When a person who does not possess the Dharma stands before a community that does not possess the Dharma and claims, "I possess wisdom and universal knowledge," and if within that assembly there are those who speak of such matters of wisdom, this is called a non-Dharma assembly.
What is the assembly of the Dharma?

There may be one who practices the Dharma and teaches the Dharma, and that assembly likewise practices the Dharma and teaches the Dharma. That person of the Dharma stands before the assembly of the Dharma; based on what he himself knows, he speaks without falsehood, declaring what is true and real, manifesting and analyzing it, establishing its practice, and proclaiming it in successive order. Desiring to sever the faults and evils in the minds of others, he may speak when subjected to difficult questioning.

Within the True Dharma, one may establish what one knows for oneself; that person, standing before the assembly of the Dharma, declares, "I possess wisdom and universal knowledge. If, within that [assembly], there are those who speak thus regarding matters of wisdom, it is called an assembly of the Dharma.

Therefore, you should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and what is meaningless. Having known what is Dharma and non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and meaningless, you should train yourselves in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, he rose from his seat and entered his room to sit in quiet meditation.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Venerable friends!..."
"You should know that the Blessed One has briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis, and has then risen from his seat and entered his room to sit in private meditation.

Therefore, you should understand what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and what is meaningless. Having understood what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and what is meaningless, you should train yourselves in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning."
They further thought: "Virtuous ones!
Who among you is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated?"
He further thought:
"The Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant and knows the Buddha’s mind; he is constantly praised by the World-Honored One as well as by all wise practitioners of the holy life."
The Venerable Ānanda is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly explained.
Friends, let us go together to the Venerable Ānanda and request him to explain this meaning.
“If the Venerable Ānanda would analyze this for us, we shall receive and uphold it well.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:
“Venerable Ānanda!”
"You should know that the Blessed One has briefly stated this meaning without detailed analysis, and has risen from his seat, entered his dwelling, and sat in private meditation.

'You should all know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and what is meaningless. Having known Dharma and non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and meaningless, you should train yourselves in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning.'"
We then thought to ourselves:
"Venerable friends!
Who among us is able to explain in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated?"
We further thought to ourselves:
"The Venerable Ānanda is the Buddha’s attendant and knows the Buddha’s mind; he is constantly praised by the World-Honored One as well as by all wise practitioners of the holy life."
"The Venerable Ānanda is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has briefly explained.
We pray that the Venerable Ānanda will, out of compassion, explain it at length."
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Virtuous ones!
Listen as I speak a parable; for the wise understand the meaning through a parable."
Venerable friends!

It is just as if there were a person who, desiring to seek out the core of a tree, entered a forest for that purpose carrying an axe. Seeing a great tree consisting of roots, trunk, joints, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, that person does not touch the roots, the trunk, the joints, or the fruit, but touches only the branches and leaves.
What you venerable ones have said is likewise so.
While the World-Honored One is present, he has left him to come to me and inquire about this matter. Why is that?
"Venerable friends!

You should know that the Blessed One is the eye, he is wisdom, he is the meaning, he is the Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, and the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of the truths and manifests all meanings through him. Venerable friends, you should go to the Blessed One and ask about this matter:
'Blessed One!'"
"What does this mean?
What is the significance of this?
As the Blessed One has spoken it, you venerable ones should properly receive and uphold it.
Then the bhikṣus replied:
"Indeed it is so,
Venerable Ānanda!"

The Blessed One is the eye, he is wisdom, he is the meaning, he is the Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, and the General of Dharma; he proclaims the meaning of the ultimate truth, and it is from that Blessed One that all meanings are revealed.

However, the Venerable Ānanda was the Buddha’s attendant and understood the Buddha’s intentions; he was constantly praised by the World-Honored One as well as by all wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life.
The Venerable Ānanda is able to analyze in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has just briefly stated.
We pray that the Venerable Ānanda will, out of compassion, explain it at length.
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!
Listen together to what I shall say."
"Venerable friends!
Wrong view is non-Dhamma; right view is the Dhamma.
If, due to wrong view, immeasurable evil and unwholesome states arise, this is called 'not beneficial'."
Venerable friends, if immeasurable wholesome qualities arise because of right view, this is called "the meaningful.

Furthermore, up to the point where false knowledge is what is not the Dharma and right knowledge is the Dharma: if immeasurable evil and unwholesome qualities arise because of false knowledge, this is called "the meaningless."
"Venerable friends, if immeasurable wholesome qualities arise because of right knowledge, this is what is meant by that meaning.
The Blessed One spoke this matter in brief without detailed analysis, then rose from his seat and entered his dwelling to sit in meditation."

"Therefore, you should know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and what is meaningless. Having known what is Dharma and non-Dharma, and what is meaningful and meaningless, you should train yourselves in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the meaning."

"This was briefly stated by the Blessed One without a detailed analysis of its meaning; I have explained it extensively according to these words and this text. Venerable friends, you may go before the Buddha and present this in full. If the meaning is indeed as the Blessed One has spoken, then you, venerable friends, may accept and uphold it."

Then, having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, those bhikṣus received and recited it well; they rose from their seats, circumambulated the Venerable Ānanda three times, and departed for the place where the Buddha was. Having arrived, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!..."
Having briefly explained this meaning to the Blessed One without detailed analysis, he rose from his seat, entered his dwelling, and sat in private meditation.
The Venerable Ānanda then expounded it at length using these very phrases and these very words.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One sighed in praise:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Among my disciples, there are those who possess vision, wisdom, the Dharma, and its meaning. Why is this?
It is because when the Teacher has briefly explained this meaning to his disciples without extensive analysis, those disciples elaborate upon it through these very phrases and these very words.
As Ānanda has spoken, you all should receive and uphold it in this way.
Why is this? Because the meaning of contemplation should be understood in accordance with what he has said.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Āyāraṇa Sūtra*, the second, ends here, totaling 1,828 characters. 189. *The Noble Path Sūtra* (189), Middle Discourses, Twin Section, *The Noble Path Sūtra*, the third, the fifth recitation section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Kuru people at the Kuru capital of Kammāsadhamma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikkhus:

"There is a single path that leads sentient beings to purification, to freedom from sorrow, lamentation, and weeping; it brings about the cessation of grief, suffering, and despair, and leads to the attainment of the Dharma as it truly is—namely, noble right concentration."

There is practice, there is assistance, and there is also equipment; these constitute seven factors. Regarding noble right concentration, they speak of practice, they speak of assistance, and they also speak of equipment.
What are the seven?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.

If one possesses these seven factors—cultivating, supporting, and fulfilling them—and thus rightly inclines toward the mind’s unification, this is called noble right concentration, which has cultivation, support, and fulfillment.

Why is this so? Right view gives rise to right intention; right intention gives rise to right speech; right speech gives rise to right action; right action gives rise to right livelihood; right livelihood gives rise to right effort; right effort gives rise to right mindfulness; and right mindfulness gives rise to right concentration. When a noble disciple’s mind is thus rightly concentrated, lust, anger, and delusion are instantly exhausted. When a noble disciple’s mind is thus rightly liberated, they immediately know, in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence. Among these, right view stands foremost.
"If one perceives wrong view as wrong view, this is called right view; if one perceives right view as right view, this also is called right view.
What is wrong view?"

This refers to the view that there is no giving, no sacrifice, and no recitation of spells; that there is no wholesome or unwholesome karma, nor any fruit or result of wholesome or unwholesome karma; that there is no this world or the next world; that there is no father and no mother; and that in the world there is no true person who has reached the good destination, who has fared well and is heading toward the good, who has personally known, awakened to, and realized for themselves through direct experience in this world and the next. This is called wrong view.
What is right view?
It is this view:
"There is giving, there is sacrifice, and there are also incantations;..."
There are wholesome and unwholesome karmas; there are results of wholesome and unwholesome karmas;
there is this world and the other world; there is father and mother;

in the world there are true persons who, having gone to the good destination, having gone well and directed themselves well, dwell having personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized for themselves this world and the other world.
This is called right view.
To see that wrong view is indeed wrong view is called right view;
to see that right view is indeed right view is also called right view.
Having understood this, he then seeks training, desiring to abandon wrong view and accomplish right view; this is called right effort.
The bhikṣu abandons wrong view through mindfulness and accomplishes right view; this is called right mindfulness.
These three factors follow right view and proceed from the application of vision; therefore, right view comes first.
"If one perceives wrong intention as being wrong intention, this is called right intention."
If one perceives right intention as being right intention, that is also called right intention.
What is wrong intention?
Thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness—these are called wrong intention.
What is right intention? It is the thought of non-desire, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-harming;
this is called right intention. Thus, seeing wrong intention as wrong intention is what is called right intention.
To see right intention as right intention is also called right intention.
Having known this thus, one then seeks to train, desiring to abandon wrong intention and to accomplish right intention; this is called right effort.
A bhikṣu uses mindfulness to sever wrong intention and accomplishes right intention; this is called right mindfulness.
These three factors follow right intention and proceed from the application of vision; therefore, right view is foremost.
"If one perceives wrong speech as wrong speech, this is called right speech.
If one perceives right speech as right speech, this also is called right speech.
What is wrong speech?"
False speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—these are called wrong speech.
What is right speech?
Abstinence from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—this is called right speech.
To see wrong speech as wrong speech is called right speech;
to see right speech as right speech is also called right speech.
Having known this, one then seeks to train, desiring to abandon wrong speech and accomplish right speech—this is called right effort.
A bhikṣu uses mindfulness to sever wrong speech and accomplishes right speech; this is called right mindfulness.
These three factors follow right speech and derive from the application of insight; therefore, right view comes first.
"If one perceives unwholesome action as unwholesome action, this is called right action.
If one perceives wholesome action as wholesome action, this also is called right action.
What is unwholesome action?"
Killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct—these are called wrong action.
What is right action?
Refraining from killing, refraining from taking what is not given, and refraining from sexual misconduct—these are called right action.
To see that unwholesome action is indeed unwholesome action is called right action;
to see that wholesome action is indeed wholesome action is also called right action.
Having known this, one then seeks to train, desiring to abandon unwholesome action and accomplish right action; this is called right effort.
A bhikṣu uses mindfulness to sever unwholesome actions and accomplishes right action; this is called right mindfulness.
These three factors follow from right action and originate from the application of vision; therefore, right view comes first.
"If one perceives wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood, this is called right livelihood.
If one perceives right livelihood as right livelihood, this too is called right livelihood.
What is wrong livelihood?"

If there are those who seek but find no satisfaction, they sustain their lives through various animal incantations and wrong livelihoods; such persons seek clothing and bedding in a manner that is not according to the Dharma, for it is unrighteous.
To seek food, drink, bedding, medicine, and various requisites for life in an unrighteous manner—because it is contrary to the Dharma—is called wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
What is right livelihood (*samyagājīva*)?

If one does not seek with dissatisfaction, does not employ various kinds of spells for animals, and does not maintain life through wrong livelihood, but seeks clothing and bedding in accordance with the Dharma, then it is by means of the Dharma.
Seeking food, drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, and all articles of livelihood in accordance with the Dharma—this is through the Dharma;
this is called right livelihood. To see wrong livelihood as wrong livelihood is what is called right livelihood.
To see right livelihood as right livelihood is also called right livelihood.
Having known this thus, one then seeks to train, desiring to abandon wrong livelihood and to accomplish right livelihood; this is called right effort.
A bhikṣu uses mindfulness to sever wrong livelihood and accomplishes right livelihood; this is called right mindfulness.
These three factors follow right livelihood and proceed from the application of vision; therefore, right view is foremost.
“What is right effort?
Here, a bhikkhu generates desire, exerts himself, applies energy, uplifts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil states that have already arisen.”
In order that unarisen unwholesome states do not arise, one generates desire, seeks skillful means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.
In order that unarisen wholesome states arise, one generates desire, seeks skillful means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.

In order that wholesome states already arisen may endure, not be forgotten, not regress, but rather increase, expand, and become fully perfected through cultivation, one generates desire, seeks skillful means, exerts oneself, uplifts the mind, and strives; this is called right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
"What is right mindfulness?
A bhikkhu contemplates the body internally as body; he contemplates feelings, the mind, and phenomena as they truly are, up to and including phenomena as phenomena. This is called right mindfulness."
"What is right concentration?
Here, a bhikkhu, detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna; this is called right concentration."
"What is right liberation?
A bhikṣu is liberated from the mind of desire, and liberated from the minds of hatred and delusion; this is called right liberation.
What is right knowledge?"
A bhikkhu who knows the liberation of the mind from desire, and knows the liberation of the mind from ill will and delusion—this is called right knowledge.
This constitutes the eight factors for one in training; for an arahant whose taints are exhausted, it constitutes ten factors.
"How does a trainee accomplish the eight factors?
Training in right view up to training in right concentration—this is how a trainee accomplishes the eight factors.
How does an Arhat whose taints are exhausted accomplish the ten factors?"
From right view of one beyond training up to right knowledge of one beyond training—this is called an Arhat who has exhausted the taints and is accomplished in ten factors. Why is this so?
Right view abandons wrong view; and as for those immeasurable evil and unwholesome states that arise because of wrong view, those too are abandoned.
If immeasurable wholesome dharmas arise from right view, he cultivates them so that they become fulfilled and complete.
When he reaches right knowledge, he abandons wrong knowledge; and if immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas arise from wrong knowledge, he likewise abandons them.
If immeasurable wholesome qualities arise from right knowledge, one then cultivates them until they are fulfilled and perfected.

These are the twenty categories of wholesome factors and the twenty categories of unwholesome factors; these are called the forty great dharma-categories for turning the Brahma-wheel, which no ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can obstruct or declare to be incorrect.

If there be any śramaṇas or brahmins regarding whom I have turned the Brahma-wheel within the forty great Dharma-chapters that I have taught, no śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain it or declare it to be false.
Regarding that which is in accordance with the Dharma, there are ten forms of censure. What are these ten?
They are: if one reviles right view and praises wrong view.
If there are recluses or brahmins with wrong views whom one honors and praises;

and if there are recluses or brahmins for whom I have proclaimed the forty great Dharma-topics that turn the Brahma-wheel, which no recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain or declare to be false—then such [honoring and praising] those with wrong views is called the first reproach regarding what is in accordance with the Dharma.
"If one disparages right knowledge while praising false knowledge;
or if there are recluses and brahmins who possess false knowledge, and one makes offerings to them and praises them."

If there are any śramaṇas or brahmins who, regarding the forty great Dharma-topics by which I have turned the Brahma-wheel—concerning which no śramaṇa, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can rightfully challenge or deny them—they are, with respect to suchness, subject to this tenth censure.

If there are recluses or brahmins regarding whom I have turned the Brahma-wheel of the forty great dharma-topics, and no recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world can restrain me or declare it to be wrong—this is called the ten grounds for censure regarding what is in accordance with the Dharma.

If there are other recluses or brahmins who, while crouching, speak of crouching; who, while asserting non-existence, speak of non-existence; who speak of causelessness, speak of lack of action, and speak of the absence of karma—claiming that the various designations of good and evil deeds performed here and there are cut off and destroyed, and that the Great Wheel of Dharma turned by me in the forty-fold discourse on the Dharma cannot be obstructed or declared false by any recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—they too will face censure, sorrow, and fear.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikkhus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third discourse, the *Ariyapariyesanā Sutta*, ends here, totaling one thousand eight hundred and five characters. 190. The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness (*Cūḷasuññata Sutta*), the fourth in the Twin Section of the *Madhyama Āgama*. Fifth Recitation Section. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and was staying at the Eastern Park in the Hall of Mṛgāramātṛ.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his meditation in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One, on one occasion while you were traveling among the Śākyas at the city named Śāketa, I heard such a teaching from the World-Honored One.”
"Ānanda! 'I have practiced emptiness extensively.
Regarding what that Blessed One has spoken, do you well understand it, well receive it, and maintain it well?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied:
"Ānanda! Regarding what I have taught, you truly know it well, have received it well, and have retained it well."
Why is that? From that time until now, I have practiced emptiness extensively. Ānanda!
Thus, this Sāḷha Hall is empty and devoid of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, wealth, grain, servants, and laborers; yet it is not empty, for it is filled solely with the community of bhikṣus.
This is it, Ānanda!
If something is not present here, for that reason I see it as empty; if something else remains here, I see it as truly existing.
Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion. Ānanda!

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not dwell on perceptions of village, nor should he dwell on perceptions of people; he should instead frequently dwell on the perception of solitude.
He thus knows that [the mind] is empty of the perception of a village and empty of the perception of people; yet it is not empty of one thing alone: the perception of non-existence.
If there were any fatigue caused by the perception of a village, I do not possess such a thing.
If there were weariness due to the perception of persons, I too would not have it;
there is only weariness due to the perception of a single state of non-action (*apravṛtti*).
If that [person] does not exist therein, for this reason he sees it as empty; if something else remains therein, he sees it as truly existing.
"Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not dwell on the perception of a person, nor should he dwell on the perception of non-existence; rather, he should repeatedly dwell on the perception of the single earth.
If that bhikṣu sees this ground as having elevations and depressions, clusters of snakes, thickets of thorns, sand, stones, precipitous mountains, or deep rivers, he must not dwell upon them.
If one sees this ground as level as the palm of a hand and finds the location for observation to be excellent, one should repeatedly bring that to mind.
Ānanda! It is just like a cowhide stretched out with a hundred nails; once it has been fully stretched and taut, it is without wrinkles and without shrinkage.
If you see that this ground has elevations and depressions, clusters of snakes, thickets of thorns, sand, stones, treacherous mountains, or deep rivers, do not fixate your mind upon them.
If one sees this ground as level as the palm of a hand and the location for observation is favorable, one should repeatedly bring that to mind.
Thus knowing it, one perceives it as empty of the notion of persons and empty of the notion of things; yet there is that which is not empty: the singular notion of earth alone.
If there is weariness, it arises from the perception of persons; I have no such thing.
If there is weariness, it arises from the perception of non-entities; I likewise have no such thing.
There is only weariness, caused by the perception of a single ground.
If there is nothing therein, for that reason he sees it as empty; if there is something remaining, he sees it as truly existent.
"Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not dwell on the perception of non-existence, nor should he dwell on the perception of earth; rather, he should repeatedly dwell on the perception of the base of infinite space.

He knows thus: it is empty of the perception of objects and empty of the perception of earth; yet there is that which is not empty—the singular, immeasurable perception of the sphere of infinite space.
If there were weariness due to the perception of objects, I do not have that.
If there were weariness due to the perception of earth, I would not have it either;
there is only weariness due to the perception of the sphere of infinite space.
If that [earth] does not exist therein, for this reason he sees it as empty; if something else remains there, he sees that as truly existing.
"Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of earth, nor should he attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite space; rather, he should repeatedly attend to the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Knowing thus, he is empty of the perception of earth and empty of the perception of the base of infinite space; yet there is that which is not empty: namely, the single perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
If there were fatigue caused by the perception of earth, I would not have it;
if there were fatigue caused by the perception of the sphere of infinite space, I likewise would not have it.
There is only weariness, due to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
If there were nothing therein, he would see it as empty because of that; if there were something remaining, he would see it as truly existing.
"Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not dwell on the perception of the base of infinite space, nor should he dwell on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness; rather, he should frequently dwell on the perception of the base of nothingness.

He knows thus: the perception of the base of infinite space is empty, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness is empty; yet there remains that which is not empty—the singular perception of the base of nothingness.
If there is any fatigue resulting from the perception of the sphere of infinite space, I have none of that.
If there is any fatigue resulting from the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, I likewise have none of that.
There is only weariness due to the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
If there were nothing therein, one would see it as empty because of that; if there were something remaining, one would see that as truly existing.
Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"

If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should not attend to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, nor should he attend to the perception of the base of nothingness; rather, he should repeatedly attend to a single concentration of the mind without perception.

He knows thus: the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is empty, the perception of the sphere of nothingness is empty; yet there is that which is not empty—namely, the single concentration of mind without perception.
If there were any fatigue arising from the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, I do not have that.
If there were any fatigue arising from the perception of the sphere of nothingness, I likewise do not have that.
There is only weariness resulting from the concentration of the mind of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*).
If there were nothing therein, he would see it as empty; if there were something remaining, he would see that as truly existent.
Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion.
He forms this thought:

“I was originally in the concentration of the mind free from perception; as for what was originally practiced and what was originally contemplated—if it were that which was originally practiced and originally contemplated, I would not delight in it, I would not seek it, and I should not abide in it. Knowing thus and seeing thus, my mind was liberated from the outflow of sensual desire, and my mind was liberated from the outflows of existence and ignorance. Being liberated, I knew I was liberated: ‘Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence,’ knowing this as it truly is.”

Thus he knows: the outflow of sensual desire is empty, the outflow of existence is empty, and the outflow of ignorance is empty; yet there is that which is not empty—namely, this body of mine, consisting of the six sense bases, as long as life remains.
If there is weariness caused by the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), I have none of that.
If there is weariness caused by the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) or the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*), I likewise have none of that.
There is only weariness because my body’s six sense bases and life-force persist.
If there were nothing therein, he would see it as empty;
if there were anything remaining, he would see that as truly existent.
Ānanda! This is called practicing reality, emptiness, and non-perversion;
that is to say, the exhaustion of outflows, the outflow-free, the unconditioned, and the liberation of the mind.

“Ānanda! All those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past practiced this reality, emptiness, and non-perversion—namely, the exhaustion of outflows, the outflow-free, the unconditioned, and the liberation of the mind.”

Ānanda! All those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future—all of them practice this reality, which is empty and non-perverted; namely, the exhaustion of outflows, the state of being without outflows, the unconditioned, and the liberation of the mind.

Ānanda! Even now, as I, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, I too practice this reality—empty, non-perverted—which is the exhaustion of outflows, the outflow-free, the unconditioned, and the liberation of the mind.

Ānanda! You should train yourself thus: "I too shall practice this reality—empty, non-perverted—which is the exhaustion of the outflows, the outflow-free, the unconditioned, and the liberation of the mind."
"Therefore, Ānanda, you should train yourselves in this way.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikkhus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Fourth Discourse on the Lesser Emptiness ends here, totaling one thousand four hundred and twenty-three characters. 191. The Great Emptiness Discourse (191), Middle Collection, Twin Section, The Fifth Discourse on the Great Emptiness, Part Five of the Fifth Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Śākyas at Kapilavatthu, staying at the Nyagrodha Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having passed the night, dressed in the early morning and taking his bowl, entered Kapilavastu to beg for food. Having finished his meal after midday, he proceeded to the Kālādamya Śākya monastery.
At that time, the Śākya Kālāmas had prepared many seats and couches in their monastery, and many bhikṣus were residing there.
Then, the Blessed One emerged from the Śākya Kālāma monastery and proceeded to the Śākya Kāla monastery.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was together with a great many bhikṣus in the Karakaṇḍa Śākyan Monastery, gathered there to perform work on robes. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the Venerable Ānanda went out to meet him; he took the Buddha’s robe and bowl, returned to arrange the seat, and drew water to wash his feet.
After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat upon the seat prepared by the Venerable Ānanda in the Karakaṇḍa Śākya Monastery and said: “Ānanda,
many beds and seats have been spread out in the Karakaṇḍa Śākya Monastery, and many bhikṣus are residing there.”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
Kālakhemaka the Śākyan prepared many seats and couches in his vihāra, and many bhikṣus stayed there.
Why was this? Because I am currently engaged in the work of making robes.
Then the Blessed One again addressed Ānanda, saying:

“A bhikṣu should not desire clamorous discourse, delight in clamorous discourse, or engage in clamorous discourse; he should not desire a crowd, delight in a crowd, or associate with a crowd; he should not wish to be separated from a crowd, nor should he delight in dwelling alone in a secluded place.”

If there is a bhikṣu who desires frivolous talk, delights in frivolous talk, engages in frivolous talk, desires a crowd, delights in a crowd, assembles with a crowd, does not wish to leave the crowd, and does not delight in dwelling alone in seclusion—then he is said to lack the joy that is noble, the joy of dispassion, the joy of renunciation, the joy of cessation, the joy of awakening, the joy of non-nutriment, and the joy that transcends birth and death.
If such happiness were easy to obtain rather than difficult, it would never be possible. Ānanda!

If there is a bhikkhu who does not desire idle talk, does not delight in idle talk, and does not engage in idle talk; who does not desire the company of others, does not delight in the company of others, and does not engage with the company of others; who desires to be apart from the company of others and always delights in dwelling alone in seclusion—then he is said to possess happiness: noble happiness, the happiness of dispassion, the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of cessation, the happiness of enlightenment, the happiness of being without food, and the happiness that is beyond birth and death.
"If such happiness were easy to obtain and not difficult to attain, it would certainly be possible. Ānanda!

A bhikṣu who desires clamorous speech, delights in clamorous speech, engages in clamorous speech, desires crowds, delights in crowds, assembles with crowds, does not wish to leave the crowd, and does not delight in dwelling alone in seclusion—[for him, such happiness is impossible]."

If there is a bhikṣu who desires frivolous talk, delights in frivolous talk, engages in frivolous talk; who desires a crowd, delights in a crowd, assembles with a crowd, does not wish to leave the crowd, and does not delight in dwelling alone in seclusion—then for such a person to attain liberation of mind through love at the proper time, or liberation of mind that is timeless and immovable, is absolutely impossible.

Ānanda! If there is a bhikṣu who does not desire clamor, does not delight in clamor, and does not engage in clamor; who does not desire the assembly, does not delight in the assembly, and does not engage with the assembly; who desires to be apart from the assembly and always delights in dwelling alone in seclusion—then it is certainly possible that he will attain the liberation of mind through love at the proper time, as well as the unshakable liberation of mind that is not dependent on time.

Why is this? I do not see any form that causes me desire or pleasure; yet when that form decays and changes, at another time it gives rise to sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, and despair. For this reason, I have attained perfect awakening and full realization in this distinct dwelling place, which is called transcending all perceptions of form and proceeding in the sphere of external emptiness.

“Ānanda! Having practiced this dwelling, joy arose within me. With this joy, my entire body experienced mindfulness and clear comprehension; gladness arose, tranquility arose, happiness arose, and concentration arose. Just as I had this concentration, my entire body experienced mindfulness and clear comprehension.”

Ānanda! There may be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who come together to visit me; I then direct such and such a state of mind toward them—detachment, delighting in the absence of desire—and I also preach the Dharma to them and encourage them.

Ānanda! If a bhikṣu wishes to practice emptiness extensively, that bhikṣu should maintain the internal mind in a state of stillness and bring it to one-pointed concentration. Having maintained the internal mind in a state of stillness and brought it to one-pointed concentration, he should then contemplate internal emptiness.

Ānanda! If a bhikṣu speaks thus: "I do not maintain the inner mind in stillness, nor do I bring it to one-pointed concentration, yet I am mindful of internal emptiness," you should know that this bhikṣu is merely exhausting himself greatly.
“Ānanda! How does a bhikṣu maintain the internal mind so that it abides in one-pointed concentration?

Here, Ānanda, a bhikṣu’s body is saturated, steeped, drenched, and thoroughly suffused with the joy and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his body that is not pervaded by this joy and happiness born of seclusion.”

Ānanda! It is like a person bathing who takes a vessel filled with cleansing powder, pours water over it to mix it, kneads it into a ball, and soaks it until it is thoroughly saturated; it becomes completely filled throughout, dense both inside and out, with no place where moisture can leak away.

In this way, Ānanda, the bhikṣu’s body is saturated, thoroughly soaked, and completely filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his body that is not pervaded by this joy and happiness born of seclusion.

Ānanda! In this way, a bhikṣu maintains the internal mind in stillness so that it attains one-pointed concentration. Having maintained the internal mind in stillness so that it is concentrated, he should then contemplate internal emptiness.
Having contemplated internal emptiness, his mind wavers; it does not incline toward it, nor does it attain clarity, nor does it abide in or comprehend internal emptiness.

Ānanda! If, when a bhikṣu contemplates, he perceives that his mindfulness of internal emptiness causes his mind to waver, does not incline toward it, fails to attain clarity, and neither abides in nor resolves upon internal emptiness, then that bhikṣu should practice mindfulness of external emptiness. Having practiced mindfulness of external emptiness, if his mind still wavers, does not incline toward it, fails to attain clarity, and neither abides in nor resolves upon external emptiness—[he should proceed further].

“Ānanda! If, when a bhikkhu observes, he knows that his mindfulness of external emptiness is shifting, does not incline toward it, does not attain clarity, and neither abides nor resolves within external emptiness, that bhikkhu should practice mindfulness of internal and external emptiness.”

Having contemplated internal and external emptiness, his mind wavers; it does not incline toward it, it does not attain clarity, and it neither abides in nor understands internal and external emptiness.

Ānanda! If, when a bhikṣu observes, he knows that his mindfulness of internal and external emptiness wavers, does not incline toward proximity, fails to attain clarity, and neither abides in nor understands internal and external emptiness, then that bhikṣu should practice mindfulness so that it does not waver.
Once that mindfulness is no longer shifting, his mind still moves; it does not incline toward proximity, nor does it attain clarity, nor does it abide in or understand non-shifting.

“Ānanda! When a bhikkhu observes thus, he knows that while mindfulness does not waver, his mind wavers; it does not incline toward the proximate, nor does it attain clarity, nor does it abide in or understand the unwavering state. That bhikkhu, regarding those various states of mind and those various concentrations, repeatedly masters them, repeatedly practices them, makes them supple again and again, making them excellent, pliant, and malleable; he takes delight in their withdrawal and seclusion.”

If that mind, regarding those various concentrations, has been repeatedly guided and repeatedly practiced, repeatedly made supple, well-prepared, pliant, and gentle, and having attained the joy of withdrawal through mastery, one should dwell having accomplished internal emptiness.
Having accomplished and dwelled in that inner emptiness, his mind does not waver; it moves toward proximity, attains a clear and pure abiding, and realizes inner emptiness. Ānanda!

When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that he dwells having accomplished internal emptiness; his mind does not waver, it inclines toward the proximate, and he attains a clear and pure abiding. One who understands internal emptiness in this manner is said to possess right knowledge.

“Ānanda! A bhikkhu should dwell having accomplished the emptiness of the external; having dwelt having accomplished the emptiness of the external, his mind does not waver, it inclines toward the proximate, attains a clear and pure abiding, and understands the emptiness of the external.”

Ānanda! When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that he dwells having accomplished the external emptiness; his mind does not waver, it inclines toward the proximate, and he attains a clear and pure abiding. One who understands external emptiness in this manner is said to possess right knowledge.

Ānanda! A bhikkhu should dwell having accomplished the emptiness of the internal and external; having dwelt having accomplished that emptiness of the internal and external, his mind does not waver, he inclines toward the proximate, attains a clear and pure abiding, and understands the emptiness of the internal and external.

Ānanda! When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that he dwells having accomplished internal and external emptiness; his mind does not waver, it inclines toward the proximate, and he attains a clear and pure abiding. One who understands internal and external emptiness in this manner is said to possess right knowledge.

Ānanda! One should dwell having achieved immovability; having dwelt having achieved immovability, the mind becomes unshakable, inclines toward the proximate, attains a state of purity, and realizes immovability.

Ānanda! When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that he dwells having accomplished non-distraction; his mind is undisturbed, it inclines toward the proximate, and he attains a clear and pure abiding. One who understands non-distraction is said to possess right knowledge.

“Ānanda! When that bhikkhu practices this dwelling-mind and wishes to practice walking meditation, he emerges from his meditation cell and practices walking meditation on the open ground within the shadow of the cell. His sense faculties are turned inward, and his mind does not turn outward. He maintains the perception of what was behind as he moves forward. Having practiced walking meditation in this way, no covetousness, sorrow, or unwholesome, evil states arise in his mind; this is called right knowledge.”

Ānanda! When that bhikṣu practices this dwelling of the mind and wishes to sit in meditative concentration, he leaves the walking path and goes to its end, where he spreads his sitting mat, sits cross-legged, and having thus sat down in concentration, no covetousness, sorrowful distress, or evil unwholesome states arise within his mind; this is called right knowledge.
Ānanda! When that bhikṣu dwells with this state of mind, if he should have any thoughts, and if those thoughts of his are these three evil and unwholesome thoughts—
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness— he should not entertain these three evil and unwholesome thoughts.
If one has these three wholesome thoughts—thoughts of non-desire, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harming—one should attend to these three wholesome thoughts.
When one attends in this way, covetousness, grief, and evil unwholesome states do not arise in the mind; this is called right knowledge.

"Ānanda! When that bhikṣu dwells with this state of mind, if he wishes to speak, that bhikṣu should not engage in un-noble discourse that is inconsistent with the goal—namely, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of wars, talk of food and drink, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of maidens, talk of courtesans, talk of the world, talk of false paths, talk of the ocean, or various other such kinds of talk concerning animals."

If one discusses noble discourse that accords with the true meaning, it makes the mind supple and free from the hindrances (āvaraṇa). This refers to discourse on generosity, discourse on ethical discipline, discourse on meditative concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation, discourse on gradual reduction, discourse on non-contention, discourse on few desires, discourse on contentment, discourse on dispassion, discourse on relinquishment, discourse on cessation, discourse on solitary meditation, and discourse on dependent origination—such is the discourse of a śramaṇa.
Having deliberated in this way, no covetousness, sorrow, or unwholesome, evil states arise in the mind; this is called right knowledge.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

There are five bases of sensual pleasure that are delightful, cherished by the mind, associated with craving and passion: forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body.
If a bhikṣu, with his mind fully engaged, contemplates these merits of the five desires, and if those merits of desire proceed within his mind— why is this so?
Without beginning or end, these five strands of sensual pleasure follow after those very sensual pleasures as they move within the mind. Ānanda!
When a bhikkhu contemplates in this way, he knows that these five strands of sensual pleasure follow after those very sensual pleasures as they move within the mind.

That bhikṣu contemplates those various qualities of sensual desire as impermanent, as subject to decay, as free from desire, as something to be severed, as something to be extinguished, and as something to be relinquished. If there is any desire or defilement regarding these five qualities of sensual desire, he immediately extinguishes it.

Ānanda! When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that these five strands of sensual pleasure possess desire and defilement, and that he has already abandoned them; this is called right knowledge.
"Furthermore, Ānanda, there are five aggregates of clinging:

the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. A bhikṣu contemplates their arising and passing away in this way: 'This is form, this is the origin of form, this is the cessation of form; these are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is consciousness, this is the origin of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness.'"
If there were any conceit of self regarding these five aggregates of clinging, it would have ceased. Ānanda!
When a bhikṣu contemplates in this way, he knows that the conceit of self within the five aggregates has already ceased; this is called right knowledge.

Ānanda! This Dharma is consistently wholesome, consistently blissful, and consistently conducive to right reflection; it is without outflows and without grasping. It is beyond the reach of Māra, beyond the reach of evil, and beyond the reach of all unwholesome and non-virtuous states—those defiled things which are the root of future existence and the cause of birth, old age, sickness, death, and the arising of feverish suffering. That is to say, it is the accomplishment of this heedfulness.

Why is this so? It is because by means of heedfulness, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, have attained awakening; and from the root of heedfulness, all immeasurable wholesome dharmas arise.
Ānanda, if there are factors that accord with the path, you should train yourself thus:
"I too shall accomplish heedfulness; I shall train myself in this way."
“Ānanda!
For what reason do faithful disciples follow the World-Honored One in service until the end of their lives?
Venerable Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma originates from the Blessed One. We pray that he will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: “Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in full detail.”
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!
Because he has not mastered the discourses, the songs, and the records, a faithful disciple follows the World-Honored One in service until the end of his life.
However, Ānanda!

Or perhaps, throughout a long night, they have repeatedly heard this Dharma, reciting and practicing it up to a thousand times; they contemplate it with their minds, seeing it clearly and penetrating it deeply. If this discourse is a noble discourse that accords with the meaning, it makes the mind supple and free from the hindrances—namely, discourses on giving, morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, gradual reduction, non-attachment, fewness of desires, contentment, dispassion, abandonment, cessation, solitary meditation, and dependent origination.
Such is the discourse of the śramaṇa: it is attainable, easy, and not difficult to obtain. For this reason, the faithful disciple follows the World-Honored One, serving him until the end of life.
"Ānanda! In this way, one becomes a teacher who causes affliction, a disciple who causes affliction, and one who causes affliction to the holy life. Ānanda!"
What is meant by a "teacher who causes agitation"?

It is when a teacher has appeared in the world who possesses deliberation and reflection, who frequents grounds of deliberation, and whose practice is mixed with discursive thought and observation. Although such a person possesses eloquence, they dwell in a secluded place—among the mountains, forests, or at the foot of trees, or perhaps on high cliffs—where it is silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people. There, they sit in meditation in accordance with the Dharma, or dwelling in that place, they train in seclusion and diligence, attaining the higher mind and abiding in happiness in this very life.
Having practiced seclusion, exerted himself with diligence, and wandered in peace and happiness, he returned to his disciples, as well as to the brahmins, householders, villages, and townspeople.
When he has followed his disciples back to the brahmins, householders, villages, towns, and countries, he then returns home with a sense of high achievement.

This is what it means to be a "bothersome teacher. It is also a bad and unwholesome state, a defilement that serves as the root for future existence, a cause of the suffering of feverish distress, and the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death. This is called a bothersome teacher.
“Ānanda! What is meant by a ‘bothering’ disciple?

It is when a teacher’s disciple trains in that seclusion, dwelling in a secluded place—among the mountains, forests, or at the foot of trees, or staying on high cliffs, silent and soundless, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited—sitting in meditation accordingly, or staying in such places, training in seclusion with diligence, attaining the higher mind, and dwelling in happiness in this very life. Having trained in seclusion with diligence and living in peace and joy, he then returns to the disciples, brahmins, householders, villages, and towns. This is called a ‘bothering’ disciple.”
When he has followed his disciples back to the brahmins, householders, villages, towns, and kingdoms, he then returns home with a sense of self-importance.

To be thus preoccupied with one's disciples is a defilement, an evil and unwholesome state, a source of future existence, a cause of feverish suffering and the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death; this is what is meant by being "preoccupied with one's disciples."
“Ānanda! What is the corruption of the holy life?
