It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—worthy, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One—and he dwells in a secluded place, in the forest or at the foot of a tree, or stays on a high rocky crag, silent and free from noise, remote, without evil, devoid of people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.

Ānanda! For what purpose does the Tathāgata dwell in places devoid of affairs—among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees, or atop high cliffs—in silence and stillness, far removed from noise, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditative composure in accordance with the Dharma?
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying:

“The Blessed One is the root of the Dharma; the Blessed One is the master of the Dharma; the Dharma proceeds from the Blessed One. We pray that you will explain it, so that having heard it now, we may gain a broad understanding of its meaning.”
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Ānanda!
Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in full detail."
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said: “Ānanda!

It is not because the Tathāgata has not yet attained what he wishes to attain, nor has yet acquired what he wishes to acquire, nor has yet realized what he wishes to realize, that he dwells in secluded places, among the mountains and forests, beneath trees, or on high cliffs—silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and devoid of people—sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.

Ānanda! It is for two reasons that the Tathāgata dwells in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees, or high upon rocky crags—where it is silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditation in accordance with his practice: first, so as to manifest for himself a dwelling in the bliss of the Dharma; second, out of compassion for future generations.

Or there may be people born later who emulate the Tathāgata by dwelling in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and beneath trees; or they may dwell on high cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and devoid of people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.

Ānanda! For this reason, the Tathāgata dwells in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and trees, or on high cliffs—silent and free from noise, remote, free from evil, and devoid of people; there he sits in meditation in accordance with the Dharma, or dwelling in those places, he trains in seclusion and diligence, attaining the higher mind and abiding in the happiness of the present life.
Having practiced seclusion, exerted himself with diligence, and wandered in peace and happiness, he returned to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who follow the holy life.
Having followed the holy life and returned [to their respective states] as monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, they do not consider themselves superior and do not return to the household life.
Ānanda! If one realizes the unshakable liberation of mind, I do not say that there is any obstacle for them.

If one attains the four higher states of mind that dwell in happiness in the present life, this is due to having been diligent and practicing without negligence; however, because many disciples gather around such a person, there may be occasions for failure.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

That teacher and his disciples dwell in imitation [of the Buddhas] in secluded places—among the mountains, forests, and under trees, or dwelling on high cliffs, silent and without sound, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people, sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.

Or, dwelling there, he trains in the diligence of seclusion, attaining the higher mind and the blissful abiding in the present life. Having trained in the diligence of seclusion and having wandered in peace and happiness, he returns to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who follow the holy life.
When he has returned to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who were following the holy life, he then returns home with a sense of self-importance.

This is what it means for the holy life to be troubled; this is also what it means to be troubled by evil and unwholesome states, by defilements, by the root of future existence, and by the causes of birth, old age, sickness, death, and the retribution of feverish suffering. This is called "the holy life being troubled."
Ānanda! Among a teacher who is defiled and a disciple who is defiled, this defiled holy life is most undesirable, unpleasant, unlovely, and most disagreeable to the mind.
"Ānanda! For this reason, you should perform acts of loving-kindness toward me and not perform acts of enmity. Ānanda!"
How does a disciple act with hostility toward the teacher and fail to act with kindness?

If the honored teacher teaches the Dharma to the disciple out of compassion and pity, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace and happiness, and giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion—this is for their benefit, this is for their happiness, and this is for their benefit and happiness. Yet [the disciple] acts otherwise. This is how a disciple acts with hostility toward the teacher and fails to act with kindness.

If a disciple is disrespectful and does not practice in accordance [with the teaching], does not establish himself in wisdom, and his mind does not incline toward the Dharma that follows the Dharma; if he does not receive the true Dharma, violates the teacher’s instructions, and is unable to attain concentration—such a disciple performs hostile acts toward the teacher and does not perform acts of loving-kindness.
“Ānanda! How does a disciple practice acts of loving-kindness toward the teacher and not acts of enmity?

If the venerable teacher teaches the Dharma to the disciple out of compassion and pity, seeking their welfare and benefit, seeking their peace, security, and happiness, and giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion—this is for their benefit, this is for their happiness, this is for their benefit and happiness.”

If that disciple practices with reverence and compliance, establishing himself in wisdom, directing his mind toward the Dharma and its successive stages, upholding the True Dharma, not contradicting the teacher’s instructions, and being able to attain concentration—such a disciple performs acts of loving-kindness toward the teacher and does not perform acts of enmity.
Ānanda! For this reason, you should perform acts of kindness toward me and not act with hostility. Why is that?
I do not speak in this way, as a potter makes his pots. Ānanda!
I say that it is rigorous and extremely painful; yet if one possesses truthfulness, one will certainly be able to go [to the goal].
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The first section, the "Paired Discourses" (*Yamaka-vagga*), ends here, totaling 11,580 characters. This is the end of the fifth subsequent recitation.

Section Two: The Great Division (Mahāvarga). This section contains ten sūtras; it is the fifth recitation section.
Kālo Udāyī, Māluṅkyaputra Bhadda, Aśvajit, Cunda, Upāli the Tamer,
Maudgalyāyana, Ariṣṭa, and Revata.
192. The Kālāmasūtra (192). Middle Āgama, Mahāvagga, The First Kālāmasūtra. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅga together with a large community of bhikṣus, and arrived at Aṭṭhakanāgara, where he stayed at the Gaddula-bālagāma monastery.

At that time, when the night had passed and at dawn, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered Āḷavī to beg for food. Having finished eating after midday, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (*niṣadana*) over his shoulder, and went to a certain grove, wishing to practice walking meditation during the day.

The Venerable Udāyin also, when the night had passed and at dawn, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Āpaṇa to beg for food. After he had finished eating and it was after midday, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) over his shoulder, followed behind the Buddha, and thought to himself:
"If the World-Honored One goes on his midday walk now, I too shall go to that place for my midday walk."
Thereupon, the Blessed One entered the grove, went to the foot of a tree, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.
Venerable Udāyin also entered that grove; not far from the Buddha, he went to the foot of a tree, spread out his sitting mat, and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was sitting alone in seclusion, reflecting in meditation, and this thought arose in his mind:
"The Blessed One has brought us great benefit; the Sugata has brought us great peace and security."
The Blessed One has removed for me the various dharmas of suffering and increased for me the dharmas of happiness.
The Blessed One has removed from me immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas and increased for me immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas.

Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Udāyin rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side. The World-Honored One said to him: “Udāyin!”
“Are you free from want, living in peace and happiness, and is your physical strength as it usually is?
Venerable Udāyin replied, “Indeed so.”
“World-Honored One!
I lack for nothing; I am peaceful, secure, and happy, and my physical strength is as usual.
The World-Honored One asked again:
“Udāyin! How is it that you lack nothing, are at peace and happy, and possess your usual vigor?
Venerable Udāyin replied:
“World-Honored One!
While I was sitting alone in seclusion in quietude, reflecting in my mind, this thought arose:
‘The World-Honored One has brought us great benefit; the Sugata has brought us great peace and security.’”
The Blessed One has removed from me the various dharmas of suffering and increased for me the dharmas of happiness.
The Blessed One has removed from me immeasurable evil and unwholesome dharmas and increased for me immeasurable wholesome and sublime dharmas.
"World-Honored One, in the past you told the bhikṣus:
'You should abstain from eating after midday.
World-Honored One!"
Having heard this, we find it unbearable and intolerable; we do not desire it nor do we delight in it.

If there are faithful brahmins or householders who go to the monastery grove to perform extensive acts of merit and give food with their own hands, we ourselves would receive such food; yet now the World-Honored One instructs us to abandon this, and the Sugata instructs us to cut off this practice.
Furthermore, they made this claim:
"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food.
However, we were unable to endure our veneration for the World-Honored One’s majestic power and wondrous virtue; therefore, we abstained from food after midday.
"Furthermore, in the past, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
'You should abstain from eating at night.
World-Honored One!"

Having heard this, we were unable to endure it, could not bear it, did not desire it, and took no pleasure in it; for among the two kinds of food, these were the most superior, the most exquisite, the most excellent, and the most beautiful, yet the World-Honored One now instructs us to abandon them, and the Sugata instructs us to sever them, further saying:
"This Great Śramaṇa cannot digest such food."
“World-Honored One!
Formerly, there was a householder who, having brought back various kinds of pure and exquisite food and drink from his travels, returned to his home and instructed his attendants, saying:
‘You all receive this and set it aside in one place; I shall join you all for a night meal, not for the morning.’”
"World-Honored One!

When the most exquisite and supreme food is prepared in various households, there is only the evening meal; yet for my sake, [the family] provides it during the morning. Now the World-Honored One instructs me to abandon this, and the Sugata instructs me to cut it off, further saying:
'This Great Śramaṇa cannot digest food.'"
"However, we were unable to bear the weight of the World-Honored One’s majestic power and sublime virtue; for this reason, we have ceased eating at night.
World-Honored One!
We further had this thought:"

"If there is a bhikṣu who enters a village at an improper time to beg for food, he may encounter thieves—whether they are active or inactive—or he may encounter tigers, deer, or both tigers and deer; or he may encounter leopards, bears, or both leopards and bears. Or he may go to such places and encounter wild elephants, wild horses, wild oxen, or wild dogs; or he may come upon a swarm of snakes; or he may be pelted with clods of earth, or struck with sticks; or he may fall into a ditch or a moat, or fall into a latrine; or he may mount a cow that is lying down, or fall into a deep pit, or enter among thorns. Or, seeing an empty house, he may enter such a house; and once he has entered, if a woman sees him, she might call out to him to engage in unwholesome, impure conduct."
“World-Honored One!
Once, during the darkness of night when fine rain was falling and lightning flashed repeatedly, a certain bhikṣu went out of his time to enter another’s house to beg for food.

At that moment, a woman of the household had gone outside to wash the eating vessels. Seeing the bhikṣu from afar in the flash of lightning, she took him to be a ghost; filled with terror, her hair stood on end, and she let out a loud cry. She immediately suffered a miscarriage and spoke these words:”
"Venerable sir, you are a ghost!
Venerable sir, you are a ghost!
At that time, the bhikṣu said to the woman:
“Sister! I am not a ghost; I am a śramaṇa who has come now to beg for alms.
At that time, the woman reviled the bhikṣu with words of extreme bitterness and malice, speaking thus:

"May this śramaṇa’s life-force be cut short; may this śramaṇa’s parents die early; may this śramaṇa’s lineage be extinguished; may this śramaṇa’s belly split and be destroyed! This bald-headed śramaṇa, wrapped in black, childless and of broken seed—would you rather take a sharp blade and slit your own belly than go out for alms at an improper time during the night, sitting upon this śramaṇa and causing me to fall pregnant?"
"World-Honored One!
Having recollected that, joy arose within me.
World-Honored One!"
Because of this, my body was completely filled with joy; with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, there arose rapture, tranquility, bliss, and concentration.
World-Honored One!
Because of this concentration, my body was completely filled; I possessed right mindfulness and right clear comprehension.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
I lack for nothing; I am at peace and happy, and my physical strength is as usual.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent, Udāyin!"
"You are not like that foolish person now.
To that deluded person, I said:
'You must sever this.'"
He spoke thus: "This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off."
It was also said thus:

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; he does not abandon this [fault], and he merely conceives dislike and intolerance toward me, as well as toward other bhikṣus who well protect and uphold the precepts."
"Udāyin! That fool is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they grow ever tighter and more constricting, cannot be severed, and he shall not attain liberation."
Udāyin! It is just as if there were a fly caught by mucus or spittle; it would suffer or die therein. Udāyin!
If someone were to say that the fly’s bondage is not firm, not solid, does not become increasingly tight, and can be severed so that one attains liberation—is that a correct statement?
The Venerable Udāyin replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
Why is this so? Because the fly is bound by the mucus and saliva; therein it either suffers or dies.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
"That fly is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they grow tighter and more constricting, cannot be severed, and it finds no liberation.
"Udāyin! [he said.]
To those foolish people, I say:
"You must sever this.
They, however, speak as follows:
"This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off.
He spoke thus.

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; he does not cease this [behavior]. He merely harbors resentment and intolerance toward me, and likewise harbors resentment and intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well protect and uphold the precepts."
"Udāyin! That fool is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they grow tighter and more constricting, cannot be severed, and he shall not attain liberation."
"Udāyin! If I were to say to a son of good family,
'You should sever this,' [he would understand]."
He does not say: "This is a trivial matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off."
Nor does he speak thus:

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; therefore, I shall cut it off. He does not give rise to displeasure or intolerance toward me, nor does he give rise to displeasure or intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well protect and uphold the precepts.
"Udāyin! The bonds by which that son of good family is bound are neither firm nor strong; they do not increase in intensity, and being capable of being severed, he shall attain liberation."

Udāyin! It is just like a lordly elephant sixty years of age, possessing the pride of a mahānāga, with tusks, feet, and body complete, and its strength and vigor at their peak; when it is bound by firm fetters, if it turns its body with the power of its rage, those firm fetters will then snap and break, and it returns to its original place.
"Udāyin! If someone were to say this:

'That great elephant king has reached sixty years of age; though he possesses the pride of a mahānāga, with tusks, feet, and body complete, and his physical strength at its peak, his bonds are extremely firm and solid, becoming tighter and tighter, impossible to sever, and he cannot attain liberation'—would that be a correct statement?"
The Venerable Udāyin replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
Why is this? That great elephant king, having reached sixty years of age, was a haughty Mahānagna, fully endowed with tusks, feet, and body, and possessed of vigorous strength.
If that great elephant king, though firmly bound, turns his body with the power of his wrath, those firm bonds will immediately snap and he will return to his original place.

World-Honored One, for this reason, when that great elephant king reaches the age of sixty, he remains possessed of pride, with the Mahānagna’s tusks, feet, and body complete, and his physical strength still flourishing.
"That bond is neither firm nor strong; it does not tighten further and can be severed, whereby one attains liberation. "It is so, Udāyin!"
To those sons of good family, I say:
"You must sever this.
Yet they do not speak thus:
"This is but a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off.
Nor should one speak in such a manner:

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; therefore, I shall cease providing it to him. He will not give rise to displeasure or resentment toward me, nor will he give rise to displeasure or resentment toward other bhikṣus who well-guardedly maintain the precepts."
"Udāyin! The bonds by which that son of good family is bound are neither firm nor strong; they do not increase in intensity, and being capable of being severed, he shall attain liberation."
Udāyin! If there is a foolish person for whom I say,
"You should abandon this," [and he does not do so].
He spoke thus: “This is but a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet now the Blessed One instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off.”
It was also said thus:

"This Great Śramaṇa cannot digest his food; he does not abandon this [fault]. He merely gives rise to displeasure and intolerance toward me, and likewise gives rise to displeasure and intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well protect and uphold the precepts."
"Udāyin! That fool is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they grow ever tighter and more urgent, cannot be severed, and he shall not attain liberation."
"Udāyin! It is just as if there were a poor man who possessed neither wealth nor power.

He had a wife whose eyes were blind, who was ugly and unattractive. He had only one house, which was dilapidated, leaking, inhabited by crows and birds, and so wretched that it was unfit for habitation."
He had a single bed that was broken and shattered, worn out and unfit for lying upon; he had only a single water jar, chipped and unusable.

Seeing that the bhikṣu had finished his meal after midday, had washed his hands and feet, and had spread out his *niṣīdana* to sit beneath a tree, he observed him practicing the higher mind (*adhicitta*) in a state of cool composure and harmony.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas are happy; the śramaṇas are like nirvāṇa. I am evil and devoid of virtue. Why is this so?"
I have a wife whose eyes are blind, who is so ugly as to be unlovely, yet I cannot bear to abandon her.
I have but one house, which is dilapidated and leaking, where crows and birds take up residence; it is so wretched that it is unfit for habitation, yet I cannot bear to abandon it.
Yet there was a single bed, moreover broken and shattered, so dilapidated it could not be used for lying down, yet he could not bring himself to abandon it.
There was also a single water jar, chipped and unusable, yet he could not bring himself to abandon it.
"Out of love and delight, a bhikkhu shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the Path.
Thus spoke Udāyin.
If someone were to say this:
"That poor person has neither wealth nor power; the bonds that bind him are neither firm nor strong, they do not tighten further, and can be severed, whereby he shall attain liberation."
“Is this what constitutes a correct teaching?
Venerable Udāyin replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One! Why is this?
That poor man possesses neither wealth nor power; he has a blind wife who is so ugly as to be unlovely, yet he cannot bring himself to abandon her.”
There was only a single house, dilapidated and leaking, inhabited by crows and birds; it was so decrepit that it was unfit for habitation, yet he could not bring himself to abandon it.
There was also a single bed, broken and shattered, so worn out that it was unfit for lying upon, yet he could not bring himself to abandon it.
I have a single water jar that is chipped and unusable, yet I cannot bear to part with it.
I love and delight in how a bhikkhu shaves off his hair and beard, dons the saffron robes, and out of deep faith leaves the home life for homelessness to train in the Path.
"World-Honored One!
For this reason, that poor man possesses neither wealth nor power; his bonds are extremely firm and solid, becoming ever tighter and more urgent, impossible to sever, and he finds no liberation."
“Thus it is, Udāyin! If there is a foolish person for whom I say:
‘You should abandon this,’ [and he does not do so].”
He said this: "This is but a minor matter; why should it be worth abandoning?
Yet now the Blessed One instructs me to abandon it, and the Sugata commands me to sever it."
He spoke thus:

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; he does not abandon this [fault]. He merely conceives aversion and intolerance toward me, and likewise conceives aversion and intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well-guardedly maintain the precepts."

"Udāyin! For this reason, that foolish person is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they become ever more intense and ever more urgent, cannot be severed, and liberation is not attained."
"Udāyin! If I were to say to a son of good family:
'You should sever this.'"
He does not say this:
"This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut off this."
Nor should one say: "This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food;

therefore, he has ceased [eating this]. He will not give rise to displeasure or intolerance toward me, nor will he give rise to displeasure or intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well-guard and uphold the precepts."
"Udāyin! For this reason, the bonds of that son of good family are neither firm nor strong; they do not become increasingly tight, but can be severed, whereby he attains liberation."

"Udāyin! It is just as if there were a householder or a householder’s son who was extremely wealthy and prosperous, possessing vast amounts of wealth and property, with livestock and enterprises beyond counting; with fiefs, food-grant villages, and an abundance of rice and grain; and with various kinds of articles for living, slaves, and elephants and horses, their number being immeasurable."

He saw that after the bhikṣu had finished his meal, he washed his hands and feet, spread out his sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat beneath a tree, cultivating the higher mind (adhicitta) in a state of cool serenity and harmony.
Having seen this, he thought to himself: "The ascetic life is happiness;

the ascetic life is like Nirvana. I should indeed renounce my immense wealth and pleasure—gold and jewels, grain and cattle, elephants and horses, and my male and female slaves—and out of faith, shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and go forth from the home into the homeless state to practice the holy life."
"Udāyin! If someone were to say this:
'The bonds of those householders and sons of householders are extremely firm and extremely strong; they grow tighter and more constricting, cannot be severed, and liberation is not possible.'"
“...is this a correct exposition?
Venerable Udāyin replied, “No.”
World-Honored One! Why is this so?

Those householders and sons of householders are able to renounce their immense wealth and luxury—gold, treasures, grain, elephants, horses, servants, and concubines—and out of love for the bhikṣus, they shave off their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, and with deep faith, leave their homes for the homeless life to study the Path.
World-Honored One!
For this reason, the bonds of that householder or householder’s son are neither firm nor strong; they do not increase in intensity, but can be severed, whereby one attains liberation.
“Thus it is, Udāyin! If I were to say to a son of good family:
‘You should sever this.’”
He does not say this:
"This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut off this."
Nor should one say: "This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food;

therefore, he has ceased eating it. One should not give rise to displeasure or resentment toward me, nor toward other bhikṣus who well-guard and uphold the precepts, by thinking that they too have ceased eating it.
"Udāyin! Therefore, the bonds of that son of good family are neither firm nor strong; they do not increase in intensity, and being capable of being severed, he attains liberation."

Udāyi! When a bhikkhu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, a thought associated with desire arises, a bond of craving and delight; he delights in that, does not sever it, does not abide in its relinquishment, and does not reject it.
"Udāyin! I speak of this as bondage; I do not speak of it as liberation. Why is that? Because..."
"Udāyin, the fetters are unwholesome.
Because the fetters are unwholesome, I say they are bonds, not liberation."

Udāyi! When a bhikkhu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, a thought associated with desire arises, a bond of craving and delight; he does not delight in that, but abandons it, dwells in its relinquishment, and casts it out.
Udāyin! I say that this, too, is bondage; I do not say it is liberation. Why is that?
"Udāyin, all fetters are unwholesome.
Because the fetters are unwholesome, I say they are bonds; I do not say they are liberation."

Udāyin! When a bhikkhu practices equanimity, having practiced equanimity, at times his mind may forgetfully give rise to a thought associated with desire, which is bound by attachment and fondness; this is slow to observe and quick to vanish.

Udāyin! It is just as if there were an iron ball or an iron plowshare that had been scorched by fire all day long; if someone were to drop two or three drops of water upon it, and those drops were slow and not continuous, the water would quickly evaporate.

Udāyin! Thus a bhikkhu practices equanimity; having practiced equanimity, at times his mind may forget, and there arise thoughts associated with desire, accompanied by attachment and fetters, which are slow to observe and quick to subside.
Udāyin! I say that this too is bondage; I do not say it is liberation. Why is that?
"Udāyin, all fetters are unwholesome.
Because the fetters are unwholesome, I say they are bonds, not liberation."
"Udāyi! While still within the faculty of suffering, one wanders without birth-and-death; having reached the unsurpassed exhaustion of craving, the mind is well-liberated. Udāyi!"
I speak of liberation; I do not speak of bondage. Why is this?
Because all fetters have been exhausted.
Udāyin! Because all fetters are exhausted, I say there is liberation; I do not say there is bondage. Udāyin!

There is a pleasure that is not the noble pleasure; it is the pleasure of ordinary worldlings, the root of disease, the root of abscesses, and the root of arrows and thorns. It involves nutriment, involves birth and death, and cannot be cultivated, practiced, or developed. Regarding such pleasure, I say it should not be cultivated.

Udāyin! There is a pleasure that is noble, a pleasure free from desire, a pleasure of renunciation, a pleasure of tranquility, and the pleasure of perfect awakening; it is without sustenance, without birth and death, and can be cultivated, practiced, and fully developed—I say that such a pleasure should indeed be cultivated.

Udāyin! What is that pleasure which is not noble, but is the pleasure of ordinary worldlings—the root of disease, the root of abscesses, the root of thorns and arrows; which has nutriment, involves birth and death, and cannot be cultivated, practiced, or developed? Is it not my teaching that such pleasure should not be cultivated?

If pleasure and goodness arise from the five objects of desire, such pleasure is not the noble pleasure; it is the pleasure of ordinary worldlings, the root of disease, the root of abscesses, and the root of thorns. It is accompanied by nutriment, accompanied by birth and death, and cannot be cultivated, practiced, or developed. Therefore, I say that it should not be cultivated.

"Udāyin! What kind of pleasure is there that is noble, free from desire, a pleasure of renunciation, a pleasure of peace, and the pleasure of the Perfectly Awakened One—a pleasure that is without nutriment, free from birth and death, which can be cultivated, practiced, and developed, and which I say should indeed be cultivated?"

"Udāyin! If a bhikkhu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, this is happiness, this is the noble happiness, the happiness of dispassion, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of the perfectly awakened ones; it is without nutriment, free from birth and death, and can be cultivated, practiced, and fully developed. I say that such a state is indeed to be cultivated."

Udāyin! When a bhikkhu, detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna—this, the Noble Ones call "shifting."
Among these, what does the Noble One describe as movement?
Herein, there is applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); this is what the Noble One describes as movement.
Among these, what does the Noble One describe as movement?

"Udāyi! When a bhikkhu has stilled initial application and sustained application, and with internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, is without initial application and without sustained application, and attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and happiness—this, the Noble Ones call 'shifting.'"
In this context, what does the Noble One describe as "shifting"?
If one attains joy therein, the Noble One describes that as shifting.
In this context, what does the Noble One describe as "shifting"?

"Udāyin! A bhikkhu, detached from the desire for joy, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as 'equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness. This, Udāyin, is what the Noble Ones call 'shifting.'"
In this context, what is it that the Noble Ones describe as "shifting"?
If one says that the mind delights in shifting, this is what the Noble Ones describe as shifting.
In this context, what is it that the Noble Ones describe as "not shifting"?

"Udāyi! When a bhikkhu has the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither-painful-nor-pleasant, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, and utterly pure—this is called 'immovability' by the Noble Ones."

"Udāyi! A bhikkhu, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
Udāyin! I say that this cannot be non-existent, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended.
What, in this context, is meant by "transcending"?

"Udāyi! When a bhikkhu has stilled initial application and sustained application, with internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, free from initial and sustained application, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss; this is what is called 'transcending' in this context."
Udāyin! I say that this, too, cannot be non-existent, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended.
What, in this context, is meant by "transcending"?

"Udāyi! When a bhikkhu is detached from the desire for rapture, dwells equanimous and mindful, and experiences pleasure with the body—of which the Noble Ones say, 'He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in pleasure'—he attains and abides in the third jhāna. This, Udāyi, is called transcending in this regard."
Udāyin! I say that this, too, cannot be non-existent, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended.
What, in this context, would constitute transcendence?

"Udāyi! When a bhikkhu, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—neither-painful-nor-pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity—this is called transcending within this context."
"Udāyin! I say that this, too, cannot be non-existent, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended.
What, in this context, is meant by 'transcending'?"

Udāyin! When a bhikkhu transcends all perceptions of form, extinguishes perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity, he dwells having attained the base of infinite space, thinking "space is infinite. This is called transcending within this context.
Udāyin! I say that this, too, cannot be non-existent, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended.
What, in this context, would constitute transcendence?

Udāyin! A bhikkhu, having transcended the base of infinite space, [perceives] infinite consciousness; he dwells having attained the base of infinite consciousness—this is called "transcending" in this context.
Udāyin! I say that this, too, cannot be attained through non-existence, cannot be attained through cessation, and cannot be attained through transcendence.
What, in this context, is meant by "transcendence"?
"Udāyi! A bhikkhu, having transcended the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness; this is called 'transcending' in this context."
"Udāyi! I say that this, too, cannot be attained as non-existent, cannot be abandoned, and cannot be transcended. What, Udāyi, could there be to transcend within this?"
A bhikkhu, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, enters and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called "transcending" in this context.
Udāyin! I say that even reaching the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one cannot obtain non-existence, cannot obtain cessation, and cannot obtain transcendence. Udāyin!

Is there any single fetter, whether small or great, that remains for a long time, such that I say it cannot be abandoned, cannot be severed, and cannot be transcended—would you say that I am saying it is not severed?
The Venerable Udāyin replied:
"No, World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Udāyin! You are not like that foolish person. To that deluded person, I say:
"You should abandon this."
He spoke thus: "This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet the World-Honored One now instructs me to sever this; the Sugata commands me to cut this off."
It was also said thus:

"This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food; he does not abandon this [fault]. He merely gives rise to dislike and intolerance toward me, and likewise gives rise to dislike and intolerance toward other bhikṣus who well-guard and uphold the precepts."

"Udāyin! Therefore, that foolish person is bound by bonds that are extremely firm and extremely strong; they become ever more intense and ever more urgent, cannot be severed, and he shall not attain liberation."
"Udāyi! If there is a son of good family for whom I say:
'You should abandon this.'"
He does not say: "This is a minor matter; why should it be severed?
Yet now the World-Honored One instructs me to sever this, and the Sugata commands me to cut off this."
Nor should one say: "This great śramaṇa cannot digest his food;

therefore he has cut it off. One should not give rise to dissatisfaction or resentment toward me, nor toward other bhikṣus who well protect and uphold the precepts, nor should one give rise to dissatisfaction or resentment toward him.
"Udāyin! Therefore, the bonds of that son of good family are neither firm nor strong; they do not increase in intensity, but can be severed, whereby he attains liberation."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Udāyin rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Kāḷudāyī Sūtra*, the first, ends here, totaling 4,467 characters. 193. The Mūlapariyāya Sūtra (193) Middle Āgama, Mahāvagga, Mūlapariyāya Sūtra, the second [of the five], the fifth recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Mūlapaśuna frequently gathered together with several bhikṣuṇīs.
If someone speaks of a bhikṣuṇī to the bhikṣu Mūli-pakkaṇa, upon hearing it, he will become angry, resentful, and jealous, even to the point of quarreling.
If anyone speaks ill of the bhikṣu Mūlaprakaṇṇa to the bhikṣuṇīs, once the bhikṣuṇīs have heard it, they will become angry, hateful, and envious, even to the point of quarreling and disputing.
Having heard this, a great number of bhikṣus went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, sat down to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Mūlaprakaṇḍa frequently assembles with bhikṣuṇīs."
If someone speaks of a bhikṣuṇī to the bhikṣu Mūli-pakula, upon hearing it, he will become angry, resentful, and jealous, even to the point of quarreling.
If anyone speaks ill of the bhikṣu Mūlaprakaṇḍa to the bhikṣuṇīs, once the bhikṣuṇīs have heard it, they will become angry, resentful, and jealous, even to the point of quarreling and disputing.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to where the bhikṣu Mūlapaśyana is and say to him:
'The World-Honored One calls for you.'"
Having heard this, a certain bhikṣu replied,
“So be it, World-Honored One!
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
He went to where the bhikṣu Mūli-paryāpanna was and said to him,
"The World-Honored One calls for you!
Having heard this, Mūli-paryāpanna came to the place where the Buddha was, paid homage to the Buddha, and sat down to one side.
The World-Honored One said:
“Pāṭandaka! It is true that you frequently gather together with bhikṣuṇīs.”
If someone speaks ill of you to the bhikṣuṇīs, and upon hearing it, you become angry, resentful, and envious, even to the point of quarreling;
or if someone speaks ill of you to the bhikṣuṇīs, and upon hearing it, the bhikṣuṇīs become angry, resentful, and envious, even to the point of quarreling.
“Pakudha! Is it truly so? Pakudha replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One questioned him again, saying:
“Pakudha! Have you not gone forth out of firm faith, having left your home for the homeless life, to study the Path?
Pakudha replied:
“Yes, World-Honored One,” [he replied]. The World-Honored One said:
“Pūraṇa! Therefore, you who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of deep faith to study the Path, you should train yourself thus:
if there is any desire or thought dependent upon the household life, abandon it.”
If there is desire and mindfulness based upon non-desire, this is practice, this is cultivation,
this is extensive development. Pūraṇa,
you should train yourself in this way.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus:
"Have you not all, out of faith, left the home life for homelessness to study the Way?
The bhikṣus replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Therefore, you who have with supreme faith left the home life for homelessness to train in the Path, you should train yourselves thus:
if there is any desire or thought dependent upon the household life, abandon it."
"If there is desire and mindfulness that rely upon non-desire, this is what should be practiced, cultivated, and expanded; you all should train yourselves in this way.
In the past, I once told the bhikṣus: 'You all!'"

Whether there be bhikṣus who have many acquaintances or bhikṣus who have few acquaintances, if they all train in eating in a single sitting, having trained in eating in a single sitting, they will be unconditioned and free from seeking; they will be free from illness and pain, their bodies will be light and agile, their physical strength will be robust and healthy, and they will dwell in peace, security, and happiness.

Those bhikṣus, whether they were of great renown or little renown, all practiced eating in a single sitting. Having practiced eating in a single sitting, they became free from conditioned activity and free from seeking; they were without illness or pain, their bodies were light and agile, their physical strength was robust and healthy, and they dwelt in peace, security, and happiness.
Those bhikṣus may take confidence in my mind, for I do not instruct or reprove them excessively.

Because of this, those bhikṣus give rise to mindfulness directed toward the Dharma and its successive stages, just as a charioteer riding a horse-drawn carriage holds the reins with his left hand and the whip with his right, proceeding along the Eightfold Path wherever his will leads him.
"In this way, O bhikṣus, you may take confidence in my mind, for I do not instruct or reprove you excessively.

Because of this, the bhikṣus give rise to mindfulness directed toward the Dharma and the successive stages of the Dharma. It is like a fertile field where there is a grove of sāla trees; a caretaker of that grove who is intelligent, wise, and diligent, tends to the roots of the sāla trees according to the season, repeatedly weeding and manuring them, irrigating them with water, digging up what is too high, and filling in what is too low."

If weeds grow at the edges, they are weeded out and discarded; if there are those that grow together, crooked, warped, or not straight, their roots are pulled up and cast outside; if branches grow crosswise or curved, they are pruned away; if new growth near the edge is upright and fine, it is tended according to the season, repeatedly hoed and manured, and irrigated with water. In this way, that excellent grove of sāla trees becomes increasingly lush and flourishing.
In this way, those bhikṣus may place their trust in my mind, and I do not need to instruct or reprimand them much.

It is not because of their skillful speech or respectful compliance regarding robes, alms-bowls, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, or other articles of daily life that I speak of them as such.
Why is that? If a bhikṣu does not obtain this [state], he fails to achieve skillful speech and respectful compliance; he does not fulfill the qualities of skillful speech and respectful compliance.

"If there is a bhikṣu who dwells in seclusion, relies upon seclusion, and abides in seclusion, and who speaks with skillful speech and respectful compliance, fulfilling the qualities of skillful speech and respectful compliance—I say that he is one who speaks with skillful speech and respectful compliance."
Why is that? There may be one who is well-guarded in the practice of the Sugata, meaning he is free from malicious speech by others.

If others do not speak maliciously to him, he does not become angry, nor does he feel hatred or envy; he is not bound by the fetter of sorrow, he does not harbor resentment, and he does not reveal his own faults.
Having seen him, those bhikṣus thought:
"This worthy one is patient, gentle, and enduring; he is well-restrained, well-concentrated, and well-at peace."
If another speaks harsh words, he becomes angry, resentful, and envious; he remains bound by anxiety, and his hatred gives rise to evil.
When the other monks see this, they think:
"This worthy one is of an evil nature, impetuous, base, and coarse; he is undisciplined, unrestrained, and finds no rest."

"Why is that? 'Monks! In the past, there was a householder’s wife named Vedehī, who was exceedingly wealthy and prosperous. She possessed vast amounts of money and property, with livestock and enterprises beyond counting; she held fiefs and food-grant villages, and had an abundance of rice, grain, and various kinds of household requisites.'"

At that time, the housewife Viḍūḍabī was so renowned that her fame spread in all directions: "The housewife Viḍūḍabī is patient, enduring, gentle, well-restrained, well-concentrated, and well-composed."
At that time, the householder’s wife Vaddha had a maidservant named Kali, who was formerly her attendant; she was eloquent and had performed some small measure of wholesome deeds.
That maidservant Kali thought to herself:

"My mistress, the householder’s wife Vaddha, has such great renown spread in all directions, that she is patient, enduring, mild, well-restrained, well-composed, and well-at-ease. I should now test my mistress, the householder’s wife Vaddha, to see whether she is truly angry or truly not angry."
Thereupon, the maidservant Kālī lay down and did not rise early.
The lady called out to her,
saying, "Kālī!"
"Why do you not rise early?
Upon hearing this, the black maidservant thought to herself:
"My mistress, the householder’s wife Vaidhātrī, is truly angry; it is not that she is not angry."

However, because I am skilled at managing the household affairs, skilled in administration, and skilled in maintenance, my mistress, the housewife Vedehikā, has acquired such great renown that it spreads in all directions: "The housewife Vedehikā is patient, enduring, gentle, well-restrained, well-composed, and well-at-ease."
"I should now test the housewife Vaddhaki further to see whether she is truly angry or truly not angry.
Thereupon, the maidservant Kali lay down very late and did not rise.
The lady called out,
"Black slave!
Why do you not rise so late?"
Having heard this, the maidservant Kali thought to herself:
"My mistress, the householder’s wife Vedehī, is truly angry; it is not that she is not angry.

However, because I am skilled at managing the household affairs, skilled at conducting business, and skilled at maintaining order, my mistress, the householder’s wife Vedehī, has acquired such great renown spread in all directions as 'The householder’s wife Vedehī is patient, enduring, gentle, well-restrained, well-composed, and well-at-ease.'"
"I should now once again subject the housewife Vedehikā, the lady of this great family, to an ultimate test to see whether she is truly angry or truly not angry.
Thereupon, the maidservant Kali lay down until the time of the afternoon meal, when she finally arose.
The lady called out, "Black slave!

Why have you not risen until the hour of *pradoṣa*? Since you neither do the work yourself nor instruct others to do it, this black slave does not follow my instructions; this black slave treats me with contempt."

He then became greatly incensed and gave rise to hatred and envy; the three veins on his forehead stood out as he knit his brows and went there himself. He closed the door and lowered the bolt, then seizing a large staff in his hand, struck him on the head until it was split open and blood flowed.
Thereupon, the maid Kālī’s head was split open and blood flowed; she went out and told her neighbors, and a clamor of litigation arose as many things were recounted:
"O honorable ones!..."
Seeing this practitioner of patience, who was capable of enduring with gentleness and who practiced skillful restraint, skillful concentration, and skillful tranquility,
he reviled me, saying:
"Black slave!"

"Why has she even risen until the hour of *pradoṣa*? She neither does it herself nor instructs anyone else to do it. This slave girl Kālī does not follow my instructions; this slave girl Kālī treats me with contempt."

He then became greatly incensed and gave rise to hatred and jealousy; the three veins on his forehead stood out as he knit his brows and came toward me. He bolted the door from within, took up a large staff in his hand, and struck my head, so that it was split open and blood flowed.

At that time, the householder’s wife Vīṭhaddhī became widely notorious for her great evil reputation throughout all directions; it was said that the householder’s wife Vīṭhaddhī was of a wicked nature, impetuous, cruel, and coarse, being unstable, unrestrained, and unceasing.
"It is so. There may be one who practices the well-guarded conduct of the Sugata, meaning that he does not engage in malicious speech toward others.

If others do not speak maliciously to him, he does not become angry, nor does he feel hatred or envy; he is not bound by the fetter of sorrow, he does not increase his anger, and he does not manifest evil."
Having seen this, those bhikṣus thought:
"This worthy one is patient, gentle, and enduring; he is well-restrained, well-concentrated, and well-at peace."
If another speaks harsh words to him, he becomes angry, hateful, and envious, remaining bound by anxiety; his hatred and anger give rise to evil.
When the other bhikṣus see this, they think:
"This worthy one is of an evil nature—impetuous, corrupt, and coarse; he is unsettled, unrestrained, and finds no rest."

"Furthermore, there are five kinds of speech: when another speaks, it may be at the proper time or the improper time; it may be true or untrue; it may be gentle or harsh; it may be spoken with loving-kindness or with malice; and it may be meaningful or meaningless."
"You all! Regarding this path of the fivefold speech, if others speak it and your minds become disturbed, or if you utter evil words, I say that because of this, you will certainly suffer decline."

"You should train yourselves in this path of the fivefold speech: when others speak, your mind remains unchanging and your mouth utters no harsh words; toward those who are your enemies, you direct thoughts of loving-kindness and compassion, and with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, you dwell having pervaded one direction."

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Thus one achieves and abides in this state.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—you should dwell pervading the entire world; you should train yourselves in this manner.
It is as if someone were to bring a large hoe and say:
"I can cause this great earth to become non-earth.
He then digs and digs everywhere, defiling it with spittle and urine, uttering evil words, and speaking thus:
"Suppose one were to say, 'Let the great earth become non-earth. What do you think?
Could that person, by such means, cause this great earth to become non-earth?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Because this great earth is profoundly deep, exceedingly vast, and immeasurable; therefore, by such means, that person cannot cause this great earth to become something other than earth.
“World-Honored One!
That person would merely exhaust himself in vain. “It is so.

These five kinds of speech, if spoken by another—whether at the proper time or the improper time, whether true or untrue, whether gentle or harsh, whether compassionate or angry, and whether meaningful or meaningless—[are all such].”

"You! Regarding this path of fivefold speech, if others speak it and your minds become agitated or you utter evil words, I say that because of this you will surely suffer decline; therefore, you should train yourselves in this path of fivefold speech."

If others speak [harshly], your mind shall not waver and your mouth shall utter no evil words. Toward those who speak thus, you should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; let your mental conduct be like the earth—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading the entire world as you dwell in its accomplishment. You should train yourselves in this way.
It is just as if someone were to carry a large grass torch and say:
"I shall use this grass torch to heat the waters of the Ganges until they become boiling hot."
"What do you think?
Could that person, by such means, cause the waters of the Ganges to become hot boiling water?
The bhikṣus replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
“World-Honored One!
Those waters of the Gaṅgā are extremely deep and vast, beyond measure.
Therefore, by such means, that person cannot cause the waters of the Gaṅgā to become hot or turn them into boiling water.”
“World-Honored One!
That person would merely exhaust himself in vain. “It is so.”

Regarding this path of speech, if another person speaks—whether at the proper time or the improper time, whether true or untrue, whether gentle or harsh, whether with loving-kindness or with anger, and whether meaningful or meaningless.
"O you! Regarding this path of the fivefold speech, if others speak it and your minds become disturbed, or if you utter evil words, I say that because of this, you will surely suffer decline."

"You should train yourselves in this Way of the Fivefold Path: when others speak, let your minds not be disturbed and let no harsh words issue from your mouths. Toward those who speak thus, give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Let your mental conduct be like the waters of the Ganges—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, exceedingly vast and great, immeasurably well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as you dwell therein. You should train yourselves in this way."
It is just as if a painter or a painter’s apprentice were to bring various pigments and say:
"I shall paint figures upon this empty space and embellish them with these colors."
"What do you think?
Could that painter or his apprentice, by such means, ever paint a form or image in the sky and embellish it with colors?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
This space is not form; it is invisible and non-obstructive.
Therefore, by such means, that painter or the painter’s disciple is unable to paint a form or embellish it with colors upon empty space.
“World-Honored One!
It would merely cause that painter or the painter’s disciple to exhaust themselves in vain.

“It is so. These five kinds of speech, if spoken by another—whether at the proper time or the improper time, whether true or untrue, whether gentle or harsh, whether compassionate or angry, and whether meaningful or meaningless—[are all likewise].”
"O you! Regarding this path of the fivefold speech, if others speak it and your minds become disturbed, or if you utter evil words, I say that you will surely suffer decline because of this."

"You should train yourselves in this Way of the Fivefold Path: when others speak, let your minds remain unchanging and your mouths free from harsh words. Toward those who speak, give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; let your mental conduct be like space—without fetters, without enmity, without ill will, and without contention. Let it be exceedingly vast, immense, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, pervading and suffusing the entire world as you dwell therein. You should train yourselves in this way."
It is just like a cat-skin bag that has been thoroughly tanned and made extremely soft, such that it lacks the rustling sound and produces no rustling sound.
Suppose someone were to strike it with their fist, throw stones at it, beat it with a staff, slash it with a knife, or even throw it to the ground—what do you think?
"That cat-skin bag has been so thoroughly softened that it is free from rustling; there is no rustling sound.
Could it possibly have any rustling sound again? The bhikṣus replied, "No, sir."
World-Honored One! Why is this so?
World-Honored One!
"That cat-skin bag has been treated so thoroughly that it is extremely soft;
it eliminates the rustling sound, so that there is no longer any rustling sound. It is thus."

"O monks! If others should strike you with their fists, hurl stones at you, beat you with sticks, or cut you with swords; if, when others thus strike you with their fists, hurl stones at you, beat you with sticks, or cut you with swords, your minds should become disturbed or you should utter evil words, I say that because of this, you will surely come to ruin."

"You should train yourselves thus: even when others strike you with their fists, hurl stones at you, beat you with sticks, or cut you with swords, let your mind not be disturbed and let no harsh words escape your mouth. Toward those who strike you, give rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion. Let your mental conduct be like a cat's skin bag—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated. Abide pervading the entire world with this attainment. You should train yourselves in this way."

"If bandits come and cut you limb from limb with sharp saws and knives, should your minds change or should you utter evil words when such bandits come and cut you limb from limb with sharp saws and knives, I say that because of this, you will surely suffer decline."

"You should train yourselves thus: even if bandits should come and sever you limb from limb with a sharp saw or blade, your mind shall not waver, nor shall you utter evil words toward those who cut you. Instead, you should give rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward them; with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, you should dwell pervading one direction, having accomplished it thoroughly."

In this way, toward the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading everywhere—one dwells having suffused the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, one attains and abides therein.

In this same way, you should train yourselves so that with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—you dwell having pervaded the entire world and attained mastery therein.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"You should repeatedly reflect upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw. Having repeatedly reflected upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw, do you see that when others direct unpleasant and malicious words toward you, upon hearing them, are you unable to endure it?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One again praised the bhikṣus, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"You should repeatedly reflect upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw. Having repeatedly reflected upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw, if you travel to the east, you will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction;
if you travel to the south, the west, or the north, you will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction."
Excellent! Excellent!

You should repeatedly reflect upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw. Once you have repeatedly reflected upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw, I would not even say that your wholesome qualities remain, much less that they decline.
One should simply cause wholesome qualities to increase day and night without decline.
Excellent! Excellent!

"You all should repeatedly reflect upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw. Having repeatedly reflected upon the teaching of the śramaṇa likened to a sharp saw, you will surely attain one of two fruits: either you will attain ultimate knowledge in this very life, or else you will become a non-returner (anāgāmin) with some remainder."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Mūlapariyāya Sutta*, the second [sutta], ends here, totaling 3,358 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, scroll fifty-seven, totals 7,825 characters.
