194. Bhaddekaratta Sutta (194). Third Sūtra of the Great Section; Fifth Subsequent Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, observing the rains retreat.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I eat in a single sitting; having eaten in a single sitting, I am without conditioned activity or seeking, free from illness and pain, with a body that is light and agile, and with physical strength that is robust, peaceful, and happy."

You, too, should train yourselves in eating in a single sitting; having eaten in a single sitting, you will be without affliction or seeking, free from illness, with bodies light and agile, and with strength and vigor restored, dwelling in peace and happiness.
At that time, the Venerable Bhaddāli was also present in the assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhaddāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
"World-Honored One!..."
I am not capable of eating in a single sitting. Why is this?
If I were to eat in a single sitting, I would fail to complete my tasks, leading to a heart of distress and regret.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I am unable to undertake eating at a single sitting.
The World-Honored One told him:
"Bhadraharī! If I accept the invitation, you shall follow me; I permit you to take food from my meal and carry it away for a single sitting meal. Bhadraharī!"
"If it is so, one will live a truly happy life.
The Venerable Bhadrika then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In this way, I am also unable to eat in a single sitting. Why is that?
If I were to eat in a single sitting, I would fail to complete my tasks and would feel distress and regret in my heart.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I am unable to undertake eating in a single sitting.
The World-Honored One repeated this to the bhikṣus a second and a third time:

"I eat in a single sitting; having eaten in a single sitting, I am free from artifice and desire, free from illness and pain, my body is light and agile, my energy is robust and strong, and I dwell in peace and happiness."

You, too, should train yourselves in eating in a single sitting; having eaten in a single sitting, you will be free from busyness and seeking, free from illness and pain, with bodies light and agile, and with strength, health, peace, and happiness.
The Venerable Bhaddāli also rose from his seat a second and a third time, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
I am unable to subsist on a single sitting of food. Why is this?
If I were to eat in a single sitting, I would fail to complete my tasks, leading to distress and regret in my heart.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I am unable to undertake eating at a single sitting.
The World-Honored One repeated his words a second and a third time:
"Bhadraharī! If I accept the invitation, you shall follow me; I grant you permission to request food and take it away for a single sitting meal. Bhadraharī!"
"If it be so, one may live life happily.
For a second and a third time, the Venerable Bhaddāli addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
In this way, I too am unable to eat in a single sitting. Why is that?
If I were to eat in a single sitting, I would fail to complete my tasks, leading to a heart of distress and regret.
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, I am unable to undertake the practice of eating in a single sitting.

At that time, the World-Honored One established the precept of eating in a single sitting for the community of bhikṣus. All the bhikṣus received and studied this precept as well as the various subtle and wondrous dharmas within the sphere of the World-Honored One; however, the Venerable Bhadrika declared himself unable to undertake it, rose from his seat, and departed.
Why is this? Because he had not studied the complete precepts nor the various subtle dharmas within the sphere of the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhaddāli remained hidden for an entire summer retreat, without seeing the World-Honored One.
Why is this? It is because they have not studied the complete precepts or the various subtle dharmas that constitute the domain of the World-Honored One.

At that time, the bhikṣus were making robes for the Buddha. Having completed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī, and after three months had passed, the World-Honored One finished mending his robes; he then took up his robes and bowl, intending to travel among the people.

The Venerable Bhaddāli heard that the bhikṣus were making robes for the Buddha, and that after the World-Honored One had completed his summer retreat in Śrāvastī and the three months had passed, he would finish mending his robes, take up his bowl and outer robe, and set out on a journey through the human world.
Having heard this, the Venerable Bhaddāli went to where the bhikkhus were; seeing the Venerable Bhaddāli coming from afar, the bhikkhus said to him: "Friend Bhaddāli!"

"You should know that this is for making a robe for the Buddha. When the World-Honored One has completed his summer retreat in Śrāvastī and the three months have passed, having finished mending his robes, he will take up his robes and bowl and travel through the human world."
"Bhadraharit, you must guard that place well yourself; do not cause much trouble at a later time.
Having heard these words, the Venerable Bhadraharit went immediately to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
I truly have committed a fault; I truly have committed a fault. I am as foolish, as deluded, as ignorant, and as unskilled as one might be. Why is this?

The Blessed One has established the rule of eating in a single sitting for the community of bhikṣus, and while all the bhikṣus have respectfully trained in that precept and in the various subtle and wondrous dharmas within the sphere of the Blessed One’s teaching, I alone declared myself incapable and rose from my seat to depart.
"Why is this? Because they have not studied the complete precepts nor the subtle dharmas that are the domain of the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"Bhadraharit! At that time, you did not know that many bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs were observing the rains retreat in Śrāvastī; they knew me and saw me, [saying], 'There is a bhikṣu named Bhadraharit, a disciple of the World-Honored One, who does not train in the complete precepts nor in the various subtle and wondrous dharmas that are the domain of the World-Honored One.'"
Bhadraharī! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadraharī!

At that time, you did not know that there were many upāsakas and upāsikās living in Śrāvastī who knew me and saw me; nor did you know of the bhikṣu named Bhadrayāśas, a disciple of the World-Honored One, who had not yet mastered the complete precepts or the various subtle and wondrous dharmas within the realm of the World-Honored One.
Bhadraharī! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadraharī!

At that time, you did not know that many heterodox śramaṇas and brahmins were observing the rains retreat in Śrāvastī; they knew me and saw me, [thinking]: "There is a bhikṣu named Bhadrika, a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama, who does not train in the complete precepts or the various subtle dharmas of the World-Honored One’s domain."
Bhadraharī! Did you not know this at that time? Bhadraharī!
Bhadraharit! If there is a bhikṣu who is liberated both ways, I would say to him:
"Come, enter the mud. Bhadraharit!
"What do you think?
If I instruct that bhikṣu, would that bhikṣu be able to remain there or should he move away and avoid it?
Venerable Bhaddāli replied:
"No, World-Honored One," [he replied]. The World-Honored One said to him: "Bhadrapāla!

If there is a bhikṣu who, though not liberated in both ways, is liberated by wisdom; or one who, though not liberated by wisdom, is a body-witness; or one who, though not a body-witness, has attained vision; or one who, though not having attained vision, is liberated through faith; or one who, though not liberated through faith, is a practitioner of the Dharma; or one who, though not a practitioner of the Dharma, is a practitioner of faith—I say to him: "Come, enter the mud."
"Bhadraharit! What do you think?
When I instruct that bhikṣu, would that bhikṣu ever remain where he is or move away to avoid it?"
The Venerable Bhaddāli replied, “No,
World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
“Bhadraharitī! What do you think?

At that time, did you attain the stage of faith-practice, the stage of dharma-practice, liberation through faith, vision-attainment, bodily witness, liberation through wisdom, or both-fold liberation?”
The Venerable Bhaddāli replied,
“No, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“Bhaddāli! At that time, were you not like one in an empty house?

Thereupon, having been rebuked face-to-face by the Blessed One, the Venerable Bhaddāli harbored inner grief; with his head bowed, he remained silent, deprived of speech and unable to utter a word, as if searching for something to say.
Thereupon, having rebuked the Venerable Bhaddāli face-to-face, the Blessed One, wishing to gladden him, addressed him thus: "Bhaddāli!
At that time, you had no serene confidence in me regarding the Dharma, no serene confidence in the Dharma, and no serene confidence in the tranquility of the Dharma. Why was this?

Because I established the precept of eating in a single sitting for the community of bhikṣus, and while all the bhikṣus in the community respectfully studied that precept and the various subtle and wondrous dharmas within the sphere of the World-Honored One, only you declared yourself incapable of it, rose from your seat, and departed.
"Why is this? Because they have not studied the complete precepts and the various subtle dharmas that are the domain of the Blessed One.
Venerable Bhadrika replied:
"It is indeed so.

Why is this? The Blessed One has established the precept of eating in a single sitting for the community of bhikṣus, and while all the bhikṣus have respectfully studied this precept as well as the various subtle dharmas within the sphere of the Blessed One’s domain, I alone declared that I was incapable of it, rose from my seat, and departed."
Why is this? Because I have not studied the complete precepts nor the subtle and wondrous dharmas that are the domain of the World-Honored One.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my transgression; having recognized my fault, I shall repent of it myself, guard against it from now on, and never commit it again.
The World-Honored One said:
“Bhadrika! It is so; you are indeed foolish and deluded, ignorant and unskilled.”

Why is this? I have established the precept of eating in a single sitting for the community of bhikṣus, and all the bhikṣus have respectfully studied this precept as well as the various subtle and wondrous dharmas within the sphere of the World-Honored One; yet you alone declared yourself incapable of it, rose from your seat, and departed.
Why is this? It is because you have not studied the complete precepts and the subtle dharmas that constitute the domain of the World-Honored One. Bhadrapāla!
If you have committed a transgression, having seen it, you should repent of it yourself and from now on guard against it, so as not to do it again.
Bhaddāli! In this way, you will benefit and not be diminished within the Noble Dharma and Discipline.
If you have committed a transgression, and having seen it, you repent of it yourself and from now on guard against it so as not to do it again—
Bhadrahalī, what do you think?

If there is a bhikkhu who does not train in the full precepts, yet dwells in a secluded place—among the mountains, forests, or at the foot of a tree; or on a high crag, silent and soundless, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people—and sits in meditation accordingly; if he dwells in such seclusion, practicing with diligence, attaining the higher mind and dwelling in happiness in this very life; and if, while dwelling in such seclusion and practicing with diligence in peace and joy, he falsely slanders the Blessed One’s precepts, as well as the wise fellow practitioners among the devas, and likewise falsely slanders his own precepts.

Having falsely slandered the Blessed One’s precepts, as well as the wise and holy practitioners among the devas, and having likewise falsely slandered his own precepts, he does not experience joy. Not experiencing joy, he does not experience rapture. Not experiencing rapture, his body is not stilled. His body being unstilled, he does not experience happiness. Not experiencing happiness, his mind is not concentrated.
"Bhadraharī! When the mind of a noble disciple is not concentrated, he does not see things as they truly are, nor does he know them as they really are. Bhadraharī!"
What do you think?

If there is a bhikṣu who trains in the complete precepts, he dwells in a secluded place—among the mountains, forests, or at the foot of trees, or high upon a rocky crag that is silent and soundless, remote, free from evil, and uninhabited by people—sitting in meditation in accordance with the Dharma.
Dwelling in seclusion, practicing with diligence, he attains the higher mind and abides in happiness in this very life.

Having dwelt in seclusion, practicing with diligence, and having attained peace and joy, he does not misrepresent the Blessed One’s precepts, nor does he misrepresent the deities, the wise, or his fellow practitioners of the holy life, nor does he misrepresent his own precepts.

Having not slandered the World-Honored One regarding his precepts, nor slandered the devas or other wise practitioners of the holy life, and having likewise not slandered his own precepts, he then gives rise to joy. Having given rise to joy, he then gives rise to rapture. Having given rise to rapture, his body becomes tranquil. His body being tranquil, he experiences happiness. Experiencing happiness, his mind becomes concentrated.

"Bhadraharī! When a noble disciple’s mind has become concentrated, he sees things as they truly are and knows them as they really are. Having seen things as they truly are and known them as they really are, he becomes detached from desire and detached from evil and unwholesome states; with directed thought and evaluation, born of detachment, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by joy and bliss."

Bhadraharī! This is called his attainment at that time of the first *adhicitta*; he attains a dwelling in peace in this very life, easily and without difficulty, abiding happily and without fear, secure and joyful, leading him to ascend to *nirvāṇa*.

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he becomes inwardly tranquil and one-pointed; free from directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

Bhadraharī! This is called his attainment of the second higher state of mind at that time; he attains a dwelling in happiness in this very life, which is easy to obtain and not difficult, a joyful abode free from fear, secure and blissful, leading to the ascent into Nirvāṇa.

With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He who is equanimous, mindful, and dwells in happiness. Thus he attains and abides in the third dhyāna.

Bhadraharī! This is called his attainment of the third higher state of mind at that time; namely, dwelling in happiness in this very life, which is easily attained and not difficult to obtain, abiding in joy without fear, secure and blissful, leading to the ascent into Nirvāṇa.

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and possesses equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.

Bhadraharitī! This is called his attainment of the fourth higher mind at that time; he attains a dwelling in happiness in this very life, which is easily obtained rather than difficult, a joyful abode free from fear, secure and blissful, leading to the ascent into Nirvāṇa.

Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, stainless, and untroubled—supple, well-established, and immovable—he realizes and witnesses the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives. With its specific modes and characteristics, he recollects his manifold former existences: one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births; aeons of world-formation, aeons of world-destruction, and countless aeons of both formation and destruction.

"Those beings were named so-and-so; I have previously experienced them, having been born among them with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such a long duration of life, and such an end to my lifespan. From here I died and was reborn there; from there I died and was reborn here; I am now born here with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such a long duration of life, and such an end to my lifespan."

Bhadraharī! This is called his attainment of this first clear penetration at that time. Because he was originally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligence, ignorance was extinguished and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light was established; nescience was extinguished and wisdom arose—namely, the clear penetration of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives as a witness.

Having thus attained concentration, with a mind that is pure, stainless, and free from affliction—supple, well-established, and unshakable—he trains in and realizes the supernormal knowledge of the cognition of birth and death.

With the purified divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he sees these beings as they die and are reborn—whether of beautiful or ugly appearance, sublime or unrefined—as they pass away from or proceed toward favorable or unfavorable destinations, seeing them exactly as they are according to the karma these beings have performed.

If these sentient beings accomplish misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind; if they revile the noble ones, hold wrong views, and accomplish the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and, possessing right view, accomplish the karma of right view—by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will surely ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in the heavenly realms.

Bhadraharitī! This is called his attainment of the second clear knowledge at that time: because he was fundamentally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligence, ignorance was extinguished and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light was established; nescience was extinguished and wisdom arose—namely, the clear knowledge and realization of the wisdom regarding birth and death.

Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, stainless, and free from affliction—supple, well-established, and unshakable—he trains in the realization of the superknowledge of the destruction of the outflows.

He knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. He knows these taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—this he knows as it truly is.

Bhadraharī! This is called his attainment of the third clear knowledge at that time: because he was fundamentally free from negligence, delighted in dwelling in seclusion, and practiced with diligence, ignorance ceased and knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed and light was established; nescience ceased and clarity arose—namely, the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows as a realization.
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhaddāli rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"By what cause and by what condition, World-Honored One, do these bhikṣus equally violate the precepts, yet some are treated with harsh discipline while others are not?
The World-Honored One replied: "Bhadrapāla!"

There may be a bhikṣu who repeatedly violates the precepts; because of these repeated violations, he is rebuked by his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Having been rebuked by his fellow practitioners and having become subject to what they have seen, heard, or suspected regarding him from others, he then speaks of various other matters and external topics, becoming angry, resentful, and envious, giving vent to wrath and widespread malice, harassing the assembly and showing contempt for the assembly, and speaking thus:
"I shall now act in such a way as to please and satisfy the assembly; I shall form such an intention."
“Bhadraharit! Then those bhikṣus thought: ‘Indeed, this worthy one repeatedly violates the precepts;

because he repeatedly violates the precepts, he is censured by his fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin). When he is censured by his fellow practitioners of the holy life for what they have seen, heard, or suspected of him from others, he then speaks various other matters and external topics, becoming angry, resentful, and envious; he gives way to rage and widespread malice, harassing the assembly and showing contempt for the assembly, speaking as follows:’”
"I shall now act in such a way as to gladden and satisfy the assembly.
Having seen this, he spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"You should contemplate this so that it may endure for a long time. Bhadrapāla!
In this way, the bhikṣus contemplated it so that it might endure for a long time.

"Suppose there is a bhikkhu who repeatedly violates the precepts. Because of these repeated violations, he is rebuked by his fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*). Having been rebuked by them, and having been seen, heard, or suspected by others, he does not engage in various discourses or talk about other matters; he does not become angry, resentful, or envious, nor does he give vent to wrath or harbor ill will; he does not harass the assembly or treat the assembly with contempt. He does not speak thus:
'I shall now act in such a way as to please and satisfy the assembly,' nor does he entertain such an intention."
"Bhadraharī! Then those bhikṣus thought: 'Indeed, this worthy one repeatedly violates the precepts;

because he repeatedly violates the precepts, he is rebuked by his fellow practitioners of the holy life. When he is rebuked by his fellow practitioners of the holy life regarding what he has seen, heard, or suspected from others, he does not speak of various other matters outside of that; he does not become angry, resentful, or envious, nor does he give way to widespread malice; he does not harass the assembly nor treat the assembly with contempt, nor does he speak in such a manner as follows:'"
"I shall now act in such a way as to bring joy and satisfaction to the assembly.
Having seen this, he spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"One should contemplate them so that they may be extinguished early. Bhadrika!
Thus do the bhikṣus contemplate so that [defilements] may be extinguished early.
A slight transgression of the prohibitive precepts is likewise so. "Bhadrapāla!
There may be a bhikṣu who possesses faith, affection, and tranquility; this present bhikṣu possesses faith, affection, and tranquility."

"If we were to treat this worthy man with harsh discipline, he now possesses faith, affection, and tranquility; because of these qualities, he will surely sever [the defilements]. Therefore, we should rather protect this worthy man together with care."
The bhikṣus then carefully protected him together. Bhadrapāla!

It is just as if there were a person who had only one eye; his kinsmen and relatives, out of compassion and pity, seeking his profit and benefit, seeking his peace, security, and happiness, would carefully protect him together, so that this person would not suffer from cold or heat, hunger or thirst, illness, or sorrow, nor from the afflictions of illness and grief, nor from dust, nor smoke, nor the combination of dust and smoke.
Why is this? Furthermore, fearing that this person might lose one eye, his relatives protect him well. Bhadrapāla!
When a bhikkhu has little faith, little affection, and little serenity, the other bhikkhus think:

"Now this bhikkhu has little faith, little affection, and little serenity. If we were to discipline this worthy man harshly, since he now has little faith, little affection, and little serenity, he will surely be broken because of it. We would rather collectively and properly protect this worthy man."
"Therefore, monks, you should well protect one another, just as relatives would protect a man with only one eye.
Thereupon, the Venerable Bhaddāli rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"World-Honored One!"
For what cause and for what reason did, in the past, few precepts being laid down, many bhikṣus follow and uphold them?
