"If there is a bhikṣu who is neither liberated both ways nor liberated by wisdom, who is neither a bodily witness nor one who has attained vision, who is neither liberated through faith nor a Dharma-follower, yet is a faith-follower..."
What is a bhikṣu who possesses conduct based on faith?

If there is a bhikṣu who, with single-minded determination, has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; and who, regarding the Dharma as he has heard it, contemplates and accepts it with wisdom, yet does not act in accordance with that Dharma—such a bhikṣu is one who possesses conduct based on faith.
"I teach this bhikṣu to practice heedfulness; having seen that this bhikṣu practices heedfulness, what fruit do I see that leads me to teach this bhikṣu to practice heedfulness?"

Alternatively, if this bhikṣu seeks mastery over the sense faculties, associates with virtuous friends, and dwells in accordance with the practice, he will certainly attain one of two fruits: either he attains ultimate knowledge in this very life, or, if there remains some residue [of clinging], he attains the state of an anāgāmin.
I see that for this bhikṣu who practices heedfulness, there is such a fruit as this.
Therefore, I speak of the practice of heedfulness to this bhikṣu;
I speak of the practice of heedfulness to all these bhikṣus.

“I do not say that all bhikṣus have attained ultimate knowledge, nor do I say that all bhikṣus first attain ultimate knowledge; rather, by gradually training in the path, receiving instruction and reproof, it is only then that the bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge.”

Regarding this ultimate knowledge attained by these bhikṣus, how do they gradually train, follow the path, receive instruction, and receive admonition, before finally attaining that ultimate knowledge?
"Have these bhikṣus attained ultimate knowledge? Some, having gained faith, would go to him; having gone, they would practice under him;

having practiced, they would listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus; having listened with a single-minded focus, they would uphold the Dharma; having upheld the Dharma, they would reflect upon it; having reflected, they would weigh it; having weighed it, they would investigate it. Once the noble disciple has investigated it, he realizes it directly with his own body and contemplates it through the predominance of wisdom.

He then thinks: "This truth was never before realized by me with my own body, nor contemplated through the predominance of wisdom; now this truth is realized by me with my own body, through contemplation by the predominance of wisdom."
"In this way, by gradually training in and following the path, receiving instruction and admonition, the bhikṣus attain ultimate knowledge; such is the ultimate knowledge attained by these bhikṣus."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed them, saying:
“Āśvalāyana! Pūrṇaśaila!”
“There is a teaching called the ‘Fourfold Array’ that I wish to explain to you; do you wish to know it?
Āśvajit and Punarvasu replied, “World-Honored One!”
"Who are we? By what means shall we come to know the Dharma?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One had this thought:
“O foolish man! You have transgressed against this Dhamma and Discipline of mine by a very great distance.

If there were a teacher of the Dhamma and Discipline who was attached to food and did not abandon food, his disciples should not quickly fall into negligence; how much less so for me, who am unattached to food and have abandoned food?”
A faithful disciple should speak thus:
"The Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple of the Blessed One. The Blessed One has taught me the Dharma;
the Well-Gone One has taught me the Dharma, so that I may for a long night attain its meaning, gain benefit, and find peace and happiness."

"Those faithful disciples who have much to do within the domain of the World-Honored One, who bring great benefit within the domain of the World-Honored One, who practice extensively within the domain of the World-Honored One, and who enter and abide within the domain of the World-Honored One—whether they travel to the east, they will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction;
whether they travel to the south, west, or north, they will surely attain peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction."

If a faithful disciple has much practice within the domain of the World-Honored One, much benefit within the domain of the World-Honored One, and much conduct within the domain of the World-Honored One—entering the domain of the World-Honored One and abiding in the domain of the World-Honored One—I would not say that even their wholesome qualities remain, let alone that they decline.
One should simply increase wholesome qualities day and night without decline.

If a faithful disciple performs much within the domain of the Blessed One, brings great benefit to the domain of the Blessed One, practices extensively within the domain of the Blessed One, enters the domain of the Blessed One, and abides in the domain of the Blessed One, they will surely attain one of two fruits: either they will attain ultimate knowledge in this very life, or, if there remains some residue of clinging, they will become a non-returner (anāgāmin).
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The fourth Āśvalāyana Sūtra ends here, totaling 4,199 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 51, totals 8,506 characters. Fifth Subsequent Recitation.
Madhyama Āgama, Scroll 52.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
196. Cunda Sūtra (196). Chapter 5: The Great Section. Cunda Sūtra, Part 5, Subsequent Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Vajjis and was staying at the village of Sāmagāma.
At that time, the novice Cunda was observing the rains retreat at Pāvā. In Pāvā, there was a Nirgrantha named Puttaka who passed away there.

Not long after his passing, the disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta each broke apart and no longer lived in harmony; they spoke of their own divisions and discordant matters, engaging in strife, litigation, and mutual entanglement, hating one another and contending together, saying:
"I know this Dharma, but you do not."
"What dharma do you know that is like what I know?
I am disciplined, while you are undisciplined.
I am consistent, while you are inconsistent."
That which should have been stated first was stated last, and that which should have been stated last was stated first.
I am superior; you are not my equal.
When I question you on a matter, you are unable to answer.
"I have already subdued you; I shall ask further questions.
If you move, I will bind you again.
Thus they vied with one another in arrogance, seeking only to prevail in their discourse, and there was no one to rebuke them.
If Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta has any lay disciples who are white-robed householders, they all feel weary of and disgusted by these disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta. Why is that?
Because of the evil Dharma and discipline they have taught, it is not the essential path of deliverance; it does not lead to perfect enlightenment, nor was it spoken by the Well-Gone One (Sugata).
It is collapsing and without support, and the teacher whom they revere is neither a Tathāgata, nor an Arhat, nor a Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Thereupon, the śrāmaṇera Cunda, having completed his summer retreat and the three months having passed, finished mending his robes; then, taking up his robes and bowl, he went to the village of Śrāvastī and stayed in the Siṃsapā Grove to the north of the village.
The novice Cunda went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and having arrived, he prostrated at his feet and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Ānanda asked him: "Worthy Cunda!"
“From where have you come, and where did you spend the summer retreat?
The novice Cunda replied,
“Venerable Ānanda!”
"I have come from Pāvā; I observed the rains retreat there in Pāvā.
Venerable Ānanda!
In that Pāvā, there was a Nirgrantha named Puttamṛgīputra who passed away there."

Not long after his passing, the disciples of the son of Nigaṇṭha each broke apart and ceased to live in harmony; they each spoke of divisive and discordant matters, engaging in strife, litigation, and mutual entanglement, hating one another and disputing together:
"I know this Dharma; you do not know it."
"What dharma do you know that is as I know it?
I am well-composed, while you are not well-composed.
I am in accordance with the teaching, while you are not."
That which should have been stated first was stated last; that which should have been stated last was stated first.
I am superior, and you are not equal to me.
When I question you on a matter, you are unable to answer.
"I have already subdued you; you shall be questioned further.
If you move, I will bind you again.
Thus they took turns in arrogance, seeking only to prevail in debate, with no one offering any rebuke.
If the Nirgrantha Putraka has any lay disciples who are householders, they all feel weary of and distressed by these various disciples of the Nirgrantha Putraka. Why is that?
Because of the evil Dharma and Vinaya they have taught, it is not the essential path of deliverance; it does not lead to perfect enlightenment, nor was it spoken by the Well-Gone One (Sugata).
It is collapsing and without pillars, offering no refuge; even the teacher they revere is not a Tathāgata, Arhat, or Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Having heard this, the Venerable Ānanda said: "Worthy Cunda!
You may go to see the Buddha on account of this very teaching and offer it to the World-Honored One."
"Venerable Cunda!
Let us now go together to the Buddha and report this matter in detail to the World-Honored One; perhaps we may thereby hear some extraordinary Dharma from the World-Honored One."

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda went together to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and then the Venerable Ānanda withdrew to stand to one side, while the novice Cunda withdrew to sit to one side.
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"World-Honored One!
Today the novice Cunda came to where I was, prostrated at my feet, and sat down to one side. I asked him:"
“Venerable Cunda!
From where have you come?
Where did you spend the summer retreat?”
The novice Cunda replied to me, saying:
"Venerable Ānanda!
I have come from Pāvā; I have observed the rains retreat in Pāvā."
Venerable Ānanda!

Among those Nigaṇṭhas there was one named Putta, who passed away there. Not long after his death, the disciples of the Nigaṇṭha Putta each became divided and ceased to live in harmony. They each spoke of divisive and discordant matters, engaging in strife, litigation, and mutual entanglement;
they harbored hatred and contended with one another, saying: "I know this Dharma, but you do not!"
"What dharma do you know that is as I know it?
I am disciplined, while you are undisciplined.
I am consistent, while you are inconsistent."
That which should have been stated first was stated last; that which should have been stated last was stated first.
I am superior, and you are not my equal.
When I question you on a matter, you are unable to answer.
"I have already subdued you; you shall be questioned further.
If you move, I will bind you again.
Thus they alternately displayed arrogance, seeking only to prevail in debate, yet there was no one to rebuke them.
If the Nirgrantha Putraka has any lay disciples who are householders, they all feel weary of and disgusted with these disciples of the Nirgrantha Putraka. Why is that?
Because of the evil Dharma and discipline they have taught, it is not the essential path of deliverance; it does not lead to perfect enlightenment, nor was it spoken by the Well-Gone One (Sugata).
It is collapsing and without pillars, offering no refuge; and their revered teacher is likewise not a Tathāgata, Arhat, or Samyaksaṃbuddha.
“World-Honored One!

Having heard this, I was struck with terror and alarm; my hair stood on end. May no bhikṣu, after the World-Honored One has departed, give rise to such strife within the assembly. For such strife does not benefit many people, brings suffering to many, is neither righteous nor beneficial, and is not conducive to peace, security, or happiness—even leading to the ultimate suffering and affliction for gods and humans alike.”
"Bhagavān!
I see a bhikṣu sitting before the Bhagavān, with a mind of sincere reverence for the Bhagavān, skillfully protecting the Sugata.
Bhagavān!"
Having seen this, I thought to myself:

"If I allow this bhikṣu, after the Blessed One has passed away, to incite such strife within the Saṅgha—strife that is of no benefit to many people, brings suffering to many, is contrary to the Dharma and not conducive to welfare, nor to peace and happiness, even resulting in extreme misery for gods and humans."
Thereupon, the Blessed One asked: “Ānanda!

What kind of assembly have you seen in which there is strife and contention—strife that does not benefit many people, brings suffering to many, is unrighteous and non-beneficial, and is not conducive to peace, security, or happiness, even resulting in the ultimate misery and affliction for both gods and humans?”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One,
it is said that there are disputes which arise among the assembly on account of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher insight.”
World-Honored One!

This quarreling does not benefit many people; it brings suffering to many, being neither righteous nor beneficial, neither peaceful nor pleasant, even resulting in the utmost suffering and affliction for both devas and humans.
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, these disputes are very few, namely those arising on account of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher insight."
Ānanda! If there should be disputes arising within a community on account of the Dhamma or the path to the Dhamma, Ānanda, such disputes are not for the benefit of many people;
they bring suffering to many, and are contrary to what is righteous, beneficial, peaceful, and happy.

Ānanda! Do you see those two bhikṣus therein, each with a different intention, giving rise to quarrels and disputes: "This is the Dharma, this is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, this is not the Vinaya; this is an offense, this is not an offense; it is light, it is heavy; it is expiable, it is inexpiable; it is curable, it is incurable; it has a remainder, it is without remainder; it arises, it does not arise"?
Ānanda! What do you think?

Regarding my collection of teachings—those which I have known for myself, realized for myself, and witnessed for myself: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
Ānanda! The son of Nigaṇṭha is truly not omniscient (sarvajña), yet he claims to be omniscient. Ānanda!
If the son of Nigaṇṭha were all-knowing and all-seeing, he would not have established for his disciples these six bases of dispute, saying, "One should hear them and then stop."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One,
now is precisely the right time."
"Sugata, now is precisely the right time.
If the World-Honored One were to explain the six roots of dispute to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus, having heard them from the World-Honored One, would properly receive and uphold them."
The Blessed One said:
“Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it to you in full detail.”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Indeed, sir.
We shall receive your instruction and listen."
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda, there may be a person who is bound by the fetter of ill will.”

Ānanda! When a person is afflicted by anger and resentment, they are bound by fetters; such a person does not revere the teacher, does not see the Dharma, and does not protect the precepts. Having failed to revere the teacher, see the Dharma, and protect the precepts, they then give rise to such disputes within the assembly.

That is to say, this strife does not benefit many people; it brings suffering to many, it is neither righteous nor beneficial, neither peaceful nor happy, and it results in extreme suffering and affliction for both gods and humans.

Ānanda! Regarding such disputes, if you perceive them within or without but have not yet exhausted them, then for the sake of severing these disputes, you should swiftly seek skillful means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endure so as not to let yourself regress.
Ānanda! It is just as if a person whose head or clothing were on fire were to urgently seek means to save their head or clothing.

In the same way, regarding this dispute—if you see that it has not been fully eliminated within or without—you should, for the sake of severing this dispute, quickly seek skillful means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and exercise patience so as not to let it regress.

Ānanda! Regarding such disputes, when you perceive their exhaustion within and without, you should protect those minds with renewed care and remain ever vigilant, desiring to bring this dispute to an end; in this way, you shall sever the very root of this dispute.

Ānanda! Just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire would urgently seek a means to save their head or clothing, so too, regarding this dispute, when you see that it has been exhausted within and without, you should protect that person’s mind with renewed care and always remain free from negligence, desiring to bring this dispute to an end; in this way, you shall sever the root of this dispute.
"Likewise, there are the fetters of silence, stinginess, envy, flattery and deception, lack of shame, lack of dread, evil desire, wrong view, and an unruly, wicked nature."

Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who has evil desires, wrong views, and a wicked nature that cannot be restrained; he does not respect his teacher, does not see the Dharma, and does not guard the precepts. Having failed to respect his teacher, see the Dharma, and guard the precepts, he then gives rise to such disputes within the assembly, saying: "This quarreling is of no benefit to many people; it brings suffering to many, it is neither righteous nor beneficial, nor is it peaceful or happy, leading even to the ultimate suffering and affliction for gods and humans."

Ānanda! Regarding such disputes, if you perceive them internally or externally and have not yet brought them to an end, then for the sake of severing these disputes, you should swiftly seek skillful means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and exercise patience so as not to let yourself regress.
Ānanda! Just as a person whose head or clothes are on fire would urgently seek means to save their head or clothes,

so too, regarding this dispute— whatever you see within or without that has not been fully abandoned— you should, for the sake of ending this dispute, quickly seek means, train with extreme diligence, maintain right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, and endure without allowing yourself to retreat.

Ānanda! Regarding such disputes, when you see that they have been exhausted within and without, you should guard their minds with great care and always remain free from negligence, desiring to bring these disputes to an end; in this way, you shall cut off the very root of these disputes.

Ānanda! Just as a person whose head or clothing is on fire would urgently seek a means to save their head or clothing, so too, regarding this dispute, when you see that it has been exhausted within and without, you should protect those minds with renewed care and remain constantly free from negligence, desiring to bring this dispute to an end; in this way, you shall sever the root of this dispute.
"Furthermore, Ānanda, there are seven methods for settling disputes: first, the legal procedure for settling a dispute in the presence of the parties;
second, the legal procedure for settling a dispute through recollection."
Third, the legal procedure for settling disputes through the verdict of "not being deranged" should be applied.
Fourth, the legal procedure for settling disputes through self-confession should be applied.
Fifth, the legal procedure for settling disputes through the majority vote should be applied.
Sixth, one should apply the legal procedure for settling disputes through successive mediation.
Seventh, one should apply the legal procedure for settling disputes by casting them aside like refuse. Ānanda!
How should the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) be applied?
How is this dispute to be settled?
It is by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya*.
Ānanda! One person may instruct and admonish another, protecting them with the Dharma and the Vinaya according to the teaching of a venerable teacher, bringing them to joy in their presence.

One person may instruct and admonish two people, one person many people, or one person a multitude, protecting them with the Dharma and the Vinaya according to the teaching of a venerable teacher, bringing them to joy in their presence.
When two people admonish two others, protecting them with the Dharma and the Vinaya according to the instruction of a venerable teacher, they cause them to rejoice in their presence.

When two people admonish many, when two people admonish a multitude, or when two people admonish a single person, protecting them with the Dharma and the Vinaya according to the instruction of a venerable teacher, they cause them to rejoice in their presence.
When many people are to be admonished by many people, they are protected by the Dharma and the Vinaya, as taught by the Venerable Teacher, and are made to rejoice in his presence.

When many people are to be admonished by a multitude, or by one person, or by two people, they are protected by the Dharma and the Vinaya, as taught by the Venerable Teacher, and are made to rejoice in his presence.
The community admonishes the individual, protecting them by means of the Dharma and the Vinaya, just as a venerable teacher would instruct, so that they may find joy in their presence.

Whether it be one person, two people, or many people of the community who admonish, they protect by means of the Dharma and the Vinaya, just as a venerable teacher would instruct, so that they may find joy in their presence.
"Ānanda! This is called the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of), by which such a dispute is settled; that is, it is due to the *saṃmukhavinaya*. Ānanda!"
What is the legal procedure for settling a dispute by means of recollection (*sativinaya*),
and how is this dispute resolved?
It is through the legal procedure for settling a dispute by means of recollection.
Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who has violated the precepts but does not remember it. When the bhikṣus see this, they say to him:

"You have violated the precepts but do not remember it; you should request from the Saṃgha the *smṛtivinaya* (the legal procedure for restoration of memory), and the Saṃgha shall collectively grant the *smṛtivinaya* to the worthy one."

"Ānanda! If there is a gathering of the assembly, that bhikṣu should go there, adjust his robe to bare one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, prostrate at the feet of the elder and most venerable bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder and most venerable bhikṣus, saying:
'Venerable sirs!'"

‘Listen, I once committed an offense but do not remember it; I now seek from the Saṃgha the restoration of my memory regarding the Vinaya. May the Saṃgha, being in harmony, grant me the restoration of my memory regarding the Vinaya. Ānanda!

For the sake of that bhikṣu, the community should assemble in harmony and grant him the *smṛtivinaya* (verdict based on memory), according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, in accordance with the Teacher’s instruction, so as to bring him joy in their presence.

"Ānanda! This is called the legal procedure for settling a dispute by means of recollection; in this way, such a dispute is settled, namely by the legal procedure for settling a dispute through recollection. Ānanda!"
How should the legal procedure for settling a dispute through "absence of delusion" (amūḷhavinaya) be applied?
How is this dispute to be resolved?
It is by means of the legal procedure for settling a dispute through absence of delusion.

Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who has become deranged and whose mind is inverted; having become deranged and mentally inverted, he engages frequently in impure conduct, which is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and speaks in violation of the practice of the Dharma.
At a later time, he regained his original mind. When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to him:

"You were seized by madness and your mind was inverted; having been mad and mentally inverted, you committed many impure acts that are not the way of a śramaṇa, and you spoke in violation of the Dharma, acting contrary to the practice of the Dharma."

"When the wise person later regains his original mind, he may request from the community the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of sanity); the community should collectively grant the wise person the *amūḷhavinaya*.
Thus spoke Ānanda.

If there is a gathering of the assembly in a certain place, that bhikṣu should go there, expose one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, prostrate at the feet of the elder and most venerable bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder and most venerable bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!"

Listen, for I was once deranged and my mind was inverted; having been deranged and my mind inverted, I engaged in many impure practices that were not the way of a śramaṇa, and contrary to the practice of the Dharma, I spoke of transgressions.
"At a later time, I regained my original mind; I now seek from the assembly the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of sanity). May the assembly, being in harmony, grant me the *amūḍha-vinaya*.
Thus, Ānanda!

For the sake of that bhikṣu, the community should assemble in harmony and grant him the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the verdict of sanity), in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, following the instructions of the Venerable Teacher, so as to bring him joy in their presence.

"Ānanda! This is called the 'Legal Procedure for Settling Disputes through Non-delusion,' by which such a dispute is settled; that is to say, it is settled by means of the Legal Procedure for Settling Disputes through Non-delusion. Ānanda!"
What is the legal procedure for settling a dispute through one’s own confession?
How is this dispute resolved?
It is resolved by means of the legal procedure for settling disputes through one’s own confession.
Ānanda! Suppose there is a person who has violated the precepts; whether someone speaks of it or does not speak of it, whether they remember it or do not remember it.

Ānanda! Wherever there is an assembly of monks gathered together, that bhikṣu should approach them, adjust his robe by exposing one shoulder, remove his sandals, enter the assembly, prostrate at the feet of the elder and senior bhikṣus, kneel with palms joined, and address the elder and senior bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!"
Listen!

I have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess it with a sincere heart before you, Venerable Elder Bhikṣu; I openly declare it and do not dare to conceal it. I shall henceforth maintain it well and never commit it again.
"Ānanda! The community of bhikṣus should ask that bhikṣu:
'Venerable one, do you yourself see what you have committed?'"
He should reply:
"I truly see what I have transgressed.
The assembly should then say to him:
"Guard it well from now on; do not commit it again. Ānanda!

This is called the *Pratideśanīya* (Rule for Confession) for settling a dispute by means of one's own confession; in this way, the dispute is settled through the *Pratideśanīya* rule of self-confession.
“Ānanda! How should the *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (rules for settling disputes) be applied to you?
How is this dispute to be resolved?”
This refers to the *yebhuyyasika* (majority) rule for settling disputes with you. Ānanda!

Suppose there is a person who is shameless and does not repent for what he has seen or heard, following the evil desires of those who doubt him. Having committed an offense, he claims to have known it in one instance and claims to have seen it in another; having claimed to have known it in one instance, he claims to have seen it in another; having claimed to have seen it in one instance, he claims to have known it in another. In the midst of the assembly, he claims to have known it in one instance and claims to have seen it in another; having claimed to have known it in one instance, he claims to have seen it in another; and having claimed to have seen it in one instance, he claims to have known it in another.

Ānanda! For the sake of that bhikṣu, the community should assemble in harmony and grant him the *tassa-pāpiyasika* (censure) procedure: "You are without principle and without reason; you are evil and unwholesome."

Why is this so? It is because after you have transgressed the precepts, you claim to know in one instance and claim to see in another; having claimed to know in one instance, you claim to see in another; having claimed to see in one instance, you claim to know in another. Within the assembly, you claim to know in one instance and claim to see in another; having claimed to know in one instance, you claim to see in another; and having claimed to see in one instance, you claim to know in another.
"Ānanda! This is called the *yebhuyyasika* (majority decision) legal procedure for settling a dispute; it is by means of this *yebhuyyasika* legal procedure that such a dispute is settled. Ānanda!"
How should the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) be applied?
How is this dispute to be settled?
It is by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya*.

Ānanda! There were two bhikṣus who, in the midst of this, gave rise to various disputes of mind, saying: "This is the Dharma, that is not the Dharma; this is the Vinaya, that is not the Vinaya; this is an offense, that is not an offense; it is light, or it is heavy; it is speakable, or it is unspeakable; it is protectable, or it is unprotectable; it has a remainder, or it has no remainder; it is confessable, or it is non-confessable."

Ānanda! That bhikṣu should settle this dispute in private. If it is settled in private, one should say that this dispute is settled. If it is not settled in private, he may bring it before the assembly. If it is settled within the assembly, one should say that this dispute is settled. If it is not settled within the assembly, Ānanda!

Regarding those who dwell nearby: if among them there is a bhikṣu who upholds the Sūtras, upholds the Vinaya, or upholds the Mātṛkā, one should go together with this bhikṣu to him and speak of this dispute. If it is settled while on the road, this dispute should be said to be settled; if it is not settled on the road, this dispute should be brought before the assembly again. If it is settled within the assembly, this dispute should be said to be settled; if it is not settled within the assembly, Ānanda!
Ānanda, if there are many companions who are upholders of the Sūtras, upholders of the Vinaya, and upholders of the Mātrikās,
that bhikṣu should cease this dispute by means of the Dharma and the Vinaya, according to the Teacher’s instruction, so as to bring about reconciliation in their presence.
Ānanda! This is called the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of), by which this dispute is thus settled; that is to say, it is through the *saṃmukhavinaya*. "Ānanda!"
What is the *yebhuyyasika* (decision by majority) method for settling disputes?
How is this dispute to be resolved?
It is through the *yebhuyyasika* method for settling disputes.
Ānanda! If there is a dwelling place where the community of bhikṣus quarrels, disputes, feels hatred and jealousy, and contends with one another out of mutual animosity— Ānanda!

Those bhikṣus divided themselves into two groups. Having divided into two groups, in one group there were elders and senior venerables, or those who were next in rank, or presiding leaders, or those who were next in rank.
Ānanda! This bhikkhu said to that bhikkhu:
"Venerable friends!"
Listen!
We are without the Way and without principle; we are evil and unwholesome. Why is this so?

While we have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya to practice the path, we engage in quarrels, disputes, malice, and envy, hating one another and contending together.
Venerable friends!

Because of this dispute, we have committed offenses—excluding those of *sthūlātyaya* and those associated with the householders. For my own sake and for the sake of you, venerable friends, I now confess these to you with a sincere heart, openly declaring them and not daring to conceal them; I shall henceforth guard myself well and never commit them again.
"Ānanda! If there is not even one bhikkhu in this group who is qualified, Ānanda! That bhikkhu should go to that second group;
having arrived, he should prostrate himself, pay homage at the feet of the elder, most venerable bhikkhus, kneel with palms joined, and say to those elder, most venerable bhikkhus: "
"Venerable sirs!
Listen!
We have been without the Path and without principle; we have committed evil and unwholesome deeds."

Why is this? Because although we have, out of faith, gone forth from the home life into homelessness to train in this well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, we engage in quarrels, disputes, malice, and envy, hating one another and contending together.
Venerable friends!

Because of this dispute, we have committed offenses—excluding those of *sthūlātyaya* and those associated with the household life. For my own sake, and for the sake of you venerable friends as well, I now confess before the elders and seniors with a sincere heart, openly declaring and revealing it; I dare not conceal it, but shall henceforth guard myself well and never commit it again.
"Ānanda! That bhikṣu should say to this bhikṣu:
'Venerable friend!'"
"Do you yourself see that you have committed an offense?
He should answer:
"Truly, I see what I have committed."
He should say this to him:
"Guard and maintain [the precepts] even more carefully;
do not commit them again. The second section is also like this.

Ānanda! This is called the *pātimokkha* for settling disputes by way of "discarding like refuse"; in this manner, one settles this dispute, namely by means of the *pātimokkha* for settling disputes by way of discarding like refuse.
“Ānanda! I now instruct you to explain the six modes of consolation. Listen closely, listen closely, and reflect upon them well.
Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Yes, indeed.
We shall receive and listen to the instruction.
The Buddha said:

"What are the six? They are: compassionate bodily action directed toward fellow practitioners of the holy life; this is a dharma that provides consolation, a dharma of affection, a dharma of joy, which causes them to feel love, to feel respect, to offer service, and to show reverence; it causes them to practice and to be gathered together; it leads to the attainment of the state of a śramaṇa, to the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, to the attainment of diligence, and to the attainment of nirvāṇa. [Likewise] there is compassionate verbal action and compassionate mental action."

If one obtains gains in accordance with the Dharma, and having received food for oneself until it is placed within the alms bowl, distributes such gains to fellow practitioners of the holy life—this Dharma is a source of consolation, a source of affection, and a source of joy; it causes one to love and revere, to honor and respect, to cultivate and embrace, thereby attaining the state of a śramaṇa, attaining single-mindedness, attaining diligence, and attaining nirvāṇa.

If one possesses the factors of morality that are unbroken, untorn, unstained, and unblemished; like the earth, independent of others, praised by the noble ones, and fully and rightly undertaken—then by giving such moral discipline to fellow practitioners of the holy life, this Dharma becomes a source of consolation, a source of affection, and a source of joy. It inspires love, inspires reverence, inspires veneration, inspires cultivation, and inspires integration. Through it, one attains the state of a śramaṇa, attains single-mindedness, attains diligence, and attains nirvāṇa.

If there is a noble vision that leads to transcendence, which is clear, profound, and penetrative, capable of rightly exhausting suffering—such a vision is distributed and shared with fellow practitioners of the holy life. This Dharma is a source of consolation, a source of affection, and a source of joy; it inspires love and respect, inspires veneration and reverence, inspires cultivation and integration, leading to the state of a śramaṇa, to one-pointedness of mind, to diligence, and to nirvāṇa.
Ānanda! It is for this reason that I have spoken of the six modes of consolation which I previously mentioned. Ānanda!

If you should completely eradicate these six roots of dispute and apply these seven methods for settling disputes—using the legal procedures for settling disputes that cast out quarrels like discarded refuse—and furthermore practice these six methods of consolation.

Ānanda! Thus, after my passing, you shall remain together in harmony, joyful and without dispute, with a single mind and a single teaching, blending as one like water and milk, dwelling in happiness just as you do now while I am still here.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifth discourse, the Cunda Sutta, ends here; it contains four thousand two hundred and thirty characters. 197. Upāli Sutta (197), Middle Discourses, Great Chapter, Upāli Sutta, the sixth; the fifth subsequent recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Campā and stayed on the bank of the Ganges Pond.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Upāli rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!”
“If a community of bhikkhus is in concord, yet performs different actions and pronounces different actions, are those actions in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the Vinaya?
The Blessed One replied: “No.”
"Upāli! The Venerable Upāli asked again:
"World-Honored One!"

If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and grants the *paṭiññātakara* (decision in the presence) to one for whom the *sativinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness) should be granted, or grants the *sativinaya* to one for whom the *paṭiññātakara* should be granted, is this an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?
The Blessed One replied, “No, Upāli.”
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
"World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, and they grant the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict for one not insane) to one who should receive the *sativinaya* (verdict based on memory), or grant the *sativinaya* to one who should receive the *amūḷhavinaya*, is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?"
The Blessed One replied: “No, Upāli.”
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
"World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in harmony, and they grant the *pāṭidesanīya* (formal acknowledgment) to one for whom the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of sanity) should be granted, or grant the *amūḷhavinaya* to one for whom the *pāṭidesanīya* should be granted— is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?"
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:

“World-Honored One, if a community of bhikṣus is in concord and, when they ought to grant the *svavavāda* (self-disclosure) discipline, they instead grant the *saṃvara* (restraint) discipline; or when they ought to grant the *saṃvara* discipline, they instead grant the *svavavāda* discipline—is this an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, and they grant a formal act (*kamma*) to one who should be censured, or censure one who should be granted a formal act— is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they demote one who should be censured and censure one who should be demoted— is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they suspend one who should be reinstated and reinstate one who should be suspended, is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, and they suspend one who should be suspended and suspend one who should be suspended— would this be an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied, “No, Upāli.”
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they perform an act of formal remembrance against one who should be expelled, or perform an act of expulsion against one who should be granted formal remembrance— is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
"World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in harmony, and they grant a formal act of *smṛti* (remembrance) to one who should be subject to a formal act from the root, or grant a formal act from the root to one who should be subject to *smṛti*, is that an action in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya?"
The Blessed One replied: “No, Upāli.”
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One!

If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they expel one who should be disciplined from the root, and discipline from the root one who should be expelled—is this an act in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
“World-Honored One!

If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they expel one who should not be expelled while failing to expel one who should be expelled—is this an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?”
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."
The Venerable Upāli asked again:
"World-Honored One,

if a community of bhikṣus is in concord and treats with non-insolence those who should be treated with non-insolence, while treating with discipline those who should be disciplined, is this an action in accordance with the Dharma and an action in accordance with the Vinaya?"
The Blessed One replied: "No, Upāli."

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord yet performs a separate action and pronounces a separate action, that is an action not in accordance with the Dharma and an action not in accordance with the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they grant a *paṭiññātakara* (decision in the presence) where a *sativinaya* (verdict based on mindfulness) should be granted, or grant a *sativinaya* where a *paṭiññātakara* should be granted, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; the assembly is also at fault.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they grant a *smṛtivinaya* (verdict based on memory) when a *amūḍhavinaya* (verdict for one who was not insane) should be granted, or grant an *amūḍhavinaya* when a *smṛtivinaya* should be granted, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and an action contrary to the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they grant a *pārivāsika* (probation) for one who is not insane when it should be a *pratideśanīya* (confession), or grant a *pratideśanīya* when it should be a *pārivāsika* for one who is not insane—this is an act contrary to the Dharma and an act contrary to the Vinaya, and the community is also at fault.

"Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and should grant a *svavavāda-vinaya* when a *yadbhūya-vinaya* is required, or grant a *yadbhūya-vinaya* when a *svavavāda-vinaya* is required, that is an action contrary to the Dharma and an action contrary to the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt."

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and should grant a *tajjaniya-kamma* (an act of censure) where a *tajjaniya-kamma* ought to be granted, or should grant a *tajjaniya-kamma* where a *tajjaniya-kamma* ought to be granted, that is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya, and the assembly is also at fault.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they should reprimand and censure one who ought to be demoted, or should demote one who ought to be reprimanded and censured—this is an action contrary to the Dharma and an action contrary to the Vinaya, and the assembly is also at fault.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they should demote one who ought to be suspended, or suspend one who ought to be demoted, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; the assembly is also at fault.

"Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they should suspend one who ought to be suspended, or suspend one who ought not to be suspended, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt."

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they perform an act of formal remembrance (*smṛti*) against one who should be expelled (*pravāsanīya*), or perform an act of expulsion against one who should be granted formal remembrance, this is an action not in accordance with the Dharma and an action not in accordance with the Vinaya; the assembly, too, incurs guilt.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord, yet they grant a formal act of remembrance (*sativinaya*) when they should apply a disciplinary measure from the root (*mūlāpakarṣa*), or apply a disciplinary measure from the root when they should grant a formal act of remembrance—this is an action contrary to the Dharma and an action contrary to the Vinaya, and the assembly is also at fault.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and should apply a fundamental disciplinary measure to one who ought to be expelled, yet instead expels one who ought to be subjected to a fundamental measure, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; the assembly is also at fault.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and they expel one who should be granted the *amūḷhavinaya* (the verdict of not being insane), or grant the *amūḷhavinaya* to one who should be expelled, this is an action contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt.

Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in concord and should instead treat one who ought to practice humility as one deserving of discipline, or treat one who deserves discipline as one who practices humility, this is an act contrary to the Dharma and an act contrary to the Vinaya; the community also incurs guilt.

“Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in harmony and, in accordance with the action they have performed, declares that very action, then that action is in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, and the community is without fault.”

"Upāli! If a community of bhikṣus is in harmony, and they grant the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) when it should be granted; the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) when it should be granted; the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) when it should be granted; the *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by admission) when it should be granted; the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīya* (settlement by investigation of the nature of the act) when it should be granted; the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement by majority decision) when it should be granted; the *tarjanīya* (reprimand) when it should be imposed; the *nigarhaṇīya* (censure) when it should be imposed; the *pratisaṃharaṇīya* (banishment) when it should be imposed; the *utkṣepanīya* (suspension) when it should be imposed; the *pravāsanīya* (expulsion) when it should be imposed; the *āvarhaṇīya* (requiring to live in dependence) when it should be imposed; the *pratyanta-vāsa* (requiring to dwell in a remote area) when it should be imposed; and the *parivāsa* (probation) when it should be administered—then these are actions in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya, and the community is without fault."

“Upāli! You should train yourself thus: whatever action has been committed, you must declare that very action. When the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) is appropriate, you should grant the *sammukhavinaya*; when the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) is appropriate, you should grant the *smṛtivinaya*; when the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) is appropriate, you should grant the *amūḍhavinaya*; when the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya* (settlement by confession) is appropriate, you should grant the *pratijñākāraka-vinaya*; when the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement according to the majority) is appropriate, you should grant the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*; when censure (*tarjanīya*) is appropriate, you should censure; when demotion (*nigarhaṇīya*) is appropriate, you should demote; when suspension (*pravāsanīya*) is appropriate, you should suspend; when banishment (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*) is appropriate, you should banish; when reconciliation (*āpattiyā saṃvāsa*) is appropriate, you should reconcile; when treatment from the root (*mūlāpakarṣa*) is appropriate, you should treat from the root; when expulsion (*niḥsaraṇa*) is appropriate, you should expel; when the practice of non-insolence (*tassapāpiyasikā*) is appropriate, you should practice non-insolence; and when formal discipline (*parivāsa*) is appropriate, you should discipline.”
"Upāli! You should train yourself in this way.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Upāli and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

This concludes the sixth sūtra, the Upāli Sūtra, totaling one thousand five hundred and sixty-one characters. 198. The Sūtra on the Ground of the Tamer (198). Majjhima Nikāya, Mahāvagga, The Seventh Sūtra on the Ground of the Tamer, Fifth Sub-recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.
At that time, the novice Āyupāla was also wandering in Rājagṛha, staying in a meditation hut in a secluded place.

At that moment, the prince Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya, having finished his midday meal, was strolling about when he came to where the novice Āyupāla was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:
"Venerable Ākīśana!..."
"I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
The novice Āyanaṃdika replied, "O noble prince!"
"Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
The Prince asked: "Āḷāra Kālāma!"
"Is it true, bhikkhu, that within this Dhamma and Discipline you have attained heedfulness, practiced with diligence, and achieved one-pointedness of mind?
The novice replied,
"O noble prince!"
"Indeed, Bhikkhu, in this Dhamma and Vinaya, one who is heedful and practices with diligence attains one-pointedness of mind.
The Prince asked again:
"Venerable Ajjhāsaya!"

"You should tell me everything according to what you have heard and according to what you have recited and practiced—just as a bhikkhu, through heedfulness in this Dhamma and Discipline, practices with diligence and attains one-pointedness of mind."
The novice replied:
"Worthy Prince!

I am not capable of explaining to you in detail, according to what I have heard and according to what I have studied and recited, how a bhikṣu, through heedfulness within this Dharma and Vinaya, practices with diligence and attains one-pointedness of mind."
"O Prince Kalyāṇabhadrika!

If I were to speak to you, Prince Kalyāṇabhadrika, according to the Dharma as I have heard it and as I have studied and recited it—such that a bhikṣu, through heedfulness in this Dharma and Vinaya, practices with diligence and attains one-pointedness of mind—it may be that Prince Kalyāṇabhadrika would not understand it, and thus my efforts would be in vain."
The prince said to the novice:
"Venerable Ajjunna!
You have not yet been defeated by another; for what reason do you withdraw of your own accord?"
"Venerable Ajjhāsaya!

Just as you have heard the Dhamma and as you have studied and recited it, please explain it to me, so that a bhikkhu, through heedfulness in this Dhamma and Discipline, may practice with diligence and attain one-pointedness of mind."
"If I know it, that is well; if I do not know it, I shall no longer inquire further about those dharmas.

Thereupon, the novice Āyupāla, according to the Dharma he had heard and according to what he had studied and recited, spoke to Prince Jīvaka Śreṇya as follows: "In this Dharma and Vinaya, O Bhikṣu, one attains single-mindedness by practicing with heedfulness and diligence."
Then the young prince Jīvaka Śreṇyaka said: "Venerable Ājīvas!
It is impossible that a bhikṣu, being heedless within this Dharma and Vinaya, yet practices with diligence and attains one-pointedness of mind."
Having declared that such a thing was impossible, he rose from his seat and departed without taking leave.
Not long after the young prince Jīvaka Śreṇyaka had left,

the novice Ājñātakauṇḍinya went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself in salutation, withdrew to sit at one side, and related to the Buddha everything that he had discussed with the young prince Jīvaka Śreṇyaka.
Having heard this, the Blessed One said to the novice: "Aciravata!
Stop!"
"How could Prince Jīvaka Śyāma attain such a state?
He practices sensual desire, is attached to sensual desire, is devoured by the craving for sensual desire, and is burned by sensual desire.

It is impossible that there could be a place where Prince Jīvaka knows, sees, or perceives a state in which sensual desire is severed, the craving for sensual desire is severed, and the burning heat of sensual desire is severed—a state free from the knowledge of desire, free from the vision of desire, and free from the awakening to desire."
Why is that? Ācchāna!
The young prince Jīvaka Śyāmaputra constantly indulges in sensual desires.
"Āciṣṇa! It is just as there are four types of tamers:
the tamer of elephants, the tamer of horses, the tamer of oxen, and the tamer of humans; among these, two tamers are unable to tame, while two tamers are able to tame."
Āṇiḍḍhāna! What do you think?
If these two tamers were untamable—such that they were untamed, belonging to the state of the untamed, and incapable of receiving the task of taming—it would simply be impossible.

If these two trainers are capable of training, are skilled at training, and can guide those who have been trained as well as those who are yet untrained, it is certainly possible for them to receive the task of training.
Thus it is, Ācchāna! Enough!
How could Prince Jīvaka Śyāmaputra possibly obtain it?

Practicing desire and being attached to desire, one is devoured by the craving for desire and burned by desire. As for this stage where desire is severed, the craving for desire is severed, and the fever of desire is severed—where there is no more knowing of desire, no more seeing of desire, and no more perceiving of desire—it is impossible that Prince Rājakumāra could know it or see it.
Why is that? Ācchāna!
Prince Jīvaka Śreṇya constantly indulges in sensual desires.
"Ācittaka! Suppose there were a great stone mountain not far from a village—without fissures, without holes, solid and not hollow, firm and immovable, all joined together as one.
Suppose there are two people who both wish to see [the mountain]. One of them quickly climbs the mountain, while the second person remains at the foot of the mountain.

From atop the rocky mountain, the first person sees level ground by the side of the mountain, with gardens, groves, forests, clear springs, lotus ponds, long-flowing streams, and rivers. Having seen this, the person on the mountain says to the one below:
"Do you see the level ground by the side of the mountain, with its gardens, groves, forests, clear springs, lotus ponds, long-flowing streams, and rivers?"
The man from the foot of the mountain replied:
"If I were to see on that side of the mountain level ground, gardens, groves, forests, clear springs, lotus ponds, long-flowing streams, or rivers, such a thing could never be."
Thereupon, the man on the rocky mountain quickly descended, while the man at the foot of the mountain was swiftly taken up by him; having reached the top of the rocky mountain, he asked:
"Did you see by the side of the mountain a fine level plain, gardens, groves, clear springs, lotus ponds, long-flowing streams, and rivers?"
That person replied,
"I see it now for the first time.
He asked that person again:
"What you previously stated—that you saw—is ultimately impossible.
Now that you say again that you saw, what do you mean by this?
That person replied:
"I was previously obstructed by a mountain, and for that reason I did not see it.
Thus it is, Ājīveśana! Enough!
Prince Jīvaka Śyāmaputra, how could this be?

One who practices desire, is attached to desire, is devoured by the craving for desire, and is burned by desire—such a person, regarding that state where desire is severed, the craving for desire is severed, the fever of desire is severed, and there is no more knowing of desire, no more seeing of desire, and no more perceiving of desire—that Prince Jīvaka should know it or see it is simply impossible.
"Āḷavaka! In the past, King Mahāsudassana, the Kṣatriya born from the crown of the head, had an elephant-trapper to whom he said:
'You, elephant-trapper, go catch a wild elephant for me and bring it here; once you have found one, report back to me.'"
Then, having received the king’s command, the elephant trainer mounted the royal elephant and went to the forest.
There in the wilds, the trainer saw a large wild elephant; having seen it, he captured and bound it, attaching it to the neck of the royal elephant.
At that time, the king’s elephant trainer led the wild elephant out into the open air; the elephant catcher then returned to King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja and said to him:
"O Great King!..."
"Having captured the wild elephant, it has been tethered in the open air according to the King’s wish.
Upon hearing this, the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja said:
"O skilled elephant trainer!"
“You should now quickly tame this wild elephant and subdue it until it is well-trained. Once it is well-trained, return and inform me.

Thereupon, the elephant trainer, having received the king’s command, took a massive goad, slung it over his right shoulder, and went to where the wild elephant was. He set the goad on the ground, secured the elephant by its neck, and restrained its wild impulses; he removed its wild desires, stilled its wild exhaustion, and caused it to delight in the village and become accustomed to human society. Then, the elephant trainer first gave the elephant food and drink.
"Āḷavaka! When that wild elephant first receives food and drink from the elephant trainer, the skilled trainer thinks:
'Now this wild elephant will surely survive.'"
Why is that? It is because this wild elephant is receiving food and drink for the first time.

If that wild elephant receives food and drink from the elephant trainer for the first time, the skilled trainer then addresses it with gentle and pleasing words regarding its lying down and rising, its coming and going, its taking and setting aside, and its bending and stretching.

If that wild elephant follows the elephant trainer, then with gentle and pleasing words, [the trainer directs it] regarding lying down and rising, going and coming, taking up and setting aside, and bending and stretching; in this way, the wild elephant complies with the instructions of the elephant trainer.

"Āḷavaka! If that wild elephant follows the instructions of the elephant trainer, the skilled trainer then binds its two forelegs, its hind legs, its two thighs, its two flanks, its tail and spine, its head and forehead, its ears, and its tusks; he also binds its trunk and has a man hold a hook while riding upon its head. He then stations many men before it, holding swords, shields, spears, lances, halberds, axes, and battle-axes. The skilled trainer, holding a sharp spear in his hand, stands before the wild elephant and speaks these words:
'I shall now discipline you so that you do not move; discipline you so that you do not waver.'"

When that wild elephant, under the training of the elephant trainer, remains motionless, it does not lift its forefeet nor move its hindfeet; its two thighs, two flanks, tail, spine, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk all remain unshaken. Thus, the wild elephant stays with the elephant trainer, remaining unmoving.

“Āḷavaka! If that wild elephant, following the elephant trainer, does not move away, then at that time it can endure swords, shields, spears, lances, halberds, axes, and battle-axes; it can endure loud shouts and cries, as well as the blowing of conchs, the beating of drums, and the striking of bells.”

If that wild elephant is able to endure it, then at that time he is tamed, well-tamed; he attains superior taming and the most supreme taming; he is of superior swiftness and unsurpassed swiftness; he is fit to be the king’s mount, receives food from the royal granary, and is celebrated as the king’s elephant.
"So it is, Āciṣa! When a Tathāgata appears in the world—

one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a well-gone one, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people capable of being tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One— then [this occurs]."

In this world, among its gods, Māras, Brahmās, recluses, and brahmins, from humans up to the devas, he dwells having personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized [this] for himself.

He teaches the Dharma that is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is meaningful and well-phrased, complete and pure, and fully reveals the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
When the son of a householder hears the Dharma he teaches, having heard it, he gains faith in the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
Having gained faith, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and out of deep conviction left the home life for homelessness to study the Path. Ācitta!

At that time, the noble disciple goes out into the open air like a wild elephant of a king; as for that wild elephant who is greedy for and attached to sensual pleasures, it is said to be in the forest.
Āḷavaka! In this way, gods and humans are greedily attached to sensual pleasures, namely the five objects of desire: forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
When the Tathāgata first guides that bhikṣu, he says:
"You should guard the purity of your body and life; you should guard the purity of your speech, mind, and life.
If a noble disciple guards the purity of his body and life, and guards the purity of his speech, mind, and life, the Tathāgata further disciplines that bhikṣu:
"You should contemplate the internal body as body, and so on, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena.

If a noble disciple contemplates the internal body as body, and so on, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena, these four foundations of mindfulness abide within the mind of the noble disciple; they bind the mind, restrain the inclination toward the household life, eliminate thoughts of domestic desire, cease the exhaustion of worldly life, cause one to delight in the True Dharma, and cultivate the noble precepts.

Āḷavaka! It is just as when an elephant trainer, having received instructions from a Kṣatriya king born from the crown of his head, takes a massive goad, places it upon his right shoulder, and goes to where a wild elephant is; he plants the goad on the ground, fastens it around the wild elephant’s neck, restrains its wild impulses, removes its wild desires, stops its wild weariness, and causes it to delight in the village and become accustomed to loving human society.
Thus it is, Ācchana!

These four foundations of mindfulness, when present within the minds of the noble disciples, bind the mind, restrain the inclination toward the household life, eliminate thoughts of domestic desire, cease the weariness of the household, cause delight in the True Dharma, and lead to the cultivation of noble ethical discipline.

"If a noble disciple contemplates the internal body as body, and so on, up to contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena, the Tathāgata further disciplines that bhikṣu: 'You should contemplate the internal body as body;

do not attend to thoughts associated with sensual desire. Up to: you should contemplate feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena; do not attend to thoughts associated with what is contrary to the Dharma.'"

"If a noble disciple contemplates the internal body as body and does not dwell on thoughts associated with desire, and likewise contemplates feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena and does not dwell on thoughts associated with what is contrary to the Dharma, such a noble disciple follows the teaching of the Tathāgata."

Āḷavaka! It is just as when a wild elephant follows the instructions of a trainer, responding to him with gentle and pleasing words regarding his lying down and rising, his coming and going, his taking up and putting down, and his bending and stretching; in this way, the wild elephant complies with the trainer’s teaching.
In this way, Ācchana!

If a noble disciple contemplates the body internally as body, without dwelling on thoughts associated with desire, and likewise contemplates feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena, without dwelling on thoughts associated with what is not the Dharma—in this way, the noble disciple follows the teaching of the Tathāgata.
“If a noble disciple follows the teaching of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata further trains that bhikkhu:
‘You should become detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, and attain and abide in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.’”

"If a noble disciple, having detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome and evil states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna, such a noble disciple then dwells following the Tathāgata, remaining immovable."

"Āḷavaka! Just as when a wild elephant, being trained by a trainer, remains motionless, neither lifting its forefeet nor moving its hindfeet, and with its two thighs, two flanks, tail, spine, head, forehead, ears, tusks, and trunk all remaining still—thus does the wild elephant abide following the trainer without moving."
In this way, Ācchana!

If a noble disciple, having become detached from sensual desires and detached from unwholesome and evil states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna, such a noble disciple dwells following the Tathāgata, remaining immovable.

"If a noble disciple dwells in accordance with the Tathāgata and remains unshakable, then at that time he is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the oppression of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh words and the striking of staffs. Even when his body encounters various illnesses of extreme pain, such that his life is about to cease, he is able to endure all that is unpleasant."

Āṇiṣaṇḍa! It is just as when a wild elephant follows a trainer and remains stationary without moving; at that time, it endures swords, shields, spears, javelins, halberds, axes, and battle-axes, as well as loud shouts and cries, or the blowing of conchs, the beating of drums, and the striking of bells—all of which it is able to endure.
In this way, Ācchana!

If a noble disciple dwells following the Tathāgata without wavering, then at that time he is able to endure hunger and thirst, cold and heat, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, and the oppression of wind and sun; he can also endure harsh words and the striking of sticks. Even when his body encounters various diseases of extreme pain, such that his life is about to end, he is able to withstand all that is unpleasant.

"Āṇiṣaṇḍa! If a noble disciple is able to endure in accordance with the Tathāgata, at that time he is tamed and well-tamed; he attains supreme taming and the highest taming, supreme tranquility and the highest tranquility. Having eliminated all crookedness, evil, fear, delusion, and flattery, he is pure, stilled, free from dust, stainless, and unsullied. He is worthy of being invoked and invited, worthy of honor and respect, truly worthy of offerings, and serves as a fertile field of merit for all devas and humans."

Āḷavaka! Just as a wild elephant that is capable of endurance is, at that time, tamed, well-tamed, supremely tamed, most excellently tamed, swift, and unsurpassedly swift; fit for a king’s mount, receiving food from the royal granary, and celebrated as a royal elephant—so it is with you.
Thus it is, Ācittika!

If a noble disciple is able to endure in accordance with the Tathāgata, at that time he is tamed, well-tamed; he has attained supreme taming and the highest taming, supreme tranquility and the highest tranquility. Having removed all crookedness, evil, fear, delusion, and flattery, he is pure, stilled, free from dust, stainless, and unsullied. He is worthy of being addressed and invited, worthy of honor and respect, truly worthy of offerings, and serves as a fertile field of merit for all devas and humans.
“Āḷavaka! When a young wild elephant dies while unsubdued, it is said that it died unsubdued; when a middle-aged or old wild elephant dies while unsubdued, it is said that it died unsubdued.”

Ācchanna! When a junior noble disciple dies without having been disciplined, it is said that he died undisciplined; when a middle-aged or elderly noble disciple dies without having been disciplined, it is said that he died undisciplined.

Āḷavaka! When a young wild elephant dies having been well-trained, it is said that it dies well-trained; when a middle-aged or old wild elephant dies having been well-trained, it is said that it dies well-trained.
Ācittasena!

When a junior noble disciple who has well-trained himself passes away, it is said that he passes away having been well-trained; when a middle-aged or elderly noble disciple who has well-trained himself passes away, it is said that he passes away having been well-trained.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the novice Āyana and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* (or *Dharanī-dhātu-sūtra*), the seventh, ends here. [Total: 2,891 characters]. The *Madhyama Āgama*, scroll fifty-two, [total: 8,682 characters]. Fifth Subsequent Recitation.
