Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Kasmīra during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. 199.
The Discourse on the Grounds of Delusion and Wisdom (199). Section on Great Discourses, Discourse on the Grounds of Delusion and Wisdom, the Eighth; Fifth Subsequent Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now explain to you the dharmas of delusion and the dharmas of wisdom; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon them well.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"What are the dharmas of delusion?
A person of delusion has three marks, signs, and characteristics of delusion; that is to say, one who is accomplished in delusion is called a person of delusion."
What are the three?
A foolish person thinks evil thoughts, speaks evil words, and performs evil deeds; it is for this reason that a foolish person is called "foolish."
If a foolish person does not think evil thoughts, does not speak evil words, and does not perform evil deeds, one should not call that foolish person "foolish."
Because foolish people think evil thoughts, speak evil words, and perform evil deeds, it is for this reason that foolish people are called "fools.
Such foolish people, in this very life, experience three kinds of mental and physical suffering.
How is it that a foolish person experiences three kinds of mental and physical suffering?
A foolish person, whether walking about, sitting in a gathering, on a road or alley, in a marketplace, or at a crossroads, speaks of matters associated with foolishness.

The foolish person kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehoods, and even holds wrong views, as well as accomplishing other immeasurable evil and unwholesome states.
If one has accomplished immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, others, upon seeing this, will speak of those evils.
When that foolish person hears this, he thinks:

"If others, having seen someone who has accomplished immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, speak of their evils, and I too possess these same immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, then if others were to know of them, they would likewise speak of my evils."
"This is what is meant by a foolish person experiencing the foremost physical and mental suffering in this very life.
Furthermore, that foolish person sees royal officers seize a criminal and subject them to various forms of torture,
such as cutting off the hands, cutting off the feet, cutting off both hands and feet, or cutting off the ears and nose."
Furthermore, they cut off their ears and noses, or slice them into pieces; they pluck out their mustaches and hair, or pluck out both mustache and hair;
they place them in wooden cages, wrap them in cloth, and burn them with fire; or they bury them in sand, bind them with straw, and roast them with fire;
or they place them within the belly of an iron donkey, or inside the mouth of an iron pig, or within the mouth of an iron tiger to be burned.
Some are placed in copper cauldrons, or cooked in iron cauldrons; some are cut into pieces, or pierced with sharp forks, or hooked with hooks;
some are laid upon iron beds and doused with boiling oil, or seated in iron mortars and pounded with iron pestles;
some are stung by venomous dragons, or whipped with whips, or beaten with staffs.
They are beaten with clubs, or impaled alive, or their heads are decapitated and displayed.
Upon seeing this, that foolish person thinks:

"If one who has accomplished immeasurable evil and unwholesome states is caught by the king and thus punished, and I too possess these same immeasurable evil and unwholesome states, then if the king learns of them, he will likewise punish and torture me."
"In this way, it is said that the foolish person, in this very life, experiences a second kind of sorrow and suffering in body and mind.

Furthermore, when that foolish person has practiced evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, at the time he suffers from illness—whether sitting or lying on a bed, a couch, or on the ground—extreme and intense pain arises in his body, even to the point where his life is about to cease."

Whatever unwholesome conduct he has engaged in through body, speech, and mind, at that time it hangs suspended above him; just as in the late afternoon, when the sun descends behind a high mountain, its shadow hangs suspended upon the ground, so too do his unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind hang suspended above him at that time.
He thinks to himself:
"These were my own evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, which now hang suspended above me.

In the past, I failed to perform merit and committed much evil. If there is a place for those who commit evil, who are violent and act unrighteously, who fail to perform merit, fail to do good, and fail to feel dread—wherever one must go for refuge and reliance—I shall go to that evil destination."
From this, remorse arises; having given rise to remorse, one dies unvirtuous and passes away with an unwholesome end.
This is called the third kind of sorrow and suffering that a foolish person experiences in this present life, affecting both body and mind.

"Furthermore, that foolish person engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. Having engaged in such misconduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will certainly go to a state of misery and be reborn in hell."
Having been born there, one undergoes painful retribution that is entirely unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable to the mind. If one were to say:
"That which is entirely unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable to the mind is called hell."
"Why is this? Because that hell is exclusively unlovely, unpleasant, and not to be thought of with a favorable mind.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the suffering of hell?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Monks! The hells cannot be fully described, namely the suffering of the hells. Monks!”
"However, the suffering of hell consists solely of suffering.
The bhikṣu asked again:
"World-Honored One!"
"It may be possible to illustrate this meaning through a simile.
The World-Honored One replied,
"It may indeed be possible to illustrate this meaning through a simile."
"Monks! It is just as when royal officers arrest a thief and bring him before the Kṣatriya King Mūrdhaja, saying:
'O Heavenly King!'"
"This man is a thief and guilty; we pray that the Great King will punish him.
King Kṣatriya Śiromaṇi replied, "Take him away and punish this man’s crime: in the morning, pierce him with a hundred spears."
The king’s men received their instructions and took him away to be executed; they pierced him with a hundred spears at dawn, yet the man continued to live.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked:
"What is the state of that man?"
The king's men replied:
"O Heavenly King!
That man is still alive."
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja spoke again, saying:
"Go! At midday, pierce them once more with a hundred spears."
The king’s men followed these instructions; at midday they pierced the man again with a hundred spears, yet he remained alive.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked again:
“What is the state of that man?”
The king’s men replied,
“O Great King!
That man is still alive.”
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja spoke again, saying:
"Go! At sunset, pierce him once more with a hundred spears."

The king’s men followed these instructions; at sunset they pierced him again with a hundred spears. Although that man remained alive, his entire body was perforated, pierced, shattered, and utterly destroyed, such that not a single spot remained intact, appearing like holes for coins.
King Kṣatriya Mūrdhaja asked again:
"What is that person like?
The royal official replied:
"O Heavenly King!
That person continues to live, yet his entire body is pierced, split, shattered, and utterly destroyed, such that there is not a single spot remaining intact, even as small as a hole for a coin."
“Bhikṣus! What do you think?
If that person were pierced by three hundred spears in a single day, would that person’s body and mind suffer affliction and extreme distress because of it?”
The bhikṣu replied, “World-Honored One!

If one were pierced by a single spear, one would still experience extreme suffering; how much more so when receiving three hundred spear thrusts in a single day—would that person’s body and mind not be afflicted with intense distress and suffering?”
Thereupon, the Blessed One took a pebble from his hand, which was like a small bean, and said: "Bhikkhu,
do you see this pebble I have taken from my hand, which is like a small bean?"
The bhikkhu replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One asked again:
"Bhikkhu, what do you think?"
“I have taken up a pebble, like a small bean; compared to the King of Mountains, the Himālayas, which is the greater?
The bhikṣu replied:

“World-Honored One, the pebble held in Your hand, like a small bean, when compared to the King of Mountains, the Himālayas, falls short by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and even a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold. It cannot be counted, it cannot be calculated, it cannot be illustrated, and it cannot be compared; the King of Mountains, the Himālayas, is simply immense and exceedingly great.”
The World-Honored One said:

"Bhikṣus! If I were to take a pebble the size of a small bean and compare it to the King of Mountains, the Himavat, it would not come close by even a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold. It could not be counted, nor calculated, nor illustrated by analogy, nor compared; the King of Mountains, the Himavat, is simply immense and exceedingly great."
In this way, bhikṣus!

Even if such a person were pierced by three hundred spears in a single day, the extremely heavy suffering and grief experienced by body and mind on account of that would not—by any measure—approach even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the suffering of hell; it cannot be counted, it cannot be calculated, it cannot be illustrated, and it cannot be compared, for the suffering within hell is simply ultimate and most intense.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and, with iron axes blazing and glowing with heat, fashion their bodies—either making them octagonal, or hexagonal, or square, or round; or making them high, or low, or beautiful, or ugly.”

Thus they are interrogated and tortured, oppressed by painful sensations for many years, even up to hundreds of thousands; they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and intense, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and, with iron axes blazing and glowing all over, they fashion their bodies—making them octagonal, or hexagonal, or square, or round; making them high or low, or beautiful or ugly.”

Thus subjected to such interrogation and punishment, oppressed by pain for many years—even up to hundreds of thousands—they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and extreme suffering, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and force them to sit upon iron spears that are glowing and blazing with heat. Then, using iron tongs, they pry open their mouths and place glowing, blazing iron balls inside. These burn the lips, burn the tongue, burn the gums, burn the throat, burn the heart, and burn the stomach, passing out through the lower part of the body.”

Thus subjected to such interrogation and torture, oppressed by painful sensations for many years—even up to hundreds of thousands—they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and intense, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hands and force them to sit upon iron spikes that are glowing and blazing all over. Then, with iron tongs, they pry open their mouths and pour molten copper into their mouths; it burns the lips, burns the tongue, burns the gums, burns the throat, burns the heart, and burns the stomach, before exiting from below the body.”

Thus subjected to such interrogation and torture, they are oppressed by suffering for many years, even up to hundreds of thousands; they undergo immeasurable suffering, most heavy and extreme pain, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.
“Bhikṣus! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hands and force them to lie face up upon an iron ground that is glowing and blazing all over. They are subjected to the ‘five-fold binding’ torture: their two hands, two feet, and their abdomen are each pierced with iron nails.

Thus subjected to such interrogation and torture, oppressed by pain for many years—up to hundreds of thousands—they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and intense, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Bhikṣus! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and force them to prostrate upon the ground of iron, which is glowing and blazing all over. They pull their tongues from their mouths and stretch them out with a hundred nails until they are without wrinkles or shrinkage, just like a cowhide stretched out with a hundred nails until it is without wrinkles or shrinkage.”

Thus, when beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and force them to prostrate upon a floor of iron that is glowing and blazing all over; then, having pulled their tongues from their mouths, they stretch them out with a hundred nails so that they are neither wrinkled nor shriveled.

Thus subjected to such tortures and oppressed by agony for many years—up to hundreds of thousands—they undergo immeasurable suffering, most heavy and extreme, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Bhikṣus! What is the suffering of the hells? Beings are born in the hells;

once born there, the wardens seize them by the scalp with their hands and flay the skin down to their feet, then flay the skin from their feet up to their heads. They then bind them to iron chariots that are blazing and glowing with heat, and lead them back and forth across an iron ground that is likewise blazing and glowing with heat.”

Thus subjected to such tortures and oppressed by pain for many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, they undergo immeasurable suffering—extremely heavy and intense suffering—yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Bhikṣus! What is the suffering of the hells?

When beings are born in the hells, once they have been born there, the wardens take blazing, fiercely burning fire, make them toss it onto the ground, and then make them take it up with their hands and pour it over their own bodies.”

Thus subjected to such tortures and oppressed by painful sensations for many years, even up to hundreds of thousands, they undergo immeasurable suffering—extremely heavy and most intense—yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted; this is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of the hells?

When sentient beings are born in the hells, once they have been born there, the wardens take a mountain of fire, blazing and fiercely aflame, and make them walk up and down upon it. If they set their feet down, their skin, flesh, and blood are instantly consumed by the flames; when they lift their feet, their skin, flesh, and blood grow back just as they were before.”

Thus subjected to such interrogation and torture, they are oppressed by pain for many years, even up to hundreds of thousands; they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and intense, yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell?

When beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hands and, taking a great iron cauldron that is glowing and blazing with heat, they lift their bodies upside down—feet up and head down—and place them inside the cauldron. There, within it, they move either upward or downward, or toward the cardinal directions; from their own bodies, froth emerges and boils back over them. It is just as when black beans, mung beans, kidney beans, bitter beans, or mustard seeds are placed in a cauldron filled with much water and a fire is lit fiercely beneath it; those beans within move either upward or downward, or toward the cardinal directions, being boiled while enveloped by their own froth.”

Thus, when beings are born in hell, once they have been born there, the wardens seize them by the hand and, with a great iron cauldron blazing with intense heat, lift their bodies up and place them inside with feet above and heads below. Within that cauldron, whether moving upward or downward, or toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, froth issues from their own bodies and boils back upon them.

Thus subjected to such interrogation and torture, oppressed by pain for many years—even up to hundreds of thousands—they undergo immeasurable suffering, most grievous and intense; yet they do not die until their evil and unwholesome karma is exhausted. This is called the suffering of hell.
“Monks! What is the suffering of hell? Within that hell there is a place called the Sixfold Contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

If a being is born there, once born, whatever forms they see with the eye are neither pleasant nor agreeable, not such as to be delightful; the mind is not moistened by them, not such as to be moistened; the mind does not find joy in them, not such as to find joy. Whatever sounds are heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, tastes tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, or mental phenomena known by the mind, these are neither pleasant nor agreeable, not such as to be delightful; the mind is not moistened by them, not such as to be moistened; the mind does not find joy in them, not such as to find joy. This is called the suffering of hell.”

“Monks! For you, I have used countless skillful means to describe those hells and to speak of the matters of hell; yet the suffering of these hells cannot be fully described—there is only suffering in hell.”
“Bhikṣus!
If a foolish person, at some time, emerges from hell and is born among animals, the state of being an animal is also extremely painful.
“Bhikṣus! [he said.]
What is the suffering of animals?
If a being is born among animals—meaning they are born in darkness, grow up in darkness, and die in darkness—what is that like?
This refers to the worms born from the earth.

As for the foolish person, because they were formerly attached to the flavors of food, they committed evil deeds of body, and committed evil deeds of speech and mind. Having committed those evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, on that account and by that condition, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among animals—specifically, being born in darkness, growing in darkness, and dying in darkness; this is called the suffering of animals.
“Monks! What is the suffering of animals?
It is when beings are born among animals—born within their bodies, grow within their bodies, and die within their bodies.”
What is it? It is called the "wound-worm.

As for the foolish person, because they were formerly attached to the flavors of food, they committed evil deeds of body, and committed evil deeds of speech and mind. Having committed those evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, on account of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among animals—meaning they are born within a body, grow within a body, and die within a body; this is called the suffering of animals.
“Monks! What is the suffering of animals?
It is when beings are born among animals—born in water, grow in water, and die in water.”
What are they? They are the fish, the makara, the tortoise, the crocodile, the *pāruṇī*, the *tibi*, the *tibigāra*, and the *titibigāra*.
The foolish person, due to their former attachment to the taste of food, engages in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind.

Having engaged in such misconduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among animals—specifically those born in water, growing in water, and dying in water; this is called the suffering of animals.
“Monks! What is the suffering of animals?
If a being is born among animals, they are those that live by gnawing with their teeth and eat grass and trees.”
What are they? They are elephants, horses, camels, oxen, donkeys, deer, water buffaloes, and pigs.

A foolish person, due to their former attachment to the taste of food, engages in bodily misconduct and misconduct of speech and mind. Having engaged in such bodily, verbal, and mental misconduct, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among animals—namely, those that live by gnawing on grass and trees for food; this is called the suffering of animals.
“Bhikkhus! What is the suffering of animals?

If a being is born among animals, they smell the scent of human excrement and urine and immediately run toward it to eat that food. It is just as when men and women smell the fragrance of food and drink and immediately go toward it; in this same way, it is said that they eat that food.”
In this way, bhikṣus!
If a being is born among the animals, upon hearing the scent of human excrement and urine, it immediately runs toward it and eats that food.
What are they? They are chickens, pigs, dogs, jackals, crows, *kūlīras*, and *kuraṅgas*.
As for the foolish person, because of their prior attachment to the flavors of food, they engage in misconduct of body, and misconduct of speech and mind.

Having engaged in misconduct of body and misconduct of speech and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn among animals—namely, those that eat excrement and impurities; this is called the suffering of animals.

“Monks! For you, I have used countless skillful means to speak of those animals and to speak of the affairs of animals; yet the suffering of these animals cannot be fully described—there is only suffering in the realm of animals.”
“Monks! It is extremely difficult for a foolish person who has emerged from the animal realm to be reborn as a human being. Why is that?

Among those animals, benevolence and righteousness are not practiced; rites and laws are not observed; and sublime goodness is not cultivated. Those animals devour one another: the strong eat the weak, and the large eat the small.

"Monks! Suppose this earth were filled with water, and there was a blind turtle whose lifespan lasted for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years. Upon that water floated a small, light wooden board with only a single hole, being driven about by the wind."
"Monks! What do you think?
Would that blind turtle’s head ever manage to enter the single hole of this small, light wooden plank?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“World-Honored One!
It may indeed be possible to enter, but it would take a very long time and be exceedingly difficult.”
The Blessed One said:

"Monks, suppose that at some time, after a hundred years have passed, a blind turtle should emerge from the east and raise its head once; meanwhile, that small wooden board with a single hole, driven by an easterly wind, has been moved to the south."
Suppose that at some time, after a hundred years have passed, a blind turtle surfaces once from the south, and that single-holed board, driven by a southern wind, has moved to the west.

Suppose that at some time, after a hundred years have passed, a blind turtle should emerge from the west and raise its head once; meanwhile, that single-holed board, driven by a westerly wind, has been moved to the north.
Suppose at some time a blind turtle were to come from the north and raise its head once, while that single-holed board, driven by the north wind,
were drifting in all directions. Bhikṣus, what do you think?
“Would that blind turtle’s head ever manage to enter this single hole in the plank?
The bhikṣu replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"Or one might be able to enter it, but only after a very long time and with great difficulty. Bhikṣus!
In this same way, it is also extremely difficult for that foolish person to emerge from the animal realm and be reborn as a human."

Why is this so? Among those animals, benevolence and righteousness are not practiced; ritual and law are not observed; and sublime goodness is not cultivated. Those animals prey upon one another: the strong devour the weak, and the large devour the small.

"Monks! If a foolish person should at some time emerge from the animal realm and be reborn as a human, if he has a family, it will be of low standing and humble birth, wretched and impoverished, with little food and drink—meaning that obtaining food is extremely difficult."

What are they? They are the families of jailers, craftsmen, artisans, and potters; such other low-caste families as these, who are wretched, evil, and impoverished, possessing little food and drink, meaning that it is extremely difficult for them to obtain food.

Born into such a family, once born there, they may be blind or lame, have short arms or elbows, or be hunchbacked; they may be left-handed, have a foul complexion, or the face of a sheep; being ugly and short-lived, they are employed by others. They engage in bodily misconduct, as well as verbal and mental misconduct.

Having engaged in misconduct of body, and having engaged in misconduct of speech and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he returns to a state of woe and is reborn in hell.

"It is just as if two people were playing a game of dice together, and one of them, having first taken such a course of action, lost his slaves and servants, lost his wife and children, and further took himself and hung upside down in a smoke-filled room.
He would think: 'I shall neither eat nor drink, for I have already taken such a course of action.'"
"Consequently, he loses his slaves and servants and loses his wife and children; furthermore, he takes his own body and hangs it upside down inside a smoke-filled house. Monks!

This practice yields very little fruit, resulting in the loss of slaves and servants, the loss of wife and children, and further taking one's own body and hanging it upside down inside a smoke-filled house."
"Monks! This is what is practiced by one who practices: practicing bodily misconduct, and practicing verbal and mental misconduct.

Having practiced bodily misconduct and practiced verbal and mental misconduct, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he goes to a state of misery and is reborn in hell."
"Monks! These conditioned phenomena are utterly unlovely, truly not delightful, and not to be cherished by the mind. Monks!"
"Is it not for the sake of fully explaining the dharma of delusion?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Indeed it is."
“World-Honored One!
Are you teaching the dharma of folly in its entirety?
The World-Honored One replied:
"What is the dharma of wisdom?
That person of wisdom possesses three characteristics of wisdom, marks of wisdom, and images of wisdom; that is to say, the person who has accomplished wisdom speaks of wisdom."
What are these three?
A person of wisdom thinks wholesome thoughts, speaks wholesome words, and performs wholesome deeds; it is for this reason that a person of wisdom is called "wise."

If a wise person does not contemplate what is worthy of contemplation, does not speak what is worthy of being spoken, and does not perform what is worthy of being performed, one should not call that wise person "wise."
Because a wise person thinks what is wholesome, speaks what is wholesome, and acts what is wholesome, that wise person is said to possess wisdom.
Such a wise person, in this very life, experiences three kinds of joy and happiness within body and mind.
How does a wise person experience three kinds of joy and happiness in this very life, both physically and mentally?
A wise person—whether walking about, sitting in an assembly, on a road or in an alley, in a marketplace, or at a crossroads—speaks of matters corresponding to the wisdom of the wise.

A wise person abandons killing, desists from killing, abandons taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech; they even abandon wrong view to attain right view, and further accomplish immeasurable other wholesome dharmas.
If one has accomplished immeasurable wholesome qualities, others, upon seeing them, will praise them.
When that wise person hears this, they think:

"If others, upon seeing someone who has accomplished immeasurable wholesome qualities, praise them, then I too possess these immeasurable wholesome qualities; if others were to know of them, they would surely praise me as well."
This is called the wise person experiencing the foremost joy and happiness of body and mind within this present life.
Furthermore, that wise person also sees the king’s men inflicting various punishments upon criminals, namely:
cutting off hands, cutting off feet, cutting off both hands and feet; cutting off ears, cutting off noses, and cutting off both ears and noses.
Some are cut into pieces; their beards are plucked out, their hair is plucked out, or both beard and hair are plucked out.
Some are placed inside wooden cages, wrapped in cloth, and burned with fire; some are buried in sand, bound in straw, and roasted by fire;
some are placed within the belly of an iron donkey; some are put into the mouth of an iron pig; some are set within the mouth of an iron tiger to be burned; or they are placed in a copper cauldron.
Within [the hells], some are boiled in iron cauldrons; some are cut into pieces; some are pierced with sharp forks;
some are hooked with iron hooks; some are laid upon iron beds and doused with boiling oil; some are seated in iron mortars and pounded with iron pestles;
some are stung by venomous dragons; some are whipped with whips; some are beaten with canes; or some are struck with clubs.
They beat them, or impale them alive on stakes, or decapitate them.
When a wise person sees this, they reflect:
"If one has committed immeasurable evil and unwholesome deeds, the king, having learned of it and apprehended them, subjects them to such punishment."
"I do not possess such immeasurable evil and unwholesome states; if the King were to know this, he would never punish me with such severity.
This is called the second kind of joy and happiness that a wise person experiences in this very life, pertaining to both body and mind.

"Furthermore, when that wise person practices sublime conduct of body and practices sublime conduct of speech and mind, at a time when he is afflicted by illness—whether lying on a bed, or lying on a couch, or lying on the ground—and his body experiences extreme pain and very heavy suffering, even to the point where life is about to cease."

Whatever wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind he possesses at that time hangs suspended above him; just as when the sun descends a high mountain in the late afternoon, its shadow hangs suspended upon the ground, so too do his wholesome conducts of body, speech, and mind hang suspended above him at that time.
He thinks to himself:
"These are my own bodily, verbal, and mental wholesome deeds that hang suspended above me; in the past, I did no evil and performed much merit."

If there is a place where one does no evil, is not violent, and performs no irrational acts; where one performs merit, performs good, and performs what inspires awe; which is a refuge and a reliance—may I go to that auspicious place.
"And he does not give rise to regret; having not given rise to regret, he dies as a noble one with a good passing.
This is called the third kind of joy and happiness that a wise person experiences in this very life, pertaining to both body and mind.

"Furthermore, that wise person practices sublime conduct of body, and practices sublime conduct of speech and mind. Having practiced sublime conduct of body, speech, and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn in a heavenly realm."
Having been born there, one experiences pleasant retribution that is entirely desirable, entirely delightful, and agreeable to the mind. If one should think:
"That which is entirely desirable, entirely delightful, and agreeable to the mind is called a wholesome state."
"Why is that? Because that which is a wholesome state is entirely lovely, entirely delightful, and worthy of being cherished by the mind.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“World-Honored One!
What is the bliss of the well-placed?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Bhikkhus! The good destination cannot be fully described; that is to say, the good destination is happiness, and in the good destination there is only happiness.
The bhikkhus asked again:
“World-Honored One,
may an analogy be used to manifest this meaning?
The World-Honored One replied:
"This can also serve as a metaphor to manifest its meaning.
It is like a wheel-turning monarch who has attained the seven treasures and the four bases of supernormal power.
O Bhikṣus!"
What do you think?
Does that wheel-turning monarch, having accomplished the seven treasures and the four bases of supernormal power, experience extreme joy and happiness in body and mind because of them?
The bhikkhu replied:
“World-Honored One!

If one who possesses a single treasure and the supernormal power of a single person still experiences supreme joy and happiness, how much more so for a Wheel-Turning King who possesses the seven treasures and the four kinds of supernormal powers of a person—would he not experience supreme joy and happiness?”
Thereupon, the Blessed One took a pebble from his hand, about the size of a small bean, and said: "Bhikkhu,
do you see this pebble I have taken from my hand, which is like a small bean?"
The bhikkhu replied:
“I have seen them,
World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One asked again:
"Bhikkhu, what do you think?"
“I have taken up a pebble, like a small bean; compared to the King of Mountains, the Himavat, which is the greater?
The bhikṣu replied:

“World-Honored One, the pebble held in Your hand, like a small bean, compared to the King of Mountains, the Himavat, falls short by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousand-ten-thousandfold. It cannot be counted, it cannot be calculated, it cannot be illustrated, and it cannot be compared; the King of Mountains, the Himavat, is simply immense and exceedingly great.”
The Blessed One said:

“Monks, if I were to take a pebble the size of a small bean and compare it to the King of Mountains, the Himālayas, it would not come within a hundredth, a thousandth, or even a hundred-thousand-millionth part; it could not be counted, calculated, illustrated by analogy, or compared at all. Only the King of Mountains is truly great and exceedingly vast.”
Thus it is, bhikṣus!

If a wheel-turning monarch possesses the seven treasures and the four bases of supernormal power, the physical and mental bliss he experiences exceeds that of the gods by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or even a hundred-thousand-millionfold; it can never be equaled. It is beyond counting, beyond calculation, beyond analogy, and beyond comparison. This is what is called the bliss of the auspicious realm, for in the auspicious realm there is only bliss.
“Monks! What is the happiness of the good destination?
There is a good destination called the six bases of contact (ṣaḍ-āyatanāni).”

If beings are born therein, once they have been born there, if their eyes see forms that are pleasing to the mind, those are pleasing; if they are objects of mental moisture and affection, those are objects of moisture and affection; if they are objects of mental delight, those are objects of delight.

The sounds heard by the ear, the odors smelled by the nose, the flavors tasted by the tongue, the tangibles felt by the body, and the mental objects known by the mind—whatever is pleasing to the mind is indeed pleasing; whatever is cherished and beloved by the mind is indeed cherished and beloved; whatever is well-liked by the mind is indeed well-liked. This is called the happiness of the wholesome state.

"Monks! For you, I have used countless skillful means to speak of that auspicious realm and the matters pertaining to that auspicious realm. Yet, the bliss of this auspicious realm cannot be fully described; there is only bliss in the auspicious realm."
“Bhikkhus! Suppose a wise person, having at some time come from a good destination, is reborn here among humans.

If he belongs to a family that is extremely wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable wealth and property, many livestock, fiefdoms and food-grant villages, abundant rice and grain, as well as various kinds of household requisites—what do you think of him?”

That is to say, among the families of great kṣatriya householders, great brahmin householders, and great householder householders, as well as others who are exceedingly wealthy and prosperous, possessing immeasurable riches, numerous livestock, fiefdoms, food estates, and abundant rice and grain, along with various kinds of articles for daily life.

Born into such a family, he is handsome and lovely, respected and compliant by all, possessing great renown, great majesty and virtue, beloved by many, and cherished by many; he practices sublime conduct of body, and practices sublime conduct of speech and mind.

Having practiced excellent conduct of body and having practiced excellent conduct of speech and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, he returns to a good destination and is reborn among the devas.
"It is just as if two people were gambling together, and one of them, having initially adopted such a practice, won much wealth. He would think to himself:
'I did not engage in farming, yet by initially adopting such a practice, I have won much wealth.'"
"Monks! This practice is very meager, namely, the acquisition of much wealth. Monks!"
This refers to one who practices these courses of action: practicing excellent conduct of body, and practicing excellent conduct of speech and mind.

Having practiced excellent conduct of body and excellent conduct of speech and mind, because of this and conditioned by this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they go to a good destination and are reborn among the devas.
"Monks! These formations are the most beloved, the most delightful, and the most cherished of all formations. Monks!"
“Is it not for the sake of fully explaining the Dharma for those who possess wisdom?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed it is.”
“World-Honored One!
Please explain in full the Dharma for those who possess wisdom.
The World-Honored One replied:

"These are called the qualities of foolish people and the qualities of wise people. You should know the qualities of foolish people and the qualities of wise people; having known the qualities of foolish people and the qualities of wise people, you should abandon the qualities of foolish people and adopt the qualities of wise people. You should train yourselves in this way."
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Dhīprajñābhūmi Sūtra*, the eighth, ends here; it contains 5,638 characters. The *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 53, contains 5,638 characters. This concludes the fifth subsequent recitation.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 54.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
200. The Ariṣṭa Sūtra (200). The Ninth Sūtra of the Great Section, The Ariṣṭa Sūtra; Fifth Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, formerly a gaṇadhara, gave rise to this evil view:
"I understand the Blessed One to have taught that one who indulges in sensual desires encounters no obstacles.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa and asked him, "Ariṣṭa!"
"Is it true that you have spoken thus:
'I understand the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in such a way that one who engages in sensual desires encounters no obstacles'?
At that time, Ariṣṭa replied:
“Venerable friends!
I truly know that the Blessed One has taught the Dharma in this way: ‘For one who engages in sensual desires, there is no obstruction.
The bhikṣus rebuked Ariṣṭa, saying:
"Do not speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One does not speak in such a way, Āḷavaka!"
Sensual desire is an obstacle; the Blessed One has taught through immeasurable skillful means that sensual desire is an obstacle.
Ariṭṭha! You should quickly abandon this evil view.
After the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa had been rebuked by the other bhikṣus, he stubbornly clung to this evil view with great force and spoke categorically:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
Thus they spoke a second and a third time.

Being unable to cause the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to relinquish this evil view, the many bhikṣus rose from their seats and departed. They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, sat down to one side, and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa gave rise to this evil view:
"I understand the World-Honored One to have taught this Dharma:
'There is no obstacle for one who engages in sensual desires.'"
"World-Honored One!
Having heard this, we went to where the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was and asked him: 'Ariṣṭa!'"
Do you truly say this:
"I understand the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma thus:
'For one who engages in sensual desires, there is no obstruction'?"
The bhikkhu Ariṭṭha replied to us, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I truly know that the Blessed One has taught the Dharma in this way:"
"One who indulges in sensual desires has no obstacles.
World-Honored One!
We rebuked him, saying:
"Āḷavaka! Do not speak thus;
do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak in such a way."
Āḷavaka! Sensual desire is an obstacle;
with immeasurable skillful means, the Blessed One has taught that sensual desire is an obstacle. Āḷavaka!
"You should quickly abandon this evil view.
After we had thus rebuked him, he stubbornly clung to that evil view with great force and spoke resolutely:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
"World-Honored One!
Just as we were unable to cause the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to abandon this evil view, we rose from our seats and departed."
Having heard this, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa and say to him:
'The Blessed One calls for you!'"

Thereupon, a certain bhikṣu, having received the instruction of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was and said to him:
“The Blessed One calls for you!”
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One asked him: “Ariṣṭa!”
Indeed, he spoke thus:
"I understand the Blessed One to have taught this Dharma:
'For one who indulges in sensual desires, there is no obstruction.'"
"Is this so? Āḷavaka replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"I truly understand the Blessed One to have taught this Dharma:
'For one who indulges in sensual desires, there is no obstruction.
The Blessed One rebuked him, saying:
"Āḷavaka! How do you know that I have taught the Dharma in such a way?
From whose mouth did you hear me teaching the Dharma in this manner?"
"You foolish person!
I do not speak categorically; you, however, speak categorically?
You foolish person!"
"I have heard that when the bhikṣus reproached you together, you should have answered them in accordance with the Dharma at that time, saying:
'I shall now question the bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One questioned the bhikṣus:
"Do you also understand my teaching of the Dharma in this way:
'For one who engages in sensual desires,
there is no obstacle'?"
At that time, the bhikṣus replied,
“No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked:
"How do you understand the Dharma I have taught?
The bhikṣus replied,
"We understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma in this way:"
"Sensual desires are an obstacle," so the Blessed One has said; sensual desires are an obstacle.
"Sensual desires are like a chain of bones," so the Blessed One has said; sensual desires are like a chain of bones.
Sensual desires are like a piece of meat; the World-Honored One has said that sensual desires are like a piece of meat.
Sensual desires are like a torch; the World-Honored One has said that sensual desires are like a torch.
Sensual desires are like a pit of fire; the World-Honored One has said that sensual desires are like a pit of fire.
Desire is like a venomous snake; the World-Honored One has said that desire is like a venomous snake.
Desire is like a dream; the World-Honored One has said that desire is like a dream.
Desire is like a borrowed thing; the World-Honored One has said that desire is like a borrowed thing.
“Sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree; the Blessed One has said that sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree.
We understand the Blessed One to have taught the Dharma in this way.
The Blessed One praised them, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent, monks!”
"You all should understand that I teach the Dharma in this way. Why is this?
For I also teach it thus:"
"Sensual desires are obstacles," I say; sensual desires are obstacles.
"Sensual desires are like a chain of bones," I say; sensual desires are like a chain of bones.
Sensual desire is like a piece of meat; I say sensual desire is like a piece of meat.
Sensual desire is like a torch held in the hand; I say sensual desire is like a torch held in the hand.
Sensual desire is like a pit of fire; I say sensual desire is like a pit of fire.
Sensual desire is like a venomous snake; I say that sensual desire is like a venomous snake.
Sensual desire is like a dream; I say that sensual desire is like a dream.
Sensual desire is like a borrowed object; I say that sensual desire is like a borrowed object.
"Sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree; I say that sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
You all understand my teaching of the Dharma in this way.
However, this foolish man Ariṣṭa has misunderstood both the meaning and the letter in a distorted manner.

Because he has understood and accepted this through his own perversion, he slanders me to his own detriment; he commits an offense and incurs guilt, which is displeasing to all wise practitioners of the holy life, and he thereby incurs great demerit.
"You foolish man!
Do you know that there is such an evil and unwholesome state?

Thereupon, having been rebuked face-to-face by the Blessed One, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa harbored grief within; with his head bowed and silent, he lost his eloquence and remained speechless, as if brooding over something.
Thereupon, having rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa face-to-face, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you fully understand the meaning of the Dharma as I have taught it, you should uphold it in this manner."
If there are those who do not fully understand the meaning of the Dharma I have taught, they should question me and other wise fellow practitioners of the holy life.

Why is this? There may be foolish people who misinterpret both the meaning and the phrasing; because they have misinterpreted them for themselves, they come to understand that Dharma—namely the discourses (*sutta*), songs (*geyya*), prophecies (*veyyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), causal narratives (*udāna*), legends (*itivuttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), past lives (*abbhutadhamma*), and expositions (*vedalla*)—in such and such a way. They contend over their understanding of this meaning and do not accept the understanding of liberation regarding this meaning. Though they claim to know this Dharma, they do not attain its true meaning; they merely undergo extreme suffering and exhaust themselves in vain.
Why is this? It is because they have received and understood the Dharma through inversion.
"It is like a person who, wishing to catch a snake, goes about searching for one."

While seeking a snake, he was walking through a forest wilderness when he saw an enormous serpent. He immediately stepped forward and seized it by its waist with his hand; the snake turned around and raised its head, perhaps biting his hands, feet, or other limbs.
That person’s endeavor to seek and seize the snake fails to achieve its purpose; he merely undergoes extreme suffering and exhausts himself in vain.
Why is this? It is because he does not properly understand the method for seizing a snake.

In this way, there may be some deluded persons who misinterpret both the meaning and the phrasing. Because they have misinterpreted them for themselves, they understand those teachings—namely, the discourses (*sūtra*), songs (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), causal narratives (*nidāna*), legends (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), past lives (*vaipulya*), marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*), and expositions (*upadeśa*)—in such and such a manner.

Those who dispute know this meaning, yet they do not accept it for the sake of liberation; those who act upon knowing these teachings fail to attain their true meaning, undergoing only extreme suffering and exhausting themselves in vain.
Why is this? It is because they have received and understood the Dharma through inversion.

However, there may be sons of good family who do not invert [the truth] and properly receive and understand both the meaning and the phrasing. Because they do not invert and properly receive and understand, they know those teachings accordingly—namely, the discourses (*sūtra*), songs (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), causal narratives (*nidāna*), legends (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), past occurrences (*vaipulya*), marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*), and expositions of the meaning (*upadeśa*).

He does not strive to know this meaning; rather, he knows this meaning solely through the acceptance of liberation. He knows this Dharma for its own sake and attains this meaning without undergoing extreme suffering or becoming exhausted.
Why is this? It is because they understand and comprehend the Dharma without inversion.
"It is like a person who, wishing to catch a snake, goes about searching for one."

When he was searching for snakes, he carried an iron staff in his hand and walked through the wild forests; there he saw an extremely large snake. First, he pressed down on the snake’s head with the iron staff and seized its head with his hand. Although the snake turned its tail back and coiled around his hands, feet, and other limbs, it was unable to bite him.
That person, seeking to catch a snake, achieves this objective without undergoing extreme suffering or becoming exhausted.
Why is this? It is because he has skillfully mastered the method for seizing snakes.

In this way, there may be a son of good family who correctly and skillfully receives and understands both the meaning and the phrasing. Because he correctly and skillfully receives and understands them, he comes to know those teachings as they truly are—namely, the discourses (*sūtra*), chants (*geya*), prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), causal narratives (*nidāna*), legends (*itivṛttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), past events (*vaipulya*), marvelous accounts (*adbhutadharma*), and expositions (*upadeśa*). He does not dispute over the knowledge of this meaning; rather, he accepts and understands this meaning solely for the sake of liberation.
One who knows this Dharma and attains this meaning for that purpose will not undergo extreme suffering, nor will they become weary. Why is this?
Because they receive and understand the Dharma without inversion.
"For a long night, I have taught you the Dharma through the parable of the raft, desiring that you abandon it, not that you should grasp it.
How is it that for a long night I have taught you the Dharma through the parable of the raft, desiring that you abandon it, not that you should grasp it?"
It is like a mountain river that is exceedingly deep and vast, with a long current flowing so swiftly that it sweeps away much;
within it there is neither boat nor bridge. Suppose a person comes who has business on the other bank and wishes to cross; while seeking to cross, he thinks to himself:

"This mountain river is exceedingly deep and vast, with a long current flowing so swiftly that it sweeps away much; within it there is neither boat nor bridge by which one may cross. Since I have business on the other bank and wish to cross, by what skillful means can I reach the other bank in safety?"
Again, he thought:
"I would rather now gather grass and wood on this bank, bind them together to make a raft, and cross over by means of it."
He then gathered grass and wood on the bank and bound them together to make a raft. Mounting it, he crossed over and reached the other shore in safety.
He then thought to himself:

"This raft of mine has been of great benefit; having mounted it, it has enabled me to come safely from the far shore and cross to this shore. I should now perhaps place it upon my right shoulder or carry it on my head as I go."
"He would then place the raft on his right shoulder or carry it on his head as he departed.
What do you think?
Having done such a thing, would that raft be of any benefit to him?"
At that time, the bhikṣus replied,
“No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"How does that person find benefit from what was done with the raft?
That person reflects thus:
'This raft of mine has been of great benefit; having mounted this raft, it has brought me safely from the further shore to this shore.'"
"Shall I now rather place this raft back into the water, or set it on the bank, and then depart?
That person then placed the raft back into the water, or set it on the bank, and abandoned it before leaving.
"What do you think?
By doing such a thing, would that raft be of any benefit?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied:
"It is beneficial.
The World-Honored One replied, "It is so."
For a long night, I have taught you the Dharma through the parable of the raft, desiring that you abandon it, not that you should cling to it.
If you understand this Dharma of mine taught for a long night as being like a raft, you should abandon even this Dharma, let alone what is not the Dharma.
"Furthermore, there are six bases for views. What are the six?

A bhikṣu, regarding all forms—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; fine or coarse; sublime or base; near or far—all of these he regards with wisdom as they truly are: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. "

Whatever perceptions there are, whatever notions there are, and whatever views there are—none of these are mine; I do not belong to them; they shall not be mine; I shall not exist as them. All of those are not mine, I do not belong to them, nor are they my self (*ātman*). Thus, one observes with wisdom and knows it as it truly is.

Whatever views there may be—whether seen, heard, cognized, or known; attained or observed; or whatever is thought upon by the mind regarding this world and the next, or the next world and this one—all of that is not mine, I do not belong to it, and it is not my self. Thus, one should observe with wisdom and know it as it truly is.

Whatever views there may be such as: "This is the self, this is the world, this is my soul; I shall exist in a future life, eternal, unchanging, and of an indestructible nature"—all such things are not mine, I am not they, nor are they the self. Thus one should observe with wisdom and know them as they truly are.
Thereupon, a certain bhikkhu rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
"Is there, perhaps, any cause for fear within?
The Blessed One replied, "There is."
The bhikkhu asked again:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that fear arises because of the internal?”
The Blessed One replied:
“A bhikkhu sees thus and speaks thus: ‘That which did not exist for me in the past, even if it were to exist, I would not obtain it.’”
Seeing things thus and speaking thus, he becomes sorrowful and distressed, weeping, beating his breast, and falling into madness and delusion.
Monks! In this way, there is fear on account of the internal.
After the bhikkhu had praised the Blessed One, he asked again:
“Blessed One,
is there perhaps a cause for being without fear within?”
The Blessed One replied, “There is.
The bhikkhu asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that one has no fear on account of the internal?
The World-Honored One replied:
"A bhikkhu does not hold such a view nor speak thus: 'Perhaps it did not exist for me in the past, or even if it existed, I did not obtain it.
Because he does not hold such a view nor speak thus, he does not grieve, does not suffer, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness."
“Monks! Thus, because of this internal state, there is no fear.
After the monks had praised the Blessed One, they asked him again:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps a cause for fear that arises from what is external?
The World-Honored One replied:
“There is. The bhikkhu asked again:
“World-Honored One!
"How is it that one has fear and dread due to external things?
The World-Honored One replied:
"A bhikṣu sees thus and speaks thus: 'This is the self; this is the world; this is my self; I shall exist in a future life.'"
Holding such views and speaking thus, he may encounter either a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata—one who is intelligent, wise, eloquent, and accomplished in wisdom.

Whether it be a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, they teach the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all notions of a self; they teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints, all notions of "I" and "mine," and for the sake of extinguishing the underlying tendency of conceit. When such a Tathāgata or disciple of the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all notions of a self—abandoning all taints, all notions of "I" and "mine," and extinguishing the underlying tendency of conceit—one who experiences grief, distress, and exhaustion, weeping, beating one's breast, and falling into madness, might say: "I am annihilated and no longer exist."

Why is this? Because that which the bhikṣu calls "the long night" is unlovely, unpleasant, and unworthy of mental attention; when a bhikṣu practices that excessively, he becomes sorrowful and distressed, weeping, beating his breast, and falling into madness and delusion.
"Monks! Thus, there is fear due to external things.
After the monks had praised the Blessed One, they asked again:
“World-Honored One!
Is there perhaps a cause for fear that does not arise from external things?
The World-Honored One replied:
“There is. The bhikkhu asked again:
“World-Honored One!
"How is it that one has no fear on account of external things?
The Blessed One replied:
"A bhikkhu does not see in such a way, nor does he speak in such a way: 'This is the self, this is the world, this is my soul, and I shall exist in a future life.'"
They do not hold such views nor speak in such a manner; rather, they may encounter a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata who is intelligent, wise, eloquent, and perfected in wisdom.

Whether it be a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, they teach the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all notions of a self; they teach the Dharma for the sake of abandoning all taints (*āsrava*), all [conceptions of] "I" and "mine," and for the sake of extinguishing the underlying tendencies of conceit (*māna-anuśaya*). When these Tathāgatas or disciples of the Tathāgata teach the Dharma for the sake of extinguishing all notions of a self, for the sake of abandoning all taints, all [conceptions of] "I" and "mine," and for the sake of extinguishing the underlying tendencies of conceit, they do not grieve, do not suffer, do not weep, do not beat their breasts, and do not fall into madness or delusion, nor do they speak thus: "I am annihilated and shall no longer exist."

Why is that? Because, bhikkhu, that which is for a long night desirable, pleasant, and agreeable to the mind—when a bhikkhu practices it extensively, he does not become sorrowful, distressed, or weeping; he does not beat his breast or fall into madness and delusion. Bhikkhu!
"In this way, there is no fear due to external causes.
At that time, the bhikṣu praised the World-Honored One, saying:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
Having praised him thus, and having heard what the Buddha had spoken, he received and recited it well, and then remained silent.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One praised the bhikṣus, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!

A bhikkhu who accepts what is to be accepted in this way, having accepted it, does not give rise to sorrow or distress, does not become weary or fatigued, does not weep, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into madness or delusion.”

Do you see that regarding what has been received and what is to be received, you do not give rise to sorrow or distress, do not become weary or troubled, do not weep, do not beat your breasts, and do not fall into madness?
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

Relying upon such a view as that which is worthy of reliance, once you have seen it, do not give rise to sorrow or grief, do not become distressed, do not weep, do not beat your breasts, and do not fall into madness or delusion.

Having seen that which is to be relied upon according to such views, do you not, having seen it, give rise to sorrow and grief, nor become distressed, nor weep, nor beat your breasts, nor fall into madness?
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You have received such a body; is this entire body a dharma that is eternally abiding, unchanging, and indestructible?
Having seen and received such a body as you have, do you perceive it as a dharma that is eternally abiding, unchanging, and indestructible?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

That which is called "the self exists because of the soul" (jīva), or "seeing no-self when there is no soul"—these are the soul and what belongs to the soul; they are neither obtainable nor can they be designated. Furthermore, the bases for views, fetters, attachments, and underlying tendencies within the mind are likewise neither obtainable nor can they be designated.
"Monks! Is it not the case that I have fully explained the view and the continuity of that view, just as in the case of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, who was formerly a Gārgīputra?"
The bhikkhu replied: “So it is,
World-Honored One.”
"I shall explain for you in full the views and the continuity of those views, just as the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was formerly a gāthā-reciter.
"Furthermore, there are six bases of views."

What are the six? A bhikṣu considers whatever forms there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; fine or coarse; excellent or inferior; near or far—all of these are not mine, I am not they, and they are not my self.
Observing with such wisdom, one knows it as it truly is:

whatever perceptions, mental formations, ideations, or views there may be—these are not mine, I am not these, they shall not be mine, they shall not exist, and all of them are not mine, I am not theirs, nor are they the self (ātman).
Observing with such wisdom, one knows it as it truly is:

whatever views there may be—whether seen, heard, cognized, known, attained, or contemplated; whatever is thought of by the mind regarding the passage from this world to that world, or from that world to this world—all of that is not mine, I am not that, and it is not my self.
Observing with such wisdom, one knows it as it truly is:

"Whatever views there may be—'This is the self,' 'This is the world,' 'This is me,' 'I shall exist in a future life,' 'It is eternal, unchanging, and imperishable'—all of these are not mine, I am not they, and they are not my self."
Observing with such wisdom, he knows it as it truly is:

"Any bhikkhu who does not perceive a self in these six bases for views, nor perceives anything belonging to a self—having thus not perceived them—he does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, he is free from fear. Being free from fear, he attains parinibbāna, knowing as it truly is: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence.'"
This is called the bhikṣu who has crossed the moat, passed over the moat, broken down the wall, and is without a gate—the mirror of noble wisdom.
How does a bhikṣu cross the moat?
When the moat of ignorance is exhausted and fully known, its root is uprooted and severed, and it is shattered so that it shall never arise again; in this way, the bhikṣu has crossed the moat.
How does a bhikṣu cross over the moat?
When craving has been exhausted and fully understood, its root uprooted and severed, and it shattered so that it shall not arise again—in this way, a bhikṣu crosses over the moat.
What is it for a bhikṣu to break through the wall?

When birth and death have been exhausted and fully understood, and their root has been uprooted and severed, so that the wall is broken through and he shall not be born again—thus does a bhikṣu attain the breaking through of the wall.
What is meant by a bhikṣu who is "without a gate"?
It is when the five lower fetters have been exhausted and fully known, their root severed, broken asunder so that they shall never arise again; in this way, a bhikṣu attains being "without a gate."
What is the mirror of noble wisdom for a bhikṣu?

It is when he has fully understood that his conceit (*māna*) is exhausted, uprooting it by the very root, shattering it so that it shall never arise again—this is the mirror of noble wisdom for a bhikṣu.
This is called the bhikṣu who has crossed the moat, passed over the moat, broken down the rampart, and is without a gate—the mirror of noble wisdom.

Thus, when the Tathāgata is rightly liberated, even Indira and the god Īśāna, as well as Brahmā and his retinue, though they seek it, cannot find the consciousness upon which the Tathāgata relies. The Tathāgata is Brahmā; the Tathāgata is cool; the Tathāgata is without feverish distress; the Tathāgata is immutable.
I have spoken thus:

"Various śramaṇas and brahmins slander me with false and untrue words, saying: 'The śramaṇa Gautama teaches a doctrine of non-positing; he asserts that there truly exist sentient beings who undergo annihilation and destruction, and because there is no self herein, he does not speak of it; yet that Tathāgata speaks of the state beyond sorrow in this very life.'"

If others should revile the Tathāgata, strike the Tathāgata, or, out of anger, reproach and accuse him, the Tathāgata, because of that, would not become angry or resentful, and would never harbor a harmful intent.
"If someone reviles the Tathāgata, beats him, or angrily reproaches him, what does the Tathāgata think?
The Tathāgata reflects thus:
'If this has come about because of what I myself originally did and originally created.'"
"If others revile the Tathāgata, beat him, or angrily reproach him, the Tathāgata forms this thought:

'If there were others who honored the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying homage, and respecting him, the Tathāgata would not on that account feel gratified, nor would he feel joyful, nor would his heart find pleasure.'"
If others were to revere the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying homage, serving, and honoring him, what would the Tathāgata think?
The Tathāgata would reflect thus:
"Whatever I have now known and abandoned was brought about by that."
"If there are others who revere the Tathāgata, making offerings, paying homage, serving, and honoring him, the Tathāgata forms this thought.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If others revile you, beat you, or angrily reproach you; or if others revere you, make offerings to you, pay homage to you, and honor you—because of these circumstances, you should likewise not give rise to anger, hatred, or envy; do not harbor a mind of malice, nor should you feel delight or joy, nor should your hearts be pleased."

Why is that? We have no self, nor anything belonging to a self, just like this dry grass and withered wood outside the gate of this Jeta Grove. Suppose another person were to take it away, burn it with fire, or use it as he pleases; what do you think?

"Would those dry grasses and withered wood ever think: 'Someone is taking me away to burn in fire for their own use as they please'? The bhikṣus replied: "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "In the same way, bhikṣus, you have left your parents, abandoned your wives and children, sold yourselves into servitude, and have come forth from home into homelessness. You have shaved off your hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and taken up the bowl. You have renounced all worldly affairs and now dwell in the forest. Do you not think: 'The World-Honored One has taught us the Dharma for the sake of liberation; we must practice it diligently so that we may attain the fruit of the path? The bhikṣus replied: "Yes, World-Honored One. The Buddha said: "Bhikṣus, you should train yourselves thus: 'We have left our parents, abandoned our wives and children, sold ourselves into servitude, and have come forth from home into homelessness. We have shaved off our hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and taken up the bowl. We have renounced all worldly affairs and now dwell in the forest. The World-Honored One has taught us the Dharma for the sake of liberation; we must practice it diligently so that we may attain the fruit of the path. Bhikṣus, you should train yourselves in this way. The Buddha then spoke these verses: "If one does not abandon desire, One will surely fall into the three evil realms. If one abandons desire, One will surely attain the state of peace. If one does not abandon desire, One will surely fall into the three evil realms. If one abandons desire, One will surely attain the state of peace. If one does not abandon desire, One will surely fall into the three evil realms. If one abandons desire, One will surely attain the state of peace. At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
