"In this way, if others should revile you, beat you, or angrily reproach you; or if others should honor, provide for, pay homage to, and respect you—you should, because of these, neither become angry, hateful, or envious, nor give rise to a mind of malice, nor feel joy or delight, nor find pleasure in your heart."

Why is this? Because we have no self and nothing belonging to a self; we possess the well-expounded Dharma, which has been revealed and widely disseminated without omission, circulated and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.
In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, widely disseminated, without deficiency, and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.

If one who has attained liberation through right wisdom passes away, it cannot be said that they have reached an end; for my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, widely disseminated, without deficiency, and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.
In this way, my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, widely disseminated, without deficiency, and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.

If one whose five lower fetters are exhausted passes away, they will be reborn in that realm, where they shall attain parinirvāṇa, reaching the state of non-retrogression and no longer returning to this world.
My Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulating and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.
Thus my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulating and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.

Having exhausted those three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, one attains the state of "once-returning" between the heavens and the human world; having returned once more, one then reaches the end of suffering.
My Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulated and proclaimed even unto devas and humans.
Thus my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulated and proclaimed even unto devas and humans.

Having exhausted those three fetters, he has attained the stage of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); he is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms and is destined for full enlightenment. At most, he will wander seven times between the heavens and the human world, and after those seven wanderings, he shall reach the end of suffering.
My Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulated and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.
Thus my Dharma is well-expounded, revealed, and widely disseminated; it is without deficiency, circulated and proclaimed even unto gods and humans.
"If there are those who have faith and joy in me and pass away, they shall all be born in a good destination, as described above with remainder.
Thus the Buddha spoke.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Āḷavaka Sutta, the ninth, ends here, totaling four thousand five hundred and seventy characters. 201. The Cūḷa-vedalla Sutta (201), the tenth in the Mahāvagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the fifth subsequent recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kevaddha, son of Kātyāyana, gave rise to this evil view:
"I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus:
'This consciousness, upon rebirth, does not become something else.'"
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to where the bhikṣu Lāḍita was and asked him:
"Lāḍita, did you truly speak in such a manner?"
"I understand the Blessed One to have taught this Dharma:
'Is this consciousness not different from that which is reborn?
Thus did the bhikṣu Kevaddha reply.
"Venerable friends!
I truly know that the Blessed One has taught the Dharma in this way:
'This present consciousness, when reborn, does not become something other.'"
At that time, the bhikṣus rebuked the bhikṣu Kālāmas, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One. It is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One, for the World-Honored One does not speak in such a manner."
"Venerable Bhadrika!

This consciousness now arises due to causes and conditions. The World-Honored One has taught through immeasurable skillful means that consciousness arises by way of causes and conditions: when there are conditions, it is born; when there are no conditions, it ceases."
"Vādi Bhikṣu! You should quickly abandon this evil view.
Although Vādi Bhikṣu was thus rebuked by the bhikṣus, he stubbornly clung to that evil view with great force and spoke resolutely:
"This alone is true; all else is false.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.

The many bhikṣus were unable to cause the bhikṣu Kevaddha to abandon this evil view, so they rose from their seats and departed, going to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
The bhikṣu Kevaddha has given rise to such an evil view:
‘I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma in this way:’”
"Regarding this consciousness, there is no difference between its passing away and its rebirth.
"World-Honored One!
Having heard this, we went to where the bhikṣu Kevaddha was and asked him:"
"Vāseṭṭha! You have indeed spoken thus:
'I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One in this way:'"
"Regarding this consciousness, its rebirth is not otherwise.
Thus did the bhikṣu Lāḍita answer us, saying:
"Virtuous ones!..."
"World-Honored One, I truly understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One thus:
'This present consciousness, when reborn, does not become something else.
World-Honored One!
We rebuked him, saying:
"Venerable Bhaddiya! Do not speak thus;
do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak in such a manner."
"Venerable Ānanda!

This consciousness now arises due to causes and conditions. The World-Honored One has taught through immeasurable skillful means that consciousness arises due to causes and conditions; when there is a condition for consciousness, it is born, and when there is no condition, it ceases."
"Venerable bhikṣu!
You should quickly abandon this evil view.
After we had thus rebuked him, he stubbornly clung to that evil view with great force and spoke persistently:
"This is the truth; all else is false.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, World-Honored One!
"Just as we were unable to make the bhikṣu Kevaddha abandon this evil view, he rose from his seat and departed.
Having heard this, the World-Honored One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to where the bhikṣu Kevaddha is and speak these words:"
“The World-Honored One calls for you!

Thereupon, a certain bhikṣu, having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He went to where the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin was and said to him:
“The World-Honored One calls for you!”
The bhikṣu Lāḍita immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One asked him:
“Is it true that you spoke thus?”
"I understand the World-Honored One to have taught the Dharma thus:
'This consciousness that now transmigrates and is reborn is not something other.
Thus did the bhikṣu Kevaddha reply.
“World-Honored One!
I truly understand the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma thus:
‘This present consciousness, when reborn in another existence, does not become something different.’”
The World-Honored One asked:
"What is consciousness?
The bhikṣu Kevaddha replied:
“World-Honored One!
This consciousness is said to speak, perceive, act, cause others to act, arise, and co-arise; it is that which performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds and thereby undergoes their retribution.”
The World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"Cunda! How can you understand my teaching of the Dharma in such a way?"
"From which mouth did you hear me teaching the Dharma in such a way?
You foolish person!
I do not teach exclusively [in one way], yet you speak as if I do?"
"You foolish man!
When you hear the bhikṣus collectively reproaching you, you should answer them in accordance with the Dharma, saying:
'I shall now question the bhikṣus.'"
Then, the World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus:
"Do you also understand me as teaching the Dharma in this way:
'Is this consciousness not different when it undergoes rebirth?'"
At that time, the bhikṣus replied, “No,
World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then asked:
"How do you understand my teaching of the Dharma? The bhikṣus replied, "We understand the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma thus:

consciousness arises conditioned by its causes and conditions. The World-Honored One says that consciousness arises conditioned by its causes and conditions; when there are conditions, consciousness is born, and when there are no conditions, it ceases. We understand the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma in this way."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"O bhikṣus!
You should understand that I teach the Dharma in this way. Why is that?

I also speak in this way: consciousness arises with conditions. I say that consciousness arises with conditions; when there are conditions, consciousness is born, and when there are no conditions, it ceases. Consciousness arises in accordance with its object; that very object is its condition.

It is said that consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and forms; once consciousness has arisen, it is called "eye-consciousness. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body; and when consciousness arises conditioned by the mind and mental objects, once consciousness has arisen, it is called "mind-consciousness."
It is just like fire, which arises depending on its respective conditions: when fire arises depending on wood, it is called "fire from wood" or simply "wood-fire";
when fire arises depending on a heap of grass or dung, it is called "fire from grass and dung."
In this way, consciousness arises in accordance with its object; that very object is said to be the condition for the arising of consciousness.

Having arisen, it is called "eye-consciousness. Likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, and body. With the mind as condition and mental phenomena as objects, consciousness arises; having arisen, it is called "mental consciousness."
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"You should understand that I have taught the Dharma in this way.
Yet this foolish bhikṣu, Kālāmas, has misunderstood both the meaning and the letter in a perverted manner.

Because he has misunderstood them perversely, he slanders me; he brings harm upon himself, commits an offense and incurs guilt, is displeasing to wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life, and incurs great demerit."
"You foolish man!
Do you know that there is such an evil and unwholesome state?

Thereupon, the bhikṣu Kāḷudāyin, having been rebuked by the Blessed One to his face, harbored grief within; with his head bowed, he remained silent, his eloquence lost and speechless, as if searching for something to say.
Thereupon, having rebuked the bhikṣu Kevaddha face to face, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"I shall teach you the Dharma that is ultimate, free from vexation, free from fever, and eternally immutable. Those of wisdom contemplate it thus: listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well."
Then, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"Do you truly see what is spoken?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One asked:
"Do you truly see what the Tathāgata has spoken?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:
“After the Tathāgata has passed away, do you see that all those dharmas which are subject to extinction are also extinguished?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, I do.”
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied,
"Have you truly seen what was spoken?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One asked,
“Monk, have you truly seen that which the Tathāgata has spoken?
The monk replied:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said to him:
“After the Tathāgata has passed away, do you see that all those dharmas which are subject to cessation have also ceased?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed, I do.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied,
“Is this true teaching free from doubt?”
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One asked:
"Is the Tathāgata’s true teaching free from doubt?
The bhikṣu replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
“After the Tathāgata has passed away, will all those dharmas that are subject to cessation also cease?
Is there no doubt about this? The bhikṣu replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
“If one speaks thus according to reality and perceives with wisdom as it truly is, are all doubts extinguished?”
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One said:
“If the Tathāgata speaks thus in accordance with reality, and one perceives it with wisdom as it truly is, are all doubts extinguished?
The bhikkhu replied:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said to him:
“After the Tathāgata has passed away, will all those phenomena that are subject to cessation likewise be seen by wisdom as they truly are, so that all doubts regarding them are extinguished?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed, it is so.”
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied,
“Have you truly understood my teaching and are now free from doubt?”
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One asked,
"Is there no longer any doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s true teaching?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Yes, indeed,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said to him:
“Since the Tathāgata has already passed away, have you now no further doubt regarding the fact that all things are subject to cessation?
The bhikṣu replied,
“Indeed, I do.”
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

If you know thus and see thus, thinking, "This view of mine is so pure," and yet you cling to it, treasure it, guard it, and do not wish to relinquish it, do you then understand my teaching of the parable of the raft, and having understood it, do you open the blocked flow?
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

If you know thus and see thus—thinking, "This view of mine is so pure"—and if you do not cling to it, do not cherish it, and do not guard it, desiring rather to relinquish it, then do you understand that I have long taught the Dharma as a simile for a raft? Having understood this, is the flow that was blocked now opened?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
If any followers of other teachings should come and ask you:
"Venerable ones!
If you possess such pure vision, what is its purpose, what is its function, and what are its merits?"
"How would you answer? The bhikṣus replied,
"World-Honored One!"
If any follower of another school should come and ask me:
"Venerable sir!
If you possess such a pure vision, what is its meaning, what is its purpose, and what is its merit?"
To this, we should answer: "Virtuous ones!
It is for the sake of disenchantment, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of seeing and knowing things as they truly are."
“World-Honored One!
If followers of other teachings were to come and question us, we would answer them in this way.
The World-Honored One praised them, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If followers of other teachings come to question you, you should answer them in this way.”
Why is this so? This contemplation that has been explained consists of four things: first, gross and subtle edible food; second, contact; third, mental volition; and fourth, consciousness.
What is the cause and what is the condition for these four nutriments?
From what do they arise,
and by what do they exist?
Those four nutriments have craving as their cause, craving as their condition; they arise from craving and exist because of craving.
What is the cause of craving, what is its condition, and from what does it arise?
By what does craving exist?
Craving is conditioned by feeling, practiced through feeling, born from feeling, and exists by virtue of feeling.
What is the cause and what is the condition for feeling?
From what does it arise?
By what does it exist?
Awareness arises from contact and is conditioned by contact; it is born from contact and exists by means of contact.
What is the cause of contact, what is its condition?
From what does it arise,
and by what does it exist?
Contact (phassa) has the six sense bases as its cause, is conditioned by the six sense bases, arises from the six sense bases, and exists because of the six sense bases.
What is the cause and what is the condition for the six sense bases?
From what does it arise?
By what does it exist?
As for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), they have name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their cause; they are conditioned by name-and-form, born from name-and-form, and exist by virtue of name-and-form.
What is the cause and what is the condition for name-and-form?
From what does it arise?
By what does it exist?
Regarding name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): it is conditioned by consciousness (*vijñāna*), cultivated by consciousness, born from consciousness, and exists because of consciousness.
What is the cause and what is the condition for consciousness?
From what is it born?
By what does consciousness exist?
Consciousness is conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), practiced through volitional formations, born from volitional formations, and exists by virtue of volitional formations.
What is the cause and what is the condition for volitional formations?
From what does it arise?
By what does it exist?
Practitioner, it arises from ignorance and exists by means of ignorance; it is produced through ignorance and comes into being because of ignorance.

"Thus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. In this way, this entire mass of suffering comes into being."
“With birth as condition, there is aging and death; this is said to be ‘with birth as condition, there is aging and death. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"It is our view that aging and death have birth as their condition. Why is this?
Because aging and death arise conditioned by birth."
“With existence as condition, birth comes to be; this is what is said regarding ‘with existence as condition, birth comes to be. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"It is because of existence that there is birth; such is our view. Why is this?
Is it not the case that birth arises conditioned by existence?"
“With feeling as condition, there is existence; this is what is meant by ‘with feeling as condition, there is existence. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"It is conditioned by feeling that there is existence;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because it is conditioned by feeling that there is existence."
“With craving as condition, there is feeling; this is what is said regarding ‘with craving as condition, there is feeling. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"It is because of craving that there is feeling;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because it is conditioned by craving that feeling arises."
“The pratyekabuddhas have craving; this is said to be the case that pratyekabuddhas have craving. What do you think of this?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
We believe that Pratyekabuddhas possess craving. Why is this?
Because Pratyekabuddhas do indeed possess craving.
“With contact as condition, there is feeling; this is called ‘with contact as condition, there is feeling. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"It is because of contact that there is feeling;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because it is conditioned by contact that there is feeling."
“With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; this is what is called ‘with the six sense bases as condition, there is contact. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"It is our view that contact arises conditioned by the six sense bases. Why is that?
Because contact arises conditioned by the six sense bases."
“With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases; this is said to be ‘with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases. What do you think about this?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases;
such is our view. Why is that?
Because with name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases.
“With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form; this is what is said regarding 'with consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.
What do you think about this? The bhikṣus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"Conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form."
“‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be. This is what is said regarding ‘with volitional formations as condition, consciousness comes to be. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"Conditioned by volitional formations (saṅkhāra), consciousness (viññāṇa) comes to be;
such is our view. Why is that?
Because consciousness comes to be conditioned by volitional formations."
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be; this is called ‘with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"It is our view that volitional formations arise conditioned by ignorance. Why is this?
Because volitional formations arise conditioned by ignorance."

Thus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises; and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering arises.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Monks! You should speak thus. Why is that? Because—"

I also speak in this way: conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases there is contact; conditioned by contact there is feeling; conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is clinging; conditioned by clinging there is existence; conditioned by existence there is birth; conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Thus does this entire great mass of suffering come into being.
"With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death. "What do you think about this statement, 'With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death'?
The bhikkhus replied, "World-Honored One!"
With the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death;
such is our understanding. Why is this?
Because with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
“When there is the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth. Regarding this statement that with the cessation of existence there is the cessation of birth, what do you think?
The bhikṣus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"With the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth."
“When feeling ceases, existence ceases; this is what is meant by ‘when feeling ceases, existence ceases. What do you think about this?
The bhikṣus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"When feeling ceases, existence ceases;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because when feeling ceases, existence ceases."
“When craving ceases, feeling ceases; this is what is said regarding the cessation of craving leading to the cessation of feeling. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"When craving ceases, feeling ceases;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because when craving ceases, feeling ceases."
“When feeling ceases, craving ceases; this is what is meant by ‘when feeling ceases, craving ceases. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
When feeling ceases, craving ceases;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because when feeling ceases, craving ceases.
“When contact ceases, feeling ceases; this is what is meant by ‘when contact ceases, feeling ceases. What do you think about this?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
When contact ceases, feeling ceases;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because when contact ceases, feeling ceases.
“With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. This is what is meant by ‘with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases. What do you think about this?
The bhikṣus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
such is our view. Why is that?
Because with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases."
“When name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease. Regarding this statement that with the cessation of name-and-form the six sense bases cease, what do you think?
The bhikkhus replied, “World-Honored One!”
"With the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
such is our view. Why is that?
Because with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease."
“When consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease; this is what is meant by ‘when consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease. What do you think about this?
The bhikṣus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases;
such is our view. Why is this?
Because with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases."
“When formations cease, consciousness ceases. Regarding this statement that with the cessation of formations consciousness ceases, what do you think?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One! [It is so.]”
When volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases;
such is our view. Why is that?
Because when volitional formations cease, consciousness ceases.
“When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease. Regarding this statement that with the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of volitional formations, what do you think?
The bhikkhus replied:
“World-Honored One!”
"When ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease;
such is our understanding. Why is this?
Because when ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease."

This is how, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease. Thus, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are brought to cessation; in this way, this entire great mass of suffering is extinguished.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Monks! You should speak thus. Why is that? Because—"

I also speak in this way: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease, as well as sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
If you know thus and see thus, would you perhaps form such a thought regarding the past as:
"I existed in the past, or I did not exist in the past"?
"How does there exist a past time?
By what means does there exist a past time?
The bhikṣu replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If you know thus and see thus, would you perhaps form such a thought regarding the future:”
"I shall exist in the future; I shall not exist in the future.
How will there be existence in the future?
By what means will there be existence in the future?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
If you understand thus and see thus, do you perhaps have any doubt or confusion within yourselves as to what this is,
what this is like,
or from where these sentient beings have come?
To where does one go?
By what cause has it already come to be?
And by what cause will it come to be?
The bhikṣu replied,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

If you know thus and see thus, would you ever intentionally kill your parents, harm a disciple who is an Arhat, cause a schism in the Saṅgha, or with an evil intent toward the Buddha draw blood from the Tathāgata?
The bhikkhu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"If you understand thus and see thus, would you ever intentionally violate the precepts, renounce the training,
or abandon the path? The bhikṣus replied, "No."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent!”
“Excellent!
If you understand thus and see thus, would you perhaps abandon this and seek another external object of veneration or seek another field of merit?
The bhikṣus replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If you know thus and see thus, would you, as śramaṇas or brahmins, speak in such a manner?”
"Venerable sirs!
Do you know what should be known, and see what should be seen?
The bhikṣus replied:
"No, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!
If you know thus and see thus, do you consider yourselves to be auspicious and pure?”
The bhikkhu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

If you know thus and see thus, would you then associate yourselves with those recluses and brahmins whose views are associated with auspiciousness, yet are mixed with suffering, mixed with fever, and mixed with anguish—claiming that they are the truth?
The bhikṣu replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”

What is called the "cowherd's fast"?
Suppose a cowherd releases his cattle into a marsh in the morning and gathers them back to the village in the evening. When he returns to the village, he reflects:
"Today I tended the cattle here; tomorrow I shall tend them there."
"Today I shall water my oxen here; tomorrow I shall water them there.

"Householder’s wife!

"Today I drink such a drink; tomorrow I shall drink such a drink as that.

If that person remains attached to sensual pleasures throughout this day and night, it is called the "cowherd’s fast.
One who observes such a cowherd’s fast does not obtain great benefit, does not attain great fruit, possesses no great merit, and does not achieve widespread renown.
"Laywoman! What is called the Nigaṇṭha fast?
If there are those who have gone forth to train as Nigaṇṭhas, they exhort people, saying: "

“If there are sentient beings to the east beyond a hundred yojanas, you shall lay aside your swords and staves for their protection; likewise, if there are sentient beings to the south, west, or north beyond a hundred yojanas, you shall lay aside your swords and staves for their protection. Some protect sentient beings through perception, while others do not protect sentient beings because they lack perception. On the fifteenth day, when you recite the *Prātimokṣa*, you should strip off your clothes, stand naked, face the east, and speak as follows:

"I have no father or mother; I am not possessed by father or mother. I have no wife or children; I am not possessed by wife or children. I have no slaves or servants; I am not born of slaves or servants."
"Householder’s wife!

Using this desire, he uses what has not been given rather than using what has been given; this is called the Nigaṇṭha vow.

Householder’s wife!

Householder’s wife!

Householder’s wife!

"Householder's wife!

If one thousand six hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), and thirty such days and nights make a month, and twelve such months make a year, then sixteen thousand such years constitute the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations."

Thereupon, Mṛgāramātṛ Viśākhā joined her palms toward the Buddha and said:

This Noble Eightfold Fast is truly marvelous!”
How extraordinary!
It possesses great benefit and great fruit; it has great merit and great widespread dissemination.
World-Honored One!
"From this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall observe the noble eightfold fast and, according to my capacity, practice giving and cultivate merit.

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through Nālandā and was staying in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.

At that time, the householder Pūtila, dressed in pure white garments, with his head wrapped in a white cloth, leaning on a staff and holding a parasol, wearing secular sandals, wandered from garden to garden, from park to park, and from grove to grove, roaming about at leisure.
If he sees any śramaṇas or brahmins, he speaks thus: "Virtuous ones!
You should know that I have departed from the secular, severed the secular, and abandoned all worldly affairs."
Those śramaṇas and brahmins spoke with gentle, soft, and conciliatory words:
"Indeed, worthy Pūtila,
you have distanced yourself from the mundane, severed ties with the mundane, and abandoned all worldly affairs."

Thereupon, the householder Potaliya, wandering about on his rounds, went to where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings, he stood before the Buddha leaning upon his staff. The World-Honored One addressed him, saying:
"Householder!"
"There is a seat; sit if you wish to sit.
The householder Potaliya said, "Gautama!..."
"This is not so; this is impossible. Why is that?
I have left the world and severed worldly ties, having abandoned all mundane affairs; yet the śramaṇa Gautama calls me a 'householder'?"
The Blessed One replied:
"You possess the marks and insignia of a householder; therefore, I address you as 'Householder!'"
"There is a seat; sit whenever you wish to sit.
For a second and a third time, the World-Honored One spoke thus, saying:
"Householder!"
"There is a seat; sit if you wish.
The householder Potaliya also spoke a second and a third time, saying:
"Gautama!..."
"This is not so; this is impossible.
I have departed from the mundane, severed the mundane, and abandoned all worldly affairs—how then can the śramaṇa Gautama address me as a 'householder'?"
The Blessed One replied:

"There is a seat; when you wish to sit, you may sit.
The World-Honored One asked:
"How have you distanced yourself from the mundane, severed the mundane, and abandoned all worldly affairs?"
The householder Potaliya replied: “Gautama!

All the wealth and property I possess have been given entirely as gifts to my sons. I wander without purpose or desire, merely going to seek food and sustain my life; in this way, I am detached from the world, severed from the world, and have abandoned all worldly affairs.”
The Blessed One said:
"Householder,
in the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, worldly affairs are not severed in such a manner."
“Householder!
In the Noble Dharma and Discipline, there are eight factors for abandoning worldly affairs.
Thereupon, the householder Potaliya cast aside his staff and removed his sunshade, took off his lay shoes, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, said:
“Gautama! In what way are the eight factors for abandoning worldly affairs taught in the Noble Dharma and Discipline?
The Blessed One replied:

"Householder! A well-taught noble disciple relies on abstaining from killing and abandons killing; relies on abstaining from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given; relies on abstaining from sexual misconduct and abandons sexual misconduct; relies on abstaining from false speech and abandons false speech; relies on non-attachment and abandons attachment; relies on non-malice and abandons malice; relies on non-envy, resentment, and vexation and abandons envy, resentment, and vexation; relies on the absence of overweening pride and abandons overweening pride."
"Householder!
How does a learned noble disciple rely on abstaining from killing and bring about its cessation?
A learned noble disciple reflects thus:"

"The killer will surely receive an evil retribution in both this life and the next. If I were to kill, I would be harming myself and falsely slandering others; the devas and wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my lack of precepts, and my evil reputation would be heard in all directions; when the body perishes at the end of life, I would certainly go to an evil destination and be born in hell."
"Since a killer receives such an evil retribution in both this life and future lives, should I not now rely upon abstaining from killing and severing it?
Thereupon, he relied upon abstaining from killing and severed it.
"In this way, the learned noble disciple relies upon abstaining from killing and abandoning killing.
Householder!
How does the learned noble disciple rely upon abstaining from taking what is not given and abandoning taking what is not given?"
The learned noble disciple reflects thus:

"One who takes what is not given will certainly undergo an evil retribution, both in this present life and in future lives. If I were to take what is not given, I would thereby bring harm upon myself and falsely slander others. The gods and those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my lack of virtue; my evil reputation would be heard in all directions. When my body breaks up at the end of life, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."

"Since one who takes what is not given receives such an evil retribution in both this life and future lives, should I now rather rely on abstaining from taking what is not given and severing the practice of taking what is not given?"
Thus, he abides by refraining from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given.
In this same way, the well-taught noble disciple abides by refraining from taking what is not given and abandons taking what is not given.
"Householder!
How does a well-taught noble disciple rely on abstaining from sexual misconduct and abandon sexual misconduct?
A well-taught noble disciple reflects thus:"

"One who commits sexual misconduct will inevitably receive an evil retribution, both in this life and in future lives. If I were to commit sexual misconduct, I would thereby bring harm upon myself and falsely slander others. The gods and those wise practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my violation of the precepts; my evil reputation would be heard in all directions. When my body perishes and my life ends, I will surely go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."
Since one who commits sexual misconduct receives such evil retribution in both the present life and future lives, should I now rather rely upon abstaining from sexual misconduct and severing it?
Thus, he relies on abstaining from sexual misconduct and abandons sexual misconduct.
In this way, the learned noble disciple relies on abstaining from sexual misconduct and abandons sexual misconduct.
"Householder!..."
How does the learned noble disciple rely on abstaining from false speech and bring false speech to an end?
The learned noble disciple reflects thus:

"One who speaks falsely will certainly undergo an evil retribution in both the present life and future lives. If I were to speak falsely, I would thereby harm myself and slander others; the devas and wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my lack of virtue, and my ill repute would be heard in all directions; at the breaking up of the body after death, I would surely go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."

Since one who speaks such falsehoods receives this evil retribution both in the present life and in future lives, should I not now rather rely upon abstaining from false speech and severing false speech?
Thus, one relies upon abstaining from false speech and the abandonment of false speech.
In this way, the learned noble disciple relies upon abstaining from false speech and the abandonment of false speech.
"Householder!..."
How does the learned noble disciple rely on non-attachment and abandon attachment?
The learned noble disciple reflects thus:

"Attachment inevitably brings about an evil retribution, both in the present life and in future lives. If I were to become attached, I would thereby harm myself and falsely slander others; the gods and wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my lack of virtue, and my ill reputation would be heard in all directions. At the dissolution of the body after death, I would surely go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."
"Those who are thus greedily attached receive this evil retribution in both the present life and future lives; should I not now rather rely on non-attachment and sever attachment?"
"Thus, by relying on non-attachment and abandoning attachment,
the well-taught noble disciple relies on non-attachment and abandons attachment,
householder."
How does a well-taught noble disciple rely on non-harming and non-ill will to abandon harming and ill will?
A well-taught noble disciple reflects thus:

"One who harbors harm and ill will will surely experience an evil retribution, both in this present life and in future lives. If I harbor harm and ill will, I shall thereby bring harm upon myself, and I shall also slander others. The gods and wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life will proclaim my lack of virtue; my evil reputation will be heard in all directions. When my body breaks up and my life ends, I will certainly go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."
Since those who harbor malice and anger receive such evil retribution in both this life and future lives, should I now rather rely on non-malice and non-anger, and abandon malice and anger?
"Thus, one relies on non-harming and non-ill will, and abandons harming and ill will.
In this same way, the well-taught noble disciple relies on non-harming and non-ill will, and abandons harming and ill will.
Householder!"
How does a learned noble disciple rely on the absence of malice, envy, and resentment, and how does he abandon malice, envy, and resentment?
A learned noble disciple reflects thus:

"One who harbors malice, envy, and resentment will certainly undergo an evil retribution, both in this present life and in future lives. If I harbor malice, envy, and resentment, I shall thereby bring harm upon myself and slander others. The gods and those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life will proclaim my lack of virtue; my ill fame will be heard in all directions. When my body breaks up at the end of life, I will surely go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."

Since those who harbor hatred, envy, and affliction receive such evil retribution in both this life and future lives, should I not now rely upon being free from hatred, envy, and affliction, and instead sever hatred, envy, and affliction?
"Thus, one relies on the absence of malice, envy, and vexation, and abandons malice, envy, and vexation.
In this same way, the learned noble disciple relies on the absence of malice, envy, and vexation, and abandons malice, envy, and vexation."
“Householder!
How does a learned noble disciple rely on the absence of overweening pride and abandon overweening pride?
A learned noble disciple reflects thus:”

"One who possesses overweening pride will inevitably suffer an evil retribution in both this life and the next. If I were to possess overweening pride, I would thereby bring harm upon myself and falsely slander others. The gods and those wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life would proclaim my lack of virtue; my ill repute would be heard in all directions. When my body perishes and my life ends, I will surely go to an evil destination and be reborn in hell."

Since those with such overweening pride receive this evil retribution in both the present life and future lives, should I not now rely upon being free from overweening pride and severing overweening pride?
"Thus, one relies on the absence of overweening pride and abandons overweening pride.
In this same way, the learned noble disciple relies on the absence of overweening pride and abandons overweening pride."
"This is what is called the eightfold severance of worldly affairs within the Noble Dharma and Discipline.
The householder asked: "Gautama!"
"In the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, is there only the abandonment of worldly affairs, or is there more?

The Blessed One replied, "In the Noble Dharma and Vinaya, there is not only the abandonment of worldly affairs; furthermore, there are eight factors for the abandonment of worldly affairs that lead to realization."
Having heard this, the householder Potaliya removed his white turban, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Gautama,

The Blessed One replied:

"Householder, it is just as if there were a dog, hungry and emaciated, who went to a place where oxen are slaughtered. There, the butcher or his apprentice, having cleanly stripped away the flesh, threw a bone to the dog."
"Once the dog has obtained the bone, it gnaws at it here and there; its lips are torn and its teeth are broken, or perhaps its throat is wounded, yet the dog cannot thereby satisfy its hunger.
Householder!"
The learned noble disciple also reflects in this way:
"Sensual desire is like a skeleton.
The World-Honored One has said that sensual desire is like a skeleton: it offers little pleasure but much suffering, and is fraught with many calamities; one should keep far away from it."
"If there is this relinquishing of desire and the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, that all worldly food and drink are forever exhausted without remainder—one should cultivate that."
"Householder!

It is just as if, not far from a village, there were a small piece of meat fallen upon the open ground; a crow or an owl would seize that meat and carry it away, while other crows and owls would compete to pursue it."
"What do you think, householder?
If this crow did not quickly let go of that small piece of meat, would it not cause other crows to compete and pursue it?
The householder replied:
“Yes, indeed,
Gautama! What do you think, householder?”
“If this crow were able to quickly abandon this small piece of meat, would other crows and birds still compete for it?
The householder replied, “No.”
"Gautama! Householder,
the learned noble disciple also reflects in this way:"
“Desire is like a piece of meat;
the World-Honored One has said that desire is like a piece of meat—there is little pleasure and much suffering, and it brings many calamities and afflictions; one should keep far away from it.
If there is this relinquishing of desire and abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—that is, the complete exhaustion of all worldly nutriment without remainder—one should cultivate that.
"Householder!
It is just as if there were a person holding a torch in their hand and walking against the wind.

The householder replied,

"What do you think, householder?

The householder replied:

The learned noble disciple also reflects in this way:

"If there is this relinquishing of desire and the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, that all worldly food and drink are forever exhausted without remainder—one should cultivate that."

"Upon seeing that pit of fire, he would immediately think of staying far away, wishing for its abandonment and escape. Householder,

"Upon seeing that poisonous snake, he would think of staying far away from it, wishing for its abandonment and separation.

If there is this relinquishing of desire and abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, the complete exhaustion of all worldly food and drink without remainder—one should cultivate that.
"Householder!

It is just as if there were a person who, in a dream, obtained the five sensory pleasures in their entirety and amused himself with them; yet once he has awakened, not a single one of them is to be seen.
Householder!"
The learned noble disciple also reflects in this way:

"Since pleasure is little and suffering is much, and there are many calamities and afflictions, one should distance oneself from it.
If there is this relinquishing of desire and the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, that all worldly food and drink are forever exhausted without remainder—one should cultivate that.
“Householder!

"If there is wealth or property, one should enjoy it to the utmost for oneself.

Then the owner of that property, either seizing it himself or inciting others to seize it, would take it away; or inciting others to take it, he would have it taken. When many people saw this, they spoke together, saying:

Why is this so? Because the owner of those goods may take them away himself as he desires, or incite others to take them; he may take them himself, or incite others to take them.
"Householder!

"If there is this relinquishing of desire and the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, that all worldly food and drink are forever exhausted without remainder—one should cultivate that."
"Householder!
It is as if there were a large fruit tree not far from a village, a tree that always abounds in many fine and delicious fruits.
Suppose a person comes along, hungry, weak, and exhausted, desiring to eat its fruit; he would think thus:"

However, there are no fallen fruits beneath this tree by which I might satisfy my hunger or take some with me. Since I am able to climb trees, would it not be better for me to ascend this tree now?"
Having thought this, he climbed up.
Then another man arrived, emaciated and exhausted by hunger, wishing to obtain fruit to eat. Carrying an extremely sharp axe, he thought to himself:

"This tree always has many fine and delicious fruits; however, there are no fallen fruits under this tree from which I can eat my fill or take home. I cannot climb the tree; would it not be better for me to cut this tree down?"

What do you think, householder?
If the person in the tree did not quickly come down, would his arm or other limbs necessarily be broken when the tree fell to the ground?
