The householder replied, “No, Gautama.”

"Householder! A learned noble disciple also reflects in this way: 'Sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree; the World-Honored One has said that sensual desires are like the fruit of a tree—yielding little pleasure but much suffering, and fraught with many calamities and afflictions; one should keep far away from them.'"

If there is this relinquishing of desire and abandoning of evil, unwholesome states—namely, that all worldly food and drink are forever exhausted without remainder—one should cultivate that; this is called another of the eight factors for severing mundane affairs and attaining realization within the Noble Dharma and Discipline.
"Householder!

With the subsiding of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), he becomes inwardly tranquil and one-pointed; without applied thought or sustained thought, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss."

Having already become detached from desire for joy, he dwells in equanimity, free from seeking, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing bliss with the body; that which the Noble Ones describe as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in bliss," he attains and abides in the third dhyāna.

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.

Having thus attained a concentrated mind that is pure, stainless, and free from affliction—supple, well-established, and unshakable—he cultivates and realizes the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
He knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are.
He knows these taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; he knows according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
When this Dharma was being taught, the householder Pūtila became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.

Thereupon, the householder Pūtila saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma; he realized the pure and white Dharma, severed doubt, crossed over uncertainty, and had no further reliance on others. No longer depending on another, free from hesitation, and having already established himself in the realization of the fruit, he attained fearlessness in the Dharma of the Blessed One. He prostrated at the feet of the Buddha and said:
"Blessed One!"

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.
"Bhagavān!

Formerly, I was dressed in pure white garments, with my head wrapped in a white cloth, leaning on a staff and holding a parasol, wearing secular sandals, and wandering from garden to garden, from park to park, and from grove to grove. Whenever I saw any śramaṇas or brahmins, I would speak to them thus:
'O worthy ones!'"
"I have departed from the worldly, severed the worldly, and abandoned all worldly affairs.
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, gentle and mild-tempered, said to me:
"Indeed so."
"The worthy Pūtila has left the world and severed worldly ties; he has abandoned all mundane affairs.
"World-Honored One!

At that time, although he truly lacked wisdom, he was established in the station of the wise; though he truly lacked wisdom, he offered sacrifices as if possessing wisdom; and though he truly lacked wisdom, he served others as if he were a person of wisdom."
"Blessed One!

From this day forward, among the assembly of bhikṣus and the disciples of the Blessed One, I shall truly possess wisdom; I shall abide in the station of wisdom, truly possess the sacrifice of wisdom, truly possess the food of wisdom, and truly possess wisdom as I serve those who possess wisdom."
"Bhagavān!

I now once again take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray only that the Bhagavān accept me as an upāsaka; from this day forth, until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live."
"Blessed One!
From this day forth, I shall sever all faith, respect, and veneration for the non-Buddhist śramaṇas and brahmins whom I formerly held in such regard.
Blessed One!"

From this day forth, I take refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. I pray only that the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day until the end of my life, I shall take refuge for as long as I live.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the householder Potaliya and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The second discourse, the Potaliya Sūtra, ends here, totaling 3,642 characters. The Madhyama Āgama, Volume 55, totals 7,691 characters. Fifth Recitation Section.
Madhyama Āgama, Volume 56.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Gautama Saṃghadeva of Jibin during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
204. Rāma Sūtra (204). Chapter on Potaliputta, Third Sūtra: The Rāma Sūtra; Part Five, Subsequent Recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, in the Eastern Park, at the Mṛgāramātṛ Hall.
Then, in the late afternoon, the Blessed One rose from his meditation, descended from the hall, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"I shall now go with you to the river Ajiravatī to bathe.
Venerable Ānanda replied, "So be it."
Venerable Ānanda, taking the keys, went about visiting all the dwellings; seeing the bhikkhus there, he spoke to them thus:
"Virtuous ones!..."
"We should go together to the house of the brahmin Rāma.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went together to the house of the brahmin Rāma.

The World-Honored One, taking the Venerable Ānanda with him, went to the river Ajiravatī; he removed his robes on the bank, entered the water to bathe, and having bathed, came back out, wiped his body, and put on his clothes.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and fanning the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!"
The house of the brahmin Rāma is extremely well-ordered and very pleasant; we pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will go to the house of the brahmin Rāma.
The Blessed One accepted the request from the Venerable Ānanda by remaining silent.
Thereupon, the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda with him and went to the house of the brahmin Rāma.

At that time, many bhikṣus were gathered and seated at the home of the brahmin Rāma, preaching the Dharma. The Buddha remained outside the gate, waiting for the bhikṣus to finish their discourse on the Dharma.
When the many bhikṣus had finished preaching the Dharma, they remained silent.

Knowing this, the World-Honored One cleared his throat and knocked at the door. Hearing him, the bhikṣus went immediately to open the gate, and the World-Honored One entered the house of the brahmin Rāma. He spread out a seat before the assembly of bhikṣus and sat down, asking:
"Bhikṣus, what were you discussing just now?"
"For what reason have you gathered and sat here?
At that time, the bhikṣus replied:
"World-Honored One!"
"Just now I taught the Dharma, and for this purpose of the Dharma you have gathered and sat here.
The World-Honored One praised them, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent!
When bhikṣus are gathered in assembly, they should practice two things:
first, preaching the Dharma; second, remaining silent.
"Why is that? I shall also teach the Dharma to you; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus said:
“Yes, indeed.
We shall receive and listen to the instruction.
The Buddha said:
“There are two kinds of seeking: first, noble seeking; second, ignoble seeking. What is ignoble seeking? There is one who, being truly subject to the nature of illness, seeks the nature of illness;
being truly subject to the nature of aging, the nature of death, the nature of sorrow, lamentation, and dejection, and the nature of defilement, seeks the nature of defilement.”
What is meant by "seeking the nature of illness within the nature of illness"?
What is the nature of illness?
Sons and brothers are the nature of illness.

Elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, money, wealth, precious gems, rice, and grain are phenomena that cause affliction; yet sentient beings become defiled by contact with them, becoming arrogant and attached, failing to perceive their calamities and failing to see the way of escape, as they take them up for use.
What are the phenomena subject to aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and dejection; what are the phenomena that are defiled? Sons and brothers are defiled phenomena.

Elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, money, wealth, treasures, and grain are defiled and harmful phenomena. Sentient beings become stained by contact with these, becoming greedily attached, arrogant, and absorbed in them; they do not see their dangers nor the way of escape, yet they take them up and use them.

If that person desires to seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness, yet attains that unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness—such a thing is simply impossible.

If they seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, yet attain that unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement—such a thing is simply impossible.
This is called the non-noble quest.
"What is the noble quest?
There is one who reflects thus:"

"I am truly subject to the nature of illness and, though innocent, I seek out the nature of illness; I am truly subject to the nature of aging, the nature of death, the nature of sorrow, lamentation, and dejection, and the nature of defilement, and though innocent, I seek out the nature of defilement."

I would rather now seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from illness; I would seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from aging, free from death, free from sorrow, lamentation, and distress, and free from all defiled phenomena.
That person then seeks the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness; that they shall attain this unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness is certainly possible.

For one who seeks the unsurpassed, secure Nirvana—free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, lamentation, and despair, and free from defilement—it is certainly possible that they shall attain this unsurpassed, secure Nirvana, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, lamentation, and despair, and free from defilement.
"Before I had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I also thought thus:

'I am truly subject to the nature of illness and yet I seek the nature of illness; I am truly subject to the nature of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, and yet I seek the nature of defilement. Would it not be better for me now to seek the unsurpassed, secure nirvana that is free from illness, free from aging, free from death, free from sorrow and lamentation, and free from defilement—the unsurpassed, secure nirvana? "
At that time, I was a young boy with pure, dark hair, in the full bloom of youth at twenty-nine years of age; at that time, I took great delight in play and would go about adorned with ornaments.

At that time, while my parents wept and my relatives were distressed, I shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Way, maintaining purity in the life of the body and purity in the lives of speech and mind.

Having accomplished this aggregate of virtue, desiring to seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana—free from illness, free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement—I went to where Āḷāra Kālāma was and asked him: "Āḷāra!..."
"I wish to practice the holy life under your teaching;
would that be permissible? Āḷāra replied to me, saying, "Worthy one!..."
"I have no objection; if you wish to go, then go.
I then asked again: "Āḷāra!"
"How is it that you have known this Dharma for yourself, awakened to it for yourself, and realized it for yourself?
Āḷāra replied to me, saying:
"Worthy one!"
"I have transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness and attained the sphere of nothingness, dwelling in its accomplishment.
Therefore, regarding my Dharma, I know it myself, realize it myself, and witness it for myself.
Then, I further had this thought:

"It is not only Āḷāra who alone possesses this faith; I too possess this faith. It is not only Āḷāra who alone possesses this diligence; I too possess this diligence. It is not only Āḷāra who alone possesses this wisdom; I too possess this wisdom."
"Āḷāra has personally known, personally awakened to, and personally realized this Dharma.
Desiring to realize this Dharma myself, I then dwelt alone in seclusion, in a quiet and peaceful place, my mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.
Dwelling alone in a secluded, empty, and tranquil place, with a mind free from negligence and practicing with diligent effort, I soon realized that Dharma.
Having realized that Dharma, I went again to where Āḷāra Kālāma was and asked him: "Āḷāra!..."

"Having known this Dharma for oneself, realized it for oneself, and witnessed it for oneself— namely, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, does one attain and dwell in the accomplishment of the sphere of nothingness?
Āḷāra Kālāma replied to me, "Worthy sir!..."

"I have realized, known, and personally witnessed for myself this Dharma, namely: having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, I attained and dwell in the accomplishment of the sphere of nothingness.
Āḷāra Kālāma then said to me again:
"Worthy one!..."
"In this way, as I have realized this Dharma, so have you; as you have realized this Dharma, so have I.
Worthy one!
Come, lead this assembly together with me."
This was my dwelling with the teacher Āḷāra Kālāma; there, I was treated as his equal, receiving the highest respect, the highest offerings, and the highest joy.
I further thought:

"This teaching does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, and does not lead to nirvāṇa. I would rather now abandon this teaching and seek instead the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvāṇa that is free from illness; I seek the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvāṇa that is free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement."

I then abandoned this teaching and sought instead the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana, free from illness; having sought the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana, free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, I went to where Udraka Rāmaputra was and asked him: "Udraka!..."
"I wish to train in your Dharma; would that be permissible?
Udraka Rāmaputra replied to me, "Venerable one!..."
"I have no objection; you may learn as you wish.
I then asked again: "Udraka!"
"Udraka Rāmaputra, what dharma do you yourself know, yourself realize,
and yourself witness? Udraka Rāmaputra replied to me,
"Venerable sir!"
Having transcended the sphere of nothingness, he attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Worthy one!
This is the Dharma that my father Rāma knew for himself, realized for himself, and witnessed for himself.
I further thought: "It is not only Rāma who possesses this faith; I too possess this faith.
It is not only Rāma who possesses this diligence; I too possess this diligence."
"It is not only Rāma who possesses this wisdom; I too possess this wisdom.
Since Rāma has known, realized, and personally witnessed this Dharma for himself, why should I not also know, realize, and personally witness this Dharma for myself?"
Desiring to realize this Dharma, I dwelt alone in seclusion, in a place that was empty, quiet, and peaceful, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort.
Having dwelt alone in seclusion, in a place that was empty, quiet, and peaceful, with a mind free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort, I soon realized that Dharma.
Having realized that Dharma, he went again to where Uddaka Rāmaputta was and asked: "Uddaka!

Did your father Rāma, having known it for himself, awakened to it for himself, and realized it for himself, claim to have transcended the sphere of nothingness and attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"
Uddaka Rāmaputta replied to me, saying: "Worthy one!

My father Rāma knew this Dharma for himself, realized it for himself, and witnessed it for himself; that is to say, having transcended the sphere of nothingness, he attained and dwelt in the accomplishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Uddaka further said to me:
"Just as my father Rāma realized this Dharma through direct realization, so have you; just as you have realized this Dharma, so did my father."
"Worthy one!
Come, lead this assembly together with me.
At the place where Uddaka Rāmaputra was my teacher, I likewise treated him as my teacher, offering him the highest respect, the highest offerings, and the highest joy.
I further had this thought:

"This Dharma does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, and does not lead to Nirvana. I would now rather abandon this Dharma and seek instead the illness-free, unsurpassed peace and security of Nirvana; I seek the old-age-free, death-free, sorrow-free, grief-free, and defilement-free, unsurpassed peace and security of Nirvana."

I then abandoned this teaching and sought instead the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana, free from illness; having sought the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana, free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, I went to the south of Mount Hatthigiri to the brahmin village of Uruvelā, named Senāni.
That place was exceedingly delightful, with lush and verdant mountain forests and the clear, flowing waters of the Nairañjanā River filling its banks.
Upon seeing it, I thought to myself:

"This place is exceedingly delightful, with its lush and verdant mountain forests and the clear, flowing waters of the Nairañjanā River filling its banks. If a son of noble family wishes to train, he may do so here; I too shall train, and I should now indeed train here."

He then took the grass and went to the Bodhi tree; having arrived, he spread out the *niṣīdana* mat, sat down cross-legged, and vowed not to break his posture until the destruction of the outflows was attained: "I shall not break this sitting posture until I have attained the destruction of the outflows. I, too, did not break my sitting posture until I had attained the destruction of the outflows.
Seeking the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from illness, I have attained the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from illness.

Seeking the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, I have attained the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana that is free from old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement.

Possessing innate knowledge and innate vision, he has established the factors of the path; birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows, in accordance with reality, that there will be no further existence.
"When I had first awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I thought:
'For whom should I first teach the Dharma?
Then I thought again:"
"I should now perhaps preach the Dharma first to Āḷāra Kālāma.
At that time, a deva dwelling in the midst of the sky spoke to me, saying:
"Great Seer!..."
"You should know that seven days have passed since Āḷāra Kālāma’s death.
"I too know for myself that seven days have passed since Āḷāra Kālāma’s death."
I further had this thought: "Āḷāra Kālāma!
That man has long been deprived of hearing this Dharma; had he heard it, he would have quickly understood the Dharma and its sequence."
"After I had first awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I had this thought:
'For whom should I first preach the Dharma?
Then I further had this thought:"
"I thought to myself: 'Should I now first teach the Dharma to Udraka Rāmaputra?
Then a deva, stationed in the air, spoke to me, saying:
'Great Seer!'"
"You should know that it has been two weeks since Udraka Rāmaputra passed away.
"I too know for myself that it has been two weeks since Udraka Rāmaputra passed away."
I further had this thought:
"Udraka Rāmaputra! That man is long deprived of hearing this Dharma;
had he heard the Dharma, he would have quickly understood the Dharma and the sequence of the Dharma."
"After I had first awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I had this thought:
'For whom should I preach the Dharma first?
Then I further had this thought:"

"In the past, the five bhikṣus labored for me and benefited me greatly; while I was practicing austerities, those five bhikṣus attended upon me. Should I not now preach the Dharma first to these five bhikṣus?"
I further thought to myself:
"Where are the five bhikṣus now?

With the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, I saw the five bhikṣus at the Deer Park in the Abode of Seers at Vārāṇasī. Remaining beneath the Bodhi tree, I gathered my robes, took up my bowl, and set out for the city of Kāśi in Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the heterodox teacher Udāyin saw me coming from afar and said to me:
"Venerable Gautama!
Your faculties are pure, your complexion is most exquisite, and the light from your face shines radiantly."
Venerable Gautama!
Who is your teacher?
Under whom have you studied the Path?
"In whose dharma do you place your faith?
At that time, I immediately spoke a verse in reply to Udāyin:
"I am the most supreme and most excellent; I am unattached to all phenomena."
With all cravings extinguished, liberated, and having awakened for himself, who could be called his teacher?
Peerless and unsurpassed, he has awakened to the supreme enlightenment;
the Tathāgata, Teacher of Gods and Humans, possesses the power of universal knowledge and accomplishment.
"Udāyin asked me: 'Venerable Gautama!
Do you claim to be superior? "
I further replied to him with a verse:
"A Victor is one who is thus: having attained the exhaustion of all taints (*āsrava*), I have destroyed all unwholesome dharmas;
O Udaya, for this reason I am the Victor."
Udāyin asked me again:
"Venerable Gautama,
where do you wish to go?"
At that time, I replied to him with these verses:
"I have gone to Vārāṇasī To beat the wondrous drum of the Deathless (amṛta),
To turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, Which has never before been turned in the world."
Udāyin said to me: "Venerable Gautama,
it may indeed be so."
When he had spoken thus, that heretical discourse immediately vanished, and I proceeded on my own to the Deer Park, the dwelling place of the seers.

At that time, the five bhikṣus saw me coming from afar and, having consulted one another, established a rule, saying: "Venerable friends! [Do not greet him with the title 'Āyuṣmat,' but rather address him as 'O monk' (bhante) or 'O recluse' (samaṇa).]"

"You should know that this śramaṇa Gautama has come; he is full of desire and full of seeking, eating exquisite food and fond of fine rice, parched grain, ghee, and honey, and now he has arrived again with his body anointed with sesame oil. You should simply remain seated; be careful not to rise to meet him, nor offer him salutation. Set aside a seat in advance, but do not invite him to sit."
Having arrived, he said:
"Sir! If you wish to sit, do as you please."
I then went to where the five bhikṣus were.

At that time, the five bhikṣus could not endure my supreme and wondrous majesty; they immediately rose from their seats—some took up their robes and bowls, some spread out mats, some fetched water, and some wished to wash my feet.
I thought to myself: "These foolish people!"
"Why is it not firm?
You have established your own regulations that contradict the original essentials.
Having understood this about them, I sat upon the seat prepared by the five bhikṣus.
"At that time, the five bhikṣus addressed me by my clan name and personal name, and spoke to me as an equal.
I said to them:
'O five bhikṣus!'"
I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; you should not address me by my original family name or clan, nor should you address me as "you. Why is this?
I sought the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness, and I have attained the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from illness.

I sought the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement, and I have attained the unsurpassed peace and security of nirvana free from aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, and defilement.

Possessing innate knowledge and innate vision, he has established the factors of the path; birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows with suchness that there will be no further existence.
He said to me: "O Gautama!

If, by practicing such conduct, following such a path, and performing such asceticism as you did in the past, you were still unable to attain the superhuman states, the distinguished qualities, the noble knowledge, and the noble vision—how much less so today, when you have many desires and many cravings, eating choice foods, fine rice, parched grain, ghee, honey, and anointing your body with sesame oil?"
I spoke again, saying:
"O five bhikṣus!
Did you previously see my faculties thus purified and radiating such brilliance?"
Then, the five bhikṣus replied to me again, saying:
"We have never before seen your faculties so pure and your radiance so brilliant.
You, Gautama!"
"Now his faculties are pure, his form and color are most exquisite, and the radiance of his face shines forth.
At that time, I immediately said to them:
"O five bhikṣus!..."
One should know that there are two extreme practices which those who seek the Path ought not to study:
first, attachment to sensual pleasures and base activities, which is the conduct of ordinary people;
second, self-inflicted affliction and self-mortification, which is not the pursuit of the Dharma by the Noble Ones and is inconsistent with the meaningful.
"O five bhikṣus!

Abandoning these two extremes, there is a Middle Way that brings about vision, brings about knowledge, leads to the attainment of concentration, and results in mastery; it leads to wisdom, leads to awakening, and leads to Nirvāṇa. This is called the Eightfold Noble Path, from Right View through to Right Concentration—these are the eight."
He intended to follow the instruction to teach the five bhikṣus: he would instruct two of them while three went for alms, and when those three brought back the food, it would suffice for the six;
or he would instruct three of them while two went for alms, and when those two brought back the food, it would suffice for the six.
I have thus instructed and transformed him; seeking the illness-free, unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa*, he has attained the illness-free, unsurpassed peace of *nirvāṇa*.

Seeking the unsurpassed peace and security of *nirvāṇa*—which is without aging, without death, without sorrow, lamentation, or distress, and without defilement—one attains that unsurpassed peace and security of *nirvāṇa* which is without aging, without death, without sorrow, lamentation, or distress, and without defilement.

Possessing innate knowledge and innate vision, he has established the factors of the path; birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and he knows, as it truly is, that there will be no further existence.
Then the Blessed One spoke again to them, saying:
"O five bhikṣus!
There are five strands of sensual pleasure that are lovely, delightful, agreeable to the mind, and associated with wholesome desire."
What are the five? The eye cognizes forms;
the ear cognizes sounds; the nose cognizes odors; the tongue cognizes tastes; the body cognizes tangibles.
These, O bhikṣus!

Foolish worldlings who are not of much learning do not see virtuous friends; they do not know the noble Dharma and do not practice the noble Dharma. They encounter defilements with greedy attachment, becoming arrogant and absorbed in them; failing to see their peril and failing to see the way of escape, they take them up and employ them.

You should know that such a person follows the evil Māra, becomes an evil Māra himself, falls into the hands of the evil Māra, is entangled in the net of Māra, and is bound by the snare of Māra, unable to escape the snare of Māra.
"O five bhikṣus!

It is just as when a wild deer is caught in a snare; you should know that it follows the hunter, acts as the hunter's own, falls into the hunter's hands, becomes entangled in the hunter's net, and once the hunter has arrived, cannot escape."
Thus it is, O five bhikṣus!
The foolish worldling is of little learning, does not see virtuous friends, does not know the noble Dharma, and does not practice the noble Dharma.

He comes into contact with these five strands of sensual pleasure, becoming defiled by them and greedily attached; he becomes arrogant and absorbed in them, failing to see their peril and failing to see the way of escape, yet he continues to take them up and use them.

You should know that such a person follows the evil Māra, becomes an evil Māra himself, falls into the hands of the evil Māra, is entangled in the net of Māra, and is bound by the snare of Māra, unable to escape the snare of Māra.
“O five bhikṣus!

A learned noble disciple sees a virtuous friend, understands the noble Dharma, and practices the noble Dharma. Regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, he does not touch them, is not defiled by them, does not crave them, and does not cling to them; nor does he become arrogant or absorbed in them. Seeing their peril and seeing the escape from them, he makes use of them.”

You should know that such a person does not follow the evil Māra, does not act as a Māra himself, does not fall into the hands of Māra, is not entangled in the net of Māra, and is not caught in the snare of Māra; they are thus liberated from the snare of Māra.
"O five bhikṣus!

It is just as when a wild deer escapes from a snare; you should know that it does not follow the hunter, it is not subject to the hunter's will, it does not fall into the hunter's hands, and it is not entangled by the hunter's net. Once the hunter has come, the deer is able to escape."

In this way, O five bhikṣus! A well-heard noble disciple perceives the true friend and knows the noble Dharma; furthermore, he masters the noble Dharma. Regarding these five strands of sensual pleasure, he does not touch them, is not defiled by them, does not crave them, and does not cling to them. He neither views them with arrogance nor undergoes their influence; rather, seeing their peril and seeing the escape from them, he makes use of them.

You should know that such a person does not follow the evil Māra, nor the Māra of non-sovereignty; they do not fall into the hands of Māra, are not entangled by the net of Māra, and are not ensnared by the snare of Māra, but are instead liberated from the snare of Māra.
“O five bhikṣus!

When a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—he abandons, even unto the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind and weakness of wisdom—and being detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, he attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.”

With his mind thus concentrated, pure, stainless, and free from affliction, supple, well-established, and unshakable, he trains in and realizes the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
He knows this suffering as it truly is; he knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are.
He knows these taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of these taints, the cessation of these taints, and the path leading to the cessation of these taints as they truly are.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), and his mind is liberated from the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Being liberated, he knows he is liberated; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence—he knows this as it truly is.
At that time, he moves with mastery, stands with mastery, sits with mastery, and lies down with mastery.
Why is this? Because he has personally seen that immeasurable evil and unwholesome states have been exhausted.
Therefore, he walks at will, stands at will, sits at will, and lies down at will.
"O five bhikṣus!
It is just as in a desolate place devoid of people, where there are wild deer that walk at will, stand at will, lie down at will, and rest at will."
Why is this? Because that wild deer is not within the hunter's domain.
Therefore, it moves at its own will, stays at its own will, crouches at its own will, and lies down at its own will.
Thus it is, O five bhikṣus!

A bhikṣu whose taints are exhausted attains the taintless state; his mind is liberated and his wisdom is liberated. Having known, realized, and witnessed this for himself, he dwells having achieved it: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence"—he knows this as it truly is.
At that time, he moves with mastery, stands with mastery, sits with mastery, and lies down with mastery.
Why is this? Because he personally perceives that his immeasurable evil and unwholesome states have been exhausted.
Therefore, he moves with mastery, stands with mastery, sits with mastery, and lies down with mastery.
O five bhikṣus!

This is called liberation without remainder; this is called the illness-free, unsurpassed peace and security of *nirvāṇa*; this is called the unsurpassed peace and security of *nirvāṇa* that is free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, lamentation, and distress, and free from defilement.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The third *Rāma Sūtra* ends here, totaling 4,121 characters. 205. The Discourse on the Five Lower Fetters (205). *Madhyama Āgama*, *Purindada-varga*. The Fourth and Fifth Recitations of the *Pañca-avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana Sūtra*. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I have previously spoken of the five lower fetters; do you all uphold them?”
The bhikṣus remained silent and did not answer.
The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus a second and third time:
"Do you accept and uphold what I have taught regarding the five lower fetters?"
The bhikṣus likewise remained silent and did not answer, even after being asked a second and a third time.
At that moment, the Venerable Māṇava was present in that assembly.
Thereupon, the Venerable Māṇava rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
“The Blessed One has spoken of the five lower fetters; I have received and uphold them.
The Blessed One asked, “Māṇava!”
“I have spoken of the five lower fetters; do you uphold them?
The Venerable Māṇava replied:

“The Blessed One has spoken of the first lower fetter, which I uphold: sensual desire. Hatred, identity view, adherence to rules and observances, and doubt—the Blessed One has spoken of these as the fifth lower fetter, which I uphold.”
The Blessed One rebuked him, saying:
"Māṇava! How can you claim to have received and upheld my teaching on the five lower fetters?"
Māṇava! From which mouth did you receive and uphold my teaching on the five lower fetters? Māṇava!
Is it not because many heterodox practitioners have come to reprimand, reproach, and interrogate you with the analogy of an infant? Mañca-putta!
An infant is young and small, soft and lying on its back; it has no thoughts of desire, let alone being bound by the fetters of a lustful mind.
However, because that nature is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it is called the "latent tendency of desire.
Boy Mañjuṣaka!
When an infant is very young, soft, and lying on its back, it has no perception of a sentient being; how much less could it be bound by the fetter of a mind of ill will?
However, because that nature is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it is called the latent tendency of ill-will (*vyāpādānuśaya*). Mañjukeśa!
When an infant is very young, soft, and lying on its back, it has no perception of a self; how much less could the mind be bound by the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
However, because that nature is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it is called the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-anuśaya*).
Mañjuśrī-kumāra!
When an infant is very young, soft, and lying on its back, there is no perception of precepts; how much less could there be the mental entanglement of clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
However, because that nature is a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it is called the latent tendency of clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-anuśaya*). Maṇicūḍa!
When an infant is very young, soft, and lying on its back, there is not even the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*); how much less could there be the entanglement of a doubting mind?
However, because that is his underlying tendency (*anuśaya*), he speaks of the underlying tendency of doubt. Boy Wreath!
Was it not for the sake of many heterodox teachers who have come here to reproach and interrogate you with this parable of the infant?

Thereupon, having been rebuked face-to-face by the Blessed One, the Venerable Māṇava stood with inner grief, his head bowed in silence; deprived of his eloquence and speechless, he remained as if lost in thought.
At that time, having rebuked the youth Māṇava in the presence of the World-Honored One, the Blessed One remained silent.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda stood behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and fanning the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time."
“Sugata, now is the very time.
If the Blessed One were to explain the five lower fetters to the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus, having heard them from the Blessed One, would receive and uphold them well.”
The World-Honored One said:
“Ānanda! Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.”
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
"Indeed. I shall receive your instruction and listen."
The Buddha said:

“Ānanda, suppose there is one who is entangled by desire; once a thought of desire has arisen, he does not know how to relinquish it as it truly is. Because he does not know how to relinquish it as it truly is, his desire becomes increasingly intense and cannot be restrained or eliminated; this is a lower fetter.”

Ānanda! Suppose there is one who is entangled by anger; once the thought of anger has arisen, he does not know, as it truly is, how to relinquish it. Because he does not know, as it truly is, how to relinquish it, his anger flares up even more intensely and cannot be restrained or eliminated. This is a lower fetter.

Ānanda! Suppose there is one who is缠縛 (bound) by the view of a self-identity; once the thought of the view of a self-identity has arisen, he does not know how to abandon it as it truly is. Because he does not know how to abandon it as it truly is, the view of a self-identity increases further and cannot be restrained or eliminated; this is a lower fetter (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Ānanda! There may be one who is entangled by the clinging to precepts and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*). Once such a mind of clinging to precepts and observances has arisen, he does not know, as it truly is, how to relinquish it. Because he does not know, as it truly is, how to relinquish it, his clinging to precepts and observances increases further and cannot be restrained or eliminated; this is a lower fetter (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*).

Ānanda! Suppose there is one who is entangled by doubt; once doubt has arisen in the mind, he does not know how to abandon it as it truly is. Because he does not know how to abandon it as it truly is, his doubt increases and becomes more intense, such that it cannot be restrained or eliminated. This is a lower fetter (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
“Ānanda! If one relies on the path and relies on the track to abandon the five lower fetters—
there is no possibility that one could abandon the five lower fetters without relying on this path and without relying on this track.”

Ānanda! It is just as if there were a person who, desiring to obtain fruit, entered a forest for that purpose carrying an axe. If that person, seeing a tree fully developed with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit, were to fail to cut through the roots and trunk and instead returned home with only the fruit—it is simply impossible that such a thing could happen.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If one relies on the path and relies on the track, one severs the five lower fetters.
It is impossible that one who does not rely on this path and does not rely on this track could sever the five lower fetters; such a thing can never occur. Ānanda!
If one relies on the path and relies on the track, then for one who relies on this path and relies on this track to sever the five lower fetters, that is certainly possible.

Ānanda! It is just as if there were a person who, desiring to obtain fruit, entered a forest for the sake of seeking that fruit, carrying an axe. That person sees a tree fully developed with roots, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruit; if that person cuts through the roots and trunk and returns having obtained the fruit, such a thing is certainly possible.

It is so, Ānanda! If one relies on this path, relies on this track, and severs the five lower fetters— relying on this path and relying on this track to sever the five lower fetters— such a thing is certainly possible.
“Ānanda! By what path and by what track does one abandon the five lower fetters? Ānanda!”

There may be one who is not bound by desire; if the bond of desire arises, he immediately knows its relinquishment as it truly is. Having known its relinquishment as it truly is, his bond of desire is then extinguished.

Ānanda! Suppose there is one who is not entangled by ill will; if the entanglement of ill will arises, he immediately knows the relinquishing of it as it truly is. Having known the relinquishing of it as it truly is, that entanglement of ill will is then extinguished.

Ānanda! There may be someone who is not bound by the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi). If the bond of the view of a self arises, he immediately knows its relinquishment as it truly is. Having known its relinquishment as it truly is, that bond of the view of a self is then extinguished.

Ānanda! There may be one who is not bound by the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances; if the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances should arise, he immediately knows its relinquishment as it truly is. Having known its relinquishment as it truly is, that attachment to precepts and observances is then extinguished.

Ānanda! There may be one who is not entangled by doubt; if the entanglement of doubt arises, he immediately knows the relinquishing of it as it truly is. Having known the relinquishing of it as it truly is, that entanglement of doubt is then extinguished.
"Ānanda! By relying on this path, by following this track, one severs the five lower fetters. Ānanda!"
It is like the Ganges River, whose waters overflow its banks.
Suppose there were a person on this side who, having business on the other bank, wished to cross the river. He would think to himself:
"This Ganges River has waters overflowing its banks; I have business on the far shore and wish to cross, yet my body lacks the strength to float safely to the other side."
"Ānanda! You should know that such a person lacks power.
It is thus, Ānanda!"
If there is someone who has awakened to, extinguished, and attained nirvana, yet their mind does not incline toward it, is not purified, and does not abide in liberation— Ānanda,
you should know that such a person is like that weak man who lacks strength.
Ānanda! It is as if the waters of the Ganges River were overflowing its banks.
Suppose a person were to come to the far bank, having business that required them to cross the river, and they were to think this:

"This River Gaṅgā has its waters overflowing the banks; I have business on the opposite shore and wish to cross over. My body now possesses the strength to enable me to float safely to the other side."
"Ānanda! You should know that such a person possesses great power.
It is thus, Ānanda!"
If there is someone who has awakened, attained cessation, and entered nirvana, whose mind is directed toward purity and who abides in liberation— Ānanda,
you should know that such a person is like that strong man.
“Ānanda! It is like a mountain river, exceedingly deep and extremely wide, with a long-flowing, rapid current that sweeps away much; yet within it there is neither boat nor bridge.”
Suppose someone comes to the other shore and, having business there, seeks to cross over. While seeking to cross, he thinks to himself:
"This mountain river is very deep and extremely wide; its current flows swiftly and violently, carrying many things away. Within it there is no boat, nor is there any bridge by which one may cross."
"I have business on the other shore and wish to cross over; by what means may I reach that other shore in safety?
He then thought further:
"I should now gather grass and wood from this shore, bind them together to make a raft, and cross over by riding upon it."
He then gathered grass and wood by the bank, bound them together to make a raft, and crossing upon it, reached the other side in safety.
In this same way, Ānanda!

If there is a bhikṣu who takes disenchantment as his object of focus, relies upon disenchantment, and abides in disenchantment, then because he has stilled bodily misconduct and his mind has entered into seclusion and concentration, he—detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states—with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the first dhyāna.

Relying on this basis, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings; having relied on this basis and contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, he dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints; or, if he does not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, he will certainly advance further to attain the state of rest.
"What is the further advancement that attains the state of tranquility?

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he becomes inwardly settled and one-pointed; without directed thought or evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and happiness."

Relying on this basis, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings; having relied on this basis and contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, he dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints. Should he not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, he will certainly advance further to attain the state of cessation.
How does one progress to attain the state of rest?
Detached from joy and desire, dwelling in equanimity and seeking nothing, with right mindfulness and right clear comprehension, he experiences happiness with the body.
This is what the Noble Ones describe as the noble state of equanimity, mindfulness, and dwelling in happiness; thus he attains and dwells in the fulfillment of the third dhyāna.

Relying on this basis, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings; having relied on this basis and contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, he dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints. Should he not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, he will certainly advance further to attain the state of rest.
How does one advance to attain the state of rest?

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.

Relying on this basis, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings; having relied on this basis and contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, he dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints; even if he does not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, he will certainly advance further to attain the state of rest.
"What is the further advancement that leads to the attainment of the state of rest?

One transcends all perceptions of form, ceases perceptions of sensory resistance, and no longer attends to perceptions of diversity; one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Relying upon this state, one contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings. Having relied upon this state to contemplate the arising and passing away of feelings, one dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints. Should one not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, one will certainly advance further to attain the state of rest."
What is the further advancement that leads to the attainment of the state of rest?
Having transcended the sphere of infinite space, one attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Relying on this basis, he contemplates the arising and passing away of feelings; having relied on this basis and contemplated the arising and passing away of feelings, he dwells therein and will certainly attain the destruction of the taints; should he not attain the destruction of the taints while dwelling therein, he will certainly advance further to attain the state of cessation.
How does one advance to attain the state of rest?
Having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness entirely, there being nothing whatsoever, one dwells having attained the sphere of nothingness.
If he experiences any feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he contemplates that feeling as impermanent;
he contemplates its arising and passing away, its dispassion, its cessation, its abandonment, and its relinquishment.

Thus observing this consciousness as impermanent, having observed its arising and passing away, its dispassion, its cessation, its abandonment, and its relinquishment, he does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, he is not terrified. Because he is not terrified, he attains parinirvāṇa, knowing according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."

"It is like this: not far from a village there is a large plantain tree. Suppose a person were to take an axe and split the plantain tree, breaking it into pieces, dividing it into ten parts, or even into a hundred parts."
Having broken it into ten parts, or even a hundred parts, and then splitting it leaf by leaf, one does not see its joints, much less its core.

Ānanda, in this same way, if a bhikṣu experiences any feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he contemplates that feeling as impermanent; he contemplates its arising and passing away, its dispassion, its cessation, its abandonment, and its relinquishment.

Thus observing this perception as impermanent, having observed its arising and passing away, its dispassion, its cessation, its abandonment, and its relinquishment, he does not cling to this world. Not clinging to this world, he is not afraid. Being without fear, he attains parinirvāṇa, knowing according to reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"World-Honored One!
How extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary!

The Blessed One has established for the bhikṣus a reliance based on reliance, teaching the relinquishing of outflows and the transcending of outflows; yet the bhikṣus do not quickly attain the unsurpassed, which is called the ultimate end and exhaustion."
The Blessed One said: "So it is, Ānanda!"
"So it is, Ānanda! How extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary!

I have established for the bhikṣus a reliance upon reliance, taught the relinquishing of outflows, and taught the transcending of outflows; yet these bhikṣus do not quickly attain the unsurpassed, which is called the ultimate end and exhaustion."

Why is this so? Because there are distinctions of superiority among persons, the cultivation of the path consequently possesses degrees of refinement and coarseness; because the cultivation of the path possesses these degrees of refinement and coarseness, persons consequently possess distinctions of superiority.
"Ānanda! For this reason, I say that among persons there are distinctions of superiority.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Ānanda and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Fourth Discourse on the Five Lower Fetters ends here, totaling two thousand three hundred and twenty-six characters. 206. The Discourse on Mental Defilement (Cittasavaka Sutta) The Fifth Discourse on Mental Defilement, from the Puḷina-vagga of the Madhyama Āgama. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī does not uproot the five impurities within the mind and does not untie the five fetters within the mind, I declare this to be the dharma of inevitable decline for that bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī."
What is meant by not extracting the five impurities from the mind?
It is when someone harbors doubt regarding the World-Honored One, being hesitant, lacking clarity of mind, lacking understanding, and having a restless mind.

If one harbors doubt regarding the Blessed One—hesitating, lacking clarity of mind, lacking understanding, and having an unsettled mind—this is called not extracting the first defilement of the mind, namely, [doubt] regarding the Blessed One; and likewise regarding the Dharma, the Discipline, and the Teaching.

If there are fellow practitioners of the holy life who are praised by the Blessed One, yet one reproaches them, treats them with contempt, harasses them, and harms them—being displeased, dissatisfied, and mentally unsettled—this is called the fifth impurity not extracted from the mind, namely, regarding fellow practitioners of the holy life.
"What is meant by not understanding the five fetters within the mind?
There may be one whose body is not free from passion, not free from desire, not free from craving, and not free from thirst."

If there is a person whose body is not free from defilement, not free from desire, not free from craving, and not free from thirst, their mind will not incline toward it; it will not be tranquil, will not abide, and will not be liberated, such that they abandon their own practice of meditative seclusion through their own effort.

If one possesses such a mind that does not incline toward it, is not settled, does not abide, and is not liberated, yet one attempts to sever [distractions] through one's own efforts while sitting in meditation, this is called the first unliberated mental bond, namely, the body.
Furthermore, regarding sensual desires, one is not free from defilement, not free from desire, not free from craving, and not free from thirst.

If one is not free from defilement, not free from desire, not free from craving, and not free from thirst regarding sensual desires, then that mind does not incline toward [the goal], is not tranquil, does not abide, and is not liberated; thus, through one's own effort, one abandons the practice of meditative seclusion.

If one possesses such a mind that does not incline toward [the goal], being unsettled, non-abiding, and unliberated, and who abandons solitary meditation through their own efforts, this is called the second bond of the unliberated mind, namely desire.

"Furthermore, there is another case where what is spoken is consistent with the noble meaning, gentle, and free from the hindrances of doubt—namely, discourse on virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, on reduction, on non-association, on fewness of desires, on contentment, on relinquishment, on dispassion, on cessation, on solitary meditation, and on dependent origination. Yet, regarding such speech by a recluse, the mind of that bhikkhu does not incline toward it; it is not settled, not established, and not liberated therein, as he personally exerts himself to abandon solitary meditation."

If one possesses such a mind that does not incline toward it, and which is not settled, not abiding, and not liberated, yet one attempts to sever [the defilements] through one's own efforts while in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*), this is called the third unliberated mental bond; thus it is said.
Furthermore, there are frequent assemblies of monastics and laypeople that are characterized by restlessness, arrogance, and a lack of inquiry.

If there are such frequent assemblies of monastics and laypeople that are characterized by restlessness, arrogance, and a lack of inquiry, one’s mind will not incline toward [the goal], will not be settled, will not abide, and will not be liberated; thus, one abandons the practice of solitary meditation through one's own efforts.

If this mind does not incline toward it, is not settled, does not abide, and is not liberated, yet one attempts to sever it through one's own effort while in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*), this is called the fourth unliberated mental bond, namely, social assembly (*saṃsarga*).
"Furthermore, because one has attained something slight, one dwells therein and no longer seeks further advancement.

If, because of having attained something slight, one dwells therein and no longer seeks further advancement, that mind does not incline toward [the goal]; it is not tranquil, not settled, not liberated, and one’s own skillful means for solitary meditation are severed."

If this mind does not incline toward it, is not settled, does not abide, and is not liberated, such that one abandons meditative seclusion through one's own efforts, this is called the fifth non-liberation of the mind’s bondage, namely, the failure to advance.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who do not extract these five impurities from within their minds, nor untie these five fetters within their minds, they are said to be bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs subject to inevitable decline.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who have skillfully uprooted the five impurities within their minds and skillfully untied the five fetters within their minds, this is called the pure dharma of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
"What is meant by 'skillfully uprooting the five corruptions from within the mind'?
It is when someone does not doubt the Blessed One, is without hesitation, has an open mind, possesses understanding, and has a tranquil mind."

If there is one who does not doubt the World-Honored One, who is without hesitation, whose mind is opened, whose mind is liberated, and whose mind is tranquil—this is called the first excellence in uprooting the defilements from the heart, namely with respect to the World-Honored One; and likewise with respect to the Dharma, the Discipline, and the Teaching.

If there are those who practice the holy life (brahmacariya) praised by the Blessed One, and one does not reproach them, treat them with contempt, harass them, or harm them, but instead opens their mind, liberates their mind, and calms their mind—this is called the fifth thorough extraction of impurity from the heart, namely, regarding the holy life.
"What is the liberation from the five fetters within the mind?
There may be one whose body is free from passion, free from desire, free from craving, and free from thirst.

If there is one whose body is free from passion, free from desire, free from craving, and free from thirst, their mind inclines toward tranquility, abides in it, and is liberated; they personally apply the means to sever [the fetters] while sitting in meditation."

If one possesses this mental orientation—tranquil, stable, and liberated—and through one's own skillful means abandons idle sitting, this is called the first liberation from the bond within the mind, namely, the body.
Furthermore, one becomes free from passion for sensual desires, free from desire, free from craving, and free from thirst for them.

If one is thus free from passion for sensual desires, free from desire, free from craving, and free from thirst, their mind inclines toward, settles in, and is liberated in tranquility; through their own skillful means, they abandon worldly distractions and dwell in meditative seclusion.

If one possesses this mental inclination toward tranquility, stability, and liberation, and through one's own skillful means abandons secluded meditation, this is called the second liberation from the bond of the mind, namely, desire.

"Furthermore, there is another teaching that is consistent with the noble meaning, gentle, and free from doubt or obscuration; namely, the teaching on virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, on diminution, on non-association, on fewness of desires, on contentment, on abandonment, on dispassion, on cessation, on solitary meditation, and on dependent origination. When a bhikkhu thus hears what is spoken by a recluse, his mind inclines toward it, becomes tranquil, settled, and liberated, and he applies himself through his own effort to the practice of solitary meditation."

If one possesses this mental orientation—tranquility, stability, and liberation—and personally applies skillful means to sever [the bonds] while in meditative seclusion, this is called the third liberation from the bonds of the mind; that is to say, it is "discourse."
Furthermore, one does not frequently congregate with monastics and laypeople, nor does one study with a distracted mind or with arrogance.

If there is one who does not frequently congregate with monastics and laypeople, and who studies without distraction or arrogance, their mind will incline toward tranquility, stability, and liberation, as they personally apply the means to cultivate solitary meditation.

If one possesses this mental orientation—tranquility, stability, and liberation—and through one's own skillful means abandons secluded sitting, this is called the fourth liberation from the bond of the mind, namely, non-assembly.
"Furthermore, because one has attained something slight, one does not abide therein but seeks further advancement.

If, because one has attained something slight, one does not abide therein but seeks further advancement, that mind inclines toward tranquility, stability, and liberation, and through its own skillful means, it abandons secluded meditation."

If this mind inclines toward tranquility, stability, and liberation, and one abandons seated meditation through one's own skillful means, this is called the fifth liberation from the bonds of the mind, namely, spiritual advancement.

If there are bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who skillfully uproot these five defilements within the mind and skillfully understand these five fetters within the mind, this is called the pure dharma of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
Having established himself in these ten factors, he further cultivates five dharmas. What are the five?

He cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of the concentration of desire and the accomplishment of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and relying on relinquishment, tending toward the state beyond the categories; he cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation and the accomplishment of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and relying on relinquishment, tending toward the state beyond the categories. Being capable of the fifth, he accomplishes these fifteen dharmas, including the capability itself.

One who has achieved self-realization necessarily knows, necessarily sees, and necessarily attains perfect and complete awakening; having reached the gate of the Deathless and dwelling near Nirvana, I declare that there is no such person who will not attain Nirvana.

It is like a hen that has laid ten or twelve eggs, which she covers at the proper time, warms at the proper time, and watches over at the proper time. If the hen should become negligent, among those eggs there might be a chick that, using its beak and feet, pecks through the shell and emerges safely; such a one is the foremost.

Thus, when a bhikkhu accomplishes these fifteen qualities, beginning with capability, he will necessarily know, necessarily see, necessarily attain right and full awakening, and necessarily reach the gate of the Deathless; he dwells near to Nirvana. I declare that such a one shall not fail to attain Nirvana.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The fifth discourse, "The Discourse on Mental Defilement," ends here, totaling 1,399 characters. The fifty-sixth fascicle of the Madhyama Āgama ends here, totaling 7,846 characters. Fifth Recitation Section.
