207. Śaraśāṭhya Sūtra (207). Chapter on Potaliputra, Śaraśāṭhya Sūtra, the sixth [sūtra] in the fifth subsequent recitation.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty persons, observing the rains retreat.
At that time, when the night had passed and at dawn, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.

Having finished begging for food, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and went to the park of the heterodox teachers in the Māluṅgya Grove.

At that time, within the heretical grove of the Peacock Forest, there was a certain heterodox teacher named Śarabha. He was a preeminent leader, a master revered by the multitude, possessed of great renown, and highly esteemed by all; he led a large assembly of followers and was honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners.

Amidst the clamor and commotion of the great assembly, he let out loud voices and spoke various kinds of animal-like discourses; that is to say, he spoke of kings, of thieves, of battles, of food, of clothing, of women, of maidens, of courtesans, of the world, of wildernesses, of the ocean, and of the people of the country.
They were sitting together in assembly discussing such matters concerning animals.
From afar, the heterodox teacher Śarabha saw the Buddha approaching and commanded his own followers, saying:
"Remain silent, for that śramaṇa Gautama is coming."
That assembly was silent; they always delighted in silence and praised silence.
If they saw this assembly in silence, they might come to meet him.
Having caused the assembly to be silent, the heterodox teacher Śarabha remained silent himself.
The Blessed One went to where the heterodox teacher Śarabha was; the heterodox teacher Śarabha immediately rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said:
"Welcome, Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"It has been a long time since the Śramaṇa Gautama has come here; please sit upon this seat.

The World-Honored One then sat upon the seat spread out by the heterodox teacher Śarabha. The heterodox teacher Śarabha then exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what were you discussing just now?"
"For what reason have we gathered here together?
The wanderer Śarabha replied, "Gautama!"
"Let us set aside this discussion; it is not excellent. If the śramaṇa Gautama wishes to hear this discussion, it will not be difficult for him to hear it later.
The Blessed One asked a second and a third time: "Udāyin!"
"What were you discussing just now?
For what reason have you gathered here and sat together?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied a second and a third time:

“Gautama! Let us set aside this discussion; it is not excellent. If the Śramaṇa Gautama wishes to hear this discussion, it will not be difficult to hear it later. If the Śramaṇa Gautama asks a second or even a third time, and he still wishes to hear it, I shall speak of it now.”
"Gautama!
We, along with many brahmins of the Kosalans, were all gathered together sitting in the Kosalan schoolhouse, discussing such a discourse."

The people of Aṅga and Magadha have gained a great and wholesome benefit; the people of Aṅga and Magadha have attained a great and wholesome benefit, for such a great field of merit as this assembly is now dwelling together in retreat during the rains at Rājagṛha—namely, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
Why is this so? Gautama!

Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is a master of virtue and renown, a teacher for all people, possessed of great fame and highly respected by the multitude; he leads a great assembly of followers and is venerated by five hundred heterodox practitioners.
In this city of Rājagṛha, they observed the rains retreat together: namely, Māṣika Ghoṣila, Sañjayī Vairaṭīputra, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, Sañjayin Belaṭṭhiputra, and Ajita Keśakambalin.

"Gautama! Ajita Kesakambalin, a master of renown and virtue, a teacher to the multitude, of great fame and highly esteemed by all, who leads a large assembly and is honored by five hundred heterodox practitioners, is currently observing the rains retreat here in this city of Rājagṛha."
"Previously, we were also discussing the śramaṇa Gautama!

This śramaṇa Gautama is a preeminent master of name and virtue, a teacher to all people, one of great renown, and highly revered by the multitude. Leading a great assembly of bhikṣus—honored by these one thousand two hundred and fifty men—he too is currently staying here in Rājagṛha, observing the rains retreat."
"Gautama! We further had this thought:
'Among these venerable śramaṇas and brahmins, who is the one honored, revered, supported, and served by his disciples?'"
It is not the way of a disciple to revile one who reviles him, nor is it for a disciple to challenge his teacher; this is entirely improper and inconsistent. Having spoken thus, he departed.
"O Gautama! We further thought this:

'This Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is not honored, respected, venerated, or served by his disciples; he is reviled by his disciples with verbal abuse. Many disciples challenge their teacher, saying, "This is improper, this is inconsistent, this is not rightly taught," and having said this, they depart. "
“Gautama! In the past, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa would frequently stand among his assembly of disciples, raising his hand and shouting:
‘You all should stop! No one has come to question you about such matters; it is people who ask me about them. You cannot resolve these matters, but I can resolve them.’”
"But while we were in the midst of discussing other matters, our disciples did not wait for the teacher to finish his discourse.
Gautama! We further thought to ourselves:"
"In this way, this Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was not honored, respected, venerated, or served by his disciples; he was reviled with verbal abuse by them, and many disciples challenged their teacher, saying:
'This is improper; this is inconsistent.'"
Having spoken these unequal words, he departed and left.
In this same manner, Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Kesakambalin [did likewise].
"Gautama! We have had this thought:
'This Ajita Keśakambalin is not honored, respected, venerated, or served by his disciples; he is reviled by his disciples with verbal abuse, and many disciples challenge their teacher.'"
"This is untenable; this is inconsistent; this is not rightly taught. Having said this, he would depart. Gautama!
In the past, Ajita Kesakambalin used to stand among his assembly of disciples, raising his hand and shouting loudly:
"You all may stay; no one will come to question you on this matter. It is I whom people question regarding this matter; you are unable to resolve it, whereas I am able to resolve it."
"But while we were in the midst of discussing other matters, our disciples did not wait for the teacher to finish his discourse.
Gautama! We further thought to ourselves:"
"In this way, Āḷāra Kālāma was not honored, respected, venerated, or served by his disciples; he was reviled by his disciples with verbal abuse, and many disciples rebuked their teacher, saying:
'This is improper, this is inconsistent, this is an unequal teaching,' and having said this, they departed."
“Gautama! We further thought this:
‘This śramaṇa Gautama is honored, respected, venerated, and served by his disciples; he is not reviled by his disciples with verbal abuse, nor do his disciples challenge their teacher.’”
"This is untenable; this is inconsistent; this is not rightly spoken. Having said this, he would depart. "Gautama!

In the past, when the śramaṇa Gautama was frequently in the midst of a great assembly surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people preaching the Dharma, there was one person among them who snored while sleeping. Then another person said to that person:"
"Do not snore while sleeping and make such a noise!
Do you not wish to hear the World-Honored One preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, which is like nectar?
Thereupon, that person immediately became silent and made no sound.
"Gautama! We further thought this:

'In this way, this śramaṇa Gautama is honored, respected, venerated, and served by his disciples; he is not reviled by his disciples with verbal abuse, nor do his disciples pose difficult challenges to their teacher.'"
"This is unacceptable, this is inconsistent, this is not rightly spoken"—having said this, he departed.
When the Blessed One had heard this, he asked the wanderer Sāṇavāsi: "Udāyin!..."
"Do you see what qualities I possess that cause my disciples to revere, respect, make offerings to, and serve me, always following me without leaving?"
The wanderer Sāṃjīva replied:
“Gautama! I see five qualities in Gautama that cause his disciples to revere, respect, honor, and serve him, following him constantly without ever leaving.”
What are these five?

The ascetic Gotama is content with coarse robes and commends being content with coarse robes; since the ascetic Gotama is content with coarse robes and commends being content with coarse robes, this is what I see as the first quality of the ascetic Gotama that causes his disciples to revere, respect, honor, serve, and constantly follow him without leaving.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is content with coarse food and praises being content with coarse food. If the śramaṇa Gautama is content with coarse food and praises being content with coarse food, this is what I call the second quality found in the śramaṇa Gautama, by which his disciples revere, respect, make offerings to, and serve him, constantly following him without leaving.

"Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama eats little and praises eating little. Since the ascetic Gautama eats little and praises eating little, this is what I see as the third quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, respect, honor, serve, and constantly follow him without leaving."

Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse lodgings and seats, and he praises being content with coarse lodgings and seats. If the ascetic Gautama is content with coarse lodgings and seats and praises being content with coarse lodgings and seats, this is what I call the fourth quality in the ascetic Gautama by which his disciples revere, respect, honor, and serve him, constantly following him without leaving.

Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama practices meditative seclusion and speaks in praise of meditative seclusion. Since the ascetic Gautama practices meditative seclusion and speaks in praise of meditative seclusion, this is what I see as the fifth quality of the ascetic Gautama that causes his disciples to revere, respect, honor, and serve him, constantly following him without leaving.
This is what I mean when I say that the śramaṇa Gautama possesses five qualities because of which his disciples revere, respect, honor, and serve him, constantly following him without ever leaving.
The Blessed One said:
"Udāyin! It is not by these five qualities that I cause my disciples to revere, respect, honor, and serve me, following me constantly and never parting from me."
Udāyin! The robes I wear have been cut according to the noble power and dyed in unattractive colors; such, Udāyin, are the noble robes, dyed in unattractive colors. Udāyin!
Or some of my disciples, who throughout their lives have discarded ordinary clothing and wear only rag-robes, also say:
"Our Blessed One is content with coarse clothing; he praises being content with coarse clothing."
“Udāyin! If my disciples were to praise me on account of being content with coarse robes, they would not, for that reason, honor, respect, make offerings to, or serve me, nor would they follow me.”
Furthermore, Udāyin!
I eat well-ripened rice that is free of husks and possesses immeasurable varieties of flavor. Udāyin!
Or perhaps my disciples, throughout their entire lives, practice alms-gathering and eat discarded food, yet they also say:
"Our World-Honored One is content with coarse food; he praises being content with coarse food."
"Udāyin! If my disciples were to praise me because they are content with coarse food, they would not, on that account, honor, revere, make offerings to, or serve me, nor would they follow me."
"Furthermore, Udāyin!
I eat as much as one *vīra* of food, or perhaps half a *vīra*. Udāyin!
Or my disciples eat as much as one *kuḍava*, or perhaps half a *kuḍava*, and they also speak in this way: [that they eat only a little]."
“‘My Blessed One eats little; he praises eating little. Udāyin!
If my disciples praise me on account of eating little, they do not, for that reason, honor, respect, make offerings to, or serve me, nor do they follow me.”
Furthermore, Udāyin!
I may dwell in a high tower, or I may dwell in a multi-storied pavilion. Udāyin!
Or perhaps my disciples, after nine or ten months have passed, might spend a single night in a sheltered place and say:
"Our World-Honored One is content with coarse lodgings and seats; he praises being content with coarse lodgings and seats."

"Udāyin! If my disciples, because they are content with coarse dwellings and seats, praise me for that reason, they do not thereby show me respect, honor, offerings, or service, nor do they follow me."
"Furthermore, Udāyin!
I am constantly busy with monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; or my disciples enter the assembly once every half-month for the sake of the purity of the Dharma, and they also say this:
'Our Blessed One practices solitary meditation (pratisaṃlayana) and praises solitary meditation.'"

"Udāyin! If my disciples, because of their practice of solitary meditation (pratisaṃlayana), were to praise me on that account, they would not, for that reason, show me reverence, respect, honor, or service, nor would they follow me."
"Udāyin! I do not possess these five qualities that cause my disciples to revere, respect, make offerings to, and serve me, following me constantly without ever leaving."
"Udāyin! I have five further qualities by which my disciples revere, respect, honor, and serve me, always following me without departing."
"What are the five? Udāyin!
I have disciples who proclaim me as one possessing unsurpassed virtue."
“The World-Honored One practices the great precepts of morality; as he speaks, so he acts, and as he acts, so he speaks. Udāyin!
If my disciples praise me on account of this unsurpassed morality, they will, for this reason, revere, respect, make offerings to, and serve me, following me constantly without ever departing.
Furthermore, Udāyin!
I have disciples who, regarding my unsurpassed wisdom, declare of me:
"The World-Honored One practices wisdom; his wisdom is exceedingly great."

If anyone comes to engage in debate with him, he will certainly be able to subdue them; that is to say, they will find it impossible to speak against the True Dharma and the Discipline, nor will they be able to refute what he himself has spoken.

"Udāyin! If my disciples, because of their unsurpassed wisdom, speak of me in praise, they do so on this account: that they revere, respect, honor, and serve me, always following me without ever leaving."
"Furthermore, Udāyin!
I have disciples who, on account of my unsurpassed knowledge and vision, proclaim of me:

'The Blessed One moves in knowledge, not in ignorance; he moves in vision, not in blindness. He teaches the Dharma to his disciples as having causes and not without causes, as having conditions and not without conditions; it is answerable and not unanswerable; it involves renunciation and not non-renunciation.'"

"Udāyin! If my disciples praise me because of their unsurpassed knowledge and vision, they do so on this basis, and they revere, honor, make offerings to, and serve me, constantly following me without ever leaving."
Furthermore, Udāyin!
I have a disciple who, having become weary of the arrow of craving, came to question me:
"Suffering is suffering; its origin is its origin; its cessation is its cessation; the path is the path."
I then replied to him:
"Suffering is suffering; its origin is its origin; its cessation is its cessation; the path is the path. Udāyin!

If my disciples come and question me, and I answer them in a way that is pleasing and brings them joy, they will, on that account, revere, respect, honor, and serve me, constantly following me without leaving.
"Furthermore, Udāyin!

For my disciples, I have sometimes declared the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives as a realization attained through direct experience, and I have sometimes declared the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of the taints as a realization attained through direct experience."

Udāyin! If my disciples, within this True Dharma and Discipline, have attained reception and liberation, have reached the further shore, are free from doubt and confusion, and possess no hesitation regarding wholesome qualities, they honor, revere, make offerings to, and serve me on that account, constantly following me without separation.
Udāyin! These are the five further qualities by which my disciples revere, respect, honor, and serve me, always following me and never departing.
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Śarabha rose from his seat, draped his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Gautama!
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!
You have so skillfully expounded this sublime matter that it moistens my very being, just like nectar."
"Gautama!
Just as when it rains heavily, this earth—whether high or low—is everywhere moistened and nourished;
so too, Śramaṇa Gautama, you have well explained wonderful matters for us, nourishing our bodies like nectar."
“World-Honored One!
I have understood. Sugata!”
"I have understood, World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. May the World-Honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth, until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the wanderer Śarabha rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The sixth discourse, the Śarabha Sūtra, ends here; it contains two thousand eight hundred and seven characters. 208. The Śarabha Sūtra (II). Madhyama Āgama, Bhāradvāja Vagga. The Śarabha Sūtra, the seventh. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Garden.
Then, when the night had passed and it was dawn, the World-Honored One dressed, took his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha to beg for food.

Having finished his almsround, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) over his shoulder, and went to the park of the heterodox teachers in the Peacock Grove.

At that time, in the park of the non-Buddhist ascetics within the Peacock Grove, there was a certain teacher named Śarabha. He was a preeminent leader, a master revered by the multitude, possessed of great renown, and held in high esteem by all; he led a large retinue and was honored by five hundred non-Buddhist ascetics.

Amidst the clamor and commotion of the great assembly, he let out loud voices and spoke various kinds of animal-like discourses; that is to say, talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of clothing, talk of women, talk of maidens, talk of courtesans, talk of the world, talk of wildernesses, talk of the ocean, and talk of the people of the country.
They were sitting together in a group discussing such matters as those concerning animals.
From afar, the heterodox teacher Śarabha saw the Buddha approaching and commanded his own assembly, saying:

"Remain silent, all of you! That śramaṇa Gautama is coming; he and his followers delight in silence, praise silence, and commend silence. If he sees that this assembly is silent, he may perhaps come to visit us."
When the heterodox teacher Śarabha had commanded the assembly to remain silent, he himself sat in silence.

The Blessed One approached the place where the heterodox teacher Śarabha was; the heterodox teacher Śarabha immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "Welcome!
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
It has been a long time since Śramaṇa Gautama last came here; please, sit upon this seat.
The Blessed One then sat upon the seat spread out by the heterodox teacher Śarabha. The heterodox teacher Śarabha then exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what were you discussing just now?"
"For what reason have we gathered and sat here together?
The wanderer Śarabha replied, "Gautama!"
"Let us set aside this discussion; it is not excellent. If the śramaṇa Gautama wishes to hear this discussion, it will not be difficult for him to hear it later.
The Blessed One asked a second and a third time: "Udāyin!"
"What was the subject of your recent discussion?
For what reason have you gathered here and sat together?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied a second and a third time:

"Gautama! Let us set this discussion aside; it is not a profound matter. If the Śramaṇa Gautama wishes to hear this discussion, it will not be difficult to hear later. If the Śramaṇa Gautama requests it a second or even a third time, I shall now speak of what he wishes to hear."

"Gautama! I possess strategic deliberation and reflection; I abide in the stage of deliberation and the stage of reflection. I possess wisdom and eloquence. I speak of what truly exists: that there is one who is omniscient (*sarvajña*), all-seeing, possessing knowledge without remainder and vision without remainder. When I went to question him about these matters, he did not know them."
"Gautama! I had this thought: 'What is this? "
The World-Honored One asked:
"Udāyin! You possess strategic planning and reflection;

you abide in the state of strategic planning and the state of reflection; you possess wisdom and eloquence. Who is it that claims to truly possess *sarvajñatā*—all-knowingness and all-seeingness, knowing everything without remainder and seeing everything without remainder—that you went to question about matters, yet he did not know?"
The heterodox teacher Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta replied: “Gautama,
it was Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.”
Why is that? Gautama! Pūraṇa Kāśyapa himself declares that he truly possesses *sarvajñatā*—all-knowingness and all-seeingness, with no knowledge remaining and no vision remaining.

I possess strategic deliberation and reflection; I abide in the state of strategic deliberation and the state of reflection; I possess wisdom and eloquence. When I go to inquire about matters, they do not know them.
"Gautama!
For this reason, I have this thought: 'What is this? "
In this way, there were Makkhali Gosāla, Sañjaya Vairaṭīputra, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, Pakudha Kaccāyana, and Ajita Keśakambalin.
"Gautama!
Ajita Keśakambalin himself declares that he truly possesses *sarvajñatā*—all-knowingness and all-seeingness; that there is no knowledge remaining and no vision remaining."

I possess strategic reflection and contemplation; I abide in the stage of strategic reflection and the stage of contemplation; I possess wisdom and eloquence. When I go to inquire about matters, they do not know them.
"Gautama!
For this reason, I have this thought: 'What is this? "
"Gotama! I further had this thought:
'If I were to go to the place where the śramaṇa Gotama is and inquire about matters of the past, the śramaṇa Gotama would surely be able to answer me regarding those past matters.'"
"I shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and inquire about matters of the future; the śramaṇa Gautama will surely be able to answer me regarding the future.
Furthermore, whatever matter I may ask the śramaṇa Gautama about, the śramaṇa Gautama will surely answer me according to what I have asked."
The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin, stop!
"Stop!

Because for a long night you have held different views, different tolerances, different inclinations, different desires, and different intentions, you are unable to fully understand the meaning of what I have taught."

"Udāyin! My disciples, possessing causes and conditions, recollect their immeasurable past births—namely, one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births; aeons of formation, aeons of destruction, and immeasurable aeons of both formation and destruction. They remember: 'A sentient being named so-and-so—I was once born there; such was my clan, such my name, such my birth, such my food and drink, such the suffering and pleasure I experienced, such my longevity, such my duration of stay, and such was the end of my life.'"

"Dying here, one is born there; dying there, one is born here. I was born here, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such an end to my lifespan."

He came and questioned me about the past; I answered him regarding the past. I also went and questioned him about the past; he also answered me regarding the past. Whatever matter I asked him about, he likewise answered me according to what I had asked.
"Furthermore, Udāyin!

I have disciples who, with the purified divine eye that surpasses that of humans, see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether they are beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior, and as they pass away from and take birth in good or bad destinations—seeing them truly according to the karma these beings have performed."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, and have accomplished misconduct of speech and mind; if they have slandered the noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished the karma of wrong views—by reason of these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, accomplish excellent conduct of speech and mind, do not slander the noble ones, possess right view, and accomplish the karma of right view, then by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn among the devas.

He comes to me and asks about future matters; I answer him regarding future matters. I also go to him and ask about future matters; he also answers me regarding future matters. Whatever matter I ask him about, he likewise answers me regarding that very matter.
The heterodox teacher Śarabha said:
"Gautama! If this is so, I am increasingly ignorant, I am increasingly sightless, and I have become more deluded and fallen into delusion, since you, the ascetic Gautama, speak thus."
"Udāyin! Stop! Stop!"

"Because for a long night you have held different views, different tolerances, different inclinations, different desires, and different intentions, you are unable to fully understand the meaning of what I have taught, Udāyin!"

I have disciples who, possessing the causes and conditions, recollect their immeasurable past origins and former births—namely, one birth, two births, a hundred births, a thousand births; through eons of formation, eons of destruction, and immeasurable eons of both formation and destruction—they remember that sentient beings were named so-and-so, and I was born there, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such longevity, such duration of stay, and such an end to my life.

"Dying here, one is born there; dying there, one is born here. I was born here, with such a clan, such a name, such a birth, such food and drink, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such an end to my life."

He came and questioned me about past events, and I answered him regarding past events; I also went and questioned him about past events, and he answered me regarding past events. Whatever matters I asked him about, he likewise answered me concerning those very matters.
"Furthermore, Udāyin!

I have disciples who possess the purified divine eye, surpassing that of humans; they see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether beautiful or ugly, excellent or inferior—as they pass from good or bad destinations, seeing them truly according to the karma these beings have performed."

If these sentient beings have accomplished misconduct of body, and have accomplished misconduct of speech and mind; if they have slandered the noble ones, held wrong views, and accomplished the karma of wrong views—due to these causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly go to a miserable destination and be born in hell.

If these sentient beings accomplish excellent conduct of body, accomplish excellent conduct of speech and mind, do not slander the noble ones, possess right view, and accomplish the karma of right view, then by reason of this, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will certainly ascend to a happy destination and be reborn among the devas.

He comes to ask me about future matters, and I answer him regarding future matters; I also go to ask him about future matters, and he answers me regarding future matters. Whatever matter I ask him about, he also answers me regarding that very matter as it was asked.

“Gautama! Regarding this present life, I cannot even recall what I did in my past lives or what I attained in my past lives; how much less could I recall the infinite matters of my former births, which were conditioned by causes and conditions?”
"Gautama!

I cannot even see the wind-demon; how much less could I, with the pure divine eye that surpasses that of humans, see these beings as they die and are reborn—whether of beautiful or ugly appearance, sublime or base, and as they pass to a good destination or a bad destination—and see them truly according to the karma these beings have performed?"
"Gautama!
I thought to myself:
'If the ascetic Gautama were to ask me about the Dharma learned from my teacher, perhaps I would be able to answer him in a way that would satisfy his mind.'"
The World-Honored One asked:
"Udāyin! How did you learn that Dharma from your teacher?"
The wanderer Sāṃjīva replied: “Gautama!
He speaks of form as surpassing form; that form is the most excellent, that form is the supreme.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyi! What kind of form is it?"
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama!
If there were no other form that was more supreme, more exquisite, or more excellent than this form."
"That form is most excellent; that form is supreme.
The World-Honored One said: "Udāyin!"
It is just as if someone were to say:
"If there is a woman in this country who is most excellent, I wish to obtain her.
If someone were to ask him thus:
"Do you know that there is a woman in the country who is most excellent—of such a clan, such a name, and such a birth?
Is she tall or short, stout or slender, fair-skinned, dark-skinned, or neither fair nor dark?"
Is she the daughter of a kṣatriya, or the daughter of a brahmin, a householder, or a craftsman?
Is she from the east, the south, the west, or the north?
That person replied, "I do not know.
He questioned that person again:

"Do you not know, do you not see that in this country there is a most exquisite woman—of such a clan, such a name, such a birth; tall or short, stout or slender, fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark; a daughter of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman; from the east, the south, the west, or the north—and yet you say:
'I wish to obtain that woman'?"
"In this way, Udāyin, you have said:
'He speaks of form as surpassing form; that form is the most excellent, that form is the supreme.'"
He asked, "Do you know that form? But he did not know.
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied, "Gautama!

It is just like the finest refined gold, the essence of purple-gold, which a skilled goldsmith has polished and cleansed until it is pure; when placed upon white silk in the midst of the sun, its color is most exquisite and its radiance shines forth."
"In this way, Gautama, I say that this form surpasses all other forms; it is the most excellent, it is the supreme.
The Blessed One replied:
“Udāyin! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit. Udāyin!”
"What do you think?

Suppose there were a piece of refined purple-gold set upon white silk and placed in the midst of the sun; its color would be most exquisite and its radiance would shine brilliantly. Then suppose there were a firefly shining with light in the darkness of night. Between these two lights, which is the superior and which is the most excellent?"
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: “Gautama!
The light of a firefly is the most excellent and supreme compared to the light of refined purple-gold.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what do you think?"

Suppose there were a firefly shining with light in the darkness of night, and an oil lamp shining with light in the darkness of night; between these two lights, which would be the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama!
The light of a burning lamp is the most excellent and the most superior compared to the light of a firefly."
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what do you think?"

Suppose there were an oil lamp shining with brilliant light in the darkness of night, and a great bonfire of stacked wood shining with brilliant light in the darkness of night; between these two lights, which would be the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: “Gautama!
The radiance of a fire fueled by a great pile of wood is superior and more excellent than the radiance of an oil lamp.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what do you think?"

Suppose there were a great bonfire of piled wood blazing with light in the darkness of night, and the planet Venus shining with unclouded brilliance at dawn; of these two lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Māṭhara replied, “Gautama!
The light of Venus is the most excellent and supreme among the light of a fire burning a great pile of wood.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what do you think?"
Suppose the planet Venus shines with unobstructed radiance at dawn, and the lunar palace shines with unobstructed radiance at midnight; among these lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Śāṇavāsa replied: “Gautama!
The radiance of the lunar palace is the most supreme and the most excellent compared to the light of Venus.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin, what do you think?"

It is asked: between the light of the lunar palace at midnight when the sky is cloudless and the radiance of the solar palace at midday during autumn when the heavens are clear and cloudless, which of these lights is the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama!
The radiance of the sun’s palace is superior and more excellent than the radiance of the moon’s palace."
The Blessed One said:
“Udāyin! There are many devas;
although these sun and moon possess great supernormal power (ṛddhi), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, their radiance nonetheless does not equal the radiance of those devas.”
In the past, I once gathered with various devas and discussed matters with them; what I spoke accorded with the inclinations of those devas, yet I did not say:
"That form surpasses all forms; that form is the most excellent, that form is the supreme."

"Udāyin! Regarding the light and color of a firefly—which is the most inferior and the most ugly—you claimed that its color surpasses all other colors, that it is the most excellent and the most supreme; yet when questioned, you did not know."
The heterodox teacher Śarabha said:
“World-Honored One!
I repent for these words.”
“O Sugata,
we repent for these words!
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin! With what intention do you speak thus:
'World-Honored One!'"
I repent of these words.
Well-gone One!
I repent of these words.
"Is it so? The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama!"
I have made this claim:
"That form surpasses all other forms; that form is the most excellent, that form is the supreme.
Now, the śramaṇa Gautama has thoroughly examined me, skillfully instructed and reproved me, so that my falsehoods are rendered void and non-existent.
"Gotama! For this reason, I say thus:
'World-Honored One!'"
I repent of these words,
Sugata! I repent of these words!
The heterodox teacher Sāṇavāsi said:
"Gautama! There is a path leading to the unalloyed happiness of the future world, which can be personally realized in this very life."
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin! What is the state of uniform happiness in future lives?"
"What is the single path of practice that leads exclusively to direct worldly realization?
The wanderer Sāṇa Māṇava replied: "Gotama!"

"Or there may be someone who abstains from killing and has abandoned killing, abstains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, and so on, up to abstaining from wrong view and attaining right view,
O Gotama!"
"This is called the state of unalloyed happiness in future lives; this is called the one path leading to the realization of the world in the present.
The World-Honored One said, "Udāyin!"
I now ask you; answer as you see fit.
Udāyin, what do you think?
"If there is one who has abandoned killing and is free from killing, is he subject exclusively to pleasure, or is he subject to a mixture of suffering?
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama! [He is subject to a mixture of suffering]."
"This is mixed with suffering.

"If there is one who abstains from taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, and false speech, up to abstaining from wrong view and attaining right view—is that exclusively happiness, or is it mixed with suffering?"
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied:
“Gautama, it is a mixture of suffering.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Udāyin! Is it not for the sake of such a path of practice that leads to mixed pleasure and pain that you bear witness to the world?"
The heterodox teacher Sāṃjīva replied:
“Gautama! It is thus that the path of practice involving both suffering and pleasure serves as a worldly realization.”
The wanderer Śarabha said,
"World-Honored One!
I repent for these words."
“O Sugata,
we repent for these words.
The Blessed One asked:
“Udāyin! With what intention do you speak thus:
‘World-Honored One!’”
"Does he say, 'I repent this statement,
O Sugata; I repent this statement'?"
The heterodox teacher Śarabha replied: "Gautama!
Previously, I spoke of a state of unalloyed happiness in the future life, and of a path leading thereto that can be personally realized in this very life."
"Śramaṇa Gautama has now skillfully examined me, skillfully instructed and skillfully rebuked me, so that my falsehoods have been rendered non-existent.
Gautama! For this reason, I speak thus:"
“World-Honored One!
We repent for these words. Sugata!”
"Renounce this statement.
The World-Honored One said, "Udāyin!"
"In the world, there is that which is exclusively pleasant, and there is a path leading to its realization in this very life.
The wanderer Sāṇa asked: "Gautama!"
"What is that which is exclusively pleasant in the world?
And what is the single path leading to its realization as a worldly attainment?
The Blessed One replied:

“Udāyi! When a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a well-gone one, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—he abandons, up to, the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and being detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, born of seclusion, accompanied by joy and happiness; yet he does not share with those devas an equality of virtue, an equality of mind, or an equality of view.”

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is inner tranquility and unification of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and accompanied by rapture and bliss; yet he does not share with those devas an equality of virtue, an equality of mind, or an equality of view.

With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he attains and abides in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness. He achieves this without sharing it with those devas in terms of virtue, mind, or view.
"Udāyin! This is what is called 'unilateral happiness in the world.
The wanderer Sāṇavāsi asked:
"Gautama! Is this singular happiness in the world truly the ultimate?
The Blessed One replied:
“In this world, there is not only the one-sided pleasure that is supreme. Udāyin!
There is yet another path leading to the direct realization of the world.”
The wanderer Sāṇavāsi asked: “Gautama,
what further is that single path leading to direct realization in this very life?”
The Blessed One replied: “Udāyi!

A bhikkhu, secluded from sensual desires and secluded from unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna; he attains equality in virtue, equality in mind, and equality in view with those devas.”

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is inward tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and accompanied by joy and bliss; he attains equality with those devas in terms of virtue, mind, and view.

With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he attains and abides in the third dhyāna, which the Noble Ones describe as "equanimous, mindful, and dwelling in happiness," and he acquires the same morality, mind, and view as those devas.
"Udāyin! This is called the one path, the single track that leads directly to realization in this very life.
The wanderer Sāṇavāsi asked:

"Gautama! Do the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama for the sake of one-sided happiness in this world, and because there is a single path that leads exclusively to direct realization in this very life?"
The Blessed One replied:
"Udāyin! My disciples do not train in the holy life under me for the sake of one-sided worldly pleasure, nor for the sake of one-sided worldly realization of the path leading to the goal."
"Udāyin! There is something further—most supreme, most exquisite, and most excellent—for the sake of realizing which my disciples train in the holy life under me."
Thereupon, that great assembly raised a loud cry:
"He is the most supreme, the most exquisite, and the most excellent! It is for the sake of realizing this that the disciples of the ascetic Gautama practice the holy life under the ascetic Gautama."
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Śarabha commanded his own assembly to remain silent and addressed [the Buddha],
saying: “Gautama,
for the sake of realizing what is most supreme, most exquisite, and most excellent, why do the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama?”
The Blessed One replied:

"Udāyin! A bhikkhu, with the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity."
"Udāyin! This is called the highest, the most sublime, and the most excellent; it is for the sake of realizing this that my disciples train in the holy life under me."
Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Śarabha rose from his seat, intending to bow at the Buddha’s feet.
Then, the heterodox disciples and fellow practitioners of the holy life said to the heterodox teacher Śarabha:
"Venerable sir, it is now the time for you to act as a teacher; do you wish to become a disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama?"
"Venerable sir, it is not fitting that you should act as a teacher while serving as a disciple to the ascetic Gautama.

This constitutes an obstacle for the disciples of the heterodox teacher Śalīna who practice the holy life, in that they would learn the holy life from the Venerable One instead of from the heterodox teacher Śalīna."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, the heterodox teacher Śarabha rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The seventh discourse, the Śarabhasūtra, ends here, totaling three thousand eight hundred and thirty characters. 209. The Vammīkasutta (The Ant-hill Discourse) Middle Āgama, Bhāradvāja-vagga, The Vammīkasutta, the eighth discourse. Fifth Subsequent Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the wanderer Vaimanasi, having wandered about after the midday meal, approached the place where the Buddha was. After exchanging greetings, he asked:
"Gautama!..."
Most beautiful, most beautiful, Gautama!
Most beautiful!
The Blessed One asked:
"Kaccāna, what kind of form is it?"
The wanderer Vemacitra replied: “Gautama!
If there were no other form that was more supreme, more exquisite, or more excellent than that form, Gautama!”
"That form is most excellent; that form is supreme.
The World-Honored One said, "Kaccāna!"
It is just as if someone were to say:
"If there is a woman in this country who is most excellent, I wish to obtain her.
Should someone then ask him:
"Do you know that there is a woman in the kingdom who is most exquisite—of such a clan, such a name, and such a birth?
Is she tall or short, stout or slender, fair-skinned, dark-skinned, or neither fair nor dark?"
Is she the daughter of a kṣatriya, or the daughter of a brahmin, a householder, or a craftsman?
Is she from the east, the south, the west, or the north?
That person replied, "I do not know.
He asked that person again:

"Do you not know, do you not see that in this country there is a woman most exquisite—one of such a clan, such a name, such a birth; one who is tall or short, stout or slender, fair, dark, or neither fair nor dark; whether she be the daughter of a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a craftsman; or one from the east, south, west, or north—and yet you say:
'I wish to obtain that woman'?"
"So it is, Kātyāyana! You have spoken thus."
"That form is beautiful, most beautiful; that form is supreme, that form is unsurpassed.
When you were asked about that form, you did not know it.
The heterodox teacher Vaimanasi replied:

"Gautama! It is just like the finest essence of purple-polished gold, skillfully ground and polished by a master goldsmith until it is pure; when placed upon white silk in the midst of the sun, its color is most exquisite and its radiance shines forth."
"Thus it is, Gautama!
I say that his exquisite form is the most exquisite of forms; that form is the most excellent, that form is the supreme.
The Blessed One replied:
“Kaccāna! I shall now question you; answer as you see fit. Kaccāna!”
"What do you think?

Suppose there were a piece of refined purple-gold placed upon white silk in the midst of the sun; its color would be most exquisite and its radiance would shine brilliantly. Then suppose there were a firefly shining with its light in the darkness of night. Between these two lights, which is superior and more excellent?"
The heterodox teacher Vaimanasi replied: “Gautama!
The light of a firefly is the most excellent and the most supreme compared to the light of refined purple-gold.”
The World-Honored One asked:
"Kaccāna, what do you think?"

Suppose there were a firefly shining with light in the darkness of night, and an oil lamp shining with light in the darkness of night; between these two lights, which would be the most excellent and supreme?
The wanderer Vaimanasi replied: "Gautama,
the light of a burning lamp is the most excellent and supreme compared to the light of a firefly."
The Blessed One asked:
"Kaccāna, what do you think?"

Suppose there is an oil lamp shining with bright light in the darkness of night, and a great bonfire of piled wood shining with bright light in the darkness of night; between these two lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The wanderer Vaimanasi replied: “Gautama!
The radiance of a great bonfire of stacked wood is the most excellent and supreme compared to the radiance of an oil lamp.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Kaccāna, what do you think?"

Suppose there were a great bonfire of stacked wood blazing with light in the darkness of night, and the planet Venus shining with light at dawn when the sky is cloudless; between these two lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Vemacitra replied: “Gautama!
The light of Venus is the most excellent and supreme among the light of a great mass of wood burning with fire.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Kaccāna, what do you think?"

That is to say: when the planet Venus shines with unobstructed radiance at dawn, and when the lunar palace shines with unobstructed radiance at midnight—of these two lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The heterodox teacher Vāmama answered, “Gautama!
The radiance of the lunar palace is the most supreme and the most excellent compared to the light of Venus.”
The Blessed One asked:
"Kaccāna, what do you think?"

That is to say: when the light of the lunar palace shines at midnight on a cloudless night with its radiance illuminating all, and when the light of the solar palace shines at midday in autumn when the sky is clear and cloudless with its radiance illuminating all—of these two lights, which is the most excellent and supreme?
The wanderer Vemacitra replied, “Gautama!
The radiance of the solar palace is superior and more excellent than the radiance of the lunar palace.”
The Blessed One said:
"Kaccāna! There are many devas.

Although these sun and moon possess great supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), great majesty, great merit, and great spiritual authority, their radiance nonetheless does not equal the radiance of those devas."

In the past, I once gathered with the devas and discussed matters with them; what I said accorded with the inclinations of those devas, yet I did not say that "this exquisite form is the most exquisite form," or that "this form is the most excellent, the most supreme."
"Kātyāyana!

Regarding the light and color of a firefly, which is most wretched and most ugly, you have declared it to be a beautiful color, the most beautiful color, that color is supreme, and that color is unsurpassed; yet, having been questioned, you do not know."

Thereupon, the wanderer Vāmaka, having been rebuked face-to-face by the Blessed One, was inwardly filled with grief; he lowered his head and remained silent, deprived of his eloquence and speechless, as if brooding over something.
Thereupon, having rebuked him face-to-face, the Blessed One further caused him to rejoice and said: "Kaccāna!

There are five strands of sensual pleasure that are desirable, agreeable, delightful, and accompanied by passion: forms known by the eye, sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body."
Kātyāyana! Regarding form, there may be that which is beloved and that which is not beloved.

Suppose there is a person who finds a certain form agreeable, pleasing, delightful, satisfying, and fulfilling; even if there were other forms that were more supreme and more excellent than it, he would have no desire for them, no thought of them, no wish for them, and no pursuit of them. For him, that very form is the most supreme and the most excellent.
Kātyāyana!
Such are sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. Kātyāyana!
Regarding tangibles, some are pleasant and some are unpleasant.
Suppose there is a person who finds a certain contact to be agreeable, pleasing, delightful, satisfying, and fulfilling.
Toward other contacts, even those that are most excellent and supreme, he has no desire, no thought, no wish, and no seeking.
"He is the most excellent and supreme regarding this contact.
Thereupon, the wanderer Vaimanasi joined his palms toward the Buddha and said:
"Gautama!..."
"How marvelous!
How extraordinary!
The śramaṇa Gautama has, through immeasurable skillful means, taught me that sensual pleasure is the foremost."
"Gautama!

Just as a fire that burns grass can ignite a fire that burns wood, and a fire that burns wood can ignite a fire that burns grass, so too has the ascetic Gautama, by means of countless skillful methods, spoken to me of sensual pleasure and declared sensual pleasure to be supreme."
The World-Honored One said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Kātyāyana!

Because for a long night you have held different views, different tolerances, different inclinations, different desires, and different intentions, you are unable to fully understand the meaning of what I have taught."

"Kaccāna! My disciples, throughout the first and last watches of the night, remain constantly awake and do not lie down to sleep; with right concentration and right intention, they cultivate the factors of enlightenment. They know according to reality: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence. They fully understand all that I have taught."

Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vaimanasi became enraged toward the Buddha; he gave rise to hatred, envy, and resentment, desiring to slander and undermine the World-Honored One. Thus slandering and thus undermining the World-Honored One, he spoke, saying:
"Gautama!..."

There are recluses and brahmins who do not know the prior limit of the world, do not know its subsequent limit, and do not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet they claim to have attained ultimate knowledge, knowing in accordance with reality: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"Gautama! I think thus:

'How is it that these śramaṇas and brahmins, who do not know the prior limit of the world, nor the subsequent limit of the world, nor the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge, saying: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence"—do they know this as it truly is?'"
Then, the Blessed One thought to himself:

"This heterodox teacher Vaimanaputra has become angry with me; he has conceived hatred, envy, and resentment, wishing to slander me and wishing to bring about my downfall. Thus he slanders me and thus seeks my downfall, saying to me:
'Gautama!'"

There is a certain ascetic or brahmin who does not know the prior limit of the world, does not know its subsequent limit, and does not know the endless cycle of birth and death; yet he declares that he has attained ultimate knowledge, truly knowing: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
"Gautama! I had this thought:

'How can this śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, who does not know the prior limit of the world, does not know the subsequent limit of the world, and does not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge—truly knowing that "birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence"? "
The World-Honored One, having understood this, said: “Kaccāna!

If there were any śramaṇas or brahmins who do not know the prior limit of the world, who do not know the subsequent limit of the world, and who do not know the endless cycle of birth and death, yet claim to have attained ultimate knowledge—knowing truly that ‘birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence’—they should speak as follows:”
"Setting aside the prior limit of the world, setting aside the posterior limit of the world," Kaccāna!
This is what I have taught.
"Setting aside the prior limit of the world and the subsequent limit of the world:

even if one does not recall a single lifetime, when my disciple-monks come to me—free from flattery and deceit, honest and straightforward—I shall instruct them. If they follow my instruction and practice accordingly, they will certainly come to know the True Dharma."
"Kātyāyana!

It is just as when an infant child, young and tender, lies on its back, and the parents bind its hands and feet. Later, as it grows up and its faculties mature, the parents release its hands and feet; the child remembers only the time of being released from the bonds, not the time of being bound."
In this way, Kaccāna! I speak thus:
"Setting aside the prior limit of the world, setting aside the posterior limit of the world."
"Even if they do not recall a single lifetime, when my disciple-monks come to me—being free from flattery, free from deception, and straightforward—I shall instruct them."
"If you follow my teaching and practice in this way, you will surely come to know the True Dharma.
Kātyāyana!

It is like a lamp that burns because of oil and a wick; if no one adds more oil and no one replaces the wick, once the previous oil is exhausted and no further oil is supplied, it will naturally and quickly go out."
In this way, Kātyāyana! I speak thus:
"Setting aside the prior limit of the world, setting aside the posterior limit of the world."

"Even if they do not recall a single lifetime, when my disciple-monks come to me—being free from flattery, free from deception, and upright—I shall instruct them. If they follow my instruction and practice accordingly, they will surely come to know the True Dharma."
Kātyāyana!

It is just as if there were a heap of ten logs, or twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty logs, which are set ablaze by fire until they burn fiercely and intensely, and one sees the flames; yet afterwards, no one adds more grass, wood, husks, or sweepings. When the previous fuel is exhausted and no more is added, having nothing further to receive, it is extinguished of its own accord.
In this way, Kaccāna! I speak thus:
"Setting aside the prior limit of the world, setting aside the posterior limit of the world."
"Even if they do not recall a single lifetime, when my disciple-monks come to me—free from flattery, free from deception, and upright—I shall instruct them."
"If you follow my instruction and practice in this way, you will certainly come to know the True Dharma.
When he spoke these words, the heterodox practitioner Vimalakṣa was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him.

Thereupon, the heterodox teacher Vaimanasi saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the pure and white Dharma; he recognized no other as supreme, was no longer dependent on others, severed doubt, transcended delusion, became free from hesitation, and having established himself in the realization of the fruit, attained fearlessness regarding the Dharma of the Blessed One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“Blessed One!”
"I wish to go forth from the household life under the Buddha to study the Path, receive full ordination, become a bhikṣu, and practice the holy life.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent!"
"Monks! Practice the holy life.
Having gone forth from the household life to study the Path under the Buddha, that follower of another school received full ordination, became a monk, and practiced the holy life.
The Venerable Vimalakṣa went forth to study the Path; having received full ordination, he knew the Dharma and saw the Dharma, until he attained the state of an Arhat.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Venerable Vīmaṇasī and the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
