Dharma-rati Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra (210), Chapter 9: The Section on Pūtila, Part Five of the Latter Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the female lay follower Viśākhā went to where the bhikṣuṇī Dharmavatī was, prostrated at her feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the bhikṣuṇī Dharmavatī, saying:
“Noble One!”
"I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmā replied, "Viśākhā!"
"Ask whatever you wish to ask; once I have heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
Then the laywoman Viśākhā asked:
"Noble One!"
"One speaks of 'self';
what is meant by 'self'?
The bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā replied:

“The Blessed One has spoken of the five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of clinging to bodily form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is what the Blessed One has called the five aggregates of clinging.”
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable and noble one.
Having offered this praise, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
What is the view of a self-body?
The bhikkhunī Dhammā answered:

“The unlearned, foolish worldling does not see a true spiritual friend; he does not know the noble Dharma and does not practice the noble Dharma. He regards form as the self, the self as possessing form, form as being within the self, or the self as being within form.”
To view feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as the self; to view the self as possessing consciousness; to view consciousness as being within the self;
and to view the self as being within consciousness—this is called the view of selfhood (*sakkāya-diṭṭhi*).
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having offered this praise, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
What is the absence of the view of a self-existent body?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied:

“The well-heard noble disciple sees a true friend, knows the noble Dharma, and is skilled in practicing the noble Dharma; he does not view form as the self, nor the self as possessing form, nor form as being within the self, nor the self as being within form.”

One does not see feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness as the self; one does not see the self as possessing consciousness; one does not see consciousness within the self; nor does one see the self within consciousness.
"This is what is called being free from the view of a self-existent body.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed in praise:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
O Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
How does one extinguish the self?"
The bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā replied:
"The aggregate of form, when severed without remainder, is relinquished, vomited out, exhausted, unstained, ceased, stilled, and vanished."
When the aggregates of grasping—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are severed without remainder, abandoned, vomited out, exhausted, unstained, ceased, stilled, and vanished;
this is called the extinction of one's own self.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the female lay follower Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir!

Is it that ‘the aggregates (skandha) are the clinging-aggregates (upādānaskandha)’ and ‘the clinging-aggregates are the aggregates,’ such that the aggregates are identical to the clinging-aggregates and the clinging-aggregates are identical to the aggregates?
Or are the aggregates one thing and the clinging-aggregates another?”
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
“Sometimes the aggregates (khandha) are themselves the clinging-aggregates (upādānakkhandha), and sometimes the aggregates are not the clinging-aggregates.
In what way are the aggregates themselves the clinging-aggregates?”

If form is with outflows and with grasping, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are with outflows and with grasping, this is called "aggregates" (skandha) which are "burdensome aggregates" (upādānaskandha).
What are aggregates that are not burdensome aggregates?

“Form that is untainted and without grasping; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness that are untainted and without grasping—these are called aggregates, but not aggregates of grasping.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent!”
“Excellent!
O Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the upāsikā Viśākhā joyfully practiced his instructions.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
What is the Noble Eightfold Path?"
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
“The Noble Eightfold Path consists of right view up to right concentration; these are the eight, and this is called the Noble Eightfold Path.”
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir! Is the Noble Eightfold Path conditioned?
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
“Thus, this Noble Eightfold Path is conditioned.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed, “Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent!
O Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully put his words into practice.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
How many aggregates are there?"
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
"There are three aggregates:
the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom."
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having offered this praise, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced it.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
Does the Noble Eightfold Path subsume the three aggregates, or do the three aggregates subsume the Noble Eightfold Path?
The Bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
"The Noble Eightfold Path does not subsume the three aggregates;
rather, the three aggregates subsume the Noble Eightfold Path.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three path factors are subsumed within the aggregate of noble ethical discipline."
Right mindfulness and right concentration—these two path factors are subsumed under the noble aggregate of concentration.
Right view, right intention, and right effort—these three path factors are subsumed under the noble aggregate of wisdom.
"This is called the three aggregates not being subsumed by the Noble Eightfold Path, while the three aggregates do subsume the Noble Eightfold Path.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
O Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā joyfully practiced his instructions.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
Is cessation with opposition?"
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied,
“Cessation is without a counterpart.
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent,
O Worthy and Noble One!”
Having praised them, the laywoman Visākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She asked again:
"Noble ones!..."
“How many factors are there in the first dhyāna?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied:

“The first dhyāna has five factors: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), rapture (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā). These are called the five factors of the first dhyāna.”
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Worthy and Noble One!
Having offered this praise, the laywoman Viśākhā, filled with joy, respectfully practiced [his teaching].
She then asked again:
“Venerable Sir!
What is concentration?
What are the characteristics of concentration?”
What is the power of concentration?
What is the efficacy of concentration?
How does one cultivate concentration?
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
“If a well-directed mind attains singleness, this is called concentration.
The four foundations of mindfulness are called the characteristics of concentration.”
The four right efforts are called the power of concentration.
The four bases of psychic power are called the function of concentration.
If one practices these various wholesome dharmas as garments, cultivating them repeatedly with focused diligence, this is called the cultivation of concentration.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
How many qualities must one possess so that, after birth and death, when the body is cast away in a cemetery, it is as insentient as a log?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmā replied:
“There are three factors by which, once a living body has died and been cast away in a cemetery, it becomes as insentient as a piece of wood.
What are these three?

First, life; second, warmth; and third, consciousness. These are the three factors by which, once a living body has died and been cast away in a cemetery, it becomes as insentient as a piece of wood.”
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
What is the difference between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmā replied:
“In one who has died, the life-span has been exhausted, warmth has departed, and the faculties have disintegrated.

For a bhikkhu who has entered the attainment of cessation, the life-span is not exhausted, warmth does not depart, and the faculties do not disintegrate. This is the distinction between one who has died and one who has entered the attainment of cessation.”
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his words.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir!
If one enters the attainment of cessation and one enters the attainment of non-perception, what is the difference between them?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied:
“When a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, perception and feeling cease.
When one enters the attainment of non-perception, perception and feeling do not cease.
This is the distinction between entering the attainment of cessation and entering the attainment of non-perception.”
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir!
What is the difference between one who arises from the attainment of cessation and one who arises from the attainment of non-perception?
The bhikkhunī Dhammā answered:
“When a bhikkhu arises from the attainment of cessation, he does not form the thought:
‘I am arising from the attainment of cessation.
When a bhikkhu arises from the attainment of non-perception, he forms such a thought:”
"Am I possessed of perception? Am I without perception?
If one arises from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or arises from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), this is called the distinction.
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
She then asked again:
“Worthy sirs!
When a bhikṣu enters the attainment of cessation, he thinks thus:
‘Have I entered the attainment of cessation?’”
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:
"When a bhikkhu enters the attainment of cessation, he does not form the thought:
'I am entering the attainment of cessation.'"
"However, it is because he has cultivated his mind in this very way that he thus inclines toward it.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
O Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
When a bhikkhu arises from the attainment of cessation, he forms this thought:"
"Did I arise from the attainment of cessation?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmā replied:
"When a bhikṣu arises from the attainment of cessation, he does not form this thought:"
"I have arisen from the attainment of cessation.
"However, it is because of this body and the six sense bases as conditions that the life-faculty exists; therefore, one arises from meditative absorption.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent,
O Noble One!"
Having praised [him], the upāsikā Viśākhā, filled with joy, respectfully practiced his instructions.
She then asked again:
"O Noble One!"
“After a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation, what does his mind delight in, what does it incline toward, and what does it conform to?
The bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā replied:
“After a bhikkhu has emerged from the attainment of cessation, his mind delights in seclusion, inclines toward seclusion, and conforms to seclusion.”
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir!
How many kinds of applied thought are there?
The bhikkhunī Dhammā answered:
“There are three feelings:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
By what cause do these exist?”
“With contact as condition,
there is feeling. Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed,
“Excellent!”
“Excellent!
O Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Venerable sir!
What is pleasant feeling?"
"What is the feeling of suffering?
What is the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant?
The bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā replied:
"If one is touched by a pleasant contact, there arises in body and mind a pleasant and wholesome perception; this perception is called a pleasant perception.
If one is touched by an unpleasant contact, there arises in body and mind an unpleasant and unwholesome perception; this perception is called an unpleasant perception."

When one is touched by a contact that is neither painful nor pleasant, there arises in body and mind a state that is neither painful nor pleasant—a perception that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; this perception is called the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir!
Regarding pleasant feeling, what is pleasant and what is painful?”
What is impermanence?
What is affliction? What is the underlying tendency?
Regarding the perception of suffering: what is pleasure?
What is suffering?
What is impermanence?
What are the calamities and afflictions?
What are the latent tendencies?
And regarding the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, what constitutes pleasure?
What is suffering?
What is impermanence?
What is calamity?
"What is the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*)?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmaratī replied:

"Regarding pleasant feeling: its arising is pleasant and its persistence is pleasant; however, its transformation is suffering, and its impermanence is a calamity—this is the underlying tendency of desire."

Regarding the painful feeling: it arises as suffering and persists as suffering; its transformation is pleasure, and its impermanence is itself a calamity—the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*).

Regarding the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling: one does not know suffering and does not know pleasure; its impermanence is itself transformation—the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*).
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
She then asked again:
“Venerable sir, are all pleasant feelings driven by the underlying tendency of sensual desire?
Are all painful feelings driven by the underlying tendency of aversion?
And are all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings driven by the underlying tendency of ignorance?”
The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied:

“Not all pleasant feelings are driven by the underlying tendency toward sensual desire; not all painful feelings are driven by the underlying tendency toward aversion; and not all neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings are driven by the underlying tendency toward ignorance.”
What is the pleasant feeling that is not driven by the underlying tendency of sensual desire?

If a bhikkhu, detached from sensual desires and detached from evil and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and possesses joy and happiness, this is called the pleasant feeling that is not driven by the underlying tendency of sensual desire.
Why is this so? Because this is the abandonment of desire.
How is it that a painful feeling is not driven by the underlying tendency of aversion?

If one seeks the bliss of supreme liberation, yet gives rise to distress and suffering through longing and anxiety, this is called the perception of suffering that is not driven by the latent tendency of hatred. Why is this so?
Because it has severed hatred.
What is the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is not driven by the underlying tendency of ignorance?

When pleasure has ceased and pain has ceased, and joy and sorrow have already been extinguished, one attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna—equanimity, mindfulness, and purity; this is called the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure that is not driven by the underlying tendency of ignorance.
"Why is this? It is because this cuts off ignorance.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed in praise:
“Excellent! Excellent,
O Noble One!”
Having praised these words, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She asked again:
"O Noble One!"
"What is the counterpart to the perception of pleasure? The bhikkhunī Dhammā replied,
"The perception of suffering is the counterpart to the perception of pleasure."
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"O Worthy and Noble One!
Having offered these words of praise, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
What is the antidote to the perception of suffering?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmaratī replied:
"The perception of suffering has the perception of pleasure as its counterpart.
Upon hearing this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed,
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
O Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
What is the antidote to pleasant feelings and painful feelings?"
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied,
“The perception of pleasure and the perception of pain have the perception of neither-pain-nor-pleasure as their antidote.
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent,
O Worthy and Noble One!”
Having praised these words, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
She asked again:
"Noble One!..."
"What is the counterpart to the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied,
"The feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant has ignorance as its counterpart."
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the laywoman Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his words.
She then asked again:
“Venerable ones!
What is the antidote to ignorance?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmaratī replied:
"Regarding ignorance, clarity is its opposite.
Having heard this, the laywoman Viśākhā exclaimed,
"Excellent!"
"Excellent!
O Worthy and Noble One!
Having thus praised him, the upāsikā Viśākhā rejoiced and respectfully practiced his instructions.
He asked again:
"Venerable ones!
What is the counterpart of the wise?"
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied,
“The wise take nirvāṇa as their counterpart.
Having heard this, the upāsikā Viśākhā exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent,
O Noble One!”
Having praised him, the upāsikā Viśākhā, filled with joy, respectfully practiced his teaching.
She then asked again:
"Noble One!"
"What is the counterpart to nirvāṇa?
The bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā replied:
"You wish to ask an endless question; however, though you may ask, you shall not be able to reach my limit."
Nirvāṇa is without opposition.
Nirvāṇa is so called because it is free from the fault of the snare and because the binding of snares has been extinguished.
For this reason, one practices the holy life under the Blessed One.

Thereupon, having heard what the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā had said, the upāsikā Viśākhā received it well, retained it well, and mastered it through recitation; she then rose from her seat, prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā, circumambulated her three times, and departed.

Thereupon, not long after the laywoman Viśākhā had departed, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat down to one side. She related to the Buddha in its entirety the discussion she had shared with the laywoman Viśākhā, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, she said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"In speaking and answering thus, am I not slandering the Blessed One?
Am I speaking what is true, speaking in accordance with the Dharma, and speaking the Dharma that accords with the Dharma?"
"In accordance with the Dharma, is there no contradiction, dispute, or fault?
The World-Honored One replied, "Bhikṣuṇī!"

Since you have spoken and answered in this way, you do not misrepresent me; you speak what is true, you speak in accordance with the Dharma, you speak the Dharma that follows the sequence of the Dharma, and within the Dharma you have not contradicted it, nor is there any fault or dispute.

“Bhikṣuṇī! If the upāsikā Viśākhā had approached me with these very phrases and these very words to ask this question, I would have answered the upāsikā Viśākhā with this same meaning, these same phrases, and these same words.”
"O Bhikṣuṇī!
This meaning is just as you have stated; you should hold it thus. Why is that? Because..."
"This teaching is itself the meaning.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā and the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Dhamma-saṃvāsa Bhikkhunī Sutta, the ninth, ends here; 3,049 characters. 211. The Mahākoṭṭhita Sutta (211), the tenth in the Puḷina Vagga of the Madhyama Āgama, for the fifth subsequent recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Nivāpa.

At that time, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his meditation and went to where the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita was. They exchanged greetings with one another and sat down to one side.
The Venerable Sāriputta said: "Worthy Koṭṭhita!
I wish to ask a question; will you allow me to ask?"
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied: “Venerable Sāriputta!
Ask whatever you wish; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.”
The Venerable Sāriputta asked: "Worthy Koṭṭhita!
You have spoken of what is unwholesome as unwholesome, and you have spoken of the roots of the unwholesome as the roots of the unwholesome."
"What is unwholesome, and what are the roots of the unwholesome?
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:
"Bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct—these are unwholesome."
"Greed, hatred, and delusion are the unwholesome roots.
These are called 'unwholesome,' and these are called 'unwholesome roots.
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent,
worthy Koṭṭhita!”
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
"Worthy Koṭṭhita!..."
“The virtuous speak of virtue; those with roots of virtue speak of the roots of virtue.
What is virtue? And what are the roots of virtue?
Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:
“Wholesome conduct of body, wholesome conduct of speech, and wholesome conduct of mind—these are wholesome.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—these are the roots of the wholesome.
These are called ‘the wholesome,’ and these are called ‘the roots of the wholesome.’”
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Kūṭadanta!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
“Worthy Koṭṭhita!
When those possessed of wisdom speak of wisdom, what is wisdom?
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:
“Because one knows thus, it is called wisdom. What does one know?
One knows this suffering as it truly is;
one knows the origin of this suffering, the cessation of this suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of this suffering as they truly are. Because one knows thus, it is called wisdom.”
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Venerable Kūṭadanta!
Having uttered this exclamation, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
“Venerable Cūḷa Kaccāyana!
Regarding what is called ‘consciousness,’ what is consciousness?
Venerable Mahā-Kaccāyana replied:
"It is called consciousness because it cognizes.
What does it cognize? It cognizes forms;
it cognizes sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. It is called consciousness because it cognizes."
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Worthy Koṭṭhita!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
“Venerable Kaccānagotta!
As for these two phenomena—wisdom and consciousness—are they conjoined or distinct? Can these two phenomena be designated as separate?”
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhila replied:
"These two phenomena are conjoined and not separate; these two phenomena cannot be designated as distinct. Why is that? Because..."
"That which is known by wisdom is precisely that which is cognized by consciousness.
Therefore, these two phenomena are conjoined and not distinct; these two phenomena cannot be established as separate.
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent,
worthy Koṭṭhita!"
Having praised these words, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
"Worthy Koṭṭhita!"
"What do you know, sir? Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied,
"I know, sir, through wisdom."
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Kūṭadanta!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
“Venerable Cūḷa Kaccāyana!
What is the meaning of wisdom? What is its excellence? What are its virtues?
Venerable Mahā Kaccāyana replied:
“The wise possess the sense of disenchantment, the sense of dispassion, and the sense of seeing things as they truly are.
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent,
worthy Koṭṭhita! Having praised him thus,
the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Venerable Kaccānagotta!
What is right view?"
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:
“To know suffering as it truly is, and to know the origin, cessation, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering as they truly are—this is called right view.”
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Venerable Kūṭadanta!
Having thus praised him, the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He then asked again:
“Venerable Cūḷa Kaccāna!
Through how many causes and through how many conditions does right view arise?
The Venerable Mahā Kaccāna replied:
“Right view arises from two causes and two conditions. What are these two?
First, hearing from others; second, internal reflection.”
"These are called the two causes and two conditions by which right view arises.
Having heard this, the Venerable Sāriputta exclaimed:
"Excellent!"
"Excellent,
worthy Koṭṭhita! Having thus praised him,
the Venerable Sāriputta rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
He asked again:
"Venerable Kaccāyana!

How many factors comprise right view so that one attains the fruit of liberation of mind and the fruit of liberation by wisdom, and the qualities of liberation of mind and the qualities of liberation by wisdom?"
The Venerable Mahākoṭṭhita replied:

“There are five factors that encompass right view, which lead to the fruit of liberation of mind and the fruit of liberation by wisdom, and to the qualities of liberation of mind and the qualities of liberation by wisdom.”

It is just as a lamp is ignited because of oil and a wick; therein, because of the flame there is light, and because of the light there is the flame. If there were no flame, there would be no light; if there were no light, there would be no flame.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Uruvelā, in the forest of Senāni.

At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was traveling through Uruvelā and was staying in the Ātaviya Sāla Grove. Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a man, saying:

"Go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and inquire on my behalf whether his holy body is healthy and strong, whether he is at ease and free from illness, whether his daily activities are light and convenient, and whether his strength is as usual?"
He spoke these words:
"King Pasenadi of Kosala inquires after your venerable health—whether you are strong, at ease, free from illness, light and nimble in your movements, and whether your vigor remains as it was?"
Again, he spoke, saying:
"King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come and see you.
Having received these instructions, that man went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with him, sat down to one side, and said:

"Gautama! King Pasenadi of Kosala inquires after your venerable health: Are you strong and well? Are you free from illness? Is your daily life easy and comfortable? Is your physical strength as it was before?"
"King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come and see you.
The World-Honored One replied, "Now King Pasenadi of Kosala is at peace and happy; today, gods and humans, asuras, gandharvas, rākṣasas, and various other beings are all at peace and happy."
"If King Pasenadi of Kosala wishes to come, he may do as he pleases.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, the messenger received and memorized it well, rose from his seat, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding a fly-whisk and attending to the Buddha.

the Blessed One took the Venerable Ānanda to that large hall facing east, opened the windows, closed the doors, arranged a seat in a secluded spot, spread out a sitting mat (niṣīdana), and sat down cross-legged.

"The Śramaṇa Gautama is now waiting for the Great King; may the Great King himself know the proper time.

“Is there any other teaching or any other reception?
Does the śramaṇa Gautama remember what he has said?

"Great King!
I recall having spoken thus.
Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed:

King Pasenadi of Kosala asked:

The Blessed One replied:
"There are four such types—the kṣatriya, the brāhmaṇa, the householder, and the craftsman—and among them there is superiority and distinction."
The Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa castes are of the highest virtue among humans; the Vaiśya and Śūdra castes are of inferior virtue among humans.
"There are four such types: the kṣatriya, the brahmin, the householder, and the craftsman; these are called their distinctions, these are called their differences.
Having heard this, King Prasenajit of Kosala exclaimed:
"The words spoken by the śramaṇa Gautama are like those of a teacher; the words spoken by the śramaṇa Gautama are like those of a virtuous teacher."
King Pasenadi of Kosala said: “Gotama!
I do not ask only about the meaning of this present life; I also wish to ask about the meaning of future lives. Will you allow me to ask?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Great King!
If you wish to ask anything, feel free to ask as you please."
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: “Gotama, among these four classes—
the kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans— is there any superiority or distinction between them in regard to future lives?”
The Blessed One replied:
"There are four such types—kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—and among them there is superiority and distinction, namely, with respect to future lives."

There are four such types: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans. If they accomplish these five factors of abandonment, they will certainly find a good teacher who is a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha; they will certainly find what is pleasing and avoid what is displeasing; and for a long night, they will obtain meaningful benefit, peace, and happiness.
What are the five?

The learned noble disciple has faith and devotion toward the Tathāgata; it is rooted, established, and firm, such that no one can take it away—not even śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world. This is called the first factor of abandonment.

Furthermore, Great King, the learned noble disciple has little illness and is free from disease; he achieves a balanced diet that is neither too hot nor too cold, which is pleasant and free from conflict—meaning his food and drink are digested and properly digested with ease. This is called the second factor of abandonment.

Furthermore, Great King, a learned noble disciple is without flattery and without deceit, being upright and sincere toward the True World-Honored One and those living the holy life as they truly appear; this is called the third factor of abandonment.

Furthermore, Great King, the learned noble disciple constantly practices diligence, abandoning evil and unwholesome states and cultivating all wholesome dharmas; he always rouses his own intention with single-mindedness and firm resolve for the sake of all roots of goodness, never relinquishing skillful means—this is called the fourth factor of abandonment.

Furthermore, Great King, the learned noble disciple practices wisdom, contemplates the phenomena of arising and passing away, and attains such knowledge—noble, penetrative, clear, and fully understood—thereby rightly bringing an end to suffering; this is called the fifth factor of abandonment.

There are four such types—kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—who, if they accomplish these five factors of abandonment, will certainly encounter a True Teacher, a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened One; they will certainly find what is pleasing and avoid what is displeasing, and for a long night they will obtain meaningful benefit, peace, and happiness. These four types—kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—are what is meant by superiority and distinction in future lives.
Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed:
“The teaching of the ascetic Gotama is like that of a teacher; the teaching of the ascetic Gotama is like that of a good teacher.”
"I wish to ask further; will you allow me to ask?
The World-Honored One replied, "Great King!"
"If you wish to ask, feel free to ask whatever you desire.
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama!..."
"There are four kinds—kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—is there any superiority or distinction among them regarding the cultivation of abandonment?"
The Blessed One replied:
"There are four such types—Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, householders, and artisans—and among them there is superiority and there is distinction in their practice of abandonment."
Great King!
What do you think?
That what is severed by one who has faith could be severed by one who lacks faith—such a thing is simply impossible.
If that which is abandoned by one who has little illness were abandoned by one who is frequently ill, such a thing could never be.
If that which is abandoned by one who is neither sycophantic nor deceitful were abandoned by one who is sycophantic and deceitful, such a thing could never be.
That which is abandoned by one who is diligent cannot possibly be abandoned by one who is indolent;
that which is abandoned by one who possesses wisdom cannot possibly be abandoned by one who possesses evil wisdom.

"It is just as with four charioteers: an elephant-charioteer, a horse-charioteer, an ox-charioteer, and a human-charioteer; among them, two charioteers cannot be tamed or controlled, while two charioteers can be tamed and controlled."
"Great King!
What do you think?
If these two charioteers are untamable and cannot be guided, it is simply impossible that they could come to tame the earth, guide the earth, or undertake the task of governance."

If those two charioteers were capable of being trained and guided, and had reached the stage of training and the stage of guidance such that they could undertake the task of driving, this would certainly be possible.
It is even so, Great King!
"What do you think?
Is that which is abandoned by one who has faith abandoned by one who lacks faith?
Such a thing is absolutely impossible."
If that which is abandoned by one who has little illness were abandoned by one who is frequently ill,
such a thing could never be.
If that which is abandoned by one who is neither sycophantic nor deceitful were abandoned by one who is sycophantic and deceitful, such a thing could never be.
This is absolutely impossible.
If that which is abandoned by one who is diligent were abandoned by one who is indolent,
this would be absolutely impossible.
If that which is abandoned by one of wisdom were abandoned by one of evil wisdom,
such a thing could never be.
Thus, among these four types— kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans— there is this distinction and difference regarding their practice of abandonment.
Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed:
"The words spoken by the ascetic Gotama are like those of a teacher; the words spoken by the ascetic Gotama are like those of a true spiritual friend."
"I wish to ask further; will you allow me to ask?
The World-Honored One replied, "Great King!"
"If you wish to ask, feel free to ask whatever you desire.
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama!..."

There are four kinds of people: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans; is there superiority among them, is there a distinction between them—namely, that one has severed [the fetters] while another has not?
The Blessed One replied:

“There are four such types—kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans—and when they have equally severed [the fetters], there is no superiority or inferiority among them, nor is there any distinction in their severance.”
"Great King!
It is just as if a young Kṣatriya from the east were to come and take dry sāla wood to serve as the fire-drill base, rubbing and churning it to produce fire;
or a young Brahmin from the south were to come and take dry sāla wood to serve as the fire-drill base, drilling and churning it to produce fire."
A young householder’s son from the west arrived; he took dry *candana* sandalwood as the fire-drill base and produced fire by drilling and rubbing it.
A young artisan’s son from the north arrived; he took dry *pāṭalī* wood as the fire-drill base and produced fire by drilling and rubbing it.
"Great King!
What do you think?
Suppose various people take various kinds of wood as fire-drills and produce fire by drilling; among them, some might place dry grass or wood, whereupon smoke arises, flames arise, and color arises."
"Great King!
Regarding smoke and smoke, flame and flame, and color and color, what distinction do you speak of?
King Pasenadi of Kosala replied:

"Gautama! Suppose those various kinds of people take various kinds of wood to serve as fire-drills and, by rubbing them together, produce fire. Among them, some might add dry grass and wood, whereby smoke arises, flames arise, and color arises."
"Gautama!
I do not say that there is a distinction between smoke and smoke, flame and flame, or color and color. "It is so."
"Great King!

There are these four kinds: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and craftsmen. All of them are equal in their abandonment; there is no superiority or inferiority, and no distinction among them regarding that abandonment."
Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed:
“The teaching of the śramaṇa Gautama is like that of a teacher; the teaching of the śramaṇa Gautama is like that of a true spiritual friend.”
“I wish to ask further; will you grant me leave to question you?
The World-Honored One replied, “Great King!”
"If you wish to ask, feel free to ask whatever you desire.
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked:
"Gautama!..."
"Are there devas?
The World-Honored One asked:
"Great King!"
"With what intention do you ask whether there exists a heavenly realm?
King Pasenadi of Kosala replied, "Gautama!"
If there are devas who harbor disputes and delight in disputes, they should come here.
If there are devas who are free from disputes and do not delight in disputes, they should not come here.
At that time, the general Viśvāmitra was standing behind King Prasenajit of Kosala, fanning the king with a whisk. General Viśvāmitra addressed him, saying: “Gautama!
If there are gods who are without contention and do not delight in contention, they do not come to this world; let us set those gods aside for now.

If there are gods who are contentious and delight in contention who do come to this world, the śramaṇa Gautama will certainly say that the merit of those gods is superior and their holy life is superior, [and that] these gods have attained mastery over them, causing those gods to decline and driving them away.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was behind the Blessed One, holding a fly-whisk and attending upon the Buddha.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda thought to himself:
"This General Bhūriñjaya is the son of King Prasenajit of Kosala, and I am the son of the Blessed One; now is the very moment for the sons of our respective fathers to converse together."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda said to General Bhūriśara:
"I wish to question you; answer as you see fit.
General!..."
What do you think?

Within the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala, and wherever his commands reach, because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in the holy life (brahmacarya), would he not have the power to dismiss or send away those [who oppose him]?
The general Bhūriṇḍaka replied: “Śramaṇa!

As for the realm of King Prasenajit of Kosala, wherever his commands reach, because King Prasenajit of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in holy life, he has the power to dismiss or send them away.”
“General! What do you think?
If it were not within the domain of King Prasenajit of Kosala, such that his commands did not reach it.”
"Since King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in the holy life (brahmacarya), can you, with the mastery of your mind, cause him to fall away or send him away?
The general Bhūriśravas replied,
"O Śramaṇa!"

If it were not within the domain of King Pasenadi of Kosala, where his commands do not reach, then because King Pasenadi of Kosala is superior in merit and superior in the holy life (brahmacarya), he would be unable to exercise authority over them to withdraw them or send them away.
The Venerable Ānanda asked again:
"General, have you heard that there are the Thirty-three Gods?"
The general Vīrūḍhaka replied:
“When King Prasenajit of Kosala was out on a pleasure excursion, I heard that there are the Thirty-three Gods. “General!
"What do you think?

Because King Pasenadi of Kosala excels in merit and excels in the holy life, could he exercise such mastery as to cause those gods of the Thirty-three to retreat or even expel them from the Heaven of the Thirty-three?"
The general Vīrūḍhaka replied: "O Śramaṇa!
Even King Prasenajit of Kosala cannot even see the Heaven of the Thirty-three, much less dismiss or send away its inhabitants."
"It is impossible that those gods of the Thirty-three would ever be driven away. "It is so, General!
If there are gods who are free from strife and take no pleasure in strife, and do not come to this place, it is because the merit of those gods is superior and their holy life is superior."
If there are gods who delight in strife and come to this realm, these gods cannot even see those gods in their own abode, let alone have them expelled by the gods of that realm.
"It would be impossible for him to dismiss them.
Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala asked:
"Gotama!..."
"What is the name of this śramaṇa?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Great King!"
"This bhikkhu is named Ānanda; he is my attendant.
Upon hearing this, King Pasenadi of Kosala exclaimed:
"What Ānanda has said is like the Teacher himself; what Ānanda has said is like that of a true spiritual friend."
"I wish to ask further; will you allow me to ask?
The World-Honored One replied, "Great King!"
"If you wish to ask, feel free to ask whatever you desire.
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked: "Gotama!..."
"Is there perhaps a Brahmā?
The World-Honored One asked,
"Great King!"
With what intention do you ask whether Brahmā exists?
Great King!
If I were to designate a Brahmā, that Brahmā would be pure.
While the Blessed One was discussing this matter with King Pasenadi of Kosala, the messenger returned, bringing the young man Soṇadaṇḍa, and approached King Pasenadi of Kosala, saying:
"Your Majesty! [Soṇadaṇḍa has arrived]."
“Thinking that the youth Maṅgala has been here since long ago,” King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard this, asked the youth Maṅgala:
“The other day, when the King was seated together with a great assembly, who was the first to say that the śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus?”

"Was it not the case that he said: 'In the past there was nothing, in the future there will be nothing, and even now in the present there is nothing—were there any other śramaṇas or brahmins who possessed all-knowledge and all-vision'?"
The youth Śrīgarbha replied:
“O Heavenly King!
It was the Great General Vairūḍhaka who spoke previously.”
Having heard this, General Viśvāmitra said to him:
"O Great King!
This was previously taught by the youth Maṅgalya."
Thus those two men continued to dispute this argument with one another. In the meantime, the charioteer prepared the carriage and went to King Prasenajit of Kosala, reporting to him:
"Your Majesty!..."
"The carriage is prepared and we have arrived; Your Majesty, the King of Devas, please know that the time has come.
Having heard this, King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"I asked the Gautama about the matter of omniscience, and the ascetic Gautama answered me regarding the matter of omniscience."
I asked the śramaṇa Gautama about the four kinds of purity, and the śramaṇa Gautama answered me regarding the four kinds of purity.
I asked the śramaṇa Gautama about what has been attained, and the śramaṇa Gautama answered me regarding what has been attained.
I asked the ascetic Gautama about Brahmā, and the ascetic Gautama answered me regarding Brahmā.
If I were to ask him about other matters, the ascetic Gautama would certainly answer me regarding those other matters.
"Gautama!
I have many affairs now and wish to take my leave.
The World-Honored One replied:
"Great King!
You yourself should know the proper time.
Having heard what the Blessed One had said, King Pasenadi of Kosala received and retained it well, rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
King Prasenajit of Kosala, the Venerable Ānanda, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Sarvajña-sūtra*, the first [chapter], ends here, totaling three thousand seven hundred and seventy-three characters. 213. *Dharmālaṃkāra-sūtra* (213), Saṃyukta Āgama, Chapter on Examples, *Dharmālaṃkāra-sūtra*, the second [sūtra], the fifth [section] of the latter recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas, staying in a Śākya city named Mithilā.
At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala, accompanied by Jīvakambavana, went out to the town of Ambaṭṭha for some business.

Upon arriving at that park, King Pasenadi of Kosala saw that beneath the various trees there was profound silence; it was secluded, free from evil, devoid of people, and conducive to solitary meditation. Having seen this, he called to mind the Blessed One.
King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Long-wa!

This place beneath the tree is tranquil and silent, secluded, free from evil, and devoid of people; it is a place conducive to sitting in meditation. It is here that I have frequently gone to see the Buddha."
"Longca! Where is the Blessed One now?
I wish to go and see him."
Dīrgha replied: "Great King!
I have heard that the World-Honored One is traveling among the Śākyas, staying in the capital city of the Śākyas named Mithilā."
King Pasenadi of Kosala asked again:
"Long-waist!
How far is Mithilā, the capital city of the Śākya clan, from here?"
Dīrgha replied,
"Great King!
It is three krośas from here."
King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Dīgha!
Order the carriage to be prepared; I wish to go to the Buddha."
Dīrgha-kāra received the instruction and immediately ordered the chariots to be prepared, reporting:
"Your Majesty!
The chariots are ready; it is as Your Majesty wishes."
King Pasenadi of Kosala immediately mounted his carriage and departed from the city, traveling to the Śākya capital named Mithilā.
At that time, many bhikṣus were walking in meditation in the open air outside the gates of Mithilā. King Pasenadi of Kosala approached those bhikṣus and asked:
"Venerable sirs!"
“Where is the Blessed One walking about during the day now?
The many bhikṣus replied,
“Great King!”
"That great hall facing east has its windows open and its doors closed; the World-Honored One is currently walking about within it during the day.
Great King!
If you wish to see him, go there at once. Upon arrival, stand outside, clear your throat, and knock on the door. If the World-Honored One hears you, he will surely open the door for you."
King Pasenadi of Kosala immediately descended from his chariot.

When a Kṣatriya king of the royal lineage comes to occupy the human station and commands the great earth, he possesses five regalia: a sword, a parasol, a flower garland, a fly-whisk with a jeweled handle, and ornate sandals. Having removed them all, he handed them to Dīgha Kārāyaṇa, who thought to himself:
"The Heavenly King will surely enter alone; we should remain here together and wait."

Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala, surrounded by his retinue, proceeded on foot to the great hall facing east. Upon arrival, he stood outside, cleared his throat, and knocked at the door. Having heard this, the World-Honored One opened the door for him. King Pasenadi of Kosala then entered the hall, approached the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and three times announced his own name:
“I am King Pasenadi of Kosala.”
"I am King Pasenadi of Kosala.
The Blessed One replied, "It is so."
Great King!
You are King Pasenadi of Kosala. You are King Pasenadi of Kosala.
After King Pasenadi of Kosala had stated his name and lineage a second and a third time, he bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.
The World-Honored One asked him:
“Great King!”
"What meaning do you see in me that you have humbled yourself to bow your head at my feet and to serve and honor me?
King Pasenadi of Kosala replied,
"World-Honored One!..."
I have found peace in the Dharma of the Buddha; for this reason, I have this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent, and the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-directed."
"World-Honored One!

Whenever I am seated in the assembly hall, I see mothers disputing with their sons and sons disputing with their mothers; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen all dispute with one another. When they are thus quarreling, the mother speaks ill of the son, and the son speaks ill of the mother; fathers and sons, brothers, sisters, and kinsmen speak ill of one another—how much more so toward others?"

I have observed that among the community of bhikṣus who are disciples of the World-Honored One practicing the holy life under him, there may be some bhikṣus who, having given rise to various disputes to a greater or lesser extent, abandon the precepts and leave the path; yet they do not speak ill of the Buddha, do not speak ill of the Dharma, and do not speak ill of the Saṅgha, but instead reproach themselves, saying:
"I have done evil; I am devoid of virtue."
"Why is this? Because I am unable to practice the holy life under the Blessed One for as long as my life lasts.
This is what I call having a sense of spiritual tranquility toward the Buddha; for this reason, I have this thought:
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-directed.
Furthermore, Blessed One:

I have seen a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who, for nine or ten months, practiced the holy life to a greater or lesser extent; yet he has cast off his robes and returned to his former dress, becoming defiled by desire, stained by desire, and bound by desire. Arrogant and immersed in it, he perceives neither its peril nor the way of escape, and thus delights in the practice of sensual desire.
“World-Honored One!
I see that among the World-Honored One’s disciples, the community of bhikṣus, there are even as many as hundreds of millions who practice the holy life (brahmacarya) for as long as they live.

Beyond this, I do not see such pure holy life as that found within the World-Honored One’s own family. This is what I mean by having ‘dharma-serenity’ toward the Buddha; for this reason, I have formed this thought:”
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-directed.
Furthermore, Blessed One:

I saw a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who was emaciated and haggard, his appearance extremely wretched, with white pustules breaking out on his body, such that people did not delight in seeing him. I thought to myself:
"Why are these venerable ones so emaciated and haggard, their appearance so extremely wretched, with white pustules breaking out on their bodies, such that people do not delight in seeing them?"

"These venerable ones surely do not delight in practicing the holy life; perhaps their bodies are afflicted by illness, or perhaps they commit evil deeds in secret. For this reason, these venerable ones have become emaciated and haggard, their appearance is extremely wretched, white blisters have broken out on their bodies, and people take no pleasure in seeing them."
I went to them and asked:
"Venerable sirs, for what reason are you so emaciated and haggard, with such an extremely wretched appearance, white blisters breaking out on your bodies, such that people do not wish to see you?"
Do you venerable ones not delight in practicing the holy life?
Is there some ailment in your bodies?
Or have you committed evil deeds in secret?
"For this reason, these venerable ones are emaciated and haggard, their appearance is extremely foul, white blisters have broken out upon their bodies, and people take no pleasure in seeing them.
He replied to me, saying:
"Great King!..."
This is the white disease,
Great King!
This is the white disease.
"World-Honored One!

I see the community of bhikṣus, the disciples of the World-Honored One, who delight in upright conduct, whose complexions are radiant and pleasing, and whose bodies are pure and clean. They are unconditioned and free from seeking; they guard against the food of others' wives like deer, and throughout their entire lives they practice the holy life (brahmacarya). Having seen this, I thought:

'For what reason do these venerable ones delight in upright conduct, have such radiant and pleasing complexions, and possess such pure and clean bodies? Why are they unconditioned and free from seeking, guarding against the food of others' wives like deer, and practicing the holy life for as long as they live? "

"These venerable ones have attained either freedom from desire or the higher mind, dwelling in happiness in this very life; they have attained these easily and without difficulty. For this reason, these venerable ones delight in upright conduct;

their countenances are serene and radiant, and their bodies are pure and clean. They are unconditioned and free from seeking; they guard the wives and food of others like deer, and throughout the duration of their lives, they practice the holy life.
If those who practice the pursuit of sensual pleasures are handsome, then I too should delight in practicing for handsomeness.
Why is this? Because I shall obtain the merits of the five desires easily, without difficulty.

If these venerable ones have attained freedom from desire and attained the higher mind, dwelling in happiness in this very life, which they obtain easily and without difficulty; therefore, these venerable ones delight in upright conduct, their complexions are radiant, their bodies are pure and clean, they are unconditioned and free from seeking, guarding the wives and food of others like deer, and practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for as long as they live—this is what I mean by having "peace in the Dharma" regarding the Buddha.
For this reason, I have this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent; the Saṅgha of the World-Honored One’s disciples is well-directed."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One! I see a certain śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa who is intelligent and wise, claiming himself to be intelligent and wise; one who is widely learned and decisive, well-versed in all the sūtras, who subdues powerful adversaries, and whose discourse is clear and penetrating. His fame and virtue are spread abroad, such that there is no one in the entire world who does not know of him. Wherever he travels, he destroys the tenets of various views and immediately establishes his own doctrines, saying:
'We shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such and such questions; if he can answer them, we shall challenge and interrogate him.'"
"If he cannot answer, and after having been cross-examined, he abandons the matter and departs.

When he heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through a certain village or town, he went to where the Buddha was; yet he did not even dare to ask the World-Honored One about the matter, much less wish to cross-examine him.
This is what I call having a settled conviction in the Dharma regarding the Buddha; for this reason, I have this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent, and the Saṅgha of the World-Honored One’s disciples is well-directed."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One!

I see a certain śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa who is intelligent and wise, claiming for himself intelligence and wisdom; one who is widely learned and decisive, well-versed in all the sūtras, who subdues powerful adversaries, and whose discourse is clear and penetrating. His fame and virtue are spread abroad, such that there is no one in the entire world who does not know of him. Wherever he travels, he demolishes the tenets of various views and immediately establishes his own arguments, saying:
'We shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such-and-such questions; if he can answer them, we shall cross-examine him.'"
"If he cannot answer, or even after having been cross-examined, he abandons the matter and departs.

When he heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through a certain village or town, he went to where the Buddha was and questioned the World-Honored One about certain matters. Having heard the Buddha's response, he attained great joy, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed. This is what I mean by "having a settled mind in the Dharma regarding the Buddha."
For this reason, I have formed this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is excellent; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is well-directed."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One! I see a śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa who is intelligent and wise, claiming for himself intelligence and wisdom; one who is widely learned and decisive, well-versed in all the sūtras, who subdues powerful adversaries, and whose discourse is clear and penetrating. His fame and virtue are widespread, such that there is no one in the entire world who does not know of him. Wherever he travels, he destroys the tenets of various views and immediately establishes his own doctrines, saying:
'We shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such and such questions; if he is able to answer them, we shall cross-examine him.'"
"If he cannot answer, and after having been cross-examined, he abandons the matter and departs.

When he heard that the World-Honored One was traveling through a certain village or town, he went to where the Buddha was and questioned the World-Honored One about these matters. Having received the World-Honored One’s answers, he attained great joy and immediately took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. The World-Honored One accepted him as a lay follower (*upāsaka*), who took refuge for the rest of his life until the end of his days. This is what I mean by "having the Dharma-tranquility in the Buddha."
For this reason, I have this thought:
"The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One is excellent; the Saṅgha of the World-Honored One’s disciples is well-directed."

"Furthermore, World-Honored One! I have seen a śramaṇa-brāhmaṇa who is clever and wise, claiming for himself that he is clever and wise; one who is widely learned and decisive, well-versed in all the sūtras, who has subdued powerful adversaries, and whose discourse is clear and enlightened. His fame and virtue are spread abroad, such that there is no one in the entire world who does not know of him. Wherever he travels, he destroys the tenets of various views and immediately establishes his own doctrines, saying:
'We shall go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is and ask him such and such questions; if he can answer them, we shall then cross-examine and challenge him.'"
"If he cannot answer, and after having been cross-examined, you should leave him and depart.

Hearing that the World-Honored One was traveling to a certain village or town, he went to where the Buddha was and questioned the World-Honored One on certain matters; the World-Honored One then provided answers.

Having heard this reply, he was filled with joy and immediately sought from the World-Honored One to go forth and train; he received full ordination and attained the status of a bhikṣu. The Buddha then delivered him, conferred full ordination upon him, and he attained the status of a bhikṣu.

"If those venerable ones go forth to study the Path and receive full ordination, having attained the status of a bhikṣu, they dwell alone in seclusion, their minds free from negligence, practicing with diligent effort."

Dwelling alone in seclusion, his mind free from negligence, having practiced with diligence, that son of noble family—who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and out of deep faith left the home life for homelessness to study the Path—having reached the culmination of the unsurpassed holy life, realizes it for himself through direct knowledge and personal experience, attaining it while living in this very life: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence," knowing this as it truly is.

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin who had an only son whom he cherished with the utmost affection; his mind was patient and gentle toward him, never weary of gazing upon him, until the boy suddenly passed away.

After his life ended, the brahmin was overcome with grief and distress; he could neither eat nor drink, he no longer wore clothes, nor did he apply perfumes, but went only to the cemetery to wail, remembering the place where his son had lain.
Thereupon, the brahmin wandered about until he arrived at the place where the Buddha was staying. After exchanging greetings with one another, he withdrew to sit at one side.
The World-Honored One asked him: "Brahmin!
"Now, do your faculties not seem to abide in accordance with your own mind?
The brahmin replied,
"How could my faculties possibly abide in accordance with my own mind now?"
Why is this? He had only one son, whom he cherished with the utmost love; his mind was patient and gentle toward him, never weary of gazing upon him, yet suddenly the boy passed away.

If those two kingdoms—Kāśi and Kosala—in which I enjoy myself, fully endowed with the fivefold qualities of sensual pleasure, were to undergo change and transformation, I would not even spare my life; how much less could I avoid sorrow, lamentation, grief, distress, and despair?
Mallikā replied:
"By this matter, it is known that when craving arises, there arise sorrow, lamentation, grief, suffering, vexation, and despair."
Mallikā asked the king,
"What do you think? Do you love me?"
The king replied again,
"I truly love you.
Mallikā asked once more:
"If I were to undergo change and become otherwise, what would you do,
O King? He replied,
"Mallikā!..."
"If you were once to change and become otherwise, I would surely give rise to grief, lamentation, sorrow, suffering, vexation, and despair.
Mallikā replied, "For this reason,
I know that when craving arises, there arise grief, lamentation, sorrow, suffering, vexation, and despair."
King Pasenadi of Kosala said: "Mallikā!

"Malunkyāputra!
