The *Piyajātika Sutta*, the fifth, ends here, totaling one thousand six hundred and seventy-eight characters. 217. The *Aṭṭhaka Sutta* (217), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Similes, the sixth discourse in this section. Fifth Subsequent Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, not long after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, a great number of highly venerable and renowned bhikṣus were traveling through the city of Pāṭaliputra and were staying at the Kukkuṭārāma.
At that time, the householder Daṭṭhābhaya of Aṭṭhakanāgara, taking many excellent goods, went to the city of Pāṭaliputta to conduct trade and commerce.

There, the householder Daṭṭhābhaya of Aṭṭhakanāgara quickly sold those many excellent goods and gained great wealth and profit. Elated and full of joy, he departed from the city of Pāṭaliputta and went to the Jeta Grove to visit the many highly venerable and renowned bhikkhus. He prostrated at their feet, paid his respects, and sat down to one side.

Then, those venerable and renowned bhikṣus preached the Dharma for him, exhorting him to aspire with longing and bringing him to a state of joy; having used immeasurable skillful means to preach the Dharma for him, exhorting him to aspire with longing and bringing him to a state of joy, they remained silent.
Then, after those senior bhikṣus had taught the Dharma to him, incited in him a sense of longing, and brought about joy, the householder Aṭṭhaka of Daṇḍakappaka addressed them, saying:
"Venerable sirs! "
"Where is the Venerable Ānanda now?
I wish to go and see him.
The senior bhikṣus replied:
“Householder!
The Venerable Ānanda is currently at the high tower on the bank of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī. If you wish to see him, you may go there.”

At that time, the tenth householder of Aṭṭhakanāgara rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the most venerable bhikṣus, circumambulated them three times, and departed. He went to where the Venerable Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and said:
"Venerable Ānanda!..."
"I wish to ask something; will you allow me to ask?
The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Householder!"
"Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.
The householder asked:
"Venerable Ānanda!"

"Bhagavān, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you who have accomplished the eye of wisdom and perceive the ultimate truth—do you perhaps teach even a single dharma by which a noble disciple, abiding therein, attains the exhaustion of the outflows without remainder and achieves liberation of mind?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied, “It is so.
The householder asked:
“Venerable Ānanda!
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has attained the eye of wisdom and perceives the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

How can it be said that there is one dharma by which a noble disciple, abiding therein, attains the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*) without remainder and achieves liberation of mind (*cittavimukti*)?
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Householder!
A learned noble disciple, having abandoned sensual desires and abandoned unwholesome and evil states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.”

Relying upon this basis, he contemplates phenomena as they truly are; relying upon this basis, he contemplates phenomena as they truly are. It is possible that, by abiding therein, one may attain the destruction of the taints.

If one dwells there but does not attain the exhaustion of outflows, then by means of this dharma—desiring it, loving it, delighting in it, and finding peace in it—and through that joyful appreciation, one completely severs the five lower fetters, is reborn there by transformation, and attains parinirvāṇa; having attained the state of non-retrogression, one never returns to this world again.
"Furthermore, householder,
a learned noble disciple dwells having suffused one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), accomplished and pervasive. In this same way, he dwells having suffused the second,

third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below— everywhere all around, everywhere extending— the mind imbued with loving-kindness, free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated, dwelling having suffused the entire world."

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.

Relying on this basis, he contemplates phenomena as they truly are; relying on this basis, he contemplates phenomena as they truly are. For one who dwells therein and attains the destruction of the taints, there is indeed such a possibility; yet for one who dwells therein and does not attain the destruction of the taints, it may be that through these teachings—desiring them, loving them, delighting in them, and finding peace in them—he, with joyful affection, completely severs the five lower fetters, is reborn spontaneously in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, having reached the state of non-retrogression and never returning to this world again.

This is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has accomplished the eye of wisdom, sees the ultimate truth, and teaches that there is one dharma by which a noble disciple, abiding in the exhaustion of the outflows without remainder, attains liberation of mind.
"Furthermore, householder!
A learned noble disciple transcends all perceptions of form, and so on, up to and including attaining and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
In this regard, he contemplates phenomena as phenomena; in this regard, he contemplates phenomena as phenomena. It is possible that by abiding therein, one may attain the destruction of the taints.

If one dwells there but does not attain the exhaustion of outflows, yet through this Dharma desires it, loves it, delights in it, and finds peace in it—rejoicing with affection and joy—one will sever the five lower fetters, be reborn there by transformation, and attain parinirvāṇa, having attained the state of non-retrogression and never again returning to this world.

This is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who has accomplished the eye of wisdom, sees the ultimate truth, and teaches that there is one dharma: if a noble disciple abides therein, their outflows will be exhausted without remainder, and they will attain liberation of mind.
Thereupon, the householder Aṭṭhaka of Aṭṭhakanāgara rose from his seat, adjusted his robe to bare one shoulder, and with palms joined, said:
"Venerable Ānanda!
"How marvelous!
How extraordinary!

I asked Venerable Ānanda about a single gate of ambrosia, yet Venerable Ānanda has at once explained twelve gates of ambrosia for me. Now, by means of these twelve gates of ambrosia, one will surely attain peace and security according to what they rely upon."
Venerable Ānanda!
Suppose there were a large house not far from a village, with twelve doors open, and a person, for some purpose, entered that house.
Suppose another person comes who does not seek the welfare or benefit of that person, nor seeks their peace and security, but instead sets fire to that house.
Venerable Ānanda!
That person will certainly find one of these twelve openings to escape by, thereby attaining their own safety and security.

Thus, when I asked the Venerable Ānanda for a single gate of ambrosia, the Venerable Ānanda immediately taught me twelve gates of ambrosial Dharma. Now, these twelve gates of ambrosial Dharma will surely lead to safety and deliverance, depending upon what one relies upon.
Venerable Ānanda!

Even in the Dharma and Vinaya of the brahmins, which speak of what is unwholesome, it is said that one must honor one's teacher; how much more so should I honor my great teacher, the Venerable Ānanda?

Thereupon, that night, the tenth householder of Aṭṭhaka-pura prepared an abundance of most excellent, pure, and delicious food and edibles. Having prepared the meal, at dawn he arranged the seats and invited the assembly from the Kukkutārāma and the assembly from Vaiśālī to gather in one place. He personally provided water for washing, then with his own hands served them the most excellent, pure, and delicious food and edibles until they were fully satisfied. When they had finished eating, the vessels were cleared away, and after the water for washing was finished, he purchased a house with five hundred kinds of goods and offered it specifically to the Venerable Ānanda.
Having received it, the Venerable Ānanda bestowed it upon the Saṅgha of the four quarters.
Such were the words spoken by the Venerable Ānanda.
Having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, the householder Aṭṭhaka of Aṭṭhakanāgara rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Aṣṭapurī-sūtra*, the sixth, ends here, totaling one thousand one hundred and seventy characters. 218. The *Anuruddha-sūtra* (218), from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Section on Similes, the seventh sūtra of the fifth recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī and staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣus rose from their meditative seclusion in the late afternoon and went to where the Venerable Anuruddha was. Having prostrated at his feet and sat down to one side, they said to him:
"We wish to ask a question; if you would grant us leave, we shall venture to speak."
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Virtuous friends!
Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it."
Then the bhikkhus asked:
"In what way does a bhikkhu die nobly and pass away nobly?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!

If a bhikkhu, having detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna, this is called a bhikkhu who dies nobly and passes away nobly."
Then the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is it the case that a bhikkhu dies a noble death and passes away nobly?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
It is not only when a bhikkhu dies or passes away that he is truly excellent.
Furthermore, venerable friends!"

If a bhikkhu has attained the power of the bases of psychic potency, the divine ear, knowledge of the minds of others, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and knowledge of the destruction of the taints; if he has attained the taintless state and dwells having realized for himself through direct knowledge in this very life the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, knowing truly: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
"This is what is called a bhikkhu’s noble death and noble passing away.
Then, the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is this the ultimate noble death and noble passing away for a bhikkhu?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied, "Virtuous ones!
A bhikkhu’s death is truly a noble death; his passing is a noble end."

Then, having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha had said, those bhikṣus received and recited it well; they rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
This is what the Venerable Anuruddha said.
Having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Anuruddha Sutta, the seventh, ends here with three hundred and fifty-three characters. 219. The Anuruddha Sutta (219), Middle Discourses, Chapter on Similes, the eighth discourse of the fifth sub-recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus rose from their meditation in the late afternoon and went to where the Venerable Anuruddha was. They prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said:
"We wish to ask a question; if you will grant us leave, we shall venture to speak."
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Virtuous friends!
Ask whatever you wish to ask; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it."
Then, the bhikkhus immediately asked:
"In what way does a bhikkhu die without feverish distress and pass away without feverish distress?
The Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
If a bhikkhu is upright and has attained the precepts beloved by the noble ones, this is called a bhikkhu who dies without fever and passes away without fever."
Then the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is it the case, bhikkhu, that one dies without fever and passes away without fever?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu does not die in a state of feverish distress, nor does he pass away in a state of feverish distress.
Furthermore, venerable friends!"

If a bhikṣu contemplates the internal body as body, and likewise contemplates feelings, mind, and phenomena as phenomena, this is called a bhikṣu who dies without feverish distress and passes away without feverish distress.
Then, the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is it the case that a bhikkhu dies without feverish distress and passes away without feverish distress?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu does not die in a state of feverish distress, nor does he pass away in a state of feverish distress.
Furthermore, venerable friends!"

If a bhikkhu, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, dwells pervading one direction, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, above and below, all around and everywhere; with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—free from fetters and resentment, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells pervading the entire world.

In this way, with a mind imbued with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—free from fetters and enmity, free from ill will and contention, vast, exalted, immeasurable, and well-cultivated—he dwells having pervaded the entire world.
"This is what is called a bhikkhu who dies without fever and passes away without fever.
Then, the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is this the absolute case for a bhikkhu who dies without fever and passes away without fever?"
The Venerable Anuruddha replied: "Virtuous ones!
A bhikkhu does not die nor pass away from life without being free from fever."
Furthermore, worthy friends!
If a bhikkhu transcends all perceptions of form, and so on, up to attaining and dwelling in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is called a bhikkhu who dies without fever and passes away without fever.
Then the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is it the case, Bhikkhu, that one dies without feverish distress and passes away without feverish distress?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu does not die in a state of feverish distress, nor does he pass away in a state of feverish distress.
Furthermore..."
"Venerable friends!

If there is a bhikkhu who, having transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, dwells having attained through bodily contact the cessation of perception and feeling, and who, through wisdom, perceives that all taints are exhausted—this is called a bhikkhu who dies without fever and passes away without fever."
Then the bhikkhus asked again:
"Is it the case that a bhikkhu dies without fever and passes away without fever?
Venerable Anuruddha replied:
"Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu indeed dies without fever and passes away without fever.

When the bhikkhus heard what the Venerable Anuruddha had said, they received and recited it well; then they rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the feet of the Venerable Anuruddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
This is what the Venerable Anuruddha said.
Having heard what the Venerable Anuruddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Āniruddha Sūtra, the eighth, ends here; 651 characters. 220. The *Dassana* Sūtra (220), the ninth in the *Vagga* section of the *Madhyama Āgama*, for the fifth subsequent recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, not long after the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Nivāpa.

Then, there was a certain wanderer, a brahmin who had been a friend of the Venerable Ānanda before he went forth. In the afternoon, while wandering about, he approached the Venerable Ānanda; after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"I wish to ask a question; will you allow me to ask?"
The Venerable Ānanda replied:
“Brahmin! Ask whatever you wish; having heard it, I shall reflect upon it.”
The wandering ascetic brahmin then asked:

"Regarding this view which is set aside and rejected, and not fully explained—namely, that the world is eternal, the world is not eternal, the world is finite, the world is infinite, the life-principle is identical to the body, the life-principle is one thing and the body another, the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—is this what you mean?"
“Does the ascetic Gautama know these various views as they truly are?
Venerable Ānanda replied: “Brahmin!”

Regarding this view, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has set it aside and rejected it, and has not fully explained it: namely, that the world is eternal, the world is not eternal, the world is finite, the world is infinite, the life-principle is identical to the body, the life-principle is one thing and the body another, the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
“World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, you understand these various views as they truly are.
The wandering ascetic brahmin asked again:

“Regarding this view which the śramaṇa Gautama sets aside and discards, not fully explaining it—namely, that the world is eternal, the world is not eternal; the world has an end, the world has no end; the life-principle is identical to the body, the life-principle is one thing and the body another; the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—is this what you mean?”
“How does the śramaṇa Gautama know these various views as they truly are?
The Venerable Ānanda replied: “Brahmin!”

Regarding these views—namely, that the world is eternal, the world is not eternal, the world is finite, the world is infinite, the life-principle is identical to the body, the life-principle is one thing and the body another, the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sets them aside and rejects them, rather than explaining them exhaustively. Is this what you mean?

"Is it that a heterodox brahmin, being thus equipped, thus receiving, thus proceeding, thus born, and thus arriving in a future world, is one whom the Blessed One—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—sets aside and rejects, not fully explaining [the matter], namely: 'The world is eternal,' 'the world is not eternal,' 'the world is finite,' 'the world is infinite,' 'the life-principle is the same as the body,' 'the life-principle is one thing and the body another,' 'the Tathāgata exists after death,' 'the Tathāgata does not exist after death,' 'the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,' or 'the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death'?"
"Thus one should understand these views; these views should be understood in this way.
The heterodox brahmin then said:
"I now take refuge in Ānanda."
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Brahmin! Do not take refuge in me; rather, just as I have taken refuge in the Buddha, you too should take refuge in him."
The heterodox brahmin said:

“Ānanda! I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the World-honored One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); from this day forth until the end of my life, I take refuge for as long as I live.”
Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda.
Having heard what the Venerable Ānanda had said, those heterodox brahmins rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

At one time, the Buddha was wandering in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Māṇava, alone in a secluded place, sat in meditation and reflected, his mind forming this thought:

“Regarding these views—which the World-Honored One has set aside and rejected, and which he does not fully explain—namely: ‘the world is eternal,’ ‘the world is not eternal,’ ‘the world is finite,’ ‘the world is infinite,’ ‘the life-principle is the same as the body,’ ‘the life-principle is one thing and the body another,’ ‘the Tathāgata exists after death,’ ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ and ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
"I do not desire this; I cannot endure this; I cannot accept this.
If the Blessed One were to categorically declare to me that the world is eternal, I would practice the holy life under him."
If the Blessed One does not categorically declare to me that the world is eternal, I shall cross-examine him and then depart. Likewise, [if he does not declare]:

"the world is not eternal," "the world is finite," "the world is infinite," "the life-principle is identical to the body," "the life-principle is one thing and the body another," "the Tathāgata exists after death," "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"?

"If the Blessed One were to declare categorically to me that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, I would practice the holy life under him; if the Blessed One does not declare categorically to me that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, I shall challenge him and depart."
Thereupon, in the late afternoon, the Venerable Māṇava Kumāraputta rose from his meditation, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at his feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!
"Today, while sitting alone in a secluded and peaceful place, I sat in meditation and reflected, and this thought arose in my mind:

'Regarding these views—which the World-Honored One has set aside and rejected, and which he does not fully explain: namely, that the world is eternal, the world is not eternal, the world is finite, the world is infinite, the life-principle is identical to the body, the life-principle is one thing and the body another, the Tathāgata exists after death, the Tathāgata does not exist after death, the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death—'"
"I do not desire this; I cannot endure this; I find this unacceptable.
If the Blessed One knows with certainty that the world is eternal, then, Blessed One, please explain this to me."
If the Blessed One does not know categorically that the world is eternal, he should simply say that he does not know.

Likewise, [what of] whether the world is non-eternal, finite, or infinite; whether the life-principle is identical to the body or the life-principle is distinct from the body; whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not exist after death, both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death?
If the Blessed One knows with certainty that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, then, Blessed One,
please explain it to me.
If the Blessed One does not know with certainty that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, then he should simply say that he does not know.
The World-Honored One asked:
"Māṇava! Did I ever say to you, 'The world is eternal,' and did you then come to me to practice the holy life?"
The youth Māla replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”

"In this way, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is endless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?"
“Have I ever said to you, ‘This alone is the true truth; all else is false speech; come, follow me and practice the holy life’?
The youth Māṇava replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
Māṇava, did you ever previously say to me:
‘If the World-Honored One were to categorically declare to me that the world is eternal, then I would follow the World-Honored One to train in the holy life’?”
The youth Māla replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”

“In this way, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is endless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?”
Māṇava! Did you ever previously say to me:
"If the Blessed One were to declare to me categorically that this alone is the absolute truth and all else is false speech, then I would follow the Blessed One to train in the holy life"?
The youth Māla replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One said:
"Māṇava, I have never spoken anything to you, nor have you ever spoken anything to me, you foolish man!"
"Why do you falsely and maliciously slander me?

Thereupon, having been rebuked and censured face-to-face by the Blessed One, the Venerable Māṇava felt inner sorrow and distress; with his head bowed, he remained silent, losing his eloquence and speechless, as if brooding over something.
Then, having rebuked the youth Māṇava face-to-face, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“If there were a foolish person who thought thus:
‘If the Blessed One does not definitively declare to me that the world is eternal, I will not train in the holy life under the Blessed One.’”
That foolish person never comes to know [the truth], yet passes away in the interim.

Thus, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has a limit, or that the world is limitless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
If there were a foolish person who thought thus:
"If the Blessed One does not declare to me categorically that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, I shall not train in the holy life under the Blessed One."
That foolish person will ultimately fail to understand it and will pass away in the interim.
It is just like a man who has been struck by a poisoned arrow; because of that poisoned arrow, he experiences extreme suffering.
Seeing that his kinsmen were filled with affection and compassion for him, seeking to bring him profit, benefit, welfare, and security, he sought out a physician to remove the arrow.
However, that man first thought to himself:

"The arrow must not be pulled out until I have first learned of this person's clan, their name, and their birth; whether they are tall or short, stout or slender; whether they are dark, fair, or neither dark nor fair; and whether they belong to the Kṣatriya caste, the Brahmin, the householder, or the artisan caste; and whether they come from the east, the south, the west, or the north."
"One must not yet pull out the arrow; I should first know whether that bow is made of *śiṃśapā* wood, mulberry, *kīcaka*, or horn.
One must not yet pull out the arrow; I should first know the bowstring—is it made of ox-tendon, deer-tendon, or silk?"
"One must not yet pull out the arrow; should I first know whether the color of the bow is black, white, red, or yellow?
One must not yet pull out the arrow; should I first know whether the bowstring is made of sinew, silk, hemp, or flax?"
"One must not yet extract the arrow; I should first know whether the shaft of the arrow is made of wood or bamboo.
One must not yet extract the arrow; I should first know whether the wrapping of the arrow is made of ox-tendon, deer-tendon, or silk."
"One must not yet pull out the arrow; I should first know whether the feathers of the shaft are those of a pheasant, a vulture or eagle, a wild goose, or a crane?"
"One must not yet pull out the arrow; I should first know whether the arrowhead is a barb, a spearhead, or a dagger-blade. One must not yet pull out the arrow;

I should first know the maker of the arrowhead—his clan name, his personal name, and his birth; whether he is tall or short, stout or slender; whether he is black, white, or neither black nor white; and whether he is from the east, the west, the south, or the north."
That person ultimately fails to find out, and passes away in the interim.
"If there were a foolish person who thought:
'If the World-Honored One does not definitively declare for me that the world is eternal, I will not follow the World-Honored One in training in the holy life.'"
That foolish person never comes to know [the truth], and in the interim, his life comes to an end.

In this way, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has a limit, or that the world is limitless; that the life-principle is identical to the body, or that the life-principle is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
If there were a foolish person who thought thus:
"If the Blessed One does not declare to me with absolute certainty that this alone is the truth and all else is false speech, I shall not train in the holy life under the Blessed One."
That foolish person ultimately fails to know it and passes away in the interim.
Because of this view that "the world is eternal," those who train in the holy life under me find this to be not so.

In this way, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is endless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
Because of this view, it is not the case that those who practice the holy life under me do so for this reason.
Because of the view that "the world is eternal," it is not the case that those who do not practice the holy life under me do so for this reason.

Is it thus that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is endless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
Because one holds this view, it is not the case that those who train in the holy life under me do so; such a thing is impossible.
Because one does not hold the view that "the world is eternal," it is not the case that those who train in the holy life under me do so; such a thing is impossible.

In this way, is it that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is without end; that the life-principle is identical to the body, or that the life-principle and the body are different; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
Because they do not hold this view, it is not the case that those who train in the holy life under me [would say] that the world is eternal;
because they do not hold this view, it is not the case that those who train in the holy life under me [would say] that the world is eternal.

Is it thus that the world is eternal, or that the world has an end, or that the world is endless; that life is identical to the body, or that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death, or that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death?
Because this view does not exist, it is not the case that those who do not train under me in the holy life [attain liberation].
"The world is eternal; there is birth, aging, sickness, and death, as well as sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair; thus this entire great mass of suffering arises. This is not so.

In this way, there is the view that the world is impermanent; that the world has a limit; that the world is limitless; that life is identical to the body; that life is one thing and the body another; that the Tathāgata exists after death; that the Tathāgata does not exist after death; that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death; or that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. There is birth, aging, sickness, and death; sorrow, lamentation, grief, and despair—in this manner, this entire mass of suffering arises.
"The world is eternal; I do not categorically declare this.
For what reason do I not categorically declare this?

Because it is not connected with the goal, not connected with the Dharma, not the foundation of the holy life, and does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, and does not lead to Nirvāṇa; therefore, I do not categorically declare this."

In this way, I do not categorically declare that the world is eternal, nor that the world has an end, nor that the world is infinite; nor that life is identical to the body, nor that life is one thing and the body another; nor that the Tathāgata exists after death, nor that the Tathāgata does not exist after death, nor that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death, nor that the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death. I do not speak of these with absolute certainty.
For what reason do I not categorically declare this?

Because it is not associated with the meaningful, not associated with the Dharma, not the foundation of the holy life, and does not lead to wisdom, does not lead to awakening, and does not lead to Nirvana; therefore, I do not categorically declare this.
What kind of dharma do I teach categorically?
Regarding this matter, I teach categorically: suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering—I teach these categorically.
For what reason do I declare this categorically?

Because it is consistent with the meaning, consistent with the Dharma, and is the foundation of the holy life; it leads to wisdom, leads to awakening, and leads to Nirvana. Therefore, I declare this categorically.
"This is that which is inexpressible shall not be spoken, and that which is expressible shall be spoken; you should uphold it thus, and you should learn it thus.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The *Sāropama-sūtra*, the tenth, ends here, totaling 2,027 characters. 222. *Dvayamukha-sūtra* (222), *Madhyama Āgama*, *Varga on Examples*, *Dvayamukha-sūtra*, the eleventh; Fifth Subsequent Recitation. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one wishes to sever ignorance, one should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
How is it that one who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?"

At a time when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is Worthy, Truly Self-Awakened, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Leader of Men to Be Tamed, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the Blessed One—then [this teaching arises].

He abandons them, even unto the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and contemplates the body internally as body, up to contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena. This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness."

In this way, having repeatedly severed, liberated, transcended, uprooted, ceased, fully understood, and specifically discerned [the afflictions], one who wishes to specifically discern ignorance should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One.

He abandons these, up to and including the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and contemplates the body internally as body, up to contemplating feelings, the mind, and phenomena as phenomena. This is what is meant by one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.
“Those who wish to sever ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts.
How is it that those who wish to sever ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts?

When a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One—”

He abandons them, up to and including the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind and weakness of wisdom—and for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen, he arouses desire, seeks skillful means, and with diligent effort and uplifted mind, he abandons them.
For the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, he generates desire, seeks means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.
For the sake of bringing about arisen wholesome states, he generates desire, seeks means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.

In order that wholesome states already arisen may endure, not be forgotten, not regress, but rather increase, expand, and reach full cultivation and perfection, he arouses desire, seeks after skillful means, exerts himself with diligence, uplifts his mind, and applies effort.
This is called: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Likewise, for the sake of repeatedly abandoning it, for liberation from it, for transcending it, for uprooting it, for its cessation, for knowing it as a whole, and for knowing it in detail—one who wishes to know ignorance in detail should cultivate the four right efforts.
How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the four right efforts?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One.

He abandons them, up to and including the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen, he arouses desire, seeks after skillful means, and with diligent effort, exerts his mind to abandon them.
For the sake of preventing unarisen evil and unwholesome states from arising, he arouses desire, seeks means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.
For the sake of bringing about arisen wholesome states, he arouses desire, seeks means, exerts effort, uplifts the mind, and strives.

In order that wholesome states already arisen may endure, not be forgotten, not decline, but rather increase, expand, and reach full cultivation, he generates desire, seeks skillful means, exerts himself with diligence, uplifts his mind, and applies effort.
This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance should cultivate the four right efforts.
"One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four bases of psychic power.
How does one who wishes to abandon ignorance cultivate the four bases of psychic power?"

At a time when a Tathāgata appears in the world—an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Bhagavat.

Having abandoned those [hindrances], up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through desire, accomplishing the exercise of abandonment; he relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and inclines toward relinquishment. In this same way, he cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through energy, and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through the mind.

One cultivates the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through volition, accomplishing the formations of abandonment; relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment—this is what is meant by "one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the four bases of psychic power."

In this way, having repeatedly severed, liberated, transcended, uprooted, ceased, fully understood, and specifically discerned [the defilements], one who wishes to specifically discern ignorance should cultivate the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*).
How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

When a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One—he abandons, up to, the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and cultivates the basis of power consisting of concentration through desire, accomplishing the exercise of abandonment.
Relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment, one thus cultivates the concentration of energy and the concentration of mind.

Cultivating the basis of psychic power that is the concentration of intention, one accomplishes the formations of abandonment, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment. This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the four bases of psychic power."
"One who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas.
Why is it that one who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Bhagavān."

Having abandoned these, up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he becomes detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attaining and dwelling in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
This is called: one who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas.

Likewise, for the sake of repeatedly severing it, being liberated from it, transcending it, uprooting it, extinguishing and ceasing it, knowing it in its totality, and knowing it in its particulars—one who wishes to know ignorance in its particulars should cultivate the four dhyānas.
How is it that one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the four dhyānas?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat.

Having abandoned these, up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he becomes detached from sensual desires and detached from evil, unwholesome states, attaining and dwelling in the accomplishment of the fourth dhyāna.
This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance should cultivate the four dhyānas.
One who wishes to eradicate ignorance should cultivate the five faculties.
How does one who wishes to eradicate ignorance cultivate the five faculties?"

At a time when a Tathāgata appears in the world—an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of people, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Blessed One—

He abandons them, even unto the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and cultivates the faculty of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five faculties."

Thus, for one who has brought about abandonment, liberation, transcendence, uprooting, cessation, full knowledge, and specific knowledge, and who desires to specifically know ignorance, they should cultivate the five faculties.
How should one who desires to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the five faculties?
It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat.

Having abandoned those [hindrances], up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he cultivates the faculty of faith, the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance should cultivate the five faculties."
"One who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the five powers.
How does one who wishes to sever ignorance cultivate the five powers?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people according to the Dharma, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavān."

He abandons them, even unto the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and cultivates the powers of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is what is meant by: one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the five powers.

In this way, having repeatedly severed, liberated, transcended, uprooted, ceased, fully understood, and specifically known [the defilements], one who wishes to specifically know ignorance should cultivate the five powers.
How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the five powers?
It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Having abandoned these, up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he cultivates the power of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. This is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the five powers."
"One who wishes to sever ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
How does one who wishes to sever ignorance cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a well-gone one, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One."

Having abandoned those [hindrances], up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he cultivates the awakening-factor of mindfulness, which relies on seclusion, relies on dispassion, relies on cessation, and leads to relinquishment; and he likewise cultivates the awakening-factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, and concentration.

One cultivates the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and leads to relinquishment; this is what is meant by saying that one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.

Thus, having repeatedly severed, liberated, transcended, uprooted, ceased, fully understood, and specifically known [the defilements], one who wishes to specifically know ignorance should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of persons, a teacher of gods and humans, called Buddha and Bhagavat.

Having abandoned those [hindrances], up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—he cultivates the awakening-factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and results in relinquishment; he likewise cultivates the awakening-factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, and concentration.

One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and tending toward relinquishment; this is what is meant by saying that one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment.
"One who wishes to eradicate ignorance should cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
How does one who wishes to eradicate ignorance cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?
It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—Anāgāmin, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

He abandons these, up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and cultivates right view through to right concentration, making eight; this is called "one who wishes to abandon ignorance should cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path."

Thus, through repeated severing, liberation, transcending, uprooting, cessation, full comprehension, and specific discernment—should one wish to specifically discern ignorance, one should cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path.
"How should one who wishes to discern ignorance specifically cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path?

It is when a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is free from attachment, a perfectly awakened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader, a trainer of people to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, called a Buddha and a Blessed One."

He abandons these, up to the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind and the weakness of wisdom—and cultivates right view through to right concentration as the eightfold path; this is what is meant by: "One who wishes to discern ignorance specifically should cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path."
"One who desires to sever ignorance should cultivate the ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*).
How is it that one who desires to sever ignorance should cultivate the ten universal bases?
